New Island adds giant eggs capable of smashing through entire stretches of scenery and several levels using the console's tilt via the motion sensor. The stereoscopic 3D effect gives the hand-painted world a pleasant spatiality.

The visual style is the game's greatest asset – the scenery resembles a child's drawing in pastel and chalk, with rough paper textures and adorable details. This artistic approach continues the series' characteristic aesthetic, where charm and playfulness always took precedence over technical perfection.

Culturally, New Island banks on the enormous popularity of the Yoshi brand and on nostalgia for the original SNES game, which many consider one of the best platformers of the era. Although it bears the heavy burden of expectation in the shadow of its famous predecessor, it offers a gentle, accessible, and visually lovely ride that will especially please players seeking a relaxed but still inventive platformer.

**Why play:** A gentle, visually enchanting platformer with a pastel art style and classic Yoshi egg mechanics, ideal for casual and nostalgic players alike.
3ds__yoshi-s-new-island.teaser: A direct sequel to the beloved Yoshi's Island; the green dinosaur once again carries a crying baby.

3ds__rhythm-heaven-megamix.article:
Sing along with frogs, cut hair in rhythm, knock baseballs precisely on the beat – and the best is yet to come. **Rhythm Heaven Megamix** is an explosion of pure, undiluted joy, a compilation of the best minigames from the entire series plus a heap of new ones, stitched together into one insanely catchy package. If there is a game guaranteed to brighten your day, this is the one.

The principle is brilliantly simple and at the same time devilishly addictive: each minigame is built on a single thing – feeling the rhythm. You press buttons on the exact beat, and crucially, often with your gaze averted from the visual action, guided only by the music and your hearing. Megamix gathers dozens of these "rhythm games" from previous entries (from Game Boy Advance, Nintendo DS, and Wii) and supplements them with new ones, connected by a central storyline full of adorably wacky characters.

The series is a child of studio **Nintendo SPD** and behind it stands the musician **Tsunku**, a Japanese pop icon and producer whose sense for a catchy melody permeates every single note of the game. It is his musical instinct that makes Rhythm Heaven something exceptional – the tunes burrow into your head and won't let go.

Megamix adds a new progression system, a rewards shop, and a shorter, friendlier difficulty curve, so it serves as an ideal gateway for newcomers. The controls were simplified to buttons (compared to the touch controls of the DS entry), which many players consider more precise.

Culturally, the series has built a devoted cult of fans thanks to its distinctive, surreally adorable aesthetic and unmistakable humor. Megamix is the most comprehensive declaration of love to this brand – a kind of best-of with extra reach that can entertain for five minutes or absorb you for hours.

**Why play:** An immensely catchy and funny rhythm compilation with Tsunku's melodies, perfect for short bursts of pure gaming joy as well as passionate chasing of a perfect score.
3ds__rhythm-heaven-megamix.teaser: A compilation of the best minigames from the series, plus new ones; pure, infectious rhythmic joy.

3ds__cave-story-3d.article:
A story written and programmed by a single person in their spare time became one of the most influential independent titles in gaming history – and **Cave Story** is shining proof of it. This melancholic, action-packed adventure platformer about a nameless robot awakening in underground caves gained cult status long before the term "indie game" was in vogue.

The gameplay is a classic combination of nimble action and exploration in the metroidvania style. You fight your way through branching caves, collect and upgrade various weapons, and gradually uncover a touching story about a nation of rabbit-like creatures called the Mimiga and a malevolent doctor. The weapon mechanic is unique: each weapon gains experience, but drops a level when you take a hit – so every injury hurts twice as much. The game is famous for its multiple endings and hidden areas for the most persistent players.

The original was created by Japanese developer **Daisuke "Pixel" Amaya** entirely alone over the course of five years and released for free in 2004. This act of pure creative passion inspired a whole generation of independent creators. The **Cave Story 3D** version for the Nintendo 3DS was created by studio **Nicalis** in collaboration with the author, converting the originally two-dimensional game into fully 3D-rendered scenery with stereoscopic depth.

This reinterpretation preserves the original gameplay but rebuilds the environments into spatial dioramas – caves, cemeteries, and laboratories now recede across several layers, and the handheld's 3D effect lends them tangible volume. The game also includes the option to switch to an arranged or original soundtrack, whose catchy chiptune melodies are among the icons of the indie scene.

Culturally, Cave Story foreshadowed an entire wave of independent games and proved that a single passionate creator can make a work comparable to the output of major studios. Its influence on the genre and on the entire indie culture is undeniable, and the 3DS version offers one way to experience this classic on the go.

**Why play:** A cult indie classic with a touching story and precise metroidvania gameplay, reworked on the 3DS into spatial scenery with stereoscopic depth.
3ds__cave-story-3d.teaser: Programmed by one person in their spare time; one of the most influential indie titles ever.

3ds__shovel-knight.article:
A knight armed not with a sword but with a shovel, who bounces on enemies like Scrooge McDuck on his cane and collects treasures in levels that look straight out of the eight-bit era – **Shovel Knight** is a perfect loving tribute to the golden age of Nintendo that became a modern classic in its own right. This game proved that retro aesthetics are not just a nostalgic crutch, but a fully-fledged artistic language.

The gameplay masterfully blends the best of legends like Mega Man, DuckTales, Castlevania, and Super Mario Bros. 3. The burial knight digs his way through levels, jumps down on enemies with a bounce attack of his shovel, and collects gems, for which he upgrades his equipment. The game is famous for its flawless controls, inventive level design, and an unforgettable gallery of bosses – the Order of No Quarter. Added to this is a semi-open world map in the style of Super Mario 3 and little towns full of quirky characters.

Behind the game stands the American studio **Yacht Club Games**, which funded the project through Kickstarter and raised many times more than it asked for. The developers took enormous care with authenticity: the game honors the technical limitations of the NES but cleverly circumvents them where it makes sense, and the result is pixel-art graphics that look like a memory of eight-bit games – more beautiful than they actually were. The music was composed by **Jake Kaufman** with contributions from the legendary **Manami Matsumae**, composer of the original Mega Man.

The Nintendo 3DS version adds a stereoscopic 3D effect and use of the lower screen for the map and inventory. Shovel Knight was released on a staggering number of platforms and gradually expanded with standalone campaigns for individual bosses, turning a single game into an entire sprawling saga.

Culturally, Shovel Knight became the benchmark for how to make a retro game right – with respect for its models, but with modern artistic and gameplay sensibility. It reaped enthusiastic reviews and numerous awards and is still considered one of the best indie titles ever.

**Why play:** A flawless tribute to the eight-bit era with precise controls, inventive level design, and unforgettable bosses, on the 3DS supplemented with a 3D effect and use of the lower screen.
3ds__shovel-knight.teaser: A knight with a shovel instead of a sword; a loving tribute to Nintendo's golden age, now a modern classic.

3ds__super-street-fighter-iv-3d-edition.article:
When the Nintendo 3DS hit the market, Capcom was among the first to bet on its stereoscopic screen in grand style. **Super Street Fighter IV: 3D Edition** was part of the console's launch lineup and thus became the very first full-fledged Street Fighter in your pocket that was not merely a trimmed-down version, but a true port of the ambitious fourth-generation fighting game.

The core of the game remains faithful to its arcade and console predecessors. You will find a complete roster of over thirty fighters from Ryu and Chun-Li to characters added in the Super edition, an elaborate system of Focus Attacks, EX moves, super combos, and devastating Ultra Combos. Capcom became famous for building its combat system on readability and depth at the same time: even a beginner can manage a few blows, but mastery of timing, animation cancels, and reading the opponent runs deep.

Two essential innovations were added on the 3DS. The first is the so-called Dynamic View, a camera behind the fighter's back that uses the console's 3D effect and offers a striking close-up view of the fight. The second is the ability to map special moves to the touch screen, which makes the game accessible to players who do not want to wrestle with the precise input of quarter-circle motions on the small D-pad. For veterans, the classic side view and manual input remain.

The development context is key here. Street Fighter IV in 2008 practically resurrected the genre of 2D fighting games, which until then had been languishing, and returned it to mainstream attention. The 3D Edition carried this wave to the handheld and showed that even a demanding tournament fighter could work on the go. The game also supported local and online matches, so players could test their strength outside the campaign against the computer.

Culturally, Street Fighter remains one of the pillars of the entire esports and tournament fighting-game scene, whose events like EVO are watched by thousands of viewers. Having a full-blooded version of this saga right at the launch of a new Nintendo console was reason enough for many to buy it, and the game is still considered one of the more solid launch titles of the 3DS.

**Why play:** A full-fledged Street Fighter IV in your pocket with clever use of the 3D effect and touch controls that ease newcomers in without stripping away depth for veterans.
3ds__super-street-fighter-iv-3d-edition.teaser: The first full-fledged Street Fighter in your pocket, part of the console's launch lineup.

3ds__tekken-3d-prime-edition.article:
If Capcom staffed the 3DS with its Street Fighter, Namco could not stay behind with its flagship three-dimensional fighting game. **Tekken 3D: Prime Edition** brought the famous Iron Fist saga to the Nintendo handheld and used the stereoscopic screen to give the King of Iron Fist Tournament matches real spatial depth.

Tekken has always differed from its rivals in its conception of the combat system. Instead of universal buttons for weak and strong strikes, it works with controls per individual limb: each button corresponds to one hand or leg. From this grows an enormous repertoire of combinations, juggling the opponent in the air, and the characteristic moves of individual fighters. Prime Edition offers an extensive roster of characters drawing on the series' rich history, so fans will find their favorites across generations of the tournament.

The package had one more big draw, however. Alongside the game itself, it also contained the feature-length film **Tekken: Blood Vengeance** in a format that used the console's 3D screen. It was an ambitious attempt to combine interactive matches with an animated film and offer series fans a complete experience on a single cartridge. This combination of game and film was of an unusual kind on a handheld and made Prime Edition more of a collector's package than a mere port.

Development-wise, Tekken is among the longest-running and commercially most successful fighting games ever, and the Namco brand built an enormous fan base around it all over the world. Bringing such a technically demanding 3D fighter to a handheld console was no small task, and Prime Edition showed that the 3DS hardware was up to it.

Culturally, Tekken stands side by side with Street Fighter as one of the pillars of the fighting-game tournament scene. The 3DS version was not a full-fledged sequel to the main line, but for fans on the go it represented a welcome extension and proof that even on a small screen the Iron Fist could strike hard.

**Why play:** A spatial fighting game with its signature per-limb controls and a rich roster, plus the bundled animated film Blood Vengeance as a bonus for series fans.
3ds__tekken-3d-prime-edition.teaser: The famous Iron Fist saga on a Nintendo handheld with stereoscopic depth to the fights.

3ds__mario-sports-superstars.article:
Nintendo has a long tradition of sending its mascots straight from adventures onto the sports field. **Mario Sports Superstars** takes this idea to the extreme: instead of a single discipline, it crams five different sports into a single title, making it a sort of festive mix for the whole family and for players on the go with the Nintendo 3DS.

The lineup is genuinely broad. Football, tennis, baseball, golf and horse racing, each discipline with its own rules, controls and pace. Mario's cast of characters, from Luigi through Peach and Yoshi to Bowser and Donkey Kong, appears across all the sports, so you can take your favorite hero onto the pitch as well as the green. The game aims for accessibility: the rules are easy to grasp, yet each discipline hides enough tactics to keep you entertained for the long haul.

A particularly interesting element is horse racing, where caring for your own horse, feeding and stroking it, feels closer to a light simulation than pure arcade. This discipline lends the otherwise brisk sports package a surprisingly calmer dimension. Football and baseball, by contrast, bank on team action, while tennis and golf stay faithful to the tried-and-tested Nintendo recipes that series like Mario Tennis and Mario Golf have honed over the years.

In terms of development, the game follows a long line of Mario sports titles that Nintendo has been releasing practically since the days of the Nintendo 64. Merging five distinct sports into a single title meant balancing the fun and depth of each one so that none felt like a hastily thrown-in side dish. The game also supported local and online matches for players who wanted to test their skills against others.

Culturally, Mario Sports Superstars fits neatly into the proven concept of Mario party games designed to appeal to a broad family audience. It isn't a title that breaks records for depth in any individual discipline, but as a five-pack of accessible sporting fun featuring the best-known mascots in the gaming world, it fulfills its purpose without a hitch.

**Why play:** Five sports in one with the whole Mario crew, ideal for family-friendly, accessible fun on the 3DS, where everyone can find their favorite discipline.
3ds__mario-sports-superstars.teaser: Five sports in one package, from soccer to horse racing; a festive mix for the whole family.

nes__super-mario-bros-3.teaser: One of the greatest platformers in history; the genre's benchmark of quality.
nes__super-mario-bros-3.detail: Under the leadership of Miyamoto and Tezuka, one of the finest platformers ever came to life, and the best-selling non-bundled NES game (over 17 million). It introduced a world map, costumes that change your abilities (tanuki, frog, boot) and enormous variety. In the US it was also made famous by the film The Wizard, which worked like one big advertising trailer. The design benchmark of the genre.
nes__super-mario-bros-3.article:
There exists a platformer that even people who had never heard of video games wanted to play, and its name is **Super Mario Bros. 3**. In America it was also made famous by the feature film The Wizard, which functioned like one big two-hour advertising trailer and stirred up mass hysteria even before the game reached stores. And when it did arrive, it showed just how far the genre could go.

Under the leadership of Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, one of the greatest platformers ever came to life, and at the same time the best-selling non-bundled game for the NES, selling over **17 million copies**. That is no accident. The third installment introduced a world map that gave the adventure structure and a choice of routes, and above all costumes that change Mario's abilities: the tanuki, the frog, the boot and the legendary tanuki statue.

What is truly ingenious is the variety. Each of the worlds has its own theme, its own enemies and its own ideas that rarely repeat. The game constantly surprises you, and the moment you think you've seen everything, it throws a flying airship, a giant version of a familiar setting, or an entirely new trick at you. It is a nonstop stream of creativity of a kind you simply didn't see back then.

In terms of design, the third game set a bar that others had to clear for decades afterward. Precise controls, clean pacing and balanced difficulty turned it into the quality benchmark of the entire genre. Even today it holds true that if you want to explain what makes a platformer great, you simply point to Super Mario Bros. 3.

It is no wonder, then, that it appears at the top of practically every list of the best games in history and that its influence is felt to this day. It is the crowning work of the NES era and proof that Nintendo knew how to spark timeless fun from a simple concept.

**Why play:** Because it is one of the greatest platformers of all time, unsurpassed in variety, pacing and pure joy of play.

nes__super-mario-bros.teaser: The game that saved the games industry after the '83 crash.
nes__super-mario-bros.detail: The NES pack-in title that in the US practically resurrected the games market after the 1983 crash. Over 40 million copies were sold. Its first level (World 1-1) is a textbook example of 'level design as tutorial' — it teaches you all the mechanics without a single word of text. Miyamoto's revolution in movement and pacing.
nes__super-mario-bros.article:
One game, one plumber and one jump that changed the history of entertainment. **Super Mario Bros.** arrived in 1985 as a pack-in title for the NES and in the US practically resurrected a games market that had hit rock bottom after the 1983 crash. If there is a single game we can thank for the fact that we still have consoles at all, it is this one.

The numbers speak clearly: over **40 million copies** were sold, making it one of the best-selling games ever. But the real magic lies not in the numbers, but in the design. The famous first level, World 1-1, is still cited today as a textbook example of „level design as tutorial“ — it teaches you all the game's mechanics without a single word of text. A Goomba approaching from the right teaches you to jump, a question-mark block rewards you with a mushroom, a pipe tempts you to explore.

Miyamoto's revolution lay in movement and pacing. Mario has weight, inertia and precision, and running, jumping and braking respond so satisfyingly that the mere act of moving from left to right becomes a joy in its own right. This tangibility of the controls became the template for whole generations of platformers and still counts as the gold standard today.

The cultural impact is immeasurable. Mario became not only the face of Nintendo but one of the most recognizable fictional characters on the planet, recognizable across continents and generations. The melody from the first level is among the most famous compositions in the history of media. Video games suddenly became mainstream.

Playing Super Mario Bros. today means touching the cornerstone of an entire industry. It is a game that seems simple, yet is perfectly polished, and it is precisely in that simplicity that its immortality lies.

**Why play:** Because it is the game that saved the games industry and defined platformers — timeless, perfectly controllable and still fun.

nes__legend-of-zelda.teaser: The birth of the open-world adventure; exploration in its purest form.
nes__legend-of-zelda.detail: The first great open-world action adventure: it drops you into a world without guidance and rewards experimentation (burning bushes, uncovering secrets). It was the first console game with a battery in the cartridge to save your progress. The famous 'It's dangerous to go alone! Take this.' A more influential game is hard to find; over 6.5 million copies were sold.
nes__legend-of-zelda.article:
"It's dangerous to go alone! Take this." With this single sentence and an old man in a cave, an adventure began that forever changed the notion of what a video game could be. **The Legend of Zelda** from 1986 dropped you into an open world without ceremony, gave you no guidance and left you to find your own way, and the reward was the sheer joy of discovery.

This was the first great open-world action adventure. Hyrule lay before you whole, open and full of secrets: you burned bushes, pushed gravestones, searched for hidden entrances and uncovered caves that no one told you about. The game rewarded curiosity and experimentation in a way no one had seen before, and thus created the archetype that adventures still follow today.

Technically it was a breakthrough: it was the first console game with a battery in the cartridge, which made it possible to save progress. That sounded trivial, but in reality it opened the door to larger, longer and more complex games that had previously been impossible. Suddenly you could explore a world in stages, come back and build up your progress.

Its cultural significance is enormous — over **6.5 million copies** were sold and one of the most influential and enduring gaming brands ever came into being. The principle of dungeons, the gradual acquisition of items that open new areas, and the combination of action with puzzles became the foundation of the entire genre.

Playing the original Zelda today is both a challenge and a lesson: it reminds you what it is like to explore a world without arrows and pointers, purely by the force of your own curiosity. It is the cornerstone on which countless later legends stand.

**Why play:** Because it is the birth of the open-world adventure — exploration in its purest form and one of the most influential titles in the history of games.

nes__zelda-ii-adventure-of-link.teaser: The black sheep of the series — a platformer with RPG elements; demanding, but fascinating.
nes__zelda-ii-adventure-of-link.detail: The black sheep of the series and the biggest detour in its history: instead of top-down, it's a side-scrolling platformer with RPG elements (experience, levels, spells, extra lives). Demanding to the point of ruthless. Controversial among fans, but with a devoted base; some elements (magic, towns) returned in later installments.
nes__zelda-ii-adventure-of-link.article:
Every great series has its black sheep, and in Zelda's case it is, without question, **Zelda II: The Adventure of Link**. After the triumph of the first installment, Nintendo did something unexpected: it took the successful formula and threw it out the window. Instead of the top-down view we get a side-scrolling platformer with RPG elements, and the result still splits fans into two irreconcilable camps to this day.

When you appear in the side view, Zelda II offers surprising depth. You collect experience, raise levels, learn spells and gain extra lives. Combat demands precise blocks and high or low strikes, so fencing with enemies takes on an unexpectedly tactical flavor. Between the action sequences you return to the top-down map and pass through towns where you gather advice and magic.

And then there is the difficulty. Zelda II is demanding to the point of ruthless — enemies punish mistakes harshly, the dungeons are treacherous, and the final challenges will test even seasoned players. It is precisely this uncompromising nature that is the reason the game earned both stubborn detractors and a devoted base that considers it an underrated gem.

From a historical perspective it is fascinating how much of this detour the series eventually took back. Magic, towns and deeper RPG elements returned in various forms in later installments, even if the platformer format itself never got a second chance in the main line. Zelda II thus remains a unique experiment.

Today it is a title for the brave and the curious — for those who want to know the series in all its breadth and aren't afraid of a challenge that gives no quarter. It may be the black sheep, but it is an unforgettable black sheep.

**Why play:** For a fascinating and demanding experiment that shows a completely different face of Zelda — a platformer with an RPG soul, one the series never repeated.

nes__mega-man-2.teaser: The peaks of the classic series; perfect music and design.
nes__mega-man-2.detail: The second game saved the series (the first one sold poorly, the team made it during their nights as a last attempt) and became the best-selling classic Mega Man, with famously perfect music. You choose the order of the eight bosses and steal their weapons into a rock-paper-scissors strategy. The third added the slide and the dog Rush. The definition of the genre.
nes__mega-man-2.article:
When the team at Capcom was finishing the first Mega Man, no one expected a bright future — the first game sold miserably. The sequel was therefore made at night, in free time, as a last desperate attempt to give the blue robot a chance. And out of that desperation was born **Mega Man 2** — the best-selling classic Mega Man and, in the eyes of many, the peak of the entire series.

The game's genius lies in its structure. You choose the order of the eight robot bosses and, after defeating them, steal a weapon that you then use against the next enemy in a game of rock-paper-scissors. Seeking out the right weaknesses and building up your arsenal is immensely satisfying and gives the game an almost puzzle-like dimension beyond pure action and platforming skill.

And then there is the music. The soundtrack of Mega Man 2 is among the most famous in video game history — the melody from Dr. Wily's stage became iconic and is known to this day even by people who have never played the game. Together with a sharp, legible graphical style and precise controls, it forms a work that ages exceptionally well.

This game's influence on action platformers is impossible to overlook. It established the formula that the series would then refine for decades — the third game added sliding and the robot dog Rush, but it was the second that laid the core. It became the definition of the genre and the benchmark against which even modern successors are measured.

Playing Mega Man 2 today means experiencing the NES era in its purest, most polished form: demanding but fair, addictive and musically unforgettable. A last attempt became an immortal classic.

**Why play:** For the peak of the classic action platformer with an ingenious weapon system, perfect controls and one of the best soundtracks in the history of games.

nes__mega-man-3.article:
The Blue Bomber returns — and this time he slides. **Mega Man 3** follows up on the legendary second game at a time when the series was at its peak, and adds elements that became a permanent part of the brand. For many fans, the third game is just as strong a candidate for the best classic installment as its famous predecessor.

The game's core remains faithful to the proven formula: you choose the order of the eight robot bosses, steal their weapons and forge them into a rock-paper-scissors strategy against the other enemies. This loop of choice, experimentation and reward is still one of the smartest designs in the genre, and the third game develops it with the confidence of a series at the height of its powers.

The key innovation is the slide, which gives Mega Man an entirely new move — dodging projectiles, sliding under obstacles and a faster pace of combat. The robot dog Rush was also added, a loyal companion able to transform into a springboard or a means of transport. Both of these innovations became so iconic that the series carried them for the rest of its existence.

Visually and musically, the third game holds to the high bar of the NES era: sharp, legible graphics and a catchy chiptune soundtrack that beautifully underscores the pace of the action. The difficulty remains present, but fair — the game rewards skill and knowledge of the mechanics, not chance.

Mega Man 3 is thus proof that even a sequel in the shadow of a revered second game can bring meaningful innovations and an identity of its own. It belongs in the essential kit of anyone who wants to know the golden era of action platformers on the NES.

**Why play:** For a top-tier action platformer that adds the slide and the dog Rush to the proven formula — elements that forever changed the face of the series.
nes__mega-man-3.teaser: The Blue Bomber returns and can slide for the first time; for many, the strongest classic entry in the series.

nes__castlevania.teaser: Gothic action; the third game adds branching and characters. Pillars of the genre.
nes__castlevania.detail: The first game founded the gothic action series (Simon Belmont vs. Dracula), famous for its stiff, 'committed' jump and excellent music. The third (Dracula's Curse) is the peak of the classic era: branching paths, four playable companions including Alucard, and in the Japanese version an expanded sound chip for better music.
nes__castlevania.article:
Dracula's castle looms against a mesmerizingly red sky, and you, vampire hunter Simon Belmont, step into it alone, armed only with a strip of leather whip. Thus begins **Castlevania** by Konami, a game that in 1986 (on the Famicom Disk System, reaching the West a few years later) laid the foundations of an entire gothic action legend.

At first glance it is a straightforward platformer, but the devil is in the details of the controls. Simon jumps in a so-called „committed“ way — once he leaves the ground, you can no longer change his trajectory, so you have to plan every jump in advance. This deliberation transforms the game from reflexive action into a tense duel with space. In addition to the whip there are sub-weapons powered by hearts: holy water, throwing axes, daggers or the clock that stops time. The boss battles — from Medusa through Mummies to the final Dracula, who transforms into a winged beast after being defeated once — are among the best the early NES had to offer.

An inseparable part of the experience is the music. Tracks like **Vampire Killer** burrow into your memory and to this day rank among the most cited video game motifs ever. Here Konami demonstrated how deeply a soundtrack can shape atmosphere — each level has its own mood, from catacombs to the clock tower.

Castlevania stood at the birth of a brand that lives on to this day. From straightforward action grew, over time, a branching genre that a game named Symphony of the Night would later christen. Without this first ascent of the castle there would be none of what followed — no Alucard, no exploration of an interconnected manor, no decades-long rivalry between the Belmont bloodline and the prince of darkness.

Anyone who takes retro seriously must go through Castlevania at least once. It is stiff, it is merciless, but every honestly conquered stretch tastes like a small victory over the night itself.

**Why play:** A founding cornerstone of gothic action with unforgettable music and an honestly tough design that has held up even after four decades.

nes__castlevania-iii-dracula-s-curse.article:
The year is 1476 and Dracula is not yet the fallen prince of later installments — he is a powerful threat, one that Trevor Belmont, ancestor of Simon from the first game, must stand against. **Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse** pushes the series' classic era to its very peak and to this day counts as one of the most technically and mechanically advanced titles on the NES.

Konami took the proven core — the whip, sub-weapons powered by hearts, committed jumps — and enriched it with two crucial innovations. The first is branching paths: at forks you decide which way to go, and each route leads through different levels with different bosses. The game thus offers markedly higher replayability than its linear predecessors. The second is a trio of companions you can recruit along the way and switch between with Trevor at any time: the pirate Grant DaNasty who climbs walls, the sorceress Sypha with her destructive elements, and — perhaps most famous — the vampire Alucard, Dracula's son, who can transform into a bat.

Each character plays entirely differently and opens up new ways to traverse the levels. Your choice of companion thus affects not only the style of play but also which sections you can even get through. It is a clever layer of tactics laid over fast-paced action.

The Japanese version also contained an expanded VRC6 sound chip right in the cartridge, which added extra sound channels and gave the soundtrack a richness that the standard NES couldn't manage. The Western versions lost this luxury due to different hardware, so the Japanese original sounds markedly fuller — music fans still seek out precisely the Akumajō Densetsu version because of it.

The tough difficulty remains, but the branching design and playable companions make the third game perhaps the richest experience of classic Castlevania ever.

**Why play:** The peak of the series' old school — branching levels, four distinct playable characters and, in the Japanese version, first-class music on top.
nes__castlevania-iii-dracula-s-curse.teaser: A prequel featuring Trevor Belmont against the mighty Dracula; the most technically advanced entry on NES.

nes__metroid.teaser: The beginning of the 'metroidvania'; lonely exploration and mystery.
nes__metroid.detail: Along with its name it gave rise to an entire genre (metro-id + castle-vania). Lonely exploration of an interconnected world where new abilities open up previously inaccessible places. The famous reveal after a fast finish: beneath the helmet is a woman, Samus Aran — groundbreaking for its time. Dark atmosphere and unconventional nonlinearity.
nes__metroid.article:
You wake up on the alien planet Zebes, alone, without a map and without a hint of where to go. This solitude and sense of being lost are not a flaw — they are the whole point of the game. **Metroid**, from the Nintendo R&D1 workshop in 1986, did something almost no one did at the time: it made exploration the main game mechanic.

Instead of linear levels you get one large, interconnected world full of locked doors and inaccessible shafts. The key to progress is newly gathered abilities — the Morph Ball for squeezing through narrow corridors, Bombs, the Ice Beam that freezes enemies, the High Jump. Each new piece of gear opens up previously inaccessible nooks and forces you to backtrack and rethink locations you've already passed. From this principle of „an ability unlocks the world“ later grew an entire genre whose name arose from the union of Metroid and Castlevania — **metroidvania**.

The atmosphere is dark, lonely and oppressive. Hirokazu Tanaka's music is not a pleasing melody but rather the sonic backdrop of a hostile planet that breeds unease in you. No rush, no crowds of enemies — just you, the echo of your footsteps and the sense that something unpleasant lurks behind the next wall.

And then there is the legendary finale. After finishing quickly enough, it is revealed that beneath the bulletproof armor of hunter Samus Aran hides a woman — a reveal that in the mid-1980s hit like a bolt from the blue and to this day ranks among the most cited moments in gaming history. Samus became one of the first and most striking female heroines in the medium.

Metroid is not the most welcoming game of its time — there is no map, saving was handled by passwords, and it is easy to get lost. But it is precisely that harsh nonlinearity that makes the first trip to Zebes an unforgettable and, to this day, influential experience.

**Why play:** The game that literally named an entire genre — lonely exploration, the gradual unlocking of the world and one of the most famous reveals in the history of games.

nes__kirby-s-adventure.teaser: Visually stunning on the NES; the birth of Kirby's ability copying.
nes__kirby-s-adventure.detail: It came out near the end of the NES's life and visually pushed the hardware to its maximum (colors, effects, smoothness that early NES games didn't have). Here, for the first time, Kirby copies the abilities of swallowed enemies — the mechanic that defined the series. Directed by Masahiro Sakurai.
nes__kirby-s-adventure.article:
When **Kirby's Adventure** came out in 1993, the NES should have long since been in retirement — and yet this game showed just how much could still be squeezed out of ancient hardware. Color gradients, smooth animations and visual effects that early NES titles never knew still take the breath away of anyone who knows what limited iron it runs on.

HAL Laboratory, under the leadership of Masahiro Sakurai, made a crucial step here in the development of its pink puffball. Whereas in the previous Kirby's Dream Land on the Game Boy, Kirby could only swallow enemies and spit them out, here the mechanic that would forever define the series is born: **ability copying**. Swallow an enemy with fire power and you'll start spewing flames yourself; devour one with a sword and you gain a blade; another gives you the ability to float or hurl sparks. Suddenly you hold dozens of play styles hidden within a single character.

This turns an otherwise gentle platformer into a playground full of experiments. The game is kind and accessible — Kirby can fly, so chasms aren't a death sentence as in tougher titles — but hidden nooks, minigames and secrets reward the curious. It is a platformer that a beginner and a veteran seeking pleasant relaxation alike will happily finish.

Here Sakurai built the foundation on which he later constructed not only the entire Kirby series but also his sense for playability and character, which he later cashed in on in the Super Smash Bros. phenomenon. Kirby's Adventure is thus not only the swan song of the NES but also an important milestone in the career of one of the most influential Japanese designers.

If you want to see the NES at the peak of its abilities and at the same time witness the birth of one of the most beloved gaming icons, this is a mandatory stop.

**Why play:** A technically stunning swan song of the NES and the birthplace of Kirby's ability copying — kind, inventive and timelessly playable.

nes__ducktales.teaser: Disney action with a pogo cane; iconic music (Moon Theme!).
nes__ducktales.detail: Based on the Disney series; Scrooge McDuck bounces on his cane like a pogo stick and explores levels in any order. Famous especially for its music — 'The Moon Theme' is among the most beloved video game tracks ever (composer Hiroshige Tonomura). It received an HD remake (2013).
nes__ducktales.article:
There is music that millions of people remember without ever having turned the game on — and **DuckTales** by Capcom has just such a track. The famous **Moon Theme** from the moon level became one of the most beloved and most cited video game melodies ever, and on its own it is enough to earn this 1989 game a place in the gaming hall of fame.

But DuckTales is not just one brilliant motif. Based on the Disney series of the same name, you take on the wealthy Scrooge McDuck, who sets off after treasure across exotic locations — from the Amazon through the Himalayas all the way to the Moon. His main weapon is the cane, on which he hops like a pogo stick: press down and jump and Scrooge bounces off the ground, off enemies and off boxed-up objects. This pogo mechanic gives movement a unique rhythm and serves both as an attack and as a way to reach higher.

The levels can be tackled in any order, which lends the game a pleasant sense of freedom and the chance to choose your own path to riches. The level design carries that typical Capcom quality from the era when the studio churned out one excellent licensed title after another — solid controls, clean graphics and honestly tuned difficulty that punishes carelessness but never feels unfair.

The game enjoys such respect that in 2013 it received a careful HD remake, **DuckTales: Remastered**, which reworked the graphics, re-recorded the music into an orchestral form and brought back the original voice actors from the series. Few NES games received such a modern accolade.

DuckTales is proof that a licensed game based on a cartoon series need not be a cheap cash grab, but a genuine gem that holds up even after decades.

**Why play:** A top-tier Disney platformer with an inventive pogo mechanic and perhaps the most beloved soundtrack of the NES era — you'll hear the Moon Theme and never forget it.

nes__chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers.teaser: Superb two-player co-op; a family classic.
nes__chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers.detail: One of the best cooperative NES games: two players pick up and hurl crates at enemies (and at each other). A Disney license paired with Capcom-grade level design. A family classic, ideal for playing in a pair.
nes__chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers.article:
Grab a friend, sit down in front of a single screen, and fire up **Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers** — because this 1990 game is among the very best you could play in two on the NES. Once again Capcom proved it understands Disney licenses and cooperative fun like almost no one else.

As the chipmunks Chip and Dale, you make your way through colorful levels inspired by the beloved cartoon, and your main mechanic is picking up and throwing crates. Grab a box, aim, and hurl it at an enemy — and in co-op the best (and most treacherous) fun is born: you can also throw a crate at your partner, plop them on your head, and carry them past a dangerous spot. This little interaction between two players turns an ordinary platformer into a series of funny situations and small betrayals.

The level design carries Capcom's typical precision: the levels are clear, the controls snappy, and the difficulty gentle enough that even younger kids can handle it, yet interesting enough to entertain adults. This isn't a brutally hard title like Ninja Gaiden — it's a family joy built for playing together, for laughter, and for the occasional argument over who dropped whom into the pit again.

It's precisely this accessibility and the emphasis on co-op that make Rescue Rangers a timeless classic. In an era when most games were played solo, it offered a genuinely well-crafted two-player experience that holds together to this day — all you need is a second controller and the will to have fun.

Anyone looking for an NES game to spend a pleasant evening with a friend, partner, or kids is looking in exactly the right place.

**Why play:** One of the best cooperative games on the NES — throwing crates at enemies and at your partner makes it an immortal family classic.

nes__contra.teaser: The definition of run & gun; legendary code and difficulty.
nes__contra.detail: The definition of the run & gun genre. Its notorious difficulty gave rise to the most famous cheat in history — the **Konami Code** (↑↑↓↓←→←→BA), which granted 30 lives. The iconic „spread gun“, two-player co-op, and a brutal pace. In Europe it was released as Probotector (humans replaced by robots due to censorship).
nes__contra.article:
Two commandos, endless hordes of enemies, and a difficulty that knocks you flat before you can blink — welcome to **Contra**, the game that in 1988 (1990 on the NES) defined the run & gun genre once and for all. Konami created the benchmark against which run-and-gun action is still measured today.

The principle is brilliantly simple: you run, jump, aim in eight directions, and mow down anything that moves. Along the way you collect upgraded weapons, of which the iconic **spread gun** spewing a fan of bullets ranks among the most beloved arsenals in gaming history. The levels alternate a classic side view with pseudo-3D sections where you run into the depth of the screen, culminating in battles against inventive bosses. The pace is merciless — a single hit means death.

And it was precisely that brutal difficulty that gave rise to perhaps the most famous cheat of all time. The **Konami Code** — up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A — handed you thirty lives at the start and became so legendary that you'll still find it hidden in dozens of games, apps, and websites all over the world. Few gaming sequences have embedded themselves so deeply into pop culture.

Contra is also a showcase cooperative title: with two players it takes on a whole new dimension, where you cover for each other, share weapons, and fight your way through the alien invasion together. Cooperation (and the occasional getting in each other's way) only multiplies the fun.

A bit of trivia for European players: because of the censorship of the day, Contra was released on the old continent under the name **Probotector**, where the human soldiers were replaced by robots. Under a different name, though, the same merciless heart was beating.

**Why play:** The definition of run & gun with the iconic spread gun, excellent co-op, and the most famous cheat in history — the Konami Code that has survived generations.

nes__super-c.article:
The alien threat has returned, and with it the pair of indestructible commandos — **Super C**, the direct sequel to the legendary Contra, brings another dose of merciless run-and-gun action to the NES. Konami didn't tamper with the proven foundation, it merely polished and toughened it.

The principle stays true to its predecessor: you run right to left (and up too), aim in eight directions, and eliminate everything that appears on screen. A single hit means the loss of a life, so survival depends on lightning reflexes and memorizing enemy layouts. The beloved power-ups return, including the spread weapons, without which it's hard to stand a chance in that deluge of gunfire. If you know the first installment, you'll jump right in — and die right away too, because Super C takes no prisoners.

Compared to the first game, this one reworks the level structure: the pseudo-3D corridors where you ran into the depth are this time replaced by top-down views of sprawling bases you advance through. Visually the game is a notch richer, and the bosses are even more spectacular — giant alien forms that fill half the screen and demand precise targeting of weak points.

As with Contra, it shines best in two-player co-op. Advancing together through the storm of enemy fire, sharing weapons, and coordinating movement make it a great experience for two — though even solo it offers a serious challenge for players who like a game that pushes them to improve.

Super C is exactly the sequel fans wished for: more of the same, only sharper. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it perfects the run & gun recipe and remains one of the most honest action titles on the NES.

**Why play:** A polished sequel to Contra with everything that made the original great — tough run & gun action, excellent co-op, and spectacular bosses.
nes__super-c.teaser: A direct sequel to Contra with another dose of ruthless run-and-gun shooting.

nes__ninja-gaiden.teaser: Cinematic cutscenes on the NES + brutal pace; a milestone.
nes__ninja-gaiden.detail: It brought cinematic, anime-style cutscenes between levels to consoles — storytelling that was groundbreaking for 1988. Brutally fast ninja action with wall climbing. Notoriously demanding (especially the final stretch). Influential for the entire genre and the later 3D reboot.
nes__ninja-gaiden.article:
Instead of throwing you straight into the action, **Ninja Gaiden** first sets the story in motion — and does so cinematically, in a way consoles in 1988 practically didn't know. Between the levels, animated, anime-style cutscenes unfold, with detailed shots, dramatic cuts, and a tale of the revenge of the ninja Ryu Hayabusa. For its time it was a small revolution in how a game could tell a story.

When you set down the controller after the cutscene, action awaits that is every bit as intense as the story. Tecmo created a lightning-fast ninja platformer here in which Ryu climbs walls, leaps from wall to wall, and cuts down enemies with his katana and throwing techniques picked up along the way. The movement is nimble and elegant, but the environment is merciless — enemies reappear the moment you shift the camera, and a single mistimed jump can knock you back whole sections.

It was precisely the difficulty that became legendary. The game's final stretches rank among the hardest the NES had to offer: the last bosses, being sent back to the start of a level after death, and precise timing that forgives not even the slightest hesitation. For many players, beating Ninja Gaiden remains a badge of honor to this day.

This game's influence reaches far beyond 1988. The combination of cinematic storytelling and fast, technical action inspired entire generations of action titles, and the franchise itself later received a highly acclaimed 3D reboot that introduced Ryu Hayabusa to a new generation as one of the toughest fighters in the genre.

So Ninja Gaiden is a double milestone at once — as a pioneer of video-game storytelling and as a test of reflexes that still challenges even seasoned players today.

**Why play:** A pioneer of cinematic cutscenes on consoles and brutally fast ninja action — a storytelling milestone and a merciless test of reflexes in one.

nes__punch-out.teaser: Boxing as a reflex puzzle; hasn't aged.
nes__punch-out.detail: Boxing conceived as a reflex puzzle: every opponent has a learnable pattern you must read and counter. The original version featured the licensed Mike Tyson as the final boss (replaced by Mr. Dream after the contract expired). Charismatic characters; hasn't aged a day.
nes__punch-out.article:
Boxing as a game of brute strength? Forget it. Nintendo's **Punch-Out!!** proved in 1987 that the ring can actually be a puzzle — and that the most important muscles in boxing are the ones that govern perception and memory. This game elevated the fistfight into an elegant riddle of reflexes.

As the diminutive Little Mac, you step up against a lineup of charismatic, wildly caricatured opponents — from Glass Joe through King Hippo to Bald Bull. Each of them has their own fixed pattern of attacks and movements. Your task isn't to swing away blindly, but to **read** that pattern: to notice a tiny twitch of an eye, the tilt of a shoulder, or some other warning sign that gives away where the blow is coming from. Then, in a split second, you dodge, block, and land your fist exactly where your opponent is exposed. It's a dance of reading and reaction, not a slugfest.

The opponents are designed with such a feel for character that they burn themselves into memory — their animations, taunts, and dance moves make them icons that fans recognize to this day. The gradual discovery of how to outwit each one gives the game a great rhythm: every new boxer is a small standalone puzzle you have to crack by trial and error.

The original version bore a subtitle with a licensed name — **Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!** — with the final boss being the real Mike Tyson at a time when he was among the most feared boxers in the world. After the licensing contract expired, he was replaced in later editions by the fictional character Mr. Dream, but Tyson's presence in that opening version made the game a phenomenon of its era.

Unlike many titles of its era, Punch-Out!! has practically not aged. Its principle of reading the opponent is so clean and timeless that you'll gladly fire the game up even today.

**Why play:** Boxing conceived as a brilliant reflex puzzle — charismatic opponents, timeless gameplay, and a piece of boxing history in the form of Mike Tyson as the final boss.

nes__battletoads.teaser: Notoriously the hardest NES game; a challenge for masochists.
nes__battletoads.detail: Rare's answer to the Ninja Turtles, notorious for its extreme difficulty — the third level, the „Turbo Tunnel“ (a hoverbike race with obstacles you must memorize), is an internet symbol of frustration. Varied level styles and co-op (with notoriously problematic friendly fire). A memetic classic.
nes__battletoads.article:
There are games that will give you a hard time, and then there's Battletoads — a game that wants to break you. For an entire generation of NES players it became synonymous with pure, cunning, at times downright sadistic difficulty, and that's exactly why it lodged itself in memory more deeply than hundreds of more polished titles.

At first glance it's a classic beat 'em up in the style that was in vogue back then thanks to the success of the Ninja Turtles — three amphibian heroes, green skin, a lightly mutant vibe, and humor. But the studio **Rare**, then at the peak of its technical prowess, refused to be boring. Every level mixes in a different style of play: one moment you're pummeling enemies with fists that comically transform into giant hammers at the instant of impact, the next you're sliding down ropes, climbing walls, or fighting your way through a snake tunnel.

And then comes the **Turbo Tunnel**. The third level, a hoverbike race in which walls, holes, and obstacles loom up before you at ever-increasing speed. It's not a test of reflexes, it's a test of memory — you have to learn the exact placement of every barrier by heart, because a single mistake means instant death. Decades after its release, this level became an internet symbol of gaming frustration, a meme and a badge of honor all at once.

Two-player co-op paradoxically makes things worse. The friendly fire here is infamous: your partner can accidentally (or on purpose) drag you across the entire screen, quickly turning a friendly party into an argument on one couch. Many pairs never got past certain sections, and it's precisely these shared defeats that today rank among the platform's most fondly remembered experiences.

Battletoads is something of a paradox: a game most players never finished, and yet almost everyone knows it. Its technical inventiveness, animations, and cheeky personality made it a cult classic whose name, even decades later, is spoken with both a smile and a shudder.

**Why play:** If you want to experience the legendary NES difficulty firsthand and understand where half of gaming's frustration memes come from, Battletoads is a must — just brace your nerves.

nes__bionic-commando.article:
What if a platformer had no jump? This single, daring question makes Bionic Commando one of the most distinctive action titles on the NES — a game that takes away your most basic ability and hands you something far more interesting in its place.

The hero, you see, can't jump. His only means of moving upward and across chasms is the bionic arm — a grappling hook you use to latch onto platforms, swing over enemies, and literally pull yourself through the world. It sounds like a limitation, but it actually changes the entire logic of play. Instead of mindless hopping, you have to plan every grab, judge the trajectory, and perceive space in a completely different way than in an ordinary platformer.

The structure is likewise unconventional. You advance across a map divided into areas that you move between, communicate with units over the radio, and infiltrate enemy bases. This layer of tactics and espionage atmosphere gave the game a pleasantly more serious, military flavor for its time, one that set it apart from the more colorful competition.

The graphics are snappy, the music catchy, and the combat system — a combination of shooting and skillful swinging — rewards those who learn to control the arm instinctively. At first you'll hang helplessly in place and plunge into chasms, but once the mechanic gets into your blood, movement becomes unexpectedly fluid and satisfying.

Bionic Commando is exactly the kind of game that stands on a single bold idea and carries it through to the end. That's precisely why it earned a reputation as a hidden gem of the NES library, and its hook became a model for a whole host of later games.

**Why play:** For the unforgettable feel of movement based purely on the bionic hook — once you get used to the absence of a jump, you won't want anything else.
nes__bionic-commando.teaser: The hero can't jump; the only upward movement is the bionic arm's grappling hook, which defines the entire game.

nes__crystalis.teaser: A post-apocalyptic action RPG; ambitious and beloved.
nes__crystalis.detail: A post-apocalyptic action RPG (a world after a nuclear war in the year 2097) with fluid top-down combat, chargeable elemental swords, and spells. Often compared to Zelda, but with its own identity and a deeper RPG system. Highly regarded and underappreciated; it got a (controversial) GBC remake.
nes__crystalis.article:
The world ended in nuclear fire, and you awaken from a hundred-year sleep into a post-apocalyptic landscape where technology and magic have collided into one wondrous world. So begins Crystalis — an action RPG that to this day ranks among the most ambitious and at the same time most underappreciated titles on the NES.

The story unfolds after a devastating war in the year 2097, and from the very start it breathes a distinctive atmosphere: the ruins of civilization, nature come back to life, tribes and mysterious towers. Here the studio **SNK** blended a top-down action combat system with fluid controls that in many respects recalls the Zelda series, but it charts its own course. You have at your disposal swords of the four elements, which can be charged for stronger attacks, along with a set of spells and a gradually growing arsenal.

Against purely action-based clones, Crystalis sets itself apart with a deeper RPG layer. Your character gains experience, grows stronger, learns new incantations, and so combat carries weight — it's not just swinging a sword, but the gradual building of a hero capable of facing ever more dangerous threats. The chargeable elemental swords also force you to think about which element to deploy against which enemy.

On the NES the game excels both technically and in design: a vast world to explore, a decent amount of text and storytelling, fluid animations, and a soundtrack that burrows into memory. It's no wonder Crystalis built up a devoted fan base that to this day calls it one of the console's best but little-appreciated works.

The game later received a remake on the Game Boy Color, which is, however, controversial among fans — it changed the story and the atmosphere, and for many the original remains the clearly better version.

**Why play:** For a post-apocalyptic world full of ideas and the combination of action with a real RPG — Crystalis is a quiet gem of the NES that deserves far more attention.

nes__final-fantasy.teaser: The beginning of a legend; the roots of the entire JRPG genre.
nes__final-fantasy.detail: The game that saved the failing Square (hence „Final“) and became the foundation of the biggest JRPG franchise. It defined the genre's conventions: choosing and combining the party's classes, side-view turn-based combat, an epic quest with a twist in time. Hironobu Sakaguchi bet everything on a single card and won.
nes__final-fantasy.article:
When the founding team at the studio **Square** was putting together its last chance in 1987, no one suspected that a name was being born that would go on to carry dozens of games across generations of consoles. The word „Final“ sounded like a farewell back then — instead it became the beginning of one of the greatest legends of the gaming industry.

Final Fantasy arrived with a simple but powerful idea: assemble your own party of heroes and lead them on an epic quest to save the world. At the start the player chooses and combines classes — fighter, black and white mage, monk, and others — and each combination fundamentally changes the style of play. The turn-based combat shown from the side, where your foursome faces off against the enemies, became one of the defining conventions of the entire JRPG genre.

For its time it was a remarkably sprawling adventure: you explore the world map, sail ships, fly an airship, and gradually uncover a story that isn't afraid even of a twist in time. This ambition, combined with the atmospheric music of composer Nobuo Uematsu, gave the game a depth few expected on consoles.

Legend has it that Square was on the brink of collapse at the time and Hironobu Sakaguchi bet everything on a single card. The game's success saved the studio and launched a franchise that to this day ranks among the most important in the whole field. The game reached the West in 1990 and helped open the door there for Japanese RPGs.

Today Final Fantasy is above all a historical milestone — the root from which the entire tree of modern JRPGs grew. To play it is to return to the basics, to the moment when the rules that still hold today were being written.

**Why play:** For an encounter with the roots of the entire JRPG genre and with a game that literally saved Square and founded an immortal franchise.

nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.teaser: The building blocks of the JRPG; the third game was a phenomenon in Japan.
nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.detail: The building blocks of the JRPG from Yuji Horii (design) and Akira Toriyama (characters, creator of Dragon Ball). The third game introduced a class system and a day/night cycle; in Japan it was such a phenomenon that its sale flooded the streets. The fourth introduced a chapter structure with multiple protagonists. In the West they were released as „Dragon Warrior“ due to a trademark dispute.
nes__dragon-warrior-iii-iv.article:
In Japan the story goes that when the third game came out, the streets filled with people heading off for their copy — a phenomenon so powerful that legends of schoolchildren and queues weave around it. Dragon Quest, released in the West at the time as Dragon Warrior, wasn't merely a game but a genuine cultural event.

Behind the series stand two names that together created the magic. Designer Yuji Horii gave the genre a comprehensible, accessible structure, and the artist Akira Toriyama, creator of Dragon Ball, dressed the world in unmistakably friendly, iconic characters and enemies. This combination made the Japanese RPG into something that could reach the masses.

**Dragon Warrior III** pushed the series fundamentally further. It introduced an elaborate class system, where the player assembles a party and changes its professions, and brought in a day and night cycle that changed both the world and the possibilities. It was a grand adventure whose scope and freedom astonished in 1988 and turned it into a national event in Japan.

**Dragon Warrior IV** then set off in a different direction — toward storytelling. It divided the game into chapters, each of which follows a different protagonist before the story lines converge. This structure gave the characters room and personality and foreshadowed the emphasis on storytelling that became typical for the JRPG.

By the way, the name „Dragon Warrior“ in the West didn't come about by chance — the original name Dragon Quest couldn't be used there due to a trademark dispute, and so the series long bore a different name than in the rest of the world.

**Why play:** To understand what the entire JRPG genre stands on — these installments laid the cornerstones, from the class system to chapter-based storytelling.

nes__tetris.teaser: The two best puzzle games on the console.
nes__tetris.article:
Some games age, others remain eternal — and Tetris belongs to that second, rare category. The falling tetrominoes, the filling playfield, and that unmistakable melody made it one of the purest and most perfect gaming ideas of all time.

Almost everyone knows the principle today: variously rotated combinations of four blocks fall from above, and your task is to rotate and slot them so they form solid rows. Every filled row vanishes and frees up space, but the pace speeds up inexorably. The genius of it is that you grasp the rules in a few seconds, but you spend a lifetime seeking mastery of them.

The NES version offers exactly what you'd expect from a home console — comfortable controls on a big screen, a clean presentation, and catchy music that makes it easy to lose track of time. It's the ideal game for a short break and for marathons alike, when you just keep telling yourself „one more try“.

Tetris has gone down in history as one of the most influential and successful games ever, and became a symbol of the entire puzzle genre. Its simple beauty transcends the boundaries of platforms, age, and languages — it works for absolutely everyone.

That's precisely where its strength lies: it needs no story, no characters, no effects. All it takes is falling blocks and your urge to assemble the perfect row.

**Why play:** Because Tetris is timeless puzzle perfection — one of the best games ever made, and on the NES it's in an ideal form for endless play.

nes__dr-mario.article:
What does a plumber do when he doesn't feel like playing with pipes? He cures viruses. Dr. Mario took the famous hero, dressed him in a white coat, and sent him into battle against colorful microbes — and the result is one of the most addictive puzzle games on the NES.

The principle is brilliantly simple and yet deep. Two-color pills fall from above into a bottle, and you rotate and stack them so that four of the same color in a row or column destroy the matching viruses. The bottle is full of colorful little critters, and your task is to wipe them out to the last one — except that new pills fall ever faster and space keeps running out.

The two-player variant is what makes Dr. Mario immortal. Duels side by side, where you make each other's lives difficult, can unleash passions and joy as fierce as any racing game. It's the kind of title the whole family easily takes turns at.

The music also contributes to the overall charm — the catchy tracks „Fever“ and „Chill“ burrow into memory and are themselves among the console's iconic melodies. The controls are instant and precise, so you quickly settle into a smooth, almost hypnotic rhythm of stacking.

Dr. Mario showed that Nintendo can turn even its mascots into the foundation of a great puzzle game, and it became a permanent part of its puzzle legacy, followed by further installments across consoles.

**Why play:** For instantly graspable but hard-to-put-down puzzle fun — and above all for the two-player duels that will put friendships to the test.
nes__dr-mario.teaser: A plumber in a white coat fights colorful viruses; one of the most addictive games on NES.

nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.teaser: Pure logic in an adorable package; jewels of the genre.
nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.detail: A puzzle series that a young Satoru Iwata (later president of Nintendo) worked on at HAL. You push blocks, wipe out enemies and solve one screen at a time — brilliantly designed puzzles that ramp up steadily. Based on the Japanese Eggerland series. Some of the finest puzzles on the NES.
nes__adventures-of-lolo-1-3.article:
No rush, no reflexes — just you, a single screen and a puzzle that looks innocent until you start racking your brain. Adventures of Lolo is pure logic wrapped in a cute coat, and it ranks among the very best the genre offered on the NES.

The series grew out of the Japanese Eggerland line and its premise is elegantly simple: you control the round blue hero Lolo, collect hearts on every screen, dodge enemies, push blocks and cleverly use the environment to reach the exit. Each room is a self-contained puzzle with a single correct solution you must uncover before you make an irreversible move.

The beauty of this series lies in its perfectly measured difficulty curve. You start with trivial tasks, but every new screen introduces fresh elements, combinations and pitfalls. The game never cheats you — everything you need is right in front of you, you just have to figure it out. That moment when the solution to a seemingly impossible room finally clicks is pure joy.

The development at **HAL Laboratory** involved a young Satoru Iwata, the later legendary president of Nintendo. Thanks in part to his contribution, the series has that distinctive blend of friendliness, cleverness and precise design that HAL's other titles would later become famous for.

The trio of games offers dozens upon dozens of well-thought-out puzzles and together they form a little puzzle textbook. It is ideal entertainment for calm evenings when you want to put your head to work, not your fingers.

**Why play:** For brilliantly designed, gradually escalating puzzles in an adorable package — some of the best logic games of the entire NES era.

nes__kickle-cubicle.teaser: Another great puzzle for your brain-teaser evenings.
nes__kickle-cubicle.detail: Kickle freezes enemies and builds ice bridges across chasms. Wario's Woods is famous as the very last licensed NES game in North America (1994, long after the SNES arrived) — an action puzzler where Toad lines up enemies and bombs. Both are clever logic games.
nes__kickle-cubicle.article:
Freeze an enemy into a block of ice and build a bridge across a chasm out of it — that is the idea Kickle Cubicle is built on, one of those lesser-known but all the more delightful logic games on the NES.

You control the grinning hero Kickle, who has one crucial ability: his breath turns enemies into ice blocks. He can then push these blocks around, use them to fill holes and build himself a path across the level. The goal is to collect the hidden items scattered on each screen and open the exit, with every room a self-contained puzzle requiring the right sequence of steps.

The charm of the game lies in the combination of cute, colourful graphics and a surprisingly thoughtful level design. What looks like a children's trifle can keep you genuinely busy — you have to work out where and when to freeze an enemy, how to position the ice bridges and how not to block yourself in. It is pleasantly contemplative logic without needless stress.

Kickle Cubicle belongs to the kind of titles that can easily get lost among the big names on a console, but that all the more reward anyone who gives them a chance. It offers exactly that calm, puzzle-solving fun you can spend a long evening with, never feeling that the game is cheating you.

If you enjoy puzzle games whose main asset is a clever idea and its clean execution, this icy classic deserves a place in your library.

**Why play:** For the original mechanic of freezing enemies and building ice bridges — clever, calm logic in an adorable package for laid-back puzzle evenings.

nes__wario-s-woods.article:
Wario's Woods holds one indisputable distinction: it is famous as the very last licensed game ever released for the NES in North America, in 1994 — long after its successor the SNES had already taken the throne. In its own right it feels like a charming farewell to an entire era.

Unlike most puzzle games, you do not stack or rotate blocks falling from above. Instead you directly control the character Toad, who moves around the playfield, picks up and shifts enemies and bombs, and lines them up so that the right combination destroys them. This action-driven, spatial perspective makes Wario's Woods an unconventional and refreshing entry in the genre.

The task is to clear the screen by joining enemies and explosives into rows and columns, while more critters keep dropping in from above. The blend of action-based movement and logical planning creates a pleasantly hectic rhythm — you have to think and react nimbly at the same time, a combination you won't meet in more static puzzlers.

And of course Wario is on hand as the antagonist, giving the game just the right playful, slightly mischievous atmosphere and the colourful presentation typical of Nintendo. It is a title that keeps an infectious energy and that „one more try“ pull.

Its historical context lends it a special charm: to play Wario's Woods today is to touch the last official moment of a famous console, the full stop after an era that defined home gaming.

**Why play:** For its unconventional action puzzling, where you yourself push enemies and bombs — and for its symbolic status as the very last licensed NES game in North America.
nes__wario-s-woods.teaser: The last licensed NES game in America (1994); instead of blocks, you control Toad.

nes__kid-icarus.detail: Built on the same engine as Metroid and by the same team, but with Greek mythology and vertical climbing. Pit collects upgrades and climbs toward the sky. Difficult and underrated in its day; it only gained cult status and a comeback with the Uprising installment (3DS) and appearances in Smash Bros.
nes__kid-icarus.article:
From Greek mythology Nintendo borrowed a winged hero and sent him into hell — not downward, though, but upward. **Kid Icarus** ranks among the most challenging and, at the time, most underrated titles of the early NES, yet it grew out of exactly the same workshop and at the same time as the legendary Metroid.

That is no coincidence. The game was created at Nintendo R&D1 and runs on an engine related to Metroid's, only instead of the claustrophobic corridors of planet Zebes it offers a vertical climb toward the heavens. The hero Pit, an archer with angelic ambitions, climbs upward screen by screen, collecting upgrades and hearts he spends at merchants. That climbing is itself a mechanic: falling off the bottom of the screen means death, so every jump is a little drama.

What makes the game stand out is its uncompromising difficulty and its structure. Vertical stretches alternate with side-scrolling dungeons complete with maps and bosses, changing the pace and the demands on the player. Pit starts weak and vulnerable, but as the game goes on he grows strong enough that at the summit he faces the goddess of darkness herself. That arc — from helplessness to triumph — is part of why fans remember the game.

For many years Kid Icarus was more of a footnote in Nintendo's history, a curiosity in the shadow of the big brands. The comeback came later and grandly: thanks to Pit's presence in the **Super Smash Bros.** games and especially the modern installment **Kid Icarus: Uprising** on the 3DS, the brand gained a new cult status and a whole generation of new fans who traced their way back to the original.

Today the eight-bit original is regarded with respect — as a tough, ambitious game that took mythology seriously and did not go easy on players. It is a title for those who love a challenge and are not afraid to die.

**Why play:** A demanding, atmospheric platformer from Nintendo's golden era that stands at the roots of the metroidvania and today is finally reaping its deserved respect.

nes__blaster-master.teaser: Tank + on-foot, two play styles; ambitious hybrid.
nes__blaster-master.detail: An ambitious hybrid: you drive the SOPHIA tank in a side view and step out on foot into top-down caves (switching between two play styles). An interconnected, explorable world à la metroidvania. Great music and technical work from Sunsoft. It got a modern sequel (Blaster Master Zero).
nes__blaster-master.article:
Step out of the tank and go into a cave on foot — few eight-bit games gave the player such freedom of movement as **Blaster Master**. This is no ordinary platformer but an ambitious hybrid of two gaming worlds fused into a single interconnected adventure.

At its core is the SOPHIA tank, in which you roam sprawling levels from a side view — jumping, climbing walls, collecting upgrades that give the tank new abilities and open up previously inaccessible areas. But when you hit a door to the underground, you step out of the vehicle and continue on foot in a top-down view, in caves full of enemies and bosses. That switch between two distinct play styles was bold for its time and still works surprisingly smoothly today.

The world of Blaster Master is interconnected and explorable in a way that foreshadows the metroidvania genre — a new ability means a new route, a return to old places and the gradual uncovering of the map. The game is further driven by the craftsmanship of **Sunsoft**, one of the NES's technical elite: it looks great, moves smoothly and the soundtrack has swagger.

The story of a boy searching for his lost frog, which turns into a fight against mutants, is of course just a pretext — and in the West it got a different flavour than in Japan. But that hardly matters. What counts is the feel of playing: that moment when you first climb a vertical wall in your tank, or when you tensely head out on foot into an unknown cave.

Blaster Master earned a cult reputation and got a modern sequel, **Blaster Master Zero**, which dusted off the original concept for a new generation and confirmed that the tank/on-foot switching idea ages well.

**Why play:** A technically polished hybrid of action, exploration and metroidvania from the masters at Sunsoft — one of the most inventive games on the NES.

nes__little-samson.teaser: A rare, technically top-tier platformer; a collector's grail.
nes__little-samson.detail: Released at the very tail end of the NES in a tiny print run, so it is today one of the most expensive NES titles of all (a complete copy runs into the tens of thousands). You play four characters with different abilities (a boy, a dragon, a mouse, a golem) that you switch between. Technically top-tier and excellent to play — emulation is the only reasonable path.
nes__little-samson.article:
There is a handful of cartridges collectors crave like a holy grail — and **Little Samson** is one of them. It came out at the very tail end of the NES era in 1992, at a time when the world had long since turned its gaze to sixteen-bit consoles, and so it sold desperately few copies.

The result? Today it ranks among the most expensive NES titles of all, and a complete, well-preserved copy sells for the equivalent of thousands of dollars. But the price tag should not overshadow what matters: Little Samson is, in purely gameplay terms, an absolutely outstanding platformer, one of the most technically advanced titles of the entire eight-bit generation.

Its gameplay rests on a clever idea of four playable characters you switch between freely during play. The titular Samson can climb walls and ceilings, the dragon Kikira flies and breathes fire, the mouse Gamm slips through narrow gaps, and the stone golem Ko can soak up enormous punishment. Every level thus becomes a little puzzle: which character to deploy, where it pays to risk the dragon and where it is better to send in the durable golem.

The graphics are detailed and colourful, the animation smooth and the level design thoughtful — you can tell the creators at **Takeru** knew exactly where the NES's limits were and pushed them to the max. The soundtrack and overall craftsmanship hold to the same high bar.

The sad truth is that owning an original is unrealistic for most people today — the physical cartridge simply costs a fortune.
