It is a title that rewards patience and planning yet never lets you get bogged down in a single repetitive loop.

Graphically and sonically it is a solid representative of its era — colorful ports, a world map you gradually reveal, and music that underscores the atmosphere of distant lands. The pace is deliberate, but that is precisely what feels today like a pleasant counterpoint to frantic modern games. You sit down for the evening thinking you will just quickly reach the next port, and suddenly it is midnight.

New Horizons belongs among titles that were never as massively popular on consoles as action hits, but among fans of strategy and simulation it built a solid reputation as one of the more accessible gateways into the genre of trade and discovery. If you love the feeling that the world is open and you write your own story within it, this is the game for you.

**Why play:** An open naval simulation with several paths to glory that combines trade, exploration, and adventure into an addictive whole.
snes__uncharted-waters-new-horizons.teaser: A strategy game from the age of great discoveries with multiple captains and a freedom the genre didn't offer back then.

snes__aerobiz-supersonic.article:
Running an airline may sound dull — until you discover how much adrenaline goes into deciding whether to open a route to Tokyo or buy a new aircraft instead. Aerobiz Supersonic is a strategy and economic simulation for the Super Nintendo in which you become the head of an airline competing for dominance over the global skies.

The core of the game is building a network of routes between real-world metropolises. You must negotiate landing rights, buy and renew your fleet of aircraft, set ticket prices, and track demand, which shifts with the economy, politics, and the season. The game runs across several decades, so technology advances — from piston-driven machines through jet aircraft to the supersonic transport that the Supersonic subtitle references.

What makes Aerobiz so gripping is its degree of interconnection. Every decision has consequences: overly aggressive expansion can drain you financially, while caution hands lucrative markets to the competition. Random events enter the game — recessions, oil crises, wars, and Olympics that temporarily change the demand for travel to a given region. So you must not only plan but also react flexibly.

Visually the game bets on clarity: a world map, tables, charts, and aircraft icons. It is not a visual spectacle, but that only makes it lean harder on the depth of its systems and on that sweet feeling when your long-term gamble finally pays off and your rivals start to retreat. The game also supports multiplayer, which turns the battles over markets into a genuinely tense affair.

Among fans of economic simulations, Aerobiz Supersonic has a reputation as a surprisingly deep and balanced title that arrived on the console at a time when similar genres reigned mainly on computers. It is proof that even a strategy about tables and tariffs can be captivating on the SNES.

**Why play:** A deep airline business simulation with real metropolises, decades of development, and thrilling competition for the global skies.
snes__aerobiz-supersonic.teaser: An economic simulation of an airline company; routes, planes, and the fight for dominance over the skies.

snes__lemmings.article:
Hundreds of little green-haired creatures march toward certain doom, and the only thing standing between them and the abyss is you. Lemmings on the Super Nintendo brings one of the most ingenious puzzle ideas of its time to the Nintendo console and proves that a simple premise can grow into an utterly addictive game.

The principle is touchingly simple and devilishly clever at the same time: the lemmings hurl themselves forward with no instinct for self-preservation, and your task is to lead a sufficient number of them to the exit. On their own they do nothing clever, but you can assign them roles — diggers, bridge builders, blockers, climbers, or the one who sacrifices himself in an explosion. From these few abilities you assemble solutions to ever more fiendish levels.

The beauty of Lemmings lies in the tension between planning and time. The creatures do not stop, so you must think ahead and often improvise when a single badly issued command sends the whole procession to its doom. The levels gradually add traps, differences in height, and the need for precise timing, until an unassuming game becomes a genuine test of logic and a cool head.

On the SNES the game benefits from colorful graphics, clear controls, and catchy music that burrows into your memory. Controlling it with a gamepad instead of a mouse takes some getting used to, but once you master the rhythm of switching between roles, play flows smoothly. Every solved level brings that peculiar kind of satisfaction where you feel clever precisely because the game was, for a moment, cleverer than you.

Lemmings became one of the most influential puzzle games ever and was ported to practically every platform of its era. Its simple yet endlessly variable mechanics are still cited today as a textbook example of great game design.

**Why play:** A brilliantly simple logic classic where you rescue suicidal little creatures and every solved level tastes like a small victory.
snes__lemmings.teaser: Hundreds of adorable little creatures marching toward certain doom; your job is to save as many as possible.

snes__street-fighter-ii-turbo-hyper-figh.article:
Bringing the arcade marvel Street Fighter II into the living room was the holy grail of the early nineties. The Super Nintendo proved to be its ideal home, and Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting on it was one of the main reasons people bought the console. For many players it was the first chance to have those legendary fights at home, anytime and without feeding coins into a machine.

This version cleverly combined the best of two arcade editions. It offered both the normal speed matching Champion Edition and the frantic Turbo mode inspired by Hyper Fighting, and moreover, for the first time on the SNES, it let you play as the four grand bosses — Balrog, Vega, Sagat, and M. Bison. Players could thus choose the pace as well as the entire roster of fighters and get a feel for the specials they were used to from the arcades.

The conversion was among the most faithful home consoles offered at the time. Large sprites, fluid animation, and a decently preserved feel of the controls made this cartridge one of the most prized in the SNES library. The Super Nintendo's six-button controller was made for Street Fighter, giving the platform a tangible comfort advantage over the standard three-button Mega Drive pad.

In development terms it was a continuation of Capcom's strategy to squeeze the maximum out of the brand's huge success. After the first home Street Fighter II, which became one of the console's best-selling titles of all time on the SNES, this improved Turbo edition arrived as the logical next step for players hungry for a faster and more complete version.

The cultural significance of the home ports cannot be overstated. It was precisely thanks to them that Street Fighter II became a true mass phenomenon that penetrated pop culture, T-shirts, comics, and later the silver screen as well. The ability to play at home against a friend on the couch created countless rivalries and memories and cemented the brand's standing in players' hearts.

Compared to the first home conversion, this Turbo edition brought a tangible leap forward. Whereas the original Street Fighter II on the SNES offered only normal speed and did not allow playing as the bosses, Turbo: Hyper Fighting added a faster mode and the playable quartet of grand fighters. For many it was reason enough to buy the game again, even though they already had the previous version at home. Capcom thus cleverly monetized a single brand several times over, and players did not protest, because they were getting a measurably more complete and livelier experience that was also closer to what they knew from the arcades.

Today this cartridge is a sought-after piece among collectors and still plays wonderfully. It represents the moment when the arcade elite truly moved into living rooms and when home consoles proved they could faithfully deliver an experience once paid for in arcades. For Super Nintendo owners it was one of the defining experiences of the era.

**Why play:** Home Street Fighter II in its most complete form, with a choice of pace, playable bosses, and the comfortable six-button controls of the SNES.
snes__street-fighter-ii-turbo-hyper-figh.teaser: A home port of the arcade marvel, combining the best of two versions of Street Fighter II.

snes__mortal-kombat-ii.article:
When Mortal Kombat II moved from the arcades to home consoles in 1994, tension ran high. The previous installment had suffered humiliating censorship on the Super Nintendo, blood was turned into sweat, and the game lost commercially to the bloody Mega Drive version. But with the sequel the tables turned, and Nintendo learned from the mistake that had cost it both reputation and revenue.

The Mortal Kombat II version for the Super Nintendo now included blood. After a wave of criticism and the creation of the ESRB rating system, Nintendo relaxed its strict policy and allowed the game to be released faithful to the arcade original. Players finally got an uncensored experience on the powerful console, with spurting blood and complete fatalities — an enormous leap and a satisfaction compared to the embarrassment of the first game.

And it was the technical power of the Super Nintendo that shone here. The conversion was among the most faithful the home systems offered. Large digitized sprites, rich colors, and decently preserved sound made this cartridge one of the technically most impressive fighting games on the console. The game faithfully carried over the expanded roster, the new fatalities, Babalities and Friendships, and all the secrets for which the sequel was so loved.

In development terms the conversion was overseen by Acclaim, and the whole situation perfectly illustrates how quickly the market changed. Within a single year, the censorship that had sunk the game commercially became a thing of the past, and blood became the standard, albeit newly fitted with a rating label. Mortal Kombat II on the SNES thus symbolizes the victory of player demand and the beginning of an era in which more mature content earned a legitimate place on consoles.

Culturally it was one of the defining experiences of the late Super Nintendo era. Couch battles against a friend, discovering hidden fighters, and pulling off fatalities were among the highlights of console gaming in the mid-nineties. The cartridge became one of the must-have titles and is today a beloved piece among collectors.

Compared to the competing Mega Drive version, this time it was the SNES that came out on top. The Super Nintendo's more powerful graphics hardware offered a richer color palette and cleaner digitized sprites, so the characters and backdrops looked more detailed and overall more faithful to the arcade original. Whereas with the first installment the winner was decided by censorship, with the sequel — where blood now flowed on both platforms — it was pure technical quality that decided, and there the SNES fared better. For players it was a one-hundred-eighty-degree turnaround from the situation of the previous year.

Compared to the first, censored version, SNES Mortal Kombat II represents the righting of a wrong. It is proof that players eventually got what they wanted, and that even conservative Nintendo had to yield to the reality of the market and the changing expectations of an audience maturing alongside its favorite medium.

**Why play:** A faithful and this time uncensored conversion of the great sequel, technically impressive and with the blood and fatalities just as they were always meant to be.
snes__mortal-kombat-ii.teaser: After the censored first game, finally uncut blood; Nintendo learned from its own mistake.

snes__prince-of-persia.article:
The sand in the hourglass drains away relentlessly, and you have exactly one hour to fight your way through treacherous dungeons, rescue the princess, and overthrow the evil vizier Jaffar. Prince of Persia on the Super Nintendo is a polished console version of the game that forever changed the idea of what character movement in a platformer could look like.

The original was created by Jordan Mechner and first appeared on the Apple II computer in the late eighties. Mechner used rotoscoping, filming his brother's movements and animating the hero from the footage, so that running, jumps, and falls looked unusually fluid and realistic. The SNES version took that fluidity up a notch, adding more colorful graphics, new levels, and improved sound, making it one of the best console conversions of the entire series.

The gameplay rests on a combination of precise platforming and sword fights. Every jump must be timed, because floors collapse, spikes lurk, and blades spring out. The fights require a feel for attack and parry, not frantic button-mashing. All of this under the pressure of a time limit that turns the game into a tense race against your own memory and dexterity.

Prince of Persia had a fundamental influence on the entire cinematic platformer genre, and its rotoscoped animation inspired a host of later games. The brand later grew into the sprawling 3D series The Sands of Time by Ubisoft, which breathed new life into the genre in the modern era, but the roots of it all lie in these tense two-dimensional dungeons.

The console version for the SNES is still beloved today precisely for its expanded content and its refined feel of control. It is a title that rewards patience, memorization, and precision, and where every successful jump brings a small victory.

**Why play:** A model example of the cinematic platformer with timelessly fluid animation and tension that grips your heart to this day.
snes__prince-of-persia.teaser: An hour to save the princess; the movement animation that forever changed platformers.

snes__another-world.article:
Lightning strikes a particle accelerator and the young scientist Lester finds himself on an alien planet where he knows neither the language, nor the enemies, nor the rules. Another World is one of the boldest and most distinctive titles of its time, and the Super Nintendo version brought this cinematic vision to Nintendo's consoles.

The game was created practically single-handedly by the French author Éric Chahi at the turn of the eighties and nineties. He used vector polygon graphics, which made the characters and environments look fluid and cinematic at a time when most games relied on pixel sprites. The result was a unique visual style and storytelling without a single word, relying purely on image, animation, and atmosphere.

The gameplay is a mix of platforming, action, and logic puzzles, where death lurks literally around every corner. The game does not hold your hand, shows no lives or tutorials; instead it lets you discover the world by trial and error. Observation, timing, and improvisation are key, whether you are fleeing a predator, using a laser weapon, or figuring out how to get further. An important role is also played by the silent ally you meet in captivity.

Another World, released in North America under the title Out of This World, became a cult title and fundamentally influenced the concept of an atmospheric, visually narrated gaming experience. It inspired later creators of independent games, and its influence is evident in works that emphasize mood and direction rather than the number of enemies. The game was ported to a countless number of platforms and even received modern remakes.

On the SNES it is a demanding but unforgettable experience for players seeking something more than reflexive action. It is an interactive film from a time when it was still being discovered just what games could do.

**Why play:** A quiet, cinematic, and still unique experience that proves a game could be art as early as the beginning of the nineties.
snes__another-world.teaser: A cinematic sci-fi adventure practically created single-handedly by Éric Chahi using vector graphics.

snes__micro-machines.article:
Imagine a world seen from the height of a kitchen counter, a breakfast table, or a workshop bench. That is exactly where one of the most original racing ideas of its time takes place. Micro Machines puts you behind the wheel of tiny cars, motorboats, hovercraft, and bulldozers that tear around the giant backdrops of an ordinary household. Amid scattered cereal, puddles of spilled milk, and pencils, the magic of perspective comes fully into its own, making every corner funny and treacherous at once.

The gameplay is built on a top-down view and the unexpectedly demanding physics of the little vehicles. The tracks are not just a backdrop but an active obstacle: if you fall off the table or end up in a puddle, the camera waits relentlessly and your rival gains a lead. The racing model is simple to control but hard to master, which makes the title an ideal game for short but repeatedly addictive runs. It is precisely this immediacy that made Micro Machines synonymous with arcade fun racing.

The series is based on a license of the real collectible Micro Machines toy cars, which were a popular toy at the time. The developer Codemasters managed to build a distinctive gaming brand out of a tiny toy, one that spread across many platforms from eight-bit computers through consoles to later titles. The Super Nintendo version brings this concept into a colorful sixteen-bit coat.

The series became legendary above all thanks to its multiplayer. Later installments became famous for letting even four players play at once on a single controller, with a pair sharing one gamepad. This communal, noisy, and competitive living-room atmosphere made Micro Machines a fixture of gaming parties and one of the few racers that can be played as a ruthless elimination arena as well.

The cultural footprint of this brand is significant mainly because it showed that a racing game need not be about realism or supercars. All it takes is a good idea, humor, and perfectly tuned controls. For many players of the European school of the eighties and nineties, Micro Machines was the first racing game over which they burst out laughing just as often as with rage.

**Why play:** For timeless, instantly understandable fun and some of the best battles on a single couch that the racing genre has to offer.
snes__micro-machines.teaser: Miniature cars racing across kitchen counters; the magic of a giant perspective in a tiny world.

snes__top-gear-2.article:
There are racing games you remember for their graphics, and then those that stick with you for their music and sense of speed. Top Gear 2 belongs unequivocally to the second group. This sequel to the popular sixteen-bit racer hurls you into a series of tracks across continents, where speed mixes with an unexpected dose of strategy and where every mistake hurts on the results table.

The core of the game is racing from a behind-the-car view along winding tracks full of rivals. Compared to plain arcade driving, Top Gear 2 adds a layer of depth: between races you spend your earned money on upgrades to the engine, tires, transmission, or nitro. You have to reckon with fuel consumption, varying weather, and vehicle damage, so each event is a bit of a managerial calculation too. This combination of arcade action and light car building made the game an above-average complex experience for its time.

Behind the game stands the studio Gremlin Graphics, a British developer with a rich racing tradition, and it builds on the success of the first installment. The Top Gear series (known under different names in some regions) was one of the flagships of the racing genre on the Super Nintendo at a time when the console did not yet have many strong representatives of this style.

An inseparable part of its renown is the stirring music. The dynamic soundtrack is among the most cited examples of how the SNES sound chip could conjure an energetic, almost rock-like atmosphere that drives the player forward perhaps even more than the speed on screen itself. Many fans to this day rank these tracks among the best that sixteen-bit racing had to offer.

Top Gear 2 earned a reputation as an honest, addictive, and surprisingly extensive racer for one or two players in split-screen. For a whole generation of players who had no access to the later 3D racers, it represented the peak of what they expected from the genre, and it is remembered to this day as one of the gems of the SNES library.

**Why play:** For the feeling of pure speed, an infectious soundtrack, and unexpected tactical depth in upgrades and car management.
snes__top-gear-2.teaser: Speed and music on the track; a sequel renowned more for its sense of tempo than its graphics.

snes__wild-guns.article:
The Wild West meets a steam-powered future, and from the resulting collision emerges one of the most stylish action games on the entire Super Nintendo. Wild Guns combines cowboy romance with steampunk robots and creates a world where you face not only bandits but also giant mechanical guardians and steam engines spewing lead. Even the idea alone is bold enough for the game to stick in one's memory.

The gameplay is brilliantly simple yet masterfully tuned. Your character stands at the front of the scene and moves side to side, while with a cursor you aim anywhere on the screen and eliminate enemies. The key to survival is the dodge and roll with which you evade bullets, and the well-timed use of dynamite. This combination of shooting from a rear view and manual aiming makes Wild Guns something between a classic shooting-gallery game and hectic run-and-gun action.

Behind the game stands the Japanese studio Natsume, known for its feel for pixel craftsmanship. Wild Guns came out in 1994, at the very end of the SNES golden era, and belongs among titles that did not break through on a mass scale in their original release; all the more, however, did its reputation grow among collectors and connoisseurs. Original cartridges eventually became a sought-after and expensively traded item.

The game's cultural significance was confirmed by the fact that, years later, it received an improved return. The Wild Guns Reloaded version brought the title to modern players on contemporary platforms, added new characters, weapons, and levels, and proved that an idea from the mid-nineties had lost none of its charm even after more than two decades.

Wild Guns is today rightly ranked among the hidden gems of the sixteen-bit era. It is a game that makes sense both in solo and in co-op for two players, where the chaos and the joy of blasting the entire screen multiply. The combination of an original theme, perfect controls, and high but fair difficulty makes it a must for every fan of arcade action.

**Why play:** For a phenomenal mix of Western and steampunk and for one of the most addictive shooting-action games the SNES offers, ideal in co-op too.
snes__wild-guns.teaser: The Wild West meets steampunk; a stylish shooter with cowboys against mechanical robots.

snes__nhl-94.article:
For an entire generation of hockey fans there is a game where just saying two digits instantly brings a warm feeling of nostalgia. NHL '94 is the title that many to this day consider the moment when the sports arcade on consoles definitively broke through into perfection. Fast, fluid, and incredibly addictive hockey made it the benchmark of the genre.

The gameplay tunes exactly that delicate line between accessibility and depth. Movement on the ice is fast, passes whistle by, and goals fall in bursts that please even the uninitiated viewer. NHL '94 is legendary in part for introducing the one-button attack in the form of the wrist deke and puck control, which gave the game an unmistakable rhythm. Battles along the boards and the ability to knock down an opponent gave the matches the juice that players loved.

Behind the series stands Electronic Arts and their EA Sports brand, which with this very installment launched its long-term dominance in the genre. NHL '94 came out simultaneously on the Super Nintendo and the competing Sega Mega Drive console, and both versions earned an enthusiastic reception. The game featured an official NHL license as well as the players' association, so you could take the ice with the real teams and stars of the time.

The cultural significance of this installment reaches beyond the boundaries of video games. Its fame was further amplified by the film Swingers, in which NHL '94 became a literal cult prop and the subject of one-liners between characters. For many players it is to this day synonymous with perfect retro hockey and appears at the top of countless polls of the best sports games of all time.

Dozens of annual NHL editions have been added since then, technology has advanced by light-years, but NHL '94 holds a special status as an untouchable classic. It is a game that veterans return to not for realism but for the pure joy of play, which later installments, with all their complexity, often struggle to match.

**Why play:** For instantly understandable, lightning-fast hockey that many to this day consider the most fun installment of the entire series.
snes__nhl-94.teaser: The benchmark of arcade hockey; fast, fluid gameplay that defined the genre for years to come.

snes__nba-jam.article:
Boomshakalaka! A single word is enough to trigger an avalanche of memories in anyone who grew up in the nineties next to an arcade cabinet or a console. NBA Jam is not a basketball simulation, it is its explosive, exaggerated and utterly unbridled celebration. Two on two, no fouls, no whistled travels and jumps so high that the stars' heads literally catch fire.

The gameplay rests on speed, spectacle and instant reward. The game abandons the rulebook and instead aims for a pure show: wild dunks, mid-air somersaults and the famous heated-up player mechanic, where after three baskets in a row the ball bursts into flames and your shots become all but unstoppable. This simplicity combined with the spectacle turned NBA Jam into an arcade phenomenon and one of the highest-grossing coin-op games of its era.

Originally an arcade title, it was created by the studio Midway with Mark Turmell as its designer. NBA Jam capitalized on an official NBA license, so real league stars took the court in cartoonishly inflated proportions. The game also became famous for its many hidden characters and jokes, among them the inclusion of the then-current American presidential couple as unlockable players.

The versions for Super Nintendo and other home systems brought the arcade experience into living rooms and became the backbone of many a gaming night. Commentary lines like He's on fire or the aforementioned Boomshakalaka etched themselves into pop culture so deeply that even people who never played the game still quote them today. Few sports titles ever left a comparable linguistic mark.

NBA Jam defined an entire sub-genre of over-the-top, two-on-two arcade sports and inspired a host of successors as well as later remakes and reboots. Its legacy is simple but powerful: it proved that a sport in a video game doesn't have to be faithful in order to be fun. It just has to be unpredictable, fast and full of show.

**Why play:** For timeless two-on-two arcade fun, flaming basketballs and one of the best party experiences any sports game has ever offered.
snes__nba-jam.teaser: Boomshakalaka! Over-the-top, explosive 2-on-2 basketball where players' heads catch fire on a hot shot.

snes__killer-instinct.article:
When the icy Combo Breaker rings out on screen at the very start and the characters begin chaining together endless strings of blows, it's clear this is no ordinary fighter. Killer Instinct arrived with the ambition to astonish, and it succeeded completely. This dark, aggressive and visually stunning brawl became one of the most distinctive brands of the mid-nineties.

At the heart of the game lies an elaborate combo attack system. Killer Instinct built its identity on long, flashily chained sequences of hits that an opponent could interrupt using the so-called Combo Breaker. This interplay of attack and defense gave fights a unique tactical layer and a visual flourish, with the hit counter climbing into dozens of strikes to the accompaniment of a roaring announcer. There was no shortage of brutal finishing moves in the spirit of its rival Mortal Kombat, either.

Behind the game stands the British studio Rare in cooperation with Nintendo, with the arcade version using pre-rendered 3D graphics that felt otherworldly at the time. This visual style, similar to the technology used in Donkey Kong Country, turned the characters and environments into a breathtaking spectacle. Killer Instinct came out for the Super Nintendo and became one of the most anticipated titles on the console.

The game's cultural impact was considerable. The home version for the SNES shipped with a bonus music album titled Killer Cuts, which contained remixed tracks from the game and underscored its energetic, almost soundtrack-like identity. The roster of fighters ranged from a skeleton and an ice warrior through a dinosaur to cybernetic beings, setting the game apart from the genre conventions of the day.

Killer Instinct received a sequel as well as a much later modern reboot, which successfully brought the brand to a new generation of players and confirmed that its combo system truly was timeless. For those who remember it, though, the original remains a symbol of the era when fighting games competed over which would dazzle more, and in that battle Killer Instinct was among the loudest.

**Why play:** For the adrenaline-fueled combo system, the iconic announcer and one of the technically most impressive fighting games of its time on the SNES.
snes__killer-instinct.teaser: A dark, aggressive fighter famous for its endless combos and the phrase Combo Breaker.

snes__seiken-densetsu-3.article:
Three heroes, six possible stories and a world that changes depending on who you choose as your main character. Seiken Densetsu 3 belongs among the legends of the 16-bit era, ones that were long only whispered about in the West. This sequel to Squaresoft's Mana series never left Japan back in its day, so players around the world enjoyed it for many years only thanks to fan translations.

The game builds on the action combat system of its predecessor Secret of Mana but expands it in every respect. Battles play out in real time right in the environment, and an elaborate class system was added, where characters can advance along a path of light or darkness and change their classes. The day-and-night cycle and the rotation of the days of the week, which affect gameplay, are also ingenious. Choosing your opening trio from six heroes fundamentally changes the angle of the narrative as well as the final enemy, giving the game enormous replay value.

Seiken Densetsu 3 came out in Japan in 1995, at a time when Squaresoft was churning out one technically and artistically polished title after another. The pixel art, animation and color palette rank among the finest the Super Nintendo was ever able to display, and Hiroki Kikuta's music enriches the game with an atmospheric, at times dreamlike tone.

The game's cultural significance is twofold. On one hand it is the peak of the classic branch of the Mana series, on the other it became a textbook example of a game the Western audience loved long before it officially received it. An official English release didn't come until much later, in 2019, under the title Trials of Mana as part of the Collection of Mana for Nintendo Switch, and later also as a full 3D remake. For years it circulated only in the form of a fan translation that enthusiasts created themselves in order to make accessible a title that in Japan enjoyed a reputation as one of the finest RPGs on the console.

Also worth noting is how the game handles the party. From the six heroes, from the fighter Angela through the warrior Duran to the wolf-girl Riesz, you assemble a trio, and it is your first choice that determines the main villain and the overall arc of the story. This structure was exceptionally ambitious for its time and makes every playthrough a slightly different experience, a concept the genre returned to only gradually.

For many collectors and JRPG fans, Seiken Densetsu 3 remains one of the most beautiful and most ambitious games of its generation. The combination of action combat, a branching story and artistic splendor makes it a title that even today holds up as a demonstration of what a 16-bit console was capable of.

**Why play:** An action JRPG with a branching story and gorgeous graphics that was long among the most sought-after unavailable treasures of the Super Nintendo.
snes__seiken-densetsu-3.teaser: Three heroes, six stories, a world that changes with your choice. It reached the West only thanks to fans.

snes__donkey-kong-country.article:
When Donkey Kong Country arrived in 1994, players couldn't believe their eyes. The characters and environments looked as if they had been rendered on an expensive workstation, not like something running on a console from 1990. With it, the British studio Rare proved that the Super Nintendo still had plenty of untapped potential inside it, and brought the gorilla Donkey Kong back into the spotlight.

In terms of gameplay it's a precise 2D platformer. You control Donkey Kong and his nimbler nephew Diddy, switching between them depending on the situation, collecting bananas and the letters K-O-N-G, searching for hidden bonus rooms and fighting your way through traps, barrel cannons and enemies led by the reptile King K. Rool, who stole the banana hoard. Animal helpers like the rhino Rambi or the bird Expresso aid you, and every level is designed with an emphasis on pace, precision and rewarding attentive players. The game also doesn't skimp on variety: from mine carts hurtling along rails through underwater passages to caves and snowy peaks, it offers a colorful palette of situations that regularly shift the pace and the demands on the player.

The technical sensation was the so-called pre-rendered graphics. Rare modeled the characters and objects in 3D using Silicon Graphics technology and converted them into 2D sprites, creating a plastic look unheard of at the time. It was accompanied by David Wise's ambient soundtrack, which to this day ranks among the most acclaimed in the genre's history.

Donkey Kong Country became an enormous commercial hit and one of the best-selling titles on the Super Nintendo ever. It helped Nintendo stay competitive in the so-called console wars against Sega and its Mega Drive and effectively gave birth to a successful new gaming brand that lives on to this day. Its huge success subsequently opened the door to two sequels on the same console and later to further returns on newer platforms. It is precisely the variety of environments together with the carefully measured difficulty that holds the game together and makes it an experience that even after decades feels fresh and playable.

The story of its creation is important too. Rare, a small British studio previously known more for smaller titles, impressed Nintendo with its technical experiments to such an extent that Nintendo entrusted it with one of its most precious brands. The bet paid off: the game arrived in 1994, that is at a time when Sega with its Mega Drive was at its peak, and it helped Nintendo catch its breath again in the fight for players' favor precisely through the power of its audiovisual presentation.

Culturally, it was the moment when it became clear how important presentation and marketing are. The game became Nintendo's flagship in the mid-nineties and its visuals helped define what players thought a next-generation game should look like, even before fully 3D consoles arrived. Donkey Kong became a first-rate star once more, and the series Rare launched lives on in various forms to this day.

**Why play:** A technically groundbreaking platformer that plays superbly to this day, with a legendary soundtrack, which showed what the Super Nintendo could really do.
snes__donkey-kong-country.teaser: Pre-rendered graphics that looked impossible on a 16-bit console back in 1994.

snes__donkey-kong-country-2.article:
This time it's Donkey Kong himself who's in trouble. The crocodile king K. Rool has kidnapped him, and it's up to the nimble Diddy and his friend Dixie to rescue him. Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest from 1995 is considered by many players and critics to be the peak of the whole trilogy, and in a series as strong as this one that's quite a statement.

The studio Rare took the excellent foundation of the first installment and refined it in every way. You play as the new duo of Diddy and Dixie, who once again complement each other, with Dixie able to use her hair to glide and slow her fall, opening up new level-design possibilities. The pirate theme, ships, lava caves, thorny thickets and spiky arenas bring a varied range of environments, and the game is generally more demanding, more inventive and denser than the first. Collectible goals were also added for players who want to reach one hundred percent completion. The world is threaded with hidden rooms and bonus challenges, so simply finishing the game is only the beginning, and true full completion demands careful exploration of every nook.

Technically the game continued in the pre-rendered visual style that Rare had mastered and pushed it even further in detail and atmosphere. David Wise's soundtrack ranks among the absolute best of the 16-bit era; tracks like the melancholic swamp theme became cult favorites and to this day appear in rankings of the best game music ever.

Diddy's Kong Quest sold superbly and cemented the position of the Donkey Kong Country brand as one of Nintendo's pillars in the mid-nineties. There is broad agreement among series fans that the second installment best balanced difficulty, level design and music, and it often appears in rankings of the best platformers ever.

The new environments also give the game an unmistakable atmosphere. The pirate theme, sunken wrecks, spooky swamps and abandoned amusement parks give each group of levels its own mood, further heightened by the musical accompaniment. The result is an adventure that feels cohesive while never ceasing to surprise with new ideas right up to the very end.

Culturally it is a textbook example of a sequel that surpasses its already outstanding original. For many players, Diddy's Kong Quest remains the yardstick against which all other 2D platformers of the era are measured, and it still enjoys a reputation as one of the best games on the entire console.

**Why play:** A masterfully polished sequel with inventive level design and one of the best soundtracks of the 16-bit era, often called the peak of the series.
snes__donkey-kong-country-2.teaser: Diddy and Dixie rescue the kidnapped Donkey; many rank it as the peak of the entire trilogy.

snes__donkey-kong-country-3.article:
Donkey Kong and Diddy have vanished, and this time it's Dixie together with the burly little Kiddy who take up the search. Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble from 1996 closes out Rare's famous trilogy on the Super Nintendo, at a time when the gaming world was already fixing its eyes on the arrival of fully 3D consoles.

The gameplay stays true to the proven recipe. Once again it's a demanding 2D platformer with two characters you switch between, collecting secrets and carefully designed levels. The new addition is the duo of Dixie and Kiddy, where the small Dixie uses her gliding abilities and the robust Kiddy uses strength, meaning some puzzles require thoughtful alternation of the two. The game also adds an explorable overworld map with side activities and a greater emphasis on searching for hidden items. The relationship between the two characters gives the game a specific rhythm: the small Dixie is fast and agile, while the burly Kiddy is useful wherever brute force is needed, and switching between them becomes part of solving many passages.

Visually Rare once again wrung the maximum out of the pre-rendered graphics and pushed the Super Nintendo to its limits in the final years of its lifespan. This time the environments are tuned to a more northern, lakeside and mountainous tone. The soundtrack here was handled by Eveline Fischer along with other composers and offered a different mood than the previous installments.

Commercially and critically it was a successful title, even though it came out late in the console's life cycle, when players' attention was already beginning to turn to the new generation. Even so, it proved the brand still had something to offer and closed out one of the best-rated platformer series of its time. Later re-releases on Nintendo's handheld consoles also gave the game a second life with a new audience, and this dynamic of the hero duo gives the third installment its own face within an otherwise very consistent trilogy.

Culturally, the third installment represents a dignified full stop to the era in which Rare defined what a technically top-tier 2D platformer could look like. For fans of the series it is an essential piece of the puzzle and proof that even the last installment at the end of the generation managed to maintain a high bar.

**Why play:** The conclusion of a legendary trilogy with a new hero duo and honestly demanding level design, ideal for anyone who finished the first two installments.
snes__donkey-kong-country-3.teaser: Dixie and little Kiddy close out Rare's trilogy just as fully 3D consoles were arriving.

snes__super-mario-rpg.article:
What happens when Nintendo, a master of its craft, joins forces with Squaresoft, the king of Japanese RPGs? You get Super Mario RPG: Legend of the Seven Stars, one of the most unusual and at the same time most beloved adventures of the plumber Mario. Released in 1996 for the Super Nintendo, it is the first true RPG featuring Mario and a title that laid the foundations for many later spin-offs.

The game combines classic turn-based battles with something that wasn't a given at the time: action commands. If you press a button at the right moment of an attack or defense, you boost its effect, so combat stays tense and active. Add to that an isometric view, jumping and exploration in a platformer style, item collecting and a band of unexpected companions, among them the doll Geno and even Mario's eternal rival Bowser, who this time joins your side.

The story breaks the status quo: a giant sword crashes into the Mushroom Kingdom, scattering seven star fragments, and Mario must team up with unlikely allies to set right the wishes of the people. From a development standpoint it was the last major collaboration between Nintendo and Squaresoft on Nintendo hardware before Square headed to the PlayStation with its Final Fantasy series, which makes this game a symbolic full stop to an era.

Super Mario RPG, from what was then a top-tier studio, is a gem in terms of humor, design and music (composed by Yoko Shimomura). Its influence is undeniable: it launched the tradition of Mario RPGs, which continued with the Paper Mario and Mario & Luigi series. The game even received a modern remake for the Nintendo Switch in 2023, proving just how much popularity it retains to this day.

The game's overall tone is also worth noting. Super Mario RPG is saturated with humor, playfulness and unexpected moments, from bizarre enemies to lighthearted dialogue, while retaining an honest role-playing structure with levels, equipment and special attacks. This combination of accessibility and depth made it an ideal gateway into the genre for players who until then knew Mario only from platformers.

Culturally it is a crossroads of two gaming philosophies, from which something fresh and timeless emerged. For fans of Mario as well as classic RPGs it is a mandatory stop and one of the most accessible entries into the genre ever.

**Why play:** A witty, accessible and cleverly designed RPG in which Mario's charm meets Squaresoft's craftsmanship, and which kicked off a whole tradition of Mario role-playing games.
snes__super-mario-rpg.teaser: The first RPG starring Mario; a collaboration between Nintendo and Squaresoft that kicked off a later line of spin-offs.

snes__mega-man-x2.article:
The robotic hero X is back, and this time he must face the remnants of Sigma's army as well as the mysterious group of X-Hunters. Mega Man X2 from 1994 follows on from the revolutionary first installment, which reworked the Mega Man series in a more mature direction, and advances it not only in story but also technically.

The core of the gameplay stays true to the proven formula. You fight your way through action-platformer levels, at the end of each waits a boss Maverick, and after defeating him you gain a new weapon that can be used against the next enemy. X can dash, climb walls, charge shots and collect armor upgrades that expand his abilities. The new addition is the hunt for the X-Hunters, who appear in levels carrying the dismantled parts of your friend Zero, so careful players can unlock special content.

A technical curiosity is the Cx4 chip right in the cartridge, which made it possible to display simple vector and rotating effects beyond the Super Nintendo's usual capabilities. Capcom used it to spice the game up with flashy fights and animations that were not a given on a 16-bit console.

Mega Man X2 came out at a time when Capcom was keeping the Mega Man brand at the peak of productivity, developing both the classic and the more modern branch of the series in parallel. The X line brought a faster pace, more elaborate movement and a more mature tone, and the second installment further cemented this identity. Capcom at the time was able to release games under this brand almost annually without their quality dropping significantly.

The choice of the order in which you take on the individual bosses also gives the game a strategic dimension. Every defeated monster gives you a weapon to which a different enemy is especially vulnerable, so a thoughtful player can make progress considerably easier. On top of that, collecting armor upgrades, hearts that increase endurance and hidden abilities noticeably transforms the character and rewards players who go through levels attentively and return with new weapons to previously inaccessible places. This loop of constant strengthening is the heart of the whole series, and in X2 it works just as well as in its best installments.

Culturally, the Mega Man X sub-series belongs among the favorite pillars of 16-bit action platformers, and X2 is a solid sequel that maintains a high standard. For fans of precise, fast and demanding gameplay it is a welcome dose of proven fun with an extra technical touch.

**Why play:** A fast and precise action platformer with weapon and armor upgrades, plus a special graphics chip that pushed the boundaries of the Super Nintendo.
snes__mega-man-x2.teaser: X faces the remnants of Sigma's army and the mysterious X-Hunters; a follow-up to the revolutionary first X game.
snes__mega-man-x2.detail: The classic (non-X) series dressed in 16-bit clothing: big, colorful robots, boss-order selection, and precise jumping and shooting. An overlooked but excellent entry.

snes__mega-man-x3.article:
The Mavericks rise once again, and this time the robotic hunter X doesn't have to go to the battlefield alone. Mega Man X3 from 1995 closes out the Mega Man X series trilogy on the Super Nintendo and brings a long-awaited novelty: for the first time you can also play as Zero in the main game.

The gameplay builds on the solid foundations of the previous installments. You go through freely selectable levels, at the end of which you defeat the boss Mavericks, collect their weapons and armor upgrades, and use the dash, wall climbing and charged shots. Zero is playable here to a limited extent and offers a different fighting style with a light saber, which was a big deal for fans. The game also features so-called Ride Armor, robotic suits, and more paths to progress, rewarding experimentation.

Mega Man X3 was the last installment of the X line released on the Super Nintendo before the series moved on to new console generations. Capcom once again used an expansion chip in the cartridge for some effects, and the game ranks among the visually and difficulty-wise more demanding pieces of the sub-series. For many players it's quite a challenge that tests reflexes as well as patience.

In development terms the game falls into the period when Capcom was simultaneously running the classic Mega Man series and the more modern X branch, and the brand was among its most reliable pillars. The third installment thus represents the culmination of the 16-bit era of this sub-series, before the action moved into the world of 32-bit consoles. A later port to the PlayStation and Saturn then brought the game closer to some players outside the original platform.

The ability to play, even if only in a limited way, as Zero was much more than just a technical trifle. For fans it was a symbolic step that foreshadowed how important a role this character would play in later installments, and it gave the third game a special significance within the whole series. Together with expansion elements like the robotic suits, X3 thus offers a somewhat richer and more varied experience than its predecessors. At the same time, however, it escalates the difficulty: the bosses are tougher and the levels more intricate, which makes it a title that will be most appreciated by players already familiar with the previous installments, while for newcomers it can be merciless at times. Yet it is precisely in that challenge that a piece of its charm and long lifespan lies.

Culturally it is a valuable piece for collectors and fans, among other reasons because the original release was among the rarer and more sought-after titles. As a full stop to the 16-bit chapter of the Mega Man X series, it holds up to this day.

**Why play:** A demanding conclusion to the 16-bit Mega Man X trilogy, where for the first time you also get to play as Zero with his light saber.
snes__mega-man-x3.teaser: Closes out the Mega Man X trilogy on SNES and, for the first time, offers Zero as a playable character.

snes__gradius-iii.article:
The classic spaceship Vic Viper hovers over the scorching surface of an enemy planet, and you know that a single hit is enough and you're done. This is **Gradius III**, one of the most demanding and at the same time most elegant horizontal shoot 'em ups on the Super Nintendo, and a game that to this day remains a byword whenever talk turns to the shmup genre.

The Gradius series was brought into the world by Konami, and its console version, Gradius III, follows on from the arcade original from the late eighties. At the heart of the game is the now-iconic upgrade system: you collect capsules that gradually light up a bar at the bottom of the screen, and you yourself choose when and into what to invest the energy. Speed, missile, double shot, laser, accompanying Option modules and a shield put combinations in your hands that few shooters of the era offered. A mistimed squandering of your bonuses, meanwhile, can spell ruin, so every advance requires a plan.

Gradius III is notoriously known for its difficulty. Bosses, narrow corridors full of obstacles and the legendary level with spewing volcanoes test even seasoned players, and death means the loss of most of your upgrades, so the return to action tends to be painful. It is precisely this uncompromising nature, though, that turned the game into a summit that genre fans want to conquer. Visually, the console version makes full use of the Super Nintendo's capabilities, including colorful backgrounds and smooth scrolling.

The game is also an important piece of the retro mosaic because of its role in the launch of the Super Nintendo in Japan, where it was among the early titles accompanying the console's arrival. For many players it was the first encounter with what Nintendo's new machine could handle in the action-shooter genre, and it underscored that Konami was among the top developers of the era.

Anyone who picks up Vic Viper today gets pure, fast and honestly hard action without needless frills. It's a game about reflexes, memory and cool-headed decision-making, not about story, and that is precisely where its enduring appeal lies. Gradius III has aged with the grace that only a true classic deserves.

**Why play:** If you want to understand why the Gradius series is spoken of with respect, and you're not afraid of a challenge, this is an essential shmup of the golden 16-bit era.
snes__gradius-iii.teaser: A mercilessly demanding horizontal shmup from Konami, a port of the famous arcade original.

snes__lufia-ii-rise-of-sinistrals.article:
To begin a game with the defeat of the heroes and only then return to the very start of their journey takes courage, and that is exactly how **Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals** opens its narrative. This JRPG on the Super Nintendo is a prelude to the events of the first installment and belongs among those titles that lovers of the genre pass on to one another as a secret tip.

Lufia II came out on the Super Nintendo in the mid-nineties and combines classic turn-based battles with something that wasn't a given in the genre at the time: elaborate puzzles right inside the dungeons. Rooms full of sliding boulders, arrows, timed switches and logic riddles turn traversing a dungeon into a brain-teaser, not just a sequence of random skirmishes. The game also features the famed Ancient Cave, a randomly generated hundred floors where you lose your equipment and have to work your way up relying only on what you find along the way, a feature that foreshadows the later roguelike elements in JRPGs.

The story follows the swordsman Maxim and his companions in their fight against the Sinistrals, a quartet of powerful enemies. The narrative heads toward an exceptionally powerful and emotional ending that became legendary among players and is still spoken of to this day as one of the most emotionally affecting finales of the 16-bit era. The characterful cast and the calm pace give the drama room to resonate.

The series is the work of a Japanese studio, and in the days of its release Lufia II remained a more intimate title that didn't gain the mass attention of the big names of the genre. That is precisely why it earned a reputation as a hidden gem: players who discovered it often rank it among the best and at the same time most underrated JRPGs on the Super Nintendo. The collector's value of the original cartridges reflects this.

The combination of clever combat, an addictive dungeon puzzle and a narrative that gets to you makes Lufia II a game that stands up to comparison with far more famous names. It's a title for someone who wants more than just bashing monsters in random battles, and who appreciates it when a game can strike right at the heart toward the end.

**Why play:** A hidden gem of 16-bit JRPGs with addictive puzzles and one of the most powerful finales of the whole era. If you love turn-based role-playing, don't overlook this one.
snes__lufia-ii-rise-of-sinistrals.teaser: A JRPG prequel that begins with the heroes' defeat and returns to the origin of their story.

snes__tetris-attack.article:
Forget about falling blocks; here the blocks shift sideways and the game flies at such a pace that it leaves you dumbfounded. **Tetris Attack** is, despite its name, an entirely different kind of puzzle than you'd expect, and it belongs among the most addictive puzzle games ever released on the Super Nintendo.

The principle is ingeniously simple: colored blocks keep shifting upward from the bottom, and you swap them in pairs side by side so as to line up three or more of the same in a row, causing them to disappear. The key to mastery, though, lies in chain reactions and combos, where the destruction of one set of blocks triggers an avalanche of others and dumps piles of garbage on top of your opponent. In two-player mode this turns into a merciless duel of reflexes and foresight, where it comes down to who overwhelms the other first.

In the version for the Super Nintendo the game is wrapped in the world of Yoshi and characters from the Mario games, so instead of stark abstraction you're accompanied by charming graphics and catchy music. This aesthetic turns an otherwise intensely competitive game into something accessible and friendly that will settle in with even players who usually steer clear of puzzlers. Beneath the colorful surface, though, beats a surprisingly deep strategy.

The game has its roots in the Japanese title Panel de Pon and reached the West precisely in the guise of Yoshi's world. The principle proved so timeless that it survived in dozens of further incarnations and variations across later platforms, which testifies to just how perfectly tuned a mechanic it is. The competitive multiplayer was ahead of its time and foreshadowed the later wave of competitive puzzle games.

Tetris Attack is proof that the best puzzles are easy to learn but hard to master to perfection. Whether you tune it solo and chase a higher score, or you battle a friend over who lasts longer, it draws you into a state of utter concentration that's hard to step out of. It's the pure joy of play in its most distilled form.

**Why play:** A timelessly addictive puzzler with a brilliant competitive multiplayer. Grab a second controller and get ready for the evening to slip away before you even notice.
snes__tetris-attack.teaser: Blocks shift sideways instead of falling; an addictive puzzle game with a dizzying pace.

snes__zombies-ate-my-neighbors.article:
Your neighbor is grilling in the backyard, except instead of sausages he is turning you over the fire, and in the pool, lurking in place of inflatable mattresses, are snapping monsters. Welcome to **Zombies Ate My Neighbors**, a gloriously fun action game that grew out of a love for B-movie horror into a cult classic of the Super Nintendo.

The game is a top-down action shooter in which you fight your way, solo or in pairs, through suburban streets, supermarkets, pyramids and castles, mainly rescuing surviving neighbors before an army of monsters gets to them. And what an army: zombies, chainsaw-wielding maniacs in hockey masks, giant babies, spitting plants, mummies and aliens. The arsenal is just as zany, from water pistols through tomatoes to bazookas, and every rescued victim also means points, so caution pays off.

Zombies Ate My Neighbors was made by the studio LucasArts, and Konami handled its release. The game is literally a monument to a love of the horror pop culture of the 1980s and early 1990s: every enemy is a tribute to some movie monster and the overall tone is confidently parodic. This playfulness and humor set the title apart from the more seriously minded shooters of its time and gave it an unmistakable personality.

Interestingly, because of the amount of blood and horror motifs, the game was censored in some regions or even renamed to pass stricter content rules. This history made it an even more sought-after piece among collectors and fans, and to this day it is spoken of as one of the most distinctive titles on the Super Nintendo. Over the years it earned a firm place in players' hearts and became a coveted title.

Anyone who wants to play something that does not take itself seriously while offering honest cooperative action will find a treasure in Zombies Ate My Neighbors. It is a game full of surprises, dark humor and chaos that is best experienced with two people on one couch. A few hours in its company will reliably lift your mood.

**Why play:** Funny, inventive and perfect for two players, plus packed with tributes to B-movie horror. An ideal choice for an evening when you want action with a smile on your face.
snes__zombies-ate-my-neighbors.teaser: A top-down action game inspired by B-movie horror; solo or in pairs, you save the neighbors.

snes__aladdin.article:
A leap across a chasm, a slide beneath a blade and a scimitar in hand — this is not just a film turned into a game, this is one of the finest platforming experiences of its day. **Aladdin** on the Super Nintendo pulled off what film adaptations rarely manage: becoming a genuinely great game.

At its core is a brisk platformer in which Aladdin runs, jumps and climbs through the marketplaces, dungeons and cellars of Agrabah, and even flies through the Cave of Wonders themselves on a carpet. Unlike many adaptations of the time, Aladdin holds a scimitar, so fights with enemies are an equal part of the game alongside precise jumps and finding your way through the levels. Add to that throwing apples at range and sliding down ropes, so the action has a nice pace and variety.

Visually the game was among the best of its generation. The character animation is unusually smooth and the art faithfully captures the style of the source, with vivid colors and fluid motion that at the time felt almost like an animated cartoon in motion. It was precisely this smoothness of animation that was one of the main reasons the Super Nintendo version earned praise and became a reference example of what a well-made film license should look like.

It is worth knowing that there were two distinctly different Aladdin games, one for Sega consoles and another for the Super Nintendo, and each was created by a different studio with its own interpretation. The Super Nintendo version is a work in its own right, with an emphasis on combat platforming action, and it places honest demands on the player, especially in the later levels. Both versions, however, still fuel fan debates to this day over which is better.

Aladdin is proof that a licensed game need not be a corner-cutting product for a quick profit. It is a carefully tuned platformer that honors its source while standing firmly on its own feet as an honest challenge. For anyone who loves 16-bit platformers, it is a title that deserves a place in the library.

**Why play:** A beautifully animated and brisk platformer, one of the best film adaptations of the 16-bit era. A great choice when you want a colorful platformer with an edge.
snes__aladdin.teaser: A platformer based on the film in which you slice through the Agrabah marketplace with a scimitar and acrobatics.

snes__lion-king.article:
The lion's roar echoes across the savanna and you realize for the first time just how merciless a childishly cute-looking game can be. **The Lion King** on the Super Nintendo went down in history not only as a handsome adaptation of the famous animated film, but above all as a symbol of almost inhuman difficulty.

The game is a platformer in which you move through scenes from the film while growing up alongside the main hero. In the fur of a little lion cub you first jump, roll over enemies and let out a roar that scares animals away, while later, as a grown lion, you gain strength, claws and harder-hitting attacks. The game thus cleverly ties the character's transformation to the development of gameplay abilities and tries to mirror the dramatic arc of the film level by level.

Visually The Lion King benefited from above-standard animation and rich colors, thanks to which the game looked like a film brought to life on screen. The backgrounds, the fluid movement of the characters and the film-inspired soundtrack turned playing into an audiovisual experience that felt exceptionally striking in the mid-1990s and appealed to players across age groups.

The game became a legend, however, because of its notorious difficulty. The very second level, in which you have to precisely time jumps across swinging monkeys, etched itself into the memory of an entire generation as the point where a great many players ran aground. Among fans it is said that the difficulty was deliberately cranked up, among other reasons so the game could not be beaten on a single rental — which was a real commercial consideration for publishers at the time.

Today The Lion King is a reminder of an era when platformers pulled no punches and when finishing a game was a genuine badge of honor. Beneath the pretty surface lies a hard test of patience and precision that will challenge even seasoned players. For nostalgics and challenge-hunters alike it is a title that is not forgotten, whether for its beauty or for the sleepless evenings at that cursed second level.

**Why play:** A gorgeously animated platformer with legendary difficulty that became a legend. Dive in if you love both nostalgia and a challenge that gives nothing away for free.
snes__lion-king.teaser: A platformer based on the film, notorious for its almost inhuman difficulty and faithful recreation of its scenes.

snes__pocky-and-rocky.article:
A young Shinto priestess with sacred talismans and, at her side, a raccoon in a kimono, together facing a horde of Japanese spirits and demons. **Pocky & Rocky** is an adorably zany action shooter that pumps a dose of folklore, color and uncompromising two-player action into your veins.

The game is a top-down run-and-gun affair in which you advance through levels and repel waves of enemies by throwing talismans or leaves, complemented by a melee strike and a roll to dodge. The key to survival is constant movement and thinking about where to turn, because enemies attack from all sides and the screen quickly fills with projectiles. The game carries a cheerful tone inspired by Japanese folk tales and yokai demons, so despite the hectic action it radiates a distinctive charm.

It was made by Taito and builds on that maker's arcade tradition. The Super Nintendo version became famous for its two-player cooperation, in which one player controls the priestess Pocky and the other the raccoon Rocky, with the teamwork of both being necessary to overcome the dense waves of enemies and inventive bosses. Playing together makes it a sought-after title for anyone who wants honest cooperative action on one couch.

Among retro game fans, Pocky & Rocky earned a reputation as a well-made but fairly demanding title that rewards teamwork and patience. The cute graphics can be misleading, for beneath them hides brisk and at times genuinely tough action that tests both players' reflexes. Original cartridges are today among the more prized pieces in genre enthusiasts' collections.

Anyone looking for a game that combines a specific Japanese charm with adrenaline-fueled shooting action will not go wrong with Pocky & Rocky. It is a title best savored in pairs and one that reminds you how diverse and colorful the Super Nintendo library could be beyond the big Western names. A few rounds with a friend easily stretch into a whole evening.

**Why play:** Brisk run-and-gun action with Japanese folklore charm and great co-op for two. Ideal when you want something distinctive and unexpectedly challenging.
snes__pocky-and-rocky.teaser: A Shinto priestess and a raccoon in a kimono face demons; a colorful run & gun for one or two players.

snes__u-n-squadron.article:
A fighter jet cuts through the sky, enemy territory spreads out beneath its wings, and you know that every downed machine means money for better equipment. **U.N. Squadron** is a horizontal aerial shooter that brought an unusual layer of strategy to the shmup genre and became one of the favorite titles for the Super Nintendo.

The game is based on a Capcom source and at its core is a classic horizontal shmup in which you pilot a combat plane, mow down waves of enemies in the air and on the ground, and fight your way through to massive bosses. What sets it apart is the money system: kills earn you funds that you spend between missions on weapons, special armament and upgrades, so to a certain extent you plan your own progress. This economic dimension gives the game a depth that shooters of the time usually lacked.

The player also chooses between several pilots and types of aircraft that differ in their attributes and durability, which affects the play style and difficulty. Choosing your machine and shopping wisely for equipment makes you not just a pilot but a bit of a strategist too, one who has to weigh how to handle limited funds ahead of the more demanding stretches. This makes U.N. Squadron a game worth returning to and trying different approaches.

Visually and sonically the game makes good use of the Super Nintendo's capabilities and offers brisk, readable action across varied environments. Among fans of the genre, U.N. Squadron holds a good reputation as a solid and cleverly designed shooter that, thanks to its shopping system, has aged better than many a more straightforward rival. For fans of aerial shmups it is a title worth getting to know.

The combination of adrenaline-fueled aerial action and thoughtful resource management makes U.N. Squadron a pleasantly refreshing piece. It is neither the hardest nor the most famous shooter on the console, but it is well thought out and fun, and it gives you the feeling that you decide your success even beyond the battle itself. That is precisely why it earned its firm place among the 16-bit classics of the genre.

**Why play:** A horizontal shmup with an unusual equipment-buying system that adds a layer of strategy. A great choice for anyone who loves aerial action with a bit of planning.
snes__u-n-squadron.teaser: A horizontal shmup from Capcom that added weapon purchasing and upgrades to the genre.

snes__axelay.article:
The spaceship Axelay races alternately over a planet's surface and straight down into the depths of dark space. And this very game managed something on a sixteen-bit console that long looked like science fiction: blazing planetary surfaces that undulate beneath you like a gigantic sphere, and immediately afterward classic side-scrolling against swarms of enemies. Axelay is Konami's technological pride and one of the most visual arguments for why the Super Nintendo took graphics seriously.

Konami released Axelay in 1992 and the alternation of two perspectives made it an unmistakable title. The horizontal levels used the so-called Mode 7, so the ground beneath the ship curved into a round shape and created the illusion of a giant planet underfoot. The vertical missions, on the other hand, returned to the traditional vertical shmup, but with splendidly animated parallax layers and enormous bosses who filled half the screen.

Mechanically Axelay is more accessible than the Japanese bullet-hell infernos tend to be. Instead of a single instant death you get a weapon arsenal that you choose before each mission, and a hit means the loss of your current weapon, not an immediate end. That gives room for learning and a comeback even for less hardened players. Taro Kudo's sound rounded out the atmosphere of a sinister machine enemy named Armada.

Culturally, Axelay fits into an era when Konami was among the most technical studios on the market and churned out one visual marvel after another. The game never became as much of a phenomenon as Gradius or Contra, but among connoisseurs it earned a reputation as a hidden gem that proved just what the SNES hardware could do when the right people got their hands on it.

To this day Axelay is a favorite title among collectors and emulator enthusiasts and often appears in rankings of the best shooters of its generation. Its transitions between 2D and pseudo-3D perspectives remain striking even after more than thirty years.

**Why play:** If you want to see how the SNES bent planets underfoot, Axelay is a technically dazzling shooter that still plays smoothly and looks great.
snes__axelay.teaser: Alternates pseudo-3D flight over a planet with side-scrolling; a technological showcase from Konami.

snes__rock-n-roll-racing.article:
Imagine a race where it is not just about crossing the line first, but also about shooting your rivals to pieces on the way there to the sound of Black Sabbath and Deep Purple. Rock n' Roll Racing is not a pure racing simulator, it is an isometric brawl on four wheels with rockets, mines and turbo jumps, underscored by catchy rock riffs. And it was precisely this combination that made it a cult title in 1993.

Behind the game is the studio Silicon & Synapse, which later renamed itself Blizzard Entertainment. Rock n' Roll Racing came out on the Super Nintendo (and later on the Mega Drive as well) and was built on an engine related to their earlier game RPM Racing. The isometric view, upgradable vehicles and planets with varying gravity gave the racing unexpected depth.

At the heart of the fun is aggressive combat. You collect money for your placing and for destroying rivals, and buy better cars, armor, weapons and turbo. The commentator Larry Huffman announces the action with the enthusiasm of a sports host, and the game even fit in split-screen for two players. The soundtrack featured adapted versions of tracks like Paranoid or Highway Star, which was an absolute rarity on a console of that time.

Culturally, Rock n' Roll Racing is interesting mainly as an early showcase of the future Blizzard's signature, namely a sense for playability, humor and the polishing of details. For many players it was the first game where real rock classics rang out of the speakers, albeit in a simplified form due to the limitations of the sound chip.

The game received remasters and re-releases, among others as part of the Blizzard Arcade Collection. This only confirms that it is remembered not just by veterans, but that the studio itself considers it worth commemorating.

**Why play:** The combination of isometric racing, destroying rivals and rock hits makes Rock n' Roll Racing great fun for two players on one couch.
snes__rock-n-roll-racing.teaser: Isometric racing with rockets and mines, set to riffs from Black Sabbath and Deep Purple.

snes__tiny-toon-adventures-buster-busts-.article:
The rabbit Buster Bunny bursts out of the Acme Looniversity classroom straight into a crazy ride full of slapstick, and Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster Busts Loose is one of the most underrated platformers on the Super Nintendo. Konami took the popular cartoon series and turned it into a fast, artistically rich and surprisingly inventive game that was not afraid to experiment with pacing.

Konami released the title in 1993 and built it on what it did best: precise gameplay and visual flair. Buster controls not only jumps but also his characteristic dash and sliding kick, thanks to which the game moves faster than most competing mascot platformers. Every level has a different theme and a different gameplay twist, so the action never begins to repeat itself.

Mechanically the game brilliantly varies the pace. In one level you run along the roofs of a train, in another you play American football, elsewhere you find yourself in a space parody. The bonus phases and comic-book interludes faithfully carry over the atmosphere of the series, including its typical looney humor and the exaggerated animations of the characters, which Warner Bros. oversaw.

Culturally, Buster Busts Loose belongs to the wave of licensed games derived from cartoon series that flooded consoles in the nineties. Unlike many quick cash-ins, however, Konami did honest work and created a title that holds up even without nostalgia for the brand. For fans of Tiny Toons it was a dream come true of how their favorites should look in a game.

Thanks to its quality execution, the game made its way into many retro recommendations as an example that even a licensed title can be great if a capable studio stands behind it. For SNES collectors it is still a sought-after piece.

**Why play:** A fast, funny and visually delightful platformer from Konami that shows how a game based on a cartoon series should be made.
snes__tiny-toon-adventures-buster-busts-.teaser: Buster Bunny romps through a wild platformer based on the show; an underrated gem from Konami.

snes__joe-and-mac.article:
Two cavemen, clubs in hand and hordes of dinosaurs all around — Joe & Mac is a prehistoric platformer that breathes primeval bizarreness and humor. Beneath the colorful skin hides a brisk action game where you chew your way through levels full of predatory lizards to rescue kidnapped cave girls. It is an undemanding but incredibly addictive affair.

The game was created by the studio Data East and was originally an arcade machine from 1991 that subsequently made its way to a number of consoles including the Super Nintendo. The subtitle Caveman Ninja gives away the tone of the whole thing: prehistory treated with great exaggeration, where the cave heroes throw stone axes, bones and wheels like real warriors.

Mechanically Joe & Mac combines platforming action with throwing weapons in several directions. You collect various types of ranged strikes, face enormous bosses in the shape of dinosaurs, and in co-op you can play it in two players. The pace is fast, the controls simple, and the whole thing is laced with charming comic-book humor that sets the game apart from the more serious titles of its time.

Culturally, Joe & Mac benefited from the popularity of arcade machines at the start of the nineties and became successful enough to kick off a small series with several sequels and spin-offs. Its prehistoric theme and cartoonish approach made it an easily recognizable brand that found fans across platforms.

The conversions differed slightly depending on the hardware, but the SNES version was among the more colorful. To this day Joe & Mac is a pleasant choice for short, undemanding sessions, when you just want to cheerfully clobber dinosaurs and not think about anything more complicated.

**Why play:** A brisk prehistoric platformer with humor and co-op for two, ideal for undemanding retro fun.
snes__joe-and-mac.teaser: Two cavemen bash dinosaurs with clubs and rescue kidnapped cavewomen.

snes__goof-troop.article:
Before Capcom got into Resident Evil, one of its young designers named Shinji Mikami honed his skills on a cute game with Goofy and his son Max. Goof Troop is a cooperative action adventure based on the Disney series, and surprisingly it is one of the first titles on which the future father of the horror series worked. For that reason alone it deserves attention.

Capcom released Goof Troop in 1993 on the Super Nintendo and bet on the then-not-so-common combination of puzzles, exploration and simultaneous cooperation of two players on one screen. Goofy and Max set off for a pirate island to rescue kidnapped friends, with each location being essentially a small logic puzzle.

Mechanically the game does not build on combat, but on cleverness. The characters have no classic weapons; instead they pick up and throw objects, pull levers, push crates and search for keys. The cooperation of two players is crucial, because many puzzles require coordination. This emphasis on logic and teamwork makes the game a pleasantly different piece in a sea of action platformers.

Culturally, Goof Troop fits into the rich period of Disney games from Capcom, which includes for instance the Aladdin series or DuckTales on the NES. From today's perspective, however, it is most interesting as an early work of Shinji Mikami, who would later forever change the shape of the horror genre.
