The union of a cute Disney license and a future legend is trivia that fans love.

The game remains popular mainly for the cooperative experience and as a curious fragment of gaming history. It is neither long nor extremely demanding, but it offers a laid-back shared evening at one console.

**Why play:** A pleasant cooperative adventure full of puzzles, and on top of that an early work by the creator of Resident Evil, which makes it a delicacy for fans of gaming history.
snes__goof-troop.teaser: A co-op adventure starring Goofy and Max, directed by a young Shinji Mikami.

snes__street-fighter-alpha-2.article:
Between the first Street Fighter and the cult sequel there yawns a story gap, and it was filled precisely by the Alpha series. Street Fighter Alpha 2 is its second installment and for many fans the peak of the entire prequel branch. Stylized anime graphics, a brisk pace and a thoughtful combat system make it one of the best fighting games of the nineties.

Capcom released Alpha 2 in 1996, originally into arcade machines on the CPS2 board, and subsequently onto home consoles including the Super Nintendo. The conversion to the SNES was technically demanding and used an add-on chip in order to faithfully carry over the colorful and animated world of the arcade original. Even so, it was one of the most ambitious fighting games on the console.

In combat, Alpha 2 stands on the Super Combo gauge system and especially on the new Custom Combo mechanic, which lets players chain their own attacks and create devastating series. The roster offers the return of classics and characters like Dhalsim, Sagat or Rolento, and each fighter has their own destructible background and musical theme. The pace and control over the match feel tuned and fair.

Culturally, Alpha 2 cemented Capcom's position as the king of fighting games in the mid-nineties, at a time when the genre was peaking in arcades all over the world. The anime-reminiscent stylization and the emphasis on the characters' story backgrounds gave the series its own identity, distinct from the main Street Fighter II line.

The game received many ports and re-releases across generations of consoles and to this day appears in tournament retro communities. For many players Alpha 2 remains a showcase of how tuned and stylish a 2D fighting game could be.

**Why play:** A stylish, technically tuned fighting game with the depth of the Custom Combo system, one of the peaks of the genre's golden era.
snes__street-fighter-alpha-2.teaser: A prequel between the original Street Fighter and the second game; anime visuals and a deep fighting system.

snes__super-tennis.article:
There are games that never earned the fame of the big blockbusters but count among connoisseurs as hidden gems. Super Tennis for the Super Nintendo is exactly such a case. This tennis title from the early years of the sixteen-bit console still ranks among the most playable sports games of its time, and many players consider it one of the best retro tennis games of all.

The secret to its success is perfectly tuned controls. The game offers a whole range of strokes, from powerful forehands through fierce volleys to delicate lobs and drop shots, and each of them is controlled intuitively, yet with room for a tactically led rally. Moving the player around the court, timing your stroke and reading the opponent's return — all of this you have to learn to master if you want to succeed in the higher rounds. Beneath the simple surface hides a surprising depth.

Super Tennis also bets on variety. Available is a range of male and female players with differing attributes, various types of surfaces that affect the bounce and speed of the ball, and a clear tournament mode where you fight your way up the ladder of opponents. This diversity ensures that the game does not get boring for a long time and that each match can have a different character depending on whom and where you play.

The absolute peak, however, is the two-player match. Tennis duels against a friend are among the most thrilling things sixteen-bit sport has to offer. Long rallies, tactically testing your opponent and the winning ball played into an empty court can unleash proper emotions at one screen. It is right here that you see how timelessly the game is built.

Super Tennis is proof that perfect playability requires neither photorealistic graphics nor dozens of modes. One discipline taken to flawlessness is enough. For fans of tennis and sports games in general it is a title that deserves a place in every retro collection. Even after years it controls so naturally that you quickly forget just how old it actually is.

**Why play:** For its excellently tuned controls and thrilling two-player duels, which make it one of the best retro tennis games of all.
snes__super-tennis.teaser: A hidden gem; famously well-tuned controls make it one of the best retro tennis games.

snes__international-superstar-soccer-del.article:
For an entire generation of players, the abbreviation ISS meant the same thing that a big football brand means today. International Superstar Soccer Deluxe by Konami became the benchmark on the Super Nintendo against which all sixteen-bit football was measured. And for many it remains, to this day, the best kick-around ever released on the console.

In ISS Deluxe, Konami managed to blend arcade accessibility with surprising depth. The game flows briskly and goals are scored in style, yet beneath the surface hides an elaborate system of passes, crosses, dribbles and shots that rewards precise timing and reading of the game. You can learn the basics in a moment, but mastering all the tricks that let you outwit the opponent's defence takes a hefty dose of practice.

Another great asset was the selection of game modes and options. Players could enjoy exhibition matches, league and tournament competitions and a roster of national teams that included the famous footballing powerhouses. On top of that, the game added tactical settings, so you could adjust the formation and playing style to your own taste. For its time it was a surprisingly rich package.

But International Superstar Soccer Deluxe truly came alive in multiplayer. A duel with a friend belongs to the legendary experiences of the sixteen-bit era, when a friendly match turned into a matter of honour within moments. The shouting over a conceded goal, the celebratory leaps and the eternal arguing about offside all belong inseparably to this game. It was multiplayer that made it a fixture at many a house party.

ISS Deluxe confirmed Konami as a master of sports arcades and, for years to come, defined what fun console football should look like. For those who remember it, it is an inseparable part of childhood; for new players, it is a showcase of how brilliantly old games could combine simplicity with lasting fun. It holds a firm place in the retro football hall of fame.

**Why play it:** For legendary sixteen-bit football that combines arcade fun with depth and excels above all in multiplayer.
snes__international-superstar-soccer-del.teaser: The benchmark of 16-bit football from Konami; for many, still the best soccer game on SNES.

snes__nhl-96.article:
The siren, the roar of the crowd and the puck flying into the top corner of the net. Electronic Arts' NHL series was one of the flagships of sports games in the nineties, and NHL '96 brought this hockey merry-go-round to the Super Nintendo too. For many players it was their first real encounter with licensed hockey featuring genuine teams from the North American league.

NHL '96 built on the proven combination of brisk arcade action and rules realistic enough to make a match feel like real hockey. Passes, breakaways, hard body checks and the option to commit fouls and land in the penalty box all came together to create a lively, dynamic game. It was accessible enough for newcomers, yet at the same time offered plenty of room for those who wanted to polish their play to perfection.

A major strength of the series was the licence, thanks to which you could play with real clubs and pit your strengths against each other in matches as well as longer competitive modes. The feeling of leading a real team to victory added to the game's appeal and set it apart from generic hockey arcades. EA Sports was building its reputation as a brand that delivered sport as faithfully as possible, and NHL was one of its pillars.

As with most sports titles of the era, the most fun is to be had against a live opponent. A hockey derby with a friend at a single screen can push emotions to the maximum, whether it is a nail-biting duel down to the last second or a one-sided rout you keep bringing up long afterwards. It is precisely this couch rivalry that keeps retro sports games alive to this day.

NHL '96 is today part of a long and famous line that continues to this day and ranks among the longest-running sports series ever. As a sixteen-bit stop along this journey, it is a pleasant reminder of a time when hockey on consoles was only just getting established. For fans of retro sport and hockey alike it is a solid, playable classic.

**Why play it:** For licensed hockey with real teams and heated two-player derbies, which belong to the pillars of the famous NHL series.
snes__nhl-96.teaser: Licensed hockey from EA with real teams from the overseas league and brisk arcade action.

snes__super-soccer.article:
The stadium roars, the camera sits somewhere high behind the goal and the players spread across the pitch in a perspective nobody expected on a home console back in 1992. **Super Soccer** by Human Entertainment is among the first football games to fully exploit the Super Nintendo's graphics chip and its famous Mode 7 to draw the pitch in a semi-pseudo-3D view instead of a flat top-down one. The result is an experience that still feels surprisingly dynamic today.

Mechanically it is old-school arcade football. You always control the player nearest the ball, pass with one button, shoot with another, and the rest is handled by semi-automatic switching. The game doesn't bet on the simulation depth of later titles, but on speed, clarity and instant fun. The goalkeeper got his own save animations, and long-range goals are accompanied by a satisfying shake of the net.

The visuals were a period draw. The pseudo-3D pitch tilts and scrolls, players grow larger depending on their distance from the camera, and it all runs smoothly. For players used to the static football of the eight-bit era it was an obvious leap forward and one of the reasons Super Soccer became one of the first sports arrivals in the console's library.

There is a range of national teams to choose from and a tournament mode that guides you all the way to the final. Without FIFA licences, the teams are marked by colours and abbreviations, which doesn't hurt the arcade approach at all. A duel between two players at a single console is exactly the kind of fun that had enthusiasts gathering around the television.

The game was released in Japan, North America and Europe and became one of the early pillars of the Super Nintendo's sports offering, before the big annual brands took over the market. For many European console owners it was the very first football they played on the SNES, and for that very reason it retains its nostalgic value to this day.

Today Super Soccer is more of a historical exhibit than a rival to modern football games, but as a demonstration of how far the Super Nintendo could push the sports genre in the early nineties, it stands up wonderfully. It is a fast, loud and friendly game that nobody gets bored with.

**Why play it:** For brisk arcade football with an eye-catching pseudo-3D perspective and instant two-player fun at a single screen.
snes__super-soccer.teaser: One of the first football games to use Mode 7 for a pseudo-3D view of the pitch.

snes__top-gear.article:
The starting light goes out, the engine roars and the screen splits into two halves even when you're playing alone. **Top Gear** is a Super Nintendo racing classic developed by the British-Argentine studio Gremlin Graphics and published by Kemco in 1992. For plenty of players it remains synonymous with fast arcade racing at the eight-bit to sixteen-bit turning point.

At the core of the game is a pseudo-3D view from behind the car, along which corners, hills and rivals come hurtling toward you. You race across a series of tracks inspired by real cities and countries, keeping an eye on your fuel consumption and refilling the tank in the pits. Fuel is precisely what adds a tactical layer: do you risk skipping a stop, or would you rather slow down? Four cars with different characteristics push you to experiment with your driving style.

Top Gear became famous for its sense of speed and, above all, its music. The soundtrack was composed by Barry Leitch, and his energetic tracks became one of the most memorable parts of the whole game. The melody from the opening track ranks among the most-cited chiptune memories of SNES owners.

A big draw was the cooperative and competitive two-player mode on a split screen. Racing through the championship together, overtaking a friend on the finishing straight and battling for a better placing gave the game long-lasting appeal far beyond a single playthrough.

The game earned a sequel and gave rise to the entire Top Gear series, which was one of the mainstays of the racing genre on the Super Nintendo. Thanks to its combination of accessible controls, distinctive music and multiplayer, it built a strong fan base that still remembers it with a smile.

Even after decades Top Gear remains a demonstration of how much a sense of speed can be squeezed out of relatively simple technology. It's not a simulator, it's pure adrenaline arcade, and that is exactly how it won its place in the hearts of retro gamers.

**Why play it:** For an unforgettable soundtrack, a sense of speed and superb two-player split-screen racing.
snes__top-gear.teaser: Pseudo-3D racing from Gremlin Graphics with a split screen even in single-player mode.

mega-drive__sonic-hedgehog-1-3.detail: Sega needed a mascot to take on Mario, and Naoto Ōshima designed a blue hedgehog with „attitude“. Sonic 1 (1991) became the pack-in that drove Genesis sales in the US. The third game + Knuckles use the famous „lock-on“ cartridge — you slot Sonic 3 into Sonic & Knuckles and they combine into one giant game. Michael Jackson supposedly contributed to the music of Sonic 3 (still disputed to this day). A symbol of speed and the 90s.
mega-drive__sonic-hedgehog-1-3.article:
Sega needed a mascot who wouldn't just snap at Mario's heels but overtake him outright — and Naoto Ōshima gave it a blue hedgehog with a cheeky grin and a speed that platformers had never known before. Sonic the Hedgehog became a symbol of the nineties and of the entire Mega Drive era, and its first three instalments form one of the finest platforming chains ever.

Sonic 1 from 1991 arrived as a pack-in title that literally drove Genesis sales in the US. Its magic lay in movement: loops, springs, steep slopes and a sense of speed where the camera barely manages to bend after the hero. Where Mario rewarded precision, Sonic rewarded courage and momentum — and a generation of players loved it.

Each subsequent instalment added layers. The second introduced Tails and the spin dash, which turned launches into rocket starts. The third then brought grander levels, story elements and, above all, the famous \"lock-on\" cartridge: you slot Sonic 3 into Sonic & Knuckles and both games combine into one giant adventure. This technical trick was astonishing for its time.

Around the music of Sonic 3, moreover, one of the most enduring gaming legends still circulates to this day — that Michael Jackson supposedly contributed to it. The evidence is indirect and the whole matter remains disputed, but that is exactly what makes it a spicy topic of fan debate. Either way, the soundtrack ranks among the best the console offered.

Together these games defined what a fast platformer means, and Sonic hatched out of them into an icon that has survived decades, remasters and transformations into 3D. To play them today is to touch the very core of the nineties console wars.

**Why play it:** A trio of platformers that defined speed, gave Sega an iconic mascot and remain, to this day, among the very best on the Mega Drive.
mega-drive__sonic-hedgehog-1-3.teaser: The trilogy that turned Mega Drive into a phenomenon; the first game as a pack-in title kicked off sales.

mega-drive__sonic-and-knuckles.teaser: Sega's mascot; speed, loops, iconic music. The third game + Knuckles is the peak.
mega-drive__sonic-and-knuckles.article:
What if a cartridge weren't just a box with a game, but a key that unlocks other games? Sonic & Knuckles on the Mega Drive became famous not only as a first-rate platformer but also thanks to the ingenious \"lock-on\" technology that turned it into one of the most inventive pieces of the era of eight-bit and sixteen-bit legend.

At first glance it is a classic Sonic as you know it: speed, loops, springs and iconic music that burrows into your head. But it added the character of Knuckles, a burly echidna who can glide through the air and climb walls, opening up entirely new paths through the levels and changing both the pace and the approach to the game.

The real magic, however, hides on the back of the cartridge. When you slot Sonic 3 into Sonic & Knuckles, both games combine into one giant campaign — and it is precisely this combination, often described as the peak of the whole series, that offers the best of both worlds. You can also \"lock on\" older instalments and play as Knuckles where he wasn't before. For its time it was a small technical miracle.

The levels of Sonic & Knuckles itself rank among the best designed in the series: sprawling, full of hidden paths and tuned to reward both a fast run-through and careful exploration. Visually and sonically it is the peak of what the Mega Drive could squeeze out, and the boss battles have the necessary dose of grandeur.

Thanks to the linking trick and the quality of the game itself, Sonic & Knuckles earned a reputation as one of the console's cleverest and most beloved titles. It is a game that showed hardware, too, can be part of a creative idea.

**Why play it:** A top-tier Sonic platformer with an ingenious lock-on cartridge that combines it with Sonic 3 into the crowning experience of the whole series.

mega-drive__streets-of-rage-2.teaser: Perhaps the best 2D beat 'em up ever; a legendary soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro.
mega-drive__streets-of-rage-2.detail: Regarded by many as the best 2D beat 'em up ever. The music was composed by the then 24-year-old Yuzo Koshiro in his own programming language — a pioneering dance/house soundtrack still cited today as a high point of game music. Fluid combat, four characters, superb co-op. Essential.
mega-drive__streets-of-rage-2.article:
Sometimes a few seconds of the title music are enough and you know you're home. Streets of Rage 2 from 1992 opens with a pulsing beat and within an instant drags you into streets full of thugs who are practically asking for a proper beating. Many still call it the best 2D beat 'em up ever made — and they have solid reasons for it.

The combat here is fluid, readable and satisfying: every blow has weight, throws and special attacks land exactly where you need them, and the game rewards you for rhythm and positioning. There are four characters with distinct styles — from the balanced Axel through the nimble Blaze to the slow but crushing Max — so each choice changes the pace and tactics.

An enormous strength is co-op. Playing through the game as a pair is one of the best couch co-op experiences of its era; a well-drilled duo covers each other, combines attacks and works together through crowds of enemies and inventive bosses. The level design leads you from lit streets through fairground attractions to the final villain's lair, and the pace never lets up.

A legend was made, however, above all by the soundtrack. The then twenty-four-year-old Yuzo Koshiro composed it in his own programming language and created pioneering dance and house music that sounds raw, energetic and still modern. To this day it is cited as one of the high points of game music altogether, and it is in itself a reason people return to the game.

Streets of Rage 2 is an essential Mega Drive title — a combination of a flawless combat system, superb co-op and an immortal soundtrack makes it a game against which the whole genre is measured. If you want to understand why we love beat 'em ups, start right here.

**Why play it:** Perhaps the best 2D beat 'em up ever — flawless combat, superb co-op and Yuzo Koshiro's legendary soundtrack.

mega-drive__streets-of-rage-3.teaser: Faster, harder; reassessed today as excellent.
mega-drive__streets-of-rage-3.detail: Faster and tougher than the second game, with running, upgradable strikes and a branching ending. The Western version was censored and made harder (different colours, cut content), which long marred its reputation — today reassessed as an excellent instalment. Koshiro's more experimental soundtrack.
mega-drive__streets-of-rage-3.article:
If the second game felt fast to you, wait until you hit the streets a third time. Streets of Rage 3 from 1994 pushed harder on the pedal — it is faster, tougher and more ambitious than its famous predecessor, and after years of an unfair shadow it has earned a deserved reassessment as an excellent instalment of the series.

The combat got new options: characters can run, strikes can be upgraded and stronger versions of special attacks are unlocked over time. The game also offers a branching progression and several endings depending on how you do, which gives repeated play meaning. The pace is brisker and the enemies more aggressive, so it demands sharper reflexes and better use of space from the player.

The instalment's reputation was long marked by the Western localisation. The version for that market was censored and at the same time made markedly harder — character colours were changed, part of the content vanished and the difficulty cranked to the extreme put off a number of players. Only with hindsight and thanks to comparison with the original Japanese version, Bare Knuckle III, did it become clear what a quality game hid beneath those alterations.

Koshiro's soundtrack takes a more experimental path this time. His generative, almost techno-like tracks sound at times strange to the point of futuristic and divide fans to this day — some don't warm to them, others see in them a bold, distinctive shift. Either way it is an unmissable authorial signature that lends the game a unique atmosphere.

Streets of Rage 3 is today seen as an underappreciated gem of the Mega Drive: fast, deep and more inventive than its contemporaries granted it. For fans of the genre it is a mandatory stop and proof that the first impression need not be the last.

**Why play it:** A faster and deeper sequel with upgradable attacks and a branching ending, which after years won a reputation as an excellent beat 'em up.

mega-drive__gunstar-heroes.teaser: Treasure's debut; an explosion of ideas and action. A gem of the console.
mega-drive__gunstar-heroes.detail: The debut of studio Treasure, founded by former Konami employees who wanted to make creative action instead of sequels. An explosion of ideas — each level a different principle, combinable weapons (4 types × mix = unique projectiles), crazy bosses (a die with minigames!). Pushes the hardware to the max. One of the best run & gun games ever.
mega-drive__gunstar-heroes.article:
There are games that save their ideas for the sequel — and then there is Gunstar Heroes, which dumps them all out in the first five minutes and then adds more. The debut of studio Treasure from 1993 is literally an explosion of creativity, one of the best run & gun titles ever and a gem that made owning a Mega Drive worthwhile.

Treasure was founded by former Konami employees who had had enough of endless sequels and wanted to make bold, creative action. That is evident in every pixel of Gunstar Heroes. Each level stands on a different idea — one moment you're hurtling forward, another you're solving a board minigame on a gaming die with bosses, another the game flips over entirely. Boredom simply doesn't get a chance here.

The heart of the fun is the combat and weapon system. There are four basic weapon types that can be combined with one another, giving rise to unique kinds of fire — from guided lasers to devastating streams of flame. You can also choose between free and fixed shooting, which changes the play style and opens room for experimentation. The combat is fast, readable and incredibly satisfying, especially in co-op.

And then there are the bosses. Treasure downright feasted on them: huge, multi-phase, full of animations and surprises, including the already-mentioned bizarre die with minigames. The game also pushes the Mega Drive's hardware to its very limit — the amount of objects on screen, effects and animations feels as if the console were about to explode with enthusiasm along with you.

Gunstar Heroes laid the foundation of studio Treasure's reputation as masters of inventive action and is to this day celebrated as one of the peaks of the genre. It is a game that never slows down and never repeats itself — and that is exactly why players return to it decades after release.

**Why play it:** A dazzling debut from studio Treasure — an endless supply of ideas, combinable weapons and crazy bosses make it one of the best run & gun games of all time.

mega-drive__castlevania-bloodlines.teaser: The only MD Castlevania; fast and stylish.
mega-drive__castlevania-bloodlines.detail: The only Castlevania on the Mega Drive, set during the First World War across Europe. Two playable characters (John Morris with a whip, Eric Lecarde with a spear) with different gameplay. Impressive graphical effects (rotation, warping) exploiting the Genesis hardware. Atmospheric and underrated.
mega-drive__castlevania-bloodlines.article:
What if vampire hunting took place not in a dusty castle, but across a Europe convulsed by the First World War? Castlevania: Bloodlines from 1994 is the only Castlevania that ever came out on the Mega Drive, and Konami mined that exceptionality into an atmospheric, fast and stylish piece that deserves more attention than it gets.

The story takes the hunt for Dracula out of the usual settings into real European locations against the backdrop of the great war, which lends the series an unusual, gloomy tinge. There are two playable characters with different gameplay to choose from — John Morris with his whip in the style of the classic Belmonts, and Eric Lecarde with a spear that offers longer reach and its own movement tricks. Each of them changes the way you make your way through the levels.

The gameplay is brisker and more fluid than you'd expect of a Castlevania of that time, yet it still retains the need for deliberation during jumps and fights. The game varies the pace, offers inventive levels and boss fights that test your timing. The whip and the spear have a different rhythm, so replaying as the second character feels fresh.

Visually Bloodlines makes proper use of the Genesis hardware. You'll encounter eye-catching pieces such as rotation and warping of the image, collapsing and crumbling scenery and atmospheric environments that breathe gothic horror transplanted into a modern era. This is accompanied by music that can create tension as well as heroic pathos where needed.

Among fans of the series Bloodlines has a reputation as an underrated instalment — the only Castlevania on a Sega console, moreover with a distinctive wartime setting and honest craftsmanship. For anyone who likes atmospheric action platformers, it is a little treasure.

**Why play it:** The only Castlevania on the Mega Drive — fast, stylish and atmospheric, with two heroes and impressive graphical effects against the backdrop of the First World War.

mega-drive__shinobi-iii-return-of-ninja-.teaser: Smooth ninja action; one of the console's best titles.
mega-drive__shinobi-iii-return-of-ninja-.detail: The peak of the Shinobi series: exceptionally fluid ninja action with varied pacing — wall-running, horseback riding and surfing, throwing shuriken. Superb level design and music. One of the console's best action titles.
mega-drive__shinobi-iii-return-of-ninja-.article:
A true ninja is recognised not by the quantity of moves, but by how smoothly they merge into one fluid dance of death — and Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master from 1993 is exactly such a dance. Sega's peak of the Shinobi series belongs to the absolute top tier of action titles on the whole Mega Drive and remains, years on, a textbook of what fast ninja action should look like.

What elevates the game is its exceptional fluidity. The hero Joe Musashi moves like he's oiled — he runs along walls, double jumps, slashes with the katana and throws shuriken with a precision that makes movement itself a joy. The controls respond instantly, so even more demanding passages feel fair, and every successful run brings a sense of perfect mastery.

The level design, moreover, superbly varies the pace so as not to let you catch your breath in monotony. Between classic platforming and combat passages appear brisk interludes — riding a galloping horse, surfing on waves or a forward sprint where reflexes are what matter. The game thus constantly offers something new and keeps you on edge from start to finish.

Visually and sonically it is a polished piece of work. The environments have style and atmosphere, the enemies and bosses are inventive and the soundtrack underscores the tension and action of every scene. Everything fits together so that the game feels like one focused, self-assured experience with no dead spots.

Shinobi III is to this day celebrated as one of the console's best action and platforming titles and as a dignified finale to its series. If you want to feel what it's like to be a real ninja master, this game gives you that feeling like few others.

**Why play it:** Exceptionally fluid ninja action with varied pacing and superb level design — one of the best action titles on the Mega Drive.

mega-drive__phantasy-star-iv.teaser: The culmination of a classic JRPG saga; gorgeous comic-book-style panels.
mega-drive__phantasy-star-iv.detail: The culmination of a classic sci-fi JRPG saga, famous for the comic-book panels that tell the story (a presentation unique for its time). Refined turn-based combat with combo attacks (Combination Techniques) and a satisfying conclusion to the whole story arc. One of the best JRPGs outside Square.
mega-drive__phantasy-star-iv.article:
There are saga endings that burrow under your skin so deeply that you remember them even decades later — and Phantasy Star IV is exactly such a case. The culmination of the sci-fi JRPG line Sega had nurtured arrived at the twilight of the Mega Drive era and felt like the swan song of a whole generation: mature, self-assured and surprisingly emotional.

The game's most striking hallmark are the **comic-book panels** through which the story is told. Instead of static text windows, key moments unfold into hand-drawn frames like a page of manga — a solution that, on a 16-bit console, felt unusually cinematic and lent the storytelling both momentum and atmosphere. The journey through the Algol planetary system, its cursed past and the gradual uncovering of the true enemy hold the tension from the first hour to the last.

The combat is classically turn-based, but honed to a shine. The star of the system is **Combination Techniques** — when you use certain abilities of individual characters in the right order, they merge into a spectacular joint technique with a far greater effect. This layer rewards experimentation and gives otherwise conventional battles a tactical depth you'll want to keep exploring further and further.

The party of heroes is unforgettable — from the hunter Chaz through mysterious companions to characters whose fates can genuinely strike you. The game moreover elegantly wraps up motifs that ran through the previous instalments, so for fans of the series it is the settling of a long-promised debt.

At a time when the JRPG genre was dominated by Square with its Final Fantasy, Sega managed something of its own: Phantasy Star IV is to this day named as one of the best Japanese RPGs outside the Squaresoft workshop and ranks among the most prized titles in the whole Mega Drive library.

**Why play it:** A mature sci-fi JRPG with inventive comic-book storytelling and clever combat, which isn't afraid to stand alongside the genre's greatest legends.

mega-drive__shining-force-i-and-ii.teaser: Approachable turn-based tactics; a gateway into the genre.
mega-drive__shining-force-i-and-ii.detail: Approachable turn-based tactics with charismatic characters and a fantasy story; you combine battles with exploring towns and recruiting dozens of army members. A great gateway into the genre — less punishing than Fire Emblem. The second game is more expansive and more polished.
mega-drive__shining-force-i-and-ii.article:
If tactical RPGs have always tempted you but Fire Emblem felt like a harsh test of nerves, Shining Force is the right gateway. This pair of turn-based tactics games released by Sega offers all the charm of the genre without its sharpest edges — and that is exactly why it won over an army of fans.

At its core is **grid-based turn-based tactics**, where you pit heroes against enemies while watching ranges, terrain and turn order. But Shining Force adds something extra: between battles you **explore towns**, talk to people, shop and, above all, recruit new members into your army. Over time you gather dozens of fighters of all sorts of professions, from knights through mages to downright bizarre creatures.

Compared with the harsher representatives of the genre, Shining Force is more welcoming — fallen allies can be revived, progress is readable, and the game does not punish you for a single mistake by taking away a favorite character forever. That makes it an ideal textbook of tactics without losing its strategic juice.

The studio Climax was involved in development, and the charismatic fantasy world together with the well-tuned pacing turned these games into evergreens. **The second game** is in many ways more expansive and more refined — a bigger army, a more elaborate story and better battles — so releasing both parts together is a little treasure chest of tactical adventure.

The Shining series later branched out into many forms, but this original tactical line remains what fans remember most fondly.

**Why play:** Approachable, readable and charismatic turn-based tactics that teach you to love the genre instead of driving you away from it.

mega-drive__shadowrun.teaser: Cyberpunk action RPG with an open world; cult classic, deep.
mega-drive__shadowrun.detail: An adaptation of the tabletop RPG, a cyberpunk action RPG with an open world in an isometric view. You hack into the Matrix, hire companions and complete jobs in the gloomy future of Seattle. Deep and atmospheric; together with the SNES version (an entirely different game) it ranks among the most revered adaptations of the setting. A cult classic.
mega-drive__shadowrun.article:
Near-future Seattle, where megacorporations tower over the streets, magic mixes with technology and you scrape by in the gray zone as a hired shadowrunner — Shadowrun on the Mega Drive is one of those titles that cyberpunk devotees pass around like a secret password.

It is an **open-world action RPG** in an isometric view, an adaptation of the famous Shadowrun tabletop system. Instead of a linear story you get freedom: you take jobs, hire companions, arm yourself and gradually uncover a conspiracy hidden beneath the city's surface. The atmosphere of a gloomy, rainy future breathes from every screen.

The most enticing part is **hacking the Matrix** — a virtual space you jack into, where combat of a completely different kind takes place than on the street. This dual track between the physical world and cyberspace gives the game a depth that few things on consoles of the era could offer.

Interestingly, the SNES version is an entirely different game with a different approach and story — and fans to this day carry on friendly disputes about which one is better. The Mega Drive variant scores precisely with its openness and its emphasis on player freedom.

Both adaptations today rank among the most revered treatments of the Shadowrun setting ever, and this console version has earned a firm cult standing among lovers of cyberpunk and classic RPGs alike.

**Why play:** An atmospheric cyberpunk RPG with an open world and Matrix hacking — a cult gem for anyone who loves a neon-lit future.

mega-drive__arcus-odyssey.teaser: Isometric action RPG for two; underrated.
mega-drive__arcus-odyssey.detail: An isometric action RPG with two-player co-op and a choice of four heroes with different styles. From Wolf Team (later creators of the Tales series). Nice style, brisk action; an underrated hidden treasure.
mega-drive__arcus-odyssey.article:
Some games deserve far more attention than they ever received — and Arcus Odyssey is exactly this kind of quiet underdog in the Mega Drive library. An isometric action RPG that shines the moment you sit a second player down next to it.

The biggest draw is **two-player co-op**. You dive into the adventure together, choosing from **four heroes** with different combat styles and approaches to enemies, and make your way through levels from a bird's-eye isometric perspective. Combat is brisk, the action clear, and the shared adventure gives the game a completely different energy than playing solo.

Behind the game stands the studio **Wolf Team**, whose people later helped give birth to the famous Tales series. Even here you can see a feel for style and character — the visual side has its own expression and it all holds together at a pleasant pace.

Arcus Odyssey never belonged among the console's big names, and perhaps that is why it radiates the charm of discovery today. It is the type of title that collectors and enthusiasts know while the mainstream barely heard of it — and it brings all the more joy when you stumble upon it.

**Why play:** An underrated isometric action RPG with terrific two-player co-op — a hidden treasure for those who love hunting forgotten gems.

mega-drive__story-of-thor-beyond-oasis.teaser: Action RPG with fluid combat; beautiful.
mega-drive__story-of-thor-beyond-oasis.detail: An action RPG from the studio Ancient (Yuzo Koshiro and his sister Ayano as designer) with exceptionally fluid, animated combat and summonable elemental spirits (fire, water, shadow, plant). Visually one of the most beautiful action games on the console.
mega-drive__story-of-thor-beyond-oasis.article:
There are action games that simply look good, and then there is Story of Thor — known in the West as Beyond Oasis — which ranks among the most visually beautiful titles on the entire Mega Drive. A few minutes are enough to understand why old-timers speak of it with such respect.

In gameplay terms it is an **action RPG** with exceptionally **fluid, richly animated combat**. The hero's movement, his attacks and enemy reactions feel soft and natural, which was by no means a given on a 16-bit console. The combat is a joy to control, and thanks to it the game still plays wonderfully today.

A unique mechanic is the **summonable elemental spirits** — fire, water, shadow and plant. Each offers different abilities and combinations, so you approach combat and puzzles creatively and switch approaches according to the situation. This layer gives the otherwise straightforward action a pleasant depth.

Behind the game stands the studio **Ancient**, tied to the composer Yuzo Koshiro; his sister Ayano Koshiro contributed to the design. A feel for detail and style shows in the result at every turn — from the color palette through the animation to the atmosphere.

In the shadow of more famous action adventures, Story of Thor remains somewhat underappreciated, but for connoisseurs it is one of the most beautiful and most pleasantly controllable action games the Mega Drive offered.

**Why play:** A gorgeously animated action RPG with inventive elemental spirits — a visual and gameplay delight that ages with grace.

mega-drive__ristar.teaser: A platformer where you grab with your hands; charming and original.
mega-drive__ristar.detail: From the creators of Sonic, near the end of the console's life. Instead of jumping on enemies you use elastic arms — you grab, climb and attack with a headbutt. Charming style, great music and an original mechanic. A quiet gem that slipped through the cracks due to its late release.
mega-drive__ristar.article:
When a platformer came out near the end of the console's life in which you get rid of enemies not by jumping but by **grabbing them with your own hands**, it should have been clear that this was something special. Ristar is exactly this kind of quiet gem — and the team behind it was none other than the creators of Sonic.

Instead of the classic stomping on heads, the hero uses **elastic, stretching arms**. You grab enemies with them and pull yourself toward them to defeat them with a headbutt, you climb pillars and swing across chasms. This single but brilliantly executed mechanic changes the rhythm of the platformer and gives it its own, instantly recognizable character.

Visually Ristar is adorable — colorful, rounded and full of cute details — accompanied by **excellent music** that easily burrows into old-timers' heads. The levels are inventive and the grabbing mechanic is used creatively within them, so the game never grows stale.

Ristar's misfortune was its **late release** in 1995, when players' attention was already being drawn to newer 32-bit consoles. The game thus slipped through the cracks somewhat, even though it deserves to be named in the same breath as the console's best platformers.

Thanks to re-releases in various collections, anyone can easily reach it today — and almost every time it is a pleasant surprise.

**Why play:** An original and charming platformer from the creators of Sonic with an unmistakable grabbing mechanic — a gem that deserves a second chance.

mega-drive__vectorman-1-and-2.teaser: Pre-rendered action; a technical showpiece of the late era.
mega-drive__vectorman-1-and-2.detail: Pre-rendered „claymation/3D“ graphics — Sega's answer to Donkey Kong Country — and brisk shooting action with hero morphing. A technical showpiece of the late MD era, when the console tried to keep pace with 32-bit.
mega-drive__vectorman-1-and-2.article:
When Nintendo dazzled the world with the pre-rendered graphics of Donkey Kong Country, Sega did not fall behind — and its answer was Vectorman, a technical showpiece that squeezed everything it could out of the Mega Drive.

The hero is a robot composed of **pre-rendered, glossy spheres** whose 3D look was strikingly, even unexpectedly, effective on a 16-bit console. This „claymation“ style was a direct effort to keep pace with the competition at a time when the era of 32-bit machines was already knocking at the door.

In gameplay terms it is a brisk combination of **run & gun and platformer**. Vectorman shoots in all directions, jumps and, moreover, can **transform** into various forms — from a sphere into a drill, into a car and others — which spices up both the combat and traversal of levels. The pace is fast and the action satisfying.

The second game followed up with further ideas and improvements, and together the two games form one of the console's last great technical flagships, with which Sega tried to show that the old hardware still had something to offer.

Today Vectorman radiates the charm of an era when consoles competed with graphical trump cards — and as brisk action shooters they hold up even without nostalgia.

**Why play:** Technically impressive run & gun action with hero transformations — a late flagship of the Mega Drive that still entertains.

mega-drive__comix-zone.teaser: You fight inside a comic book; visually unique.
mega-drive__comix-zone.detail: You fight literally inside the pages of a comic book — you leap between panels, the artist paints you into the action and makes enemies with a pencil in real time. Visually absolutely unique. Short and brutally hard (you take damage even from destroying panels). A cult classic for its originality.
mega-drive__comix-zone.article:
Imagine an artist squeezing you right onto the page of a comic book — and you have to fight your way out, panel by panel, while the same author sketches enemies into your path with a pencil. That is exactly what Comix Zone is, one of the most visually original games ever released on the Mega Drive.

The entire game takes place **inside the pages of a comic book**. You **leap between individual panels**, the action runs within frames as if on paper, and the artist „paints“ you into the plot in real time — enemies literally come into being with a stroke of the pencil. This presentation had no equal in 1995 and still takes your breath away today.

The gameplay is a classic **beat 'em up**: you punch, kick and use objects to fight your way onward. But Comix Zone is **short and downright brutally hard** — and this is underscored by a cruel detail where you hurt yourself even by destroying the very panels around you. Every fight is thus a little test of nerves.

It was precisely the combination of merciless difficulty and an incredibly distinctive visual that turned the game into a cult affair. It is not a title everyone finishes, but it is an experience you never forget.

With its idea, Sega proved that even in an established genre you can come up with something that looks and plays like nothing before it.

**Why play:** A visually absolutely unique beat 'em up set inside a comic book — a short, cruel and unforgettable original.

mega-drive__rocket-knight-adventures.teaser: A Konami platformer with a rocket pack; brisk and clever.
mega-drive__rocket-knight-adventures.detail: The opossum Sparkster in rocket armor with which you charge up and ricochet off walls like a projectile in every direction — a unique movement mechanic. Brisk design, beautiful graphics and Konami music at its best. Underrated gems.
mega-drive__rocket-knight-adventures.article:
Take a charming opossum, dress him in rocket armor and let him ricochet off walls like a living projectile — and you have Rocket Knight Adventures, one of the cleverest and most underrated platformers from Konami.

The hero Sparkster carries a **rocket thruster** on his back that can be charged up and then fired off in any direction. He crashes into walls and bounces off them, hurtles through levels and attacks — this **movement mechanic** is the core of the whole game and gives it an unmistakable rhythm. Mastering the timing of the dives is a joy that other platformers of the era did not offer.

The level design is brisk and inventive, full of moments that cleverly exploit the rocket-thruster mechanic. Added to this is **beautiful graphics and excellent music** — in the mid-nineties Konami was simply among the elite, and it shows in every detail.

Despite its quality, Rocket Knight Adventures remained more of a connoisseurs' secret tip than a big commercial hit. But for platformer fans it is one of those games recommended onward with enthusiasm.

Sparkster later received a sequel and his adventures returned in a modern form as well, but the original Mega Drive installment remains for many the best.

**Why play:** A brisk, clever and beautiful platformer from Konami with a unique rocket-thruster mechanic — an underrated gem that deserves to be discovered.

mega-drive__sparkster.article:
The opossum in rocket armor returns — Sparkster continues the legacy of Rocket Knight Adventures and delivers another helping of brisk action platforming from Konami's workshop on the Mega Drive.

At the core of the experience remains the **rocket thruster on the hero's back**: you charge up energy and then launch yourself in a chosen direction, ricochet off walls and hurtle through levels like a guided missile. This movement mechanic gives the game its characteristic rhythm, where it is not just about jumping but about the right timing of dives and the deft use of space.

As an action platformer, Sparkster bets on what suits both the genre and the platform — a brisk pace, clear action, and combat and traversal situations built around the abilities of the rocket armor. The Mega Drive was an ideal home for this type of fast, reflexive game, and Konami was among those who knew how to get a lot out of its hardware.

For fans of the previous adventure it is a sequel in the established spirit: more of what worked, set into new challenges. Anyone who took a liking to the feel of rocketing and ricocheting across the screen will find a reason to return to it.

As part of the wider family of games around Sparkster, this title represents another chapter in one of the charming, characterful brands of the nineties platforming scene.

**Why play:** If the feel of the rocket thruster caught you, Sparkster offers another dose of brisk action platforming in Konami's characteristic style.
mega-drive__sparkster.teaser: An opossum in rocket armor bounces off walls; the sequel to Rocket Knight Adventures.

mega-drive__contra-hard-corps.teaser: Brutal run & gun with branching; for hardcore players.
mega-drive__contra-hard-corps.detail: The most demanding classic Contra, with a choice of four characters (each with different weapons), a branching story and several endings. Insane pace, giant bosses every moment. The Japanese version had a health bar, the Western one just one hit = death. For hardcore players.
mega-drive__contra-hard-corps.article:
One hit and you are done. So simple, so cruel — and it is exactly this philosophy that makes Contra: Hard Corps the toughest chapter of one of the most famous run & gun series of all time. In 1994 Konami took its legendary brand, packed it with adrenaline to the bursting point and sent it to the SEGA Mega Drive, where it immediately ranked among the most demanding titles on the console.

Unlike the older installments, here you choose from **four playable characters**, each of whom wields their own set of four weapons — from classic spread shot to homing missiles and risky melee weapons. Right from the first choice the game opens up an enormous space for experimentation and repeated playthroughs, because each character changes the combat style from the ground up.

The heart of the experience, however, is the **branching story**. At key moments you choose which way to go, which leads to completely different level sequences and several different endings. The pace is insane, something is constantly happening on the screen, and giant bosses roll in one after another at such a frequency that a moment of rest practically does not exist. Visually it is one of the flashier action games of its time — explosions, mechanical monsters and dynamic scenery use the Mega Drive hardware to the fullest.

An interesting detail is the difference between regions. The **Japanese version** gave the player a health bar and the ability to withstand several hits, whereas the **Western release** returned to the series' merciless tradition, where a single touch means instant death. This adjustment turned an already difficult game into a proving stone of reflexes and memorization, remembered to this day by everyone who dared to complete it without cheats.

Hard Corps is not a game for everyone, and it was never intended to be. It is a celebration of the old school, pure action and a hard challenge that rewards precision and patience. For hardcore players it represents one of the peaks of the genre in the 16-bit era.

**Why play:** If you crave uncompromising, fast and stylish run & gun action with a choice of characters and a branching story, this is the peak of the genre on the Mega Drive.

mega-drive__thunder-force-iii-iv.teaser: The pinnacle of the console's shmups; speed and music.
mega-drive__thunder-force-iii-iv.detail: The pinnacle of the console's horizontal shmups. Weapon selection by switching, fluid multi-layered scrolling and a phenomenal hard-rock soundtrack (Technosoft were masters of sound). The fourth game (Lightening Force in the USA) ranks among the technically best shooters of the entire 16-bit era.
mega-drive__thunder-force-iii-iv.article:
There is a handful of games whose soundtrack you remember before anything else — and Thunder Force belongs squarely in this category. The studio Technosoft was renowned as masters of sound, and their series of horizontal shooters on the SEGA Mega Drive proves it with every note and every pixel. The third game from 1990 and the fourth from 1992 represent the absolute pinnacle of the genre on this console.

At the heart of the gameplay is a **weapon-switching** system. Instead of linear upgrading, you choose on the fly between different types of fire depending on the situation, which turns survival into a tactical game of the right weapon at the right moment. Add to this the smooth, **multi-layered scrolling** that gave an illusion of depth and motion far beyond what was expected of a 16-bit machine.

Technically both games went to the edge of the possible. Backgrounds pile over one another, enemy formations roll in in well-thought-out waves, and the overall pace keeps the player in constant tension. **Thunder Force IV** (released in the West as Lightening Force) is to this day cited as one of the technically most advanced shooters of the entire 16-bit era — huge bosses, detailed animation and a smoothness the competition could hardly catch up to.

And then there is that music. Technosoft's hard-rock soundtrack was not just accompaniment but a full-fledged part of the experience, driving the player forward and underscoring every explosion. The Mega Drive's sound chip got here one of the best uses it ever received, and fans remember the tracks to this day.

The Thunder Force series became something of a flagship of what the Mega Drive could do in the world of shmups. For fans of the genre it is a must, and for anyone who wants to understand why this console built its reputation as a paradise of action games, it is an ideal gateway.

**Why play:** Top-tier horizontal shmups with tactical weapon switching, a dazzling technical side and one of the best soundtracks of the 16-bit era.

mega-drive__alien-soldier.teaser: A Treasure boss-rush; intensity to the max.
mega-drive__alien-soldier.detail: Essentially one boss fight after another (25 bosses) at a dizzying pace, with a minimum of ordinary levels. Treasure took the intensity to the max; notoriously demanding. Released only in Japan and Europe. For lovers of challenge and boss fights.
mega-drive__alien-soldier.article:
Forget ordinary levels, forget catching your breath — Alien Soldier is essentially one endless chain of boss fights that grabs you by the throat and does not let go. The studio Treasure, renowned for pushing the SEGA Mega Drive to extremes, created here in 1995 one of the most intense works of its entire legendary career.

The concept is brilliantly simple and brutal at the same time: the game leads you through **roughly twenty-five bosses** with an absolute minimum of classic connecting passages between them. Almost every moment is thus a fight to the death against a giant, aggressive monster. The pace is dizzying, the screen overflows with projectiles, and you must constantly switch weapons, dodge and search for opponents' weaknesses.

Treasure were famous for their feel for boss fights, and here they took their skill to the absolute maximum. Every enemy has its own attack patterns that must be learned, and the game mercilessly punishes any inattention. It is a **notoriously demanding** title that assumes you will learn from your mistakes and return repeatedly until you master every pattern in detail.

Visually and mechanically it is a showcase of what the Mega Drive could do in the hands of true experts. The game runs briskly, the explosions and effects are impressive, and the overall sense of intensity is exceptional to this day. It is no wonder that Alien Soldier built a cult status among lovers of challenge.

An important fact is that the title was released only in **Japan and Europe**; the North American market did not officially get it. That long made it a semi-hidden treasure in the West, known only to the initiated. Today, thanks to digital re-releases, it is more accessible, but its reputation as a relentless challenge remains.

**Why play:** If you love boss fights and seek pure, uncompromising intensity from the masters at Treasure, this is boss-rush in its purest form.

mega-drive__dynamite-headdy.teaser: A Treasure platformer bursting with ideas at every turn.
mega-drive__dynamite-headdy.detail: A platformer where the little guy Headdy attacks and solves puzzles by swapping his head for dozens of types (bomb, hammer, question mark…). A Treasure explosion of creativity with a theatrical theme (it all takes place „on stage"). Underrated thanks to confusing marketing.
mega-drive__dynamite-headdy.article:
What if the hero's main weapon were his own head? This crazy idea is exactly what Dynamite Headdy is built on, a platformer in which Treasure unleashed one of its most playful explosions of creativity on the SEGA Mega Drive. Released in 1994, it pours out original ideas at literally every step.

The main draw is the **head-swapping system**. Headdy attacks by launching his head at enemies, and throughout the game he can swap it for dozens of different types – a bomb, a hammer, a question mark and many more, each offering different abilities and often solutions to specific puzzles. This mechanic gives the game unexpected depth and constantly surprises the player with new possibilities.

The entire game unfolds in a **theatrical setting**, as if everything were happening on the stage of a puppet show. Backgrounds shift and slide like scenery, bosses feel like oversized stage props, and the overall visual style is unmistakably bizarre and enchanting. Here Treasure showed off its full flair for artistic imagination and for choreographing action scenes.

As with the studio's other titles, there is a heavy emphasis on inventive boss battles and constantly changing gameplay situations, so the player is practically never bored. Platforming sections are interspersed with puzzles that make use of that very head system, and the pace changes so often that every level brings something fresh.

Despite its quality, the game remained somewhat in the shadows – partly due to confusing marketing that failed to clearly convey what it was actually about. That is why today it is often labeled an underrated gem that deserves far wider attention than it ever received.

**Why play it:** An inventive and visually enchanting Treasure platformer with the original mechanic of swappable heads – an underrated Mega Drive gem.

mega-drive__earthworm-jim-1-and-2.teaser: Cartoon humor and insane design; a 90s icon.
mega-drive__earthworm-jim-1-and-2.detail: Doug TenNapel designed a bizarre world and an earthworm hero in a robotic suit; the team had animation experience, so the game looks like a cartoon. Insane humor (a cow, a blind cat, „Groovy"). It became a 90s icon with its own TV series and merch.
mega-drive__earthworm-jim-1-and-2.article:
An earthworm in a robotic suit saving the universe – if that sounds like something out of a Saturday-morning cartoon lineup, you're absolutely right. Earthworm Jim looks and plays exactly as if an animated film had come to life, and it is precisely this distinctiveness that made it one of the icons of gaming's nineties on the SEGA Mega Drive.

Behind the bizarre world and the hero stands artist **Doug TenNapel**, whose quirky imagination gave rise to a gallery of unforgettable characters – from a blind cat and a cosmic cow to catchphrases like „Groovy". The creative team had experience with animation, so the game boasts fluid, wildly exaggerated movements that give it that signature cartoon flair.

The gameplay mixes **platforming with run & gun action**. Jim shoots his blaster pistol, uses his own body as a whip to grapple and climb, and works his way through a series of inventive, often utterly insane levels. The 1995 sequel pushed the absurdity even further and added a range of completely madcap gameplay situations that broke the conventions of the genre.

Humor is absolutely essential here. Earthworm Jim pokes fun not only at its enemies but also at the medium itself and at genre clichés. This relaxed, slightly zany atmosphere combined with precise gameplay made it an instant hit and a beloved favorite of many players.

The success was so great that Jim outgrew the boundaries of games – he got his own **television series** as well as a range of merchandise, joining the ranks of the true pop-culture phenomena of his time. The first two installments remain the best this franchise ever offered.

**Why play it:** An iconic pair of action platformers with cartoon humor and insane design that defined the atmosphere of gaming's nineties.

mega-drive__toejam-and-earl.teaser: A funky roguelite about two aliens; a unique chill vibe.
mega-drive__toejam-and-earl.detail: Two cool, funky aliens search for pieces of their ship across randomly generated levels — a roguelite structure years before the genre boomed. Inspired by Rogue + hip-hop culture + quirky humor. Best in co-op. Nothing else plays like this game.
mega-drive__toejam-and-earl.article:
Two wacky aliens, funky music and planet Earth as a bizarre playground – Toejam & Earl is a game that plays like absolutely nothing else, and that was already true back in 1991. It arrived on the SEGA Mega Drive with a recipe so idiosyncratic that it still holds its utterly unique laid-back atmosphere to this day.

The story is simple: a pair of cool aliens crash-lands on Earth and has to collect **the pieces of their wrecked ship**, scattered across the individual levels. The catch is that the levels are **randomly generated**, so every playthrough looks different. This roguelite structure, openly inspired by the classic game Rogue, arrived years before the genre had its big boom – in this respect the game was truly ahead of its time.

Around this framework the creators built a world steeped in **hip-hop culture and funk**. Instead of enemies in the sense of classic opponents, bizarre earthlings lie in wait for you – rampaging dentists, devilish imps, or tomato-throwing hazards – and the game's humor is quirky, lazy and unmistakably cool. The pace is leisurely, the atmosphere relaxed, and the whole thing breathes an unmistakable chill.

The game truly comes alive in **co-op mode**. When two players explore the planet at once on a split screen, a unique shared experience arises, full of discovery, laughter and unexpected situations. Cooperation and mutual ribbing make co-op the very best way to experience Toejam & Earl.

Few games have managed to build such a distinctive identity. The combination of roguelite structure, funk aesthetics and downright good cheer made it a cult favorite that fans love precisely because it stands entirely outside all the established categories.

**Why play it:** A uniquely laid-back funky roguelite about two aliens that plays like nothing else – and in co-op it's unforgettable.

mega-drive__ghouls-n-ghosts.detail: An excellent home port of an arcade classic; the knight Arthur (left in his underpants after a hit) against hordes of the undead. Legendary old-school difficulty. The Mega Drive port was an impressive showcase of the console's power for its time.
mega-drive__ghouls-n-ghosts.article:
A knight who, after a single hit, is left standing in nothing but his underwear – if there's one image that sums up the merciless difficulty of the old school, this is it. Capcom's Ghouls 'n Ghosts became synonymous with an unforgiving challenge in 1989, and its home port on the SEGA Mega Drive was among the best players could have wished for at the time.

In the role of the knight **Arthur** you fight your way through hordes of the undead, demons and all manner of vermin toward saving the world. Your armor withstands a single hit; after a second one Arthur falls – this dual durability became cult and is still recalled by anyone who encountered the game for the first time. Various weapons come into play, from spears to shield-throwing projectiles, and choosing the right one often decides survival.

The difficulty is downright legendary. The game demands memorizing enemy placement, precision and nerves of steel, and even finishing it usually requires a repeated playthrough. It is the classic arcade school, where every death teaches and every bit of progress is a well-earned reward.

The home conversion for the Mega Drive was, for its time, an **impressive showcase of the console's power**. The port came very faithfully close to its arcade original, animated smoothly and displayed detailed backgrounds and enemies – for many it was one of the first proofs that the 16-bit SEGA could bring a genuine arcade experience right into the home.

The Ghosts 'n Goblins series to which this game belongs remains a legend to this day precisely for its combination of atmospheric horror design and brutal difficulty. For players seeking a pure old-school challenge, Ghouls 'n Ghosts remains one of the defining titles of the genre.

**Why play it:** Mercilessly demanding arcade action with the iconic knight in his undies and an excellent period port that showed off the power of the Mega Drive.

mega-drive__mega-man-wily-wars.teaser: A remake of the first three games in 16-bit; nice.
mega-drive__mega-man-wily-wars.detail: A remake of the first three NES Mega Man games in 16-bit graphics and sound, plus the bonus „Wily Tower" campaign with new challenges. In the US it was released only through Sega's subscription service Sega Channel, so the cartridge is rare. Nice for fans of the classics.
mega-drive__mega-man-wily-wars.article:
What if you could relive the blue robot's first three adventures, but this time in full 16-bit splendor? This is exactly the offer brought by Mega Man: The Wily Wars, a compilation in which Capcom transferred the classics from the NES to the SEGA Mega Drive in 1994 and wrapped them in a new coat.

At the heart of the package are **remakes of the first three installments** of the Mega Man series, originally released on Nintendo's 8-bit console. Capcom reworked them into richer graphics and improved sound, so the familiar levels, bosses and gameplay gained a fresh 16-bit sheen without losing their spirit. For fans of the classics it is a pleasant look back at the series' roots.

Besides the three reworked games, the compilation also adds a bonus campaign called **„Wily Tower"**. It offers new challenges and gives players the chance to combine weapons and abilities across installments, bringing content that was not in the original versions. It is a nice little cherry on top that makes the package more than a simple re-release.

What is especially interesting is its distribution history in North America. There the game was never released in regular retail on a cartridge, but was available only through Sega's subscription **Sega Channel** service, which delivered games over the cable network. As a result, the physical cartridge is very rare and collectible in the US today.

For lovers of classic Mega Man, Wily Wars is both a pleasant curiosity and a full-fledged way to revisit the series' fundamentals in a new guise. It's no revolution, but an honestly crafted tribute that will please anyone fond of the blue robot.

**Why play it:** A nice 16-bit remake of the first three Mega Man games with a bonus campaign – a treat for fans of the classics and a rare collector's piece.

mega-drive__landstalker.teaser: An isometric action RPG; the predecessor of Beyond Oasis.
mega-drive__landstalker.detail: An isometric action RPG with spatial jumping and puzzles — the predecessor of Beyond Oasis by the same people (Climax). Charming and expansive, though the isometric perspective sometimes complicates precise jumps. For fans of exploration.
mega-drive__landstalker.article:
An isometric world full of treasure, puzzles and precise jumps – Landstalker is an adventure that brought a fresh take on the action-RPG genre to the SEGA Mega Drive. In 1992 (it reached the West a year later), studio Climax built an expansive journey whose perspective and gameplay departed from the standard of the time.

The most striking feature is the **isometric view**, which gives the world spatial depth and opens up room for jumping in three dimensions. The game combines combat, exploration and the solving of **spatial puzzles**, where you have to carefully judge jumps between platforms, push objects and search for paths through hidden nooks. It is a mix of action and logic that keeps the player attentive.

Landstalker is also considered **the predecessor of Beyond Oasis**, which people from the same studio later worked on. Already here you can sense a feel for blending action with discovery and for building an expansive, charmingly designed world that invites a thorough exploration of every corner.

Charm and scope are the game's strong points, but the isometric perspective also has its price. Judging jumps precisely can, due to the distorted view, occasionally be frustrating and requires a bit of getting used to. Once the player masters the spatial perception, however, an inventive and rewarding adventure opens up before them.

For fans of exploration and the action-RPG genre, Landstalker represents an interesting and today somewhat forgotten choice that shows how diverse a catalog the Mega Drive built up even beyond the action and shooter genres.

**Why play it:** An expansive isometric action RPG with spatial puzzles and jumping, the predecessor of Beyond Oasis – ideal for lovers of discovery.

mega-drive__light-crusader.article:
When a studio manages to combine brisk action with clever puzzles and wrap it all in an isometric world, the result is an adventure that keeps head and fingers equally busy. Light Crusader is exactly such a game for the SEGA Mega Drive – a title on the border of action RPG and logic challenge that bet on exploration and thinking just as much as on combat.

As an action-puzzle-flavored RPG, the game combines two layers of experience. On one side there is combat and progression through the world, on the other the solving of **puzzles** that punctuate the adventure and force the player to stop and think. This combination gives the game its specific rhythm, distinct from the console's purely action titles.

The isometric perspective, typical of this kind of game, underscores the atmosphere of exploration and gives the spaces depth. The player moves through carefully designed locations, discovers hidden nooks and gradually reveals everything the world has to offer. The emphasis on discovery and logic makes the game an experience for patient players who like to take their time.

On the SEGA Mega Drive, the action-RPG genre with puzzle elements was a welcome change of pace alongside the omnipresent shooters, platformers and run & gun action. Games of this type expanded the console's catalog toward a slower, more contemplative experience and showed that the 16-bit machine could handle more than just fast reflex titles.

For players who enjoy the blend of action, adventure and logic, Light Crusader represents a pleasant piece from the console's rich catalog – a title that rewards curiosity and the appetite for solving mysteries as much as skill in combat.

**Why play it:** An action RPG with an emphasis on puzzles and isometric exploration – a pleasant change of pace for players who enjoy thinking as much as action.
mega-drive__light-crusader.teaser: An isometric action RPG from Treasure that puts as much emphasis on puzzles as on combat.

mega-drive__golden-axe.teaser: A fantasy beat 'em up; an arcade legend.
mega-drive__golden-axe.detail: A fantasy beat 'em up where you ride dragons and magical creatures and use spells gathered from goblins. An arcade legend and one of the MD launch titles. Best in co-op. Simple but iconic brawling.
mega-drive__golden-axe.article:
There is a sound that every Mega Drive owner recognizes instantly: the booming roar of a giant axe swing and the crackle of lightning as the hero spends his gathered magic. **Golden Axe** is the essence of what arcades did best at the turn of the eighties and nineties — fast, readable and brutally satisfying brawling wrapped in a fantasy garb that borrows so much from Conan the Barbarian that Robert E. Howard might be jealous.

The game was created at Sega and conquered arcades in 1989, from where it headed straight to the Mega Drive as one of the titles meant to sell the console. And sell it did. You pick one of three heroes — the barbarian Ax Battler, the dwarf Gilius Thunderhead with a thirst for revenge, or the amazon Tyris Flare — and set out after the evil Death Adder, who holds the king and princess captive. Each character wields a different type of magic and differs in strength and reach, so the choice is not cosmetic.

The heart of the fun is gathering magic. At night, little thieves and goblins with pouches of potions sneak between the levels, and whoever kicks them squeezes out blue vials. The more you collect, the more devastating the spell you can unleash — from a tiny spark to a screen-filling apocalypse. This creates an eternal dilemma: waste the magic right away, or save it for the boss? Added to this is the joy of riding beasts. Goblins can be knocked off their lizard steeds and off a fire-breathing dragon, and the saddle instantly changes the pace of the fight.

**Golden Axe** comes alive best with two players. The shared screen, joint kicks into enemies and the occasional accidental hit on your teammate — that is exactly the kind of cooperation that created arcade legends and later countless home evenings at the console. The battles are simple, built on the trio of attack, jump and magic, but it is precisely that simplicity that makes the game so accessible and timeless.

Culturally, Golden Axe ranked among the pillars of the beat 'em up genre alongside Final Fight and Streets of Rage, while its fantasy coat gives it a distinctive identity to this day. The series continued with further installments and later reboot attempts, and the game became a staple of Sega's retro compilations, so even today's player can easily reach it. It is a title that ages with grace — it may not be deep, but it is honest, energetic and immediately intelligible.

**Why play it:** For pure, ageless arcade brawling in a fantasy setting that, with two players, is still among the best the Mega Drive has to offer.

mega-drive__aladdin.teaser: Two of the console's best Disney platformers; beautiful animation.
mega-drive__aladdin.detail: Aladdin (the MD version) was animated by real Disney artists and the hero can even slash with a saber — visually stunning for its time (there is a completely different, also good SNES version by Capcom). Castle of Illusion with Mickey is a charming Sega adventure. Both beautiful.
mega-drive__aladdin.article:
Sometimes the stars align so perfectly that the result looks as if it had fallen off a movie screen — and that is exactly how **Aladdin** felt on the Mega Drive in 1993. At a time when most film licenses meant a rushed horror, along came a platformer whose animation involved real artists from the Disney workshop, and players couldn't believe their eyes. The characters moved with a fluidity home consoles had scarcely known until then.

A key difference from the competition lay in the gameplay too: this Aladdin wields a saber. Instead of merely jumping over enemies or landing on them from above, he can slash his way through rows of guards, snakes and desert beasts, while hurling apples as a throwing weapon. This creates a brisk mix of action and jumping that has bite and pace. The levels lead you through the marketplace of Agrabah, a Cave of Wonders full of falling rocks and an escape from lava, and it is all held together by a flawless sense of movement and timing.

It is worth mentioning that there is also a completely different **Aladdin** for the SNES by Capcom — also excellent, but built on a different philosophy where the hero carries more of a rope and jumps on enemies. Two studios, two versions, two camps of fans who argue to this day over which is better. The Mega Drive one, however, remains an icon precisely thanks to its cinematic sheen and bold action.

Aladdin ranked among the best-selling and most acclaimed titles on its console and remains to this day a textbook example of how to do a film license properly — with respect for the source and for the player. It showed that an animated film and a video game can speak the same visual language, and it foreshadowed an era when games began to be produced with almost studio-level care.

Anyone who fires up the cartridge today will find a platformer that, while demanding on jump precision, rewards with a fairy-tale spectacle and the feeling of controlling a cartoon character who has just run out of the cinema. It is a title that ages more slowly than most of its contemporaries — the colors glow, the animations flow and the magic remains.

**Why play it:** For the most audiovisually striking film platformer of its time, where a saber, apples and Disney animation form a whole that is still enchanting today.

mega-drive__castle-of-illusion.article:
Before Mickey Mouse became the symbol of a corporate empire, he was simply an adorable adventure hero — and **Castle of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse** is one of the loveliest proofs of that. This Sega platformer from the early nineties is a charming, tender and surprisingly inventive adventure in which Mickey sets out to rescue his Minnie from the clutches of the evil witch Mizrabel.

The gameplay rests on the classic principle of jumping on enemies' heads and throwing objects, but the magic lies in the execution. Each world has its own artistic identity — from a forest with giant apples and cookies to a toy landscape and the spooky chambers of the castle. Sega demonstrated here a mastery of color and level design that is welcoming enough for children yet inventive enough to entertain an adult player as well. It's a platformer you recognize by its atmosphere within a few seconds.

Castle of Illusion is among the titles Sega built as a family counterweight to Nintendo's mascots, and Mickey serves in it as a dignified ambassador. The game received sequels and a later modern remake that reminded a new generation of it in a 3D coat, but the original keeps its magical, hand-painted charm.

The difficulty is kind but not insultingly low — there are passages that will test timing and precision, especially in the later levels and against the bosses. It is precisely that balance that makes Castle of Illusion an ideal gateway into the genre and at the same time a pleasant return for veterans looking for something heartwarming.

Together with the other Disney titles of its time, it forms a small golden era when licensed games were not a dirty word but a promise of quality spectacle. Castle of Illusion is among its brightest stars and holds up to this day as a work that loved both its hero and its player.
