Culturally, Pole Position II confirmed that the qualify-and-race format wasn't a lucky fluke but a genuine cornerstone of the genre. It strengthened the whole brand's position as one of the pillars of arcade racing and helped spread its popularity to the next wave of players.

Today we see both Pole Position games as communicating vessels, proof that a good sequel doesn't have to turn the rules upside down; it's enough to cleverly expand on what worked. For fans of retro racing it's a mandatory stop.

**Why play:** For an improved and more varied version of the classic that defined arcade racing, now with a choice of multiple tracks.
arcade__pole-position-ii.teaser: An expansion of Pole Position with more tracks; more content, the same proven formula.

arcade__super-sprint.article:
A top-down view, three cars on the track and you frantically turning the wheel so you don't slide out in a sharp corner. Super Sprint is a racing game that goes against the pseudo-3D trend of its time and bets on something completely different: a clear bird's-eye view and pure, instant fun. And that's exactly how it won players' hearts in the arcades.

The mechanic is brilliantly simple. You see the whole track at once, control a little car and try to complete as many laps as possible before your rivals. The routes are full of corners, junctions and obstacles, so it's not enough to floor the gas; you have to learn the ideal line and master the car's inertia. The game also let several people play at once, which made it a great social experience where emotions ran high.

What makes Super Sprint stand out is its pace and competitiveness. The races are short, intense and immediately understandable, so players came back again and again. Between individual runs you could upgrade your car and earn advantages, which gave you motivation to keep going and conquer ever more demanding tracks full of oil slicks and other traps.

Culturally, Super Sprint carries on the tradition of classic top-down racers and became one of the best-known representatives of this style in the arcades. It reminded us that not every racing game needs to imitate the cockpit view to be gripping; sometimes perfectly tuned gameplay and the chance to test your strength against friends at a single cabinet is enough.

Today Super Sprint is seen as a benchmark of bird's-eye arcade racing and as proof that a simple idea taken to perfection can last for decades. For lovers of local multiplayer it's an ageless gem.

**Why play:** For fast, addictive top-down races and terrific duels with friends at a single cabinet.
arcade__super-sprint.teaser: A top-down view, three cars, and a trackball; the controls deliver raw, instant fun.

arcade__nba-jam.article:
BOOMSHAKALAKA. One word that defined an entire genre and burned itself into the memory of a generation of players. NBA Jam wasn't a basketball simulation, it was a celebration of the impossible, a game where two players a side leapt several meters into the air, set the ball on fire and made the whole cabinet dance with their pure, over-the-top energy.

The gameplay was gloriously simple: two on two, no fouls apart from exceptions, no basketball offside, just speed, dunks and points. When a player sank three baskets in a row, the ball literally caught fire and the character entered the on fire state, when almost every shot went in and the dunks got even more absurd. This mechanic made NBA Jam the perfect party experience, one that was mainly about joy and laughter, not tactics. Dunks from half court, characters flying through the air like superheroes and instant feedback turned every play into a little explosion.

NBA Jam was developed by Midway, and the game used digitized likenesses of real NBA players, which lent it authenticity despite its utterly unrealistic gameplay. The cabinet became a huge financial success and was among the highest-grossing arcade games of its time, earning arcade operators considerable sums. Its popularity led to a string of ports to home consoles and to a whole series of sequels that kept this style of basketball alive for many years.

Culturally, NBA Jam had an enormous reach. It helped popularize basketball among gamers and became a textbook example of how an arcade sport can be more fun than a realistic simulation. The announcer's catchphrases, including the legendary boomshakalaka and he is on fire, entered pop culture and fans still quote them today. The game also featured a host of hidden characters and funny secrets that players passed on by word of mouth, further cementing its status as a phenomenon.

Arcade cabinets were at their peak at the time, and sports titles were an important part of them because they drew multiple players to competitive play at a single machine. NBA Jam perfectly exploited this social dimension of the arcades, where little crowds gathered around the cabinet, took turns dueling for points, and where every spectacular dunk drew a loud reaction from the onlookers.

It's exactly this combination of instant fun, exaggerated style and social experience that made NBA Jam one of the most beloved arcade games of all time. The game showed that a sports title doesn't have to be a serious simulation to captivate, and that exaggeration can be far more entertaining than faithfully copying reality.

NBA Jam's legacy is still vividly felt in every arcade sports game that bets on spectacle and fun over accuracy. Its style, its catchphrases and its two-on-two spirit became the yardstick for what a sports game should look like, one you play mainly to have fun and laugh, whether you win or lose.

**Why play:** For the pure, over-the-top joy of dunks from half court and the boomshakalaka catchphrase that turns every match into a party.
arcade__nba-jam.teaser: The iconic BOOMSHAKALAKA and over-the-top dunks; 2-on-2 arcade basketball with no brakes.

arcade__punch-out.article:
The ropes rise, the crowd roars and in the ring stands a giant who looks like he could knock you into next week with a single punch. Punch-Out!! was a boxing game that wasn't built on realistic combat but on precise observation, timing and reflexes. It was essentially a kind of rhythmic puzzle dressed up in boxing gloves.

The mechanic was brilliantly readable. Every opponent had his own set of attacks and so-called tells, tiny gestures or flashes that gave away the incoming blow. The player had to learn these patterns, dodge the punches by weaving to the sides or blocking, and counter at just the right moment. The fights therefore weren't about hammering a button but about patience and gradually decoding each opponent like a logic problem. Every bout was like a chess game, where a single mistake meant a harsh punishment.

Punch-Out!! was born at Nintendo and became one of the company's most distinctive arcade titles outside its best-known platformer series. The arcade version was remarkable technically too, using two stacked displays to show information and the fight. The series later got famous versions on home consoles that became cult favorites and to this day rank among the best the boxing genre has offered. So an arcade cabinet became the foundation of one of Nintendo's respected brands.

Culturally, Punch-Out!! is remembered above all for its distinctive, almost cartoonish opponents, who had strong personalities and became iconic. The fight with each of them was like a little story, a challenge players remembered and told each other about. The series became synonymous with clever, addictive gameplay built on learning and repetition, where a defeat didn't mean the end but a lesson for the next attempt.

The arcade setting was ideal for a game of this type, because it offered an instant, intense challenge that lured players into repeated attempts to beat the next opponent. Every victorious bout brought a sense of deserved success achieved through your own skill, not luck. It was exactly this earned quality of victory that made Punch-Out!! such a satisfying experience.

To this day Punch-Out!! is a textbook example of how to make an action game that tests the mind as much as the fingers, and how to turn a simple principle into a thoughtful challenge. Each opponent is really a puzzle that has to be solved by observation, and only once the player understands his rhythm does the path to victory open up.

This philosophy sets Punch-Out!! apart from most fighting and sports games that bet on finger speed or the force of an attack. Here it's about reading, patience and the precise moment, and it was exactly this distinctiveness that guaranteed the series a long and respected existence across generations of consoles.

**Why play:** For a clever boxing puzzle where victory isn't about strength but about finally seeing through your opponent and timing that perfect punch.
arcade__punch-out.teaser: Boxing as a rhythm puzzle; what decides it is watching the opponent's tells and precise timing.

arcade__tehkan-world-cup.article:
Imagine football controlled not by a joystick but by a huge rotating trackball you spin with your palm to send the ball exactly where you want. Tehkan World Cup was one of the first games to bring football into the arcades in a form that laid the foundations for many later titles of the genre.

The game's genius lay precisely in its controls. The trackball allowed intuitive, analog steering of movement and kicks, which gave players surprisingly fine control over the ball at a time when most games made do with eight-way joysticks. The top-down view of the pitch, the fast pace and the option to play two against each other made Tehkan World Cup an extraordinarily addictive and competitive affair. The power of a kick depended on how hard the player spun the trackball, which lent the play surprising depth.

The game was created by the Japanese company Tehkan, known today more by its later name Tecmo. It was a pioneering title that showed football could work in the arcade setting as fast, accessible and exciting fun. Many of the elements introduced here, including the view of the pitch and the emphasis on fast competitive play, appeared in later football games for decades. Tehkan thus indirectly influenced the whole direction football games would take.

Culturally, the game mattered as one of the cornerstones of the football genre in video games. At a time when developers were still figuring out how best to translate the sport into digital form, Tehkan World Cup offered a convincing solution built on clever controls and competition between two players. It thus became an important forerunner of the whole tradition of football games that later grew into one of the biggest sports genres in the industry.

The arcades were the ideal place for such a title, because football is by its nature a contest played against another person. The trackball controls tempted passers-by to give it a try, and duels between two players drew spectators who gathered around the cabinet and cheered. The game wasn't just entertainment but a little social event that played out right there in the arcade.

Today Tehkan World Cup is a fascinating window into a time when the conventions we now take for granted were only being born, and its trackball controls remain unique and, to this day, surprisingly pleasant. For players used to classic controllers it's a small revelation of how natural a feel for the ball a trackball can offer.

As a pioneer of football games, Tehkan World Cup deserves a place in the history of the genre. It showed that football could work in digital form as fast, accessible and deeply competitive fun, and thereby opened the door to the dozens of football titles that came after it and gradually grew into one of the biggest genres in the industry.

**Why play:** For a nostalgic look at the roots of football games and the unique trackball controls that give the ball a surprisingly natural feel.
arcade__tehkan-world-cup.teaser: Football controlled with a giant trackball; it laid the groundwork for later arcade soccer games.

arcade__hat-trick.article:
Ice hockey is fast, brutal and full of moments where everything is decided in a fraction of a second. Hat Trick was an arcade game that tried to bring that speed and tension into the arcades, offering hockey in an accessible, straightforward form meant for fast competitive play.

Mechanically it was direct, action-packed hockey with a view of the ice, where the player controlled his team, passed, shot and tried to beat the opposing goalie. Part of the experience was also controlling the goalie on defense, which added a tactical dimension, since the player had to handle both attack and defense at once. The emphasis was on speed and instant action rather than complex rules, so anyone who stepped up to the cabinet could handle the game without long learning or reading a manual.

Hat Trick belonged to the wave of arcade sports games that were bringing various sports into the arcades at the time. Hockey was a natural choice in this context, because its fast pace and physical contact suited the arcade, action-packed gameplay perfectly. The game allowed a duel between two players, which was the key to its appeal in the social environment of the arcades, where the main point was to test your strength against a friend or an unknown challenger.

Culturally, Hat Trick was part of the wide offering of sports cabinets that complemented the dominant action and platform titles of the eighties. Sport was popular in the arcades precisely because it offered a natural competition between people and didn't require lengthy learning; you just came and played against a friend. Hockey, with its dramatic nature where a goal can fall at any moment, was made for this format.

The arcade setting made sense for such sports games, because they bet on instant fun and a competitive spirit. Hockey, with its speed and the chance to score at any moment, was an ideal candidate for a game where players took turns, cheered and came back for a rematch. Every match was short, intense and invited another attempt at a better result.

Hat Trick thus remains a reminder of a time when the arcades offered a whole fan of sports experiences, and when even a sport as swift as hockey found its place among the cabinets luring players with fast, straightforward fun. For hockey fans it was a welcome chance to experience their favorite sport in a form that required nothing more than the desire to test their strength.

In a sea of action and platform games, Hat Trick offered a pleasant change of pace and proof that sports titles have their firm place in the arcade world. Its simplicity was also its strength, because it let anyone jump straight into the battle for goals and enjoy the pure joy of the game.

**Why play:** For fast, straightforward arcade hockey that needs no complex rules and puts you straight into a battle for goals against your opponent.
arcade__hat-trick.teaser: Fast, straightforward arcade hockey built on instant head-to-head competition between two players.

neogeo__metal-slug-2.article:
The very first screen of Metal Slug 2 is a parade of detail: soldiers march, explosions tear apart the scenery and you claw your way through a flood of enemies with both exaggeration and endearing brutality. This run and gun gem from SNK is still a benchmark of the genre and one of the most beautiful titles ever to appear on the Neo Geo.

Metal Slug 2 was created at SNK as a sequel to the successful original and came out on both the arcade and home Neo Geo system. Genre-wise it's a classic side-scrolling shooter where you fight your way through levels left to right with a foot soldier, collecting weapons, freeing prisoners and hopping into the iconic Metal Slug tank and other vehicles. Visually the game excels with detailed pixel art animation that ranks among the best of its time.

The series became famous for its sense of humor and over-the-top action. Your character comically fattens up after eating food, enemies react in an exaggeratedly theatrical way, and every level is packed with hidden details and easter eggs. Metal Slug 2 added new vehicles, transformations and more varied environments, though the second game is also known for the Neo Geo hardware noticeably slowing down at times on crowded screens.

The cultural significance of the Metal Slug series is beyond dispute. It became synonymous with the run and gun genre, and to this day developers and fans alike cite it as the pinnacle of hand-drawn pixel art animation in action games. Sequels and remakes appeared on a range of platforms and the series' characters found their way into other SNK titles.

Metal Slug 2 is a joy to look at and to play, especially in two-player mode, when the on-screen chaos multiplies. It's a monument to honest craft from a time when visual impact was decided by the animator's hand, not the power of a graphics card.

**Why play:** A gorgeous, witty and jam-packed run and gun classic that still defines what top-tier pixel art in action should look like.
neogeo__metal-slug-2.teaser: Hand-drawn animation and dense action; one of the most beautiful run & gun titles on the Neo Geo.

neogeo__fatal-fury-special.article:
If you want to understand how SNK built its fighting empire even before the King of Fighters era, Fatal Fury Special is the perfect guide. This enhanced version of the packed roster of fighters from the city of South Town is among the most played fighting games of the golden Neo Geo era and still has its devoted fans.

The game was created by SNK as an expanded and fine-tuned version of the previous installment Fatal Fury 2 within the Garou Densetsu series. It came out on the Neo Geo system and brought an expanded roster of fighters, including the return of popular characters from the first game. Players especially loved the Bogard brothers, Terry and Andy, and the charismatic Joe Higashi, who later became pillars of the whole SNK universe.

Mechanically, Fatal Fury stood out with its two-plane fighting system, where characters could hop between the foreground and background of the arena, which added a tactical layer to the genre that the competition didn't have. Special fine-tuned the balance of the characters, sped up the pace and added special attacks, placing it among the most accomplished installments of the series in terms of gameplay.

The cultural significance is considerable. Terry Bogard became one of SNK's most iconic faces and still appears across other games and crossovers to this day. Fatal Fury Special was also one of the titles that helped establish the Neo Geo as the home of serious, hardcore fighting games at a time when the genre was ruled by Street Fighter II.

Fatal Fury Special remains a great choice for fans of classic fighters who want to get to know the roots of later legends. It's a title with character, distinctive personalities and a depth that even today's players seeking an honest retro battle will appreciate.

**Why play:** A fine-tuned classic fighter that laid the foundations of the SNK legend and still entertains with distinctive characters and its two-plane fighting system.
neogeo__fatal-fury-special.teaser: An improved collection of South Town fighters; one of the most-played fighting games of the Neo Geo's golden era.

neogeo__real-bout-fatal-fury.article:
With Real Bout, the Fatal Fury series entered a new, more confident era. SNK rewrote the rules of its combat, sped up the pace and added new mechanics that made this fighter one of the most dynamic in the Neo Geo family. For fans of South Town it was a big step forward.

Real Bout Fatal Fury was developed by SNK as part of the long-running Garou Densetsu series and came out on the Neo Geo system. It brings back a cast of familiar faces led by Terry Bogard, to whom the game added a reworked combat system. Real Bout simplified and at the same time sharpened the controls compared to older installments, making the game accessible to new players without losing its depth for veterans.

The most striking novelty is how it works with the arena environment. Real Bout introduced a system where you can knock your opponent out of the ring and thereby cause his defeat, which added tension and strategy to the fights. The proven system of switching between two combat planes also returned, this time in a smoother and more refined form, and the faster pace gave the matches extra bite.

Real Bout Fatal Fury is among the titles that cemented SNK's reputation as a master of fighting games alongside rival Capcom. The series as a whole significantly influenced the genre's development, and its characters live on in crossovers and in the King of Fighters series. For many fans this very line represents the heart of the SNK fighting tradition.

To this day Real Bout is prized as one of the most playable installments of the series and a great entry point for anyone who wants to learn what set SNK fighters apart from the mainstream. Speed, style and character are all at a top level here.

**Why play:** A dynamic, fine-tuned sequel to a legendary series with tense ring-outs and a top-tier combat feel.
neogeo__real-bout-fatal-fury.teaser: SNK rewrote the series' rules and picked up the pace; it's among the fastest fighting games on the Neo Geo.

neogeo__art-of-fighting.article:
When huge, intricately animated fighter characters first appeared on the Neo Geo screen, players couldn't believe their eyes. Art of Fighting arrived with a visual spectacle without parallel in early-nineties fighting games, and added to it several ideas that pushed the genre further.

The game was created by SNK for the Neo Geo system and set in the same world as the Fatal Fury series, in the city of South Town. The story follows young fighters Ryo Sakazaki and Robert Garcia, who are searching for Ryo's kidnapped sister. This connection later resulted in one of SNK's best crossover details, since the characters from Art of Fighting and Fatal Fury share a common history.

Art of Fighting brought several pioneering elements. Famous were the giant, impressively scaled character sprites that grew larger as the camera zoomed in, and the spirit gauge system for special attacks, which drained as they were used and could be recharged. The game also introduced facial damage to characters during a match and bonus challenges for improving skills, showing its ambition to push the genre's presentation forward.

The cultural significance of Art of Fighting lies mainly in its influence on later SNK titles. Mr. Karate, Ryo and Robert became fixtures of the universe, and the connection to the Fatal Fury world laid the groundwork for the later big crossovers in the King of Fighters series. The game is now seen as an important link in the evolution of SNK fighters.

Art of Fighting is thus a fascinating stop for anyone who wants to see how developers experimented with the presentation and mechanics of fighting games in the early nineties. It's a title full of ambition that was ahead of its time in its emphasis on visual impact.

**Why play:** A visually pioneering fighter with giant sprites and an innovative spirit gauge that significantly shaped the SNK fighting universe.
neogeo__art-of-fighting.teaser: Giant, intricately animated characters and a camera that zoomed into fights like nothing before it.

neogeo__world-heroes-2.article:
When hundreds of fighting games filled the arcades in the mid-nineties, every title needed something extra to survive. World Heroes 2 bet on a crazy idea: what if fighters from across history clashed in a single tournament? This series from studio ADK, published under the SNK banner on the Neo Geo hardware, pitted characters inspired by real legends against purely fictional figures, and it was precisely this mix that gave the game a distinctive character at a time when the competition was churning out one serious fighter after another.

The second installment significantly expanded the roster compared to the original game and fine-tuned the combat system. Alongside classic matches it also offered so-called Death Match modes, where the arena itself dealt damage – spikes, explosives and other traps turned the fight into a bloody farce. This gimmick set World Heroes apart from the austere realism of Street Fighter and from the ghostly mysticism of other titles, and gave players room for a proper show.

The Neo Geo was the ideal home for this type of game. Mighty sprites, a vivid color palette and smooth animations gave the characters a distinctive comic-book flavor. Players lucky enough to own the home Neo Geo AES console brought the arcade experience home practically without compromise, right into the living room – albeit at a price that made this platform a privilege of wealthier fans.

World Heroes 2 never reached the prestige of Street Fighter II or the fame of the later King of Fighters, but in its day it built up a loyal group of supporters. For Neo Geo connoisseurs it's a typical example of how SNK and allied studios experimented with the genre and searched for their own path amid the clouds of nineties fighters. The series continued with further installments that gradually added mechanics and characters.

Today the game is interesting mainly as testimony to the variety of the arcade scene of the time. Anyone wanting to work through the genre's history will come across World Heroes 2 as an honest, playable fighter with a touch of tongue-in-cheek that didn't take itself quite as seriously as its more famous competitors.

**Why play:** For brisk fights with historical and fictional fighters and crazy Death Match arenas that still entertain today.
neogeo__world-heroes-2.teaser: ADK brought fighters from across history and fiction together into one wacky Neo Geo tournament.

neogeo__magician-lord.article:
Magician Lord ranks among the very oldest titles for the Neo Geo and remains famous to this day for its merciless difficulty. This action platformer from the Alpha Denshi (ADK) studio launched among the first games of SNK's new platform at the turn of the eighties and nineties, and its job was to show what the expensive, powerful hardware could do as it tried to bring the arcade experience straight into the home.

The player takes on the role of the wizard Elta, who sets out to defeat a dark ruler. The key mechanic is transformation: by collecting items, Elta changes into several forms — from a dragon to a ninja to an elemental warrior — each with different abilities and a different way of attacking. This variability gave the game depth and forced players to think about which form to use when as they fought their way through hordes of enemies.

Visually, Magician Lord dazzled. Large, detailed sprites, multi-layered backgrounds, and giant bosses demonstrated the power of the Neo Geo at a time when ordinary home consoles could not manage such a spectacle. The dark fantasy atmosphere, with its Gothic settings and monstrous adversaries, felt extraordinarily evocative for its era.

The game earned its reputation above all through its harsh difficulty. A single hit usually meant losing a transformation or your life outright, and progress required patience, memorized patterns, and steady nerves. It was precisely this uncompromising nature that turned Magician Lord into a cult title, often cited as an example of the old-school arcade tradition.

Thanks to later compilations and digital releases on modern platforms, a new generation can try the game as well. For Neo Geo fans, Magician Lord remains an iconic launch title that set the bar for audiovisual quality across the entire platform.

**Why play:** For its stylish dark fantasy, inventive transformation system, and honest old-school difficulty that will test your patience.
neogeo__magician-lord.teaser: One of the first Neo Geo games from Alpha Denshi, notorious for its merciless difficulty.

neogeo__blazing-star.article:
If there is one game that can convince you within a few seconds that the Neo Geo knew how to make dazzling shooters, it is Blazing Star. This horizontal shoot 'em up from the Yumekobo studio arrived in the mid-nineties as a spiritual successor to the older title Pulstar, and it became one of the most sought-after shooters on the entire platform — not least because of the prices the original cartridges fetch today.

Blazing Star bet on pre-rendered graphics that gave the ships and backgrounds a plastic, almost three-dimensional look. The result was an explosion of color, detailed enemies, and spectacular bosses that filled the whole screen. The player could choose from several ships, each with different weapons and a different play style, which added to the replayability.

The key mechanics were the charged shot and, above all, a bonus system that rewarded fast and precise destruction of enemies. Anyone who could chain hits and use charge attacks was rewarded with a higher score and more impressive effects — and it was precisely this chase for points that made Blazing Star a favorite among players focused on performance and leaderboards.

The game is also notoriously famous for its imperfect English in the text, some phrases of which became internet memes among retro gaming fans. Paradoxically, this small detail contributed to its cult reputation, and enthusiasts around the world still bring it up today.

Thanks to digital releases within collections of classic Neo Geo games, Blazing Star reached a modern audience that otherwise had no chance to taste this originally expensive arcade treasure. For lovers of the genre, it is one of the best-looking 2D shooters of its era.

**Why play:** For the gorgeous pre-rendered graphics, the addictive scoring system, and one of the finest visual experiences the Neo Geo had to offer.
neogeo__blazing-star.teaser: Yumekobo's dazzling horizontal shooter, a spiritual successor to Pulstar and a pricey rarity.

neogeo__pulstar.article:
Before the dazzling Blazing Star came along, the Aicom studio laid the foundation of this line of shooters with a game called Pulstar. This horizontal shoot 'em up for the Neo Geo from the mid-nineties is often compared to the legendary R-Type series, and that is no coincidence — it shares with it a slower, more tactical pace as well as an emphasis on memorizing the layout of enemies and hazards.

Pulstar stood out with pre-rendered graphics that gave the ships and biomechanical bosses a plastic, organic look reminiscent of the work of H. R. Giger. Backgrounds full of tentacles, sinews, and cosmic monsters created an oppressive atmosphere that differed markedly from the more colorful, action-packed shooters of the time.

In terms of gameplay, the game rested on the charged shot: holding the button accumulated energy for a powerful attack, so the player constantly had to weigh when to fire normally and when to save up a devastating salvo. This mechanic, together with the merciless difficulty and the need to learn the levels by heart, made Pulstar a title for patient and determined players.

Pulstar built a reputation as one of the most demanding and, at the same time, most beautiful shooters on the platform. As with a number of Neo Geo exclusives, its high purchase price turned it into a rarity that collectors still crave today, and original cartridges are among the prized pieces.

Thanks to later digital reissues and collections, it also reached a new generation of players who appreciate its atmosphere as well as its tough but fair challenge. For connoisseurs of the genre, Pulstar remains an unmissable gem among 2D shooters.

**Why play:** For the oppressive biomechanical atmosphere, the tactical charged-shot system, and an honest R-Type-style challenge.
neogeo__pulstar.teaser: Aicom's shooter often compared to R-Type; a tactical pace and pre-rendered graphics.

neogeo__sengoku-3.article:
A brawler that blends feudal Japan with ninjas and supernatural powers — that is how you could briefly sum up Sengoku 3, the third installment of the beat 'em up series from SNK for the Neo Geo platform. It came out at the turn of the millennium, when the beat 'em up genre had already passed its golden age, which made it all the more surprising how brisk and polished the action it offered was.

Unlike the two older, somewhat stiff installments of the series, Sengoku 3 turned into a fast, fluid slaughter with an emphasis on combos and mobility. Players could choose from several fighters with distinct styles, chain combos, use special attacks, and coordinate in co-op. The result was one of the most playable late brawlers of all.

Visually, the game benefited from the mature Neo Geo hardware. Detailed sprites, dynamic animations, and stylish environments combining historical Japanese motifs with fantastical elements gave the game a distinctive look. The pace was fast, the blows had punch, and the boss fights did not lack imagination.

Sengoku 3 was created at a time when the Neo Geo hardware was already on its way out and the beat 'em up genre was fading into oblivion, pushed aside by 3D action games. That is precisely why it is prized as one of the last great representatives of the classic brawler, showing that even in the cramped 2D format you could create fresh and entertaining action.

For fans of cooperative brawlers, Sengoku 3 represents a smaller hidden treasure worth discovering — especially thanks to later digital releases that made the game accessible to a wider audience beyond the expensive original hardware.

**Why play:** For the brisk, polished cooperative slaughter that ranks among the best late brawlers and stylishly mixes history with fantasy.
neogeo__sengoku-3.teaser: Feudal Japan, ninjas, and the supernatural; an SNK beat 'em up from a late but sprightly release.

neogeo__twinkle-star-sprites.article:
What if a shooter and a puzzle game collided in one competitive game for two players? That is exactly what Twinkle Star Sprites offers, an original title from the ADK studio for the Neo Geo from the second half of the nineties, which earned a reputation as one of the most inventive and entertaining competitive games on the entire platform.

The principle is ingeniously simple: two players each have their own split screen and shoot at swarms of enemies and stars. By destroying groups in the right way, you trigger chain reactions that send attacks onto the opponent's half. The goal is not to complete a level but to overwhelm your opponent so they cannot withstand the onslaught — so it is a kind of cosmic duel in the style of falling blocks, only dressed up as a colorful shooter.

Twinkle Star Sprites combines the reflexes of a classic shoot 'em up with the tactical chain planning known from puzzle games. Cute cartoon graphics, bizarre little characters, and a playful atmosphere give the game an unmistakable charm that stands in pleasant contrast to the otherwise often serious and hard Neo Geo titles.

With two people, it is one of the most gripping competitive games the platform had to offer — it was the one-on-one duels that gave the game a devoted fan base. A solo mode against the computer does exist, but the real magic fully reveals itself only against a live opponent.

Thanks to reissues and digital releases on modern consoles, Twinkle Star Sprites found its way to a new generation of players who appreciate its original blend of genres. For fans of local multiplayer, it is a little gem that still delivers fun.

**Why play:** For the ingenious fusion of shooter and puzzle and the unforgettable competitive duels between two players.
neogeo__twinkle-star-sprites.teaser: ADK combined a shooter with a puzzle game into a competitive duel; an inventive Neo Geo one-of-a-kind.

neogeo__baseball-stars-2.article:
Baseball was never as colorful and accessible in video games as in the Baseball Stars series from SNK, and its second installment for the Neo Geo raised the bar even higher. Baseball Stars 2 from the first half of the nineties is often called one of the best arcade sports games on the platform, and fans still recall it today as the benchmark for entertaining, uncomplicated baseball.

Unlike simulation-oriented sports titles, Baseball Stars 2 bet on brisk, instantly graspable action. Large, expressive player sprites, exaggerated animations, and a colorful presentation gave the game a comic-book touch that fit the arcade spirit perfectly. The duel between pitcher and batter had momentum, the hits were spectacular, and the matches flowed without unnecessary downtime.

The game benefited from the power of the Neo Geo: detailed characters, smooth animations, and vibrant graphics looked extraordinarily good at a time when other sports games looked far more austere. It was precisely the audiovisual side, together with the easy-to-grasp controls, that made Baseball Stars 2 an ideal title for quick duels with a friend.

Thanks to the combination of accessibility and entertainment, the game built a reputation among Neo Geo enthusiasts as an evergreen that is a joy to pull out at any time. It requires neither deep knowledge of baseball rules nor patient study of statistics — all you need is the desire to have fun and match your skills.

For players looking for arcade sport in its purest form, Baseball Stars 2 remains a reliable choice. Even after decades, it offers exactly what it promises: fast, colorful, and entertaining baseball with no unnecessary fuss.

**Why play:** For the brisk, colorful arcade baseball that is instantly fun and ideal for two-player duels.
neogeo__baseball-stars-2.teaser: Colorful, accessible baseball from SNK; the benchmark for fun arcade sports games.

neogeo__nam-1975.article:
NAM-1975 is among the very first titles that accompanied the launch of the Neo Geo platform, and for many players it was their first contact with SNK's extraordinarily powerful hardware at the turn of the eighties and nineties. This action shooter set against the backdrop of the Vietnam War showed what the new platform could do and became a symbol of the Neo Geo's arrival in arcades and living rooms alike.

In terms of gameplay, it is a shooter in which the player controls a soldier moving along the bottom of the screen and shoots at enemies deep in the scene. In addition to ordinary fire, he can dodge bullets and grenades and use devastating attacks to clear the screen. This combination of movement, aiming into the distance, and dodging gave the game a brisk, tense pace.

Visually, NAM-1975 was stunning for its time. Pseudo-three-dimensional environments, explosions, burning helicopters, and detailed backgrounds demonstrated the graphical power of the Neo Geo that the home consoles of the day could not match. Two-player co-op moreover increased both the fun and the chaos on screen.

As a launch title, NAM-1975 played a crucial role: it showed why it was worth investing in SNK's expensive but technically advanced system. Today, fans remember it as one of the pillars of the early Neo Geo library and evidence of the ambitions with which the platform entered the market.

Thanks to later collections and digital releases, the game remains available even to modern players who want to taste the beginnings of one of the most legendary gaming platforms. For connoisseurs of retro action, it is a small piece of history.

**Why play:** For the brisk cooperative action, the atmosphere of the early Neo Geo era, and a piece of history from the very launch of a legendary platform.
neogeo__nam-1975.teaser: The Neo Geo's launch title set in the Vietnam War; it showed what SNK's new hardware could do.

neogeo__king-of-fighters-94.article:
The year 1994 brought a bold idea: what if heroes from different SNK games met in one big tournament? The King of Fighters '94 turned this idea into reality and founded one of the most influential fighting-game series of all time. For the mighty Neo Geo, it was a title that combined a crossover of stars with an entirely new team mechanic.

The biggest innovation is the three-on-three combat system. Instead of a single fighter, you choose a team of three combatants, and the clash proceeds gradually until one team loses all its members. This structure gave fighting games a new tactical layer: you have to consider the order of characters, their strengths and weaknesses, and the team's overall strategy. The game offers a roster made up of preset teams, among which you will also find familiar faces from earlier SNK titles such as Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting.

In development terms, it was SNK's flagship on the Neo Geo hardware, which was famous for its 2D power and its large, finely animated characters. Thanks to this platform, SNK long ranked among the elite of arcade fighting games, and King of Fighters became its cornerstone brand, released practically every year. The crossover concept moreover celebrated the studio's rich history and connected its worlds into one.

Culturally, KOF '94 kicked off a franchise that became a symbol of competitive gaming, especially in Asia and Latin America, where it built a huge and loyal community. The team format became the hallmark of the entire series and inspired other creators as well. A long line of sequels grew out of this game, shaping the genre for decades to come.

Today, The King of Fighters '94 is prized as the founding title of one of the longest-running fighting-game series. For fans of the genre, it is a cornerstone worth getting to know not only for its gameplay but also for its historical significance as the first meeting of SNK's stars on one stage.

**Why play:** The founder of a legendary series and pioneer of three-on-three team battles, in which SNK's stars met for the first time on Neo Geo hardware.
neogeo__king-of-fighters-94.teaser: SNK brought its heroes together in one tournament for the first time; the new 3-on-3 system founded a famous series.

neogeo__king-of-fighters-95.article:
Barely a year after the first tournament, SNK returned with a sequel that pushed the series an important step further. The King of Fighters '95 built on the success of the founding installment and added a feature that fans had been calling for: the ability to assemble your own team. Thus a crossover novelty began to turn into a sophisticated competitive fighting game with its own identity.

The key change from its predecessor is team editing. Whereas in the first installment the trios of fighters were fixed, KOF '95 allowed players to mix combatants to their own liking and create strategic combinations across the original groups. The three-on-three team system remained the foundation, but this freedom added depth and replayability to the game. Moreover, the striking character Rugal entered the story as a recurring villain, and the roster saw adjustments and additions.

In development terms, it was once again a title from SNK for the arcade and home Neo Geo hardware, a platform famous for its large animated sprites and its faithful transfer of the arcade experience into the home. SNK continued its strategy of annual installments, thanks to which King of Fighters quickly established itself as one of the studio's main brands and an evergreen of arcade cabinets around the world.

Culturally, KOF '95 confirmed the series as a serious rival to the other fighting-game giants and cemented the team format as its characteristic trait. The character of Rugal and other story elements became part of the franchise's mythology, which fans followed across the individual annual editions. The community around KOF grew, and the series built a reputation as a hardcore fighting game for demanding players.

Today, The King of Fighters '95 is seen as an important milestone that shaped the series into the form its fans love. For connoisseurs of the genre, it is a title that shows how quickly SNK tuned its format toward perfection, and at the same time a solid link in one of the longest-lived fighting-game lines of all.

**Why play:** A sequel that introduced editing your own teams and definitively refined the team format of one of SNK's most legendary fighting-game series.
neogeo__king-of-fighters-95.teaser: A year after the first tournament, SNK added the ability to build your own team of fighters.

neogeo__king-of-fighters-97.article:
There are tournaments, and then there is The King of Fighters '97. For many fighting-game fans from the late nineties, this very edition is the moment when SNK brought its ambitious crossover series to perfection. After two years of tuning, you have a game that plays fast, cleanly, and with absolute confidence in every blow.

The foundation is three-on-three team combat, where you assemble a trio of characters from a rich roster uniting heroes from Fatal Fury, Art of Fighting, and original fighters created specifically for KOF. The '97 edition introduced a major novelty: two selectable play styles, Advanced and Extra. The Advanced mode works with rolling, short hops, and a gradually filling Power gauge, while Extra continues the older system of charging energy by holding. This choice gave players the ability to adapt the pace to their own nature, and passionate debates about it still rage among tournament players today.

In narrative terms, KOF '97 closes the so-called Orochi saga, a story arc stretching back to 1995. The climax surrounding the dark god Orochi and his servants gave the series a dramatic charge that went beyond mere brawling in the ring. Characters like Iori Yagami or Leona came here to the center of events and gained a depth that was rather exceptional in the genre at the time.

The Neo Geo was expensive arcade and home hardware, but it was precisely thanks to it that KOF '97 looked luxurious. Large, finely animated sprites, hand-painted backgrounds full of movement, and SNK's characteristic sound design turned every match into a little show. Moreover, the game ran smoothly even in demanding moments, which was a hallmark of first-rate craftsmanship for its time.

Today, the '97 edition is considered one of the milestones of the series and returns in all sorts of compilations and digital reissues. For retro players, it represents an ideal gateway into the world of KOF: accessible enough not to overwhelm you, and at the same time deep enough to hold you for months.

**Why play:** A top-tier team fighting game that closes the legendary Orochi saga and to this day ranks among the best the Neo Geo had to offer.
neogeo__king-of-fighters-97.teaser: For many fans the peak of the series: a fast, clean, and perfectly tuned team fighting game.

neogeo__king-of-fighters-98.article:
If someone forced you to pick a single installment of The King of Fighters that you simply must have, most connoisseurs would point without hesitation to the ninety-eighth. KOF '98 carries the subtitle Dream Match, and that is exactly what it is: a celebration of the entire series without the weight of a story, where practically every fighter you had come to love up to then gathered.

Because the game detached itself from a continuous storyline, SNK could cram an enormous number of characters into the roster, including those who had died or were unavailable in previous installments. The result is one of the richest fighter lists of its time. The gameplay builds on the proven three-on-three team format and offers two styles similar to the previous edition, Advanced and Extra, so everyone finds the pace that suits them.

What makes the eighth installment so prized is its balance and smoothness. The combat system feels polished, the controls are precise, and the game forgives fewer mistakes than many a competitor without being inaccessible. That is precisely why KOF '98 became a long-standing evergreen of the tournament scene, and the community still plays it today, often in the Ultimate Match version, which expanded the roster and options even further.

Visually, it is the peak of what the Neo Geo managed in the field of 2D fighting games. Striking sprite animations, carefully drawn arenas, and energetic sound give every match its juice. The game runs briskly and clearly, which is absolutely crucial in a fighting game where a fraction of a second decides everything.

For retro players, KOF '98 has one huge advantage: it is ubiquitous. It received countless ports and reissues on modern platforms, so you can easily get to it and see why fans call it the peak of the series' classic era.

**Why play:** A carefree celebration of the entire series with a giant roster and a perfectly tuned combat system that the tournament scene still loves today.
neogeo__king-of-fighters-98.teaser: The subtitle Dream Match fits perfectly: a celebration of the whole series with no story, just the best roster.

neogeo__last-blade.article:
While most fighting games on the Neo Geo settled duels with fists and kicks, The Last Blade drew a katana. Here SNK abandoned modern brawlers and transported us to the twilight of the Bakumatsu period, when feudal Japan was crumbling under the pressure of modernization. The atmosphere is melancholic, dignified, and unmistakable.

The core of the game is weapon-based combat, predominantly with cold blades, which places emphasis on timing and distance control. The Last Blade added an elegant system of two styles, Speed and Power, between which the player chooses depending on whether they want fast series of strikes or hard individual hits. Added to this is a defensive parry and spectacular special techniques, thanks to which the duels feel like the choreography of a samurai film.

Visually, the game belongs to the most beautiful that appeared on the Neo Geo. The backgrounds breathe the mood of the late Edo period, leaves fall, lanterns burn, and the scenery changes with the seasons. The sprite animation of the characters is fluid, and the sound design with traditional Japanese motifs underscores the serious, almost poetic tone of the whole game. SNK evidently cared not just about combat here but about mood.

The Last Blade received a direct sequel and gradually built a firm cult standing. Among SNK fans, it is regarded as a stylish alternative to the faster and more hectic fighting games, appreciated above all for its atmosphere and aesthetics. It is not the most famous title of its time, which makes its discovery all the more pleasant a surprise for retro players.

Thanks to reissues within collector's collections and on modern platforms, the game is easily accessible today. If you are drawn to a fighting game that bets on grace and mood instead of brute force, you have an ideal candidate.

**Why play:** An atmospheric katana fighting game set in the twilight of old Japan that bets on style, timing, and unforgettable aesthetics.
neogeo__last-blade.teaser: A katana instead of fists and the twilight of the Bakumatsu; a melancholic, unmistakably Japanese fighting game from SNK.

neogeo__sengoku.article:
Before SNK became famous for fighting games, it was conquering arcades with on-screen brawling. Sengoku is one of the early beat 'em up titles for the Neo Geo, and right from the start it makes clear that this won't be your ordinary street-thug bashing. Its heroes slip between past and present and face down an army of the ghosts of ancient warriors.

The basic premise is pure genre: you advance left to right, clear the screen of enemies, and use combinations of punches and kicks. But Sengoku adds its own twist in the form of transformations. On the fly, the player can change their character into different fighters — for example a swordsman or a dog-like companion — each with different abilities and reach. This mechanic gives the otherwise straightforward action a tactical layer and sets the game apart from the competition.

Visually and thematically, Sengoku blends a modern city with the ghostly scenery of feudal Japan, which lends it a distinctive, slightly bizarre atmosphere. On the early Neo Geo hardware it delivers solid sprite presentation and the brisk pace you'd expect from an arcade beat 'em up. The difficulty is traditionally arcade — that is, uncompromising, counting on you to feed another coin into the machine.

The game kicked off a small series and got a sequel, confirming there was appetite for genre action on the Neo Geo. In the context of its time it was one of the titles that helped build the library of SNK's new and expensive system, back when beat 'em ups enjoyed great popularity.

Today Sengoku is more a matter for enthusiasts and collectors than for the general public, but that's exactly where its charm lies. It's a piece of early SNK history that shows the studio before it turned its focus to fighting games.

**Why play:** A distinctive arcade beat 'em up with a character-transformation mechanic and an unconventional clash between the modern world and the ghosts of feudal Japan.
neogeo__sengoku.teaser: An early Neo Geo beat 'em up where heroes travel through time and fight the ghosts of samurai.

neogeo__top-hunter.article:
Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy is one of those titles that prove the Neo Geo wasn't just about fighting and shooting games. This colorful action platformer from SNK bets on snappy fun, cartoon humor, and a clever idea that sets it apart from the flood of similar games from the nineties.

The player controls bounty hunters Roddy or Cathy, who set out across varied worlds full of enemies. The key mechanic is stretchy arms: the characters can extend their hands, grab enemies and objects, and hurl them around. This elastic interaction gives both the fights and the platforming parts a playful, rubbery character that's instantly likable. On top of that comes the option to play in pairs, making Top Hunter a pleasant cooperative affair.

Visually the game benefits from a bold, almost cartoon-like style with large and adorable sprite characters. The levels aim to be varied and imaginative, alternating ordinary platforming sections with ideas that break up the routine. Here SNK shows a sense for lightness and humor that we don't see nearly as often in their later, more serious fighting games.

At the time of release Top Hunter got somewhat lost among the Neo Geo's flagships, so it remains more of a hidden gem for those who aren't afraid to dig deeper into the system's catalog. But it's precisely this relative obscurity that makes it a rewarding discovery for retro players looking for something lighthearted and original.

Thanks to re-releases within Neo Geo collections, the game can be tried more easily today than ever before. Anyone who enjoys platformers with a good idea and a pinch of humor shouldn't overlook Roddy and Cathy.

**Why play:** A lighthearted cooperative platformer with the witty mechanic of stretchy arms, showing the more playful face of the Neo Geo.
neogeo__top-hunter.teaser: SNK bet on a colorful platformer with bounty hunters and their stretchy arms.

neogeo__waku-waku-7.article:
Sometimes the best fighting game is the one that doesn't take itself seriously. Waku Waku 7 from the Sunsoft studio is exactly such a case: an exuberant, zany, and colorful game that takes the genre's conventions and turns them into a comic full of exaggerated gestures and giant attacks.

The foundation is classic — one-on-one combat — but presentation is everything. The characters are drawn in an adorable, manga-inspired style with oversized sprite animations, and the roster of seven fighters offers a colorful collection of eccentric oddballs, from the cute to the utterly crazy. The combat system works with exaggerated super moves and generous energy, so even a less experienced player will enjoy flashy pile-ups full of over-the-top explosions.

Technically, Waku Waku 7 shows what the Neo Geo could do in the field of lively, cartoon-like 2D graphics. There are lots of sprites, they're large, and they move with an exaggerated springiness that gives the whole game a cartoon energy. It's all rounded out by energetic music and sound effects that underline the lighthearted, almost parodic tone.

The game arrived at a time when the fighting-game market was oversaturated, and perhaps that's why it bet on personality instead of competitive depth. Among fans it built a cult reputation precisely thanks to its charm and unmistakable atmosphere. It's not a title chasing tournament prestige, but the sheer joy of play — and in that it's unbeatable.

Because it was a relatively less mainstream piece, Waku Waku 7 is today among the more sought-after items among collectors and Neo Geo lovers. Fortunately it has appeared in digital re-releases too, so anyone can savor its high-spirited energy.

**Why play:** An adorably zany fighter with a cartoon style and exaggerated attacks that bets on fun and personality instead of competitive seriousness.
neogeo__waku-waku-7.teaser: Sunsoft didn't take fighting games seriously: comic-book graphics and wildly over-the-top special moves.

neogeo__metal-slug-1-x-3.article:
When the first bullet fires and hand-painted explosions scatter across the screen, it's immediately clear why Metal Slug is still, decades later, the benchmark for run & gun action. The series that the Nazca studio launched and SNK took over on the Neo Geo hardware brought pixel animation to a level that takes your breath away to this day — every soldier reacts to a hit differently, explosions roll in cascades, and the characters' facial expressions add an unexpected dose of personality to the game.

The gameplay is the essence of arcade fun: you run forward, shoot everything that moves, collect weapons, and free prisoners who gratefully thrust more arsenal into your hands. The pace is merciless, the difficulty classically arcade — get ready for the game to push you to feed the machine „one more credit.“ And that's exactly the point: that addictive cycle of death and the instant urge to try again.

The visuals are the star of the whole series. Hand-drawn backgrounds, detailed animation, and the trademark black humor — from overeating prisoners to absurd bosses — make Metal Slug an audiovisual treat you'll relish even just as a spectacle. Hidden bonuses and alternate paths additionally reward exploring every corner of the levels.

The cooperative mode is invaluable too. Metal Slug is made for two-player play, where you and a buddy cover each other's backs, race for score, and laugh together at the on-screen chaos. It's precisely this sociability that made it a firm fixture of arcades and of later console and digital releases.

Whether you start with the first game, the tuned-up „X,“ or the third installment that many consider the peak of the series, you'll get clean, brilliantly crafted action. It's one of those cases where the word „classic“ fits absolutely precisely.

**Why play:** The peak of hand-drawn run & gun action with unforgettable animation, humor, and superb co-op — the essence of the very best of arcades.
neogeo__metal-slug-1-x-3.teaser: Nazca and SNK set the benchmark for run-and-gun action; the hand-drawn explosions still take your breath away.

neogeo__king-of-fighters-98-2002.article:
Assemble a team of three fighters, choose from more than forty characters, and throw yourself into battles that for many connoisseurs represent the peak of SNK fighting games — The King of Fighters '98 and 2002 are the so-called „Dream Match“ installments, freed from story constraints and built purely on the best possible roster. No narrative, just the purest form of team-versus-team tournament brawling.

The 3v3 format is the heart of the experience. You send three fighters into battle one after another, managing energy and building super attacks, with every exchange of blows a game of positioning, timing, and reading your opponent. SNK honed its combat system into a form that rewards precision and depth — and that's exactly why '98 still holds up as a respected competitive standard, played at tournaments even after many years.

The enormous roster is another asset. Characters from various SNK franchises meet here in one melting pot, each with their own style, moves, and personality. For fans it's a gallery of icons; for newcomers a varied offering in which they'll easily find their favorite. Visually the series benefits from characteristic SNK detail and fluid 2D animation.

The 2002 variant built on the proven concept with another „dream match“ lineup and a tuned system, thereby strengthening KOF's position as one of the pillars of the competitive fighting scene. Together these two installments form the roots from which the modern shape of the series and the community around it grow.

Anyone who enjoys technical 2D fighters with an emphasis on the battle of minds and precise execution will find here one of the genre's most honest representatives.

**Why play:** Top-tier SNK fighting games with the 3v3 team format and an enormous roster — '98 is still a respected competitive standard and the heart of the KOF scene.
neogeo__king-of-fighters-98-2002.teaser: Later entries dropped the story, offering just 3-on-3 battles with the series' best possible roster.

neogeo__garou-mark-of-wolves.article:
Few 2D fighters look as gorgeous and play as finely tuned as Garou: Mark of the Wolves from 1999 — SNK's swan song at the peak of its powers and, for many connoisseurs, an almost sacred title. As the culmination of the long Fatal Fury line, it brought a new roster, fresh design, and one of the most elegant combat systems of its era.

The key novelty is the „Just Defend“ mechanic. If you block an attack at the precise moment, you gain small advantages — such as replenishing health or room for an instant counterattack. This single mechanic gives fights unexpected depth and rewards the player for courage and precision instead of passive defense. Together with the finely tuned pace, this creates a fighter that flows like butter.

Visually it's one of the pinnacles of the hand-drawn 2D era. The character animation is fluid and full of personality, the backgrounds carefully drawn, and the overall style elegant without needless flamboyance. The new fighter roster also brought fresh faces and opened a new chapter for the series, even if fate ultimately didn't allow it to fully develop.

The historical context adds another dimension to the game. Garou was one of the last great SNK fighters before the company's crisis, so it carries a whiff of a final masterpiece — everything the studio knew about the genre, brought to a brilliant form. Among fans it therefore enjoys almost cult reverence.

Anyone looking for a beautiful, technically rich, and gorgeously balanced 2D fighter will find in Garou one of the genre's absolute gems, one that doesn't age and still keeps its elegance.

**Why play:** A gorgeously animated and brilliantly tuned 2D fighter with the „Just Defend“ mechanic — the peak of the Fatal Fury line and one of the most beautiful SNK fighters ever.
neogeo__garou-mark-of-wolves.teaser: SNK's 1999 swan song, with an elegant fighting system and the Just Defend mechanic.

neogeo__samurai-shodown-ii.article:
When the sound of a drawn katana rings out on screen, you know that a single wrong step means the end. **Samurai Shodown II** from SNK brought a fighter to arcades in 1994 that consciously turned its back on frantic button-mashing. Instead of endless combos, timing, distance, and cold calculation rule here. One well-timed slash can strip half of an opponent's life, so every exchange resembles a battle of nerves more than a dance.

The Samurai Shodown series was born on the Neo Geo board and from the start positioned itself as the counterpoint to fast fighters like Street Fighter. The second installment brought this philosophy to perfection: a slower, more tactical pace where players circle each other, wait for an opening, and punish mistakes with a hard blow. The emphasis on weapons gives fights a different dynamic than fist-based fighters, because reach and the angle of a slash decide life and death.

Visually it's one of the most beautiful games of its time. The characters are large, carefully animated, and set into scenery inspired by feudal Japan. The Edo-era aesthetic, blossoming cherry trees, and stormy sky create an atmosphere that the competition of the day could hardly match. The music and sound design underline the gravity of every clash, where the tension can be cut with a knife.

Mechanically the game offers a system that rewards patience and precision. Working with distance, evasive rolls, and the option to disarm your opponent bring an almost chess-like depth to fights. Anyone who comes with a button-masher mentality will soon take a hard lesson. It's precisely this difficulty and emphasis on clean execution that made the second installment a legend among fighting fans, remembered to this day as one of the peaks of the entire series.

Samurai Shodown II is today considered one of the best installments of the brand and regularly appears in SNK retro collections for modern platforms. For players who lived through the Neo Geo era it represents a nostalgic classic; for newcomers, an ideal entry into the world of weapon-based fighters, where every blow means something.

**Why play:** If you're tired of mindless button-mashing and want a fighter where deliberation, timing, and nerves decide, Samurai Shodown II is an elegant lesson in the art of combat.
neogeo__samurai-shodown-ii.teaser: SNK's 1994 title moved away from combo-mashing; one precise katana slash can take half your health.

neogeo__last-blade-2.article:
The aesthetic of an epoch's turning point, the edge of a katana, and the melancholy of the vanishing world of the samurai. **The Last Blade 2** ranks among the gems of the weapon-based fighters that SNK created for the Neo Geo hardware. The game follows on from the first installment and pushes its atmospheric concept even further, while retaining an unmistakably Japanese, faintly nostalgic tone.

The Last Blade 2 is built on weapon fights, where timing, reach, and clean execution play the key role. A characteristic element of the series is the option to choose between two fighting styles that change both the pace and the approach to your opponent: a more aggressive variant focused on offense, and a more defensive, technical style. Added to this is a parry system that rewards precise timing and opens room for quick counter-actions. Fights thus feel tactical and dramatic at once.

Visually it's one of the prettiest 2D fighters of its time. Hand-drawn characters, fluid animation, and backgrounds steeped in the atmosphere of the late samurai period create a strong aesthetic impression. The color palettes and the music underline the tone of a game that carries itself more in the spirit of pensive poetry than thunderous action. This sets the series apart from most of the competition.

Thanks to the Neo Geo hardware, which allowed detailed sprites and rich animation, The Last Blade 2 ranks among the titles that demonstrate what SNK could do at the twilight of the golden era of 2D fighters. For genre fans it's a respected and sought-after piece that appears in modern re-releases and collections.

Over time the game built a reputation as a cult affair among connoisseurs. The combination of technical depth in its fights and an exceptional artistic side makes it a title players return to not only out of nostalgia, but for the sheer quality of the craft.

**Why play:** For devotees of weapon-based fighters with soul and style, who will appreciate a tactically clean battle wrapped in one of the most beautiful 2D aesthetics of the Neo Geo era.
neogeo__last-blade-2.teaser: The sequel deepens the atmosphere of a vanishing samurai world, with weapon-based duels.

neogeo__puzzle-bobble-bust-move.article:
One shot that decides everything. Puzzle Bobble, known in the West as Bust-A-Move, took the cute little dragons from the Bubble Bobble series and placed them into a logic game so addictive that it became one of the most cited puzzle titles of the nineties. The principle is ingeniously simple: you aim and fire colored bubbles upward, and when you connect three or more of the same color, they pop and disappear.

The magic is in what happens next. Bubbles that lose their connection to the ceiling break free and drift down, earning you huge bonuses for a single well-aimed shot. This chain-collapse mechanic rewards planning and spatial imagination, because the best players don't shoot at the nearest target but set up whole cascades to fall.

The game's strength lies in the tension of the two-player battle mode. There, every successful combo of yours sends a row of annoying extra bubbles into your opponent's field and pushes the ceiling relentlessly downward. A duel between two skilled players is a game of nerves where fate turns on a single shot, and it's precisely this drama that made Puzzle Bobble a fixture of both arcades and living rooms.

Behind the game stands the Taito studio, home to many arcade classics, along with its trademark cute visuals and a catchy melody you'll be humming long after switching off the machine. The series got countless sequels and ports to practically every existing platform, from consoles through computers to mobile phones.

An accurate aiming reticle with a hinted flight path, a gradually descending ceiling, and instantly understandable rules make it a textbook example of what a perfect puzzle game should look like: easy to learn, impossible to leave. It belongs in the same league of immortal logic classics as Tetris.

**Why play:** For instantly addictive bubble-matching and for nerve-wracking two-player duels where a single shot flips the whole match.
neogeo__puzzle-bobble-bust-move.teaser: The dragons from Bubble Bobble star in a puzzle game so addictive it defined an entire genre.

neogeo__money-puzzle-exchanger.article:
A puzzle game where every penny counts. Money Puzzle Exchanger takes the classic falling-block genre and dresses it in the unexpected garb of financial arithmetic. Instead of colors, coins of various values fall here, and your task is to exchange them: gather enough smaller coins and they merge into a larger denomination, and by cleverly chaining these exchanges you set off a devastating combo.

This exchange system gives the game fresh tactical depth. It's not enough to just stack identical pieces side by side; you have to think about values and about how to accumulate coins so that at the right moment they transform and drag as many others as possible along with them. It's a puzzle for the head, where greed becomes a virtue and the biggest combo goes to whoever calculates furthest ahead.

As with most arcade logic games, the heart of the fun is the competitive mode against another player or a computer-controlled opponent. Successful exchanges send obstacles into your rival's field and push them toward being overwhelmed, so every match is a race over who sets off the avalanche of exchanges first. The cute mascot character and colorful cartoon style are typical of this kind of Japanese arcade.

In its day it was one of many attempts to stand out in the oversaturated falling-block genre that flooded arcades after the enormous success of Tetris and Puzzle Bobble. The idea of exchanging currency instead of simple color-matching was refreshing, and the game thus found its loyal admirers among puzzle-arcade aficionados.

Today it belongs more among the hidden gems you'll stumble upon in emulator collections and which enthusiasts speak of with affection. If you enjoy logic games with their own distinctive mechanic and aren't afraid of a little arithmetic, it's a pleasant surprise off the beaten path.

**Why play:** For the original coin-exchanging mechanic that gives the falling-block genre a fresh tactical layer, and for snappy duels for puzzle-game aficionados.
neogeo__money-puzzle-exchanger.teaser: An unconventional falling-block puzzle — coins are exchanged for higher denominations, chaining combos.

neogeo__magical-drop-ii-iii.article:
Speed is everything here. Magical Drop is not among the puzzle games where you have time to calmly weigh every move. It's a frantic, action-packed affair where your character stands beneath columns of colored balls, pulls them down to itself and shoots them back up with a single button, and whoever has quicker fingers and a sharper eye wins. The pace is so fierce that in a good match you'll forget to breathe.

The series from the Data East studio built its identity precisely on this ferocity. Connect three or more balls of the same color and they pop, and with skillful catching and throwing you set off giant chain combos that roll one after another. Unlike its more sedate competitors, it rewards pure skill and the ability to read the field a fraction of a second ahead.

**Magical Drop II and III** honed this formula to perfection. They brought a colorful gallery of opponents inspired by tarot cards, each with their own personality and behavior, and a competitive mode that's among the sharpest in the whole genre. By sending annoying balls into your opponent's field, it becomes a brutal race where the lead flips every second.

Visually the series shines with garish colors, bold characters, and an overall over-the-topness typical of nineties Japanese arcades. The music drives the pace forward and the whole experience feels like an adrenaline ride rather than a contemplative diversion.

Among connoisseurs of the puzzle genre, Magical Drop has a reputation as one of the most demanding and rewarding series for those who love head-to-head battles. It's not a title for Sunday relaxation; it's a discipline for players who want to test their reflexes and nerves against a live opponent.

**Why play:** For the fastest and fiercest duels the falling-puzzle genre offers, and for a colorful gallery of tarot opponents on whom you'll cut your teeth.
neogeo__magical-drop-ii-iii.teaser: A lightning-fast action puzzle from Data East — one button to pull down and launch balls.

neogeo__aero-fighters-2.article:
Fighter jets, crazy pilots, and a screen full of colorful gunfire — **Aero Fighters 2** (known in Japan as Sonic Wings 2) is a vertical shmup that may not play a serious note, but all the more an unfeigned arcade fun. It's a title that grabs you with its pace and doesn't let go.

The game is built on **choosing from various nationalities and pilots**, each of whom brings a different plane, different fire, and — which is half the charm — a different personality and humorous quips. This lightness and self-irony set Aero Fighters apart from its gloomier competitors and give the game an instantly likable character. It's not a military epic; it's an exuberant ride.

In terms of play it's a snappy, accessible vertical shmup with an emphasis on **fast action and readable patterns**. The screen fills with enemies and projectiles, but the pace stays fun rather than crushing — which makes the title a great entry gate for players who want to fall in love with the genre without being punished right away. The boss fights are spectacular and the game doesn't skimp on visual fantasies.

The series built a devoted fan core precisely thanks to this combination of accessibility, character, and classic arcade action. Aero Fighters 2 is among the things people sought out on compilation sets and in arcades, where it comes in handy for a quick, energetic round.

It's a reminder that a shmup doesn't always have to be a trial of suffering — sometimes a good plane, generous firepower, and a pinch of humor are enough.

**Why play:** A snappy, accessible, and pleasantly lighthearted vertical shmup with a varied selection of pilots — ideal for quick arcade fun and for newcomers to the genre.
neogeo__aero-fighters-2.teaser: A quirky vertical shmup with a colorful cast of pilots; released in Japan as Sonic Wings 2.

neogeo__neo-turf-masters.article:
Golf in the arcade? It sounds like a contradiction in terms — and yet **Neo Turf Masters** from 1996 is one of the most addictive sports games the Neo Geo cabinet ever offered. Studio **Nazca** (under the **SNK** banner) showed here how to make golf fun even for someone who has never held a club in their life.

The secret lies in a brilliantly simple **three-click control system**: the first click starts the power meter, the second locks it in, and the third sets the accuracy and spin of the shot. It is instantly understandable, yet it hides surprising depth — mastering the wind, the slope of the green and the right timing of your swing takes feel and practice. This elegant balance between accessibility and precision is the whole magic of the game.

Visually it is a beauty — colourful, clean and sunny presentation, six courses scattered across the whole world, and fluid animation that turns every shot into a little pleasure. The game breathes that laid-back atmosphere where you just want to have a pleasant time, and yet it quietly draws you into the chase for a better score.

It is precisely this **addictiveness** that makes Neo Turf Masters a legend. It is the ideal game for short rounds as well as head-to-head duels, where every well-placed shot brings a smile and every botched one an angry grumble and an immediate „one more time“. You do not need to be a golf fan — the game wins you over all on its own.

Among connoisseurs of the Neo Geo catalogue, Neo Turf Masters is regularly cited as the pinnacle of arcade golf and proof that even a seemingly placid sport can spark a genuine addiction in the arcade.

**Why play it:** The best arcade golf ever — brilliantly accessible, beautiful and frighteningly addictive, fun even for complete non-fans of the sport.
neogeo__neo-turf-masters.teaser: Arcade golf from Nazca with brilliantly simple three-click swing controls.

neogeo__windjammers.article:
You throw the frisbee across the court, your opponent returns it at a sharp angle, you catch it at the last second and unleash a smash that whistles into the corner — and suddenly you realise that **Windjammers** is no silly beach trifle but one of the deepest competitive titles the arcade has ever seen. This gem from **Data East**, released in 1994, is a cult classic for good reason.

At first glance it is a simple thing: two players, a court divided into zones, and a flying disc that must be sent into the opponent's goal area. But beneath this simple surface hides surprising tactical depth. **Bounce angles, spin, lobbed passes, smashes and special shots** — every throw becomes a little psychological battle where you read your opponent and try to outsmart them. Easy to grasp, masterfully hard to master.

Each character has their own speed and power, which leaves room for different play styles, from nimble dodgers to power artillery. The pace is lightning-fast, the rounds short and intense, and the feeling when you send a perfect smash right into the gap in the defence is indescribably satisfying.

Windjammers has a lovely second-chance story behind it: for a long time it was an insiders' treasure before the **e-sports and competitive community** rediscovered it and lifted it into the spotlight. Thanks to modern ports and remasters it reached a new generation of players and to this day it ranks among the best local versus games for two that you can fire up.

It is a textbook lesson in how to strike immortal competitive fun from a simple idea.

**Why play it:** An unexpectedly deep frisbee arena for two, easy to grasp and masterfully hard to master — a cult versus gem rediscovered by the e-sports community.
neogeo__windjammers.teaser: A frisbee sport from Data East that's deeper and more competitive than it first appears.

neogeo__shock-troopers.article:
If you love Metal Slug and are looking for where to head next, **Shock Troopers** should be right at the top of the list. This action gem for the Neo Geo from 1997 is among the very best the run & gun genre offered in the arcades — and yet it remains undeservedly in the shadow of its more famous siblings.
