Unlike classic horizontal shooters, **Shock Troopers** bets on a multi-directional top-down view, where you push forward, sideways and into the depth of the screen. This freedom gives the fights a different rhythm: you take cover behind obstacles, flank an enemy nest from the side and constantly weigh where to cut through the infantry assaults and armoured vehicles. The game is brisk, readable and packed with action from the very first second.

Behind the game stands studio Saurus under the wing of SNK, a master of two-dimensional arcade action. You recognise the game by its typically rich hand-drawn pixel graphics and fluid animation, the kind the Neo Geo pulled off like few other pieces of hardware of its time. A signature element is the choice of multiple characters, each with their own strengths and weaknesses, so it pays to experiment with weapons and play style.

The second draw are the branching paths. Before missions you choose the route you will take to the goal, and each offers a different environment, different enemies and different traps. This dramatically boosts replayability — playing through the game a different way each time is by itself a reason to come back. And since it is an arcade classic, you can set out solo or in co-op with a buddy.

**Shock Troopers** is a showcase of craft at its peak. It brings no revolution, but it does everything you expect from honest run & gun action superbly. For fans of the Metal Slug style it is a mandatory stop.

**Why play it:** Top-tier multi-directional action from SNK with character selection and branching paths — the ideal next step for anyone who has finished Metal Slug.
neogeo__shock-troopers.teaser: A run-and-gun living in Metal Slug's shadow, but with its own multi-directional top-down view.

cps__ghouls-n-ghosts.article:
The knight Arthur stands in a graveyard, the wind drives the clouds and in a single moment a zombie strips him of his armour – he is left in his underwear and runs on. This iconic scene from **Ghouls 'n Ghosts** perfectly captures why it ranks among the most legendary and hardest action platformers of all time. Capcom took the concept of its arcade hit and brought it to perfection here.

The game is a sequel to **Ghosts 'n Goblins** and ran on the Capcom CP System board, which at the end of the eighties raised the bar for arcade graphics. Arthur once again sets out to rescue the princess and fight his way through hordes of the undead, demons and monsters. The gameplay stands on merciless difficulty: two hits and it is over, with the first hit stripping your armour and the second meaning death. The creators also added the ability to shoot upward and downward, which broadened the tactical options of combat.

A key element is collecting weapons – lances, daggers, axes or the magic bow – and above all the Golden Armour, which lets Arthur cast devastating spells. Each weapon suits something different and a bad choice before a boss can really torment you. The level design is full of traps, disappearing platforms and enemies coming from all sides, so the game demands memorisation as well as precise timing.

Also notorious is the final twist: to see the true ending, the player must beat the whole game twice and moreover obtain a special weapon, otherwise they are thrown back. This uncompromising philosophy made the series a symbol of arcade toughness and inspired generations of developers. You will find references to Ghouls 'n Ghosts in plenty of modern games that pay tribute to the tradition of demanding titles.

The series continued with **Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts** on the Super Nintendo and later Arthur appeared even in Capcom's fighting games as a bonus character. Conversions came out on countless home systems from the Mega Drive to the Amiga, and the game still appears in retro collections today. For many players Ghouls 'n Ghosts remains the yardstick of what a real challenge means.

**Why play it:** If you are looking for an honest, uncompromising action platformer that will test your nerves and reflexes, this is a classic you simply must play.
cps__ghouls-n-ghosts.teaser: Arthur in his underwear after losing his armor is the iconic image of one of the toughest platformers in history.

cps__strider.article:
The ninja Hiryu leaps from a flying wing straight into a snow-covered Kazakhstan, his plasma katana flashes and within a second the fight turns into a ballet of movement. **Strider** was a revelation in the year of its release – an action platformer that felt faster, smoother and more cinematic than anything around it.

The game was created at Capcom on the CP System board as a lavishly conceived arcade project, tied at the same time to a manga. Hiryu is an elite agent of the Strider organisation and his mission takes him across a futuristic Soviet Union all the way to the mysterious ruler Grandmaster. His main weapon is the Cypher, an energy sword whose whistling slashes became the trademark of the series.

What enchanted with Strider was the movement. Hiryu climbs walls, swings across ceilings, slides down slopes and clambers practically anywhere, which turned the levels into an acrobatic playground. Added to this were inventive bosses – a giant snake made of robotic technicians or a gigantic gorilla – and exotic settings from Siberia through the Amazon jungle to a space station. The visual sweep and pace were extraordinary for their time.

Culturally Strider is remembered as one of the defining arcade action games of the turn of the eighties and nineties. The character of Hiryu later became a Capcom fixture and appeared as a playable fighter in the Marvel vs. Capcom series, where his fast combos and the Cypher fitted in perfectly. This kept Strider popular even with players who never played the original arcade version.

The game received conversions to home systems such as the Mega Drive or Amiga-line computers, and later even a more modern reboot. Even so, the arcade version still holds a special charm thanks to its pace and atmosphere. Strider remains a textbook example of how to make an action game that both looks and plays like a comic book in motion.

**Why play it:** For brisk, acrobatic action with an unmistakable style and one of the coolest gaming characters of its era.
cps__strider.teaser: A ninja with a plasma katana, in action faster and smoother than anything else around at the time.

cps__1943-battle-of-midway.article:
The sky over the Pacific is full of enemy fighters and in a single aircraft you face an entire army – this is the essence of **1943: The Battle of Midway**, one of the most influential vertically scrolling shooters of the late eighties. Capcom here built on its earlier hit and pushed the genre toward a more elaborate upgrade system.

The game is a sequel to the legendary **1942** and ran on the Capcom CP System board. The player controls a fighter plane in a fictionalised air battle over Midway and gradually shoots down waves of aircraft, ships and giant bombers. Unlike many shooters of the time, 1943 was built not just on lives but on an energy gauge that thinned out from hits and even from ordinary flight and could be replenished.

The most interesting mechanic was the upgrade system: between missions and during them you could boost your weapons, endurance and special abilities, such as a devastating strike sweeping the whole screen or temporary rolls dodging bullets. With this the game brought elements of gradual progression that were fresh at the time and foreshadowed the later evolution of the genre. Fights against giant ships and aircraft split into destructible parts were the highlight of every level.

Culturally 1943 earned its place as one of the pillars of Capcom's arcade era and a respected jewel among vertical shoot 'em up games. The World War II theme in the Pacific resonated and the game became a favourite in arcades around the world. Its balanced difficulty and emphasis on strategic resource management set it apart from purely reflex-based titles.

The game received a number of conversions to home consoles and computers, including an NES version, and it was followed by further sequels in the series. It still appears in Capcom's retro collections today and belongs among the names every fan of classic aerial shooters knows.

**Why play it:** For a finely tuned vertical shooter that adds a pleasant layer of upgrades and strategy to classic action.
cps__1943-battle-of-midway.teaser: The sequel to the legendary 1942 pushed vertical shooters forward with better ship upgrades.

cps__darkstalkers-night-warriors.article:
Forget street brawlers in jeans – here vampires, werewolves, mummies and monsters from horror B-movies square off against one another. **Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors** brought something to the fighting genre that had not been there before: a gothic, comic-book-exaggerated atmosphere full of supernatural creatures and wildly fluid animation.

The game was created by Capcom on the more powerful CP System II board and bet on a visual style that stood on sharply stylised, lavishly animated characters. In the base roster you find the charismatic vampire Demitri, the succubus Morrigan, the werewolf Jon Talbain or an ice spirit. Each character has their own horror archetype and a distinctive moveset, which made choosing a fighter an experience in itself.

Mechanically Darkstalkers built on the foundations of Street Fighter but added new elements: a faster pace, air blocks and systems that foreshadowed Capcom's later fighting games. Special moves and super attacks were spectacular and the combat system rewarded an aggressive, offensive style. The character animations were among the best that 2D fighters offered at the time.

The cultural significance of the series lies in how it broadened the notion of what a fighting game can look like. Morrigan Aensland became one of Capcom's most iconic characters ever and to this day ranks among the company's favourite representatives in crossover games. You can feel the visual DNA of Darkstalkers even in Capcom's later projects, especially in the emphasis on expressive animation.

The series continued with instalments like Night Warriors and Vampire Savior, and its characters repeatedly appear in the Marvel vs. Capcom crossovers. Although the main series has long awaited a new instalment, the cult around Darkstalkers has never faded and fans keep returning to it. It is a jewel of the golden era of 2D fighters.

**Why play it:** For an unmistakable horror atmosphere and superbly animated characters that turn a fighting game into a little comic-book theatre.
cps__darkstalkers-night-warriors.teaser: A fighting game with vampires and werewolves instead of street brawlers; the gothic atmosphere the genre was missing.

cps__vampire-savior.article:
The music plays, the screen pulses with colour and two monsters lay into each other in one of the fastest and most stylish fights the 2D era offered. **Vampire Savior** is the pinnacle of Capcom's Darkstalkers series and for many connoisseurs at the same time one of the best-tuned fighting games of the nineties.

The game came out on the Capcom CP System II board and followed the previous instalments about the supernatural Night Warriors. Iconic characters like Morrigan, Demitri, Jon Talbain or Felicia return and new faces were added. Vampire Savior is renowned for its striking artistic style, lavish animation and music that rounds out the gothic circus atmosphere.

At the heart of the game is its combat system. Vampire Savior introduced a system where, instead of the classic rounded rounds, the match continues fluidly until one of the fighters falls, and it brought aggressive mechanics like the Dark Force mode and fast combos. The pace is high, offence pays off and the game rewards players who can keep up the pressure. It is precisely this depth that made it a fixture of the tournament community.

Culturally Vampire Savior confirmed that Darkstalkers is not just an exotic detour but a fully-fledged fighting series with its own identity. Its characters and visual style influenced Capcom's later games and to this day a number of fighters from this instalment are represented in crossovers. Among fans of 2D fighters it has a reputation as a hidden gem.

The game appeared in various compilations, among others in the Darkstalkers collections, and remains popular in the community of players who appreciate its mechanical sophistication. Even after decades it feels brisk and modern. For fans of the genre it is a mandatory item.

**Why play it:** For a fast, deep and visually enchanting fighting game that connoisseurs rank among the best 2D titles of its time.
cps__vampire-savior.teaser: The pinnacle of Capcom's Darkstalkers series and one of the best-balanced fighting games of the nineties.

cps__marvel-super-heroes.article:
Spider-Man, Hulk, Captain America and Iron Man could finally face one another in the arena – and Capcom added the mighty Infinity Stones to it. **Marvel Super Heroes** was a fighting game that joined the world of superheroes with a combat system honed over years by the Japanese studio, creating a combination fans had long yearned for.

The game ran on the Capcom CP System II board and drew on the comic saga The Infinity Gauntlet. Players chose from a plethora of Marvel characters, from Spider-Man through Wolverine to the villain Thanos, and each had their own special attacks inspired by their comic-book abilities. Capcom drew on its experience from Street Fighter and the X-Men games and transferred it into a spectacular superhero show.

The unique mechanic was precisely the Infinity Stones. During a match you could collect six stones, each granting temporary advantages – increased strength, speed, regeneration or defence. This added a tactical layer and chaotic unpredictability to the fight, because a well-timed stone could turn a seemingly lost match around. Coupled with this were spectacular super attacks and Capcom's typically fluid animation.

Culturally the game was an important step on the road to the legendary crossovers. It followed X-Men: Children of the Atom and opened the door to the Marvel vs. Capcom series, which later became one of the most popular fighting brands ever. Marvel Super Heroes showed that a licensed superhero fighting game can have real depth and style.

The game made it to the home consoles of the time and later into digital collections. For fans of comics and fighting games alike it is a milestone that joined two worlds in a way that influenced a whole further decade of crossover games. To this day it is a treasured classic.

**Why play it:** For the joy of battles between iconic Marvel heroes spiced up with the tactics of the Infinity Stones.
cps__marvel-super-heroes.teaser: Marvel superheroes in a fighting game featuring the Infinity Stones as a core mechanic.

cps__giga-wing.article:
In a single instant the screen turns into a dense wall of enemy bullets – and you deflect it back with a single gesture. This scene defines **Giga Wing**, one of the most spectacular bullet hell shooters ever to fly through the arcades. Capcom, in collaboration with studio Takumi, pushed the genre to the edge of visual madness here.

The game ran on the Capcom CP System II board and belongs among the so-called danmaku, that is, shooters that flood the screen with enemy fire. The player controls a flying machine and fights their way through waves of enemies in a fantastically toned world. What set Giga Wing apart from the competition, however, was not just the density of bullets but a brilliant defensive system.

The key mechanic is the Reflect Barrier – the ability to create a shield that not only absorbs enemy bullets but reflects them back as your own devastating counterattack. This loop turned survival into offence and opened the door to astronomical scoring. Giga Wing became famous precisely for its outrageously high score numbers, which reached dizzying values and made the chase for a record the main draw.

Culturally Giga Wing ranked among the favourite titles for fans of bullet hell shooters and, together with the work of studio Takumi, helped define the turn-of-the-millennium era of this genre. Its visual excess and emphasis on the reflexive mastery of chaos made it an unforgettable experience for anyone who values precise fire-based action.

The game was released on the home console of its time and was followed by a sequel. Among collectors and fans of the genre it remains a respected name associated with extreme scoring and inventive defensive mechanics. For lovers of shoot 'em up it is a little jewel.

**Why play it:** For adrenaline-fuelled bullet hell action, where deflecting bullets becomes an art and the chase for an incredible score will not let you go.
cps__giga-wing.teaser: A bullet hell where a single move reflects a wall of enemy bullets straight back at the attacker.

cps__super-puzzle-fighter-ii-turbo.article:
Cute versions of the fighters from Street Fighter and Darkstalkers grin at each other across the screen while colourful gems rain down – and suddenly you realise this game is just as addictive as any great puzzle classic. **Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo** is a brilliant marriage of falling blocks and the competitive spirit of fighting games.

The game was created by Capcom on the CP System II board as a light-hearted but surprisingly deep variation on the genre of competitive puzzle games. Players choose from cutely caricatured versions of characters like Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li or Morrigan and compete against one another in a style reminiscent of legendary duels like Tetris or Puzzle Bobble, only with its own clever mechanic.

The core of the game is stacking gems of the same colour. When you stack gems and break them with a so-called Crash Gem, whole blocks disappear at once and chain reactions send annoying Counter Gems onto the opponent's field, which harden and complicate their game. This creates tense rounds full of combinations and countermoves, where a well-prepared chain explosion can bury the opponent and decide the match in an instant.

Culturally Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo became a player favourite thanks to its combination of accessibility and depth. The use of popular Capcom characters in an adorable super deformed style gave it flair and humour that appealed even to those who otherwise do not play puzzle games. Among competitive puzzlers it carved out a firm place.

The game received many conversions to home consoles and computers and repeatedly appears in Capcom's retro collections. Its principle is so timeless that it entertains even after decades and still ranks among the best-designed competitive puzzle games ever. It is proof that even a detour from the big series can spawn a little jewel.

**Why play it:** For catchy, competitive puzzle action with Capcom's cute heroes, where you will lose all track of time.
cps__super-puzzle-fighter-ii-turbo.teaser: Street Fighter and Darkstalkers characters in a falling-block puzzle game; an addictive crossover.

cps__armored-warriors.article:
Imagine a battlefield where colossal war robots rise from the ashes of a city and where every blow flings enemies across the whole screen. That is Armored Warriors, one of the most ambitious beat 'em ups Capcom ever built on its CPS-2 arcade hardware. Instead of muscular street brawlers, here you control piloted combat mechs and the whole game breathes a robust mechanical energy you rarely meet in the genre.

The greatest asset is the parts-swapping system. From defeated enemies and from bosses you can seize their limbs, weapons and chassis and thus assemble your own robot in real time right in the middle of battle. One moment you fight as a walking tank, the next you put on wheels and turn into a fast gunnery platform. This mutability gives the game a depth that static beat 'em ups lack, and it rewards players for experimenting with the arsenal.

The game was created in the mid-nineties, at a time when Capcom dominated the arcades thanks to the CPS-2 boards and series like Street Fighter II or Final Fight. Armored Warriors belongs to the mecha universe that the company followed up with the later title Cyberbots, which moved the same robots into the one-on-one fighting genre. The visual style with its detailed animated machines and explosion pyrotechnics shows how far the two-dimensional pixel art of the time could go.

Culturally Armored Warriors captures Japanese pop culture's fascination with giant robots, rooted in the anime tradition, and transfers it into brisk cooperative action for up to three players at once. Crushing enemy legions together, sharing captured parts and coordinated salvoes are among the best that arcade beat 'em ups of the era offered.

Thanks to CPS-2 emulation the game today comes alive in full glory, with sharp graphics and instant control response. It is a title that perhaps never reached the fame of Final Fight, but among connoisseurs of the genre it has a firm and well-deserved place.

**Why play it:** If you want a beat 'em up with an extra idea, where you assemble your own robot from captured parts during the fight, Armored Warriors is a unique experience.
cps__armored-warriors.teaser: A beat 'em up where you pilot colossal combat mechs instead of street brawlers.

cps__progear.article:
The sky darkened with a swarm of enemy machines and the only thing standing between you and a flood of projectiles is the precision of your finger on the trigger. Progear is a vertical shooter that brought together two legends of the Japanese gaming industry: publisher Capcom and studio Cave, regarded as the king of so-called bullet hell shooters.

The game runs on Capcom's CPS-2 arcade hardware and is renowned for its dense yet readable enemy-fire design. You control small flying machines in a world that blends a steampunk aesthetic with cogwheels and diesel-powered mechanics. The key mechanic is a shooting-and-collecting system, where destroying enemies in rhythm and gathering bonuses raises your score and rewards aggressive but calculated play.

Progear was born from a collaboration in which Cave brought its mastery of designing bullet patterns and Capcom provided its proven platform. For Cave it was a chance to reach a wider audience, since their titles otherwise appeared on their own or other hardware. The result is a game that fans of the genre still treasure for its elegant balance of difficulty and visual clarity.

In a cultural context, Progear represents one of the bridges between mainstream arcades and the hardcore community of score chasers. Bullet hell shooters demand patience, memorization and a cool head, and Progear offers exactly the blend of tension and satisfaction that keeps this subgenre alive long after the arcade era.

Thanks to emulation, this otherwise rare board is now accessible even to players who would never have encountered the original cabinet. It is a great entry point into the world of Cave and at the same time a title that holds up even before the most demanding veterans.

**Why play:** The collaboration between Capcom and Cave gave rise to an elegant steampunk bullet hell shooter that makes an ideal gateway into the demanding world of score chasing.
cps__progear.teaser: A vertical bullet hell from genre masters Cave, famous for its readable bullet-pattern design.

cps__street-fighter-iii-3rd-strike.article:
One perfectly timed press and the whole situation flips — the parry system in Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike from 1999 is proof that a fighting game can be both brutally demanding and beautifully elegant. With this game Capcom took the 2D Street Fighter to its absolute peak: masterfully crafted action where deflecting an opponent's attack at the exact moment can turn around even a seemingly lost exchange.

The parry is a mechanic that changed the perception of the genre. Instead of blocking, which drains energy, you can „deflect" a blow with a precise motion at the right split second — and open a path to a counterattack. It takes nerves of steel and a deep reading of your opponent, but the reward is intoxicating. It is precisely this depth that made 3rd Strike a sacred title among competitive players.

Proof of this is the legendary „EVO Moment 37", when Daigo Umehara parried an entire super combo on his last sliver of health and the crowd literally exploded. It is the most famous moment in competitive gaming ever, a clip that circled the globe and became a symbol of why fighting games are such thrilling spectacle.

Beyond the depth of its system, the game dazzles with its animation. The characters move with a fluidity and personality few could match at the time — every blow, dodge and victory pose is hand-tuned down to the smallest detail. It is the visual peak of Street Fighter's 2D era and a spectacle that has not aged a day.

The difficulty will deter anyone looking for casual fun, but for anyone who longs to dig beneath the surface and master true skill, 3rd Strike is one of the deepest and most rewarding fighting games ever made.

**Why play:** A masterful 2D fighter with a legendary parry system and timeless animation — the pinnacle of Street Fighter and the cradle of e-sports' most famous moment.
cps__street-fighter-iii-3rd-strike.teaser: The parry system made 3rd Strike a fighting game where precise timing can turn around any exchange.

cps__street-fighter-alpha-3.article:
Street Fighter Alpha 3 is among the most ambitious things Capcom produced in the 2D fighting era — an entry that poured so many characters, choices and system layers into the proven formula that it became one of the richest tournament experiences of its time. If you were looking for a Street Fighter that lets you play your way, this was the answer.

The key is the fighting-style system. Before a match you choose from various modes that change how your super energy, defense and offensive options work — one choice favors aggressive pressure, another patient play and meter building. This flexibility gives the game unexpected depth and opens space for different play philosophies even with the same character.

The roster is vast and varied, full of familiar faces and less common fighters from the Alpha series. Capcom added its trademark signature: distinctive 2D animation, readable moves and duels that reward knowledge of timing and spatial awareness. The pace is brisk and the combo system leaves room for both beginners and technically skilled players.

Visually, the game benefits from the colorful, energetic style of the Alpha line, which stood apart from the later and darker entries. It is a polished, confident spectacle that represents the era when Capcom set the direction of the genre.

Among fans of 2D fighters, Alpha 3 holds a firm place precisely because of the breadth of options and the depth it offers a willing player. Anyone unafraid to experiment with the modes and find their own style gets one of the most versatile Street Fighters ever.

**Why play:** A rich 2D fighter with selectable fighting styles and a vast roster — one of the most versatile and deepest entries in Street Fighter.
cps__street-fighter-alpha-3.teaser: Alpha 3's selectable fighting-style system offered perhaps the richest tournament experience of its era.

cps__marvel-vs-capcom.article:
Spider-Man against Ryu, Wolverine amid a barrage of hadoukens and a screen that literally overflows with colors and explosions — Marvel vs. Capcom took comic-book heroes and Capcom's stars, threw them into one melting pot and produced one of the most spectacular fighters the arcades ever saw. This is a game built on pure spectacle.

The team format is its engine. You assemble a duo of fighters, switch between them, call your partner in for an assist and chain attacks into long, staggering combos. The pace is insane, aerial action is everywhere and the super attacks are so over-the-top they fill the entire screen with lights and effects. It is excessive in the best sense of the word — a joy that is not meant to hold back.

The magic of the crossover lies in meeting characters who would otherwise never clash. Seeing Marvel icons side by side with faces from Capcom games was a small miracle back then and it still holds an irresistible charm. Each character carries its own style and fan appeal, so building a team is fun in itself.

Visually the game shines with Capcom's characteristic 2D animation, only polished into an even more exuberant, bombastic form. The speed, colors and chaos on screen turn every match into little fireworks that are a joy to watch even as a mere onlooker.

Marvel vs. Capcom laid the foundations of the entire „vs." subgenre and inspired a string of sequels and imitators. For lovers of fast, flashy and unbridled action it is a staple worth returning to again and again.

**Why play:** A bombastic team crossover fighter full of combos and effects that founded the entire „vs." subgenre — pure, unbridled fun.
cps__marvel-vs-capcom.teaser: Team battles between hero duos with on-the-fly switching; pure comic-book spectacle.

cps__x-men-children-of-atom.article:
Mutants from Marvel comics unleash combat chaos on a scale that had no equal at the time — X-Men: Children of the Atom is the game in which Capcom first fully showed how brilliantly it could translate superhero action into a fighter. For the entire later „vs." phenomenon it is a key predecessor.

The gameplay rests on a grand take on superpowers. Characters hover, chain long combos and fire staggering super attacks that fill the screen with effects. The pace is fast and aerial, with an emphasis on flashy execution and the feeling that you truly command the mighty mutants from the comic pages. The fights have the energy and juice for which Capcom became renowned in the genre.

The character selection draws on the world of the X-Men, so you face familiar heroes and villains alike. Each has its own recognizable style of movement and abilities, faithful to the comic source. It is precisely this love of detail and respect for the license that make the game a feast for fans of the mutant tales.

Visually the game dazzles with Capcom's characteristic 2D animation — bold, colorful and full of motion. The grand effects and dynamic presentation place it among the technically advanced arcade fighters of its day, and confident craftsmanship radiates from it to this day.

Its historical significance is undeniable: this is where the style was born that Capcom carried into the legendary crossovers with its own characters. Anyone who wants to understand the roots of the entire „vs." line, or simply enjoy a fast superhero brawl, has an excellent starting point here.

**Why play:** A grand superhero fighter with Marvel's mutants and the typical Capcom animation — a key predecessor of the entire „vs." subgenre.
cps__x-men-children-of-atom.teaser: A key predecessor to the whole Capcom vs. series, where mutants first flew freely across the screen.

cps__capcom-vs-snk-2.article:
Two fighting dynasties, one ring — Capcom vs. SNK 2 is the dream bout in which the icons of Street Fighter and King of Fighters finally clash in a grand crossover that fans of the genre long awaited. Here Capcom joined the best of both worlds into one exceptionally rich fighter.

At the heart of the game is the system of choosing fighting styles, the so-called „grooves". Before a match you pick a mode that determines how your energy, defense and attack options work — one matches the rules of Capcom games, another the SNK style. Thanks to this, every player can assemble a match exactly according to their play philosophy and the game offers enormous tactical depth.

The roster is a feast for fans of both camps. Characters from the Street Fighter and SNK universes meet side by side here, each with its own style and distinctive signature. Building a team, finding the ideal „groove" and tuning strategy against a specific opponent turns every duel into a little chess game at full speed.

Visually the game benefits from the precision of 2D animation that Capcom was expert at, and from a readable, dynamic presentation. The fights are fast yet deep — they reward knowledge of both systems and the ability to combine them cleverly.

Among connoisseurs, Capcom vs. SNK 2 has a reputation as one of the deepest and most balanced crossover titles, one the competitive community has returned to for many years. For anyone who loves technical 2D fighters and dreams of a clash between the two giants, it is a wish come true.

**Why play:** A dream crossover of Capcom and SNK with a deep system of fighting styles and a huge roster — one of the most technical and balanced fighters ever.
cps__capcom-vs-snk-2.teaser: The dream crossover of Street Fighter and King of Fighters, with a selectable groove system.

cps__cadillacs-and-dinosaurs.article:
Full throttle, a shotgun in hand and a tyrannosaurus at your back. **Cadillacs and Dinosaurs** from 1993 is one of the juiciest excursions into the golden era of the Capcom beat 'em up. The game was based on the comic and animated series of the same name and takes the player into a post-apocalyptic world where modern people contend with gangs of villains and with reawakened dinosaurs.

In gameplay terms it is a textbook side-scrolling brawler from early-1990s Capcom, from the era when the studio dominated this genre. Excellent character animation, a varied gallery of heroes with different combat styles and superb multiplayer co-op make it an ideal title for sitting down at the cabinet with friends. Capcom moreover added the ability to pick up and use weapons, including firearms, which gives fights against dinosaurs and human opponents a juicy dynamic.

The game belongs to the wider family of Capcom brawlers of the time. While Knights of the Round added blocking and an experience system with growing equipment (a certain RPG flavor), Cadillacs bet on firearms and prehistoric beasts and Captain Commando on a sci-fi team of heroes. Together these titles form the peaks of the genre, on which Capcom showed its mastery of animation, enemy design and the feel of blows.

Visually the game shines with colorful environments, large and carefully drawn sprites and imaginative opponent design, from street thugs to giant reptiles. The feel of combat is tangible and every blow has weight, which is exactly what you expect from an arcade brawler.

Thanks to its tie to the comic source, the game has a distinctive atmosphere that sets it apart from other titles in the genre. The blend of car chases, dinosaurs and classic street brawling creates a unique cocktail that retains its magical retro charm to this day.

**Why play:** For a genuine experience of the golden era of the Capcom beat 'em up, where you pummel gangs and tyrannosaurs alike and where co-op with a friend is the greatest fun.
cps__cadillacs-and-dinosaurs.teaser: A post-apocalypse with a shotgun in hand and a tyrannosaurus on your tail, based on the comic of the same name.

cps__alien-vs-predator.article:
Two icons of horror sci-fi, one cabinet and endless hordes of xenomorphs. **Alien vs. Predator** from Capcom is one of the highest-rated arcade brawlers ever, one that fans of the genre and of both film series pass on like a treasure. The game blends the brutal atmosphere of cosmic horror with polished early-1990s Capcom action.

The core of the experience is a classic side-scrolling beat 'em up in which you hack through legions of Aliens. The playable team mixes human soldiers with Predators, so you can choose between raw human resilience and the deadly technologies of the alien hunters. Each character has its own combat style, reach and weapons, from blades to firearms to special attacks, which gives the fights against enemies a pleasant variety.

The game draws on what Capcom did best in the genre: excellent animation, a tangible feel of blows and imaginatively designed enemies and bosses. The pace is fast and chaotic in the best sense, especially when teammates join you and the screen fills with action. Co-op is once again the right spice that turns playing into an adrenaline ride.

Visually the title carries a dark, industrial style that faithfully evokes the atmosphere of the film sources. Dark environments, hissing xenomorphs and iconic Predators together create the tension that inseparably belongs to the Alien vs. Predator license. Here Capcom showed that it can handle a brand with respect and craftsmanlike care.

Due to complicated licensing, the game long remained unavailable outside arcades, which made it a sought-after and almost cult title. For many players it is one of the peaks of Capcom brawlers and one of the best ways to experience the clash of these two sci-fi icons.

**Why play:** For fans of both film series and lovers of arcade brawlers who want a brutal, atmospheric and perfectly polished slugfest in Capcom's style.
cps__alien-vs-predator.teaser: One of the highest-rated arcade brawlers ever made — hordes of xenomorphs against the legends.

cps__punisher.article:
Frank Castle knows no mercy and this game makes that clear from the very first seconds. **The Punisher** from Capcom, released in 1993, takes the beloved avenger from Marvel comics and hurls him into a raw, violent arcade brawler that ranks among the hidden gems of the genre. Alongside the Punisher, Nick Fury also fights, so you play as a pair of uncompromising warriors against crime.

In gameplay it is a classic side-scrolling beat 'em up in the early-1990s Capcom style, from the era when the studio set the tone in this field. To the usual punching and weapon-collecting was added a pronounced shooting element: in some passages you can switch to a mode with firearms and mow down enemies at range. This combination of close combat and shooting gives the game a brisk and brutal dynamic.

The game benefits from Capcom's typical strengths of the era, namely excellent animation, a tangible feel of blows and a varied gallery of enemies and bosses. The pace is fast and uncompromising, which fits the dark tone of the source. Co-op for two players again raises the fun, because carving a path through legions of villains as a duo is the best choice.

Visually the game faithfully captures the gritty atmosphere of the Punisher comics. Gloomy urban environments, bloody action and the characteristic figure of the avenger in his black skull shirt create a distinctive, more mature tone that was not a given in arcade brawlers.

Thanks to the Marvel license and its quality execution, The Punisher built a reputation among genre fans as a respected, if somewhat overlooked, title. For connoisseurs of Capcom beat 'em ups it is one of the unforgettable ones.

**Why play:** For lovers of gritty arcade brawlers and comic-book antiheroes who will appreciate the brisk combination of fists, guns and an uncompromising atmosphere.
cps__punisher.teaser: Frank Castle alongside Nick Fury in a raw, uncompromising brawler based on Marvel comics.

cps__dungeons-and-dragons-shadow-over-my.article:
Imagine a beat 'em up with the soul of an adventurous RPG campaign. **Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow over Mystara** from 1996 is exactly what Capcom used to prove that the street-brawler genre can have unexpected depth. The game follows the previous title Tower of Doom and pushes its concept of a fantasy brawler with role-playing elements to its peak.

Instead of a single hero template, the player chooses from six classes, from a fighter through a cleric and a mage to an elf, a dwarf and a thief. Each character has its own abilities, combat style and role in the party. Added to this are spells, an inventory with items, scrolls and potions, and the ability to collect and use various weapons. The game moreover offers branching paths, so you can head in different directions through the adventure, which markedly increases replayability.

Mechanically it is still a brisk action brawler for up to four players, in which you fight, cast spells and combine equipment on the move. It is precisely the fusion of addictive arcade action with elements of tabletop Dungeons & Dragons that gives the game its unique character. Fights against varied fantasy creatures, from goblins to dragons, feel epic and co-op in a full foursome is breathtaking fun.

Visually the game shines with the typical Capcom quality of the mid-1990s. Detailed sprites, fluid animation and colorful fantasy environments evoke the atmosphere of a classic adventure. The enemy and boss design draws on the rich world of Dungeons & Dragons and every location has its own flavor.

Because of the Dungeons & Dragons license, the game was long hard to obtain outside arcades, which made it a sought-after title. Today you can find it in an official collection for modern platforms, so everyone can finally enjoy this unusually deep brawler.

**Why play:** For players who want a beat 'em up with the soul of an RPG, where the choice of class, spells and branching paths make every playthrough a different adventure.
cps__dungeons-and-dragons-shadow-over-my.teaser: A beat 'em up with the soul of an RPG campaign; choose from six classes and level up your character.

cps__final-fight.article:
The slums of Metro City cry out for justice and you deal it out with your bare hands. **Final Fight** from 1989 is the forefather of modern beat 'em ups, a title that literally defined the template of the entire genre: a band of heroes fights through the streets and clears the city of a criminal gang. With this concept Capcom created a model that countless later games merely imitated.

The game's origin is already intriguing. Final Fight was originally meant to be Street Fighter '89, that is, a sequel to the famous fighter. In the end, though, it became a standalone brand that steered the development of street brawlers for a decade to come. The story of the kidnapping of Jessie, daughter of the mayor and former wrestler Mike Haggar, by the criminal gang Mad Gear gave players clear and juicy motivation to join the fight.

The player chooses from three characters: the burly mayor Haggar, who relies on brute strength and grapples, the nimble Cody with a balanced combat style and the fast fighter Guy. Each offers a different feel of play and a different approach to crowds of enemies. The fights rest on tangible blows, grapples and the ability to grab weapons or smash objects in the environment for bonuses.

Visually the game impressed for its time with large sprites, striking characters and a lively rendering of a decaying metropolis. A varied gallery of opponents and bosses and imaginative bonus stages, where you demolish a car, for example, make playing a brisk and enjoyable ride that you can still enjoy in two-player today.

The historical significance of Final Fight is enormous. It became the benchmark of the genre, received many ports, sequels and references in other games (characters like Haggar and Guy appeared in the world of Street Fighter). Even after decades it remains superbly playable and reminds us where the roots of street brawlers lie.

**Why play:** Because this is the source from which the entire beat 'em up genre grew, and at the same time a still-entertaining and tangibly satisfying street brawl for one or two players.
cps__final-fight.teaser: The forefather of modern beat 'em ups, which literally defined the genre's entire template.

cps__captain-commando.article:
A sci-fi team of superheroes, a futuristic city and hordes of villains waiting for a beating. **Captain Commando** from Capcom expands the studio's famous family of street brawlers with a colorful touch of science-fiction comics. The game builds on the legacy of Final Fight, but moves the action into the future and offers a foursome of unforgettable heroes.

Instead of ordinary street thugs, the title's Captain Commando and his crew are in command here: a ninja, a mummy and a small warrior piloting a robotic suit, or an alien depending on the interpretation. Each team member has its own combat style, reach and special attacks, so the choice of character markedly affects how the game will play for you. This variety gives the pummeling of enemies a pleasant diversity.

In gameplay it is a classic side-scrolling beat 'em up in the proven early-1990s Capcom style. You punch, use grapples, collect weapons and items and fight through waves of opponents up to the bosses. Multiplayer co-op is once again the best way to experience the game, because a full band of heroes on screen turns the action into a fun melee.

Visually the game shines with typical Capcom quality. Large and carefully animated sprites, colorful futuristic environments and imaginative enemy and boss design create a fresh sci-fi atmosphere that sets it apart from the more realistically tuned brawlers of the time. The feel of blows is tangible and the pace brisk.

Captain Commando belongs to the wider group of Capcom beat 'em ups that together form the peaks of the genre. Alongside Final Fight, Knights of the Round or Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, it takes its place as a colorful, sci-fi-flavored piece that fans fondly remember.

**Why play:** For lovers of Capcom brawlers who want a brisk street brawl spiced with a sci-fi team of heroes and superb co-op with friends.
cps__captain-commando.teaser: A sci-fi twist on the Final Fight family: led by title hero Captain Commando and his colorful crew.

cps__knights-of-round.article:
Knights of the round table, blocking blows and a sword that grows stronger with every victory. **Knights of the Round** by Capcom brings the legend of King Arthur into the world of arcade brawlers and enriches the genre with features that were far from standard at the time. The game belongs to the famous family of Capcom beat 'em ups from the early nineties.

Unlike most street brawlers of the era, the game added two distinctive elements. The first is the ability to block attacks, which brings a tactical dimension to the fights and rewards players for well-timed defense. The second is a character development system: defeating enemies earns you experience, you level up, and both your gear and appearance change. This role-playing touch gave the game a sense of progression that was uncommon in the genre.

The player chooses from a trio of knights, among them King Arthur himself and his companions, each offering a different fighting style and a different balance between speed and strength. The combat is built on sword slashes, blocking and grapples, rounded out by battles against inventive bosses drawn from Arthurian legend. Co-op once again boosts the fun and turns the fight toward the round table into a shared adventure.

Visually the game benefits from Capcom's trademark quality. Detailed sprites, fluid animation and environments inspired by medieval England create the atmosphere of a heroic saga. The characters' changing gear as they level up is a pleasant visual bonus that underscores the feeling of progress.

Knights of the Round ranks among the titles with which Capcom pushed the boundaries of the genre. Together with Final Fight, Cadillacs and Dinosaurs and Captain Commando it forms the peak of street brawlers and proves that even brisk arcade action can carry real depth.

**Why play:** For fans of Capcom brawlers who will appreciate blocking, character progression and Arthurian legend wrapped in a snappy co-op scrap.
cps__knights-of-round.teaser: An Arthurian brawler where your sword grows stronger with every victory, and attacks can be blocked for the first time.

cps__alien-progear.article:
Among arcade shooters there exists a narrow, fanatically beloved circle of so-called „manic shooters“, and **Progear** is one of its jewels. This horizontal shooter from the revered studio CAVE was released in 2001 as one of the few titles where the masters of Japanese bullet hell teamed up with the publisher Capcom — and the result remains a byword among connoisseurs of the genre to this day.

Unlike many of CAVE's vertically oriented games, **Progear** plays out in a horizontal layout and drops the player into a steampunk world of airships and steam engines. At the heart of the gameplay is the interplay between a pilot and a gunner: in addition to your main fire you also control a support unit whose angle and focused shots are the key to a high score. The screen quickly fills with dozens of slowly drifting projectiles, and the whole art lies in weaving between them through a narrow sliver of safety.

It is precisely the scoring system that makes **Progear** more than just a test of reflexes. Collecting gems, chaining hits and risky play at the very edge of fire range reward bold players with a dizzying score — and the chase for the record is what keeps the community around the game together even now. Visually it is classic CAVE splendor: detailed pixel bosses, a rich palette and spectacular explosions.

Because it was an arcade title with limited distribution, **Progear** was for a long time hard to obtain outside the original boards. That changed thanks to later official releases within collections and digital re-releases, so today a far wider audience can reach it than back then.

For a newcomer bullet hell can be intimidating at first, but **Progear** is one of the more approachable gateways into the genre — it is readable, fair and immensely satisfying once you grasp its rhythm.

**Why play:** An elegant horizontal bullet hell from the masters at CAVE, where the dance between projectiles and the chase for score never stop being fun.
cps__alien-progear.teaser: A manic shooter from CAVE, prized by bullet-hell connoisseurs as a hidden gem of the genre.

cps__street-fighter-ii-world-warrior.article:
There are few games of which one can say without exaggeration that they reinvented an entire genre. Street Fighter II: The World Warrior is exactly that. When Capcom launched this cabinet in Japanese and later North American arcades in 1991, no one suspected that it had just kicked off the golden era of fighting games and a phenomenon that for a few years literally rescued the declining arcade business.

The magic lay in a combination that no one had put together before. Eight playable characters, each with a completely different style, speed and reach, and above all a set of special moves entered with precise joystick motions. Ryu and Ken's legendary Hadoken (quarter-circle forward and a punch button), the Shoryuken or Guile's Sonic Boom became the vocabulary of an entire generation. Six buttons distinguishing light, medium and heavy punches and kicks gave the fights a depth that players dissected for years. The concept of the combo was born too, originally a programming bug that Capcom deliberately left in.

The most important thing, however, was player-versus-player combat. The ability to challenge an opponent by tossing a coin into the machine and immediately squaring off with them turned arcades into bustling arenas full of crowds. People stood in lines, placed bets and forged rivalries. This was a genuine social dimension that had been missing before.

Development was led by producer Yoshiki Okamoto and a team in which designer Akira Nishitani and artist Akiman shone. The game ran on the CP System (CPS-1) board and its large, bold sprites and colorful backdrops representing various countries of the world looked breathtaking at the start of the nineties. Capcom hit the mood of a time when players craved something fast, skill-based and competitive.

The cultural impact was enormous. Street Fighter II became the best-selling fighting cabinet of its era and set off an avalanche of competitors and imitators, from Mortal Kombat to countless others. It defined the rules by which fighting games abide to this day: character select, health bars, best-of-two rounds, motion specials. The game saw countless revisions and versions, of which The World Warrior was the very first, still without mirror matches and without playable bosses. That came only in later editions, which addressed the imbalance and the so-called infinite combos.

The success was so enormous that Capcom soon launched a whole cascade of follow-up editions, from Champion Edition through Hyper Fighting to Super Street Fighter II. Each of them added characters, tuned the balance or sped up the pace, keeping the brand at the top for years. The game also became one of the most-ported titles of the nineties, with the home version for Super Nintendo ranking among the console's best-selling cartridges of all and helping Capcom build an empire. Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li and the others became lasting icons that carry the brand to this day.

Today World Warrior is more of a historical artifact surpassed by its own successors. Yet it is that fundamental turning point, the starting point from which everything else unfolds. Without it the competitive scene and the esport of fighting games would not look the way we know them.

**Why play:** To feel with your own thumbs the original spark from which the entire modern genre of fighting games sprang.
cps__street-fighter-ii-world-warrior.teaser: The game that literally reinvented fighting games in 1991 and kicked off their golden era.

cps__street-fighter-ii-hyper-fighting.article:
When the competition began snapping at Capcom's heels and arcades were flooded with pirated modified boards of the original Street Fighter II sporting a faster pace, Capcom answered in its own way. In 1992 came Street Fighter II: Hyper Fighting, officially Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting, a version that took everything good and pressed the speed button all the way down.

The main draw was speed. The fights ran noticeably brisker than in previous editions and demanded lightning reflexes and precise execution of specials. For the hardcore players of the day it was paradise; the game turned into a test of pure skill where fractions of a second decided everything. Capcom also fine-tuned the balance, added new color variants for the characters and gave some fighters new abilities, such as Dhalsim's teleport or Chun-Li her own fireball.

Hyper Fighting was a direct reaction to the phenomenon of home modifications. Players craved a faster game and pirate hacks of the original version offered exactly that, so Capcom delivered an official, tuned variant that legitimized these modifications and pushed them further. To this day many veterans regard this edition as one of the best-balanced and cleanest installments of the entire Street Fighter II series, precisely for its emphasis on the speed and fairness of the fights.

Technically it still stood on the proven CPS-1 board and visually it did not differ from its predecessors; the magic was in the tuning and the pace. With it Capcom proved how cleverly it could tend to a living product. Instead of one release and done, it kept coming with iterative revisions that sustained player interest and money in the machines for months on end.

Culturally Hyper Fighting confirmed that Street Fighter II was not a one-off hit but a long-term platform. This version became a tournament favorite and later saw ports to home consoles. Among other things it appeared as one of the few truly faithful arcade conversions on the Super Nintendo and, much later, in compilations and on services like Virtual Console, where another generation got to play it.

It is worth noting how fast Capcom iterated back then. Barely a year and a half passed between the first World Warrior and Hyper Fighting, and yet Champion Edition with its mirror matches and playable bosses still fit in between. Hyper Fighting logically capped off this line with an emphasis on speed and tuned combos. For players it meant a constant stream of novelties and a reason to keep returning to the machine, and for Capcom a steady flow of coins and the building of a brand reputation that the era of Super Street Fighter II and further sequels would later build upon.

For understanding the evolution of fighting games, Hyper Fighting is a key intermediate step. It shows how the genre shifted within a single year from relatively measured tactics to fast, nerve-racking action that then defined players' expectations for years to come. It is the version for those who wanted to really stretch their reflexes.

**Why play:** If you crave the fastest and, according to many, most balanced version of the classic Street Fighter II, this is it.
cps__street-fighter-ii-hyper-fighting.teaser: Capcom's answer to sped-up bootleg copies of SF II — the official version with turbo cranked all the way up.

cps__captain-commando-2.article:
A futuristic metropolis of the future has been flooded with villains, and the only hope lies in the hands of a superhero in a blue cape and his three-member crew. **Captain Commando** by Capcom from 1991 is one of the most colorful and stylish brawlers ever released on the famous CPS board.

The game belongs to the golden era of the beat 'em up genre, which Capcom co-created with the Final Fight series. The principle is classic: you advance through streets and levels from left to right and wipe out waves of enemies with punches, kicks, throws and special attacks. But Captain Commando stands out with its unmistakable quartet of characters: besides the titular captain you can play as the knife-wielding mummy Mack the Knife, as the infant in a robotic suit Baby Head, or as the alien ninja Ginzu. Each hero has a different fighting style, reach and strength, which lends the game pleasant variety.

Visually Captain Commando draws on the best that Capcom's hardware of the time could offer: detailed sprite animations, vivid backgrounds and enormous bosses. The gameplay is snappy and shines especially in co-op, when up to four players gather for the fight at once and the screen turns into a colorful chaos of fists and explosions.

An interesting fact is that the main hero's name references Capcom itself; the character had served as a sort of unofficial company mascot even earlier. Captain Commando later appeared in the crossover fighting games Marvel vs. Capcom, where he recalled his role in the studio's history. The game saw ports to a number of home systems and remains a favorite of arcade brawler fans.

Captain Commando is a celebration of unbridled action from the days when it was enough to drop a coin into the machine, call over some friends and dish out justice together. It is a title full of energy, style and honest gaming fun that has not aged.

**Why play:** For a stylish co-op brawl with a quartet of quirky heroes from the masters of the beat 'em up genre.

cps__knights-of-round-2.article:
Arthurian legend as told by Capcom does not begin in a library but on a battlefield full of clashing steel. **Knights of the Round** casts you in the role of a knight for whom more is at stake than surviving to the next round: it is a journey from a youth to a king. And it is one of the most stylish brawlers the arcades of the time had to offer.

The game was released on the **CPS (Capcom Play System)** boards, the famous arcade platform that gave rise to a whole generation of side-scrolling brawlers. You choose from a trio of heroes from the Arthurian cycle, each with different weaponry and fighting style. The mechanics rest on the genre's classic scheme of the beat 'em up: you advance from left to right, mow down waves of enemies and fight your way to the bosses. But Capcom added several elements here that elevated the game above the ordinary average.

The most striking is the blocking system. Unlike most brawlers of the era, where you could only dodge enemy blows, here the strikes can be actively parried with a shield or weapon. The fights thus take on an almost fencing-like rhythm, where judging the timing of the opponent's lunge decides whether you get through without a scratch. To this the game adds gradual character upgrades: as you collect experience, your armor and gear change and grow stronger, giving the playthrough a sense of real growth.

Visually the game benefits from a rich medieval palette, detailed backgrounds and large, boldly animated enemies. The boss battles are among the highlights, crowned by a spectacular final clash. All of this is accompanied by rousing music and the sound of weapons that gave arcade halls the proper atmosphere. Multiplayer co-op, typical of this genre, moreover turns the game into a shared expedition where both the advantages and the dangers multiply.

Culturally we rank **Knights of the Round** among the titles that helped define the golden era of arcade brawlers. At a time when arcades competed for players' attention with the flashiest machines possible, a medieval subject was a welcome refreshment amid street scraps and sci-fi themes. For many fans of the genre it remains one of those titles they gladly return to for its atmosphere and its refined combat.

**Why play:** A stylish medieval brawler with blocking and character growth that shows why Capcom was at home on the arcade CPS boards like few others.

cps__cadillacs-and-dinosaurs-2.article:
Cars with fin-like fenders, submachine guns and a Tyrannosaurus scampering around them. **Cadillacs and Dinosaurs** is exactly the kind of unbridled idea that could only have been born in the arcades of the early nineties, and Capcom mined it into one of its most characteristic brawlers.

The game runs on the arcade boards **CPS (Capcom Play System)** and genre-wise belongs to beat 'em up titles, that is, to side-scrolling brawlers in which you fight your way forward through endless waves of opponents. Capcom was one of the most experienced creators in this genre and it shows here: the controls are snappy, the blows carry proper weight and the pace of the action does not let up for a moment. There are several playable characters to choose from, so everyone finds a style that suits them.

What sets the game apart from typical street scraps is its world. The story takes place in a post-apocalyptic future where humanity lives side by side with dinosaurs, and this premise seeps into every fight. Alongside ordinary villains, prehistoric reptiles hurl themselves at you and you get your hands on a varied stock of weapons, from melee to firearms. The ability to grab a rifle and empty a magazine into an approaching enemy gives the fights a juice that purely fist-based brawlers lacked.

The visual side is another strong card. Capcom was renowned for detailed, bold pixel graphics and here it played it to the full: colorful backgrounds of a scorched world, massively animated dinosaurs and characterful character design give the game an unmistakable flair. The boss fights and the rotation of environments make sure the playthrough does not slide into monotony, and multiplayer co-op tips the whole experience toward the best that the arcades of the time had to offer.

Culturally it is a title that combined a beloved genre with an attractive licensed source and became one of the iconic arcade brawlers of its time. For arcade veterans **Cadillacs and Dinosaurs** remains synonymous with carefree, action-packed fun where logic gives way to style and every minute of play ends with another explosion, gunshot or roar of an ancient reptile.

**Why play:** A juicy post-apocalyptic brawler where you pound gangsters and dinosaurs alike with a gun in hand; the pure essence of why arcades were so addictive.

pc-engine__bonk-s-adventure.teaser: The console's mascot; platformers about headbutting.
pc-engine__bonk-s-adventure.detail: The console's mascot: a caveman kid who attacks by ramming with his giant head and climbs walls by biting into them. Playful, colorful platformers with their own identity; the platform's symbol in the fight against Mario and Sonic.
pc-engine__bonk-s-adventure.article:
Every console of the eight- and sixteen-bit era needed its mascot, and while Nintendo had a plumber and Sega a hedgehog, NEC and Hudson bet on a caveman kid with a disproportionately large head. Bonk's Adventure from 1990 and 1991 became the face of the PC Engine, or the TurboGrafx-16 in the West, and to this day ranks among the most characteristic platformers of its time.

Bonk's main weapon was literally his head. Instead of jumping on enemies, Bonk bit into walls to climb them and attacked with a fierce headbutt, whether from below or with a slam from above that stunned everything around him on landing. This single, but cleverly developed mechanic gave the game its own rhythm, unlike anything from the competition. Collecting pieces of meat moreover temporarily turned Bonk into a furious, invincible state.

Visually the game shone with a colorful, playful prehistoric world full of dinosaurs, which after being stunned often became friendly. The graphics leveraged the strengths of the PC Engine, a console that Hudson and NEC built as a direct challenge to Nintendo, and it celebrated great success in Japan. Bonk became a symbol of the whole platform and appeared even in the TurboGrafx advertising campaigns.

Behind the game's development stood a collaboration of the studios Atlus, Red Company and Hudson Soft, experienced creators who knew how to squeeze the maximum out of the hardware. The birth of the mascot was no accident: the PC Engine desperately needed an iconic character to give it an identity in the battle for living rooms, and Bonk filled that role perfectly.

The success of the first game kicked off a small series of sequels and spin-off titles, and Bonk became one of the few mascots who managed to compete with the established stars. Although the PC Engine never broke through in the West the way it did in Japan, Bonk's Adventure remains a beloved classic and a gateway into the library of one of the most underrated consoles of that era.

**Why play:** For a fresh, original platformer with the unmistakable headbutt mechanic and to get to know the iconic mascot of a console that deserves more attention.

pc-engine__bonk-s-revenge.article:
When a mascot scores a hit, a sequel follows, and Bonk's Revenge was exactly what PC Engine fans had hoped for. The second adventure of the caveman kid with the mighty head took everything that worked in the original and honed it into an even more colorful, refined and entertaining form. For many players it is the peak of the entire series.

The foundation remained faithful: Bonk attacks by headbutting, climbs by biting into walls and stuns enemies with a slam from above. But the sequel added new abilities, more varied levels and smarter boss-fight design. Pieces of meat once again triggered Bonk's furious transformations and the game brimmed with witty details, hidden rooms and minigames that extended the fun far beyond simply clearing the levels.

The visual side again showed what the PC Engine could do: vivid colors, fluid animation and a playful prehistoric world full of personality. The team around the studios Red and Hudson Soft bet on what carried the first game and fine-tuned the pace and difficulty so that the title was accessible yet still offered a challenge for more experienced players.

Culturally Bonk's Revenge cemented its hero's standing as the platform's flagship. At a time when mascots became a tool of the marketing wars between console makers, Bonk represented NEC and Hudson in a league dominated by Mario and Sonic. That he held his own in it testifies to the quality and distinctiveness of the series.

Today Bonk's Revenge is prized as one of the best platformers on the PC Engine and proof that a sequel can not only match the original but even surpass it. For anyone discovering this console's library, it is a mandatory stop right after the first installment.

**Why play:** Because it takes a great original and improves it in every respect, thus offering the peak of one of the most distinctive platformer series of the sixteen-bit era.
pc-engine__bonk-s-revenge.teaser: The second adventure of big-headed Bonk is, for many fans, the high point of the whole series.

pc-engine__blazing-lazers-gunhed.article:
If there were a textbook on what a perfect vertical shooter on a 16-bit console should look like, it would be called **Blazing Lazers**. Under the Japanese title **Gunhed** this gem came out on the PC Engine and instantly proved why Hudson had built a reputation as the king of shmups. The game was created in connection with the eponymous Japanese sci-fi film, but that is actually the last thing on your mind while playing — here everything serves a single purpose: relentless, deafening fire.

At the heart of the experience is a weapons system that ranks among the best-tuned of its time. You pick from several types of main firing system — from a focused laser to scattered salvos covering the whole screen — and on top of that you collect support modules, shields and cleverly designed power-ups. The gradual accumulation of power is addictive to the point of pain: each further upgrade changes the feel of the ship so much that losing lives hurts twice as much. The pace is brisk, enemies arrive in well-readable waves and the bosses at the end of the levels present exactly the right measure of challenge.

Visually the game shone for its time. The PC Engine could render an enormous number of objects on screen without significant slowdown, so Blazing Lazers is not afraid to flood the player with shots, explosions and colorful effects. Parallax backgrounds, varied cosmic scenery and detailed enemy design showed that the little console from Hudson and NEC was a match for the arcades in the shooter genre.

In the context of the PC Engine's early history it is one of the titles that defined the platform. While Western audiences knew the console as the TurboGrafx-16, it was shooters like this one that made the machine a cult choice for fans of the genre. Blazing Lazers appears to this day in rankings of the best shmups of the late eighties and early nineties and belongs among the titles that collectors hunt with enthusiasm.

It is the type of game you return to not for the story but for the pure, rhythmic flow of the action — for the chase after a better score and the feeling that this time you will finally push it one level further. It is the essence of why we love 16-bit shooters.

**Why play:** If you want to see what a textbook vertical shooter with an excellent weapons system and an uncompromising pace looks like, Blazing Lazers is a mandatory stop.
pc-engine__blazing-lazers-gunhed.teaser: A textbook vertical shooter from Hudson, released in Japan under the name Gunhed.

pc-engine__soldier-blade.teaser: Top-tier shmups; the console was their paradise.
pc-engine__soldier-blade.detail: Top-tier vertical shmups; the PC Engine was a paradise for the genre. Fast, addictive, with an excellent system of weapons and power-ups. Soldier Blade even has caravan modes (timed score challenges). Mandatory stops for shooter fans.
pc-engine__soldier-blade.article:
There are shooters that grab you within the first ten seconds and do not let go until you finish — and **Soldier Blade** is exactly such a case. This vertical shmup from Hudson, on which the genre masters from **Compile** collaborated, represents the culmination of the famous Soldier series on the PC Engine and to this day counts as one of the most playable titles of its kind on the console.

At the heart of the game is a weapons and power-up system so intuitive you will learn it in a moment, yet so deep you will keep polishing it for hours. You collect three types of main fire, each of which gradually upgrades, and on top of that you have stashed „bombs“ at your disposal in the form of a temporary mighty attack that pulls you out of the worst situations. The pace is fast and clean, the game runs smoothly even in the moments when the screen is flooded with dozens of enemies and shots.

What sets Soldier Blade apart from the competition is its perfect balance. The game does not punish the player excessively, but neither does it rest on its laurels — the difficulty curve rises exactly as it should, and each level brings new visual motifs and enemy formations. The bosses are inventive and the fights against them have the right momentum.

An entirely separate chapter is the so-called **caravan modes** — time-limited challenges for the highest score, typically two or five minutes. This tradition carried enormous cultural weight in Japan: Hudson held competitions where players fought for the best possible result in a limited time, and Soldier Blade is designed directly for these contests. For lovers of the score chase it is a little treasure that offers endless replayability.

Within the Soldier line it is the title fans remember with the greatest love — it combines the technical maturity of the platform's later years with that unmistakable Compile touch for playability. If you ever wanted to understand why the PC Engine was a paradise for shooter fans, here you have the answer in concentrated form.

**Why play:** A superbly tuned shooter with an addictive weapons system and caravan modes for the score chase — a mandatory stop for every fan of the genre.

pc-engine__super-star-soldier.article:
Before Soldier Blade came, there was **Super Star Soldier** — and it was precisely this one that laid the foundations for why the Soldier series became a household name on the PC Engine. This vertical shooter continued the tradition of Hudson's shmups and demonstrated what snappy, readable and addictive action on a 16-bit console, adored by fans of the genre, should look like.

In gameplay Super Star Soldier sticks to the proven recipe but perfects it. You advance up the screen, collect power-ups and gradually build your ship into a flying fortress. The weapons system offers several types of fire that you switch between depending on the situation, and it is all held together by a smooth pace that gives no chance to catch your breath. Enemies arrive in well-designed waves and the bosses at the end of levels present just the right dose of challenge.

Technically it was a showcase of what the PC Engine could do — a large number of objects on screen, varied cosmic backgrounds and spectacular explosions. The console felt right at home in the shmup genre and Super Star Soldier was one of the titles that built this reputation.

Just as with the other games in the series, here too the spirit of the Japanese **caravan competitions** is present — time-limited challenges for the highest score that turn playing into almost a sporting discipline. It was precisely this philosophy of „one more try, this time it will be better“ that defined the whole genre, and Super Star Soldier embodies it in its pure form.

Today this game is more for connoisseurs and collectors than for a mass audience, but among shooter fans it holds a firm place. It is one of those titles that earned the platform its cult status — a fast, honest and endlessly replayable piece of classic.

**Why play:** A classic Hudson shooter with a smooth pace and the spirit of the caravan competitions — ideal for anyone who loves the chase for a high score.
pc-engine__super-star-soldier.teaser: Laid the foundations of the famous Soldier series before the acclaimed Soldier Blade arrived.

pc-engine__ys-book-i-and-ii.teaser: One of the first CD RPGs with voice acting and redbook music; a milestone.
pc-engine__ys-book-i-and-ii.detail: One of the first CD-ROM RPGs with voiced scenes, animated cutscenes and redbook (CD-quality) music — for 1989 a stunning leap that showcased the potential of the CD. A brisk „bump" action RPG with a phenomenal soundtrack. Historically pivotal and still excellent.
pc-engine__ys-book-i-and-ii.article:
Picture the year 1989 — and a game in which voiced characters speak to you through the speakers, animated scenes play out, and music of the quality you know from an audio CD plays in the background. For players of the era it must have felt like a revelation. **Ys Book I & II** in its CD-ROM version for the PC Engine rightfully went down in history as one of the titles that revealed the potential hidden within the new medium.

The foundation is made up of two games from the legendary series by the Japanese studio **Falcom**, brought to the PC Engine in collaboration with **Hudson**. It is a brisk action RPG built on the unmistakable „bump" combat system — you don't defeat enemies with an attack button, but by charging into them from the side or from behind. It may sound odd, but in practice the result is an incredibly fluid and fast combat that keeps up the pace even during the sprawling adventure of the hero Adol.

What made this version a milestone, however, was the presentation. Thanks to the capacity of the CD-ROM, players got voiced dialogue, animated cutscenes and, above all, a **redbook soundtrack** in CD quality — and the music of Ys ranks to this day among the most acclaimed video game soundtracks of all time. The energetic melodies underscoring the battles became iconic, and fans have returned to them for decades.

In the context of the era it was a staggering leap. While cartridge games on competing platforms were limited by size and by the sound of chip music, Ys Book I & II showed just how far the medium could advance. It is no exaggeration to say that this version helped kick-start the era of CD games and influenced how RPGs on consoles were viewed.

The beautiful thing is that the game holds up even today. The story of a journey after the mystery of the lost sacred books, the brisk gameplay and the timeless music make it a title played not just out of nostalgia, but for pure joy. The Ys series continues to this day, after all, and the original installments have seen a number of remakes and ports — but this CD version remains historically pivotal.

**Why play:** A historic milestone of the CD-ROM era with a timeless soundtrack and a brisk action RPG that is great even after more than three decades.

pc-engine__castlevania-rondo-of-blood.article:
Many Castlevania fans will tell you that the best classic whip game never officially came out in the West at the time of its creation — and they would have in mind precisely **Rondo of Blood**. This CD title for the PC Engine remained for many years a legend, whispered about only abroad, and today it ranks among the most revered installments of the entire series.

In gameplay terms it is the pinnacle form of the classic, linear Castlevania — that is, before the series turned toward the metroidvania structure. You control the vampire hunter Richter Belmont, cracking the iconic whip, collecting secondary weapons like holy water or throwing axes, and fighting your way through a series of beautifully designed levels to Dracula himself. The boss battles are memorable and the difficulty is honestly demanding, as befits a classic installment of the series.

What makes Rondo of Blood exceptional are the hidden paths and alternative levels, thanks to which the game has unexpected replayability. You'll even find captives who can be freed — including the playable character Maria, who offers a completely different style of play. Add to that the fantastic presentation made possible by the CD medium: animated scenes and an excellent arranged soundtrack in which the iconic melodies of the series ring out in full glory.

The visual side ranks among the best that was created on the PC Engine — detailed Gothic environments, fluid animation and an atmosphere that breathes horror romanticism. It's no wonder the game acquired an almost mythical status among collectors and fans.

The influence of Rondo of Blood is unmistakable: the character of Richter and the entire story backdrop became the foundation for the famous Symphony of the Night. Thanks to later remakes and ports, the game finally reached a wider audience as well, which understood why fans had spoken of it with such reverence for years.
