Because of their ties to the Dreamcast and its limited reach, both games remained something of a hidden treasure and today rank among the rare, collector-sought titles. For those who discover them, though, they're still one of the most refreshing takes on the fighter.

**Why play it:** For chaotic 3D arena fun for up to four players that still has few equals today.
dreamcast__power-stone-1-and-2.teaser: Capcom turns the static fighting stage into a full 3D arena full of chaos.

dreamcast__marvel-vs-capcom-2.detail: An insane crossover with 56 characters and 3v3 teams in an explosion of effects and super attacks. Long considered the pinnacle of „team-based" fighters; the competitive scene still plays it today. The Dreamcast version was the best home port.
dreamcast__marvel-vs-capcom-2.article:
Fifty-six characters, three-on-three teams and a screen so crammed with effects that at times you can't tell where you're standing — **Marvel vs. Capcom 2** is a celebration of the unbridled madness a fighting game can allow itself. And yet beneath that explosion of color pulses a surprisingly deep and competitive system.

The game from **Capcom** united heroes from the Marvel comics with icons from the studio's own franchises into a single colossal crossover. The three-on-three format, letting you swap characters in a flash, call teammates in for assist attacks and chain combos, gave the game incredible speed and depth. The fights resemble a colorful storm more than a classic round of a fighter.

It's precisely this blend of spectacle and tactical depth that made it a long-standing pinnacle of „team-based" fighters. Players kept discovering new combos, character synergies and strategies for years after release, and the competitive scene returns to it to this day, making it one of the most enduring tournament titles of its kind.

The Dreamcast version was the best home port at the time — faithfully bringing the arcade experience, including its smoothness and vast roster, straight into living rooms. For console owners it was a ticket into a world that otherwise lived mainly in the arcades.

The combination of casual spectacle and enormous mechanical depth makes Marvel vs. Capcom 2 a one-of-a-kind — a game equally enjoyed by a random button-masher and a seasoned tournament fighter hunting for the perfect combo.

**Why play it:** For an insane crossover of dozens of characters and a timeless fighting system that the competitive scene still loves today.
dreamcast__marvel-vs-capcom-2.teaser: 56 characters, 3-on-3 battles, and a screen overloaded with effects; crossover madness.

dreamcast__shenmue.article:
Few games were as ambitious in their day as **Shenmue**. Sega didn't take the path of fast action with it, but instead tried to create a living, breathing world in which time flows, the weather changes and people live by their own schedules — a vision whose scope outran much of what only arrived years later.

The game combines adventure with action elements and places enormous emphasis on atmosphere and detail. You stroll the streets, talk to the residents, examine objects, follow clues and gradually uncover a story driven by the hero's personal motivation. The pace is deliberately slower, betting on immersion in the environment rather than nonstop action.

It's precisely this striving for a believable world that makes Shenmue a milestone. Characters have their own daily routines; you can drop into an arcade, go shopping or just watch the town's life flow by. Action sequences then spice up the storytelling with combat scenes and hectic moments that break the calmer rhythm of the investigation.

Shenmue became synonymous with ambitious, so-called „immersive" gaming, and its influence on genres focused on open, believable worlds is cited to this day. Many elements we now take for granted — living NPCs, day cycles, small interactive details — were introduced here in a form players of the time had never seen.

Still, it was a title tightly bound to the fate of the Dreamcast, so its vision was fully enjoyed by a devoted minority rather than the masses. That's exactly what turned it into a cult legend, still talked about today as a game ahead of its time.

**Why play it:** For an uncommon immersion in a living world and ambitions that foreshadowed the future of open-world gaming experiences.
dreamcast__shenmue.teaser: An ambitious living world with its own weather and daily rhythm; ahead of its time.

dreamcast__skies-of-arcadia.detail: An optimistic JRPG about sky pirates in a floating world, with the discovery of new territories and airship battles. Charismatic characters and an adventurous tone (rare in a genre full of darkness). Highly acclaimed but, due to the Dreamcast's failure, little-played — cult status.
dreamcast__skies-of-arcadia.article:
In a genre that at the time so often bet on darkness and melancholy, **Skies of Arcadia** blew in like a gust of fresh wind beneath an airship's sails. This optimistic JRPG about sky pirates wagered on adventure, exploration and an indomitable zest for life — and won over the heart of everyone who gave it a chance.

The game from **Overworks** under Sega's wing takes you into a floating world divided into aerial continents, between which you travel aboard your own airship. Exploring uncharted territories, seeking hidden islands and uncovering treasures gives the game an air of pure exploration that many other JRPGs lacked. The world literally invites you to head over the horizon.

Battles take place on two levels. Classic turn-based fights with your characters are complemented by grand **airship** clashes, where entire flying vessels face off in a duel of cannons and maneuvers. This duality gives the combat system its edge and underlines the game's pirate theme.

Most of all, though, Skies of Arcadia lives through its characters and tone. A charismatic crew, adventurous humor and infectious optimism create an atmosphere rare in the genre. Instead of a brooding hero, you're pulling a story along with a crew you'll be delighted to spend dozens of hours with.

Critics prized the game highly, but due to the Dreamcast's commercial failure relatively few players got to try it. From that contradiction — high quality and small reach — grew its cult status as a game connoisseurs recommend as a hidden gem that deserves far more attention.

**Why play it:** For adventurous optimism, exploring a world in the clouds and airship battles — a JRPG that simply roots for the joy of the journey.
dreamcast__skies-of-arcadia.teaser: An optimistic JRPG about sky pirates; a refreshing counterpoint to the dark JRPGs of its time.

dreamcast__grandia-ii.detail: Famous for one of the best combat systems in the genre — a combination of turns and positioning on a timeline, where you can interrupt an enemy's attack (cancel/counter). Brisk and visually pleasing. A must for fans of JRPG combat.
dreamcast__grandia-ii.article:
If what you always loved most about JRPGs was the combat, **Grandia II** is a game that can grip you from the very first encounter. This sequel to a beloved series became famous for one of the best combat systems the genre has offered — so clever and dynamic that fans still point to it today.

The magic lies in linking turn-based strategy with positioning on a **timeline**. The actions of your characters and enemies advance along a gauge, so it's not just about which attack you choose, but also exactly when it lands. A key element is the ability to **interrupt** an enemy's attack the moment it's about to strike — a well-timed hit cancels the opponent's move, knocks them back down the gauge and turns the tide of battle in your favor.

This mechanic adds a layer of rhythm and anticipation to combat that static turn-based systems don't offer. You watch the gauge, plan your movement around the battlefield and the timing of spells and hits, so every fight turns into a little tactical puzzle where every moment matters.

Alongside its polished combat, Grandia II is also a visually pleasing and brisk game from **Game Arts**. The pace flows, the environments are varied and the overall experience doesn't hold the player up with needless delays, making the play a smooth and satisfying ride.

Grandia II may not have made a name for itself with mass sales, but among JRPG connoisseurs it earned a firm place thanks to the quality of its combat. It received re-releases on other platforms, so its combat system could be discovered by later generations of players looking for something more than plain hammering of the attack button.

**Why play it:** For one of the best and most tactical combat systems in JRPG history — a must for lovers of turn-based battles.
dreamcast__grandia-ii.teaser: One of the best battle systems in any JRPG; turn-based action on a timeline bar.

dreamcast__resident-evil-code-veronica.article:
When the Dreamcast received a major new Resident Evil chapter exclusively in 2000, it was a huge asset for Sega – the series that stood at the birth of the entire survival-horror genre abandoned fixed, pre-rendered backdrops for the first time and built its whole world from full-fledged 3D polygons. **Code Veronica** thus looked dramatically different from the previous PlayStation installments: the camera could move smoothly, the environments breathed with depth and, thanks to the Dreamcast's power, the game felt a generation ahead.

Storywise it follows on from the events of the first installments and tracks **Claire Redfield**, who's searching for her brother Chris. From a prison island controlled by the Umbrella corporation she makes her way to a snowbound Antarctic base, and later you take the controls of Chris himself. The storytelling here is more ambitious than before – the series fully develops the theme of the Ashford family and pits you face to face with one of the most theatrical villains of the entire franchise.

In gameplay it stays true to the proven recipe: limited ammunition and healing items, tank controls, puzzles involving the collection of keys and objects, and the permanent feeling that every bullet is precious. That very tension between exploration and fear of the next corner made Resident Evil such an addictive experience. The limited-capacity inventory forces you to think about what to carry and what to leave in the chest, and backtracking becomes a little logic game in itself.

The move to real 3D also brought new possibilities for horror direction. A freely tilting camera could reveal a threat at an unexpected moment, and the designers played with light and shadow in ways static backdrops didn't allow. The game was at the same time one of the flagship titles meant to demonstrate what the Dreamcast could do as hardware.

Today **Code Veronica** is remembered as one of the key installments of the series, which later came out in an expanded version and reached other platforms, so players outside the Dreamcast community got to enjoy it too. For fans of the franchise it represents an important link between the classic era and the later direction of Resident Evil.

**Why play it:** Classic survival horror at the moment the series fully transitioned to 3D for the first time – tense atmosphere, ammo conservation and a theatrical story that belongs in the Resident Evil canon.
dreamcast__resident-evil-code-veronica.teaser: The first Resident Evil with fully 3D environments instead of pre-rendered backgrounds.

dreamcast__ikaruga.detail: The spiritual successor to Radiant Silvergun and perhaps the most revered modern shmup. A brilliant polarity mechanic: you switch your ship between black and white, absorb bullets of your own color and destroy enemies with the opposite one — turning bullet-hell into almost a logic game. Treasure mastery.
dreamcast__ikaruga.article:
There's a handful of games that fans speak of in a hushed, almost sacred tone – and **Ikaruga** is one of them. This vertical shooter from the legendary **Treasure** studio is the spiritual successor to the revered Radiant Silvergun and to this day counts as one of the most respected modern shmups of all. It first appeared as an arcade game in 2001, then came to the Dreamcast in 2002.

At the core of the whole experience is a brilliant polarity mechanic. Your ship switches between two states – black and white – and this choice changes absolutely everything. Bullets of your own color don't harm you; on the contrary, you absorb them and charge up a powerful attack, while enemies of the opposite color take double damage. What would elsewhere be a chaotic bullet-hell thus becomes a game that resembles a logic puzzle in real time.

Each screen is a carefully designed sequence you learn to read, anticipate and master. The game also rewards chaining enemies in trios of the same color with bonus score, which turns the pursuit of a high score into a discipline of its own that players dig into for years. Ikaruga isn't so much about reflexes as about rhythm, planning and almost meditative focus.

Visually it's a clean, elegant game where the contrast of black and white isn't just aesthetics but the very game principle. Treasure was famous for building action around a single idea taken to perfection, and Ikaruga is perhaps the best proof of that approach – minimalist in its basic idea, infinitely deep in execution.

That's exactly why the game built a cult standing and over the years appeared on other platforms too, where a new generation of players found it. For the shmup community it remains a kind of benchmark against which other games of the genre are measured.

**Why play it:** A masterful shmup from Treasure, where the polarity mechanic transforms bullet-hell into an elegant puzzle – one of the deepest and most respected representatives of the genre.
dreamcast__ikaruga.teaser: The spiritual successor to Radiant Silvergun from Treasure; one of the most acclaimed shmups ever made.

dreamcast__bangai-o.detail: A Treasure action game where you pilot a mech firing in all directions and unleash giant „smart bomb" attacks (the more bullets around you, the stronger) — an explosion of hundreds of projectiles on screen. Chaotic, inventive, addictive.
dreamcast__bangai-o.article:
If you've ever wished to see hundreds of explosions on screen at once and still feel like it makes sense, **Bangai-O** from **Treasure** is exactly that experience. This action shooter for the Dreamcast from 1999 puts you in a robotic mech that spews bullets in every direction at once and fills the screen with such a density of projectiles that your eyes can barely keep up.

The heart of the game is a „smart bomb"-style mega-attack whose power depends on how many enemy bullets are around you at that moment. The greater the risk you take and the more you let yourself be surrounded by fire, the more devastating the salvo you can then unleash. This mechanic actively pushes you into danger and flips the usual logic of shooters on its head – instead of dodging, you actually want to throw yourself into the thickest fire.

The levels are sprawling and full of enemies, so the action constantly escalates into chaotic shootouts where the screen literally lights up with explosions. Yet behind all that visual maelstrom stands Treasure's typically inventive design, which rewards the player for boldness and improvisation. It's a fast, intense and surprisingly addictive game.

Treasure built a reputation as a studio that doesn't make boring things, and Bangai-O is further evidence of that – it combines action, a touch of tactics and a sense of exaggeration into a package that doesn't take itself entirely seriously but plays superbly. It's one of those titles that defined the quirky identity of the Dreamcast library.

Thanks to its originality and insane density of action, Bangai-O found devoted fans and became another of the cult pieces that made retro players so fond of the Dreamcast. It's a game you only need to switch on for a few minutes to know at once that you're not playing anything ordinary.

**Why play it:** A crazy action shooter from Treasure where the more bullets around you, the more devastating the counterattack – chaotic, inventive and instantly addictive.
dreamcast__bangai-o.teaser: Hundreds of explosions on screen and mechs spraying projectiles in every direction, from Treasure.

dreamcast__chuchu-rocket.detail: A fast puzzle where you use arrows to direct mice into rockets and avoid cats. It was the first online-playable console game in Europe (the Dreamcast had a built-in modem). Insane multiplayer chaos; a clever single-player puzzle mode.
dreamcast__chuchu-rocket.article:
Few games pair an adorable look with such merciless chaos as **ChuChu Rocket!** from **Sonic Team**. This brisk puzzle from 1999 sets you a seemingly simple task: use directional arrows to guide swarms of mice into rockets while protecting them from cats, which move across the same grid with bloodthirsty simplicity.

In the single-player part it's a clever logic game where you place a limited number of arrows so the mice find their way to the goal and the cats end up out of the picture. The solutions require foresight and an understanding of how all the little creatures move across the board at once. It's an elegant, gradually tangling puzzle that rewards careful thinking about every move.

But ChuChu Rocket became legendary thanks to its multiplayer. With four players, the tranquil puzzle turns into a frenzied battle where you sabotage each other, steal one another's mice and turn your opponents' own arrows against them. The pace is merciless and the winner changes within seconds – it's exactly the kind of game that provokes both laughter and shouting in a single room.

The title also holds extraordinary historical significance. The Dreamcast was the first console with a built-in modem, and ChuChu Rocket! went down as one of the first online-playable console games in Europe. At a time when networked play on consoles was still exotic, it was a small technological miracle and proof that Sega meant the future seriously.

Thanks to the combination of an accessible look, a clever single-player and insane multiplayer, ChuChu Rocket! remains one of the most beloved and most fondly remembered pieces in the Dreamcast library – a game that can still entertain to this day.

**Why play it:** An adorable but merciless puzzle with legendarily chaotic multiplayer and a place in history as one of the first online console games in Europe.
dreamcast__chuchu-rocket.teaser: Adorable chaos from Sonic Team; use arrows to guide mice into rockets while dodging cats.

dreamcast__rez.detail: A synesthetic rail shooter where every hit and action generates music and visuals — the act of playing itself composes an electronic track. Inspired by abstract art (Kandinsky) and the idea of synesthesia. An original that was ahead of its time; influential, it received a VR remake (Rez Infinite).
dreamcast__rez.article:
Some games you want to play, others you want to feel – and **Rez** clearly belongs to the second group. This synesthetic rail shooter from 2001 by **United Game Artists**, led by the visionary **Tetsuya Mizuguchi**, doesn't ask only about your reflexes but tries to link sight, hearing and touch into a single flowing stream of sensation.

The principle is simple at first glance: you move a reticle across the screen, target enemies and fire off salvos of shots. The magic, though, lies in the fact that every action, every hit and every explosion generates sound and a visual effect in rhythm with the music. As you progress through the levels you literally compose an electronic track through your play – the better and more rhythmically you play, the richer and more satisfying the resulting wall of sound and image.

The visual side draws on abstract art, and Mizuguchi made no secret of his inspiration from the painter **Kandinsky** and the very idea of synesthesia, the blending of the senses. The world of Rez is built from wireframe models, glowing points and geometric shapes that pulse to the music and draw you into an almost trance-like state. It's an experience that eludes the usual categories and feels more like an interactive work of art.

At the time of its release Rez was significantly ahead of its time and became one of those titles referenced whenever the conversation turns to games as art. Its influence is felt across a whole wave of later rhythm and audiovisual games.

Its lasting significance is attested by the fact that much later it received a reworked version, **Rez Infinite**, with virtual-reality support that carried the original vision into an environment it seemed made for from the start. But on the Dreamcast this whole remarkable journey began.

**Why play it:** A synesthetic shooter where you compose both music and visuals through your play – a timeless, artistically ambitious work that was ahead of its time and inspired a whole wave of followers.
dreamcast__rez.teaser: Tetsuya Mizuguchi's synesthetic rail shooter; a game you feel more than play.

dreamcast__space-channel-5.detail: A rhythm game where reporter Ulala saves the world through dance (you repeat movement sequences Simon-says style) in a retro-futuristic 60s sci-fi setting. Michael Jackson makes a cameo as a character. Stylish, quirky, cult.
dreamcast__space-channel-5.article:
Save the world by dancing? In **Space Channel 5** it's the most natural thing under the sun. This 1999 rhythm game from **United Game Artists** slips you into the pink hair of reporter **Ulala**, who faces an alien invasion in the most stylish way imaginable — through precise dance sequences in the spirit of Simon says.

The gameplay is built on repeating commands. Enemies perform a string of moves and directions, and you have to echo them back in the right rhythm and order. As you progress, the sequences grow longer and faster, so what begins as playful dancing turns into an increasingly demanding test of focus and timing. Every duel you pull off is a little performance that makes you want to bounce right along.

Where Space Channel 5 truly stands out, though, is its inimitable atmosphere. The game is wrapped in a retro-futuristic sci-fi style cut straight from the 1960s' vision of what the future would look like — pastel colors, cosmic stations, a fashion show in zero gravity. It's a feast for both eyes and ears, one with its own distinctive personality.

A special mention goes to the fact that the game features a cameo by **Michael Jackson** himself, who appears as a character. Given his relationship with dance and music, it was an entirely logical and flattering tribute to the very style the whole game is built on.

Space Channel 5 was never a mass hit, but it built a solid cult following and to this day counts as one of the most distinctive and charismatic titles the Dreamcast had to offer. It's a game that breathes joy and style in every single frame.

**Why play it:** A stylish rhythm game full of retro-futuristic charm where you fend off aliens with dance — a quirky, charismatic cult favorite with a Michael Jackson cameo.
dreamcast__space-channel-5.teaser: Rhythmic dance moves save the world; Ulala faces an invasion in a Simon Says style.

dreamcast__crazy-taxi-2.article:
Hop in, buckle up and hold on tight — **Crazy Taxi 2** once again puts you behind the wheel of the craziest cab in town and sends you into the streets with a single goal: get your fares where they want to go, as fast and as stylishly as possible. This sequel to the arcade hit on the Dreamcast keeps everything that made the original such a blast and adds a few tricks of its own.

The foundation stays unchanged and just as addictive. You pick up passengers, follow the arrow to their destination, and try to weave through dense traffic before time runs out. You rack up points for speed, risky maneuvers and flashy driving, so the game constantly pushes you to ride the edge — leaping over guardrails, drifting around corners and slipping between cars at the last second.

The arcade pedigree shows at every turn. The pace is brisk, the controls immediately intuitive, and the whole design is built on quick doses of adrenaline and the chase for a high score. It's exactly the kind of game you fire up for five minutes and before you know it, it's midnight and you're still trying to beat your record.

Crazy Taxi 2 belongs to that wave of arcade conversions that earned the Dreamcast its reputation as the console that brought the arcade to life right in your living room. Sega was porting its arcade prowess to home hardware back then, and Crazy Taxi was one of the flagship brands of that approach.

For fans of carefree, fast and downright fun driving without needless complications, the Crazy Taxi series remains a benchmark of the genre. The second installment is another serving of that pure, unbridled arcade joy.

**Why play it:** Pure arcade joy behind the wheel — a fast, crazy chase for score and time, ideal for short but endlessly replayable runs.
dreamcast__crazy-taxi-2.teaser: The sequel to the arcade hit; the same crazy driving, with a few new tricks on top.

dreamcast__capcom-vs-snk-2.detail: The culmination of a crossover between two fighting-game giants, with 48 characters and a system of six "grooves" (each mimicking the mechanics of a different series). Deep, finely tuned; a competitive classic.
dreamcast__capcom-vs-snk-2.article:
When the two biggest rivals in the fighting genre come together on one screen, you get something like **Capcom vs. SNK 2** — the culmination of a crossover saga in which the worlds of Capcom and SNK clash in one grand battle. This 2001 fighter from **Capcom** is a celebration of decades of both brands' history crammed into a single loaded game.

The roster boasts a respectable **48 characters** from both companies' legendary series — from Ryu and Chun-Li to Terry Bogard and other icons. The variety is enormous, and fans can finally pit against each other heroes who otherwise never met, which was always the main draw of the entire crossover line.

What gives the game its real depth, however, is the system of six so-called **grooves**. Each one mimics the mechanics of a different famous series, so you choose not only your characters but also your overall fighting style — a different groove means different options for defense, super attacks and energy management. This layer offers a huge number of combinations and turns the game into an exceptionally versatile battlefield where every decision matters.

It's precisely this depth and careful balancing that put Capcom vs. SNK 2 among the competitive classics players keep returning to for years. It's not a game you'll figure out in an afternoon — it rewards study, practice and an understanding of the individual systems.

The Dreamcast was an ideal home for 2D and hybrid fighters, and Capcom vs. SNK 2 is one of the titles that confirm that reputation. For anyone who loves fighters with a big roster and a deep system, it's an essential piece of genre history.

**Why play it:** A massive crossover with 48 characters and six fighting styles that delivers both depth and variety — a competitive classic uniting the two biggest names in fighting games.
dreamcast__capcom-vs-snk-2.teaser: 48 characters from two legendary companies in one jam-packed crossover fighter.

dreamcast__street-fighter-iii-3rd-strike.detail: Two of the most beautiful and finely tuned 2D fighters ever, in perfect ports on the Dreamcast. 3rd Strike is famous for its parry system (the legendary Daigo moment), Garou for its "Just Defend" mechanic and gorgeous animation. Peaks of the 2D genre.
dreamcast__street-fighter-iii-3rd-strike.article:
If there's a peak that 2D fighters spent decades striving toward, then **Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike** embodies it perhaps more purely than any other. On the Dreamcast, this game reached households in a port that managed to carry over practically all the beauty and fluidity of the arcade original, making it one of the most faithful conversions of its time.

Visually, it's one of the most gorgeous 2D games ever made. The character animation is admirably rich and fluid, every strike and movement carrying its own weight and personality. Capcom took the hand-drawn fighter to an absolute peak here, and the result hasn't aged a day — many consider it the aesthetic pinnacle of the entire genre.

In terms of gameplay, 3rd Strike is best known for its **parry system**. Instead of passive blocking, you can deflect a strike with a precise movement at just the right moment, which completely changes the dynamic of the duels and raises the skill ceiling to dizzying heights. It was this very mechanic that gave rise to perhaps the most famous moment in fighting-game history — the legendary comeback by player Daigo, still talked about to this day.

This depth means 3rd Strike isn't about memorizing a few combos, but about reading your opponent, timing and risk. Every match unfolds like a game of chess at high speed, where a single well-executed parry can turn a losing duel into victory. No wonder the game maintained a solid competitive scene for many years.

On the Dreamcast, which was practically made for 2D fighters, 3rd Strike represents one of the absolute peaks of the library. For lovers of the genre it's a mandatory stop — a game you have to experience to understand just how far 2D fighters were able to go.

**Why play it:** One of the most beautiful and deepest 2D fighters ever, renowned for its parry system and legendary moments — a peak of the genre in an excellent Dreamcast port.
dreamcast__street-fighter-iii-3rd-strike.teaser: The pinnacle of 2D fighting games; a port that faithfully carried over the beauty and fluidity of the arcade original.

dreamcast__garou-mark-of-wolves.article:
There are games that stand at the end of an era as its perfect crowning achievement — and **Garou: Mark of the Wolves** is exactly such a case. This fighter from SNK is regarded by connoisseurs as one of the best and most beautiful 2D fighters ever created, and on the Dreamcast it found a home that fully matched its qualities.

Garou introduces a new generation of fighters and, with them, a fresh, carefully balanced combat system. The character animation ranks among the finest the 2D genre has offered — fluid, expressive and full of personality, with backgrounds and an art style that lend the game an unmistakable atmosphere. It's a visual feast that reveals the mastery of SNK's creators.

The gameplay core rests on the **Just Defend** mechanic. If you block an opponent's strike at the precise moment, you take no damage, restore a bit of energy and gain the upper hand for a counterattack. This mechanic rewards courage and perfect timing and gives the duels exceptional depth — just like related systems in other top-tier fighters, it pushes the skill ceiling very high.

The result is a game that's approachable at first glance yet hides enormous room for mastery. The duels are fast, clean and full of tactical decisions, so Garou is among the titles the competitive community returns to again and again, discovering new layers within it.

On the Dreamcast, which became a refuge for the top 2D fighters of its era, Garou: Mark of the Wolves stands as one of the absolute gems. For fans of the genre it's an essential title — an elegant farewell to SNK's classic era and proof that 2D fighters could age gracefully.

**Why play it:** One of SNK's most beautiful and finely tuned 2D fighters, with the Just Defend mechanic — an elegant peak of the genre that deservedly holds its cult status.
dreamcast__garou-mark-of-wolves.teaser: One of the most beautiful 2D fighting games ever made, a perfect close to one era of SNK.

dreamcast__virtua-tennis.detail: Arcade tennis perfected — simple controls, addictive pace and superb multiplayer. A "Tour" mode with minigames. The defining tennis game of its era.
dreamcast__virtua-tennis.article:
Just a few seconds with the controller and you'll understand why **Virtua Tennis** still holds its reputation as the purest tennis game the arcades ever spat out. No lengthy tutorials, no menus full of statistics — just the ball, the court and an instant plunge into a game that's hard to walk away from.

Sega AM3, led by Mie Kumagai, showed here what a perfectly tuned arcade feel looks like. The controls rest on just two buttons — topspin and lob — but the depth emerges from timing, positioning and reading your opponent. The game runs on the NAOMI hardware, which shares its architecture with the Dreamcast, so the 2000 home port was practically a lossless transfer of the arcade cabinet into the living room. The fluidity and pace felt revolutionary.

The heart of the home version, however, is the **World Circuit (Tour)** mode, which enriched the tennis with a career woven through with bizarre minigames. You'd knock down bowling pins with your serve, hit targets, smash giant balls — training disciplines that became just as addictive as the matches themselves. It was this layer that turned a short arcade ride into a game worth dozens of hours.

Where **Virtua Tennis** truly shines is multiplayer. Four-player doubles on a single console is one of the legendary social experiences of the era — immediately understandable to anyone, yet tactical enough to spark dramatic rallies and bitter defeats by a single point. It's the kind of game people shout over.

The title's influence on the genre was fundamental: it set the bar for arcade tennis and defined how such a game should look and play. The series continued with a string of installments, and Virtua Tennis became one of the pillars on which the Dreamcast built its reputation as a console of top-tier arcade conversions.

**Why play it:** The purest and most addictive arcade tennis of its era, one that reliably gets a whole room going around a single console.
dreamcast__virtua-tennis.teaser: The purest arcade tennis; just two buttons and instant pick-up-and-play.

dreamcast__samba-de-amigo.detail: A rhythm game originally played with maracas controllers (a different experience on emulation/pad), where you shake and position them in time with Latino hits. Energetic party fun; iconic for the Dreamcast.
dreamcast__samba-de-amigo.article:
Maracas in hand, a Latino rhythm in the speakers and a room full of people laughing like crazy — **Samba de Amigo** is joy distilled into game form. This game never pretended to be anything more than a pure party explosion, and that's exactly why it stuck in memory.

It originally appeared as an arcade cabinet with a pair of maraca-shaped motion controllers, complete with sensors detecting the height at which you shake them. The principle is brilliantly simple: you hit the rhythm and position your hands into three levels — up, middle, down — precisely according to the markers on screen. On emulation or a classic pad the experience is naturally different, since part of the magic lies precisely in the physical waving, but the rhythmic essence remains.

Behind the game stands **Sonic Team**, the studio that otherwise spun the blue hedgehog, and that playful, colorful energy is felt in every pixel. The soundtrack builds on catchy Latino hits and covers, the monkey Amigo grins from the screen, and the whole presentation bursts with such optimism that it's almost impossible not to start smiling.

On the Dreamcast, **Samba de Amigo** became one of the console's iconic calling cards — proof that Sega wasn't afraid to experiment with alternative controls long before motion controllers went mainstream. It was a showcase game, the one you'd put on for a visitor so they'd grasp what the Dreamcast could do.

Today it's a title that works best in company — alone in front of the screen it loses half its magic, but once a group gathers, it transforms into an unforgettable show. It's the pure joy of play, without ambition and without inhibition.

**Why play it:** Indestructible party fun with a Latino rhythm that gets any gathering going and reminds you why the Dreamcast was such a bold console.
dreamcast__samba-de-amigo.teaser: Maracas in hand and Latin rhythm; a pure party explosion with no grand ambitions.

dreamcast__sega-bass-fishing.article:
Fishing as an adrenaline sport? At first glance a contradiction — and yet **Sega Bass Fishing** pulled off exactly that, turning a patient hobby into brisk arcade fun that has your heart pounding with every bite.

The game falls into that specific Sega school of arcade simulations, where realism gives way to immediate, comprehensible enjoyment. Instead of hours waiting over a still surface, it's all about quick reactions here: cast, hook at the right moment and then wrestle a fish that thrashes, changes direction and tries to break free. The line has its tension, the rod its limit, and you learn to feel when to give and when to reel in.

On the Dreamcast, the game was paired with a fishing controller in the shape of a reel, which added a physical dimension to the experience — you'd guide the lure with movement and feel the reel's spin in your own hand. But the principle works with a classic pad too, keeping its brisk, lightly casual character.

The platform context matters here: the Dreamcast was a console that loved bringing arcade cabinets straight into the living room, and fishing in this rendition fit perfectly into the philosophy of instantly graspable fun. You don't need to know any rules — you sit down and within a minute you're fishing.

It's a title that best captures why Sega had the reputation back then of a creator of unexpectedly addictive games from non-gaming subjects. Beneath the undemanding surface hides a surprisingly satisfying loop of catching, upgrading and beating your own records.

**Why play it:** Brisk arcade fishing that turns a patient hobby into unexpectedly tense and addictive fun for a few minutes or a whole evening.
dreamcast__sega-bass-fishing.teaser: Fishing turned into an adrenaline-fueled arcade sport with snappy reactions.

dreamcast__house-of-dead-2.article:
Zombies emerge from the darkness, you raise your light gun and that unmistakable dance begins — **The House of the Dead 2** is the essence of the arcade light-gun shooter in its purest, bloodiest form.

The House of the Dead series was among the flagship arcade experiences of the late nineties, and the second installment pushed the formula to its peak: you advance along a predetermined path full of the undead, aiming, shooting and rescuing ambushed civilians, while every miss or hit on an innocent costs you precious points or health. The genre rests on reflexes, precision and pressure that never lets up.

On the Dreamcast the game was paired with a light gun, thanks to which the home port's experience strikingly resembled the arcade — you'd aim directly at the screen and the game turned into an intense physical battle against waves of enemies. Without the gun, on a pad or emulation, part of the magic naturally fades, but the pace and atmosphere remain.

An inseparable part of the legend is also the unforgettably overacted voice lines and the B-movie horror atmosphere, which turned the game into an object of loving cult status. This imperfection eventually became a trademark — fans quote the dialogue to this day.

The series' influence was considerable: it helped define what a modern rail shooter looks like, and its legacy lived on in sequels and later adaptations on other platforms. On the Dreamcast it was yet another proof that the console was a paradise for faithful arcade conversions.

**Why play it:** Pure, addictive light-gun action with B-movie horror flavor, which on the Dreamcast best showed the magic of arcade shooters at home.
dreamcast__house-of-dead-2.teaser: The essence of the arcade light-gun shooter; zombies, a pistol, and an unmistakable rhythm.

dreamcast__dead-or-alive-2.detail: A 3D fighter emphasizing a fast counter system (hold) and interactive multi-level arenas (you knock opponents off heights). Visually top-tier for its time. Tomonobu Itagaki.
dreamcast__dead-or-alive-2.article:
The fight neither begins nor ends on a flat floor — in **Dead or Alive 2** your opponent kicks you off a balcony, you fly a level down and the battle continues amid showering sparks. This game turned the arena from a backdrop into an active player.

**Team Ninja**, led by Tomonobu Itagaki, built the combat system on an elegant trio of strike–grab–throw, complemented by the famous **counter (hold) system**. Instead of blocking, you bet on prediction here: if you correctly read the type of incoming strike and react in time, you turn your opponent's force against them. This produces fast, psychologically tense exchanges where every hesitation is punished and reading your adversary is rewarded.

Visually it was one of the prettiest games of its time. Fluid animation, detailed characters and above all the multi-level, interactive arenas you fly through across several floors — knocking opponents off heights became the series' hallmark and gave the duels a dynamism its contemporary rivals didn't have.

The game first appeared in the arcade in 1999, and the home version for the Dreamcast (2000) delivered a faithful, technically impressive port that ranked among the console's visual showcases. For many players it was their first contact with the series in full glory.

**Dead or Alive 2** fundamentally shaped the direction of the entire brand and set out its identity: speed, visual gloss and a counter system based on risk and reward. It made Tecmo and Team Ninja a respected name among fighting-game creators.

**Why play it:** A fast, visually dazzling 3D fighter with a brilliant counter system and multi-level arenas that defined the identity of the entire series.
dreamcast__dead-or-alive-2.teaser: Team Ninja turns the arena into an active participant; battles crash through balconies and floors.

dreamcast__sword-of-berserk-guts-rage.article:
A giant sword sweeping through throngs of enemies, blood spraying across the screen and a dark, bleak atmosphere — **Sword of the Berserk: Guts' Rage** brought the harsh world of the Berserk manga straight to the Dreamcast, and it spared none of the rawness.

The game is an action hack-and-slash in which you take on the role of Guts, a warrior with a superhumanly large blade, cutting your way through waves of foes in a series of brutal clashes. The emphasis lies on a fast, bloody combat system where massive sweeping attacks mow down hordes of enemies at once and where a raw satisfaction arrives with every hit. The pace is uncompromising, the atmosphere gloomy.

What sets the title apart is its close bond with the source material. Between the action passages, the game tells its story through extensive dialogue and animated sequences, so it works as an interactive expansion of Kentaro Miura's dark world. For fans of the series it was a chance to experience Berserk's atmosphere with their own hands.

On the Dreamcast the game represented one of the few attempts to bring a popular manga into action form on this platform, thus rounding out the console's diverse library with a title of a distinctly adult, brutal tone that wasn't for everyone.

Thanks to its faithfulness to the source and its uncompromising action, the game found its audience among Berserk fans and lovers of raw hack-and-slash experiences alike, those seeking something darker than the mainstream of the time.

**Why play it:** A brutal, atmospheric hack-and-slash ride faithful to the dark world of Berserk, ideal for fans of the source and lovers of raw action alike.
dreamcast__sword-of-berserk-guts-rage.teaser: A bloody carve-up based on the dark manga Berserk, starring the giant sword Dragonslayer.

dreamcast__cannon-spike.detail: A twin-stick arena shooter with Capcom stars (Mega Man, Cammy, Charlie) in anime style. Fast, intense arcade action. Rare and sought-after.
dreamcast__cannon-spike.article:
Cammy, Charlie and Mega Man in one arena where bullets hover from all sides and anime style bursts from every frame — **Cannon Spike** is a crossover madness that only makes sense thanks to how great it plays.

The title arose from a collaboration between **Capcom** and the studio **Psikyo**, masters of arcade shooters, and the result is fast twin-stick arena action. You move in one direction and aim and shoot in another, while the screen floods with enemies and their projectiles. The pace is merciless and demands constant movement, weaving between salvos and timed attacks.

The biggest draw is the cast of characters made up of Capcom stars — a fighter on roller skates, familiar faces from Street Fighter and Mega Man himself — all rendered in brisk anime stylization. This mix gives the game the air of a fan celebration and sets it apart from other arena shooters of its time.

On the Dreamcast, **Cannon Spike** fit right in among the titles that benefited from the console being a refuge for arcade action. It was a niche, purely player-focused affair — short, intense and designed for repeated runs in pursuit of a higher score.

It's precisely because of its marginality and limited print run that the game gradually became a sought-after and rare collector's item. For connoisseurs of arcade action and lovers of Capcom crossovers it remains a small, sharply honed gem in the Dreamcast library.

**Why play it:** Fast twin-stick arena action with Capcom stars in anime style — short, intense and today a sought-after rarity for fans of the genre.
dreamcast__cannon-spike.teaser: A wild crossover between Capcom and Psikyo — Cammy, Mega Man, and Charlie all in a twin-stick arena.

dreamcast__mars-matrix.detail: A trio of acclaimed shmups from the late Dreamcast era, when the console became a haven for the genre (after the death of the arcades and the Saturn). Mars Matrix is bullet hell, Under Defeat is helicopter action, and Border Down is a strategic horizontal shmup. Treasures for genre connoisseurs; pricey today.
dreamcast__mars-matrix.article:
A screen drowned in a curtain of enemy fire, and somewhere among it you hunt for that one safe gap — **Mars Matrix** is bullet hell in its purest form, a game that tests your reflexes and your nerves down to the last pixel.

The title was created in collaboration between the studios **Takumi** and **G.rev** and earned its place among the prized shmups of the late Dreamcast era. As the arcades declined at the turn of the millennium and the Sega Saturn bowed out, this very console became an unexpected refuge for the genre of vertical and horizontal shooters — and Mars Matrix stands among its flagship representatives.

The game is built on intense dodging of dense projectile patterns, complemented by its own mechanics of absorbing and returning enemy fire. Scoring is a religion here: every run is a chase for perfection, for a higher number, and for mastering patterns that look impassable at first glance. It is a genre for the patient and for those who love memorization and honing their skills.

Together with titles like Under Defeat and Border Down, **Mars Matrix** forms a trio for which collectors still hunt down Dreamcast shmups to this day. These games were released in limited print runs and today rank among the pricey, sought-after pieces whose value on the collector's market climbs high.

For genre connoisseurs it is a treasure — proof that in its final years the Dreamcast hosted one of the best shmup collections of its generation, despite the fact that the console was already commercially on the wane.

**Why play:** A merciless bullet hell with its own fire-absorbing mechanics, one of the jewels of the Dreamcast shmup era for aficionados of the score chase.
dreamcast__mars-matrix.teaser: Bullet hell in its purest form from Takumi and G.rev; a screen drowning in enemy fire.

dreamcast__under-defeat.article:
The rotor slices the air, a lavishly modeled battlefield spreads out below you, and you weave between the gunfire — **Under Defeat** took the classic vertical shooter and wrapped it in a wartime atmosphere the genre never expected.

The game belongs to the group of prized shmups of the late Dreamcast era, when the console became the genre's natural home after the departure of the arcades and the Saturn. Instead of abstract spaceships, here you pilot a combat helicopter over realistically styled battlefields, which gives the game a more tangible, almost cinematic feel.

Its signature mechanic is directional fire: your shots tilt according to how you move, so positioning and the timing of your attacks gain tactical depth. It is not just about dodging — it is about reading space, angles, and eliminating enemies efficiently at the right moment. The pace is more deliberate and thoughtful than in frantic bullet hell shooters.

The visuals bank on atmosphere — smoke, explosions, and detailed backdrops evoke real wartime chaos and round out the distinctive character that sets **Under Defeat** apart from other titles in the genre. It is a game with a mood, not just reflexes.

Together with Mars Matrix and Border Down it forms one of the trio of Dreamcast shmups that collectors still seek out today and for which high sums are paid due to their limited print runs. For lovers of the genre it is a little treasure of the late Dreamcast.

**Why play:** An atmospheric helicopter shooter with clever directional fire and a wartime feel, one of the sought-after shmup jewels of the Dreamcast.
dreamcast__under-defeat.teaser: A vertical shmup with a war atmosphere; instead of a spaceship, you pilot a combat helicopter.

dreamcast__border-down.article:
The color of the screen's border tells you how close you are to death — **Border Down** built its entire identity on a brilliantly simple idea that turned failure from a punishment into part of the strategy.

The title from the studio **G.rev** ranks among the prized shmups of the late Dreamcast era, when the console served as the genre's last bastion after the departure of the arcades and the Saturn. It is a horizontal shooter, but with a clever structural twist: the game is divided into three difficulty tiers — the „borders“ — and depending on how you fare, you move between them and encounter different versions of the levels.

The key idea goes like this: death does not knock you out but drops you down a level, to an easier „border“ where you face a milder version of the same stretch. A great performance, on the other hand, keeps you up top, in the more demanding and more rewarding variant. This creates a dynamic system where every decision is a strategic choice between risk and certainty — do you want a higher score, or a safer run?

This structure makes **Border Down** a more thoughtful experience than most frantic shooters. You memorize, you plan, and you decide when to take risks and when to play it safe, which lends the genre an unexpected tactical layer.

Together with Mars Matrix and Under Defeat it completes the trio of Dreamcast shmups that are rare and pricey among collectors today. For genre connoisseurs it is one of the most inventive titles the late Dreamcast had to offer.

**Why play:** A strategic horizontal shmup with an ingenious system of borders where even death serves the game — an ingenious and sought-after jewel of the late Dreamcast.
dreamcast__border-down.teaser: A shmup from G.rev built on a brilliant idea — the screen border's color reveals how close death is.

dreamcast__shenmue-ii.article:
There are games, and then there is **Shenmue II**, an ambitious sequel that pushed the boundaries of what interactive storytelling could encompass at all. Yu Suzuki and his team at SEGA AM2 continued here the story of the young Ryo Hazuki and his search for his father's killer, this time set against the breathtaking backdrops of Hong Kong and Kowloon. If the first game was a revolution, the second is its grand, far more sprawling fulfillment.

Shenmue became famous for the term FREE, that is Full Reactive Eyes Entertainment, and the second installment carried this concept to perfection. The world lives by its own rhythm, characters have daily routines, shops open and close, and the weather changes. The player can spend hours exploring the streets, playing arcade machines, gambling, looking for a part-time job, or simply soaking up the atmosphere of a city that feels incredibly alive even years later.

At the core of the gameplay remain investigation, a combat system derived from the fighting game Virtua Fighter, and the so-called Quick Time Events, that is action sequences requiring quick button reactions. It was Shenmue that made this element famous and influenced countless later action games. The beat 'em up style fight sequences, in turn, gave the player the feeling that Ryo was truly growing as a fighter.

The series' development was legendary for its budget, which ranked among the highest of its time and, according to many sources, contributed to SEGA's financial troubles in the hardware arena. Shenmue II was released in Europe on the Dreamcast, while in North America it appeared only as a port on the Xbox, which made the European Dreamcast version an especially prized piece among fans. For the whole platform it became one of its flagships.

The cultural significance of Shenmue is enormous. It is often called a forerunner of modern open worlds, and its influence can be felt in works like Yakuza. The story, which ended on an open note, left fans waiting nearly two decades before a crowdfunding campaign brought them the sequel Shenmue III. Few series can hold on to such a devoted community for so long.

**Why play:** For immersion in an unforgettably alive world and a piece of gaming history that was generations ahead of its time.
dreamcast__shenmue-ii.teaser: Yu Suzuki's ambitious sequel, which pushed the boundaries of interactive storytelling.

dreamcast__power-stone.article:
When the SEGA Dreamcast was looking for a game to show off everything that little white console could do, Capcom answered with **Power Stone**, a fighting game unlike any that had existed before. Forget static duels on two planes. Here the brawlers move freely in fully three-dimensional arenas, climb walls, hurl furniture at each other, and the entire environment becomes part of the battle.

The game was created at Capcom and originally appeared in arcades on the Naomi system, which shared its architecture with the Dreamcast, so the conversion to the home console was almost lossless. In 1999 that was a stunning lure: arcade quality right in the living room. Power Stone immediately captivated players with its freshness and colorful, slightly comic-book style that distinguished each of its vivid characters.

A key mechanic gave the game its name. Gems, the so-called Power Stones, appear around the arena, and once a player collects three, their character transforms into a super-powered version of themselves with devastating special attacks. This transformation turned the course of a fight on its head and forced players to fight not only against each other but also for control of the scattered stones. The bouts were thus chaotic, fast, and always unpredictable.

Thanks to the ability to use objects from the environment, from chairs and barrels to explosives, Power Stone became the ideal game for two players on the couch. It was not a title for tournament veterans hunting frame-perfect combos, but spontaneous, action-packed fun where even an inexperienced player could beat a friend through a lucky break. This accessibility became its greatest asset.

Power Stone quickly became one of the darlings of the Dreamcast library and today ranks among the games fans cite as proof of why the SEGA console was so exceptional. The series continued with Power Stone 2, and both games later received a collector's compilation on the PSP. For many players it remains a symbol of the era when SEGA could still afford to experiment.

**Why play:** For the freedom of fully 3D arenas and chaotic, instantly graspable fun that excels above all with two players.
dreamcast__power-stone.teaser: Capcom's fighting game without flat arenas; battles in 3D space with destructible surroundings.

dreamcast__power-stone-2.article:
If the first installment showed what a fighting game freed from two dimensions could look like, **Power Stone 2** took the whole concept and shot it into the stratosphere. Capcom did not stop at one-on-one bouts here, but crammed up to four players into the arenas at once and turned the battles into utterly insane, euphoric chaos with no equal on the Dreamcast. It is a celebration of unbridled party fun in its purest form.

The biggest novelty is the interactive, shifting arenas, which function as an opponent in their own right. The floor may collapse, an airplane may crash down on the players, the scene may turn into a flight from a surging flood or a fight aboard a plummeting airship. The environment is no longer just scenery but an active threat you must flee from as fiercely as from your rivals. This unpredictability makes every round a little drama.

Besides expanding to four players, Power Stone 2 added a more elaborate item system. Dozens of weapons lie scattered around the arenas, from swords and cannons to collectible materials from which players can forge even stronger equipment at a smithy. The classic mechanic of three stones and the ensuing transformation into a super version of the character of course remained, so even among four players there is a constant battle for the upper hand.

This game never pretended to be a serious tournament fighter. It is a deliberately accessible, boisterous brawl where the winner is whoever best exploits the surrounding mayhem. It is precisely thanks to this that it became a legendary title for shared evenings, where even a complete newcomer could beat a seasoned player through the right timing and a bit of luck. Few games of the era matched the energy of its four-way battles.

Together with the first installment, Power Stone 2 forms a pair that fans still cite among the best reasons to own a Dreamcast. Both games later appeared in the Power Stone Collection on the PSP, bringing them to a new generation of players. For connoisseurs they remain a symbol of the daring and playfulness Capcom could afford at the time.

**Why play:** For unbeatably crazy battles of up to four players in arenas that try to kill you just as hard as your opponents do.
dreamcast__power-stone-2.teaser: A sequel supporting up to four players at once, turning battles into wild, fun chaos.

dreamcast__soul-calibur.article:
Sometimes a perfect game meets perfect hardware at the right moment, and a legend is born. **Soul Calibur** on the SEGA Dreamcast is exactly such a case, a title still called one of the best fighting games of all time and the absolute peak of what the console could do. When it came out, it felt like a revelation from the future, one that overshadowed even its arcade originals.

The game was made by the Namco studio as a sequel to the arcade title Soul Edge, and its main distinguishing feature lies in weapon-based combat. Instead of bare fists, the fighters here wield swords, katanas, scythes, whips, and nunchaku, and each weapon has its own reach and style. A key innovation was the so-called eight-way run, which let players circle freely around their opponent and turned a bout into an elegant chess match full of evasions and timing.

The 1999 Dreamcast version made history with its technical side. The graphics markedly surpassed the arcade original on the Namco System 12, ran at perfect speed, and dazzled with detailed models and environments. Many players and reviewers saw it as the first truly home port that not only caught up with its source but even surpassed it. It was a clear signal of the raw power the new hardware held.

Besides its technical splendor, Soul Calibur also offered rich content for players at home. The Mission Battle mode called the Edge Master saga stretched the game across dozens of challenges, rewarding them with new weapons and characters and giving the game surprising longevity. The easily accessible combat system meanwhile concealed enormous depth, so both Sunday players and those who polished every bit of timing got their money's worth.

Critical reception was extraordinary, and Soul Calibur ranks among the highest-rated games ever, regularly appearing at the top of lists of the best fighting games and the best Dreamcast games. The series continued with a string of installments on other platforms, and its influence on the genre is unmistakable. For many players, though, it is this Dreamcast version that remains the moment when fighting games came of age.

**Why play:** For one of the best and most elegant fighting games in history, which on the Dreamcast surpassed even its arcade roots.

dreamcast__phantasy-star-online.article:
Imagine a time when playing with people from the other side of the world was a miracle, and into the midst of it steps a console game that brought this miracle into living rooms. **Phantasy Star Online** on the SEGA Dreamcast became a pioneer in the year 2000, the first truly mass-market online action RPG on a gaming console, and it forever changed the notion of what a home machine could do.

The game was developed by the Sonic Team studio under the lead of Yuji Naka and took the name of the classic Phantasy Star series, which it however steered away from turn-based battles toward real-time action gameplay. The player creates a character from various races and classes and sets off to explore the planet Ragol, where in underground plains, caves, and ruins they eliminate monsters and gather loot. Randomly generated loot and endless equipment upgrades became the engine that pulled players along for hours and hours.

The defining element was cooperation of up to four players over the internet. Phantasy Star Online cleverly solved even the language barrier with a system of pre-prepared messages and symbols, so players from Japan, Europe, and America understood one another without a common tongue. This little detail created a remarkably friendly global community and foreshadowed a social dimension we take for granted today.

For SEGA it was the flagship of the Dreamcast's online ambitions and its network service. The game received expanded versions like Ver. 2 and later ports to the GameCube and Xbox under the name Phantasy Star Online Episode I and II, extending its reach even further. Each version added new content and kept the player community active even after the Dreamcast itself was gone.

Its cultural significance is undeniable. Phantasy Star Online laid the foundations for the entire genre of console online action RPGs, and its influence can be traced all the way to later games built on loot collection and cooperation. For many players it was the very first moment they experienced an online adventure alongside real people, and that is precisely why it holds a special place in the hearts of Dreamcast fans.

**Why play:** For the historic experience of the first great console online RPG and cooperative loot hunting that is still fun today.
dreamcast__phantasy-star-online.teaser: A pioneer of massively online RPGs on consoles; from Sonic Team and Yuji Naka, the year 2000.

dreamcast__daytona-usa-2001.article:
When the original arcade cabinet of Daytona USA rolled into the arcades in 1993, it redefined what a racing game should look like. Textured 3D models, dazzling speed, the smell of gasoline, and a chorus roaring the famous „Daytonaaa!“ - this game was a phenomenon. And it was precisely its legacy that the Daytona USA 2001 version carried onto the Dreamcast, aiming to bring the magic of the arcade into the living room with all the trimmings.

At the core of the experience remains what always made Daytona Daytona: three tracks graded by difficulty, from a simple oval for beginners to a demanding course full of turns, and above all drifting. A skid through a corner here is not a mistake but an art - a properly initiated and controlled slide launches you out of the apex faster than anything else. NASCAR stock cars jostle past one another on the track in a dense field of rivals, and the sense of speed is practically unrivaled thanks to the clean, smooth image.

The Dreamcast release had its purpose: SEGA was building its final console as a machine that could bring arcade fidelity home. The Dreamcast shared its architecture with the SEGA NAOMI cabinets, and Daytona USA was exactly the type of title meant to demonstrate this philosophy. The Dreamcast version added, compared to older conversions, improved graphics, new tracks, and extra modes, so it was not a mere port but an expanded edition of a legend.

Culturally, Daytona USA ranks among the most influential racing games ever. Together with titles like Virtua Racing and Sega Rally, it helped SEGA define the genre of nineties arcade racers and raised a whole generation of players for whom the arcade was a temple of speed. The distinctive soundtrack with its choral vocals became a cult piece of internet culture, and fans still lovingly parody and praise it to this day.

On the Dreamcast, which became a symbol of SEGA's ambitious but commercially tragic end as a hardware maker, Daytona is a reminder of what the company did best - pure, immediate arcade fun without any needless frills. You jump in, you drive, you drift, and you smile.

**Why play:** For genuine arcade speed and the art of the drift, which pulls you in within the first ten seconds and never lets go.
dreamcast__daytona-usa-2001.teaser: A home version of the legendary arcade racer that defined the genre back in 1993.

dreamcast__quake-iii-arena.article:
There are games that tell a story, and then there is Quake III Arena - a game that needs no story, because the only thing that matters is whether you are faster and more accurate than the other guy. In 1999 id Software threw out the single-player campaign and built the entire title around a single idea: multiplayer arenas where players (or bots) face off in a merciless deathmatch. And the Dreamcast received this pure distillate of competitive FPS in the year 2000.

The mechanics of Quake III are a textbook of the genre to this day. Movement is lightning-fast, mastering the art of strafe-jumping and rocket-jumps, the maps are designed around control of key items and a brutal arsenal from the railgun to the rocket launcher. There is no room for hesitation - what wins is reflex, knowledge of the maps, and the ability to anticipate the opponent. It was precisely this ruthless purity that made Quake III a pillar of the early esports scene.

The Dreamcast version was remarkable for several reasons. As one of the first consoles, the Dreamcast offered a built-in modem and online play, so Quake III Arena could be played over the network against other players - at a time when console online was still an exotic thing. The game moreover supported a keyboard and mouse connected to the console, which made it one of the few ways to play an FPS on a console with true PC precision.

The development context is a legend in itself. id Software, under the lead of John Carmack and company, was the studio that literally invented the modern FPS - Doom, Quake, technological revolutions in 3D engines. Quake III ran on the new id Tech 3 engine, which was later licensed into dozens of other games and raised the bar in rendering curved surfaces and lighting.

Its cultural significance is enormous. Quake III, together with Unreal Tournament, which came out at the same time, defined the era of arena shooters and laid the foundations of organized competition from which today's esports grew. For the Dreamcast, the port meant proof that the console took online and hardcore gaming seriously - a shame only that SEGA ran out of time before this vision could fully unfold.

**Why play:** For pure, timeless multiplayer deathmatch that has not aged - and on the Dreamcast, with mouse and keyboard support for true precision on top of that.
dreamcast__quake-iii-arena.teaser: A pure distillation of multiplayer action from id Software; no story, just deathmatch.

dreamcast__ecco-dolphin-defender-of-futu.article:
Few gaming series have an atmosphere as unmistakable as Ecco the Dolphin. When the installment subtitled Defender of the Future came out on the Dreamcast in the year 2000, it was not a nostalgic return to the old, but a complete rebirth - it carried the dolphin Ecco into a full-fledged 3D world where beneath the surface of the ocean hides a meditative, melancholic, and often surprisingly harsh adventure.

The gameplay is built on free swimming through a three-dimensional underwater space, which in itself was and remains unusual. Controlling a dolphin means learning to flow through the water, accelerate, leap above the surface, and use sonar to map the surroundings and to communicate with other creatures. The game combines exploration, puzzle-solving, and skill-based passages, with some stretches famous for their difficulty - Ecco was never a relaxing game for children, as the cute dolphin might suggest.

Behind the new installment stood the Appaloosa Interactive studio, formerly Novotrade, that is the creators of the original Ecco titles from the SEGA Mega Drive era. The visual look of the world was overseen by the renowned designer and illustrator Ed Annunziata, who was there at the birth of the whole series. The result was one of the most atmospheric titles in the entire Dreamcast library, where clear water, the play of light, and vast underwater spaces fully harnessed the console's power.

Culturally, Ecco always stood apart from the mainstream - it was a title for players seeking something other than explosions and combat. The original Ecco the Dolphin from 1992 became a cult classic precisely thanks to its peculiar blend of beauty, solitude, and frustrating difficulty. Defender of the Future carried this mood into a new generation and, for many fans, represents the peak of the series.

On the Dreamcast, a console full of bold and unconventional titles, Ecco fit in perfectly. It is a game that was not afraid to be slow, contemplative, and different - and precisely for that reason it still holds a devoted audience today that appreciates the hypnotic atmosphere of the ocean depths and the music that inseparably belongs to them.

**Why play:** For a hypnotic, beautifully eerie journey through an underwater world unlike anything else in gaming history - just expect it to give you a real hard time in places.
dreamcast__ecco-dolphin-defender-of-futu.teaser: A meditative yet surprisingly tough underwater adventure starring the dolphin Ecco, in 3D.

dreamcast__toy-commander.article:
Do you remember the feeling when an ordinary child's room turned into a sprawling battlefield and, among the furniture, you waged war with little cars and airplanes? It was exactly this fantasy that came alive in Toy Commander, one of the first titles that accompanied the European and American launch of the SEGA Dreamcast in 1999. The game put you in the role of a commander of an army of toys whose battles play out inside an ordinary house, enlarged to giant proportions.

The magic of Toy Commander lies in its variety. You control a whole palette of toys - racing cars, tanks, helicopters, and airplanes - and each behaves completely differently. In one mission you tear across the kitchen table, in the next you fly through the bedroom and shoot at enemy contraptions. The game thus mixes racing, flying, and action combat into a single package, with the domestic environment serving as an ingeniously designed three-dimensional arena full of ordinary objects elevated into gameplay elements.

Behind the game stood the French studio No Cliché, which created under the wing of SEGA Europe and specialized precisely in ambitious Dreamcast projects. Toy Commander was proof of how varied a library SEGA wanted to build for its new console - alongside the big arcade brands, original, creative ideas from European developers, which had no equal elsewhere, also got their space.

Conceptually, the game belongs to the long tradition of stories where toys come alive, and in the gaming medium it represents a distinctive contribution to this theme. The premise of a miniature war on the human scale of a household gives designers the chance to play with perspective and scale in a way that is fun in its own right - an ordinary staircase turns into a mountain pass and a kitchen counter into a fortified stronghold.

As a Dreamcast launch title, Toy Commander carried on its shoulders the task of showing what the new console could do, and it did so with infectious playfulness. Today it ranks among those Dreamcast titles that remind us how bold and imaginative the offering of this prematurely discontinued console was - games that were not afraid to be idiosyncratic and to play with fresh ideas.

**Why play:** For a cute and imaginative war of toys in a giant house that combines racing, flying, and action and breathes with the creativity of the early Dreamcast.
dreamcast__toy-commander.teaser: Toys come to life in an oversized child's bedroom; one of the Dreamcast's launch titles.

dreamcast__mr-driller.article:
Sometimes a brilliant idea hides inside the simplest of mechanics. Mr. Driller takes the classic falling-block game and turns it on its head: instead of stacking upward, you drill downward, ever deeper, counting every breath of air along the way.

The concept is charming in its purity. You control Driller, who digs through colored blocks toward the depths. Blocks of the same color merge and vanish when they touch, but beware, everything above you comes crashing down and threatens to crush you. On top of that, you manage a supply of air that you replenish by collecting capsules scattered underground. The result is a tense balance between speed, planning and a cool head, where a single mistaken drill sets off a cascade of trouble.

Mr. Driller is the work of Namco and originally appeared in arcades at the turn of the millennium, from where it spread to a number of platforms including the Dreamcast. According to the game's lore, the main hero Susumu Hori is the son of characters from the legendary Dig Dug series, an elegant way for Namco to link its old classic with a new hit and underscore the family tree of the dig-underground genre.

Culturally, Mr. Driller fits into the tradition of Japanese puzzle games that manage to be simple to grasp yet almost endless in the depth of their mastery. It became a small phenomenon that spawned its own whole series of sequels and spin-offs, which are still being released today. Its cute graphics and catchy music made it a title players love to return to.

On the Dreamcast, a console famous for excellent arcade conversions, Mr. Driller found the ideal home. It is exactly the kind of game where you plan a single round and come to an hour later, determined to beat your record. Instantly understandable, yet devilishly addictive.

**Why play:** For its fresh twist on the falling-block classic and its addictive gameplay, where every round tempts you into another attempt.
dreamcast__mr-driller.teaser: A falling-block classic turned inside out — instead of stacking up, you drill your way down.

dreamcast__super-puzzle-fighter-ii-x.article:
Take the legendary fighters from Street Fighter and Darkstalkers, shrink them into cute super-deformed versions and pit them against each other in a battle of falling gems. That is how Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo was born, one of the cleverest and most entertaining puzzle games ever made, which shone on the Dreamcast in the version marked X.

The mechanic is beautifully thought out. Players stack falling colored gems against each other along with Crash Gems, which shatter entire clusters of the same color at once. The bigger the block a player builds and detonates all at once, the more nuisance blocks they dump onto their opponent. It is a duel of nerves and foresight, where one well-timed combo can turn the whole match around while your little character on screen performs attack animations.

Behind the game stands Capcom, cleverly recycling its all-star fighting roster. Characters like Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li or Morrigan from Darkstalkers serve as mascots here, each with their own distinctive pattern of sending blocks to the opponent. Combining two very different genres, fighting and puzzle, was a brilliant marketing and gameplay move that appealed to both audiences.

Culturally, Puzzle Fighter earned a reputation as a title that is every bit as good in multiplayer as Tetris or Puyo Puyo, which clearly inspired it. It became a fixture at parties and in gaming communities and is still remembered today as one of the best competitive puzzle experiences. Its cute aesthetic turns an otherwise merciless duel into a joyful spectacle.

The Dreamcast version benefited from the console's power and smooth performance. It is a title you can understand in a few minutes, but whose mastery takes hours, and a match between two experienced players is a gripping spectacle full of twists. An ideal piece for anyone who enjoys competitive play on a single screen.

**Why play:** For the brilliant fusion of fighting and puzzle that offers one of the best competitive experiences on a shared screen.
dreamcast__super-puzzle-fighter-ii-x.teaser: Street Fighter and Darkstalkers characters in a clever falling-gem puzzle game.

zx81__3d-monster-maze.article:
Picture a green-and-purple screen, flickering characters instead of graphics, and you yourself in a cramped maze where a giant dinosaur slowly emerges from a fog of pixels. This is 3D Monster Maze, a game that managed something on the unassuming Sinclair ZX81 that few considered possible at the time: to evoke genuine fear.

The mechanic is brilliantly simple. You move corridor by corridor through a maze rendered in a simple but surprisingly legible first-person perspective. Your only goal is to find the exit before a Tyrannosaurus Rex catches you. The game keeps you informed about the predator's status with text messages in the style of „REX LIES IN WAIT“ or the dreaded „RUN HE IS BEHIND YOU“. No weapons, no potions, just flight and mounting panic as that unmistakable silhouette begins to grow on the horizon.

Technically it was a small miracle. The ZX81 had only a tiny amount of memory and no hardware for moving graphics, so rendering movement in a pseudo-3D space was a remarkable programming feat. The game used character graphics to assemble an illusion of depth, and its atmosphere fed on exactly how crudely and terrifyingly the image redrew itself.

Historically, 3D Monster Maze is often labeled one of the first representatives of what we would today call survival horror, long before the term even existed. Confined corridors, a defenseless player and a relentless pursuer are elements that appear in various forms in horror games to this day. On a machine sold as a cheap computer for enthusiasts, it was an unexpectedly powerful emotional experience.

That is precisely where the game's magic lies. It shows that atmosphere and tension do not arise from the number of pixels or colors, but from clever design and from how the game works with uncertainty and fear of the unknown. Even after decades, the ZX81 version can make your heart race.

**Why play:** To experience firsthand how little it takes to inspire real fear, and to discover one of the ancient roots of survival horror on a legendary British microcomputer.
zx81__3d-monster-maze.teaser: A survival horror maze on the ZX81, where a giant dinosaur slowly emerges from a fog of pixels.

zx81__mazogs.article:
