The gameplay builds on classic arcade racing with a behind-the-car view, in which you tear along the circuits, overtake rivals and battle for the best possible placement. The goal is to get through a season of races and win the championship, so it is not just about a single ride but about a persistent fight for points across the whole year. The game thus combines the immediate fun of fast driving with the motivation to press on toward the coveted title.

What the game tried to appeal with was the license tied to the name of a real racer and the atmosphere of Formula 1 races. At a time when Mansell was at the peak of his fame, his name carried great weight among motorsport fans, and the game benefited from the sport's popularity. The Amiga version was among those on which players could try what it is like to drive a single-seater along demanding tracks.

Culturally this game fits into the wave of licensed sports and racing titles that, at the turn of the eighties and nineties, tried to transfer the fame of real stars into the gaming world. It is a testament to a time when the brands and names of famous athletes became a lure on game covers and when Formula 1 was enjoying enormous interest in Europe.

Today Nigel Mansell's World Championship is an interesting reminder of an era when home computers like the Amiga served as a gateway to the world of motorsport. For retro enthusiasts and fans of Formula 1 history alike, it is a nostalgic ride into the past.

**Why play:** For a nostalgic return to the era when a Formula 1 champion's name adorned the box and promised a proper racing ride on the Amiga.
amiga__nigel-mansell-s-world-championshi.teaser: An F1 champion's name on the box promised speed; classic arcade racing from behind the car.

amiga__eye-of-beholder.detail: A cult first-person dungeon crawler under the AD&D rules that took the baton from the Dungeon Master series and pushed it toward crystal-clear presentation. You assemble a party of four and step by step explore the labyrinth beneath the city of Waterdeep, full of traps, puzzles and monsters. The atmosphere, hand mapping and tactical combat make it a model of the genre.
amiga__eye-of-beholder.article:
The darkness of a corridor, a flickering torch and, around the corner, something that growls before you spot it. Eye of the Beholder pulls you into an underground from which you will not easily escape, and on the Amiga it was one of the most atmospheric RPG experiences of its time. This dungeon crawler built on the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons rules pushed the genre of first-person labyrinths a great step forward.

The game's mechanics put you in the role of a four-member party of adventurers who chew their way through the layers of the underground beneath the city of Waterdeep. Movement is step-by-step, tile by tile, the view is first-person, and combat takes place in real time, when you click on the characters' weapons in the lower part of the screen. Added to that is solving puzzles and searching for hidden switches, buttons and traps. It was precisely this combination of exploration, tactical combat and constant tension that made this game an absorbing experience.

Eye of the Beholder was created at Westwood Associates, later famous under the name Westwood Studios, and was released under the SSI label, which at the time held the license for computer adaptations of Dungeons & Dragons. Westwood soon became one of the most respected developers, and Eye of the Beholder was one of the titles that built its reputation. The Amiga version benefited from colorful graphics and detailed underground textures.

The game's cultural significance is considerable. Eye of the Beholder built on the legacy of dungeon crawlers like Dungeon Master and moved the genre's presentation closer to what players expected from the AD&D brand. The game gave rise to sequels and became one of the pillars of the golden era of licensed D&D games on computers in the early nineties.

Today Eye of the Beholder remains a beloved classic for fans of old-school RPGs. Its underground still breathes atmosphere and its puzzles can still give you a real headache.

**Why play:** For an absorbing expedition into a dark underground in the spirit of classic Dungeons & Dragons, where every step could be your last.
amiga__eye-of-beholder.teaser: An atmospheric dungeon crawler on AD&D rules; dark corridors that pushed the genre forward.

amiga__ishar-legend-of-fortress.article:
An exotic island, a party of adventurers you assemble yourself, and a world in which your companions may simply walk out on you if they dislike your decisions. Ishar: Legend of the Fortress brought to the Amiga an RPG with its own distinctive identity and colorful, picturesque graphics that set it apart from the gloomy dungeons of the competition. It was a title that combined exploration of a more open world with classic party building.

In gameplay terms Ishar builds on a first-person view and step-by-step movement across a fantasy landscape full of towns, forests and mysterious locations. A peculiarity was the elaborate party system, into which you recruited characters with their own personalities. The members had their own opinions and relationships and could even refuse to obey, or leave the group, if they disagreed with your deeds. This social dynamic gave the game an unexpected dimension and set it apart from more mechanical rivals.

Ishar was created at the French studio Silmarils and followed on from its previous fantasy titles. The French development scene of the time had a reputation for creating visually inventive and distinctive games, and Ishar confirmed that reputation. The Amiga version stood out with richly colored graphics and finely painted environments that made wandering the island a visual experience.

The game left a cultural mark chiefly as the start of a successful series. Ishar received sequels and became one of the characteristic European RPGs of the early nineties, prized for its atmosphere and for the courage to come up with its own ideas instead of merely copying successful formulas.

Today Ishar recalls the variety of European game creation of that time and remains popular among fans of classic RPGs who are looking for something with a face of its own.

**Why play:** For a colorful fantasy expedition with a party that has a mind of its own, and for a distinctive European take on the RPG genre.
amiga__ishar-legend-of-fortress.teaser: An RPG with a colorful, painterly world; your companions will gladly leave you if they dislike your choices.

amiga__body-blows.article:
When the world went crazy for fighting games in the early nineties, the Amiga was not allowed to be without its champion either. Body Blows from the British studio Team17 was the home computer scene's answer to the arcade fever surrounding combat games, and on its machine it was among the best-executed representatives of the genre. For Amiga owners it was a chance to measure their strength against a genre that until then had reigned mainly in arcades and on consoles.

The gameplay relied on the proven formula. You pick one of a gallery of fighters, each with his own look, special punches and style, and progress through a tournament against the rest of the roster. There are kicks, punches and special techniques triggered by combinations of directions and buttons, and of course a two-player duel is not missing either. On the Amiga the fluidity of animations and the size of the characters were above average, which made the fights a satisfying spectacle.

Body Blows was created at Team17, which built a strong name for itself on the Amiga and later became famous for the Worms series. The team was among the most active and capable developers on the platform, and Body Blows was proof that even the demanding fighting genre could be handled with honor on a home computer. The game received further installments that developed the series.

The title's cultural significance lies in the fact that it brought the fighting game phenomenon to players who did not have access to arcades or consoles. In an era when the genre defined the whole playing field, Body Blows was an important title for the Amiga community and a source of pride that their machine too could keep pace.

Today Body Blows remains an interesting testament to how the Amiga coped with the trends of its time and how capable developers managed to squeeze the maximum out of its hardware.

**Why play:** For a proper dose of fighting action in the style of the early nineties and for a reminder that the Amiga could keep pace even in the fighting genre.
amiga__body-blows.teaser: Team17's answer to the fighting-game craze; one of the best-crafted brawlers on the Amiga.

amiga__eye-of-beholder-ii-legend-of-dark.article:
If there's a moment when Westwood Studios brought the dungeon crawl to perfection, it's **Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon**. Many consider this 1991 sequel the pinnacle of the entire series — and rightly so. Unlike the first installment, confined to the sewers beneath a city, a varied adventure unfolds here: you begin in a gloomy forest, penetrate the sinister temple of Darkmoon, and climb the floors of a tower, each with its own atmosphere and logic.

The core remains faithful to AD&D rules — movement across a square grid in a real-time first-person perspective, party management, combat, and spellcasting. But the second installment added more spells, more varied monsters, a more elaborate story full of twists, and craftier puzzles that force you to search every wall. The atmosphere is heightened by excellent graphics and sound, especially impressive on the Amiga.

Westwood polished their formula to a shine here before turning to real-time strategy and creating Dune II and Command & Conquer. For lovers of the genre, Eye of the Beholder II is an essential piece of history — a dungeon crawl that retro gamers return to again and again.
amiga__eye-of-beholder-ii-legend-of-dark.teaser: The peak of the trilogy according to many fans; a more varied world than the first game's enclosed sewers.
amiga__eye-of-beholder-ii-legend-of-dark.detail: A more mature sequel, considered by many to be the pinnacle of the series: larger and more varied environments (a forest, the Temple of Darkmoon, several floors of a tower), a better story, and more spells and enemies. Westwood polished the formula to perfection here before moving on to RTS games. An essential dungeon crawl.

amiga__eye-of-beholder-iii-assault-on-my.article:
Every trilogy needs its conclusion, and **Eye of the Beholder III: Assault on Myth Drannor** from 1993 closes out one of the most beloved dungeon series of the Amiga era. This time Westwood Studios were no longer at the helm, but an internal team of the publisher SSI itself, and the handwriting changed noticeably. The party sets out for the ruins of the once-glorious elven city of Myth Drannor to stop an ancient evil — and for the first time in the series, the adventure also moves into more open outdoor environments.

The greater expansiveness and the attempt to break away from claustrophobic corridors are welcome, but they came at the cost of rougher technical compromises — the game feels less polished than the second installment, and some mechanics don't reach Westwood's precision. Even so, it stays faithful to the proven core: real-time movement across a grid, character management under AD&D rules, combat, and spells.

For fans of the series, the third installment is more of an obligation than a revelation — a way to bring the story to a close and experience one last campaign with your party. Retro gamers take it on knowing its weaknesses, but also with respect for the fact that it closes a chapter that helped shape the dungeon crawl genre in the early nineties.
amiga__eye-of-beholder-iii-assault-on-my.teaser: The trilogy's final chapter, this time from SSI; an expedition to the ruins of the elven city of Myth Drannor.
amiga__eye-of-beholder-iii-assault-on-my.detail: The third installment, no longer developed by Westwood but by SSI's in-house team. It moves out into outdoor settings around the ruined city of Myth Drannor and brings more openness, albeit at the cost of rougher technical compromises. A must for fans of the series wanting to close out the trilogy.

amiga__dune.article:
There are games that lodge themselves in the memory not through their mechanics but through their atmosphere — and **Dune** by Cryo Interactive from 1992 is their flagship. Based on Herbert's monumental saga, an unusually beautiful hybrid emerged: half a contemplative adventure in which, as the young Paul Atreides, you travel across the planet Arrakis, negotiate with Fremen chieftains, and uncover the secrets of the desert; half a light strategy game in which you organize the mining of the precious spice and build a resistance against the cruel Harkonnens.

What elevates Dune above a mere sum of genres is its sensory side. The hand-painted vistas of Arrakis, the smooth transitions between locations, and above all the hypnotic soundtrack by Stéphane Picq create a mood without equal on the Amiga. The game gradually opens up the map, hands you ever more sietches and fighters, and leads you from intimate exploration to a broader campaign against the enemy.

Dune became a cult gem and an interesting historical bridge — it was released practically alongside Westwood's Dune II, which defined the modern RTS. While the "second" one founded the genre, this first Dune remains the more poetic, dreamlike experience that retro gamers still cherish today.
amiga__dune.teaser: Based on Herbert's saga; a contemplative adventure on Arrakis combined with a strategy game about spice.
amiga__dune.detail: An unusually beautiful hybrid game based on Herbert's saga: half atmospheric adventure of traveling across Arrakis, half light strategy of harvesting spice and building the resistance against the Harkonnens. A hypnotic soundtrack (Stéphane Picq) and painted screens made it a cult gem — and helped inspire Dune II.

atari-st__dungeon-master.article:
Imagine the year 1987, you step into a dark dungeon, on the screen a monster creeps in real time, and for the first time in your life you feel that this is not a static turn-based game. This is Dungeon Master, a title that literally redefined what a computer RPG could look like.

The game from the American studio FTL Games, released first on the Atari ST, abandoned the then-usual turn-based approach and built the entire experience on a first-person view in fluid, continuous time. You lead a four-member party, which you assemble from characters imprisoned in mirrors, descend floor by floor and solve physically conceived puzzles: levers, buttons, doors, hidden paths. Combat takes place live, so you have to nimbly click on weapons and spells, retreat and maneuver.

The magic system was revolutionary too, where you compose spells from runes according to forces and elements, and so was the system of improving skills through practice, not mere accumulation of experience. The more you fight, the better a warrior you are; the more you cast spells, the mightier a mage. This approach, where the character improves at what it actually does, influenced dozens of later games.

Dungeon Master became one of the best-selling games for the Atari ST and is generally listed among the most influential RPGs ever. It inspired a whole wave of first-person dungeon crawlers, and its DNA can be traced in series like Eye of the Beholder or later in modern titles that proudly return to grid-based dungeon crawling. For its time it also dazzled with fluid graphics and sound.

What makes the game remarkable even after decades is its coherence. It is not a jumble of systems but a thoughtfully designed world, where every puzzle, every enemy and every weapon found makes sense. The atmosphere of descending into the unknown, when you have to look after your charges' fatigue, hunger and thirst, still draws you in today.

**Why play:** It is a cornerstone of the dungeon-crawler genre and one of the most influential games of the eighties. Anyone who wants to understand where modern RPGs came from must descend right here.
atari-st__dungeon-master.teaser: A 1987 real-time dungeon crawler that redefined what a computer RPG could look like.

atari-st__oids.article:
Gravity is a merciless teacher, and Oids will remind you of that with every landing. This action shooter for the Atari ST is among the little gems that managed to turn a simple idea into hours of tension.

The principle combines inertial physics in the style of Asteroids or Thrust with a rescue mission. You pilot a small ship through cavern and planetary levels, fight enemy robots and, above all, free enslaved androids called Oids, which you have to load up and safely transport back. The ship's control is purely inertial, so every burst of the thrusters drives you on, and precise maneuvering in the tight spaces between turrets and walls is half the challenge.

Beyond the levels themselves, the game offered an editor in which players could build their own planets and share them. This gave Oids an unexpected longevity, because the community could generate new content long before it became the standard. For a computer like the Atari ST, it was a thoughtful use of its capabilities.

Culturally Oids fits into the rich tradition of gravity-based action games that flourished on eighties home computers. Players of the time loved that peculiar mix of frustration and satisfaction, when one wrong tap of the thrusters meant smashing against a wall, but a perfect landing with a cargo of androids brought a genuine feeling of piloting skill.

Compared to the big epic titles, Oids is a more modest but all the purer experience. It needs no story cutscenes or complex systems; physics, well-designed levels and the constant temptation to fly just a bit farther, despite the dwindling fuel, are enough for it. It is a game that respects the player's reflexes and patience alike.

**Why play:** If you are drawn to inertial physics and tense rescue missions, Oids offers precise gravity-based action with a level editor that gives it unexpected longevity.
atari-st__oids.teaser: Gravity-based action inspired by Thrust and Asteroids; landing is as much a challenge as combat.

atari-st__llamatron.article:
Llamas. Mutant goats. Explosions in every pixel. Welcome to the world of Jeff Minter, the brilliant British eccentric whose Llamatron from 1991 is the pure essence of arcade madness served up on the Atari ST.

Llamatron is an undisguised tribute to the Robotron: 2084 arcade machine. Ideally you control it with two joysticks, or a mouse and keyboard, one direction for movement and the other for shooting in an independent direction. Hordes of enemies pour onto the screen, you mow them down with volleys of shots, rescue defenceless llamas and try to survive in the mounting chaos. It is pure, relentless action, where reflexes and peripheral vision decide everything.

Minter, founder of the Llamasoft studio, was famous for his obsession with hoofed animals and a psychedelic aesthetic overflowing with colour. He released Llamatron as shareware, in the spirit of an era when games were spread for free and players then sent money if they liked them. This approach turned him into one of the legends of the home computer scene, and to this day he remains a symbol of an independent, auteur approach to development.

Culturally, Minter embodies the type of creator who stubbornly follows his own path. His games were never about realism or a serious story, but about the raw joy of shooting, dazzling effects and humour. Llamatron is a perfect demonstration of this: fast, loud, visually aggressive and incredibly addictive. Minter, incidentally, still creates in a similar spirit today, and his signature is unmistakable.

Anyone who experienced the golden era of arcade machines will find instant satisfaction in Llamatron. It is a game about the chase for a higher score, about getting one wave further and about pure motor joy. It needs to explain nothing, it just hurls you into the action and does not let go.

**Why play:** One of the purest arcade experiences on the Atari ST from the cult figure Jeff Minter, where the roots of Robotron merge with psychedelic madness and an endless chase for score.
atari-st__llamatron.teaser: Jeff Minter's mad tribute to Robotron; a twin-stick massacre with mutant llamas and goats.

atari-st__stunt-car-racer.article:
The peak of a metal structure, wheels dangling in the air, the engine roaring and you praying that the track beneath you does not vanish. Stunt Car Racer from 1989 is perhaps the most intense racing experience the home computers of the eighties had to offer.

The brilliant idea is that you do not race on a smooth road, but on elevated roller-coaster-like tracks built from steel girders, full of jumps, drops and huge bumps. The game runs on a full 3D engine with filled polygons, which was exceptional for its time, and thus gives rise to an intoxicating sense of speed and the weight of the car. When you fly into the air, you really fly, and hard landings damage the chassis of your car, which can even break apart.

Behind the game stands the legendary British programmer Geoff Crammond, a master of simulations who later became famous for the Formula One Grand Prix series. In Stunt Car Racer he demonstrated how convincingly he could simulate the physics of suspension, mass and inertia even on limited hardware. You compete one on one against an opponent, advance through divisions, and every mistake is punished by the loss of your damaged car and your position in the standings.

The game earned cult status, and to this day many players and critics rank it among the best racing titles of its generation. Its tension springs from the fragile balance between speed and survival, because full throttle in the wrong place means flying off the track and the end of the race. It is precisely this threat that makes every lap an adrenaline-fuelled test of nerves.

Stunt Car Racer was ahead of its time in how intensely it managed to pull you into the cockpit. It was not just a race against the clock, but a battle for the bare survival of your car's structure. Even today, when 3D graphics no longer dazzle us, that feeling of rattling along a steel track can still quicken the pulse.

**Why play:** A pioneering 3D racing experience from Geoff Crammond, where the tension springs from the struggle with gravity on elevated tracks. Adrenaline that has not aged.
atari-st__stunt-car-racer.teaser: Racing on elevated steel tracks full of jumps; perhaps the most intense retro racer there is.

atari-st__carrier-command.article:
One aircraft carrier, an island archipelago and an enemy fleet that wants the same thing you do: to control everything. Carrier Command from 1988 was a bold hybrid game for its time, one that combined action and strategy long before it became common.

You command a futuristic amphibious carrier and your goal is to seize a chain of islands, while a second, enemy-controlled ship with identical capabilities stands against you. The game seamlessly combines strategic planning with direct action, because at any moment you can switch into the cockpit of the launched fighters or amphibious vehicles and attack yourself, defend islands or build a production and defensive network. This freedom between commander's overview and direct control was exceptional.

Behind the game stands the British studio Realtime Games, and it was released under the Rainbird label. Technically it was a remarkable piece: a 3D world with polygon graphics, a simulation of resources, equipment production and logistics across the islands. You had to manage the economy, produce equipment for your vehicles and at the same time not forget the defence of your own ship, because the enemy never slept.

Carrier Command is today seen as one of the early predecessors of the genre we now call action strategy or open-world game elements. Its ambition to combine the macro level of command with the micro level of piloting was inspiring, and the game earned recognition as well as later remakes and spiritual successors. For the players of the eighties it was an experience of exceptional depth.

The magic of Carrier Command lies in the tension between overview and chaos. One moment you are planning a long-term strategy on the map, the next you are sitting in a fighter's cockpit in the middle of a firefight above an island. That constant oscillation between the role of commander and soldier makes playing an experience that forces you to think and react at the same time.

**Why play:** A visionary fusion of strategy and action, where you command an entire aircraft carrier as well as individual machines. Depth and freedom that were ahead of their time.
atari-st__carrier-command.teaser: A 1988 hybrid of action and strategy about commanding an aircraft carrier against a rival fleet.

atari-st__captain-blood.article:
A spaceship, a cloned pilot falling apart into pieces and aliens with whom you communicate through pictograms: L'Arche du Captain Blood is one of the strangest and most daring adventures ever created. And it came out of France in 1988.

The story is in its own way an existential horror. You are a programmer named Bob Morlock, who is stuck in his own game in the role of Captain Blood, whose being has split into five clones scattered across the galaxy. To survive, you must find and absorb them back, because with every passing moment your body and mind disintegrate further. You travel through space, land near planets and meet bizarre alien species.

The most famous element is the communication system Universal Protocol of Communication and Other Messages, UPCOM for short. Instead of writing sentences you assemble messages from icons that represent concepts, and the aliens answer in the same way. This iconographic conversation was utterly innovative for its time and lent the game an unmistakably alien, unsettling atmosphere where you never quite know whether you understand one another.

Behind the game stand Philippe Ulrich and especially Didier Bouchon, whose visual and technical skill gave rise to remarkable fractal graphics of the planets, which were generated procedurally. Captain Blood became a symbol of the ambitious French gaming scene of the eighties, the so-called touch française, which was not afraid of experiments, the surreal and artistic ambitions far beyond the boundaries of ordinary entertainment.

Today Captain Blood is more of a cult experience for connoisseurs than an easily accessible game. Its pace is slow, its logic alien and its atmosphere cold to the point of anxiety. It is precisely this uncompromising otherness, however, that makes it a fascinating artefact of an era when the gaming medium was still learning how far it could go in storytelling and in evoking emotions.

**Why play:** A surreal French sci-fi adventure with revolutionary pictogram dialogue and an oppressive atmosphere of disintegrating identity. An artistic experiment without equal.
atari-st__captain-blood.teaser: A strange French adventure about a programmer trapped inside his own game, alongside his clones.

atari-st__another-world.article:
You open your eyes in a laboratory, a particle accelerator discharge flashes and your character finds itself beneath the surface of an alien planet. No menus, no tutorials, no HUD. Another World throws you into a hostile world from the very first second and lets you die as many times as it takes before you grasp its rules. This opening scene is among the most famous openers in the history of games and can still draw you in to this day.

The Frenchman Éric Chahi created the game practically alone: he programmed, animated and designed it. He used his own technique of polygon vector graphics, thanks to which the characters and environments looked fluid and cinematic at a time when most games relied on pixel sprites. The movement animations of the hero Lester and his alien ally were unprecedentedly realistic for their time, and the whole game ran without a single word of text, told purely through image and situation.

Mechanically it is a cinematic platformer and an adventure at once. You run, jump, pick up a laser weapon capable of firing, creating shields and breaking through walls, and above all you solve the environment by trial and error. Death here is constant and often brutal, but the checkpoints are generous and every failure moves you closer to understanding what the world requires. The relationship between Lester and the prisoner you meet creates an emotional arc without a single line of dialogue.

The game came out in 1991, originally on the Amiga and Atari ST, and became an immediate critical success. Under the name Out of This World it also made its mark in North America and saw dozens of ports across generations of consoles and computers, including modern 20th anniversary remasters. Its influence is unmistakable: it openly inspired creators such as Hideo Kojima or the studio Playdead (Limbo, Inside).

Another World remains a textbook example of the fact that a game can be art. It is short, uncompromising and at times frustrating, but the experience of gradually uncovering its world is unforgettable. The Atari ST version was one of the first, and the Atari home computers gave it a dignified stage.

**Why play:** For the timeless, wordlessly told story and an atmosphere that defined an entire genre of cinematic games.
atari-st__another-world.teaser: A cult wordless cinematic adventure; one of the most famous intros in gaming history.

atari-st__speedball-2-brutal-deluxe.article:
Imagine football and hockey crossed with American football, set in a dystopian future where armoured players slam against metal walls and points are scored equally for goals and for knocking an opponent out of the arena. This is Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, one of the most addictive sports titles ever created on home computers. The game's slogan was clear: Ice cream, ice cream!

Behind the game stands the British studio The Bitmap Brothers, a legendary team famous for its stylish, polished metallic graphics and top-tier gameplay. Speedball 2 came out in 1990 and followed up on the original Speedball from 1988, which it significantly improved and expanded. The Atari ST version was among the platform's flagships and showed what 16-bit hardware could do in the right hands.

The core of the fun is fast, aggressive arcade action in a split arena. You control a team of robotic gladiators, you pass, shoot at the goal and at the same time physically eliminate the opposing players. Points fall from bonus targets, ramps and from sending an opponent to the ground. Between matches you buy upgrades and strengthen your players, so besides the immediate action the game also offers a light managerial layer and a long career mode in a league.

A huge draw was the two-player mode, one of the best of its kind on the ST and Amiga. A duel of two people at a single keyboard or on joysticks could keep players glued to the screen for hours. The metallic, industrial visuals and the raw soundtrack created an unmistakable atmosphere that fans remember to this day.

Speedball 2 collected enthusiastic reviews and repeatedly appeared among the best games for 16-bit computers in the polls of the day. It saw a number of ports as well as later remakes and remasters, thereby confirming that its gameplay aged far better than that of many a more modern sport.

**Why play:** For the two-player mayhem that never ages, and for a perfect mix of arcade action, violence and team building.
atari-st__speedball-2-brutal-deluxe.teaser: Bitmap Brothers' brutal sports mashup, where you score points for taking out opponents too.

atari-st__xenon-2-megablast.article:
As soon as you launch Xenon 2: Megablast, the bassline of the covered track Megablast by the group Bomb the Bass rings out and you know this is going to be a different kind of shooter. This vertically scrolling cosmic shoot 'em up sends you deep into organic-looking worlds full of alien giants, where every level pulses with life and music.

The game was created in 1989 by the studio The Assembly Line in collaboration with The Bitmap Brothers, who supplied their typical sense of style. They followed up on the original Xenon from 1988 and pushed the visuals and atmosphere to a new level. The Atari ST version, together with the Amiga one, was among the best and showed how impressively 16-bit hardware could combine detailed graphics with a resonant soundtrack.

The gameplay is classically demanding: you fly through five extensive levels, shoot swarms of enemies and spend the cash you collect in the shop of the eccentric merchant Crispin between rounds. Here you buy weapon upgrades, additional drones, missiles and shields. An interesting and unconventional element is the ability to reverse backwards, so the game does not only push you forward but lets you fly back through places you have already passed. The battles with gigantic bosses are among the highlights.

Visually, Xenon 2 stands out with a darkly organic, at times almost repulsively biological design of the environments. Together with the iconic music it creates an atmosphere that differs markedly from the colourful Japanese shooters of that era. It is a European shoot 'em up with its own identity and a distinctive aesthetic signature.

The game met with a very positive reception and became one of the defining titles of the genre on home computers. It saw ports to a range of platforms including consoles, and it remains in players' memory mainly thanks to that opening music, which is indelibly written into the history of game sound.

**Why play:** For the unmistakable atmosphere, the iconic soundtrack and the honestly tough old school of the vertical shooter.
atari-st__xenon-2-megablast.teaser: A vertical shoot 'em up with Bomb the Bass's Megablast remix and organic worlds.

atari-st__gods.article:
Step through the gates of an ancient temple as a mythical hero striving for immortality. Gods is no ordinary platformer, it is tactical action where the enemies are not stupid sprites but adversaries driven by a thoughtful artificial intelligence that reacts to your behaviour. This game expects you to think, not just to mash jump and shoot.

Gods was created in 1991 by the British studio The Bitmap Brothers, masters of the 16-bit era known for their characteristic metallic style. The Atari ST version was released simultaneously with the Amiga one and again demonstrated how high the studio could set the bar of production quality. The music was composed by Nation 12, a project connected with John Foxx of the band Ultravox, which gave the game an unusually atmospheric sonic accompaniment.

The player passes through four extensive worlds divided into levels, jumps across platforms, throws weapons at enemies and solves a host of ingenious puzzles with hidden rooms, traps and treasures. The key to success is the economy: you collect treasures which you then spend at the merchant for better weapons and upgrades. The aforementioned enemy AI is cited to this day; the adversaries can retreat, lie in ambush and adapt to the way you play.

Gods became famous for its high difficulty and depth, which set the clever player apart from the one who merely forces his way forward. Visually it relied on a sombre, monumental palette of antiquity with an emphasis on detail, as was customary with The Bitmap Brothers. It was not a title for everyone, but those who gave it time were rewarded with one of the most thoughtfully designed action games of its era.

The game collected strong reviews and became another of the respected titles in the studio's collection. It saw ports to further platforms and it holds a firm place in the community of 16-bit computer fans as proof that an action platformer can be clever.

**Why play:** For the combination of stylish action, clever enemy AI and depth that rewards the thoughtful player.
atari-st__gods.teaser: A tactical action platformer from Bitmap Brothers with opponents controlled by clever AI.

atari-st__populous.article:
What if you were a god? Not metaphorically, but literally, with the power to raise and level the landscape, to send down disasters and to lead your faithful against a rival deity. Populous is the game that first truly grasped this concept and thereby practically created the entire genre of the so-called god games. Out of a small settlement grow cities, out of cities grow armies, and you look down on it all from the heavens.

Populous was created in 1989 by Peter Molyneux with his studio Bullfrog and became its first great hit. The Atari ST version was among the original ones, alongside the Amiga, and launched a dizzying career, one of the first strategies where the player did not control units directly but shaped the conditions under which his people prospered. It was an entirely new way of thinking about strategy games.

The core of the gameplay is terraforming. You level the land so that your people can build houses and multiply, thereby gaining mana, divine energy. You then invest this into abilities ranging from earthquakes and floods through swamps to volcanoes and the apocalyptic Armageddon. The goal is to crush the rival's population on each of the many hundreds of levels. The game also offered play for two players connected by a cable, which at the time was a small miracle.

Populous sold in large numbers of copies and became an international phenomenon that kick-started an entire genre and inspired later titles from Black & White to endless variants of building and god strategies. Peter Molyneux became, thanks to it, one of the best-known game designers of his generation.

To this day Populous is a textbook example of innovation: a simple premise, deep mechanics and a concept no one had seen before. The Atari ST version was at the birth of this revolution, and for fans of the platform it is one of the absolutely key titles of the library.

**Why play:** For the birth of the god game genre and the feeling of true divine power over an entire world and its people.
atari-st__populous.teaser: Peter Molyneux's god game that founded the entire genre of god games in 1989.

atari-st__bubble-bobble.article:
Two adorable little dragons, Bub and Bob, imprisoned in the Cave of Monsters, have only one way to fight their way out: blowing bubbles. In these they trap enemies and then, with a pop, turn them into fruit and treasures. Bubble Bobble is pure joy of playing wrapped in a colourful, irresistibly catchy arcade platformer that has enchanted whole generations.

Originally it was an arcade hit from the Japanese studio Taito from 1986, whose author was Fukio Mitsuji. The game quickly became a classic and in the following years saw ports to practically every platform of the time, the Atari ST not excepted. The home conversions brought arcade fun to players' homes and the versions for 16-bit computers were among the favourites.

The gameplay is ingeniously simple: each of the hundred single-screen levels asks you to clear the area of enemies. You blow bubbles, trap monsters in them, jump on them and collect falling treasures and bonuses. The game is famous for the number of hidden secrets, the EXTEND letters which, once they spell the word, grant an extra life, and the secret doors. And above all: it plays best in two, the co-operation of Bub and Bob is the very heart of the experience.

Bubble Bobble also became famous for its tricky system of endings. The true ending and the encounter with the true boss can only be unlocked by a pair of players who finish the game together, which was an ingenious way to motivate players to co-operate. The catchy musical loop that plays round and round wrote itself into the memory of everyone who ever tried the game.

The game's success gave birth to an entire series, followed up by titles such as Rainbow Islands or Bubble Symphony, and Bub and Bob became iconic mascots of Taito. To this day Bubble Bobble is synonymous with indestructible, time-proof arcade fun, and on the Atari ST it represents one of the loveliest pieces of the library.

**Why play:** For carefree co-operative fun in two and an infectious arcade charm that never ages.
atari-st__bubble-bobble.teaser: A cute Taito arcade game where dragons Bub and Bob trap enemies inside bubbles.

atari-st__prince-of-persia.article:
The character takes a run-up, jumps across a chasm and grabs the edge of a ledge with a fluidity no one had seen at the time. Prince of Persia, released in 1989, brought to the Atari ST a cinematic platformer that, thanks to the technique of rotoscoping, raised the bar of animation in games to an entirely new level.

The game principle combines agility with deliberation. You control a nameless young man who has a mere hour to fight his way through the dungeons and the tower of the palace, rescue the princess from the hands of the evil vizier Jaffar and defeat him. Progress consists of precise jumps, climbing, avoiding deadly traps in the form of spikes and collapsing floor plates, and sabre duels in which the timing of attacks and blocks matters. The time limit gives the whole adventure a tension that was not customary in platformers at the time.

The game was created by Jordan Mechner, who had already broken through with the title Karateka. For Prince of Persia he filmed the movements of his brother and transferred them into the game using rotoscoping, thereby achieving unprecedentedly realistic and fluid animation of the character. This work made the game both a technical and an artistic milestone. The conversion for the Atari ST was among the platforms where the game excelled and spread the reputation of Mechner's work among European players.

The cultural significance of Prince of Persia is fundamental. The game became a model for the entire genre of cinematic platformers and inspired titles such as Flashback or the later Another World. The brand later came back to life in 2003 with the three-dimensional game Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, which turned the series into one of the most successful brands of the Ubisoft studio, and it also saw a film adaptation.

Today Prince of Persia is recognised as one of the most important titles of the late 1980s, which showed that games could offer cinematic fluidity and storytelling. For every lover of gaming history it is an essential classic.

**Why play:** For the pioneering rotoscope animation and a thrilling cinematic platformer that defined an entire genre.
atari-st__prince-of-persia.teaser: A cinematic platformer from 1989 famous for its rotoscoped character animation.

atari-st__lemmings.article:
A swarm of little green-haired creatures marches blindly towards its doom and only you can save them. Lemmings, released by the studio DMA Design in 1991, is one of the most addictive and inventive puzzle games of all, and on the Atari ST it was among its home platforms.

The principle of the game is ingeniously simple. A stream of lemmings pours from an entrance, going ever forward regardless of chasms, lava or traps, and your task is to bring a sufficient number of them to the exit. To do this you assign professions to individual lemmings: one digs a tunnel, another builds stairs, another blocks the rest, yet another turns into a climber or a parachutist. From these simple elements arise levels requiring careful planning and precise timing, often under the pressure of a ticking clock.

DMA Design, the Scottish studio that later became famous as the creator of the Grand Theft Auto series, created an unexpected worldwide hit with Lemmings. The game enchanted players with a combination of a cute appearance, black humour and surprisingly deep gameplay. Hundreds of levels divided into difficulty categories offered an enormous portion of fun, and the game quickly spread to dozens of platforms, from home computers to consoles.

Culturally, Lemmings became one of the defining titles of its time and one of the most ported video games in history. The characteristic sound of Let's go and the moment when a lemming blows itself up with the cry Oh no wrote themselves into players' memory. The series continued with a number of installments and add-ons and the brand has survived to this day in various forms, including mobile games.

Today Lemmings remains a textbook example of timeless game design that works regardless of the graphical possibilities of the era. Its magic lies in a perfect balance between accessibility and depth.

**Why play:** For the ingeniously simple and timeless puzzle concept from the future creators of GTA, which entertains even after decades.
atari-st__lemmings.teaser: A puzzle game from DMA Design in which you rescue hordes of blindly marching lemmings.

atari-st__double-dragon.article:
The two Lee brothers head out into the streets to wrest a kidnapped girl from the hands of the Black Warriors street gang. So begins Double Dragon, one of the titles that in the second half of the 1980s defined the beat 'em up genre and gave it clear rules: move from left to right, hit everything that moves, and pick up the weapons your enemies drop.

The original arcade game from Japan's Technos in 1987 became famous not only for its fluid combat but above all for two-player cooperation and the clever detail that after defeating the villains, the two friends could ultimately fight each other for the girl. On the Atari ST, as on most home computers of the era, the port came about through British publishers and arcade license conversions that filled the shelves of gaming software shops at the time.

In terms of gameplay, Double Dragon rests on a simple but satisfying repertoire of punches, kicks, throws, and grapples. Picked-up whips, knives, barrels, or stones give the fights an edge and force the player to strategize about when to use a weapon and when to leave it lying. On the 16-bit Atari ST, the port grappled with the typical compromises of arcade conversions, but the spirit of the original and its tense atmosphere of grimy streets remained intact.

The cultural significance of the original is hard to overstate. Double Dragon kicked off an entire wave of brawlers, inspired later classics like Streets of Rage and Final Fight, and became a brand that spawned sequels, conversions to countless platforms, an animated series, and a feature film. For Atari ST owners, it offered the chance to play one of the most influential arcade hits of its generation at home.

Today Double Dragon is more of a historical milestone than a technical showcase of the ST's capabilities, but that is precisely why it deserves attention. It is a game that shows what the beginnings of a genre looked like — a genre that would later dominate arcades and living rooms around the world.

**Why play:** To meet the forefather of the brawler genre and to cooperate with a friend in the style of the good old arcades.
atari-st__double-dragon.teaser: A foundational beat 'em up from Technos, 1987; the Lee brothers punch their way through gangs from left to right.

atari-st__golden-axe.article:
A barbarian, a dwarf, and an amazon set out against the evil Death Adder, who has kidnapped the king and his daughter and taken over the land of Yuria. Golden Axe is a fantasy brawler that took the proven beat 'em up formula and spiced it up with sword and sorcery, rideable beasts, and the unmistakable atmosphere of heroic fantasy.

Sega created the original for its arcades in 1989 and it quickly ranked among its iconic arcade titles. The game's strength lies in the combination of three distinct characters with their own abilities, the ability to mount fire-spewing enemy creatures, and magical attacks whose power the player replenished by collecting vials from goblins. All of this in two-player cooperation.

On the Atari ST, Golden Axe arrived as part of the wave of home conversions of Sega arcade hits, which were among the most sought-after products at the time. Sixteen-bit computers like the ST and Amiga were a natural choice for these conversions, even though they too could not fully match the performance of specialized arcade hardware. Nevertheless, the port delivered a colorful fantasy world and its characteristic battles.

Culturally, Golden Axe became one of the pillars of Sega and its arcade era. It spawned a series of sequels and ports, appeared in later compilations, and to this day remains a symbol of the golden era of fantasy-flavored brawlers. Together with titles like Double Dragon and Final Fight, it forms a cornerstone of the genre.

For Atari ST players, Golden Axe was a ticket to a colorful adventure that combined action, cooperation, and a bit of that sword-and-magic romance. Even today it ranks among the best that 1980s arcade fantasy had to offer.

**Why play:** For a brisk fantasy brawler with three heroes, beast riding, and magic, best enjoyed as a duo.
atari-st__golden-axe.teaser: A fantasy brawler from Sega with rideable beasts and magic spells; an arcade icon from 1989.

atari-st__out-run.article:
Get behind the wheel of a red convertible, seat a blonde beside you, and set off across an entire continent for the sheer joy of driving. Out Run is not a race for position or points in the classic sense — it is a celebration of speed, freedom, and the sunny atmosphere that defined one of the most famous arcade machines of the 1980s.

The Sega original from 1986, from Yu Suzuki's workshop, brought a revolutionary sense of driving, dynamic music selectable straight from the car radio, and above all a branching track where the player chose which way to continue at every junction. This gave rise to several different endings and enormous replayability. The arcade machine also became famous for its moving cabinet, which tilted into the turns.

On the Atari ST, Out Run arrived as one of many home conversions that filled the catalogs of the era. Converting the arcade graphics and smoothness to a 16-bit computer was a challenge, and the port had to contend with the platform's limitations, but it strove to preserve the essentials: the feeling of the road rushing by, the branching tracks, and the characteristic laid-back mood.

Culturally, Out Run is a seminal game. It laid the foundations of the so-called arcade racer genre focused on the driving experience rather than simulation, influenced countless later titles, and its aesthetic and music became a symbol of an entire era. The brand continued with further installments and to this day is synonymous with summery, carefree driving.

Even on the Atari ST, Out Run retained its charm. It is a game you return to not for the challenge but for the feeling it leaves behind — that moment when the road opens up before you and you simply step on the gas.

**Why play:** For the timeless feeling of free driving and the branching tracks of one of the most influential arcade racing games of all time.
atari-st__out-run.teaser: It's not about winning, it's about the drive; Suzuki's arcade legend with a choice of route and music.

atari-st__ghouls-n-ghosts.article:
Knight Arthur dons his armor once again to save a kidnapped princess, and once again hell on earth awaits him — literally. Ghouls 'n Ghosts is the sequel to the notoriously demanding Ghosts 'n Goblins and ranks among the most challenging action platformers the arcades ever produced.

Capcom released the original on its arcades in 1988 and built on its predecessor's reputation as a game that punishes every mistake. Arthur can take only two hits — after the first he loses his armor and runs around in his underwear, after the second he crumbles into a skeleton. The game also introduced new mechanics, such as shooting up and down and a mighty golden armor capable of charging special attacks.

On the Atari ST, a port was created that ranked among the prized home conversions of Capcom arcades. Sixteen-bit computers were capable of conveying the colorful, gloomy atmosphere of graveyards, windmills, and castles full of the undead, even though converting the hellishly difficult gameplay was never easy. Nonetheless, the port retained the merciless challenge of the original.

The cultural significance of the series is enormous. Ghouls 'n Ghosts cemented the brand's reputation as a symbol of hardcore difficulty, influenced generations of designers, and to this day is referenced whenever the conversation turns to games that truly torment the player. The series continued with further installments including Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts and lives on in the modern era.

Anyone seeking an honest, old-fashioned, merciless challenge will find exactly that in Ghouls 'n Ghosts. It is a game that will kill you a hundred times over, and you will keep coming back for another try.

**Why play:** For the legendary difficulty and darkly fairy-tale atmosphere of one of the most demanding action platformers of the arcade era.
atari-st__ghouls-n-ghosts.teaser: A hellishly difficult sequel to Ghosts 'n Goblins; double jump and armor from Capcom, 1988.

atari-st__r-type.article:
The lone fighter R-9 hurls itself against the biomechanical horror of the Bydo empire, and the player soon discovers that surviving here means learning every pixel by heart. R-Type is one of the most influential horizontal shooters ever and the yardstick against which the entire genre is still measured today.

Irem introduced the original in arcades in 1987 and brought with it a revolutionary idea: a detachable auxiliary unit called the Force, which the player attached to the ship from the front or the back, used as both a shield and a weapon, and maneuvered strategically. Added to this was a charged shot and an elaborate, organically styled enemy design inspired by the works of H. R. Giger.

On the Atari ST, R-Type arrived as one of the prestigious home conversions and was among the titles that owners of 16-bit machines took pride in. Converting the demanding, pattern-recognition-based gameplay and detailed graphics was difficult, but the port strove to preserve that tension where a single hit means death and where every level is a carefully designed trap.

Culturally, R-Type defined what a serious shoot 'em up should look like. Its Force mechanic became a textbook example of innovation, the game spawned a series of sequels and spin-offs, and it inspired countless followers. The boss of the first level, the giant Dobkeratops, ranks among the most iconic enemies in the history of the genre.

R-Type is not a relaxing game — it is a test of reflexes, memory, and patience. And that is precisely why, even after decades, it retains respect as one of the absolute peaks of arcade shooters.

**Why play:** For a masterfully designed horizontal shooter with the revolutionary Force unit, which still sets the tone for the entire genre today.
atari-st__r-type.teaser: An iconic horizontal shoot 'em up with a detachable Force pod; Irem, 1987.

atari-st__shadow-of-beast.article:
Few games could take your breath away on first launch quite like Shadow of the Beast. Smoothly scrolling background layers, a staggering number of colors, and David Whittaker's hypnotic soundtrack turned this platformer into a technological showpiece of its time — a work whose main purpose was to show what 16-bit computers were capable of.

The British studio Reflections released the game through Psygnosis in 1989 and it immediately became an icon, especially on the Amiga, where it fully exploited that machine's graphics hardware. On the Atari ST, a port was created that had to cope with different sound and parallax scrolling capabilities, but it still carried that unmistakable, fantastically dark visual style with its monstrous hero who was once a human.

In terms of gameplay, it is a demanding platformer combined with elements of combat and exploration of a vast, surrealistically tinged world. The game was notorious for its difficulty and how mercilessly it punished mistakes, which in many players evoked admiration for the graphics rather than joy at progress. It was here that the eternal tension between audiovisual splendor and playability became apparent.

The cultural significance of Shadow of the Beast lies in the fact that it became synonymous with the graphical pinnacle of the home computer era and with Psygnosis's reputation as a publisher of visually lavish titles. It spawned sequels and to this day is remembered as one of the most breathtaking technical demonstrations of its generation.

Whether you judge it as a brilliant work of art or as a frustrating trial, Shadow of the Beast remains unforgettable. It is a game you remember mainly for how it looked and sounded.

**Why play:** For an audiovisual experience that in 1989 showed the limits of what home 16-bit machines could do and still captivates today with its dark magic.
atari-st__shadow-of-beast.teaser: A technological showcase for the Atari ST with a hypnotic soundtrack by David Whittaker.

atari-st__rainbow-islands.article:
From the adorable spewing of bubbles, the heroes moved on to conjuring rainbows — and one of the loveliest and at the same time cleverest arcade platformers of the late 1980s was born. Rainbow Islands is the sequel to the cult Bubble Bobble, this time with a different, climbing mechanic based on rainbows.

Taito released the original in arcades in 1987 (with the subtitle Bubble Bobble 2) and brought an inventive gameplay principle: the hero shoots rainbows that serve as steps for climbing upward, as a weapon against enemies, and as a means of revealing hidden bonuses. The goal is to climb to the top of each level before the rising water catches up with you. Added to this was a rich system of hidden items and secret endings.

On the Atari ST, a port was created as part of the wave of home conversions of Taito hits. The 16-bit platform could convey the colorful, cheerful visuals and addictive gameplay well, although converting the precise timing from the arcade was always delicate. The port, however, retained that unmistakable, playful character of the original.

Culturally, Rainbow Islands ranks among Taito's most precious gems and is often placed among the best arcade platformers of all time. It became famous for its depth hidden beneath a cute surface, its system of secret diamonds unlocking the true ending, and its overall addictiveness. Together with Bubble Bobble it forms one of the most beloved gaming lineages.

Rainbow Islands is proof that cute graphics and serious gaming depth go hand in hand. Beneath the colorful surface hides a surprisingly thoughtful and demanding game that players return to even today.

**Why play:** For the inventive rainbow mechanic, the hidden secret endings, and the best combination of cuteness and gameplay depth the arcades had to offer.
atari-st__rainbow-islands.teaser: A colorful sequel to Bubble Bobble; instead of bubbles, the heroes climb their own rainbows.

atari-st__rick-dangerous.article:
An adventurer with a hat, whip, and pistol crawls through traps full of spikes, falling boulders, and arrows shooting out of the walls. Rick Dangerous is an unmistakably British platformer that cheerfully parodied Indiana Jones while at the same time punishing the player with one of the most insidious collections of hazards in the history of the genre.

The game was created by the studio Core Design and released in 1989, among others precisely on the Atari ST and Amiga. Core Design, later famous for the Tomb Raider series, bet here on the trial-and-error method: moving forward means running into a trap, dying, memorizing its location, and avoiding it next time. Rick defends himself with a pistol, dynamite, and a club with which he can stun enemies.

In terms of gameplay, Rick Dangerous became famous precisely for this merciless, memorization-based difficulty. Traps often come without warning and surviving the first run through a level is almost impossible, which makes the game a test of patience and a sense of humor. It was this combination, however, that made it unforgettable for an entire generation of home computer players.

Culturally, Rick Dangerous became one of the defining platformers of the British computer scene at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s. It got a sequel, Rick Dangerous 2, and to this day is remembered as a symbol of an era when games were made in small studios and when difficulty was considered a virtue, not a flaw.

Anyone who loves an old-fashioned challenge spiced with adventurous atmosphere and a pinch of English humor will find exactly that in Rick. It is a game that will kill you again and again, and you will be smiling all the while.

**Why play:** For a classic British trap platformer with an Indiana Jones vibe and a difficulty that is a legend in its own right.
atari-st__rick-dangerous.teaser: A British parody of Indiana Jones full of treacherous traps, from the future creators of Tomb Raider.

atari-st__kick-off-2.article:
A ball that doesn't stick to your feet, breathtaking speed, and a top-down view that turns football into a game of perception and anticipation. Kick Off 2 is for many old-timers not just a great football game but a downright sacred classic, and on the Atari ST it ranked among the best experiences you could have on the pitch. This game redefined what computer football could look like and how it could play.

The key innovation of the series was the way the ball was controlled. Unlike games where players glued the ball to their feet, in Kick Off 2 the ball moved independently and you had to control your running and kicks with a far greater dose of skill and timing. This resulted in a fast, almost relentless pace of the match, where reflexes and a sense of positioning decided everything. The bird's-eye view gave an overview of the whole pitch and the game offered extensive options from friendly matches to tournaments.

Behind the game stood designer Dino Dini and it was released under the Anco brand. Kick Off 2 built on the successful first installment and pushed its concept toward perfection, adding new options, tactics, and details such as corner kicks and cards. On machines like the Atari ST and Amiga it became the benchmark of the genre and sparked passionate debates among fans of competing football series.

The cultural significance of Kick Off 2 is enormous. The game built a devoted community that is still dedicated to it today, holds tournaments, and considers it the pinnacle of arcade football. For many players it remains the yardstick against which they measure all other football games, and its influence on the genre is undeniable.

Today Kick Off 2 can still get the blood pumping. Its controls have a high skill ceiling and reward those who learn to tame them with an experience that modern arcade football can hardly offer.

**Why play:** For demanding, fast, and immensely satisfying arcade football with legendary ball control that retains a devoted community to this day.
atari-st__kick-off-2.teaser: A cult football game where the ball doesn't stick to your feet; the top-down view redefined football games.

atari-st__international-karate.article:
Two figures facing each other, the calm before the strike, and then an explosion of movement, where a single well-timed kick decides victory. International Karate + brought martial arts on home computers to elegant perfection and on the Atari ST offered one of the purest and most polished takes on the fighting game. It was a work that pushed the genre beyond mere button-mashing.

Compared to older fighting games, International Karate + brought a fundamental novelty, namely a fight of three fighters at once. In the ring you had to deal with two opponents at the same time, which dramatically changed the dynamics of the match and forced you to watch your position on both sides. Scoring followed a system taken from real karate, where points were awarded for accurate and well-timed hits, so it was about elegance and precision, not frantic pounding. Between rounds there were also lighthearted bonus minigames.

Behind the game stood programmer Archer Maclean, who had already become famous with the first installment of International Karate, and IK+ is generally regarded as the peak of his work in this field. Maclean was among the most talented British creators of his generation, and his sense of animation fluidity and gameplay balance came fully to the fore in International Karate +. The game was released on a number of platforms and earned acclaim everywhere.

The cultural significance of the title is considerable. International Karate + is ranked among the best fighting games of the 8-bit and 16-bit era of home computers and for many players remains the definitive treatment of karate. Its balance, purity, and emphasis on skill made it a lasting classic.

Today International Karate + still ranks among the titles worth rediscovering. Its fight of three fighters remains fresh and its controls reward precision in a way that is satisfying even after years.

**Why play:** For elegant, skill-based combat of three karateka from one of the best British developers and for a timeless classic of the fighting game genre.
atari-st__international-karate.teaser: An elegant one-on-one fighting game where victory is decided by a single, precisely timed kick.

game-watch__ball.detail: The very first Game & Watch and Nintendo's first handheld game. You juggle balls and try not to drop them. Primitive, but a historically priceless start to all of portable gaming and to Yokoi's philosophy of cheap, reliable fun.
game-watch__ball.article:
This is where it all began. If you want to understand where portable gaming as you know it today came from, you have to go back to a single device with a silver body and a simple LCD display — the first Game & Watch, called Ball, from 1980. This is literally the zero point of the history of Nintendo's handheld games.

The gameplay principle is disarmingly simple: you control a character juggling balls, and your only task is to not let any of them fall. By moving your hands left and right you catch and toss the balls in a rhythm that gradually speeds up. No levels, no story — just pure reflexive challenge and the pursuit of the highest possible score. But it is precisely this simplicity that makes Ball immortal.

Behind the whole concept stands the legendary Gunpei Yokoi, a designer whose philosophy of "lateral thinking with seasoned technology" shaped Nintendo for decades to come. Yokoi bet on cheap, reliable, and accessible components — LCD displays and simple electronics from calculators — and turned them into entertainment that almost anyone could afford. Ball was proof that a game does not need power but a good idea.

The cultural significance of this device is enormous. Game & Watch kicked off an entire era of handheld electronic games and laid the foundations on which the Game Boy and all of Nintendo's later handheld consoles would later grow. Without Ball and its successors, the gaming industry would have taken quite a different path. It is a relic that shows how little it took for a phenomenon to be born.

Thanks to its historical significance, Ball was even commemorated later — Nintendo never forgot it, and this title remains a symbol of the beginning of the entire line. For collectors and fans of retro hardware, it is an iconic piece around which the story of portable gaming revolves.

**Why play:** To touch the very beginning of handheld gaming with your own hands — a primitive but historically priceless moment when an entire category of entertainment was born.
game-watch__ball.teaser: The first Game & Watch from 1980 by Gunpei Yokoi; ground zero for handheld gaming.

game-watch__fire.article:
Some games make you build empires, others simply want you to not let anyone hit the ground — and Fire belongs precisely to that second, purely nerve-racking category. This classic Game & Watch game from the early era of Nintendo's portable LCD devices puts the player in the role of a rescuer and turns a simple principle into a surprisingly stressful race against time.

The game mechanics are a model of the exemplary simplicity on which the entire Game & Watch series was built. People jump out of a burning building and you, with a pair of firefighters holding a rescue tarp, run along the bottom of the screen to catch them. Every bounced person must be safely delivered to the ambulance on the other side. The pace relentlessly speeds up, more and more figures appear, and a single miss means a loss. It is a pure reflexive challenge where every fraction of a second counts.

Fire was created during a period when Nintendo, under the leadership of Gunpei Yokoi, was only just discovering what could be done with a cheap LCD display and simple electronics. The philosophy was clear: no levels or story, just one perfectly tuned principle that drives the player to chase higher and higher scores. It was precisely this purity of design that made Game & Watch a phenomenon.

Culturally, Fire fits into the mosaic of titles that defined what portable gaming looked like before the arrival of the Game Boy. These little devices were immensely popular among children and adults alike, and the principle of catching falling objects became one of the archetypes of the genre — you will find variations on it in electronic games all over the world.

The simplicity and immediate comprehensibility make Fire an ideal illustration of why Game & Watch worked. You don't need instructions, you don't need time to learn — just a few seconds and you are already desperately chasing the figures across the screen so that no one hits the pavement.

**Why play:** For pure, addictive reflexive fun from one of the archetypal titles of portable gaming, where every second decides between rescue and a fall.
game-watch__fire.teaser: Catch jumpers from a burning building in a safety sheet; a simple mechanic, brutal pace.

game-watch__octopus.article:
Beneath the surface lurks a giant octopus, and you have a single task: retrieve the treasure from the sunken wreck before its tentacles drag you into the depths. Octopus is one of the best-known titles in the entire Game & Watch series and remains one of the games that fans of portable LCD classics recall first.

The gameplay combines greed with evasive agility. You control a diver who sets out from the boat to the seabed for gold coins and jewels. On the way there and back, however, you must weave between the moving tentacles of the giant octopus, which stretch tirelessly across the screen. The longer you linger at the treasure and the more coins you gather, the higher your score — but also the greater the risk that a tentacle will catch you. The game is thus essentially a constant gamble between greed and caution.

Octopus was created in the early phase of Game & Watch under the direction of Nintendo and Gunpei Yokoi, whose approach consisted of distilling a single idea into a perfectly playable form. No story, no levels — just mounting tension and the desire to beat your own record. It was precisely this purity and instant comprehensibility that made Octopus one of the most beloved pieces of the whole line.

Culturally, Octopus became something of a flagship for the Game & Watch aesthetic. Its simple yet striking silhouette of a diver and tentacles imprinted itself on the memory of an entire generation, and the principle of "go for the loot and come back alive" is repeated in countless later games. When people say classic Game & Watch, many picture exactly this underwater chase.

Thanks to its popularity, the Octopus motif appeared in various commemorations and tributes to the classic era of Nintendo's portable games. For collectors and nostalgics alike, it remains one of the iconic symbols of what handheld entertainment looked like in the early eighties.

**Why play:** For a thrilling game of greed versus survival that ranks among the most iconic titles of the entire Game & Watch series.
game-watch__octopus.teaser: A diver collects treasure from a wreck while dodging tentacles; one of the best-known Game & Watch games.

game-watch__oil-panic.detail: Dual-screen games using the fold-out format. Oil Panic is about catching drops of oil, Mario Bros. is cooperative bottle-packing on a conveyor belt (the first game where Mario and Luigi work together). Clever design within the strict limits of LCD.
game-watch__oil-panic.article:
Two screens, one disaster, and you in the middle — Oil Panic showed that even with a strictly limited LCD display, something surprisingly ingenious could be devised. This Game & Watch title from the first half of the eighties made use of the fold-out dual-screen format and managed to extract gameplay from it that single-screen devices could not offer.

The principle of Oil Panic is based on catching drops of oil. On the top screen you catch escaping oil in a container and make sure it does not overflow; when it is full, you must pour it down at the right moment onto the bottom screen, where a helper waits with containers. The game thus cleverly links the action on both displays — you have to watch the upper and lower parts at the same time and coordinate two activities at once. That is precisely what made it an unusually demanding and clever title.

Dual-screen Game & Watch devices of this type were an example of how Nintendo pushed the boundaries of its own platform. Instead of a single display, they offered a fold-out construction with two screens, thereby expanding design possibilities. This format proved to be such a strong idea that it foreshadowed Nintendo's later dual-screen thinking. The same family also includes the cooperative Mario Bros., the first game where Mario and Luigi work together on a conveyor belt packing bottles.

The cultural significance of these titles lies in the fact that they expanded the notion of what a pocket game could do. The player no longer watched just one field of the screen but had to divide their attention — a concept that proved extraordinarily viable and returned to Nintendo many years later.

Clever design within the strict limits of LCD is exactly what Oil Panic excels at. It shows that the creativity of the designers was able to overcome technical limitations and turn the simple mechanic of catching drops into a tense interplay of both hands and both eyes.

**Why play:** For clever dual-screen gameplay that squeezed a surprisingly fresh and demanding experience out of the strict limits of the LCD display.
game-watch__oil-panic.teaser: A dual-screen Game & Watch where you catch oil drops on both the top and bottom screen; a clever LCD trick.

game-watch__donkey-kong.detail: A key title for two reasons: it was the first dual-screen Game & Watch (the fold-out "multi screen" that directly inspired the later Nintendo DS) and, above all, this is where Yokoi invented the **D-pad** — the cross-shaped controller that became the worldwide standard on all game controllers. A condensed version of the arcade Donkey Kong.
game-watch__donkey-kong.article:
There are games that are fun, and games that change an entire industry — and Donkey Kong in its Game & Watch version clearly belongs to the second group. This 1982 device was not just a clever pocket adaptation of the famous arcade game but the cradle of one of the most important inventions in the history of game controls altogether.

From a gameplay standpoint, it is a condensed version of the arcade Donkey Kong. As Mario you climb up the structure, dodge obstacles, and try to reach the kidnapped girl while the giant gorilla makes your path harder. The Game & Watch version cleverly recast the arcade experience into a limited LCD format and spread the action across the two screens of the fold-out device.

And this is exactly where two fundamental milestones come in. Donkey Kong was the first dual-screen Game & Watch of the "multi screen" type — a fold-out construction with two displays, which decades later directly inspired the Nintendo DS concept. Even more importantly, Gunpei Yokoi invented the **D-pad** here, the cross-shaped directional controller. This unassuming plate with four directions became the worldwide standard that you have since found on practically every game controller on the planet.

The cultural significance of this device is therefore hard to overstate. The D-pad fundamentally changed how players control games — it replaced clumsy joysticks and levers with an elegant, intuitive solution that caught on immediately and has survived to this day. The fact that it was born on a small pocket Game & Watch with Donkey Kong is one of the best pieces of trivia in all of gaming history.

Donkey Kong as a brand was, moreover, one of the pillars on which Nintendo built its popularity, and its portable version helped spread the fame of the gorilla and Mario into the palms of players' hands. The combination of an iconic character, technical innovation, and design genius makes it one of the most significant titles of the entire series.

**Why play:** Because you are holding in your hand the device on which the D-pad and the idea of two screens were born — a piece of gaming history in the form of a brisk pocket classic.
game-watch__donkey-kong.teaser: The handheld Donkey Kong from 1982, birthplace of the D-pad; a turning point in controls.

game-watch__donkey-kong-jr.article:
When the gorilla ends up behind bars, it is time for its offspring to step onto the scene — and that is exactly what Donkey Kong Jr. in the form of a pocket Game & Watch is about. This platformer casts the player in the role of the young Donkey Kong Jr., who sets out to free his imprisoned father, and converts the famous arcade game into an economical yet cleverly designed LCD format.

The gameplay is built on climbing and dodging. As DK Jr. you move upward along vines and structures, gather your way to the goal, and dodge the enemies and obstacles that the villain places in your path. The Game & Watch version had to condense the arcade original into the confines of a simple display, and so it relies on readable, instantly comprehensible movement and increasing difficulty that tests your reflexes and timing.

The title was created under Nintendo's direction in an era when the Game & Watch series was experiencing the peak of its popularity and Nintendo was systematically converting its arcade hits into pocket form. Donkey Kong Jr. was a logical continuation of the phenomenon that Donkey Kong itself had started — and so fans got the chance to experience the other side of the story, where the hunter becomes the rescuer.

Culturally, Donkey Kong Jr. is interesting also in that it represents one of the few cases where the player controls a character from the "opposite" side of the conflict — instead of Mario you stand against him as a young gorilla saving his father. This inversion of roles was fresh for its time, and the Donkey Kong brand thereby grew further into one of Nintendo's pillars.

As part of the extensive line of portable LCD games, this title too helped shape the notion of what gaming on the go looked like in the early eighties. For collectors and nostalgics it remains a pleasant reminder of the days when a small display and a good idea were enough to create addictive entertainment.

**Why play:** For a brisk pocket platformer in which you command the young Donkey Kong for the first time and experience the other side of the famous duel with Mario.
game-watch__donkey-kong-jr.teaser: DK Jr. climbs to reach his imprisoned father; a compact but cleverly designed port of the famous arcade game.

game-watch__mario-bros.article:
If you recall the name Mario today, a jumping platformer most likely comes to mind.
