The Xbox version added new tracks over the arcade original, game modes focused on time trials and drifting, and online leaderboards letting players compare times with others around the world.

OutRun 2 is still cited as one of the best arcade racers ever made and as proof that pure driving joy doesn't need realism or an open world to work. A run lasts just a couple of minutes, but it tempts you into replaying it immediately in search of a better line and better sequence of turns. Sega later followed up on the concept with the sequel OutRun 2006: Coast 2 Coast, but the 2004 Xbox version is still remembered as the purest transfer of the arcade classic to a home console.
xbox__outrun-2.teaser: An arcade machine from Sega AM2; the goal isn't to win the race, but to enjoy a scenic drive.

xbox__conker-live-and-reloaded.article: A remake of the notorious squirrel game from the Nintendo 64, brought by Rare to the Xbox in dazzling graphics. Behind the cute exterior hides a vulgar, boozy, parodic ride full of movie references and black humour — definitely not for kids. The campaign serves up crazy situations and famous moments, while the reworked multiplayer added online battles. Live & Reloaded is a visually gorgeous showcase of what the Xbox could do, and the last great classic of Rare's old era.
xbox__conker-live-and-reloaded.teaser: A remake of the vulgar, drunken-parody-filled squirrel classic from the Nintendo 64.

ps2__tekken-4.article:
**Tekken 4**, the fourth installment of Namco's famous fighting series, arrived on PlayStation 2 after the series had established itself as an arcade classic, bringing a major leap forward in the form of fully three-dimensional arenas with obstacles, walls, and height differences that could be used tactically in fights. For the first time players could corner an opponent against a pillar, knock them down stairs, or use uneven terrain to their advantage, which felt revolutionary at the time and set Tekken apart from rival series like Virtua Fighter and Soulcalibur. Walls also enabled entirely new combos, since a bounced-off opponent stayed briefly defenseless, and for the first time players could move more freely to the sides of the arena.

Visually, the game benefited from the PS2's power and offered more realistic character models and more elaborate animation, though the controls turned out somewhat slower and less fluid than in previous entries, earning mixed reactions from hardcore fans. Story-wise, the game continued the King of Iron Fist tournament and expanded the Mishima family mythology with new characters such as Steve Fox and Christie Monteiro. The Story Battle mode gave individual fighters short cinematic interludes, while Tekken Force added beat 'em up sections between fights, in which the player fought through waves of enemies in simple levels.

Although Tekken 4 is viewed today more as a transitional entry between the classic and modern eras of the series, its environmental experiments influenced later titles, and the game remains an important milestone in the history of fighting games on Sony consoles. Reviews of the time praised the cinematic intro and graphical precision, though they objected to the slower pace compared to the arcade-born Tekken 3. Today the entry is remembered as a bold transitional step toward the later Tekken 5, which took its interactive environments but restored the speed players were used to. That's exactly why Tekken 4 remains interesting today: it offers a glimpse of the moment the series tried to find itself in a new generation.
ps2__tekken-4.teaser: For the first time, fully three-dimensional arenas with walls and stairs that can be used tactically in fights.

ps2__tekken-tag-tournament.article:
As one of PlayStation 2's launch titles in Japan, **Tekken Tag Tournament** showed what the new console could do, becoming a literal showcase for the generation. Namco chose not to build a new story but instead based the game on a simple yet brilliantly functioning tag team combat principle, where the player picks a pair of fighters and can swap between them at any time during a match, while the benched fighter slowly regenerates health. Tagging can also be triggered mid-combo, producing spectacular joint attacks by both characters, and the whole system rewards players who master two different styles instead of just one.

Practically the entire history of the series made it into the roster, including bosses and bonus characters from previous installments, turning the game into a giant showcase of the Tekken universe. The visuals were stunning for their time, with detailed models, fluid animation, and spectacular two-on-two battles that had no equal on other platforms at the time; the console version also offered a sharper image and higher character detail than the arcade original. The game also included the beloved Tekken Bowl bonus mode, bowling with the series' characters, serving as light relief between more serious fights.

Although formally a spin-off without its own canonical story, Tekken Tag Tournament became an extraordinary commercial success and is still remembered as a title that convinced players the jump to a new console generation was worth it. The game also offered an elaborate training mode and an extensive gallery of unlockable costumes and characters, motivating repeated play beyond the fights themselves, and it is often cited as one of the best-selling PlayStation 2 launch titles of all time. The popularity of the format eventually led to a sequel, Tekken Tag Tournament 2, a whole generation later, and tag battles remain something fans still occasionally wish would return to the series.
ps2__tekken-tag-tournament.teaser: A launch showcase for the PlayStation 2; tag team fights with instant fighter switching.

ps2__soul-reaver-2.article:
**Soul Reaver 2**, the sequel to the cult Legacy of Kain series, picked up directly from the end of the first Soul Reaver and threw players back into the role of the vampire Raziel, who falls through time rifts into Nosgoth's past to uncover the dark secrets behind his own curse and the fate of the entire realm. Crystal Dynamics bet on a cinematic storytelling form with elaborate dialogue, high-quality voice acting, and a script full of twists, ranking among the most ambitious narratives of action-adventure games of the era.

Gameplay-wise, the game combined platforming, puzzles based on switching between the material and spectral worlds, and a combat system in which Raziel could absorb the souls of defeated enemies. Shifting into the spectral plane changes not only the appearance but also the shape of the environment — walls warp and inaccessible passages open up — and most puzzles are built around this dual nature of the world. Compared to the first entry, less emphasis was placed on collecting upgrades and open-world exploration; the game instead became more linear and focused more on storytelling and the atmosphere of a decaying gothic world.

Visually, it was one of the technically most impressive titles of the early PS2 era, with striking lighting, long sightlines, and architecture inspired by Victorian gothic style; loading between areas was also hidden within seamless movement, making the world feel like one continuous whole. Although the story ended on a cliffhanger that frustrated fans awaiting resolution, Soul Reaver 2 is still valued today as one of the most atmospheric and best-written action titles of its time. Kurt Harland's musical score perfectly underscored the melancholic atmosphere of the decaying Nosgoth and lent individual locations significant emotional weight, which is why the game still serves today as an example of how powerfully sound can shape a told story.
ps2__soul-reaver-2.teaser: A direct sequel with cinematic storytelling; Raziel falls into the past through rifts in time.

ps2__legacy-of-kain-defiance.article:
**Legacy of Kain: Defiance** became the grand finale of the series and, for the first time, let players switch between two protagonists of the entire saga — the vampire Raziel and his creator Kain — whose fates stretch across millennia of Nosgoth's history. The game finally tied together the previously fragmented storylines from Blood Omen, Soul Reaver, and Soul Reaver 2, delivering a satisfying, if dark and morally ambiguous, resolution appreciated especially by longtime fans of the series. The two characters play very differently: Kain relies on brute vampiric strength and the blood of his enemies, while Raziel draws on spiritual abilities and soul manipulation.

The combat system underwent a significant shift toward a more action-oriented approach closer to hack-and-slash games, with combos, special abilities, and the option to equip Raziel with various weapons, bringing a more dynamic pace than the contemplative earlier entries. The game also abandoned a free camera in favor of fixed cinematic angles, which limited combat visibility somewhat but significantly heightened the theatrical impact of individual scenes. Puzzles based on switching between the material and spiritual worlds remained a key gameplay element, and together with the gothic atmosphere of a crumbling kingdom, formed the core of the experience.

High-quality voice acting, an ambitious script full of philosophical musings on fate and free will, and sensitive musical work gave the game the mark of mature storytelling that was rare on consoles at the time. Defiance may not have achieved the commercial success of the era's major action blockbusters, but critics and players alike still rank it among the best-written and most atmospheric titles of the entire PlayStation 2 generation. Reviewers particularly praised the performances of Simon Templeman and Michael Bell, whose vocal delivery gave the age-old dispute between Raziel and Kain the weight and drama it deserved, and many fans still hope for a sequel the franchise has yet to receive.
ps2__legacy-of-kain-defiance.teaser: The series' grand finale, for the first time alternating between Raziel and Kain, tying up the saga's storylines.

ps2__prince-of-persia-warrior-within.article:
After the unexpected success of Sands of Time, Ubisoft Montreal opted for a bold shift and delivered a darker, more brutal sequel, **Prince of Persia: Warrior Within**, in which the Prince flees from the Dahaka itself, a personification of fate that has come to claim him for disrupting the flow of time. The game abandoned its predecessor's fairy-tale tone in favor of a gothic, industrial aesthetic underscored by an official soundtrack collaboration with the band Godsmack. The chases with the Dahaka, against which there is no defense and only fleeing is possible, rank among the most tense passages of the entire trilogy.

Acrobatic parkour remained the core of the gameplay — the Prince runs along walls, swings on poles, and manipulates time — but the combat system was significantly reworked toward rougher, bloodier fights, with the ability to finish off enemies, wield two weapons at once, and collect found swords and axes that wear down and break during battle. The game also introduced, for the first time, a mechanic of traveling between two time periods of the same fortress, enabling clever puzzles based on comparing past and present; the very same room can look like a well-preserved palace one moment and a ruin the next.

The presence of a more revealing version of Shahdee and the overall more mature tone proved controversial, dividing fans of the original trilogy. The vast fortress also forms an interconnected labyrinth easy to get lost in, which some players welcomed as a liberating freedom and others saw as a step back from the first game's tight design. Nonetheless, Warrior Within became commercially successful, and its harsher approach influenced the direction of the whole series toward a more action-oriented style, which culminated in the following installment, Two Thrones. Despite mixed reception from fans of the original fairy-tale trilogy, it ranks among the series' best-selling entries, and its tone still sparks debate today about which direction the Prince of Persia brand should take next.
ps2__prince-of-persia-warrior-within.teaser: A bold, darker turn after Sands of Time; gothic aesthetics inspired by metal music.

ps2__prince-of-persia-two-thrones.article:
**Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones**, the concluding chapter of the trilogy about the Prince and the Sands of Time, brought players back to Babylon, where the hero returns after inadvertently bringing back with him the consequences of his interference with the flow of time, as well as a malicious dark twin born of the sand. Ubisoft Montreal combined the best of both previous games in this installment — the elegant acrobatics and fairy-tale atmosphere of Sands of Time with the darker, more action-oriented combat system of Warrior Within — creating a more balanced entry that became the best received by both players and critics in the whole series.

New to the game were so-called Speed Kills, spectacular quick-time events unfolding during fluid movement through the environment, where the Prince ambushes an enemy unexpectedly, and a single timing mistake sends him back into open combat. The game also introduced the option to temporarily play as the dark twin, who possesses different, more aggressive abilities including shadow movement and a chain weapon, with these sections chasing the player because of constantly depleting health. The game expanded the acrobatic repertoire with new moves such as sliding down ropes or fighting while riding a chariot, adding even greater dynamism to the pace, and the ruined Babylon offered a more open, urban scenery instead of enclosed palaces.

The story, told partly in retrospect through the Prince's memories, elegantly closed the plotline established in the first game and offered a satisfying resolution to the relationship between the Prince and Shahdee, complemented by the twin's inner voice acting as both conscience and temptation. The Two Thrones is still considered a dignified and technically polished conclusion to one of the most acclaimed action trilogies of the PlayStation 2 generation. Critics also praised the balance between acrobatics, combat, and storytelling, which is why many fans consider this the best-tuned entry in the entire trilogy, and composer Stuart Chatwood's score earned numerous accolades.
ps2__prince-of-persia-two-thrones.teaser: The trilogy's conclusion combines the acrobatics of Sands of Time with the darker style of Warrior Within.

ps2__baldur-s-gate-dark-alliance-ii.article:
**Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance II**, the sequel to the console hack-and-slash RPG set in the Forgotten Realms, took players to the area around the city of Baldur's Gate shortly after the events of the first game, where a band of adventurers embarks on a search for a lost artifact and uncovers a conspiracy involving demonic forces. The game stayed true to the proven formula — an isometric view, two-player split-screen co-op, and an elaborate system of loot, crafting, and character upgrades based on Dungeons & Dragons rules.

Compared to the first game, it offered a wider selection of classes including barbarian, druid, monk, and necromancer, each with its own skill trees and unique fighting style, increasing replayability. Combat plays out in real time and is controlled directly with the stick and buttons like an action game, so D&D rules operate in the background without slowing the player down; spells and special attacks are assigned to quick-select slots. Visually, the game felt more polished thanks to better lighting and more varied environments, ranging from city streets through swamps to underground caves full of monsters.

Co-op mode remained the series' main draw, letting two players progress through the campaign together and share loot, making the game a popular pick for game nights, and a tougher difficulty level awaited fully built-up characters after completion. Despite a modest graphical and technical step forward compared to its competition, Dark Alliance II confirmed that console action RPGs rooted in Dungeons & Dragons had a solid place on PlayStation 2 with a loyal fan base. The game also offered an elaborate crafting system for combining runes and gemstones into weapons and armor, deepening the incentive to collect and experiment with loot even after finishing the main campaign, keeping many players hooked for dozens of hours.
ps2__baldur-s-gate-dark-alliance-ii.teaser: A sequel to the console hack-and-slash RPG set in the Forgotten Realms, playable cooperatively by two.

ps2__champions-of-norrath.article:
Snowblind Studios, creators of the successful engine behind Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, brought a similar recipe to the world of EverQuest and created, with **Champions of Norrath**, one of the most beloved console action RPGs of the generation. The game offered players a choice of several classes such as warrior, wizard, or necromancer and sent them across the diverse continent of Norrath, where they battle armies of undead, demons, and other monsters from EverQuest's rich mythology. Each class is also tied to a specific race with its own opening background, so even a repeat playthrough of the campaign feels different.

The game's key strength was an elaborate item system with randomly generated properties, making loot hunting and character building addictive in a way similar to PC hack-and-slash classics like Diablo, something with little competition on consoles at the time. Combat is fully action-based, controlled directly with the stick, and complemented by a skill tree in which points are invested at every level. The game supported co-op for up to four players on a single screen, making it a popular party game, and it also offered online multiplayer through the PlayStation 2 Online service of the time, where characters and items could be shared with friends.

Visually, the game benefited from colorful and varied environments ranging from deserts through ice fields to underground temples, with the engine handling large numbers of enemies on screen without noticeable slowdown. Critics particularly praised the depth of itemization and replayability, which made Champions of Norrath one of the longest-played titles of the genre on PlayStation 2 and the predecessor to the successful sequel Champions: Return to Arms. The game later received a digital re-release on modern platforms, confirming its lasting popularity among action RPG fans even more than two decades after its debut.
ps2__champions-of-norrath.teaser: An action RPG from the creators of Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, set in the world of EverQuest.

ps2__dark-cloud.article:
**Dark Cloud**, the debut title of the then-unknown studio Level-5, was among PlayStation 2's launch games and immediately showed its ambition to combine dungeon crawling with the unusual element of town building. The player takes on the role of young Toan, who sets out to rebuild a world destroyed by the demon Dark Genie — quite literally, since he collects individual buildings, inhabitants, and landscape features as so-called Atla stones while making his way through randomly generated dungeons, then places them back into abandoned towns using the Georama tool.

This unique hybrid of action RPG and town-building simulation gave the game unexpected depth and staying power, since correctly placing houses and objects affected inhabitants' satisfaction and unlocked further possibilities; residents have their own wishes about neighbors and views, and fulfilling them rewards the player with bonuses and new quests. The combat system ran in real time, weapons wore down as the game progressed and had to be forged and upgraded at blacksmiths, adding another layer of resource management. On top of that, the player had to keep an eye on the hero's thirst and continually find water, giving even dungeon exploration its own rhythm and tension.

The graphics may look simpler compared to later PS2 titles, but the colorful, fairy-tale visual style has aged surprisingly well, and the randomly generated levels ensured dungeons never repeated the same way twice. Dark Cloud laid the foundation for Level-5's distinctive style, which the studio later developed further in the more successful sequel Dark Cloud 2, and it is still valued today as one of the most original RPG titles of the console's early era. Composer Tomohito Nishiura's melodic soundtrack perfectly complemented the game's fairy-tale atmosphere, and thanks to its success, Level-5 earned Sony's trust for further ambitious projects. The combination of endless descent into the dungeons and the calm assembly of villages on the surface created a pleasant rhythm alternating tension and relaxation that has since appeared in many other games.
ps2__dark-cloud.teaser: Level-5's debut game; it combined dungeon crawling with building your own town.

ps2__maximo-ghosts-to-glory.article:
**Maximo: Ghosts to Glory** was created as a spiritual successor to the classic arcade series Ghosts'n Goblins, and Capcom's developers made no secret of wanting to bring the tough difficulty and gothic atmosphere of the old hit into three dimensions for a new console generation. The player takes on the role of the knight Maximo, who, after being betrayed, sets out into the realm of the dead to rescue his fiancée from the dark sorcerer Achrius, passing along the way through graveyards, locked castles, and hellish landscapes full of skeletons, zombies, and other gothic monsters.

Gameplay-wise, it was an action platformer emphasizing precise sword-and-shield combat, collecting keys to unlock new areas, and the genre's typical black comedy, in which Maximo loses pieces of his armor after being hit before finally dying, running around meanwhile only in his underwear. Besides regular lives, the game also works with a limited number of continues that must be bought from Death himself, so every failure carries a tangible price and the player has to weigh whether to risk further progress. The difficulty was intentionally high, harking back to the tradition of arcade cabinets, setting it apart from the then-prevailing trend of more accessible action games.

The visual style combined cartoonish grotesqueness with elaborate environments, and the game earned praise for sensitively building on the legacy of Ghosts'n Goblins while maintaining its own identity; levels are also designed to reward memorizing enemy and trap placement. Maximo became commercially successful enough to earn a sequel, Maximo vs. Army of Zin, and established itself as one of the genre's icons on PlayStation 2. The game was also accompanied by a distinctive narrator commenting on Maximo's failures with dark humor, lending even the more frustrating passages a lighter tone and setting the title apart from more seriously toned competition. Today Maximo is remembered as one of the rare cases where the uncompromising arcade school was successfully translated into three-dimensional space without the game losing the readability and fairness that the old Ghosts'n Goblins was built on.
ps2__maximo-ghosts-to-glory.teaser: A spiritual 3D successor to Ghosts 'n Goblins; harsh difficulty and a gothic atmosphere.

ps2__ratchet-and-clank-going-commando.article:
**Ratchet & Clank: Going Commando**, the second installment in the adventures of the lombax Ratchet and the robot Clank, significantly expanded the concept of the first game and transformed the series from a linear platformer with shooter elements into a more open action-adventure with RPG elements. For the first time, players could return to already-visited planets, buy weapon upgrades with experience points, and watch as their arsenal gradually evolved, changing both appearance and effects, bringing deeper motivation for repeat play and experimentation. The hero himself also gains experience, so his stamina gradually increases, turning a simple action game into a title with tangible progression.

Insomniac Games also added so-called research missions and minigames, expanded space combat, and introduced arena battles in which the player fights through waves of enemies using their collected arsenal for rewards of money and rare items. The series' humor, built on Clank's sarcastic quips and the genre's self-irony about space adventures, remained core to its appeal and was backed by quality voice acting and cinematic cutscenes full of fictional advertisements and media inserts.

Visually, the game raised the bar for colorful, intricately animated worlds, from snowy planets to industrial complexes, and technically ranked among the best PS2 had to offer at the time; the engine handled sprawling locations with dozens of enemies and effects without noticeable stutter. Going Commando is still viewed by many fans as the peak of the trilogy thanks to its ideal balance of action, humor, and meaningful character progression, and it cemented the series' position as one of Sony's flagship franchises for the generation. Critics today still often call it the best-balanced entry of the entire original trilogy and the moment the series found its definitive shape. It's here that the principle the series still builds on today took hold: every weapon has its own personality, grows along with the player, and it pays to rotate through all of them instead of relying on a single tried-and-true favorite.
ps2__ratchet-and-clank-going-commando.teaser: Expanded the first game with RPG elements, revisitable planets, and weapon upgrades.

ps2__ratchet-deadlocked.article:
**Ratchet: Deadlocked**, the fourth entry in the Ratchet & Clank series, brought a dramatic stylistic shift as Insomniac Games abandoned the traditional platforming elements in favor of a more action-heavy, more mature shooter inspired by reality television and gladiatorial combat. Ratchet is here without his robotic sidekick Clank, forced to fight in the arenas of the broadcast show DreadZone, where a sadistic producer decides his fate, and he's backed up by two combat robots that can be given orders in battle. The whole proceedings are further narrated by a pair of cynical hosts, giving the game a satirical edge.

The emphasis on team tactics, enemy waves, and arena combat set Deadlocked apart from earlier entries focused on exploration and platforming, which drew mixed reactions from part of the fanbase, while others appreciated the fresh change of pace and more intense action. Missions are structured as a series of challenges with optional additional conditions that reward better prizes when completed, letting the player set their own difficulty level. The weapon system remained the core of the fun, offering a wide array of extravagant instruments of destruction that could be upgraded, and the game also featured online cooperative and competitive multiplayer, a fairly ambitious feature for the series at the time.

Visually, the game felt darker and more industrial than previous entries, emphasizing metallic arenas and the technological aesthetic of a futuristic show business, while the engine kept things running smoothly even with large numbers of enemies and explosions on screen. Deadlocked showed the flexibility of the Ratchet & Clank brand, even though the series wouldn't return to its platforming roots until the following generation on PlayStation 3. The game also offered a sophisticated upgrade system for the combat robots, who gained experience and new abilities much like the main hero in previous entries of the series. In retrospect, Deadlocked feels like an interesting dead end in the brand's development, yet also one of the most fast-paced and best-controlling action titles Insomniac released on PlayStation 2.
ps2__ratchet-deadlocked.teaser: Without Clank, in the arenas of a bloody reality show; the harshest entry in the series.

ps2__jak-x-combat-racing.article:
For their final Jak and Daxter title on PlayStation 2, Naughty Dog opted for an unexpected genre leap, offering with **Jak X: Combat Racing** a full-fledged racing game with combat vehicle elements, drawing inspiration from the successful racing sequences within Jak 3. The story takes place after Jak is unjustly accused and, as punishment, is forced to take part in deadly races organized by the underworld, which serves as a framework for tying the career mode together with the series' distinctive humor and colorful cast.

Gameplay-wise, the game offered a wide range of weapons and power-ups, destructible tracks inspired by earlier locations in the series, and a deep vehicle upgrade system, letting races combine speed with tactical use of offensive and defensive abilities. Besides classic races, players also face arena battles and time trials, so the career mode offers a more varied program than just lapping tracks, and handling relies on brisk drifting and boosting rather than simulation-grade precision. The graphics engine, built on Jak 3 technology, allowed large numbers of vehicles on track at once and visually striking destructible environments, which was impressive for the hardware of the time.

The game also offered online multiplayer, still a relatively new feature for console racing titles at the time, along with classic split-screen play for duels on a single console. Although Jak X didn't commercially overshadow the series' main platforming entries, it was received by critics as a competent and enjoyable racing spin-off that gave a fitting close to the story of the Jak and Daxter trilogy on PlayStation 2. Critics especially praised the depth of the vehicle upgrade system and the game's fidelity to the series' signature humor even in its new racing-game guise. For Naughty Dog, it was also a farewell to the world of Jak and Daxter, as the studio subsequently went in a completely different direction and made its mark on PlayStation 3 with more realistically styled action-adventures.
ps2__jak-x-combat-racing.teaser: The last PS2 entry in Jak and Daxter; an unexpected leap into a full-blooded racing game.

ps2__gradius-v.article:
The legendary horizontal space shooter series Gradius returned after years of dormancy in the form of **Gradius V**, created by the acclaimed studio Treasure, renowned for its technically brilliant and visually spectacular shoot 'em up titles. The game preserved all the series' traditional elements, namely collecting power-ups through the iconic gradual upgrade-selection system, the accompanying Option modules orbiting the Vic Viper ship, and the notoriously high difficulty that forced players to memorize enemy layouts and traps.

A new addition was the ability to choose, at the start, one of four ways to control the Option modules, ranging from a fixed lock direction to rotation around the ship, which fundamentally changes tactics in individual stages and gives the player room to find their own style. Treasure also brought its own distinctive signature, evident in elaborate boss battles, a dynamic camera changing angles during stage flights, and extremely dense waves of enemy projectiles typical of the studio's work.

Visually, the game ranked among the most technically impressive 2D shooters on PlayStation 2, with intricately detailed backgrounds, transparency effects, and smooth animation even with an enormous number of objects on screen. Despite the genre's relatively low commercial potential during a period dominated by 3D action games, Gradius V earned praise from both the specialist press and loyal fans of classic arcade shooters as one of the peaks of the genre for its generation, and proof that a traditional 2D shoot 'em up can still find an audience on modern hardware. Studio Treasure also brought its tradition of extremely elaborate boss fights requiring precise recognition of attack patterns, which is why the game remains one of the most-cited showcases of this development team's mastery to this day. It's also the last major entry in the classic Gradius line, so Gradius V is viewed as a fitting full stop to one of the oldest shooter franchises of all.
ps2__gradius-v.teaser: The return of the legendary space shooter, made by Treasure, masters of the shoot 'em up.

ps2__r-type-final.article:
**R-Type Final** was officially presented by Irem as the closing chapter of the long-running horizontal space shooter series R-Type, which was reflected in the game's extraordinarily generous content. The title offered an incredible over one hundred playable ships, from classic models from previous entries to experimental and bizarre machines, with each ship having its own characteristics, beam type, and Force module behavior, effectively turning the game into a museum of the series' history. New ships were also gradually unlocked based on flight hours logged and conditions met, so building up the hangar was in itself a long-term goal.

The gameplay remained faithful to the traditional recipe, that is, slow, deliberate progress through stages full of organic alien constructs, precise handling of the Force module, which can be attached to the ship from the front or back or launched forward as a standalone shield, and the need to memorize the layout of hazards, which was especially appreciated by longtime fans of the genre. The visual side combined detailed 2D sprites with three-dimensionally modeled environments and bosses, so the game felt visually current despite its nostalgic nature, and a dark, oppressive visual style inspired by biomechanical art gave it an unmistakable atmosphere.

The presence of secrets, unlockable ships, and several alternate endings increased replay value for collector-minded players. Although it was a niche title aimed primarily at devoted series fans, R-Type Final is still remembered today as a dignified and content-packed farewell to one of the most influential shooters in video game history and a milestone for the genre on PlayStation 2. The game also included an extensive gallery describing the history and characteristics of each ship, making it a genuine celebration of the series' history, and Irem shelved the franchise for a long time after its release.
ps2__r-type-final.teaser: The official closing chapter of the R-Type series; over a hundred playable ships, possibly a genre record.

ps2__armored-core-silent-line.article:
**Armored Core: Silent Line**, full title Armored Core 3: Silent Line, expanded the world established in Armored Core 3 and offered players another dose of the deep combat mech customization the series is famous for. The player assembles their own Armored Core robot from dozens of components, from the core frame through legs to weapons and generators, with each choice affecting weight, speed, energy consumption, and combat style, creating an almost endless number of possible configurations and making the game equally a strategic puzzle and an action shooter. The decision between a light, nimble machine and a lumbering colossus with massive firepower is reflected in every second of combat: the generator's energy is quickly consumed by maneuvering, an overloaded mech moves like a target on a shooting range, and a poorly balanced build fails before it even manages to target the enemy.

The game's story takes place in a parallel timeline to Armored Core 3 and introduces factional conflicts, in which the player's decision about which side to join affects available missions as well as the resulting story development. The missions themselves place emphasis on tactical planning of loadout before combat as much as on agility during the actual fights in industrial and underground environments; cramped corridors demand a completely different configuration than open plains, so the player learns to read the briefing before even leaving the hangar. Rewards for completed contracts also flow straight back into repairs and part purchases, creating a separate layer of economic tension.

FromSoftware, later famous for the Dark Souls series, was already demonstrating in this game its inclination toward demanding, uncompromising difficulty and rewarding patient mastery of the game's systems. Armored Core: Silent Line became a beloved title within a narrow but devoted community of mech simulator fans, and is still valued today for the depth of its customization system, which in many respects surpassed the competition. The game also offered asynchronous exchange of mech build data between players, which deepened the series' community aspect, and FromSoftware continued in it its tradition of an extremely detailed customization system that also influenced later entries.
ps2__armored-core-silent-line.teaser: Deep customization of combat mechs; build a robot exactly to your own specifications.

ps2__zone-of-enders.article:
The first entry in the **Zone of the Enders** series was created under the supervision of Hideo Kojima, creator of Metal Gear Solid, and became one of Konami's most distinctive experiments with the action mech genre on PlayStation 2. The player takes on the role of a young boy, Leo Stenbuck, who accidentally comes into possession of the advanced combat robot Jehuty and is drawn into a conflict between Earth and the Martian colonies, forced to face a dilemma between his fear of war and the necessity of fighting. Leo's reluctance to kill isn't just window dressing, but permeates the entire narrative, giving an otherwise action-heavy game an unexpectedly urgent anti-war undertone.

Gameplay-wise, the game offered brisk, acrobatic combat taking place in three-dimensional space, where the player dodges, flies, and attacks both from a distance with laser weapons and up close with melee attacks, which was exceptionally dynamic and fluid for its time. Automatic targeting keeps the opponent locked on even during sharp dodges and boosting, so the player can focus on the rhythm of strikes, blocks, and counterattacks instead of wrestling with the camera. The game also tracks damage inflicted on the colony's defenses, so carelessly fighting enemies between residential blocks is reflected in the final rating, adding an element of responsibility to every battle.

The short playtime was partly offset by high replay value and bonus content, including access to a demo of the then-upcoming Metal Gear Solid 2, which helped the game sell beyond fans of the mech genre. The visual style combined anime aesthetics with technically advanced particle effects and explosions, placing the game among the most technically impressive titles of the console's early era. Zone of the Enders laid the groundwork for the more successful sequel The 2nd Runner and remains valued to this day as a stylistically distinctive and innovative entry in the action mech genre. The game's music was composed by Norihiko Hibino, and the atmosphere was rounded out by the striking visual style inspired by designer Yoji Shinkawa's work, which earned the title a loyal fanbase despite its short runtime.
ps2__zone-of-enders.teaser: Mecha action from the studio of Hideo Kojima, creator of Metal Gear Solid.

ps2__contra-shattered-soldier.article:
After years of dormancy for the legendary Contra series, Konami brought it back in the form of **Contra: Shattered Soldier**, which preserved the brutal difficulty and run-and-gun action of the classic entries, but set it in a darker, more mature sci-fi story with more pronounced violence and gore, earning the game a stricter age rating. Players once again control mercenaries Bill and Lance, who after years in prison get a chance at pardon in exchange for eliminating an alien threat, and progress through classic scrolling stages full of giant bosses, mechanical enemies, and extremely dense waves of gunfire.

A major change from the older entries was limiting the arsenal to a fixed set of weapons, between which the player switches depending on the situation, and which can be charged for a stronger attack by holding the trigger, turning the choice of the right type of fire against a specific boss into a puzzle of its own. The game introduced a performance rating system based on accuracy and speed of kills, motivating players to replay and memorize stages in order to achieve the highest possible score, in the spirit of the arcade tradition; only a sufficiently high rating unlocked the game's true ending. Two-player co-op on a single console was retained, and in practice it was among the most enjoyable ways to actually finish the game.

The visual side combined pre-rendered backgrounds with detailed 3D models of characters and bosses, giving the game a visually striking, cinematic feel while retaining two-dimensional gameplay. The soundtrack relied on brisk, electronically tinged themes, including variations on the series' classic melodies. The difficulty was deliberately extreme and uncompromising, in keeping with the series' tradition, but at the same time limited its accessibility to new players. Shattered Soldier is still valued today as one of the best returns of a classic arcade series to modern hardware, and proof that the run-and-gun shooter genre still has its firm place even in the era of 3D action. The entry also brought the series back into the awareness of a new generation of players and paved the way for the following title, Neo Contra, released two years later.
ps2__contra-shattered-soldier.teaser: The return of a legend with a darker sci-fi story and the same brutal difficulty.

ps2__castlevania-lament-of-innocence.article:
**Castlevania: Lament of Innocence** represented a major turning point for the series, being the first to bring it into a fully three-dimensional environment, setting the story in the eleventh century, where we follow the knight Leon Belmont as he sets out into Dracula's castle to rescue his fiancée, unknowingly founding the tradition of the cursed family of vampire hunters. Gameplay-wise, the game combined exploration of a gothic castle full of puzzles and hidden rooms with action combat, in which the player uses the iconic whip supplemented with secondary weapons and magic orbs, whose combinations unlock a whole range of special attacks and give the combat an experimental dimension.

The developers drew inspiration from the structure of the series' so-called metroidvania entries, but simplified navigation through fast travel between key areas of the castle, which made getting around the three-dimensional space easier. Individual wings of the castle could be traversed in essentially any order, and each was capped off by its own boss, giving progress a pleasant sense of choice. The combat itself built on whip combos, dodging, and precisely timed counterattacks, rewarding the player for an aggressive, fluid fighting style rather than cautious waiting.

The game's atmosphere drew on gothic architecture, dark lighting, and a classic musical score connecting the new entry with the legacy of the series' previous games. Boss battles, from giant gargoyles to legendary figures such as Death, were among the game's most visually striking moments. Although the shift to 3D drew mixed reactions among fans compared to the beloved 2D entries on Game Boy Advance, Lament of Innocence is now valued as a dignified and atmospheric start to a new era of the series on home consoles. Composer Michiru Yamane's score elegantly combined orchestral arrangements with the series' classic melodies, reinforcing the sense of continuity with Castlevania's long-standing legacy.
ps2__castlevania-lament-of-innocence.teaser: The first fully 3D Castlevania; it founded the legend of the cursed Belmont bloodline.

ps2__castlevania-curse-of-darkness.article:
**Castlevania: Curse of Darkness** followed the three-dimensional line of the series established by Lament of Innocence, setting the story in 1479, shortly after the events of Castlevania III, where we follow the mercenary Hector, a former devil forgemaster capable of summoning and controlling demons, who sets out after a betrayal to avenge the death of his beloved and confronts his former ally Isaac. The key new feature was the so-called Devil Forge system, which lets the player capture defeated demons and use them as summonable companions in battle, and further upgrade them by combining items and materials obtained from enemies, bringing a depth comparable to RPG crafting systems.

The combat system remained based on melee weapons supplemented by help from summoned demons with specific abilities, ranging from offensive to supportive, allowing for different approaches to combat tactics. Collecting materials from fallen enemies and forging them into new swords, spears, or gauntlets drew the player into an endless cycle of upgrading and gave meaning even to ordinary battles, since every defeated opponent could be hiding material for the next tier of gear. The demon companions also evolved based on how they were treated, so the player effectively raised their own combat retinue.

The game's environments ranged from frozen forests to underground dungeons, adorned with the series' typical gothic aesthetic and accompanied by a quality orchestral soundtrack. Although the graphics didn't seem exceptional for their time and the technical execution was criticized for a certain stiffness, the depth of the demon system and the engaging story of betrayal and revenge secured the game a lasting place among the beloved action titles of the Castlevania series on PlayStation 2. The game also became the last entry of the series released for PlayStation 2 before the Castlevania brand moved for a long time to handhelds and the new generation of consoles.
ps2__castlevania-curse-of-darkness.teaser: A 3D sequel in the series with a Devil Forging system for controlling demons.

ps2__devil-may-cry-2.article:
**Devil May Cry 2** arrived with enormous expectations following the revolutionary first entry, which had defined the stylish hack-and-slash genre, but ultimately became one of the series' most controversial titles due to a marked departure from what fans had loved about its predecessor. Dante becomes a much colder and less charismatic hero in this entry, the game's pace slowed down, and the combat system, though technically expanded to feature two characters, Dante and the newly playable Lucia, with distinct fighting styles, lacked the depth and responsiveness that fans expected from the series. A large portion of enemies could be eliminated simply by holding down the gun trigger from a safe distance, removing the pressure that pushed players to take risks and build stylish combos.

Still, the game brought some positive innovations, such as the Devil Trigger system allowing temporary transformation into a more powerful demonic form with its own abilities, and it expanded the acrobatic moves with the ability to run along walls and leap between buildings both during and outside of combat. The camera shifted from the static cinematic angles of the first entry toward a freer, player-controlled view, which better suited the more open spaces the game leads through. The visual style and urban environments inspired by a modern metropolis gave the game a different visual identity compared to the first entry's gothic castle.

Critics received the game with mixed feelings, and many called it the series' biggest disappointment, which led Capcom to a strong return to its roots in the excellent third entry, which brought both difficulty and combat depth back to their maximum. Despite its reputation, Devil May Cry 2 remains an interesting historical chapter in the development of one of the most influential action series in video game history. Many players still cite the game as a cautionary example of how easily a sequel can lose the identity of a successful predecessor, even though from a purely technical standpoint it was a solidly crafted title.
ps2__devil-may-cry-2.teaser: A controversial entry after the revolutionary first game; a colder Dante, a slower pace.

ps2__resident-evil-code-veronica-x.article:
**Resident Evil Code: Veronica** was originally created for the Sega Dreamcast as the first entry in the series set fully in a 3D environment rather than pre-rendered backgrounds, and the expanded X version, supplemented with new scenes and improved graphics, arrived on PlayStation 2, allowing a much wider audience to experience a key chapter in the story of the Ashford family and the continuation of Claire and Chris Redfield's fates following the events of Resident Evil 2. The player follows Claire, imprisoned on an island facility belonging to the Umbrella Corporation, from which she tries to escape amid a zombie apocalypse while uncovering the dark secrets of the family behind the creation of the T-virus.

Gameplay-wise, the game remained faithful to the series' classic survival horror recipe, that is, limited ammunition, key-and-item-based puzzles, and a tense atmosphere reinforced by cinematic camera angles, though the full 3D environment allowed for a more dynamic camera than in earlier entries. The genuine room geometry also brought small but significant changes to the feel of the game: the camera could smoothly follow the character, lights cast moving shadows, and threats could now emerge from the depth of the space, not just from behind a fixed frame edge. The item chests, however, aren't linked together, so a poorly organized inventory can punish the player for dozens of minutes to come.

Switching between playable characters, Claire and later Chris, brought shifting perspectives on the same story and expanded the narrative scope with background on the Umbrella Corporation. The X version's visuals were improved on PS2 with sharper textures and new cutscenes explaining connections to later entries in the series. Code: Veronica X remains valued today as an important bridging point in the Resident Evil mythology and one of the last classic survival horrors before the arrival of the more action-focused fourth entry. The X version also added several new cutscenes clarifying Albert Wesker's relationship to the Umbrella organization, which was especially appreciated by longtime fans of the entire saga.
ps2__resident-evil-code-veronica-x.teaser: An expanded version of the first fully 3D Resident Evil; a key chapter in the Ashford family story.

ps2__resident-evil-outbreak.article:
**Resident Evil Outbreak** brought a significant innovation to the series in the form of cooperative multiplayer, in which up to four players together make their way through a zombie apocalypse in Raccoon City, taking place in parallel with the events of previous entries in the series. The game offered several short scenarios, in which players choose from eight civilian characters, ranging from a waitress to a police officer to an actor, with each character possessing unique abilities and weaknesses affecting their survival style. The choice of character thus fundamentally changes the playthrough: one can open locked doors, another can carry more items or handle treating the wounded, so the same map offers a slightly different way out each time.

Online multiplayer, still rare on consoles at the time, allowed players to cooperate on solving puzzles, share limited resources, and jointly face hordes of infected, bringing a completely new social dimension based on communication and cooperation under pressure into the classic survival horror. Because the game lacked voice chat, players communicated using a set of predefined commands and gestures, which paradoxically created tense, almost silent teamwork amid the chaos. The game also introduced a virus infection system, where a character could become infected and their condition would gradually worsen if the player didn't find a cure in time, adding urgency to the whole playthrough of a scenario.

The visuals matched the series' standard, emphasizing the dark atmosphere of an abandoned city, and the scenarios, from a burning restaurant to a hospital and sewers, offered strikingly varied settings. Due to the technical limitations of the network infrastructure at the time and the need to purchase a network adapter for the PS2, the online features suffered from limited availability, yet Outbreak remains a significant experiment that foreshadowed later cooperative horror games and demonstrated the genre's potential for a shared experience. The game also received a direct sequel, File 2, which expanded the roster of playable scenarios and characters with further chapters of the zombie apocalypse in Raccoon City.
ps2__resident-evil-outbreak.teaser: A cooperative survival horror game for up to four players in Raccoon City.

ps2__fatal-frame.article:
**Fatal Frame**, known in Japan as Zero, brought a distinctive and unmistakable twist to the survival horror genre: the only weapon protagonist Miku Hinasaki has against ghosts is not a gun, but an ancient camera, the Camera Obscura, capable of harming and repelling supernatural entities by capturing their likeness on film. The story drops the player into the abandoned Japanese mansion of Himuro, cursed after a tragic ritual that spiraled into a massacre years earlier, where the heroine searches for her missing brother amid haunted corridors filled with the spirits of the ritual's victims.

The photography mechanic created a truly unique combat system, requiring the player to wait for the right moment to snap a ghost for maximum damage, demanding nerves of steel and the courage to move closer to a supernatural threat instead of fleeing. The viewfinder switches the game to a first-person view, so the player loses awareness of their surroundings at exactly the moment they are most vulnerable, and must rely on the trembling of the image and sound cues that betray an approaching presence. Camera film is also a limited resource, and players instinctively save the strongest types for later, creating the same tension of managing ammunition found in classic horror games.

The game's atmosphere, built on traditional Japanese yūrei mythology and the claustrophobic setting of the old mansion, ranked among the most terrifying experiences of the entire console generation, heightened by minimalist sound design and the absence of music during tense moments. Diaries and scraps of notes found along the way pieced the story of the ritual together gradually, leaving many horrors only hinted at. Fatal Frame became a cult classic of J-horror video games, and its unique concept influenced later entries in the series as well as numerous other horror titles that tried to imitate its unmistakable atmosphere of fear. Years later the game received a remastered version for modern platforms, confirming the lasting popularity of its concept.
ps2__fatal-frame.teaser: The only weapon against ghosts is a camera; a distinctive survival horror game.

ps2__fatal-frame-iii-tormented.article:
The third installment in the series, **Fatal Frame III: The Tormented**, linked the characters and storylines of the two previous games through the Dream House, a mysterious mansion into which the heroines are transported every time they fall asleep, and from which they risk never waking again. The protagonist is photographer Rei Kurosawa, scarred by the trauma of a car accident that killed her fiancé, and her nightly visits to the cursed house connect past and present through a tattoo that gradually appears on her body and draws the attention of malevolent spirits.

The game retained the proven mechanic of fighting ghosts with the Camera Obscura, this time expanded with new types of film and camera upgrades, and added a system in which the character falls asleep in her own room, serving as the transition between the real world and the mansion's dreamlike nightmare. This alternation between the two planes is one of the game's strongest ideas: the apartment in the waking world functions as a calm home base where the player examines findings, reads notes, and prepares, yet the horror of the house gradually seeps in here too, and the safe haven stops being safe. Linking three playable characters with different abilities and perspectives on the same story gave the narrative depth and emotional weight, especially through themes of loss, guilt, and fear of sleep, which the game handles with unusual sensitivity for the horror genre.

The visual and audio presentation remained at the high level typical of the series, emphasizing quiet, claustrophobic dread over cheap jump scares; the camera moves slowly, the corridors are dark, and the most frequent sound is the player's own breathing. The Tormented is still considered the most emotionally powerful and thematically cohesive entry in the entire Fatal Frame series. Composer Ayako Toyoda completed the unsettling atmosphere with a minimalist, quiet musical score that further heightened the sense of loneliness and vulnerability felt by the main heroines.
ps2__fatal-frame-iii-tormented.teaser: Connects the previous entries through a dream house from which there is no escape.

ps2__siren.article:
**Siren** was created under the direction of Keiichi Toyama, creator of the original Silent Hill, and became one of the most demanding and darkest survival horror games of its generation, set in the isolated Japanese village of Hanuda, whose inhabitants were transformed into undead beings called Shibito after a mysterious ritual. The game follows ten interconnected characters whose fates intertwine across a non-linearly told story divided into short, difficult missions, and the player often has to figure out the connections between individual chapters alone, without explicit explanation. The chronological mission map, on which further branches gradually unlock, thus functions as a puzzle whose meaning only becomes clear after several playthroughs.

The game's key and most distinctive mechanic was the so-called Sightjack, allowing the player to temporarily see through enemies' eyes and thereby track their movement as well as whether they had spotted the player, which became an essential survival tool in an environment where direct combat was extremely risky and often best avoided entirely. The player literally learns to read the village through the eyes of others: depending on where a patrolling Shibito is currently looking, they plan short dashes between hiding spots, wait lying in the grass, and pray that the flashlight beam doesn't fall the wrong way. The characters are mostly ordinary civilians with no combat training, so even a plain pipe or a shovel feels like a desperate improvisation.

The game's atmosphere, built on oppressive silence, a static camera perspective, and extremely limited resources, ranked among the most terrifying and also most frustrating experiences of its time due to its notoriously high difficulty. Thanks to its raw, uncompromising approach and original Japanese folklore foundation, Siren earned cult status among horror fans and is still praised today as one of the most nerve-wracking titles of the genre on the PlayStation 2. The game was later followed by a loose sequel, Siren 2, and a reworked remake, Siren: Blood Curse.
ps2__siren.teaser: From the creator of Silent Hill; one of the darkest and most demanding horror games of the generation.

ps2__haunting-ground.article:
**Haunting Ground** cast the player as Fiona Belli, a young girl who wakes up locked inside an ancient castle after a mysterious car accident, inhabited by a strange family harboring dark secrets, and unlike most survival horror games of its time it completely lacks any weapon, meaning the only means of survival is running, hiding, and using the environment to break away from pursuers. Fiona is accompanied on her journey by a dog named Hewie, who can be tamed and used to attack enemies, find hidden items, or warn of approaching danger, creating an unusual relationship element between the player and a virtual companion built on trust and care.

The game focused on a permanent sense of vulnerability, heightened by the fact that pursuers can appear almost anywhere, forcing the player to improvise hiding places rather than confront them directly, which created a dread different from traditional combat-based survival horror. Fiona also succumbs to panic: the longer someone chases her, the less control she has, the screen blurs, her breathing quickens, and the heroine stops obeying commands, so the player loses control exactly when they need it most. Wardrobes, barrels, and cramped spaces under tables thus become more valuable than any weapon, and the game regularly forces the player to hold their breath and wait for footsteps beyond the door to fade away.

The sexualized design of the main heroine and the game's themes of abuse of power sparked some controversy in the press at the time, but they also contributed to the work's unmistakable, unsettling atmosphere. The visually gothic castle, full of symbolism and dark corners, completed the claustrophobic sense of helplessness, and several different endings rewarded the player based on how well they had taken care of Hewie throughout. Haunting Ground is still valued today as one of the last purebred survival horror games of the PlayStation 2 era before the genre's shift toward a more action-oriented approach.
ps2__haunting-ground.teaser: Without a single weapon - survival is only possible through running and hiding from your pursuers.

ps2__gitaroo-man.article:
**Gitaroo Man** ranks among the most distinctive rhythm games ever released on PlayStation 2, and it became a cult favorite despite never becoming a commercial hit. The player takes control of an awkward boy named U-1, who in a dream obtains a mystical guitar and becomes the hero Gitaroo Man, whose task is to defeat a series of bizarre enemies in musical duels resembling a combination of a guitar showdown and a classic rhythm game with notes scrolling across the screen. Each level offered a completely different musical genre, from rock through Latin rhythms to electronic music, and a unique visual style inspired by Japanese anime, with colorful, exaggeratedly expressive character animation.

The game's system demanded not only precise timing of button presses following the note chart, but also simultaneous control of attack and defense via two analog sticks, creating a much more dynamic and demanding experience than competing rhythm games of the time. The duels are further divided into alternating phases: in the offensive phase the player follows a winding line along which a tone travels, in the defensive phase the player deflects the opponent's incoming blows, and in the final phase the winner is decided. Both sides' life gauges rise and fall according to accuracy, so the musical piece itself serves as the dramaturgy of the duel, and the player can literally hear how well they are doing.

The story, full of humor as well as surprisingly emotional moments, wove the individual musical duels into a coherent coming-of-age journey for the main hero, and at one point manages to shift from wild comedy to a quiet acoustic ballad that many players still remember today. Although the game never received a direct sequel outside Japan due to low sales, Gitaroo Man is still remembered as one of the most creative and beloved rhythm titles of its generation, prized above all for its unmistakable style and musical inventiveness.
ps2__gitaroo-man.teaser: A cult rhythm game about guitar duels, a commercial failure at the time, legendary today.

ps2__frequency.article:
**Frequency**, from Harmonix — the studio that a few years later created the phenomenon of Guitar Hero and Rock Band — introduced a completely original rhythm game concept in which the player doesn't play a single track linearly but literally composes and remixes music by alternately activating individual sound tracks, such as drums, bass, synth, or vocals, arranged in separate lanes around a central cylinder. Successfully holding the rhythm on one track locked it in permanently, and the player could then jump to another, gradually building the complete song out of individual layers, creating the feeling that the player was simultaneously a musician and a DJ composing their own version of the song.

The controls used three shoulder buttons for three note lanes, plus a separate switch for changing tracks, so the player had to constantly decide which layer of the song to keep playing and which to let fall silent for a while. A mistake didn't just cost points — it left an audible hole in the music, a brilliantly direct way of giving feedback without a single number on screen. The soundtrack combined electronic music, hip hop, and rock from both independent and better-known artists, allowing the game to appeal to an audience seeking an alternative to mainstream musical offerings.

The visual style, with its futuristic neon design of the tunnel and cylinder, perfectly complemented the electronic aesthetic of the music selection and created a hypnotic audiovisual experience that, during longer sessions, could induce an almost trance-like state. Frequency did not achieve major commercial success, partly due to its demanding controls requiring rapid switching between tracks, but it was received extremely warmly by critics as an innovative work that anticipated the future direction the music game genre would later actually take. Harmonix indeed later admitted that the experience of developing Frequency directly shaped the design of their later, globally successful Guitar Hero and Rock Band series.
ps2__frequency.teaser: From Harmonix, the future creators of Guitar Hero; the player remixes the track on the fly.

ps2__amplitude.article:
**Amplitude** built on the concept of its predecessor Frequency and expanded it with more elaborate visuals, a wider range of musical styles, and more accessible controls, making it a more polished and balanced version of the original idea of remixing tracks on the fly. The player again flies through a futuristic tunnel and activates individual music tracks, from drums through bass to vocal lines, while successfully maintaining the rhythm builds the complete song and failure returns the track to an inactive state, requiring constant switching of attention between several parallel rhythmic patterns.

Compared to Frequency, the playing field expanded from a closed cylinder into a more open, flatter track that makes it easier to see what's coming, and new bonuses were added that temporarily slow the game down, auto-complete a track, or multiply the score, adding a tactical layer to the songs. Multiplayer for several players on one console, where opponents could trip each other up with sabotage bonuses, ranked among the most entertaining parts of the game. The soundtrack this time was even more varied and included tracks from acclaimed artists across the genres of electronic music, rock, and pop, moving the game closer to a mainstream audience.

The game also offered an editor that let players create their own levels and share them, putting it ahead of its time in terms of user-generated content for rhythm games. The visual design remained faithful to its predecessor's neon, futuristic aesthetic, but with improved effects and smoother animation making full use of the PlayStation 2's power. Although Amplitude never achieved commercial success comparable to the later Guitar Hero, its musical innovations and emphasis on remixing are still valued today as an important stepping stone in the development of the entire music game genre. The game received a modern remake for PlayStation 4 in 2016, confirming that the concept of remixing music tracks had lost none of its originality even after all those years.
ps2__amplitude.teaser: A polished sequel to Frequency with richer visuals and more accessible controls.

ps2__guitar-hero-ii.article:
**Guitar Hero II** expanded and polished the concept with which the first game launched the phenomenon of guitar rhythm games, and became the entry that definitively catapulted the genre into the mainstream. Players once again hold a plastic guitar with colored buttons and try to hit notes scrolling down the fretboard in time with the music, and the second installment added a more elaborate Star Power system for temporarily multiplying score, improved visuals with more pronounced effects during great performances, and, for the first time, a cooperative two-player mode where one player handles the melody and the other the bass line or rhythm guitar.

The note charts themselves were noticeably more precise and true to actual guitar playing compared to the first game, with greater emphasis on chords, transitions across several frets, and so-called hammer-ons and pull-offs that allowed fast passages to be played without a pick. The drawn-out training in the form of a career progressing through ever-larger clubs and arenas gave the player a sense of real band growth, and the money earned could be spent on new guitars, outfits, and bonus songs. The setlist, made up of both rock classics and more modern hits, ranked among the game's strongest features, spanning several decades of rock history, complemented by bonus cover versions recorded specifically for the game.

The difficulty curve was carefully tuned from accessible beginner levels all the way up to extremely demanding expert difficulties requiring virtuoso control of the peripheral. The game's commercial success, boosted precisely by the bundling with a plastic guitar, proved the enormous market potential of music peripheral games and directly paved the way for the following mega-hit Guitar Hero III as well as the competing Rock Band series. Guitar Hero II is still remembered as the peak of the original era of guitar rhythm games on PlayStation 2. The bonus band Harmonix Allstars and a number of hidden songs further gave the game long-term replay value.
ps2__guitar-hero-ii.teaser: It refined the formula of the first game and catapulted guitar rhythm games into the mainstream.

ps2__ssx-tricky.article:
**SSX Tricky** built on the successful launch title SSX and pushed arcade snowboard racing toward even more extreme, over-the-top fun full of acrobatic tricks, electronic music, and colorful, almost comic-book stylization, definitively setting the series apart from the more realistic sports simulations of its competitors. The key novelty was the so-called Tricky mode system, in which, once the trick meter was filled, the player could perform extravagant super tricks accompanied by exaggerated animations and character one-liners, further heightening the arcade, adrenaline-fueled character of the game compared to its more serious predecessor.

The roster of distinctive riders, each with their own visual identity, humor, and riding style, was a key draw of the series, and characters like Mac Fraser or Elise Riggs became icons of that console generation's sports arcade games; well-known actors even provided some of their voices, which was unusual for a sports game at the time. Tracks full of shortcuts, jumps, and destructible elements offered high replay value and motivated players to memorize ideal lines for the highest possible score and the longest trick combos. The downhill runs are designed like giant roller coasters: long tubes, ice caves, and jumps across entire valleys chain together without a single pause, and the game constantly demands that the player land cleanly and keep chaining tricks.

A soundtrack made up of electronic and dance music perfectly complemented the game's energetic pace and became an integral part of its identity. Technically, the game ran briskly and smoothly, which was essential for the feeling of speed. SSX Tricky is still widely considered the peak of the entire series and one of the best arcade sports titles of the entire PlayStation 2 generation. The commentator character DJ Atomika, accompanying players with witty remarks during races, became an inseparable part of the series' identity and lent it his voice in the following installments as well.
ps2__ssx-tricky.teaser: Extreme arcade snowboarding with over-the-top tricks; the iconic Tricky mode.

ps2__ssx-on-tour.article:
**SSX On Tour**, the fourth installment of the arcade snowboarding series, added a brand-new element in the form of skiing alongside the traditional board disciplines, letting players choose for the first time between a snowboard and skis with different handling and riding styles, which expanded the tactical options when picking a riding style. The game left behind the fictional mountains of previous installments and set its races on more realistically styled, though still over-the-top, mountains around the world, tied together by a music-tour theme in which riders travel between locations like rock bands on a concert circuit.

The most striking change was the visual stylization, which abandoned Tricky's neon futuristic aesthetic in favor of a rough, hand-drawn sketchbook look in the spirit of punk poster art, with scribbled lettering and drawings right in the user interface. The player also created their own character and worked their way up from a nobody to a star, moving the series closer to the career model of the skateboarding games of the time. The soundtrack was assembled in cooperation with specific musicians and bands, who also appeared as playable characters alongside the traditional series roster, further strengthening the connection between music and gaming culture characteristic of the entire SSX series.

The trick system and Tricky mode remained the core of the gameplay, supplemented by new acrobatic combinations and interactive track elements, such as a crowd reacting to riders' performances. The visuals faithfully captured the series' energetic, colorful aesthetic, though some reviews pointed to a certain repetitiveness compared to the high point that was Tricky. Interestingly, the GameCube version offered Mario, Luigi, and Princess Peach as playable characters. Although On Tour never reached the cult status of its predecessor, it remains a beloved and entertaining conclusion to the arcade snowboarding series on PlayStation 2 before its long hiatus.
ps2__ssx-on-tour.teaser: The fourth entry added skiing alongside snowboarding, for the first time in the whole series.

ps2__burnout-revenge.article:
**Burnout Revenge** pushed the series of arcade racing games built on risky, aggressive driving another step further, adding a mechanic that let the player ram slower traffic vehicles from behind and literally blast them off the road, fundamentally changing the dynamics of races and rewarding players for bold, aggressive driving through heavy traffic instead of merely dodging it. This change split the series' fanbase: for some it was a liberating acceleration, for others a loss of the tension that in previous installments came from every car in the lane posing a deadly danger.

The series' signature Takedown system, the destructive elimination of opponents through violent collisions, remained the core of the gameplay and was supplemented with improved crash physics, making vehicle collisions even more spectacular and visually satisfying, with emphasis on slow-motion shots of the destruction from several camera angles. The game expanded its selection of game modes with new variants of races focused specifically on destruction and scoring for damage inflicted on opponents and traffic, matching the series' philosophy of favoring chaos and adrenaline over realistic simulation. Even after their own crash, the player stays in the game: the wreck can still be blasted, sending an opponent into the barriers as one last act.

Track design offered denser traffic and more alternate shortcuts than previous installments, requiring players to make split-second decisions while driving at high speed, and motion blur at full boost gave the sense of speed an almost uncomfortable urgency. Critics especially praised the excellent sense of speed and the unrivaled vehicle destruction system. Burnout Revenge is still ranked among the peak entries of the series and one of the best arcade racing titles of the entire PlayStation 2 generation. The game was released on Xbox 360 a year later, making it one of the series' first titles on the new console generation.
ps2__burnout-revenge.teaser: Ramming civilian traffic as an offensive weapon; the most aggressive Burnout yet.

ps2__burnout-dominator.article:
**Burnout Dominator** was created as a transitional title within the series, developed primarily for PlayStation 2 and PSP at a time when the main development team at Criterion Games was already focused on the next-gen sequel Burnout Paradise, yet the game tried to return to the series' core values after the more experimental Revenge. Instead of ramming civilian traffic as an offensive weapon, Dominator returned to an emphasis on clean, smooth track handling and the so-called Burnout system, a special nitro ability charged by risky driving against oncoming traffic, drifting, and safe near-misses around opponents.

The game introduced a new Maniac system, allowing the player, once the meter was filled, to perform spectacular stunts without direct risk of crashing, rewarding stylish, smooth driving instead of pure destruction. The career structure was built around a series of so-called Burnout Driving Challenges, short challenges tied to specific vehicle classes, which made the game work excellently in short bursts and suited the handheld PSP version well. Anyone able to hold an unbroken nitro chain across an entire track was rewarded with the hypnotic feeling of speed the series had always been built on.

Track design drew on locations from previous series installments, adapted and expanded for the new game modes, including the return of the popular Crash mode focused on causing the most effective possible traffic pileup at intersections. The visuals, though limited by PS2 hardware at a time when next-gen consoles were already on the market, remained solid and smooth, accompanied by an energetic licensed soundtrack in the series' spirit. Burnout Dominator, though less innovative than Revenge, remains an honest and craftsmanlike farewell for the series to the PlayStation 2 generation. Many reviewers praised the return to a purer take on the series, even though the game itself brought no major gameplay innovations.
ps2__burnout-dominator.teaser: A transitional entry between Revenge and Paradise; a return to pure, fluid driving.

ps2__need-for-speed-underground.article:
**Need for Speed: Underground** marked a decisive turning point for Electronic Arts' long-running racing series, abandoning its previous focus on exotic supercars and police chases to dive fully into the subculture of illegal street racing and tuning of Japanese and American compact cars, inspired by the then-popularity of the Fast and the Furious film series. Players could modify their cars in extensive detail, both mechanically, through engines, transmissions and nitro systems affecting performance, and visually through body kits, spoilers, paint jobs, neon underglow and vinyl wraps, creating a depth of customization unmatched on consoles at the time.

The driving model was distinctly arcade-like and forgiving, with cars sticking to the road like glue while the game rewarded the player at every moment with a tremendous sense of speed. This was underscored by motion blur at the edges of the screen when nitro was engaged, glossy wet asphalt reflecting shop-window lights, and deliberately tight track design squeezed between buildings and lampposts. The career mode motivated players to gradually earn money for expensive parts through various race types, from classic circuits to drag races with manual gear shifting where a single missed shift could end the run, to drift competitions scored on angle and smoothness of the slide.
