The Palico feline companions are joined by new dog-like riding creatures called Palamutes, on which the hunter can traverse the map much faster than on foot. The Rampage defense mode casts the player as a commander defending the village against waves of monsters using installable towers and traps, combining traditional hunting with elements of tower defense.

The Sunbreak expansion added a new, tougher faction of monsters as well as the Elgado stronghold. Thanks to its more accessible pace, pronounced Japanese style, and the Wirebug mechanic, Rise became one of the most successful entries in the series and brought many new players to Monster Hunter who might not have taken to the slower pace of earlier generations of the series. On Switch, it also works as an ideal game for short sessions, since a single hunt typically lasts only a few dozen minutes, and up to four hunters can team up both locally and online. Visually, the game does lag behind competitors on more powerful platforms in terms of detail on Switch hardware, but the stylized Japanese backdrops of temples, bamboo forests, and flooded plains more than make up for it.
switch__monster-hunter-rise.teaser: A branch of the hunting series tailored for Switch; feudal Japan, new monsters.

switch__shin-megami-tensei-v.article:
**Shin Megami Tensei V** is a dark, philosophically charged JRPG from Atlus, in which a Tokyo student becomes a Nahobino after merging with a mysterious entity named Aogami inside a post-apocalyptic version of Tokyo called Da'at, devastated and turned into a sandy wasteland full of skyscraper ruins after a catastrophic event. In this parched world, a war between angels and demons rages over the fate of humanity, and the player, as the demigod-like Nahobino, must choose a side and confront philosophical questions about order, chaos, and human free will typical of the Shin Megami Tensei series.

The battle system uses the classic Press Turn system, where exploiting an enemy's elemental weakness grants a bonus turn, while a poorly aimed attack costs a turn instead, making every fight a risky tactical calculation. Because the same rules apply to opponents as well, a single mistake can spell the end of the entire party within a single round, and the game punishes inattention far more harshly than most modern JRPGs. A key element of the series remains negotiating with demons directly in battle, where they can be persuaded to join the player's side and subsequently fused into stronger forms in the Cathedral of Shadows; demons have their own personalities and respond to clumsy answers with mockery or by fleeing with stolen money.

A more open world structure compared to previous entries allows freer exploration of vast desert areas full of hidden treasures and optional bosses. Progression isn't linear: the player runs into significantly stronger enemies before being ready for them and must decide whether to risk it or come back later better equipped. The visually dark but detailed world is accompanied by atmospheric music by Ryota Kozuka, alternating heavy ambient stretches with rhythmic battle motifs. On Switch, this was one of Atlus's technically most ambitious games, and the hardware occasionally exacts a toll on smoothness, though this doesn't diminish the atmosphere of the abandoned, sun-scorched Tokyo. Thanks to its demanding battles, moral ambiguity, and raw themes, the game is clearly aimed at older, more experienced JRPG players.
switch__shin-megami-tensei-v.teaser: A dark, philosophical JRPG from Atlus; Tokyo transformed into a desert full of ruins.

switch__untitled-goose-game.article:
**Untitled Goose Game** is a short but infectiously funny puzzle game from the small Australian studio House House, in which the player controls an ordinary, devious goose terrorizing a peaceful English village. The goal in each of several interconnected locations is to complete a list of small, seemingly innocent but hugely annoying tasks for the villagers — steal the gardener's hat, lock him out of his own garden, scare a shopkeeper so badly he ends up in his own stall, or smuggle forbidden items where they don't belong.

The goose has no special abilities beyond a beak for grabbing objects, flapping its wings, and loud, annoying honking that can startle characters and distract them, so solving every puzzle rests on clever observation of the environment, timing, and a bit of mischievous ingenuity. The villagers behave according to simple but readable rules: what goes missing, they go looking for; what lies on the ground, they tidy away — and it's precisely from anticipating these reactions that room for elaborately planned chains of mischief emerges. The task list also doesn't need to be completed in order, so every player discovers solutions at their own pace.

The game's humor springs precisely from the contrast between the idyllic, watercolor-looking English village and the utterly shameless chaos wrought by the titular goose, accompanied by playful piano music arranged by Dan Golding and inspired by Debussy, whose tempo and intensity dynamically adapt to whatever's happening on screen. Although fairly short, the game became a viral internet phenomenon shortly after release thanks to easily shareable, comedic moments, and it also offers a cooperative mode for a second player controlling a second goose, turning organized mischief into proper chaos. After completion, a list of optional challenges is also unlocked, forcing tasks to be done faster or in unusual ways, so the game has something to offer even those who've already finished it once. On Switch, it works exceptionally well thanks to its undemanding, immediately understandable controls.
switch__untitled-goose-game.teaser: A short, infectiously funny game about a devious goose terrorizing an English village.

ps-vita__muramasa-rebirth.article:
**Muramasa Rebirth** is a remake of the action game by studio Vanillaware, originally released on Wii, which received sharper visuals, a new translation, and later a series of additional chapters on PlayStation Vita. It takes place in a stylized Japan of the Genroku era and offers two intertwined stories: the ninja Kisuke, who has lost his memories, and the princess Momohime, whose body is possessed by the spirit of a foreign swordsman. Both cut their way through a land full of demons, gods, and cursed swords, with each of them seeing the same events from a different side. Both storylines can be played through independently of each other.

The gameplay is two-dimensional action with RPG elements: movement is fast, jumps are high, and combat takes place on a single plane against dozens of opponents at once. The core mechanic is juggling three swords at once — each has its own durability gauge, and after a few blocked or heavy attacks it breaks, forcing the player to switch to the next one immediately so the first can regenerate in the meantime. On top of that there's soul collection, forging hundreds of new weapons along a branching tree, and cooking food that temporarily boosts stats. Boss fights are a showcase of patterns that must be read. Outside of combat, you travel across long horizontal maps between which fast travel is available, and the game offers several possible endings depending on the player's choices.

The main reason to fire up the game, though, is its art direction. Vanillaware paints hand-drawn backgrounds with layered planes, bamboo groves, blooming cherry trees, and temples in the mist; on Vita's small screen it looks at least as good as it did on television. The music draws on traditional Japanese instruments and complements the slow, almost painterly pacing between battles. Reception at the time was very positive, with the main complaint being repetitive environments during the long journey. The additional chapters released later also brought new playable characters with their own combat styles. Today Muramasa is one of the most beautiful games ever released on a handheld console, and it still plays completely fresh.
ps-vita__muramasa-rebirth.teaser: A remake of Vanillaware's action game from the Wii; two intertwined stories in Japan's Genroku era.

ps-vita__dragon-s-crown.article:
**Dragon's Crown** is a return to a genre that seemed long extinct — the arcade beat 'em up, in which a party of heroes works its way through ever more dangerous dungeons, smashing everything that moves. Vanillaware combined it with RPG progression: six distinct classes ranging from the fighter and amazon to the sorceress and elf, gear collection and upgrades, repeated runs through the same dungeons in harder variants, and a story told in the spirit of a classic fantasy adventure with an old narrator. The path to the true ending also runs through several repeat playthroughs, so the game is built from the start for long-term play.

Combat is simple to grasp and deep to master. Each class plays noticeably differently: the elf manages her ammo supply, the sorceress positions spells and must stay covered, the fighter belongs on the front line, and the dwarf slams enemies into the ground. Up to three companions can be brought along into the dungeons, whether online or as summoned helpers made from the bones of fallen adventurers, and loot is split after every run. The PlayStation Vita version offered cross-play with the PlayStation 3 and the ability to continue a save on either device depending on where you happened to be. Between expeditions the player returns to town to shop, revive the bones of fallen adventurers, and take on new commissions, which gives the whole loop the rhythm of a board game.

Visually it's one of the most striking games of its generation — giant hand-drawn characters, richly decorated backdrops, and animations that preserve the weight of every hit. The stylization also sparked disputes at the time over the exaggerated proportions of some characters, something that followed the game into practically every review. The music, complete with orchestra and a narrator who comments on events like a read-aloud fairy tale, gives the whole thing a theatrical tone. Reviews praised both the gameplay and the art direction, less so the repetition of the same dungeons. Today Dragon's Crown is ideal on Vita: twenty-minute expeditions fit a handheld console perfectly. The whole game can also be completed solo without a connection, though a four-player party is clearly the most fun.
ps-vita__dragon-s-crown.teaser: An arcade beat 'em up combined with RPG progression; six classes, dungeons, and Vanillaware's signature style.

ps-vita__ys-memories-of-celceta.article:
**Ys: Memories of Celceta** is an action RPG from the Japanese studio Nihon Falcom and one of the few major games made directly for PlayStation Vita rather than ported from elsewhere. Adol Christin wakes up in a border town with no memories, and the only way to get them back is to set out and map Celceta — a vast, dangerous forest from which, according to the locals, no one returns. Progressing through the game therefore literally means drawing the map: each newly explored section brings back another memory while also opening new paths into previously inaccessible areas. The map thus serves as both a progress indicator and a collecting discipline in its own right.

Combat is real-time and built around a party of three characters that can be switched between instantly. Each has a different attack type effective against a different group of enemies, so battle is mainly about swapping roles on the fly. Add to that a last-moment dodge and a precisely timed block, both rewarded with a brief advantage. The series is known for its pace, and here too movement is fast, dungeons are short, and bosses are about reading movement patterns. Alongside the main story, players gather materials, upgrade gear, and complete townsfolk requests that gradually unlock further parts of the forest. The game is accompanied by a large cast of companions, from whom the player assembles a trio depending on what's coming up, and each character has their own special skills tied to an energy gauge.

Technically the game is very well made on Vita: large open forest areas, smooth performance, and a clean look without unnecessary slowdown. Its strongest point, though, is the music — Falcom has its own in-house sound team, and its rock and symphonic compositions rank among the best the genre has to offer; some of them have become a signature of the entire series. Reviews at the time received it very warmly as one of the best action RPGs on the console. Today Memories of Celceta is an excellent entry point into the world of Ys: it assumes no knowledge of previous entries and has a beautifully balanced pace. The narrative is also straightforward and doesn't drag, which is rather the exception for a Japanese RPG of that era.
ps-vita__ys-memories-of-celceta.teaser: An action RPG from Nihon Falcom made directly for the Vita; progressing through the game means drawing the map of the forest.

ps-vita__severed.article:
**Severed** is a game that couldn't have been designed for a gamepad. The Canadian studio DrinkBox Studios has players lead the one-armed warrior Sasha through a strange, dreamlike world as she searches for the remnants of her family, and all combat plays out by swiping a finger across the screen. Enemies surround the player and attack from every side, and each hit means swiping precisely where and in the direction the opponent is vulnerable. The game punishes imprecision but rewards anyone who learns to slash cleanly and rhythmically.

Exploration takes the form of a classic first-person dungeon crawler, in which the player moves across a grid between intersections and solves logic puzzles, hidden passages, and shortcuts. Combat has its own rhythm: block attacks, swing to the correct side in time, and activate a time-slowing ability at the right moment to hit several enemies in succession. The key mechanic is severing the limbs of defeated opponents — after a hit, the player cuts off a specific body part, and these pieces are then assembled into new abilities and upgrades, so combat is also a collecting discipline. Progress opens not only new areas but also shortcuts back through older sections, so the map makes sense as a whole and invites revisiting.

Visually it's typical DrinkBox style — richly colored, flat stylization with sharp outlines, but here turned toward a feverish, sickly tone; the world is beautiful and unsettling at once. Sound and music play with silence, heartbeat, and piercing enemy noises, keeping the tension alive even in empty corridors. Reviews at the time praised the game as one of the best late Vita titles and one of the few cases where touch controls aren't a bolt-on but the entire foundation. The game came out in the console's late life, when major publishers had already lost interest in the platform, and stood out all the more for it. A runtime of around six hours is just right. Today Severed is the strongest argument for why Vita can't be fully replaced by anything else.
ps-vita__severed.teaser: Combat by dragging your finger across the screen, designed specifically for touch; inaccuracy is punished harshly.

ps-vita__persona-4-golden.article:
**Persona 4 Golden** is an expanded version of the cult JRPG from PlayStation 2, and on PlayStation Vita it became the single strongest argument for owning the console at all. You play a student who moves for a year to stay with relatives in the sleepy rural town of Inaba, only for the quiet backwater to soon be stirred up by a series of mysterious deaths linked to a strange television channel that appears after midnight. The hero and his classmates discover that it's actually possible to step into the television, and they find themselves in a foggy world where the suppressed sides of human personalities take the shape of monsters.

This is where the game's dual rhythm comes from. During the day you go to school, take tests, work part-time jobs, and above all cultivate relationships with the people around you — the so-called Social Links, which directly strengthen your combat abilities. In the afternoons and at night you descend through the randomly arranged floors of the television world, using a weakness system in turn-based battles: hitting an opponent with the right element knocks them down and opens the door for a devastating all-out attack from the whole party. Collecting and fusing Personas, the summoned beings reflecting each character's psyche, gives builds surprising depth.

The Golden version added a new character, extra story threads, an epilogue, new social activities, and online features that let you see how other players chose to act in the same situations. On Vita the game looks great: a stylized yellow-and-black interface, a sharp display, and smooth performance make it a showcase of what the small console can do. The soundtrack, mixing pop, jazz, and funk, is among the most distinctive in the genre, and the small-town atmosphere with its rains, fog, and changing seasons remains unmatched to this day. Critics received the game enthusiastically, and it ranks among the highest-rated titles on the entire platform. Even today it remains the ideal entry point into the Persona series, because the combination of detective story, school-life routine, and turn-based combat has aged remarkably well.
ps-vita__persona-4-golden.teaser: An expanded version of the cult JRPG from the PS2; possibly the strongest reason to get a Vita.

ps-vita__legend-of-heroes-trails-of-cold.article:
**The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel** brought the sprawling chronicle of the world of Zemuria to PlayStation Vita and became, for Western players, the most accessible entry point into the Trails series. You play as Rean Schwarzer, a fresh student at the Thors Military Academy, who along with other newcomers is placed into the experimental Class VII. Instead of the usual division by noble birth, this class puts aristocrats' children side by side with ordinary townsfolk, and their field training across the Erebonian Empire gradually reveals just how deep the tension dividing the country runs.

The game's structure mirrors a school year: between missions you spend free days at the academy, deepen relationships with classmates, and complete small tasks, before heading out on a several-day field study in one of the empire's regions. Combat is turn-based with a positional element, since where characters stand matters, area attacks hit everything nearby, and bonus turns appear on the timeline that are worth fighting for. The Orbment system lets you assemble spells from quartz stones, allowing significant customization of each character, and combination attacks tied to relationships reward building up the party. On top of that there's a free-time system where you can only spend it with certain companions at a time, so each playthrough reveals a slightly different part of the class and gives you a reason to come back.

On Vita the game runs noticeably more modestly than on the big consoles, but the handheld version makes perfect sense precisely because of that: the enormous amount of dialogue, text, and side conversations is easy to take in bit by bit, and the game carefully remembers who you've talked to and when. Its strongest point is the world-building — newspapers, small side-character plots, and political background that pays off in the sequels. Critics praised the characterization and the well-thought-out combat system, with complaints aimed at the slower start and the fact that the story ends mid-sentence. Today Cold Steel is a recommended gateway into one of the most sprawling narratives in the whole genre.
ps-vita__legend-of-heroes-trails-of-cold.teaser: The most accessible entry point into the extensive Trails series; students of the Thors Military Academy.

ps-vita__final-fantasy-x-x-2-hd-remaster.article:
**Final Fantasy X/X-2 HD Remaster** packed two major games from the PlayStation 2 era into a single package on PlayStation Vita and became one of the strongest reasons to have the console on hand while traveling. Final Fantasy X tells the story of a young man named Tidus, who is swept from his home city into the strange world of Spira, plagued by a seemingly indestructible threat called Sin. He joins the pilgrim Yuna and her party on a journey whose destination is shrouded from the start by a sacrifice no one dares speak of aloud. Final Fantasy X-2 then shows the same world two years later, in a much lighter, more adventurous tone.

Combat in the first game is turn-based with a visible timeline and the ability to swap in any party member at any time, turning every encounter into a small tactical puzzle. The Sphere Grid replaces classic levels with a sprawling grid along which characters travel, unlocking stats and abilities, giving you full control over development. X-2, by contrast, relies on a fast ATB system and on Dressspheres that can be swapped mid-battle, resulting in surprisingly brisk, experimental gameplay with plenty of room for your own combinations.

The remaster brought reworked character models, sharper textures, and newly recorded music, and the result looks exceptionally good on Vita's small display. A colorful Spira with its water temples and lush vegetation ranks among the most beautiful things ever to run on the console. The emotional storytelling, the iconic melody accompanying the main duo, and scenes that stuck in players' memories retain their power even years later. Critics praised both the content and the technical quality of the conversion, though some compromises compared to the big-console versions were noticeable. Today this pair remains one of the best ways to remember what Final Fantasy looked like at the peak of its classic era. Vita also lets you suspend the game at any time and continue later, which fundamentally changes how you return to a dozens-of-hours-long journey through Spira.
ps-vita__final-fantasy-x-x-2-hd-remaster.teaser: Two great games from the PlayStation 2 era in one package; Tidus and Yuna against a threat called Sin.

ps-vita__odin-sphere-leifthrasir.article:
**Odin Sphere Leifthrasir** is a complete rework of the action RPG from the late PlayStation 2 era, and on PlayStation Vita it stands as one of the most beautiful titles in the console's entire library. The story unfolds across five books, each belonging to a different main character, all of them intersecting in a war over the fate of a world inspired by Norse mythology. Only once you've finished all the storylines does the whole picture fall into place, including scenes you previously saw from the opposite side of the barricade, giving the game a structure closer to theatrical tragedy than to a typical fantasy adventure.

Battles take place in two-dimensional arenas, and the reworked version is markedly more fluid than the original: combos flow, characters have distinct styles ranging from spear to chain to a spellcaster's ring, and old, cumbersome elements have been removed. What remains is the reliance on food and potions. Ingredients are grown from seeds right in combat using the souls of defeated enemies, cooked into meals that permanently raise health or mana. Alchemy and mixing potions from found ingredients add another layer of preparation before boss fights. Each of the five characters also has their own pace, reach, and weaknesses, so the game never settles into a single reliable strategy, and key encounters demand a different preparation and approach every time.

Vanillaware's hand-painted art, with giant, finely animated characters and layered backgrounds, is still stunning today and looks practically flawless on the small display. Orchestral music with prominent strings underscores the fairy-tale-tragic tone of a story about families, prophecies, and an inevitable end of the world. Reviewers praised especially how sensitively the remake removed the original's weaknesses without losing its charm, and how thoroughly it opened up gameplay that used to be cumbersome. For Vita owners it's one of the best ways to play an action RPG that also happens to be a work of art.
ps-vita__odin-sphere-leifthrasir.teaser: A rework of an action RPG from the late PS2 era; one of the most beautiful titles in the Vita's library.

ps-vita__toukiden-kiwami.article:
**Toukiden: Kiwami** is an expanded version of the hunting action game from Omega Force, which on PlayStation Vita builds on Japanese mythology and demons called Oni. The world is fractured by rifts through which the Oni pour into human lands, and you play as a Slayer, a warrior from the village of Utakata, who must stand against what an ordinary army cannot defeat. The Kiwami version added a new story thread to the original game, additional weapon types, new hunting grounds, and extra content for players who had already finished the main campaign.

Battles combine fast action with tactics. Every monster has body parts that can be severed individually, and only once they've been cleared away is the demon unable to regenerate. This is supported by the Mitama mechanic — souls of ancient heroes that you place into your weapons to gain active abilities ranging from healing to slowing down time. There's a wide range of weapon types with their own rhythm, from sword and spear to chain sickles or bow, and missions can be accompanied by up to three AI-controlled companions, or by live players in co-op. Body parts looted from demons are then used to forge and upgrade gear, turning repeated hunts of the same opponent into targeted preparation for the next, stronger foe.

On Vita the game runs smoothly, and missions have a short, well-paced length, making it an ideal title for travel. Visually it leans on Japanese historical stylization with temples, snow-covered mountains, and jagged cliffs, and the music is suitably bombastic with prominent drums. Reviews highlighted its accessibility compared to tougher genre rivals and the clever Mitama system, which allows a lot of customization of playstyle, while complaints pointed to recycled environments. Toukiden helped establish an entire wave of hunting games on handheld consoles and remains one of the most pleasant ways for a newcomer to enter the genre without being scared off in the first few hours.
ps-vita__toukiden-kiwami.teaser: A hunting action game from Omega Force built on Japanese mythology and demons called Oni.

ps-vita__digimon-story-cyber-sleuth.article:
**Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth** is a turn-based JRPG that restored the Digimon franchise's good name and became an unexpected hit on PlayStation Vita even among players with no attachment to the original show. After an accident in digital space, the main character ends up half in real Tokyo and half in the network, where his body loses its physical form. He therefore joins a private detective agency and investigates cases straddling both worlds, from urban legends spreading online to people who have fallen into a mysterious coma.

The core of the gameplay is collecting and developing Digimon. Scanning opponents yields data from which you raise a creature, then guide it through a branching evolution tree where progress can also be reversed. Digivolving down a stage while retaining stats produces a gradually much stronger creature, a mechanic characteristic of the series and surprisingly deep. Battles are classically turn-based, with types and elements that counter one another, and a trio of active creatures drawn from a larger roster. A farm where Digimon train and complete small tasks even while you're away gives the game a pleasant pet-raising rhythm. The collection numbers in the hundreds, and obtaining many of them requires meeting specific conditions, so completing it is a very long-haul pursuit that keeps the game alive well after the main story is finished.

Technically it's a clean, colorful game with striking neon visuals for the digital world and a faithfully rendered Tokyo, whose districts you walk between cases. The music alternates calm jazz motifs from the detective agency with energetic battle tracks. Critics praised the unexpectedly serious storytelling about digital identity and the depth of the evolution system, with complaints aimed at repetitive dungeons and their plain design. Cyber Sleuth proved that Digimon could be a full-fledged collecting RPG for a more adult audience too, and it opened the way for further entries in the series.
ps-vita__digimon-story-cyber-sleuth.teaser: A turn-based JRPG that restored Digimon's good reputation even among players with no connection to the series.

ps-vita__disgaea-4-promise-revisited.article:
**Disgaea 4: A Promise Revisited** is a portable, content-expanded version of the tactical RPG from Nippon Ichi Software, and on PlayStation Vita it stands as one of the most content-packed games ever released on the console. The main hero, Valvatorez, is a vampire who once swore an oath never to drink human blood, and lives on sardines instead. As a lowly official within the Netherworld's demonic bureaucracy, he gradually takes a stand against the corrupt leadership of the entire realm, and his crusade for justice is as absurd as it is surprisingly touching.

Battles play out on grid-based maps, where terrain height, unit positioning, and colored Geo Panels all matter, and chain-destroying them can transform the entire map in a single turn. Characters can be lifted and thrown, stacked into towers for combined attacks, or sent into the Item World — randomly generated floors hidden inside every item. Numerical values grow to absurd heights, levels stretch far beyond the usual hundred, and the game knowingly celebrates this escalation as both its main joke and its main draw. You also build your own units from a wide range of classes, and nothing stops you from fielding a party made entirely of oddities, which you then experiment with in later, much harder maps.

This unlimited depth is the game's greatest asset. The main story takes dozens of hours, but the real content for dedicated players runs into the hundreds. The Vita version added new characters, scenarios, and interface improvements, and is ideally suited to playing in short bursts, since battles are self-contained and the game can be put down at any time. Visually it relies on sharp hand-drawn sprites on three-dimensional maps, which stand out nicely on the small screen. Humor, parodies of anime clichés, and exaggeration are typical for the series, and critics praised precisely the combination of comedy with an exceptionally elaborate tactical layer that holds up against anything else in the genre.
ps-vita__disgaea-4-promise-revisited.teaser: An expanded tactical RPG from Nippon Ichi; the vampire Valvatorez, who eats only sardines instead of blood.

ps-vita__demon-gaze.article:
**Demon Gaze** is a first-person dungeon crawler from Experience Inc., a studio that specialized on PlayStation Vita in classic old-school exploration RPGs. The hero Oz wakes up with no memories and an eye capable of binding demons. That's precisely why the Dragon Princess inn takes him in and sends him out into the surrounding labyrinths. Lodging isn't free, though, and the rent climbs with every due date, so pressure to earn and progress quickly is baked directly into the game's structure.

Exploration happens tile by tile through grid-based mazes, where you gradually uncover the map, search for hidden passages, and dodge traps. You place gems in designated spots to summon both enemies and treasure. The more you place at once, the greater the reward and the risk, turning every such room into a small gambling decision. Defeated demons get bound to you and become party members with powerful abilities that can, however, spiral out of control mid-battle. You build your own party from scratch by choosing races and classes, and combat is turn-based, tough, and merciless in the opening hours. Gear can also be upgraded and passed between characters, so even a failed dive into deeper floors usually yields something that pushes the next attempt a bit further.

Visually the game leans on bold character and demon artwork that contrasts with fairly plain maze corridors, as is typical for the genre. The music is energetic and rock-driven, the atmosphere more lighthearted than scary despite the constant risk of wiping the whole party. Reviewers praised the clever gem system and the way the game manages to be tough without being unfair, while criticizing the repetitive environments. For the Vita, Demon Gaze was one of the titles that brought classic grid-based crawlers back to a modern handheld, and today it's an ideal pick for players who like to plan their progress and count their resources.
ps-vita__demon-gaze.teaser: An old-school first-person dungeon crawler; rising rent pushes you to progress quickly.

ps-vita__ys-viii-lacrimosa-of-dana.article:
**Ys VIII: Lacrimosa of Dana** is an action RPG from Nihon Falcom that originally launched on PlayStation Vita and is often called the series' high point. Adol Christin is shipwrecked off the shores of the forbidden island of Seiren, from which, according to legend, no one returns. Alongside exploring the unknown land full of prehistoric wildlife, the game is also about building a castaway camp. You gradually find more survivors, who open shops, workshops, and services in the settlement, turning it from a few tents into a small functioning town.

Combat is fast and action-driven, built around switching between three characters with distinct attack types, dodging with time slowdown, and a counterattack that rewards reading enemy animations. Beyond the standard story progression, the game offers defense battles where the camp fends off monster assaults, exploration runs for resources, and even fishing and cooking. In parallel, a second storyline unfolds around a girl named Dana, whose chapters take place in an entirely different era and gradually reveal what really happened on the island long ago. The map opens up progressively based on what gear and abilities the camp acquires, so exploration has a clear rhythm and payoff, and finding a new survivor can feel just as satisfying as finding a better sword.

On the Vita this is a technically ambitious game, with sprawling outdoor areas, plenty of enemies on screen, and decent draw distance, though at the cost of softer graphics than on home consoles. Falcom's music is a highlight here too: energetic rock tracks during battles alternate with melancholic themes accompanying Dana's chapters. Critics praised the pacing, the joy of discovery, and an unexpectedly powerful resolution, though the western release was accompanied by debate over the quality of the first translation, which was later reworked. Today Ys VIII is one of the best action RPGs of its generation and practically the flagship title of the Vita.
ps-vita__ys-viii-lacrimosa-of-dana.teaser: According to many fans, the pinnacle of the Ys series; the shipwrecked Adol builds a camp on a forbidden island.

ps-vita__shiren-wanderer-tower-of-fortun.article:
**Shiren the Wanderer: The Tower of Fortune and the Dice of Fate** is the fifth entry in the classic Japanese roguelike series from Spike Chunsoft, and on PlayStation Vita it's one of the few games of its kind that made it to the West at all. The wanderer Shiren and his talking weasel companion set out for the Tower of Fortune, where fate itself can supposedly be rewritten, specifically to save a girl whose death has been foretold. The path there runs through dozens of randomly generated dungeons governed by strict, unforgiving rules.

Every step you take is also a turn for the enemies, so the game plays more like a chess problem than an action game. Hunger drains with every move, found items are unidentified, and a herb can just as easily heal you as blind you, while death means losing levels and most of your gear and starting over from scratch. That's exactly where the tension comes from. Every item thrown, every dash up the stairs, every decision on whether to risk another floor carries real weight. You can ease the grind by storing supplies in a warehouse and forging blades, but the game always remains fundamentally a fight over resources. There are also companions to hire along the way, shops inside the dungeons, and a number of special floors with their own rules, so even after dozens of runs you'll still stumble onto something you haven't seen before.

The Vita suits a game like this perfectly, since descending a few floors takes only a few minutes and the game can be put down at any time. Visually it's a clean, drawn style with clearly readable icons and hand-painted character portraits, and the music is calm and folk-flavored, providing a pleasant contrast to the constant threat of failure. Critics praised the depth of the rules and the fairness of the randomness, but noted a steep difficulty curve for newcomers unfamiliar with the genre. Today this Shiren is regarded as one of the best entries into the mystery dungeon genre and a quiet gem of the Vita library.
ps-vita__shiren-wanderer-tower-of-fortun.teaser: A classic Japanese roguelike, rarely released in the West; Shiren seeks a path to the tower of fate.

ps-vita__danganronpa-trigger-happy-havoc.article:
**Danganronpa: Trigger Happy Havoc** locks a group of high school talents inside the elite Hope's Peak Academy building, from which there's only one way out: kill one of your classmates and get through the subsequent investigation without being caught. Watching over it all is the plush bear Monokuma, whose gleeful voice frames the entire game and keeps it balanced on the edge between black comedy and pure dread. The narrative splits between looser school segments, where the player talks to classmates, learns their personalities, and divides up free time with them, and tightly structured chapters that always culminate in a discovered body, a crime scene investigation, and a courtroom trial.

It's the trial that makes Danganronpa more than just an illustrated text. Debate runs in real time, other characters' statements fly across the screen like targets, and the player shoots them down with so-called Truth Bullets to disprove a lie or confirm a contradiction. Along the way there are rhythm minigames, matching puzzles, and a comic-style crime reconstruction that must be assembled into the correct sequence of panels. The system turns detective reasoning into an arcade-like form and keeps the pace up where long dialogue might otherwise put you to sleep. Missed shots cost you influence with the jury, so even a plain conversation carries the tension of a duel.

On PlayStation Vita the game visibly benefits from the contrasty display: the flat, paper-styled character designs combined with neon-pink blood and richly saturated backgrounds look remarkably sharp on the small screen. The soundtrack blends jazz motifs with restless electronica, and the voice acting ranks among the best ever released on a handheld. The 2014 western release turned what had until then been a Japanese curiosity into a cult brand and sparked a wave of interest in detective visual novels on the Vita. Besides the main storyline, the game also offers a lighter school mode where you gather materials, build up facilities, and calmly chat with characters who have long since died in the main story. It remains an ideal entry point into the genre today, combining readability, playfulness, and one of the best-constructed twists of its era.
ps-vita__danganronpa-trigger-happy-havoc.teaser: A deadly game at an elite academy, where murder investigations decide life and death.

ps-vita__danganronpa-2-goodbye-despair.article:
**Danganronpa 2: Goodbye Despair** moves the deadly game from school hallways to the tropical Jabberwock Island, where a fresh batch of talented students is meant to enjoy an idyllic school trip. The idyll lasts exactly until Monokuma emerges from underground and offers the same deal as in the first game: kill and leave. The island setting isn't just a fresh coat of paint. The individual beaches, hotels, and abandoned facilities function as separate scenes with their own internal logic, the player travels between them more freely than in the first game, and part of the islands only opens up as the story progresses.

The structure stays true to the tried-and-tested rhythm of free chatting, investigation, and courtroom trial, but mechanically the game has noticeably sharpened. Alongside shooting down contradictory statements, direct verbal showdowns with one specific classmate have been added, the crime reconstructions have grown longer, and a new logic dive sends the player down a path of questions where the correct answer must be chosen at full speed. There's also now the option to build relationships with classmates outside the main storyline and unlock their backstories, which makes their later deaths considerably more painful. Overall, the sequel is longer, denser, and noticeably darker in its second half than its predecessor.

Technically it's a very similar but polished package: two-dimensional characters over stylized environments, sharp colors, and smooth performance without slowdown, which matters on the Vita. The music again leans on jazz and electronic motifs, this time laced with falsely carefree summer melodies that contrast with what's actually happening on the island. Alongside the main storyline there's also a more extensive relaxation mode involving island-building and raising small creatures, which serves as a counterweight to the heavy plot. Critics mostly called the sequel the better entry, mainly thanks to more elaborate cases and a more emotional payoff. Today it reads as proof that a visual novel can stay gripping even after twenty hours, provided it has the nerve to make the player genuinely doubt their own conclusions.
ps-vita__danganronpa-2-goodbye-despair.teaser: The same deadly game of Monokuma, this time on a tropical island with its own carefully crafted setting.

ps-vita__danganronpa-v3-killing-harmony.article:
**Danganronpa V3: Killing Harmony** is a reboot that doesn't pretend otherwise: a new cast, a new building full of cages and machines, and new rules for the killing game that demand not just the player's attention but a willingness to have everything they thought they knew about the series called into question. Sixteen students wake up in a locked compound, Monokuma introduces five of his offspring, and the whole cycle of investigation and trial begins again, this time with a considerably crueler sense of humor and a narrative ending that became one of the most debated in the genre.

The trial segment gained the most new tools. Alongside the usual disproving of statements, there's now mass panic debate, where several characters talk at once and the player has to follow multiple streams of speech simultaneously, a group argument that splits the jury into two camps, and above all the option to knowingly lie, firing a false bullet to steer the debate in a direction that isn't true but opens up a new angle. Investigations in the environment are more open-ended, the cases more tangled, and individual chapters happily build on distrust not just between characters but between the game and the player. There's also a large amount of bonus content, from a board-game minigame through settlement building to a mode where the player assembles their own cast of characters and pits them against each other, so there's still a reason to keep coming back even after finishing the main story.

The PlayStation Vita version runs smoothly, and the color-tuned environments with pink blood on the display still look great, though in busier scenes it shows that this is older hardware pushed to its limit. The music builds on previous entries but leans more often into abrasive, dissonant motifs, and the voice acting again carries much of the atmosphere. Reception was strong, even though the ending split the audience into camps. Today V3 feels like the most ambitious entry in the series, one that isn't the best starting point but offers the most food for thought about why we play detective visual novels in the first place.
ps-vita__danganronpa-v3-killing-harmony.teaser: A no-holds-barred reset of the series; new rules and a willingness to question everything players thought they knew about it.

ps-vita__zero-escape-virtue-s-last-rewar.article:
**Zero Escape: Virtue's Last Reward** is one of the first truly great reasons to own a PlayStation Vita. Nine people wake up in a locked complex, where a masked figure calling himself Zero forces them to play a game of trust and betrayal: everyone has a point account, pairs decide behind closed doors between cooperation and backstabbing, and only those who accumulate nine points are allowed to leave. On top of that, you first have to get out of each individual room, which splits the game into long dialogue passages and classic escape-room puzzles.

The escape rooms are the best thing the puzzle side has to offer. Each has its own theme, set of objects, combination locks, and hidden codes, and they're solved through real deduction, not random clicking. The Vita's touch controls make sense here, since examining objects and combining inventory items is fast and intuitive. The story side runs on a branching flowchart that remembers the game for the player: at any point you can jump back to any decision, take a different branch, and carry knowledge gained elsewhere into it. This isn't just a convenience, it's literally part of the plot. The game also keeps a clear log of information found and a glossary of terms, without which it would be easy to get lost in the tangle of clones, viruses, and timelines, and any unfinished room can be left and returned to later.

Graphically the game swapped the predecessor's drawn portraits for three-dimensional models, which cost it a bit of character but allowed full voice acting and much more dynamic direction. The sound design works with silence and a claustrophobic electronic loop that turns empty corridors into an unpleasant place to be. Critics received the game very well, praising above all how the puzzles and the storytelling reinforce rather than get in each other's way. Today Virtue's Last Reward remains an essential title for anyone who likes detective and sci-fi plots built on paradoxes, and on a handheld the short-session format suits it even better than it does on a big screen.
ps-vita__zero-escape-virtue-s-last-rewar.teaser: Nine people, a game of trust and betrayal, and escape rooms; one of the reasons to get a Vita.

ps-vita__zero-escape-zero-time-dilemma.article:
**Zero Escape: Zero Time Dilemma** closes out the trilogy, and it does so in the harshest way possible. Nine people are split into three teams of three, locked inside an underground facility, and forced to play a game where what's at stake isn't points but lives, directly. The participants' memories are regularly wiped, so the characters keep losing context that the player, by contrast, keeps accumulating. The result is a narrative chopped up into dozens of short fragments that can be played back in almost any order, and only gradually pieced together into a timeline.

Compared to the previous entries, the long static dialogues are gone, replaced by fully voiced, cinematic scenes with three-dimensional models. The escape rooms remain and rank among the genre's solid entries: hunting for codes, working with objects, and several genuinely clever puzzles built around tracking time. New decision moments appear where the game openly flips a coin or lets the player choose who survives, pushing the whole series from logical tension toward moral discomfort. The fragmented structure is at once the game's greatest strength and its greatest weakness, since without patience it's easy to get lost. Progress is also tied to what the player knows rather than to the order on the timeline, so some fragments only unlock once you've filled in a missing piece of information elsewhere and can ask the right question.

On PlayStation Vita the game runs at a lower resolution, and the character models and animations show signs of a modest budget, but the sharp display and the ability to play in short fragment-sized bursts suit it very well. The sound design works with silence and industrial humming, with music stepping in only where it needs to land a blow. Reception was more divided than for its predecessor, mainly due to the technical execution and a more rushed narrative, though fans appreciated that the series got a genuine conclusion. Today it's a title recommended mainly for those who've been through both earlier entries and want to see where the whole plot was heading.
ps-vita__zero-escape-zero-time-dilemma.teaser: The harshest conclusion of the Zero Escape trilogy; three teams, erased memory, and decisions about who lives.

ps-vita__steins-gate.article:
**Steins;Gate** is one of the best-known visual novels of all, and its release on PlayStation Vita was for a long time the most convenient way for western players to experience the story. We follow a group of young enthusiasts from Tokyo's Akihabara district who, in a rented workshop above a shop, accidentally build a device capable of sending messages into the past. What starts as playful experimentation quickly turns into a nightmare, since every change to the past rewrites the present, and the hero is the only one who remembers the previous versions of the world.

Gameplay rests almost entirely on reading, but the key element is the mobile phone system. The game doesn't offer classic dialogue choices; instead the player decides whether to answer an incoming call, who to text back and how, and it's precisely these seemingly minor details that determine which of several paths the story ultimately takes. This creates an unusually natural feeling of making decisions in everyday life rather than through a menu. Alongside the main storyline there are several standalone endings devoted to individual characters, and one path the game considers the true one. Backtracking through already-read passages and fast-skipping text are handled conveniently, which helps, since without repeated playthroughs you won't reach the true ending. The game also keeps building a glossary of terms from internet culture and physics, which can be opened directly from the text.

Technically it's a classic novel with drawn portraits and richly illustrated scenes, but it's on the Vita's display that the warm color palette and hand-drawn style really shine. The Japanese voice acting is complete, and the music stays in the background with minimalist, mildly oppressive motifs that come in full force during the twists. The title contributed massively to visual novels being taken seriously in the West, and its influence can be seen across an entire wave of later sci-fi stories. Today it remains one of the best-constructed time-travel plots in the medium, though the first hours require patience before the comedy tips over into drama.
ps-vita__steins-gate.teaser: One of the best-known visual novels; a group from Akihabara accidentally invents a time machine.

ps-vita__steins-gate-0.article:
**Steins;Gate 0** follows up on its famous predecessor from an unexpected angle: instead of a continuation, it follows the branch where the hero failed and gave up on further attempts to rewrite the past. The once-confident tinkerer has become a withdrawn student trying to live a normal life while unable to shake memories of worlds that no longer exist. Into the story steps an artificial intelligence research project built on the stored memories of a real person, and it's from there that both the game's strongest emotional thread and its darker sci-fi layer grow.

The structure stays faithful to the original recipe. The player reads, watches illustrated scenes, and makes decisions mainly through the mobile phone, this time via a messaging app with conversation threads, choosing which message to respond to and in what tone. Seemingly small decisions once again split the story into several endings. Compared to the first game, the storytelling is slower and more melancholic, leaning less on Akihabara-flavored jokes and more on an atmosphere of guilt, though it offers several scenes that rank among the strongest in the whole series. It also includes a clear diagram of unlocked scenes, making it easy to go back to branch points and track down missing sections, plus a glossary of terms accessible directly from the text, which helps a lot given how dense the sci-fi plot is. The narrative also switches between several points of view, so the player consistently knows more than any single character.

The PlayStation Vita release offers complete Japanese voice acting, a visually clean presentation, and enough text volume that it suits long evening reading sessions better than short breaks. The music is noticeably more intimate, leaning heavily on piano and silence, underscoring the sense that the hero is living in an in-between period. Critics praised the storytelling and the music above all, with reservations about the slow pace and the fact that the plot is almost impossible to follow without knowledge of the first game. Today Steins;Gate 0 is a recommended second step, not a first one, and the reward for it is a considerably broader view of the whole plot.
ps-vita__steins-gate-0.teaser: A branch into a timeline where the main hero failed; instead of a confident tinkerer, an introverted student.

ps-vita__corpse-party-blood-drive.article:
**Corpse Party: Blood Drive** closes out the horror series about a cursed elementary school and is also the first entry that didn't launch on older handhelds but directly on PlayStation Vita. Survivors from the previous games try to break the curse, but the way back into Heavenly Host Elementary School is one-way, and the game makes clear from the start that a happy ending isn't a given. The narrative splits between dialogue segments with drawn portraits and stretches through dark corridors, where you search for keys, note fragments, and a way to the next section.

Compared to earlier entries, the series has moved from a two-dimensional pixel perspective to a fully three-dimensional environment. The heroine moves with a flashlight whose battery drains, so light has to be rationed while also avoiding ghosts that can only be outrun or hidden from. There's more item collecting, simpler puzzles for opening up paths, and a system of multiple endings, the bad ones described in disgusting detail. The game is openly cruel, leaning on audio horror and helplessness rather than action, and practically requires headphones for the full experience. It also includes collectible diary fragments and side chapters that flesh out the school's background, along with several segments played as other characters in other time periods. Saving is only possible at designated spots, so even a short stretch of corridor can generate real tension.

Technically Blood Drive is the most divisive entry in the series. The environments are visually unremarkable and the game occasionally stutters, but the binaural audio ranks among the best on the whole platform and can turn a simple floor creak into full-blown panic. The music is minimalist and often steps aside for nothing but footsteps and breathing. Reception was cooler than for the older entries, mainly due to the technical state and the characters' slow movement, though fans appreciated that the story got a proper conclusion. Today it's a title for a dedicated audience that wants raw Japanese horror and doesn't mind the game prioritizing atmosphere over comfort.
ps-vita__corpse-party-blood-drive.teaser: Closes out the horror series about a cursed school; the first entry made specifically for the Vita.

ps-vita__root-letter.article:
**Root Letter** starts unassumingly: the hero finds, after many years, letters from a girl he used to correspond with as a student, and the last of them contains a confession to murder. He sets out to find her in Shimane Prefecture, only to discover that no one by that name ever lived at the given address, and the school she supposedly attended has no record of her. The game develops as a search for a person who, according to every official record, doesn't exist, and the player gradually visits former classmates, confronts them with the contents of the letters, and pieces together what happened in that class years ago.

Gameplay combines reading with classic adventure-game legwork. Locations are picked on a map, details are examined on the spot, and in conversations you choose which word or object to bring up to get a witness talking. The investigative sections take the form of confrontations, where you must pick the one piece of evidence, out of everything gathered so far, that breaks through an excuse. The game offers several distinct endings depending on how the player steers the conversations, and some of them change the meaning of the whole story surprisingly dramatically. The pace is slower, calmer, and rests on small interpersonal revelations. There's also a collection of letters you can return to at any time and reread with what you've since learned, which gradually changes their meaning, and the map fills in with locations that only open up after a correctly steered conversation.

Visually the title stands out by using edited photographs of real locations in Shimane as backgrounds, over which drawn characters move. On the PlayStation Vita's display, the combination of real landscape and illustration feels unusual and adds a lot to the sense of searching for a real person in a real place. The music is nostalgic, heavily acoustic, and restrained. Reviews praised the atmosphere, the visual approach, and the mystery itself, with reservations about some endings whose sharp genre swerve breaks with the tone of the rest of the game. Today Root Letter is a pleasant, travelogue-flavored detective story for players who want to investigate without rushing.
ps-vita__root-letter.teaser: A search for a girl whose existence has no records; a quiet, melancholic detective story.

ps-vita__code-realize-guardian-of-rebirt.article:
**Code: Realize ~Guardian of Rebirth~** sets a romance visual novel in a steampunk London hiding a girl with poison in her body: anything she touches disintegrates. That's why she lives in seclusion until a band of adventurers drawn from classic adventure literature comes to fetch her, among them a gentleman thief and an inventor. The result is an unusual blend of romance, conspiracy, and the story of someone who, for the first time in her life, is allowed to touch another person, even if only through gloves.

The gameplay is purely novel-based: long passages of text, illustrated scenes, and decision points that determine which character the heroine grows close to and how her own storyline unfolds. The game has six main routes, and they genuinely differ from one another, with some fundamentally changing the perspective on what lies behind the plot. The recommended order isn't mandatory, but it rewards patient players, since the final route pieces together information scattered across the others. Alongside the romance there's a surprisingly solid adventure line with intrigue and the question of what society allows itself to do to inconvenient people. The decision points are clearly marked, and the game lets you quickly jump back to earlier choices, so going through all the routes never feels like a chore but a natural part of progression. Besides the main routes, there's also a collection of short side vignettes.

On PlayStation Vita the game looks very good. The drawn portraits and illustrations are detailed, the color palette works with muted brass and purple tones, and they stand out beautifully on the sharp display. The Japanese voice acting is complete, and the music alternates orchestral motifs with more intimate pieces that support the quieter scenes well. The title was among those that helped establish otome novels in the Western market, where they had been a niche affair until then, and reviewers praised it precisely because, alongside the romance, it offers a genuinely well-built story. Today it's recommended even to those who never had any interest in the genre.
ps-vita__code-realize-guardian-of-rebirt.teaser: A romance novel set in steampunk London; a girl with poisonous skin and a group of heroes.

ps-vita__amnesia-memories.article:
**Amnesia: Memories** builds its entire story on a simple yet remarkably sturdy idea. The heroine wakes up without any memories and discovers she has a boyfriend, a job, friends, and a past she knows absolutely nothing about. To avoid giving herself away, she must act in everyday situations as if she remembered everything, all while piecing together a picture of her own life from other people's hints. So the player isn't just uncertain who to trust, but who the played character actually is, which turns ordinary dialogue into gripping detective work.

The game is divided into several parallel worlds that differ in who the heroine's past is tied to. Each has its own tone, ranging from lighthearted romance through jealousy to a decidedly oppressive line, and the level of danger varies quite a bit between them too. Alongside classic dialogue choices, the game tracks trust and affection meters, so a poorly judged answer can lead to a breakup, an accident, or a bad ending. The calendar structure divides the plot into days and forces the player to plan whom to spend time with. The number of endings is high, and repeat playthroughs genuinely pay off. The game keeps track of unlocked endings and a memory diary, so it's immediately clear what's still missing, and it offers a collection of short bonus scenes where the characters appear in a more relaxed light. The small added minigames serve more as a breather between chapters.

The PlayStation Vita version offers complete Japanese voice acting, clean drawn illustrations, and an interface that handles comfortably on the touchscreen. The music is delicate and leans heavily on the mood of each world, from calm motifs to unsettling loops in the darker routes. The title was among the first otome novels to reach a wider English-speaking audience, and it helped pave the way for others. Today it stands out mainly for how cleverly it uses memory loss as a game mechanic, and some of its darker routes read more like a psychological thriller than a romance.
ps-vita__amnesia-memories.teaser: A heroine with no memories pretends to remember her own life. An otome game with a good idea.

ps-vita__grim-fandango-remastered.article:
**Grim Fandango Remastered** brings one of the most acclaimed adventure games of all time to the handheld console. The protagonist Manny Calavera works as a travel agent in the land of the dead, selling the recently deceased packages for their four-year journey to eternal rest. When he discovers that someone is gaming the system and cheating honest souls out of their deserved ticket, he sets out to uncover the conspiracy. The result is a story that blends the Mexican Day of the Dead with the aesthetics of 1930s noir detective fiction, and it does so with such ease that the combination retroactively seems like the only possible one.

The gameplay is classic adventure fare: collecting items, combining them, talking to bizarre characters, and solving puzzles that rank among the most inventive as well as the toughest in the genre. The original release used direct character control, but the remaster thankfully added classic point-and-click controls too, which on PlayStation Vita means comfortable tapping right on the screen. It also added lighting, reworked character models, and the option to switch between the new and original graphics at any time, making it easy to see just how much work went into it.

On Vita's small screen the game works surprisingly well. The hand-painted backgrounds are crisp, touch controls cut down on fumbling, and the shorter chapters can be played in pieces. What still matters most is the music: the jazz and mariachi motifs rank among the best soundtracks in the genre's history, and the lead character's voice acting remains a textbook example. The remaster also added developer commentary that can be listened to while playing, discussing how individual scenes came together, which is reason enough on its own for genre fans to dive in. The original release from the nineties was not a commercial success, but critics ranked it among the pinnacles of adventure gaming, and the remaster brought it back into the spotlight. Today it's a mandatory stop for anyone who wants to know how far storytelling in adventure games can reach, though it's worth expecting some puzzles to demand a good deal of patience.
ps-vita__grim-fandango-remastered.teaser: One of the most acclaimed adventure games of all time; a traveling salesman in the land of the dead.

ps-vita__day-of-tentacle-remastered.article:
**Day of the Tentacle Remastered** is a meticulous restoration of a comedic adventure that has ranked among the pinnacles of the genre since its original release. A trio of very different friends try to stop a mutated tentacle from taking over the world, but their attempt to travel back in time fails, and each of them ends up in a different era. One gets stuck in the colonial past, another in a haunted present, and the third in a future ruled by tentacles. The player switches freely between them, solving puzzles that interlock across the centuries.

It's precisely this interlocking that makes the game an unmatched logic puzzle to this day. An item sent into the past changes history so that something different appears in the future, and many puzzles require thinking several steps ahead about the consequences. Yet it's a thoroughly cheerful game, full of absurd ideas, caricatures, and one-liners, so even a tricky solution is rewarded with a funny scene. The remaster added redrawn high-resolution graphics, reworked music, developer commentary, and the option to switch to the original pixel-art version at any time. The controls remain pleasantly simple: all interaction happens through a short verb menu and an inventory shared among all three heroes, so you can focus on thinking rather than hunting for hotspots. The package also includes a complete copy of an older game that can be run from a computer in one of the rooms.

On PlayStation Vita the game controls very comfortably, since the touchscreen replaces the mouse practically without any loss, and the drawn style looks great on the compact display. The music, in the spirit of old cartoon slapstick, combined with full voice acting, creates the impression of an interactive Saturday-morning cartoon. The original release became the benchmark for what a comedic adventure should look like, and its influence can be seen in dozens of later games. The remaster secured it a place on modern platforms, and it particularly shines on the handheld console, since it's short, playful, and can be comfortably finished over a few evenings.
ps-vita__day-of-tentacle-remastered.teaser: A comedic classic of the genre; three friends get stuck each in a different era after a failed attempt at time travel.

ps-vita__machinarium.article:
**Machinarium** is a Czech adventure game that won a worldwide audience mainly through its visual design. A small robot gets thrown onto a scrapyard outside the city, and the only thing it can do is return, piece itself back together, and find out who hurt it. The whole story is told without a single word, using only picture bubbles, gestures, and sounds, so the game needs no translation and anyone can understand it. The world is entirely hand-drawn, rusty and dusty, yet surprisingly cozy, and it's full of small animations worth watching longer than strictly necessary.

The gameplay is classic adventure fare with a strong helping of logic puzzles. The robot stretches and shrinks to reach items placed up high, combines items it finds, and solves standalone puzzles that often take the form of mechanical jigsaws, sliding puzzles, or sequence-tracking tasks. The difficulty is higher than it first appears, but the game offers a two-tier hint system: first a picture hint for the current scene, and finally a hand-drawn walkthrough, which must first be unlocked with a short action minigame. The game also isn't afraid to veer off into small pleasures, whether it's a hidden arcade game on one of the machines or a band that plays on a rooftop when the player helps it out. There's no time pressure anywhere, nor any way to lose, so you can explore at your leisure.

The PlayStation Vita version is one of the most pleasant the game has received, since touch controls match the original mouse-clicking almost exactly, and the sharp display does the hand-painted scenery a good service. Tomáš Dvořák's music is one of the best parts of the whole package, blending muted electronics with acoustic machine sounds, and together with the sound design it creates a calm, slightly melancholic atmosphere. The game earned a number of awards and helped show that an independent studio can compete with major brands. Today it's a short but exceptionally lovely experience that ages more slowly than most games of its time.
ps-vita__machinarium.teaser: A wordless Czech adventure game that conquered the world with its art style; a robot searches for the way home.

ps-vita__escape-plan.article:
**Escape Plan** was among the first games to show what PlayStation Vita could really do once its design was built directly around the console's own controls. Two characters, the skinny Lil and the pudgy Laarg, try to escape a bizarre facility full of traps, blades, and dangerous machines. The player doesn't control them directly in the usual sense; instead, they guide them through touches, taps, drags, and the rear touch panel, which can, for example, bend the floor or push an obstacle out of the way.

Every room is a standalone puzzle with one correct solution and a whole range of very nasty ways to fail. The characters can be sped up with a tap, put to sleep, inflated, or sent into the gears, and the game openly plays with the idea that death is part of the experimentation. New mechanisms, combinations of both characters, and levels that require split-second timing keep getting added along the way. A rating for the number of touches and speed then encourages replaying already-solved rooms in search of a more elegant approach. There are several dozen levels split into chapters with their own settings, and the game manages to tell it all without a single word, just through movement, sound, and short scenes between rooms. Alongside the main campaign, additional sets of rooms were added that ramp up the difficulty and assume the player already has full command of all the mechanisms.

The visual design is what players remember most. The game is entirely black and white, drawn with bold outlines and clearly inspired by surrealist and silent film, joined by a soundtrack made of jazz pieces and jittery piano. On Vita's sharp display, this high-contrast style looks fantastic and still feels fresh today. Reviews praised its inventiveness, atmosphere, and use of the hardware, but criticized its brevity and the fact that part of the content was sold separately. Today Escape Plan remains one of the best demonstrations of what Vita's hardware could do the moment someone actually worked with it, rather than simply porting a game from another platform.
ps-vita__escape-plan.teaser: A puzzle solved only through taps, swipes, and tilting the console; there's no direct control.

ps-vita__lumines-electronic-symphony.article:
**Lumines: Electronic Symphony** launched alongside PlayStation Vita's debut and quickly became the title used to show off the console. The principle is simple and addictive at once: square blocks made of two colors fall from above, the player rotates and arranges them so that solid-colored two-by-two squares form. These are then swept away by a timeline that sweeps across the playing field from left to right in time with the currently playing track. The better the player times large clusters, the bigger the chain cleared in a single pass.

The result is a game that plays more like a musical instrument than a classic puzzle game. Each field has its own track, its own color scheme, and its own timeline speed, and moving up a level changes all of it at once, so the player must constantly relearn both their eyes and their hands. Special blocks, an avatar system with small abilities, and an experience meter that unlocks further content were added, giving the game a reason to keep coming back to even after mastering the base mode. Alongside an endless mode, timed and battle variants are also available. Transitions between fields happen seamlessly too, without interrupting the game, so a single session can last tens of minutes and still feels like one long track.

The soundtrack is the main star. Electronic music forms the backbone of the experience, and every block touch produces a sound that fits into the track, so even ordinary play sounds like improvisation. The visuals are accompanied by backgrounds that react to what's happening on the field, so that even simple block-stacking plays out like a music video. On Vita the game is controlled with both buttons and touch, and the sharp display with vivid colors suits the abstract visual style perfectly. Reviewers received the title very well, and many of them called it the best reason to pick up the console right from launch. Today it remains one of the best-fitting handheld games ever made, since it combines short sessions with the feeling that the player isn't shaping the music by accident.
ps-vita__lumines-electronic-symphony.teaser: A music puzzle game where the track grows with every colored square cleared.

ps-vita__guacamelee.article:
**Guacamelee!** takes the classic metroidvania structure and dresses it in Mexican folklore, luchador masks, and colors that practically glow off Vita's screen. The hero is farmer Juan Aguacate, who, after dying at the hands of a skeletal villain, receives a magical mask and transforms into a wrestler. The goal is to rescue the mayor's kidnapped daughter and prevent the realm of the dead from merging with the world of the living. The script doesn't take itself seriously at all, pouring out references to other games and internet culture, and regularly reaches for downright loose humor between fights.

The core system combines a brawler with a platformer. Juan learns special strikes that serve simultaneously as weapons and as keys: each has its own color and only breaks blocks of the matching hue. As the game progresses, combat and movement merge together, since enemies are protected by colored shields and the platforming sections demand chaining double jumps, dashes, and mid-air strikes. Add the ability to switch between the world of the living and the dead, where platforms appear and disappear, plus a transformation into a rooster for squeezing through narrow gaps, and you get one of the most demanding acrobatic games of its generation. The optional final sections rank among the toughest the genre offers.

The Vita version launched simultaneously with the PlayStation 3 release and was offered bundled together, which wasn't a given at the time. The vector-based graphics get along well with the smaller screen, and the game runs smoothly even in the busiest bursts of color. The music blends Latin American motifs with electronica and manages to be as danceable as it is dramatic. Critics mainly praised the precision of the controls and the inventive visual identity, and the title quickly became one of the most frequently recommended indie picks on Sony's handheld console. A later expanded edition added new areas and abilities. Even today it's an exceptionally slick game that works exactly as well in short sessions as a portable console demands.
ps-vita__guacamelee.teaser: A metroidvania dressed in Mexican folklore; luchador masks, humor, and brawls.

ps-vita__rayman-origins.article:
**Rayman Origins** was one of the titles that accompanied PlayStation Vita's launch in Europe, and it immediately showed how well the new display could handle hand-painted graphics. Ubisoft's handless mascot's return to 2D platforming was built on the UbiArt engine, which let artists' own drawings be animated directly, so every bush, enemy, and background looks like an illustration from a children's book brought to life. The story is just a pretext: Rayman and his friends wake dark forces with their snoring and must journey through worlds full of musical instruments, deserts, sinking wrecks, and living kitchens.

The gameplay relies on purity. At first the hero can only run and jump, and gliding, swimming, wall-running, and strikes are added over time, with each new move getting its own set of levels that thoroughly put it through its paces. Collecting small Lums and freeing trapped Electoons opens up further areas while also giving a reason to return to already-completed levels. The real test comes in the timed sections, where the game speeds the pace into a race against the screen and demands absolutely precise timing. The controls are supple and forgiving enough that death never feels unfair.

The Vita version focuses on solo play and adds small touch interactions, but otherwise offers virtually the complete content of the big consoles in your pocket. Smooth performance and rich color on the small screen were, in 2012, among the best demonstrations of the device's capabilities. The music is playful, funny, and often becomes part of the level design itself, especially in rhythm-driven passages. Critics received the game enthusiastically and ranked it among the best 2D platformers of its time, even though sales never matched the acclaim. Origins made a major contribution to reviving interest in hand-drawn platformers and showed that a major publisher can still build a solid 2D game even in the age of 3D blockbusters. Today it plays just as well as it did on release day, and for Vita owners it remains one of the best ways to recall what the console promised at the start of its journey.
ps-vita__rayman-origins.teaser: A hand-painted platformer built on the UbiArt engine; the screen feels like a children's book come to life.

ps-vita__rayman-legends.article:
**Rayman Legends** built on Origins and, in many ways, surpassed it, taking the proven foundation and adding an even broader range of ideas. It's once again a hand-painted 2D platformer powered by the UbiArt engine, but this time with an even richer palette of settings, from underwater temples through medieval fortresses to snow-capped peaks. The story framework consists of paintings that the heroes enter to free the Teensies trapped inside them. The structure is thus looser than a classic linear progression, and players often choose which of the open paths to try first.

The strongest move is the musical levels that close out each world. The player races forward in precise sync with the track, with jumps, strikes, and destroyed obstacles landing right on the beat, so an ordinary platformer suddenly turns into a dance choreography. Alongside that, the game leans on sections where you control the environment instead of the hero, cutting ropes, rotating platforms, and stunning enemies. On Vita this role is taken over by the touchscreen, one of the most natural uses of the hardware a handheld console ever offered. Also added are daily and weekly challenges with leaderboards, plus a large selection of reworked levels from the previous entry.
