The portable version keeps very solid smoothness and crisp drawing and comes close to the big consoles in content. The soundtrack is playful, varied, and in the musical passages even allows itself some cheeky cover versions of famous melodies, which turned these sections into one of the most-quoted moments of the whole generation. Critics received the game exceptionally well, and many still consider it the pinnacle of the modern 2D Rayman. For Vita it was one of the best reasons to pull the console out on a train, since individual levels take only a few minutes and the game can be set aside at any time. The content is also generous enough that finishing absolutely everything takes considerably longer than you'd expect from a platformer. Even years later, Legends feels remarkably fresh and is regularly mentioned among the best 2D platformers of its generation.
ps-vita__rayman-legends.teaser: An improved successor to Origins with a richer palette of worlds and even more generous content.

ps-vita__shovel-knight.article:
**Shovel Knight** is a tribute to the eight-bit era that didn't stop at nostalgic packaging but truly understood why the old platformers were so good. The hero is a knight armed with a shovel, which he uses to slash enemies, dig treasure out of walls, and above all as a spring, aiming it downward to bounce off enemies' heads, lamps, and falling rocks. This single move defines the entire game: the pogo bounce is a weapon, a means of movement, and a way to clear a trap, and the game builds most of its ideas around it.

The structure draws on the classics. On the map you select levels that end with a fight against one of the members of the Order of No Quarter, each with their own theme, their own set of mechanics, and their own musical motif. Between expeditions you can shop in towns, expand your stamina, buy relics with side abilities, and upgrade your armor. The difficulty is high but fair, since checkpoints are placed sensibly, and the player can voluntarily smash them for treasure, which is one of the most elegant ways to offer extra challenge without separate difficulty settings.

The graphics honor the limits of consoles of the era but allow themselves a wider palette and smoother animation, so it looks the way we remember old games looking, not how they actually looked. The chiptune soundtrack ranks among the most highly praised in the modern indie scene, and its melodies stick in your head long after finishing the game. The Vita version was released alongside other Sony console versions and looks excellent on the small display, since pixel art doesn't need a large screen. The game came out of a very successful Kickstarter campaign and became a textbook example of how to see such a project through to completion, including free expansions with playable villains that gradually turned the original game into a large package of several campaigns. Critics received the title enthusiastically and ranked it among the best games of its year regardless of budget. To this day, Shovel Knight remains one of the best modern platformers ever made, and on Vita it plays perfectly naturally.
ps-vita__shovel-knight.teaser: A tribute to the eight-bit era, where a pogo-bounce with a shovel is a weapon, a movement tool, and almost a philosophy.

ps-vita__axiom-verge.article:
**Axiom Verge** is a rare case of a game created almost entirely by a single person, and yet it feels like a full-fledged successor to the classic metroidvanias of the sixteen-bit era. The player takes on the role of a scientist named Trace, who, after a lab accident, wakes up in a foreign world full of organic machines, silent giants, and messages from beings whose motives stay unclear for a long time. The storytelling is fragmentary and oppressive, and it deliberately leaves plenty of questions open, so the atmosphere of isolation lasts all the way to the end.

The foundation is classic exploration of an interconnected map, where new equipment unlocks previously inaccessible paths. There's an unusually large number of weapons, differing not just in power but also in the shape of their fire, so it's worth switching between them depending on the situation. The truly original element, though, is a tool that can damage reality itself: aim it at an enemy or a piece of the environment, and the game starts generating visual and logical glitches, textures vanish from walls, enemies change behavior, and passages appear in the damaged blocks. Where other games treat a graphical bug as a problem, Axiom Verge turned it into its core mechanic. On top of that, the world is scattered with modifications that alter weapon properties, plus a good number of well-hidden secrets.

The visual side deliberately imitates the limitations of old machines, including color palettes and flicker, which lets the damaged areas blend naturally into the overall picture. The music is dark, synthetic, and industrially cold, offering more of a bleak sonic backdrop for exploration than melody. Critics praised the game mainly for the courage to build its whole concept around one strong idea and for its expansive, densely designed world. On Vita the title has an ideal home, since it suits both short and long sessions, and the smaller screen serves the sharp pixel art well. The game also reached a wide audience thanks to a PlayStation Plus subscriber offer, which helped it break out beyond the circle of old-metroidvania enthusiasts. To this day, Axiom Verge is regularly mentioned among the best the genre has produced since 2010.
ps-vita__axiom-verge.teaser: A metroidvania made by a single developer; oppressive and mysterious like a classic of the 16-bit era.

ps-vita__spelunky.article:
At first glance, **Spelunky** looks like a cute platformer about an adventurer with a whip, but it is actually one of the strictest and smartest games of its time. Every descent into the caves generates a completely new layout of rooms, traps, enemies and treasures, so nothing can be memorized. What you can learn is how the individual parts of the world react to one another, and that is where all the magic lies. Death is instant, final, and you start again from the very first level, usually feeling that you alone are to blame.

Your equipment consists of bombs, ropes and a whip, and you can find or buy further items, from climbing gloves to boots that protect against traps. The real depth, however, comes from how the systems are interlinked. A fire trap ignites a crate, the crate sets a shopkeeper alight, the shopkeeper flies into a rage and hunts the player for the rest of the whole expedition. A stone block dropped onto an enemy opens up a path, but at the same time wakes the inhabitants of the neighbouring room. These chain reactions create stories players still tell today, and helped make Spelunky one of the most cited templates for the entire roguelike wave.

The PlayStation Vita version was offered together with the home console release, and the handheld format suits it exceptionally well, since a single run takes only a few dozen minutes and invites you to try it again at any moment. A daily challenge was also added, where everyone gets the same cave layout and a single attempt, which turned it into a popular ritual. The pixel art is legible even on the smaller screen, the music alternates adventurous motifs with tension, and the audio feedback tells you exactly what has just woken up nearby. Critical reception was enthusiastic, and the game is still cited today as a textbook example of perfectly balanced random design. Beneath the surface there are also several well-hidden paths and alternative endings whose existence most players remain unaware of for a long time. Anyone who gives Spelunky enough time gets one of the most durable games that exist on the Vita.
ps-vita__spelunky.teaser: A roguelike platformer where the caves regenerate on every descent; death is instant.

ps-vita__velocity-2x.article:
**Velocity 2X** is an unusual hybrid that alternates a vertical space shooter with a two-dimensional action platformer within a single level, and above all does both excellently. The player controls Captain Kai Tana, whose ship, the Quarp Jet, can teleport a short distance, and when needed lands so the heroine continues on foot through the narrow corridors of enemy stations. The transition between the two modes is seamless, with no loading, and the game uses it to maintain a pace that practically never drops.

The core of the gameplay is speed and precision. In the shooter sections you can speed up or slow down the screen scroll, teleport through walls and send out homing probes that let you jump back to a previously seen spot, turning every level into a small logic puzzle about the order in which to open colour-coded doors. The on-foot sections have their own version of the teleport and their own pace, but the same rule applies: the best result goes to whoever can plan the route ahead of time. The rating at the end of each mission tracks time, the number of navigation points collected, and survivors rescued, which encourages repeated attempts to improve your results and compete on the leaderboards.

On the Vita the game runs very smoothly, and its clean, brightly neon look really shines on the display. The electronic soundtrack pulses in precise rhythm and can turn even repeating a single level into an almost hypnotic experience. The title reached a wide audience partly because it was offered to PlayStation Plus subscribers at launch, and critics received it very favourably, praising above all the courage to combine two genres without either getting in the other's way. The British studio earned itself a reputation as a specialist in precise arcade action with this release. The game follows on from an earlier, purely shooter-focused title by the same team, but feels noticeably more confident and cohesive by comparison. Today, Velocity 2X is among the titles that best show what could be achieved on the Vita with a small budget and a clear vision.
ps-vita__velocity-2x.teaser: A hybrid of a vertical shooter and a platformer with a teleporting ship; it excels at both.

ps-vita__steamworld-dig.article:
**SteamWorld Dig** combines platforming, digging and gradually unlocked abilities into a surprisingly addictive whole that can be finished in a single evening and still leaves a strong impression. The player takes on the role of the steam-powered robot Rusty, who inherits a mine from his uncle and gradually works his way deeper and deeper beneath the town of Tumbleton. The setting has a western flavour, with cacti, a desert sky and robotic inhabitants who come across as laconic and dryly funny.

The game's loop is simple and exceptionally well tuned. You descend, dig sideways and downward, collect ores and gems, keep an eye on your light and water reserves, and return to the surface in time to sell your finds. With the money earned, Rusty upgrades his pickaxe, stamina, lantern and movement, so the next descent goes faster and reaches further. Special caves hold technologies that change the rules: drilling through hard blocks, running along walls, or a steam-powered jump. Digging also creates your own map, since every passage you carve out remains and becomes your own personal way back.

The PlayStation Vita version launched alongside the release for the big console, and the handheld form suits it well, since each descent is short and offers a natural point to put the game down. The hand-drawn art is clean and legible, the music alternates calm western motifs with tenser tones in the deeper levels, where the surroundings stop being friendly. Critics praised above all the pacing and how the game never drags, and the title became the foundation of a series that continued with further entries in different genres. It is also interesting how, without a single word of explanation, the game teaches the player to plan the way back up, since reckless digging downward eventually catches up with you. Today, SteamWorld Dig still plays just as well as it did back then, and remains one of the best entry points for anyone wanting to start exploring independent games on the Vita.
ps-vita__steamworld-dig.teaser: Digging, platforming, and gradual upgrades; it can be finished in a single evening.

ps-vita__olliolli.article:
**OlliOlli** took skateboarding, flattened it into two dimensions, and turned it into a test of timing that can be just as frustrating as it is satisfying. The player rides through a level from left to right, jumping over obstacles, grinding rails, and chaining tricks into one long combo that must not be broken by a fall. The controls are built around the analogue stick: a trick is input with a motion, but what really matters is pressing the button at the exact moment of landing. Whoever nails it perfectly gets the full score and keeps their speed; whoever mistimes it crashes to the ground and starts again.

The structure is split into short tracks with five tasks each, from reaching a certain score to performing a specific trick at a specific spot. Completing all of them unlocks a harder variant, where scoring is based on a single unbroken run and any fall means immediate failure. It is precisely this design that makes OlliOlli a game players repeat for tens of minutes because of a single stretch, without ever feeling cheated, since every mistake is clearly their own. Daily challenges with leaderboards give players further reason to return even after finishing the campaign.

The game was originally made for the PlayStation Vita, and it shows that it was designed with it in mind. Short tracks, instant restarts, and the ability to put the console to sleep at any moment make the handheld an ideal home for it. The pixel art is deliberately spare so as not to interfere with judging distances, and the main role is played by a soundtrack of electronic tracks that keeps the pace and, at its best moments, blends with the rhythm of the ride. Critics received the title very well and praised above all the cleanness of the controls, which places the game among the best-controlling arcade titles on this platform. A sequel followed, and the series gradually grew into the form known to today's players, but its roots lie right here. Anyone who gets used to its particular rhythm will find that OlliOlli plays more like a music game than a sports simulation, and that this is exactly where its greatest strength lies.
ps-vita__olliolli.teaser: Two-dimensional skateboarding built on precise trick timing, not luck.

ps-vita__fez.article:
**Fez** rests on a single idea that changes everything: the world looks like a two-dimensional pixel-art platformer, but is actually three-dimensional, and the player can rotate it by ninety degrees. Platforms that seemed miles away turn out, once the view is rotated, to be right next to each other; a chasm disappears, and a path leads where nothing was before. The hero Gomez receives a magical cap that grants him this ability and sets off to collect the fragments of a shattered cube that hold his world together.

The jumping itself is calm and forgiving; the game never punishes you for falling, and enemies barely exist. The real substance lies elsewhere: in observation, mapping, and figuring out everything hidden within the world. Alongside the usual collectible tasks, there is an entire layer of puzzles built on its own alphabet, number system, hidden patterns and signals that the game never explains anywhere. Anyone who wants to reach all the way to the very end really does have to take notes on paper. This second half of Fez is still cited today as one of the most ambitious attempts to turn an entire audience into one big puzzle-solving community.

The visuals combine nostalgic pixel art with spatial effects and, above all, with a gradually expanding scale that manages to surprise even after hours of play. The audio is one of the strongest elements; ambient electronica with echoes and gentle melodies creates a dreamlike, slightly melancholic mood rarely found in platformers. The release on Sony's consoles came with cross-buy across platforms, so the game could be carried over to the Vita, where the smaller screen and the ability to pause at any moment suit it well. Critics received Fez very warmly, and it is still discussed today as one of the titles that, in the first half of the last decade, defined what an independent game could mean. So many discussions grew up around its creation and around the author himself that Fez became part of a wider narrative about how small teams were making their mark at the time. But the game holds up on its own merits too, and nobody has repeated its central trick better since.
ps-vita__fez.teaser: A seemingly 2D platformer that turns into a 3D puzzle when you rotate the view by 90 degrees.

ps-vita__thomas-was-alone.article:
**Thomas Was Alone** is a game where the player controls coloured rectangles, and yet it is one of the most cited examples of how a moving story can be told with minimal means. The main character, Thomas, is a red rectangle who one day wakes up inside a computer system and starts looking around. He gradually meets other shapes, each with a different size, a different form and a different ability, and through a narrator the game turns them into real characters with worries, vanity and loyalty. The narration is dry, British in its humour, and surprisingly kind.

In terms of gameplay, it is a calm logic platformer. The goal is to get all the characters to their target spots, which requires making use of their differing properties. A small rectangle jumps high but not far; a large block serves as a step and as a bridge; one shape floats on the surface of a dangerous liquid, another can reverse gravity. The player switches between them, building a living scaffold out of them. The difficulty stays gentle, since the game's centre of gravity lies in atmosphere and rhythm rather than a test of dexterity, and the levels are short, which suits short sessions well.

The graphics are deliberately reduced to simple shapes on a dark background, so all the meaning is carried by movement, narration and music. The piano and string soundtrack is understated but remarkably effective, and contributes to the overall impression just as much as the writing does. The Vita version launched alongside the PlayStation 3 release, and gave the game a home where it works beautifully in moments when there is only time for a few levels. Critics received the title very warmly, praising above all the writing and the voice performance, and the game became one of the symbols of that era's wave of small independent projects. It also showed that a narrator's commentary can be a fully fledged gameplay mechanic in its own right, since it is precisely this that gives otherwise neutral shapes motivation and weight. To this day, Thomas Was Alone manages to leave an impression in two to three hours that much bigger productions fail to achieve.
ps-vita__thomas-was-alone.teaser: A story told about colored rectangles; minimalism that can genuinely move you.

ps-vita__rogue-legacy.article:
**Rogue Legacy** built its entire concept on a simple idea: when the hero dies, the game is not taken over by them again, but by their descendant. Before each expedition, the player chooses from several heirs, who differ in class, abilities and, above all, inherited quirks. One is colour-blind and sees the whole castle in black and white, another is a giant who barely fits through the corridors, another has reversed controls or suffers from excessive flatulence, a purely cosmetic joke. This small detail gives every attempt its own personality and keeps a sense of humour alive even after dozens of deaths.

The castle is regenerated each time from four interconnected areas, and the player fights, jumps, dodges projectiles and searches for treasure within it. The gold earned, however, does not carry over; upon returning it is entirely swallowed by the construction of the family manor, where new classes, spells, blacksmith and rune upgrades and permanent stat increases are unlocked. Progress therefore works in two ways: the bloodline as a whole improves, and at the same time so does the player's own ability to read enemies and time their attacks. Combat is fast and demands discipline, since even a weaker enemy can punish carelessness.

The pixel art is clean and colourful, the music alternates heroic motifs with tenser tracks in later areas, giving the expeditions the right amount of drive. The Vita release was part of a cross-buy with other Sony consoles, and the handheld format suits the game well, since a single expedition is short and can be stopped at any point in between. Critics received the title very well, and Rogue Legacy is today considered one of the games that helped bring roguelite principles beyond a narrow circle of enthusiasts. The combination of permanent progression and randomized runs became a model for a whole line of successors and still works remarkably well. After finishing it, a New Game Plus mode with tougher enemies also awaits, so there is reason to keep returning long after the last of the original castle guardians has fallen.
ps-vita__rogue-legacy.teaser: A roguelite where, after the hero dies, their descendant takes over the game with their own mutation.

ps-vita__salt-and-sanctuary.article:
**Salt and Sanctuary** took the structure and mood of the Souls games and translated them into two dimensions without losing any of their weight. The player is shipwrecked on a grim island full of monsters, crumbling fortresses and silent priests, and gradually discovers an interconnected world in which shortcuts open from the inside, and every new path feels like a genuine victory. The story is not told directly; it is pieced together from item descriptions, fragments of conversation, and what the environment itself suggests about what once happened here.

The combat system is slow, weighty and demands patience. Every strike costs stamina, every roll has its windows, and enemies punish greed. Weapons are divided into many categories with differing reach and rhythm, joined by shields, bows, spells and prayers. Experience, in the form of salt, is lost on death and can only be recovered by returning to the place you fell. Character progression runs through an extensive skill tree that resembles a constellation and offers considerable freedom in how you build your character. Instead of bonfires, sanctuaries serve as rest points, where the player chooses an order that influences the services on offer and the nature of resting.

The hand-drawn graphics with sharp, dark silhouettes give the game a distinctive face and set it apart from imitators. The audio is restrained, relying more on silence, wind and the clash of weapons than on grand music, which only heightens the sense of loneliness. The PlayStation Vita version launched shortly after the release on the big console, and despite being a technically demanding title, it runs surprisingly well on the handheld and offers the complete content. Critics received the game favourably and called it the finest two-dimensional take on soulslike principles of its time. It is also worth appreciating that the game did not simply imitate its inspiration but added its own ideas, such as moving along walls and ceilings, or the order system that changes the entire course of the game. For players who enjoy a hard and deliberate style of progress, it is one of the most substantial experiences on the Vita altogether.
ps-vita__salt-and-sanctuary.teaser: A two-dimensional Souls game; the same weight, an interconnected world, and storytelling through items.

ps-vita__sound-shapes.article:
**Sound Shapes** is a platformer in which the player does not collect coins but notes, and every note picked up instantly becomes part of the composition playing through the level. As the level progresses, the music layers up and grows; a simple rhythm becomes a full song, and the player feels as though they are composing it themselves through movement. The character you control is a simple ball that can stick to certain surfaces and detach from them, which turns movement into a question of timing whenever the platforms move in rhythm with the track.

The campaign is divided into albums, each with its own artist and its own musician, so they differ significantly not only in sound but also in visual style. One album looks like abstract graphics, another like an industrial landscape, another like a gloomy city. Well-known musicians and artists took part in creating them, giving the game a reputation as a project somewhere between a video game and a music album. Alongside the campaign, the title offers a fully featured editor where the player builds their own level and composition at the same time, since the placement of notes directly determines the melody. Modes focused on speed and survival are also included, using the same material in a considerably more aggressive way.

The Vita version launched alongside the PlayStation 3 release and offered shared progress between the two devices, an appealing novelty in 2012. The touchscreen makes the editor considerably more pleasant to use, and the handheld form suits a game whose individual levels last only a few minutes. Critics received the title very well, praising above all how naturally it linked playing with composing music without turning into a rhythm game in the usual sense. Sound Shapes remains one of the most original things ever released on the Vita, and stays one of the best examples of a game that is just as important to listen to as it is to play. With headphones on, it becomes an experience with few equivalents on a handheld console, and even after years it still manages to surprise with how naturally it weaves together movement, image and sound into a single whole.
ps-vita__sound-shapes.teaser: A platformer where collected notes directly compose the level's playing track.

ps-vita__resistance-burning-skies.article:
**Resistance: Burning Skies** was the first genuine first-person shooter on the PlayStation Vita to fully make use of the dual analogue sticks, showing that a handheld console could handle a genre long treated as merely a tolerated guest on portable devices. The story unfolds in the alternate history known from the Resistance series, where an alien Chimera invasion overruns America, casting the player as an ordinary firefighter who, over the course of a single night, becomes an armed resistance fighter. The campaign runs through linear settings of shattered cities, tunnels, factory halls and improvised refugee camps, moving between an arsenal ranging from a standard rifle to inventive Chimeran weapons with alternate fire modes. The touchscreen is not just decoration: it is used for quickly switching grenades, for brutal close-range finishing moves, and for weapon upgrades that gradually unlock new abilities through use.

Technically, in 2012 this was an important demonstration of the new console's capabilities. Environments are detailed, enemies arrive in larger groups, and the lighting plays with contrast between dark interiors and muzzle flashes, at the cost of occasional frame-rate drops and simpler background textures. The atmosphere builds on the oppressive mood of a depopulated America, where the enemy feels more like a predatory force of nature than an army, and the music holds the dark orchestral tone familiar from the main series. Multiplayer offered classic modes for eight players and ran surprisingly smoothly on the handheld.

Contemporary reception was mixed. Reviewers praised the very fact that a console-style shooter works on the Vita and controls naturally, but criticized its short and narratively flat campaign, enemy behaviour, and the fact that production values fell short of the main series entries. Even so, it remains an important milestone, since it defined the control standard that more ambitious titles would later build upon. Today it is best appreciated as a brisk adventure for a few evenings and as proof of just how far portable action could go at the time.
ps-vita__resistance-burning-skies.teaser: The first major dual-stick FPS on a handheld; the Chimera invasion of America.

ps-vita__unit-13.article:
**Unit 13** is a third-person action shooter that, instead of a long story campaign, relies on dozens of short, precisely designed missions built for repeat play and chasing a better score. The player commands a squad of six operatives with different specializations, from a silent sniper through a heavy-armoured trooper to a specialist skilled in close combat, choosing whoever best suits the type of task at hand. Missions are divided into categories that dictate the style of play: some call for a silent infiltration without raising the alarm, others for a loud, timed firefight, or for completing the advance without taking a single hit. Every attempt earns a grade and a score, so the main motivation is to refine your own approach into the cleanest possible run.

Zipper Interactive, the studio behind the SOCOM and MAG series, built the controls around both analogue sticks and complemented them with touch input for quick commands, loadout selection and interacting with the environment. The structure of short missions proved to be a clever solution for a handheld console, since you can finish one mission during a tram ride, while the room for improvement remains almost limitless. The game was rounded out by daily challenges, online leaderboards and two-player co-op, which turned many missions into an entirely different experience.

Reviews praised the precise controls, brisk pace and technical presentation, which ranked among the better showcases of the Vita's early library, but criticized the generic environments and the lack of a narrative that might have given the action greater weight. The title also ended up being one of the last works of the studio, which closed shortly after release, lending it a somewhat melancholic edge. Today, Unit 13 feels surprisingly modern: a structure built on short, repeatable runs and leaderboards is exactly what action games commonly do today, on both mobile and home platforms. Anyone who enjoys polished repetition and measuring themselves against others will find a surprisingly addictive game here, one they keep returning to for missions they already know by heart.
ps-vita__unit-13.teaser: A third-person action game built on short missions and chasing a better score.

ps-vita__ultimate-marvel-vs-capcom-3.article:
**Ultimate Marvel vs. Capcom 3** was one of the strongest weapons in the PlayStation Vita launch lineup and still stands as proof of how well a handheld can handle a fast team fighter. Battles are fought in three-on-three teams, with characters swapping on the fly, chaining attacks together and covering each other with assists. The roster mixes heroes and villains from the Marvel comic universe with icons of Capcom's gaming history, from Ryu and Dante to Morrigan, creating matchups that would make no sense anywhere else. The pace is extremely fast, the screen is often flooded with effects, and a single well-timed hit can turn an entire match around, turning every bout into a small drama.

The Vita port kept a surprising amount of fidelity. The art style, inspired by comic panels and inked linework, remains legible even on a smaller screen, animation runs smoothly, and button controls stay precise. A new touch mode let players trigger special attacks directly with a finger on the screen, so even an inexperienced player could enjoy flashy combo strings without having to practice complex inputs. The game was rounded out with an online mode and the option to train against a dummy anytime between matches.

At the time it was received very well, often noted as one of the best reasons to own the console. Players praised the near-complete content parity with the home versions, including the expanded roster and adjusted balance. The Marvel vs. Capcom series shaped the entire team-fighter genre with its emphasis on fast character switching and aggressive pacing, and this portable version remains one of the best ways to play it on the go. It stays fun even after all these years, whether you're playing a few matches against the CPU or trying to grasp the depths of team combos. An energetic soundtrack and over-the-top presentation keep the feel of a grand comic-book showdown alive from the first second to the last.
ps-vita__ultimate-marvel-vs-capcom-3.teaser: A fast three-on-three team fighting game with assists; an ace of the Vita's launch lineup.

ps-vita__street-fighter-x-tekken.article:
**Street Fighter X Tekken** is a crossover that brought together the two biggest fighting franchises of its time, and on PlayStation Vita it offered the most content-rich take on this clash. The foundation is two-on-two team battles where you can switch between your pair at any point during a combo and chain attacks seamlessly, so matches feel like a constant stream of pressure and counterattacks. Tekken characters were adapted into two-dimensional combat while keeping their signature strike chains, while Street Fighter contributed its precise special-move system. A special chapter of its own were the so-called gems, boosts that adjust a character's traits before the match, which split the community into a camp enjoying the experimentation and a camp of purists.

The Vita version arrived with the complete set of additional fighters included right in the base package, including guest characters from other gaming worlds, making it the most content-rich variant of the game. Technically the port succeeded: the resolution is lower, but the style with bold outlines and colorful effects looks good on the Vita's screen, and the controls stay precise enough even on the small directional pad. The game was rounded out with an online mode and the ability to play against owners of the home console, which felt like a nice bonus at a time when cross-platform connectivity wasn't common.

Reception was mixed but leaned positive: reviewers praised the pacing, the team system and the generous amount of content, while criticism was aimed mainly at the gem system and at the fact that the game never built as strong a competitive scene as classic Street Fighter IV. Today it gets a surprising rehabilitation: team fighting with character switching has become a standard part of modern fighters, and on Vita it's still one of the most nimbly playable fighting games you can pick up anywhere. Watching icons from two completely different gaming worlds face off also has a charm that hasn't aged a bit.
ps-vita__street-fighter-x-tekken.teaser: A crossover of two fighting-game giants; Tekken characters translated into the Street Fighter plane.

ps-vita__mortal-kombat.article:
**Mortal Kombat** appeared on PlayStation Vita in a version that took the successful 2011 revival of the legendary series and added a heap of extra content on top. The game returns to a two-dimensional plane of combat and to the brand's roots: a tournament between worlds, brutal fights, and the infamous finishing moves that once helped push the genre onto newspaper front pages. Battles work with a meter that can be spent on a boosted special attack, breaking the opponent's combo, or a devastating X-ray hit that shows bones breaking in close-up detail. Systemically it's a surprisingly deep fighter that's also accessible, since anyone can grasp the basics within a few minutes.

The Vita version includes the full story campaign, which walks the player through a narrative that switches between characters across chapters, plus added fighters that were sold elsewhere as paid content. It also arrived with an expanded challenge tower holding several hundred tasks, including new ones built specifically around the handheld's abilities, namely touch and tilt controls. Technically it was a solid port: resolution and some effects took a step back, but the pace of the fighting stayed intact, and the dark, grimy atmosphere of the arenas works even on a smaller screen.

Reviews welcomed the portable version warmly, highlighting especially the sheer amount of content that made it one of the most content-rich fighters on the console. Criticism was aimed at the technical compromises and a less stable online mode. The 2011 revival of the series had a major impact on the whole genre with how heavily it leaned on a large story campaign and companion modes, which quickly became the standard. In the Vita version, it's still a fighter you can sink dozens of hours into even solo, since there's enough content to last for weeks. At the same time, it's a game that nicely reminds you why the series once stirred up such heated debates about violence, and why it managed to keep its audience regardless.
ps-vita__mortal-kombat.teaser: A return to the 2D plane of combat and to the fatalities that once sparked a moral panic.

ps-vita__injustice-gods-among-us-ultimat.article:
**Injustice: Gods Among Us Ultimate Edition** brought superhero fights from the DC comic universe to PlayStation Vita, and showed that even a technically demanding fighter can be ported to a handheld with dignity. The story mode is built on a dark alternate reality in which Superman, after a personal tragedy, becomes the world's authoritarian ruler, and Batman leads a resistance against him, which explains why the heroes end up beating each other up. Fights take place on a plane, but rely heavily on the environment: characters bounce off walls, throw cars at each other, and a strong attack can send an opponent flying through several floors of a building in a flashy animation. Each hero also has a unique ability that changes their style, whether it's a temporary boost, projectiles, or a change in movement.

The port by studio Armature ranks among the technically most interesting pieces on the console. Character models and arenas stayed detailed, the pace of combat holds up, and the game added options built around touch, including a mini-game during special attacks. The Ultimate Edition release also includes all fighters and costumes released afterward, so it doesn't fall behind the home versions in terms of content.

Reception was largely positive, with emphasis on how good the game looks on the handheld and how smoothly it runs. Criticism pointed to certain details and effects logically stepping back, and to the online scene staying small. Injustice had a major impact on the genre: it confirmed that a fighting game can also work as a full-fledged narrative adventure with cinematic sequences, and it opened the way for a sequel that became one of the pillars of the genre. Today, the Vita version is a pleasant way to revisit this era, especially if you enjoy the comic-book source material. Alongside the campaign, the game also offers a series of challenges and side tasks that unlock costumes and other extras, so there's no shortage of motivation to come back. The music holds a dark, cinematic tone matching the serious take on the source material, and together with the fight direction it turns every clash into a small comic-book scene.
ps-vita__injustice-gods-among-us-ultimat.teaser: Battles of DC heroes in a dark alternate reality where Superman becomes a tyrant.

ps-vita__blazblue-chrono-phantasma.article:
**BlazBlue: Chrono Phantasma** is the third major chapter in Arc System Works' stylized fighting series, and on PlayStation Vita it stands as one of the best-looking games in the entire library. The foundation is two-dimensional fights with hand-drawn sprites carrying an incredible number of animation frames, so every character feels like a living animated series. The fighters are deliberately very different from one another: one fights with the help of a phantom, another controls gravity or sets traps on the field, so learning a new character essentially means learning a new game. Systemically the game works with defensive mechanics that let you break out of an opponent's pressure, and a boosted mode that changes the properties of attacks near the end of a match.

Beyond the fighting itself, the game offers an enormous amount of story content. The narrative unfolds through extensive text and voiced scenes that continue from previous entries and develop a tangled plot about time loops and fates that repeat themselves. Anyone who wants to see it all can easily spend dozens of hours on the story alone. The music is typically rock and energetic, with distinctive themes for individual characters, and it's one of the series' hallmarks.

Reviews praised the visual execution, the depth of the fighting system, and the generosity of the content; criticism pointed to it being an extremely complex game for newcomers, with a dense story that's hard to jump into. The BlazBlue series had a major impact on the more modern generation of two-dimensional fighters by showing that hand-drawn graphics can be technically top-notch and timeless at once. That's exactly why Chrono Phantasma still looks great on Vita today and ranks among the titles worth showing off on the console. It's helped by a wealth of extra modes, from tutorial lessons through challenges to lighthearted mini-games, giving the player plenty to do even without an internet connection.
ps-vita__blazblue-chrono-phantasma.teaser: A stylized 2D fighting game with hand-drawn sprites and animation like an anime series come to life.

ps-vita__dead-or-alive-5-plus.article:
**Dead or Alive 5 Plus** is the portable version of a fighting series that has always been built on fast pacing, counterattacks, and arenas where the environment itself is dangerous. The core of combat is a simple yet surprisingly tactical trio: strike, throw, and counter beat each other like rock, paper, and scissors, so every match is a guessing game about the opponent's intentions. On top of that come multi-level arenas where characters fall through floors, get swept away by explosions, or tumble down a slope, adding theatrical drama to the fights while also changing the game's positioning.

The PlayStation Vita version was prepared with care. Besides the complete content package, including the story mode and fighters from later updates, it brought expanded training options that guide players step by step through building combos and reacting to pressure. Control modes built around the touchscreen were also added, letting attacks be triggered directly with a finger, lowering the entry barrier for complete beginners. The game could be linked with the home version, so progress and matches weren't stuck on just one platform.

Technically the game ranks among the console's better ports: character models are detailed, the pace of combat stays brisk, and the stylized arenas, from temples to factory floors, look striking. Reviews at the time praised mainly the fact that it was a full-fledged fighter without major compromises, while critical comments were aimed at the visual presentation of the characters, something that has long followed the series. Today, Dead or Alive 5 Plus is a good example of an accessible fighter where even a less experienced player can enjoy flashy fights while gradually discovering a deeper tactical layer. The series has had a notable influence on the genre through its counterattack system, which put defense on equal footing with offense, and through interactive arenas that later became a common part of competing games. On a handheld, the model of short matches, where you can put the console to sleep between rounds at any time, works especially well.
ps-vita__dead-or-alive-5-plus.teaser: A fighting game built on a strike-throw-counter triangle; even the arenas themselves are dangerous.

ps-vita__ninja-gaiden-sigma-plus.article:
**Ninja Gaiden Sigma Plus** was among the PlayStation Vita launch titles and brought one of the most demanding action games of its time to the handheld. The player takes on the role of the ninja Ryu Hayabusa, who sets out on a bloody quest for revenge and for a lost demonic sword. The fights are fast, precise, and merciless: enemies attack from every direction, block, catch the player in combos, and even a common foe can kill within a few seconds if the player forgets to dodge and guard. An arsenal ranging from a katana to a scythe and combat staves changes the style of combat, and every weapon has its own set of combos that can be developed through upgrades.

The Vita version is based on an earlier remaster of the game and adds its own new features. It came with an easier difficulty for players who want to see the story without dozens of deaths, a mode focused on quickly blitzing through levels, and controls using touch and tilt for aiming a bow or performing special attacks. The technical side had a cost, however: the game runs at a lower frame rate than the home versions, which is noticeable in such fast action and takes a while to get used to.

Reviews at the time received it as a solid launch title and as proof that Vita could handle even demanding console-style action, but they did criticize its smoothness and an at-times chaotic camera. The Ninja Gaiden series had a major influence on modern action games through how high it set the difficulty bar and how firmly it insisted on precise, defense-oriented combat, a line later followed by other demanding action franchises. Today, Sigma Plus is a challenge for players seeking tough, honest action without compromises. The atmosphere shifts between Japanese mythology, European cathedrals, and underground temples full of demons, while the music moves from quiet tension to fierce drums the moment the arena seals shut and the fight for survival begins. It's exactly this combination of high difficulty, precise controls, and stylish violence that makes this series, for many players, the yardstick by which other action games are measured.
ps-vita__ninja-gaiden-sigma-plus.teaser: A merciless action game starring the ninja Ryu Hayabusa; even an ordinary enemy kills quickly.

ps-vita__god-of-war-collection.article:
**God of War Collection** brought two key chapters of the story of the Spartan warrior Kratos, who rebels against the gods of Olympus in ancient Greece, to PlayStation Vita. Both games are built on a combination of fast combat with chained blades, logic puzzles set within monumental temples, and spectacular battles against giant beings that often fill the entire screen. The combat is accessible yet has depth: the player combines light and heavy attacks, dodges, uses magic abilities granted by the gods, and gradually upgrades their arsenal. Boss fights culminate in sequences where you must press a displayed button or perform a gesture on the touchscreen at just the right moment.

The handheld port kept the essence of both games, including the meticulously directed camera work that leads the player through the environment like a film. The touchscreen took over the role of certain quick actions, and the rear touchpad handles additional gestures, a solution some players took longer to get used to. Technically it's a compromise; reduced resolution and less stable frame rates are noticeable, but the monumental mythological settings and the mighty orchestral score lose none of their power.

Reviews at the time welcomed the collection warmly, mainly because it was an extraordinarily valuable content package on a single card. Criticism was aimed at the technical side and at occasionally awkward use of touch. The God of War series fundamentally shaped the modern action-adventure genre through how it combined brutal action with grand direction, and its early entries rank among the best the genre had to offer at the time. On Vita, it's still a great way to go through the story that later received a very differently conceived sequel. For newcomers, it's also an ideal entry point, since both games maintain an understandable pace and explain their mechanics on the fly. Anyone familiar with the more modern take on the series will be surprised how different Kratos appears here: wrathful, uncompromising, and driven by revenge, without a trace of the reconciliation that came much later.
ps-vita__god-of-war-collection.teaser: Two key chapters of Kratos's revenge against the gods of Olympus in one package.

ps-vita__super-stardust-delta.article:
**Super Stardust Delta** was one of the first games to show on PlayStation Vita that arcade action loses nothing coming from a handheld. The player controls a small ship orbiting a round planet and must defend it from an avalanche of asteroids and enemy vessels that accelerate and multiply with every wave. The key to survival lies in choosing the right weapon: rocky asteroids need to be shattered with one type of fire, icy ones melted with another, and metallic ones torn apart with a third, so the player is constantly switching modes depending on what's flying at them at that moment. The result is a game that looks simple but demands total concentration and the ability to read the chaos on screen.

The Vita version made use of the console's capabilities beyond the usual dual-stick control. Touch can release a shockwave that blasts everything nearby away, and tilting the console controls some of the bonus modes, a solution some players embraced enthusiastically and others preferred to turn off. Besides the main arcade mode, the game offers time-limited challenges and survive-as-long-as-possible modes, plus leaderboards that turn every attempt into a contest against your friends' results.

Visually it's a fireworks show: planet surfaces are detailed, explosions flood the screen with light, and on the Vita's high-contrast display it looks especially striking, backed by rhythmic electronic music. Reviews received the title very well as one of the best launch titles, with the caveat that the tilt-controlled modes aren't always pleasant. Today it remains a perfect example of a game you switch on for ten minutes and don't put down until an hour later. Housemarque has long kept the tradition of arcade shooters alive with this series at a time when major publishers tended to avoid them, and Super Stardust Delta is one of its most finely tuned entries. It also shows nicely why the genre thrives especially on portable devices: you grasp the rules within a few seconds, but mastering every last detail takes months.
ps-vita__super-stardust-delta.teaser: Arcade defense of a planet against waves of asteroids; the weapon has to match the type of fragment.

ps-vita__hotline-miami.article:
**Hotline Miami** is a brutal top-down action game that casts the player as a nameless man in Miami in 1989, who, following cryptic messages left on an answering machine, sets out in a mask to clear out one house after another. Each level is a small tactical playground: you kill enemies in a single hit, but you're just as fragile, so getting through means dozens of quick deaths and instant restarts. Success rests on planning and improvisation at once, since one wrong step is enough to collapse a carefully prepared approach. Animal masks worn before each mission change the rules of the game, letting you kill with your bare fists, move faster, or altering enemy behavior.

The PlayStation Vita port turned out excellent, since quick restarts and short levels are practically made for playing in bursts. Dual-stick controls are precise, the touchscreen is used for quick switching, and the game runs smoothly. But its strongest weapon is the atmosphere: pixel art in toxic neon colors, pulsing synthwave music, and a narrative that, through hallucinatory interludes, keeps asking why the player is killing so much in the first place, together creating something between a fever and a dream.

At the time it received major attention and became one of the most influential independent titles of its era. It influenced an entire wave of fast, brutal action games built around instant restarts, and its soundtrack proved just how powerfully music can define a game's identity. Today Hotline Miami still feels fresh, since neither its pace nor its aesthetic have aged, and on a handheld it's one of the best ways to play it. Because of its extreme brutality and dark tone, though, it's certainly not a game for everyone. It's also one of the rare cases where violence isn't just spectacle: the game repeatedly forces the player to walk back through empty rooms full of bodies, leaving it up to them to answer what they're actually doing. A points score at the end of every level also rewards risky, fast, uninterrupted runs, quietly pushing the player toward an even more aggressive style.
ps-vita__hotline-miami.teaser: A brutal top-down action game; one hit kills, and the restart comes instantly.

ps-vita__need-for-speed-most-wanted.article:
**Need for Speed: Most Wanted** on PlayStation Vita is one of the most ambitious attempts to squeeze an open world full of fast cars into your pocket. The game is built on the same foundation as the home console versions, namely the city of Fairhaven, which you drive around freely, without any menus or loading screens between events. Cars aren't bought but found parked on the streets, and as soon as the player gets in one, it's immediately theirs. The goal is to earn points in sprints, circuits, and speed trials, smash through billboards, hunt down hidden shortcuts, and finally take on a top ten of most-wanted drivers whose cars need to be taken out of commission for good.

The heart of the experience remains the police chases. Just drive past a radar too fast, and a long game of cat and mouse begins, with police setting up roadblocks, using spike strips, and trying to push the player into a wall. The driving model is arcade-style, with long drifts and aggressive collisions accentuated by impressive slow-motion camera work. Porting it to the handheld demanded compromises in environmental detail and traffic density, yet it's still an impressive technical feat, helped by a beautifully lit nighttime Fairhaven. The soundtrack leans on rock and electronic tracks that match the nervous pace of the chases. Every car has its own set of upgrades unlocked by repeatedly driving specific events, so the game gradually opens up mechanically as well, without forcing the player into side collecting or menu purchases.

Reviewers praised the Vita version especially for not being a stripped-down spin-off but a genuinely equivalent game adapted to a smaller machine. Criticism focused mainly on smoothness in the busiest sections and on the fact that the campaign has no classic narrative, relying purely on the freedom of exploration. Today, Most Wanted on Vita is an example of how far this console could be pushed, and at the same time a pleasant game for short bursts, since a single event can be driven in a few minutes before closing the console again right away.
ps-vita__need-for-speed-most-wanted.teaser: The open world of Fairhaven with no loading, brought to your pocket without losing scope.

ps-vita__ridge-racer.article:
**Ridge Racer** accompanied the launch of PlayStation Vita the same way it accompanied the launch of practically every previous Sony console, bringing along everything players associate with the series. The driving model is built on drifting, triggered not through delicate balance but a sharp yank of the wheel with the throttle held to the floor. The reward for long drifts is nitro, and managing it well decides whether a race ends in victory. Anyone who grasps the rhythm at which a car dives into a corner and shoots back out of it gets one of the purest arcade racers ever made.

Technically the Vita version is well executed, running smoothly, holding a stable image, and the tracks keep the series' characteristic look, with highway overpasses, tunnels, and coastal vistas. The controls suit a handheld very well, since drifting gets by with just a few buttons and doesn't demand delicate throttle work. The music is the traditional mix of house, drum and bass, and dance electronica, exactly what belongs to this series' driving experience as inseparably as the announcer's voice counting down the start. The game is also rounded out with an unusual feature where the player picks a team and contributes to its colors in an overall competition against other players through races completed, meant to give an otherwise solitary drive a sense of belonging to a wider community.

Reception, however, was noticeably marred by an unusually small amount of content at launch. The game offered only a handful of tracks and cars, with more added via downloadable packs, which sparked strong criticism at the time, even though some of the content was later released for free. Reviews mostly agreed that the core gameplay itself is excellent, but that the path to it was strangely stingy. Today, with the game available together with its later additions, it can be viewed more forgivingly, offering exactly what you want from a handheld console: short, fast, and instantly satisfying races without unnecessary preamble.
ps-vita__ridge-racer.teaser: Sony's launch classic; drifting pulled off with a sharp wrench of the wheel and nitro floored.

ps-vita__motorstorm-rc.article:
**MotorStorm RC** took the wild off-road racing series and shrank it down to remote-controlled models racing on tracks viewed from above. The change in perspective looks like a minor gimmick at first, but it fundamentally changes the nature of the game. Instead of a tense scramble through a pack of rivals, the player focuses on driving the perfect line, hunting for the ideal racing line, and shaving off a tenth of a second in every corner. Individual races usually last only around a minute, so the game can be turned on and off literally while waiting for a bus.

The structure is built on sets of challenges divided by environment and vehicle type, from buggies through pickups to monster trucks, with each one handling differently on the surface. Completing objectives unlocks further events, and the main driving force is the leaderboards, which instantly show the times of friends and players from around the world. This quiet battle over tenths of a second is what makes the game most addictive, because the difference of one badly taken corner is visible immediately. The environments stay true to the series' roots — dusty canyons, snowy slopes, and muddy coastlines — just at a miniature scale. The top-down view also reveals the whole course at once, so the player sees ahead, and a mistake can only be blamed on their own impatience, not an unexpected turn beyond the horizon.

The game launched as an inexpensive digital title and offered a purchase valid for both PlayStation 3 and Vita at once, including shared progress, which felt like a generous move at the time. Critics praised the precise controls, clean look, and fair price, with reservations mainly aimed at the experience being rather compact and repetitive. Today, MotorStorm RC is a pleasant reminder of how well Evolution Studios understood the feel of driving, and it remains one of the best Vita games for short moments between other activities.
ps-vita__motorstorm-rc.teaser: The wild off-road series shrunk down to RC models, viewed from above for a perfect line.

ps-vita__f1-2011.article:
**F1 2011** was the first attempt to bring a full-fledged Formula 1 simulator to a handheld console, complete with all the licensed drivers, teams, and circuits of that season's championship on PlayStation Vita. The game offered a complete career across the championship, practice sessions, qualifying, and races with adjustable length, so everyone could choose whether they wanted a sprint of a few laps or a proper full race weekend. It also included the rules of the time, namely the movable rear wing for overtaking and a temporary power boost system, which required thinking about when to let a rival get closer and when to strike instead.

The driving model is adjustable across a wide range, from heavy assists that make the game feel like a brisk arcade racer, to a no-assist mode where you must respect braking points and tire temperature. Tire management and pit stop strategy form the core of the longer races, since rain can turn the running order upside down. Technically, the game was an impressive showcase at the console's launch, the circuits are well recognizable, and the interface stays readable even on the smaller screen, though with some concessions in trackside detail. The career mode also includes a bit of rivalry within the team, since the game tracks how the player performs against their own teammate, and better results open the door to offers from stronger outfits, which gives meaning to individual race weekends even when you're not fighting for the front of the pack.

Contemporary reception was mildly positive. Reviewers particularly praised the fact that this was a genuinely substantial game rather than a simplified spin-off, and praised the ability to drive a whole season anywhere. Criticism was aimed at the controls on the small sticks, which demand a finesse the handheld's hardware only offers to a limited degree, and at occasionally uneven frame rate. Today, F1 2011 is interesting mainly as a period document of a season that can be relived, and as proof that the Vita could handle genres you wouldn't expect from a handheld console.
ps-vita__f1-2011.teaser: The first full-fledged Formula 1 simulator with licensed teams on a handheld.

ps-vita__motogp-13.article:
**MotoGP 13** brought an officially licensed motorcycle championship to PlayStation Vita, including the lower classes, so a player could start in a junior category and gradually work their way up to the premier class elite. The career mode is built on the classic path from offers from smaller teams to a seat with the front-running outfits, with bike setup tuned and team objectives fulfilled between races. Besides the championship, there's also a quick race, time trials, and bonus challenges that emphasize precise riding more than wheel-to-wheel duels.

Riding a motorcycle is more sensitive than in car games, since it involves leaning, weight transfer, and the risk that opening the throttle too aggressively coming out of a corner will send bike and rider alike into the gravel. The game offers several levels of assists, letting complete beginners manage the first laps, while more experienced players can turn off braking and stability aids and ride in an almost simulation-like fashion. Visually, the handheld version is somewhat more modest than on the big consoles, but the circuits are faithful, the riders recognizable, and the sense of speed close to the ground is convincing. The engine sound is among the best things the game offers, since the difference between the classes is audible immediately. It also helps that you can rewind a few seconds after a crash, so a failed attempt doesn't ruin the whole race, and the player can push the limits of risk without having to start over from the grid.

Reviews were mostly favorable, noting that this was a solid, honestly made effort that doesn't pretend to be more than it is. Reservations concerned the repetitive career structure and the fact that the game doesn't offer much beyond the track. Still, for fans of road racing motorcycles, MotoGP 13 on Vita remains one of the few ways to play this sport in a handheld format, and that's where its value lies.
ps-vita__motogp-13.teaser: A licensed motorcycle championship from the junior class all the way to the premier class.

ps-vita__modnation-racers-road-trip.article:
**ModNation Racers: Road Trip** accompanied the launch of PlayStation Vita and tried to bring the series' full concept to a handheld console: kart racing combined with extensive tools for creating your own content. Besides the racing itself, the game offers an editor where you can assemble your driver character, paint and rebuild your vehicle, and above all model your own track. The track is drawn directly with your finger on the touchscreen, the terrain rises and falls with a drag, and the game itself fills in guardrails, spectators, and surrounding scenery, so a rough sketch becomes a usable circuit within moments.

The races themselves are arcade-style, with drifting that charges up energy and a set of items ranging from rockets to shields. An interesting element is that accumulated energy can be spent either on attack, or on defense and a speed boost, so the player is constantly choosing between aggression and safety. Finished tracks can be shared with others and other players' creations downloaded, which was the main draw at the time of release. Visually, the game relies on a colorful cartoon style with bold outlines that shows off very well on the console's screen, and the music keeps a light, friendly mood. Character creation goes into surprising detail, since besides the face and clothing you can also change small things like helmet accessories, and the finished character can then be seen in other players' races.

Reception was mixed. The editor and its inventiveness earned praise, but criticism targeted long loading times, inconsistent frame rate, and rival AI that could be unpleasantly stubborn. Still, Road Trip remains an interesting title, since it shows how early a game built around content creation and sharing appeared on a handheld console. Today it's judged mainly on how well the editor itself works, and it remains surprisingly pleasant to use even after all these years. For Vita owners, Road Trip remains a fond memory of a time when people were still figuring out everything a touchscreen could do on a new console.
ps-vita__modnation-racers-road-trip.teaser: Kart racing combined with a track editor drawn by finger on the display.

ps-vita__fifa-13.article:
**FIFA 13** was the most complete form of football PlayStation Vita ever offered, and for a long time it also remained the last one, since subsequent entries never made it to this platform in the same way. The game brought licensed competitions, clubs, and players, along with the usual set of modes led by manager career, quick matches, tournaments, and building your own team from collected cards. That collecting mode proved to be the most enduring, since it offers virtually endless motivation to improve your squad and look for chemistry between players of different leagues and nationalities.

The controls mirror the conventions of the big-console versions — short and long passes, crosses and shots split across buttons — while the console also added touch-based extras. You could send the ball to a specific spot by dragging a finger across the rear touch pad, and quick instructions could be entered on the front screen, an interesting though not essential option for everyone. The pace of the game is somewhat slower than on the big consoles and the opponent's defense less consistent, which keeps matches flowing briskly and makes it well suited for short sessions. Commentary, crowd voices, and club chants convey the stadium atmosphere surprisingly well. It's also worth noting that the game offers several levels of passing and aiming assistance, so it suits both someone who hasn't played a football game in years and a player used to fully manual controls.

Contemporary reviews rated the game as a decent but not particularly bold step forward from the previous year, noting that its main value lies in the amount of content and in the ability to have a complete football game in your pocket. Today the situation is different, the online features no longer run the way they used to, and the squads are long out of date. Still, FIFA 13 on Vita remains a good foundation for a quick match, and for fans of the console it's an obvious choice when they want to kick a ball around.
ps-vita__fifa-13.teaser: The last full-fledged football entry on the Vita, with career mode and team card collecting.

ps-vita__virtua-tennis-4-world-tour-edit.article:
**Virtua Tennis 4: World Tour Edition** arrived on PlayStation Vita within the console's first days on the market and presented players with tennis in a form that's easy to understand while still offering plenty of room for improvement. The foundation is arcade-style — the player mainly handles the timing of the shot and its direction, while movement around the court is largely handled by the game itself. Still, winning requires understanding when to play long shots into the corners, when to shorten the point at the net, and how to gradually pull the opponent out of position, since points are earned through patiently building a rally.

The main content is a world tour, in which you travel across a map, plan your tournament calendar, top up your stamina, and complete inventive minigames between matches. Those minigames are among the series' traditional highlights and make use of the console's capabilities, since they involve collecting items, hitting balls at targets, or solving situations that demand quick decisions. Visually, the game looks clean and clear, player animations are smooth, and the distinct styles of individual tennis players give matches character. The sound relies on ball impacts, squeaking shoes, and understated crowd applause, which is enough to carry the atmosphere. Matches can be played in both singles and doubles, where suddenly positioning and teamwork with a partner matter more than raw power, and doubles tends to be the most enjoyable option for playing with another person.

Reviews welcomed the Vita version favorably as a well-executed port of a game already proven on the big consoles, with the reservation that it doesn't bring anything fundamentally new. What was praised, on the other hand, was the ability to play a quick set practically anywhere, and the presence of licensed players of the era. Today, Virtua Tennis 4 on Vita comes across as one of the best-aging sports titles on the platform, since its playability doesn't depend on how up to date the rosters are. A match lasts exactly as long as the player sets it to, and that's a quality anyone who plays in bits and pieces on the way home from work will appreciate on a handheld console.
ps-vita__virtua-tennis-4-world-tour-edit.teaser: Arcade tennis where the player mainly manages timing and shot direction, while the game handles movement.

ps-vita__hot-shots-golf-world-invitation.article:
**Hot Shots Golf: World Invitational**, released in Europe under the name Everybody's Golf, was one of the titles that accompanied PlayStation Vita from the very start, and it quickly proved to be one of the best games in its entire library. Golf here is presented in a colorful, slightly cartoonish style with caricatured characters, but beneath the friendly surface lies a surprisingly deep game. The shot is set using the classic three-stage meter, where power and the accuracy of the ball strike are chosen separately, so there's still room for improvement even after hundreds of shots.

The player progresses through a series of tournaments, earns new clubs, outfits, and other characters, and learns to read the course, since wind, green slope, and the surface the ball lies on change the outcome significantly. Reading the break on the green, where you estimate the ball's path across uneven ground, is among the game's most tense moments. The courses are varied, from open coastal layouts to wooded, mountainous ones, and each demands different tactics. Visually, the game looks very clean and smooth, the music is cheerfully light, and the overall pace fits the handheld console perfectly, since a single round can be paused at any time. The characters also develop, gaining experience and changing their attributes, so the player gradually forms an attachment to one particular golfer and to the set of clubs that suits them best.

Critics received the game excellently and repeatedly noted that it was the ideal title for travel, one that could entertain for dozens of hours. The ability to measure yourself against other players through recorded results was also praised. Today, World Invitational is a classic for Vita owners, one they return to after years, because its charm lies in constant small improvement and in a relaxed mood that similar sports titles rarely offer today. It's also one of the few games where it doesn't matter that the player has no idea about golf, since everything essential is learned naturally during the first few tournaments.
ps-vita__hot-shots-golf-world-invitation.teaser: Cartoon golf with a three-stage swing; surprising depth beneath the cheerful surface.

ps-vita__persona-4-dancing-all-night.article:
**Persona 4: Dancing All Night** took the beloved cast from Persona 4 and placed them in the middle of a rhythm game where dance wards off a supernatural threat. It sounds like an odd idea, but it works surprisingly well, since the series has always been strongly tied to music, and the dance concept suits it more naturally than it might seem. The game has a full story mode told as an extensive visual novel, in which the characters get tangled up in a mystery connected to a popular idol group and a mysterious internet video, with individual dance battles playing out between the dialogue scenes.

The gameplay itself is unusual and cleverly makes use of the controller's layout. Markers fly out from the center of the screen toward its edges, where they're hit using the directional buttons on the left side and the face buttons on the right, with longer notes held down and, at certain moments, the stick also used to boost the score. Anyone who manages to keep their accuracy triggers a battle tempo increase, and another dancer appears on stage. The visuals retain the series' typical black-and-yellow stylization with sharp outlines, and the music is its biggest draw, since these are carefully crafted dance remixes of well-known tracks from the original game. Outside the story, there's a free mode where you can pick any song, dancer, and costume and just chase a better score.

Reception was favorable, especially among fans of the series, who appreciated that the story portion wasn't just a weak excuse for rhythm tracks but a genuine continuation of the characters' fates. Criticism mainly targeted the story being long-winded and hard for newcomers to follow. Today the game is considered one of the best rhythm games on Vita, and also a lovely gift for anyone who fell in love with the original Persona 4. Those with no attachment to the series can skip the story and focus purely on the music, since the individual tracks work on their own and quickly draw players in even without knowing the backstory. It's precisely this dual nature that makes it a title worth returning to even years later.
ps-vita__persona-4-dancing-all-night.teaser: The characters from Persona 4 dance against the supernatural; rhythm gameplay delivered as a visual novel.

ps-vita__hatsune-miku-project-diva-f.article:
**Hatsune Miku: Project DIVA f** brought to PlayStation Vita a rhythm game built around virtual singers whose voices are generated through voice synthesis and whose songs are created by a community of authors. The gameplay foundation is simple: symbols move across the screen and must be confirmed with the matching button exactly when they reach their mark. Higher difficulties add rapid sequences, combinations of several buttons at once, and long held notes, so what starts as a pleasant, relaxing game quickly becomes a genuine test of concentration and peripheral vision.

A peculiarity of the Vita version is its use of the touchscreen for special notes, which are collected with a finger swipe and rewarded with bonus points. Good results unlock further songs, costumes, and accessories, and the game also offers an extensive mode in which the player builds their own music video, setting up the camera, environment, and character movements. A fully animated performance runs in the background of every song, and it's precisely the combination of music with carefully edited visuals that turns playing into a small show. The songs cover a wide spectrum, from upbeat pop to calmer, more melancholic pieces, so the selection is more varied than one might expect. Each song comes with its own scene and costume, and many of them originated as community creations, so the game also functions as a showcase of everything that has grown up around the virtual singers.

The game was released first in Japan and only later reached a Western audience, where critics received it very warmly as one of the best rhythm games on the console. The precision of the controls, the amount of content, and the clean visuals were praised. Reservations concerned mainly the steep difficulty jump and the fact that it's a title best enjoyed by people with an attachment to this particular musical scene. Today, Project DIVA f is one of the reasons players associate the Vita with the Japanese gaming scene.
ps-vita__hatsune-miku-project-diva-f.teaser: A rhythm game with virtual Vocaloid singers; the melodies are created through voice synthesis.

ps-vita__djmax-technika-tune.article:
**DJMAX Technika Tune** is a rhythm game built primarily around touch controls, which makes it one of the most distinctive titles in the entire PlayStation Vita library. Instead of buttons, you play with your fingers directly on the screen, across which a vertical line moves from left to right, and the player must hit the markers exactly as the line passes them. Alongside simple taps there are sideways swipes, held notes, and combinations requiring both hands at once, so at higher difficulties, playing looks from the outside like rapid work on a musical instrument.

The game draws on an arcade-machine series that was very popular in Asia, and carries over its music library made up of electronic dance music, drum and bass, pop, and calmer songs. Stylized videos play in the background, and the interface relies on bold colors and clean shapes, keeping the screen readable even during the densest passages. As you progress, further songs and difficulties unlock, and the game also offers a mode played with classic buttons, which those who don't take to the touch variant will appreciate. It also lets you build your own playlists and compare results with other players. Each song's score tracks both the accuracy of individual touches and the length of an unbroken combo, so achieving a top result requires not just finishing the song, but playing it without a single slip.

Reviews received the game favorably as a well-made and unusually bold attempt to use the touchscreen for something more than a mere add-on. Reservations concerned the fact that the screen's glass quickly picks up fingerprints and that touch accuracy is stretched to its limits in the toughest songs. Still, it's a title that simply couldn't exist in the same form on another platform, and that's exactly why it remains popular among Vita owners to this day. Anyone looking for a reason to pull out the console and spend half an hour in full concentration will find one here immediately.
ps-vita__djmax-technika-tune.teaser: A rhythm game controlled purely by touch on the display; a distinctive piece of the Vita's library.

ps-vita__super-monkey-ball-banana-splitz.article:
**Super Monkey Ball: Banana Splitz** brought to PlayStation Vita the series' simple yet incredibly addictive idea: a monkey enclosed in a transparent ball doesn't move on its own — instead, the player tilts the whole world beneath it, and gravity does the rest. The goal of each level is to reach the finish before time runs out, without falling off narrow walkways, rotating platforms, and moving bridges suspended over empty space.
