There are also plenty of collectibles, from bottles that unlock each episode's vault to masks, so anyone wanting to see everything will spend considerably more time in the game.
ps-vita__sly-cooper-thieves-in-time.teaser: The master thief travels through time to save the family book of tricks; released simultaneously with the PS3 version.

ps-vita__assassin-s-creed-iii-liberation.article:
**Assassin's Creed III: Liberation** was, in 2012, the main argument for why a PlayStation Vita owner should pick up a big licensed action-adventure game. The game runs parallel to the series' third entry, but instead of colonial New England, it takes place in 18th-century New Orleans, its surrounding swamps, and Mayan ruins. The lead character is Aveline de Grandpré, daughter of a French merchant and an African mother — an unusual perspective for the series, one the game manages to use not just in the story but directly in the gameplay.

The key mechanic is a set of three personas. In a lady's dress, Aveline doesn't arouse suspicion and can bribe people, but she can't climb; disguised as a slave, she blends in among laborers and moves unnoticed; in her assassin outfit she has full freedom of movement and her whole arsenal, but she instantly draws the guards' attention. The rest is classic Assassin's Creed of the era — rooftop parkour, combat counterattacks, silent kills from above, and an open city full of side quests, including a trading network and sending shipments by boat. The persona system comes with a suspicion meter that behaves differently for each disguise, so the player has to think not only about where to go but also how to look while doing it.

Technically, it was an impressive feat: on Vita, New Orleans has a dense crowd, a day-night cycle, and vegetation that wasn't common on a handheld at the time, though at the cost of minor hiccups and a shorter draw distance. Touch controls are used more out of obligation, for rowing or opening letters. Besides the city, the game also plays out in the open swamps of Louisiana, where the player moves along branches and treetops much like in the third game's colonial wilderness. The atmosphere is helped by music with Creole motifs and the sultry, damp swamp setting. Contemporary reviews praised the scope and the lead character while criticizing the simplified and poorly told story. Aveline later got a remaster for home consoles, but the original version remains a showcase of just how far portable gaming could be pushed at the time.
ps-vita__assassin-s-creed-iii-liberation.teaser: A major adventure tailored for the Vita; the heroine is Aveline de Grandpré, an exception in the series.

ps-vita__metal-gear-solid-hd-collection.article:
**Metal Gear Solid HD Collection** brought two of its era's most ambitious action-adventure games — Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty and Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater — to PlayStation Vita in reworked resolution and with all their bonus missions intact. For console owners, this meant getting games in their pocket that previously required a television and hours-long blocks of time, without losing anything essential. It was thus one of the most generous packages ever released on this platform. Both games also include extensive bonus and virtual missions, which push the total content into the dozens of hours.

Both games are built around stealth: the player skirts around guards, watches their fields of view and the sound of their own footsteps, and uses boxes, disguises, and a tranquilizer pistol, with direct combat generally being an admission of failure. The third game adds jungle terrain, camouflage matched to the environment, treating wounds, and managing your own food supply, making it one of the series' most detailed entries. The Vita lacked analog triggers and a second pair of shoulder buttons, so Armature Studio's port shifted part of the controls to the touch panels — aiming and certain actions are handled with your fingers, and it takes a while to get used to. The third game is also one of the few where a boss fight plays out as a long, silent wait in the grass, and on a small screen that feels surprisingly intimate.

Technically, the collection was one of the better ports on the console: the image is sharp, performance is mostly stable, and save transfers between Vita and PlayStation 3 worked. The audio remains extraordinary — cinematic orchestral themes, long codec conversations, and silence that works better during stealth than any music could. Contemporary reviews recommended the collection as one of the best reasons to own a Vita, with reservations about the controls. Today it's the most convenient way to play through Snake Eater on the go, a game that fundamentally shaped the entire stealth genre.
ps-vita__metal-gear-solid-hd-collection.teaser: Two ambitious Metal Gear Solid games in reworked resolution, squeezed into your pocket.

ps-vita__ninja-gaiden-sigma-2-plus.article:
**Ninja Gaiden Sigma 2 Plus** is a portable version of one of its generation's toughest action games, and on PlayStation Vita it kept everything that made the original an uncompromising experience. Ryu Hayabusa once again sets out against a demonic conspiracy, this time backed by several playable companions, and from the first minutes the game demands that the player learn its precise combat rhythm. This isn't a game you can button-mash your way through; every fight requires focus and a good knowledge of your own equipment. The series has a reputation as one of the genre's most demanding, and this version doesn't let up on that at all.

The combat system ranks among the most elaborate in the genre. Each of Ryu's weapons has its own strings of attacks, blocking, dodging, and counterattacks are essential, and once an enemy loses an arm or a leg, its behavior instantly changes — maimed opponents throw themselves into suicidal attacks. Battles pit the player against large numbers of enemies at once, mistakes are punished mercilessly, and the difficulty is high even on the base setting. The port added an easier mode for newcomers, reworked enemy placement, and missions that let you play as characters outside the main storyline. Alongside Ryu, you also get to play as Ayane, Rachel, and Momiji, each with her own arsenal and pace, which expands the game with several standalone segments.

Technically, this involved trade-offs: resolution and the number of enemies on screen had to be scaled back, and smoothness isn't always ideal — noticeable in a game built around reflexes. Still, the sense of power remains — the animation, weapon sounds, and movement speed are still exceptional, and the drum-and-orchestra soundtrack keeps pushing the pace forward. Contemporary reviews treated it as a decent but technically compromised port of a big action game; genre fans forgave it, since nothing else that demanding existed on the console. Besides the main storyline, there are also single-player challenge missions that make the whole package feel more like an arcade trainer than an adventure. Today it's mainly of interest to players who want portable action that forgives not a single mistake.
ps-vita__ninja-gaiden-sigma-2-plus.teaser: Ryu Hayabusa's uncompromising action in portable form; the game demands absolutely precise combat rhythm.

ps-vita__atelier-rorona-plus-alchemist-o.article:
**Atelier Rorona Plus: The Alchemist of Arland** brought the first entry in Gust's Arland trilogy to PlayStation Vita in a reworked form with new graphics and improved systems. The titular Rorona inherits an alchemy workshop from her teacher, only for the kingdom to immediately hand her an ultimatum: if she doesn't complete a series of assigned commissions within three years, the workshop will be shut down. So instead of saving the world, you handle fairly ordinary concerns — supplying the town with medicine, baking a cake for the queen, gathering materials, and trying not to go broke in the process.

The game is built on three interlinked activities. You gather materials at surrounding locations, synthesize items from them following recipes where the quality and properties of the ingredients genuinely matter, and all the while keep an eye on the calendar, since every action consumes days. Battles are turn-based and mainly serve as a way to get better materials. You recruit townsfolk into your party, and their goodwill grows depending on how you treat them and how much time you spend with them. There are several endings, and they hinge precisely on these relationships and on how well you handled your commissions. The workshop itself offers plenty of small optimizations, since a higher-quality intermediate product feeds into the final item's properties, and an experienced player can squeeze far more out of the same raw materials.

The Plus version added new characters, difficulty levels, costumes, and the option to keep playing after finishing the main story, and above all it adjusted the pacing, which felt rushed in the original release. The visuals are pastel, relaxed, and pleasantly unconfrontational, while the music leans on light acoustic and jazz motifs that make Atelier one of the most soothing series in the genre. Critics praised the depth of the alchemy system and the charming atmosphere, with reservations aimed at the time limit, which won't suit everyone. On Vita, it's a model game for evening play sessions when you don't want tension, just a well-designed system you can keep optimizing endlessly.
ps-vita__atelier-rorona-plus-alchemist-o.teaser: The alchemist Rorona handles ordinary commissions instead of saving the world; the first part of Gust's trilogy.

ps-vita__borderlands-2.article:
**Borderlands 2** ranks among the most ambitious ports ever to appear on PlayStation Vita, since it squeezed a full, sprawling shooter with dozens of hours of content and endless weapon generation into your pocket. The game takes place on the harsh planet Pandora, where four mercenary vault hunters fight against the corporate tyrant Handsome Jack, whose caustic commentary accompanies the whole journey. Its foundation blends shooter and RPG: characters level up, develop skill trees, and above all collect weapons that the game randomly assembles from different parts, so every chest might hide something slightly different. On top of that comes a comic-book art style with bold outlines that stays clear and colorful even on a smaller display.

The move to a handheld required compromises. The frame rate is lower than on home consoles, detail density in the open plains dropped, and co-op was limited to two players instead of four, turning the chaotic shared firefights into a more intimate experience. On the other hand, the release included the extra characters and part of the expansions, so the sheer volume of content remained staggering, and the touchscreen took over the map, inventory, and quick weapon swapping, which made managing the enormous collection much easier.

Contemporary reviews were split: critics praised the sheer nerve of bringing a game this big to a portable console, and the fact that the fun loop of collecting and shooting still worked here, but the technical side was frequently criticized. With hindsight, the Vita version is interesting mainly as proof that the looter shooter is a genre practically made for playing in short bursts: a few missions in the evening, an interesting new weapon part, and the urge to come back tomorrow. Anyone unfamiliar with Pandora gets one of the most wittily written shooters of its time, along with a distinctive soundscape full of one-liners and a desert guitar atmosphere. It was precisely that humor and stylization that set the series apart from the competition and helped define the whole loot-shooter genre that many later games built on.
ps-vita__borderlands-2.teaser: A vast looter shooter squeezed into your pocket without losing its weapon generation.

ps-vita__legend-of-heroes-trails-of-cold.article:
**The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel II** picks up exactly where the first game left off, at the moment the Erebonian Empire is torn apart by civil war and Class VII is scattered across the country. Rean Schwarzer wakes up alone in the mountains, and his first task isn't to save the world but to find his former classmates, convince them to reunite, and only then try to intervene in a conflict far larger than himself. As a result, the game naturally combines the collect-the-party structure of its opening chapters with a map that gradually opens up. As allies and modes of transport are added, the whole territory becomes accessible, along with a wealth of side quests through which Falcom, as always, builds a sense of a lived-in world.

The combat system remains turn-based with a strong tactical layer. Positioning on the battlefield determines who gets caught by area attacks, a turn-order gauge reveals upcoming bonuses worth fighting for, and a linked-partner system lets you chain finishers as well as shield allies from lethal blows. Orbments can be tuned into very specific roles, so even routine skirmishes leave room for optimization. The second game also adds several entirely new modes, including battles in mechanical armor that serve as flashy climaxes to key chapters. Technically, it's solid work on Vita: the game runs smoothly and keeps a legible interface even on a small screen.

The soundtrack from Falcom's in-house sound team ranks among the strongest the series has offered, blending rock themes for battles with calmer melodies for traveling, and handling callbacks to the previous game with sensitivity. Reviewers praised the narrative cohesion and the way the game rewards familiarity with earlier stories, while noting a slower start and a heavy amount of text. Today, Trails of Cold Steel II is among the titles worth hunting down a Vita for: the portable format suits a long conversational chronicle, and the game proved that a sprawling story about politics and school friendships doesn't get lost on a handheld console.
ps-vita__legend-of-heroes-trails-of-cold.teaser: A direct sequel to the first game; Rean gathers the scattered Class VII after the civil war.

ps-vita__disgaea-3-absence-of-detention.article:
**Disgaea 3: Absence of Detention** brought one of the most distinctive tactical series ever made to Vita, right in the console's first few months of life. The story takes place at a demonic academy, where the model student is the one who consistently skips class and breaks the rules. Thanks to this, the protagonist Mao is the top of his class, and he decides to become a hero in order to defeat his own father, the ruler of the underworld. A cast full of parodic figures gradually gathers around him, from an overenthusiastic human hero to a girl who stubbornly insists she's an angel. The script pokes fun at Japanese RPG and school-story clichés throughout, keeping a light tone, even though a surprisingly sensitive plot about parents and expectations hides beneath it.

The gameplay is built on grid-based turn-based battles, to which the series has added quite a few inventions of its own. Colored panels change the rules of battle, since they multiply damage, heal enemies, or ban magic, and chain-destroying them can flip the course of a fight in a single turn. Characters can be picked up and thrown across half the map, stacked into towers, and attack together, turning every turn into a small logic puzzle. On top of all that sits the series' famed depth of progression: levels that reach far beyond the usual limits, item enhancement done from the inside in separate procedurally generated dungeons, and damage numbers that balloon to utterly absurd proportions.

The Vita version includes content that was sold separately on the earlier console, so it offers a broad roster of characters, including guests from previous entries. The handheld's sharp display suits the colorful 2D portraits and spell animations well, and the ability to put the game to sleep at any moment fits perfectly with a play style where you fight one battle and set it aside. Contemporary reviews praised the content's generosity and its wit, with criticism aimed at repetitive environments and the fact that the true depth only opens up after finishing the main storyline. That's precisely why Disgaea 3 still works today as a demonstration of just how endless a tactical RPG can be.
ps-vita__disgaea-3-absence-of-detention.teaser: A tactical RPG set at a demon academy, where the model student is the one who breaks the rules.

ps-vita__tales-of-hearts-r.article:
**Tales of Hearts R** is a remake of a Japanese game from the previous generation's handheld console, and for Western players it marked the very first chance to play this entry in the Tales series. It tells the story of a young man named Kor Meteor, who tries to save a girl named Kohaku from an attack and accidentally shatters her soul into a multitude of fragments in the process. The rest of the adventure is about searching for these shards, and with them the emotions the girl lost. The game's world rests on the idea that the human soul is a tangible substance that can be wounded, healed, and even wielded as a weapon, and the script uses this metaphor to tell a story about how easily people shut themselves off from their own feelings.

Battles take place in real time on a two-dimensional plane, across which characters move freely, chaining basic strikes with special techniques and being able to launch enemies into the air to continue combos mid-jump. It's precisely these aerial fights that give the entry its own identity, since a correctly timed transition from ground to air unlocks longer attack strings and flashier finishers. Each character has their own skill tree and an extensive weapon upgrade system, so the party can be customized fairly freely. The remake replaced the original two-dimensional graphics with three-dimensional models, added new characters, and expanded the script with segments missing from the original release.

On the Vita the game runs smoothly and the colorful, cartoonish art style shines on the screen, even though it's clearly a remake of an older title. The Western release shipped with Japanese voice acting only and without some of the extras, which disappointed part of the audience at the time, but otherwise reviews praised the brisk action and the likable cast of characters, while criticism was aimed more at the conventional story structure and repetitive environments. Today, Tales of Hearts R is interesting mainly as evidence of how the Tales series gradually refined its action combat system, and as one of the few entries in the brand that made it to the Vita in a Western release at all.
ps-vita__tales-of-hearts-r.teaser: A remake of an older handheld game; the first chance for Western players to experience this Tales entry.

ps-vita__world-of-final-fantasy.article:
**World of Final Fantasy** is a celebration of the entire Final Fantasy brand, retold in the charming language of a monster-catching game. Siblings Lann and Reynn wake up in a world called Grymoire, having lost their memories, and discover they have the ability to tame local creatures called Mirages. Grymoire is stitched together from environments and characters players know from individual entries in the series, so during the journey they'll encounter heroes spanning decades of history. The whole thing works as a sentimental guided tour, but one that doesn't forget to have its own plot about memory, guilt, and responsibility, and is deliberately written to make sense even to someone unfamiliar with the older games.

The core of the gameplay is stacking. Captured monsters come in three size categories, and the player builds towers out of them together with their own heroes, with the assembled formation sharing stats and abilities. Taking a tower apart, on the other hand, grants a greater number of independent actions per turn, so there's a genuine choice between stability and flexibility. Battles are turn-based with a classic action-preparation gauge, capturing happens by fulfilling a specific condition against a weakened enemy, and every monster has its own skill tree. Collecting and upgrading the bestiary makes up a large portion of the content, and players who enjoy it can easily extend the game far beyond the main story.

The Vita version runs at a lower resolution than the home console variant and had to sacrifice some detail in crowded scenes, yet it remains colorful and legible, and the portable format suits monster-catching well. The music blends new compositions with reworked themes from older entries, and these callbacks are often the strongest experience the game has to offer. Reviewers praised the inventive battle system and the gentle tone, with criticism aimed at the chattier passages and the slower opening pace. Today, World of Final Fantasy remains an unusually accessible entry point into the series and one of the last big Japanese RPGs the Vita received.
ps-vita__world-of-final-fantasy.teaser: A cute celebration of the entire Final Fantasy series built around catching Mirage monsters.

ps-vita__dragon-quest-builders.article:
**Dragon Quest Builders** starts from a simple idea: what if, in the story of the first Dragon Quest, the hero had failed and the world was left in ruins? The player awakens into such a world as the last person who remembers how to build, and their task is to restore civilization piece by piece. The broken landscape gradually becomes a village, inhabitants arrive, and with them come new tasks, recipes, and reasons to keep building. The structure is divided into chapters set in different regions, each starting almost from scratch, which keeps up the pace and prevents the game from becoming aimless block-clicking.

Building takes place in a block-based world, but unlike open sandboxes, the game has clearly defined goals. Villagers ask for specific rooms, and when the player assembles the right combination of furniture and dimensions, the room activates and starts providing bonuses. On top of that, the base needs to be defended, since waves of enemies arrive at regular intervals and a poorly designed fortification will collapse. Combat consists of simple action skirmishes tied to the durability of materials and tools, so the depth isn't in the fighting itself but in how well prepared you are. The combination of set tasks and free-form creation makes the game something between a building simulation and a classic adventure.

The Vita version runs at a lower resolution and with shorter draw distance than the home version, but the gameplay remains complete, and portability suits this type of game exceptionally well. The visuals retain the series' typical style thanks to instantly recognizable monster designs, and the music works with Dragon Quest's orchestral themes. Critics received the game very well, praising how it gave block building a clear goal and narrative. Today, Dragon Quest Builders is seen as one of the smartest attempts to combine a signature Japanese RPG with a sandbox, and on the Vita it represents one of the most pleasant games for long evenings.
ps-vita__dragon-quest-builders.teaser: What if the Dragon Quest hero lost? The player then rebuilds the world piece by piece.

ps-vita__atelier-sophie-alchemist-of-mys.article:
**Atelier Sophie: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Book** opened a new era for the long-running series about alchemists and is a welcoming entry point for anyone who has so far been intimidated by its reputation. Sophie Neuenmuller inherited her grandmother's workshop along with unfinished knowledge, and one day discovers that an empty book on the shelf can talk. The book, named Plachta, doesn't remember who she was, and her memories return each time Sophie discovers a new recipe. The story therefore isn't about saving the world, but about a craftsman's journey from clumsy beginner to master, and about a friendship between two characters who teach each other. The tone is calm, gentle, and deliberately intimate.

The key novelty compared to earlier entries is the removal of the strict time limit that used to force players to plan every single day. Sophie can take her time, experiment, and go back, which makes the game significantly more accessible. Alchemy itself has become a spatial puzzle: ingredients have shapes resembling puzzle pieces, and the player places them into the cauldron's grid to activate colored fields and get the best possible properties for the result. Brewing potions has thus become the main game in itself, and combat mostly serves as a source of materials, though it does have its own turn-based system with support from characters in the back row. Gathering ingredients across the landscape, their quality, and chaining effects together form a loop that can absorb dozens of hours.

On the Vita the game runs at a lower resolution and with simpler lighting than on the home console, but the pastel art style handles it well, and the alchemy interface is pleasant to control on the touchscreen. Gust's music is traditionally a strong point of the series, alternating peaceful workshop themes with more energetic pieces for battles. Reviews praised the welcoming nature and pleasant atmosphere, criticizing the lower dramatic stakes of the story. Today, Atelier Sophie is a recommended starting point for the whole brand, and on the Vita it's one of the best games for slow, unstressful play.
ps-vita__atelier-sophie-alchemist-of-mys.teaser: A new era of the alchemist series; a welcoming starting point for anyone put off by its reputation.

ps-vita__oreshika-tainted-bloodlines.article:
**Oreshika: Tainted Bloodlines** is among the most original Japanese RPGs ever released on the Vita, because it turned generational character turnover into the very core of the gameplay. The main characters' family has been cursed, and its members only live to be two years old. The player therefore doesn't lead a single party, but an entire bloodline: characters age, weaken, die, and their descendants continue the vendetta against the demon who cast the curse. To keep the family from dying out, the heroes form marriages with gods, and from these unions come new family members who inherit abilities and weapons from their ancestors. Death, then, isn't a punishment but a planned part of progression.

The game is split between a calm segment at the family estate, where marriages to gods, raising descendants, and equipment are handled, and expeditions into dungeons, where turn-based battles take place. Party formation and positioning determine who can strike whom, so even a simple encounter requires careful thought. Because every character has a limited number of months to live, the player must decide when it's still worth investing in their training and when it's better to prepare a successor. This rhythm gives the game a peculiar melancholy, underscored by an art style inspired by Japanese woodblock prints and paper painting.

The audiovisual side is the game's greatest asset. Muted colors, outlined shapes, and stylized environments create the impression of an animated scroll, and the music uses traditional Japanese instruments, giving an unusually dignified atmosphere to a game that is otherwise full of humor. Contemporary reviews praised the boldness of the concept and the depth of the family system, with criticism aimed at the repetitive dungeons and the fact that the game doesn't explain much to the player at first. Today, Oreshika is valued as a title that made great use of Japanese cultural heritage as well as an unusual mechanic, and it's one of the games that make the Vita remembered as a console with an unusually varied lineup.
ps-vita__oreshika-tainted-bloodlines.teaser: A cursed bloodline dies out after two years; the player doesn't guide a single hero but entire generations of descendants.

ps-vita__tokyo-xanadu.article:
**Tokyo Xanadu** is Falcom's attempt to combine its own action-adventure tradition with a setting of modern Japan and the structure of school life. The player takes on the role of high schooler Kou Tokisaka in the fictional town of Morimiya, which looks like an ordinary suburb until cracks begin opening into a parallel dimension called Eclipse. Beyond them lurk monsters drawn by human anxiety, and Kou, together with other students, becomes one of those who drive them back. The alternation between two worlds is the game's core axis: during the day school matters, side quests for the town's residents, and relationships with classmates are handled, and in the evening a dungeon opens up.

Combat takes place from a top-down perspective in isometric levels and is built around rapidly switching between several heroes right in the middle of battle. Each character has a different element and a different range, so the party is chosen based on what a given dungeon calls for. Combining attacks, dodges, blocking, and special techniques tied to an energy gauge give the battles a brisk pace, and the game consistently rewards bold play with bonuses for unbroken combos. Outside of combat, bonds with characters develop, unlocking passive bonuses and story scenes, which is clearly inspired by the structure of Japanese school-set RPGs.

On the Vita this was one of the last major Japanese titles, and technically it's clear the game fit within the console's capabilities with room to spare: it runs smoothly, but the environments are rather plain and repetitive. This is offset by the music, an area where Falcom has long excelled, alternating energetic rock pieces with urban themes. Reviews rated the game favorably, highlighting the fun combat and the likable cast, with criticism aimed at the predictable plot and repetitive dungeons. Today, Tokyo Xanadu is seen as a pleasant, if not groundbreaking title, and as proof that Falcom could carry its signature style into a modern setting as well.
ps-vita__tokyo-xanadu.teaser: Falcom combines action-adventure with school life and rifts into another dimension.

ps-vita__grand-kingdom.article:
**Grand Kingdom** puts the player in the role of a mercenary company commander at a time when four powers are fighting over the remnants of a collapsed empire. The game has no single hero, but rather an assembled squad: the player hires soldiers of various classes, assigns them equipment, skills, and roles, and sends them on contracts that may be for any of the warring factions. The narrative is therefore more of a framework than a driving axis. The real engine is unit management, the economics of expeditions, and the sense that success depends on how well the company is assembled and equipped. Soldiers also wear down over time, and the fallen must be replaced with new recruits, so personnel planning carries its own weight.

The combat system is the most striking part of the whole package. Battles take place on a two-dimensional battlefield divided into four lanes, between which characters move, and it matters who stands in which lane and what their range is. Archers can hit across the entire field, but allies standing in the line of fire block the shot, mages create area-of-effect spells, and infantry try to close the distance. Movement between turns takes place on a board-game-style field with traps, bonuses, and obstacles that can also be placed against the enemy. Alongside single-player contracts, the game also offered asynchronous warfare, in which the results of players' companies fed into battles between nations.

On the Vita the game stands out visually, since the hand-drawn characters and backgrounds resemble illustrations from an old book and look excellent on the small screen. The sound is accompanied by orchestral compositions that lend the battles appropriate gravitas. Reviewers praised the tactical depth and unusual combat system, with criticism aimed at the repetitive structure of contracts and the way the game overwhelms the player with numbers and offers. Today, Grand Kingdom is considered one of the last seriously intentioned tactical titles for the Vita, and a game best appreciated by those who enjoy building and fine-tuning their own unit.
ps-vita__grand-kingdom.teaser: You command a mercenary company amid a war between four powers; managing your unit is the core.

ps-vita__natural-doctrine.article:
**Natural Doctrine** is remembered by players mainly for its uncompromising difficulty. It takes place in a harsh world where people survive in fortified cities and venture into mines in search of a rare mineral that enables the use of magic. The main character, Geoff, belongs to a group of hunters whose expedition into the depths goes wrong and reveals that the line between humans and monsters is more permeable than it seemed. The narrative is terse, raw, and makes no effort to be likable, which matches the overall tone of a game that forgives the player nothing. The characters bicker with one another and their motives are petty, so even the dialogue feels harsher than in most Japanese RPGs.

Battles take place turn-based on a grid, but with rules that differ significantly from the genre's conventions. The key is the link system, where units standing in the right position relative to each other gain additional actions and can attack in a chain even before their turn comes up. The same rule, however, applies to enemies as well, so a poorly arranged group can be crushed by a chain of follow-up attacks in a single round. The harshest rule is that the death of any unit means the immediate end of the battle and a return to the last save. The game therefore demands planning ahead, discipline, and a willingness to repeat encounters until the player understands exactly where they went wrong.

Technically, this is a functional but modest production on the Vita, with a dark palette and rather austere environments, which nonetheless suits the grim atmosphere of the underground. Contemporary reviews were mixed: critics faulted the game for insufficiently explaining its own rules and for difficulty that felt unfair, while part of the audience embraced it as a welcome challenge in a genre that was otherwise leaning toward simplification. Today, Natural Doctrine is more of a cult item for players seeking a tactical game with no compromises, and a good example of how fundamentally a single rule can change the character of an entire genre.
ps-vita__natural-doctrine.teaser: A tactical RPG known for its uncompromising difficulty and raw, austere story.

ps-vita__stranger-of-sword-city.article:
**Stranger of Sword City** opens with a plane crash, after which the hero wakes up in the world of Escario, where people transported from our reality end up. Surviving outsiders gain supernatural abilities here and become monster hunters, since that is the only way to keep a place in the fragile human settlement. The story is told sparingly, through conversations in the city and scraps of notes, and it doesn't try to hold the player's hand. What matters is building your own party, since the main character can't manage alone and can't get by underground without a well-assembled group.

The game is a classic first-person dungeon crawler with grid-based movement and a map that reveals itself through exploration. Alongside ordinary battles there is a trap system: the player picks a spot to wait for a rare enemy, positions the party, and tries to catch it off guard to obtain the crystals needed for further progress. Characters have a limited number of lives in the form of spheres, and once these run out, they disappear for good, forcing the player to weigh every risky decision. Each class has its own role within the formation, where the difference between the front and back row really matters, and character growth is slow and tangible. Returns to the city serve to hand in loot, restock supplies, and rearrange the party before the next descent.

Visually the game leans on a dark, faded palette and character art that gives it a grim, weary tone matching a world with no hope of returning home. The music is understated and mostly deepens the sense of dread underground. On the Vita it's an ideal title for short play sessions, since exploring the dungeons breaks down nicely floor by floor. Reviewers praised the honest difficulty and thoughtful party management, while criticism targeted the repetitive environments and terse storytelling. Today Stranger of Sword City ranks among the best Experience Inc. delivered on the Vita, and among the pillars of the entire handheld revival of dungeon crawler RPGs.
ps-vita__stranger-of-sword-city.teaser: After a plane crash, the hero wakes up in a strange world and becomes a monster hunter.

ps-vita__operation-abyss-new-tokyo-legac.article:
**Operation Abyss: New Tokyo Legacy** transplants the classic dungeon RPG into present-day Tokyo, where beneath the city's streets lie spaces called Abyss, full of monsters that threaten the population. A government organization deploys students with special abilities against them, gathered into a unit called the Xth Squad, and the player assembles and leads that very group. The combination of school setting, secret official organization, and classic maze gives the game an unusual character: between expeditions the player returns to the city, takes on assignments, restocks equipment, and reads fragments of investigation reports that gradually piece together what is really happening beneath Tokyo.

The core of the game is thoroughly old school. Exploration happens in first person on a grid, the map reveals itself step by step, and the dungeons are full of hidden doors, teleporters, and traps. Characters are created by choosing a class and a so-called code, which determines their abilities, and a party of six is arranged into two rows, where position determines attack range. Battles are turn-based, with orders issued to the whole group at once, and the game doesn't hold back from situations where a single misjudged skirmish sends the party straight back to the city. Character injuries only heal once you return, moreover, so managing resources matters just as much as the fighting itself.

On the Vita the game makes good use of the handheld format, since exploring floor by floor can comfortably be split into short sessions and the map stays clear on the display. Visually it relies on character art and simple but legible corridors, while calmer electronic music fills out the atmosphere. Reviews acknowledged it as a solid, accessible representative of the genre, while also pointing out the flat storytelling and how quickly the environments repeat. Today the game is a good entry point for anyone who wants to try classic map-drawing without being punished for it right away.
ps-vita__operation-abyss-new-tokyo-legac.teaser: A classic dungeon crawler set beneath the streets of modern Tokyo, full of monsters.

ps-vita__god-eater-2-rage-burst.article:
**God Eater 2: Rage Burst** is an expanded version of the second entry in the hunting action series, in which humanity survives amid the ruins of a world overrun by creatures called Aragami. The player belongs to a unit of so-called God Eaters, fighters equipped with living weapons capable of devouring enemies and drawing strength from them. The game's structure is mission-based: between expeditions the player moves around the base, talks with fellow soldiers, takes on contracts, and prepares equipment before heading out on a time-limited hunt for a specific monster. Compared to the first game, the story is darker and gives more room to the psychological toll on soldiers who know their weapon is also their affliction.

Combat relies on fast action with the ability to switch the weapon between several forms right in the middle of an attack. The player alternates between a sword, a cannon, and a form meant for devouring enemies, which replenishes ammunition and activates boosting states. The expanded version added a system of so-called blood arts, which unlock and improve according to how the player actually fights, along with a new burst mode for turning the tide in tough battles. The Aragami have readable attack patterns and destructible body parts, and the materials harvested from them are used to craft better gear, creating the classic hunting loop where you play for the sake of gradually improving your equipment.

Technically the game ranks among the better action titles the Vita produced. It keeps a brisk pace, the animations are fluid, and the design of both weapons and monsters is inventive, even though the mission environments repeat. The music leans on dramatic orchestral and rock themes that give the hunts the urgency they need. The game was very popular in Japan and found a dedicated audience in the West as well, although reviewers pointed to the volume of text between missions and the fact that newcomers lack context from the first game. Today it stands as one of the most substantial cooperative action titles the handheld ever offered.
ps-vita__god-eater-2-rage-burst.teaser: An expanded version of the hunting action game, where fighters devour giant Aragami with living weapons.

ps-vita__utawarerumono-mask-of-deception.article:
**Utawarerumono: Mask of Deception** is an unusual hybrid in which most of the playtime is taken up by an extensive visual novel, with tactical battles arriving as the climax of individual chapters. A man with no memory, who comes to be called Haku, wakes up in the middle of a snowy wilderness in a world inhabited by people with animal-like features. He is rescued by a girl named Kuon, and together they travel to the capital, where Haku becomes entangled in court intrigue against his will. A substantial part of the game is calm, humorous, and devoted to everyday life, food, and relationships between the characters, which is a deliberate setup that makes later twists sting all the more.

Battles play out turn-based on a grid, where range, direction of attack, and how long it takes for a unit's turn to come round again all matter. The most distinctive mechanic is chaining attacks through precisely timed button presses, which lets the player extend an attack combo and increase damage, so that even passively watching a fight demands attention. Characters have their own roles, from heavy infantry to support mages, and their development comes from assigning points into skills. There are fewer battles than in classic tactical RPGs, but they are longer and serve as the story's dramatic moments rather than ordinary filler. The pace is therefore slow, and the game demands patience.

On the Vita the game works very well, since extensive reading suits a handheld console, and the fully voiced dialogue turns it into something close to a listening experience. The character and background art is meticulous, and the music draws on both traditional Japanese instruments and orchestra, shifting sensitively from peaceful melodies to themes of war. Reviews pointed out that the game is clearly the first half of a larger whole and ends just as the plot is really getting started, while also praising the writing and atmosphere. Today Mask of Deception is recommended as an entry point into one of the best-written Japanese series the Vita ever received.
ps-vita__utawarerumono-mask-of-deception.teaser: A hybrid of an extensive visual novel and tactical battles as the culmination of each chapter.

ps-vita__hotline-miami-2-wrong-number.article:
**Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number** took the brutal formula of its predecessor and scaled it up, and on the PS Vita it became one of the most intense experiences the handheld ever offered. The game again relies on a top-down view, on a single hit meaning death, and on the constant repetition of short, extremely fast confrontations. The difference is that the second game splinters the story into a mosaic of several characters and timelines, so the player finds themselves at various points in the shoes of a film crew, a journalist, a soldier, and even the copycat gang from the first game. Each character has its own rules, one starts with a pistol, another cannot use firearms, another moves in a pair, and these small variations reshape the tactics of every level from the ground up.

The level design is more sprawling and open than in the first game, leading to more frequent ranged firefights and the need to keep an eye on the edges of the screen. On the Vita this initially feels like a complication, since the smaller display shortens the sightline, but the game offers a look-around function, and the player quickly learns to combine fast rushes with cautious waiting in doorways. Aiming with the right stick is precise and reloading after death is nearly instant, which is absolutely essential for a game built around dozens of rapid restarts. The pixel art, with its bold color filters and strobe effects, looks remarkably vivid and contrasty on the Vita's display.

The biggest weapon remains the music. A soundtrack made of dark synthwave and electronica sets the pace for the whole game, and combined with headphones it creates a hypnotic, faintly unpleasant trance that the on-screen violence oddly fits into. Reception was mixed: some players praised the greater scope and bolder storytelling, others criticized the difficulty stemming from confusing situations and the departure from the tightness of the first game. The influence of both games on the wave of retro-styled action titles is nonetheless undeniable. Today Hotline Miami 2 works as a harsh, stylistically self-assured piece that makes sense on the Vita precisely because of short sessions spent on a single chapter.
ps-vita__hotline-miami-2-wrong-number.teaser: A brutal sequel with even faster clashes, this time told through a mosaic of multiple characters.

ps-vita__helldivers.article:
**Helldivers** is a cooperative top-down shooter in which four soldiers of an elite corps try to spread so-called managed democracy across a hostile galaxy while trying not to shoot each other. The game rests on a simple principle: a mission lasts ten to twenty minutes, the team drops onto a planet's surface, completes objectives, and must make it to evacuation in time. The key mechanic is the stratagem, support called in by entering a short sequence of directional button presses, ranging from air strikes and defense turrets to a personal exoskeleton. Entering combinations under pressure, while an insect swarm or robotic units close in from every side, is the source of most of the tension as well as most of the comic disasters.

Crucially, friendly fire is always on. Every bullet, grenade, and orbital strike can kill a teammate, turning what would otherwise be straightforward action into an exercise in communication and discipline. Progress unfolds on a galactic map shared by all players across platforms, and a joint campaign against several factions gives individual missions meaning beyond a single sitting. On the Vita the game runs smoothly and clearly, and it makes use of cross-play with the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation 4 versions, so a character in progress can be carried from the television to the palm of your hand. The smaller display makes reading dense combat situations a bit harder, but legible icon and effect stylization largely compensates.

The atmosphere is carried by exaggerated military pathos, propaganda one-liners, and orchestral music that openly pokes fun at the military blockbuster genre. Reviewers praised the cooperation above all and the idea behind the stratagems, while criticism targeted the repetitive mission structure. In hindsight, the game clearly foreshadowed the same brand's later enormous success in a different form, and on the Vita it remains one of the few big online action games that truly worked there. Today it plays best with a familiar group; solo it's an honest challenge, and with four players it's the best kind of chaos there is.
ps-vita__helldivers.teaser: A cooperative top-down shooter; a squad of four soldiers calls in stratagems and watches the mission clock.

ps-vita__resogun.article:
**Resogun** is a pure arcade shooter that takes the classic side-scrolling principle and bends it around a cylinder. The player flies along the inner wall of a rotating game world, shooting down waves of enemies while trying to save the last surviving humans, who run around on the surface waiting to be carried to safety. It's precisely this rescue of civilians that turns the game into something more than mere shooting: whenever key enemies appear, the player must interrupt the attack, fly to the other side of the cylinder, and pick up the humans before the enemy destroys them. The tension between greed for score and the duty to protect civilians drives the whole design.

The arsenal is spare but well balanced: an upgradeable main weapon, an overcharged shot, a temporary shield, and a bomb that pays off to save for the right moment. The game runs at a high tempo and rewards keeping the multiplier alive, so the best results belong to players who can keep firing continuously while moving around the entire circumference of the level. The Vita version was released later than the original PlayStation 4 edition and is a separately adapted port that sacrificed some effects but kept what matters: smooth performance, legibility, and a huge amount of voxel particles that break apart into individual cubes during explosions.

Sound and music matter just as much as the visuals. The electronic backing intensifies as the pressure on screen grows, and the terse synthetic voice announcing the imminent loss of the last human ranks among the most memorable audio motifs of its generation. The title was received as an example of what a modern arcade game should look like: short, demanding, and built around leaderboards. Besides the main arcade progression, it also offers rule-altered variants and the option to cooperate in pairs, so there are more reasons to come back than the chase for a better ranking alone. Today Resogun is ideal handheld entertainment: a single round lasts a few minutes, but the pursuit of a better score keeps you at the console considerably longer than originally planned.
ps-vita__resogun.teaser: An arcade shooter on the inner wall of a cylinder, where rescuing civilians interrupts the shooting.

ps-vita__txk.article:
**TxK** is a hypnotic arcade shooter in which the player controls a spider-like ship at the edge of an abstract geometric tube, shooting down everything that crawls up from within it. The basic principle is simple yet unforgiving: movement is confined to the rim of the track, shots are fired into the depth, and enemies must be destroyed before they reach the edge and start blocking movement. Each of the dozens of levels has a different track shape, a different mix of enemies, and a different color filter, so progressing feels like flying through an endlessly shifting tunnel. A bomb, a temporary speed boost, and a jump that briefly lifts you off the tube's surface are all available.

The game was created as a Vita exclusive and is clearly tailored to the handheld console. Short rounds, instant restarts, and a checkpoint system encourage playing in a few-minute bursts, while leaderboards, conversely, lead to long sessions chasing a better ranking. Technically it's an impressive demonstration of what modest hardware can handle: the screen fills with glowing vector shapes, particles, and light trails, yet it remains legible and runs perfectly smoothly. On the display of the original Vita, the result looks almost like a glowing neon toy you don't want to put down.

Sound is a crucial part of the experience. The electronic music intertwines with the sound effects so that shooting and explosions become part of the rhythm, and combined with headphones a state players describe as trance sets in. This exact combination of image and sound turns individual levels into something closer to a musical composition than a classic shooter, and it explains why players return to the game even after hundreds of playthroughs. Critics received the game very well and often called it one of the best reasons to own a Vita. The title's fate was later complicated by a legal dispute over its similarity to older games by the same creator, so TxK never received wide distribution on other platforms. That makes it all the more valuable right here, where it still ranks among the pinnacles of the console's entire arcade lineup.
ps-vita__txk.teaser: A hypnotic shooter from Jeff Minter; a ship shoots down enemies crawling out of a tube.

ps-vita__terraria.article:
**Terraria** brought to the PS Vita a massive two-dimensional sandbox where digging, building, fighting, and exploring go on practically without end. The world is randomly generated, and the player digs through it from the grassy surface through caves and underground lakes down to hellish layers full of lava. The core loop is addictive: gathered ore turns into better tools, better tools open deeper layers, deeper layers yield rarer materials and with them access to new bosses. Combat happens in real time and demands nimble jumping, precise timing, and clever use of built platforms, so the game leans closer to an action platformer than to calm building.

The Vita version offers extensive content, including building homes for merchants, wide-ranging crafting, seasonal events, and several difficulty levels. The touchscreen handles quick item selection and targeted digging, while the sticks and buttons take care of movement and combat, a combination that works surprisingly well on a small display. The port also supports playing together with other players, so a world can be shared. Technically it's very solid work: large maps load briskly and the game keeps a stable framerate even during dense fights with dozens of enemies at once. Progress isn't tied down in any way either, the game doesn't dictate an order or a single goal, and leaves it up to the player whether to dive into deep mining, build a sprawling town, or head straight for hunting giant bosses.

Visually, Terraria rests on pixel art with a strong sense of detail, the music changes according to environment and time of day, and especially the night and underground themes manage to evoke a feeling of desolation. The title was received on Vita as one of the best possible choices for handheld play, since it can be played in short bursts or across whole hours without losing momentum. The game's influence on the entire sandbox exploration genre is fundamental, and to this day you can spend hundreds of hours in it without running out of new things to craft or new places to dig through.
ps-vita__terraria.teaser: A giant 2D sandbox of mining and building, where better tools open up deeper layers.

ps-vita__minecraft-playstation-vita-edit.article:
**Minecraft: PlayStation Vita Edition** managed to do what had long seemed impossible: cram an entire block world into a device that fits in a backpack, and have it run decently. The game offers both classic sides of the experience, a survival mode where you gather wood, build shelter before the first night, and gradually build up a base with a furnace, a farm, and mines, and a creative mode with unlimited resources that serves as a pure building set. Gamepad controls are complemented by the touchscreen and rear touchpad, so selecting items and managing the inventory is faster than it used to be on older console versions.

The console edition differs from the PC version mainly in bounded, pre-generated worlds and a guide that explains basic recipes to newcomers. That's exactly what made the Vita version, for many players, a gateway into the entire brand. The port supports multiplayer for several players and offers importing saved worlds from the PlayStation 3 version, so an in-progress fortress could be taken along outside. The technical compromise comes at the cost of a shorter draw distance and occasional dips in smoothness in densely built areas, but overall it's an exceptionally well-made conversion of an extensive game. It's also worth noting how well the interface is adapted for handheld play, switching between building and combat is quick and doesn't require lengthy menu navigation.

Atmosphere is carried above all by sound and music: calm piano motifs during the day, heavy silence and distant enemy sounds in the caves. The combination of headphones and a small screen surprisingly heightens the sense of confinement underground, where the player watches only a small circle of light around a torch and hopes nothing explosive is waiting around the next corner. The Vita edition was very well received and for a long time ranked among the console's best-selling titles. Today it feels like a reminder of a time when Minecraft was still split into separate console editions, and like one of the few truly bottomless sources of fun the handheld PlayStation had to offer.
ps-vita__minecraft-playstation-vita-edit.teaser: The entire blocky world of Minecraft shrunk down into a handheld console and still working.

ps-vita__binding-of-isaac-rebirth.article:
**The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth** is a reworked version of the cult roguelike action game in which a crying boy flees from his own mother into a basement full of monsters and defends himself with his own tears. The structure is simple and endlessly variable: every attempt generates a new sequence of rooms, the player advances through the floor, searches for treasures, shops, and secret chambers, and faces a boss at the end of each level. The key lies in hundreds of items that combine with one another, one increases range, another turns tears into a laser, a third adds familiars, and the resulting builds are often completely unbalanced, which is the main source of joy in every new run.

The PS Vita version is based on a completely rewritten form of the original game. The new engine foundation brought smooth performance, far more effects on screen, two-player co-op, and extensive content expansion compared to the original web version. On a handheld console the game works ideally, since a single run lasts roughly thirty to fifty minutes and can be put to sleep at any point and finished later. The pixel art is deliberately crude and gross, with plenty of bodily fluids and disfigured creatures, so the title certainly isn't aimed at the youngest audience. Two-stick control is precise and the game runs without a hitch even when the screen fills with dozens of projectiles, which for a title built around dodging determines whether the player perceives death as fair.

The audio side is unexpectedly strong, melancholic and aggressive tracks underscore the descent into ever darker floors and, together with the religious symbolism, create a strangely oppressive fairy tale about childhood anxiety. The game was received as one of the cornerstones of the modern roguelike wave, and its influence can be seen across an entire generation of titles built on randomly assembled items and short repeated runs. Today Rebirth remains an exceptionally strong choice on the Vita: there's so much content that unlocking all characters and items takes dozens of hours, and every attempt looks different.
ps-vita__binding-of-isaac-rebirth.teaser: A reworked cult roguelike, where a crying boy fights monsters with his tears.

ps-vita__bastion.article:
**Bastion** begins with a boy waking up in a world that has broken apart into floating fragments, and from the very first moment a gravelly narrator accompanies him, commenting on his every step. The game is an isometric action ride in which the path literally forms beneath his feet, tiles rise out of the void just ahead of the character, creating the impression of a world being born only through the player's movement. Combat combines two chosen weapons, a special ability, and a dodge, with an entire range of weapons available from a hammer and a rifle to a bow and a machete, each upgradable at the arsenal and testable in special challenges.

Progress leads through the individual fragments of the world back to a base, which the player gradually rebuilds. Here decisions are made about upgrades, about tonics that change the game's rules, and about so-called idols that raise difficulty in exchange for better rewards, an elegant way of letting players set their own challenge level. The Vita version contains the complete game including additional modes, and adds touch controls for quick selection, but above all it uses rich colors so the hand-painted backgrounds stand out even on a small screen. The game runs smoothly and loading is short, which suits shorter sessions well. Also included are optional challenges for individual weapons and special memorial levels that flesh out the backstory of the main characters, giving players a reason to return outside the main line and experiment with equipment combinations.

The strongest asset remains the pairing of narrator and music. The commentary reacts to what the player is doing at that very moment, so the storytelling feels like a living blues tale, and the soundtrack blending guitars, folk motifs, and vocals ranks among the most acclaimed in independent creation altogether. The game is often cited as one of the titles that, at the time of its release, helped push the independent scene into the mainstream and showed that small studios could pull off their own storytelling style. On Vita, Bastion is ideal for several longer evenings, and even after years its storytelling idea still feels fresh.
ps-vita__bastion.teaser: An isometric action game where the path literally builds itself beneath your feet, narrated by a storyteller.

ps-vita__limbo.article:
**Limbo** is a black-and-white platformer about a small boy who wakes up in a dark forest and, without a word of explanation, sets out to find his sister. The game uses not a single line of text or dialogue, all the storytelling is carried by image, sound, and whatever the player discovers through their own mistakes. Progress consists of running, jumping, pulling crates, and triggering mechanisms, with each section bringing a new physics puzzle: a rocking boat that must be used as a floating platform, a gravity field that reverses the direction of weight, or giant spiders that can only be escaped through absolutely precise jump timing.

The approach to death is essential. The game assumes the player will die several times before understanding the rules of a given trap, so it restarts instantly and right in front of the obstacle. The deaths themselves are raw and unpleasantly graphic, which keeps a constant sense of threat and forces careful progress. The PS Vita version contains the complete original game and works remarkably well on the small screen, since the main character's silhouette remains perfectly legible even at a small scale. The grainy film-like stylization and depth of field give the image the feel of an old film frame. The game is also short in the best sense, no passage repeats needlessly, and every new mechanism appears, exhausts its possibilities, and disappears to make room for the next idea. Thanks to that it keeps its pace from beginning to end, and the player never feels like they had to suffer through anything.

The audio side is just as restrained as the visuals. Instead of music, mostly ambient sounds play, wind, creaking wood, and distant mechanisms, musical motifs only appear at key moments and hit all the harder for it. The title was among the games that helped establish the idea that an independent platformer could be a work of art with its own authorial vision, and it is often ranked among the most influential releases of its time. Today Limbo can be finished in two or three evenings, and its oppressive atmosphere works just as well as it did at the time of its original release.
ps-vita__limbo.teaser: A wordless black-and-white platformer; a boy searches for his sister using only image and sound.

ps-vita__shantae-and-pirate-s-curse.article:
**Shantae and the Pirate's Curse** is a colorful action platformer in which the half-genie Shantae loses her magical powers and has to make do with equipment looted from pirates. That's the central idea of the whole game: instead of transforming into animals, the player collects a pirate hat for gliding through the air, a scimitar for a downward strike, a pistol for hitting distant switches, boots for fast running, and a cannon for a high jump. Each item retroactively opens previously inaccessible spots on already-visited islands, so the game works as a lighter, more straightforward variant of the structure known from metroidvanias.

Progress leads across several islands, traveled between by ship, and each has its own town with merchants, its own theme, and its own maze capped off by a boss. Combat rests on the hair-whip attack the whole series is built around, and on the smart use of gathered gear; the difficulty is welcoming, but collectibles and hidden nooks give more experienced players a reason to explore every screen. On the PS Vita the game looks excellent, the hand-drawn animations and rich palette look even sharper on the smaller screen, and it runs completely smoothly without a hitch. Alongside the main line there's also a range of side quests, dance abilities, and items that extend stamina or attack power, so it's worth talking to town residents and returning to places where something was previously out of reach. The game thus keeps a pleasant pace between action, exploration, and calmer moments in towns.

The music ranks among the best the series has to offer, catchy melodies with an oriental flavor and striking loops that stay in your head long after the console is switched off. Critics considered this installment the moment the series finally found its ideal form, and the game became the best-received title of the entire brand. Today it stands as a textbook example of a well-measured platformer, long enough to be worth it and brisk enough not to start dragging before the player reaches the final battle.
ps-vita__shantae-and-pirate-s-curse.teaser: Shantae loses her magic and has to make do with pirate gear she's plundered.

ps-vita__olliolli2-welcome-to-olliwood.article:
**OlliOlli2: Welcome to Olliwood** pushes two-dimensional skateboard trick riding into movie-set scenery and adds a depth that turned the original idea into a full genre of its own. The core remains: the skater rides left to right, the player calls up tricks with the stick, and a precisely timed button press on landing determines whether they land clean or end up on the ground. New here are manuals, which allow chaining individual tricks into one unbroken combo across the whole level, and branching routes offering several paths through a single level.

Every level contains a set of objectives, from reaching a certain score through performing specific tricks to finishing without falling, and completing them unlocks a harder professional version of the same track. It's precisely this structure that makes the game an ideal handheld title: a single attempt takes under a minute, but the pursuit of a perfect run without a single stumble stretches into dozens of repetitions. The Vita version runs perfectly smoothly, which is absolutely essential for a game built on precise timing, and the controls are instantly legible. Visually it's clean silhouette graphics with striking colorful backgrounds referencing film studios, jungle, and western settings. Besides career mode, the game also offers a daily challenge with a single attempt and several purely sport-focused modes that push players toward the longest possible unbroken trick sequence and constant comparison against others.

The sound consists of an electronic selection that keeps the pace and subtly reinforces the rhythm of the ride; a properly long combination of tricks comes with a quiet satisfaction that few other games offer. Reviewers praised above all the precision of the controls and its addictiveness, criticism targeted the high difficulty of later tracks. The series' influence is visible across the whole wave of later two-dimensional skateboarding games. Today OlliOlli2 remains one of the best-fitting titles for short sessions the Vita ever offered, and also a game where the player visibly improves from attempt to attempt.
ps-vita__olliolli2-welcome-to-olliwood.teaser: 2D skateboard tricks in movie sets; manuals link individual tricks together.

ps-vita__sonic-and-all-stars-racing-tran.article:
**Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed** is an arcade racing game that takes the tried-and-true model of item-based racing and adds vehicle transformation on the fly. The track changes during the lap, part of it is raced in a car, part on a boat amid churning water, and part in a plane through the air, and with every lap the layout of obstacles shifts, so the second lap already looks different from the first. Each of the three modes has its own physics: the car slides into drifts, the boat bounces on waves, and the plane requires managing tilt, so the player must constantly switch between three styles of driving.

The roster of characters spans the publisher's history and includes both expected faces from the blue hedgehog's world and representatives of older, less common brands. The career mode runs across a branching map of tasks, where alongside classic races there are also time trials, duels, and missions with special rules. Split-screen play and online racing are also available. The Vita version contains extensive content including several exclusive racers, and it's a very solid conversion that, at the cost of lower resolution and slightly simplified effects, maintains the necessary smoothness even on more demanding tracks. Controls are responsive and offer drifts with a gradually charging boost, so even after dozens of completed races there's still room to improve how cleanly corners are taken. The game also rewards bold driving with airborne tricks that likewise fill the acceleration meter.

The tracks themselves are the biggest asset: each is built around a specific game world, has its own musical arrangement of classic melodies, and can surprise with a dramatic environment change on the final lap. The game was received as one of the few racing titles that managed to stand alongside the genre's benchmark from the competition, and many reviewers called it the best work of its kind outside the genre's biggest brand. Today it's still the first choice on Vita if the player is looking for fast arcade racing with items and doesn't want to race alone.
ps-vita__sonic-and-all-stars-racing-tran.teaser: Arcade racing where the vehicle transforms on the fly between a car, a boat, and a plane.

ps-vita__retro-city-rampage-dx.article:
**Retro City Rampage DX** is a wild top-down action game that looks like a lost title from the eight-bit era and behaves like a parody of the entire pop culture of the nineties. The player moves around an open city, steals cars, completes missions for shady clients, and along the way bumps into dozens of references to movies, TV shows, and older games. The structure combines story missions with free-roaming mayhem, arcade time trials, and collectibles scattered across the whole map, so alongside the main line there's plenty of reason to just wander the streets.

Shooting and driving follow the classic pattern of older top-down games, but the game adds a range of unexpected weapons and abilities that change the pace of individual missions. The DX version that the Vita received brought improved clarity, a new aiming mode, added missions, and the ability to customize the main character's look. It's precisely on the handheld that the game makes exceptional sense: missions are short, arcade challenges last a few minutes, and the pixel art looks sharp and clean on the small screen. There are also several visual filters mimicking old televisions and portable consoles. The package also includes a number of short minigames and nods to older genres, from simple platforming interludes to parodies of action games of the era, which gives the whole thing surprising variety and keeps the city driving from wearing thin quickly.

The audio side works with chiptune music that alternates fast action motifs with calmer melodies and nails the period mood precisely. Reception was mostly favorable, with reservations that the density of jokes sometimes outweighs the actual game design and some missions lack more careful polish. The title is one of the best-known examples of how a large game can be built by almost a single person. Today it feels like a charming time capsule that can be played in short bursts and that pokes fun at its own nostalgia just as gladly as it celebrates it.
ps-vita__retro-city-rampage-dx.teaser: An eight-bit-looking top-down action game, full of references to nineties pop culture.

ps-vita__papers-please.article:
**Papers, Please** puts the player in the booth of a border official of a fictional eastern state and has him decide who may cross the border and who may not. The game looks stark: on one side a desk with documents, on the other a line of people. But the rules multiply every day — first it's enough to check a passport, then a work permit is added, a fingerprint, comparing a photograph, and finally a list of wanted persons. The player must compare data across documents under time pressure, look for discrepancies, and decide with a stamp, while every mistake brings a warning and a further offense costs docked pay.

It's precisely the economy that turns the game into something far more uncomfortable than mere spot-the-difference. Processed people bring pay, from which rent, food, and heating for the family are covered, so slow and careful decision-making means hunger at home. On top of that come the personal stories of travelers, bribe offers, and pressure from an organization that wants the player to knowingly break the rules. The game has several different endings depending on how one behaves over the course of a few weeks. The PS Vita version came out several years after the original release and uses the touchscreen for handling documents, which is probably the most natural possible control scheme for this game. Alongside the main story campaign, the game also offers an endless mode where the only goal is the longest error-free shift possible, so it's worth returning to even after finishing it. It's there that the whole system of checks really shows how well it's tuned.

The visuals are deliberately gray and roughly pixelated, the music plays only sparingly, and the main soundtrack is the pounding of the stamp and the rustling of papers. Reception was extraordinarily strong, and the title became one of the most cited examples of a game telling a political story through mechanics rather than text. Its influence on the wave of games about bureaucracy and moral compromise is clear to this day. On the Vita it's an ideal title to play in small pieces, ironically exactly as the game itself frames it.
ps-vita__papers-please.teaser: The player acts as a border checkpoint officer deciding on entry, while the rules keep growing day by day.

xbox-360__burnout-paradise.article:
**Burnout Paradise** took the tried-and-tested arcade series about speed and crashes and transplanted it into an open city where you never stop in a menu. Paradise City is one continuous stretch of map with highways, a harbor, mountain switchbacks, and construction sites, and a race simply starts by hitting the gas and brake at an intersection at the same time. The game tells you the destination and you have to find your own way there, which turns every race into a test of how well you know the city. Alongside this come other event types: takedown races where you have to wreck opponents, escapes from pursuers, stunt runs for points, and the famous mode where you deliberately crash and try to cause the greatest possible damage.

The driving model is purely arcade but exceptionally well tuned. Reckless driving against traffic, long drifts, and near misses fill up the boost meter, so the game directly pushes the player to drive irresponsibly. Crashes are a spectacle of their own: the camera slows down, sheet metal crumples, and the car tumbles among other vehicles. Victory rewards include new cars that appear on the streets and have to be chased down and wrecked to be unlocked. There's also a genuinely generous online component where you can just roam around one shared world and complete challenges together.

Technically it was one of the most impressive achievements of its time on Xbox 360, since the city runs smoothly and without visible loading even at extreme speeds. Criterion also kept expanding the game for a long time after release with free updates that added motorcycles, day-night cycles, and an entire new island. The atmosphere is carried by laid-back rock and alternative music and an iconic title track that every player instantly associates with this city. Reception was very positive, though some fans regretted the classic menu with a one-button race start. Today Burnout Paradise remains one of the most fun arcade rides there is.
xbox-360__burnout-paradise.teaser: Arcade racing transplanted into an open city with no menus between races.

xbox-360__project-gotham-racing-4.article:
**Project Gotham Racing 4** is the final entry in a series that spent its whole run trying to find its own place between arcade and simulation, and it managed that better than anyone else. At its core is the Kudos system, points for style. It's not enough to cross the finish line first; the game rewards long controlled drifts, driving the inside line, close passes on opponents, and clean laps without a scratch. Whoever just drives fast gets little. Whoever drives fast and elegantly unlocks new cars and tracks. This principle turns every lap into a small improvisation, because taking risks pays off, but a single hit against the barriers wipes out your whole chain of points.

The fourth installment added two crucial new features. The first is weather, which is not just decoration: rain, snow, and fog fundamentally change grip and visibility, so the same track in London or Tokyo is a completely different experience in a downpour. The second is motorcycles, which mix in with cars in races and handle very differently, with more sensitive braking and a completely different sense of speed. The career is put together from short challenges, which suits the game well because it can be played in half-hour sessions. There's also a sophisticated photo mode and a solid online component.

On Xbox 360 the game looked excellent, especially thanks to reflections on wet asphalt and honestly lit cities, which remain the main star. The engine sound is convincing, and the music draws on a selection across genres that you can switch between like a radio. Contemporary reviews were very favorable; the game was rated one of the best racing rides on the console, and the only thing critics held against it was its excessive similarity to its predecessor. The influence of the Kudos system is still visible today wherever racing games reward style rather than just time. Today PGR4 feels like a reminder that the series ended at its peak and never got a sequel. The gap it left behind was never fully filled, because racing games built on elegance of driving rather than perfection of simulation remain rare even years later.
xbox-360__project-gotham-racing-4.teaser: A racing game built on style; Kudos points reward elegant driving more than raw speed.

xbox-360__need-for-speed-hot-pursuit.article:
**Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit** is the series' return to what it always did best: chases between luxury supercars and police vehicles on wide country roads.
