Health is scarce, healing is limited, and enemies can kill within a few hits, so every encounter demands full concentration. The world is divided into four main regions that can be visited in any order, each offering a different environment, a different set of enemies, and a demanding boss. Beyond that, the game is riddled with hidden rooms, secret passages, and modules that unlock new moves, none of which is marked by an arrow or a quest log.

The Special Edition for Switch adds a further region, new equipment, and several control adjustments, and the console's hardware suits it well, since the pixel-art graphics with their striking palette of purple, cyan, and crimson look exceptionally good on a smaller screen. Disasterpeace's audio accompaniment relies on dark ambience and low synthetic tones that often weigh down the mood rather than accompany the action, further intensifying the atmosphere of decay. Critics praised the game for its visual style and sense of movement, with reservations aimed at occasionally unclear navigation. Today Hyper Light Drifter is regarded as one of the formative games of its era's independent scene, and its aesthetic has been imitated by numerous later titles.
switch__hyper-light-drifter-special-edit.teaser: Top-down action without a single line of dialogue; only visuals and environmental finds tell the story.

switch__gris.article:
**GRIS** is a short platformer that builds its entire experience on visuals, music and feeling rather than challenge. The player guides a young girl through a world that has collapsed along with her, moving through a landscape that begins almost colourless and gains a new part of its palette with each new area. The game uses no dialogue, no text and no quest markers, relying entirely on the player understanding where to go and what is happening from the composition of the scene itself. The theme is clearly about coping with loss, yet the game never states this directly and leaves the interpretation open.

The gameplay is deliberately non-confrontational. There is no way to die, no enemies in the usual sense and no time limits; instead the player jumps, climbs, swims and solves undemanding environmental puzzles. Along the way she gains new abilities, such as turning into a heavy stone block that withstands gale winds and breaks through fragile surfaces, or the ability to swim and later move through currents. Each ability opens up a different kind of environment, and the game introduces it, develops it and lets it fade away within a few minutes, so the pacing is always in motion.

The audiovisual presentation is the main reason the game earned so much attention. Hand-painted watercolour visuals combine flat colour fields with delicate animation and sweeping panoramas, where the character is often a tiny speck within an enormous vista. On Switch the game looks great both handheld and on the TV, and the smooth performance reinforces the sense of a painted film. The music by the Catalan group Berlinist, with piano, strings and a female vocal, is timed to the scenes so closely that it often shifts mood at the exact moment of transition between screens. Critics praised the game especially for its aesthetics and its sensitive way of guiding the player, while more critical voices took issue with its low difficulty. Today GRIS is one of the most frequently cited examples of a game experienced as an artistic work, one that can be finished in a single evening and yet stays in memory much longer.
switch__gris.teaser: A short platformer built on visuals and music rather than challenge; the world gains color alongside the heroine.

switch__rayman-legends-definitive-editio.article:
**Rayman Legends Definitive Edition** brought to Switch, shortly after the console's launch, one of the best-reviewed 2D platformers of the modern era, and it still ranks among the best the genre has to offer on the console. The game is built on very fluid movement, with the hero running, sliding, gliding on his hair, punching enemies and bouncing off walls, and the levels are designed so that a skilled player can clear most of them without ever stopping. The structure is split into worlds with distinct themes, ranging from fairy-tale groves through medieval castles to underwater and oriental settings.

The standout feature is the musical levels that form the finale of each world. The entire progression, jumps, enemies and environmental movement are precisely synced to the rhythm of a well-known song, turning the platformer into a rhythm game for a few minutes. Alongside the main campaign, the Switch version also includes reworked levels from the previous game, Rayman Origins, daily and weekly challenges, and extensive collecting of small Teensies that unlock further content. Local four-player co-op works excellently and is one of the main reasons to bring the game out for a group evening.

Technically it's a showcase of what the UbiArt Framework engine can do. The visuals look like a moving illustration, with hand-drawn characters, delicate animation and richly decorated backgrounds, all while running perfectly smoothly in both handheld and TV mode. The Switch version also adds touch controls for the Murfy sections and a few small extras, including local races. Critics received the original release extremely warmly, praising above all the amount of content, the variety of ideas and the precision of the controls. Today the game hasn't aged a bit, because its visual style doesn't rely on technical specs, and for Switch owners it's one of the easiest platformers to recommend outright.
switch__rayman-legends-definitive-editio.teaser: One of the modern era's best-reviewed 2D platformers; brisk movement that never stops.

switch__hat-in-time.article:
**A Hat in Time** is an independent 3D platformer that openly embraces the legacy of games like Super Mario Sunshine and Banjo-Kazooie, aiming to revive the collect-a-thon adventures of the turn of the millennium. The player controls a small girl with a hat whose spaceship has lost its fuel in the form of scattered hourglasses, forcing her to explore the planet below. Each world is a self-contained chapter with its own tone, ranging from a mafia-run port town through a film studio of rival directors to a haunted forest, and individual goals within the same map vary widely enough that repeated returns never grow stale.

Movement is the core, and the game leans heavily on it. The character jumps, performs a roll into a follow-up leap, uses an umbrella both as a weapon and as a way to grapple onto ropes, and collects hats with different abilities, such as summoning an arrow pointing to the next objective, an explosive, or the ability to slow down time. Badges add further passive upgrades, letting the player build their own personal movement style. Chapters are divided into full-fledged levels and shorter tasks, and the game also offers time trials for those who want to fully master the controls.

On Switch the game arrived later than on other platforms, and handheld mode suits it well, since individual missions typically last around ten to twenty minutes. The visuals go for a soft, cartoonish style with bold colours and exaggerated character expressions, while the music leans on playful orchestral and jazz motifs that shift with each chapter. The project came about thanks to a successful Kickstarter campaign, and critics and players alike praised how it managed to capture the mood of classic platformers without being mere nostalgia. Occasional technical rough edges and an imperfect camera are the main complaints, but overall it's one of the few modern games that truly deliver on this nearly extinct genre.
switch__hat-in-time.teaser: A collectible-driven 3D platformer in the spirit of Mario Sunshine and Banjo-Kazooie; each world has its own tone.

switch__cave-story.article:
**Cave Story+** is the console incarnation of one of the most important independent games ever made, a project that a single author developed over several years in his spare time and released for free in 2004. The game tells the story of a memoryless robot who wakes up in the caves of a floating island inhabited by the peaceful Mimigas, gradually uncovering why the entire island is in danger. The storytelling is surprisingly elaborate, with side characters the player will remember, and several endings, the best of which requires meeting non-obvious conditions and skipping one seemingly tempting item.

Gameplay-wise it blends platforming with shooting in the spirit of classics like Metroid or Blaster Master. Weapons level up by collecting energy triangles, but getting hit costs the character her progress, which pushes the player to play cleanly. The arsenal is varied, and some weapons change how the character moves, such as a rocket launcher that lets her launch herself upward with her own explosion. The final stretches rank among the harder parts of the game and also offer optional tough levels for those who want to see the game truly through to the end.

The Plus version adds improved graphics, new modes and the option to switch back to the original look and original music, which matters a great deal to longtime fans. On Switch the game runs perfectly smoothly, supports two-player play, and handheld mode suits it well thanks to short stretches between saves. The chiptune soundtrack, which the author also composed himself, ranks among the most memorable in all of independent gaming and can shift within a single hour from a carefree melody to a thoroughly oppressive theme. The game's influence is hard to overstate, since it showed that a single individual could create a title comparable to professional production, opening the way for an entire wave of later independent projects. Today it still plays excellently and belongs on the genre's required reading list.
switch__cave-story.teaser: A legendary indie game by a single author, originally released entirely for free.

switch__owlboy.article:
**Owlboy** is a pixel-art platformer about a mute owl boy named Otus, who struggles to hold his own in a world of floating islands while constantly falling short of what those around him expect. The main thing that sets it apart from most games in the genre is movement: Otus can fly almost anytime and without restriction, so the game doesn't take place on platforms but in the air. The environments are shaped accordingly, with caves and temples built vertically, full of shafts, draughts and narrow passages, and the player moves through them more like through open water than across solid ground.

Combat is handled cleverly. Otus himself has essentially no attack of his own; instead he can pick up one of his companions and use their weapon, whether a gunner with a ranged shot or a character able to break through solid surfaces. Switching between companions mid-flight is the basis of both combat and puzzles, since each one opens up different paths. The game constantly combines exploration, simple puzzles and firefights against pirates threatening the islands. The structure is fairly linear and story-driven rather than open, which actually suits it, since it lets the game focus on its narrative.

Visually it's one of the most striking pixel-art games ever made. Development took nearly ten years, and it shows in the sheer number of hand-animated details, the colour gradients of the sky and the large panoramas built from several layers of background. On Switch the game runs without a hitch, and handheld mode really highlights the care put into the scenery. The music works with orchestral and chamber motifs and carries most of the emotional weight in key scenes, since the game barely uses spoken dialogue at all. The story of feeling inadequate and searching for one's own place among others is unexpectedly melancholic, and it ends more powerfully than the setting of floating islands might suggest. Critics received the game warmly, and it's still cited today as an example of just how far pixel art can be pushed.
switch__owlboy.teaser: A pixel platformer about an owl boy who flies without limits; played mostly in the air.

switch__crash-team-racing-nitro-fueled.article:
**Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled** is a complete rebuild of the kart-racing classic from the late nineties, prepared for modern consoles by Beenox. The core remains untouched: tracks full of shortcuts, beach curves, volcanic caves and futuristic highways, raced by characters from Crash the wombat's world. The main draw, though, is a driving model built around chaining boosts. The player charges boost by drifting and must release it with precisely timed hops to keep the acceleration going, and anyone who nails the rhythm can drive an entire lap essentially without ever slowing down. This one mechanic alone makes the game something more than relaxed family fun, splitting players into those who simply enjoy the colourful spectacle and those who hone the ideal racing line as a technical discipline.

There's an unusually large amount of content here. Alongside the tracks from the original, courses from the sequel Crash Nitro Kart were added, and there's a classic story mode with bosses and relic collecting, time trials, battle arenas and online matches. The developers also kept adding further tracks, karts and costumes in seasonal waves for months after release, so the offering grew far beyond the source material. On Switch the game runs at a lower resolution and with more noticeable compromises in detail than on more powerful consoles, but the smoothness of the driving remains intact, and in handheld mode it's one of the best-looking racers of its generation. The preserved local split-screen also makes the console an ideal machine for couch gaming.

The atmosphere is held together by cartoonish visuals with a bold palette and music that plays with the original themes in modern arrangements. Reception was very favourable, with reviewers praising above all the amount of content and the fidelity of the demanding driving model, while criticism was mainly aimed at unpolished online services in the first weeks after launch. Today it's the strongest competitor to Mario Kart on Nintendo's platform, a game that relies not on chaos and luck but on genuine driving skill and knowing the tracks down to the last corner.
switch__crash-team-racing-nitro-fueled.teaser: A rebuild of the nineties kart-racing classic; the driving model is built around drift-chained turbos.

switch__team-sonic-racing.article:
**Team Sonic Racing** is an attempt to bring the idea of a team-based game into the kart-racing genre, and it does so quite thoroughly. The player doesn't race alone but as part of a three-member team that shares a combined finishing result. When a teammate is out in front, they leave behind a yellow trail that others can ride to pick up extra speed, while whoever is lagging behind receives items from the team and can, in turn, send their own items forward to whoever needs them more. Filling the team gauge unlocks a shared ultimate manoeuvre that pits the whole trio against their rivals for a few seconds. The result is a racer where it pays to watch the others and share, rather than focusing solely on your own line.

Mechanically it's a classic kart racer with drifting, jump boosts and items built around the Wisps from the main series. Three car types, speed, technique and power, differ in how they handle shortcuts and collisions with obstacles, which forces the player to think when assembling a team. The Team Adventure campaign leads the player through dozens of tasks that, besides regular racing, add slaloms, target-destruction runs or time-limited driving, and unlock parts for kart customisation. The Switch version is the most technically scaled-back of the whole release, with lower resolution and less smoothness than the other consoles, but handheld mode works well, and local four-player split-screen has been kept intact.

The visuals lean on the colourful environments typical of the newer Sonic games, while the music draws on rock and electronic motifs characteristic of the series. Reception was fairly good: reviewers praised the team system as a fresh idea, but criticised the smaller variety of tracks and characters compared to the same studio's earlier Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed. Today, Team Sonic Racing is an interesting alternative for group play, since it forces even people who otherwise just stay quiet and floor the gas in races to actually communicate.
switch__team-sonic-racing.teaser: A kart racer built on teamwork — whoever's in the lead leaves a slipstream for teammates.

switch__burnout-paradise-remastered.article:
**Burnout Paradise Remastered** brings to Switch one of the most free-roaming racing games ever made. Paradise City isn't a set of separate circuits but an open city with no loading screens, where the player simply drives off and the game itself offers up races, time trials, chases or tasks in which a hulking car has to be delivered across town without a scratch. Routes aren't marked with arrows on the ground, only by the finishing intersection, so the player chooses their own path. That's exactly why it pays to learn the city, searching for shortcuts through construction sites, ramps on rooftops and shortcuts through narrow alleys.

The driving model is built on aggression. Driving into oncoming traffic, close near-misses with other vehicles and drifting all fill the boost gauge, so the game practically punishes caution. The series' signature feature remains takedowns, ramming an opponent into a wall or guardrail, accompanied by a slow-motion shot of the bodywork tearing apart. Crashes are part of the fun, not a failure state, and a standalone mode centred on finding the most efficient way to cause a pile-up was one of the most popular parts of the original release. The remaster includes all the later expansions, including an island with rough off-road driving and motorbikes, and the Switch version sacrifices resolution and some effects to keep things smooth. In handheld mode it's a surprisingly well-executed port of a game from 2008.

The atmosphere is recognisable at first glance: a sun-soaked city, a radio host commenting on the player's exploits, and a soundtrack made up of rock and punk tracks. The original Burnout Paradise was very well received at launch and is considered one of the high points of arcade racing, since it convincingly dissolved the boundary between menu and driving by opening up the city. Today the game feels remarkably fresh precisely because it explains nothing and simply lets the player drive, and on a handheld console it becomes an ideal title for short bursts of play, since one great chase lasts just a few minutes and can start anywhere on the map.
switch__burnout-paradise-remastered.teaser: An open racing city with no loading and no arrows on the ground; you choose your own route.

switch__grid-autosport.article:
**GRID Autosport** is one of the most ambitious ports on Switch ever: a full-fledged circuit racer from Codemasters, brought to the handheld by Feral Interactive. It's neither arcade nor a hardcore simulator, but a middle ground between the two. The cars have noticeable weight, tires lose grip when the player pushes too hard into a corner, and damage affects handling. At the same time, the game offers so many assists that it can be tuned from a relaxed ride to a mode where every mistake is final.

The career consists of five disciplines that play completely differently. Touring cars are overtaken through nudging and body contact, GT cars demand a smooth racing line, single-seaters tolerate no contact at all, drift events score angle and fluidity, and endurance races force the player to watch tire wear over long distances. The player races under a team's colors alongside a teammate who can be sent ahead or ordered to drive safely via radio. Feral split the game into smaller data chunks and lowered the resolution, yet still managed to keep the full grid of rivals and stable smoothness. Wheel support, a touch menu, and later added online multiplayer made it a complete release rather than a stripped-down demo.

The visuals rely on clean lighting and honest car models, and engine sound plus crowd noise do more for the atmosphere than the music, which mostly plays in the menus. The original 2014 release was well received as the series' return to racing without unnecessary spectacle, and the Switch port earned admiring reactions precisely because of its technical achievement. Today it remains one of the few racing titles on the platform that offer serious circuit racing, and for players who want something other than go-karts on the go, it's practically a mandatory choice. At the same time, it's a showcase of how much can be squeezed out of the Switch hardware when a studio that knows exactly what to sacrifice and what to keep handles the port.
switch__grid-autosport.teaser: A circuit racer between arcade and simulation; one of the most ambitious ports on Switch.

switch__fast-rmx.article:
**Fast RMX** was one of the first games Switch owners downloaded right after turning on the console, and for a long time it stood as the platform's best technical showcase. It's an anti-gravity racer in the style Nintendo's own F-Zero series once represented: vehicles hover above the track, race at several hundred kilometers per hour, and colliding with a wall means an instant loss of momentum. The tracks run through deserts, frozen canyons, futuristic cities, and orbital structures, and include loops, jumps, and sections where the player clings to a tunnel wall.

The whole game is defined by a single mechanic: phase switching. Boost panels on the track glow either orange or blue and only work when the vehicle is set to the matching color. Switching is done with a single button and must be timed mid-race, so besides holding the ideal line, the player is constantly reading the colors ahead. On top of that, energy is collected into a separate turbo boost, which is also consumed when returning to the track after a crash, forcing a choice between risk and reserve. The mode selection is modest, there are championships, time trials, local split-screen for up to four players, and online races, but the quality of the driving itself carries it a long way.

Technically it was something of a minor sensation: the game ran smoothly at high resolution docked and without any visible drop in handheld mode, which was surprising for a launch title from a small German studio. The audio consists of a hard electronic soundtrack that matches the speed on screen precisely. Reviews were largely favorable, praising the speed, visuals, and price, while mainly criticizing the limited mode selection and the high difficulty at higher speed classes. Today Fast RMX is a reminder that the anti-gravity racing genre didn't die, it just moved to smaller developers who keep it alive. For Switch owners it remains the fastest thing you can launch on the console, and for newcomers a decent lesson in what it means to drive with precision.
switch__fast-rmx.teaser: An anti-gravity racer in the spirit of F-Zero; it showed what Switch could do right at launch.

switch__doom-eternal.article:
**DOOM Eternal** is the sequel to the rebooted series that pushed first-person shooting into the form of a fast action game about resource management. The player once again takes on the role of the Doom Slayer, blasting through hordes of demons on Earth and beyond, but this time it's not just about aiming. Every weapon and ability gives something different: the chainsaw restocks ammo, the flamethrower knocks armor off hit enemies, and brutal melee finishers restore health. If the player stops or starts holding back, resources run out and death follows, so the only way forward is to keep attacking and switch tools according to what's needed at that moment.

Compared to its predecessor, mobility is far more pronounced. A double jump, air dash, grappling hook, and monkey bars turn arena fights into a three-dimensional dance where the player is constantly moving above enemies' heads. Stronger demons have weak points that can be shot off, giving combat a logic of priorities: disable the healer first, then the one shooting from range. Between arenas, the game weaves in platforming sections and searches for hidden upgrades. The Switch port was handled by Panic Button, and the result is a remarkable compromise, that is, lower resolution scaled to the load and a lower frame rate than on other platforms, but combat readability and the full campaign content are preserved.

The atmosphere is built from a combination of raw metal music, metallic environments, and a story that deliberately takes itself with comic-book seriousness. Reception was strongly positive, the game was called one of the best action titles of its generation, though some players had reservations about the sheer number of mechanics piled on top of each other and the platforming inserts. Today Eternal stands as the peak of one approach to shooters: no cover, no rest, just constant motion. On Switch, it's also one of the most demanding titles ever gotten running on the console, and for that alone it deserves attention even from people who already know it from elsewhere.
switch__doom-eternal.teaser: A fast action shooter about resource management; the chainsaw refills ammo, melee finishers restore health.

switch__wolfenstein-ii-new-colossus.article:
**Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus** continues B. J. Blazkowicz's story in an alternate history where Nazi Germany won the Second World War and occupies the United States. The player joins the resistance and pushes through devastated cities, secret bases, and bizarre locations that couldn't exist in a more realistic game. The story is told far more cinematically than in most shooters: long dialogue scenes, dark satire, and characters with their own arcs alternate with extremely brutal action. It's precisely that contrast between quiet interludes at the base and the massacre in the following mission that gives the game its distinctive tone.

Gameplay is built on the choice between stealth and open combat. Officers patrol every larger map and can be eliminated with a knife or a silenced weapon. Whoever kills them in time prevents reinforcements from being called in; whoever fails faces an endless wave of enemies. Dual-wielding weapons, reloading on the move, and extensive weapon upgrades allow for very aggressive play, yet the game doesn't tolerate reckless charging, since the health pool doesn't refill above its base level on its own. In the second half, the player gains special equipment that opens up alternative routes and retroactively changes how earlier locations can be traversed. The Switch version by Panic Button lowers resolution and effect detail and is noticeably softer visually, but keeps a stable pace and even offers motion controls for aiming.

The audio is one of the game's most distinctive elements: period-styled German-language cover songs, heavy industrial motifs, and loud weapon sound. Reviews were very favorable, praising above all the boldness of the storytelling and the quality of the shooting, with unbalanced difficulty and a short campaign length as the most common complaints. Today it stands as one of the few big shooters on the platform bold enough to be both a brutal spectacle and a politically outspoken game, and it definitely doesn't belong in the hands of the youngest players.
switch__wolfenstein-ii-new-colossus.teaser: An alternate history where the Nazis won the war; its storytelling is more cinematic than the competition.

switch__elder-scrolls-v-skyrim.article:
**The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim** arrived on Switch as one of the first big third-party ports and proved that a sprawling open-world RPG could work on a handheld console. The player wakes up as a condemned prisoner on the chopping block in a northern province, only to discover they carry a dragon's soul and the ability to use the dragon tongue as magic. What follows, though, is mainly freedom: the main quest can be shelved for dozens of hours in favor of joining the thieves' guild, the college of magic, the war between the empire and the rebels, or simply wandering mountain trails and digging up old tombs.

The character system has no classic classes. The player improves at whatever they actually do, meaning whoever shoots a bow gets better with a bow, whoever steals gets better at sneaking, and on top of that they pick perks from skill constellations. Combat is simple but has weight: blocks, power attacks, and spells in both hands, plus dragon shouts that can knock an opponent off a cliff or slow down time. The Switch version includes all three major expansions, motion control support for sword swings and bow aiming, and bonus content tied to Zelda in the form of Link-inspired gear. Technically it's a compromise, meaning lower resolution and simpler effects than on other consoles, but it's a fully playable version in your hands, which changes how a player returns to a game of this scope.

The atmosphere rests on the Nordic landscape, mist between the mountains, and music with sweeping choirs that even someone who's never launched the game remembers. The original 2011 release ranks among the most influential RPGs ever, since it opened the genre to a wide audience, and its modding scene keeps the game alive to this day. The Switch version's reception was favorable, with complaints about the price and the aging technical side. Today it's the easiest way to carry the entire province of Skyrim in your bag, and the game keeps its main strength: the player decides for themselves what actually matters in it.
switch__elder-scrolls-v-skyrim.teaser: A vast open-world RPG about a dragonborn hero; the main quest can be shelved for dozens of hours.

switch__diablo-iii-eternal-collection.article:
**Diablo III: Eternal Collection** is the complete edition of the action RPG about hacking through hordes of demons and collecting ever more absurd gear, and it works surprisingly naturally on Switch. The player chooses from several classes, from the barbarian and monk to the wizard and necromancer, each with its own set of abilities that can be further customized with runes. The core loop is simple: run through a location, cut down everything that moves, pick up better gear, and move on. But the game tunes this loop for so long that it becomes an extraordinarily satisfying rhythm, where picking up a new pair of gloves can change a character's entire build.

Once the campaign is finished, the main content opens up: an endless scaling of difficulty. Rifts generate randomly assembled levels with a boss at the end, higher tiers punish the player with steadily rising enemy stats, and the seasonal system regularly resets progress so players start fresh under new rules. The Switch release includes both the Reaper of Souls expansion and the later-added necromancer class, and above all local four-player co-op on a single screen. Just plug in controllers and you're playing instantly. Technically it's a well-executed conversion that keeps smooth performance even in the densest fights, topped off with a handful of cosmetic items referencing Nintendo brands.

The atmosphere is dark, gothic, and quite loud: blood, torches, cathedrals, and the roar of dying monsters accompanied by orchestral music that pulls back into quiet motifs during calmer moments. The original Diablo III had a troubled reception at its 2012 launch because of the auction house and mandatory internet connection, but after being reworked and expanded, it became the genre's benchmark on consoles. Today the Switch version is the most convenient way to get a short dose of this loop, even though a short evening threatens to turn into an all-nighter. For playing together on a single console, it also has few competitors on the platform, since the co-op here works without a single compromise.
switch__diablo-iii-eternal-collection.teaser: Demon-slaying and gear collecting that works surprisingly naturally on Switch.

switch__streets-of-rage-4.article:
**Streets of Rage 4** is the sequel to the legendary Sega Mega Drive beat-'em-up, arriving decades after the last installment, yet most players still embraced it as a true successor. The setting stays the same: a city under the control of a criminal organization, streets, subway, galleries, and rooftops through which a group of heroes moves, solving problems with their fists. Axel and Blaze return to the roster, joined by new characters, each with their own speed, reach, and special attacks, so the choice of fighter significantly changes the play style.

The combat system runs deeper than it first appears. Special attacks drain health, which can be earned back by hitting enemies without taking a hit yourself, creating a risky bet on how long to stay on the offensive. Combos are tracked, and a scoring system rewards keeping a chain going, throwing enemies into each other, and bouncing them off walls, turning an ordinary playthrough into a game about clean execution. Two-player local co-op is preserved, and there's also an online mode, a single-life arcade run, and a battle arena. Character versions from the classic games can also be unlocked, complete with their original pixel art and behavior, which follow their own rules. On Switch, the game runs without a hitch, and the sharp hand-drawn art gets along well with handheld mode.

The visuals from Lizardcube rank among the most striking in the genre, since the drawn backgrounds look like an illustration brought to life. The music was led by Olivier Deriviere, with contributions from composers tied to the original series, so the soundtrack alternates modern electronica with nods to nineties sound. Reviews were very favorable, and the game is considered proof that the classic beat-'em-up still has a place today. Today it's the ideal game for an evening with friends: short, tough, and the kind players return to for a better score. On Switch, it's enough to unplug the Joy-Cons and a second player joins within seconds.
switch__streets-of-rage-4.teaser: A sequel to the Sega Mega Drive brawler; players embraced it as its true successor.

switch__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-shr.article:
**Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Shredder's Revenge** is a beat-'em-up that deliberately returns to the arcade and console takes on the Turtles from the turn of the eighties and nineties. The player chooses from a roster of characters, that is, all four turtles, Splinter, April, and others, and fights through the streets of New York, sewers, construction sites, and a TV studio against members of the Foot clan and familiar villains from the animated series. Each character has a different reach and speed, so the choice isn't purely cosmetic: whoever plays as Donatello keeps enemies at range, whoever plays as Raphael has to go in for close contact.

Combat is simply readable but has enough depth to hold up over repeated playthroughs. Besides basic combos, there are dodges, deflecting projectiles back at the shooter, throws, and a chargeable special attack that briefly makes the player invulnerable. The game comes most alive in co-op, which supports up to six players at once, both locally and online, including the ability to revive each other and pull off joint moves. Alongside the arcade run, there's a story mode with a map, character quests, and gradual fighter leveling, giving a reason to return to individual missions. On Switch, it's a completely trouble-free title that looks just as good handheld as on a TV.

The pixel art nails the style of the original cartoon, including its animations and color palette, the music was composed by Tee Lopes and alternates funky and synth sounds with loud drums. Reception was very favorable, reviewers called it one of the best licensed beat-'em-ups ever and praised above all the co-op and the precision of the controls, with criticism aimed at its short length. Today Shredder's Revenge shows what a genre tribute should look like, one that doesn't rely solely on nostalgia but on genuinely well-designed combat. In a group of four or six, it ranks among the safest bets you can boot up on Switch, since everyone grasps the rules instantly.
switch__teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-shr.teaser: A brawler returning to the arcade Turtles games of the late 80s and early 90s against the Foot Clan.

switch__overcooked-2.article:
**Overcooked! 2** is a cooperative cooking game that really tests your ability to communicate under pressure. Two to four players run a shared kitchen where orders keep coming in on one side while the clock runs down on the other. Every dish demands a sequence of steps: chop, cook, plate, serve, and finally wash the dishes that keep piling up. Nobody has enough hands to manage alone, so everything depends on splitting roles and shouting instructions like who grabs the rice and who puts out the burning pan.

The series' main joke is that the kitchens themselves work against the player. The floor moves on drifting ice floes, tables ride conveyor belts, the path between the stove and the serving hatch splits apart over a chasm, or the whole room rotates. The second game added the ability to throw ingredients across a distance, which fundamentally changes tactics in split kitchens, and crucially it added online multiplayer, which the first game lacked. Alongside a campaign with levels that unlock progressively, there's also a scoring mode where players return to individual kitchens trying to earn three stars. On Switch the game works exactly as it should, since two people can split a pair of Joy-Cons and start playing instantly, with no setup and no extra hardware.

The visuals are deliberately cute, with a colorful cartoon world and characters scurrying around each other in a panic, while the music keeps a light, quick rhythm that pushes players forward as time runs out. Reception was very positive, and the series became one of the most common answers to the question of what to play with a partner or with kids. At the same time it has a reputation as a game that can make even well-matched couples argue, and that's exactly why people keep coming back to it. Difficulty ramps up gradually, and the final kitchens demand a rehearsed routine, so what started as easygoing fun can easily turn into a multi-hour session repeating the same level until that third star finally drops. For Switch it's one of the best party titles around, and proof that a cooperative game doesn't have to be a stripped-down version of something bigger.
switch__overcooked-2.teaser: Cooperative cooking that tests how well you communicate under pressure; nobody has enough hands.

switch__puyo-puyo-tetris.article:
**Puyo Puyo Tetris** is an unusual crossbreed of two completely different puzzle classics, released on Switch in the console's very first year and becoming one of its best titles for a train ride. On one side stands Tetris with its four-piece blocks and line clears, on the other Puyo Puyo, where colorful blobby drops fall and the player must link them in groups of four or more. The two games run on completely different logic: Tetris is about space and speed, Puyo is about setting up chain reactions, where one well-placed piece triggers a cascade.

The game finds its true purpose in versus play. Every successful move sends obstacles to the opponent, so the match becomes a question of who can keep up the pace longer. The mode selection is broad: there's a classic duel within the same game, but also one where one player plays Tetris and the other Puyo simultaneously on a single screen, plus Swap, which regularly switches between the two games, and Fusion, where blocks and drops fall onto one shared field together. The story mode, with voiced anime cutscenes, mainly serves as a tutorial that gradually teaches players advanced techniques. On Switch there's the option to play two players on one console with detached Joy-Cons, plus a snappy online mode, which keeps the game a reliable pick for a group.

The visuals are loud and colorful, full of animated characters commenting on the match as it unfolds, and the music adapts to how close a player is to losing. Reception was very positive, with reviewers especially praising the sheer number of modes and the quality of both base games, while frequent criticism was aimed at the price and having to sit through a repeated story thread. Today Puyo Puyo Tetris ranks among the best things you can play on a handheld console in short bursts, and at the same time among the toughest competitive puzzle games out there. Anyone who gets used to both rulesets at once ends up with a game that can be played for years while there's still room to improve. For newcomers, it's also nice that either half can be played entirely on its own.
switch__puyo-puyo-tetris.teaser: A crossover of two puzzle classics with completely different logic; great for train rides too.

switch__super-bomberman-r.article:
**Super Bomberman R** was one of the first games available on Switch and marked the return of a franchise that had essentially been dormant for several years. The principle hasn't changed since the eighties: the player moves across a grid, plants bombs that explode into a cross shape after a moment, and tries to catch opponents in the blast before ending up caught in their own trap. Destroying blocks unlocks upgrades, meaning more bombs at once, longer blast range, faster movement speed, or the ability to kick and throw bombs, and gathering that loadout from every match creates an escalating race for the advantage.

The core of the game is battles for up to eight players, playable both locally and online, and this is where the game truly shines. The arenas have their own obstacles, conveyor belts, or teleporters, a round lasts roughly a minute, and once eliminated a player becomes a ghost who can still shoot into the field and return to the game, so nobody just stares at the screen for nothing. Alongside that there's a story campaign with its own bosses and voiced cutscenes, playable in two-player co-op as well, though its difficulty was a frequent target of criticism at launch. Single Joy-Con controls mean that all it takes for a group game is one console and a handful of controllers, which is exactly the scenario Bomberman suits best.

The visuals are clean and colorful, with three-dimensional arenas viewed from above, while the music leans on upbeat, fast-paced tunes including rearranged classic themes from the series. Reception at launch was mixed, with reviewers criticizing the price, the unpolished online mode, and a dull campaign, but Konami kept patching the game long after release and adding characters and modes for free, which noticeably raised its standing. Today Super Bomberman R is a simple but reliable pick when a group gets together and nobody wants to read rules. It also remains one of the few games on the platform where eight people can gather around a single console, and that quality keeps it in the library to this day.
switch__super-bomberman-r.teaser: The brand's return after years of silence; the principle unchanged since the 80s — bombs, grid, explosions.

switch__rocket-league.article:
**Rocket League** is a game whose description sounds like a joke, and yet it's one of the most precisely tuned competitive titles of the last decade: soccer played with rocket-powered cars in an enclosed arena. The rules are trivial, namely get the giant ball into the opponent's goal, and anyone can learn the controls within a minute. Underneath that, though, is a physics model that players spend years learning. The cars can jump, spin in mid-air, bounce off walls and the ceiling, and use collected boost fuel to launch upward and strike the ball out of the air, so the gap between a beginner and an experienced player is enormous, and the game is effectively played in three dimensions.

Matches last five minutes, played in lineups from one-on-one up to three-on-three, and every duel for the ball is also a duel for position, since whoever launches badly leaves their goal empty. Around that core sits extensive car customization, seasonal content, and ranked ladders. The Switch version launched in the console's first year and kept the smoothness that's essential for this game, albeit at the cost of lower resolution and simpler effects. It supports cross-play with other platforms, which significantly extends the lifespan of a competitive title on less powerful hardware, and local multiplayer on a single screen is also included.

The atmosphere rests on simple, clean graphics, explosions on impact, and an electronic soundtrack that keeps the tempo without becoming distracting. After launching in 2015, the game became a phenomenon, moved to a free-to-play model, and built a strong competitive scene with its own tournaments. Today it remains one of the few titles that work just as well as fifteen minutes of couch fun as they do as a discipline you can devote hundreds of hours to, and on Switch it's still always within reach. Crucially, the game has no purchasable content that grants any advantage, so the outcome depends solely on how well someone flies and reads the ball. Landing that first aerial hit, meanwhile, is a moment most players remember.
switch__rocket-league.teaser: Soccer with rocket-powered cars in an enclosed arena; anyone can pick up the controls, mastering the physics takes years.

switch__it-takes-two.article:
**It Takes Two** is a game that can't be played alone, and that's the entire point of it. A couple of parents on the verge of divorce are turned into rag dolls and must fight their way back together, with every step requiring the other player's cooperation. It's played exclusively by two people, either on one screen in split windows or online, and the game shows both halves at all times, so players can see exactly what the other one is doing and when they need to pull a lever or jump.

What makes It Takes Two exceptional is the pace at which it discards old mechanics and introduces new ones. Players have barely gotten used to a pair of abilities before the chapter ends and the next one starts with something entirely different, whether that's a nail and hammer, a magnet and attraction, time manipulation, or flight. Almost every section is built so that one player has the tool and the other has the target, so neither can progress alone. Scattered throughout are dozens of small competitive minigames, from tug-of-war to hockey, serving as a breather. The Switch version arrived later and is technically among the more modest, with lower resolution and softer visuals, but it's content-complete and split-screen works even in handheld mode.

Visually it's a colorful fairy-tale world seen from the perspective of shrunken characters, where a shed or a garden becomes a giant adventure, and the music gives it a cinematic touch. Reception was extremely positive, with the game collecting numerous awards including Game of the Year, and it's often cited as proof that co-op doesn't have to be a mere add-on to a single-player game. The story about a relationship falling apart never feels like an excuse for a string of minigames, since every chapter comments in some way on what's happening between the two leads. Critics especially praised the inventiveness of individual levels and the fact that the game never lets itself repeat the same trick twice. Today it's the most common recommendation for a pair who want to play together, whether that's a couple, friends, or a parent and child, and the second player doesn't even need to own the game.
switch__it-takes-two.teaser: A game that can't be played alone — parents on the verge of divorce turned into rag dolls.

pc-dos__jazz-jackrabbit.article:
**Jazz Jackrabbit** was the PC's answer to fast console platformers and still ranks among the most polished action games ever released for DOS. The hero is a green rabbit armed with an oversized weapon, setting out to rescue a princess kidnapped by the turtle Devan Shell, journeying across planets with wildly different looks, from jungles through icy slopes to mechanical mazes. Unlike most platformers of its time, the game isn't just about jumping between platforms but mainly about shooting: Jazz has several types of ammo, can run at tremendous speed, slide through narrow tunnels, and collect gems that unlock bonus levels. Each episode ends with a boss fight, and the world map between levels gives the whole game a pleasant sense of rhythm.

Technically, the game was a showcase of what a 386 processor with VGA graphics could do. It runs at a smooth pace, uses multi-layered parallax-scrolling backgrounds, large colorful sprites, and a number of effects that had until then been rare on PC. Smooth screen scrolling in particular was the biggest surprise for players of the time, since it was a discipline where home computers had long lagged behind game consoles. The music uses module tracks played through a sound card, mixing energetic, fast themes that suit the breakneck pace perfectly, and even the gunfire sounds carry a pleasantly arcade-like sharpness.

At the time, Jazz Jackrabbit was very well received precisely because it filled a long-empty niche: the PC had shooters and strategy games, but hardly any quality fast platformer. Shareware distribution made it widely known, and a sequel later followed that pushed the whole genre line even further. Today the game feels charmingly over-the-top and colorful; the difficulty at times rests on reflexes and knowledge of level layouts, but the core remains fun and the controls are surprisingly precise. Anyone who wants to see that DOS could do snappy platformers too, and not just dark corridors, should start right here.
pc-dos__jazz-jackrabbit.teaser: PC's answer to fast console platformers; a green rabbit with a giant gun on his back.

pc-dos__jill-of-jungle.article:
**Jill of the Jungle** is a platformer in which the heroine fights her way through intricate jungle levels full of lizards, bats, and spikes, wielding a throwing knife as her main weapon. The game was released as a trilogy of episodes, and its most interesting idea lies in transformation: at certain points, Jill can turn into a frog, a bird, or a fish, and with each form the way she moves changes too. Jumping in frog form, gliding through the air, or swimming underwater isn't just a cosmetic variation — it completely redraws the possibilities for getting through a level. Besides combat, the levels also feature simple puzzles with keys, switches, and moving platforms, so the pace regularly alternates between action and unhurried exploration.

Technically, the game left a pleasantly clean impression. The graphics use bright, richly saturated colors and clearly readable backgrounds, the levels are large enough that you can get lost in them for a while, and the screen scrolling is decently smooth for the standards of the time. The music is simple but catchy and contributes significantly to a slightly fairy-tale atmosphere that sets the game apart from darker action titles of the era. The controls are straightforward and the game doesn't tend to punish the player excessively, though some jumps over spikes require patience and a few extra attempts before you get used to the character's momentum.

Jill of the Jungle was one of the titles with which Epic MegaGames built its reputation on the shareware scene in the first half of the nineties. The first episode circulated freely and served as a hook for the remaining two, a model that worked brilliantly on PC at the time. The reception was warm, mainly thanks to the unconventional heroine and the transformation mechanic, which elevated the game above the average attempts to imitate console platformers. Today it's more of a short nostalgic experience that you'll get through quickly, offering less depth than the publisher's later platformers, but the transformations and the calm jungle mood are exactly what make it a title people remember fondly.
pc-dos__jill-of-jungle.teaser: A shape-shifting platformer - the heroine turns into a frog, a bird, or a fish, changing her way of moving each time.

pc-dos__cosmo-s-cosmic-adventure.article:
**Cosmo's Cosmic Adventure** tells the story of a small alien whose family ship crash-lands on an unknown planet, and when his parents go missing, Cosmo must find them on his own. The core mechanic is suction cups on his hands: Cosmo can cling to vertical walls and climb up them, turning ordinary jumping into a much more interesting spatial puzzle. Enemies are dispatched by jumping on their heads, levels are full of bonuses, hidden rooms, and explosive crates that reveal secret areas. The game is split into three episodes, and its design consistently alternates safer passages with more demanding sections where you need to carefully plan how to actually get upward.

Graphically, this was one of the more attractive titles of its time on PC. The sprites are large, rounded, and expressively animated, the environments burst with saturated colors, and the game noticeably goes beyond what players were used to from DOS platformers. Smooth screen scrolling and carefully drawn backgrounds give the world a pleasant sense of depth, and yet the whole thing runs briskly even on modest hardware. Sound through an Ad Lib card accompanies the adventure with light, almost cartoonish melodies that underscore the game's childlike, gentle tone, even though some levels can be surprisingly tricky and demand good jump timing.

Apogee distributed this game in the usual shareware fashion, with a freely available first episode and paid sequels, and Cosmo became one of its signature titles alongside the publisher's other platformers. At the time it was praised mainly for its graphics and for the wall-climbing idea that set it apart from the rest of the field. Today it's a pleasantly short adventure good for one or two afternoons, delighting mainly with how clean and readable its gameplay is. Anyone who enjoys classic platformers with an emphasis on exploration and finding secret nooks will find exactly what they're looking for here. The short runtime is, if anything, an advantage, since the game never loses pace anywhere.
pc-dos__cosmo-s-cosmic-adventure.teaser: Suction-cup hands for climbing walls turn jumping into a spatial puzzle.

pc-dos__crystal-caves.article:
**Crystal Caves** is a classic cave platformer in which the hero Mylo Steamwitz descends beneath the surface of alien planets to collect precious crystals to fund his own business. Each level has a clear goal: collect all the crystals and find the exit, with the path leading through moving platforms, laser traps, poisonous plants, and alien vermin. Mylo is no warrior — he only carries a simple weapon with limited ammo, so it often pays to go around enemies or use the environment against them instead. Between levels the player moves across a clear map with entrances to individual mines, which gives freedom in choosing the order and a pleasant sense of progress.

Technically the game runs on sixteen-color EGA graphics, which look sharp and contrasty today but were entirely standard at the time and, above all, ran smoothly even on very modest hardware. The screens don't scroll continuously but switch whole-screen by whole-screen, and the level design cleverly uses this so that each screen functions as a small standalone puzzle. The sound is limited to internal-speaker beeps and simple effects, so the atmosphere is carried mainly by the visual style of underground corridors, pipes, and machinery. This very austerity contributes to the game feeling focused and never wasting your time.

Crystal Caves belonged to Apogee's early wave of shareware titles that showed the PC could have its own platformer scene even without game-console hardware. The game was well received mainly thanks to its balanced difficulty and the careful design of individual screens, which rewards thoughtfulness more than fast reflexes. Its influence came especially from being part of the family of games that made Apogee a major publisher of action titles for DOS. Playing it today is a pleasantly old-fashioned yet honest experience: short, clear, and at times surprisingly demanding, especially if you want to collect absolutely everything.
pc-dos__crystal-caves.teaser: Collecting crystals among traps and platforms; the hero has only a weak weapon with limited ammo.

pc-dos__bio-menace.article:
**Bio Menace** puts the player in the boots of agent Snake Logan, who is shot down over a city overrun by mutated monsters and must fight his way out while figuring out who's behind the whole chaos. Compared to most platformers of the era, there's a much heavier emphasis on shooting here: the hero starts with a submachine gun, gradually finds stronger weapons and grenades, and the environment is full of enemies who walk, jump, and attack from range. Besides combat, the levels also involve finding hostages who need to be freed, as well as keys or switches that open further paths. The levels are large and intricate, so exploration plays just as big a role as accurate aim and knowing when it's better to retreat instead.

The game runs on an engine derived from Apogee's earlier platformers, which shows in the smooth scrolling, precise controls, and carefully built levels. Visually, though, it's much grittier than most colorful platformers of the time: the environments are dark, full of green slime and crumbling city sets, and the enemies are drawn with a relish for disgustingly gruesome detail. The Ad Lib or Sound Blaster soundtrack leans into tension and pace, so the overall impression is closer to an action movie than a children's adventure. This gave the game its own niche among PC platformers aimed at an older audience.

Bio Menace came out late in the life cycle of this type of game, at a time when players' attention was already being pulled toward first-person shooters, so its reception wasn't as strong as it deserved. Even so, it's one of the technically best and most enjoyable shooting-focused DOS platformers, and it kept a good reputation within the community. The authors later released it as freeware, which extended its lifespan even further. Today it delights mainly with its large levels, the pleasant weight of its weapons, and a raw atmosphere that feels refreshingly different from most modern platformers. Anyone who enjoys fast side-view shooting won't find a much better choice on DOS.
pc-dos__bio-menace.teaser: A run-and-gun platformer focused on shooting; a submachine gun and grenades instead of jumping.

pc-dos__hocus-pocus.article:
**Hocus Pocus** sends into action an apprentice of a sorcerers' order who must pass a series of trials to be accepted among true masters. The player thus goes through four episodes full of castles, caves, temples, and fantasy landscapes, dispatching skeletons, giant spiders, and other vermin with magic bolts. The core of the gameplay rests on searching: each level requires collecting a certain number of items or finding all the crystals and keys that unlock the exit. Potions, teleport pads, invisibility, and temporary weapon upgrades help along the way, turning the ordinary progression into a pleasant change of pace and rewarding players who search every corner of the map.

Graphically, this is one of the most colorful DOS platformers of its time. The game uses the VGA palette to the full, the backgrounds are detailed and built from several layers, the sprites are cleanly animated, and the whole visual side feels more mature than most cartoonish platformers. The music rests on module tracks with striking fantasy themes that fit the theme of masters and sorcerous trials well and noticeably help the atmosphere. The controls are simple; the hero isn't a particularly acrobatic character, so the game relies more on thoughtfulness and orientation within a level than on demanding jumps over chasms.

The title was released under the Apogee label at a time when the PC platformer market was already saturated and attention was shifting to other genres, yet it found a decent following and is still mentioned among the finer shareware games today. At the time, the graphics and music were praised most, while criticism pointed to the level structure repeating itself over time. Today it's a pleasantly extensive game that lasts several evenings and has a surprisingly good rhythm if you enjoy hunting for collectibles. Anyone who likes fantasy settings and a calmer platformer pace gets exactly what they wish for. Collecting every item and searching for hidden rooms also gives good reason to revisit earlier levels.
pc-dos__hocus-pocus.teaser: Four episodes of castles and temples, where magic projectiles fly instead of head-stomps.

pc-dos__monster-bash.article:
**Monster Bash** is a horror-themed platformer in which young Johnny Dash falls asleep, wakes up in a realm of monsters, and sets out to rescue kidnapped puppies and kittens. The enemies form a whole classic gallery of spooks, from skeletons through mummies and zombies to bats, and the player fends them off with a slingshot whose shots can be upgraded. Besides combat, the game is above all about exploration: the levels hide secret rooms, locked cages with animals, and bonuses tucked behind walls, so thoroughly searching the map matters just as much as reflexes. The layout of graveyards, cellars, and castle corridors is intricate, and the game happily rewards those who try even unconventional paths.

The game uses the same technological lineage as Apogee's other platformers of the time, so it runs smoothly and controls precisely. Visually, though, it stands apart with its dark palette, moonlight, cobwebs, and a wealth of small details that make it one of the most atmospheric DOS platformers. The horror charge is playful rather than truly scary, more in the style of childhood spooky tales. The soundtrack through a sound card uses gloomy themes with a dash of humor, and it's one of the reasons players remember this game so fondly. The slingshot can even fire diagonally upward, which is often the difference between surviving and a sudden end.

Monster Bash came out at a time when other genres were already gaining the upper hand on PC, so it didn't leave as strong a mark in the press of the day as the publisher's more famous titles, but it earned a solid place among shareware fans. Today it's a short yet very distinctive experience whose mood evokes an animated spooky fairy tale more than an action game. The difficulty is pleasantly balanced, the levels can be replayed, and the effort to rescue absolutely every animal gives a reason to come back. For fans of retro platformers, it's one of the best-aged pieces in the genre. Revisiting it, meanwhile, won't take more than one evening.
pc-dos__monster-bash.teaser: A horror platformer with a classic lineup of monsters and an upgradeable slingshot.

pc-dos__another-world.article:
**Another World** begins unusually: a young scientist is struck by lightning during a nighttime particle accelerator experiment and finds himself in a foreign world full of hostile creatures and unknown machines. The game has no introductory text, no tutorial, no indicators — all the storytelling happens through imagery, and the player learns through his own death. The core of the gameplay consists of running, jumping, kicking, and later an energy weapon that can shoot, build a protective barrier, and blast obstacles, turning every encounter into a small tactical puzzle. Progress happens through trial and error, with the player repeating a short section until they understand its correct solution and can execute it precisely.

Visually, this was an utterly exceptional title. Instead of the usual sprites, the game uses vector polygons, so characters and environments are made of shapes that can be smoothly animated and resized. The result feels like a moving comic-book illustration, and despite a very limited color count it manages to convey space, depth, and mood. The animation of the main character is remarkably convincing, and cinematic cuts flow seamlessly into playable sections without any pause. The sound is sparse, often leaving nothing but silence broken by footsteps or a distant roar, which only amplifies the foreignness of the whole world.

Contemporary critics received the game as proof that a video game could tell a mature story without a single word, and its influence is visible throughout the entire line of so-called cinematic platformers, as well as in later games built on atmosphere and wordless storytelling. It's also a title that essentially originated as the work of a single author, which made it a frequently cited example of an auteur game. Today it can be finished within a few hours, and its harsh trial-and-error schooling will put plenty of players off, but its visual power and the boldness of telling a story entirely without dialogue remain extraordinary even decades later. That's exactly why it still appears in surveys of games that pushed the medium forward, and its newer remakes keep arriving on further platforms even after all these years.
pc-dos__another-world.teaser: Without a single word of text; the story is told purely through imagery, and the player's death serves as a teacher.

pc-dos__flashback-quest-for-identity.article:
**Flashback: The Quest for Identity** opens with a hovercraft crash in the jungles of Titan, where the hero Conrad wakes up with no memory, his only clue a recording of his own voice leaving him a message. The game blends precise platforming action with exploration, dialogue, and simple tasks the player completes in cities and laboratories alike. Conrad moves slower and more deliberately than the heroes of arcade jumpers: he crouches, grabs ledges, carefully swings across gaps, draws his pistol, and takes cover behind force fields. It's exactly this weight of movement that creates tension, since every misjudged distance or mistimed jump hurts, and fights are won more often through positioning and anticipation than quick fingers.

Technically, the game builds on the rotoscoped animation the studio was already known for, so every character movement looks remarkably natural. The environments are drawn in fine detail, backgrounds carry their own layers with numerous small animations, and comic-book-style cutscenes tie the individual chapters into a coherent story. On PC the game uses a VGA palette, and later releases add CD audio, though even the floppy disk version holds onto a strong mood thanks to ambient melodies and economical sound effects. The structure is chapter-based, and each part has a different focus, from arena combat to infiltrating an enemy complex.

Flashback was very well received in its time and became one of the most acclaimed European titles of the early nineties, seeing ports to numerous platforms. Its influence can be seen everywhere games lean on realistic character movement, atmospheric sci-fi, and environmental storytelling. Today it demands patience, since the controls are deliberately slower and several passages can prove tricky, but the story of searching for one's own identity, along with the extraordinary animation, still ranks among the best DOS has to offer. It works best when the player takes their time and treats each screen as a small situation to solve.
pc-dos__flashback-quest-for-identity.teaser: A hero without memory, whose only clue is his own recording; his movement is slow and deliberate.

pc-dos__rise-of-triad-dark-war.article:
**Rise of the Triad: Dark War** sends five agents of a secret unit to an island where a cult is preparing an attack on the surrounding city, and before starting the player picks one of the characters, each differing in speed and stamina. The game originally began life as a sequel to an older shooter from the same publisher and grew technically beyond it too, which shows in the level design. The weapons are utterly over the top: alongside pistols and a submachine gun there are rocket launchers, homing missiles, and magical items that temporarily turn the hero into a god or a dog. On top of that come bounce pads, narrow walkways over chasms, moving platforms, and a wealth of traps, making the levels feel far more vertical and playful than the flat corridors of the previous generation.

The engine is an extended version of older technology, but with a host of additions that mask its age: characters move at different heights, there are jump pads, walls of fire, and breakable windows. What stands out most, though, is the gore, since a rocket hit turns an enemy into a shower of flying body parts, and the game clearly plays this for laughs. Digitized guard barks and exaggerated death sounds underline the overall comic-book tone. The title also offered a multiplayer mode with its own rules and modifications, which considerably extended its lifespan among players.

Rise of the Triad arrived at a time when it was already competing against far more modern shooters, so technologically it felt a bit behind, but its sheer inventiveness and over-the-top attitude won it a loyal following that has stuck with it to this day. At the time, reviewers praised the wealth of ideas in the levels and the playful weapons, while criticizing the aging graphics. Today it's one of the most fun old shooters around, because unlike serious modern shooters it never once tries to be realistic, and its chaos is exactly what keeps it alive. Thanks also to a community that still builds custom levels for it, this game hasn't been forgotten in retro circles.
pc-dos__rise-of-triad-dark-war.teaser: A choice of five agents with different speed and stamina; the weapons are utterly over the top.

pc-dos__raptor-call-of-shadows.article:
**Raptor: Call of the Shadows** is a vertically scrolling air shooter in which the player, a mercenary pilot, takes on jobs against corporations and spends the earned cash between missions on new weapons and upgrades for their ship. It's exactly this shopping element that makes the game more than a classic arcade shooter: the player has to weigh whether to invest in a stronger main weapon, a shield, or homing missiles, and every decision shows up in the next mission. The campaign is split into several sectors, each with its own set of levels capped off by a battle against a giant ship or a ground base. Downed enemy craft drop crates with bonuses and cash, so it pays to risk flying into heavier fire.

Technically, this was a very accomplished piece of work. The game runs in VGA mode with a huge number of colorful sprites, the explosions are unusually detailed, and the backgrounds shift from deserts through cities to factory complexes without the pace ever dropping. Sound Blaster audio accompanies the action with fast music and punchy explosion effects that give impacts real weight. At the time of release the game felt like proof that a PC could hold a first-class shooter of this type, a domain that until then had belonged to consoles and arcade cabinets, and it remained one of the few genre representatives to truly succeed on DOS.

Released under the Apogee label with the usual shareware model and a freely available first episode, the game was very well received by players, mainly for combining arcade action with the gradual buildup of one's own ship. It's exactly this purchasing system that gives it a structure keeping players glued to the screen longer than pure arcade action, which is why it's still mentioned among the best PC shooters of its kind. Today it delights with its straightforwardness: you take off, you fly, you shoot, and between missions you treat yourself to the joy of buying stronger gear. The difficulty rises smoothly and the game stays readable and fair. This clarity, plus the pleasure of gradually upgrading your own ship, is exactly why players keep coming back to it even after all these years.
pc-dos__raptor-call-of-shadows.teaser: A vertical shmup where a mercenary pilot buys weapons between missions with money earned in combat.

pc-dos__halloween-harry.article:
**Halloween Harry** is an action platformer about a mercenary called into an underground complex after aliens start turning people into zombies. His main tool is a flamethrower, later joined by other weapons, and above all a jetpack that lets the hero fly for short bursts. It's exactly this flying that changes the whole rhythm of the game: instead of precisely judging jumps, the player hovers above enemies, hunts for a good position, and strafes hordes of zombies from above. The main objective of each level is to find and free captured scientists and lead them to the exit, so besides combat there's also plenty of thorough exploring of sprawling bases full of elevators, pipes, and hidden nooks.

Technically the game ranks among the best of DOS platformers. It runs in a VGA palette, the screen scrolls smoothly, the sprites are large and well animated, and the game uses digitized voice lines and sound effects that give it a peculiar cinematic flair. The environments mix sterile laboratories, frozen storage areas, and organically infested sections, and the flames and explosions rank among the most impressive things the genre had to show on PC. The soundtrack goes for fast, slightly horror-flavored themes that complement the game's crazy tone well, where a serious sci-fi premise meets total over-the-top absurdity.

The game was released under the Apogee label and later also sold under the title Alien Carnage, the name by which many players know it. Reception was very positive, praising in particular the technical execution and the idea of the jetpack, which set it apart from an otherwise similar crowd of platformers. The authors later released it for free, which helped it keep a steady circle of fans. Today it's one of the most enjoyable old DOS action games around, one that requires no compromises: the pace is brisk, the controls are comfortable, and the pleasure of torching zombies with a flamethrower hasn't aged a bit. At the same time it's a good example of where DOS platformers were heading just before the shift to a three-dimensional viewpoint pushed them aside.
pc-dos__halloween-harry.teaser: A flamethrower and a jet pack for short bursts of flight change the pace of this run-and-gun platformer.

pc-dos__disney-s-aladdin.article:
**Disney's Aladdin** is a platformer based on the animated film of the same name and ranks among the best-looking games ever released for DOS. The player moves through the marketplace of Agrabah, the Cave of Wonders, the Sultan's dungeon, and the final palace, using a scimitar for close combat and apples as a throwing weapon. Besides regular jumping, Aladdin swings on ropes, slides down stall awnings, climbs poles, and in one section flees on a magic carpet ahead of rising lava. The levels are full of small secrets, hidden gems, and bonus items, so it pays to move through them more slowly than the pace of the game might suggest.

The main draw is the graphics. The characters are animated using a hand-drawn technique close to film animation, so Aladdin runs, dodges, and fights across hundreds of smoothly connected frames, and the whole thing feels like an interactive cartoon. The backgrounds are colorful and full of detail, from crackling fires to moving crowds, and the PC version makes full use of a VGA palette. The audio side borrows familiar melodies from the film and plays them through a sound card, backed by pronounced sound effects. The game demanded a fairly capable computer by the standards of its time, but the reward was a visual experience the likes of which had barely been seen on PC before.

The title originally started life on consoles and arrived on PC as a port, and for many European players this version became their first encounter with the game. At the time, reviewers praised the graphics and animation, while criticism centered on its relatively short length and on difficulty that was gentler compared to other platformers. Today it holds a reputation as one of the finest movie tie-ins in gaming history, mainly because it didn't settle for simply retelling the plot but offered its own carefully designed action game with immediately readable controls. Visually it remains one of the most charming games to appear on computer screens of its era, and many players remember it exactly for that reason.
pc-dos__disney-s-aladdin.teaser: Visually the most impressive DOS platformer; swinging on ropes, sliding down canvas sails.

pc-dos__titus-fox-to-marrakech-and-back.article:
**Titus the Fox: To Marrakech and Back** is a platformer about a fox who sets off across Europe and North Africa to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend. The gameplay rests on one distinctive feature: the hero can't defeat enemies by jumping on their heads or shooting them, but he can pick up crates, barrels, and all sorts of objects to throw at foes or use as stepping stones. Most levels are therefore, in a sense, spatial puzzles where you need to carry the right object to the right place to reach an otherwise unreachable platform. Add flying enemies, chasms, and time pressure, and the game constantly alternates between thinking and pure action.

Technically it's a typical representative of French production of the era. The graphics are colorful and stylized in a slightly comic-book manner, the settings shift from city streets through desert landscapes to strange dreamlike levels, and the screen scrolls smoothly. The sound is sparser, the game leaning more on effects than a rich musical score, and the controls have noticeable momentum that takes a while to get used to. It's exactly this control responsiveness combined with strict enemy placement that makes Titus the Fox one of the toughest platformers available on DOS.

The game was released on numerous platforms and became one of the signature titles of its European publisher, known for churning out colorful, demanding action games for home computers. At the time it was received with mixed feelings: praised for its inventive object-carrying system, criticized for its unforgiving difficulty and unpleasant enemy placement. Today it's a title for patient players who enjoy old European platformers with a distinctive personality of their own. Anyone who chews through the first levels will find surprisingly cleverly built environments and a game that forces more thought than it seems at first glance. It's exactly this combination of charm and toughness that makes it a title still remembered in Europe with decidedly mixed feelings.
pc-dos__titus-fox-to-marrakech-and-back.teaser: The hero doesn't kill by jumping on heads - instead he throws crates and barrels at enemies.

pc-dos__prehistorik-2.article:
**Prehistorik 2** is a colorful platformer about a prehistoric hunter armed with a club whose only real goal is to eat his fill. The player moves through levels full of dinosaurs, mammoths, insects, and other prehistoric inhabitants, clubbing them and collecting everything edible along the way, from roast chickens to giant cakes. Collecting food isn't just decoration, since it's exactly what makes up the score and the bonuses that decide your progress. Besides regular combat, there are hidden rooms, platforms over chasms, and enemies that need several hits, so the game gradually ramps up and can challenge even experienced players in the later levels.

Visually it's a very pleasant title. The graphics are drawn in a bold cartoonish style with strong colors, the characters are large and easy to read, and the individual worlds are clearly distinct from one another, from green prehistoric plains to caves and snowy regions.
