Today it's one of the most easily digestible old dungeon crawlers: it can be played in half-hour sessions, the map doesn't need to be drawn by hand, and exploring the islands still has a pleasant, addictive rhythm. Besides DOS, the game also made it to consoles and other computers of its era, but the core of the experience remains the same: a huge map and the constant feeling that there's something to find around the next corner.
pc-dos__might-and-magic-iii-isles-of-ter.teaser: The series traded austerity for color here; beneath the fantasy coating hides a sci-fi plot too.

pc-dos__wizardry-vi-bane-of-cosmic-forge.article:
**Wizardry VI: Bane of the Cosmic Forge** is a restart of the legendary series that keeps its uncompromising face while shedding the crutches of its era. A party of six characters enters an abandoned castle where a vanished king and his wizard have left traces leading to an artifact capable of rewriting reality. The whole game takes place within a single sprawling complex that opens up floor by floor, and its story is pieced together from journals, inscriptions, and conversations, not cutscenes. The player has to work out the full plot alone, often only after several returns to already explored parts of the castle.

The system is obsessively deep: a wide selection of races and classes, the ability to change profession mid-game, skills that grow with use, and magic split into several schools with manual control over casting power. Combat is turn-based and merciless, because a badly built party simply won't get past the first floors. Conversations are conducted by typing keywords, so the player has to keep notes as carefully as a map, and the puzzles are among the hardest the genre ever offered; several genuinely require thinking hard about what you've seen and read where. Resting isn't free either, and a badly timed pause can get the party into as much trouble as a lost fight.

Technically it was a noticeable modernization. Drawn monster portraits, an auto-map, and a clearer interface stripped away Wizardry's worst period baggage without simplifying the game. The atmosphere of an empty castle where you meet nothing friendly for a long stretch is dry and oppressive. At the time, the sixth entry was received as a return to form and remains popular among hardcore RPG fans today; a saved character can even be carried over into the sequels, so your party lives on. Today the game demands patience and paper on hand, but whoever adjusts finds one of the most honestly designed dungeons of its time. Also worth noting is how strong the series' standing was in Japan, where it influenced a whole generation of local RPG creators.
pc-dos__wizardry-vi-bane-of-cosmic-forge.teaser: A restart of the legendary series set in a single castle; the story is pieced together from diaries and wall inscriptions.

pc-dos__wizardry-vii-crusaders-of-dark-s.article:
**Wizardry VII: Crusaders of the Dark Savant** expanded the previous entry into a sprawling open world and became one of the most demanding turn-based RPGs PC ever offered. The party lands on the planet Guardia, where several factions and rival adventuring parties race after maps leading to an ancient machine. Crucially, the rivals act on their own: if you're slow, someone else grabs the artifact and the game moves on regardless of your plans. The party from the previous game can be carried over with its equipment, but you can also start completely from scratch.

Exploration happens in first-person, grid-based perspective, but the world isn't just a series of dungeons. There are forests, towns, underground areas, and whole territories you travel between on your own, with no destination marker. Conversations are again conducted via keywords, skills grow with use, and the class system with profession changes allows for building very unusual parties. Combat is turn-based, slow, and deadly; fleeing is often the only sensible tactic. Notes, your own maps, and the ability to endure even after several defeats are a necessity here, not a playstyle choice. The map is also full of places that only make sense much later, so the player learns to come back and try again.

Technically the game built on the sixth entry's engine with nicer scenery and a clearer auto-map, staying restrained musically and in sound. The charm comes more from the texts and the feeling that you're a small group on an alien planet where nobody is waiting for you. At the time the seventh entry was rated highly, though even then it was considered extremely tough and unfriendly to beginners. Its openness and rival factions moving through the world alongside you were unusual for their time and still feel modern today. Today's player has to swallow the pacing and the lack of guidance, but the reward is one of the most liberating RPGs of the nineties. A remade CD version later appeared with voiced dialogue and rougher three-dimensional graphics, but the core of the game remained just as tough.
pc-dos__wizardry-vii-crusaders-of-dark-s.teaser: An open world where rivals act on their own; whoever hesitates loses both the artifact and the pace.

pc-dos__betrayal-at-krondor.article:
**Betrayal at Krondor** is an RPG that wasn't afraid to play at literature. The game is set in the world of Midkemia from Raymond E. Feist's books and is told in nine chapters like a novel: each opens with a text introduction, changes the party's makeup and goals, and takes the player across a vast landscape from coastal towns to mountain passes. The tale of betrayal, elven politics, and a dark mage is unusually mature for the genre and written with a feel for dialogue. The chapters alternate so the player sees events from several sides and gradually pieces together a picture of a much wider conspiracy.

Krondor rests on several clever ideas. Characters have no classic levels; skills improve with use, and the player can flag which abilities they want to train preferentially. Combat is turn-based on a small chessboard-like grid, where weapon reach and positioning matter, and weapons and armor wear out and need upkeep. Chests scattered across the world are locked with word riddles whose clues are wordplay and puzzles, and to this day it's one of the game's most distinctive features. Travel is slow, with camping, healing herbs, and random encounters, which strengthens the feeling of a genuine expedition. Herbs, arrows, and money are limited, so besides combat you're also weighing whether you can afford another night out in the open.

Technically it was an interesting mix: three-dimensional landscape interspersed with digitized character portraits and extensive texts that carry most of the atmosphere. The music is quiet and melancholic and suits reading better than action. At the time the game was highly praised precisely for its story and used to be called one of the best adaptations of fantasy literature into a game. Today it feels slow, but that slowness is deliberate; anyone who likes RPGs with a lot of reading and thinking will find one of the best-written games of the entire decade. The response was such that Krondor's story even got a novelization, and the series received further sequels.
pc-dos__betrayal-at-krondor.teaser: An RPG based on the novels of Raymond E. Feist, told in nine chapters like a book.

pc-dos__lands-of-lore-throne-of-chaos.article:
**Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos** is Westwood's answer to the question of how to make a dungeon crawler accessible without losing its teeth. The player sets out into a kingdom threatened by the sorceress Scotia, who commands shapeshifting powers and is pushing the land toward collapse, and gradually assembles a small party traveling from forests and caves to castles and underground cities. At the start the player picks one of four heroes, who differ in strength, magic, and skills, so each playthrough has a slightly different focus.

The basics are classic: first-person view, grid-based movement, and real-time combat handled by clicking on weapons. But Westwood strips away most of the friction. The auto-map draws itself, the interface is large and readable, the inventory is clear, and the game guides the player clearly through a set sequence of locations you can return to. Puzzles rely more on observation and using the right item than on drawing plans on graph paper, and the steady arrival of new companions keeps the story's pace up even as the dungeons start to stretch out. There are also special items and transformations that change the rules of passage, so the game regularly flips the switch on you.

Visually it's one of the prettiest games of its kind on DOS: detailed VGA environments, boldly animated monsters, and character portraits that react to injury. The CD version also offered spoken dialogue, in which King Richard was voiced by Patrick Stewart, giving the game an unusually professional sheen. The music is melodic and adventurous, miles away from the frozen silence of Eye of the Beholder. At the time the game was praised for its fluency and presentation and founded a series that later headed toward a more action-oriented take. Today Lands of Lore is probably the best choice for someone who wants a taste of an old dungeon crawler without the frustration: it's good-looking, easy to follow, and its pace still holds up after thirty years. The series followed it with two sequels, though neither has quite as pure a fantasy mood as Throne of Chaos.
pc-dos__lands-of-lore-throne-of-chaos.teaser: Westwood's accessible answer to dungeon crawlers; a choice of four distinct heroes.

pc-dos__pool-of-radiance.article:
**Pool of Radiance** was the first computer game built directly on an Advanced Dungeons & Dragons license, and it set the template SSI would follow for its Gold Box titles for several more years. A party of newcomers arrives in the ravaged town of Phlan on the shore of Moonsea and clears it of monsters district by district in order to return it to its people. What starts as ordinary cleanup gradually turns into an investigation pointing toward a far greater threat in the background. The player builds the party from scratch, including races, classes, and attribute distribution, so the first hours are mostly about bare survival.

The game combines three layers. Moving through the town and wilderness happens in first-person, grid-based view; combat unfolds turn-based on an isometric grid where each character has its own movement and action; and part of the story is carried by long texts printed in an accompanying booklet, which the game references by paragraph number. The turn-based battles are its greatest strength: positioning the party, sleep spells, precisely dosed magic, and using chokepoints turn every larger clash into a small tactical puzzle. AD&D's rules are transferred faithfully, including initiative, brutally low starting hit points, and the need to rest to recover spells. Experience is also divided by class, and advancing a level requires a visit to a training hall, not just accumulating points.

Technically the game was modest, with simple scenery and monster portraits; the atmosphere is carried by well-written texts and the feeling that Phlan is genuinely being cleared street by street. At the time it was received excellently and kicked off a whole series of sequels on the same engine, which carried the D&D license through the rest of the eighties and beyond. Today it demands patience with the interface and the pace, but its tactical combat remains enjoyable, and many later games under the same license draw directly from it. A saved party could be carried over into the other Gold Box games, creating an unusually long continuity across the individual titles.
pc-dos__pool-of-radiance.teaser: The first computer game licensed under Advanced Dungeons & Dragons, and the foundation of the whole Gold Box series.

pc-dos__darklands.article:
**Darklands** is one of the most ambitious RPGs of its time and also a game that goes its own way in absolutely everything. Instead of elves and dragons it offers the fifteenth-century Holy Roman Empire as people of the time imagined it: knights, guilds, robber barons, and alongside them witches, alchemy, and demons, because for a medieval person all of that was just as real a part of the world. The party of four characters is created through a biography, with the player choosing individual career stages, resulting in someone with a real past, not just a list of numbers. The characters thus enter the game already aged and experienced, which is reflected in their abilities and in what they can afford.

The game has no main quest in the usual sense. You travel across the empire's map between towns, monasteries, mines, and caves, take on contracts, trade, and gradually unravel a conspiracy the player may or may not choose to pursue. Most situations are resolved through text scenes with several options, where the outcome depends on a combination of skills, reputation, and the chosen tactic. Combat runs in real time with the option to pause; magic takes the form of prayers to saints and alchemical potions that must be mixed from ingredients gathered across the whole empire. Time passes, reputation spreads, and in some towns people are already waiting for you, whether with a job offer or an accusation.

Technically the game bet on drawn screens and a lot of text, giving it the feel of an illustrated chronicle; sound-wise it's restrained, but it does a good job of building tension during a nighttime ambush on the road. At the time Darklands was loved for its ideas and atmosphere, and equally notorious for the number of bugs in its first version, which were only fixed by subsequent patches. Today it feels like a fascinating dead end of the genre: slow, text-heavy, and cluttered, but with a historical setting that has practically never been repeated since. For a player who loves history, it's still one of the few titles where you can spend an evening settling guild disputes and immediately after fighting a supposed demon.
pc-dos__darklands.teaser: A unique RPG without elves or dragons - a medieval realm full of alchemy, guilds, and demons.

pc-dos__wasteland.article:
**Wasteland** is probably the most influential post-apocalyptic RPG ever made, and its trace is still visible today. A party of Desert Rangers heads out into the ravaged American Southwest after a nuclear war to investigate strange signals and incidents, and quickly discovers that something far more organized than mere bandit gangs lies behind the collapse of the settlements. The world is harsh, ironic, and doesn't wait for the player to understand it. The base party is made up of rangers, joined along the way by other characters, though not every one of them is reliable.

The game is remarkable for how little it insists on a single solution. Locked doors can be picked, blown up, or bypassed entirely another way; you can talk to people in the settlements, bribe them, or shoot them, and the game generally takes that into account somehow. Skills like climbing, repair, medicine, or persuasion are used directly on objects and situations, party members can be recruited and lost, and the consequences of decisions get written permanently into the world, so a settlement once destroyed stays destroyed even after reloading a save. Longer descriptions are read in the accompanying booklet, which at the time also served as copy protection while letting the game tell far more than would fit on screen. Unusual approaches are also rewarded with experience, so ingenuity pays off just as much as good aim.

Turn-based combat is simple, but tense thanks to an arsenal ranging from knives to heavy machine guns and thanks to the noticeable vulnerability of characters. The presentation is austere for its time; atmosphere is carried by text and a black humor unafraid to be unpleasant. At the time the game was very successful and became a reference point for the whole genre; when Fallout was made a decade later, it openly acknowledged its debt to it. Today Wasteland demands a willingness to read and to make peace with an archaic interface, but its freedom of approach remains exceptional. It's no accident that the series returned to it years later in the form of new sequels built again on its rules and tone.
pc-dos__wasteland.teaser: The most influential post-apocalyptic RPG ever; the direct spiritual predecessor of Fallout.

pc-dos__ultima-vi-false-prophet.article:
**Ultima VI: The False Prophet** is the entry where the series first turned its own moral question against the player. Britannia is under threat from gargoyles who destroy shrines and abduct people, yet the further the player progresses, the clearer it becomes that these are a civilization with their own script, faith, and prophecy — and that in their story, the Avatar is the one who came to take. Resolving the conflict ultimately can't be done with a sword, but through understanding, an unusual solution for 1990. Key to understanding the other side is also their script, which the player gradually learns to read, and suddenly the inscriptions he's walked past so many times start to make sense.

Technically, Ultima VI unified the world into a single seamless top-down map, with no switching between an overworld map and towns, and it introduced mouse control along with an icon-based action interface. There's a huge number of objects, and most of them can genuinely be used: sacks of flour, barrels, sleds, magic lenses, or dice. Spells are mixed from reagents, townsfolk keep a daily schedule and respond to keywords, and a lot of important information is hidden only in dialogue with side characters. Turn-based combat, by contrast, is more of a hindrance than the game's highlight. The party is made up of familiar faces from the series, each with their own inventory and opinions, and some puzzles hinge precisely on having the right companion on hand.

Visually it was a major leap thanks to the VGA palette, and the music on cards like the Roland or AdLib ranks among the best Origin had composed up to that point. At the time, the sixth installment was well received, though some players missed the more enchanting atmosphere of the earlier tile-based worlds. Today it stands as an interesting middle step between classic and modern Ultima: it already has a simulated world, but not yet its full fluidity. Its central theme — an enemy who has a truth of their own — still works brilliantly. The game was also ported to other systems and remains one of the most frequently discussed entries in the series among fans.
pc-dos__ultima-vi-false-prophet.teaser: For the first time the series turned its own moral question against the player - the gargoyles have their own faith.

pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-blade-of-desti.article:
**Realms of Arkania: Blade of Destiny** is a computer adaptation of the German tabletop system Das Schwarze Auge (The Dark Eye) and ranks among the most detailed RPGs ever released on DOS. A party of six adventurers must find a legendary axe on the northern island of Thorwal before the unified orc tribes crush the local settlements. The main plot is simple, but the road to it is not: it's a long expedition across dozens of towns and villages, where you ask for directions, hire guides, and wait out the weather. The sense of an actual journey matters here more than narrative momentum, and the game makes no secret of it.

The system's level of detail is both the main attraction and the main obstacle. Characters have a wide range of attributes and skills, and rolls are made for practically everything, from swimming and climbing to cooking and haggling, while on the road you have to keep track of food, water, illness, broken bones, and whether the party has anywhere to sleep. Random events during travel are written as short text scenes with several choices, and they can delay the expedition just as easily as help it. Combat is turn-based on a grid and slow, but it's faithfully tied to the source rulebook's rules, including the harsh consequences of injury. Individual characters can also have their own personality quirks that complicate dealings with others at inopportune moments.

Technically, the game combines a world map, first-person dungeon views, and drawn town screens; the overall impression is rather sober and cold, which suits the northern setting well. At the time it was praised for its depth and faithfulness to the source material, but criticized for its pacing and for bugs that, for this first entry in the series, only got patched afterward. Today it's a game for the patient: anyone who enjoys a travel simulation where the real protagonists are logistics, supplies, and bad weather will find here one of the few titles that takes this completely seriously. Blade of Destiny was followed by two more sequels that expanded the system further, and the first installment eventually received a modern remake years later.
pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-blade-of-desti.teaser: An adaptation of the German Das Schwarze Auge; among the most detailed RPGs ever released on DOS.

pc-dos__ravenloft-strahd-s-possession.article:
**Ravenloft: Strahd's Possession** brought the darkest Dungeons & Dragons setting to PC as a gothic first-person dungeon crawler. A party is pulled into Barovia, a land sealed off by mist and ruled by the vampire Strahd von Zarovich, and must find a way out — if one exists at all. Compared to its heroic-fantasy competitors, the tone is considerably grimmer: villages are depopulated, the inhabitants terrified, and the game takes great care to never let the player feel safe. The party also doesn't arrive in Barovia by choice, which gives the whole expedition a different flavor than the usual treasure hunt.

Movement is grid-based but fluid, with the ability to turn and look around, and combat runs in real time. The system follows AD&D rules with characters, spells, and items, to which Ravenloft adds its own dread-laced logic: holy symbols, garlic, curses, and monsters like werewolves, mummies, or golems, whose defeat often depends on finding what can actually harm them. The settings alternate between crypts, decaying manors, catacombs, and Castle Ravenloft itself, and the game offers several endings depending on how the player behaves along the way. Working with items and information from the locals matters too, since without the right advice you simply won't reach certain places.

Technically it was a decent, if not groundbreaking, engine; its strength lies in the lighting and color palette, which turn the corridors into oppressive, murky spaces. The sound design works with screams, creaking, and silence, while the music surfaces mostly at key moments, hitting all the harder for it. At the time, the game received more mixed reviews than the genre's absolute top titles, but few denied it had atmosphere. Today it's mainly of interest to horror and D&D lore fans: technically it has aged worse than Eye of the Beholder, yet the oppressive mood of Barovia and the presence of Strahd, who reminds you of himself from time to time, still hold up. DreamForge followed it with another entry set in the same world, and its signature style of dark, slow-paced dungeons is recognizable in their later games as well.
pc-dos__ravenloft-strahd-s-possession.teaser: A gothic dungeon crawler in D&D's darkest setting - the misty Barovia ruled by the vampire Strahd.

pc-dos__master-of-orion.article:
**Master of Orion** is a turn-based space strategy game that defined the term 4X — explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate — for an entire generation of players. The player picks one of a dozen alien races, each with different aptitudes for research, industry, diplomacy, or combat, and starts with a single home planet in the middle of a randomly generated galaxy. From there begins a slow but immensely addictive empire-building process: scout ships search for habitable worlds, colonists settle planets with varying atmospheres and gravity, population shifts between star systems, and on each planet sliders divide production between factories, defense, ecology, shipyards, and research. Those sliders are a brilliantly simple interface that carries an entire empire's economy without a single extra spreadsheet.

The technology tree is designed so that you never unlock everything in any given category, and some discoveries are permanently lost to you. Two playthroughs with the same race therefore look different, giving technology trading, espionage, and diplomacy real purpose. The system's crowning feature is the ship editor, where unlocked components are assembled into a custom vessel class, from a small fast fighter to a giant battleship packed with shields and missiles. Battles play out on a turn-based field where range, speed, armor, and the ability to survive the first salvo all matter. Presiding over all of it is a galactic senate that votes on the ruler of the galaxy, meaning victory can also be achieved through pure diplomacy and patient alliance-building.

Technically, it's a typical DOS strategy game of its era: clean VGA graphics with striking alien portraits, mouse control, and music that plays more to atmosphere than for effect. That restraint is actually a strength, since nothing distracts from the numbers and the decisions. At the time, Master of Orion was received as one of the pinnacles of the genre, and its influence can be seen in most later space 4X games. Today it feels surprisingly fresh — you'll grasp the rules within a single playthrough, and the eternal 'just one more turn' works exactly the same as it did thirty years ago.
pc-dos__master-of-orion.teaser: A space turn-based strategy game that defined the term 4X for an entire generation: explore, expand, exploit.

pc-dos__master-of-magic.article:
**Master of Magic** took the skeleton of the space 4X genre and transplanted it into a fantasy world, where rival wizards fight for dominance over two interconnected planes of reality. Before starting a game, the player builds their own mage: distributing points among five books of magic, adding special abilities like alchemy or an innate gift for spellcasting, and picking the race to start with. Each race has its own buildings, units, and temperament, so dwarves play completely differently from elves, lizardmen, or dark orcs. The player then founds cities, builds walls and temples, explores the map, and stumbles upon ruins and towers full of monsters guarding treasure and magic items.

Magic is the heart of the game. Spells are researched from books and cast in combat, on the strategic map, and against rivals, with the most powerful ones changing the rules of the entire game. Added to this is the world's second plane, the harsh and dangerous Myrror, reachable only through special gates, offering better resources at the price of tougher enemies. Battles take place on a tactical field where units of several figures each face off, with terrain, morale, and heroes all mattering — heroes who can be recruited, equipped with forged items, and gradually improved. The combination of empire building, artifact collecting, and hero-party development gives the game a depth that no one managed to replicate for a long time.

Technically, it was a solid DOS production with colorful VGA graphics, a clear interface, and music that keeps a fairy-tale mood running beneath the calm empire-building. The game did, however, have a rocky launch due to bugs that only later patched versions gradually cleaned up. Even so, it won an exceptionally devoted audience, and a community still exists today that tunes and expands it with its own mods. Anyone who enjoys turn-based strategy with an emphasis on spellcasting and exploration will find in Master of Magic a title that, even decades later, offers more possibilities than most of its successors.
pc-dos__master-of-magic.teaser: The skeleton of a space 4X transplanted into fantasy; at the start you build your own wizard.

pc-dos__sid-meier-s-railroad-tycoon.article:
**Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon** cast the player as a nineteenth-century railroad magnate and in doing so founded an entire branch of building games still called "tycoons" today. You start with borrowed capital, an empty map, and a single decision: where to build your first station. Track is laid tile by tile across hills, rivers, and forests, every stretch costs money, and every steep grade slows the train down. Stations have different reach, and only once a town, mine, or farm falls within their radius does cargo start accumulating there that's actually worth hauling somewhere.

Out of this grows a surprisingly rich economic game. Raw materials only turn into goods at the appropriate industries, so coal and iron gain value only at the steel mill and cattle only at the slaughterhouse, and the player hunts for profitable town pairs worth connecting with a line. Add to that train scheduling, choosing locomotives that grow stronger and faster over time, building sidings and signals so trains don't block each other, and finally the stock market. Shares of your own company and of competitors can be bought, borrowed against, and, with a bit of nerve, used to take a rival over completely. Every map also runs in real time, which can be sped up or paused, so play switches between calm planning and tense watching to see whether a train will arrive on time.

On DOS, it was a very readable game: a map with clean, colorful graphics, smooth controls, and understated sound effects, where the strongest impression comes from a locomotive's whistle and the announcement that a line has been completed. At the time, the title was praised for how easily it drew players in and how deep it let them fall, and its legacy lives on in later installments and a whole host of imitators, including transport simulators. Today it still delights mainly because it emphasizes clever network planning over quick reflexes, and a single game can easily swallow a whole evening. It helps that the player can choose both the map and the historical period, and try out how differently railroads get built in mountainous Europe versus on the open American plains.
pc-dos__sid-meier-s-railroad-tycoon.teaser: It founded the genre of building games known as tycoons; you build a 19th-century railroad empire.

pc-dos__sid-meier-s-colonization.article:
**Sid Meier's Colonization** transports turn-based strategy to the age of the early modern colonization of the Americas, setting the player a task that differs from typical conquest games: the goal isn't to dominate the map, but to lead your own colonies to a declaration of independence and defend it against the mother country's army. The player picks one of four European powers, each with different advantages in trade, combat, or dealing with the native population, sets sail with a single ship, and founds the first settlement on an unfamiliar coast.

The game's focus is on production chains. A colonist placed on a forest tile harvests wood, another turns it into tools in a workshop, cotton becomes cloth, tobacco becomes cigars, and sugar becomes rum. Goods are then shipped to Europe, where their price fluctuates with supply, or traded with native villages and colonies of other nations. Settlers can be trained into specialists, part of the population works as politicians producing liberty bells that attract prominent figures with permanent bonuses to the Continental Congress. The more patriotism a colony builds up, the higher the taxes and the larger the army sent across the ocean, so declaring independence is a decision planned dozens of turns in advance. The military side is simple but ruthlessly unforgiving, since only a well-fortified and well-supplied settlement can withstand trained regular troops.

Technically, the game follows the look and controls of the original Civilization: a clear bird's-eye map, extensive advisors, and plenty of table-filled windows that nonetheless stay readable. The music is understated and period-appropriate; the atmosphere is carried more by the slow uncovering of the continent and the growing network of towns. At the time, Colonization was received as Civilization's more demanding, more distinctive sister, and it still has a loyal audience today that appreciates its emphasis on economics. Anyone who enjoys production optimization and long games with a clear climax will find here one of the best-designed strategy titles of its era.
pc-dos__sid-meier-s-colonization.teaser: A turn-based colonization strategy where the goal isn't to conquer the map but to declare independence.

pc-dos__panzer-general.article:
**Panzer General** achieved what hex-based wargames had been attempting for years: turning slow, complicated World War II simulations into fun you can grasp during the first mission and won't stop playing until sometime after midnight. The player commands German forces across a war campaign that starts in Poland and, depending on individual battle outcomes, branches into different scenarios. Every map has an objective, a time limit, and a number of turns within which key cities or mountain passes must be captured, otherwise the advance stalls and the campaign veers elsewhere.

The core of the game is the system of so-called core units. Divisions the player buys with prestige points accompany him through the entire campaign, gain experience, become more accurate and resilient, and can be re-equipped with more modern technology as research progresses. Losing a battle-hardened tank battalion therefore hurts far more than losing freshly conscripted infantry. Combat takes place on a hex map, where terrain, weather, supply, and above all weapon combination all matter, since tanks without infantry and artillery support bleed out in cities, and without fighter cover the advance is slow. Prestige is also spent on repairs and replenishing losses, so every turn is simultaneously a budgeting decision.

Technically, it was a very pleasant DOS game, controlled entirely with the mouse, with a clean VGA map, easy-to-read unit icons, and period photographs and film clips between missions that give the campaign momentum. The music is spare and march-like; the atmosphere is carried more by combat sounds and battle-result reports. Panzer General became the most successful title in its line, launched an entire series of "General" games in other eras and settings, and its veteran-unit system was adopted by many later turn-based games. Today it's the easiest entry point into the world of wargames — the rules fit into a few paragraphs, yet it still offers plenty of room for tactics.
pc-dos__panzer-general.teaser: It achieved what had failed for years - turning a complex hex wargame into an all-night obsession.

pc-dos__populous.article:
**Populous** is the game that invented the entire god-game genre and remains its purest expression to this day. The player is neither an army commander nor a mayor, but a deity who cares for its believers indirectly: it cannot order them where exactly to go, but it can reshape the world beneath their feet. By raising and lowering terrain, the player creates flat areas on which bigger, richer houses grow, and the bigger the houses, the faster the population grows and the more divine mana the player gains. An opposing deity with the same abilities stands in the way, so every map becomes a race to see who can turn the wilderness into a tidy plain faster.

Saved-up mana is spent on miracles. It starts with swamps that swallow enemy walkers, continues through earthquakes, volcanoes and floods, and ends with the apocalypse, which forces both sides into a final battle. A special place belongs to the papal magnet, with which the player designates a rallying point for their believers and picks a leader who guides the others into battle. Battles resolve themselves, the outcome decided by the number and strength of units, so the real game happens in the preparation phase, where you decide whether to invest in growth or dig a chasm under your rival's feet instead. Hundreds of levels with different worlds and difficulty settings ensured the game lasted a very long time.

On DOS, Populous was ported from home computers and looks understated, the isometric map is simple but clear and handles large numbers of little figures at once. The sound is sparser than on the Amiga, but the atmosphere is carried mainly by the ant-like swarming of believers, which is hypnotic even today. The game was received enthusiastically at the time and became studio Bullfrog's first major success, and its principle was followed up by a whole string of titles from Powermonger through Black & White to modern imitators. Anyone who fires it up today will understand within minutes why thinking through the environment instead of through orders caught on so quickly.
pc-dos__populous.teaser: The game that invented the god-game genre; you shape the terrain and help your believers.

pc-dos__powermonger.article:
**Powermonger** carries on the ideas of Populous but swaps the divine perspective for the role of a warlord without a land of his own. The player finds himself at the edge of a divided world, and his task is to gradually conquer one territory after another until no one is left to oppose him. Each map is a small region with villages, forests, sheep and headstrong inhabitants who have their own names, allegiances and occupations. No one here is just a token: the blacksmith can forge weapons, the fisherman brings food, and the farmer can be recruited into the army.

Orders are given through dispatched captains and a handful of basic commands: occupy a village, recruit, plunder, produce, attack. Everything else happens on its own, and the player watches his unit move across the countryside, watches supplies dwindle, and watches the mood of the inhabitants shift depending on whether he arrived as a liberator or a marauder. Food plays a key role, since a hungry army loses strength and scatters, so conquest is also a logistics problem. Inventions such as bows, catapults or ships gradually unlock and shift the balance of power. The whole landscape is rendered in a rotatable, tiltable isometric perspective that can be zoomed all the way down to individual characters, which was an impressive technical showcase in the early nineties.

The DOS version kept this fluid three-dimensional map along with a wealth of statistics on every inhabitant, but the controls are dense and the game makes no real effort to hold the player's hand. The sound design is restrained, and the atmosphere rests on a quiet, cold Middle Ages where wars are fought over sheep and bread. At the time, Powermonger was seen as an ambitious and technically inventive title that foreshadowed later real-time strategy games with a focus on supply lines. Today it demands patience and a willingness to learn its language, but the reward is a strategy game that, even after all these years, feels unusual and distinctive.
pc-dos__powermonger.teaser: Populous's successor, cast as a warlord; every inhabitant has their own name and occupation.

pc-dos__syndicate.article:
**Syndicate** is a cold cyberpunk work in which the player leads neither an army nor plays a hero, but instead runs four cybernetically enhanced agents from a skyscraper office and expands the reach of his corporation across the entire world. The world map is divided into territories that are conquered mission by mission, and every controlled territory pays a tax that funds research and equipment. The mission objectives are described curtly and dirtily: assassinate a rival scientist, kidnap a researcher, incite an uprising, or wipe out an entire enemy cell.

The action itself plays out in an isometric city full of billboards, cars, elevators and utterly indifferent pedestrians. The four agents can be split up or kept together, each can be assigned a weapon individually, and three sliders for addictive substances can be switched on, boosting perception, accuracy and endurance at the cost of faster exhaustion. A key tool is the Persuadertron, a device with which an agent subjugates civilians and enemy soldiers alike, turning them into an obedient escort, so that by the final mission you can walk in with an entire crowd of your own. Between missions, the lab researches better limb prosthetics, eyes and weapons ranging from shotguns to guided missiles, and the money earned is split between research and team equipment.

Technically, this was a very impressive game in 1993: the city is rendered in a dark, rainy palette, things explode and burn, and the whole screen can be rotated and zoomed. The music and sound effects create a stifling, depersonalized atmosphere in which violence is a routine business operation, which is one reason the title belongs in the hands of adult players. At the time, Syndicate earned great acclaim for its world and for its nerve in letting the player play the worse side, and its influence can be felt in later tactical games with small squads. Today the controls are clunky in places and the missions repeat toward the end, but the mood of that cold corporate world has aged remarkably well, and few later games have managed to replicate it.
pc-dos__syndicate.teaser: A cold cyberpunk game in which you control four cybernetically enhanced corporate agents.

pc-dos__transport-tycoon.article:
**Transport Tycoon** is a game about turning an empty landscape into a working transport network, and it ranks among the most addictive building games ever released on DOS. The player founds a transport company in a year of their own choosing and has four modes of transport at their disposal: railways, road vehicles, ships and aircraft. The map is dotted with towns, mines, forests, refineries and power plants that produce and consume various goods, and the task is to find profitable pairs and connect them as cheaply and quickly as possible.

The heart of the game is track building. Rails are laid by hand, embankments, bridges and tunnels are constructed, every curve slows a train down, and every badly placed signal causes a jam that the player only notices once revenue starts dropping. It's precisely the work with signals, junctions and multi-level crossings that turns the game into a construction toy in its own right, one that some players tinker with for hours regardless of profit. The economy, meanwhile, is unforgiving: cargo loses value the longer it spends in transit, a station without regular service stops producing, and towns only grow where transport actually works. Years pass, faster locomotives and more modern aircraft appear, and older technology stops paying off, so the network must be continually rebuilt. Meanwhile, rival companies grab the best routes.

Technically, the game impresses with isometric graphics packed with detail, smooth scrolling even on period computers, and sounds that make the map feel like a living place. The music, in the form of calm jazz tunes, became one of the series' hallmarks. At the time, Transport Tycoon was very well received, an expanded Deluxe version soon followed, and the game earned such a loyal community that an open-source successor was built on its foundation and remains alive to this day. That's exactly why it's worth returning to without hesitation: its design has barely aged at all, and it still offers that rare feeling of chaos gradually turning, line by line, into a machine that runs by itself.
pc-dos__transport-tycoon.teaser: An addictive DOS building game; you build a network of trains, trucks, ships, and planes.

pc-dos__theme-park.article:
**Theme Park** cast the player as the owner of an amusement park and showed that a building game doesn't have to be about cities or war, but about getting as much money as possible out of visitors while still sending them home happy. It starts with an empty plot, a small budget and a handful of basic rides. Roller coasters, carousels, haunted houses and, above all, paths gradually get added, and paths have to lead visitors exactly where the player wants, since crowds behave according to whatever you build in their way.

The economic layer is superb. The player sets ticket prices as well as prices for individual rides, hires janitors, mechanics, entertainers and security, negotiates wages with unions, and buys supplies on a commodities exchange. The game's best-known trick is the option to adjust the amount of salt in the fries and sugar in the soda, since salty food drives visitors toward the drink stands, but overly seasoned snacks make them sick right on the roller coaster. Research unlocks better rides and faster maintenance, and roller coasters let you design your own track and set the cart's speed, which is both great fun and a fine way to bankrupt your park. Once a park is thriving, it can be sold off and you can start over on a pricier, more demanding plot elsewhere in the world.

Technically, this was a typical Bullfrog game: colorful isometric graphics, an enormous number of small animations and sounds, from carousel music to a visitor throwing up after overeating. It's exactly that humor and exaggeration that hold the whole atmosphere together; the game never takes itself too seriously. At the time, Theme Park was very successful and is still regarded today as the forerunner of an entire wave of amusement park management sims. Anyone who fires it up today will find a game with a surprisingly deep economy, one that can also be played as a calm sandbox where it's enough to build paths and watch the crowds swarm between the rides. It's precisely the difficulty settings, which switch parts of the managerial worries on and off, that make Theme Park a game suited both to complete beginners and to number-crunchers.
pc-dos__theme-park.teaser: A theme park building game where the main goal is squeezing money out of visitors.

pc-dos__caesar.article:
**Caesar** is a building strategy game in which the player founds a Roman city in a newly conquered province and tries to keep its population happy, its treasury full, and the barbarians at bay. The game is split into two layers. On the provincial map, decisions concern the development of the whole region, its roads, trade with neighbors and military campaigns, while the city portion is a classic building game where, tile by tile, a network of streets, houses, wells, baths, temples and theaters takes shape.

A properly built city is an organism. Dwellings transform on their own from shacks into decent houses and eventually into villas, but only if they have access to water, food, safety and entertainment, so placing services correctly is the game's main puzzle. Warehouses, markets and workshops need to be built for this, tax collection must be watched, and care must be taken that dissatisfied citizens don't abandon the city. The other half of the game is defense. Barbarians come from the edges of the map, and the city needs walls, towers and a garrison that can be reinforced with hired troops, and sometimes it's necessary to march out into the field even beyond your own territory. Success is measured by career advancement within the Roman administration, so the player moves from smaller provinces to richer, more demanding ones.

Technically, Caesar is restrained: a clear bird's-eye map, iconic interface elements, and music that tries to evoke an antique mood without heavy pathos. The game's charm lies in watching a handful of houses gradually become a sprawling city with a forum and aqueducts. At the time, it was one of the first successful city builders with a historical theme, and the series continued with further installments, the third of which in particular influenced the entire genre of antique city builders. Today the first Caesar is more of a historical document, but it has its own calm and clarity that later, far more complex games never managed to replicate. Anyone wanting to see where antique city building on computers began will find here a surprisingly playable and still legible foundation for everything that came after.
pc-dos__caesar.teaser: A building strategy game about a Roman province; played on two levels - region and city.

pc-dos__lords-of-realm.article:
**Lords of the Realm** combines medieval estate management with conquest and turns it into an unusually honest game about the idea that whoever can feed an army wins the war. England is divided into counties, and the player starts with one of them. Each turn represents a season, and in it the player assigns subjects between working the fields, raising livestock, cutting wood and quarrying stone, mining, and armed service. Assign people badly, and winter brings famine, the population shrinks or moves elsewhere, and contentment drops so far that resentment against the lord rises.

The economic side is surprisingly detailed: fields are sown with grain, meadows serve as pasture for cattle, surpluses are bought and sold at market, and every decision only shows its effect months later. Only on top of this foundation is an army built. Weapons are forged from your own iron, soldiers are drawn from the workforce, so every peasant conscripted is missing from the fields. Castles are built from prepared plans, their cost measured in stone, timber and time, and they give defenders a decisive advantage. Battles play out on a separate screen, where units of archers, pikemen and knights face off against one another, with terrain and morale mattering, and sieges can be resolved through starvation, bombardment of the walls, or a direct assault. Diplomacy with other lords is brief and usually doesn't hold for long.

Technically, this is a pleasant DOS game with painted graphics, clear tables and calm medieval music that nicely underscores the changing of the seasons. The atmosphere is civilian; the game thinks more about granaries and herds than about heroics. At the time, the title was praised precisely for linking economy with warfare, and it became the foundation of a series that continued with further installments. Today it will please players who enjoy a slower pace, clear rules, and the feeling that every battle was already won years before it began, somewhere in a field by a granary, rather than only in the moment the armies clashed beneath the walls.
pc-dos__lords-of-realm.teaser: It combines managing a medieval estate with conquest; the war is won by whoever can feed their army.

pc-dos__battle-isle.article:
**Battle Isle** is a turn-based war game set in a stark sci-fi world that took the clarity of tabletop wargames and added several ideas that set it apart from everything else. Combat takes place on a grid of hexagons where tanks, infantry, artillery, helicopters and ships face off, each unit type having its own range, mobility and effectiveness against the others. Maps are designed as puzzles, and the goal is usually to seize factories and energy fields that supply resources and allow units to be replenished right in the middle of a battle.

The most interesting element is the way turns are resolved. The player first issues orders to all their units, and only then does the entire turn play out at once, so planning happens with the awareness that the opponent is preparing something at this very moment too. On top of that comes an emphasis on fuel and ammunition supply: once a unit runs out of supplies, it becomes a helpless target. Battles are replayed on a special screen showing the machines charging at each other, giving an otherwise abstract game a pleasant bit of flavor. The game was also designed with two players in mind, sharing one computer or two linked machines, which made it a popular social activity back before networks were widespread.

The DOS version took over colorful graphics with bold unit icons and technical music from home computers, fitting well with the cold military tone. The interface is dense but becomes fully clear after a few maps, and the difficulty ramps up briskly. At the time, Battle Isle was seen as a fresh and accomplished contribution to turn-based strategy and founded a series that continued with several sequels and expansions. Today it's a pleasant game for short sessions, since individual maps are self-contained puzzles that can be solved in a single evening, and the combat system has aged considerably better than most of its contemporaries. It helps, too, that the game never punishes slow deliberation and rewards care rather than speed.
pc-dos__battle-isle.teaser: A turn-based war game in a stark sci-fi guise; the hex maps are elaborate puzzles.

pc-dos__warlords-ii.article:
**Warlords II** is a turn-based fantasy strategy game built on a simple yet remarkably addictive foundation: the map is dotted with cities, each city produces a certain type of unit, and whoever controls more cities fields a bigger army. The player leads one of eight warring factions, from human knights through orcs to dark lords, and the goal is to gradually conquer the entire land. Production can be upgraded in every city, so a flimsy garrison grows into heavy infantry or even dragon riders after a few turns, and deciding where and what to invest in decides the whole match.

On top of plain conquest lie several layers that give the game its depth. Heroes are hired for gold, carry magic items, raise the combat value of the whole stack, and can set out to explore ruins and tombs where treasures and monsters alike await. Some cities and temples offer alliances with special creatures, other rulers can be talked into a truce or, conversely, provoked. Combat is resolved automatically based on the strength of both sides, the terrain, and the presence of heroes, so the game's center of gravity lies in movement across the map, guarding supply routes, and making sure conquered cities aren't left undefended. The whole system is clear enough that matches move quickly, yet varied enough that no two are alike.

Technically it was a restrained but very polished DOS game with a clear map, unit icons, and simple mouse control. It also shipped with a map and scenario editor, which spawned countless player-made worlds. Especially popular was the option to take turns on a single computer with multiple players, which turned Warlords II into a classic of gaming get-togethers. At the time it was hailed as one of the best turn-based strategy games of its era, and its legacy can be traced in later fantasy strategy titles. Today it can be recommended to anyone who wants to see what perfectly tuned minimalism looks like.
pc-dos__warlords-ii.teaser: A turn-based fantasy strategy game with an addictive principle: whoever controls more cities has a bigger army.

pc-dos__ancient-art-of-war.article:
**The Ancient Art of War** is one of the oldest games that can be considered a forerunner of real-time strategy, and it arrived on personal computers at a time when most strategy games were still strictly turn-based. The player commands several units on a map of the land, with units moving fluidly through time, although the game can be paused at any moment to issue new orders. The goal is usually to destroy enemy forces, capture their base, or seize a flag, and to do so the player must cleverly use terrain, mountain passes, bridges, and march length.

Units consist of three types of fighters. Knights are strong in direct combat, archers strike from a distance, and barbarians move quickly and are suited to ambushes, with each type holding an advantage over another, creating a simple but functional combat triangle. Soldiers grow tired and hungry and need supplying, so a long march through the mountains can weaken an army more than losses in battle. When two units meet, the game switches to a side-view battle screen, where the player arranges individual ranks and watches how the clash unfolds. The whole game is interspersed with quotes from Sun Tzu's Art of War, which frame the individual scenarios and at the same time hint to the player how to think.

Technically it was, for its time, an impressive title with a clear, though very sparse, color palette and sound limited by the capabilities of computers of the era, relying all the more on its concept and clear design. It also shipped with an editor in which players could create their own maps and scenarios. At the time the game earned praise and received sequels set in naval and medieval settings. Today it's interesting above all as evidence of how early someone came up with the idea of commanding armies in real time, and its basic ideas returned in a considerably richer form a decade later. The matches themselves are short and tight, so even today's player can finish one scenario in a few dozen minutes and understand why the game received so much attention back then.
pc-dos__ancient-art-of-war.teaser: One of the first games foreshadowing real-time strategy; it was released as early as 1984.

pc-dos__wing-commander.article:
**Wing Commander** brought something to the PC in 1990 that no one had tried before: a space fighter game that didn't feel like a technical manual but like a war film. The player boards the carrier Tiger's Claw as a fresh Confederation pilot and flies out into battles against the feline Kilrathi race. Individual missions consist of navigation points, escorts, reconnaissance, and sharp dogfights, but around them is built an entire campaign structure: depending on how you perform, the campaign branches into a better or worse variant, the mood aboard ship changes, and so does who from your squadron survives to the next deployment.

Combat runs on a simple but extremely readable model. The fighters behave more like World War Two aircraft than objects in zero gravity, and that's exactly what makes the dogfights so understandable even to a player who never opened the manual. Each craft has a different combination of armor, shields, speed, and weapons, so the choice of mission and wingman carries weight. Between flights you visit the ship's bar, listen to stories, and watch anonymous names turn into characters players come to care about. Technically it was a showcase for the computers of the time: a full VGA palette, scaled bitmap graphics, digitized sound, and music that reacted continuously to what was happening in combat.

At the time the game was seen as proof that the PC had caught up with, and in many ways overtaken, the Amiga and the consoles of the era, and it launched one of the most important series of the nineties. Wing Commander's influence can be felt wherever space action meets storytelling, from later space sims to modern attempts to revive them. Today the game feels archaic in its controls and in how demanding it was on period hardware, but its pacing, music, and the sense of belonging to a squadron still work. Anyone who wants to understand why such a cult formed around space simulators should start right here.
pc-dos__wing-commander.teaser: A space fighter game that in 1990 felt like a war movie, not a manual.

pc-dos__star-wars-x-wing.article:
**Star Wars: X-Wing** was the first major attempt to put the player in the cockpit of a Rebel fighter in a way that wasn't arcade-like but a genuine space simulator. The campaign takes a pilot from training flights in the simulator through escort and reconnaissance missions all the way to the attack on the Death Star, and along the way offers three craft with very different characters: the nimble A-wing, the versatile X-wing, and the slow but sturdy Y-wing. The key to survival is managing power, that is, shifting output between engines, shields, and lasers, as well as redirecting shields forward or backward depending on where the enemy is attacking from.

Missions aren't just shooting galleries. The game works with convoys, checkpoints, transports that must be protected, and hyperspace jump timing, so failure often doesn't come from being shot down but from failing to complete the main objective in time. Technically the game ran on full polygons, which at the time allowed smooth ship rotation and readable dogfights even on ordinary machines with a 386 or 486 processor. The audio side was carried by the iMUSE system, thanks to which the music continuously reacted to what was happening around the player. A strafing run, a hull hit, and a victorious flyaway each had their own musical motif, and the atmosphere of the film source gained enormously from it.

At the time X-Wing became one of the standout titles of its year and set the bar for licensed Star Wars games. It established the idea that a simulator could also be a dramatic story-driven game without sacrificing the depth of its systems. Today the game is tough, missions repeat here and there, in-flight saving options were limited, and the difficulty of some deployments is merciless, but the cockpit, the engine sound, and the tension of escorting a defenseless transport still work. For fans of space simulators it's a mandatory stop and at the same time the best introduction to what came from the same team a year later. It also helps that the game was later released in expanded versions with additional campaigns that added dozens of missions and new situations, so there's plenty of content here for a long time.
pc-dos__star-wars-x-wing.teaser: The first honest Star Wars space simulator; three fighters with completely different flight characteristics.

pc-dos__star-wars-tie-fighter.article:
**Star Wars: TIE Fighter** flipped the perspective and put the player in an Imperial fighter, a craft without shields, without a hyperdrive, and with armor that can take only a few hits. It's precisely this fragility that changes the whole style of the game. While a Rebel pilot could withstand a strafing run and pull back, an Imperial pilot must dodge, attack from favorable angles, and rely on speed. As the campaigns progress, stronger craft are unlocked, from the TIE Bomber through the heavy TIE Advanced to models with shields, so the game smoothly transitions from pure survival to the role of an elite pilot with full equipment.

The missions are noticeably more varied than in the previous game. Besides combat, players inspect ships, hunt down pirates, escort diplomats, or secretly recruit crews, and alongside the main objectives come bonus and secret tasks that the player must discover on their own. The layer of orders from a secret Imperial order gives the whole campaign an unexpectedly interesting narrative framework, where the Empire isn't just a backdrop but an organization with its own politics. Technically the game improved the polygon engine, added more detailed models and more colorful environments, and again used dynamic music that underscores every turn of a mission.

At the time TIE Fighter was received as the pinnacle of the genre and still appears in rankings of the best space simulators of all time. It showed that a game can put the player on the side of the antagonist faction and still pull them in, because the missions make sense from the perspective of the character they're playing. Even today it's a surprisingly playable title: the controls are logical, the missions have a clearly readable structure, and the feeling of flying a craft that must not take a single hit is still remarkably tense. If today's player is to try only one DOS space sim, this is the safest choice. It helps that the game explains its systems gradually, so even a newcomer learns within a few missions to work with power management, shields, and wingman orders without having to study the whole manual.
pc-dos__star-wars-tie-fighter.teaser: It flipped the perspective to the Empire's side; a fragile fighter without shields changes the whole play style.

pc-dos__falcon-3-0.article:
**Falcon 3.0** was, for its time, one of the most ambitious attempts to bring the real handling of an F-16 fighter jet to a computer. It wasn't a game you switch on for twenty minutes. The package included a hefty manual that behaved more like a training handbook, and the player had to learn to work with the radar and its various modes, the head-up display, the multifunction displays, weapon management, and countermeasures. The reward was the feeling of piloting a machine with its own logic, not an aircraft controlled with two buttons.

The game offered several theaters of war and, above all, a dynamic campaign in which the front line shifted according to the results of your flights. A destroyed bridge, a scattered convoy, or lost air superiority fed into the further development of the conflict, so missions weren't just a lineup of scenarios but part of a bigger whole. Alongside that stood quick combat and instant action for those who just wanted to fly. Technically Falcon 3.0 was demanding; the polygon graphics and complex simulation could tax even powerful computers of the day, and the game was among the titles people bought better hardware for. It also included the option to play against another human over a modem, which was a small revelation in an era before common networks.

At the time Falcon 3.0 was regarded as the benchmark of the so-called study sim, that is, a simulator that doesn't try to be accessible but faithful. Expansions for other theaters and other aircraft kept the game alive for several years and set a standard that later flight simulators measured themselves against. Today the entry barrier is high, the controls rely on dozens of keyboard shortcuts, and without the manual the player gets lost within the first minute. But whoever fights through it gets a simulation whose depth can still be taken seriously decades later. This is especially evident in the moments when the player first locks a target on radar themselves, fires a missile from long range, and watches the opponent vanish from the screen. That kind of moment can't be experienced in simpler games.
pc-dos__falcon-3-0.teaser: One of the most ambitious attempts to simulate the F-16; the box included a manual like a textbook.

pc-dos__stunts.article:
**Stunts** is a racing game that took a seriously designed driving model and let it loose on tracks full of loops, corkscrews, ski jumps, and bridges leading into thin air. The player chooses from a selection of cars based on real-world models, from sharp sports cars to circuit specials, and each handles, accelerates, and grips differently. You race either against a computer opponent or against your own time, and it's precisely the chase for a better time on a familiar track that keeps the game alive to this day.

Its strongest weapon is the track editor. Assembling a circuit from tiles is straightforward enough that a first custom track takes shape in a few minutes, while still allowing players to build monstrosities that couldn't exist in an ordinary racing game. On top of that, the game offers replay recording with switchable cameras, so players could watch back a well-landed helicopter jump from behind the car as well. The graphics are simple, fully polygonal, and run smoothly even on modest hardware, which wasn't a given at the time. Crashes have their own short animations, after which the driver climbs out of the wreck, and this small comic detail became part of the game's identity.

At the time Stunts caught on thanks to its combination of accessibility and unexpected depth. Those who wanted to just have fun could drive for fun; those who wanted more honed their braking points and hunted for shortcuts on the tracks. A community still gathers around the game to this day, running time-trial competitions and sharing custom tracks, which is exceptional for a title from the early nineties. Today's player will find the controls oddly heavy-handed until they get used to how the cars respond, but after a few laps exactly that addictive rhythm sets in, the reason people keep coming back to Stunts after all these years. It also helps that the game is undemanding, launches practically anywhere, and a single track barely takes a minute, so an attempt at a better time can be repeated endlessly. Few racing games of that era offer such a direct ratio between time invested and visible improvement.
pc-dos__stunts.teaser: A seriously intended driving model on tracks full of loops and jump ramps.

pc-dos__test-drive-ii-duel.article:
**Test Drive II: The Duel** built the whole game on a simple, tempting idea: two supercars, an open road, and a duel over who reaches the finish first. You don't race on circuits but on public roads running through mountains, deserts, and along the coast, where the player faces not only the rival's car but also oncoming traffic and police patrols. The route is divided into stages, between which you refuel, so the game feels more like an illegal street race than a sporting contest.

The driving model retains the series' typical trait, namely an emphasis on manual gear shifting and on making the player feel the difference between individual machines. An over-revved engine, a badly chosen gear, or braking too late before a bend usually ends the same way, that is, scraping against a rock face or falling off a cliff. The cockpit view with the specific car's dashboard was highly effective for its time, and the game paired it with colorful VGA graphics, a rich engine soundscape, and a suitably brisk pace. An interesting feature was support for add-on disks with more cars and more landscapes, which let players expand the game's content.

At the time Test Drive II was very popular precisely because it offered a fantasy most players couldn't experience otherwise: getting behind the wheel of a dream sports car and pushing it along mountain switchbacks to the limit of its abilities. Its influence can be seen throughout the later wave of road racing games with licensed cars and police in pursuit. Today the game shows its age; collisions are unforgiving, the roads repeat, and the opponent's artificial intelligence is very straightforward, but as a historical record of where racing games were heading at the start of the nineties it deserves attention. What's also interesting is how well its basic idea still works. A duel between two cars on a narrow road with no other rivals carries clear tension and forces the player to take risks exactly where they should rather slow down. That very principle keeps returning in racing games to this day.
pc-dos__test-drive-ii-duel.teaser: A duel of two supercars on an open road, where oncoming traffic and police are also a threat.

pc-dos__f-19-stealth-fighter.article:
**F-19 Stealth Fighter** bet on the then-mysterious topic of invisible aircraft and turned it into one of the best-designed flight games of the eighties. The star of the show was a speculation on what an American stealth aircraft might look like, and the game built its entire style of play around that premise. The main enemy isn't the opponent's fighter jet but their radar. The player has to watch how large a signature their aircraft is creating, when to open the bomb bay, whether to switch on their own radar, and from which direction to approach so as to reach the target area unseen.

Missions span several theatres of war, from the Persian Gulf through northern Europe to central Europe in a Cold War scenario, and before takeoff the player chooses the difficulty, the mission type, and the loadout. Route planning over the map is also part of it, avoiding known radar sites. Getting back to base matters just as much as hitting the target, because the pilot advances in rank, earns decorations, and risks capture if shot down. Technically the game ran on simple polygon graphics that were legible and fast, and the cockpit interface was clear by the standards of the day.

At the time, F-19 was among MicroProse's most successful simulators and did a great deal for the studio's reputation as a brand that could combine a seriously-intended simulation with playability. Its greatest legacy is the emphasis on stealth and planning, an approach that only returned to flight games much later. Today the game obviously looks primitive and the controls rely on a keyboard full of shortcuts, but the tension of watching an enemy radar trace slowly light up on the display still works surprisingly well decades on. The mission structure holds up just as well, since every flight has a clearly defined goal, a measurable outcome, and continuation in the form of the next rank. It's a game you can pick up with no preparation at all and still get a surprising amount out of.
pc-dos__f-19-stealth-fighter.teaser: Flying a fictional stealth aircraft, where the biggest enemy isn't a fighter jet but radar.

pc-dos__red-baron.article:
**Red Baron** put the player into the cockpits of World War I biplanes and showed that a flight simulator doesn't have to be all about radar and missiles. The aircraft of 1915 to 1918 are slow, fragile, and armed with nothing but machine guns, so combat plays out at close range, in constant circling and jockeying for an advantageous position over the opponent. That very slowness is the game's greatest strength: the player has time to take in what's happening, and every kill is the result of patient maneuvering rather than a single trigger pull.

At its core is a pilot's career, where the player picks a side in the conflict, advances along the front, earns ranks and decorations, and moves on to more modern aircraft as the years pass. The game tracks personal score, kill count, and whether the pilot survives, complemented by a gallery of real aces you can face in stand-alone duels. Alongside the career sit individual missions, from escorting bombers to attacking observation balloons to free hunts over the front. Technically the game relied on Dynamix's polygon engine, which handled smooth flight scenes, and the atmosphere was rounded out by period trench scenery and a simple but effective sound design.

At the time, Red Baron became one of the most popular flight simulators of its era, and for a great many players it was the very first game that drew them into dogfighting. It also opened the door to a whole wave of World War I games, and its later sequels built directly on that legacy. Today Red Baron is pleasantly accessible: the controls are simpler than in more modern simulators, the pace is slow, and the career mode can draw in even a player who knows nothing about aircraft. Few 1990 games have aged this gracefully. Behind that stands mainly the clarity of the whole situation. In the air you can always see who is where, the fight happens in a small space, and the outcome is almost always the result of the player's own decisions rather than some invisible system. That very directness makes Red Baron one of the best introductions to flight simulators there is.
pc-dos__red-baron.teaser: A flight simulator with fragile World War I biplanes and slow dogfights.

pc-dos__comanche-maximum-overkill.article:
**Comanche: Maximum Overkill** was a technical sensation in 1992. While the competition built its worlds from crude polygons, here the terrain was rendered with voxel technology, giving it genuine hills, canyons, rock towers, and smooth transitions. The player takes the seat of an RAH-66 Comanche attack helicopter and flies low over the ground, where the terrain shields them from radar and gunfire alike, and it's precisely this valley-hugging flight that makes the game what it is.

The gameplay sits somewhere between simulator and action game. The helicopter handles fairly directly, but the player has to manage ammunition, switch between the cannon, unguided rockets, and anti-tank missiles, and above all choose the order of targets. Missions feature tanks, anti-aircraft systems, enemy helicopters, and ground installations, and typically require hitting several targets and making it back safely. The rotor sound and onboard-system callouts keep the tension up, and even though the graphics look crude today, at the time they produced an effect polygon games simply couldn't offer. That spectacle came at a price in performance, though — the game was among the titles that could bring even a decent computer to its knees.

At the time, Comanche was received as a showcase of where computer graphics were heading, and it launched a whole series of sequels and expansion packs. The voxel approach ultimately lost out to accelerated polygons, but in the early nineties it showed that terrain could be rendered more organically than the engines of the day were capable of. Today the game feels simple and the missions repeat after a while, but flying just above the surface of a dam or between rock walls still has its charm and recalls a time when technical innovation alone could sell a game. Alongside the main campaign, the title also offers quick missions and a difficulty choice, so you can sit down with it for twenty minutes. That combination of instant action and then-unheard-of scenery is why plenty of players still remember Comanche as one of the experiences that convinced them of the power of the PC.
pc-dos__comanche-maximum-overkill.teaser: A technical sensation of 1992 thanks to its voxel graphics; the terrain hides the helicopter from radar.

pc-dos__indianapolis-500-simulation.article:
**Indianapolis 500: The Simulation** is a game from which you can trace the history of serious racing simulators on computers. Instead of arcade-style driving, it offered a single track, a single type of car, and an utterly uncompromising approach to physics. The player gets behind the wheel of an Indy car on the Indianapolis oval, with the choice of practice, qualifying, and a full race that, at full length, means two hundred laps and several hours of focused driving.

The key innovation was car setup. Adjusting wing downforce, spring stiffness, gear ratios, and tire type feeds directly into how the car behaves on track, and the player quickly learns that a fast lap isn't made by courage alone. On top of that comes pit-stop strategy, tire wear, and damage that changes the handling after contact with the wall. A strong point is also the replay system with the ability to switch between cameras and individual cars, which felt like a television broadcast at the time. The graphics are simple but smooth, and the field of rivals behaves variably enough that the race never feels like driving in an empty space.

At the time, the game showed there was an audience willing to spend hours tuning a chassis, and it launched the path of a studio that would go on to define computer racing simulations for years to come. The influence of Indianapolis 500 can be seen in every later game that offers telemetry, car setup, and full race distance. Today the content on offer is narrow — one track and one category of car won't hold your attention for long — but anyone who sits down at the wheel and runs a few qualifying laps will understand why this game is spoken of as a landmark title. The way the game communicates information helps too. The difference between a good and a bad setup shows up immediately in the lap times, the car's behavior in a corner is predictable, and the player learns without the game ever forcing anything on them. That very honesty is why Indianapolis 500 is still cited today as the first true racing simulator for home computers.
pc-dos__indianapolis-500-simulation.teaser: It marks the start of serious racing simulators; a single track, unforgiving physics.

pc-dos__nascar-racing.article:
**NASCAR Racing** brought American stock cars to the PC in 1994 in a form no one had offered before. Heavy cars with enormous power and minimal downforce behave completely differently from open-wheelers: oversteer arrives quickly, the tires wear down gradually, and on a long oval the most important skill is holding a consistent pace, not one heroic lap. The game offers practice, qualifying, and a full season with a points table and a wide selection of tracks, ranging from fast ovals to more demanding road courses.
