pc-9x__interstate-76.teaser: Vehicular combat set in an alternate 1976; the cutscenes imitate the grainy film look of the seventies.

pc-9x__pod.article:
**POD** was, for a lot of owners of the first Pentium MMX machines, literally the first thing they launched after building their new computer — the game was bundled with new hardware at the time and served as a showcase of what the new processors and accelerators could do. It's set on a dying planet that can only be escaped by a single ship, and futuristic races are held to decide who gets to leave. The vehicles are light, fast, and slidey, and the tracks wind through tunnels, industrial complexes, and crumbling cities, full of shortcuts, jumps, and spots where a small mistake sends you flying off the track.

The handling model is pure arcade with an emphasis on flow. There's no tire wear or suspension tuning to worry about; instead, a lot of the work goes into the track itself — banked corners, jumps that punish a bad approach by throwing you into a wall, and opponents who are more than just scenery. Technically the game impressed mainly with its high-resolution textured graphics and smooth performance, which wasn't a given back then. It also offered networked play, including racing against opponents over the internet, which made it a popular title for LAN parties of the day. The music blends electronic and industrial motifs and suits the cold, metallic aesthetic well.

Contemporary reception was very favorable, and POD earned a reputation as a technological flagship. An expanded version later shipped as POD Gold, adding tracks and vehicles, and the series got a sequel. The title's impact lay mainly in showing ordinary players just how big a difference 3D accelerators made: the gap between the jerky software mode and the smooth accelerated picture was obvious at a glance. Today it's a fast, straightforward arcade racer without unnecessary padding, and a few minutes are enough to get the hang of a lap. Above all it stands as evidence of an era when game graphics changed practically from month to month. Its track design also holds up well, relying on a legible rhythm alternating straights and technical sections rather than complex features, so players get oriented within a single lap and start chasing their time right away.
pc-9x__pod.teaser: A showcase title for the first Pentium MMX chips — a racing game demonstrating what the new hardware could do.

pc-9x__driver.article:
**Driver** built the entire game around a single idea: to capture the feel of a car chase from a seventies American movie. You play as Tanner, an undercover cop who gets himself hired as a getaway driver for a gang, and most missions boil down to driving someone somewhere, chasing someone, or losing the police within a time limit. The cities are open and drivable throughout — Miami, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New York each have their own character, hills, bridges, and intersections where regular traffic reacts to how you drive.

The handling model is deliberately heavy and lumbering, exactly like American sedans of the era. Cars lean into corners, the rear end breaks loose easily, and controlling a slide is the core skill the player has to learn — which leads to the famous opening test in an underground parking garage, where you must demonstrate a set of maneuvers, and which many people failed to clear even after dozens of attempts. The police drive aggressively, block off streets, and pin you against walls during a long chase, so the tension builds naturally. The package also includes a replay editor, where you can use virtual cameras to cut together your own movie-style chase. The music relies on funky bass lines and horns that round out the period atmosphere.

Contemporary reviews praised the game for its authenticity and for how convincingly it conveyed speed in the streets, with criticism aimed mainly at the difficulty and the repetitive structure of the missions. The title's influence was considerable: an open city full of traffic, where the car is the main character, became a template for the whole genre, and the series continued with further installments. Today Driver is above all an atmospheric experience — the graphics are rough, but the low camera angle behind the spoiler and the squeal of tires still work. Anyone who gets past the tough start gets one of the most stylish games of its time. It also helps that missions are short and restart within seconds after a failure, so the player goes right back to retrying without the frustration of waiting. That tightness and clearly defined goal feel refreshing today against sprawling open worlds.
pc-9x__driver.teaser: Built around a single idea: the feeling of a car chase in a 1970s American film.

pc-9x__grand-prix-3.article:
**Grand Prix 3** is the pinnacle of the series that Geoff Crammond made for MicroProse, and at the time of release it was the most respected Formula 1 simulator on computers. Its foundation is a complete season with licensed circuits, qualifying, practice sessions, and a race-weekend structure that can be shortened to taste or played out down to the last detail. The game insists throughout that speed is the product of work, not reflexes: without understanding braking points, correct gear selection, and smooth throttle work, nobody gets very far.

At the heart of it is detailed car setup. Downforce, gear ratios, spring stiffness, toe angle, and brake balance all have a noticeable effect on cornering and straight-line behavior, and the game pushes you to find a compromise between qualifying pace and race-day durability. The major addition over its predecessor was weather — rain changes grip, wet lines form on the track, and driving through standing water demands a completely different rhythm. The graphics already used 3D acceleration, but the biggest impression comes from the sense of speed and the behavior of opponents, who make mistakes and fight among themselves. The engine sound changes with the revs and, in the cockpit, helps you judge when to shift.

At the time the game was received as the benchmark of its genre, though some players noted that visually it lagged slightly behind the competition and that it was more a refinement of its predecessor than a revolution. Still, an unusually active community grew up around the title, spending years creating mods for seasons, cars, and circuits, extending the game's life far beyond the usual shelf life of a racing title. Its influence on the genre is unmistakable: many later simulators adopted its approach to car setup and race weekends. Today Grand Prix 3 is an uncompromising but fair game that rewards patience — and it can still teach what it's like to drive a Formula 1 car. Anyone willing to put in the work on setup and string together a few clean laps in a row experiences a satisfaction that more modern, forgiving racing games rarely offer.
pc-9x__grand-prix-3.teaser: The peak of Geoff Crammond's Formula 1 simulators; speed here is the reward for understanding.

pc-9x__nascar-racing-3.article:
**NASCAR Racing 3** is a textbook example of what was called an honest simulator in the nineties. Papyrus had a reputation for being obsessed with physics, and in this installment they took it to a very high level: the race car is heavy, understeers, and is sensitive to tire pressure and, above all, to airflow. The aerodynamic draft behind an opponent is a crucial part of the game — tucking in behind a rival gains you speed but costs you downforce, and the car starts to come apart in the corners. Ovals therefore aren't dull circling but a constant tactical fight for position.

A race weekend includes practice, qualifying, and long races with mandatory pit stops, where you deal with fuel, tire changes, and quick chassis adjustments as the track changes in the heat. Along with that comes working with an engineer, telemetry data, and endless tuning that many players find more enjoyable than the driving itself. Technically the game supported hardware acceleration, offered decent resolution, and ran smoothly even with a large field of cars on track, which wasn't easy at the time. The audio side lives mainly on the roar of V8 engines and pit-crew radio chatter, which lends the driving a professional framework.

At the time the game ranked among the best in its genre and was seen as the obvious choice for anyone who wanted to race seriously on a computer. Criticism was mainly directed at its being a fairly closed world of ovals, without immediate appeal for the uninitiated player. Its major contribution, though, lay in the community: leagues formed around the title that ran regular online seasons with rules and penalties, and modders built their own car rosters and circuits. Today NASCAR Racing 3 feels raw, but the physics model holds up even after all these years, and for fans of American oval racing it remains one of the most faithful recreations ever made. It's also helped by the fact that it can be played in short bursts of shortened races, so there's no need to sacrifice an entire evening to a single several-hundred-kilometer oval battle.
pc-9x__nascar-racing-3.teaser: A physics-obsessed simulator from Papyrus; drafting behind a rival decides the outcome of the race.

pc-9x__toca-touring-car-championship.article:
**TOCA Touring Car Championship** brought the license of the British touring car championship to computers, and with it a racing style fundamentally different from both open-wheel and oval racing. The cars are based on production sedans, slower but tremendously aggressive: races happen in tight packs, contact is part of the sport, and the fight for position is often bumper to bumper. The campaign takes the player through a whole season on British circuits, with two races per weekend, points, and rivals who remember how you treated them a moment ago.

The handling model sits somewhere between arcade and simulation. The car has weight, oversteer arrives with heavy throttle, and curbs can be used and abused, yet the game doesn't discourage players with complicated setups. Damage modeling plays an important role — a broken bumper, a dented side, or damaged steering have a visible and noticeable effect. An interesting touch is the penalty system: cutting across the grass, shortcutting the track, or outright ramming opponents earns a warning, and repeat offenses bring disqualification, which keeps the game within the bounds of fair racing. The graphics used 3D acceleration, and the sound relies on deep engine roar, the race steward's voice, and the screech of bent metal.

At the time, the game was seen as one of the most enjoyable racing titles of its generation precisely because it found the balance between accessibility and credibility. Reviewers praised the battles against the AI, the accuracy of the circuits, and the championship atmosphere, while criticism was mainly aimed at the smaller number of cars and tracks. The series became one of Codemasters' pillar brands, and its approach to contact-heavy racing influenced many later titles. Today, TOCA is a game you can sit down and drive immediately, while still offering enough depth to make chasing better lap times worthwhile. Battles within a pack of touring cars also age better than the technological flashiness of the era, because they rest on car behavior and cleverly built circuits, not on effects.
pc-9x__toca-touring-car-championship.teaser: A licensed British touring car championship; tight bumper-to-bumper racing.

pc-9x__colin-mcrae-rally.article:
**Colin McRae Rally** did for rally what other games did for circuit racing: it translated the sport into a form even someone who had never read anything about it could understand, without losing its seriousness. You don't race against opponents on a track, but against the clock on closed special stages that run through gravel, asphalt, mud, and snow across several countries. The key figure is the co-driver, who reads out the pace notes — and learning to listen to and trust his instructions is the biggest skill the game asks of the player.

The handling model is essential: the surface changes the car's behavior very clearly — on gravel the car floats and you need to brake earlier, on asphalt it grips and rewards a clean line. Jumps, cambered corners, and narrow forest sections push you to drive boldly but not recklessly, because damage carries over between stages. Between legs you get a limited amount of time for repairs and have to decide whether to fix the dampers, the gearbox, or the cooling — and what to leave be. Technically, it was a good-looking title with well-modeled cars and smooth performance on the accelerator cards of the day. The sound is understated, dominated mainly by the engine, gravel under the wheel arches, and the navigator's voice, which underlines the feeling of a lonely drive.

The game was received extremely well at the time and became one of the most popular racing brands of the turn of the millennium. Reviewers praised above all the balance between accessibility and credibility, and how well the game conveys a sense of speed in a narrow space. Its influence on the genre was enormous — many later rally games adopted the stage structure here, the repair system, and the way pace notes are handled. Today it's a compact, cleanly designed game without filler, still addictive when chasing the last few seconds. Rally is also a genre that doesn't mind older graphics: what matters is how the car reacts to the surface and how quickly you can react to the call from the passenger seat, and that still works unchanged more than two decades later.
pc-9x__colin-mcrae-rally.teaser: Made rally racing accessible beyond the sport's fans; you race against the clock, not rivals on the track.

pc-9x__midtown-madness.article:
**Midtown Madness** set racing in a simplified but surprisingly sprawling version of Chicago that you can drive through without restriction. Alongside standard point-to-point races, where you choose the route yourself, it also offers checkpoint runs against the clock and a so-called cruise mode — free roaming around the city with no goal at all. That mode was the main draw for a lot of players: the city feels alive, buses and taxis get in your way, pedestrians jump aside, and the police come after you the moment you get too wild.

The handling model is arcade-like, but with a feel for weight — a big American sedan leans differently in a corner than a small roadster, and the truck is slow but practically unstoppable. Cars visibly dent, buckle, and get dirty, and damage affects handling. The game's real charm lies in the openness of its design: there's no prescribed route in a race, so it pays to look for shortcuts through parks, underpasses, or courtyards, and knowing the city matters as much as speed. Technically it was a title built on Direct3D that handled a big city and heavy traffic well on the machines of the time. A multiplayer mode was also included, letting you play cops and robbers.

At the time, the game earned praise for its freedom, the good feel of driving, and the atmosphere of a real city, while criticism pointed to the smaller number of cars and the fact that once the career is finished, free roaming is mainly what's left. Its influence is clear — open urban racing soon became a branch of the genre in its own right, and the series got sequels set in London and Paris. Today Midtown Madness feels like a pleasantly low-pressure game where the biggest fun is simply driving out, finding a ramp, and seeing how far you can fly. Chicago doesn't have the detail of modern open worlds, but it has recognizable neighborhoods, an elevated train, and a waterfront, so players genuinely learn to find their way around. And that moment when you stop following the arrow and start driving from memory is the best thing about the whole game.
pc-9x__midtown-madness.teaser: An open Chicago with no restrictions; the goal-free cruise mode was the main draw for many players.

pc-9x__motocross-madness.article:
**Motocross Madness** took dirt bikes and turned them into a game where flying matters just as much as racing. It offers several modes: classic races on closed motocross tracks, long rides across open country, stadium racing, and above all a freestyle arena where you score points for tricks in the air. It was this combination of speed and acrobatics that made it a title players kept coming back to long after finishing the career mode.

The controls are built around shifting the rider's weight. Leaning forward and back handles landings, coming out of banked turns, and whether you stay in the saddle after a jump or end up in the dirt. The crash physics are exaggerated, and exactly that makes them fun — the rider tumbles down the slope like a ragdoll, and often the crash is funnier than a well-ridden race. The terrain is sprawling, made of hills, ravines, and jumps, which tempts you to leave the track and find your own paths. Technically the game used 3D acceleration and looked very clean for its time, with long draw distance and smooth performance. Internet multiplayer was among the best things racing games offered at the time.

The game was received very favorably at launch, praised above all for its great sense of riding, the humor of its crashes, and the freedom of movement across the terrain. Criticism pointed to the smaller amount of content and the fact that difficulty doesn't grow much once you've mastered the basics. Its influence on the genre was still considerable — the trick system and open terrain became the standard for later motocross and quad-bike games from the same studio. Today Motocross Madness is quick, no-strings-attached joy: hop on, ride up a hill, pull off a backflip, and laugh at the result. Few racing games of the era managed to be so carefree. It's also a nice example of how game spaces opened up in the late nineties: instead of a narrow track, the player got open country to ride in any direction, and the game didn't scold them for it but rewarded them with a new view.
pc-9x__motocross-madness.teaser: Off-road motocross bikes, where aerial tricks matter just as much as racing.

pc-9x__re-volt.article:
**Re-Volt** put the player in charge of remote-controlled model cars and scaled the entire world around them to match. Races take place in a supermarket between shelves, in a museum, in a parking lot, in a schoolyard, or inside a house, where you slip under furniture and hop over doorsills. The change of perspective is the main trick: an ordinary environment turns, from the viewpoint of a palm-sized car, into varied terrain full of ramps, obstacles, and shortcuts that would be invisible at real-life scale.

The handling model is unexpectedly honest for how playful the game looks. The models have a light body, flip over easily, lose grip on smooth surfaces, and the difference between electric and combustion power is clearly felt. On top of that you collect pickups — from rockets and oil slicks to a plain extra battery — so races also have a combat dimension without losing their focus on driving. A major strength is the built-in track editor, where players build their own circuits from pieces, and together with the multiplayer mode it significantly extended the game's life. Technically it was a colorful, clean-looking title with good lighting and reflections on polished floors.

The game was warmly received at the time, with reviewers praising the original idea, the well-designed tracks, and the fact that it works for both children and more demanding players. Criticism was mainly aimed at the occasionally punishing difficulty, where a single hit can knock you from first place to last. An unusually persistent community later grew up around the title, spending years creating new tracks, cars, and technical updates for modern systems. Today Re-Volt is one of those games that ages well — the idea is timeless, and driving across a carpet between table legs is just as fun as it ever was. The art direction helps too, since it doesn't aim for realism but for a colorful, readable environment, so the game doesn't feel dated, just a bit blocky. For playing together on one computer, it's still one of the best choices of its generation.
pc-9x__re-volt.teaser: Radio-controlled car races at palm-sized scale — a supermarket or a schoolyard as the track.

pc-9x__falcon-4-0.article:
**Falcon 4.0** is one of the most ambitious flight simulators ever released for computers. It models the F-16 fighter in such depth that the player works with real-world procedures: starting with cold instruments, setting the radar into individual modes, managing weapons systems, electronic warfare, and waypoint navigation. The included manual ran to hundreds of pages, and that wasn't a marketing gimmick — you practically can't function in the cockpit without reading it, because every switch has meaning.

The real revolution, however, was the dynamic campaign set in a conflict on the Korean peninsula. The war runs regardless of the player: ground units advance, both sides plan air raids, lose aircraft and airfields, and the front line shifts based on the outcome of hundreds of engagements. The player chooses which missions to fly, and success or failure has a measurable impact on the overall situation. Thanks to that, it never feels like a string of scripted scenes but like being one pilot within a huge machine. Technically it was an extremely demanding program that pushed the computers of its day to the limit, and its release was accompanied by notorious instability and bugs.

Contemporary reviews swung between enthusiasm over its scope and disappointment at the state it launched in. That, however, kicked off a unique story: the community took up the simulator, released its own fixes and expansions for years, and kept it alive far longer than anyone expected, with later community and commercial versions significantly improving both the avionics and the stability. Its influence on the genre is fundamental, since the dynamic campaign became the yardstick by which military simulators are still measured today. Falcon 4.0 remains a demanding but hugely rewarding game for anyone who wants to fly seriously. Your first solo takeoff, the first properly locked radar contact, and the first return to base in a damaged aircraft rank among the most powerful experiences computer games of the nineties had to offer. The price for that is several evenings spent learning before you even get into the air.
pc-9x__falcon-4-0.teaser: The most ambitious flight simulator; it models the F-16 in depth, down to real pilot procedures.

pc-9x__flight-unlimited-ii.article:
**Flight Unlimited II** left behind the purely aerobatic focus of the first game and turned into a civilian flight simulator set around the San Francisco Bay Area. The player gets several types of small aircraft, a map with airports, navigation aids, and essentially a free hand: you can learn the basics through training lessons, fly a pre-planned route, or simply circle over the bay looking for familiar landmarks. The environment is based on real geography, so navigating by the coastline, bridges, and hills works just as it would in reality.

The game's strength lies in how it handles flight and the world around it. The aircraft responds to wind, thermals, and power changes in a clear, unforced way, so the game can double as a teaching tool for understanding basic principles. Air traffic control also gets involved, communicating with you and assigning runways and clearances, turning a simple flight into a structured procedure. Other aircraft move through the sky, so the airspace never feels empty. Technically the game was impressive for its time, with terrain built from aerial photography, though that also meant high demands on the computers of the day.

At the time, reviews agreed it was a beautiful, atmospheric simulator that brought unusual visual quality to civilian flying, with criticism mainly directed at its performance demands and the smaller number of available aircraft compared to the competition of the day. Interestingly, the simulator came from a studio known for completely different genres, which shows in the care put into the design and the emphasis on a believable world. Today Flight Unlimited II is mostly a calm, meditative affair — taking off at dusk over the bay and just quietly circling is an experience that works regardless of how old the graphics are. It's also a reminder that civilian flying doesn't need an enemy or a score: all it needs is a route, weather, and a decision about where to land. In that sense it foreshadowed the direction modern civilian simulators would take many years later.
pc-9x__flight-unlimited-ii.teaser: A civilian flight simulator over San Francisco Bay; the freedom to fly without a script or a goal.

pc-9x__rollcage.article:
**Rollcage** took futuristic racing and added one crucial idea: the cars have huge wheels that extend beyond the bodywork, so they're fully reversible and drive equally well on their wheels or on their roof. Flipping over isn't a penalty, then, but a normal part of driving — the car turns over, keeps going, and the player naturally learns to use tunnel walls and ceilings as a full part of the track. That shapes the game's pace, which is extremely fast and at times borders on chaos.

The tracks are designed to make the most of this mechanic. They run through tunnels, tangled structures, and around destructible scenery — pillars, fences, and parts of buildings vanish under impact and change the look of the circuit mid-race. On top of that you collect weapons and pickups, from missiles to mines, turning every lap into something of a small battle for position. The controls take some getting used to, because at that speed you need to plan ahead and read the track intuitively rather than reactively. Technically it was a game using 3D acceleration with a strong sense of speed and a dark, industrial look. The soundtrack leans on electronic dance tracks that keep rhythmic pace with the races.

At the time, the game was praised for its originality, its pace, and its destructible environments, while criticism pointed to the difficult controls and the fact that in the thickest chaos it's hard to keep track of what's happening. Even so, it found a devoted audience and got a sequel that developed the idea further. The title's influence can be seen in later anti-gravity and arcade racers that play with an inverted perspective and tracks in three dimensions. Today Rollcage is above all fast, noisy fun, where a few minutes of play turns into an unexpectedly long session. It shines best with multiple players, where driving along a tunnel ceiling and smashing pillars turns into shared slapstick. And even after all these years, it's refreshing to meet a racing game that doesn't worry in the slightest about which way up you're actually driving.
pc-9x__rollcage.teaser: Futuristic racing with wheels larger than the car body — you can drive on the ceiling just like the ground.

pc-9x__thief-dark-project.article:
**Thief: The Dark Project** put players in the boots of the thief Garrett and did something that was almost heretical in 1998: it gave him a first-person view but forbade him from shooting. The game takes place in an unnamed city where medieval architecture blends with steam machinery and pagan magic, and Garrett makes his living by burgling the mansions of wealthy nobles. The jobs seem like ordinary heists at first, but they gradually get tangled up in a conflict between the rigid Hammerite cult and an old forest deity, so the second half of the campaign leaves the city rooftops behind and leads into tombs, temples, and places where the player, for the first time in the genre, learns to fear the dark from the other side.

The entire game system rests on light and sound. A gem in the bottom corner of the screen shows how visible Garrett is, and the volume of his footsteps changes with the surface underfoot: on marble and metal he can be heard from across the hall, on carpet and moss almost not at all. Supporting this is an arsenal of special arrows that has become a textbook example: a water arrow douses a torch, a moss arrow creates a silent carpet, a rope arrow opens a path upward, and a noise arrow lures a guard elsewhere. Enemies are not just scenery, they react to open doors, to lights that have gone out, and to trails of blood, and they move gradually between calm, suspicion, and active search. Technically this was powered by an engine with advanced spatial sound propagation, and the game's audio remains its strongest asset to this day: wind whistling, guards muttering to themselves, and unsettling ambient loops keep the player tense better than any musical score could.

At the time it was a title critics embraced enthusiastically and one that immediately won a devoted community, even though it never commercially outgrew the big action franchises. Its influence is nonetheless unmistakable, practically every later stealth game has borrowed at least a visibility meter or its approach to sound from it. Today fan patches and hundreds of user-made missions keep the game alive, and although the textures and character models have aged, the level design and atmosphere hold up without excuses.
pc-9x__thief-dark-project.teaser: First person without shooting — Garrett is only allowed to steal and sneak through a city full of magic.

pc-9x__thief-ii-metal-age.article:
**Thief II: The Metal Age** took everything that worked in the first game and focused it back where stealth belongs: among houses, offices, and mansions full of locks, safes, and guards. Garrett returns to a city where, in the meantime, the technocratic Mechanist order led by Karras has seized power, replacing faith with machines, placing cameras and mechanical guardians throughout the streets, and promising to purify the world. The campaign accordingly cuts back sharply on undead and supernatural locations and adds sprawling urban missions where the main obstacle is human security, locked routes, and the need to slip in and out unseen.

The gameplay stays faithful to the original, just with smoother edges. Alongside arrows come new tools like tracking devices and improved lockpicks, and inventory and objective hints are friendlier, changing depending on the chosen difficulty: on the highest setting the game forbids killing and adds further conditions, turning the mission into a genuine puzzle. The level design ranks among the genre's high points, especially the mission involving climbing across facades and rooftops during a party in the upper floors of a villa, where the player must improvise with a limited supply of rope arrows. Guard AI got finer alert stages and better search behavior, and the sound design again carries most of the atmosphere, from the clanking metal legs of automatons to the nervous chatter of patrols.

Reviews were very favorable, and to this day many players consider it the best entry in the series, since it offers the largest and most open maps of the whole trilogy. The bittersweet context is impossible to ignore, though: Looking Glass Studios shut down shortly after release, making The Metal Age its swan song. Today the game runs on modern systems thanks to community engine patches, still hosts a huge supply of fan-made missions, and even after all these years remains one of the purest examples of what stealth built on planning rather than reflexes should look like.
pc-9x__thief-ii-metal-age.teaser: Brings the series back to houses and mansions full of locks and guards; more pure stealth craft.

pc-9x__tomb-raider.article:
**Tomb Raider** introduced the world to Lara Croft and simultaneously showed that three-dimensional space could be used in an action-adventure for more than just a backdrop for shooting. The British archaeologist travels from Peruvian caves through Greek temples and Egyptian tombs to the lost city of the Atlanteans, searching for pieces of an artifact that a rival party is also after. Most of the time, though, the player isn't in gunfights but studying the space: measuring jumps, looking for levers, watching which slab in the wall moved after flipping a switch, and trying to figure out how to reach a ledge three floors up.

Lara's movement is built on a precise grid, so jumps have a fixed length and the player learns to judge them to the centimeter. Alongside this comes what's now called tank controls: the character turns in place before moving forward, which feels clunky at first, but combined with the ability to grab an edge, pull herself up, or perform a roll, it delivers a surprisingly rich repertoire. Combat with wolves, bats, bears, or dinosaurs mostly serves as seasoning between the acrobatic passages. Technically it was a flagship title of its era, released in a software version as well as versions taking advantage of the first 3D accelerators, which brought filtered textures and smoother performance. The sound is deliberately sparse, most of the time the player only hears their own footsteps and dripping water, with music arriving in short orchestral bursts exactly where something is about to happen, resulting in a feeling of total solitude in dead corridors.

At the time it was a massive commercial success, and Lara became an icon that outgrew the games themselves. The title's influence is fundamental, the very notion of a three-dimensional action-adventure built around platforming navigation and puzzles was essentially defined by it. Today the original version demands a bit of patience with the controls and camera, but the feeling of discovering empty tombs has aged far better than the technology.
pc-9x__tomb-raider.teaser: Introduced the world to Lara Croft and turned 3D space into a puzzle, not just a backdrop for shooting.

pc-9x__tomb-raider-ii.article:
**Tomb Raider II** came out just a year after the original and is a textbook example of a sequel that overturns nothing while adding everything. This time Lara is hunting for a dagger from Chinese legend, and the journey takes her from the Great Wall of China through the canals of Venice, a sunken ocean liner, and Tibetan monasteries all the way into the heart of a mountain full of molten lava. The structure stays the same, long levels full of jumps, movable crates, keys, and switches, but the environments are more varied and take place far more often among people rather than in abandoned tombs.

The most visible change is a shift toward action. Enemies are noticeably more numerous, and most of them are now armed people, new weapons have arrived including a submachine gun and a harpoon, and vehicles appear for the first time, so the player rides a motorboat through the canals and a snowmobile down Tibetan slopes. There's also a small addition that fundamentally changes the pacing, namely flares: they burn for only a limited time in dark corridors, forcing the player to decide when to light the way and when to go on blind. A bonus is the famous opening level set in Lara's mansion, where you can practice the controls, explore the house, and find a few hidden secrets. On the technical side, the game made better use of the era's 3D accelerators, adding colored lighting and greater draw distance, and the sound again relies on restrained orchestral motifs that only sound out at key moments.

Critics and players alike embraced the second entry enthusiastically, and together with the first game it made Core Design one of the most closely watched European studios of the late nineties. In hindsight it's been criticized for sometimes having too many gunfights and for difficulty that can be merciless, since death lurks even around corners the player couldn't have seen. Even so, it remains one of the series' most beloved entries, and today it's most easily accessible through a modern remaster as well as community tools that resolve compatibility with modern systems.
pc-9x__tomb-raider-ii.teaser: A sequel released a year after the original that changes nothing, only adds to it — from China to Tibet.

pc-9x__rollercoaster-tycoon.article:
**RollerCoaster Tycoon** is one of those games where it's easy for a player to look up from the monitor only to find it's past midnight. The task is simple: build and run an amusement park so it turns a profit, attracts enough visitors, and fulfills the scenario's goal, such as reaching a certain park value or guest count by a set date. The individual scenarios start from a half-empty field as well as from a neglected park that needs to be put back on its feet, and they differ in budget, terrain, and what the player has available from the start.

The heart of the game is building roller coasters piece by piece. The player assembles climbs, banked turns, loops, and braking sections, watching speed, g-forces, and above all whether the train actually makes it to the end, with the game showing graphs of excitement, intensity, and nausea. Around all this runs a full economy: admission fees, food prices, maintenance, mechanics, janitors, staff, advertising, and breakdown repairs. Visitors aren't just scenery, each one has their own wallet, mood, and opinion, you can click on them and read what they're thinking right now, which is an inexhaustible source of feedback and humor when an entire queue complains about the mess or goes looking for a trash can. Technically it's something of a small miracle, the isometric graphics with a huge number of independently simulated little figures ran smoothly even on modest late-nineties machines, and the game lets you ride through a built coaster from the cart's point of view, which is the fastest way to find out something isn't quite right.

The game became a massive hit, received two expansion packs and a whole series of sequels, and fundamentally shaped the entire genre of amusement park building simulations. Critics praised above all how easy it was to get into and how unexpectedly deep it was beneath the surface. Its combination of playful construction and a hard economic framework proved extraordinarily addictive, and an open community version still keeps it alive today, adding higher resolutions, modern controls, and an endless supply of user-made parks.
pc-9x__rollercoaster-tycoon.teaser: Building and running an amusement park, so absorbing that players easily lose track of time.

pc-9x__sims.article:
**The Sims** arrived with an idea that on paper sounded like a recipe for a flop: a game with no enemies, no score, and no ending, in which the player looks after ordinary people in an ordinary suburban house. The result was one of the most successful titles of its era and an entirely new genre in its own right. The player creates characters, assigns them personality traits, builds them a house, and then organizes their lives: cooking, sleeping, hygiene, work, friends, hobbies, and relationships. Hovering over all of this is a set of need meters that must be kept in balance, because a tired and hungry Sim won't get anywhere at work and, in the worst case, will lose their job.

The other half of the game is building. The house-building tools are surprisingly deep, the player draws walls, changes flooring and wallpaper, adds floors, pools, and gardens, and furnishes the interior with furniture where the more expensive pieces are noticeably better at satisfying needs. It's precisely this tension between a career, which brings in money, and the time a character needs for food and sleep, that forms the core economic loop. The Sims speak their own made-up gibberish language, so scenes work in any language and the player fills in the story themselves, which is the key to why playing so often turned into telling one's own little stories. Technically it combined three-dimensional characters with pre-rendered isometric environment graphics, which ran even on ordinary home computers, with the ability to rotate the view and zoom in on the scene.

The success was enormous, followed by a long line of expansion packs and an entire series that made The Sims one of the strongest brands in the industry. Its influence on the genre is clear, the game showed that a simulation of everyday life could have mass appeal and that a large part of the audience was looking for creation and storytelling rather than challenge. Today the first game feels raw and some of its mechanics are unforgiving, but its charm and dry humor remain.
pc-9x__sims.teaser: A game with no enemies, score, or ending, about ordinary people in an ordinary house — it founded a genre.

pc-9x__theme-hospital.article:
**Theme Hospital** is a management simulation in which the player builds and runs a hospital, but with one significant twist: the patients suffer from completely made-up ailments, such as Bloaty Head or Alien DNA, and treatment takes place in machines that look like they escaped from a grotesque circus. That satirical layer, however, doesn't disguise the fact that a very serious operations simulation runs underneath it. The player places consulting rooms, waiting areas, laboratories, and operating theaters, hires doctors, nurses, handymen, and cleaners, and keeps watch over the budget, treatment prices, reputation, and the satisfaction of both staff and patients.

The gameplay is built on constantly resolving bottlenecks. A patient first arrives at reception, then goes to a consulting room where a diagnosis is made, possibly followed by a series of tests, and only then to treatment, so any missing room instantly blocks the whole flow and queues start forming outside the doors. On top of this the game adds epidemics that must be hushed up or handled before a fine arrives, inspector visits, earthquakes, equipment breakdowns, and research that unlocks new equipment and improves what's already there. Individual levels have clear goals and gradually ramp up the challenge. Visually it's classic isometric graphics with a huge number of small animations, and the sound is unmistakable, especially the hospital PA announcements, which comment on events with dry humor and became the game's signature trademark.

At the time it was a very well received title that built on the studio's older management tradition and confirmed that operations management could be entertaining even for players who don't love spreadsheets. Its influence remains visible today, a whole range of modern operations simulations openly cite it as an inspiration, and one of them was created directly as its spiritual successor. The original game is still playable thanks to an open engine that runs it in high resolution on today's systems, and its pace and humor hold up without losing a beat.
pc-9x__theme-hospital.teaser: A hospital management simulation with made-up diseases and bizarre-looking equipment.

pc-9x__commandos-behind-enemy-lines.article:
**Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines** is a game that looks like a real-time strategy title but plays like a demanding logic puzzle. The player commands a small squad of Allied commandos behind enemy lines during the Second World War, and each mission has a specific goal to accomplish, such as destroying a bridge, freeing a prisoner, stealing documents, or getting to a designated location in one piece. No base building, no unit production, just a handful of men against overwhelming numbers, where a single spotted movement usually means reloading a saved position.

The charm lies in the fact that each member of the team is skilled at something different, and a mission can only be pulled off through their combined efforts. The Green Beret handles silent takedowns and hiding bodies, the Sniper has a limited supply of ammunition and must use it carefully, the Sapper plants charges and traps, the Diver moves through water, and the Driver operates vehicles and heavy weapons. A key element is the guards' fields of view, shown as rotating, overlapping cones, so the player spends a long time observing patrol routes before planning who to move and when. The game allows pausing and issuing orders on the fly, which is essential since timing is often a matter of seconds. Technically it excelled with hand-painted two-dimensional maps packed with detail and smooth zooming that let you inspect every barrel and crate, complemented by restrained military music and soldier barks that quickly lodge themselves in the player's memory.

The game was very well received, especially in Europe, where it became one of the biggest successes of the Spanish games industry and kicked off an entire series as well as a standalone expansion with additional missions. Its reputation comes above all from its difficulty, missions are solved through trial and error, and a player can easily wrestle with a single one of them for an entire evening before finding the right sequence of steps. It's precisely this tightness, though, that keeps its charm alive today, and modern tactical games about small squads cite it as their model.
pc-9x__commandos-behind-enemy-lines.teaser: Looks like a real-time strategy game, plays like a demanding logic puzzle.

pc-9x__hitman-codename-47.article:
**Hitman: Codename 47** introduced a bald contract killer with a barcode tattooed on the back of his head, and with him an idea that no other series has replicated quite the same way since: a level as an open-ended murder puzzle. The player gets a target, a map, an equipment budget, and total freedom in how to reach the victim. You can go in guns blazing, which usually ends badly and fast, or slip into a chef's, security guard's, or delivery driver's uniform, walk past the guards, set up a trap, and leave before anyone realizes what happened. The story takes the player from Hong Kong through the South American jungle and Rotterdam, back to the question of who actually created Agent 47.

The gameplay is unusually uncompromising for its time. There's no saving mid-mission, so a single mistake means replaying the entire level from scratch, disguises only work until you get too close to someone who sees through them, and the crowd's and guards' behavior can be unpredictable. That's exactly where the tension comes from: the player learns the map by heart, tries variations, and finds a new detail on every playthrough. Technically, it was a showcase for the studio's own engine, which offered impressively populated environments and physical body behavior that was unusual for the year 2000. Jesper Kyd composed the score, and its cold orchestral and choral motifs gave the game a signature tone the series still carries today, which together with the stark, almost sterile art direction creates the impression that the player isn't following a hero, but a tool.

Contemporary reviews were mixed, praising the concept, atmosphere, and freedom, but criticizing the awkward controls, missing save function, and uneven difficulty. Even so, the game sold well and founded one of the longest-running stealth franchises ever, whose later entries polished its ideas to perfection. Today the first Hitman feels rough and unforgiving, but its core idea remains legible, and some of its missions still deserve a look even after all these years.
pc-9x__hitman-codename-47.teaser: Introduced the bald hitman; each level is an open-ended murder puzzle.

pc-9x__metal-gear-solid.article:
**Metal Gear Solid** arrived on PC two years behind the console original, but in a version that could take advantage of higher resolutions and sharper visuals than had previously been available. Playing as Solid Snake, the player infiltrates a remote military facility in Alaska, where a group of renegades has seized the base along with a secret weapon of mass destruction and is holding hostages. The goal isn't to shoot your way through the facility, but to slip through unnoticed, rescue the hostages, and find out what's really going on inside.

The gameplay is built around a top-down view with a fixed camera, a radar showing guards' fields of vision, and patient creeping along walls. Snake hides inside boxes, knocks on walls to lure guards away, uses a suppressor, crawls through ventilation shafts, and must break line of sight and flee when spotted until the alert dies down. The game is further defined by boss fights, each governed by its own rules and often forcing the player to think outside the usual conventions, along with extensive radio dialogue that carries the story forward through themes of genetics, nuclear deterrence, and a soldier's duty. It was precisely this cinematic direction of scenes, editing, voice acting, and music that made Metal Gear Solid a revelation on release, since almost nobody had seen an action game told with this much confidence before. The PC version also included an extensive package of training challenges that let players practice individual mechanics separately from the campaign.

The original ranked among the best-reviewed games of its generation and is essential to the entire stealth genre, having shown that sneaking around could carry a big story and strong characters. The PC port was received mostly positively, with objections aimed at the controls and its late arrival. Today the game is best found in later collections, but even so, its pacing, humor, and fourth-wall-breaking ideas age remarkably slowly, and many of its scenes still stick in players' memories two decades on.
pc-9x__metal-gear-solid.teaser: The PC version arrived two years later, but in sharper resolution than the original.

pc-9x__oddworld-abe-s-oddysee.article:
**Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee** is a platformer whose hero can't fight, can barely carry anything, and dies after a single hit. Abe is a slave at the giant meat-processing plant Rupture Farms, where he stumbles onto the fact that the company's next product is meant to be his own kind, and decides to escape while freeing as many of his fellow workers as possible along the way. The game combines platforming acrobatics with patient sneaking past guards, since the only weapon Abe has is his own voice and the ability to make an enemy make a mistake.

The core mechanic is a speech system that lets Abe greet another Mudokon, tell him to follow or wait, and lead him to a rescue gate. Freeing them is optional but crucial, since the number of fellow workers saved determines which ending the player sees. On top of that, Abe can temporarily possess the body of an enemy Slig, walk it through a guarded area, and clear out sentries he could never have gotten past on his own. The levels are built as a sequence of carefully arranged situations solved through precise jump timing, sneaking, dodging mines, and finding hidden secret areas. Visually the game relies on pre-rendered backgrounds and remarkably rich character animation, so it looks more like an animated film than a game from 1997, accompanied by a dark, industrial soundscape of drums and whispers.

At the time, the game was praised above all for its original world, dark humor, and the boldness of building a platformer around a defenseless hero, while criticism targeted its high difficulty and the need to repeat screens over and over. Its influence on the genre is undeniable, since it fused logical platforming with a story that has something to say about exploitation and industry. Today it will mostly delight players who don't mind trial and error, and its art style remains as distinctive as ever, along with the feeling that this time the hero is someone with no power at all.
pc-9x__oddworld-abe-s-oddysee.teaser: A hero who can't fight and dies after a single hit; a platformer built around sneaking.

pc-9x__championship-manager-3.article:
**Championship Manager 3** is a game in which the player never sees a single second of actual on-pitch action, and yet it manages to devour more evenings than most action titles of its time. You take on the role of a football manager, choose a club anywhere from the English elite to a half-forgotten third-division existence, and from that moment on you handle absolutely everything: the lineup, tactics, training schedule, transfers, contracts, dressing-room morale, injuries, and pressure from a board that has its own ideas about where the team should go.

The series' strength has always lain in its database. It contains tens of thousands of players from many countries and leagues, each with their own set of abilities, personality traits, and hidden potential the manager only glimpses at first. Hunting for an unknown youngster from a second-rate league who blossoms into a star within three seasons became almost a discipline of its own, and the names of these discoveries were passed around the community like legends. Matches unfold as a text broadcast, with the clock running and commentary lines accumulating, while the player can intervene at any moment with substitutions or a formation change. Paradoxically, it's exactly this sparseness that generates the tension, since imagination fills in the rest, and the final minutes of a tight match are read with a pounding heart. Hardware demands were minimal, yet saving and processing the next in-game day could still tax a decent machine, especially with several competitions running at once.

At the time it was an extraordinarily popular game, especially in the United Kingdom, where it became a phenomenon reaching well beyond the gaming crowd. Its influence is visible across the entire sports management genre, since it set the bar for simulation depth that its successors, under a later series name, would go on to inherit. Today the interface feels archaic, but the core itself, building a team and battling the league table, still works just as quietly and just as relentlessly.
pc-9x__championship-manager-3.teaser: Not a single real moment of action on the pitch, and yet it eats up more evenings than action games.

pc-9x__fifa-98-road-to-world-cup.article:
**FIFA 98: Road to World Cup** is the entry many players remember as the moment the series finally found the balance between arcade fun and at least basic footballing credibility. The main new feature is hinted at in the subtitle: a full qualification campaign for the World Cup, in which the player picks any of a huge number of national teams and works their way through the groups all the way to the final tournament. Alongside that, club leagues, cups, friendlies, and an indoor mode with adjusted rules and a faster pace are all present.

On the pitch, the game leans on fast but readable controls, emphasizing short passing combinations, crosses, and first-time shots. Set pieces gained manual, aimed setup, tactical options let you adjust formation and playing style, and the lineup could be tweaked to suit the opponent. Technically, it was one of the first entries to draw heavily on 3D accelerators on PC, so with acceleration enabled it offered smoother motion, sharper player models, and better stadium lighting than software rendering could manage. An inseparable part of the experience is the sound: crowd reactions, commentary, and above all licensed music that an entire generation of players associates so strongly with the menu screen that the tracks became part of collective memory.

At the time it was one of the best-selling sports games and cemented the FIFA brand's position in Europe, where it became almost synonymous with football on the computer. Its influence is clear in how the series settled into the structure it would keep for years: a huge roster of licensed teams, tournament modes, and an emphasis on broadcast atmosphere. Today the game is of course dated in every respect, from crude models to simplistic opponent defending, but anyone who fires it up quickly remembers why an entire afternoon could vanish into it, and why two-player tournaments used to run late into the night.
pc-9x__fifa-98-road-to-world-cup.teaser: The entry where the series found the balance between arcade fun and football authenticity.

pc-9x__transport-tycoon-deluxe.article:
**Transport Tycoon Deluxe** is an improved release of the transport simulation in which the player founds their own shipping company and tries to turn it into an empire over the course of decades. It starts with an empty landscape dotted with a few towns, mines, forests, and factories, a small bank loan, and a decision about where to begin. Gradually you build railway lines and stations, bus routes, ports, and airports, connect raw materials to buyers, and watch the little settlement by your stop grow into a city.

The game's strength lies in how a complex system emerges from simple rules. Cargo is generated based on industrial output and city demand, and shipping revenue depends on distance and how quickly a shipment arrives, so it pays to plan routes carefully, build double-track lines, and manage signals and sidings so trains don't jam up. The Deluxe version added various climate settings, including desert and snowy environments, plus an entirely different world with its own cargo types, alongside a longer time span in which vehicles gradually age and get replaced by newer, faster, and pricier machines. Rival companies try to carve out their own share, which pushes the player to expand faster. The isometric graphics are modest but remarkably clear, and the whole simulation model ran smoothly even on the modest hardware of the mid-1990s.

The game was very well received at the time and became a long-term favorite among fans of building simulations. Its influence is visible across a whole range of later logistics and transport titles, and its author carried its principles into his subsequent projects as well. Most importantly, though, it lives on: an open-source community successor has expanded it with higher resolutions, multiplayer, smarter signaling, and a vast range of add-ons, so it's played more today than at release. Anyone who boots it up usually finds that planning just a single rail line can eat up an entire evening.
pc-9x__transport-tycoon-deluxe.teaser: An enhanced edition of Chris Sawyer's transport simulation — from an empty field to a transport empire.

pc-modern__half-life-2.article:
**Half-Life 2** arrived on PC in 2004 and instantly raised the bar for what storytelling could look like in a first-person shooter. The player once again takes on the role of the taciturn physicist Gordon Freeman, waking up in the grim City 17 under the rule of the alien Combine regime, gradually turning from a defenseless refugee into a symbol of resistance. The game does without classic cutscenes: everything important happens right in front of the player without ever taking control away from them, and it's precisely this uninterrupted perspective that gives the story an unusual urgency. Characters speak, gesture, and react while the world collapses around them, so the storyline feels more like an experience than a reward tucked between firefights.

The engine driving the experience is Source, and its physics never stay mere set dressing. Planks, barrels, bricks, and saw blades can all be picked up, thrown, and used against enemies, and once the player gets hold of the gravity gun, the entire world turns into an ammunition supply. The level design carries the player through shelled streets, flooded canals, an airboat ride down a river, a desert full of antlions, and above all the horror stretch of Ravenholm, still one of the most-cited passages in the genre. The shooting is sharp and direct, but the game regularly alternates it with puzzles built on weight, levers, and buoyancy, so the pacing never slides into monotony.

Technically, it was one of the most advanced games of its time, especially thanks to detailed facial animation and interior lighting. The sound is restrained, the music only kicks in at the most intense moments, and the atmosphere is carried instead by silence, distant guard chatter, and creaking metal. Critics received the game with exceptional warmth, and the title quickly became one of the pillars supporting the reputation of Valve and of the Steam platform through which it was distributed. Today Half-Life 2 remains perfectly playable, runs on virtually anything, and its handling of pacing, environment, and a silent protagonist remains a textbook example that shooter designers still return to.
pc-modern__half-life-2.teaser: Storytelling without a single cut, and the gravity gun, which redefined shooter gameplay.

pc-modern__portal-2.article:
**Portal 2** expanded the original Portal's compact idea into a full-fledged adventure without losing its elegance. The player once again wakes up inside the crumbling Aperture Science complex, equipped with a gun that fires a pair of linked portals, and must shoot, or rather puzzle, their way out of the testing chambers. The basic rule is simple: whatever enters one portal exits the other, keeping its momentum. From this single idea the game wrings dozens of situations in which the player launches themselves across chasms, dodges lethal turrets, or steers laser beams through complex room geometry.

The sequel added surface-altering gels, light bridges, propulsion tubes, and moving platforms to the puzzle mix, so the layers of the puzzles interweave and solutions often require thinking about both speed and direction of fall. Alongside the campaign, the game offers a cooperative mode for two robots, where both players have to communicate and synchronize their portals; it's one of the finest cooperative experiences Valve has ever released. The package also includes an editor, which the community still uses today to build its own chambers.

Technically the game runs on a finely tuned Source engine, performs smoothly even on modest hardware, and its clean, laboratory-sterile environments contrast with the dusty innards of the complex's abandoned sections. The music is electronic, playful, and reactive to events, while humor plays an absolutely central role: the artificial intelligence GLaDOS ranks among the best-written characters in gaming history, and dry sarcasm runs through the entire game. Reviews were rapturous, and the title repeatedly appears on lists of the greatest games of all time. Today Portal 2 ages remarkably well, because its strength lies not in graphical effects but in its perfectly graduated difficulty curve and in how patiently it teaches players to think in three dimensions. For anyone who enjoys logic games with a story, it's a required stop.
pc-modern__portal-2.teaser: Smarter and funnier than the first game; GLaDOS and Wheatley steal every scene.

pc-modern__doom.article:
**Doom** from 2016 is a reboot of the legendary series that deliberately turned its back on the era's cautious modern trends and returned to what made the original games from the nineties so addictive. The player wakes up as the Doom Slayer at a Martian base belonging to the UAC corporation, where experiments with hellish energy have, predictably, ended in a demonic invasion, and the only answer is relentless forward momentum. No cover, no regeneration around the corner, no two-weapon limit: the game forces you to run, jump, and attack, because standing still means death.

The key mechanic is the so-called glory kill, a finishing execution on a weakened enemy that restores health, while the chainsaw replenishes ammo. This simple economic loop turns combat into a constant aggressive dance through arenas full of elevation changes, jump pads, and crawlspaces. The arsenal ranges from the shotgun through the plasma rifle to the iconic BFG, and every weapon can be upgraded with mods, just like the suit and its abilities. Between arenas the game offers exploration, secret rooms referencing the original levels, and collectibles, so the pace regularly gets a chance to breathe.

Technically, this was a showcase piece of work: the id Tech 6 engine managed to hold a high frame rate even with dozens of enemies on screen, and the game was one of the first major titles on PC to bet on the Vulkan API. Visually it's a mix of a metallic industrial station and blazing hell, Mick Gordon's music combines industrial metal with synthesizers and can time the onset of combat with precision. Critics and players alike embraced the series' return, and Doom became proof that old-school fast action still has something to say on the modern PC. Today the game is held up mainly by its flawless controls and combat readability, so it still works great as a short evening's entertainment. At the same time, it's a title that reopened the door to fast, cover-free action games and inspired an entire wave of successors.
pc-modern__doom.teaser: A return to the pure speed of the nineties. No cover, just constant forward momentum.

pc-modern__doom-eternal.article:
**Doom Eternal** took the principles of the 2016 reboot and pushed them into a shape that resembles a rhythm game more than a classic shooter. This time demons have occupied Earth, and the Doom Slayer drives them out across ruined cities, frozen orbital stations, and hell itself. The story is more expansive and full of mythology, but the main focus stays on the combat, which the developers rebuilt into a carefully thought-out resource system: the chainsaw supplies ammo, the flamethrower shakes armor loose from enemies, and executions restore health. The player must therefore constantly switch between tools and can never settle into a single favorite weapon.

Movement has gained new emphasis: a double jump, an air dash, monkey bars, and climbable walls turn the arenas into three-dimensional playgrounds you fly through at high speed. Each type of enemy also has a weak point whose destruction changes the course of the fight, so encounters resemble a puzzle solved in real time. Between battles the game offers platforming sections, secret areas, and challenges that stretch its length well beyond the campaign itself. It also included an asymmetric multiplayer mode and, later, an extensive story expansion.

Technically, it's a very finely tuned title: the id Tech 7 engine handles enormous, visually striking spaces at high frame rates, and the game keeps excellent readability even in the middle of chaos. The visual style moved away from grey industrial aesthetics toward saturated colors and comic-book exaggeration, and the music once again builds on hard electronic metal. Reviews were very favorable, though some players objected that the game is more demanding and less relaxing than its predecessor. It's precisely that demanding edge, however, that makes it one of the best-designed action games on PC today, one worth trying again on a higher difficulty. Anyone who learns to switch weapons without thinking gets an experience found nowhere else in the genre: combat turns into fluid motion in which every button press has its exact reason.
pc-modern__doom-eternal.teaser: Combat rebuilt around a resource system: the chainsaw grants ammo, not just blood.

pc-modern__crysis.article:
**Crysis** etched itself into players' memory twice over: as an excellent open-ended shooter and as the benchmark against which new graphics cards were tested for years. The story sends a squad of American soldiers to a tropical island in the South China Sea, where something considerably older and stranger lurks alongside the North Korean army. The player commands a character in a nanosuit that allows switching between enhanced strength, speed, armor, and cloaking. This single mechanic reshapes the whole structure of the game, because there's always more than one way to attack a base, and the player chooses whether to shoot their way in, sneak through, or drive around the enemy along the beach in a vehicle.

The environment is varied and open, with tall grass, dense jungle, and buildings that can be shot to pieces. Enemy AI tries to flank, shouts to warn each other, and falls back, so even repeated attempts on the same objective play out differently each time. In the second half the game transforms, the pace speeds up, and the tropical island gives way to frozen interiors and weightless gravity; some players welcomed the change, others mourned the loss of the early missions' freedom.

The technical side was utterly exceptional in 2007. The CryEngine 2 engine offered dynamic lighting, light filtering through foliage, convincing water, and extensive vegetation destruction. The game managed to bring even the most expensive rigs to their knees, and the phrase "can it run Crysis" became a permanent fixture of gamer vocabulary. The sound design underlines the tension with jungle ambience and an orchestral motif that surfaces at key moments. Critics praised the freedom of approach and the visual execution above all. Today the game runs without a hitch, still looks good, and its system of tactical choices anticipated many later shooters with more open design. Anyone who wants to remember the era when a single game measured a whole computer's performance has an extra reason to install it again.
pc-modern__crysis.teaser: Open-ended nanosuit action that spent years as the go-to graphics card benchmark.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-4-modern-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare** moved the series from the Second World War into the present day, and in doing so reshaped what action games would look like for years afterward. The campaign alternates between two storylines, the British SAS and American Marines, taking the player from a night-time boarding of a ship in a storm through the streets of a Middle Eastern city to a nuclear catastrophe that ranks among the genre's most powerful moments. The narrative is tight, cinematic, and unafraid to briefly strip away the player's agency to underscore the impact of events.

In terms of gameplay it's a brisk, corridor-based shooter that still puts weight on precise weapon handling, aiming down sights, suppressive fire, and cooperation with squadmates. The iconic mission "All Ghillied Up," in which the player creeps through a contaminated zone in a ghillie suit, shows that the developers also knew how to turn the pace down. The real revolution, though, was the multiplayer. Its system of levels, weapon unlocks, perks, and kill-streak rewards created an addictive progression loop that virtually the entire competition has copied ever since.

On PC the game ran beautifully even on the mid-range hardware of the time, offering sharp visuals with elaborate lighting and very good weapon sound design that still ranks among the best the series has ever produced. Music and sound design build tension without ever drowning out the action. Critics received the title enthusiastically, and it became one of the most successful games of its generation, kicking off the franchise's yearly release rhythm. Today the campaign is still excellent to play, though it's on the shorter side and some of its scripted moments read as predictable after all these years. Compared to later entries in the series it feels surprisingly restrained, since it doesn't yet chase endless effect escalation and instead relies on pacing and precisely timed twists. As a historical milestone that shaped the direction of modern military shooters and the shape of online progression in dozens of other games, it's impossible to overlook.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-4-modern-warfare.teaser: Moved the series into the present day and set the cinematic standard for war shooters.

pc-modern__battlefield-3.article:
**Battlefield 3** was a major technical and marketing comeback for the series, and on PC it became one of the best-looking titles of its time. Its center of gravity is the multiplayer mode, where two teams clash over control points on sprawling maps, with infantry supported by tanks, armored transports, helicopters, and fighter jets. It's precisely this combination of infantry combat with vehicles and air support that gives its matches a scale the competition couldn't offer; a single map can contain dozens of simultaneous engagements that feed into each other.

The game is built on a system of four classes: the assault trooper with healing gear, the engineer with anti-armor equipment, support with a machine gun and ammo, and the recon soldier with a sniper rifle and target marking. Progression unlocks scopes, attachments, and new weapons, giving the player a reason to keep coming back. Environmental destruction plays a crucial role, changing available cover as the match unfolds, toppling walls, and erasing entire floors of buildings. The single-player campaign is shorter and more cinematic, complemented by a cooperative mode.

Technically, the game ran on the Frostbite 2 engine, which delivered quality lighting, dusty interiors, convincing explosions, and sound design that ranks among the genre's finest. Gunfire in enclosed spaces sounds completely different from an open field, and the echo of shots can give away an enemy's direction. The PC version supported more players than the console release, making it the reference platform. Reviews were very favorable, with criticism aimed mainly at the external game launcher of the time. Today Battlefield 3 still delivers the unique feeling of a large-scale battle, and its sound design and destruction remain a benchmark against which later entries are measured. For anyone who wants to experience what a shooter feels like when a single soldier is just a small part of a much bigger battle, this is one of the best opportunities available, and at the same time a reminder of an era when big online shooters bet on scale instead of seasonal content.
pc-modern__battlefield-3.teaser: Sprawling maps where infantry is backed up by tanks, helicopters, and jets on a massive scale.

pc-modern__battlefield-bad-company-2.article:
**Battlefield: Bad Company 2** is, for many players, the high point of the entire series, because it managed to combine a relaxed tone with very well-balanced combat across sprawling maps. The campaign follows a squad of soldiers whose humor and friendly ribbing lighten an otherwise serious story about a secret weapon, taking the player from snowy mountains through jungle to desert cities. It's entertaining and well put together on its own, but the main reason to install the game always was, and still is, its multiplayer.

The key innovation was environmental destruction, which here made full tactical sense for the first time. Building walls can be shot through, blown apart with explosives, or leveled by artillery support, so a team defending a house can never feel truly safe, and attackers can always create their own entrance. The Rush mode, in which one side defends pairs of objectives while the other destroys them, became iconic precisely because of how the map gradually turns into ruins over the course of a match. Four classes with their own gear, plus vehicles and helicopters, round out a rich variety of situations, and the unlock system keeps players engaged for dozens of hours.

On PC it was a good-looking title with engaging lighting and dust effects, though it wasn't as demanding as later entries. Weapon and explosion sound design was top-notch, and the game could convey through audio alone that a battle was raging somewhere the player couldn't see. Reviews were very positive, and many looking back highlight precisely the balance, in which no single weapon or vehicle dominated. Today Bad Company 2 mainly serves as a reminder of how well a shooter works when built on simple rules and a changeable environment; its pace is slower and easier to read than that of many current competitors. The player has time to decide, read the map, and coordinate with the team, instead of just reacting to blinking icons. That's exactly why many people return to it even years later, and its name still comes up regularly whenever the best entries in the series are discussed.
pc-modern__battlefield-bad-company-2.teaser: The campaign's laid-back humor and balanced multiplayer make it the series' peak for many.

pc-modern__f-e-r.article:
**F.E.A.R.** combined two things that don't seem related at first glance: the best-crafted firefights of its time and a Japanese-flavored horror story centered on a girl in a red dress. The player takes on the role of an unnamed member of a special unit investigating an incident at a corporate compound, where something far worse than an armed uprising has been unleashed. Moving through the buildings alternates between sharp confrontations with cloned soldiers and quiet passages in which reality falls apart, corridors fill with blood, and the player is never quite sure what was real.

Combat is the heart of the game. The enemy AI ranks among the most highly praised in the genre's history: soldiers inform each other, flank the player through a side corridor, flip tables to create cover, and retreat once they lose the upper hand. The player can compete with them thanks to a time-slowing ability that turns a brief firefight into a choreography full of sparks, dust clouds, and flying chunks of plaster. There aren't many weapons, but each has clear weight, especially the shotgun and the rail gun, after whose hit practically nothing remains of an opponent.

Technically, the game relied on very good dynamic shadows and particle effects that turned every post-fight room into a demolished ruin. That came at a cost to performance, making it one of 2005's more demanding titles. Sound and music work with silence and sudden jolts, keeping the horror alive even between fights, though the repetitive office corridors are among its most common criticisms. Critics praised the game especially for its combat and atmosphere. Today F.E.A.R. feels surprisingly modern precisely because of its enemy behavior, which plenty of newer shooters still can't replicate. On a modern computer the game runs without a hitch, and its firefights in office spaces retain a raw dynamism that's hard to find elsewhere. The horror has lost some of its surprise over the years, but the feel of combat remains first-rate, and many still consider it an unmatched peak of the genre.
pc-modern__f-e-r.teaser: The best firefights of its era paired with Japanese-inspired horror about a girl in red.

pc-modern__far-cry.article:
**Far Cry** was a revelation in 2004, because it showed that a shooter didn't have to be just a series of corridors. Playing former sailor Jack Carver, the player ends up on a tropical archipelago where he was originally only supposed to ferry a journalist, and soon discovers that mercenaries working for a dubious scientist have taken over the islands. The environment is open and readable over long distances, and the game cleverly makes use of that: through binoculars the player can mark patrols, plan a route, and decide whether to break into a camp at night, arrive by boat, or go around it through the jungle.

Combat is merciless and fast. Enemies aim well, call in reinforcements, and behave aggressively, so a direct assault against superior numbers usually ends badly. The game therefore rewards patience, use of elevation, and vehicles ranging from a buggy to a boat with a mounted machine gun. Later sections introduce mutated enemies who pick up the pace and shift the action into laboratory interiors; this change remains a subject of debate to this day, since it takes away the game's greatest strength, namely freedom.

Technically, it was a showcase for the first CryEngine. Sweeping views of the sea, dense vegetation, quality water reflections, and sharp long-distance visibility weren't common in games at the time, and Far Cry quickly became a standard fixture of graphics card benchmarks. The sound of the jungle, the distant calls of patrols, and tense music round out the feeling of isolation in a foreign environment. Reviews were very favorable, and the game's success led both to further entries under the Ubisoft banner and, indirectly, to the creation of Crysis.
