Graphically the title is clean and legible, even though the Wii's resolution shows its age today, and the music alternates between upbeat Latin American and jazz themes that stick in your head. Mario Kart Wii became one of the best-selling racing titles ever, and to this day it's the ideal game to switch on when a group of people gets together and nobody feels like explaining anything.
wii__mario-kart-wii.teaser: The entry with a plastic steering wheel that made racing accessible to the widest audience yet.

wii__wii-sports-resort.article:
**Wii Sports Resort** is a sequel that exists mainly to show off a new add-on. Sold alongside the game was the Wii MotionPlus attachment with a gyroscope, which finally allowed the remote's rotation to be tracked in real time, with a precision the original Wii Remote could only dream of. The difference is felt immediately. Turn your wrist in the game, and an object on screen turns by the very same angle, which for the first time makes the controller a genuine extension of your hand rather than just a swing detector. The opening calibration ritual of placing the remote flat on a table became something every console owner remembers.

Everything takes place on a tropical island, and the range of disciplines is wide: fencing, table tennis, archery, frisbee, basketball, jet skiing, bowling, wakeboarding, cycling, or flying a plane over the island. The ones that shine brightest are those where angle and subtle motion decide the outcome. Fencing turns into a game of feints and guards, since you have to work around a defense that your opponent holds exactly where you're aiming. Archery demands a steady hand and a read on the wind, and table tennis quickly turns into a battle over ball spin. Flying the plane, by contrast, is a calm, almost relaxing discipline in which you can simply soar over the island and hunt for hidden spots.

The visual style follows on from its predecessor, meaning Mii characters and clean, colorful graphics without unnecessary detail, only the setting is more elaborate this time, and the island feels like a single, unified place with its own geography. The music is light, summery, and unobtrusive, exactly as befits a holiday island. Critics received the game very well and often noted that only now was the Wii's control scheme what it should have been from the start. Commercially it was a huge success, even though the add-on represented an extra expense. Today Wii Sports Resort is perhaps the best proof of what motion controls could do, and for a group of people in one room it still works without the slightest need for explanation.
wii__wii-sports-resort.teaser: The sequel showcasing MotionPlus; for the first time the controller faithfully mirrors wrist rotation.

wii__new-super-mario-bros-wii.article:
**New Super Mario Bros. Wii** brought Mario back to the big screen after years in the form people knew from the 8-bit era, a side-scrolling platformer. The major new feature was simultaneous play for up to four people on a single screen. While previous entries only offered cooperation by taking turns, here four characters crowd onto the same platform, jump on each other's heads, collect the same coins, and quite often knock each other into pits. The result sits somewhere between cooperation and chaos, provoking loud laughter and plenty of mutual finger-pointing.

The controls are deliberately simple: the Wii Remote is held sideways like a classic pad, so all you need is the d-pad and two buttons. A flick of the remote is used to pick up a teammate or to spin a propeller, one of the new abilities. Alongside the classic power-ups comes a penguin suit for sliding on ice and swimming better, a propeller suit for launching upward and gently floating back down, or a giant ice ball. Levels are built in traditional fashion, with secret exits, three big coins on each map, and bonus worlds for those willing to put in the effort. The difficulty is higher than you'd expect from an accessible title, especially in the final worlds, where the game already assumes the player can land precise jumps on the first try.

The game also introduced a feature that plays through a difficult section for the player and lets them continue afterward, one of the first such concessions to frustrated players at the time. Graphically, it's a clean, colorful two-dimensional presentation with three-dimensional models, and the music builds on playful, catchy themes topped with choral humming, which has returned to the series ever since. Reception was very good, and the title became one of the console's best-selling games. Today it remains one of the best games for an evening with four players, though playing solo will leave you feeling like you're missing out on a good half of the fun the game has to offer.
wii__new-super-mario-bros-wii.teaser: A return to 2D Mario, with the option to play with up to four people on one screen at once.

wii__donkey-kong-country-returns.article:
**Donkey Kong Country Returns** is an unusual project: a studio famous for grim sci-fi adventures was tasked with reviving a classic platforming series from the nineties, and it pulled it off with remarkable respect for the source material. Donkey Kong and his buddy Diddy once again race across an island that someone has raided of its banana supply, and the game sticks to a side-on view, precise jumping, and a fast pace. Diddy rides on the back of the bigger gorilla, and his jet-pack barrel allows for a brief hover in mid-air, which during tricky jumps is often the difference between success and a fall.

The game is demanding and doesn't try to hide it. The levels are full of traps, vanishing platforms, and enemies that appear at exactly the moment you're airborne, and several of the final maps rank among the hardest Nintendo has ever released. At the same time, everything reads clearly, and mistakes feel like your own failure rather than injustice. Alongside the classic jumping, the mine-cart ride and the rocket barrel return, silhouette passages have been added where the entire screen turns into a black shadow against a colorful background, and there are scenes where the action spills between foreground and background. The controls lean on motion a bit forcibly: the drum-thump and the roll are performed by shaking the controller, which most players considered unnecessary when a single button would have done the job.

The audiovisual presentation is one of the finest showcases of what Wii could do. Environments have depth, dynamic lighting, and a wealth of background detail, and the music reworks classic themes from the original trilogy into fuller, drum-driven arrangements that instantly trigger nostalgia. Critics received the game very well, praising exactly the fact that it isn't a mere trip down memory lane but an honest, tough, and carefully designed platformer. Today it still holds up excellently, only the shake-based controls feel more dated than they need to. Later releases on other platforms accordingly offered classic button controls and showed just how little the game needed to be perfect.
wii__donkey-kong-country-returns.teaser: A studio known for grim sci-fi adventures revived the classic series with respect for the original.

wii__legend-of-zelda-skyward-sword.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: Skyward Sword** is the series' boldest attempt to rewrite its own rules around the possibilities of motion control. The game requires the Wii MotionPlus add-on, and the sword genuinely swings in whatever direction you move your hand. Enemies have their guards set up so that you must find an opening and strike precisely, say vertically from above or diagonally from the right, and some use alternating defenses that force the player to read their stance. Combat thereby shifts from a rhythmic action into something closer to a puzzle, and it is the biggest departure from everything that came before in the series.

The world is split between a floating island above the clouds, where Link lives and flies on a large bird, and three sprawling regions down on the ground. These aren't classic open landscapes but rather extensive puzzles that unlock gradually, where every stretch of space is designed with intent. The temples rank among the most inventive in the entire series, and there are frequent moments where an entire room transforms based on a single switch. The storytelling is more personal than usual, since Zelda is this time Link's childhood friend and the main motivation is to find her, which gives the whole thing an unexpected emotional weight. Flying on the bird between islands works as a calm interlude and, at the same time, as the only truly open environment in the game.

Visually the game leaned into soft, watercolor-like colors that blur into the distance, which helped work around the console's limited resolution, and the result has aged well. For the first time in the series, the music was recorded by an orchestra, and the central theme ranks among the best ever written for Zelda. Reception was very warm at launch, though the game later became a target of criticism for its amount of repetition, a talkative guide, and occasional motion-detection failures. A later release on newer hardware offered classic controls and showed that underneath it all lies a strong, carefully built entry whose story additionally lays the foundation for the entire series mythology and explains the origin of its best-known symbols.
wii__legend-of-zelda-skyward-sword.teaser: The series' boldest attempt at motion controls; the sword strikes exactly where your hand swings.

wii__super-mario-galaxy-2.article:
**Super Mario Galaxy 2** grew out of a surplus of ideas that didn't fit into the first game, and it ended up as a full-fledged title that many consider even better than the original. The core principle remains: small planetoids with their own gravity, jumping between them, and collecting stars. Gone, however, is the sprawling observatory that served as a hub, replaced by a simple world map in the style of older entries. Thanks to that, the player gets straight to the substance and doesn't linger running through empty corridors between levels.

The main novelty is Yoshi. He catches enemies and distant points with his tongue, puffs up and rises after eating a certain plant, and at other times charges forward fast enough to run along even steep walls. Alongside him, further transformations arrive, such as a drill tool that pulls Mario through a planetoid to its far side, or a cloud that lets him create a few temporary platforms in mid-air. The levels are even denser and more inventive than before, each built around one strong idea that it then abandons right after. Toward the end, the game opens a genuinely demanding extension that tests even experienced players and ranks among the hardest Mario has ever offered. Collectors also have a reason to walk through levels again for hidden stars and comets that change the rules of galaxies already explored.

Technically it was once again a showcase of the console's peak, with a clean color palette, smooth animation, and clear design that always makes obvious where you can jump. The music again builds on orchestral recordings, and several tracks, especially during flight and space passages, rank among the best in the entire series. Critics received the game excellently and often cited it as an example of what a sequel should look like when it deepens rather than repeats. Today Galaxy 2 still feels remarkably fresh, and it's one of the strongest reasons to get a Wii or one of its successors at all. Anyone who has played only the first game is missing out on half of the best of it.
wii__super-mario-galaxy-2.teaser: A sequel born from the first game's surplus of ideas; many consider it even better.

wii__kirby-s-epic-yarn.article:
**Kirby's Epic Yarn** is one of the most visually distinctive games on the entire console. The whole world is made of fabric, yarn, and buttons, environments are stitched together out of patches and seams, and Kirby himself is just an outline made of a single thread. The story sends him to a realm where he loses his famous ability to suck up enemies and instead transforms into various objects: a yarn whip that catches and unravels things, a car, a parachute, a weight, or a rocket. Every transformation has simple controls, and the game switches between them fast enough that you never get bored.

A key decision is that in Epic Yarn you cannot die. When hit, Kirby simply loses part of the gems he's collected, which completely changes the nature of play. Tension is replaced by the joy of discovery and collecting, since every level hides fabric treasures that furnish an apartment and unlock further tasks. The title is therefore an ideal choice for younger children or for playing together with someone who doesn't normally play video games, since a second player can join in at any time without sinking anyone. Experienced players, on the other hand, will find a challenge in clearing a level with everything it offers, without losing a single gem. Alongside the main path, short minigames and tasks for the town's residents have been added, extending playtime by a few pleasant extra hours.

The audiovisual presentation is the main reason you'll remember this game. The fabric style is not only inventive but also technically elegant, since the illustrated look worked around the console's limited resolution, and the result has aged better than most realistically rendered titles of the time. The music is gentle, piano-led, and dreamy, matching the overall tenderness of the presentation. Critics received the game warmly and highlighted exactly its visual approach, though some reviewers noted that the complete absence of risk takes away tension. Today Kirby's Epic Yarn feels like a friendly, relaxing title to return to when you don't feel like anything demanding and just want to look at everything that can be assembled out of yarn and buttons.
wii__kirby-s-epic-yarn.teaser: The most visually distinctive Kirby; the entire world is made of fabric, yarn, and buttons.

wii__punch-out.article:
**Punch-Out!!** isn't a boxing simulation but a puzzle disguised as a fight. Little Mac stands against a series of opponents who are bigger, stronger, and each has their own set of attacks with a fixed order and a tell just before the blow lands. The player's job is to read that pattern, learn it, and respond with the right dodge or block, which opens a window for a counterpunch. Anyone who just tries to swing away loses within a few seconds. Anyone who breaks the fight down gets through it with remarkable ease.

The Wii version takes over the basic framework of the classic entry from the eight-bit console and adds new attacks and a second phase for each opponent, so just as you think you've got the pattern down, the opponent changes behavior. The game can be controlled in several ways. Classically, the Wii Remote is held sideways like a pad, which is the most precise option, or you can use motion controls and genuinely swing your arms through the air with the remote and nunchuk in your fists. The latter option is physically exhausting and less reliable, but surprisingly well captures the tension of the ring. A mode was also added where two people box against each other, and after completing the career mode, a tougher variant of the fights unlocks, where a single hit means the end and all the patterns you've learned have to be used flawlessly.

Graphically the game leans on a bold cartoon style with thick outlines and exaggerated caricatures of opponents, each with its own animated entrance and a personality expressed through mere gestures. Sound and music work with the tension and rhythm of the bout, and several themes are directly carried over from the original. Critics received the title very well, praising exactly the fact that it lost nothing of its toughness while still feeling contemporary. Today Punch-Out!! is one of those games you switch back on again and again after a first loss, because defeat is always clearly your own mistake and never bad luck or an unfair system. That is precisely the charm that has kept the series alive for decades.
wii__punch-out.teaser: A boxing puzzle disguised as a fight; success depends on reading your opponent's patterns.

wii__sin-and-punishment-star-successor.article:
**Sin and Punishment: Star Successor** is a dense, loud, and uncompromising action game from a studio famous for technically demanding shooters. The game carries you along a fixed path through the environment, while you aim a cursor across the screen and simultaneously dodge with a character who runs, jumps, and slides along the ground. The result is an unusual combination of a classic rail shooter and platforming action, in which you have to track two things at once: where you're shooting and where you're standing. It's exactly this split attention that makes the title a challenge you need a while to get used to.

The screen is almost constantly filled with projectiles. Most of them can be deflected back at the attacker with a swing, which turns defense into an additional source of points, and the game constantly offers the player a choice between going for score or going for survival. The boss fights are the main draw and surpass most of what the genre has produced in both scale and inventiveness. Each one has several transformations, changes the environment around itself, and often feels like a standalone game in its own right. Aiming with the Wii Remote suits this type of action superbly and is noticeably faster and more precise than an analog stick. The game also supports a classic controller, but with a pointer in hand the whole concept makes far more sense. A two-player mode on a single screen was also added.

Technically it's an impressive feat on Wii. The screen can handle an enormous number of objects and effects without noticeable slowdown, and the color scheme of the sci-fi world is bold and stylized. The music is energetic, electronic, and drives the action forward. The title is one that critics received very well, but the wider audience passed it by, since the genre was niche at the time and the game comes across as off-putting at first glance. Today it's one of the console's most valuable lesser-known gems and an ideal choice for a few hours of intense action where every second and every hit counts. Anyone who gets through it once usually comes back for a better score.
wii__sin-and-punishment-star-successor.teaser: Intense action from Treasure combining a rail shooter with platformer-style character movement.

wii__xenoblade-chronicles.article:
**Xenoblade Chronicles** is one of the most ambitious games ever released on Wii, and also one that came within a hair's breadth of never reaching the West at all. The whole world stands on the bodies of two petrified giants who once fought each other and now form the continents people walk across. This idea isn't just window dressing: the map is genuinely built on the anatomy of those beings, and journeying from the feet all the way up to the head gives the game an unusual sense of direction and scale. The main hero obtains a sword that shows him fragments of the future, and both the story and the combat grow out of that.

The combat system runs in real time and with movement across the battlefield, but with cooldowns on individual abilities, so it feels more like an action-leaning take on a classic Japanese RPG. The trick is that the game shows an impending disaster before it lands, and the player has a few seconds to avert it, say by warning an ally or repositioning. The world is huge and open, full of freely roaming creatures of every level, meaning that even early on you can run into something immensely powerful and have to avoid it. There are hundreds of side quests, and a relationship system between characters unlocks further scenes and upgrades. Equipment can additionally be customized with gems the player crafts themselves, so even gathering materials has a point.

Technically the game forced compromises. Resolution is low and textures are rough in the distance, but the view over a vast landscape from a high vantage point still lands even today. The music is one of the main reasons people remember this title: an extensive soundtrack alternates orchestral motifs with rock and jazz pieces, and the themes for the day and night versions of the same place rank among the best in the genre. Critics received the game excellently, and the fan campaign for its Western release became legendary. Today Xenoblade Chronicles is the foundation of an entire franchise and one of the strongest arguments that Wii wasn't just a console for family game nights.
wii__xenoblade-chronicles.teaser: An ambitious JRPG set on the bodies of two petrified giants that form the world.

wii__super-paper-mario.article:
**Super Paper Mario** is the strangest member of the Paper Mario series and, at the same time, one of the most interesting experiments released on Wii. Previous entries were classic turn-based RPGs with a papercraft aesthetic; here, though, the game turned into a platformer that kept from role-playing games only the experience points, character levels, and an emphasis on storytelling. The magic trick everything hinges on is switching between two and three dimensions: pressing a button rotates the flat level into space, and the player suddenly sees paths, platforms, and objects that were hidden behind one another from the side view.

This gives rise to puzzles you won't find anywhere else, and the game alternates them with classic jumping and simple touch-based combat. Additional playable characters gradually join in, each with its own ability, along with small helpers called Pixls, who can, say, explode, lift a heavy object, or shrink the hero down to the size of a bug. The structure is divided into chapters, with a small town serving as the hub between them, and individual chapters aren't afraid to get quite unconventional, including passages deliberately stylized into an eight-bit look or a level built around a single unconventional mechanic.

But it's the story that gets talked about most. A villain named Count Bleck wants to destroy every world, and the narrative around him is unusually serious, at times almost bitter, even though the humor typical of the series never disappears anywhere. Several scenes in the closing chapters rank among the most emotionally powerful moments in all of Mario's history. Graphically the game leans on a flat papercraft style with bold colors that has aged better than most more realistically rendered titles of the time, and the music mixes chiptune callbacks with playful orchestral pieces. Reviews were very favorable, though some fans regretted the departure from turn-based combat. Today Super Paper Mario is more of a cult item worth getting to know mainly for its ideas and its storytelling. On a modern television it still looks good thanks to its bold colors, and it ranks among the titles that carry the most distinctive signature on Wii.
wii__super-paper-mario.teaser: The strangest Paper Mario; switching between 2D and 3D turns the platformer into a puzzle.

wii__kirby-s-return-to-dream-land.article:
**Kirby's Return to Dream Land** is a return to what the series does best, after the previous Kirby on Wii experimented with a fabric-style look and shelved enemy-inhaling altogether. Here everything is back: the pink hero swallows foes, copies their abilities, and with them gains a hammer, sword, electricity, a leaf saw, or a whip. The story is simple, the player helps a stranded traveler named Magolor gather the pieces of his ship, and it mainly serves as a reason to work through colorful worlds at a familiar pace.

The main new feature is so-called super abilities, temporary exaggerated versions of the usual weapons that take up half the screen and literally smash entire chunks of the level, background included. They're designed as a celebration of power and always lead to a hidden area with more collectibles. The other big addition is co-op for up to four players on one screen, where the other players control familiar characters from the series, each with their own fighting style. With more people the game turns into a pleasantly chaotic affair where nobody needs to worry, since a knocked-out player is back in a moment.

Difficulty stays very mild for most of the game, which is typical for the series, but after finishing it a substantially harder mode and several challenges unlock that surprisingly put up a fight. Technically the game never pushed the Wii to its limits, but it has clean, clearly readable graphics and a smooth pace that never stutters even with four characters on screen. The music mixes new compositions with rearranged classics from the series and ranks among the catchiest ever heard on the console. Reviews welcomed the game warmly, with the usual reservation about low difficulty and conservative design. Today it's one of the best choices for playing with kids or with someone who doesn't play platformers regularly. In hindsight, it's clear this very installment set the template the series still follows today, since later Kirby games borrowed its level structure and its handling of copied abilities. It also later got a port to newer Nintendo consoles.
wii__kirby-s-return-to-dream-land.teaser: A return to traditional inhaling and copying abilities after the fabric experiment.

wii__wario-land-shake-it.article:
**Wario Land: Shake It!** is the last classic entry in Wario's platforming branch and also one of the best-looking titles released in two dimensions on Wii. The whole game is hand-drawn, animated in the style of a traditional cartoon, and topped off with cinematic cutscenes that could easily air on television. Wario sets out into a world trapped inside an old globe toy to pull out every last bit of gold he can reach, since the main hero's motivation is, as always, pure greed.

The gameplay is built on the fact that Wario isn't vulnerable in the usual sense. Enemies knock him around, set him on fire, or squash him flat, but he just turns into a ridiculous shape and keeps going, which makes the main levels feel more like spatial puzzles than tests of reflexes. The controller is held sideways like a classic gamepad, and the only motion-control element is shaking it, which makes Wario spill coins from his sack, shake the whole screen, or break the ground beneath him. Every level has the same structure: the player fights their way to a final cage, frees a small creature, and that triggers a countdown during which they must retrace their way back through every room to the entrance. This dash is the heart of the game and forces you to memorize your route.

Completed tasks and collected gold unlock further levels and upgrades, so replaying pays off. The music is playful and jazzy, matching the overall comedic tone that has always set the Wario series apart from the Mario branch. Contemporary reviews praised the artistic execution and thoughtful level design, while criticizing the shorter length and lower difficulty of the main line. Commercially it never ranked among the console's biggest hits, and today it's a somewhat forgotten gem that holds up well against far more famous two-dimensional platformers of its time. For Wii owners it's one of the few titles where the value hides more in execution than in scope, and anyone who loves hand-drawn animation won't find many better representatives on the console. The series never returned to this style again.
wii__wario-land-shake-it.teaser: The last classic Wario Land, hand-drawn like a traditional cartoon.

wii__sonic-colors.article:
**Sonic Colors** arrived at a time when the blue hedgehog was going through one of the worst periods in its history, and it turned into a surprising return to form. Sonic Team dropped the experiments with side characters, swords, or nighttime transformations and focused on a single thing: fast movement through well-designed levels. The story frames it as an amusement park that Doctor Eggman built on the orbits around several planets, of course with an ulterior motive. Each planet has its own visual theme, from a candy world through a tropical beach to a neon city, and the color palette ranks among the most vivid the series has ever had.

Gameplay alternates three-dimensional stretches with side-view passages, and the transitions between them are smooth, which had been the most common stumbling block in previous entries. The new feature is the Wisps, alien beings that lend Sonic temporary abilities: a laser shot that bounces off walls, a drill for moving underground, a rocket firing upward, or a transformation into a heavy ball. Thanks to them, levels have more alternate paths than they seem to at first glance, and replaying them genuinely pays off. Controls do without motion elements, and the game supports a classic gamepad too, so precision suffers not at all.

Technically, Sonic Colors ranks among the top-tier titles on Wii. The pace stays smooth even in the fastest passages, the colors shine, and the level design remains readable despite the speed. The music mixes electronica with big-band motifs, and the title song became one of the most beloved in the whole series. Reviews were noticeably more favorable than for previous three-dimensional entries, and many players still call it the best modern Sonic game to this day. A remastered edition later came out for newer platforms, but the original Wii version remains a fully valid experience and still plays beautifully today. For console owners it's clearly the first Sonic game to reach for. It also showed that Sonic works best when it sticks to a simple idea and lets speed speak for itself.
wii__sonic-colors.teaser: A return to form after weak years; just fast movement through well-designed levels.

wii__epic-mickey.article:
**Epic Mickey** is one of the most ambitious attempts to turn Mickey Mouse into the hero of a genuine gaming adventure, and at the same time a demonstration of how a strong idea can be undone by execution. Mickey finds himself in the Wasteland, a world where Disney discarded forgotten characters and cancelled attractions. It's ruled by Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, Mickey's older and long-overlooked predecessor, and the whole world is made up of warped versions of familiar places, giving it a strange, at times almost melancholic atmosphere.

The core of the gameplay is a brush loaded with paint and thinner. With paint the player fills in missing platforms, bridges, and whole sections of the environment; with thinner they dissolve them instead, revealing what's behind. The same choice applies to enemies: they can be destroyed, or won over with paint so they help instead. The game tracks these small choices and reflects them in how the Wasteland's inhabitants treat Mickey and in how the endings play out. Between the main areas, the player walks through short two-dimensional levels built on classic cartoons, one of the best-received ideas in the whole game.

The execution, however, doesn't reach the ambition. The camera is often unruly and actively hurts in tighter spaces, controlling the brush by aiming with the remote is fun but not always precise, and in places it shows that the Wii barely keeps up with the creators' vision. Even so, the game has a distinctive visual style, and the soundtrack, built on old orchestral motifs with a touch of the funhouse, ranks among its strongest points. Contemporary reviews were mixed, praising the idea and atmosphere while criticizing the technical shortcomings. Commercially it was a success, and a sequel followed on multiple platforms. Today Epic Mickey is interesting mainly as a reminder of a time when even major franchises dared to try unusual subject matter. Especially valued is the idea of bringing Oswald back into the game, which after decades on the sidelines returned him to wide public awareness. For collectors it's also a title tied closely to the Wii specifically.
wii__epic-mickey.teaser: An ambitious attempt to make Mickey the hero of an adventure in the forgotten Wasteland.

wii__klonoa.article:
**Klonoa** is a remake of a platformer that originally came out on the first PlayStation and has since held a reputation as one of the best-designed games of its kind. The Wii version redrew the whole world in three-dimensional, brightly colorful form, while keeping the original structure and pace. The hero, with long ears and a cap, travels through the dreamlike world of Phantomile, where something evil is stirring, and his only weapon is a ring that fires a ball of air.

The entire game rests on a single mechanic, which it wrings dry to the last drop. Klonoa doesn't hit or stomp enemies, he inflates them and lifts them overhead. From there he can throw them forward, throw them into another enemy, or throw them downward and bounce off them for a higher jump. This gives rise to puzzles, since enemies stop being obstacles and become tools. The key is the so-called two-and-a-half-dimensional path: the character moves along a clearly defined line, but that line winds through space, so the player often throws an enemy into the depth of the screen or catches them on the other side of the arena. The level design is textbook clean, each level adds one new idea and never overstays its welcome.

The atmosphere is dreamlike and unusually gentle, with its own invented language that the characters speak. The story's endings were already considered surprisingly powerful in the original version and remain untouched in the remake. The music holds the same line, playful melodies with a hint of sadness beneath the surface. Reviews of the Wii version welcomed it warmly, mainly because it made a hard-to-find classic accessible again, though they criticized its short length and low difficulty. Commercially the game never succeeded as much as it deserved, merely repeating the original's fate. Anyone who likes precise, kindly designed platformers should give it a try. On Wii it's a pleasantly short game that can be finished in an evening or two, and that's exactly why it's easy to return to repeatedly. Anyone who finishes it usually starts hunting down the sequel, which once came out on a Sony console.
wii__klonoa.teaser: A remake of the beloved PlayStation platformer; a dreamlike world and a ring-shaped weapon.

wii__boy-and-his-blob.article:
**A Boy and His Blob** is a loose reworking of an old game from the 8-bit era into a form that shares the main idea with the original while otherwise standing entirely on its own. A boy meets a white, gelatinous creature from another planet, and together they set out to save its home from a ruler who has overtaken it. The pair's strength lies in a simple rule: the boy carries a bag of jellybeans, and every flavor of jellybean turns the blob into something different.

An orange one produces a trampoline, a coconut one a coconut shell that serves as a battering ram, others create a ladder, an umbrella, a hole in the ground, or a bubble that lifts the boy upward. The player thus doesn't collect weapons but tools, and every level is really a puzzle about picking the right transformation at the right moment in the right place. There's hardly any combat, enemies are mostly avoided, and the boy is fragile, so a mistake means an instant return to the checkpoint. Besides the main path, every level hides treasure chests that unlock harder bonus levels built purely on logic.

What catches the eye most, though, is the look. The hand-drawn animation recalls a classic cartoon and, even at the time of release, was noticeably above what was typical for smaller Wii titles. One small detail matters greatly: whenever the player presses the right button, the boy hugs the blob, a simple thing that gives the whole game something like a heart. The music is subdued, orchestral, and calm, so the whole thing feels more like a fairy tale than a platformer. Reviews were very praising, but sales lagged, and the game gradually became a cult favorite that later got ported to newer platforms. Today it's one of the best smaller titles ever released on Wii. Controls do without motion elements, and the game runs smoothly, so nothing technical spoils the impression. It works best in small doses over several evenings, since the puzzles rely on careful thought rather than speed, and that's exactly what sets it apart from most platformers of its time.
wii__boy-and-his-blob.teaser: A reimagining of the 8-bit classic; jellybeans turn the Blob into tools for rescue.

wii__muramasa-demon-blade.article:
**Muramasa: The Demon Blade** is a game most people will remember first through their eyes. Studio Vanillaware drew it entirely by hand in two dimensions, with layered backgrounds, sunlit foliage, and characters animated so fluidly that on Wii it feels like something from another generation. The setting draws on Japan's Edo period blended with mythology: the player runs through bamboo groves, snowy mountain passes, rice paddies, and the underworld, meeting yokai, monks, samurai, and gods along the way.

Gameplay-wise it's a side-view action RPG with an emphasis on swordplay. The player controls one of two characters, Princess Momohime, possessed by the soul of a foreign swordsman, and the ninja Kisuke, searching for his own lost memory. Each has their own path through the world and their own endings. Combat rests on a small number of buttons and mainly on switching between three equipped katanas: a blade wears down with attacks and risks breaking, so it's necessary to switch quickly and let the edge regenerate. Switching also works as a counterattack that deflects projectiles, turning fights into a rhythmic affair reminiscent of fighting games. Progress unlocks further blades from an extensive collection, each with its own special attack, complemented by cooking meals that boost resilience.

The atmosphere is supported by a soundtrack built on Japanese instruments and drums, which recedes into the background during calm passages and picks up pace during boss fights. Contemporary reviews praised the game mainly for its artistic execution and the fluidity of the combat system, while criticizing repeated backtracking through the same areas. Even so, it became one of the titles people bought a Wii for, and it helped Vanillaware earn a reputation as a studio that outdoes much bigger competitors visually. An expanded version later came out for PlayStation Vita, but the original Wii version remains a fully valid game. Anyone looking for a Wii title that pushes the console's visuals to a completely different level should reach for exactly this one, even at the cost of a story that remains mostly a backdrop for the combat.
wii__muramasa-demon-blade.teaser: A hand-drawn action RPG from Vanillaware; the Edo period blended with mythology.

wii__okami.article:
**Okami** originally came out on PlayStation 2 from Studio Clover, and it reached Wii in a port that made use of the most important thing the new console offered: pointer aiming. The player controls the sun goddess Amaterasu in the form of a white wolf and travels through a Japanese landscape rendered as a living ink-wash painting. The world is cursed, its colors have vanished, and the task is to bring life back to trees, fields, and people, which the game shows literally: heal an area and it blossoms before your eyes.

The key mechanic is the celestial brush. At any moment the game pauses, the image turns into paper, and the player draws symbols on it that have an immediate effect in the world. A circle creates the sun and turns night into day, a horizontal line cuts through an enemy or a rope, a spiral unleashes wind, and a zigzag line calls down lightning. On Wii you draw directly with the remote, which feels more natural than the original analog stick, though somewhat less precise. The rest of the game is a classic action-adventure in the vein of Zelda: a sprawling landscape, puzzles, dungeons, collectibles, and side quests, this time built on Japanese legends, including the story of the eight-headed dragon Orochi.

The atmosphere is unmistakable. The ink-wash art style overcomes technical limitations, and the game still looks gorgeous today; the music draws on traditional Japanese instruments, and the dialogue is delivered through an odd babbling speech that surprisingly works. Contemporary reviews were enthusiastic, but commercially the game never achieved what it deserved, becoming a textbook example of an underrated classic. The Wii version has minor changes to the end credits compared to the original, but otherwise it's the complete experience. Okami's influence shows up everywhere games use art style as their main expressive tool. Its length is considerable, and the game takes its time, so the first hours may feel slow, but the patience pays off richly. High-resolution editions later came out on newer platforms, but drawing with the remote remains, for many players, the most natural way to experience it on Wii.
wii__okami.teaser: A port of the painterly PlayStation 2 hit that makes use of Wii Remote pointer aiming.

wii__no-more-heroes.article:
**No More Heroes** is a game that landed on the family-friendly Wii like a punch to the face. The main character is Travis Touchdown, an annoying otaku living in a motel in the small town of Santa Destroy, who buys a lightsaber-like beam katana over the internet and decides to become the best hired assassin in the world. To work his way up from eleventh place on the ranking to first, he must defeat the other assassins one by one, each a bizarre figure with their own scene and their own idea of how their death should look.

The combat system is simple but has style. The player attacks with a button, switches between high and low stances, and the moment an enemy is weakened, the game displays a direction to swing the controller in to finish them off. The katana is recharged the same way, leading to one of the most famous and deliberately most embarrassing animations of its time. Between fights, the player moves around an open city that is deliberately empty and dull, riding a motorcycle and taking on lowly side jobs to earn the entry fee for the next duel. This part of the game splits players into two camps: some consider it a boring filler, others a deliberate commentary on the emptiness of the hero's motivation.

Technically it was average, the city textures are thin and the framerate wasn't always smooth, but the visual style is unmistakable thanks to sharp colors, comic-book effects, and an interface stylized after eight-bit games. The music is electronic, aggressive, and the main theme sticks after the very first listen. Reviews were mostly positive and praised the game especially for its distinctiveness and humor, which constantly breaks the fourth wall. Today, No More Heroes is seen as one of the console's most important independent-minded titles and kicked off a series that has seen several sequels. For console owners it was proof that the Wii didn't have to be just a machine for family sports games, and the title still works today as a clear recommendation for anyone who likes author-driven games with a strong point of view.
wii__no-more-heroes.teaser: A bizarre action game from Grasshopper Manufacture about a hitman with a lightsaber-like katana.

wii__resident-evil-4-wii-edition.article:
**Resident Evil 4: Wii Edition** is a port of a game that already rewrote the rules of action games at its original GameCube release, and on Wii it gained exactly what it had been missing: fast and precise aiming. Leon S. Kennedy sets out to a remote European village to find the kidnapped daughter of the American president, and instead of classic zombies he runs into villagers controlled by a parasite who attack in groups, use tools, and can surround the player.

The over-the-shoulder camera, aimed shooting at specific body parts, and the alternation of tension with absolutely frantic firefights became a template for an entire generation of action games. On Wii you aim the cursor directly at the screen, which speeds up the whole rhythm, because the player can precisely hit a knee or the arm holding an axe much faster. Some contact actions also use controller shaking, whether it's shaking off an enemy or quick reactions in cutscenes. The rest remains untouched: managing the backpack, in which the player arranges weapons like a puzzle, the merchant with upgrades, protecting the escort character, and several memorable boss fights.

The Wii version also includes content that didn't make it into the original GameCube release, including the side campaign with Ada Wong and bonus modes. Technically it's a faithful rendition of the original with a sharper image, so nothing revolutionary, but smooth and legible. The atmosphere remains excellent, especially thanks to the lighting work, the echo in the castle corridors, and music that can be completely silent and then strike. Reviews were enthusiastic and many players still consider this version the best way to play Resident Evil 4. For a low price, the Wii thus gained one of the best action games ever. It's a game that both closed one chapter of the series and opened another, because later entries pulled back from its action-oriented stance and horror temporarily receded into the background. Anyone who has never played Resident Evil 4 has one of the best options to start on Wii, they just need to reckon with the brutality that ranks the game among titles for adults.
wii__resident-evil-4-wii-edition.teaser: The groundbreaking GameCube action game gained on Wii exactly what it lacked: fast aiming.

wii__monster-hunter-tri.article:
**Monster Hunter Tri** is the title that first properly established the series about hunting giant beasts outside Japan, and at the same time one of the most extensive games on the entire console. The player arrives in the fishing village of Moga, threatened by something big beneath the surface, and gradually works their way up from hunting small game to duels with dragons the size of houses. There is no experience point system here; all progress is based on equipment the player crafts from parts of hunted monsters.

Combat is slow, heavy, and utterly uncompromising. Every weapon has its own set of moves, its own speed, and its own way of returning from an attack to defense, so switching a sword for a hammer means learning the game almost from scratch. A hunt takes tens of minutes, the monster has its own behavior, gets tired, limps, flees to another area, and must be tracked by its traces. This installment's new feature is underwater combat, which adds a third dimension and is also the most frequently cited flaw, because orientation beneath the surface isn't always pleasant. Cooperation is absolutely essential: the game could be played online with other hunters, and it's precisely the shared hunt that's the reason people spent hundreds of hours on it.

Technically it was top-notch work on Wii, mainly thanks to the monster designs, their animations, and surprisingly expansive areas. The music is orchestral and switches to themes fans of the series recognize instantly when a large monster arrives. Reviews were very positive and the game became one of the few titles on Wii that also appealed to players seeking depth and difficulty. The official servers no longer function, which has closed off some content, but the game still offers a full-fledged single-player campaign. Its influence on the genre was enormous and many later monster-hunting games trace back precisely to it. The start is quite steep and the game explains very little, so the first few hours usually decide whether a player finds their way into it. But once they understand that every hunt is essentially a boss fight lasting tens of minutes, it's hard to find anything comparable. An expanded version later appeared on Nintendo's following consoles.
wii__monster-hunter-tri.teaser: The entry with which the monster-hunting series first truly broke through outside Japan.

wii__metroid-other-m.article:
**Metroid: Other M** is the most discussed installment of the entire series and also an attempt to combine two things that at first glance don't fit together: the lonely exploration typical of Metroid and the fast action of Japanese fighting games. Samus Aran arrives at an abandoned space station where she finds traces of experiments, and together with soldiers of the Galactic Federation discovers what actually happened there. The emphasis on storytelling is unusually strong; the game contains long cinematic scenes and for the first time in the series gives Samus a pronounced inner voice.

The controls are unusual. The player holds the Wii Remote sideways like a classic gamepad and moves with the d-pad, meaning only in eight directions, which gives the game the rhythm of old action games. Whenever it's necessary to fire a missile or examine the surroundings, you turn the controller toward the screen and the game switches to first person, in which, however, you cannot move. The transition is fast and looks effective, but it also forces you to change your grip at the most tense moments. Combat is rounded out by last-second dodges and finishing attacks up close, which make the action snappy and flashy. The classic exploration and upgrade-hunting remains, but it's noticeably more linear, and most abilities the player only receives with a superior's permission, which bothered a lot of people.

Technically it's one of the most beautiful games on Wii, with a clean station design, good effects, and a smooth framerate. The music is restrained and lets the environmental sounds stand out. Reviews were mixed, praising the action side and the look, but sharply criticizing the handling of the main character and the linearity. To this day the game still divides fans of the series into two camps. Anyone who approaches it without expecting another Prime will find a brisk action adventure with several very strong moments. Its length is shorter by the series' standards and the game plays briskly, which paradoxically helps it today, because it doesn't dwell needlessly. It's also interesting for remaining the only attempt to combine Metroid with the Japanese action school, while later entries returned to tried-and-true approaches.
wii__metroid-other-m.teaser: The most debated Metroid; it combines lonely exploration with fast-paced Japanese action.

wii__fire-emblem-radiant-dawn.article:
**Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn** directly continues the entry released on GameCube and continues the war between humans and laguz, beings capable of turning into animals. The storytelling itself is unusual: the game is divided into several parts, and the player gradually commands different sides of the conflict, so characters you fought alongside one day appear on the opposite side of the battlefield a few chapters later. The main new heroine is Micaiah, who leads a resistance group in an occupied land, but Ike and most of his party also return.

The gameplay is a classic turn-based tactics game on a square grid. Each unit has its class, range, weapon, and weaknesses according to the simple rock-paper-scissors rule, where sword beats axe, axe beats lance, and lance beats sword. Permanent death is crucial: when a character falls in battle, they don't come back, which makes every turn a serious decision and leads many players to restart the whole map from the beginning. Radiant Dawn ranks among the most demanding entries in the series, because the maps are extensive, there are a lot of enemies, and the player often starts with a weak group against superior numbers. On top of that come battles across three layers of terrain, weapon modifications, and a system where strong units can get a penalty for winning too easily.

Technically the game doesn't use Wii in any significant way; battles are rendered as three-dimensional animations against a flat background and the visual style is rather austere. The controls do without any motion elements. The music is orchestral, with serious and solemn themes matching the tone of the story. Reviews were positive, with criticism directed at the difficulty and at the fact that the game assumes knowledge of the previous entry. Today it's one of the most highly regarded and simultaneously most demanding entries in the series, and among fans it has a reputation as a trial to be passed. The pacing is calm, the tempo slow, and a single chapter can easily take an hour, so it's a game for long evenings. For the series it also mattered in that it remained the last entry on a home console for a long time, before the brand moved mainly to handheld systems.
wii__fire-emblem-radiant-dawn.teaser: A tactical RPG where the player alternately commands both sides of the same civil war.

wii__tales-of-symphonia-dawn-of-new-worl.article:
**Tales of Symphonia: Dawn of the New World** is a sequel to one of the most popular Japanese RPGs from the GameCube and takes place several years after its events. The two joined worlds are dealing with the aftermath of unification, the weather behaves unpredictably, and tensions are rising in the land. The main character is not anyone from the original party but young Emil, who lost his parents in an attack and blames the hero of the first game for it. Together with a girl named Marta, he sets out on a journey during which the original party appears more like guests.

The combat system remains what the Tales series has always excelled at: it takes place in real time, the player directly controls one character, runs around the battlefield, chains attacks, and unleashes special techniques, while the rest of the party acts according to set tactics. The biggest new feature is the ability to recruit monsters to your side, raise them, and evolve them into stronger forms, which brings the game closer to a collector-style RPG and gives the player freedom in assembling their party. Side content is generous, from cooking dishes to scenes between characters that deepen their relationships.

However, the game received criticisms that are still repeated today. It reuses many locations and music from the previous entry, which gives it a shorter and less ambitious feel, and some fans disliked that the original heroes stepped into the background and some of them act unusually. Technically it's a solid, though not outstanding title, visually built on a colorful style with outlines reminiscent of animation. The controls do without motion elements; the game supports a classic gamepad. Reviews were mixed, but fans of the series took a liking to it thanks to the combat and lighter tone. Today it mainly makes sense for those who know the original and want to return to its world. Its length is medium for a Japanese RPG, and the combat keeps up the pace even after dozens of hours, which is the main reason series fans still hold it dear. On Wii, it also ranks among the few full-fledged Japanese RPGs that made it onto the console at all.
wii__tales-of-symphonia-dawn-of-new-worl.teaser: A sequel to the beloved GameCube JRPG, featuring a new hero instead of the old party.

wii__excite-truck.article:
**Excite Truck** was among the first games to appear alongside the console, and remains to this day the purest demonstration of what it means to steer just by tilting the controller. The Wiimote is held horizontally with both hands, and turning it left and right steers, while tilting it forward or backward adjusts the angle of landing while airborne. You race with over-powered off-road pickup trucks across wide tracks spanning America, Asia, and icy plains, and the goal isn't just to finish first. Points are earned for jumps, drifts, close calls with trees, and flashy landings, and only the total number of stars decides whether a race advances further.

The game's biggest idea is the changeable terrain. Collecting blue symbols raises new hills and ramps beneath your wheels right during the race, so a track you just drove through looks different on the second lap. The result is racing that resembles jump acrobatics more than a fight for the ideal line, and the game supports this with generous forgiveness for mistakes: hitting a tree doesn't mean the end, just a loss of momentum. The controls take a little getting used to because the tilt sensitivity is high, but once the player adjusts, it gives a sense of direct connection to the vehicle that a classic gamepad can't offer.

Technically it's a smoothly running game with open views of the landscape, though it bets more on speed and readability than detail; the textures and surroundings were already fairly simple at the time of release. The soundtrack consists of rock tracks that could be replaced with your own music loaded from an SD card, which was a fairly unusual option on the console at the time. Reviews praised the freshness of the controls while also pointing out the sparse content and the missing full online mode. Today Excite Truck is a pleasantly straightforward title for short sessions and at the same time a historical document of how the developers played with the console's main trump card right from the start. For a newcomer, it's also one of the few games where it's enough to just take the controller in both hands and drive right away.
wii__excite-truck.teaser: A launch title showcasing tilt-steering with the Wiimote across wild off-road courses.

wii__mario-strikers-charged.article:
**Mario Strikers Charged** is soccer only in name; in reality it's an arcade sport without a referee, without out-of-bounds, and with almost no rules. It's played five-on-five on an enclosed field with an electric fence, into which opponents happily throw each other, and the difference from classic soccer comes from equipment out of the Mushroom Kingdom: shells, bananas, bombs, and stars fly around the field at the same time as the ball. Each captain has their own super shot, during which the game briefly pauses and the player must hit several flying balls into the goal, and every supporting character controls a distinctive skill that changes the pace of the attack.

Tactics revolve around regularly charging up the ball. The longer it's passed around and dribbled without being lost, the higher its charge, which increases the chance that the goalkeeper won't save the shot. Opponents of course know this and try to interrupt the buildup with a hard tackle, so matches have a fast rhythm of alternating possession and chaos. The goalkeeper is controlled with a controller motion during super shots; otherwise the game works best with the Wiimote and Nunchuk or with a classic gamepad. The matches are loud, over-the-top, and extremely fast, yet a legible hierarchy of skill between a beginner and an experienced player still functions within them.

In Europe it was one of Nintendo's first games with a full-fledged online match, which earned it a lot of attention at the time, even though the service has long since stopped working. The visuals go for a darker, comic-book-aggressive take on the characters, which stands out noticeably from the usual colorful cheerfulness, and both the music and commentary support the impression of a sports show with wrestling elements. Contemporary reviews praised the pace and the fun in a room with multiple players, but criticized the randomness and the steep start. Today Charged is one of the most entertaining competitive titles on the console, provided at least two people who aren't after victory but after revenge are sitting on the couch. A match lasts only a few minutes, so it can be played in series and returned to even after years.
wii__mario-strikers-charged.teaser: Arcade football without rules; besides the ball, bananas and bombs fly across the pitch too.

wii__warioware-smooth-moves.article:
**WarioWare: Smooth Moves** is the purest possible answer to the question of what happens when someone takes a motion controller and chops it up into hundreds of five-second ideas. The game consists of microgames that last only a few moments and offer a single terse instruction: catch, dodge, twist, blow, pull. The player has no time to think, only to react, and the pace accelerates with every success until the instructions start to blur together. The framing story is typical for the series, meaning utterly absurd, and serves mainly as glue between the blocks of microgames.

The main idea of the Wii version is the so-called grip forms. Before each group of microgames, the game shows how the player should hold the Wiimote: like a handle, like an umbrella, like a dumbbell, by the nose, on the head, or laid flat on a table. This turns a tiny change of grip into an entirely different movement language, and the game becomes entertaining for spectators too, since half the fun happens off-screen. The multiplayer section works as passing a single controller around the table and ranks among the surest ways to get a crowd moving that otherwise doesn't play video games.

Technically it's a deliberately mismatched collage: one microgame looks like a digitized photograph, another like rough pixel art, another like a felt-tip drawing. This chaos is intentional and gives the game an unmistakable visual signature that hasn't aged in the years since. The music is just as fragmented, full of short motifs, jingles, and voice clips. At the time, the game was received as one of the first titles to genuinely experiment with Wii controls instead of merely grafting them onto a classic design. Today it remains an ideal quarter-hour game and, at the same time, the best demonstration of what waving a controller around was actually good for. Anyone looking for a long campaign will leave disappointed, since the main line can be finished fairly quickly; the real longevity lies in trying to last as long as possible through the accelerating marathon, and in how reliably the game makes anyone watching burst out laughing.
wii__warioware-smooth-moves.teaser: Hundreds of five-second microgames testing everything the motion controller can do.

wii__rayman-raving-rabbids.article:
**Rayman Raving Rabbids** launched alongside the console and almost immediately rewrote the fate of the entire franchise, because in the end the attention wasn't captured by Rayman but by hordes of shrieking rabbids, who turned from minor villains into stars. The game abandoned the series' platforming roots and turned into a set of microgames framed by a story about Rayman held captive in an arena, where he must complete several events each day to earn a chance at escape. The structure is simple and addictive: finishing a round unlocks the next day, a new costume, and another batch of absurd tasks.

The minigames use the controller across its entire repertoire. In one you pull an imaginary rope, in another you balance, milk a cow, throw a cow for distance, or pound a drum in rhythm. Shooting-gallery sequences take up a prominent place, where the Wiimote is used as an aiming device and rabbids are picked off with bells, alongside music events where the player must hit the beat of well-known songs in rabbid arrangements. The multiplayer mode is built on direct competition at a single screen and is clearly where the game shines brightest, since the campaign itself tends to slide into repetition over time.

Visually it's a fast-running, cartoonish game with bold colors and excellent rabbid animation, whose facial expressions and screeches became the series' signature. The sound is deliberately exaggerated, and a single rabbid shriek managed to define the entire series. Contemporary reviews praised the inventiveness and the fun in a group, but criticized the uneven quality of individual events and the amount of repetition. Today the title is interesting mainly as a period document of the first wave of Wii games, and at the same time as a reliable party pick that nobody needs to learn for longer than ten seconds. In hindsight it's also easy to see how pivotal a decision this was for Ubisoft: the rabbids broke off into their own line of sequels, while Rayman didn't return to a classic platformer until several years later. That's exactly why the game is remembered with mixed feelings, though few would deny it was a lot of fun.
wii__rayman-raving-rabbids.teaser: The game where the side-character rabbids stole the show from the main hero and became stars.

wii__mario-party-8.article:
**Mario Party 8** carried the tried-and-true recipe of a party board game with minigames over to motion controls and became one of the console's best-selling party titles. The basics remain the same as in many previous entries: up to four players take turns rolling dice, move around the game board, collect coins, and try to buy stars, which decide the winner at the end. After each round comes a minigame, whether all-against-all, two-versus-two, or one-against-three, and it's here that most of the resources are earned. The boards have their own rules and themes, from a candy shop to a haunted house, and each brings a different kind of twist.

The minigames use the Wiimote in simple, easy-to-grasp tasks: aiming at the screen, twisting the controller, a quick flick, or holding the controller sideways like a classic gamepad. The design deliberately keeps each event down to a single idea so it can be explained during the intro screen, which is key to letting even complete beginners handle the game. Equally deliberate is the heavy dose of randomness, since the order is often decided only by the final bonus star; for some that's a source of endless laughter, for others a reason for indignation. A full match takes about an hour depending on the number of rounds, so this is an evening's affair, not a quick filler.

Graphically the game relies on bright colors, clear boards, and readable characters; technically it doesn't stand out in any way, but it runs smoothly and never leaves the player in doubt about what's happening. The music is upbeat and fairground-like, and together with the characters' lines it creates the atmosphere of a TV game show. Contemporary reviews were lukewarm and faulted the series for making little effort to renew itself, yet the public still bought the game in large numbers. Today Mario Party 8 works exactly as intended: as ready-made entertainment for four people where everyone has an equal chance and nobody needs to know how to play. On its own it's a title that wears itself out quickly in single-player, but in larger company it lasts for years.
wii__mario-party-8.teaser: A social board game with minigames adapted to the console's motion controls.

wii__wii-party.article:
**Wii Party** is a late-console title that consciously builds on what Wii did best: getting four people in front of one television and having them compete in tasks whose rules fit into a single sentence. The game uses the Mii characters stored on the console, so the faces of the guests present race right there on screen, and it's divided into several large blocks. The board modes recall a classic party board game with squares and bonuses, the competitive modes push toward direct clashes between two sides, and the so-called household games move the action into the actual room.

That last group is the most interesting. In it, the controller is used as a physical prop: it gets hidden around the room and others search for it by sound, gets set on a table while players guess who was holding it, or gets silently passed around in a circle. This way the game steps out of the screen and becomes a social activity in which the console is merely the referee. The classic minigames cover the usual range from aiming and balancing to reaction duels, and are designed so that chance keeps the odds even even among players with very different levels of experience. There's also a two-player mode that works as a quick ten-minute rematch.

The visuals are deliberately restrained and clean so the Mii characters stand out, and technically it's an undemanding game that never loses its smoothness. The music is light, upbeat, and unobtrusive, exactly in the spirit of home entertainment. At the time, the game was received as a solid, if no longer surprising, offering; reviewers praised the ideas involving the controller off-screen and pointed out that part of the roster had already been seen several times before. Today Wii Party is one of the surest choices when a group gathers that doesn't normally play video games and just wants a laugh. At the same time, it's a nice illustration of how far Nintendo took the idea that a console doesn't have to be just a source of picture, but also a tool for a game played around the table.
wii__wii-party.teaser: A late party title with Mii characters that brings four players together in front of one TV.

wii__boom-blox.article:
**Boom Blox** is a physics puzzle game born from a collaboration between Electronic Arts and director Steven Spielberg, and it ranks among the smartest uses of a motion controller ever made. The premise is easy to grasp: a structure made of blocks stands on screen, and the player must either smash it apart or, conversely, carefully take it apart safely. In some levels you throw a ball, in others blocks are carefully pulled out of the structure like in a tabletop tower game, the goal being to keep the construction from collapsing. Each level has clearly set point or move limits, so precision decides, not force.

The controls use the Wiimote very directly: winding up and swinging correspond to a throw, a gentle forward-and-back motion pulls a block out, aiming sets the target. Around this the game builds an enormous number of variants, adding an explosive block, a block that vanishes on contact, or an animal that sets its surroundings moving when hit. Alongside an extensive single-player campaign there's also co-op and competitive levels for more people, where one player demolishes and the other tries to keep the structure standing. A strong point is the editor, in which players can build their own levels and share them, extending the game far beyond the main offering.

Visually the game relies on a clean, toy-like styling with bold colors and simple shapes, which is above all functional: the player must be able to tell at a glance which block is dangerous and which is load-bearing. The physics model is convincing and rewards experimentation, since the same level can be solved in several completely different ways. At the time it was one of the best-reviewed games a Western publisher released for Wii, and reviewers often cited it as proof that motion control could support thoughtful design too. Today Boom Blox is a great choice for players of all ages, and age has taken practically nothing away from it. It's one of the few titles that can be recommended equally to a child and to a player looking for a well-thought-out puzzle for long evenings.
wii__boom-blox.teaser: A physics puzzle game from EA and director Steven Spielberg, built from block structures.

wii__guitar-hero-iii-legends-of-rock.article:
**Guitar Hero III: Legends of Rock** is the peak of the first wave of guitar-game fever, and on Wii it was sold bundled with a plastic guitar whose body took the Wiimote directly as its control unit. The principle is well known: colored notes scroll down the screen, the player holds the matching fret on the guitar's neck, and strums at the exact right moment. The longer you manage to play without a mistake, the higher your score multiplier climbs, and the stored-up energy can be released by tilting the guitar up, multiplying points even further. The campaign takes the player through a series of clubs and arenas, with increasingly complex songs along the way.

The third installment added duels against an opposing player, in which rivals send each other disruptive effects, such as a broken string or a locked fret, and the same principle also works in a face-to-face duel between two people at one screen. The songs are largely original recordings by well-known rock and metal bands spanning several decades, and the difficulty is scaled from four buttons for beginners up to an expert mode that already demands real practice. The Wii version also offered the option to play without the guitar, using a classic controller, though next to the plastic instrument that only feels like a fallback.

Technically it's a smoothly running game with a stylized, comic-book-exaggerated look for the stage and crowd, where everything is subordinated to the readability of the incoming note. The strength of the experience doesn't rest on graphics, though, but on the fact that a well-played passage creates an illusion of real performance that no other genre managed to replicate. At the time it was a massive commercial success that pushed music games into the mainstream for several years, before the market got flooded with too many sequels and accessories. Today the fun depends entirely on whether you have a working guitar; with one, it's still one of the console's best rhythm-game experiences. Finding a working instrument, however, gets harder every year, which is the main reason the whole genre stayed firmly tied to its own era.
wii__guitar-hero-iii-legends-of-rock.teaser: The peak of the first wave of guitar fever; controlled with a plastic guitar holding the Wiimote inside.

wii__beatles-rock-band.article:
**The Beatles: Rock Band** is an unusual project that, instead of a collection of songs from various bands, devoted an entire game to a single group and its story. It plays the same way as the other entries in the series: colored notes for guitar, bass, and drums scroll down the screen, and the singer follows their own line, whose accuracy the game evaluates through a microphone. The major difference is the singing, since Beatles songs are often built on multi-part harmony, and the game therefore allows up to three harmony parts to be sung at once, which in a living room makes it a completely different affair from typical rhythm games.

The campaign leads the player chronologically from the club beginnings through the famous rooftop concert to the late studio period, and is divided into chapters that correspond to specific places and stages. While the early songs are accompanied by visually faithful reconstructions of concert scenes, for the later albums the game moves into abstract, dreamlike animations that react to the music and change with every verse. The difficulty is set more gently than in other games in the series, since the goal wasn't to punish but to let the player move through the catalog; even so, expert-mode drums offer more than enough of a challenge.

The production quality is exceptional by console standards: every environment has its own artistic signature, the character animations draw on period footage, and the audio track uses separately recorded stems, so that an incorrectly played instrument really does drop out of the mix. At the time it was a critically very well-received title, often cited as an example of a video game that also functioned as a musical document. Today the game is a rare item, since both the accessories and the discs are limited, but whoever manages to find them gets one of the most tastefully produced music titles ever released on Wii. It also works well as a social experience for people who know nothing about video games but know the songs by heart.
wii__beatles-rock-band.teaser: An untraditional Rock Band entry dedicated to a single band; the singing builds on the Beatles' harmonies.

wii__just-dance-2.article:
**Just Dance 2** is a title that turned a seemingly simple idea into one of the biggest commercial phenomena of the entire console. The player holds the Wiimote in their right hand and mimics the dancer on screen; the game tracks the controller's movement and rates how accurately the player hits the choreography. No extra accessories, no rules to learn, just a song, a dancer's silhouette, and a strip of icons in the corner hinting at what's coming next. It's precisely this shameless simplicity that made the game a party staple even where most people present otherwise have no interest in video games.

The second installment significantly expanded the range of modes. It added a duel between two dancers, joint choreographies for pairs where each person dances a different line, and a mode focused on movement as exercise, which estimates energy spent and offers longer continuous routines. The songs cover both pop classics and hits of the time, and each has its own visual concept, colored background, and dancer costume. The game deliberately doesn't pretend to be a precise dance simulation; it mainly rates the movement of the hand holding the controller, which is a constant source of jokes, but also exactly why anyone at all is willing to give it a try.

Technically it's a very simple game built on filmed and stylized characters against colorful backgrounds, which can practically never slow down; the strength lies in the choreography and editing. The sound relies on licensed recordings and cover versions and is the main draw of the whole series. Contemporary reviews commonly acknowledged that as party entertainment the game works excellently, even though as a dance game the movement rating is only approximate. Today Just Dance 2 is still one of the fastest ways to get people up off the couch, and that's exactly what its creators were going for. Later sequels have since outdone it with newer songs and nicer production, but this installment is still remembered as the moment when an odd experiment turned into a brand that outlived even the console it was born on.
wii__just-dance-2.teaser: A commercial phenomenon on Wii; just hold the Wiimote and copy the dancer's moves on screen.

wii__sonic-and-sega-all-stars-racing.article:
**Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing** is a kart racer that puts characters from various Sega games on the starting line and turns their worlds into circuits. Alongside Sonic and his friends, heroes from the publisher's other well-known series get behind the wheel, each arriving in a vehicle that matches their origin, whether it's a classic go-kart, a motorbike, or something considerably more bizarre. The tracks draw on recognizable locations and alternate fast open stretches with tight passages where the standings are decided.

The driving model is built on drifting with a gradually charging boost and on collecting items that can be used for both attack and defense. Each character also has their own so-called All-Star move, a powerful moment that activates when a race is going badly and can shuffle the order completely. The game offers a series of cups, time trials against ghosts, a same-screen multiplayer mode, and the online racing of its era, with vehicles and characters gradually unlocked through points earned by racing. It can be controlled either by tilting the Wiimote or with a classic gamepad, which was appreciated by players who found motion controls a poor fit for racing.

Technically, this is a very solidly made effort for the console: the tracks are colourful, densely decorated with references to older games, and run smoothly even in split-screen. The music works with remixed themes from the original games, which is a big part of the appeal for Sega fans. At the time, the game was received as one of the few kart racers that could stand comparison with Nintendo's in-house competition without embarrassment, and criticism was aimed more at the smaller amount of content than at the quality of the driving. Today it's a pleasant alternative for those who have finished the console's main kart-racing king and want the same feeling with different faces.
