For players who grew up on Sega arcades and consoles, it's also a stroll down memory lane, since almost every corner references something.
wii__sonic-and-sega-all-stars-racing.teaser: Kart racing with heroes from across Sega's series; each vehicle matches its character's origin.

wii__mario-and-sonic-at-olympic-games.article:
**Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games** was a minor sensation in its day simply by putting two mascots side by side who had competed for the same audience for many years. The game is a collection of Olympic events, from short-distance running through long jump, javelin throw and swimming to shooting, fencing and gymnastics, and each one is turned into a short control task for the Wiimote and Nunchuk. In some you swing the controller back and forth, in others you aim at the screen, or you have to brake your movement sharply at just the right moment.

The roster of characters draws from both worlds, and every competitor has different speed, power, skill and stamina stats, so the choice sometimes genuinely decides the outcome. Alongside individual events, the game offers cup series that add up points across several races in a row, and a mode for up to four players, which is clearly the main reason the game exists. The events are deliberately short and easy to grasp, placing the game somewhere between a sports simulation and a party collection of microgames; the depth lies more in practising timing than in tactics.

The presentation is colourful and clean, the stadiums feel festive, and the commentary and crowd sound reinforce the sense of a big event. The music mixes ceremonial themes with remixed motifs from both series, a nice touch for fans. Reviews at the time were mixed: criticism targeted the shallowness of some events and the fatigue of repeated waggling, but the public bought the game in huge numbers and thereby founded a long-running series. Today it's mainly evening entertainment for a group, where simple rules and familiar faces do their job within the first minute. A solo player will admittedly get bored after a few cups, but as a historical milestone the game has a firm place: it was the first time two rival icons of the eighties and nineties came together in a single game.
wii__mario-and-sonic-at-olympic-games.teaser: The two eternal mascots together for the first time; a collection of Olympic events for Wiimote and Nunchuk.

wii__silent-hill-shattered-memories.article:
**Silent Hill: Shattered Memories** is a bold reworking of the series' first entry that takes only the basic situation from the original and rebuilds everything else from scratch. Harry Mason wakes up after a car crash in a snowbound town and searches for his daughter Cheryl, except the path to her runs through sessions with a psychotherapist who speaks directly to the player. The answers to his questions, drawing, filling out questionnaires and small choices in the environment continuously change the game: characters look different, behave differently, and entire storylines land differently. It's one of the most interesting attempts at adaptive storytelling to appear in the horror genre, and players often only discover its existence on a second playthrough.

The gameplay deliberately does away with combat. Harry has no weapon, and the moment the world turns into an icy nightmare, all he can do is run, knock obstacles down behind him and shake off pursuers with a flick of the controller. The rest of the time the game is more of a slow exploration: shining a flashlight, examining rooms, opening doors and listening. The mobile phone is used brilliantly, serving as a map, a camera and a channel for oppressive phone calls, and the player holds the Wii Remote to their ear to use it. The controller's speaker thus carries part of the sound design directly into the player's hand, and several of the game's best scares rest on exactly that.

Technically, this was an above-average title on Wii, with stylized lighting and dense snowfall that replaced the original game's memorable fog. The music and sound design keep to the series' traditional line, a mix of ambient textures, metallic screeching and a few surprisingly melodic songs. Reviewers at launch praised above all the courage to experiment and the psychological ending, which counts among the best-written moments in the whole franchise, even though some fans mourned the loss of combat. With time, Shattered Memories is now viewed as one of the strongest horror games on Wii and as proof that motion controls could serve storytelling, not just action.
wii__silent-hill-shattered-memories.teaser: A bold reimagining of the first Silent Hill; psychotherapy sessions reshape the entire story.

wii__dead-space-extraction.article:
**Dead Space: Extraction** is a prequel to the first Dead Space, telling what happened on the Aegis VII colony and aboard the Ishimura before Isaac Clarke ever entered the story. Instead of free movement, though, the developers reached for the rail-shooter format: the camera guides the player through the scene on its own, and their job is to aim, shoot, reload and above all survive. A choice that could have felt like a cheap console add-on turned out to be a surprisingly good fit, because it let the storytelling keep exactly the pace and the shots meant to instil fear.

The weapons are carried over from the main series, and the franchise's basic rule still applies: necromorphs need their limbs shot off, not their heads targeted. The plasma cutter, the ripper and other tools each have two firing modes, on top of which stasis slows enemies down and kinesis pulls objects toward you and hurls explosive canisters. The whole game can be played by two people at once, and the second player can join at any time, making it one of the best couch co-op experiences on the console. The story is told from the perspective of several alternating characters, so the loadout and emphasis of each chapter change too.

Technically, this was one of the best-looking titles on Wii, period. Dark corridors, dynamic lighting, flickering flashlights and detailed enemy models showed just how much the console could deliver when the developers focus on tightly framed scenery. The sound plays with silence and sudden clattering just as well as the source material, and the claustrophobic wreck atmosphere works without reservation. Critics received the game very warmly and often cited it as an example that even a rail shooter can have a full-fledged story. Commercially it was a disappointment, though the game was later released on PlayStation 3 with Move support. Today it's one of the strongest horror experiences Wii has to offer. Anyone who sits down to it with the lights off and decent sound gets a surprisingly intense few hours of fear.
wii__dead-space-extraction.teaser: An on-rails shooter serving as a prequel to Dead Space; a tense look at the fate of the ship Ishimura.

wii__house-of-dead-overkill.article:
**The House of the Dead: Overkill** is a prequel to the arcade series that decided not to take itself seriously at all. Agent G teams up here with the foul-mouthed Detective Isaac Washington, and together they make their way through the mud of the American South, where a criminal nicknamed Papa Caesar and his mutants run rampant. The whole game is styled as a 1970s grindhouse film: grainy picture, scratches on the film stock, exaggerated chapter titles, and a narrator introducing the next reel as if it were a double feature at a drive-in.

The gameplay sticks to the classic arcade formula. The camera moves on its own, the player sweeps a cursor across the screen, shoots, reloads with a flick of the controller and tries to keep an unbroken hit chain, since it's the combo that determines the final score. Between chapters, weapons are bought and upgraded, giving a reason to replay the game on a higher difficulty with better gear. The Wii Remote could be fitted with the plastic Wii Zapper add-on, and the game is also excellent played by two people side by side, placing it among the go-to titles for having friends over.

A distinctive hallmark of the game is its language. The dialogue is packed with profanity to such a degree that at launch the title was talked about mainly for that reason, and the humour deliberately pushes past the bounds of good taste. The music mixes funk, blues and rock motifs, and together with the garish neon lighting it creates a sharp, entertainingly over-the-top B-movie atmosphere. Critics received the game better than they themselves expected, since underneath the parody they found an honest, finely tuned shooter with a satisfying feel to the guns. It later got an expanded version on PlayStation 3 and remains to this day one of the best reasons to pick up a light gun for the Wii. The short playtime is offset by how readily people come back to it chasing a better score. Special mention goes to the character of Isaac Washington, whose one-liners became an inseparable part of the title's legend, and to the bonus levels unlocked for good results, which extend the game's lifespan by a few more evenings.
wii__house-of-dead-overkill.teaser: A grindhouse tribute to the seventies; crude humor crowns this on-rails shooter.

wii__resident-evil-umbrella-chronicles.article:
**Resident Evil: The Umbrella Chronicles** took key moments from the series' early instalments and retold them in the form of a rail shooter tailored to Wii Remote controls. The player goes through the events of Resident Evil Zero, the first game, and the third instalment set in a collapsing Raccoon City, before finally reaching an entirely new chapter that shows the fall of the Umbrella Corporation and Albert Wesker's role in it. That closing storyline is the most interesting part for fans, since it fills in events the main games never directly showed.

The game handles movement itself, so the player concentrates on aiming, reloading and picking the right weapon for a given enemy. The arsenal is gradually upgraded with points earned from precise shooting and finding hidden items in the environment, which motivates replaying the chapters. Boss fights require hitting specific weak points and sometimes dodging in time with a flick of the controller, so the pace keeps the tension up even without the freedom to move around. Two players can shoot side by side at the same time, which is the most enjoyable way to experience the game.

Technically, this was very solid work. The environments are based on models reminiscent of the GameCube originals but are lit to feel dramatic in motion, and the number of enemies on screen was decent for its time. The sound keeps the series' traditional style, with oppressive ambience, growling dogs and sudden jump-scare moments. Reviews at the time were mostly positive, with critics praising the precise aiming and the story bonus while faulting the shorter runtime and the limited freedom of movement. The game was successful enough to earn a sequel, The Darkside Chronicles, and remains among the titles that play best on Wii precisely because of controls unavailable elsewhere. For fans of the franchise, it's also valuable for neatly summarizing the plot of the early games, serving as a brisk refresher on what actually happened in Raccoon City before moving on to the later instalments.
wii__resident-evil-umbrella-chronicles.teaser: An on-rails shooter retelling the series' key moments, topped off with Umbrella's downfall.

wii__madworld.article:
**MadWorld** is one of the most distinctive games ever released on Wii, largely thanks to its look. The entire world is rendered in stark black-and-white artwork resembling a comic drawn with a heavy brush, and the only colour that appears in it is blood. The story takes the player to Varrigan City, a town cut off from the outside world and turned into the arena for a deadly television show called DeathWatch. Jack Cayman enters it with a chainsaw grafted onto his forearm and the task of fighting his way up the leaderboard of competitors to the top.

The combat isn't about ordinary brawling. The game rewards creativity: enemies can be impaled on road signs, thrown into spinning turbines, under a passing train or into the hands of giant helpers, and the longer and more bizarre the chain of actions the player pulls off, the more points they earn. It's that score which opens up further progress, turning the game into a competition of improvisation and of finding out just how much the environment will allow. The controls use Wii Remote motions both to rev up the chainsaw and for the finishing executions, while minigames parodying television game-show formats appear between levels.

The atmosphere is held together largely by the sound. A pair of announcers comments on the fights, their cynical one-liners feeling like part of the broadcast and never growing stale, and the soundtrack leans on gritty hip hop that suits the fast pace perfectly. The game is short, completable within a few evenings, yet it's dense from start to finish with no dead spots. At the time, reviewers praised its visual boldness and energy while criticizing the lesser variety of the later rounds. Commercially it didn't do especially well, yet most players rank it among the most interesting titles in the entire Wii library and as proof that the console could handle uncompromising, adult-oriented action games too. It's also worth noting that the game was made while developer PlatinumGames was still building its name, and many ideas from its combat system later resurfaced in its far more famous titles. For Wii owners, it remains one of the few ways to play merciless action on the console.
wii__madworld.teaser: A black-and-white comic-book bloodbath with one extra color – blood; a chainsaw takes the lead role.

wii__no-more-heroes-2-desperate-struggle.article:
**No More Heroes 2: Desperate Struggle** brings Travis Touchdown back to the town of Santa Destroy, this time for a personal reason. After the death of a close friend, he throws himself back into the assassin ranking, except now he starts all the way down around fiftieth place, so the road to the top is longer and full of rivals just as bizarre as in the first game. The game keeps its deliberately over-the-top tone, alternating parody of gaming clichés with moments of genuine pathos, and it's never afraid to undercut its own point with a joke before it's even finished making it.

The combat system remains built around the beam katana, fast strikes and controller gestures used to finish off combos or throw opponents over the shoulder. New this time is the option to play as two additional characters with a different style, so the pace shifts between chapters, and Travis himself now has access to more swords and the ability to switch into a berserk mode. The biggest change is structural: the tedious driving around an open city is gone, replaced by a simple map, while the side jobs for earning money have turned into charming eight-bit minigames that look like they're straight out of the NES era.

Technically, this is one of the best-looking action games on the console. The comic-book styling with bold outlines, pixel-art effects on hits, and smooth performance even with more enemies on screen keep the impression that the console is being pushed to its full potential. The soundtrack ranks among the best ever heard in an action game, combining bombastic themes with electronica and accompanying even the most absurd scenes with complete seriousness. Reviews were largely favourable, and many critics called the game better and tighter than the original. To this day it's considered one of the high points of what Wii had to offer outside the family-friendly mainstream. Players familiar with the first game will appreciate the many references and in-jokes, but newcomers won't miss anything essential, since the game stands fine on its own plot. That's exactly why it's often recommended as a first encounter with this studio's work.
wii__no-more-heroes-2-desperate-struggle.teaser: Travis Touchdown returns to the assassin ranking, starting from fiftieth place; exaggerated tone and pathos.

wii__fragile-dreams-farewell-ruins-of-mo.article:
**Fragile Dreams: Farewell Ruins of the Moon** is a melancholic adventure about loneliness of a kind rarely found in games. A boy named Seto sets out into a depopulated world after the death of the man who raised him, searching for anyone else who might have survived. He wanders through overgrown subway ruins, an abandoned amusement park, a hotel, and a department store, finding objects that carry the memories of their former owners. These small fragments of other people's lives make up most of the narrative and give the game its strange, quiet power.

The gameplay revolves around a flashlight. The player aims it directly with the Wii Remote independently of the direction of movement, so searching dark corridors is physically uncomfortable in exactly the right way, and the beam of light is the only thing separating safety from the ghosts lurking in the shadows. Combat is simple and deliberately clumsy: Seto swings whatever he has found, be it a wooden stick, a bow, or a piece of iron, and weapons wear down and break. The inventory is small, so the player has to choose what to keep, and it's possible to rest and read found diaries by a save fire.

Atmosphere is the main reason the game is still remembered today. Empty Tokyo suburbs bathed in moonlight, the rustle of wind through ruined halls, and a gentle, mostly calm soundtrack create a mood closer to poetry than horror, even though the game isn't afraid to be genuinely frightening several times. Spatial sound coming from the speaker in the controller adds to the unease, since footsteps and voices literally emanate from the player's hand. Critics received the game with mixed feelings due to its slow pace and simple combat, but it earned a devoted following among players and is often cited as one of the strongest reasons to explore the Wii library beyond its biggest names. The slow pace needs to be accepted as intentional rather than as a flaw; whoever does so is rewarded with one of the most distinctive stories to appear on the console, and an ending that stays in the mind long after the console is turned off.
wii__fragile-dreams-farewell-ruins-of-mo.teaser: A melancholic adventure about loneliness in a depopulated world; an underappreciated Wii gem.

wii__goldeneye-007.article:
**GoldenEye 007** is not a remake of the legendary Nintendo 64 game, but a new take on the same movie premise rewritten for the present day, with James Bond taking the form of Daniel Craig. Missions begin at a dam in North Ossetia and lead through Barcelona and Saint Petersburg all the way to a finale at a giant satellite dish, so fans of the original title will recognize plenty of situations, albeit in a different guise. The tone has changed: the game is tougher, more realistic, and closer to modern military shooters, but it gives far more room to stealthy approaches than its predecessor did.

The player can choose to solve a mission quietly, disabling cameras, using a silencer, and sneaking past guards, or to grab a submachine gun and blast through it head-on. Bond's watch serves as a universal tool for hacking, photographing documents, and scanning the surroundings, and using it gives the missions their rhythm. The controls offered exceptionally broad customization: aiming could be done with the Wii Remote and Nunchuk, the Wii Zapper attachment, or a classic controller, and sensitivity could be finely tuned, so both fans of motion controls and players used to analog sticks found something to suit them.

A crucial part of the game is its multiplayer. Up to four people on one screen have access to a range of modes, rules, and modifiers that directly reference the tradition of the original title, and online play was added on top of that. Technically, it was one of the best-looking shooters on Wii in 2010, with well-lit interiors and smooth performance. The music works with the famous Bond motifs, and the atmosphere of a spy thriller is captured convincingly. Reviewers received the game very well and agreed it was the best Bond video game in many years. Today it's one of the strongest arguments for not underestimating the Wii as a shooter platform. A later release of a revised version on then-newer consoles showed just how solid the foundation was, but the original Wii version remains the most interesting precisely because of the motion-aiming controller.
wii__goldeneye-007.teaser: A new take on the Bond game featuring Daniel Craig, not a remake of the N64 classic; grittier and faster.

wii__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-reflex-.article:
**Call of Duty: Modern Warfare Reflex Edition** is a port of one of the most influential shooters of the decade to Wii, released two years after the original, offering the complete campaign and multiplayer adapted to the console's capabilities. The story follows a British soldier nicknamed Soap and American marines in parallel storylines that intersect in one of the most frequently referenced moments in the whole genre, alternating firefights in narrow streets, night operations lit by night-vision, and slow crawling in a ghillie suit resembling a pile of grass.

The main added value of the Wii version is pointer aiming. Hitting targets at range is more precise and faster thanks to it than with an analog stick, and the game offered a large range of sensitivity and dead-zone size settings, so everyone could tune the controls to their liking. The classic controller and Wii Zapper attachment were also supported. The campaign remained fully intact, including bonus missions and a difficulty level that rewards careful movement and use of cover, and leaderboards for repeated timed playthroughs are also included.

Technically, it was a compromise. The graphics were adjusted for weaker hardware, so textures and effects are simpler and the resolution lower, but the game runs briskly and hasn't lost the pace the series is built on. The sound, with loud gunfire, radio chatter, and a dense orchestral backdrop, carried the atmosphere surprisingly faithfully, and some of the strongest scenes work just as well in this form. Contemporary reviews rated the version as a successful and honest port that made an otherwise unavailable game accessible to Wii owners. The online component was eventually shut down along with the console's network services, but the campaign remains fully playable and is still the best way to play a modern military shooter on Wii. Collector-wise, it's also a title that got lost in sales among family games, so today it isn't among the most common finds in secondhand shops, which makes its place in a collection all the more interesting.
wii__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-reflex-.teaser: The complete campaign and multiplayer of the legendary shooter adapted for Wii controls.

wii__conduit.article:
**The Conduit** was one of the most closely watched games of its time, because it was created with the explicitly stated goal of proving that Wii could handle a technically ambitious shooter comparable to the competition. It tells the story of agent Michael Ford, who investigates an alien attack in Washington and gets caught up in a conspiracy whose threads lead all the way to the highest places. The campaign takes the player through memorable locations of the American capital, from underground tunnels through museums to monuments that turn into battlegrounds.

The key tool is the ASE, a spherical device that reveals invisible mines, hidden messages, and control panels, and which sets the game apart from ordinary shooting. The arsenal mixes human and alien weapons with alternative firing modes, and enemies react to hits on different parts of the body. The most frequently praised element of the controls was their configurability: the player could reassign practically every button, the size of the screen's active zone, and the turning sensitivity, which made the game a benchmark for how the pointer should be handled in Wii shooters.

Technically, the game runs on its own engine with dynamic lighting, reflections, and detailed surfaces that were among the console's best in 2009. The online component offered matches for up to twelve players with custom rule selection and was one of the few places where a competitive shooter could be played on Wii with a larger number of people. Reviews were mixed: critics praised the controls and the technical side but criticized the generic story and repetitive environments that failed to make the most of the idea's potential. Even so, the game received a sequel and is still remembered as an important attempt to push the boundaries of what was expected from Wii. The studio followed up with Conduit 2, which expanded the settings and arsenal but repeated most of the original's weaknesses. Still, it's the first game that is remembered, because it showed that Wii didn't need to be as ashamed of its looks as was claimed at the time.
wii__conduit.teaser: An ambitious attempt to prove that Wii could handle a technically demanding shooter like its competitors.

wii__red-steel-2.article:
**Red Steel 2** is a game that shares only its name with its predecessor and otherwise started completely from scratch. Instead of gray Japanese interiors, it presents a colorful, comic-book-stylized world in which the desert of the Wild West meets samurai tradition. A nameless hero returns to the town of Caldera, whose inhabitants were massacred by the Jackals gang, and sets out for revenge armed with a katana and a revolver. The whole title requires the Wii MotionPlus attachment, and its precision is the foundation of everything essential the game offers.

Combat is a combination of shooting and swordplay, between which the player switches fluidly. Every vertical, horizontal, or diagonal swing of the controller is translated into the game, and enemies have guards that must be broken with the correct direction of slash, so combat feels more like a fast puzzle than mindless button-mashing. Added to that are special techniques unlocked with money found in the levels, dodges, kicks, and the ability to strip an opponent's guard. The result is combat that feels physically satisfying and noticeably more precise than anything Wii had offered up to that point, even though it requires a bit of patience before the hand gets used to it.

Visually, it's one of the best-aging games on the console, because its cel shading and bold colors don't need high resolution or complex effects. The music mixes western guitars with eastern motifs, and together with the empty streets of the desert town it creates a very distinctive mood, which also includes excellently done weapon sound. Contemporary reviews were mostly favorable, and the controls were often described as the best use of MotionPlus ever. Commercially, the game didn't do particularly well, which is a shame, because it represents exactly the kind of title that simply couldn't exist on another platform, which is why collectors keep coming back to it today. The first releases even included the MotionPlus attachment itself in the box, which opened the door for many players to other games that required it. Today, Red Steel 2 is recommended as the first title anyone with this accessory should try.
wii__red-steel-2.teaser: The Wild West meets samurai; katana and revolver controlled with the Wii MotionPlus accessory.

wii__world-of-goo.article:
**World of Goo** is a physics-based puzzle game by a two-person team from the small studio 2D Boy, which arrived on WiiWare in 2008 and became one of the strongest arguments that the console's digital store made sense. The premise is simple and instantly understandable: the player has a pile of living balls of sticky goo and must build a structure from them that reaches a suction pipe and delivers the required number of balls into it. Anyone can master the early levels within a moment, but later on it's necessary to account for weight, center of gravity, wind, and the fact that some types of goo burn or can't be reused.

The game's strength lies in how it constantly introduces new ideas and then just as quickly abandons them, so it never repeats itself even for a moment. Each chapter brings a different type of goo ball and a different environment, from pastel hills through factory pipes to zero gravity, and alongside it runs a side mode in which the player builds a single tallest possible tower out of the goo balls collected throughout the whole adventure. The Wii version is controlled with a pointer, which works surprisingly nicely for placing individual balls, and it can even be played by several people at once, each holding their own cursor.

The atmosphere is carried by the visual style and music. Hand-drawn backgrounds reminiscent of a puppet film are accompanied by a soundtrack with strong orchestral motifs, and signs from the mysterious Sign Painter appear between levels, commenting on events with ironic detachment and remarks about the world of big corporations. The game was received exceptionally well at the time and became one of the titles that helped the independent scene break through to a wide audience. It's still one of the best-designed puzzle games ever released on consoles, and its difficulty rises exactly in a way that never discourages the player. The authors also released it without any copy protection and with open trust in players, which drew a great deal of attention at the time and became part of the story told about the game to this day.
wii__world-of-goo.teaser: Physics-based building from sticky balls, made by a two-person team; a strong argument for WiiWare's purpose.

wii__cave-story.article:
**Cave Story** is a legendary platformer originally created as a freely available game by a single person, Japanese developer Daisuke Amaya working under the name Pixel, which years later received an official release on WiiWare. The player wakes up as a robot with no memories in the caves of a floating island and gradually uncovers the fate of its inhabitants, the rabbit-like Mimigas, and what a mysterious doctor intends to do with them. The story is surprisingly moving and carries several endings, the best of which requires attentiveness and well-timed decisions at moments when the game gives no hints at all.

The gameplay mixes precise action with exploration of interconnected areas. Weapons are upgraded by collecting energy crystals, but the hero loses part of their experience upon being hit, so every fight has weight, and the player learns to dodge blows instead of just soaking them up. The result is a system that rewards focus while also allowing different playstyles depending on which weapon a person prefers. The boss fights rank among the best-designed the genre has to offer, and the map opens up in a way reminiscent of classic metroidvanias with several optional areas on top.

The Wii version brought newly drawn graphics along with the option to switch back to the original pixel look, a remixed soundtrack with the same choice, and additional bonus modes including a playthrough as a different character and a time trial for record collectors. The music, which the author composed himself, ranks among the most memorable chiptune tracks ever and carries the whole mood of the game, which moves between toy-like cuteness and surprisingly dark themes. Critics received the release very well, and Cave Story became one of the icons of the independent scene, whose influence can be seen in dozens of later platformers. On Wii, it also reached an audience that had never heard of its original computer form, opening the way for other independent titles into console stores. It's still worth playing even after all these years.
wii__cave-story.teaser: A legend created for free by a single person; a touching story of a robot in an island's caves.

wii__lostwinds.article:
**LostWinds** was among the first titles to appear on the WiiWare store right after its launch, and it immediately showed what digital distribution on the console was good for. It's a fairy-tale platformer in which a boy named Toku travels through a land plagued by an evil force and joins forces with a wind spirit named Enril. The player controls both characters at once: the Nunchuk moves the boy, while the Wii Remote is used to draw gusts of wind on the screen that lift Toku upward, carry him across chasms, or blow obstacles out of his path.

This dual control is the heart of the whole game. Wind is used to solve puzzle situations, to fan flames, to carry water to a withered flower, and to deflect enemy attacks, and new techniques gradually unlock previously inaccessible parts of the land. The world is one connected whole that the player returns to with new abilities, so even at a short playtime it feels exploratory and rewards curiosity with hidden nooks. The game can be finished in one longer evening, which was the most common criticism from reviewers, for whom the story stopped right when it was picking up steam.

Visually, it's a very pleasant title with watercolor backgrounds, soft colors, and smooth animation that Wii had no trouble with whatsoever. The music is calm and orchestral, and together with the sounds of nature it creates a soothing mood rarely found in action games on the console. At the time, the game was received very well and was often cited as an example of motion controls serving as the foundation of a game idea rather than merely an alternative to buttons. It received a sequel, LostWinds: Winter of the Melodias, and still ranks among the best things ever released on WiiWare. Anyone looking for a calm title for one evening without pressure to perform will find exactly that here, and the second part continues the story directly, so both parts can be played through back to back as a single whole. It's precisely in this pair that you can see what small digital games on the console were capable of back then.
wii__lostwinds.teaser: One of the first WiiWare titles; you draw wind on the screen to propel the hero forward.

wii__bit-trip-beat.article:
**BIT.TRIP BEAT** is the first entry in a series that brought rhythm-game mechanics to WiiWare wrapped in the aesthetic of the oldest home consoles. The premise is deliberately primitive: the player controls a vertical paddle on the left side of the screen, deflecting squares that fly in from the right. Every successful hit plays a tone, so plain paddle-bouncing gradually builds into music, and conversely every missed beat causes the picture and sound to collapse into a quieter, thinner version of themselves until the player finds the rhythm again and rebuilds their score.

Controls are handled by tilting the Wii Remote held sideways, which sounds simple but demands a steady hand, since the paddle reacts instantly and later stages throw dozens of objects at once in precisely composed patterns. The game has three long levels, each capped by a boss fight, and there is no room to breathe between checkpoints, making it one of the most demanding titles in the entire store's lineup. Multiplayer cooperation is also supported, with several players sharing control of a single paddle, leading to entertaining chaos in front of one screen.

Visually the game leans on flickering geometry, pixelated backdrops, and colorful bursts that intensify with how well the player is doing, and in its best moments the screen turns into a hypnotic swirl. The chiptune soundtrack is one of its strongest assets and is still fondly remembered even outside the context of the game. Critics at launch praised the idea of tying score, visuals, and music into a single whole, though they flagged the steep difficulty as something that would put off players looking for casual fun. The series continued with further entries featuring different gameplay, and its hero Commander Video became one of the icons of the indie scene at the end of the last decade. For today's player it's more a short, intense test of reflexes than a long-term pursuit, but as a demonstration of how a minimalist form can create something genuinely distinctive, it still works beautifully. The whole series later received compilation releases on other platforms as well.
wii__bit-trip-beat.teaser: Retro pixel aesthetics and rhythm in one; you compose music by bouncing blocks back.

wii-u__super-mario-3d-world.article:
**Super Mario 3D World** took the concept of the handheld Super Mario 3D Land and expanded it into a full console experience, one where, for the first time in a three-dimensional Mario game, four players can share the same screen at once. You choose between Mario, Luigi, Peach, and Toad, and each carries their own traits: Luigi jumps higher and briefly flutters his legs in midair, Peach floats for a short moment, and Toad is the fastest but the worst jumper. Levels use a fixed, carefully guided camera and clearly readable layouts, so they keep the pace and clarity of the classic 2D entries while making full use of the added dimension. You run across floating platforms, pass through transparent pipes, and in every level hunt for three green stars and a stamp tucked away off the main path.

The headline addition is the bell, which turns your character into a cat. In cat form you can climb walls, claw at enemies, and pounce down on them from above, and a whole array of inventive levels is built around this single ability. The game never settles for milking one trick, though. Every level arrives with its own idea, demonstrates it, adds a variation, and wraps up before it has a chance to grow stale. The GamePad is used to blow away platforms with a touch, to reveal hidden blocks, and to play away from the TV, which made sense for shared living-room play. Visually it's one of the cleanest titles on the whole console, with lighting and color work that has aged exceptionally well.

The soundtrack leans on live-recorded big-band and orchestral arrangements, giving the whole game a fresh, almost variety-show mood; it ranks among the most memorable music the Mario brand has ever offered. Reviews were enthusiastic, but the game suffered from the Wii U's weak sales and long remained a title known only to a smaller circle of players. It wasn't until the later release on Nintendo Switch, with the added Bowser's Fury campaign, that it finally found the audience it deserved. Today it stands as one of the best-designed platforming experiences of its generation: welcoming to newcomers, yet with final levels that will challenge even seasoned players.
wii-u__super-mario-3d-world.teaser: The first 3D Mario for four players at once; each character has its own movement abilities.

wii-u__mario-kart-8.article:
**Mario Kart 8** is the peak the series had been building toward since the days of the Super Nintendo: a racing game that keeps the carefree item-based gameplay intact while wrapping it in technical polish unlike anything Nintendo's console lineup had seen before. The key new feature is anti-gravity. In certain sections the kart's wheels fold to the side, the vehicle sticks to a wall or ceiling, and the track curls into a loop you drive through upside down. Alongside that, gliding on a hang-glider and underwater driving both return, so a single lap can cycle through several different modes of movement without the player ever losing their bearings.

The controls remain accessible, but the depth sits just below the surface. Drifting has two stages of boost, small hops off ledges grant a brief burst of speed, and from dozens of combinations of body, wheels, and glider you assemble a kart suited to your own style, since every part changes acceleration, top speed, and grip. Colliding with an opponent during an anti-gravity section even grants a small bonus, so it's worth deliberately ramming into rivals in these stretches. The track roster blends brand-new circuits with reworked classics from earlier entries, and several of them rank among the best-designed tracks the series has ever had. Online racing ran reliably, and two major expansions added further cups, including guest characters and tracks from other Nintendo franchises.

Technically, this is the Wii U's showcase title. The game holds a stable frame rate even with two players on screen, and thanks to its work with lighting, reflections, and background detail it looks downright expensive. The soundtrack's orchestral and jazz arrangements, recorded by a live band, rank among the best Nintendo produced at the time. Reviews were exceptionally positive, and Mario Kart 8 became the console's best-selling game, though in absolute numbers it was still limited by the console's modest install base. The expanded Mario Kart 8 Deluxe later grew into one of the best-selling titles ever on Switch. Even today the original Wii U version is completely playable and just as fun in local multiplayer as it was on release day.
wii-u__mario-kart-8.teaser: The peak of the series thanks to anti-gravity; tracks twist into loops and you even drive on the ceiling.

wii-u__super-smash-bros-for-wii-u.article:
**Super Smash Bros. for Wii U** is the console half of a pair of games Nintendo released within a short span of each other on Wii U and Nintendo 3DS, and it's the flashier of the two. Fights don't run on hit points but on damage percentages: the more hits a character takes, the further the next blow sends them flying, and the goal is to knock opponents clear off the edge of the arena. That makes matches readable even for someone who's never touched a traditional fighting game, while still leaving enormous room to improve. Battles take place on moving arenas where the environment itself, falling items, and summonable characters from other games all get involved in the action.

What sets the Wii U version apart is above all its eight-player mode, which turns a battle into a chaotic but tremendously fun scrum, along with a noticeably richer offering of content beyond the fights themselves. The roster of characters was among the widest the series had ever had at launch, and it kept growing through downloadable fighters. Master Orders and Crazy Orders let you wager for rewards, Smash Tour is a board game for several players, and a classic arcade-style campaign rounds out the solo offering. The game was also among the first to make use of amiibo figures, which gradually picked up their owner's playstyle and could be sent into battle against friends.

Technically it's one of the smoothest titles on the console, holding a high frame rate even with eight characters and total chaos on screen. The soundtrack gathers hundreds of tracks, mostly new arrangements spanning Nintendo's entire history, and works on its own as a tribute to decades of game music. Series creator Masahiro Sakurai directed the game. Reception was very positive, the game became one of the console's best-selling titles, and it earned a stable place in the competitive gaming community, even though part of the older fanbase preferred the previous entry. Today it remains a great choice for an evening with friends in front of one TV.
wii-u__super-smash-bros-for-wii-u.teaser: The flashier half of the twin release with the 3DS version; percentage-based battles that even newcomers can grasp.

wii-u__splatoon.article:
**Splatoon** is the boldest new franchise Nintendo introduced during the Wii U generation, and also proof that even in an overcrowded genre like the online shooter there's still room for a genuinely fresh angle. You play as squid-like Inklings, and the goal in the core Turf War mode isn't kill count but how much of the arena's surface your team manages to cover in your own color by the end. Hitting an opponent is just a means to claim territory. And color isn't cosmetic here: while in your own color you can turn into a squid, swim quickly beneath the surface, refill your ink, and climb painted walls, whereas an opposing color slows you down and gives away your position.

Out of this single mechanic grows a surprisingly deep layer of tactics. Every weapon covers ground differently, from a roller to a sniper rifle to a spray gun, each paired with its own set of support grenades and special attacks. The result is a shooter that even a player with no aiming experience can pick up, since scoring points is possible just by painting the floor. The single-player campaign isn't merely a drawn-out tutorial, but a proper series of platforming levels that gradually introduce every mechanic and build up to several inventive boss fights. Controls aim by combining the GamePad's gyroscope with the stick, and the map on the second screen lets you jump straight to a teammate's position.

Visually the game leans on bold colors, street aesthetics, and poster-style graphics; the music mixes surf rock with pop sung in a made-up language, and the whole world has its own fashion culture and idols. For several months after launch Nintendo kept expanding the game for free with new weapons, maps, and modes, which helped keep the community together. Reviews were very positive, and the franchise became one of the console's few genuine successes, one that Nintendo went on to build further sequels around. Today Splatoon is mainly of historical importance, since the Wii U's online services are no longer running, but its core idea remains one of the smartest in modern game design.
wii-u__splatoon.teaser: A bold new Nintendo IP; in Turf War, painted territory decides the outcome, not the number of hits.

wii-u__pikmin-3.article:
**Pikmin 3** arrived after a long wait as the first new entry in the series in roughly a decade. You control a trio of tiny astronauts stranded on a planet overgrown with vegetation and insects, and their only hope lies with the Pikmin: small plant-like creatures you gather in swarms to carry objects, break down obstacles, and fight. Each Pikmin type has its own ability. Red ones resist fire, blue ones can breathe underwater, yellow ones conduct electricity, and this entry adds rock Pikmin, who shatter shells and glass, and flying Pikmin, who can carry cargo over water and off the beaten path.

Each day has a fixed length, and after dark the planet's surface turns into a deadly place, so all your Pikmin need to be brought back to the ship in time. Out of this grows a distinctive tension between planning and haste: you split your groups across parallel tasks, switch between astronauts who can work on opposite ends of the map, and keep an eye on fruit reserves, which serve as food and, by extension, as the whole expedition's time limit. Battles against giant bugs play out like small puzzles, where you need to spot the weak point and throw the right kind of Pikmin at it in the right order. Get it wrong, and you can lose dozens of helpers at once.

The visuals rank among the most beautiful the Wii U ever offered. The detailed macro-world, with water droplets, backlit leaves, and pronounced depth of field, plays like a nature documentary, and the game cleverly alternates calm and chaos. The music is understated, more atmospheric than catchy, and creates genuine tension during the nightly rush back to the ship. Critics received the game excellently, praising in particular the GamePad pointer controls and the finely tuned balance. Sales, however, were once again limited by the console's narrow install base. The later Pikmin 3 Deluxe release brought the game to a wider audience, and today it stands among the best-aged strategy games Nintendo has ever put out.
wii-u__pikmin-3.teaser: The series' return after ten years; the tiny Pikmin carry, demolish, and fight for you.

wii-u__legend-of-zelda-wind-waker-hd.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker HD** is a remaster of the GameCube entry that divided players with its art style on release and, with the passing of years, has turned out to be one of the best-aged entries in the whole series. Link sets out into a flooded world where only the tips of islands poke above the sea, sailing between them on a talking boat. Alongside the classic dungeons, puzzles, and battles fought with a weapon tailored to each boss, a substantial part of the game is simply exploring the horizon: hunting for treasure using maps, conducting the wind with a baton, and stumbling into random encounters on the open sea, where you never know what might surface.

The HD version is more than just a resolution boost. Nintendo redid the lighting, added a pronounced depth of field and richer colors that suit the cartoon-like style well, and, most notably, reworked the parts of the original most often criticized. Sailing is markedly faster thanks to a new sail, the endgame hunt for Triforce pieces is noticeably shortened, and the inventory and map moved onto the GamePad screen, doing away with constant pausing. A photo mode was also added, along with the option to play the whole game away from the TV, which works surprisingly well during long voyages. The optional Hero Mode doubles damage taken and removes potions.

Atmosphere is why people remember this game. The open sea, wind in the sails, and an orchestral score with touches of Irish and Spanish influence create a sense of adventure unlike any other entry in the series. The characters' strongly stylized, animated faces still convey emotion better than many a realistically rendered game manages. Reviews received the remaster very well, and many consider it the best way to experience Wind Waker. For Wii U it was one of the main reasons to buy the console, and even today it plays surprisingly briskly, with a clear influence on the series' later open-world approaches.
wii-u__legend-of-zelda-wind-waker-hd.teaser: A remake of the GameCube entry whose art style once divided players but has aged the best.

wii-u__legend-of-zelda-twilight-princess.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess HD** brings to Wii U the darker, more mature face of the series that originally launched on GameCube and Wii. Twilight gradually swallows Hyrule, and in its affected regions Link transforms into a wolf, forcing him to rely on smell, hearing, and the help of a mysterious being named Midna, who rides on his back. Switching between human and wolf form gives the game two entirely distinct rhythms: classic sword-and-shield combat with elaborate special strikes on one side, and tracking, platform-jumping, and trail-hunting on the other.

The dungeons rank among the largest in the entire series, and each one is built around one standout item, whether it's an iron ball on a chain, a pair of boots with increased gravity, or a hook that pulls you toward distant targets. The world is thoughtfully interconnected, riding on horseback across Hyrule field carries real weight, and mounted combat sequences rank among the game's most memorable moments. The HD version brought a higher resolution, updated textures, and reworked lighting that brightened up the original's somewhat grayish tone. The inventory and map moved onto the GamePad, and Nintendo trimmed down the most drawn-out part of the prologue as well as the light-tear-gathering section, so the game flows faster than before.

A special addition is the new Cave of Shadows mode, alongside the tougher Hero Mode variant with a mirrored world and double damage. The music works with Hyrule's rich themes and, in the twilight-covered regions, shifts into unsettling, almost ghostly textures. The original game was received with enthusiasm on release, and the remaster too earned very good reviews, though part of the fanbase pointed out its slow start and less freedom than they were used to. Today it stands as a calmer, more narratively focused Zelda, sitting at the opposite end of the spectrum from the later open-world entries, and that's exactly why it's still worth playing through. Anyone looking for a Zelda built around dungeons, combat, and atmosphere will find it here in one of its most polished forms.
wii-u__legend-of-zelda-twilight-princess.teaser: A darker, more mature Zelda; Link transforms into a wolf and relies on the spirit Midna.

wii-u__new-super-mario-bros-u.article:
**New Super Mario Bros. U** was one of the Wii U's launch titles, tasked with showing what the console could do the very first time it was plugged in. It's a classic two-dimensional platformer in the tradition the New Super Mario Bros. series established on the Nintendo DS, but this time in high definition for the first time, with a world map assembled into one continuous, seamlessly connected continent with no loading screens between areas. Bowser has seized Princess Peach's castle, and Mario fights his way toward him through forests, deserts, icy mountains, and lava-filled caves, while the map also offers detours and hidden paths.

The gameplay rests on precise, instantly readable movement and on cleverly assembled levels that first demonstrate each new mechanic safely before turning it against the player. Alongside the familiar power-ups comes a new flying squirrel suit that lets Mario glide through the air and cling to walls, plus baby Yoshi, whom you carry in your arms and who, depending on the type, inflates, glows, or swallows enemies. For Wii U, the most interesting addition is Boost Mode, where a fifth player with the GamePad doesn't fight but instead creates platforms and freezes enemies with a touch, letting them help a less experienced friend — or deliberately sabotage them.

The visuals are clean and colorful, though artistically the game stays within the boundaries the series set earlier, which is exactly what some critics held against it. The sound design leans on brisk brass arrangements and rhythmic enemy reactions to the music. Reviews were good, if not wildly enthusiastic; the most common verdict was that this is a very solid but safe game. The standalone add-on New Super Luigi U replaced every level with short, much harder variants, and is more interesting for experienced players. Today it's an honest, undemanding platformer that works brilliantly as a four-player couch game. Three collectible coins per level also give a reason to come back and hunt for paths that weren't visible on the first run.
wii-u__new-super-mario-bros-u.teaser: A Wii U launch title; a classic 2D platformer with a map joined into a single continent.

wii-u__donkey-kong-country-tropical-free.article:
**Donkey Kong Country: Tropical Freeze** is one of the most demanding, and at the same time best-designed, two-dimensional platformers of its era. The Kong family's island is overrun by Nordic wildlife that freezes everything solid, and Donkey Kong, with help from Diddy, Dixie, and Cranky Kong, sets out to reclaim his home. Each buddy you carry on your back changes how you move: Diddy hovers briefly thanks to his rocket-pack, Dixie's hair-helicopter lifts you extra high, and Cranky uses his cane as a trampoline that lets him bounce off spikes and other hazardous surfaces.

The game's strength lies in its unusually ambitious level design. The camera travels along tracks around the player, platforms break apart, ships sink, silhouettes come alive in the background, and several levels are built around a single idea taken to perfection — whether that's a mine-cart ride, swimming against the current, or fleeing an avalanche. The difficulty is high but fair. Every death is clearly your own fault, and the game offers plenty of shortcuts and helper items for anyone who gets stuck. Collectible KONG letters and puzzle pieces then unlock hidden levels that rank among the toughest in the entire series.

Technically it's one of the best-looking titles on the console, with rich lighting, ice you can see through, and background details that often become part of the gameplay itself. The most frequently praised aspect, though, is the music, composed in part by David Wise, author of the original soundtracks from the series' Super Nintendo days; his underwater tracks rank among the best game music has to offer. Reviews were excellent, but sales were again held back by the Wii U's small install base. A later Switch version with a simplified mode made the game accessible to less experienced players too. Today, Tropical Freeze is considered one of the best platformers of the last two decades and is often cited as proof that the classic genre still has plenty to say when handled by a studio that understands rhythm and camera work.
wii-u__donkey-kong-country-tropical-free.teaser: One of the most challenging and best-designed 2D platformers of its time; partners change how you move.

wii-u__xenoblade-chronicles-x.article:
**Xenoblade Chronicles X** is the largest game ever released for Wii U, and also one of the most ambitious open worlds of its entire generation. After Earth's destruction, a human ark crash-lands on the planet Mira, and the survivors found the city of New Los Angeles. Your character, whom you create yourself, joins the exploration force BLADE, tasked with mapping the planet's continents, finding the lost pieces of the ship, and deciding how humanity should relate to the native civilizations and to the warring alien fleets fighting over the planet.

The world is split into five enormous regions, all open from the very start and not gated by character level. You can therefore wander into a valley full of hundred-meter monsters right from the beginning. Combat runs in real time with automatic attacks and a set of skills on cooldowns, complemented by a system for cheering on your teammates at the right moment. Roughly halfway through the game, you obtain a Skell, a giant robotic mech that transforms, turns into a vehicle, and later even flies, opening up the whole world for a third time. There are hundreds of side quests, and many of them tell stories about the difficult coexistence of species within the city.

Technically, the achievement feels almost unbelievable on Wii U hardware: a seamless world with no loading, enormous draw distances, and dense detail, though at the cost of simpler textures and occasional pop-in at range. The music departs significantly from the rest of the series, mixing electronica, rock, and sung tracks, and it's highly divisive. Reception was very good, with reservations about the sheer amount of text and a story that remains more of a backdrop for exploration. The game remains one of the strongest reasons to pull the console out of the closet, and for a long time it was its one true home. Anyone who loves exploration for its own sake will find dozens of hours of discovery here that aren't replicated anywhere else.
wii-u__xenoblade-chronicles-x.teaser: The biggest game on Wii U and one of the most ambitious open worlds of its generation.

wii-u__bayonetta-2.article:
**Bayonetta 2** exists only because Nintendo took it under its wing after no other publisher could be found for the sequel, and it became one of the sharpest action games ever released on a Nintendo console. The witch Bayonetta descends into the underworld to save a friendly soul, wiping out ranks of angels and demons along the way in battles that combine pistols, swords, whips, and transformations of her own hair into giant spectral limbs. Combat is built around precise last-moment dodges, which trigger Witch Time, slowing the whole world down while you punish a defenseless opponent.

Compared to the first game, the system is smoother and more forgiving without losing any depth. Umbran Climax has been added, which, once its gauge is full, powers up every hit with summoned demonic attacks, and several new weapons — including a bow and a whip made of snakes — change the pace of combat. The game is built so that a beginner can get through it by mashing buttons at random, while an experienced player can break down every section into combos and chase the highest ranking. The Tag Climax mode then lets you take on selected fights in pairs online, wagering rewards, which adds hours of extra content.

The direction of the action sequences is utterly shameless: the game opens with a battle on a falling fighter jet above a city, and from that moment stacks one incredible situation on top of another without ever losing clarity. It runs very smoothly throughout and is technically one of the best showcases of what Wii U could do. The music mixes jazz, big band, and pop covers, and it fits the over-the-top style perfectly. Reviews were rapturous, but the game didn't find enough players; the package therefore included the first title as well, so newcomers could get up to speed. Today it's a genre classic that set the bar for both fluidity and for just how confidently over-the-top an action game can be. For Wii U it was an exclusive nobody expected, and it remains one of the first titles recommended alongside the console. On its own it's short, around ten hours, but built for replaying on higher difficulties, where the precision of the dodge system is only fully revealed.
wii-u__bayonetta-2.teaser: It exists thanks to Nintendo, which rescued it; one of the sharpest action games on Wii U.

wii-u__captain-toad-treasure-tracker.article:
**Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker** grew out of a handful of bonus levels in Super Mario 3D World and turned them into a standalone game that ranks among the console's most beloved surprises. Captain Toad carries a giant backpack, which means he can't jump at all. Each level is a small diorama, a compact box full of stairs, secret passages, and enemies that you can rotate freely with the camera while searching for the path to the star at the top. Without a jump, the platformer becomes a spatial puzzle where the main weapon is observation and getting the order of steps right.

On top of this foundation, the game piles on a surprising amount of variety. In one level you pull and push pillars with a touch on the GamePad, in another you ride a mine cart shooting turnips, another level goes underwater, or the whole box tilts depending on how you turn the controller. Every box hides three gems and one bonus objective that's only revealed after your first completion, so even a small level holds up for several playthroughs. The difficulty is gentle, and the game never punishes; it relies on the pleasure of noticing something that was in plain sight the whole time, just around the corner.

Visually it's a toy in the best sense of the word, with colorful materials, soft lighting, and depth of field that turns the dioramas into something close to a model railway. The music is cheerful, jazz-tinged, and has its own catchy central theme, which the hero happily hums to himself. Reviews received the game very well, praising in particular that it never pretends to be more than it is, and yet never repeats itself. Thanks to its smaller scope and lower price, it became one of the higher-rated titles in the Wii U catalog and later released on other platforms as well. Today it's the ideal relaxing game for short sessions that anyone can pick up, and at the same time a demonstration of how a single limitation — the inability to jump — can be turned into an entire genre of its own.
wii-u__captain-toad-treasure-tracker.teaser: The Captain can't jump because of his giant backpack; instead, you rotate the diorama to find a way through.

wii-u__yoshi-s-woolly-world.article:
**Yoshi's Woolly World** transplants Yoshi's adventures into a world knitted entirely from yarn, fabric, and felt. It's more than a visual gimmick: the material is part of the gameplay. Yoshi swallows enemies and turns them into yarn balls, which he then throws at obstacles; a hit can unravel a platform, reveal a hidden pattern, or knit threads together into a new bridge. Enemies unravel into individual loops, clouds are made of cotton tufts, and the background is stitched with seams and buttons, so at every step you can see that the whole world is only held together by pins and tacks.

The gameplay follows the classic Yoshi school: slower-paced, high-jump-driven platforming with a leg-flutter in midair, precise yarn-ball aiming, and above all careful searching of every level. Each one hides skeins, flowers, and hearts, and finding everything is considerably harder than simply reaching the goal. Good-Feel, the studio that previously made the similarly conceived Kirby's Epic Yarn, gives every level its own idea, whether it's transforming into an umbrella, a wheel, or a mole. A co-op mode for two players is included, in which you swallow and toss each other across chasms.

The game also offers a Mellow Mode, in which Yoshi gains wings and can practically never die, so even the youngest players can get through it without missing out on the visual side. The music is calm, playfully orchestral, and matches the overall relaxed mood that's never in a hurry. Reviews were favorable and most often praised the wonderful craftsmanship of the look and the well-hidden collectibles. Some critics, on the other hand, criticized the low difficulty of the main path. Today, Woolly World is one of the gentlest games in the whole catalog, ideal for playing with kids, and at the same time a surprisingly substantial challenge for anyone who wants to find everything. Collected skeins also unlock further Yoshi designs, from patterned ones to those inspired by other Nintendo franchises, so collecting comes with a visible reward.
wii-u__yoshi-s-woolly-world.teaser: An entire world knitted from yarn, where even the gameplay is built on thread and fabric.

wii-u__super-mario-maker.article:
**Super Mario Maker** put into players' hands a tool they'd wanted since the eighties: the ability to build their own Mario levels and share them with the whole world. The editor uses the GamePad's touchscreen so naturally that you'll place your first block before you've even finished reading the tutorial. You drag elements with your finger or stylus, combine them with each other, give enemies wings, stack them into multi-story towers, and instantly switch to test mode to check whether what you built can actually be completed at all.

The cleverest part is the ability to switch between four graphical styles: the original Super Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros. 3, Super Mario World, and New Super Mario Bros. U. Each style isn't just different graphics but different physics and different character behavior, so the same level plays completely differently depending on which style you pick. The game also unlocks tools gradually so it doesn't overwhelm beginners. The online component let you play other people's levels, give them stars, and test yourself against a hundred consecutive challenges where the number of lives is strictly limited.

An exceptionally lively community grew up around the game. Entire genres of player-made levels emerged, from music-box contraptions to precisely timed speedrun courses to infamous challenges that only a single person in the world managed to complete. The release marking the series' thirtieth anniversary was accompanied by a set of unlockable costumes tied to amiibo figures. Reviews were outstanding, and the game became one of the console's most striking successes. After Wii U's online services were shut down, level sharing came to an end, and the baton passed to its successor on Switch, but the original's historical significance remains: it showed that building levels can be more fun on its own than plenty of finished games. It was also one of the few uses of the GamePad where the second screen wasn't a bolted-on extra but the only sensible way to control the whole game, which is exactly why it made so much sense on Wii U.
wii-u__super-mario-maker.teaser: A dream fulfilled since the eighties: build your own Mario levels and share them with the whole world.

wii-u__star-fox-zero.article:
**Star Fox Zero** marked the return of Fox McCloud's space squadron after a long break, and it was also one of the most divisively received titles on the entire console. The story essentially returns to the plot of Star Fox 64: Andross once again threatens the Lylat system, and Team Star Fox flies from planet to planet to stop him. Missions alternate between corridor-style sections where you fly constantly forward, shooting down waves of enemies, and more open arenas where you can turn freely, circle giant targets, and complete objectives in any order.

The heart of the game is control split across two screens. On the TV you see the ship in third person, while the GamePad simultaneously runs a cockpit view that you aim by tilting the controller using its gyroscope. This lets you fly in one direction while shooting in an entirely different one, opening up maneuvers previous entries never allowed. At the same time, it's a habit that takes several hours to adjust to, and one that a large portion of players never fully absorbed. The Arwing also transforms into the walking Walker, joined by the Gyrowing helicopter with a small robot on a tether, and the fast ground-based Landmaster.

The game is deliberately short, built around replaying missions for better results and searching for alternative routes between planets, echoing the structure of the classic Nintendo 64 entry. Technically it's clean and smooth, since it has to render two views at once, though visually it feels more restrained than the console's other big games. The music leans on orchestral reworkings of familiar themes and works excellently. Reception was lukewarm; critics praised the mission design but considered the controls an obstacle. Today, Star Fox Zero stands as an interesting testament to just how far Nintendo pushed the dual-screen idea, and it offers a patient player an experience found nowhere else. Anyone who fights through the first few hours usually describes the feeling of piloting a machine rather than just moving a cursor on screen; for everyone else, the game mainly remains a reminder of just how risky the experiments Nintendo allowed itself in this generation could be.
wii-u__star-fox-zero.teaser: The squadron's return after years, and one of the most divisively received titles on Wii U.

wii-u__nintendo-land.article:
**Nintendo Land** launched in 2012 as Wii U's flagship showcase title, with a single core mission: to make it immediately clear what the console's second-screen controller was actually good for. The game takes the form of a virtual amusement park, guided by the chatty flying robot Monita, hiding twelve attractions inspired by classic Nintendo series — from The Legend of Zelda through Metroid and Donkey Kong to Animal Crossing and F-Zero. Each attraction is a standalone minigame with its own rules, its own visual style, and a surprisingly different feel; some are built for a single player, others for a whole couch full of people.

The strongest section is made up of the asymmetric team attractions, where the player holding the GamePad sees something completely different from everyone else watching the TV. In Mario Chase, you flee from a quartet of pursuers and only you have a clear map on your display; in Luigi's Ghost Mansion, you instead control an invisible ghost that the others must expose with flashlight cones and team up to defeat. This information imbalance creates exactly the kind of shouting, laughing, and finger-pointing that a good party night is built on. The solo attractions lean more on motion controls and the touchscreen — bow and arrow, shooting cans, sword-swinging — serving as a miniature catalogue of everything the console can do.

Technically it's a clean, colorful, smoothly running game whose playful, plastic-toy park look still feels charming and timeless today; the music recycles familiar themes from Nintendo classics in lighter arrangements. Reception at the time was largely favorable, with critics praising the inventiveness of the asymmetric modes, though it was also noted that the game needs a group of people around it — and that was exactly what the Wii U often lacked. Today, Nintendo Land reads as the most honest proof that the second-screen concept had real gaming potential; it just lacked the support. For collectors and weekend get-togethers alike, it remains one of the most entertaining games ever released on the console.
wii-u__nintendo-land.teaser: A Wii U launch showcase styled as a theme park with twelve attractions from Nintendo series.

wii-u__zombiu.article:
**ZombiU** ranks among Wii U's boldest launch titles, and also among those that most convincingly explain why the GamePad mattered at all. Ubisoft Montpellier set this first-person game in a London overrun by an infection, where the player pushes through the Underground, sewers, Buckingham Palace, and dark flats, scavenging for every tin can and every bullet individually. Combat is slow and unpleasant, a cricket bat is more reliable than a firearm, and a single careless step is enough for the crowd to tear you apart.

What still sets the game apart today is how it uses the second screen. Rummaging through your backpack, hacking locks, scanning your surroundings, or opening a chest all happen on the controller's display in real time — meanwhile the TV doesn't pause, so glancing down at your inventory is a genuine risk, and the player instinctively jerks their head back up. On top of that comes permanent death: when you fall, you take control of another random survivor, and you have to hunt down your old hero as a zombie to reclaim your gear. The base run by the mysterious Prepper serves as the only safe place to catch your breath and save your progress, so every excursion outside is planned like a small military operation.

Visually, ZombiU is dark, grimy, and claustrophobic, with an excellent soundscape full of shuffling, growling, and heavy silence — atmosphere is clearly its greatest asset. This London isn't a tourist postcard but a crumbling maze of boarded-up shopfronts, scrawled-on walls, and corridors where a flashlight barely reaches a few meters. The game also offered a peculiar mode in which one player with the controller placed undead against another player on the TV. Contemporary reviews were split: part of the critics praised the tension and the courage to swim against the tide of action shooters, while others complained about the clunky combat and technical compromises. Over the years the game gained a reputation as an underrated gem and even received a port to other platforms — though without the second screen, it lost its best idea there. That's exactly why the original Wii U release remains the only one truly worth playing.
wii-u__zombiu.teaser: The boldest Wii U launch title; a slow, uncomfortable fight for survival in a plague-ridden London.

wii-u__game-and-wario.article:
**Game & Wario** is a minigame collection from the creators of the WarioWare series, built around a single mandate: every idea has to live or die by the GamePad. Instead of hundreds of five-second micro-games, it offers roughly a dozen and a half longer, more considered disciplines, in which the controller turns into a bow, a camera, a spy's binoculars, or a sketchbook. In Arrow, you draw a bowstring by dragging a finger across the display; in Shutter, the player looks around a room by tilting the whole controller, hunting for suspicious characters; in Gamer, you hide under the covers and play on the GamePad while on the TV, mother 5-Volt circles the room and the player has to feign sleep just in time.

Gamer is the best demonstration of what a pair of screens can do: one game runs on the display in your hands, another on the TV, and your brain has to track both at once. Alongside the solo disciplines there are also party modes for a group, where one player draws on the touchscreen while the others guess, or the controller gets passed around the table like a deck of cards. The whole thing is held together by typical WarioWare humor — cluttered, ugly-cute, and full of references to older Nintendo games. Between the disciplines, small toys and trinkets also unlock, serving no purpose beyond giving you something to fiddle with for a while.

Visually it's a colorful collage of styles, alternating cartoonish stylization with pixel art and photographic parody, accompanied by a rowdy, deliberately cheap-sounding soundtrack. Contemporary reception was cooler than for the main series; reviewers praised the inventiveness of individual pieces but criticized the limited scope and uneven quality — alongside great ideas there are disciplines good for a single afternoon at best. Today the game reads more as a likeable collection of experiments than a full-fledged title, yet it remains one of the best proofs that the GamePad could offer things impossible to replicate elsewhere. As an evening game for guests, passed from hand to hand, it still works great.
wii-u__game-and-wario.teaser: Minigames from the creators of WarioWare, this time fewer but more elaborate, tailored to the GamePad.

wii-u__rayman-legends.article:
**Rayman Legends** is the pinnacle of the series' modern era and one of the best-looking 2D platformers ever made. It follows on from Rayman Origins, inheriting its hand-painted visuals powered by the UbiArt engine and expanding them into worlds inspired by fairy tales, medieval castles, ocean depths, or Mexican festivals. The player once again frees the Teensies, collects Lums, and glides through levels that combine precise jumps, timed runs, and battles against giant bosses — always with an emphasis on rhythm and fluid movement.

On Wii U, an extra role was added for the GamePad: a second player controls the fly Murfy on its screen, cutting ropes with a touch, rotating platforms, distracting enemies, and literally clearing the path for the others running on the TV. This creates an asymmetric co-op where one player plays a platformer and the other plays a timing-based puzzle game — an ideal way to get even a non-gamer to pick up a controller. Unforgettable are the musical levels closing each world, where the entire level is edited to the beat of a well-known song and every jump lands exactly on the beat. As a bonus there's the football minigame Kung Foot, daily and weekly time-trial challenges, and over a hundred unlockable levels — including reworked pieces from the previous installment — so there's an unusually large amount of content here.

Technically, the game runs smoothly, the colors are vivid, and the animation of Rayman and his companions ranks among the best ever achieved in 2D. The music alternates rowdy brass, orchestral pieces, and parody covers, and together with the art direction creates an infectiously good mood. Critics received the game very warmly, and it still shows up in rankings of the decade's best platformers; the only blemish was the delay of its Wii U exclusivity and the subsequent release on other platforms, which raised the blood pressure of console owners at the time. Today, Legends is simply a safe recommendation for anyone, and on Wii U it comes in a form no other platform offers.
wii-u__rayman-legends.teaser: The peak of the series and one of the most beautiful 2D platformers ever; hand-painted UbiArt graphics.

wii-u__mario-party-10.article:
**Mario Party 10** is a version of the famous board-game-style party series tailored directly for the second screen. The base game continues with the concept where all players ride together on a single vehicle along the board and take turns rolling the dice — a solution that sped up the pace and cut out waiting, but also took away some of the strategy that the older installments had. Between spaces you play dozens of minigames ranging from reflex-based to rhythm-based to ones that make use of the touchscreen or the controller's tilt, and their quality this time is unusually consistent. The boards are divided thematically by setting, each with its own obstacles and its own boss battle at the end, so matches have a clear dramatic arc and don't end on a random star draw.
