The true star of the package is Bowser Party mode. Four players with Wii Remotes sit in front of the TV trying to reach the finish line, while a fifth player with the GamePad plays as Bowser, sees their own view, and tries to strip the others of their hearts one by one. This creates an asymmetric cat-and-mouse game, where one side is glued to the TV and the other smirks slyly into the controller — exactly the kind of fun Wii U was supposed to be built around. There's also an amiibo Party mode added, which uses the figures like pieces on a classic board, plus a set of solid side activities.

Technically, the game is bright, colorful, and clean, with polished animations and a soundtrack that unapologetically pushes a circus-like mood. Critics received the title with mixed feelings: they praised Bowser Party and the quality of the individual minigames, but repeatedly pointed out that the shared vehicle and the reduced emphasis on stars and coins pushed the series further from its board-game roots. For families and get-togethers, though, the game still works reliably today, mainly thanks to the mode that can't be replicated anywhere else. Anyone looking for a reason to pull the Wii U out of the cabinet for a family gathering will find it right here — and the role of Bowser is, moreover, the ideal job for the most experienced player in the room.
wii-u__mario-party-10.teaser: Players ride together in a single car; a faster pace, but less tactics than before.

wii-u__wii-party-u.article:
**Wii Party U** is the sequel to the hugely successful party collection from the Wii, and its main ambition was to find as many roles for the GamePad as possible that actually make sense in a living room. The lineup includes roughly eighty minigames along with several modes that frame them into longer sessions — from a classic board-game journey to something like a bargaining game to competitions where you play for a leaderboard spot while the players' Miis pull faces at every slip-up.

The best ideas rest on the controller lying flat on the table. In the tabletop modes, the GamePad is placed screen-up and the players around it flick coins, pull on a virtual rope, or play two-finger hockey directly on the glass; elsewhere the screen serves as a card only one player sees, as a radar, a target, or an indicator of a hidden task. On top of this come games for Wii Remotes, so the lineup around the TV can vary in both the number of people and the type of input. Several activities even function as an almost screen-free social game, where the controller just keeps score and hands out secret instructions. The longer modes then frame the minigames within a story of a trip, betting on outcomes, or collecting stamps, so the evening at least has a rough structure and doesn't end in random menu-clicking.

Visually, it's clean, simple graphics with Mii characters, well suited to the audience the game targets — anyone can sit down and know what to do within thirty seconds. The music is unobtrusive and cheerful, and the commentary and sound effects reliably ramp up the tension in the final seconds. Critics rated the game mostly solid: they praised the amount of content and the clever use of the second screen, but faulted the uneven quality of individual pieces and a weaker sense of drive in the longer modes. Today, Wii Party U is one of the few games that can hold even people who otherwise don't play at all, and together with Nintendo Land it forms the pair that best shows the console's original intent. It still holds up at the Christmas table.
wii-u__wii-party-u.teaser: A sequel to the Wii hit with eighty minigames searching for a meaningful role for the GamePad.

wii-u__affordable-space-adventures.article:
**Affordable Space Adventures** is the clearest proof that the GamePad could be something entirely different from just a second screen with a map. The player sits in a cheap tourist-grade spaceship that crash-lands on an unknown planet, and their task is to make their way through a series of caves, factories, and dark depths toward freedom. The ship isn't controlled with buttons in the sense of a classic action game — the controller's display holds a full instrument panel with individual systems that get switched on, tuned, and switched off with a finger.

That's the whole joke of it. The engine, the anti-gravity drive, the lights, the scanner, and other modules can each be set independently, and each of them gives off a different amount of heat, noise, and electromagnetic radiation. Enemy sensors react to something different each time, so the player has to think about what they can get away with: sneaking past a motion detector at minimum power in the dark, or instead shutting off the electronics and letting momentum carry them down. The result is an unusually calm, technical puzzle game where the main weapon is understanding the system. With up to three players cooperating, control of a single ship gets split among several people — one has the engine, another the manipulator arm, a third the scanner — and the quiet game instantly turns into a comedy full of bickering and mutual accusations of giving the game away.

The presentation is understated and atmospheric — dark caves, dimmed spotlight, the occasional neon flicker of a sensor, all paired with a minimalist ambient soundtrack that underscores the tension rather than manufacturing it. An advertising parody of the cheapest possible product runs through the whole game, giving it an unexpectedly dry sense of humor. Critics received the title very warmly and repeatedly named it among the games that got the most out of Wii U's hardware. Today it's a game that essentially can't be faithfully ported anywhere else, which is why it remains one of the most valuable reasons to keep the console around even after all these years.
wii-u__affordable-space-adventures.teaser: The clearest proof that the GamePad can be a complete cockpit dashboard, not just a second screen.

wii-u__runbow.article:
**Runbow** is a racing platformer built on a single brutally simple idea: the background color keeps changing, and anything that currently matches that same hue stops existing. The platform you were running on turns into nothing the instant the scene shifts to purple, and the player falls. The goal is to reach the bell at the end of the track before everyone else, which in practice turns into panicked jumping, shoving, and loud finger-pointing at everyone around you.

The game bet everything on the sheer scale of local multiplayer — a big group gathers around a single console, with one player holding the GamePad and the others Wii Remotes or the Pro Controller, letting an unusually high number of characters fit onto a single track at once. Alongside the race to the finish there are also arenas, a king-of-the-hill tug-of-war for a raised spot, and other competitive modes, plus a solo campaign with time-trial challenges that works as a decent accuracy trainer. The characters are largely guest heroes from other indie games, which turns the roster into a small parade of the indie scene of its time and a pleasant game of recognition for those in the know. Unlocking further fighters and cosmetic extras keeps motivation up even outside a party setup.

Visually, it's a flat, sharply colored stylization with character silhouettes, deliberately kept simple — because in the resulting chaos, readability is the one thing that matters. The accompanying music is energetic and uncomplicated, matching the fast pace well. Critics received the game favorably and praised mainly the originality of the core idea and the fun of large matches; criticism targeted how much of the magic the game loses in single-player and how the gimmick repeats itself after longer play. Today, Runbow is an example of an independent game that found exactly the audience it needed on Wii U. In a party setup it can get a whole room laughing within ten minutes, and it belongs among the titles where nobody needs the rules explained — just point at the screen and hand someone a controller.
wii-u__runbow.teaser: The background color changes and platforms of the same color disappear; panicked jumping for multiple players at once.

wii-u__shovel-knight.article:
**Shovel Knight** is a textbook example of how to revive the eight-bit era without turning it into mere nostalgic pastiche. A knight wielding a shovel instead of a sword sets out across a fairy-tale kingdom to rescue his companion Shield Knight and defeat the members of the sinister Order of No Quarter along the way. Each of them sits at the end of their own level with their own theme, their own traps, and their own musical track, exactly according to the unwritten rules of 1980s platformers.

The controls rest on two things: a simple shovel swing and a jump in which the shovel can be aimed downward to bounce off enemies, lamps, and flying objects like a spring. This creates movement that's easy to understand and hard to master perfectly. Treasure is spent on armor upgrades and special items, there's a map between levels in the spirit of classic games, towns offer shopping and small side tasks, and the game also offers an optional higher difficulty for those who dare. Anyone who wants to can smash checkpoints in exchange for treasure, wagering their own comfort against the reward. The Wii U version also got its own guest boss fight against Battletoads found nowhere else, and the game fully supported playing directly on the GamePad without a TV.

Technically it holds to the voluntary limitations of period hardware — a limited palette, flicker, jerky background scrolling — but warms them up with modern level design and fair checkpoints. The chiptune soundtrack from Jake Kaufman ranks among the best ever heard in independent games and carries most of the atmosphere. The game came about thanks to a very successful Kickstarter campaign, earned excellent reviews, and its creators went on to release free expansions for years in which you play as the individual bosses. Today Shovel Knight is considered one of the defining independent games of its era, and it found one of its first homes on Wii U.
wii-u__shovel-knight.teaser: A revival of the eight-bit era without cheap nostalgia; every boss has its own level and track.

wii-u__wonderful-101.article:
**The Wonderful 101** is arguably the strangest and at the same time most inventive action game of its entire generation. The player doesn't control a single hero but an entire swarm of superheroes in colorful suits defending Earth from an alien invasion. The camera watches the action from above, and the individual team members stick together like a flock. The core mechanic is the Unite Morph: the player draws a shape on the touchscreen or with the right stick, and the swarm instantly merges into a giant fist, sword, gun, whip, or ladder. Each shape has different properties, different controls, and a different role in combat and puzzle-solving, so the game feels like a mix of classic action, drawing, and tactics.

The structure is divided into operations reminiscent of episodes of a TV series, complete with over-the-top twists, giant robots, and battles that switch halfway through into something else entirely — a horizontal shooter, a giant mech fight, or a scene controlled from a single hero's perspective. This willingness to change genre every few minutes is among the best things the game offers, and at the same time it's the source of its reputation. The Wonderful 101 never explains anything twice, some players never quite learned the gesture-based controls, and the first hours can be confusing. But whoever pushes through finds an unusually deep combat system with blocking, dodging, and managing the energy needed for larger shapes.

Visually the game relies on bright colors, comic-book stylization, and enormous scene scale. The orchestral music sounds like the score to a superhero series from the seventies and supports that playful pathos remarkably well. Contemporary reception was mixed precisely because of the complexity and unusual controls, but over time the title became a cult item that found a devoted audience and later got released on other platforms as well. Today it stands as a reminder of a time when a major publisher could afford to fund a completely uncompromising authorial idea.
wii-u__wonderful-101.teaser: You don't control a single hero, but an entire swarm of superheroes; drawing shapes on the screen changes their formation.

wii-u__monster-hunter-3-ultimate.article:
**Monster Hunter 3 Ultimate** brought to Wii U a series that had long been more of a cult affair than a mass hit in the West. It's an expanded version of Monster Hunter 3, augmented with additional monsters, weapons, and the highest difficulty tier called G rank. The principle is simple yet incredibly addictive: the player takes a quest, heads out into a hunting area, tracks down a giant monster, brings it down, and crafts better gear from its parts so they can hunt an even bigger monster. Around this loop is built a game spanning hundreds of hours that has no classic character levels. Instead, the player's own skill and the quality of their armor grow.

The combat system is slow, heavy, and remarkably precise. Each weapon, from the greatsword through the hammer to the bow and hunting horn, has its own set of animations, reach, and rhythm, and learning just one properly takes hours. Attacks can't be interrupted, so every swing is a commitment the player has to see through. Monsters have readable behavior, they tire, limp, flee to their lair, and can be caught in traps. The Wii U version additionally offered a noticeably sharper picture than the handheld release, a map and quick item menu on the controller screen, and the ability to play together with owners of the Nintendo 3DS version, a very unusual feature at the time.

Underwater hunting, which the series introduced in this installment, added a third dimension to combat and remains one of the most discussed elements of the whole franchise. The atmosphere is held together by a calm campsite, the loud roars of monsters, and orchestral motifs that kick in the moment the main quarry appears. At the time it was one of the best-reviewed games of the early Wii U era and, for many Western players, their first real encounter with the series. Today it's still an excellent hunting title, it just demands patience and a willingness to learn rules the game itself only explains partially. Whoever gets past that barrier gets one of the most addictive games on the console, because preparing for the next hunt is just as engaging as the hunt itself.
wii-u__monster-hunter-3-ultimate.teaser: An expanded edition with the highest G rank difficulty; hunting monsters is as addictive as it gets.

wii-u__hyrule-warriors.article:
**Hyrule Warriors** is a fusion of two worlds that makes no sense on paper and works beautifully in practice. It took the characters, settings, and props from The Legend of Zelda series and dropped them into the structure of Japanese mass-battle action games, where the player alone mows down hundreds of enemies and captures one base after another. The result is a game in which Link, Zelda, Impa, Midna, or Ganondorf perform flashy attack combos in the middle of a battlefield, and where familiar musical themes appear in rock and metal arrangements. Each character has their own weapon, tempo, and special attack, so while the core loop is simple, the differences between the heroes are substantial.

The game didn't just borrow the scenery from Zelda. Battles make use of classic items such as the boomerang, bow, bombs, or hookshot, both against giant bosses and for opening up paths across the map. Bosses have weaknesses that need to be exposed just as in classic dungeons, which brings a welcome rhythm to otherwise straightforward action. Outside the main campaign, the game offers an Adventure Mode where progress moves across tiles of a map from the very first Zelda game, and every tile hides a different task or reward. This mode adds an enormous amount of content and easily stretches play across dozens of hours.

Technically, this was a compromise. To keep such a huge number of characters on screen, the game sacrificed resolution and environmental detail, and in two-player mode smoothness dropped even further. But splitting the picture between the TV and the controller allowed two-player games without splitting the screen, a rare luxury at the time. Contemporary reception was surprisingly warm, the game became one of the console's most commercially successful titles, and it kicked off a whole line of similar crossovers with other franchises. Today it's still a pleasant, undemanding, and very generous action game for Zelda fans, one you can switch your brain off for. The title's main strength lies in how seriously it takes its source material: despite gameplay that's completely un-Zelda-like, genuine knowledge of the series shows through in every setting, sound, and small reference.
wii-u__hyrule-warriors.teaser: Characters from Zelda in a Dynasty Warriors-style mass battle; a combination that surprisingly works.

wii-u__ninja-gaiden-3-razor-s-edge.article:
**Ninja Gaiden 3: Razor's Edge** is a fairly rare case of a game that got a second chance and made the most of it. The original Ninja Gaiden 3 on competing consoles disappointed: it simplified combat, cut weapons, toned down the violence, and turned a series known for merciless difficulty into a considerably tamer experience. The Wii U version, released alongside the console itself, reversed most of these changes. Multiple weapons returned to the game, along with limb dismemberment, collecting essence to restore health instead of automatic regeneration, and above all significantly higher demands on the player. Ryu Hayabusa once again feels like a ninja who dies after a few mistakes.

Combat rests on fast attacks, blocking, and dodging at nearly the last possible moment, on precise target switching, and on finishing moves that are also the only reliable way to restore stamina. The pace is high, the camera merciless, and enemies attack from every direction, turning every larger skirmish into a test of spatial awareness. Besides the campaign, the Wii U version also offered a playable Ayane with her own missions and additional modes focused on pure action and scoring performance. The environments take the player through cities, desert, and underground areas, and giant bosses are never in short supply.

Visually the game benefits from sharp animation and fast movement, though technically it carries traces of its origins, environments are fairly empty, and the story ranks among the weakest in the series. The music is functional, reminiscent of action-movie scoring, and lets weapon sounds stand out. Contemporary reception was noticeably better than for the original release, reviewers praised the return of difficulty and content, yet the game still didn't match the reputation of the second installment. Today Razor's Edge is interesting as the best available version of the third Ninja Gaiden and as one of the few genuinely hard action games on Wii U. It's also an instructive example of how a damaged reputation can be partially repaired if the creators return to what made the series distinctive, instead of trying to court the widest possible audience.
wii-u__ninja-gaiden-3-razor-s-edge.teaser: A correction of the disappointment from other consoles; it brought back the weapons and the series' merciless difficulty.

wii-u__assassin-s-creed-iv-black-flag.article:
**Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag** is the installment in which the series briefly stopped presenting itself primarily as a game about hidden assassination and became, above all, a game about the seas. The story follows Welsh sailor Edward Kenway, who in the Caribbean at the turn of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries falls into piracy and, almost as an afterthought, into the age-old conflict between Assassins and Templars. The player gets their own ship, the Jackdaw, which they gradually upgrade, and with it freely sails a map full of islands, forts, wrecks, and trading convoys. The transition between sailing, boarding a ship, and running across a port town's rooftops happens without loading screens, which was a very powerful impression at the time.

Naval combat is the game's core: the player aims broadside cannon volleys, dodges incoming fire, rams enemy vessels, and finally boards the enemy ship to finish off the crew by hand. Damaged prizes can be captured and added to the player's own fleet, or the player can strip them for materials to upgrade the Jackdaw, so every encounter matters. Alongside this, the series' classic offerings remain — climbing tall vantage points, blending into crowds, treasure hunting, and extensive side activities including hunting, diving, and chasing legendary ships. The sheer amount of content is enormous, and the game delivers it in a relaxed way, without pressure toward a straight main line.

The Wii U version put the map, equipment management, and quick navigation on the controller screen, so the usual disruptive menu-switching disappeared, and it allowed playing entirely away from the TV as well. Visually the game benefits from striking water, changing weather, and tropical light, but what holds the atmosphere together most are the sea shanties the crew sings while sailing, which are collected like collectibles. At the time it was one of the best-received entries in the series, and many still consider it the franchise's peak today. Even years later it works wonderfully as a relaxed pirate game, one you can happily forget the main story for.
wii-u__assassin-s-creed-iv-black-flag.teaser: The series temporarily traded assassinations for pirates; the ship Jackdaw is the true star here.

wii-u__batman-arkham-city-armored-editio.article:
**Batman: Arkham City - Armored Edition** brought to Wii U one of the best-reviewed superhero games ever made, right at the console's launch. The foundation is the same as in the original version: part of Gotham has been turned into an open-air prison district where criminals including Joker, Two-Face, and Penguin have been shipped, and Batman moves through it freely, gliding between towers on his cape and dropping down into alleys full of gangs. The structure combines a main storyline, a series of side cases with classic villains, and hundreds of Riddler puzzles that push the player to explore every corner of the map.

The combat system rests on fluidly chaining strikes, counters, and dodges, where it's crucial to watch the warning icons over enemies' heads and never break the rhythm. Alongside this there's stealth work in rooms full of armed guards, where Batman uses ceiling structures, ventilation shafts, and all sorts of gadgets to pick off opponents one by one and ramp up their panic. The Wii U version added BAT mode, a temporary suit boost charged up by successful hits, and moved equipment, the map, evidence scanning, and remote-controlled gadgets onto the controller screen. Some puzzles and hacking sequences used the touchscreen directly.

Atmospherically, Arkham City is an exceptionally strong work; the city feels bleak and cold, with snow, neon signs, and the constant crackle of radio chatter that can be eavesdropped on. The music works with dark orchestral motifs, and the main characters' voice acting ranks among the best in the genre. The Wii U release also included most of the later add-ons, making it a very generous package. Reviews were very good, though some reservations came up about visual smoothness compared to older versions. Today it's still a superb action-adventure, one that for many years defined the shape of superhero games.
wii-u__batman-arkham-city-armored-editio.teaser: Free movement through a prison district and gliding between towers; a superhero game with excellent reviews.

wii-u__mass-effect-3-special-edition.article:
**Mass Effect 3: Special Edition** was the sole representative of the famous space trilogy on Wii U, and at the same time a demonstration of how complicated it was to bring a game to a console whose previous installments had never appeared there. The story follows Commander Shepard at the moment the Reapers invade the galaxy and humanity, along with the other races, faces extinction. The main task is to gather allies, resolve old disputes between nations, and assemble a fleet that has the only real chance at a counterattack. The game combines a cover-based shooter with class-specific skills, gear management, and extensive dialogue in which the fates of entire civilizations are decided.

Because the first two installments were missing on the platform, the release included an interactive comic summarizing prior events and letting the player make key decisions from the past. It was an elegant compromise, even if it couldn't replace dozens of hours of relationships built up over the previous games. The package also included the Extended Cut expansion, which reworked the game's ending after a wave of criticism, and the From Ashes add-on with a new squad member. The Wii U controller served as a map, mission list, loadout, and quick skill selection, which made combat noticeably more pleasant since the player didn't have to keep opening menus.

Atmospherically, the third Mass Effect ranks among the series' heaviest installments; it's a game about retreat, sacrifice, and farewell, and its music, built on dark synthesizer textures, underscores that. Reception of the Wii U version was decent; reviewers praised the content and the use of the second screen but pointed out the missing multiplayer co-op mode and the game's late arrival on the market. Today it's more of a collector's curiosity, since the whole trilogy is available together elsewhere, but as a standalone experience the game still works thanks to its strong characters and serious tone. It also remains the only place where Wii U owners could encounter the series at all.
wii-u__mass-effect-3-special-edition.teaser: The only entry of the space trilogy on this console; rallying allies against the Reapers.

wii-u__deus-ex-human-revolution-director.article:
**Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut** is the most complete version of one of the smartest games of its generation, and it actually arrived on Wii U before any other platform. The player takes on the role of security chief Adam Jensen, who survives a brutal attack on his company only thanks to extensive mechanical augmentations. His investigation leads him from Detroit through Shanghai to secret laboratories, and along the way he keeps bumping into the question that holds the game together: how far should a person go in upgrading their own body, and who actually profits from it. The environments are designed as small open cities full of side quests, apartments to search, and people whose worries flesh out the picture of the world.

The core of the gameplay is freedom of approach. Every mission can be completed through silent stealth, hacking, persuasion in dialogue, finding a ventilation shaft, or brute force, and the augmentation system supports all of these styles. The player chooses whether to invest in invisibility, heavier weapons, the ability to punch through a wall, or the skill to read an opponent during conversation. The Director's Cut fundamentally reworked the boss fights, which in the original release forced even stealthy players into direct shootouts, and folded The Missing Link add-on directly into the main campaign. The Wii U GamePad served as the map, inventory, and interface for the hacking minigame.

Visually the game relies on a gold-and-black palette, Renaissance motifs, and a clearly recognizable cyberpunk styling, while the music works with slow electronic soundscapes to create a melancholic, oppressive mood. Reception was very good, and the game is still cited today as a model of how to make a modern immersive sim accessible to a wider audience. Technically the Wii U version isn't the smoothest, but it is the most complete in terms of content. Today the game's theme, unequal access to technology and corporate power over the human body, feels more relevant than at launch, and the gameplay itself has barely aged at all.
wii-u__deus-ex-human-revolution-director.teaser: The most complete version of one of the generation's smartest games; Adam Jensen and the question of where humanity ends.

wii-u__darksiders-ii.article:
**Darksiders II** was part of the Wii U's launch lineup, and it's a game that unapologetically borrows from several genres at once. The player takes control of Death, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, who is trying to clear his brother War's name from the first game and, in doing so, travels between the worlds of the living, the dead, and the angels. The foundation of the gameplay is fast action with scythes, heavy weapons, and magical abilities, but built around it is a surprisingly extensive RPG with levels, two skill trees, and an endless stream of randomly generated gear that changes both the character's appearance and stats.

The second pillar of the game is exploring sprawling temples whose structure and logic clearly draw from the classic dungeons of The Legend of Zelda series. The player searches for keys, moves mechanisms, uses a hook to cross chasms, switches between the world of the living and the dead, and solves spatial puzzles that rank among the game's best parts. Death is also far more mobile than the first game's hero, running along walls, sliding down poles, and rappelling, so simply moving through the world is a pleasure. There are four worlds, each with its own character, from green plains to industrial ruin.

The Wii U version added most of the later add-ons, including extra quests and gear, and moved the map, inventory, and skill tree to the GamePad screen, which helped a great deal in a game with this much loot. Visually, Darksiders II leans on a bold, comic-book style with exaggerated proportions and strong outlines that hasn't aged much at all. The music is calmer than one might expect from a game about the apocalypse, and several of its themes are among the most memorable. Contemporary reception was good, with reservations about the length and how often the same tasks repeat in the second half. Today it's still a generous and surprisingly varied action game offering dozens of hours of content for a price a game this size would struggle to match today. A sad footnote is the fate of the studio, which folded shortly after release, forcing the series to wait years for a sequel.
wii-u__darksiders-ii.teaser: Death, one of the four horsemen of the apocalypse, blends fast action with RPG elements and exploration.

wii-u__tokyo-mirage-sessions-fe.article:
**Tokyo Mirage Sessions #FE** is one of the strangest collaborations in gaming history: a crossover between the Shin Megami Tensei series and the world of Fire Emblem, set in present-day Tokyo and wrapped in the trappings of the Japanese entertainment industry. The heroes are young people fighting their way toward careers as singers, actors, and models, while also battling creatures called Mirages that steal human creative energy. The heroes' allies are themselves Mirages, resembling familiar Fire Emblem characters, so the player fights alongside the likes of Chrom or Tharja.

Battles are turn-based and built around a weakness system: every enemy is vulnerable to a specific weapon or element, and hitting that weakness triggers a Session, a chain of follow-up attacks from other party members. At higher levels, one well-aimed blow can turn into a chain of ten or more hits, which looks spectacular while also rewarding preparation and proper team composition. Alongside combat, the game develops relationships with characters through side stories that also unlock new skills, and the individual dungeons are thematically tied to different corners of the entertainment industry, from a TV studio to a photography set.

Visually, it's one of the most colorful and sharpest-looking games on Wii U, with a bold interface, animated sequences, and a strong emphasis on style. The music blends Japanese pop with rock battle themes and is one of the main reasons the game earned a devoted fanbase. The western release underwent certain content changes, which became a subject of contemporary debate among fans. Reception was largely positive, even though fans of both series expected something a bit different from what they got. Today it's a fresh, upbeat, and unusual JRPG that doesn't take itself too seriously and whose combat system remains a lot of fun. It's also one of the few major Japanese titles to release on Wii U in the final months of its life, which is why plenty of players missed it entirely.
wii-u__tokyo-mirage-sessions-fe.teaser: A curious crossover between Shin Megami Tensei and Fire Emblem, set against the backdrop of Japanese showbiz.

wii-u__fatal-frame-maiden-of-black-water.article:
**Fatal Frame: Maiden of Black Water** is the last major Japanese horror game to release on Wii U, and also the only entry in the series to reach the West through this particular console. The story unfolds around Mt. Hikami, a place tied to death and ancient rituals, and follows several characters whose stories alternate and gradually intertwine across chapters. The player explores abandoned houses, temples, and forests shrouded in rain and mist, armed only with the Camera Obscura, a camera that can capture and harm ghosts.

Combat therefore happens through the lens. The player must let a ghost approach, focus on it correctly, and pull the trigger at the moment of greatest danger, since the later the shot, the stronger the hit. The Wii U GamePad functions directly as the camera, held up in front of the player and aimed by tilting, making it one of the best-designed uses of motion controls on the entire platform. Water is the central motif of the whole game; getting soaked increases characters' vulnerability as well as their appeal to ghosts, and the rain-soaked environments give everything a heavy, cold atmosphere.

The pace is slow, and the game relies more on long stretches of building dread than on sudden jump scares. The sound design works with silence, the patter of rain, and distant voices, and music appears only where it's truly needed, which has a far greater effect on tension than a constant score. Contemporary reception was mixed; reviewers praised the atmosphere, environments, and use of the GamePad, but criticized the stiff character controls, repeated locations, and fragmented chapter structure. Commercially it was a niche title, yet the game later saw release on other platforms. Today it's an interesting reminder of a time when Japanese horror still relied on atmosphere rather than action, and also one of the few cases where the Wii U's unusual controls served the game's central theme directly. Anyone who enjoys slow, oppressive dread without action set pieces will find exactly what they're looking for here.
wii-u__fatal-frame-maiden-of-black-water.teaser: The last major Japanese horror game for this console; a camera as a weapon against ghosts.

wii-u__lego-city-undercover.article:
**LEGO City Undercover** is the most ambitious game ever built out of bricks up to that point, and also one of the few major titles that were initially Wii U exclusives. Unlike other entries in the series, it isn't based on a film license but on an entirely original world: the player takes on police officer Chase McCain, who returns to LEGO City to catch an escaped criminal, repeatedly disguising himself as a thief, firefighter, miner, or astronaut along the way. Each disguise brings different abilities, from wall-climbing through smashing obstacles to hovering, and opens up previously inaccessible places.

The city is open and fairly large, divided into districts each with its own character, and the player moves around on foot or in dozens of vehicles that can be summoned at any time. Beyond the story missions, there's a huge number of collectibles, minigames, and hidden references, so getting to one hundred percent completion takes considerably longer than just finishing the main line. The GamePad serves as a communicator and scanner used to find clues and eavesdrop on suspects, one of the few cases where the second screen genuinely adds to the atmosphere.

The humor here is stronger than in other LEGO games, since for the first time the characters have full voice acting, and the script openly pokes fun at police movies and TV shows. Visually it's a fresh, colorful spectacle with great attention to the detail of plastic surfaces; technically, though, the game was plagued by long loading screens, which practically every review complained about. Reception was nonetheless warm, and the title long remained one of the best reasons to own the console. Today it works as a harmless, very generous game for families and collectors alike, one that can fill many evenings. Its later release on other platforms removed the features tied to the second screen, but it showed that there was interest in the LEGO City world beyond Nintendo.
wii-u__lego-city-undercover.teaser: The most ambitious LEGO game of its time, with an original story instead of a movie license.

wii-u__sonic-lost-world.article:
**Sonic Lost World** was one of the results of a deal that brought several Sonic games exclusively to Nintendo platforms, and it's also the most experimental 3D Sonic of its time. The game abandons the wide highways of previous entries and builds its levels on cylindrical and spherical bodies, around whose surfaces Sonic runs, hops between them, and climbs walls. Visually it resembles a construction set of floating chunks of landscape, each with its own rules, and the game happily switches between a side view and a behind-the-back view mid-level.

A major change was speed control. Sonic now runs slower by default, and sprinting is held on the trigger, so the player must decide for themselves when to speed up and when to slow down instead for precise platforming. Added to this is a set of moves called Parkour, allowing Sonic to run along walls and climb over obstacles. The main antagonists are a group of six called the Deadly Six, and the game also features abilities gained from Wisps, tiny aliens who temporarily transform Sonic and open up alternate paths through the levels. The Wii U version offered a map and control of certain abilities on the GamePad screen, along with a cooperative mode for a second player.

Musically it's one of the series' strongest soundtracks, with orchestral and big-band arrangements that differ quite a bit from the rock sound of previous entries. Contemporary reception was mixed; critics mainly took issue with inconsistent controls, unpredictable physics, and uneven difficulty, though some players appreciated the courage to try something completely different. Today Sonic Lost World is interesting precisely as a dead end the series later abandoned, and as a game with unusually inventive level design. Anyone who adjusts to its different pace and stops expecting nonstop speed from Sonic will find plenty of cleverly built levels and ideas that never appeared in any other entry. That's exactly why the title holds onto a small but vocal group of defenders.
wii-u__sonic-lost-world.teaser: An experimental 3D Sonic game; levels built on cylindrical and spherical shapes instead of straight highways.

wii-u__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-blackl.article:
**Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Blacklist** is the last entry in the famous stealth series and one of the few major action titles for adults to reach Wii U. Sam Fisher leads the new Fourth Echelon unit here, trying to stop a series of attacks on American targets announced by a group of ultimatums called the Blacklist. The player's base of operations is the flying command aircraft Paladin, from which missions are selected, gear is upgraded, and side objectives from team members are accepted. The structure is therefore looser than before, and the player decides for themselves what to invest their earned money into.

The core of the game remains sneaking through the dark, tracking patrols, silent takedowns, and using gadgets, from the classic cable under a door to a drone and sticky cameras. Blacklist, however, openly offers three play styles and rewards all of them: a fully silent approach without a single detection, aggressive stealth with fast on-the-move executions, and open firefights. The system of marking targets and instantly taking them out gives the action a cinematic pace, yet the hardest and most highly regarded approach remains the one where nobody even notices someone was there. Alongside the campaign, the game also offered cooperative missions and the return of the asymmetric mode, where one side plays as spies and the other as mercenaries.

The Wii U version used the GamePad screen as a map, gear selection, and drone control, which made a lot of sense in a game built around planning. Visually it relies on the contrast between darkness and pools of light, and the atmosphere is carried above all by sound, footsteps, snatches of guard conversation, and tense underscores. Reviews were very good, with reservations mainly aimed at the change of voice actor for the main character, which fans of previous entries had gotten used to. Sales, however, fell short of expectations, and the series went quiet for many years, leaving Blacklist as its final major entry. Today it's one of the best-executed stealth games of its time, one that managed to satisfy purists and players wanting a faster pace alike.
wii-u__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-blackl.teaser: The last entry in the stealth series; the command aircraft Paladin serves as a base for missions.

wii-u__injustice-gods-among-us.article:
**Injustice: Gods Among Us** brought the fighting system of the Mortal Kombat series into the world of DC comics and turned it into one of the best-received fighting games of its generation. The premise revolves around a dark version of Superman who, after a personal tragedy, establishes his own dictatorship, and the heroes from a parallel world who try to overthrow him. The campaign is told cinematically, alternating fights with short action sequences, and the player gradually takes control of most of the cast, trying out Batman, Wonder Woman, Flash, Joker, and lesser-known heroes alike.

Fights take place in two dimensions, but the environments play an unusually large role. Objects in the arena can be picked up and thrown, opponents can be bounced off walls, and a strong attack can launch them into an adjacent part of the stage, where the fight continues after a spectacular destruction sequence. Each character has a special ability tied to a single button, from a temporary shield to slowing down the opponent, and super moves are designed as short animated scenes in which Superman carries an opponent into orbit or Aquaman summons a shark. The system is readable even for newcomers while still being deep enough for tournament play.

The Wii U version was technically comparable to the competition and used the GamePad screen for an overview of moves and stats and for playing entirely off the TV. It also included an extensive S.T.A.R. Labs mode with dozens of short challenges that expand the content beyond the classic matches. Contemporary reception was very good, with the game praised for a story mode that long ranked among the genre's best, as well as its handling of the license. Today it remains a fun fighting game whose sequel brought better balance and more modern technical polish, though the first game retains its rawer, darker tone. For Wii U owners it was also one of the few cases of getting a big multiplatform game at the same time as other consoles and in a complete form, something that became increasingly rare on this platform.
wii-u__injustice-gods-among-us.teaser: The Mortal Kombat fighting system set in the DC universe; a dark, dictatorial Superman as the threat.

ps5__demon-s-souls.article:
**Demon's Souls** was a PlayStation 5 launch title and a complete remake of the game that founded the entire soulslike genre back in 2009. You return to the cursed kingdom of Boletaria, consumed by thick fog and demons that feed on the souls of its inhabitants. From the central Nexus you venture into five separate worlds, each with its own architecture, cast of enemies, and boss at the end. Progress is slow, careful, and built on learning: every trap and every alcove hiding an archer burns itself into memory, because death means losing your accumulated souls and returning to the start of the level.

Combat is built around stamina management and reading your opponent's movements. Blocking, dodging, parrying, and precisely timed retreats out of weapon range matter more than character stats, though the character can still be tuned into anything from a heavy knight to a spellcaster. A distinctive feature remains the world and character tendency system, which shifts the difficulty and content of individual locations according to your actions and opens hidden paths. The online layer is indirect and all the more effective for it: messages from other players appear on the ground, ghostly echoes of their final moments, and occasionally another player invades your world as an enemy or arrives as a summoned ally. Each player largely charts their own course, and two playthroughs rarely look alike.

Technically it was a showcase for the new console. Rebuilt models, lighting, and thick fog transformed the grim world into something the original PlayStation 3 version could only hint at, and the fast SSD cut death screens down to an instant, fundamentally changing the rhythm of repeated attempts. The orchestral music during boss fights sounds far denser than before, and the sound of footsteps in stone corridors carries the game even in its quiet moments. Reviewers praised above all the faithfulness to the original and the craftsmanship of the remake, while some players debated the changes to the atmosphere and the design of certain characters. Today, Demon's Souls remains the most comfortable way to experience the roots of a genre that has shaped a whole decade of action games.
ps5__demon-s-souls.teaser: A remake of the game that founded the entire souls-like genre in 2009; a PS5 launch title.

ps5__marvel-s-spider-man-miles-morales.article:
**Marvel's Spider-Man: Miles Morales** is a standalone sequel to the New York-set Spider-Man, putting young Miles in the role of the main hero. Peter Parker leaves town and hands him the protection of Manhattan just as a conflict flares up in the streets between a private energy corporation and organized crime. A winter New York blanketed in snow and holiday lights serves as an open playground to swing through; the movement itself remains the core of the fun, and the game never shortchanges it.

Miles has his own abilities compared to Peter. Bioelectric venom attacks can knock back a group of enemies, charge up a flashy combo finisher, or stun an armored opponent, and on top of that there's temporary invisibility, which significantly changes the stealth sections. Combat is fast, built on last-moment dodges, combos, and using the environment, while side activities take the player around the Harlem neighborhood via an app filled with reports from residents. The campaign is shorter and tighter than the first game's, focusing all the more on Miles's family, friendships, and the question of what it means to take on someone else's mask. Side threads involving the search for rare recordings of Miles's father, or following his friend, give the map purpose beyond the main story.

On PlayStation 5, the game offered a ray-traced reflections mode as well as a higher frame-rate option, near-instant loading during fast travel, and haptic feedback from the DualSense controller you feel with every web shot fired. The soundtrack leans on hip hop and modern production, setting the hero apart from the predecessor's orchestral tone and fitting well with the setting and his age. Reviews welcomed the title warmly, with reservations mainly about its length and the fact that mechanically it builds on an already familiar foundation. Today it works as an ideal entry point into the series: compact, visually striking, and with a hero the game can stand behind even for someone who never played the first game. The campaign's length is offset by the density of its individual scenes.
ps5__marvel-s-spider-man-miles-morales.teaser: A standalone continuation of the New York Spider-Man story, starring Miles Morales.

ps5__returnal.article:
**Returnal** sends pilot Selene to a mysterious planet, Atropos, where after every death she wakes up at the crash site and the world around her reshuffles into a new configuration. The effort to decipher the signal that brought her here turns into a repeated journey through six biomes full of alien architecture, overgrown ruins, and twisted creatures. The story arrives in fragments: through audio logs, through first-person sections inside a house that has no business being on an alien planet, and through the gradual revelation of what Selene is actually running from.

The gameplay combines a roguelite structure with a classic arcade-style third-person shooter. Weapons unlock permanently, but their upgraded traits and parasitic artifacts are rebuilt every run, risking a damaged suit or nasty side effects along the way. Enemies spew dense patterns of glowing projectiles, and the only solution is constant movement, precisely dashing through a barrage, and using the alt-fire mode. Boss fights rank among the toughest on the whole console and demand the same pattern memorization as old arcade games. Each run lasts hours, and losing it hurts, because part of your unlocked progress goes with it; this keeps the tension alive even after dozens of attempts.

Technically it's one of the best showcases for the DualSense controller. Adaptive triggers distinguish standard and alternate fire with a single finger, haptics convey rain hitting the helmet and the echo of explosions, and spatial audio helps reveal enemies off-screen. Visually the game combines sharp neon projectiles with a dark, cosmic-horror setting, while the music works more with dread and tension than melody. Critics praised the boldness of releasing an expensive, difficult, and author-driven game as a major exclusive title; criticism targeted the original lack of mid-run saving, which a later update addressed. Today Returnal remains one of the most distinctive and idiosyncratic games of its generation. Few titles sustain such oppressive dread for so long.
ps5__returnal.teaser: A roguelite in which pilot Selene comes back to life after every death on a differently arranged planet.

ps5__ratchet-and-clank-rift-apart.article:
**Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart** builds its entire gameplay around rifts between dimensions. Doctor Nefarious seizes a device capable of opening passages to parallel worlds, and the heroic duo find themselves in a reality where evil has won. Alongside Ratchet, the lead role is shared with Rivet, a Lombax from another dimension with her own story and tone, and the game smoothly switches between the two characters. The result is a colorful interstellar ride that isn't afraid to be, above all, fun and easy to follow.

The foundation stays true to the series: a crazy arsenal that upgrades with use, from a rocket launcher through a weapon that turns enemies into plants to a portable turret. Combat is fast, built on constant circling around groups of enemies and switching weapons to match the situation, and a short dash adds new dynamism to movement. Rifts function as part of both combat and platforming sections, since you can be pulled toward them and instantly appear on the other side of an arena. Between the action come more logic-based puzzles with the robot Glitch and calmer sections with Clank. Collectibles, armor, and bolts hidden off the main path reward attentive players and encourage revisiting already-explored levels.

The game was presented as a title that couldn't have been made on the previous console, and instant jumps between entire worlds without loading really proved it. On top of that come ray-traced reflections, several graphics modes, and quality voice acting with animation good enough that the game can be followed almost like an animated film. Orchestral music underlines the adventurous tone, while adaptive triggers split every weapon into two firing modes. Reviewers praised the technical side, the humor, and Rivet as a new character; more critical voices noted that it's a very safe sequel without major surprises. Today it's one of the best-looking family-friendly titles on the console. For families, it's also one of the few major exclusives where you can hand off the controller without worrying about the content.
ps5__ratchet-and-clank-rift-apart.teaser: An action platformer built around rifts between dimensions; Rivet joins Ratchet as a playable character.

ps5__ghost-of-tsushima-director-s-cut.article:
**Ghost of Tsushima Director's Cut** brings to PlayStation 5 the story of the samurai Jin Sakai, who during the 1274 Mongol invasion gradually abandons the code of his class in order to be able to defend the island of Tsushima at all. The open world is guided unusually subtly: instead of a map densely packed with icons, wind, golden birds, and smoke on the horizon lead you to your objectives, so you end up wandering the landscape rather than ticking off markers. The Iki Island expansion adds a separate island with its own campaign that returns to Jin's family past.

Combat combines direct clashes with sharp katana swordplay and stealth, in which you become the thing the Mongols fear. Switching combat stances against different types of opponents, duels initiated by a challenge, and tools like smoke bombs or the kusarigama give the player a choice between honor and effectiveness that the story keeps commenting on. Alongside this are extensive companion side stories, hot springs, writing haiku, and searching for shrines — activities that serve the atmosphere more than checking off a list. As the game progresses, the player assembles their own version of the hero: some stick to honorable face-to-face duels, others clear an entire camp without ever being spotted.

The PlayStation 5 version added a higher frame rate, faster loading, Japanese voice acting with synced lip movement, and haptic feedback that noticeably changes the feel of both riding a horse and every sword strike. Visually it's one of the most beautiful games of the generation: fields of red maple leaves, mist over the reeds, and lighting that clearly nods to classic Japanese cinema. The music uses traditional instruments and silence, and the black-and-white samurai filter is a tribute to old cinematography. Reviews praised the presentation and the combat system, with reservations about repetitive side quests. Today it's a safe recommendation for anyone wanting a grand historical epic. The package also includes the cooperative Legends mode, which reshapes Norse and Japanese myths into a standalone game for several players.
ps5__ghost-of-tsushima-director-s-cut.teaser: Samurai Jin Sakai during the Mongol invasion; instead of map icons, you're guided by wind and smoke on the horizon.

ps5__death-stranding-director-s-cut.article:
**Death Stranding Director's Cut** is an expanded version of the game in which courier Sam Porter Bridges reconnects the remnants of a shattered America. After a catastrophe called the Death Stranding, the world was filled with rain that accelerates time and ghostly creatures, wasteland stretched between the cities, and people sealed themselves off in underground bunkers. Your job is, quite literally, to carry deliveries, one at a time, while rebuilding a network that would reconnect isolated communities. It sounds absurd, and the game deliberately makes that its main strength.

Walking is a full-fledged mechanic here. You manage the distribution of cargo on your back, your center of balance, stamina, and whether the delivery stays dry, and while wading through a river or descending a slope you balance with both triggers. Ladders, ropes, exoskeletons, vehicles, and eventually roads gradually appear, which you build together with other players through an asynchronous shared-construction system. Encounters with ghostly creatures require sneaking and holding your breath, while clashes with raiders offer both non-lethal and harsher solutions. The Director's Cut added a firing range, a racetrack, new tools, and several extra missions. Over time, lonely toil turns into shared infrastructure, and another player's construction appears exactly where you yourself wanted to build a ladder.

On PlayStation 5 the game runs at a higher resolution and frame rate, offers a widescreen cinematic mode, and uses haptics so the player feels stones underfoot and rain on the hood. The audiovisual presentation ranks among the console's strongest: the barren Nordic-style wasteland, minimalist interface, and songs that kick in at exactly the moment the player crests a ridge and spots the destination. The game divided audiences at its original release and continues to divide them, because its pace is deliberately slow and its themes of loneliness and connection feel unusually direct. Whoever tunes into it finds an experience unlike anything else in games. The cast led by Norman Reedus and Mads Mikkelsen holds the cinematic sequences together.
ps5__death-stranding-director-s-cut.teaser: An unconventional delivery game from Hideo Kojima; you carry packages across a shattered America.

ps5__resident-evil-village.article:
**Resident Evil Village** sends Ethan Winters to a snowbound village somewhere in Eastern Europe to find his kidnapped daughter. A castle belonging to the Dimitrescu family looms over the landscape, and lycans roam around it that have little in common with the series' usual undead. The game continues with the first-person perspective introduced by the previous entry, but plays much more with horror subgenres: each of the four main locations has its own rules and mood, from a gothic fortress through a doll-maker's workshop to a factory.

The gameplay balances between action and classic survival horror. Ammunition is limited, the inventory is managed on a grid, enemy attacks can be blocked with your arms, and between chapters you shop with the merchant Duke, who also upgrades weapons and cooks food from ingredients gathered in the field. Exploration is built as an interconnected map with locked shortcuts and keys, exactly as the older entries made the series famous. The sequence in the Beneviento family's house sets action aside entirely and offers one of the most talked-about horror sequences of recent years. Weapons can be fitted with sights and larger magazines, and completing the game unlocks the Mercenaries mode with timed waves of enemies.

On PlayStation 5 the game runs smoothly at high resolution, supports ray tracing and fast loading, adaptive triggers distinguish between individual weapons, and haptics convey recoil. Sound is crucial: creaking wood, growling around a corner, and orchestral motifs that kick in during boss fights. Critics received the game very well, praising the variety of settings and the boldness of shifting tone between chapters, while some players wrote that it's the most action-heavy entry in the series and that the fear fades by the end. Today Village is one of the most accessible modern horror games and a game people remember above all for its striking characters. Capcom later added the Shadows of Rose expansion and the option to play the whole campaign from a third-person perspective, which significantly changes the feel of the game.
ps5__resident-evil-village.teaser: A horror ride through a village full of the vampiric Dimitrescu family and packs of lycans.

ps5__horizon-forbidden-west.article:
**Horizon Forbidden West** takes huntress Aloy west, into the flooded ruins of California, to find a way to stop a plague destroying the last remnants of the biosphere. The open world combines overgrown cities, desert, rainforests, and, for the first time, underwater zones you can dive into. The apocalypse here is colorful and vibrant, individual tribes have their own culture and architecture, and towering over it all move giant robotic animals, still the series' main attraction and the reason players stop and simply stare.

Combat is built on preparation. With the scanner you reveal a machine's weak points, choose the type of ammunition, shoot off a fuel tank, or tear off a weapon you can then use yourself. New tools have been added to the bow, including a glider, a grappling hook for quick traversal, and improved climbing, making movement across vertical terrain far more free than before. The character develops through branching skill trees and through crafting, which requires materials from specific machines. Alongside the main story, the game offers dense side quests, hunting challenges, and the board game Machine Strike. Aloy can choose between a silent hunt from cover and a direct clash, dodging at the last moment beneath a giant machine while aiming for individual components.

Technically it's one of the best-looking titles of its generation. Vegetation detail, facial animation, and the lighting of a sunset over the remains of skyscrapers rank among the best the console can achieve, and the player can choose between a higher-resolution mode and a smoother-running one. The music uses ethnic instruments and orchestra, and spatial audio helps well when hunting for machines hidden in foliage. Reviews praised the scope, the combat system, and the technical side, with reservations about the sheer number of systems and the pacing of the story in the first half. Today Forbidden West feels like the completion of what the first game only began. The Burning Shores expansion later added a standalone area available only on PlayStation 5.
ps5__horizon-forbidden-west.teaser: Aloy heads to the flooded ruins of California; for the first time you can also dive beneath the surface.

ps5__god-of-war-ragnarok.article:
**God of War Ragnarök** closes out the Norse duology about Kratos and his son Atreus. Fimbulwinter has already covered all nine realms, both Odin and Thor are hot on the heroes' heels, and the question of whether prophecy can be changed becomes the spine of the whole story. The game continues in the form of one long, unbroken take with no cuts, weaving together combat, exploration and conversations on the move. Atreus, for the first time, also becomes a fully playable character with his own sections and a different fighting style.

Combat builds on the previous game and expands it. The Leviathan Axe still freezes, the Blades of Chaos still burn, and a new third weapon arrives that fundamentally changes the rhythm of encounters; each one comes with its own set of skills, runes and finishing moves. Enemies are more varied than before, bosses have readable yet demanding attack patterns, and the game offers a wide range of difficulty settings along with exceptionally thorough accessibility options. The nine realms are more open, with side quests that have their own narrative arcs, puzzles hidden in ruins, and treasures tucked away behind clever use of your weapons. Both Kratos and Atreus have their own skill trees, and the game regularly switches who the player controls, so the combat rhythm never gets stale.

The title launched simultaneously on PlayStation 4 and PlayStation 5, but on the new console it offered higher resolution, smoother performance, and haptic feedback support that lets you feel every axe swing in your hands. Visually it excels through its handling of light in snowy passes and the colorful fantasy of realms like Vanaheim or Alfheim, while the music leans on choirs and Norse instruments. Critics received the game exceptionally well, praising the character writing and the performances, with the main reservations aimed at how faithfully it follows its predecessor mechanically. Today, Ragnarök stands as one of the strongest arguments for the series as a whole. The studio later added the free Valhalla expansion, which recasts the combat system in a roguelite form and returns to the hero's past.
ps5__god-of-war-ragnarok.teaser: The climax of the Norse saga of Kratos and Atreus; the son becomes a playable character for the first time.

ps5__last-of-us-part-i.article:
**The Last of Us Part I** is a complete rebuild of the original 2013 game, built on the technology the studio developed for the second installment. Smuggler Joel must escort the girl Ellie across a ravaged United States twenty years after the outbreak of a fungal infection that turned most of the population into aggressive creatures. The journey across the continent, through quarantine zones, overgrown cities and abandoned universities, mainly serves as a framework for the relationship between two people who, at first, want nothing to do with each other.

Gameplay rests on stealth, improvisation and scarcity. You gather resources bit by bit and decide whether to craft a medkit, a molotov cocktail, or a knife for a silent takedown; every encounter is short, brutal, and can turn against you fast. The infected react to sound, human enemies try to flank you, and the listen mode gives just enough information for a plan, not certainty. The remake reworked the AI of both companions and enemies, added a large number of accessibility options, and also includes the Left Behind expansion. Fights can be solved with brute force too, but the game always shows what that cost you, and a lack of ammunition reliably sends the player back into the shadows.

On PlayStation 5, the game runs in high resolution with a choice between quality and performance modes, offers practically instant loading, haptic feedback for shooting and drawing the bow, and reworked character models with far more detailed facial animation. The sound design and Gustavo Santaolalla's score, which gets by on just a few guitar notes, carry entire passages without a single word. Discussion around the game mostly focused on whether the remake was needed so soon and on its price, but the execution itself was received as technically first-rate. Today it's the most complete way to experience a story that shifted how big-budget games handle narrative. Bonus content, including a challenge mode, character models, and developer commentary, adds extra value for those who already know the story well.
ps5__last-of-us-part-i.teaser: A complete rebuild of the 2013 classic using the technology from the series' second installment.

ps5__elden-ring.article:
**Elden Ring** carried the Soulslike formula into the vast open world of the Lands Between. As a Tarnished, the player searches for fragments of the Elden Ring and a path to the throne, while the world tells you almost nothing: there are no arrows, no quest lists, only vantage points, strange structures on the horizon, and trails worth following. Writer George R. R. Martin contributed to the mythology, and it shows most clearly in the lineage of demigods whose falls form the backbone of the whole story.

Combat remains demanding and precise, but for the first time the player has far more ways to deal with an obstacle. You can flee on horseback, go around an area, come back later stronger, summon a spirit for help, or try one of dozens of combat arts that can be swapped between weapons. Underground dungeons, catacombs, and huge hidden areas beneath the surface reward curiosity just as much as the open landscape does. The online layer works as it did in the studio's earlier games: messages left on the ground, summoning helpers, and invasions by other players. The land is dotted with roaming bosses, enemy camps, and random encounters, and the game almost never tells you what counts as a fair challenge and what's a trap for an overconfident player.

On PlayStation 5, the game offers a ray-tracing mode as well as a smoother-performance option, quick reloading after death, and a more stable framerate than owners of older consoles had; the technical side was a target of criticism at launch and was addressed by later updates. Visually it excels through its handling of distant vistas and lighting, and the music mostly appears during boss fights, making all the bigger impression for it. Reception was extraordinary, and the game significantly widened the audience for a genre that used to be considered niche. The Shadow of the Erdtree expansion then showed that the developers can build an even more tightly focused experience within the same world. Today, Elden Ring is an obvious recommendation. Weapons, spells, and character builds offer so many combinations that two playthroughs barely resemble each other, and the community is still uncovering hidden details years later.
ps5__elden-ring.teaser: The souls-like formula in a vast open world; George R. R. Martin contributed to the mythology.

ps5__final-fantasy-vii-rebirth.article:
**Final Fantasy VII Rebirth** is the second entry in a trilogy retelling the classic 1997 JRPG. Cloud's party leaves Midgar and sets out across the continent in pursuit of Sephiroth, as the game opens up onto sprawling regions with their own wildlife, camps, and quests. Familiar stops like Kalm, Junon, Cosmo Canyon, and the Gold Saucer amusement park are fleshed out here into a far larger form than in the original, complemented by new scenes and much more room for the supporting cast.

The battle system builds on the previous entry: real-time action blends with a tactical pause during which you spend ATB points on spells, abilities, and items. New additions include synergy attacks between pairs of characters, which reward rotating your whole party, and progression through so-called Folios instead of a classic skill tree. On top of that comes a huge amount of side content, from the Queen's Blood card game through chocobo races to music minigames, many of which players ended up loving more than the main story itself. Each region has its own vantage points, exploration tasks, and machine and monster hunts, so simply wandering the world can easily take longer than the main plot.

On PlayStation 5, the game offers a mode favoring resolution and a smoother-performance option, though image quality in the performance mode was a target of criticism at launch and the developers later improved it. The presentation is otherwise showcase quality: grand cinematic sequences, orchestral arrangements of Nobuo Uematsu's original compositions, and a soundtrack that stretches across dozens of hours of gameplay. Critics praised the scope, the combat, and the boldness of changing a well-known story, while discussion centered on the sheer amount of side content and on an ending that leaves many questions open. Today, Rebirth is one of the biggest and most generous JRPGs of its generation. For players who know the original, the biggest draw is how the game plays with decades of expectations built up around its key scenes.
ps5__final-fantasy-vii-rebirth.teaser: The second part of a trilogy that retells the classic 1997 JRPG.

ps5__astro-bot.article:
**Astro Bot** is a full-fledged 3D platformer in which a small robot travels the galaxy searching for the scattered crew of his mothership, shaped like a PlayStation 5 console. Every planet offers several short, densely designed levels each built around its own idea, whether that's growing and shrinking, playing with time, or temporary abilities that change both movement and combat. The structure is classic and clear, the pace never lets up, and no mechanic overstays its welcome.

The controls rank among the best in the genre. Jumping, hovering with the leg thrusters, and a laser attack cover most situations, but the game keeps adding new toys: springy fists, a dog-shaped backpack that lets you run up walls, or a rocket on your back. Collecting hidden bots is the main driving force, and many of them reference PlayStation's history, so the player runs into characters from dozens of games across generations. Boss fights are short, readable, and built around a single idea that gets developed and wrapped up within the fight. Alongside the main worlds await hidden levels, time trials, and puzzles that only unlock once specific characters have been found, which keeps players happily coming back to the galaxy.

The game also doubles as a showcase for what the DualSense controller can do. Haptic feedback distinguishes the surface underfoot, the adaptive triggers create resistance when you draw back a slingshot, and the controller's built-in speaker becomes part of the puzzles. Visually, the title relies on clean colors, soft lighting, and physics for small objects; the music is upbeat and catchy without becoming tiresome. Reviews were enthusiastic, and the game picked up numerous awards, including major game-of-the-year honors, which is certainly not common for a platformer. Today it stands as the most convincing proof that a classically designed platformer can still serve as a modern showcase title for an entire console. Accessibility is high, too: both a child and an adult who last sat down with a platformer twenty years ago can handle it, yet there are still challenges here for the completionist.
ps5__astro-bot.teaser: A joyful platformer full of short, inventive levels, each with a fresh idea of its own.

ps5__stellar-blade.article:
**Stellar Blade** tells the story of the soldier Eve, who returns to an abandoned Earth overrun by creatures called the Naytiba in order to clear a path back for the rest of humanity, living in an orbital colony. The game alternates tight, linear levels set in ruins and corridors with more open desert areas where you can explore more freely, complete side quests, and search for gear. Its presentation rests on the contrast between the elegant main heroine and exceptionally unsettling, biologically styled enemies.

The combat system is the core of the whole game and relies on precisely timed parries. Every enemy type has its own rhythm, and the player learns when to block, when to sidestep, and when to use a reaction that requires a specific input; a correctly timed parry opens the enemy up and charges abilities that are spent on powerful strikes. On top of that come skill progression, suit modules, a ranged weapon for distant targets, and a solid amount of side content including puzzles and collectibles. The difficulty is noticeable, but the game also offers gentler settings for those who came mainly for the story. The game gradually adds new combat combos and exploration tools, which opens up earlier areas and makes revisiting them worthwhile.

Technically, it's a very polished title that runs smoothly on PlayStation 5 and offers several graphics modes; the environments impress mainly through their lighting and material detail. The music mixes electronic sounds with vocals and is among the things players remember most, since it underscores the melancholic tone of the depopulated world. Reception was good, with praise for the combat and the soundtrack, while reservations were aimed at the storytelling and at how the game handles the main character's visual presentation, which also sparked a wider debate. Today it's one of the most distinctive new action titles on the console. It was the South Korean studio's first major console title, and its success showed that there's room for new action franchises even outside established series.
ps5__stellar-blade.teaser: An action adventure about soldier Eve, who cleanses Earth of creatures called Naytiba.

ps5__black-myth-wukong.article:
**Black Myth: Wukong** is based on the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West and casts the player as the Destined One, a simian warrior setting out to collect the relics of the legendary Sun Wukong. The structure is more a sequence of sprawling, interconnected chapters than an open world: each has its own landscape, mythological characters, and a string of bosses who are the game's main attraction. The narrative is rounded out by hand-animated interludes at the end of each chapter, each rendered in a different art style.

Combat is faster-paced than in classic Soulslike games. The foundation is a staff and three different stances you can switch between, plus charged heavy strikes, magic that freezes enemies in place, transformations into defeated foes, and summoned animal allies. Stamina limits both dodging and attacking, but the game pushes the player toward offense rather than cautiously waiting for an opening. Progression comes through skill points, brewing elixirs, and forging gear from materials dropped by defeated bosses. Bosses have their own backstories, elaborate animations, and often several phases, turning every encounter into a small spectacle.

Built on Unreal Engine 5, the title ranks among the visually most ambitious games of its year, and on PlayStation 5 it offers a choice between image quality and performance, with the performance mode sparking discussion after launch and being further tuned by the developers. The environments draw on real Chinese architecture and landscapes, while the music mixes traditional instruments with an orchestra, opening up mythology to Western players who barely know it from games. The game became one of the biggest surprises of its generation and gave major visibility to Chinese developers; reservations were aimed at the pacing of the second half and at how understandable the story is without knowledge of the source material. Today it's worth trying mainly for the boss fights. The game first launched on PlayStation 5 and PC, and its popularity proved that a big-budget action title can succeed even without an established franchise behind it. Anyone who enjoys demanding combat has nothing to think twice about.
ps5__black-myth-wukong.teaser: An action RPG based on the classic novel Journey to the West; the main draw is its epic bosses.

ps5__final-fantasy-xvi.article:
**Final Fantasy XVI** pushed the long-running series furthest from its turn-based roots, turning it into a dark action RPG with the ambitions of political drama. The story follows Clive Rosfield, a duke's son whose life is upended by betrayal and whose fate becomes entangled with the Eikons, enormous beings who, in this world, also serve as weapons of mass destruction. The continent of Valisthea is divided among several warring houses, and the struggle over dwindling magical resources forms the backdrop of a story that doesn't shy away from cruelty, questions of slavery, or heavy losses among its main cast.

Battles are fully action-based, built around combining light and heavy attacks, last-moment dodges, and above all abilities borrowed from individual Eikons, which can be switched on the fly. Players who mainly want the story can equip ring accessories that simplify both dodging and combos. The highlight is the fights against the Eikons themselves, which alternate ordinary action with grand sequences bordering on interactive film. Classic RPG elements like party management or extensive skill trees have taken a back seat here, something part of the series' fanbase received with mixed feelings. The pacing, moreover, regularly alternates large-scale battles with calmer sections at the home base, where relationships within the group develop and equipment gets upgraded.

The game was created under producer Naoki Yoshida and on PS5 offers a choice between image quality and performance, which you'll especially appreciate during major clashes.
