Weapons are crafted and upgraded from materials collected in the environment, so exploration genuinely pays off.

The world consists of tight laboratory and testing-complex interiors linked by a more open outdoor area, where flying drones patrol and the player must choose between a quick dash and a fight. The art direction is the game's greatest asset: retro-futuristic aesthetics combine monumental statues, mosaics, and wood paneling with chrome robots, creating an environment unlike anything found in other shooters. The music is a mix of electronic tracks and rearranged period Soviet songs that feel unsettlingly contrasting during moments of carnage. On Xbox Series X|S the game runs smoothly and offers a performance-focused mode.

Reception was mixed, but with clear respect for the ambition of an independently-minded studio. Reviewers praised the visual identity, the inventive bestiary, and the combat system, while criticism pointed to sprawling dialogue, uneven pacing, and outdoor sections that lacked the density of the interiors. The game found a large audience and became one of the most talked-about titles of the year. Today it stands as an interesting alternative to conventional shooters — technically solid, visually unmistakable, and distinctive enough to be remembered even years later. Anyone who enjoys a setting that tells its own story even without characters will explore the complex with interest, even once the combat itself stops surprising them.
xbox-series__atomic-heart.teaser: An alternate USSR that has mastered robotics; a special glove freezes and lifts enemies alike.

xbox-series__ascent.article:
**The Ascent** is an isometric action shooter set in a cyberpunk arcology, a giant vertical city run by a corporation that suddenly collapses. The player starts out as an insignificant laborer in the lowest levels and gradually fights their way upward, with combat combining constant movement, cover, and switching between low and high aiming. Dual-height aiming is the most interesting mechanic: raising your weapon lets you shoot over crates and railings, while lowering it keeps you in cover. On top of that come tactical gadgets, augmentations, and stat progression, which make the game feel like a lighter action RPG.

The art direction leaves the biggest impression. The city is packed with detail — neon, advertisements, crowds of characters, and layers of trash — and the game shows it from a distance that lets you appreciate the scale of the whole construction. On Xbox Series X|S ray tracing and high resolution are available, and the environments rank among the most striking an isometric game has offered on this generation. The soundscape leans on dark electronic music that keeps a heavy mood beneath the street noise. The entire campaign can be played in co-op for up to four players, whether online or on a single console.

The game was made by a small team, which is remarkable given the scale of the world, and contemporary reviews usually highlighted that disparity. The visuals, atmosphere, and combat system were praised, while criticism targeted confusing navigation through the city's complex levels, an occasionally uneven difficulty curve, and technical issues at launch that were later addressed with patches. Today it's one of the best ways to play fast cyberpunk action with friends on console — a few dozen hours is plenty, and the visual impression of the arcology lasts long after finishing it. Playing solo is noticeably harder, since enemies attack in waves from several directions, but with two or three players the game turns into a pleasantly chaotic firefight full of improvisation. Its availability via subscription also helped it reach an audience that might otherwise never have picked up an isometric shooter.
xbox-series__ascent.teaser: An isometric cyberpunk shooter with two-tier aiming at low and high targets.

xbox-series__tunic.article:
**Tunic** looks at first glance like a cute isometric adventure about a fox with a sword, but it is actually one of the most refined puzzle games of recent years. The player finds themselves in a world with no explanation, no tutorial, and text in an unknown language; instead of a tutorial, you collect pages of the game's manual, one by one, in the style of the paper booklets bundled with console games of the eighties and nineties. Each page you find reveals a piece of the map, describes a mechanic, or shows a note scrawled in the margin, and only by gradually piecing these fragments together does the player understand what they can actually do and where to go.

Combat is straightforward, built on the tried-and-tested pattern of dodging, stamina, and timed strikes, and the difficulty can be eased in the settings for those who want to focus mainly on exploration. But the true core of the game lies elsewhere — in a masterfully designed world full of shortcuts, hidden paths, and optical illusions, where the isometric perspective itself becomes part of the puzzles. Many secrets are hidden in such a way that they cannot be found by searching for items, only by understanding the rules. Visually it's a clean, colorful, and legible environment that runs perfectly smoothly on Xbox Series X|S, accompanied by calm ambient music.

Reviews received the game enthusiastically, praising above all its courage to explain nothing and let players figure everything out for themselves. It appeared in numerous best-of-the-year lists and is often mentioned as a modern successor to the tradition of games where you keep your own notes. Today it stands as an ideal example of what a small team with one strong idea can achieve: a short, dense, and remarkably satisfying game whose greatest reward is the moment you finally realize what that strange manual page meant. That very feeling of personal discovery cannot be repeated, which is why Tunic tends to be discussed among players in hints rather than concrete walkthroughs. Anyone who wants to try, on Series X|S, a game that trusts the player's curiosity should approach it without reading anything beforehand.
xbox-series__tunic.teaser: A cute fox adventure hides one of the most refined puzzle games of recent times.

xbox-series__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-1-2.article:
**Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 1 + 2** is a remake of two skateboarding classics from the turn of the millennium that kept their controls intact while reworking everything else. The original tracks — from the warehouse through the school grounds to the mall — were rebuilt with modern graphics, but their layout stayed faithful to the original to the point that players with a memory of the era can find secret stashes blindfolded. Each level's objectives are completed in two-minute runs: collect letters, reach a target score, smash objects, or pull off a specific trick at a designated spot.

The centerpiece is the combo trick system, in which grinds, manuals, and spins link together into long chains, with the value of individual elements growing with combo length. The controls are responsive yet fair — with a bit of practice you can clear an entire level in a single unbroken run, an experience that keeps drawing people back to this series. On Xbox Series X|S, the current-gen version runs in high resolution with a 120-frames-per-second target, which genuinely helps a game built on precise timing. There's also a custom skatepark editor and character creation.

The soundtrack has always been a core part of the series' identity, and here too it combines original tracks from the late nineties with newer additions, so punk and hip hop keep the original's character alive. Reception was very favorable, and the game is often cited as an example of a remake done right: it respects the original feel of skating and adds only what helps. Today it remains the best way to relive an era when skateboarding games were among the most popular sports titles of all — and at the same time a fully functional modern arcade game you can play for ten minutes or entire evenings. The short length of individual runs makes it an ideal pass-the-controller game for two on a single console, competing for the highest score, with every failed attempt tempting you to try again. A collection of challenges, unlockable riders, and gear adds plenty of reasons to keep coming back even after finishing the main career, since perfecting a run through a track can be polished practically forever.
xbox-series__tony-hawk-s-pro-skater-1-2.teaser: A remake of two skateboarding classics with the same controls and faithfully rebuilt tracks.

xbox-series__riders-republic.article:
**Riders Republic** combines mountain bikes, skis, snowboards, jetpacks, and wingsuits into a single open world assembled from landscapes inspired by American national parks. Switching between disciplines is instant: a player can ride a bike down a forest trail, switch to a wingsuit with a single press to glide over a valley, then land in the snow and continue on skis. This fluidity is the game's main strength and sets it apart from earlier titles focused on a single discipline. The structure is built around a career divided by sport, races, trick challenges, and collecting gear that changes how you ride.

The world is persistently online and populated with other players, whose ghosts ride past you, and the main social attraction is mass races that, on Xbox Series X|S, can involve a large number of riders simultaneously. The start of such a race, with the whole field hurtling down a slope and weaving between trees, is one of the most fun moments in the game. The current-gen console ensures smooth performance and fast loading when moving across the map, which helps a lot in a game that invites constant experimentation. Visually, the environments lean on striking long-distance views, snowy peaks, and desert canyons.

Reception was largely favorable, with praise going to the variety of disciplines, the sense of speed, and the cleverly handled mass races, while criticism targeted the loose tone with a somewhat overbearing guide character and the amount of in-game store elements. In the extreme sports genre, it's one of the few current offerings with this kind of scope. Today it works best in company — the solo career offers plenty of content, but the game truly comes into its own the moment dozens of other riders show up at the start and you try to weave through the chaos to the finish. It also helps that the game never punishes you for crashing: rewinding is instant and you can retry without waiting, which keeps the pace up even on demanding tracks. For Series X|S owners, it's one of the few ways to ride a bike and ski in the same open world, and that alone remains a good reason to give it a chance.
xbox-series__riders-republic.teaser: Bikes, skis, wingsuits, and jet packs in one world with instant switching between disciplines.

switch-2__mario-kart-world.article:
**Mario Kart World** arrived on the exact launch day of the Nintendo Switch 2 in June 2025 and became the title most players picture when they think of the new console. This time, Nintendo didn't just link the individual tracks through a menu screen — it set them into a single continuous map that can be freely driven across. Highways, country roads, beaches, and snowy slopes connect the circuits, the racing field has grown to twenty-four drivers, and the classic cups are joined by an elimination Knockout Tour, where the last racers drop out at every checkpoint. The free-roam mode functions as a huge playground full of tasks, hidden panels, and collectibles, rewarding even players who just want to wander the landscape.

The driving model still feels distinctly Mario Kart, but a layer of acrobatics has been added. The kart can climb onto railings and grind along them, bounce off walls, chain jumps across bodies of water, and maintain speed even off the marked track. Items keep the familiar rubber-banding logic, but there are now foods that change the characters' outfits, along with changeable weather and a day cycle, so the same track looks a little different at dusk and in the rain each time. The online component is built around large races with twenty-four players and randomly assembled routes, split-screen for local play has been kept, and you can even race two-to-a-kart as a crew.

Technically, it's a showcase for the new console: the game runs on TV in high resolution and smooth frame rates, supports a high-refresh-rate mode, and loading between areas is practically invisible thanks to faster storage. The music relies on live-recorded big-band arrangements that change with the environment, giving the whole game a surprisingly cinematic feel. Reception was very positive, though some players argued over the price and how much the open world changes the pacing of the classic cups. Today, Mario Kart World stands as the series' most ambitious entry and a game that's just as fun in short races as during an hour of aimless wandering.
switch-2__mario-kart-world.teaser: The Switch 2 launch title that for the first time connected all the tracks into one continuous map.

switch-2__donkey-kong-bananza.article:
**Donkey Kong Bananza** launched in July 2025 as the first major three-dimensional Donkey Kong adventure in many years, and at the same time as a title showing what the Switch 2 can do beyond the original console. The core idea is simple and immensely satisfying: almost the entire world is destructible. The landscape is built from small blocks that can be smashed with your fists, torn apart piece by piece, and thrown at enemies, so the player carves a path literally through the terrain instead of following a pre-set route. If you suspect a hidden cavity somewhere, you simply dig into the ground and find out.

The story leads Donkey Kong ever deeper below the surface, through a series of underground layers, each with its own theme, inhabitants, and visual style. He's accompanied by Pauline, appearing as a young girl whose singing triggers transformations called Bananza, turning the hero into, say, a much stronger crusher or a nimble runner, with each form opening up a different path through the level. Collecting gold and crystals funds ability upgrades, side challenges offer time trials and arena battles, and a second player can join as Pauline, providing support from a distance. The combination of destruction and free exploration creates a loop reminiscent of Super Mario Odyssey transposed into dirt and rock.

Technically it's a demanding feat: the game must constantly recalculate the broken terrain, yet it maintains smooth performance and offers lighting and shadows that suit the underground caves remarkably well. The soundtrack alternates between percussive and orchestral motifs and songs that Pauline sings live during the action, giving the game an unexpectedly powerful atmosphere. Critics and players alike embraced the title very warmly and often called it the best reason to get the new console right in its first year. Even in hindsight, Bananza stands out as one of the few games to bring a genuinely fresh perspective to the 3D platformer, since here the levels aren't a given layout but raw material to be reshaped.
switch-2__donkey-kong-bananza.teaser: Donkey Kong's first big 3D adventure in years; almost the entire world can be smashed to pieces.

switch-2__nintendo-switch-2-welcome-tour.article:
**Nintendo Switch 2 Welcome Tour** is a peculiar hybrid between a tech demo and an interactive museum that launched alongside the console itself in June 2025. The player moves around a giant model of the Switch 2 itself, walking across its body as if across an exhibition floor, gradually discovering stops dedicated to specific components. Each station offers either a short minigame, a quiz, or a hands-on demonstration showing what a given feature can do and why it was designed that way. The whole thing feels like a guided tour, except here you're allowed to touch most of the exhibits.

The content consists of tasks built around the new controllers and display. One set tests the mouse mode of the Joy-Con 2, another the precision of the motion sensors, another shows the difference between various refresh rates, dynamic image range, or spatial audio. There are also simple reflex tests, small puzzles, and collectible medals for completed challenges, so the whole thing works as a light reward loop for those who want to complete everything at one hundred percent. Most of the content can be finished within a few hours, part of the stops are designed for two players on one console, and a few tasks require a connected camera or docked mode.

Technically, it's more of a showcase than a game: the presentation is clean, clear, and deliberately sparing with effects, since the goal is to show off the hardware's qualities rather than dazzle. The music is understated, electronic, and stays in the background as accompaniment in an exhibition hall. Reception was mixed, mainly because Nintendo sold the title separately instead of bundling it with the console; many players found that an odd choice for content of this kind. The content itself, though, was mostly rated as likable and informative. Today, Welcome Tour mainly stands as a period document of the Switch 2's first year and as a pleasant hour for anyone curious about how the console works inside and what the new controllers can do.
switch-2__nintendo-switch-2-welcome-tour.teaser: An interactive museum inside a giant console mock-up; minigames explain how Switch 2 works.

switch-2__legend-of-zelda-breath-of-wild.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition** is an enhanced version of one of the most influential games of the past decade, released alongside the launch of the new console in June 2025. The foundation remains untouched: Link wakes up in a devastated Hyrule with no memory, receives a tablet with a handful of abilities, and then it's entirely up to him where he goes. The world isn't divided into levels or locked chapters; instead it offers one enormous, continuous landscape that can be explored in any order, with physical and chemical rules that apply everywhere the same way.

The gameplay loop rests on curiosity and improvisation. The player climbs a tower, looks around, spots something on the horizon, and heads there; along the way they run into shrines with logic puzzles, enemy camps, cooking ingredients, or one of the four great Divine Beasts. Weapons break, forcing constant tactical changes, heat and cold require the right clothing and food, and the paraglider turns every hill into a launch pad. This very freedom is what made Breath of the Wild the yardstick against which the entire open-world category has been measured since 2017, and its influence shows even in games that have nothing to do with Nintendo.

The Switch 2 version brings higher resolution, steadier frame rates, and HDR support, which helps most with the sprawling vistas and dusk scenes where the original release sometimes lost its breath. The addition is a connection to the mobile Zelda Notes app, which can guide players toward objectives, share progress, and offer companion features away from the console screen. Owners of the original game could purchase a paid upgrade, and the title also came out in a separate boxed edition. Reception was, understandably, very positive, since this is the technically best way to play Breath of the Wild. Even today the game holds up remarkably well, and for new players it remains the ideal entry point into the series' modern era.
switch-2__legend-of-zelda-breath-of-wild.teaser: An enhanced edition of one of the decade's most influential games, for the launch of the new console.

switch-2__legend-of-zelda-tears-of-kingd.article:
**The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition** accompanied the launch of the Nintendo Switch 2 in June 2025, offering the sequel to Breath of the Wild in a form that finally handles what the game demands from the hardware. Hyrule has grown to include floating islands high above the landscape and a vast dark underground beneath it, so the map now has several layers, and the player constantly falls between them, drops down, and climbs back up through gaps in the ceiling. The familiar landscape gains an entirely new dimension without losing its sense of homeliness.

The heart of the game lies in new abilities, above all Ultrahand and Fuse. The first lets you gather planks, wheels, fans, or rockets and build vehicles, bridges, and flying machines out of them; the second fuses a weapon with any object, turning it into something stronger or utterly absurd. The result is a game that allows dozens of solutions to every obstacle and rewards ingenuity rather than adherence to a script. On top of that comes a more expansive story split across four regions, substantial dungeons, and a denser web of side quests than its predecessor had.

That very freedom was technically very demanding on the original console, and the Switch 2 version makes the biggest difference here: higher resolution, smoother performance even as complex constructions collapse, shorter loading times, and HDR support. It also adds a link to the mobile Zelda Notes app, through which you can share your own inventions and download other players' solutions, which suits the game's community side very well. The music stays restrained and atmospheric, with piano motifs that surface more in the pauses than in the action. Reception was very good, and many players consider this version to be the definitive edition. Today it's one of the most substantial games available on the console and a great demonstration of what a playground built on physics can look like.
switch-2__legend-of-zelda-tears-of-kingd.teaser: The islands above Hyrule and the depths beneath it finally run the way the game always demanded.

switch-2__super-mario-party-jamboree-nin.article:
**Super Mario Party Jamboree – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Jamboree TV** took an already packed party board game and added a bundle of content that puts the new capabilities of the Switch 2 to use. The core remains classic: players take turns around the board, roll the dice, collect coins and stars, and between rounds a minigame decides who comes out ahead. There are several boards, each with its own rules and shortcuts, plus a huge collection of minigames ranging from pure reflex tests to genuinely tactical challenges where it pays to watch what everyone else is doing.

The new addition is a segment called Jamboree TV, which plays at being a television game show and leans on the console's peripherals. It uses the connected camera, so players appear directly in the game and some contests react to their movements and facial expressions, while another set of tasks relies on the Joy-Con 2's mouse mode and the microphone. The result is a set of disciplines built around drawing, waving, shouting, and cooperating in ways the previous entry never allowed. For playing with several people on one screen it's a welcome breath of fresh air, since the fun comes as much from what happens on the TV as from what happens in the living room.

Technically, this version benefits from higher resolution and smoother performance, shorter loading times between minigames, and a stable online mode offering both casual matches and seasonal challenges with rewards. Visually it's the typically brisk, colorful Nintendo style, and the music is cheerful, poppy, and easy to get stuck in your head. Reception was largely positive, with praise for just how much new content there is and for the camera-based contests being a welcome addition, even if not everyone is thrilled about having a camera next to the console. Today it's a clear pick for family gaming nights and get-togethers, since anyone can grasp the rules within the first round, and a session can be set to last twenty minutes or an entire evening.
switch-2__super-mario-party-jamboree-nin.teaser: A packed party board game expanded with Jamboree TV and the new console's features.

switch-2__kirby-and-forgotten-land-ninte.article:
**Kirby and the Forgotten Land: Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Star-Crossed World** is the expanded release of the pink hero's first fully three-dimensional adventure, which came to Switch 2 in 2025. The original game placed Kirby in an abandoned world where nature is overtaking shopping malls, factories, and amusement parks, pairing a melancholy backdrop with utterly carefree gameplay. Kirby inhales enemies, takes on their abilities, and moves through compact levels full of hidden paths and captive Waddle Dees, who gradually bring back to life the small town serving as a hub between worlds.

The biggest draw remains the mechanic where Kirby puts on an entire object from the environment — a car, a giant traffic cone, a vending machine — and it temporarily turns into a completely different game. Add to that upgradeable abilities, arena challenges, and bosses that hit exactly the right difficulty level for family play. The Switch 2 release adds an entirely new story branch called Star-Crossed World, with additional levels, new ability variants, and content aimed at players who already know the original — so this is far more than a cosmetic touch-up of an old game.

Technically the title has moved up to higher resolution and smoother framerates, which especially benefits fast combat and scenes packed with effects. Loading is quick, and the two-player, single-screen mode has been kept. The music ranks among the series' best, alternating brisk drum-driven themes with wistfully beautiful melodies, and building into big orchestral peaks during boss fights. Reception was very positive even for the original version, and the expanded release has only cemented its reputation. Today it's an ideal game for anyone looking for an accessible yet inventive platformer that both children and adults can enjoy, and one that surprisingly works well as a relaxed evening game after work too.
switch-2__kirby-and-forgotten-land-ninte.teaser: An expanded edition of the first 3D Kirby, set in a melancholic world overgrown with nature.

switch-2__metroid-prime-4-beyond.article:
**Metroid Prime 4: Beyond** ended one of the longest waits in gaming history when it launched in late 2025 simultaneously for Switch and Switch 2. After the restart, development returned to Retro Studios, the team that originally created the Prime series, and the result stays very faithful to their work. Samus Aran once again moves through a first-person perspective, but this isn't a classic shooter: a substantial part of the game involves scanning the environment, reading logs, finding routes through an interconnected map, and gradually unlocking areas you'd merely passed through before.

The new addition is a psionic component. Samus gains abilities that let her influence objects from a distance, solve puzzles, and switch between shooting and manipulating her surroundings during combat, adding another layer to the series' classic room design. Boss fights remain a ritual of finding the weak point and the right moment, environments often loop back on themselves, and the reward for exploration is a new ability rather than just a stronger weapon. On Switch 2 the game can also be controlled using mouse mode, which sharpens aiming considerably and is a very welcome option for players used to a keyboard and mouse.

Technically, the new console offers a noticeably richer version: higher resolution, the option to play at an increased refresh rate, and steadier performance than on the original hardware. The atmosphere rests on solitude and silence broken only by ambient sounds, with the music working through ambient textures that only fully open up in the most intense moments — exactly as the Prime series has done from the start. Reception was positive, and most players appreciated that the game didn't try to modernize everything at any cost. Today Beyond feels like a reminder that first-person exploration action still has plenty to offer, even though the market has long since stopped treating it as mainstream and few similar titles get made anymore. It's also a good entry point for newcomers to the series, since the story doesn't require knowledge of earlier installments.
switch-2__metroid-prime-4-beyond.teaser: The end of the longest wait in the gaming industry; Retro Studios brings Samus faithfully back to the series.

switch-2__pokemon-legends-z.article:
**Pokémon Legends: Z-A** launched in autumn 2025, continuing the experimental line Game Freak began with Legends: Arceus. This time, though, the destination isn't the wilderness but a city. The entire game takes place in Lumiose City, the metropolis from the Kalos region, which is undergoing a massive redevelopment and gradually creating green zones where Pokémon live right among the buildings. The city serves as a single connected map that changes as the story progresses, opening new districts and filling up with more residents and wild species.

The key change is real-time combat. Instead of taking turns, the player moves around the arena, dodges attacks, keeps track of each ability's cooldown, and makes decisions based on distance and direction, turning the classic type system into a much more active affair. Catching happens directly in the world without switching to a separate screen, so it blends smoothly with exploration. At night, the city turns into the Z-A Royale competition, where the player fights their way up a ladder against other trainers, and Mega Evolution returns, functioning in battle as a time-limited trump card.

The game launched in a version for the original Switch as well as a Switch 2 edition, which brings higher resolution and smoother performance — a significant help for a densely built city full of characters. Visually it goes for a clean, mildly stylized take on Lumiose with striking night scenes and street lighting, and the music is calmer and urban, with jazz elements that suit the backdrop of cafés and boulevards. Reception was more mixed than for most entries in the series: the combat system's boldness was praised, while criticism targeted the base version's technical side and the decision to confine the whole game to a single city. Today it's an interesting detour for the series, worth attention especially for players who already found turn-based battles a bit too static. For the series, it's also an important experiment in figuring out where the main Pokémon line might head in the years ahead.
switch-2__pokemon-legends-z.teaser: The open world of Legends: Arceus, moved from the wilderness into a single city full of green zones.

switch-2__hyrule-warriors-age-of-impriso.article:
**Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment** launched in autumn 2025 exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2, marking the third meeting between the world of Zelda and the combat system known from musou-style games. This time the story reaches deep into Hyrule's past, into a period that Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom only hinted at, placing Princess Zelda at its center. The player thus goes through a war whose outcome they already know, watching how it actually came to be — which gives the whole campaign a surprisingly strong tragic undertone.

The gameplay is built around massive battles where hundreds of enemies face the player at once. Maps are divided into forts and points that need to be captured and defended, orders and crises keep arriving that demand a response, and in between, rapid combos, special abilities, and powerful finishing blows chain together. Each playable character has their own style and set of skills; between missions, abilities are upgraded, weapons are forged, and side quests are completed on the strategic map. The series thus keeps its main strength: the feeling of overwhelming power paired with a clear tactical layer that hovers over everything the whole time.

Because this is a title made exclusively for the new console, the game maintains smooth performance even when the screen is literally flooded with enemies, and it offers a cleaner image and a longer view distance than the series' older entries on the original hardware. Visually it follows the stylization of modern Zelda games, and the music reworks familiar themes into battle-ready orchestral arrangements. Reception was largely positive, with the story noted as more interesting for fans of the newer entries than in previous spin-offs. Today it's a good choice for players who want an action-focused companion to the big Zelda games and don't mind the repeating battle structure characteristic of the genre. It's also one of the few titles that launched only on Switch 2 without needing to accommodate older hardware.
switch-2__hyrule-warriors-age-of-impriso.teaser: Musou battles from Hyrule's distant past, this time with Princess Zelda in the lead role.

switch-2__kirby-air-riders.article:
**Kirby Air Riders** arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 at the end of 2025 as the long-awaited sequel to the quirky racing game from the GameCube era. It's led by Masahiro Sakurai, creator of the original Kirby Air Ride, and the project keeps its core idea intact: controls are deliberately stripped down to a minimum. The vehicle accelerates on its own, a single button handles braking and charging a boost through corners, so anyone can grasp the basics within seconds — yet truly mastering the tracks takes much longer, and the gap between players becomes obvious quickly.

Alongside classic races, the biggest draw is a mode where players first roam a sprawling area together, collecting upgrades for speed, handling, or defense, searching for hidden vehicles, and reacting to random events, before a final event kicks off whose objective they don't know in advance. This creates tension between investing time in exploration or keeping an eye on rivals, and every match plays out differently. Add to that a wide range of vehicles with very different characteristics, playable characters from the Kirby universe, and abilities taken from enemies mid-race.

Technically the game leans on clean, vividly colorful graphics and, above all, very smooth performance, which is absolutely essential for a title built around precisely judging turns. The online mode allows matches with multiple players, and local split-screen play is also supported. The music reworks classic Kirby themes and delivers surprisingly strong orchestral and rock moments. Reception was positive, with particular praise for the unusual variety of modes and for the game keeping its distinct identity instead of conforming to the standard racing template. Today it's a title that shines brightest in a group around a single console, since its simple rules let even people who otherwise avoid racing games join in.
switch-2__kirby-air-riders.teaser: Sakurai's sequel to Kirby Air Ride, with deliberately simplified, accessible controls.

switch-2__drag-x-drive.article:
**Drag x Drive** is the most unusual of Nintendo's first in-house games for Switch 2, launching in August 2025 as a purely digital title. It's a sports game featuring wheelchair basketball played in three-on-three teams, though the main draw isn't so much the sport itself as the control scheme. Both Joy-Con 2 controllers are set down on a table and used in mouse mode, so each hand corresponds to one wheel. Moving forward requires pushing both together, turning uses just one, and a sharp spin comes from moving them in opposite directions — so play physically mimics actually spinning wheels.

Getting used to it takes a while, and that's exactly where the charm lies. The first few minutes are clumsy; after an hour, a player can smoothly change direction, build up speed before a ramp jump, block opponents, and land shots with demanding timing. Matches are short, arenas include ramps and obstacles that push the sport from realistic toward arcade, and there are training challenges and smaller single-player events on offer as well. The real focus, though, is online play and the fast exchange of the ball among three teammates, where the difference between a beginner and someone who's already got a feel for the controls shows the most.

Visually the game goes for a clean, modern, mildly graffiti-inspired style with bold colors and a simple environment that doesn't distract. Performance is very smooth, which is essential given controls that depend on precisely reading hand movement. The music is upbeat, electronic, and keeps pace with the match. Reception was mixed: praise went to how inventively the game uses the new controllers, while criticism targeted the modest amount of content and the fact that it plays poorly without a suitable flat surface under your hands. Today Drag x Drive is more of an interesting experiment than a major title, but as a demonstration of what Joy-Con 2 can really do, it stands alone on the console. It's worth trying especially when you have two friends on hand and the appetite to learn something completely different from scratch.
switch-2__drag-x-drive.teaser: 3-on-3 wheelchair basketball controlled with the Joy-Con 2 controllers laid on a table like mice.

switch-2__super-mario-galaxy-1-2.article:
**Super Mario Galaxy 1 + 2** brought, in autumn 2025, a pair of games that rank among the best three-dimensional platformers ever made, bundled together in a single package for both Switch and Switch 2. Originally Wii titles, their central idea remains just as impressive as on first release: each level is built from small planetoids with their own gravity, so Mario orbits around a sphere, jumping from one side to the other, and what was up a moment ago suddenly becomes down. Spatial orientation itself becomes a gameplay discipline in its own right.

The first game builds around an observatory as a central hub and large galaxies with stars that open up gradually; the second swaps the sprawling environment for a tighter map, adds Yoshi with his own abilities, sharper difficulty, and even wilder ideas for level design. Together, both games display an extraordinary density of invention, where a given mechanic often appears in just a single level and never returns. Controls have been adapted for modern controllers, star-aiming works through motion sensors or mouse mode on Switch 2, and added assist settings let less experienced players enjoy the game too.

The technical port benefits from higher resolution and smooth performance, which lets the visual style — always built more on cleanliness and color than fine detail — really shine. The strongest weapon remains the music: fully orchestral scores that were a novelty for the Mario series back in 2007 and remain among the most-played pieces of game music of all time to this day. Reception of the collection was very positive, with reservations aimed more at the scope of the accompanying content than at the games themselves. Today it's one of the best ways to experience a classic that, in its influence on the genre and its eye for detail, still outpaces most current output. For many players, it's also the very first chance to play both games without having to hunt down an old console.
switch-2__super-mario-galaxy-1-2.teaser: The pair of Wii classics with planetoid gravity ranks among the peaks of 3D platforming ever.

switch-2__fast-fusion.article:
**Fast Fusion** was among the games available right at the launch of the Nintendo Switch 2 in June 2025, and it quickly earned a reputation as a title that squeezes more out of the new console than you'd expect from a small studio game. It's an anti-gravity racer in the spirit of futuristic classics, where vehicles glide a few centimeters above the track, speeds are extreme, and every turn demands precise timing. The Fast series, which Shin'en Multimedia had already been developing on previous Nintendo consoles, gets its fastest and best-looking entry here.

The key mechanic remains switching your vehicle's color. The track is dotted with boost panels in two colors, and you only gain a boost when your craft's color matches the panel; otherwise you slow down instead. During a race you're constantly toggling colors while also trying to hold your line, which creates extra tension on top of the usual fight for position. A new feature hinted at in the title itself is the ability to fuse vehicles, creating machines with the properties of both, so players gradually build their own set of specialists for different track types. Modes include cups, time trials, a strictly ranked hero variant, and local split-screen.

Technically, it's one of the cleanest showcases of the new hardware among the launch titles: high resolution, very smooth performance, and striking lighting on tracks running through deserts, glaciers, and futuristic cities. The music is electronic, hard-hitting, and keeps the tempo pushing forward almost nonstop. Reception was positive, with praise going mainly to the technical execution and the friendly price, while criticism pointed to a more modest scope compared to the big racing franchises. Today Fast Fusion is an ideal pick for anyone who wants pure speed after just a few minutes of play with no drawn-out setup, and who misses classic futuristic racers. As a launch title, it also served well to let new console owners immediately test what the hardware could do.
switch-2__fast-fusion.teaser: Anti-gravity racing from Shin'en that squeezes more out of the small studio than you'd expect.

switch-2__cyberpunk-2077-ultimate-editio.article:
**Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition** arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 right on the console's launch day, becoming a symbol of Nintendo's return, after years, to a platform where the big Western blockbusters land. The player takes on the role of V, a mercenary with no past and no guaranteed future, who gets tangled up in a heist for a biochip carrying the digitized personality of the legendary rocker Johnny Silverhand in the megalopolis of Night City. Silverhand settles into V's head and slowly begins overwriting it, which is both the plot and a ticking clock that gives the whole story its urgency. It plays as a first-person shooter with a deep RPG layer on top: you allocate attributes, assemble cybernetic implants, and for every job choose between a loud solution with a shotgun or a silent infiltration through hacked cameras and security turrets. The package also includes the Phantom Liberty expansion, a spy thriller set in the sealed-off district of Dogtown.

The Switch 2 version is particularly interesting from a technical standpoint. Night City is one of the most demanding cities video games have ever built, and porting it to a handheld console showcased what the new hardware can do combined with modern image upscaling. The game offers separate modes for docked and handheld play, gyroscopic aiming support, and Joy-Con mouse-mode controls that surprisingly suit the shootouts well. The atmosphere remains untouched: rainy neon streets, ads flickering through the night, radio stations with their own playlists, and a synth soundtrack that holds the city together better than its corporations do.

Cyberpunk 2077 famously had a troubled launch in 2020 and spent the following years on extensive fixes and an overhaul of its systems. That's exactly why its later release feels like a rehabilitation: a game players initially wrote off became the most-cited example of long-term care for a title actually paying off. Today it's one of the most expansive RPGs you can play on Switch 2, and also a reminder that cyberpunk was never just about neon, but about the people trying to survive in it.
switch-2__cyberpunk-2077-ultimate-editio.teaser: The complete Night City with V and Johnny Silverhand arrived on Switch 2 right at launch.

switch-2__street-fighter-6.article:
**Street Fighter 6** was among the most anticipated third-party titles at the Nintendo Switch 2 launch, and it brought something fairly significant with it: a serious tournament-grade fighting game on a Nintendo console that doesn't need to compromise on input response. Capcom built the sixth entry around the Drive Gauge, a meter that fuels several offensive and defensive techniques at once. You can spend it on enhanced attacks, parries, canceling animations, or an escape move, but once it's depleted, your character enters a state of significant weakness. That gives every match its own risk economy, one that rewards boldness and punishes waste. Alongside the classic arcade and online modes, the game offers the sprawling World Tour story mode, where you create your own fighter, walk around cities, learn techniques from masters, and complete quests.

The Switch 2 version benefits from the more powerful hardware and from the console's ability to run the game smoothly even in handheld mode, which matters a great deal in a genre built on precise timing. Capcom also added Joy-Con motion controls, where punches and kicks correspond to gestures; it's more of a fun curiosity for a shared evening than a tournament tool, but it captures the spirit of the platform well. Visually, the game leans on a bold painterly style, with brush-stroke effects accompanying every heavy hit. The soundtrack mixes electronic music, hip hop, and orchestral motifs, giving each character its own musical signature.

Reception after release was very warm, and the game quickly established itself as a pillar of the tournament scene. A major factor was the modernized control schemes, which simplify inputting special moves and open the genre up to people without years of training, along with solid online infrastructure. For Switch 2, that means the console offers a full-fledged entry point into a genre that often stayed in a simplified form on previous Nintendo hardware. Today Street Fighter 6 is the best place to learn fighting games from the ground up, and also a title that will last for hundreds of hours.
switch-2__street-fighter-6.teaser: A serious tournament fighter with the Drive Gauge system, with no compromises on response speed.

switch-2__split-fiction.article:
**Split Fiction** is Hazelight's next step on its path toward cooperative games that simply can't be played solo, and it arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 practically on the console's launch day. The story follows two writers, Mio and Zoe, who find themselves trapped inside a simulation of their own unfinished manuscripts. One writes dark sci-fi, the other whimsical fantasy, and the game constantly switches between the two worlds, so you fall from a cyberpunk metropolis into a dragon's cave and then back among spaceships. The whole game runs on split screen, where each player sees her own half, and a lot of situations hinge on the fact that both sides are looking at something different and have to describe it out loud.

The mechanics change practically every few minutes. One moment you're controlling a character with a whip while the other has a gravity ability, then it turns into a precise platformer, and moments later there's a fight against a giant boss where each player attacks from a different angle. Hazelight has also tucked a large number of optional side stories into the game, which are the wildest part of the whole package in terms of ideas and often change genre entirely, from racing to parodies of other games. In Switch 2's favor is the fact that the console handles split screen smoothly, plus the option of shared play across two consoles over the network. The game also only sets you back a few seconds after any failure, so you never end up with one weaker player holding the other back.

The game received a very strong reception and was widely called one of the highlights of 2025, in part because it keeps up a constant stream of new ideas without ever repeating itself. It also continues the tradition Hazelight established with its earlier cooperative titles, including the system where a single purchased copy lets a second player join for free. Today Split Fiction feels like the ideal title for a pair who want to spend a weekend together in front of one console, and a reminder that cooperation doesn't have to mean two identical players sitting side by side.
switch-2__split-fiction.teaser: A co-op game from Hazelight that can't be played alone; sci-fi and fantasy worlds intertwine.

switch-2__yakuza-0-director-s-cut.article:
**Yakuza 0 Director's Cut** brought one of the highest-rated entries in the entire series to Nintendo Switch 2, in an expanded form with new scenes and added dubbing. The story is set at the end of the 1980s, during Japan's economic bubble, and follows two characters: young Kazuma Kiryu, accused of a murder he didn't commit, and Goro Majima, who runs a luxury cabaret while trying to atone for his past. Both storylines revolve around a single empty lot in Kamurocho that holds inestimable value for the warring clans, and they gradually weave together into a plot about betrayal, money, and power.

The gameplay rests on two pillars. The first is street brawling, where you switch between fighting styles with different pacing and reach, and where fights break out right among the bystanders getting in your way. The second is the city itself: a small but incredibly dense and detailed district full of arcades, karaoke bars, pubs, old Sega arcade machines, and dozens of side stories that swing between absurd humor and surprisingly touching endings. That contrast between hard-boiled gangster drama and bizarre street anecdotes is the series' signature trait and the reason it built such a devoted audience.

The Switch 2 version benefits from running smoothly even in handheld mode, which suits the side activities and short episodes remarkably well; you can easily settle in for one cabaret evening, a round of mahjong, or one bout in the arena and then close the console again. Both story lines also come with extensive management minigames, in which Kiryu manages real estate and Majima runs a business, and either one could stand on its own as a separate game. The 1980s atmosphere is carried by neon storefronts, period fashion, and a soundtrack mixing funk, rock, and disco. Thanks to its place at the start of the timeline, Yakuza 0 has long been recommended as the best entry point into the series, and that reputation holds to this day. On Switch 2, it stands as one of the most extensive and most characterful titles the console offered in its first year.
switch-2__yakuza-0-director-s-cut.teaser: One of the best-rated entries in the series, now in an expanded form as a Director's Cut.

switch-2__sonic-x-shadow-generations.article:
**Sonic X Shadow Generations** came to Nintendo Switch 2 among the first major third-party titles, and it effectively offers two games in one package. The first is a remake of Sonic Generations, in which classic Sonic from the days of two-dimensional games meets his more modern three-dimensional counterpart. Each stage therefore exists in two forms: one is a classic side-scrolling platformer emphasizing momentum and finding shortcuts, the other is a fast action ride behind the character, where you drift, boost, and dodge obstacles at the last moment. You revisit environments from various eras of the series, turning the game into a kind of tour of its own history.

The second part is an entirely new campaign starring Shadow. It plays differently: Shadow has access to abilities tied to controlling time and the so-called Doom Power, which lets him glide, slow down his surroundings, or pass through certain obstacles. The stages are built so these abilities gradually stack on top of one another, opening up previously inaccessible paths, and between them you move through a connected hub area. The narrative focuses on Shadow's past and is noticeably darker and more personal than the rest of the game, since it revisits the events that made him a character standing somewhere between hero and villain.

On Switch 2, the title benefits above all from the increased power, since a genre built on speed depends directly on smooth visuals, and every hitch immediately translates into a player mistake. Visually, it's a colorful, high-contrast spectacle, and the soundtrack mixes rock tracks with electronic music in the series' tradition. Reception was largely positive, with critics often highlighting Shadow's campaign as the strongest part of the package and as proof that Sonic Team can handle three-dimensional action well. Today it's one of the most accessible ways back into the series, and a title that works just as well for a short handheld session as it does on the big screen.
switch-2__sonic-x-shadow-generations.teaser: Two games in one: classic 2D Sonic and a modern 3D version in the Sonic Generations remake.

switch-2__bravely-default-flying-fairy-h.article:
**Bravely Default: Flying Fairy HD Remaster** brought one of the most beloved Japanese RPGs of the Nintendo 3DS era to Nintendo Switch 2, reworked for the big screen. The story follows a quartet of heroes led by the young Tiz, whose village is swallowed by a chasm, and Agnès, a seer trying to restore the four crystals that keep the world in balance. At first it plays like a very classic fantasy plot about a journey to restore order, but the game deliberately toys with player expectations, and in its second half it takes a turn that is still cited in the genre to this day.

Combat rests on the Brave and Default system the game is named after. Every character can borrow turns from the future and fire off several actions at once, or instead skip a turn, take a defensive stance, and save them up for later. That creates a tactical game about risk: an aggressive opening can end a battle before the opponent even attacks, but if it fails, you're left defenseless for several turns. On top of that comes an extensive job system, where every character combines a main profession with skills from another, giving enormous room for party building and for experimenting with combinations the game itself never spells out. It also includes building your own village, which grows in real time and rewards the player with equipment.

The remaster uses the Switch 2's power to make the originally hand-painted backgrounds and paper-styled scenery look crisp even at high resolution, and adds modern conveniences like speeding up battles or adjusting difficulty. The music, built on melodic orchestral and rock motifs, is among the most consistently praised parts of the whole game. At the time of its original release, the game was considered one of the titles that breathed new life into the classic turn-based RPG at a time when the genre seemed to be fading. The series built on that success with further entries, and its battle system became a model for a number of smaller studios. Today the HD version is the natural place to experience this story for the first time, and also a reason to return to it after all these years.
switch-2__bravely-default-flying-fairy-h.teaser: An HD remaster of the beloved 3DS-era JRPG about a quartet of heroes and the world's four crystals.

switch-2__survival-kids.article:
**Survival Kids** is one of the titles Konami prepared specifically for the Nintendo Switch 2 launch, and it also marks the return of a brand that originally began back in the days of handheld consoles with monochrome displays. The premise is simple: a group of kids is shipwrecked on an unknown island and has to make do with whatever they find. You gather wood, stones, leaves, and fruit, build shelters, start fires, craft tools, and gradually open up paths to further parts of the island that were initially inaccessible because you lacked the right tool or means of transport.

What matters is that the game is built from the ground up around cooperation. Most key points require two or more players to do something simultaneously or to hand off materials to each other, and many of the crafting activities take the form of simple shared minigames that require coordination. Konami made use of the GameShare feature, which lets people who don't own the game themselves join in, even from previous-generation consoles. That makes the title a practical demonstration of how Nintendo envisions shared play on the new platform. The controls are deliberately accessible, the game has no permanent death or harsh penalties, so it works for families with younger players too. Progress still requires planning, though, since the island's resources aren't infinite and some tools wear out.

Visually, it's a bright, cartoonishly stylized game with soft shapes and bold colors, accompanied by understated, pleasantly adventurous music. Reception was moderate: reviewers praised the concept, easy accessibility, and clever use of shared play, but also often noted that for more experienced survival fans, the game is fairly soft and short. That, however, is precisely the point. Survival Kids is a gateway into the genre for those put off by harsher titles, and one of the few social games you can play with kids without a long explanation of complicated systems. At the same time, it's a case of Konami reaching for a brand left unused for years and finding a meaningful place for it.
switch-2__survival-kids.teaser: The return of an old Konami franchise; a group of kids is shipwrecked on an island and must survive from scratch.

switch-2__hitman-world-of-assassination-.article:
**Hitman World of Assassination - Signature Edition** brought the fully modernized trilogy starring Agent 47 to Nintendo Switch 2 in a form that, on the previous console, existed only as a streamed version dependent on a connection. The core remains unchanged: you get a sprawling, densely populated map, one or more targets, and complete freedom in how you approach them. You can disguise yourself as a cook, a mechanic, or a guest, slip through a service entrance, poison a drink, drop a chandelier, or solve the whole situation from a distance with a sniper rifle. Every map is a clockwork machine that runs independently of you, and the game expects you to play it again and again until you grasp its rhythm.

That very replayability is why the title is so substantial. Each level offers dozens of story opportunities, challenges, and alternative ways to complete the job, on top of modes with randomized targets or contracts that players create themselves. Signature Edition pools maps from all three entries into a single menu, so you move from an Italian town to Miami, Mumbai, or an Austrian mountain clinic without switching games and without losing progress. Progression is also tracked across the entire trilogy, so unlocking gear makes sense regardless of which map you pick.

On Switch 2, the game benefits from running locally, free of dependence on connection quality. It also makes use of the Joy-Con's mouse mode, which noticeably sharpens aiming, and gyroscopic fine-tuning. The atmosphere rests on the contrast between elegant, quiet surroundings and the cold brutality of the craft, underscored by a minimalist orchestral soundtrack that swells the moment someone spots you. The series was widely praised after its 2016 reboot for returning to the principle of a playground rather than a corridor, and it became a benchmark for modern stealth. Today it's one of the most substantial and best-designed titles you can get on Switch 2.
switch-2__hitman-world-of-assassination-.teaser: The complete Agent 47 trilogy finally runs on Switch 2 without needing to stream.

switch-2__deltarune.article:
**Deltarune** arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 on launch day and brought with it the long-awaited continuation of chapters that had previously been released piecemeal and for free. The game is loosely connected to the same author's previous title, but takes place in its own world: the protagonist Kris and his classmate Susie fall into the Dark World, where they become the heroes foretold by prophecy, and together with Prince Ralsei set out to close a fountain threatening to flood reality with darkness. It may sound like ordinary fantasy, but the game very quickly makes clear it intends to do whatever it wants with genre conventions.

Battles combine a turn-based system with elements the genre doesn't usually have. On your turn, you pick actions like in a classic RPG; on the enemy's turn, the screen turns into a miniature action game where you dodge incoming projectiles with a heart. On top of that, most encounters can be resolved without violence: every opponent has their own way of being calmed, amused, or persuaded, and the game carefully remembers how you've behaved. Alongside this there's a great deal of puzzles, side characters, and scenes that shift from absurd comedy to unexpectedly heavy moments.

Technically the game is modest, built on pixel art and simple animation, but that's exactly what suits it on a handheld console and lets you play it in short bursts. Its real strength is the music: the author composes it himself, and individual motifs return in different arrangements to carry the emotion of a specific moment. Reception was extraordinarily warm, and the franchise has long maintained one of the most active fan communities around, which is remarkable for a project built around a single creator and a small team of collaborators. Today Deltarune is one of the few games that manage to be funny, playful, and unsettling all at once, and on Switch 2 it's one of the best reasons to take the console along on your travels.
switch-2__deltarune.teaser: Toby Fox's long-assembled chapters together at last; Kris and Susie fall into the Dark World.

switch-2__star-wars-outlaws.article:
**Star Wars Outlaws** is among the titles that arrived on Nintendo Switch 2 later than on other platforms, serving as proof that the console can handle even the sprawling open worlds of the current generation. You play as Kay Vess, a small-time thief from the galaxy's fringes trying to clear a debt to criminal syndicates while carving out her own place in the universe between the events of the fifth and sixth films. She's accompanied by her animal companion Nix, who isn't just for show: you send him to distract guards, steal items, or press distant switches, making him a full-fledged part of every plan.

The gameplay blends several genres. On planets you sneak through bases, bypass locks via simple minigames, and fight with a blaster; in cities you negotiate with factions and play the card game sabacc; and between worlds you fly your own ship, engaging in space combat. The key system is reputation with individual syndicates: helping one group automatically damages your standing with another, which changes prices, access to areas, and how characters on the street react to you. The game constantly forces you to choose whom it's worth being useful to, and no choice comes without consequences.

On Switch 2, the title benefits from modern image upscaling techniques, which help maintain detailed environments even in handheld mode. The visual style deliberately embraces the aesthetic of the original film trilogy — worn-out jumpsuits, analog instruments, and grimy hangars — and the orchestral score sticks to the series' familiar sound. Reception at original launch was more mixed; a frequent complaint targeted the stealth sections, which were initially too strict, and developers later adjusted them. Today Outlaws is interesting mainly because it finally offers Star Wars from the perspective of an insignificant smuggler on the galaxy's edge — a perspective fans had been asking for for decades, instead of yet another story about chosen knights. On Switch 2 it's also one of the technically most ambitious games you'll find here at all.
switch-2__star-wars-outlaws.teaser: An open world between the Empire and criminal syndicates; Kay Vess steals her way across the galaxy.

switch-2__sid-meier-s-civilization-vii.article:
**Sid Meier's Civilization VII** launched on Nintendo Switch 2 among the console's launch titles, bringing to the console a genre that has historically struggled to gel with a standard controller. The core remains: you found cities, research technologies, build wonders of the world, forge alliances, and wage wars, all in a turn-based mode where a single decision can affect the next several hundred turns. The biggest change from its predecessors is splitting a match into separate historical ages. At each turning point you choose which civilization your society adopts next, while the leader stays the same. The result is something like a cultural rebirth that prevents the late game from becoming mere mop-up of a match decided long ago.

The second major change concerns how cities work. They start as small settlements and only become full-fledged centers through a player's decision, forcing you to think about where development is actually needed and where the existing infrastructure is enough. Diplomacy has been simplified into a system where relations with other leaders are governed by concrete actions rather than a confusing list of modifiers. Military units can be merged into formations under a commander, simplifying movement across an entire continent and cutting down on the sluggishness of late-game turns that players had long complained about.

On Switch 2, controls are crucial. The game supports the touchscreen as well as the Joy-Con's mouse mode, by far the most comfortable ways to navigate the hexagonal map, and in handheld mode the game turns into something very close to a tablet version you can put down and pick back up at any time, exactly where you left off. Reception of the seventh installment was more divided than its predecessors; frequent criticism targeted the user interface at launch and how sharply the age-change system disrupted the habits of longtime players. Even so, Civilization remains one of the most influential strategy franchises ever, and on Switch 2 it offers the most dangerous sentence in gaming: just one more turn.
switch-2__sid-meier-s-civilization-vii.teaser: The famous turn-based empire-building strategy game, adapted for a console controller for the first time.

mega-cd__sonic-cd.article:
**Sonic CD** is the strangest and at the same time the most ambitious entry in the classic hedgehog series, and remains to this day the main reason to own a Mega-CD at all. Sonic chases Doctor Robotnik to the mysterious Little Planet, a small world that appears above a lake once a year and whose fate is tied to time stones. That's exactly where the game's central idea comes from: every level exists in four time layers. When Sonic builds up enough speed and runs through a sign marked past or future, he's transported to that same location's past or future, which has different graphics, different music, and differently arranged platforms.

The game therefore doesn't rely on speed alone but mainly on exploration. Your task is to find a hidden machine in the past that manufactures Robotnik's robots, destroy it, and thereby secure a good future for that zone. The levels are more intricate and much more vertical than in the Mega Drive entries, full of loops, tunnels, and hidden nooks where it pays to slow down and search thoroughly. New additions include the so-called super peel-out, a stationary run-up as an alternative to the classic spin dash, and above all Metal Sonic, who in one of the series' most famous sequences races the player at a brutal pace.

The game made use of the CD's capabilities mainly for an animated intro and ending sequence by Japanese animators, and for music played directly from the disc. There are two completely different soundtracks, Japanese and North American, and the argument over which is better still follows fans to this day; both, however, give the levels a very distinct mood, ranging from dreamy melodies to harsher, more rhythmic tones. At the time, the game felt like proof that a compact disc didn't have to mean just cutscenes but could also mean a genuinely rich action game. Today, thanks to later re-releases, Sonic CD is one of the few Mega-CD titles that's easy to access, and it's among the best-aging things the console ever released.
mega-cd__sonic-cd.teaser: The most ambitious Sonic ever; time layers turn every level into four different versions.

mega-cd__final-fight-cd.article:
**Final Fight CD** is a conversion of Capcom's famous arcade beat-'em-up, and for Mega-CD owners it represented one of the strongest arguments for buying the add-on at all. While the Super Nintendo version had to sacrifice an entire level and one of the playable characters due to cartridge capacity, and also lost two-player co-op, the Mega-CD port offers all three fighters — Haggar, Cody, and Guy — a complete set of levels, and above all two-player cooperation, which is absolutely essential in this genre.

The principle remains purely arcade: you fight your way through the streets of Metro City through crowds of the Mad Gear gang to rescue Haggar's daughter Jessica. Each character has a different balance of speed, reach, and power; you have throws, desperate special attacks paid for with a chunk of your own health, weapons picked up off the ground, and plenty of breakable crates and barrels hiding food. The design forces players to alternate between attacking and retreating and to keep enemies at a distance, since letting yourself get surrounded means a very quick end. There's also a time-attack mode added for quick replays, plus a difficulty selection. Co-op in particular changes the whole experience: two players can split up the crowd, pin an enemy between them, and pull the other out of an encirclement, so the game feels significantly more approachable played by two than as a solo run.

On a technical level, the port surprisingly nailed the balance between fidelity to the original and what the hardware could do. The characters are large, the animation is smooth, and the action keeps a decent pace, though purists point out small concessions in the number of enemies on screen compared to the arcade cabinet. Its biggest asset is the music from disc — arrangements of the arcade soundtrack that give the grimy streets a noticeably punchier mood — plus digitized voice clips and hit sounds. At the time, the port was praised as one of the best home versions of Final Fight ever, and it's still a great way to play this early-1990s genre the way it was meant to be played: with two players, and no compromises.
mega-cd__final-fight-cd.teaser: The most complete home version of Capcom's famous beat-'em-up, with all characters and levels.

mega-cd__ecco-dolphin.article:
**Ecco the Dolphin** is one of the most unusual games of its era, and it received its most beautiful form on the Mega-CD. You play a dolphin whose entire pod is swept away by a mysterious storm, and you set out after them across the ocean, through icy seas, sunken cities, and places far stranger than what you're used to. The whole game takes place underwater, and the controls reflect that: Ecco swims in every direction, accelerates with short bursts, leaps above the surface, and must constantly keep track of two things at once — dwindling health and, above all, dwindling breath.

The gameplay is built on exploration and problem-solving rather than combat. The essential tool is sonar, which the dolphin uses to map its surroundings, talk to other creatures, and activate ancient crystals; fish serve as an energy source, and narrow tunnels act as mazes where a single mistake means drowning. Moving forward often means figuring out where you can break through an ice floe or how to use a current. The game is notorious for its difficulty and unforgiving nature, but that's exactly why it rewards patient players with the feeling of genuinely getting to know an alien world. It also regularly changes its own rules, whether by leading the dolphin into frozen caves or sending it far outside the familiar ocean.

On Mega-CD, the version benefits especially from reworked graphics and, above all, from music played from disc, which is far more spacious, dreamlike, and at times unsettling compared to the original chip-based soundtrack. The underwater backdrops layer on top of each other, with shafts of sunlight breaking through and swaying seaweed creating an atmosphere that simply wasn't common on cartridge-based consoles. At the time, the game was seen as proof that Sega could do more than just fast mascots, and it earned a cult reputation it still holds today. A modern player has to get used to the slower pace and harsh punishment for mistakes, but the reward is one of the most powerful atmospheric experiences of the entire sixteen-bit era. Few games of that time managed to so convincingly evoke the feeling of moving through an environment where you don't belong.
mega-cd__ecco-dolphin.teaser: An unusual underwater odyssey of a dolphin searching for its lost pod; atmospheric and different.

mega-cd__silpheed.article:
**Silpheed** was a Mega-CD title that got shown off on in-store demo units specifically to sell the hardware. It's a rear-view, slightly overhead space shooter in which you pilot the SA-77 fighter against a giant enemy fleet. The core is purely arcade: you dodge waves of bullets, shoot down formations of fighters, and between missions choose a combination of weapons, ranging from a wide spread shot through homing missiles to a focused beam. Your weapon choice significantly changes the game's feel and is worth tuning based on where you tend to die most often.

The main draw is how the game looks. The backgrounds are pre-rendered polygonal videos played from disc, over which classic sprite-based ships move. The result is scenes where a giant battle cruiser rotates beneath you, debris flies past, or the surface of an enemy base opens up — a spectacle consoles of the time simply couldn't manage on their own. The trick has its limits, since what happens in the background is fixed and the player has no influence over it, but at the time it felt like a revelation. The game also pays attention to pacing: calmer stretches follow the more demanding raids, giving the player time to reposition and prepare for the next boss.

The sound matches the rest of the production: orchestrally styled CD music and voiced lines from a support operator that give the missions the feel of a serious military operation rather than the usual space-arcade tone. The game is fairly short, which only encourages replaying it for a better score and surviving without losing your ship. Reviewers at the time regularly ranked it among the best things released on Mega-CD, and as one of the few titles that truly used the disc's potential for something other than filmed cutscenes. Today Silpheed is mainly a great showcase of how inventively the limits of period hardware could be worked around. It's also one of the few shooters of its era worth returning to for the spectacle alone, not just for the score.
mega-cd__silpheed.teaser: A space shooter that Sega ran in stores just to sell the hardware.

mega-cd__popful-mail.article:
**Popful Mail** is a light-hearted action RPG with platforming roots, in which the elf bounty hunter Mail chases a fugitive criminal just to finally make the rent. What starts as an ordinary hunt for cash gradually blossoms into a bigger adventure involving ancient artifacts and a threat to the whole world, told with a wink and a steady stream of humor. Alongside Mail, two other playable characters take turns joining the story, each with a different reach and a different way of fighting, and the game regularly makes you switch between them depending on what's in front of you.

The gameplay combines running and jumping across two-dimensional levels with melee and ranged combat, gathering money, and shopping for better gear in towns. Enemies have readable behavior patterns, and boss fights are more about observation and timing than raw stats, so the game feels brisk even to someone who doesn't get along with classic turn-based Japanese RPGs. Progress across the map is linear but interspersed with conversations that give the characters a surprisingly well-written personality. The maps are also designed to reward curiosity; the main path often branches into short side corridors holding a weapon or a potion that comes in handy later.

The Mega-CD version leans on the disc mainly for voiced dialogue and for music that ranks among the more melodic ever heard on the console. The English localization is famous for its loose, witty translation and quality dubbing, which turns the whole game into something closer to an animated comedy than a serious fantasy. At the time it was a title released in North America in limited numbers and quickly became a collector's rarity. Today Popful Mail is a reminder that the Mega-CD wasn't just about full-motion video, but also about carefully crafted games that hold onto their pace and charm even after three decades. For fans of the Japanese action RPG, it's one of the most pleasant entry points into the genre, since it requires no knowledge of complicated rules or hours of tedious grinding.
mega-cd__popful-mail.teaser: A lighthearted action RPG from Falcom about an elven bounty hunter, full of humor and wit.

mega-cd__flashback.article:
**Flashback** is one of the high points of the so-called cinematic platformer, and on the Mega-CD it arrived in a version that benefits from the extra disc space. The player takes on the role of Conrad Hart, a man whose memory has been wiped and who wakes up in the jungle of the planet Titan with no idea who's after him. From there, the trail leads through an illegal television contest all the way to uncovering an alien infiltration, with the story unfolding through cutscenes that were unusually cinematic for their time.

The controls are deliberately clunky and precise at the same time. Conrad breaks into a run, carefully approaches the edge of a platform, grabs onto ledges, and above all takes cover around corners, from where he fires his blaster or drops force shields. Fights are short and lethal, so it pays to scope out a room before stepping into it. Besides shootouts, the game builds on finding cards, switches, and paths through the levels, so progress is as much about logic as it is about action. The character's rotoscoped animation gives movement a weight that platformers of the time usually lacked. It's precisely this combination of cautious movement and fast, hard-hitting gunfights that spawned an entire school of games still referenced today, from later platformers emphasizing physical believability of the character to modern indie titles.

The Mega-CD version adds disc-based music and voiced dialogue, which bring the cutscenes closer to an animated film; the core gameplay itself, on the other hand, stays the same as in the original releases. The atmosphere is cold, lonely, and slightly paranoid, wonderfully supported by the sterile station corridors and the nighttime streets of New Washington. At the time Flashback was very well received across platforms and became one of the best-selling French games ever. Today it will punish anyone who approaches it with reflexes learned from modern games, but whoever accepts its slower, cautious rhythm will find an extraordinarily stylish sci-fi experience that still holds up. The hand-drawn backgrounds, meanwhile, have aged far better than the early attempts at 3D graphics of the era.
mega-cd__flashback.teaser: The pinnacle of cinematic platformers; a man without memory flees across a conspiracy about an alien invasion.

mega-cd__heart-of-alien.article:
**Heart of the Alien** is a sequel to the legendary Another World and also one of the few games released exclusively for the Mega-CD. The key twist lies in the point of view: this time you don't control the human scientist Lester, but his alien companion Buddy, who carried the hero to safety in the first game.
