The story thus picks up exactly where the original left off and develops it from the other side, including a look at Buddy's own people and his standing among them.

The gameplay stays true to its predecessor. It's a cinematic platformer where a single wrong step means death and where you progress through trial and lesson learned. Buddy has no blaster; instead he uses a whip, which he uses to pull himself up, swing over chasms, and attack enemies. Action-heavy shootout situations alternate with sequences where you need to find the right sequence of steps, pull a lever, or run past a guard while he's looking away. The segments are short, the difficulty high, and frequent deaths are part of the design, so the game is driven more by memorization than reflexes. The whip itself controls with surprising precision, and the game wrings a whole range of different situations out of a single mechanic, from swinging over a chasm to yanking an opponent off a cliff.

Visually it follows the distinctive style of its predecessor: simple flat colors, sprawling backgrounds, and rotoscoped animation that gives the characters an unusual weight. The Mega-CD is used mainly for disc-based music and for longer, calmly paced cutscenes without a single line of dialogue. At the time the game met with some skepticism, since it was made by a different studio than the original and part of the audience didn't consider it an equal sequel. With hindsight, though, it's an interesting and honestly crafted coda to one of the most influential games of the nineties, one that deserves attention if only for how boldly it shifts perspective. For anyone who finished Another World and wanted to know what happened next, it's the only possible answer, and also one of the reasons collectors still hunt down the Mega-CD library today.
mega-cd__heart-of-alien.teaser: A sequel to the cult classic Another World, this time from the perspective of the alien companion Buddy.

mega-cd__earthworm-jim-special-edition.article:
**Earthworm Jim: Special Edition** is an expanded version of one of the most distinctive platformers of the mid-nineties, and on the Mega-CD it represents arguably its best incarnation. The hero is an ordinary earthworm who has a super-conductive space suit fall on him from the sky, instantly turning him into a hero with a gun, a sarcastic running commentary, and the ability to use his own body as a whip, a rope, or a helicopter. The goal is to rescue Princess Whats-Her-Name while blasting through a gallery of thoroughly warped enemies. The humor is carried mainly through visuals rather than text, so it works regardless of language.

At its core the game is a classic platformer, but almost every level invents its own rules. One moment you're falling through a sewer full of garbage, the next you're racing on a rocket, tearing through underground tunnels, or in one of the series' most famous sections, protecting a falling puppy by bouncing it back into the air. The shooting is precise, whipping your body works as both a rope and a weapon, and the game keeps thinking up new ways to catch you off guard. The difficulty is honestly old-school, especially in the boss fights, which demand learning their patterns. The game also plays with pacing: after a hectic action sequence there's often a calmer stretch where precise jumping matters more than shooting.

The Special Edition additionally adds the Big Bruty level, missing from the original Mega Drive release, and above all a completely rearranged soundtrack played from disc, with a much fuller sound than the chip-based version. The hand-drawn animation is still a feast for the eyes even after all these years; Jim stretches, twists, and reacts to his surroundings in a way that inspired plenty of other games at the time. Back then it was a title that became the mascot of an entire wave of cheeky cartoon platformers. Today it remains an excellent showcase of the genre, only be prepared that it won't go easy on you. Especially in this version, though, it stands as one of the best-looking and best-sounding platformers of its entire generation.
mega-cd__earthworm-jim-special-edition.teaser: An expanded and probably the best version of the crazy platformer about an earthworm in a super-suit.

mega-cd__keio-flying-squadron.article:
**Keio Flying Squadron** is a horizontal shoot-'em-up that sets itself apart from most of the competition by not taking itself seriously at all. The heroine is a girl named Rami, heir to a line of guardians, who sets out in a rabbit costume on the back of a flying dragon to recover an ancient scroll stolen by a raccoon-dog villain. The whole thing is thoroughly Japanese, cute, and deliberately over the top, including anime cutscenes that tell the story between stages and are one of the main reasons the game ended up on disc in the first place. It emerged during a period when Japanese publishers were experimenting with how much animation could fit into a game, and this title is one of the ones where it actually blended well with the gameplay.

The gameplay itself is classic and highly readable. Rami shoots forward, collects power-ups that boost her attack, and is accompanied by a helper unit that can be positioned above or below the dragon. Enemy formations arrive in carefully designed waves, and the game relies more on a pleasant pace and inventive boss fights than on dense bullet curtains, making it accessible even to players who normally avoid the genre. The difficulty is well balanced and the game isn't very long, which only makes it more tempting to replay. Collected items also change the helper's behavior, so even subsequent playthroughs offer a slightly different style of play.

Graphically it's among the more colorful releases on the Mega-CD. The backgrounds are full of detail and amusing little touches, enemy animations have a cartoonish energy, and transitions between stages are accompanied by disc-based music with a strongly orchestral, at times almost folk-inflected feel. The anime cutscenes are fully voiced and at the time served as proof that CD could also be used to let a game tell its story with a sense of humor. In Europe the game was released in limited numbers and is now a sought-after collector's item. Anyone who gets their hands on it will find an undemanding, charming shooter with more personality than most far more famous titles. That personality is exactly what still keeps its value well above the genre average, even today.
mega-cd__keio-flying-squadron.teaser: A cute, deliberately over-the-top Japanese shooter with a girl riding on the back of a flying dragon.

mega-cd__robo-aleste.article:
**Robo Aleste** is a vertical shoot-'em-up from Compile, the studio that built the Aleste series' reputation as one of the most reliable brands of the genre on Sega consoles. This particular entry chose an unusual setting: the story unfolds in an alternate feudal Japan, where warring clans control giant war machines. The player pilots one of them, blasting through burning villages, castle courtyards, and flying fortresses, all of which give the game a flavor rarely seen in a genre dominated by outer space. Between missions, a story about betrayal within the clan also develops, giving the whole campaign a tighter framework than shoot-'em-ups usually have.

The foundation is the classic formula: gradually upgrading the main weapon, collectible support modules, and a sensibly designed difficulty curve that lets the player breathe between successive onslaughts. Compile was a master of this craft, and it shows in how readable the screen stays and in the fact that you can always dodge what's coming at you if you read the situation ahead of time. Boss fights are long and multi-phase, while the final levels can be downright merciless, forcing the player to know enemy layouts by heart. The game expects you to come back to it and rewards you with the fact that a once-learned section can be cleared far more elegantly the next time.

The Mega-CD's capabilities are used mainly for disc-based music, which combines rock motifs with Japanese instruments, and for illustrated cutscenes that tell the story between missions. Technically it stays very brisk, the picture remains smooth even with a large number of objects on screen, and scrolling runs without a hitch. At the time it was praised as one of the better shoot-'em-ups on the add-on precisely because it didn't rely on cinematic effects but on solid game design. Today it has become a treasure for genre fans: a short, demanding, and still excellently playable showcase of what Compile did best. For collectors it's also one of the titles that show the add-on's library in a better light than its general reputation would suggest.
mega-cd__robo-aleste.teaser: A vertical shooter from Compile, masters of the genre, set in feudal Japan with robots.

mega-cd__soul-star.article:
**Soul Star** is an action shooter from the British studio Core Design that tries to offer several different playstyles within a single game. The framing is a simple sci-fi story about a last-ditch defense against an invading alien fleet, but the missions themselves alternate between different perspectives: one moment you're flying through space with a behind-the-ship view, the next you're fighting through horizontally scrolling sections above a planet's surface, and in other segments you switch to a top-down view, controlling a vehicle or a foot soldier as you blast through the narrow corridors of a base. Transitions between the different styles flow smoothly within a single campaign.

Each mission type has its own pacing. The space sections are the fastest and revolve around dodging and quickly shooting down formations, the surface sections give more room for maneuvering, and the top-down parts feel more like classic arcade action focused on finding a path and destroying generators. The game rewards you for carefully rescuing civilians and for properly making use of weapon upgrades that carry over between missions. That variety is both its biggest draw and its biggest weakness, since not all its parts are equally polished. Still, it's precisely this switching between perspectives that keeps the game fresh and never lets any single one of its modes overstay its welcome.

Technically it's a typical showcase of how Core Design pushed the hardware. The game makes heavy use of scaling and rotating objects, something the Mega-CD handles better than the plain Mega Drive, and pairs it with disc-based music with a strongly atmospheric, at times almost dark tone. At the time reviewers praised its ambition and spectacle while also flagging its uneven difficulty. In hindsight, Soul Star is an interesting record of a period when developers tried to combine three genres into one simply because the disc finally gave them enough room, and even today it manages to entertain with its pace and inventiveness. The space sections come off best, with the most momentum and the biggest payoff from the effects the game likes to show off.
mega-cd__soul-star.teaser: An action shooter from Core Design that alternates perspectives and gameplay styles within a single campaign.

mega-cd__thunderhawk.article:
**Thunderhawk** is a combat helicopter title that on the Mega-CD counted as one of the most impressive technical showcases of the entire add-on. The player takes the seat of an attack helicopter and flies mission after mission across several war zones, from deserts to jungles to arctic seas. The objectives stay grounded — destroy a convoy, take out anti-air defenses, protect allied units, or extract a prisoner — but thanks to the varying terrain and steadily increasing enemy resilience, the individual tasks never grow stale. The missions are also ordered so that they gradually introduce new target types along with ever denser anti-air defenses.

The controls deliberately sit somewhere between arcade and simulation. The helicopter tilts, loses speed while climbing, and requires the player to keep both altitude and the timing of clearing a ridge in mind. Weapons are split between a cannon, unguided rockets, and guided missiles for air and ground targets, each in limited supply, so you need to plan your loadout before a mission and conserve ammunition in combat. The key to success is staying low, using the terrain as cover, and striking before you're targeted. Damage also affects how the machine handles, so finishing a mission on a half-wrecked helicopter is a discipline all its own.

The graphics run on a full polygonal engine enhanced with effects made possible by the Mega-CD itself, namely a smoother frame rate, digitized sound, and disc-based music that gives the missions a cinematic, tense edge. For a console of its time it was an exceptional showcase; movement over the terrain felt convincing and the sense of flight carried real weight. At the time Thunderhawk was counted among the best things released for the add-on, and as proof that the disc could serve for something other than playing back video. Today it remains an interesting piece of history that, surprisingly, still handles well once the player gets used to its heavier flight physics. Compared to the purely arcade flight games of its era, Thunderhawk feels far more mature and thoughtfully designed.
mega-cd__thunderhawk.teaser: A combat helicopter and one of the most impressive technical showcases of the entire Mega-CD.

mega-cd__lethal-enforcers.article:
**Lethal Enforcers** brings to the Mega-CD one of the most talked-about arcade shooters of the early nineties. The player takes on the role of a police officer who works through a bank robbery, dockside smugglers, a kidnapping in Chinatown, and a final assault on a weapons warehouse. The game is played by aiming at the screen and shooting targets that appear in predetermined waves, and a crucial part of it is telling apart the perpetrators from civilians, since shooting an innocent bystander costs you a life. The pace is sharp from the very start and every mistake shows immediately.

Mechanically, this is pure arcade action built on reflexes. Weapons can be upgraded by picking up a shotgun, a submachine gun, or a magnum with greater range and power, but each weapon has limited ammo, and once it runs out you fall back to your service pistol. Reloading is done by firing off-screen, which keeps the tension up, and the game supports simultaneous two-player play, which gives the whole experience a much more relaxed, different feel. Rounds are short, difficulty ramps up quickly, and the point is mainly chasing a better score. The game is built around forcing the player to judge each target in an instant, which makes it more a test of focus than finger speed.

Visually, the game relies on digitized photographs of real actors, giving it a realistic and, for its time, rather harsh look; this is exactly what made it one of the titles cited in the era's debate about violence in video games. The Mega-CD version benefits from music and voice samples played straight off the disc, and it was also sold bundled with a light gun, with which it plays incomparably better than with a gamepad. Today, Lethal Enforcers is mainly an interesting relic of an era when digitized actors passed for the peak of realism, and it still works as a short two-player action romp on a single screen. Without the light gun, though, it loses a lot, so how well you can replicate the original controls matters a great deal when playing it today.
mega-cd__lethal-enforcers.teaser: An arcade light-gun shooter about a police officer; also playable with a real toy pistol.

mega-cd__road-avenger.article:
**Road Avenger** is the console version of an arcade laserdisc game, and it's one of the finest examples of what used to be called an interactive movie. The story is simple and fast-moving: the hero's wife is killed by a gang during their wedding drive, and he then sets out in his car to hunt them down for revenge. The whole game consists of anime sequences played from the disc, into which the player intervenes at precisely timed moments — essentially a forerunner of today's quick time events. This exact type of game was the main draw of the whole add-on at launch, and Road Avenger was among the best-executed examples of it.

The gameplay lives and dies by reflexes and memory. A short prompt appears on screen telling you which way to yank the wheel, when to brake, or when to attack, and the player has a split second to react. A mistake means a crash and an immediate replay of the scene. Since the sequences are fixed, progress essentially means learning their order and starting to react before the prompt even appears. The game is short and unforgiving, but thanks to quick restarts it never feels frustrating and keeps luring you into another attempt. More complex situations gradually pile on, requiring several prompts to be handled in quick succession, and the final scenes demand a practically flawless run.

The title's strength lies in its execution. The animation is fluid, the camera dynamic, and the chases have a momentum that had no equal on a home console at the time of release; on top of that comes a rock soundtrack from the disc and dubbed scenes. At the time, it was a flagship effort to sell the Mega-CD as a device for cinematic experiences, and the game is often cited as one of the few representatives of that direction that is actually fun. Today it needs to be taken for what it is — a short interactive chase — but within its category it remains one of the best-executed pieces ever made. As proof of the era's excitement over new technology, it works brilliantly.
mega-cd__road-avenger.teaser: An interactive movie based on a laserdisc arcade game; revenge played out through anime sequences.

mega-cd__snatcher.article:
**Snatcher** is a cyberpunk detective adventure from Konami, set in the artificial island city of Neo Kobe. The player takes on the role of Gillian Seed, an investigator for the JUNKER unit who has lost his memory and must uncover the origin of the so-called Snatchers — artificial beings that murder people and take their place in everyday life. The gameplay is built around a command menu: you choose where to look, whom to address, what to examine, or which item to use, and the plot only advances once you notice a small detail that can be developed into further conversation. The investigation is interspersed with shooting sequences using a targeting reticle, which serve as tense climaxes to individual chapters.

The Mega-CD gave the game exactly what it needed. The disc's capacity allowed for detailed drawn backgrounds, extensive animated sequences, and above all a full voice cast for the English version, which was a complete exception for consoles at the time of release. The static images are rendered with a care reminiscent of period anime, and the game handles them cinematically — slow push-ins, pauses, sharp cuts to close-up. The soundtrack combines dark synthetic pieces with ambient textures and can be surprisingly melancholic in its quieter passages. The atmosphere is also helped by the fact that Neo Kobe isn't just a backdrop: the bars, offices, and apartments feel lived-in, and conversations often stray into things unrelated to the case.

At the time, it was a title that earned more of a cult following than a mass audience — the Western release came late, in limited numbers, and on a console whose star was already fading. Even so, Snatcher became one of the most-cited reasons to own a Mega-CD, and it's still talked about today as the pinnacle of that generation's storytelling ambitions. Its influence can be seen across the whole later wave of narrative-driven games built on long dialogue and cinematic direction. Today, what holds the game back is mainly its slower pace and the need to try commands repeatedly, but its mood, humor, and final reveal still work.
mega-cd__snatcher.teaser: A cyberpunk detective adventure from Hideo Kojima, full of Blade Runner-esque atmosphere.

mega-cd__lunar-silver-star.article:
**Lunar: The Silver Star** is a classic Japanese RPG about a boy from a remote village who dreams of becoming a Dragonmaster and gradually gets entangled in the fate of the whole world and its goddess. The storytelling deliberately leans on archetypes — a growing party of heroes, a mysterious singer, comic relief in the form of a flying animal companion — but handles them with such warmth that the clichés stop mattering. Battles run on a turn-based system where the positioning of characters on the battlefield matters: attacks have range, spells hit an area, and moving in the first round often decides whether the mage or the armored warrior takes the hit.

On the Mega-CD, the game made full use of the medium. Key plot turns are accompanied by hand-drawn animated cutscenes, the main characters' dialogue is voiced, and the music is recorded as audio tracks from the disc, so instead of chip tunes you get orchestral and vocal pieces. The music is in fact one of the most memorable elements — the main theme and the songs accompanying key moments carry emotion the text alone couldn't. The graphics rely on colorful, legible environments and large character portraits that change expression during conversations. The pace is slower, with honest exploration of towns and dungeons, but the game never leaves you wondering where to go next for long.

At the time, Lunar was seen as proof that CD didn't have to mean just music videos, but could genuinely mean a bigger, richer game. In the West it was helped by a careful localization that added its own humor to the text and made it one of the few Japanese RPGs to make it onto a Sega system at all. The series' influence shows mainly in how naturally later JRPGs came to use animated intros and voiced scenes. Today the game feels simple but tremendously welcoming — it's a title you can spend a long evening with without frustration, and with the sense that its storytelling has its heart in the right place. Difficulty is mild, and the game rewards exploration more than hours of repeated battles.
mega-cd__lunar-silver-star.teaser: A classic JRPG with a warm story and animated cutscenes that exceeded expectations at the time.

mega-cd__lunar-eternal-blue.article:
**Lunar: Eternal Blue** picks up centuries after the first game and tells the story of a young treasure hunter who discovers a girl bound to the blue star in the sky and to a religious order with far too much interest in her fate. Compared to its predecessor, the story is darker and more focused, with a stronger thread of faith, manipulation, and sacrifice, but it keeps the same sense of humor and characters who talk to each other like a real group of friends. Gameplay-wise it's again a turn-based RPG with positional battles, where characters move around during a round, combine the range of attacks and spells, and where choosing the order of actions often matters more than raw numbers.

Technically, it's one of the best-looking titles in the whole Mega-CD library. The animated cutscenes are longer and smoother than in the first game, character portraits have more expressions, and battle effects are strikingly colorful. Once again, the music from the disc is a major draw — the melodies are written as full-fledged compositions, and songs again carry the story's strongest moments. The dungeons are noticeably more elaborate, with traps, switches, and shortcuts, and the game gives the player more freedom in how they equip and develop the party. There's even a special rating that tracks how well you handled character situations along the way.

At the time, Eternal Blue was received as a more mature and ambitious sequel, but it arrived just as attention was already shifting to new consoles — so its reach ended up smaller than it deserved. Among genre fans it nonetheless kept a reputation as one of the best RPGs ever released on Sega systems, and the series later got remakes precisely because people remembered it. Today it delights mainly through its storytelling pace and how much time the game devotes to ordinary scenes between characters. Anyone who likes classic JRPGs will find one of the best-written stories of its era here, albeit at the cost of a slower start and more frequent battles than is common today.
mega-cd__lunar-eternal-blue.teaser: A darker sequel to Lunar, about a treasure hunter and a girl bound to a blue star.

mega-cd__shining-force-cd.article:
**Shining Force CD** brings the beloved tactical series to the Mega-CD and delivers an extensive campaign made up of several interlinked books that continue stories previously released on a handheld console. The core remains the same: you command a party of heroes on a square grid, moving each character individually and deciding whether to attack, cast a spell, use an item, or retreat to safety. Victory hinges on terrain, range, and who you send forward as a living shield. Between battles you return to towns to buy equipment, revive the fallen, and above all promote characters to higher classes, which is one of the most addictive elements of the whole series.

The move to disc shows mainly in the presentation. The game has animated cutscenes, voiced introductions to individual chapters, and music recorded as audio tracks, so the battle themes sound fuller than on a cartridge. Character sprites are larger, and the battle animations triggered in every clash have more frames and flashier spell effects. Thanks to the disc's capacity, the campaign is unusually long, and it's rounded out by a bonus mode with additional battles that offers pure tactical challenge without any story. The atmosphere stays classically fantasy — knights, elves, centaurs, and a dark cult lurking in the background — but it's delivered with a light touch and without unnecessary gravity.

At the time, it was one of the few major original RPG titles that Sega actually prepared for the Mega-CD, and among owners of the add-on it was one of the most valued reasons to own one. The Shining series as a whole contributed significantly to tactical RPGs catching on outside Japan, and this entry is an honest expansion of it. Today the game feels slow, mainly due to loading times and the length of the animations, but its tactical foundation has aged wonderfully: every move carries weight, and losing a favorite character still stings. Anyone who settles into the rhythm of battles and town returns gets one of the most substantial tactical adventures of its era.
mega-cd__shining-force-cd.teaser: A tactical RPG combining the handheld chapters of the famous series into one extensive campaign.

mega-cd__vay.article:
**Vay** is a traditional Japanese RPG that opens with a wedding interrupted by an invading army and continues into a long journey to rescue the kidnapped bride and uncover the secret of an ancient suit of battle armor. The structure is classic to the point of being textbook: you traverse a world map, visit towns, buy equipment, descend into dungeons, and fight turn-based battles with random encounters. Characters join gradually, each with their own role — healer, mage, tank — and correctly distributing items and spells is essential for surviving later areas. The game doesn't skimp on battles, so a fair share of your time necessarily goes into building up the party.

The Mega-CD version benefits from the disc mainly in presentation. The game opens with a longer animated sequence, and further drawn cutscenes appear at key story turns, with the English release getting voiced dialogue. The music runs as audio tracks, which makes the battle and town themes sound fuller than the base console's synthesizer could manage. The game's own graphics are more understated and stick to the proven genre look of the early nineties: colorful towns, darker caves, and enemies rendered as static images above a text menu. The atmosphere is more serious, with themes of loss and duty, even though the text keeps a light touch.

At the time, Vay was received as a solid but not groundbreaking RPG — its main value lay in the fact that Western Mega-CD owners had only a handful of games in this genre available to them. The localization earned a reputation for its loose translation, which gave the characters more personality than they had in the original. Its influence on the genre was small, but it's an honest representative of the era when Japanese RPGs were still gaining a foothold outside Nintendo. Today it will please mainly players who like a slow, classic pace and don't mind frequent random encounters. Anyone looking for a longer turn-based adventure on the Mega-CD who's already worked through the more famous titles will find here a solid several dozen hours with no grand ambitions, but with a clear structure.
mega-cd__vay.teaser: A traditional JRPG about a wedding interrupted by war, and the hunt for an abducted bride and an ancient suit of armor.

mega-cd__dark-wizard.article:
**Dark Wizard** is a sprawling tactical RPG in which a kingdom has fallen to a dark sorcerer and you lead the resistance from the first skirmishes all the way to the final siege. Right at the start you choose one of four heroes, and each one has their own opening chapter, different allies, and a different sequence of battles, so the game offers several playthroughs that differ by more than just the main character's name. Battles take place on a grid where terrain, range, and correct spell timing all matter. A special feature is recruiting and commanding entire units of different types — besides the heroes you have regular soldiers, cavalry, or flying creatures at your disposal, which can be promoted and reinforced between battles.

On the Mega-CD, the game uses the disc mainly for music and visual presentation: illustrated scenes introduce the chapters, animations accompany combat attacks, and the English version has voiced introductions. The soundtrack is unusually rich, with more solemn orchestral motifs that give the battles proper weight. The battlefield itself is kept plain and legible, with an emphasis on clarity, since the maps tend to be large and packed with units. The pace is slow — a single battle can easily stretch to tens of minutes — but the game compensates by giving almost every clash its own victory condition and its own trap.

At the time, it was one of the few deeper strategy titles on the add-on, and reviewers praised its scope and replayability above all, while criticizing its length and the need to replay longer stretches after a failure. Compared to the better-known Shining series, Dark Wizard remained in the shadows, but among genre fans it earned a reputation as an underrated gem. Today it's a game for the patient: anyone who takes to its unit system and pre-battle planning gets one of the most substantial adventures the Mega-CD has to offer. The choice of hero at the start also gives a real reason to come back to it again, since the allies and part of the map change as well.
mega-cd__dark-wizard.teaser: An extensive tactical RPG with four heroes and different paths through a rebellion against a wizard.

mega-cd__heart-of-alien-out-of-this-worl.article:
**Heart of the Alien: Out of This World Parts I and II** is an unusual package that combines the original Another World and its sequel, told from the perspective of the alien companion Buddy, on a single disc. The first part stays faithful to the legend of a scientist thrown by an experiment into a foreign world, while the second reverses the perspective and lets the player control a creature that navigates this environment far more skillfully. The gameplay stays the same: running, jumping, ducking, crawling, and using a weapon or whip in an environment where a single mistake means instant death. Progress is based on observation and repetition — every screen is essentially a puzzle about timing.

Technically, this is an interesting case. The vector graphics with large flat color areas and fluid character animation look just as economical and stylish on the Mega-CD as they did on computers; the disc's main contribution lies in the recorded music. It is noticeably darker and more atmospheric than the chip-tune arrangements of earlier versions, underscoring the feeling of loneliness in a hostile world. The game does not use a single line of dialogue, relying instead on facial expressions, gestures, and cinematic editing, which still gives it a peculiar dignity today. The second part is more action-oriented, less mysterious, and still difficult, at times almost unfairly so — checkpoints are far apart and some passages demand frame-perfect precision.

At the time, the first half was received as a classic worth owning in any form, while the sequel divided players and critics alike: it lacks the mystery and exploratory calm of the original. Another World's influence on cinematic platformers is undeniable and can still be felt today in the whole wave of independent games built on silent storytelling and lethal precision. Today, this version is interesting mainly for its music and for the fact that the sequel remained practically exclusive to the Mega-CD, so you won't easily find it elsewhere. The playtime is short but intense, and few games of that era manage to evoke such a sense of otherness.
mega-cd__heart-of-alien-out-of-this-worl.teaser: A compilation of both Another World installments on one disc, including Buddy's perspective.

mega-cd__rise-of-dragon.article:
**Rise of the Dragon** is a cyberpunk detective adventure set in a devastated Los Angeles of 2053, where former police officer William Blade investigates the death of a young woman linked to a new addictive drug. The investigation is conducted through a combination of moving around the city, searching crime scenes, and conversations in which you choose from a menu of lines. Time plays a crucial role — the clock keeps running, meetings happen at specific moments, and a lead you miss may be gone forever. This makes the game an unusually tense adventure where planning your day becomes a layer of gameplay in its own right, and it also means the first playthrough tends to be an exercise in learning the terrain.

Even in its original form the game relied on digitized characters and cinematic scene composition, and the Mega-CD version pushes this further with spoken dialogue and disc-based music. The screens have a dark, neon-lit palette, the character animation during conversations is unusually detailed, and the overall impression is deliberately grimy — the city feels tired, dusty, and hopeless. The soundscape, with its pulsing synthetic motifs, sustains this mood and can turn up the intensity in tenser passages. The production also includes harsher scenes and themes that were not common on consoles in the year of release.

At the time, the game belonged to a group of computer adventures with which Sega wanted to show that the add-on wasn't just a video player. Critics praised the atmosphere and the flowing-time concept, while reservations centered on the need for repetition and the fact that some dead ends only reveal themselves hours later. Its influence can be seen in later detective games that use limited time as a dramatic device. Today it's a strong atmospheric experience that benefits from the player accepting that a few attempts are part of the design. Anyone who enjoys slow cyberpunk storytelling and doesn't mind dated cursor controls will find one of the best-constructed adventures in the whole library here.
mega-cd__rise-of-dragon.teaser: A cyberpunk detective adventure from a Los Angeles of the year 2053, where both time and the investigation keep running.

mega-cd__secret-of-monkey-island.article:
**The Secret of Monkey Island** is a comedic pirate adventure about Guybrush Threepwood, a young man who wants to be a pirate and instead gets tangled up in the kidnapping of the governor and a feud with the undead Captain LeChuck. The game runs on the classic verb-command system — open, take, talk to, use — with which you combine inventory items and speak to characters through branching dialogue. The puzzles are designed to be solved through reasoning rather than random trial and error, and the series became famous for the fact that the main hero can neither die nor become permanently stuck. An unforgettable quirk is the insult sword-fighting, in which victory goes to whoever has the sharper tongue rather than the sharper blade.

The Mega-CD version uses the disc mainly for sound: the music runs as recorded tracks, so the familiar Caribbean themes sound in genuine instrumental arrangements instead of synthesizer chip music. The graphics are colorful and legible even on a television, cursor control with a gamepad is slower than with a mouse, but the game accounts for that and the verb menu is adapted to buttons. The atmosphere of Mêlée Island, with its tavern, harbor, and odd inhabitants, works because the game never takes itself seriously while still having an internally consistent world in which even absurd solutions make a certain kind of sense.

At the time, this was one of the few truly major computer adventure classics to make it onto a console at all, and for many players it was their first encounter with the genre. The original game's influence on the entire point-and-click genre is fundamental: it set the standard for humor, dialogue trees, and the conviction that players shouldn't be punished for curiosity. Today, Monkey Island is still funny and surprisingly well written, and even on Mega-CD it offers a complete experience — just with a bit of patience needed for cursor movement. The puzzles still hold up logically after all these years, the dialogue can be read aloud without embarrassment, and the whole package remains one of the best introductions to the genre ever made. For owners of the add-on, it was also a rare opportunity to play something at home on television that otherwise belonged exclusively to computers.
mega-cd__secret-of-monkey-island.teaser: The legendary comedic pirate adventure from LucasArts starring Guybrush Threepwood.

mega-cd__sherlock-holmes-consulting-dete.article:
**Sherlock Holmes: Consulting Detective** is a detective game that bet on live-action film before that was common on consoles. You get three cases set in Victorian London along with free access to the tools of a real investigator: a directory of residents, a city map, a newspaper archive, and the ability to visit anyone who might know something. Each visit triggers a short live-action segment in which a witness answers questions, and it's entirely up to the player to piece the fragments together into a coherent picture. The game never pushes you along and offers no hints — at the end of a case, you sit down for a final test where you answer questions about the culprit and motive, and your success rate is compared against Holmes's own solution.

On the Mega-CD, this meant hours of compressed video in a small window with a limited color palette, which is the first thing you'll notice today. Even so, the production holds together: the costumes, sets, and acting performances have a period theatrical dignity, and the spoken word carries almost all the information, making the technical picture quality secondary. The music and sound effects are restrained, and scenes are often accompanied by nothing more than a crackling fireplace or street noise. Calm is the game's greatest asset — it creates a sense of quiet investigation at a desk covered in notes rather than an action adventure.

At the time, this was one of the first titles used to showcase the Mega-CD, and reviews were split: the concept and atmosphere earned praise, while the small video window and complete lack of action drew criticism. Still, it's an important milestone — it showed that live-action footage could serve storytelling rather than mere spectacle. Its idea of free-form investigation without a goal marker has resurfaced in modern detective games built around archives and records. Today, the game will be best appreciated by someone who grabs a pen and paper and lets themselves be drawn into slowly assembling the connections. Anyone expecting action or a brisk pace will be disappointed, but as a calm evening puzzle for two or three people around a single screen, it still works beautifully.
mega-cd__sherlock-holmes-consulting-dete.teaser: A detective game with live-action segments, before FMV was common on consoles.

mega-cd__night-trap.article:
**Night Trap** is an interactive film in which you follow a group of girls on a weekend stay at a house where something is going on with the neighbors and the guests, and your job is to protect them. The player sits at a security system control panel, switching between cameras in individual rooms and springing traps at just the right moment to neutralize intruders. The peculiarity is that the entire plot runs in real time across all the rooms simultaneously — while you're watching the kitchen, something you'll miss is happening in the hallway right now. Part of the gameplay is also switching between color-coded traps, since without the correct code the traps won't work.

Technically, this was the flagship of the entire Mega-CD concept. The game consists overwhelmingly of live-action footage, which the console handles in a small window with a heavily limited palette, so the picture is grainy and colors break up into blocks. Even so, the production is impressive within the add-on's limits, mainly because the video runs smoothly and the player switches between cameras instantly. Sound carries the entire atmosphere: dialogue, screams, and the well-known theme song are all recorded from disc. The mood is deliberately campy — the game is more a parody of eighties B-movie horror comedies than a genuinely frightening title.

At the time, Night Trap became famous mainly outside the realm of gaming itself: it became one of the main targets of the American debate on violence in games, which ultimately led to the creation of an age rating system. Ironically, this attention brought it immortality — it remains one of the most cited symbols of the FMV era to this day. The gameplay itself is short and requires memorizing the schedule of events, which many players consider dated. But as a piece of gaming history and an entertainingly naive curiosity, it works wonderfully, especially in company, where hunting for the right camera becomes a group sport. Watching other people's scenes and commenting along the way is today the biggest fun the game offers, and it carries with it a peculiar charm: it's more an interactive film to put on for friends than a game one returns to alone.
mega-cd__night-trap.teaser: A cult interactive movie with cameras and traps; the entire plot unfolds in real time.

mega-cd__sewer-shark.article:
**Sewer Shark** is an on-rails shooter set underground in a devastated future, where surviving humanity endures in tunnels infested with mutated vermin. The player sits in the cockpit of a fighter hovercraft, shoots at targets that appear in the tunnel, and above all listens to the navigator, who shouts over the engine noise to call out which turn to take. This is the core of the game: at every junction you have a split second to turn correctly, and missing it means a crash. Progress is therefore largely about memorizing the route and reacting quickly to verbal instructions, supplemented by shooting that governs your score and access to further missions.

The game was created even before the add-on's launch and, in the year of its debut, became the very thing the Mega-CD was showcased with in stores. The entire tunnel run is a live-action, computer-augmented film running in a small window with a heavily reduced palette, so the picture is coarse and falls apart in motion. The sound, on the other hand, is a strength — the crew's recorded voice lines, the engine's roar, and bombastic music together create a surprisingly intense experience. The sewer environment is ugly and claustrophobic, and the acting performances between missions play out B-movie sci-fi with visible self-awareness.

At the time, this was a title that divided opinion: it was technologically impressive, but offered little actual decision-making in terms of gameplay, and many reviewers called it an expensive demonstration of the medium's possibilities. Even so, it was sold bundled with the hardware and became many players' first encounter with a disc-based game. As a dead-end branch of the genre's evolution, Sewer Shark is mostly of historical interest today — the gameplay is short, tough, and repetitive, but the enthusiasm with which it dives into its cheap sci-fi still gives it a certain charm. Still, it's worth booting up at least once: nothing else so precisely captures what manufacturers imagined a disc-based game to be in the early nineties, and the navigator's shouted instructions will stick in your memory for years.
mega-cd__sewer-shark.teaser: A rail shooter in underground tunnels, where a split-second turn on the navigator's cue decides everything.

mega-cd__ground-zero-texas.article:
**Ground Zero: Texas** puts the player in the role of an agent who must uncover an alien infiltration of a small Texas town from a secret base before the preparations for an invasion are complete. Gameplay takes place at a panel with several camera feeds spread across the town: you switch between views, watch for a disguised intruder to appear, and take aim and eliminate them at just the right moment. The tension arises from the fact that the scenes play out simultaneously — while you're watching one street, something is brewing elsewhere and your people in the field may get hurt. Longer cinematic passages run between the action sequences, developing the plot and introducing the characters.

In production terms, this was an unusually expensive project for its time: the game was shot with a professional crew, features elaborate exteriors, stunt scenes, and pyrotechnics, and in terms of video volume it was one of the largest titles in the entire library. On the Mega-CD, this means the usual compromise — a small window, coarse compression, and a limited palette, causing night scenes to collapse into noise. The sound side, on the other hand, is strong, with recorded dialogue and a rock-tinged score that drives the action sequences forward. The atmosphere leans toward a paranoid sci-fi thriller with a dusty American small-town backdrop.

At the time, the game was presented as proof that interactive film could reach the level of genuine television production, and reviews indeed praised the production values more than those of the studio's previous titles. Criticism, on the other hand, targeted the limited interactivity, since the player's role shrinks down to watching and aiming. The influence can be seen mainly in how the FMV format exhausted its credibility even before the technology improved. Today it's a period curiosity worth seeing for its production values — and for how confidently the whole thing takes itself seriously. The playtime is short, but having to watch several cameras at once gives the gameplay a surprisingly brisk pace.
mega-cd__ground-zero-texas.teaser: An FMV thriller about investigating an alien infiltration of a Texas town through a network of cameras.

sega-32x__doom.article:
**Doom** was, for the 32X add-on, exactly what a showcase for any new platform should be: proof that it could handle something the competition couldn't manage in the living room. As a lone marine, the player fights through bases on the moons of Mars that have been flooded with demonic creatures following a failed experiment. Progress is purely arcade-fast: you search for colored keycards, use them to unlock locked sections, press on walls suspected of hiding secret chambers, and collect an arsenal ranging from a pistol through a shotgun and chainsaw to a plasma gun. Enemies move along their own axis, so combat becomes a dance around pillars and a retreat into wider spaces, where opponents can be turned against each other and left to slaughter one another. The game handles vertical aiming for you, so all your attention goes toward dodging and never standing still.

Technically, the conversion builds precisely on what the 32X added — a pair of powerful processors on top of the Mega Drive. The picture runs in a smaller window framed by a border with the weapon and status indicators, which saves performance and keeps the pace noticeably brisker than the home conversions of the time running on weaker hardware. But that speed comes at a price: part of the levels and enemies didn't fit onto the cartridge, the textures are coarser, and the music plays through the Mega Drive's sound chip in FM form, sounding rawer than on PC. This doesn't undercut the atmosphere, though — if anything the opposite: dark corridors, metallic screeching, and the roar that sounds the moment a monster spots you still work even in this simplified form.

At the time, this was one of the main arguments for buying the add-on, and also a source of controversy, since comparisons with the computer original were merciless. For the first-person shooter genre, though, it marked an important step: it showed that console audiences were ready for this type of game. Today, the 32X version is mainly a technical curiosity and a pleasant, fast Doom for a few evenings — it still plays wonderfully, just know that it's a shortened cut of a great classic.
sega-32x__doom.teaser: The legendary FPS meant to prove that the new add-on could handle even the most demanding games.

sega-32x__virtua-racing-deluxe.article:
**Virtua Racing Deluxe** was a launch title for the 32X and, at the same time, the best possible demonstration of why the add-on existed at all. An arcade car race built on full polygons instead of sprite-scaling tricks moved over here in an expanded form: alongside the original tracks, new circuits were added, and besides formula cars you can now choose other vehicle types, which changes handling on the track as well as the optimal racing line. The driving model stays arcade-like, but not simplistic — braking before a corner pays off, you can feed the throttle gradually through a bend, and the difference between the ideal line and a sloppy one shows up on the clock immediately. The track is also less forgiving than you'd expect from an arcade game — clipping the guardrails bleeds off speed so noticeably that a single mistake in the final lap can decide the whole race.

Technically, this is a major deal: on the Mega Drive itself, the original conversion needed a special chip right in the cartridge, whereas on the 32X the polygons are handled by the new pair of processors, and the result runs smoother, in a sharper image, with a richer scene around the track. Several camera views are available, including the cockpit interior and a view from behind the car, so everyone can find their own. The sound relies on engine whine and simple melodies that, in this type of game, tend to set the mood rather than grab attention. Split-screen for two players is among the best things the cartridge offers, because racing a friend for tenths of a second is more fun here than chasing computer opponents.

Reviewers at the time praised the game as proof that the 32X had something to show, while also noting that it was an upgrade of an already-known title rather than a brand-new experience. Its influence mainly rides on its arcade original, which opened the door for polygonal racing into the gaming mainstream. Today, Virtua Racing Deluxe plays surprisingly well: the controls are legible, the races short and clean, and the roughly-hewn cars have a charm that's not so easy to find in later, more realistic games.
sega-32x__virtua-racing-deluxe.teaser: An expanded arcade classic with full polygons, new tracks, and new car types.

sega-32x__virtua-fighter.article:
**Virtua Fighter** brought the first truly three-dimensional fighting game to the 32X, and with it a different way of thinking about combat than players were used to from two-dimensional brawlers. The eight fighters have no fireballs or supernatural attacks — instead, they rely on styles drawn from real martial arts, from karate and wrestling to Chinese schools. The fight is built around a trio of punches, kicks, and blocks, on correct timing, and on whether you can push your opponent out of the circular ring. Being knocked out of the arena ends the round just as decisively as running out of health, so spatial awareness matters as much as knowing your combos. Each fighter has their own set of throws, grabs, and counters, so even after dozens of bouts there's still something to discover about what a given style can do and who it works well against.

The 32X conversion tried to preserve the essence of the arcade original and leverages the add-on's polygon power to do it. The characters are made of blocky shapes without textures, which from today's perspective looks like a moving paper statue, but the movement is legible, and that's what matters most in this game — you need to recognize whether your opponent is starting a strike or guarding. The camera stays to the side of the ring and swings into dramatic angles during throws and falls. The sound design is restrained, with hits and fighters' shouts taking the lead role, so tension mostly arises from the silence between exchanges.

At the time, the game was seen as an important argument for the add-on, even though comparisons to the arcade original and to the Saturn version were harsh. The influence of the original is hard to overstate: it defined the rules of three-dimensional fighting games, from sidesteps and throws to the emphasis on realistic styles, and its legacy carries the entire later series. On the 32X, it's an interesting period document today, at its strongest in two-player mode on a single console, where you quickly stop noticing the characters' blockiness. Anyone willing to put in the work training a single character will discover that beneath the simple controls hides a surprisingly deep fight over positioning and timing.
sega-32x__virtua-fighter.teaser: A pioneering 3D fighter built on real martial arts styles instead of magic.

sega-32x__star-wars-arcade.article:
**Star Wars Arcade** brought to the 32X an arcade experience where you sat in a cockpit and shot at Imperial fighters. The game is an on-rails space shooter: the flight path is fixed, the player aims the reticle, dodges fire, and tries to shoot down everything that appears. The campaign runs through an attack on a Star Destroyer, a fight in a hangar, and finally into the famous Death Star trench, where you need to hit the exhaust port. Weapons have limited cooling and torpedoes must be conserved, so besides reflexes it also matters when you open fire and when you wait. Difficulty rises quickly, and the game doesn't shy away from throwing more targets onto the screen than you can swing your reticle across, so the outcome depends on priority — deal first with whatever is shooting at you.

On the 32X, the game runs in full polygons, which in 1994 was the main selling point on a home console. TIE fighters turn and pass you in space, explosions break apart into simple fragments, and the cockpit frames the image much like in the arcade cabinet. The graphics are textureless and blocky, but fast and clear. The sound relies on the series' iconic effects — the whine of lasers, the screech of fighter engines — and on musical themes that, even in simplified form, immediately set the right mood. There's also a two-player mode where one pilots and the other shoots, which makes playing together a surprisingly sociable affair.

At the time, it was one of the first titles to introduce the add-on to the public, and reviews swung between enthusiasm for the technology and reservations about how short the game is and how quickly it starts to repeat itself. Genre-wise, it continues the long tradition of on-rails Star Wars shooters and belongs among the bridges between sprite-based and polygonal eras. Today it's more of a half-hour attraction than a game for long evenings, but that half hour still has punch — especially the final trench run, which even in its blocky polygonal form nails exactly the scene most players remember the game for. With two players, it also works great as an evening's social attraction.
sega-32x__star-wars-arcade.teaser: An on-rails space shooter culminating in the famous trench run at the Death Star.

sega-32x__knuckles-chaotix.article:
**Knuckles' Chaotix** is the most distinctive platformer the 32X ever got, and at the same time one of the strangest offshoots of the entire Sonic universe. The main star is Knuckles, joined by a crew who later became known as Chaotix — the crocodile Vector, the bee Charmy, or the spider Espio. The key novelty is the elastic band: characters are always played in pairs, connected by a stretchy bond that stretches, tenses, and catapults. Pulling your partner back and releasing lets you launch high into the air; a sharp move can send your buddy flying over a chasm. The entire gameplay rests on this physics, and it takes a while to get used to, because ordinary running and jumping isn't enough on its own here. The reward is a kind of movement you won't experience in other platformers: a well-timed rebound flings you across half the level, with your partner trailing behind you like a stone from a slingshot.

Visually, it's one of the most colorful titles on the add-on. Levels burst with saturated hues, funfair-style environments layer into several planes, and the game pulls off rotation and transparency effects that the Mega Drive alone couldn't manage. The sound holds onto the brisk, melodic line typical of the series, and the structure is rounded out by special bonus stages with a view into space, which again show off the hardware's polygonal capabilities. The levels are sprawling, and which set you get changes depending on how you perform, giving the game a slightly experimental edge.

At the time, the game was received with mixed feelings: it was praised for its idea and its colorfulness, while criticism targeted the less gripping pace that the bond between characters inevitably brings, and the absence of the main blue hedgehog. As a showcase of unusual game mechanics, though, it has aged well and ranks among the most sought-after cartridges of the platform among collectors. Anyone who gives the band a chance for more than a few minutes will find a platformer that plays like nothing else. And in two-player mode, where each person controls one half of the pair, it turns into a comedy full of mutual flinging and giggling.
sega-32x__knuckles-chaotix.teaser: A strange detour in the Sonic universe featuring an elastic tether linking pairs of characters.

sega-32x__kolibri.article:
**Kolibri** is an unusual shooter in which, instead of a spaceship, you pilot a hummingbird. An evil dark force in the form of a crystal is poisoning nature, and the tiny bird, armed with magical powers, sets out to stop it across meadows, caves, beehives, and strange organic innards. The game keeps the genre's skeleton — streams of enemies, collecting upgraded shots, boss fights — but instead of constant forward-scrolling, it often lets you fly freely around the level, seek out your own path, and explore the surroundings. The controls are sensitive and carry inertia, so the hummingbird really feels like a small creature fighting against the air, not like a cursor. Shots can also be strengthened and altered by collecting abilities, so progress isn't just about survival but also about what loadout you carry into the next section.

The graphics are the main reason to remember the game. The environment is drawn in soft organic shapes and lit so it looks more like an illustration from a natural-history book than the backdrop of an action game, and the add-on gets a chance to show off a color palette the Mega Drive alone couldn't manage. On top of that comes an atmospheric, moody soundtrack that gives the shooter an almost meditative tone. The result is a strange combination: a game that plays briskly yet feels calm and dreamlike, one that isn't afraid to let the player simply drift for a while.

At the time, only a fraction of players ever reached Kolibri because of the 32X's short lifespan, but those who found it generally considered it one of the most gorgeous things on the platform. Its influence on the genre therefore comes more as inspiration for later "art" shooters than as a commercial phenomenon. Today, it's one of the main reasons to return to the 32X at all — a title that neither looks nor plays like anything else from the mid-1990s. Anyone who likes games that set their own pace and aren't afraid to be fragile should give it priority over the platform's noisier titles.
sega-32x__kolibri.teaser: An unusual shooter where instead of a spaceship you control a hummingbird fighting a dark force.

sega-32x__shadow-squadron.article:
**Shadow Squadron**, released in Europe under the name Stellar Assault, is a cockpit-view space action game that tries to use the 32X for exactly what the hardware was best suited to — the smooth movement of polygonal objects in space. The player pilots a fighter craft and completes mission after mission: eliminating escorts, destroying specific components of giant ships, defending allied vessels, and finally assaulting heavily fortified targets. Two types of craft are available, with different durability and firepower, so the choice of ship changes tactics far more than is usual for this class of game. Missions have clearly defined objectives and time pressure, so there's no danger of wandering aimlessly through space — you always know what's supposed to happen and why it isn't working out.

Controls are fully free across three axes, which makes the game more of a spatial duel than a sequence of reflexive shots. What matters is managing speed and orientation: approaching a cruiser from the right angle, aiming at its generators, and disengaging in time before its defense turrets tear you apart. The image runs without textures, just in flat colors, but smoothly and with large objects that genuinely feel like they have mass around you. The sound is restrained and serious, the music holds a tense military mood, and the silence of space is broken mainly by radio chatter and explosions. That's exactly what gives rise to the atmosphere of a lonely fight far from home.

At the time, the game was seen as one of the few titles that were designed for the 32X from the ground up rather than ported from elsewhere, which helped it with reviewers — criticism targeted mainly its length and how stark the visuals are. Genre-wise, it belongs to the family of space simulators simplified for consoles, and today it's interesting precisely for how cleanly it's made. Anyone who likes space combat without unnecessary padding will find one of the platform's better games here. It also helps that the game can be finished in a few sittings, so it hasn't aged into the ailment that afflicts most period simulators today — needless length.
sega-32x__shadow-squadron.teaser: Cockpit-based space action, a technical showcase of smooth polygon movement on the 32X.

sega-32x__metal-head.article:
**Metal Head** puts the player into the cockpit of a combat robot and sends it to clear city streets of enemy machines. It's a first-person action game in a fully polygonal environment, where you walk between building blocks, search out targets according to command instructions, and progress through missions of increasing difficulty. The robot has a main weapon, secondary armament, and limited durability, so playing isn't just about pulling the trigger: you need to use buildings for cover, retreat to safety, and keep track of how much more the machine can take. Between missions there are short sequences that give the story a military-campaign framework. The machine's turning is deliberately sluggish, so the player learns to anticipate where the enemy will come from instead of relying on quickly spinning in place.

Technically, the game is one of the showcases of what the 32X could do beyond the base console: the environment is assembled from textured surfaces, which wasn't common on home consoles of the time, and movement is smooth enough to aim properly. The sprawl of the streets, however, is bought at the cost of detail — the city is rather schematic, and fog in the distance hides how far you can actually see. Sound underscores the machine's heaviness with booming footsteps and weapon blasts, while the music stays in the background and lets the noise of battle stand out. The overall feeling is slower and heavier than the brisk shooters of the era, and that's exactly the point.

At the time, Metal Head was rated as a solid demonstration of the add-on's capabilities, with reviewers valuing the technology more than the variety of missions. It contributed to the genre of mech action mainly by delivering the feeling of piloting a heavy machine on a console at a time when such games were scarce. Today it's a game for the patient — anyone who accepts its deliberate pace gets an atmospheric stroll through a concrete battlefield, while anyone expecting fast action will be disappointed. It's also interesting as evidence of where Sega's ambitions with the add-on were aimed: not toward another arcade port, but toward an original game built around what the new hardware allowed.
sega-32x__metal-head.teaser: Action from a robot's perspective in a fully polygonal city, where both cover and firepower matter.

sega-32x__space-harrier.article:
**Space Harrier** arrived on the 32X as a faithful conversion of one of Sega's most iconic arcade games. A hero with a jet pack on his back flies toward the screen through an endless fantastical landscape, shooting at everything coming at him and dodging pillars, rocks, and enemy fire. The rules are as simple as they were the year the original came out: one hit means losing a life, the path can't be slowed or stopped, and the only thing keeping the player afloat is finely honed movement and the ability to read where the shots are going to fly. Each level ends with a boss, from winged dragons to giant heads spewing projectiles. The game doesn't try to tell a story or explain where the hero came from — the whole world is simply a backdrop for the forward flight.

The add-on conversion managed to put its power to use for exactly what the game is built on — smooth, fast scaling of objects that creates the sensation of a mad flight forward. Scenery approaches without tearing, the colorful checkerboard plains rush by briskly, and the game keeps its sharp, richly colored look, complete with the typically bizarre bestiary of flying creatures. The sound picks up the arcade cabinet's famous melodies and voice samples, which still rank among the most memorable in Sega's whole catalog. It's exactly this combination of pace, color, and music that makes Space Harrier an experience whose rhythm stays in your head even after just a few minutes.

At the time, the conversion was praised as one of the most faithful home versions, though some reviewers complained that this was, after all, a mid-1980s game released in 1994. The influence of the original on the genre, meanwhile, is enormous: it defined the category of shooters viewed from behind the character, and its technology helped build Sega's reputation as the master of arcade speed. Today it's an ideal title for a short session — it has aged gracefully, because it never relied on anything but pure movement. On the 32X, it also ranks among the versions worth firing up even today, if you want to hear and see exactly why people still talk about this classic.
sega-32x__space-harrier.teaser: A faithful conversion of the iconic arcade game; a flight through a fantastical landscape with no brakes and no mercy.

sega-32x__after-burner-complete.article:
**After Burner Complete** is a conversion of the famous flight combat arcade game, in which the player sits at the stick of a fighter jet and blasts through waves of enemy aircraft. The game is pure arcade action: the plane always points forward, throttle can be briefly increased or decreased, there's a machine gun with unlimited ammo, and a limited supply of homing missiles. The crucial skill is dodging — the opponent's shots come in swarms, and the only defense is a sharp sideways evasive maneuver accompanied by a dramatic barrel roll of the whole scene. Weapons are restocked between missions, and the pace gradually escalates all the way to the final levels, where there's no moment of rest left. Missiles can't be fired recklessly either, since the supply only refills between sections, and in dense waves locking onto several targets at once is the only way out.

The 32X version draws on the add-on's power exactly where it's needed: the picture stays smooth even when dozens of objects sweep across the screen, plane scaling looks convincing, and the fast horizon rotation during dodges doesn't drop the frame rate. Compared to the plain Mega Drive version, it's a noticeable leap in both density of action and color depth. The music takes over the famous rock themes from the arcade original, and together with the voice callouts and engine roar it creates just the right atmosphere of a cinematic dogfight that the game never takes too seriously.

At the time, the title was seen as a good showcase of what the 32X was suited for — fast arcade conversions — and also a reminder that the add-on received many older games in new clothes. In the genre, the original ranks among the pillars of the so-called super scaler arcade games that Sega made famous. Today, After Burner plays exactly like it did back then: a few minutes of intense trigger-mashing that's all about reflexes, and that's exactly why it's so replayable. More experienced players can also crank up the difficulty and chase high scores, turning a short game into a discipline for weeks of practice.
sega-32x__after-burner-complete.teaser: An arcade conversion of the flight classic, where a sharp evasive maneuver is your only defense.

sega-32x__mortal-kombat-ii.article:
**Mortal Kombat II** was one of the most anticipated conversions of the mid-nineties, and it arrived on the 32X in a version that tried to stay as close to the arcade original as possible. The one-on-one fighting is built on digitized actors, a set of special moves for each fighter, and the famous finishing fatalities that let the winner dispatch the loser. The character roster grew compared to the first game, and hidden characters were added that can be found by fulfilling special conditions. The gameplay is tough and uncompromising: blocks, sweeps, jumps, and knowledge of the input commands decide the outcome before you've even had time to look around. Anyone who wants to advance through the tournament must learn not only their own commands but, above all, how to read what the opponent is doing, because the computer punishes every unnecessary jump without mercy.

The add-on gave the conversion more memory and power, which shows above all in the size and smoothness of the characters, in background details like spectators in the stands or the swaying bridge, and in sound that's richer than on older hardware. The digitized graphics keep their typical slightly muted colors, but that's exactly what belongs to the series, and together with the dark arenas and pounding music it creates an atmosphere no one else had at the time. The controls fit a six-button pad considerably better than a three-button one, so the player's equipment matters here.

At the time, the game was rated as one of the best home versions of the second installment, though the comparison to the arcade never came out completely without losses. The series' influence on the genre and on the whole debate about violence in games is well known, and the second installment is generally considered the peak of its first era. Today it's a title best played with two people — alone against the computer you'll run into a difficulty that spares no one, not even veterans. For 32X owners it was one of the few big licensed titles, and for that reason alone it remains one of the first things people try on the add-on.
sega-32x__mortal-kombat-ii.teaser: A conversion of the famous fighter as close to the arcade cabinet as possible, complete with the infamous fatalities.

sega-32x__wwf-wrestlemania-arcade-game.article:
**WWF WrestleMania: The Arcade Game** isn't a wrestling simulation but a fighting game disguised as a ring match. The stars of the WWF of the time square off here with attacks that treat physics as a mere suggestion: an opponent can be set on fire, spun to an unbelievable height, or slammed down with a blow that makes the whole screen sink. Progress runs through a series of matches against individual opponents up to a final showdown, and besides regular moves each wrestler has a set of special commands that need to be learned. Classic wrestling elements like pins and the three-count remain, just surrounded by comic-book mayhem. The pace is therefore closer to a straight-up brawler than a wrestling match: blocks, jumps, and quick combos of strikes work the same way as in other arcade fighting games.

Visually, the game relies on digitized figures of real wrestlers, who are bigger, smoother, and more colorful on the 32X than in versions for weaker consoles of the time. The crowd moves, the ring shakes, and strong effects fire off on hits. The audio side leans on the commentator's calls, the wrestlers' shouts, and blows that carry surprising weight; the music takes a back seat and lets the show shine. That very exaggeration is the main asset — the game never takes itself seriously for a moment, and that's exactly why it's still fun today.

At the time, the conversion was received warmly as one of the better versions of the arcade original, with reservations that the roster of wrestlers is fairly small and that solo play quickly slides into repetition. Its main contribution to the genre was showing a way to turn licensed wrestling into brisk arcade action instead of a slow simulation. Today it's an ideal game for two people on one console — plenty of fun can still be squeezed, years later, out of the gap between what really happens in the ring and what the wrestlers perform here. Nostalgia is further fueled by the fact that the developers cast the era's stars in their most famous costumes, so the game also works as a moving memento of a time when wrestling was at the height of its popularity.
sega-32x__wwf-wrestlemania-arcade-game.teaser: Wrestling as a fighting game; physics here is merely a suggestion, fiery moves included.

sega-32x__tempo.article:
**Tempo** is a colorful platformer in which music takes center stage, and the hero is a tall, skinny grasshopper-like creature with his own band. The player moves through levels built around musical motifs — from sheet-music staves through concert stages to environments resembling the inside of musical instruments — jumping, attacking, and collecting items that alter the character's abilities. Besides classic running and jumping, the game features moving platforms, bounce elements, and segments where you need to progress in rhythm. A companion character flies around the player and helps depending on the situation, which gives the gameplay a fresh dynamic. The levels are also structured vertically and reward exploration, so it pays to try paths that run against the main direction of progress too.

Visually, this is one of the add-on's most striking titles. The game relies on large, expressively animated characters, a rich color palette, and layered backgrounds that clearly show the 32X had a noticeable edge over the Mega Drive in the number of displayable colors. The main hero's animation has its own sense of humor — stretching, hopping, comically flopping down — and it comes paired with a musical score that's essential to the game; the tunes aren't just backdrop but set the mood and pace of each level. The atmosphere is light, playful, and slightly zany, close to the Japanese mascot platformers of the era.

At the time, Tempo reached a rather small audience, since the 32X had a short lifespan and the game came out when interest in the add-on had already faded. Reviews praised the concept and visual side, with reservations aimed at the difficulty and occasionally imprecise jumping. It brought to the genre one of the first attempts to build a platformer around a musical theme, a direction that would later be developed elsewhere. Today it's a charming curiosity worth seeing for its style and a mascot unlike any other. Among collectors, it's also one of the titles that make an otherwise short 32X library seem more interesting than the number of released games would suggest.
sega-32x__tempo.teaser: A colorful platformer with a musical theme; the hero is a grasshopper-like musician with his own band.

sg-1000__congo-bongo.article:
**Congo Bongo** accompanied the SG-1000's launch and immediately showed where Sega was headed with its eight-bit hardware. It's a home conversion of an arcade game in which a hunter sets out to track a gorilla named Bongo after the ape burned his trousers at a campfire. Instead of the usual side view, the game offers a pseudo-isometric perspective, thanks to which each screen looks like a spatial diorama built from ramps, platforms, and pits. Controls stay simple — movement in four directions and a jump — yet it's precisely the combination of the slanted view with the need to judge distance precisely that turns Congo Bongo into a game where you have to learn to read space in a completely different way than platformers of the time had accustomed you to.

The structure faithfully follows the arcade original. You progress through several standalone screens where Bongo pelts you with coconuts, boulders tumble down from cliffs, snakes slither along the ground, and in one section you must hop across the backs of hippos and fish in the middle of a river. Each screen has its own logic and rhythm, so the game works more as a set of short, repeatedly honed challenges than a continuous adventure. The home version had to cut back on color and background detail compared to the arcade, and some animations are noticeably rougher, but the isometric illusion holds together and the main character's movement stays readable. The audio relies on simple melodic loops and punchy effects that stick in memory just as reliably as the difficulty of the later screens.

At release, it was one of the flagship titles of the new console, and for SG-1000 owners it was proof that Sega could bring home some of the arcade atmosphere. The game feels raw and merciless today, since it has no saving and no in-between steps and punishes mistakes instantly, yet it's also an interesting document of how the isometric perspective fought its way into video games long before later titles popularized it. For today's player it's a short, sharp experience where the goal is more about trying for a better result than reaching an ending.
sg-1000__congo-bongo.teaser: A home port of an arcade game with a pseudo-isometric view; a hunter chases a gorilla over burnt pants.

sg-1000__zaxxon.article:
**Zaxxon** is one of Sega's most famous arcade games, and its arrival on the SG-1000 was a major event for console owners. The original 1982 arcade machine became famous for taking a classic shooter and placing it in a slanted isometric view, in which the player controls not just side-to-side movement but also flight altitude. That altitude is the whole joke of the game.
