This creates a good old game of rock-paper-scissors, where success depends on the order in which the player takes on the fights and on learning each boss's movement patterns. The core moveset stays unchanged: sliding, a charged shot, and precise jumping.

Porting the games to the Neo Geo Pocket Color required some compromises. The characters are smaller and the arenas narrower than in the arcade originals, leaving less room to dodge, and some attacks have to be avoided differently than in the original. Even so, the game stays smooth and the controls precise, which is the most important thing for platforming action built on pixel-perfect jumps. The visuals benefit from a bright color palette and clean outlines, which keep projectiles clearly visible even on the small screen. The soundtrack reuses familiar melodies from the series and, in chiptune form, keeps their energetic, rhythmic character.

The game was released only in Japan, so Western players could only get it through imports, and among collectors it's one of the more sought-after items in the library. At the time it was seen as a decent port that nonetheless couldn't replace the original arcade versions. Today it's interesting mainly as one of the few titles on the platform that doesn't come from its manufacturer's own stable, and as proof that the concept of continuous boss fights suits short handheld sessions well. Anyone who likes the classic entries in the series will find here their concentrated, considerably tougher essence. The Japanese text barely gets in the way of playing, since the whole substance takes place in the arenas and the menus are clear even without knowledge of the language.
ngpc__rockman-battle-and-fighters.teaser: A combination of two arcade boss battles against Mega Man; winning carries a weapon into the next fight.

ngpc__sonic-hedgehog-pocket-adventure.article:
**Sonic the Hedgehog: Pocket Adventure** is an unusual case: a fast Sega platformer for the Neo Geo Pocket Color, made by the console manufacturer itself. Yet the result doesn't feel like a licensed side project, but like a full-fledged handheld Sonic. The levels follow the building principles of the classic entries, meaning long slopes, loops, springs, and hidden paths both above and below, and the player runs through them across two acts capped off with a battle against Doctor Eggman. There's also the classic ring collecting as protection from hits and the ability to curl into a ball while running to gain speed from a standstill.

Technically, it's one of the platform's most impressive titles. Scrolling stays smooth even at high speed, the sprites have enough animation frames to make running feel snappy, and each level's color palette clearly distinguishes the different zones. The game also includes special stages, unlocked once certain conditions are met, where emeralds are collected, plus a bonus matching-pairs minigame that serves as a break from the action. The music rearranges well-known series motifs and, even in its economical chiptune form, keeps their upbeat, dance-inflected melodic character, so the atmosphere of the classic Sonic games remains untouched.

At the time, the game was praised as one of the main reasons to own the console, and it was often cited as proof that the Neo Geo Pocket Color had a better controller for platformers than the competition. In retrospect it's usually ranked among the best handheld Sonic games ever, putting it in the company of later entries on other platforms. Today it still works well precisely because it doesn't attempt anything groundbreaking, focusing instead on pure movement, pace, and rediscovering shortcuts. For players who want to see what the console could do beyond fighting games, this is the ideal first stop. It's also interesting as evidence of what was happening at the time Sega was giving up its own hardware and its mascot started appearing on platforms made by former competitors.
ngpc__sonic-hedgehog-pocket-adventure.teaser: A fast platformer made by Sega itself for a rival console; a full-fledged portable Sonic game.

ngpc__snk-vs-capcom-card-fighters-clash.article:
**SNK vs. Capcom: Card Fighters Clash** took the then-fashionable idea of card battles and combined it with characters from the two biggest fighting-game makers, creating one of the most beloved titles in the entire Neo Geo Pocket Color library. The game was released in two versions, each built around one of the two houses' cards, and players were meant to trade content over the link cable. The core combat is simple yet tactical: characters with attack and defense values are placed on the table, supported by action cards, and the goal is to bring the opponent's points down to zero. Managing a limited number of actions per turn is essential, since strong cards can't be played without preparation.

A whole story-driven game is built around the battles. The main character walks around town, talks to other players, accepts challenges, buys card packs, and advances through tournaments, so collecting and tuning a deck has a clear purpose and rhythm. The collection numbers in the hundreds of cards illustrated with well-known fighters from Ryu and Chun-Li to Terry and Iori, and the joy of discovering new names is exactly what keeps the game moving forward. The visuals are clean, with cutely drawn character portraits, and the music keeps a cheerful, pop-inflected tone that matches the whole story's lighthearted mood.

The game was highly praised at the time and still shows up near the top of lists of the best card games on handheld consoles. Its simple yet deep system became the benchmark against which later handheld card games were measured, and the brand even got a sequel on a different platform. Today it's probably the best choice for a player who wants to spend dozens of hours with the Neo Geo Pocket Color, not just short sessions. Anyone who enjoys deck-building will find a surprisingly modern-feeling classic here. And because the two versions contain different cards, the game still makes sense played as a pair today, where trading and complementing each other's collections still has plenty to offer.
ngpc__snk-vs-capcom-card-fighters-clash.teaser: A card battle featuring characters from both SNK and Capcom; two versions made for trading content via cable.

ngpc__snk-vs-capcom-card-fighters-clash-.article:
**SNK vs. Capcom: Card Fighters' Clash 2: Expand Edition** is a sequel that came out right at the very end of the Neo Geo Pocket Color's life, which is why only a fraction of players outside Japan ever got to it. That's a shame, because it's an expansion of the first game in the best sense of the word. The framework stays the same, meaning traveling through a world of card tournaments, collecting new cards, and gradually building a deck, but the game adds a larger number of cards, a more elaborate structure of opponents, and a longer campaign. It was again released in two cartridge variants, depending on which side of the SNK-versus-Capcom rivalry you prefer.

The battles keep the predecessor's briskness. Fighters with attack and defense values clash on the table, joined by action cards that alter the rules of a round, and by managing a resource that allows the strongest characters to be played. The second entry works with a better-balanced deck-building system and offers more situations where you need to sacrifice an immediate advantage for a plan several turns ahead. The collecting layer is deeper too, since there are noticeably more new characters from both universes, some of which can only be obtained by fulfilling specific conditions or by trading over the link cable.

On the technical side, it's the same friendly drawing style with scaled-down figures, only with a richer range of motifs and a clearer interface that better handles the larger collection. The music again relies on light, catchy loops that never overpower focus on the game. At the time, the title stayed rather in the shadow of the first game, since it arrived just as the platform was practically finished on Western markets. Among fans, though, it earned a reputation as the more refined version of the same idea, and today it's considered one of the true high points of handheld card games, albeit at the cost of high collector value for the original cartridges. Anyone who finished the first game and is looking for more of the same with better balance will find exactly what they need here, they just have to deal with the Japanese text, which fortunately acts more as a minor detail than an obstacle for navigating the menus.
ngpc__snk-vs-capcom-card-fighters-clash-.teaser: A late sequel to the card game classic that reached only a handful of players outside Japan.

ngpc__biomotor-unitron.article:
**Biomotor Unitron** was, for Neo Geo Pocket Color owners, the first proof that a full-fledged Japanese RPG could run on their console. The player becomes a young master who builds and upgrades combat machines called unitrons and sets out with them into underground labyrinths to complete jobs. The structure is simple and addictive: in town you accept a job, top up your equipment, descend into a dungeon, fight your way to the goal, and return with loot and money for further upgrades. It's exactly this cycle that makes the game ideal company for both short and long sessions.

The core of the fun lies in building the machine. A unitron is assembled from individual parts, meaning a body, limbs, a head, and weapons, and every combination changes not just the stats but also the available attacks. Battles are turn-based and take place in a small arena, where distance to the opponent matters, so choosing between a melee and a ranged weapon has an immediate effect. The blacksmith in town can upgrade and fuse parts, turning every visit into a small optimization puzzle. Dungeons are generated, which ensures the game doesn't run out of content, but it also means much of its charm rests on your appetite for endlessly tuning your own build.

Visually it's clean and pleasant work, with expressive character portraits in dialogues and clear battle scenes where the machines can be seen in full glory. The music alternates calmer town themes with tenser loops underground and keeps a good mood going even after hours of play. At the time, the game was seen as an important genre foundation for the young platform, and as a title showing that SNK's handheld console wasn't aimed only at fighting-game fans. Today it feels a bit plain, but its core, the constant improvement of your own robot, belongs to the kind of fun that doesn't age. The game also handles interruptions well, since it can be paused after every descent underground, an advantage a player of a handheld title appreciates from day one. It can last for dozens of hours without demanding them all at once.
ngpc__biomotor-unitron.teaser: The first full-fledged JRPG on the Neo Geo Pocket Color; you build combat machines for the dungeons.

ngpc__densetsu-no-ogre-battle-gaiden-zen.article:
**Densetsu no Ogre Battle Gaiden: Zenobia no Ouji** is one of the biggest surprises in the Neo Geo Pocket Color library, since it brings the acclaimed Ogre Battle strategy series to a handheld console without any substantial compromises. The player commands an army made up of smaller units, sent across the map to liberate enemy towns and fortresses. The campaign keeps the series' typical tone, meaning serious fantasy with political intrigue, where conflicts don't revolve around simple good versus evil but around the legitimacy of rule, loyalty, and the cost of liberating a country.

At its core, the system is real-time strategy with a pause for decision-making. Units move across the map on their own, and when they encounter an enemy, the game switches to a battle in which an exchange of attacks plays out automatically based on unit formation. That formation is the main puzzle: positioning characters in front and back rows determines which attacks they can use, and individual fighters' classes evolve according to their actions and character. The game also tracks the player's reputation and how they treat liberated towns, which affects the population's support as well as the shape of the ending. A careless campaign can therefore end in a victory nobody is happy about.

Shrinking the game down to a handheld format required more economical graphics, but the maps stayed readable and the unit portraits kept the series' style. The music works with solemn march-like themes that retain the necessary dignity even in chiptune form. The game was released only in Japan, so at the time it stayed off the radar of Western audiences, and among collectors it's prized to this day. For genre fans it's a remarkable proof that large-scale strategy can be handled even on a screen a few centimeters across, and one of the most valuable titles in the whole platform's library. The language barrier is the only real obstacle, since deciding the fate of towns and the development of units rests on text. Anyone who overcomes it gets a full-fledged strategy game that, at the time, had practically no equal on handheld consoles.
ngpc__densetsu-no-ogre-battle-gaiden-zen.teaser: The acclaimed Ogre Battle strategy series brought to a handheld with barely any compromises.

ngpc__puzzle-bobble-mini.article:
**Puzzle Bobble Mini**, released in Europe under the name Bust-A-Move Pocket, is one of those cases where the game concept and hardware fit together perfectly. The rules are known even to people who've never held a controller: you shoot colored bubbles from the bottom of the screen into a cluster above, and once three or more of the same color come together, they disappear. The magic lies in the fact that everything hanging beneath them falls too, so a single well-aimed shot can clear half the screen. Meanwhile the player is under constant pressure, since the ceiling keeps slowly lowering.

Controls on the Neo Geo Pocket Color benefit from the microswitch controller, which clicks into eight directions and allows aiming with pleasant precision. The key skill remains bouncing bubbles off the walls, which lets you reach seemingly inaccessible spots behind overhangs, and planning ahead based on which color comes next. The game offers a progressing campaign with dozens of layouts, an arcade mode for a quick round, and above all two-player combat over the link cable, where cleared bubbles get sent into the opponent's field. It's precisely this versus mode that made the series a classic in arcades, and it works just as well on the handheld.

Visually it's clean, vividly colorful work, where individual bubbles are perfectly distinguishable even on the small screen, an absolute requirement for this kind of game. It's accompanied by cheerful, catchy melodies that build on the series' musical motifs. At the time, it was received as one of the best puzzle games on the handheld-console market and as an ideal title for short moments of play. Today, practically nothing about it has aged, since its rules need no modernizing, and together with a handful of other puzzle games it's part of the reason the console is so often described as a great travel companion. The best part is realizing that one round never stays just one: you always feel the next shot will be the right one, and half an hour slips by in the meantime. That's exactly why the game keeps showing up in every list of the platform's best.
ngpc__puzzle-bobble-mini.teaser: Known in Europe as Bust-A-Move Pocket; a concept clear even to people who've never held a controller.

ngpc__magical-drop-pocket.article:
**Magical Drop Pocket** is the handheld version of one of the fastest-paced puzzle series of the nineties, and on the Neo Geo Pocket Color it became a game tailor-made for short but intense matches. The concept differs from most of the competition in that the player doesn't stack anything from top to bottom, but instead controls a little character below the playing field who can pull marbles from the bottom of the columns toward himself and then toss them elsewhere. Three matching colors stacked together vanish, taking everything that was resting on top of them with them, so a well-prepared move can trigger an avalanche.

The difference from calmer puzzle games lies in the pace. Magical Drop plays out at lightning speed, rows of marbles are pushed down from above, and the player has to decide instantly, often within a fraction of a second. The reward is chain reactions that dump extra rows into the opponent's field and can end a match within seconds. The game offers a campaign against computer opponents inspired by tarot cards, a survival mode, and a two-player duel, which is clearly the most entertaining form of the whole concept. The need to keep track of the entire field while acting quickly creates the pleasantly stressful rhythm the series became famous for.

Visually, the game relies on bold colors and cartoonish characters with big eyes who comment on the match with grimaces. On the small screen the marbles remain clearly distinguishable, which is essential for such a fast game. The music is energetic and helps keep up the frantic pace. At the time, the game was regarded as one of the better conversions of the arcade puzzle classic to handheld hardware, appreciated especially by players who found traditional puzzle games too slow-paced. Today it's still one of the fastest puzzle games you can carry in your pocket, and its main strength, the instant readability of its rules, hasn't aged a bit. At the same time, it's a game that's cruel to deliberate players, since a moment's hesitation is punished immediately. Anyone who gets used to the rush gets a puzzle game with such pace that most of the competition looks like a leisurely stroll next to it.
ngpc__magical-drop-pocket.teaser: A brisk puzzle series; you don't collect the balls from above, you pull them down from below with a character.

ngpc__puyo-pop.article:
**Puyo Pop** brought one of the most famous Japanese puzzle series to the Neo Geo Pocket Color and proved that a two-player duel of stacking colorful blob creatures works just as well on a small screen as it does in arcades. The rules are simple: pairs of puyos fall from above, the player rotates and places them, and once four matching colors touch, they vanish. Everything that was resting above them falls down, and if that creates another group, a chain reaction begins. Chains are the whole essence of the game, and they separate beginners from those who know what they're doing.

The competitive logic is merciless yet beautifully readable. For every link in the chain, the opponent's field gets flooded with transparent nuisance puyos, which can't be removed directly, only by clearing a colored group next to them. A match is therefore a tug-of-war in which both players try to build the longest possible cascade before the opponent's buries them first. This creates a tension that classic puzzle games simply don't offer: the screen fills up, palms sweat, and one badly placed piece decides everything. The campaign against computer opponents serves as practice, but the game finds its true purpose in a duel between two people over the link cable.

The presentation is lighthearted and colorful, with cute creatures reacting to events with facial expressions, and a clear split screen for keeping an eye on the opponent's field. The tunes are cheerful and deliberately simple, so they don't distract from the ever-increasing pace. At the time, the game was seen as an obvious staple of any handheld console's library and one of the reasons to buy a link cable for the Neo Geo Pocket Color. Today it's still one of the best-balanced competitive puzzle games there is, and a good example of how little is needed for a perfect design. Learning to build a chain of four or more links takes a long time, and that's exactly where the game's longevity hides: you'll understand the rules in a minute, but you can spend years getting better at them. The solo mode, meanwhile, mainly serves as a warm-up before the real duel.
ngpc__puyo-pop.teaser: The famous puzzle series with colorful blobs; the two-player duel works even on a small screen.

ngpc__baseball-stars-color.article:
**Baseball Stars Color** carries on one of SNK's oldest sports franchises, bringing it to a handheld console in a form that bets on speed and clarity rather than simulation depth. Baseball is played here in a lighthearted way, with short matches, easy-to-read rules, and an emphasis on instant fun. The camera switches between the pitcher's view, the batting view, and following the action in the field, so even someone who knows only the bare minimum about the American bat-and-ball sport will find their bearings within a few innings.

The game system is built on a simple yet pleasantly tactical duel between pitcher and batter. The pitcher chooses the type of pitch and its placement, the batter tries to read the trajectory and time the swing, and a small mistake is enough to send the ball straight into a fielder's glove. In the field, the player handles positioning and decides where to throw to stop the opponent's advance, which leads to the classic tense moments in the final stretch before the base. The game offers exhibition matches, a season mode, and a two-player duel over the link cable, clearly the most entertaining option, since bluffing on pitch selection only works against a live opponent.

The presentation makes good use of the color screen: the field is clearly distinguished, the characters are shrunk into a cartoonish style, and the animations for both batting and running have a pleasant snap to them. Sound fills out the action with short fanfares and stadium ambience that feels surprisingly evocative on a handheld console. At the time, it was a solid addition to the sports section of the library, appreciated especially by players looking for something other than fighting games and puzzle titles. Today it's a game that can't withstand comparison with the big sports simulations, but that's exactly why it still holds up: it offers a quick match lasting just a few minutes, understandable at a glance, with enough tension in the final innings. The season mode also gives matches purpose, since you track the team's form and the standings, so even a lost game carries weight. For fans of the series, it's a pleasant reminder of what the franchise once captivated players with on older SNK consoles.
ngpc__baseball-stars-color.teaser: SNK's oldest sports franchise in handheld form; speed over simulation depth.

ngpc__neo-turf-masters.article:
**Neo Turf Masters** is the handheld version of the golf classic players knew from Neo Geo arcade machines, and it's one of the most enjoyable sports games on the Neo Geo Pocket Color. The philosophy is simple: no lengthy simulation with dozens of parameters, just brisk arcade golf where a single hole takes a minute and a whole round can be played on the way home. The player chooses from several golfers with different attributes, plays through various courses, and tries to get as far under par as possible, or beat computer opponents in a tournament.

At its core is the classic three-press system. The first press starts the power meter, the second confirms the power, and the third fine-tunes the accuracy of the shot, with a mistake on the last step sending the ball into the rough or a bunker. On top of that comes club selection, reading the slope of the green, and above all accounting for the wind, which on some holes can turn a sure shot into a disaster. It's precisely this combination of simple controls and depth of decision-making that keeps the game interesting long after you've picked up the basic rhythm. A two-player duel over the link cable turns calm golf into pleasantly spiteful fun.

Visually, the game cleverly handles the small screen: the course is displayed clearly, with grass, bunkers, and water all clearly distinguished, and before every shot you can check the hole's layout map. The sound is understated, with soothing melodies and the distinctive sound of a well-struck ball, which accounts for half the fun. At the time, the game was seen as a fine conversion of a beloved arcade classic and as a title that offered something relaxing on a handheld console. Today it's one of the games that best demonstrates why arcade golf was so popular: you learn the rules in a minute, yet you can still spend weeks working toward the perfect round. The handheld's battery life also suits the play style perfectly, since round after round goes by without ever needing to hunt for a charger. Of all the sports titles on the platform, this is the one people come back to most often, and most gladly.
ngpc__neo-turf-masters.teaser: Handheld golf from the Neo Geo arcade machines; a hole a minute, a full round on the way home.

ngpc__pocket-tennis-color.article:
**Pocket Tennis Color** is the color version of one of the first sports games for SNK's handheld console, and it's one of the titles that makes the best use of the Neo Geo Pocket Color's microswitch controller. Tennis is played here from a behind-the-player camera, with brisk rallies and no unnecessary complexity. You pick from a roster of characters with different strengths, one faster on their feet, another stronger on serve, and set out on a tournament run in which you gradually run into tougher opponents.

The controls are built on a simple foundation that nonetheless rewards timing. Depending on which button and directional input you use, you choose between a flat shot, topspin, or a drop shot, with the exact moment of contact and the position you manage to reach playing a decisive role. Matches aren't about mashing buttons, but about gradually pushing your opponent into a corner and looking for an opening for a winning shot. Besides the tournament, the game offers quick matches and a two-player duel over the link cable, where the quality of the rally rhythm truly shines. The short length of a single set is a perfect fit for playing in a waiting room.

Graphically it's clean work, with a clearly readable court and smooth movement animation, which matters more in tennis than fine detail. The color screen helps distinguish the surfaces of the different courts, and the ball stays visible even during fast rallies. The sound stays grounded, with hits, an umpire's commentary in the form of short calls, and unobtrusive menu music. At the time, it was one of the main proofs that the Neo Geo Pocket Color could do sports too, and the game was praised especially for its precise controls. Today it comes across as pleasantly uncomplicated tennis that you can switch on any time and play a few games without it demanding anything from you. The roster of characters with differing strengths gives you a reason to try the tournament again with someone else and look for a style that suits you. Next to more demanding sports simulations, it feels simple today, but it does its job, entertaining you for a few minutes, without a moment's hesitation.
ngpc__pocket-tennis-color.teaser: Brisk tennis making full use of the Neo Geo Pocket Color's microswitch controller.

wonderswan__final-fantasy.article:
**Final Fantasy** returned on the WonderSwan Color as a completely redrawn version of the very first entry in the series. The story of the four Warriors of Light, who arrive in a world with fading crystals, stayed the same at its core, but everything around it went through a thorough modernization. At the start, the player assembles a party from six classes, from the Fighter through the Black and White Mage to the Thief, and heads out into an open world where a ship, a canoe, and eventually even an airship gradually become available. Battles are turn-based, viewed from the side, and it still holds true that the target of an attack is chosen in advance, so the way you plan out a whole round carries real weight, and a lapse in attention can send the party right back to the last save.

The overhaul touched mainly the visual side. In place of the rough eight-bit sprites came characters and enemies drawn in the style of later series entries, towns and dungeons got more detailed tiles, and battle backgrounds change depending on the environment the player is currently in. The menus were laid out more clearly, the controls account for both orientations of the console, and compared to the original, the game smoothed over some of its harshest spots, making it considerably friendlier than the repeated-death machine of the eight-bit era. Nobuo Uematsu's music appears in a new arrangement that the WonderSwan's sound chip handles surprisingly cleanly, and the famous prologue theme still carries its power even in this form.

At the time, this was more than just a remake. Square stood outside Nintendo's fold at that point, and its support for Bandai's console was the main reason the WonderSwan Color managed to establish itself in Japan at all; the return of the first Final Fantasy to a handheld machine was the flagship of that whole strategy. The WonderSwan version also became the basis for a later PlayStation compilation and, indirectly, for further ports to more modern hardware, so its influence reaches far beyond the console itself. Today it's one of the most enjoyable ways to trace the roots of the whole series: archaic enough that its era is unmistakable, yet polished enough that it doesn't play like a museum piece.
wonderswan__final-fantasy.teaser: A redrawn remake of the very first game; an open world and six classes in the party.

wonderswan__final-fantasy-ii.article:
**Final Fantasy II** arrived on the WonderSwan Color a year after the first game and brought with it the strangest progression system the series has ever had. Instead of experience levels, individual abilities improve according to how the player uses them: whoever swings a sword a lot gets better with swords, whoever takes hits builds up hit points, and whoever casts spells raises their level. On top of that comes the story of four young people from a city destroyed by the imperial army, and a keyword system that lets you talk to characters almost like in a text adventure, prying keywords out of them that open up further paths.

The remake sticks to the same philosophy as the previous entry. The graphics were redrawn in a more detailed style, character portraits gained more personality, the environments are more colorful and readable on the small screen, and the interface was rearranged so you can navigate your inventory and spells quickly even while playing on a tram. But the original's harshness stayed too: the dungeons are full of dead-end rooms, random encounters come often, and some progression segments reward patience more than cleverness. The musical score, including the famous rebellion march theme, is among the first things players remember from the console.

The second game was always seen as the black sheep of the family, and it was precisely the WonderSwan Color version that helped its reputation the most. Up to that point, practically nobody outside Japan had played it officially, and it was this version that became the springboard for later releases on other platforms, which brought the game to a wider audience. Looking back, it's clear just how much of an experiment FFII was, one that influenced the later SaGa series more than the main Final Fantasy line. Today it's worth trying mainly for how boldly it goes against the genre's established rules, and for a story that, as the first in the series, didn't spare its characters and wasn't afraid to let them die.
wonderswan__final-fantasy-ii.teaser: Forget levels – characters grow here based on what they actually do in battle.

wonderswan__final-fantasy-iv.article:
**Final Fantasy IV** was the last major stop of the series on the WonderSwan Color, and at the same time the most ambitious effort Square brought to this console. The story of the Dark Knight Cecil, who defies his king's orders and seeks a way to make peace with his own past, ranks among the strongest narratives of the sixteen-bit era. The player travels across an entire world, from desert kingdoms through the underground realm of the dwarves all the way to the Moon, and the party keeps changing throughout: characters arrive, leave, sacrifice themselves, and return, so tactics have to adapt to practically every chapter.

The battle system is built on ATB, meaning flowing gauges that determine who gets a turn and when. That's exactly what makes the fights tense, since time keeps running while you think through the menus, and strong bosses punish hesitation. The WonderSwan Color version is based on the Japanese original and adds new graphics, recolored environments, and slightly refined menus; character sprites were redrawn in a more detailed style, and the battle scenes look downright good on the small screen. The sound is naturally limited by the console's capabilities, but pieces like Golbez's theme or the airship hymn still hold onto their atmosphere even in this form.

At the time, it was proof that a handheld console could handle a full-fledged, major JRPG without trimmed-down content, and for WonderSwan owners it was one of the main reasons to buy the device. The fourth game's influence on the genre is hard to overstate: it established a storytelling style where characters have their own motivations and fixed roles within the party instead of freely assignable classes, and most Japanese RPGs of the nineties followed in that direction afterward. Today it plays surprisingly briskly, since the pace is fast, the dungeons aren't needlessly long, and the story never stalls. If someone wants to play just one single game on the WonderSwan, this is a serious contender.
wonderswan__final-fantasy-iv.teaser: The most ambitious WonderSwan JRPG; the story of the knight Cecil is among the strongest in the series.

wonderswan__romancing-saga.article:
**Romancing SaGa** ranks among the most open-ended games you can play on a handheld console. The player chooses one of eight heroes, each with their own starting environment and reason for setting out into the world, and from that point on nobody holds their hand. The continent is open, quests can be completed in any order or skipped entirely, party members are recruited in taverns and ports, and the main plot about gods and fate only comes together from what the player discovers on their own. This so-called free scenario system was, at the time the series began, something that practically didn't exist anywhere else.

Character progression is just as untraditional. There are no experience levels; instead, individual stats increase after battles, and new techniques suddenly appear in combat like a flash of inspiration, when a character mid-attack figures out on their own how to turn an ordinary slash into something stronger. This mechanism turns every battle into a small lottery of tension and rewards experimenting with weapons. The WonderSwan Color remake builds on the foundations of the sixteen-bit era release, redraws it in color, and adjusts the interface for two screen orientations; the world has a cold, slightly harsh edge, and Kenji Ito's music lends the journey a gravity you wouldn't expect from such a small device.

At the time, it was one of the titles that showed Square didn't treat the WonderSwan as a dumping ground but as a full-fledged platform. The SaGa series has a reputation for being demanding and uncompromising, and this entry confirms it: the player easily gets tangled up, runs into enemies far beyond their strength, and has to learn from mistakes. Precisely because of that, though, it has aged better than many of its more linear contemporaries. Freedom, nonlinearity, and the emphasis that the world keeps moving regardless of the player are common ambitions for big RPGs today, and Romancing SaGa was already doing this on just a few megabits of memory. The only real obstacle remaining is Japanese, because without understanding the characters' hints, the player navigates the world by instinct and map alone. Whoever gets past that barrier gets a game that can be completed eight times and looks different every time.
wonderswan__romancing-saga.teaser: An incredibly open JRPG with no hand-holding – eight heroes, quests tackled in any order.

wonderswan__makaitoushi-saga.article:
**Makaitoushi SaGa** is a remake of the game that kicked off the entire SaGa series on the Game Boy and was released abroad under the name Final Fantasy Legend. The basic idea is simple yet oddly compelling: in the middle of the world stands a giant tower said to lead to heaven, and the heroes decide to climb it. Each floor is its own separate world with its own rules, so the game drops from a classic fantasy setting straight into a post-apocalyptic city or a realm of gods. The player assembles a party from three races: humans grow stronger through purchased potions, mutants gain abilities at random, and monsters transform based on the meat they devour after battles.

Working with characters is therefore completely different from a typical JRPG. Weapons have a limited number of uses and get consumed, the right pieces of meat need to be found among enemies to trigger a monster's transformation, and there's never any certainty whether a mutant will get a useful spell or something useless. The WonderSwan Color version redrew the whole world in color, added more detailed sprites and a clearer interface, but kept the short, tight structure of the original game, which can be completed in a matter of hours. Nobuo Uematsu's music remains recognizable, and the bizarre transitions between worlds give it a peculiar dreamlike atmosphere.

At the time, it served as a reminder of where the whole offshoot came from. The original game was one of the first true RPGs on a handheld console ever and showed that the genre needed neither a big screen nor much memory. The remake made it accessible to a new generation and also confirmed that Square took the WonderSwan seriously. Today, Makaitoushi SaGa is a great entry point into the SaGa world for anyone put off by the length and sprawl of the later entries: it has the same uncompromising nature and experimental systems, but fits into a single long weekend. Its peculiar charm doesn't lie in the story, which is told sparsely and in hints, but in how unexpectedly the rules of the world change floor by floor, and how freely the player assembles their own party from beings that don't resemble each other at all.
wonderswan__makaitoushi-saga.teaser: A remake of the game that started the SaGa series; a tower where every floor is its own world.

wonderswan__front-mission.article:
**Front Mission** brought the hardest thing you could ask for on a handheld console to the WonderSwan Color: a sprawling tactical RPG with combat robots and a story that has little to do with heroism. The conflict on Huffman Island, where two great powers clash, is seen through the eyes of mercenaries whose lives the war has torn apart, and the narrative keeps a raw military tone full of political intrigue, betrayal, and people fighting for money. At the time, this was a noticeably more mature theme than what fans of Japanese RPGs were used to.

The combat takes place on a square grid, where machines called wanzers move around, take cover behind terrain, and target specific parts of the opponent: the torso, head, arms, or legs. Destroying the legs limits movement, losing an arm ends fire from that weapon, and so it's possible to defeat an even stronger opponent by aiming at the right spot. Between missions, machines are assembled from parts, weapons change, and pilots learn new skills, making preparation almost as important a part of the game as the battles themselves. The WonderSwan Color version managed to bring both the grid and the detailed combat screens to the small display, and one-handed controls feel surprisingly comfortable.

At the time, this was one of the most technically ambitious titles on the whole console and proof that Square didn't skimp on the WonderSwan. Front Mission itself is a cornerstone of the mecha tactics genre, and its combination of damaging individual robot parts with deep equipment customization influenced a whole range of later games. Today, the main obstacle is Japanese, since the story carries a large part of the experience, but the tactical layer is legible even without it. Anyone who enjoys slow, deliberate turn-based combat will find one of the best games ever released for the WonderSwan here. It's especially valuable that the game is never in a hurry: between missions there's plenty of room to rebuild machines, test weapons in the arena, and for the player to develop their own style of command. It's precisely this calm between battles that makes Front Mission a title you can keep coming back to for months of evenings.
wonderswan__front-mission.teaser: A sprawling tactical RPG with combat robots and a raw, unheroic war story.

wonderswan__blue-wing-blitz.article:
**Blue Wing Blitz** is one of the very few completely original titles Square created for the WonderSwan Color, and also its boldest attempt to push the tactical RPG genre somewhere new. It takes place in a world of floating islands where all transport and warfare happen through the air, and the player commands a squadron of machines that move above the landscape. This is the main thing that sets it apart from typical tactics games: besides position on the map, altitude and orientation matter too, so attacking an enemy from above or from behind has quite different consequences than a head-on clash.

Between battles, machines get upgraded, their weaponry changes, and crews gain experience, so assembling the squadron before a mission carries as much weight as combat itself. The game keeps a decent pace, the campaign is long, and the difficulty rises smoothly, but it never forgets it's on a handheld console, so individual engagements can be played in short bursts. Technically, Blue Wing Blitz ranks among the better offerings on the WonderSwan Color: environments are colorful and legible, machine animations are smooth, and the interface manages to display plenty of information on a small screen without overwhelming the player. The music maintains an airy, mildly adventurous mood that suits flying between islands.

At the time, the game slipped through the cracks more than it deserved. It arrived just as attention was already turning to the upcoming Game Boy Advance, and as a Japan-only exclusive it never reached a wider audience. Among collectors and tactical RPG fans, though, it holds a reputation as an interesting experiment showing what the WonderSwan could have achieved with more time. Today it still plays well, only demanding patience with Japanese and a willingness to learn the rules of aerial combat, which you won't find in quite the same form anywhere else. For collectors, it's also notable as one of the last truly major projects Square released on a third-party handheld console before its attention finally turned elsewhere.
wonderswan__blue-wing-blitz.teaser: An original Square tactical RPG with battles between floating islands; altitude decides the fight.

wonderswan__wild-card.article:
**Wild Card** emerged as Square's attempt to combine a classic Japanese RPG with a card game, at a time when card battles in Japan were just starting to become a huge topic. The player moves through a world where the card game carries social weight, talks to characters, completes quests, and gradually builds their own deck from what they pick up along the way. Battles, however, don't play out through the usual command menu selection; instead they take place on cards, so a character's strength depends not just on their level but mainly on what the player currently holds in hand and how well they can combine it.

This combination creates a pleasant rhythm. Exploration and dialogue give the whole thing an RPG's structure, while individual battles have a short, self-contained round that's great for a few minutes on the go. Collecting and upgrading the deck functions as the main motivation, and the game pays off for those who don't settle for the first strategy offered. Technically, this is a title from early in the WonderSwan Color's life, so the visuals lean on clean, hand-drawn cards and a clear interface rather than effects; the controls are simple and suited to one-handed play, which fits a card game better than more action-oriented genres.

At the time, it served as an interesting addition to Square's lineup on the console, playing the role of a smaller, more playful piece alongside the big Final Fantasy remakes. It never achieved the fame of its siblings and remained practically unknown outside Japan, so today it's known mainly within the WonderSwan community. That's exactly what makes it interesting, though: it shows how, at the turn of the millennium, Square was experimenting with blending genres and exploring everything a handheld console could do. Anyone who likes card games with a collecting layer will find here one of the earliest attempts to embed them in a full-fledged game world. Playing without knowledge of Japanese is tricky, though, since the meaning of individual cards forms a substantial part of the strategy, and without understanding the descriptions all that's left is guesswork. With a translated guide in hand, though, it turns out to be an unexpectedly addictive little game.
wonderswan__wild-card.teaser: An unusual blend of JRPG and card game – battles play out directly on the cards.

wonderswan__chocobo-no-fushigi-na-dungeo.article:
**Chocobo no Fushigi na Dungeon for WonderSwan** brought to the Bandai console the beloved Final Fantasy spin-off in which a chocobo becomes an adventurer making its way through ever-changing dungeons. The foundation follows the tradition of mystery dungeon games: every descent generates a new layout of corridors, enemies, and chests, time passes turn by turn so every step the player takes is also a step for the enemies, and death usually means losing everything collected and returning to the start. It sounds harsh, but that's exactly where the tension this genre relies on comes from.

Playing revolves around managing resources. The chocobo gets hungry as it walks, and hunger depletes with every step, so wandering aimlessly is punished; items can be used in various ways, and some start out unidentified, so the player takes a risk trying an unknown potion. On top of that, classic Final Fantasy elements appear in the form of familiar enemies and spells, giving the whole thing a more playful, friendlier tone than tougher representatives of the genre usually have. The WonderSwan version works with a monochrome display but relies on clearly readable sprites and a legible map, so you won't get lost in the dungeon because of the graphics, only because of your own carelessness.

At the time, it was one of the titles that lent the new console credibility, since Square was putting brands Japanese players already knew onto it. This chocobo roguelike is also a great example of how well the genre suits handheld play: one dungeon run doesn't take long, can be ended at any time, and the urge to try just once more works regardless of how many times the player has died. Today it feels a bit more modest than later entries on other platforms, but its addictive loop still holds up, and it remains one of the more pleasant ways to play a classic mystery dungeon. It also helps that, thanks to familiar creatures and musical motifs from Final Fantasy, it feels welcoming from the very first minute, even though hidden beneath that friendly surface is a game that can be merciless.
wonderswan__chocobo-no-fushigi-na-dungeo.teaser: Chocobo as the adventurer; a roguelike with procedurally generated dungeons on every descent.

wonderswan__riviera-promised-land.article:
**Riviera: The Promised Land** is one of the most original games ever released for the WonderSwan Color, and also proof that a Japanese RPG doesn't need to be built around walking across a world map. The player takes on the role of the angelic warrior Ecthelion, who together with his companions is meant to destroy the demons of the floating land of Riviera, only to soon discover that the orders from above aren't as clear-cut as they seemed. The story is told through scenes with large character portraits and dialogue, closer to a visual novel than to a classic journey.

Instead of free movement, the environment is explored screen by screen, where the player spends points to examine a specific spot, open a chest, or find a hidden path. Points are limited, so exploration is a puzzle in itself, and the game encourages replaying. Battles are just as untraditional: each encounter only allows the use of a limited set of items and weapons, each piece has a finite number of uses, and by wearing it down characters learn new attacks. Weapons thus become both a consumable resource and a source of progression at the same time, and deciding when to sacrifice something is among the most interesting choices in the entire game.

At the time, the game caught attention through its boldness and style: colorful hand-drawn art, a strong soundtrack, and a darker story about duty and free will earned it a devoted following. It was from the WonderSwan Color version that later releases on other handheld consoles grew, thanks to which Riviera reached players outside Japan and gained a reputation as a cult classic. Today it feels unusually fresh, since no one has really repeated its structure, and for Sting it marked the beginning of a line of games built around unorthodox gameplay systems. The original WonderSwan Color version today is mainly a collector's curiosity, since due to language and rarity of the cartridges most players reach it through later releases instead, but this is where it all began, and the core ideas are already fully in place.
wonderswan__riviera-promised-land.teaser: One of the most original JRPGs on the WonderSwan – storytelling without walking around a world map.

wonderswan__dicing-knight-period.article:
**Dicing Knight Period** is among the very last games released for the WonderSwan Color and is also one of the most sought-after items on the entire console. It's a compact dungeon crawler in which a heroine descends into the depths and fights whatever comes her way. Battles are built around dice: the values rolled determine how strong an attack will be or how good the defense is, and the player tries to piece together the best possible move from random results. Chance is thus built right into the core of the game, but it isn't all-powerful, since it's surrounded by plenty of decisions about equipment and about when to attack and when it's better to retreat.

The whole thing is deliberately short and focused. A single run can be finished in one sitting, the game pushes toward repetition and toward improving the player's own skill rather than long stat-grinding, and that's exactly why it sits on the border between a classic roguelike and an arcade game chasing the best possible score. Technically, it's a good-looking title with striking sprites, a clean interface, and snappy responsiveness that works great on the small display; the music has an unmistakable electronic flair you'd expect from a small Japanese studio.

The game came out when the WonderSwan Color was already winding down and the print run was very small, so it quickly became a collector's item, and original cartridges rank among the most expensive on the platform. Studio Qute built a reputation among handheld gaming fans for carefully polished, dense games, and Dicing Knight Period is a good example of that: it has neither a big story nor much scope, but what it does, it does with remarkable precision. Today it's mainly interesting as a forerunner of the wave of modern roguelikes built around dice and random resources that arrived a good fifteen years later. Anyone who plays it will likely be surprised to find that the principles driving the entire genre today were already worked out in fine detail at the twilight of one Japanese handheld console's life.
wonderswan__dicing-knight-period.teaser: One of the last games for the WonderSwan Color; battles here are decided by dice, not swords.

wonderswan__star-hearts-hoshi-to-daichi-.article:
**Star Hearts: Hoshi to Daichi no Shisha** was one of Bandai's attempts to build a full-fledged original Japanese RPG on the WonderSwan Color, one that wouldn't stand in the shadow of Square's remakes. It offers a classic fantasy journey with a party of heroes, world travel, towns, dungeons, and turn-based battles — exactly what a Japanese player at the turn of the millennium pictured under the genre. The story revolves around the fate of the world and a stellar power that intervenes in it, told in traditional fashion through dialogue scenes between the stages of the journey.

Gameplay sticks to a proven structure: the party grows, characters gain levels and new abilities, equipment is bought in towns, and the main activity between story beats is exploring dungeons full of random encounters. It's precisely the rhythm of short battles, easily dispatched in a few turns, that makes the game well suited to a handheld console, since it's easy to return to in small chunks. Technically it was among the better-looking RPGs on the platform, with colorful environments, legible sprites, and decently crafted battle screens that managed to keep track of the whole party even on a limited display.

At the time, the title's main job was to prove that the WonderSwan Color's library could offer a big RPG outside licensed brands and outside Square. It never made it overseas, so it remained known mainly to Japanese players and the later community of collectors who systematically comb through the console's library. Today it can't be recommended as a first stop on the platform, since without knowledge of Japanese all that's left is the combat layer, but as proof that Bandai wanted its own RPG contenders rather than relying solely on outside licenses, it has its place. For anyone mapping out everything that appeared on the WonderSwan Color beyond the best-known titles, it's one of the games that make the library richer than it might seem at first glance.
wonderswan__star-hearts-hoshi-to-daichi-.teaser: Bandai's attempt at its own JRPG, out of the shadow of Square remakes; a classic with a party and dungeons.

wonderswan__digimon-adventure-02-tag-tam.article:
**Digimon Adventure 02: Tag Tamers** is one of the best-rated games built on the Digimon brand and also a showcase of how well Bandai's own license fit its own console. The player finds themselves in a digital world, collecting and raising digital monsters and sending them into turn-based battles, and the core of the fun lies less in the story than in the effort to raise the best possible team. Digimon evolve according to how the player treats them, what battles they're allowed, and how they're cared for, so two playthroughs side by side can end up with completely different lineups.

The development system is the most interesting part of the whole. Instead of simple level climbing, a whole range of stats is tracked, and the resulting shape of the monster is a reward for long-term care, which creates strong motivation to experiment. On top of that comes trading and linking between players, which gave raising an extra dimension, and plenty of content referencing the second anime series, which was peaking at the time. Technically it's a colorful, clear title with well-executed monster portraits that manages to cram a lot of stats onto a small display without becoming illegible, and the music keeps a brisk, adventurous tone familiar from the source material.

At the time, Digimon games were part of what sold the WonderSwan to a younger audience, since the brand was at the height of its popularity in Japan and Bandai used it systematically on its own console. Tag Tamers holds a reputation among them as the most accomplished entry precisely because of the depth of raising, which surprisingly holds up well even next to later games in the series. Today it's mainly interesting for monster-collecting fans who want to see how the approach to raising creatures can differ from the Pokémon way; the language barrier is noticeable, but the system can also be understood through experimentation. The reward is the feeling that the team you've raised is truly your own creation, not just the result of how many hours you spent grinding experience in one forest.
wonderswan__digimon-adventure-02-tag-tam.teaser: One of the highest-rated Digimon-branded games; collecting and developing your own team.

wonderswan__digital-monster-ver-wondersw.article:
**Digital Monster Ver. WonderSwan** was among the titles that accompanied the console's launch and was meant to show that Bandai could carry its strongest brand from pocket eggs to a full-fledged gaming device. The game builds on what made Digimon famous at the time: the player acquires digital creatures, looks after them, trains them, and sends them into battles, except here it's all wrapped in the structure of a real game with exploration of a digital world, progression, and enemies that follow their own order. What was simple pet-raising on a keychain display thus becomes something closer to an RPG.

The core is long-term care. The creature grows and changes form depending on how the player treats it, how much training it gets, and what battles it goes through, and its final form is the result of dozens of small decisions. The battles themselves are rather short and clear, since the main tension lies in whether the upbringing is heading in the right direction. Technically it's a game for the original monochrome WonderSwan, so it relies on bold, easily readable sprites and a simple interface; the device, running on a single AA battery, lasted for long hours, which suits a title built on patient raising more than anything else.

At the time it was an important piece of the puzzle, since Digimon were at their peak in Japan and their presence on the new console helped it find an audience among younger players. At the same time, the game shows nicely how a toy turned into a game genre: the raising mechanism, where the same creature can evolve into completely different forms, remains a defining trait of the series to this day and sets it apart from competitors that rely mainly on collecting. Today it's more of a historically interesting title than one you'd return to for long, but anyone who likes slow raising and sees the charm in watching an egg turn into a monster will enjoy it. It's also a nice reminder of a time when digital pets were taken deadly seriously, and their fate depended on whether their owner made time for them.
wonderswan__digital-monster-ver-wondersw.teaser: The console's launch title; Bandai brought Digimon raising from the pocket egg into a full game.

wonderswan__gunpey.article:
**Gunpey** is among the first games Bandai released on its new handheld console, and even its name pays tribute to Gunpei Yokoi, the engineer behind the concept of portable gaming as well as the technical foundation of the WonderSwan. The principle is rarely this pure: the playing field is divided into vertical columns holding short line segments, both horizontal and diagonal. The player shifts the segments up and down, trying to assemble a continuous line connecting the left edge of the field to the right. Once a line closes, it disappears and scores points. The longer and more winding the connection you manage to create, the bigger the reward. Meanwhile new rows of segments keep appearing from below and push the screen's contents upward, so the player is always working under constant pressure.

Such a simple rule grew into a game with surprisingly large room for strategy. A skilled player doesn't place segments where the line closes fastest, but builds several unfinished paths side by side and then connects them into a chain with a single move. The controls fit the WonderSwan like a glove, since the console offers two sets of directional buttons and can be held both vertically and horizontally. Moving a segment is a matter of a single thumb flick, and the game never forces the player to shift grip. The monochrome display isn't a drawback — everything rests on shapes and contrast, not color. The music is economical, loop-based, and subtly speeds up its tempo as the field fills.

At the time, Gunpey worked exactly as Bandai intended. It was a title you could pull out for a few minutes on the subway, and just as easily spend a whole evening with, while also serving as a showcase for what the new console could do. The brand later received sequels and versions on other platforms too, which is a solid track record for a late-1990s handheld puzzle game. Today Gunpey still feels fresh mainly because it doesn't try to be anything other than a perfectly tuned mechanism. It has no story, no unnecessary modes, and its charm lies in how quickly the brain learns to read a jumble of small lines as a future path.
wonderswan__gunpey.teaser: A puzzle game named after Gunpei Yokoi, creator of the WonderSwan; a pure line-connecting concept.

wonderswan__klonoa-moonlight-museum.article:
**Klonoa: Moonlight Museum** is proof that even a monochrome handheld display can host a platformer with its own poetry. Namco sent its eared hero into a strange museum whose individual halls function as gateways to separate worlds, and built around it a game that faithfully carries over the rules of its bigger console siblings. Klonoa doesn't jump on enemies' heads. Instead, he catches them with his wind ring, inflates them, and uses them both as ammunition and as a springboard. A thrown enemy clears an obstacle or activates a switch; an enemy underfoot launches the hero a level higher. A single mechanic thus grows into a surprisingly varied toolkit of challenges, from sequences demanding precise double-jump timing to small puzzles that are more about the order of moves than reflexes.

Technically it's a purely two-dimensional game, not a backdrop with depth like the ones players know from the brand's home-console versions. That actually suits it well. The animations are legible, the characters have large, recognizable silhouettes, and the levels are designed to fit within the WonderSwan's low resolution without jittery scrolling. The music relies on simple, catchy melodies, and combined with the cute, slightly melancholic tone, it creates the atmosphere the series still carries today. The controls use only a handful of buttons, so the game can be played one-handed without learning complex combinations.

Moonlight Museum was released only in Japan, and outside it, it was long known mainly to collectors and brand fans who discovered it only in retrospect. Today it's one of the titles that make exploring the WonderSwan worthwhile at all. It's short, kind, and design-confident, and it never feels like a rushed side detour from the main series. For anyone who likes classic platformers built on an idea rather than mere jumping, it's one of the best reasons to pick up Bandai's handheld console and spend a few evenings with it.
wonderswan__klonoa-moonlight-museum.teaser: A platformer with poetry even on a monochrome display; Klonoa doesn't stomp enemies, he grabs them with a ring.

wonderswan__rockman-and-forte-mirai-kara.article:
**Rockman & Forte: Mirai Kara no Chōsensha** isn't a port of the identically named Super Famicom game, but a standalone title made specifically for the WonderSwan. Under Capcom's license, Bandai built a classic action platformer following the tried-and-true recipe: the player picks the order of levels from a selection screen, ends each one with a boss fight against a robot, and after defeating it gains a new weapon usable against the next opponent. Anyone who knows the Blue Bomber from 8-bit and 16-bit consoles knows exactly what to expect, including the need to memorize trap layouts by heart and carefully manage special-weapon energy.

The main draw is the choice of character. Rockman fires a chargeable shot and can slide, while Forte is more mobile, can aim in multiple directions, and relies on a short double jump. Both options change how the levels can be tackled and give the game a reason for repeat playthroughs. The boss lineup is entirely new for this version and keeps the playful, slightly absurd tone the series has always had. Technically the game handled the WonderSwan well. The sprites are large and legible, the pace stays brisk, and the monochrome image manages to distinguish the hero, enemies, and background even when a lot is happening on screen at once. The sound is necessarily more modest than on home consoles, yet still manages to hold onto the brand's recognizable rhythmic drive.

At the time, this was a very strong argument for owners of the new console, since Rockman was among the names Bandai needed so the WonderSwan wouldn't look like a mere collection of puzzle trifles. The game remained exclusively Japanese, though, so in the West it was long talked about more as a legend than as a title anyone had actually played. Today it's interesting precisely as a parallel branch of the series. It offers a solid, honestly challenging platformer that holds up alongside the handheld entries from the rival studio, and yet only a fraction of fans know it.
wonderswan__rockman-and-forte-mirai-kara.teaser: A standalone title for the WonderSwan, not a port of the Super Famicom game; the classic Mega Man formula.

wonderswan__makaimura-for-wonderswan.article:
**Makaimura for WonderSwan** is a handheld return to the arcade classic Western players know as Ghosts 'n Goblins. Knight Arthur sets out through a graveyard and beyond into demonic lands to rescue a kidnapped princess, armed with nothing but a lance and unbreakable resolve. The rules remain cruelly simple. The first hit knocks off his armor and the hero continues in his underwear, the second means instant death and a return to a checkpoint. Enemies appear in endless waves, flying demons disrupt jumps over pits, and weapons picked up along the way aren't always an upgrade, since a torch or a shield can turn out much worse in a given section than the basic lance.

Porting it to the WonderSwan mainly had to solve the problem of turning a wide arcade screen into a small, low-resolution display. The game therefore works with a more compact field of view, and the player often relies more on learned layouts than on what's actually visible ahead. Memorization, though, has traditionally been part of the fun in this series. The difficulty remains uncompromising, and even an experienced player counts on dozens of attempts before clearing the first two levels. The controls are thankfully precise, and the jump, which couldn't be adjusted mid-air in the original, keeps its characteristic rigidity, so every leap must be planned in advance.

From a period perspective, it was a sensible move. Bandai needed recognizable names at the console's launch, and Makaimura was one that Japanese players instantly associated with the arcade era. The title remained a Japanese exclusive, and outside Japan it's known mainly among collectors. Today it feels like an honest reminder of a time when games showed no mercy and death was part of the learning process. Anyone who likes tough platformers and doesn't mind repeating the same section will find here a concentrated version of the classic that, thanks to its short levels, surprisingly suits play in small doses. It's also a good illustration of how Capcom recycled its arcade classics across generations of hardware, and how little it had to change their substance for them to keep working.
wonderswan__makaimura-for-wonderswan.teaser: A handheld return of Ghosts 'n Goblins; two hits are enough to kill the knight Arthur.

wonderswan__guilty-gear-petit.article:
**Guilty Gear Petit** achieved something that seemed almost impossible: bringing a fast 2D fighting game full of special moves to a handheld console with a small display and simple controls. The characters from the Guilty Gear world got a shrunken, cutely caricatured look with big heads, which keeps them legible even on the WonderSwan Color's screen. The core of the fighting, though, didn't change. The player jumps, blocks, chains normal hits into specials, and tries to corner the opponent so they have nowhere left to escape. The inputs for special moves stay true to the series, so anyone who knows the moves from the arcade original carries over a good chunk of muscle memory here.

Technically the version is understandably trimmed down. The character roster is smaller than on home consoles, animations have fewer frames, and the arenas are simple. Still, the game feels surprisingly brisk and doesn't skimp on the sense of impact that matters so much in fighting games. The color display helps distinguish characters from the background, and the fast pace of combat holds up even when effects are flying all over the screen. The sound chip can't reproduce the guitar riffs the series is famous for, so the music opted for simplified arrangements that evoke the mood rather than deliver it at full strength.

At the time, it was one of the few genuinely action-oriented brands on the WonderSwan, and the title found its audience among console owners, earning a sequel that same year. Like every game on this platform, it remained Japan-only, and outside it, it long stayed among the tips fans passed along to each other. Today Guilty Gear Petit is mainly a curiosity, but a carefully made one. Nobody will play it for the depth of its fighting system, but as proof of how much could be squeezed out of Bandai's hardware, it works wonderfully, and it keeps a fresh pace in short bursts. For series fans, it's also interesting as a glimpse of what the brand looked like back when it was still building its name and could afford playful detours like this.
wonderswan__guilty-gear-petit.teaser: The fast 2D fighter Guilty Gear shrunk down to a handheld display without losing readability.

wonderswan__mr-driller.article:
**Mr. Driller** brings to WonderSwan Color one of the most addictive ideas Namco came up with at the turn of the millennium. The player controls the driller Susumu, boring ever deeper below the surface through a mass of colored blocks. The rules are simple and treacherous at the same time. Adjacent blocks of the same color merge and disappear when touched, but everything above them immediately collapses downward, so a careless drill can bury the hero. On top of that, oxygen keeps running out, replenished only by collecting capsules scattered in the depths, and the game constantly forces you to choose between the safe, slow route and a risky headlong descent for another breath.

This combination produces a pace that puzzle games usually lack. Mr. Driller isn't played calmly, it's played in mild panic, because every second spent deliberating means less oxygen. At the same time, it's a game where you can visibly improve. An experienced player reads the columns ahead, knows where to create a chain that clears half the screen, and when instead to leave blocks alone so as not to create a trap overhead. The color display of the WonderSwan Color is an absolute necessity here, since the whole game rests on distinguishing shades, and the handheld version, thanks to its short descents, fits sessions of a few minutes better than many other ports.

The original came from arcade machines and quickly spread to home and handheld platforms, so the version for Bandai's console was part of a larger brand push. At the time it helped show that the WonderSwan Color wasn't just a colored variant of the same hardware, but a console capable of hosting titles built on fast visual perception as well. Today Mr. Driller is still eminently playable, because its rules haven't aged a single day. It's the kind of game where you tell yourself "one more try" and only realize an hour later. Alongside the flood of serious action titles, it also stands out with disarming humor, since the main hero treats drilling into the depths as perfectly ordinary work, and the game happily pokes fun at its own desperate situation.
wonderswan__mr-driller.teaser: Namco's classic about drilling through colored blocks – one careless drill and the driller is buried in a landslide.

wonderswan__puyo-puyo-tsu.article:
**Puyo Puyo Tsu** is the version of Compile's franchise that most players consider its peak, and on the WonderSwan it shows that competitive colored-blob matching doesn't need a big screen to thrive. The basics are familiar to everyone. Pairs of jelly-like Puyos fall from above, the player rotates and arranges them, and once four or more of the same color touch, they vanish. Whatever sits above then collapses downward, which can trigger another vanishing, and another, and another. The chain is everything here. A single well-built setup can bury an opponent under an avalanche of transparent garbage Puyos, which can't be removed directly and must be cleared by an explosion next to them.

Compared to the first game, a rule was added that turned it into a genuine sport. An incoming attack can be countered with your own chain if you manage to respond before the garbage lands, turning the match into a tug-of-war where timing matters as much as the size of the prepared combo, and a match between two experienced players looks like a fencing duel. On the WonderSwan the game runs smoothly, and the console's control layout lets you rotate falling pairs without awkward finger repositioning. The monochrome display is the only real obstacle, since the Puyos are distinguished not only by shade but also by pattern and facial expression, which the eye needs a moment to get used to.

At the time, the franchise was among the most popular things to play in the genre in Japan, and its presence on the new console was an important signal for Bandai. The game keeps its comic-book flavor, with chatty opponents and lighthearted music that makes it pleasantly cheerful even when losing. Today Puyo Puyo Tsu is still one of the best-tuned competitive puzzle titles ever made, and the handheld version is a reminder that this system works on any hardware able to tell a few shapes apart. Anyone who pushes through the early phase, where chains form more by luck than by design, discovers a game with an enormous skill ceiling, something rarely found in the genre.
wonderswan__puyo-puyo-tsu.teaser: The pinnacle version of Compile's puzzle brand; stacking colorful puyos even on a small display.

wonderswan__judgement-silversword-rebirt.article:
**Judgement Silversword: Rebirth Edition** is the most improbable gem in the entire WonderSwan library. It was born in the environment of the WonderWitch development kit, the tool Bandai used to let hobbyists program games directly for its console, and only later received a release on an actual cartridge in a limited run. It's a vertical shooter that doesn't rely on a flood of effects but on a perfectly measured rhythm. The game is divided into short segments that flow into one another without pause, each bringing a different enemy formation, and the player learns when to dodge, when to hold position, and when to risk closing in for a higher score.

The scoring system is the heart of the whole design. The player is rewarded for efficiency and for not holding anything in reserve, so optimal play looks different from mere survival. Toward the end the game turns into a real test, where reflexes alone no longer suffice and knowing the layout becomes essential. The monochrome display, paradoxically, benefits legibility, since enemy projectiles stand out clearly against the background and the player never loses track of their own ship. The sound is spare and pulsing, underscoring a constant sense of pressure. Everything runs smoothly even when the screen is packed, which was by no means a given for handheld hardware from the turn of the millennium.

Among genre fans the title quickly earned a cult reputation, and its physical release became sought-after collector's fare. Studio Qute later revisited it, and the game appeared in a modern compilation on Xbox 360 alongside a newer shooter from the same developer, reaching an audience that would otherwise never have encountered the WonderSwan. Today Judgement Silversword is one of the reasons Bandai's console gets talked about at all outside Japan. It's a game that proves great shooter design doesn't need raw power, just a clear vision. Anyone into the genre will appreciate how little is wasted in it and how precisely every segment knows what it demands of the player.
wonderswan__judgement-silversword-rebirt.teaser: The most unlikely gem of the WonderSwan library; it grew out of the WonderWitch homebrew kit.

wonderswan__super-robot-taisen-compact.article:
**Super Robot Taisen Compact** brought to the WonderSwan the famous Japanese crossover of mecha anime franchises, in which a single campaign brings together robots from several different series to fight side by side against a common enemy. It's a tactical strategy game on a square grid. The player moves units, chooses weapons according to range and terrain type, and watches each attack trigger a short animated battle sequence typical of the series. Between battles, pilots gain experience, machines can be upgraded, and the player decides where to invest limited resources, which affects how manageable later missions become.

Bringing such a sprawling genre to a handheld console required compromises. The maps are smaller, screen scrolling handles the overview of the battlefield, and attack animations are necessarily simpler than on home platforms, yet they keep a recognizable choreography. These are, in fact, an essential part of the experience, since fans want to see their favorite robot in action. The monochrome display puts the emphasis on silhouettes, so units are distinguished more by shape than by color. The campaign is long and its pace is calm, making it well suited to playing one mission a day, which fits a handheld console nicely.

At the time, this was a significant step, since the series had until then stayed mainly on home consoles, and the handheld release opened the door to further installments. Sequels followed on the WonderSwan, along with a newer, color variant for the WonderSwan Color, turning Compact into its own line within the larger franchise. Today the game is of interest mainly to fans of mecha anime and tactics games, who will appreciate how well such a complex system fit into modest hardware. The language barrier is real, though, since the story carries most of the motivation, and without knowledge of Japanese a player is left with pure tactics. Even so, it's one of the most substantial titles ever released on the WonderSwan, and proof that the console could handle games running dozens of hours as well.
wonderswan__super-robot-taisen-compact.teaser: The famous mecha crossover tactics on a square grid; robots from multiple anime side by side.

wonderswan__shinseiki-evangelion-shito-i.article:
**Shinseiki Evangelion: Shito Ikusei** is one of the strangest games ever made based on the famous anime series, and at the same time exactly the kind of title that could only have appeared on a Japanese handheld console at the end of the nineties. The player doesn't take on the role of a pilot, but instead raises an Angel, a being the series presents as humanity's enemy. The game works as a raising simulation. The charge is fed, trained, rested, and depending on how the player treats it, its traits and appearance change.
