Over time it matures into one of many possible forms, and it then faces off in battles against the opponents the anime places on the opposing side.

The whole idea rests on the fact that the outcome is not guaranteed. Different combinations of care lead to different creatures, so the game encourages replaying and experimenting. The daily routine is short and undemanding, making it ideal company for a few minutes a day, but that's exactly why it requires patience and interest in slow progress. Technically it's a modest game that relies on static screens, simple menus, and expressive portraits. The WonderSwan's monochrome display doesn't get in the way at all, since the atmosphere is built more from a spare, cold visual style and music borrowing from the source material's mood palette.

From a period perspective, this was a typical product of Bandai's licensing policy, banking on fans buying anything bearing the logo of a beloved series. But the game offered something of its own. Flipping the perspective and letting the player raise the enemy is an idea that today's licensed productions would hardly stumble upon. Today Shito Ikusei is mainly of interest as a curiosity and evidence of how freely big franchises were handled in Japan. Without knowledge of Japanese it is, however, hard to access, since all the caretaking takes place in text menus. Fans of the source material will nonetheless find in it a distinctive artifact from an era when an enormous amount of merchandise revolved around the series, and every attempt at a game adaptation could look completely different.
wonderswan__shinseiki-evangelion-shito-i.teaser: A bizarre raising sim based on Evangelion – instead of a pilot, you raise the Angel itself.

wonderswan__digimon-adventure-anode-tame.article:
**Digimon Adventure: Anode Tamer** is one of the titles that made the WonderSwan a home for digital monsters, which were wildly popular in Japan at the time. The game builds on the world of the popular anime and turns it into an adventure combining environment exploration with battles in which the player commands a team of Digimon. A major part of the fun lies in collecting new companions. Defeated or persuaded opponents can be recruited into your own team, gradually growing stronger and evolving into more advanced forms, a mechanic the source material introduced and which serves as the main driver of progress here. The player is therefore constantly thinking about who to bring along and who to let mature.

Battles are turn-based and rely heavily on type relationships between the various creatures, so success depends on the composition of your party as much as on level. Exploration is simpler, the maps are clear, and the game guides the player fairly firmly so they don't get lost in the handheld format. Technically it stays modest. The Digimon sprites, however, are large and easily recognizable, which is essential for a licensed game, since fans want to spot their favorites at first glance. The monochrome display manages this thanks to bold outlines, and the music is simple, relying on short, repeating motifs.

At the time, this was an important entry for Bandai, which owned the franchise and could exploit it fully on its own console. Digimon games appeared repeatedly on the WonderSwan, including further variants and color versions for the WonderSwan Color, forming one of the platform's strongest series. Today Anode Tamer is mainly of interest to fans of the series who want to see how the anime's world was translated into game form at a time when it wasn't yet bound by later conventions. Japanese remains a barrier, without which a player struggles to navigate both the menus and the story. Whoever overcomes that obstacle gets a compact handheld RPG that doesn't exploit its source material but genuinely tries to mine real gameplay depth from its idea of raising creatures.
wonderswan__digimon-adventure-anode-tame.teaser: Digimon in full force on the WonderSwan; exploration, battles, and collecting companions for your team.

wonderswan__from-tv-animation-one-piece-.article:
**From TV Animation One Piece: Grand Battle Swan Colosseum** brings to WonderSwan Color an arena fighter based on one of the most popular manga and anime franchises of all. Instead of a classic single-plane fighting game, this one takes place in more open arenas where you can move around, dodge, pick up items, and use the environment. Characters from the pirate crew and their opponents each have their own set of attacks and special abilities referencing what they're famous for in the source material, and the matches are short, loud, and built more on chaotic fun than on precise mastery of a fighting system.

Porting such a large genre to a handheld console required simplification. Arenas are smaller, the number of on-screen effects at once is limited, and the roster of fighters is slimmer than in the console versions of the series. What remained, though, is the basic feeling fans loved this branch of the franchise for: fast matches, over-the-top gestures, and the chance to play as your favorite character. The color display of the WonderSwan Color is useful here, since the characters are defined in the source material by strong coloring, and in black and white they would lose half their identity. The music leans on simple, energetic motifs that give the matches the drive they need.

At the time, this was a typical licensed game, the kind Bandai released in quantity on its own platform. It didn't try to rewrite the rules of the genre and relied on the source material's popularity to do the work. Precisely for that reason, though, it fits into the WonderSwan library as evidence of how much the console lived off Japanese franchises, and how strongly its lineup was shaped by TV series. Today it's more of a curiosity for fans of the series than a game anyone would boot up for its fighting system. In short bursts, and ideally with two players, it still holds its own as fun, and as a handheld companion to the era's pirate-crew mania it makes perfect sense. Collectors, moreover, treat it as a reminder that the franchise was already huge long before it broke through outside Japan.
wonderswan__from-tv-animation-one-piece-.teaser: An arena fighter based on One Piece with free movement around the ring instead of a single fighting plane.

wonderswan__terrors.article:
**Terrors** is one of the most distinctive attempts ever seen on the WonderSwan, because it tries to evoke fear on a small monochrome display without a single loud jump scare. The game is made up of short horror episodes that place the player in uncomfortable situations and let them progress through exploring the environment, finding objects, and solving small puzzles. The pace is slow and deliberately uncomfortable. Instead of action, it relies on silence, on suggestion, and on the feeling that something is wrong, an approach much closer to the Japanese horror tradition than to the Western spooky action games of the time.

The atmosphere is carried mainly by the visuals and sound. The black-and-white image with its coarse resolution paradoxically helps, because details are left unresolved, and the imagination fills them in far more unsettlingly than any artist ever could. The soundtrack is sparse, often more a matter of noise and isolated tones than melodies, and in a quiet environment it works surprisingly powerfully. The game also plays with when the player turns it on, so playing at night isn't the same as playing in broad daylight, an idea that sets it apart from the run of ordinary handheld production.

At the time, Terrors remained a marginal affair. It was an experiment on a console that was itself a minority choice, and outside Japan almost nobody knew about it. Precisely for that reason, collectors and connoisseurs remember it today as proof that the WonderSwan wasn't just a platform for licensed anime games and puzzle trifles, but also for ideas no major console would ever have funded. Anyone able to get past the language barrier and not expect action will find here an unusual, moody game whose charm lies in what it doesn't show. It plays best in the dark, with headphones, and without haste, exactly as horror deserves, and under such conditions even simple black-and-white graphics can send an unpleasant chill down the spine. It's precisely this economy that makes Terrors a title that ages far better than period attempts at realistic horror.
wonderswan__terrors.teaser: An unusual attempt to evoke horror on a monochrome display without a single loud jump scare.

3do__road-rash.article:
**Road Rash** ranks among the best games ever released for the 3DO, and it's still remembered as a showcase of what the console could do. It's a motorcycle race on public roads, but crossing the finish line first is only half the fun — the other half comes from violence. While riding you can kick opponents, punch them, or hit them with a club or chain, which can be grabbed straight off another rider's hand mid-race. Anyone who falls has to run back to their bike and loses precious seconds. On top of that there's regular traffic, oncoming cars, cattle by the roadside, and police officers who arrest you after a stop and take your money. Winnings buy better bikes and open the way to faster classes, where opponents are more aggressive and the tracks considerably longer.

Technically, it was one of the first games to truly put the 3DO's power to use. The console version wasn't a straight port of the earlier entries but a separate build with digitized characters, smooth scrolling scenery, and a far more detailed Californian landscape stretching from coastal roads to mountain passes. What stood out most, though, was the sound: the game featured licensed tracks from real rock and grunge bands, and their music videos played from the disc in the menus and between races. In the mid-1990s that felt like a small revolution — a console game that sounded like the radio and looked like a music channel.

At the time, Road Rash became one of the main arguments for buying a 3DO in the first place, and reviewers praised above all the combination of brisk racing and raw fun. Its influence on the genre is still visible today: arcade racing with contact combat, where you don't just overtake your opponent but take them out, has its most distinctive ancestor in Road Rash. Playing it today, the controls feel harsher and less forgiving than modern arcade racers, and the longer tracks start to repeat after a while. But the immediate joy of knocking a rival into an oncoming truck still works just as well.
3do__road-rash.teaser: Motorcycle racing where you can beat your rivals with fists or a club right while riding.

3do__need-for-speed.article:
**The Need for Speed** is regarded today as the starting point of one of the longest-running racing franchises of all, and it made its debut on the 3DO. The original game was far more of a simulation than later entries: it featured a handful of exotic sports cars, each with a detailed encyclopedic section including video footage and technical specs, and a driving model that punished careless braking and overly aggressive cornering. The tracks weren't closed circuits but long stretches of country road split into stages — through mountain switchbacks, desert plains, and coastal overlooks. Regular traffic and police patrols also shared the road with you, and the police would start a pursuit and hand out a fine once they pulled you over.

On the 3DO, the game showed off what the console could do with fast 3D graphics. The car models were honestly shaped for their time, a cockpit view with working gauges was available, and the engine sounds came from real recordings of each individual vehicle, so every car sounded different. It was precisely this attention to sound and detail that made driving feel like an experience quite unlike the purely arcade racers of the day. Music took a back seat in favor of engine roar, tire squeal, and a co-driver calling out upcoming turns and road conditions.

Reviews praised the combination of technical polish, licensed cars, and the atmosphere of a lawless road race, and the game was often cited as one of the main reasons to buy the console. The series it launched later turned toward arcade drifting and police chases, but the motif of a chase with a patrol car is present right from the start. Today the original version feels slower and stricter than a player used to modern entries might expect, and the tracks are at times less readable due to the short draw distance. But anyone wanting to see where the whole franchise grew from will find a surprisingly coherent game with its own calm pace and a respect for cars that later entries never quite matched again.
3do__need-for-speed.teaser: This is where the famous racing series began; the first game was more of a meticulous simulation of exotic cars.

3do__return-fire.article:
**Return Fire** is a vehicle-based action game that was one of the most addictive two-player titles on the 3DO. The concept is simple: on a sprawling map split between two bases, the goal is to steal the enemy's flag and bring it home. Four vehicles are available — a helicopter, a tank, an armored personnel carrier, and a jeep — and each plays a different role. The helicopter flies fast and destroys targets with rockets, the tank blasts through fortifications, the carrier delivers a soldier to the flag, and the quick jeep hauls it back. Switching between them is the core of the strategy, since no single vehicle can complete the whole job alone, and losing the wrong one at the wrong moment means defeat. Vehicles can only be swapped at your own base, so every sortie is a commitment you have to see through to the end of the action.

A tilted top-down view, smooth map scrolling, and clear graphics favored readability over flashy effects, so the game ran briskly even with the screen full of explosions. But its strongest weapon is the music: Return Fire uses classical recordings that change depending on the chosen vehicle, so flying the helicopter is accompanied by a dramatic orchestral piece while driving the jeep gets a lighter tune. Pairing serious music with the destruction of entire bases created a mood players still remember today and gave the game an unexpectedly grand feel.

At the time it received a very warm reception and was often ranked among the best the 3DO had to offer; it was later released on other platforms and got a sequel. Its influence can be seen in later games that combine flag-capturing with a choice of specialized vehicles — a concept that spread through multiplayer shooters much later. Today Return Fire proves that clearly defined rules age better than technical spectacle. Played two-player on one screen, it's still one of the best fun the 3DO has to offer, even if the solo campaign feels more like training for a duel against a living opponent.
3do__return-fire.teaser: An addictive two-player capture-the-flag game; four vehicles, four different roles in battle.

3do__gex.article:
**Gex** is a platformer in which a gecko obsessed with television gets pulled into a world of TV channels controlled by an evil broadcaster. The core mechanic is his sticky tongue and tail: Gex can climb walls and ceilings, cling to surfaces, and take out enemies with a tail whip or by swallowing them with his tongue. The individual levels are styled after TV genres — a horror stage with a graveyard and a haunted mansion, a cartoon world, a kung-fu setting, and a sci-fi space station — and the player travels between them via a kind of remote control. Remotes and flies are collected as both energy and keys to further channels, giving the player good reason to explore the levels far more thoroughly than simply reaching the exit would require.

On the 3DO, this was the console's flagship platformer, and it looked excellent for its time: large hand-drawn backgrounds, smoothly animated main character, and a color palette that allowed far more shades than was common for 2D games on cartridge consoles. What set it apart was the wisecracking main character, who commented on the action with TV and pop-culture references — the very thing that built his later reputation. The music adapted to each level's theme, shifting from eerie organ pieces to faster rhythmic motifs, so every channel had its own mood.

At the time, Gex was seen as an attempt by 3DO to get its own mascot character at a time when every manufacturer had its own hedgehog or plumber, and the reception was largely positive — reviewers praised the graphics and atmosphere, with criticism aimed at difficulty and level length. The character stuck around and moved into full 3D in later entries, making it one of the few 3DO franchises with a long life. Today the game holds up as a well-tuned classic platformer with its own sense of humor, though the jumping demands patience and the maps are often bigger than a modern player might expect.
3do__gex.teaser: A gecko with a sticky tongue; levels styled after TV genres from horror to cartoons.

3do__total-eclipse.article:
**Total Eclipse** is a fast corridor-based space shooter and was one of the first games to show how smooth 3D graphics on the 3DO could be. The player sits in the cockpit of a fighter craft flying through a series of tunnels, canyons, and temple complexes above an alien planet; the route is fixed, and the task is to survive, shoot down enemies, and avoid collisions. Besides shooting, you also have to watch fuel and shield energy, so it pays to collect the bonuses scattered along the path. Turns come fast, and many stretches can only be handled once the player has memorized the track — the game is built around repetition and gradually learning the route by heart. Shooting down everything that appears isn't actually necessary; what matters more is staying centered in the corridor and not losing your shields before the next section.

Technically it was an impressive demonstration: the polygon environments scrolled briskly, the cockpit was rendered as a detailed frame with gauges, and the speed of movement was exceptional by console standards of the day. The environment changed significantly over the course of the game, from metallic tunnels to open rocky vistas, keeping alive the sense of a journey across an entire world. The music relied on dense synthetic motifs that underscored the tension and urgency; the warning sound before a crash became a lasting memory for players.

At launch, the game shipped alongside the console and served as a demo piece in stores, meant to show the difference against the sixteen-bit machines of the time. Reviewers praised its smoothness and speed, while more critical voices pointed out that the corridor structure offered little freedom and the game was fairly short. Its influence is visible across the whole line of rail-based 3D shooters that grew up on the new consoles of the mid-1990s. Today, Total Eclipse plays best in short bursts: it's unforgiving, a crash means a quick end to the attempt, but that pure sense of speed still has its charm.
3do__total-eclipse.teaser: A fast on-rails space shooter that showed off the 3DO's smooth 3D graphics.

3do__crash-n-burn.article:
**Crash 'n Burn** was the first game most 3DO owners ever saw, since it shipped bundled with the console. It's a futuristic armored-vehicle racer where speed isn't the only thing that counts — weaponry does too: cars carry machine guns, rockets, and mines, and opponents can be destroyed outright. Tracks run through tunnels, over bridges, and across industrial landscapes, with ramps and shortcuts along the way, and prize money between races upgrades engines, armor, and weapons. Damage affects how the car handles, so longer races force a choice between aggression and caution, since a wreck halfway through the track means the end of everything.

This particular game was meant to showcase 3DO's strength in an area other consoles of the time couldn't touch — playing video straight off the disc. Live-action cutscenes with actors ran between races, framing the whole thing as a broadcast TV show, and even the track itself combined polygon objects with scaled sprites. The sound leaned on harder rock motifs and a commentator's voice announcing the race. The split screen for two players also demonstrated that the console could render the scene twice without the pace completely collapsing, which was also part of the demo pitch in the year of release. The overall impression was genuinely striking at launch, though from today's perspective it's the video footage that has aged the fastest.

Reception was mixed: reviewers praised the presentation, smoothness, and sense of speed, while criticism pointed out that the game itself was shallower than it looked and that opponents lacked convincing intelligence. As a pack-in title, though, it did its job, and for many players it remained their first personal encounter with the disc-based console. Today, Crash 'n Burn is interesting mainly as a period piece — it shows what manufacturers at the dawn of the disc era promised themselves from the new medium, and you can still run a few races that entertain with raw simplicity and a pleasant sense of speed.
3do__crash-n-burn.teaser: The pack-in game bundled directly with the console; armored racing where you destroy rivals outright with weapons.

3do__super-street-fighter-ii-turbo.article:
**Super Street Fighter II Turbo** is one of the most faithful home conversions of this arcade fighting game ever released for the 3DO. The basics are familiar to everyone: a broad roster of fighters with their own special moves, matches won over two rounds, and a system where distance, timing, and reading what the opponent can do at any given moment all matter. The Turbo version added faster pace, hidden super combos charged in a bar beneath the health meter, and the mysterious fighter Akuma, who appeared only if certain special conditions were met. It was precisely the super combos and increased speed that made this the version the competitive scene stuck with for an unusually long time, and many players still consider it the best-balanced form of the entire second generation of the series.

The 3DO conversion benefited from the disc's capacity: character animations were smooth, backgrounds kept their detail along with animated background characters, and the music played at noticeably better quality than on cartridge-based consoles. The console didn't come with a six-button controller like the arcade cabinets, so serious players reached for alternative controllers; it was playable with the standard pad, but handling six strengths of attack was less comfortable. Loading between rounds was short, and the gameplay retained the sharpness of the original, including the precise timing the entire game is built on. Anyone who knew the arcade version noticed the difference only in small details.

At the time, this version was considered one of the technically best conversions available and, for 3DO owners, proof that the console could hold its own against arcade competition. Street Fighter II's influence on the entire fighting-game genre is beyond dispute — from the system of special moves through move cancels to the very format of tournaments. Today it still plays well on the 3DO, though a better controller and a second player beside you help. Playing solo against the computer is tough, and opponents in later rounds behave considerably more mercilessly than you might expect.
3do__super-street-fighter-ii-turbo.teaser: One of the most faithful home conversions of the arcade classic, plus the faster Turbo pace.

3do__samurai-shodown.article:
**Samurai Shodown** brought weapons into the world of fighting games, and that alone made it a different kind of game from the fist-based fighters that dominated arcades at the time. The fights take place in late-eighteenth-century Japan; the combatants wield katanas, spears, axes, and bows, and a single hit takes off far more health than in competing games. The pace is therefore slower and more cautious: players circle each other, wait for a mistake, and a single well-timed slash can turn an entire round around. The system rewards knocking an opponent's weapon out of their hands, temporarily disarming them, and a rage meter that fills up from taking hits and temporarily strengthens attacks. A referee running along the edge of the arena also gets involved, tossing items to the winning player, so the action on screen never feels empty.

The 3DO version was a home conversion of the arcade original and used the disc to preserve the large character sprites and detailed backgrounds, populated by minor background figures and shifting weather. The sound underscored the Japanese setting with traditional instruments and fighters' shouts, giving the atmosphere a cohesive feel. On a home console of the time, the game ranked among the best available in the genre, though a controller with more buttons and a second player across from you again helped achieve the ideal experience. The disc's capacity allowed the voice lines and longer music loops to be kept intact, which was far from a given on cartridge conversions of the era.

The original arcade version was met with an extraordinary response and the series became the main alternative to unarmed fighting games; reception of the console conversions varied depending on how well they preserved smoothness and character size. Its influence on the genre is evident in every later weapon-based fighting game that adopted the idea that a single hit has to hurt. Today, Samurai Shodown stands out for its calmer rhythm — anyone used to fast combo strings has to shift into a different mindset, but the reward is a duel where every movement carries weight and every mistake has a cost.
3do__samurai-shodown.teaser: Weapons instead of fists changed the rules of fighting games; slower, more careful, and deadlier duels.

3do__way-of-warrior.article:
**Way of the Warrior** is a fighting game best remembered for who was behind it: a small duo of developers created it for the 3DO, and the experience launched one of the most successful development careers in console history. The game is built on digitized characters captured from real people in costumes, so the fighters look like they were cut straight out of a B-movie action flick. Fights follow the classic one-on-one, best-of-three-rounds format; each fighter has their own special moves, and the game doesn't hold back on brutal finishing moves, including hazards built right into the arenas that can be used to slam an opponent into. The roster is deliberately over-the-top, and each character has a distinct look and fighting style, from giant brutes to fast swordsmen.

Technically, it was a showcase of what a small team could achieve with a disc-based format: large digitized sprites, captured backgrounds, and above all a soundtrack made up of licensed metal music that gave the game its energy and was often cited as one of its biggest strengths. The presentation felt flashy, with booming announcer calls and punchy hit sound effects, and the arenas were chosen to grab attention at first glance — a temple courtyard, a cave, or a place surrounded by a chasm. However, the combat balance fell short of the arcade fighters it was inspired by, and the controls were stiffer and less precise than genre fans were used to.

Contemporary reviews were split — some critics praised its boldness, style, and music, while others pointed out that it was more of a flashy imitation than a truly well-tuned fighter. Ultimately, though, the game's significance lies elsewhere: the earnings and experience it brought its creators let them move on to projects that fundamentally shaped the next console generation. Today, Way of the Warrior plays as a curiosity with a very strong period atmosphere, worth experiencing more for its style, music, and audacity than for the depth of its fighting system.
3do__way-of-warrior.teaser: A fighter with digitized actors, filmed by a small duo – the later Naughty Dog.

3do__killing-time.article:
**Killing Time** is a first-person shooter in which the player finds themselves on an abandoned island estate belonging to a wealthy family, where an occult ritual took place back in the 1920s. Exploration takes place across interconnected interiors and outdoor gardens; you search for keys and items that open further parts of the mansion, while fending off attacks from ghostly enemies ranging from reanimated corpses to strange mechanical creatures. The arsenal ranges from primitive weapons to more powerful ones, and part of progressing involves following clues that gradually explain what actually happened in the house. The mansion is designed as one interconnected whole, where a key found in one spot opens a door two floors away, so the player keeps returning to places they've already passed through.

The most interesting feature was the live-action video sequences embedded directly into the environment: at certain spots, ghosts of the house's former inhabitants would appear and play out short scenes from the past. This idea was ahead of its time and gave the game an exceptional atmosphere — the story wasn't told through an interrupting movie but unfolded around the player as they moved through the house. The sound design relied on oppressive silence, creaking, and sudden noises, making the island feel like a genuinely inhospitable place where no one is ever truly alone. The combination of live-action footage and game environment also showed that the disc could be used more cleverly than just for playing a long movie clip between levels.

The 3DO version was among the better-looking shooters on the console, with fairly detailed textures and large levels, at the cost of slower movement speed. Reviewers praised the atmosphere and the scale of the mansion, while criticism targeted the pacing and the fact that getting lost could drag on. Its influence is visible in later horror games that tell their story through the environment and found recordings instead of long dialogue. Today, Killing Time stands out precisely for its blend of filmed ghosts and exploration, even though the controls take some getting used to without modern aiming.
3do__killing-time.teaser: An FPS set in an abandoned mansion with an occult ritual from the 1920s; enemies range from corpses to machines.

3do__po-ed.article:
**PO'ed** is an unconventional first-person shooter in which you play a ship's cook stranded aboard a vessel overrun by monsters. Even the weapon selection hints at the game's tone: alongside regular firearms, you get to use a frying pan, a drill, and a rocket pack that lets you fly freely through space. That flight capability is the game's main distinguishing feature — the levels aren't flat corridors but vertical shafts and open spaces where you can rise to the ceiling, fly around an enemy, or reach spots a ground-bound character would never see. This significantly complicates navigation while also setting the game apart from its competition, since the player has to think about the height they're moving at and look for paths both above and below.

The environment is deliberately bizarre and repulsive, full of organic walls, fleshy structures, and enemies that look like the product of a twisted dream. At the same time, the game maintains a dark sense of humor: the exaggerated violence is presented in a way that feels more grotesque than frightening. Sound and music lean on industrial motifs and unpleasant shrieks, rounding off the atmosphere. The enemies also behave unpredictably, attacking from directions that weren't common in shooters of the time. On the 3DO, it was a technically ambitious project, since free movement across three axes was rare on consoles of that era and required a different control scheme than typical shooters.

Contemporary reception was mixed, and the game earned a reputation as a title you either fall in love with or shelve after twenty minutes. Criticism targeted the confusing level navigation and unusual controls, while praise went to its originality and boldness in going against the wave of imitators at the time. Over the years, PO'ed built up a cult status and is often remembered as one of the most idiosyncratic shooters of the nineties. Today it's an experience for players who enjoy strange games with their own internal logic and don't mind occasionally getting hopelessly lost.
3do__po-ed.teaser: An unconventional FPS starring a ship's cook; weapons include a frying pan, a drill, and a rocket thruster for flight.

3do__off-world-interceptor.article:
**Off-World Interceptor** is an action game behind the wheel of an off-road vehicle, in which the player, acting as a bounty hunter, chases fugitives across the surface of alien planets. It's not a classic race: missions have varied objectives, from destroying designated targets to surviving within a time limit or catching up with a specific vehicle, and between missions the player upgrades their car and weapons using earned rewards. The vehicle can jump, shoot, and crush smaller opponents on landing, making the driving feel more like an arcade chase across open terrain than following an ideal racing line. Fast runs over terrain waves are what players remember longest, since the vehicle stays airborne for a long time and the landing itself can be used as a weapon. The controls are deliberately heavier than is typical for circuit racers, since the vehicle has weight and easily flips onto its roof in a sharp turn.

Each planet's environment differs in color and terrain — from rocky plains to icy and volcanic regions — and uses three-dimensional rendering with a wide view that gave a sense of free movement. Speed was high, and jumps across terrain were among the things that set the game apart from the racing games of its time. The presentation was rounded out by exaggerated humor in the spirit of a TV bounty-hunting show, along with rock music that matched the pace.

Contemporary reviews were cooler toward the game than toward other titles from the same studio; praise went to the speed, the feel of the terrain, and the variety of missions, while criticism targeted the repetitive tasks and reduced clarity at high speed. Even so, it remains an interesting entry in the line of games that blend racing with combat and objectives, a genre that only fully developed in the following console generation. Today, Off-World Interceptor mainly delights with how loosely you can drive in it — it has no ambition to be a precise simulator and just lets the player barrel across the landscape, destroying everything that moves.
3do__off-world-interceptor.teaser: Action behind the wheel of an off-road vehicle; a bounty hunter crushes fugitives on alien planets.

3do__escape-from-monster-manor.article:
**Escape from Monster Manor** is a horror first-person shooter in which the player fights their way through a haunted mansion full of ghosts, monsters, and traps. The goal is to make your way through the house's floors, find fragments of a key item, and get rid of the main threat controlling the estate. The maze of corridors and rooms is navigated in the classic style of shooters of the era, except that instead of soldiers you're shooting at skeletons and specters, which often appear unexpectedly and without warning. A map in the corner of the screen helps with orientation, since the corridors look quite similar to one another and it's easy to get lost. Besides ammunition, you also search for health kits and items that open locked sections, so getting through each floor is always a combination of combat and searching.

The game was important for the 3DO as proof that the console could handle textured three-dimensional environments, which up to that point had been the domain of computers. Enemies are rendered as scaled sprites, but the environment uses fully textured walls, and the game runs smoothly even when several opponents gather at once in a tight space. Its strongest point is the mood: dim lighting, echoing footsteps, and music that works more with tension than melody managed to create a sense of dread even with the modest means available at the time. A sudden enemy appearing in a narrow corridor still reliably works today.

At the time, the game was praised as a decent showcase of the console's technical abilities and as one of the few ways to play a horror shooter on the 3DO; criticism targeted the repetitive spaces and limited enemy variety. Its significance lies mainly in the fact that it was one of the first attempts to bring this genre to a disc-based home console. Today, Escape from Monster Manor is a short but atmospheric affair, best enjoyed with the lights off and an acceptance that you'll be walking in circles a lot.
3do__escape-from-monster-manor.teaser: A horror shooter through a mansion full of ghosts and traps; instead of soldiers, you shoot at skeletons.

3do__novastorm.article:
**Novastorm** is an on-rails space shooter built around the then-new ability to play pre-rendered video straight from disc. The player controls a fighter craft moving along a fixed path above planetary surfaces, through tunnels, and among the wreckage of ships, dodging obstacles and shooting down waves of enemies. The ship can move across the whole screen, collect weapon upgrades, and must survive to the end of the segment, where a bigger opponent awaits. The game is short but unforgiving: collisions with the environment are punished harshly, and progress requires learning where each obstacle appears and where the safe path lies. Weapon upgrades are also lost after being hit, so a single mistake often means finishing the rest of the segment with basic weaponry.

Visually, it was one of the most impressive titles of its time. The background consisted of smoothly played pre-rendered animation with a level of detail that consoles of the era couldn't achieve in real time, with game objects moving over it. The result felt like a flight through a sci-fi film, though at the cost of the environment being non-interactive and the route always the same. Sound and music relied on dense electronic motifs that matched the sense of speed and helped maintain tension through to the end of each segment. Meanwhile, the console only had to handle the moving objects and overlays, which was exactly the trick that made the game look significantly better than its actual computational demands would suggest.

Contemporary reviews varied depending on how much the reviewer valued spectacle over depth of gameplay — the technical side drew admiration, while the actual gameplay was described as simple and repetitive. Novastorm is today a typical example of the first wave of games that tried to use the disc as a cinematic medium, and in that sense it has documentary value. As a game, it works best in short sessions, where the player can enjoy the speed and visual assault without being bothered by the fact that the path can't be influenced in any way.
3do__novastorm.teaser: An on-rails space shooter built on the then-new technique of video played back from disc.

3do__myst.article:
**Myst** is an adventure game set on a lonely island where the player washes ashore without explanation, without an inventory full of items, and with practically no instructions at all. The 3DO version came out in 1994 and was among the titles the console liked to show off with: it was proof of what a CD-ROM could do when, instead of pixel graphics, it offered pre-rendered images of unusual sharpness. The game is controlled as a sequence of static views, switched between by clicking; forward progress is determined not by combat or dexterity but by the ability to notice details, jot down numbers, tones, and symbols, and connect them into working wholes. The island is one big machine, and the individual puzzles are its gears — pipes, generators, a clock tower, or a rocket model.

The storytelling stays on the sidelines. Books scattered across the island lead to other worlds, and two brothers trapped within their pages take turns trying to convince the player of their innocence. You don't find out who's lying from dialogue but from what you discover in their rooms and notes. On the 3DO, sound plays an important role: the environment is mostly silence woven through with creaking wood, wind, and water, so every musical cue feels like an event. Loading times between screens are noticeable, and purists objected that the transitions weren't as smooth as on powerful computers, but the atmosphere of an abandoned place came through intact.

At the time, it was a huge phenomenon that briefly brought adventure games out of the gaming subculture and into ordinary households, kicking off an entire wave of similarly styled CD titles with pre-rendered graphics. Today, Myst feels slower than we're used to, and some puzzles require patience and a notepad. But that's precisely its strength: it's a game that doesn't rush, doesn't hold your hand, and rewards attention. On the 3DO, it also remains an important record of where the console was originally meant to head — toward a home multimedia experience player, not just another box for action games.
3do__myst.teaser: A lonely island without words or an inventory; a showcase of what CD-ROM could do with sharp graphics.

3do__7th-guest.article:
**The 7th Guest** is a horror adventure set in the mansion of toy maker Henry Stauf, to which six guests have been invited, none of them knowing who the seventh is. The 3DO version from 1994 was among the first titles to introduce home consoles to a game built almost entirely around CD: the house is modeled in 3D, the camera moves between rooms via pre-rendered flythroughs, and actors filmed against a blue screen appear directly in the rooms like ghosts of past events. For its time, it was an image that was hard to ignore in a living room.

Gameplay-wise, it's a series of logic puzzles set in individual rooms — chessboard problems, moving pieces around, a microscope in the laboratory, or a game with tombstones in the graveyard. Some rank among the best the genre has offered, others are notoriously known for their difficulty and could stop players in their tracks for days. Between puzzles, the house opens up gradually, and fragments of unfolding scenes piece together a story of greed, the loss of a child, and a deal that was unwise to make. The atmosphere is held together by music with jazz-tinged, warped motifs and a hint-giving voice that regularly mocks the player. And the hints aren't free — the game remembers every time you use one and makes sure to let you know about it.

At the time, The 7th Guest was regarded as proof that CD-ROM wasn't just an expensive floppy disk, and it became one of the titles that made people buy the drive in the first place. On the 3DO, it felt somewhat less sensational than on computers, since the console had more CD productions of that kind, but it was still a flagship of its library. Today, the game shows its age most in the acting performances — the filmed sequences come across as amusing rather than frightening — while the puzzle design and the feel of an empty, ticking house hold up surprisingly well. It's a title best played as something of a period document, but one that still makes you sweat and, after a few hours, catch yourself bringing a pencil and paper to the screen.
3do__7th-guest.teaser: A horror adventure in toymaker Stauf's house; one of the first titles built purely for CD.

3do__alone-in-dark.article:
**Alone in the Dark** brought to the 3DO in 1994 a game that a few years earlier had practically invented survival horror on computers. The player enters as either private detective Edward Carnby or Emily Hartwood into the Louisiana mansion of Derceto, meant only to look into the estate of its deceased owner — and within minutes discovers that the house is full of something that can't be beaten down with fists or shot away. The mansion quickly turns from a place to explore into a trap, with the only way out leading forward, through the attic, the cellar, and a library full of unpleasant answers.

The key lies in the technical approach: polygonal characters move across hand-painted backgrounds, and the camera is fixed, set up like a film shot. This gives the game its unease, because you often see what's coming before you know how to avoid it — or, conversely, you just hear footsteps offscreen. The inventory is limited, ammunition scarce, and the best strategy is often to flee, barricade a door, or use an entirely different trick than shooting. Books and journals scattered around the rooms aren't decoration: they carry instructions on how to defeat a specific monster and reference the Lovecraftian mythology the game openly draws from. Reading, then, isn't a delay but a full-fledged game mechanic.

The 3DO version benefited from the console handling smoother playback and better sound than typical computers of the time, so the deep tones and the silence between them came through in full. At the time, the game was praised as a breakthrough in telling horror stories in real time, and its influence can be seen across a whole line of later series, where a fixed camera, scarce ammunition, and a hostile environment remained the genre's basic grammar. Today the stiff controls are a tough nut to crack and the character models look like blocky puppets, but the tight design of the house and the feeling that the mansion is slowly swallowing you endure. Anyone with patience for the period interface will get one of the most important horror games in gaming history.
3do__alone-in-dark.teaser: A port of the game that essentially invented the survival horror genre on computers a few years earlier.

3do__d.article:
**D** is a horror adventure that came out on the 3DO in 1995 and makes clear from the first minute that it wants to be more of an interactive film than a game. Laura Harris enters a hospital where her father committed a massacre without explanation, and instead of hospital corridors finds herself in a gothic mansion full of blood, mirrors, and family secrets. The entire title is told through pre-rendered animations, through which the player moves along fixed paths, and it carries one unusual rule: it runs in a single sitting, with a two-hour time limit and no way to save. Whether the player succeeds or not, it's over after two hours.

This fundamentally changes how D plays. The puzzles aren't especially complex, but the ticking clock turns them into a tense test — and when time runs out, you start over from the beginning. The game relies on pacing, editing, and what it shows only for a moment. Controls are limited to a few directions and interactions, so attention stays on the image. Studio WARP also played with what the player expects: the title hides scenes that most people never see, and several moments that, at release, caused embarrassment even among publishers. The game gives no hint of them anywhere, and some unlock only through very specific player behavior.

Technically, it was an impressive demonstration of what CD media could do — smooth full-screen animation and music that irritates the nerves rather than scaring with a loud jolt. At the time, the game was a hit especially in Japan, where it carried the reputation of an uncompromising auteur project, and in the West it became one of the titles people remember the 3DO for at all. Today it's clear how narrow a corridor it offers players and how little real freedom it contains. Yet it remains an unusually stylish piece: short, tight, unpleasant, and played with a straight face at a time when most similar games snickered at their own B-movie origins.
3do__d.teaser: A horror adventure that wants to be an interactive film more than a game, set in a gothic mansion.

3do__policenauts.article:
**Policenauts** is a sprawling detective adventure by Hideo Kojima that reached the 3DO in 1995 and ranks among the most ambitious narrative games on the whole console. Jonathan Ingram, once a member of the police force on the orbital colony Beyond Coast, was accidentally launched into space and, after twenty-five years in hibernation, returns to a scene he no longer recognizes. An investigation into a missing man grows into a case involving smuggling, corporations, and a colony that hides its own rot beneath a polished surface. Ingram, moreover, isn't a hero arriving from outside but a man missing a quarter century of life, while everyone around him has aged in the meantime.

It plays as a cursor-driven graphic adventure: the player searches screens, questions characters on dozens of topics, and shooting sections with a reticle appear between investigations. Most of the time, though, is taken up by dialogue — long, well written, and full of tangents where you can ask about almost anything, including things entirely unrelated to the case. The anime visuals, cinematic framing of scenes, and music that shifts between calm noir passages and action motifs give the game an unusually mature tone. The pace is deliberately slow — the game wants you to ask questions, not rush.

The 3DO version mattered among ports because it was the first to bring the game from Japanese computers to a console, preceding later releases on Saturn and PlayStation. The title never received an official English translation, so in the West it long circulated as a legend most people only knew by hearsay. Today, Policenauts is fascinating precisely because it so clearly foreshadows the storytelling methods Kojima later became famous for: long conversations, technical detail, dark humor, and a tendency to hold the player up for the sake of one good scene. Anyone who likes adventures built on text and atmosphere will find one of the genre's peaks here — and one of the strongest reasons to return to the 3DO library at all.
3do__policenauts.teaser: A detective adventure by Hideo Kojima about a policeman pulled from 25 years of hibernation into a conspiracy.

3do__star-control-ii-ur-quan-masters.article:
**Star Control II: The Ur-Quan Masters** arrived on the 3DO in 1994 and brought to the console something nobody expected: a massive space game blending exploration, diplomacy, resource gathering, and arcade ship combat. The player returns to Earth with a prototype alien ship and discovers that an alien invader has since taken over the Solar System. From there, a galaxy opens up full of star systems, planets to explore, and races to deal with, trade with, or wage war on. None of it unfolds in closed chapters: the player builds their own flight plan and can easily run into things they're nowhere near strong enough to handle yet.

The structure is unusually free. Nobody tells the player where to fly; progress arises from conversations, in which every race speaks in its own, strongly characterized tone — from desperately servile to unbearably arrogant. Landing on planets and mining resources fund ship upgrades, battles play out in a two-dimensional arena with gravity, and every vessel has its own special ability, so even a weaker ship can win with the right tactics. Above it all runs a hidden time pressure: the galaxy keeps evolving even without the player, and delay only makes things worse.

The 3DO version used the CD to give characters spoken voices, which mattered a great deal for a game built on conversation. At the time, it was a critically acclaimed title that nonetheless sold rather slowly and only earned its fame gradually; a later community version built on the released source code has kept it alive to this day. Star Control II's influence shows everywhere that an open universe combines with talkative aliens and dark humor. Today it's still one of the best games of its kind, only it requires a willingness to take notes and find your own way, since nobody provided a quest marker. But that's exactly where its sense of discovery comes from — one that games an order of magnitude bigger still chase today.
3do__star-control-ii-ur-quan-masters.teaser: A sprawling space RPG blending exploration, diplomacy, and arcade-style ship combat.

3do__guardian-war.article:
**Guardian War** is a tactical RPG from studio Micro Cabin, one of the first attempts to show that the 3DO could handle slower, more thoughtful games too. In Japan it was released as Powers Kingdom, and the player leads a group of warriors against a dark power that has taken over the land. The story is classic fantasy that mainly serves as a framework for battles, where positioning of units and knowing what each character can do are what matter. The party grows over the campaign, and with it the number of ways any single encounter can be resolved.

Battles take place on a grid in an isometric view that can be rotated — an impressive trick on a console of the time, since the scene is fully polygonal and the camera circles the battlefield without stuttering. Characters upgrade into stronger classes during play, each with its own attack range and abilities, so success depends on who you send forward and who stays behind. Anyone who enjoys taking their time in turn-based battles gets exactly what they expect; anyone wanting a brisk pace will instead struggle with how long a single encounter takes. The game doesn't spare the player's time, but it rewards planning and knowledge of enemy weaknesses, of which it offers plenty.

Technically, Guardian War leaned into what the console did best: colorful three-dimensional scenes without the limits of cartridge games, smooth camera rotation, and CD music. Sound and color were exactly what the console liked to flaunt over its cartridge-based competition. At the time it was received with lukewarm to positive reviews — critics praised the look and depth, criticized the length and cluttered interface. Within the 3DO library, though, it holds a special place, since RPGs were scarce there and tactical ones even scarcer. Today it plays like an interesting detour: a game doing in the mid-1990s on a console what would commonly appear a generation later, just without the polish of later genre entries. For fans of tactical combat it's a find; for everyone else, more of a curiosity.
3do__guardian-war.teaser: A tactical RPG by Micro Cabin, released in Japan as Powers Kingdom.

3do__lucienne-s-quest.article:
**Lucienne's Quest** is a classic Japanese RPG and also one of the few that made it to the 3DO in an English version. The young sorceress Lucienne sets out on a journey during which she gathers a colorful party and faces a threat that soon outgrows her original assignment. It's told lightly, with humor and no attempt at grand drama, which sets the game apart from most of the ponderous fantasy stories of its time and makes it pleasantly undemanding company for long evenings. The characters are introduced gradually, each carrying their own reason for joining the quest at all.

Mechanically, it's a textbook JRPG: top-down view, moving through towns and dungeons, random encounters, and turn-based battles with spells, attacks, and items. Fights are clear, individual abilities have obviously readable uses, and the difficulty suits more of an entry point into the genre than a long test of patience. Progress is linear, the map opens chapter by chapter, and time between battles is filled with conversations among characters drawn with a distinctly comic-book character. Anyone who has played Japanese RPGs on other consoles will feel right at home immediately. The need to endlessly grind is present but not overdone, and the length of the whole campaign matches shorter entries in the genre rather than longer ones.

On the 3DO, the game used the CD mainly for music and for animated sequences in an anime style, which was still rare on consoles at the time. At the time, it passed without much attention — the console sold in small numbers in North America, and Japanese RPGs had no audience there waiting for them. That's exactly why it's a sought-after piece for collectors today: it's one of the few ways to play a traditional Japanese RPG on the 3DO without knowing Japanese. Mechanically it brings nothing revolutionary, but as proof of just how varied the 3DO's library actually was, it's certainly worth attention. It's a reminder of a time when Japanese developers tried to gain a foothold even on a platform that ultimately failed.
3do__lucienne-s-quest.teaser: A lighthearted JRPG starring a sorceress; one of the few 3DO RPGs also released in English.

3do__immercenary.article:
**Immercenary** is an action RPG developed specifically for the 3DO and released in 1994, set inside a digital world called Perfect. The player enters it as a hunter with a single goal: reach the ruler known as Perfect One and dethrone her. Between him and the top stands a hierarchy of other beings who hunt each other within this world and climb the ranks, so the player never moves across an empty map. The climb upward thus serves as both story and difficulty regulator — the higher you get, the tougher opponents start taking interest in you.

The world is open and entirely polygonal, which was unusual for a console in 1994; the player moves through it in first-person view, shoots, collects energy, and advances through whoever they defeat. Enemies aren't mere targets — they hold their own position in the hierarchy, and defeating someone affects who confronts you next. Visually, it's a feverish mix of neon colors and strange shapes, accompanied by music that underscores the feeling of moving inside a computer rather than a landscape. Orientation is deliberately difficult, and the game explains its rules rather grudgingly. The player learns orientation and the meaning of individual indicators mainly through trial and error.

At the time, it was a title critics treated as a display of courage: technically ambitious, visually distinctive, and unusual to play, but also confusing and unfinished in places. Commercially it sank along with the console, and today it's known mainly among people who collect 3DO hardware. That's exactly why it's worth remembering: it's one of the few attempts in the early nineties to build an open three-dimensional world with RPG elements, and although the controls are stiff and the frame rate wavers, the idea itself holds up. Anyone who likes strange, original games from a time when nobody quite knew what 3D was supposed to mean will find here a rewarding piece that, moreover, can't be mistaken for anything else.
3do__immercenary.teaser: An action RPG made specifically for the 3DO; a hunter climbs the hierarchy toward the ruler of a digital world.

3do__horde.article:
**The Horde** is a hybrid of strategy and action in which the player defends a village against a horde of ravenous creatures. The 3DO version from 1994 is famous especially for its live-action segments, in which the lead character Chauncey was played by Kirk Cameron — between rounds, a court comedy unfolds about promotion, intrigue, and an ungrateful monarch, filmed with a straight face and a B-movie budget. The narrative frame intersects with the gameplay: what happens in a scene affects what land and what options you're given.

Mechanically, two layers alternate. Between waves of attacks, the player manages resources: buying walls, ditches, towers, and traps and placing them around the property to delay the creatures as long as possible and protect villagers and livestock. When an attack begins, the game switches to isometric action, where Chauncey personally finishes off with his sword whatever the defenses failed to stop. Tension arises because preparation and combat depend on each other — a badly placed wall shows up a minute later, when the creatures break through exactly where you didn't want them to. Money for defense, meanwhile, comes from how much the village produces each season, so every lost cottage counts twice. Difficulty rises steadily, and enemies multiply faster than money does.

Technically, the game combined drawn environments with digitized actors and was among the titles the 3DO used to show off the merging of film and game. The loud, exaggerated comedy feels kitschy today, but that's exactly what gives it its period flavor. At the time, The Horde was received warmly and considered one of the few successful hybrids of base-defense and action; its scheme of build a trap, then go fight foreshadows the later wave of tower-defense-style games. Today it's short, easy to grasp, and unexpectedly addictive — and the live-action content works as a bonus worth watching, both for how unseriously the creators took themselves and how confidently they stitched the whole thing together.
3do__horde.teaser: Defending a village against a horde of monsters, famous for its cutscenes starring Kirk Cameron.

3do__syndicate.article:
**Syndicate** is a cyberpunk tactical strategy game from Bullfrog Productions that arrived on the 3DO in 1995. The player runs one of the future's corporations, tasked with taking over the world map city by city. Into every mission go four cybernetically enhanced agents — and they aren't heroes, just tools that get simply replaced if lost. Between missions, controlled territories generate tax revenue, funding further expansion and turning the world map into a layer of the game in its own right.

Missions take place in isometric cities full of pedestrians, cars, and police, and usually offer more than one approach: a quiet infiltration, an open firefight, or a device that turns bystanders into your own units. Between actions, profits are spent in the main menu on researching new weapons and on cybernetic implants that boost an agent's speed, durability, and accuracy. The arsenal also includes drugs administered mid-battle that can calm an agent down or whip them into aggression — with the risk that they'll lose control. The game's tone is cold and cynical: civilians are just a statistic to be sacrificed without hesitation, and the story never pretends otherwise. It's exactly this ruthlessness that people remember Syndicate for.

Syndicate arrived on the 3DO at a time when consoles generally steered clear of strategy games this complex, making it one of the most demanding titles in the whole library. Visually it rests on a dark, rain-soaked city lit by neon, with music that bubbles and drones rather than plays a melody. At the time it was praised as one of the studio's best games and as a title that translated cyberpunk into playable form earlier than most others. Today it shows that controlling a squad of four agents is a bit rough and missions repeat after a while, but the atmosphere of a heartless corporate future has few rivals, and the game still reads well as a forerunner of today's tactical games, which likewise combine out-of-mission preparation with in-mission improvisation.
3do__syndicate.teaser: Cyberpunk tactics from Bullfrog; agents are just tools to be replaced.

3do__theme-park.article:
**Theme Park** is a construction and management game from Bullfrog Productions in which an empty field grows into a full amusement park. The 3DO version arrived in 1995, bringing to console a title that had until then been the domain of computers. The player places rides, builds paths, hires staff, and above all watches how visitors behave — where they walk, where they bunch up, what bores them, and when their patience runs out. The park doesn't work like a plan on paper; it behaves like a living organism that reacts to every change you make.

The game's charm lies in the details of its economy. You can raise ticket prices, but people notice; you can add extra sugar to the soda so visitors get thirstier and buy more; you can build a roller coaster dangerously fast, raising both thrill and risk. Staff want raises or they go on strike, and neglected maintenance lets litter pile up across the park. Alongside the building there's also a business layer of buying land and researching new rides, so the game glides from carefree tinkering into bookkeeping without the player quite noticing. Expanding into other countries then adds different conditions and prices, so a tried-and-true approach doesn't work the same way everywhere.

On the 3DO the game leaned on CD audio: crowd noise, carousel music, and general park bustle give the screen full of tiny figures an unexpectedly lively character. Controlling it without a mouse is naturally more awkward than on a computer, and the interface takes a while to get used to, but the game itself remained untouched. At the time it was a huge success that, together with other Bullfrog titles, established the construction-and-management genre for entertainment sims and led directly to later theme-park-building games. Today Theme Park is still legible and pleasantly wicked — it's a game about turning human fun into a money machine, and that's exactly why it's still fun decades later. It suits a quick session just as well as an evening of full-scale building, because the park keeps running even while the player is just watching it for a while.
3do__theme-park.teaser: Bullfrog's classic tycoon game about building a theme park, where visitor behavior decides everything.

3do__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tiger.article:
**Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger** is a space combat game that arrived on the 3DO in 1995, bringing to console one of the most expensive productions of its era. Between cockpit flights unfolds an extensive live-action story shot with real actors, in which Colonel Blair faces the final phase of a long war against the feline Kilrathi. The player walks the decks of the carrier, talks with the crew, and his choices affect how relationships and the whole campaign play out. The conversations aren't just filler between missions — they're the main reason you want to fly the next one at all.

The gameplay itself is a classic space simulator simplified for a gamepad: pick a fighter and loadout, get briefed, jump into a sector, dogfight maneuvering enemies, and return to the carrier. Missions link together and their outcomes shape the campaign, so failure doesn't necessarily mean the end, just a worse starting position for what comes next. Flying is fast and readable, objectives simple — escort a convoy, scout, defend — and the tension comes less from the combat itself than from who makes it back to the squadron and who you won't be waiting for at the next briefing. Losing a wingman isn't just a statistic, because you'd been talking to them for a long time beforehand.

Technically this was a demanding port: the game originally shipped across several discs for computers, and bringing the live-action footage to console demanded compromises in image quality. Still, the essentials survived — the alternation of film and action at a pace that had no equal at the time. At the time, the third installment was seen as the high point of efforts to merge games and film, and also as the moment when live-action content in games reached a decent craft level. Today it's noticeable that the story scenes take up a lot of the runtime and that the dogfights themselves are simple compared to later simulators. As a period piece, though, Wing Commander III still works, and on the 3DO it ranks among the library's most lavish productions.
3do__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tiger.teaser: A space combat game with an expensive live-action story; one of the priciest productions of its time.

cd-i__hotel-mario.article:
**Hotel Mario** is one of the strangest detours in the famous Italian plumber's history, and also one of the best-known titles ever released for the Philips CD-i. It came about through a licensing deal that let Philips use characters owned by Nintendo, and the result is a logic platformer built on a single idea: closing doors. Mario and Luigi make their way through seven hotels that Bowser and his Koopalings have opened across the Mushroom Kingdom, and on every floor they must slam shut all the open doors. Once the last one closes, the floor is done and the hero moves up. It sounds simple, but as the levels progress they add elevators, moving platforms, doors that reopen on their own, and enemies that knock the player off narrow ledges. The game ends up offering more of a rhythmic puzzle than classic action, and in its two-player co-op mode it can be surprisingly fun.

Technically it's a modest title that comes nowhere near exploiting what the CD medium could offer. The graphics are simple, the controls feel clunky, and Mario responds with noticeable lag, something most contemporary reviewers complained about. What actually made the game famous were the animated cutscenes between hotels: their jerky animation, odd color choices, and overly theatrical voice acting turned them into one of the most-quoted phenomena of nineties gaming history. Plenty of people who never cared about the CD-i console can still quote lines from the opening scene.

Contemporary reception was lukewarm at best and Hotel Mario gradually became a symbol of how a licensed game turns out without the original creator's oversight. Today it can be viewed more kindly, as a curious historical item worth trying. The core mechanic starts to click after a few floors, the difficulty ramps up fairly, and it's the only Mario game that never appeared on Nintendo hardware. Collectors chase it more for the story told about it than for its gameplay, and that's exactly where its peculiar charm lies.
cd-i__hotel-mario.teaser: A Nintendo-licensed platformer built around a single idea: closing doors.

cd-i__link-faces-of-evil.article:
**Link: The Faces of Evil** is one of two action titles made for the CD-i thanks to a license letting Philips use characters from The Legend of Zelda universe. Unlike Nintendo's own games, this one has a side-scrolling view: Link hacks his way through caves, rocky passages, and villages on the island of Koridai, collecting potions, lamps, ropes, and other gear while trying to stop the wizard Ganon from imprisoning Princess Zelda. The individual stretches are linked by a map of the island the player travels across between locations, and many of them require returning with a newly acquired item. Combat relies on precisely timed sword swings that can also be aimed up and down, and the game is unexpectedly harsh: enemies have long reach, platforms tend to be narrow, and death comes quickly.

Visually the game rests on hand-drawn backgrounds and animated cutscenes, whose rough animation and quirky voice acting became the most-quoted part of the whole project. The audio makes use of the CD medium, so the music is recorded rather than synthesized, giving the levels an unusually dark, almost brooding atmosphere. The controls, however, run up against the hardware's limits: the CD-i controller was designed more for navigating multimedia catalogs than for fast action, so sluggish response and imprecise jumps complicate even otherwise simple passages.

Reviewers received the game coldly, and along with its sister title Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon, time turned it into a byword for a botched license. Over time, though, an opposite view has also emerged. Beneath the clumsy controls hides a surprisingly large and honestly designed action platformer, with exploration, item collecting, and hidden shortcuts, that with a better gamepad could have held its own alongside typical productions of its day. Today it's worth trying mainly as a curiosity and as evidence of what Hyrule looks like without Nintendo's oversight, with the understanding that it's more a historical experience than a comfortable one.
cd-i__link-faces-of-evil.teaser: A side-scrolling action platformer based on Zelda, created thanks to Philips's license for Nintendo's characters.

cd-i__zelda-wand-of-gamelon.article:
**Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon** is a sister title to Link: The Faces of Evil, and holds a special distinction in one respect: Princess Zelda is here, for the first time, a fully playable heroine controlled by the player for the entire game. While Link and her father have vanished in the land of Gamelon, where they went to help Duke Onkled, Zelda sets out on the quest alone. The game runs on the same principle as Faces of Evil — a side-scrolling platformer linked by a map the heroine crosses between castles, swamps, mines, and harbors. Her weapon is a sword supplemented by items she finds, from a lantern to a rope to magic wands, and a large part of progress comes down to talking to residents who hint where to go next and what to bring.

Compared to its brother title, Gamelon feels a bit more manageable and less punishing, though here too the controls are sluggish and the jumps imprecise. Technically the game again benefits from the CD medium: backgrounds are painted, the music recorded, and drawn animations play between chapters, whose bare-bones style and unforgettable voice acting have earned it lasting internet fame. Thanks to dark colors and calmer music, the atmosphere is surprisingly gloomy, which is unusual for a game based on a fairy-tale source.

Contemporary reviews were merciless, and the Zelda brand suffered on the CD-i a notorious blow that Nintendo never officially mentions. Yet the game has its circle of defenders: it offers a decently sized world, plenty of optional nooks, and progress that rewards patient exploration. Today most players approach it as a document of an era when Japanese franchises ended up in the hands of Western studios with no experience making action games. Anyone who pushes through the first rough hour and gets used to the sluggish controls will find an honestly expansive adventure that's more interesting than its reputation suggests. It gains extra value from the fact that a playable Zelda in the lead role wouldn't reappear for many years afterward, so for a long time this botched CD-i outing remained the only chance to actually play as the princess.
cd-i__zelda-wand-of-gamelon.teaser: A sister game to Faces of Evil; for the first time, Princess Zelda is a full-fledged playable heroine.

cd-i__zelda-s-adventure.article:
**Zelda's Adventure** is the third and strangest game to carry the Zelda name, released exclusively for the Philips CD-i. Unlike the two platformers, it returns to the top-down view that made the original The Legend of Zelda famous, and it's set in the land of Tolemac, which Ganon has conquered. In it, Zelda sets out to find the kidnapped Link, collects spells and tools, opens temples scattered across a sprawling map, and fights monsters on individual screens. Progression is classically adventure-style: each temple requires a specific ability acquired elsewhere, so the world opens up gradually and the map becomes the main tool for orientation.

The technical execution is completely different from its sister games. The environments were made by digitizing hand-built sets and models, the characters were captured from live-action footage, and the story sequences form a live-action film with costumed actors. The result feels dark, dreamlike, and at times outright eerie, aided by muted music and hissing ambient sound. Its major weakness, though, is speed: you wait for loading between screens, combat feels stiff, and the sword attack has an unpleasantly short reach, so many encounters get solved more by dodging than by fighting.

The game came out at a time when interest in the CD-i had already faded, and it remained the least known entry of the whole trio. Reviewers criticized above all its slowness and imprecise gameplay, though they praised its atmosphere and its attempt at its own visual language. Today Zelda's Adventure is interesting exactly because it looks so different from anything else in the franchise: it's a strange blend of fairy tale, live-action film, and classic action-adventure from the eighties. For collectors it's a rare piece; for curious players, a trip into a world that could only have emerged during the brief period of fascination with multimedia CDs. It's also worth noting how generous a map the developers managed to fit onto the disc: every temple has its own theme and its own monsters, and between them lies a sprawling landscape you can cross in many directions and where you can genuinely get lost even with notes in hand.
cd-i__zelda-s-adventure.teaser: The third and strangest Zelda on the CD-i; it returns to the top-down view like the original NES game.

cd-i__burn-cycle.article:
**Burn:Cycle** is the best calling card for what the Philips CD-i could do at a time when people believed the future of games lay in interactive film. The player takes on the role of data thief Sol Cutter, who picks up a virus in his head during a heist. From that moment a roughly two-hour countdown starts, after which the virus will destroy his brain, and the whole game is one long escape through a city full of corporations, hackers, and strange cybernetic beings. The gameplay combines movement through pre-rendered environments, collecting and using items, conversations, and several mini-game interludes, from flying through data tunnels to logic puzzles involving locks and security systems.

Technically it's an impressive piece of work: the combination of drawn animation, computer graphics, and smoothly played video from disc was among the best that ran on a home device in the mid-nineties. The sound is even stronger, since the game rests on an electronic soundtrack that doesn't just accompany the action but sets the whole mood and drives the pace of the escape. The atmosphere is tense, mesmerizing, and thoroughly cyberpunk, closely related to the films and books that shaped the genre at the time.

At the time, Burn:Cycle was among the best-reviewed titles on the whole platform and became a game retailers used to demonstrate what the CD-i could do. It was later ported to personal computers, reaching audiences beyond the narrow base of Philips owners. Today it's kept afloat mostly by its style: the story can be finished in one longer afternoon, the puzzles are never especially harsh, and the time limit gives the pacing an urgency that many other FMV games lack. Anyone who wants to see the one title that fully exploited what the new medium could do on the CD-i should start with this one. It has also aged better than most contemporary attempts at interactive film, because instead of relying on live actors it bets on stylized animation and a world that doesn't feel cheap even after thirty years.
cd-i__burn-cycle.teaser: A sci-fi adventure about a data thief with a virus in his head and a two-hour countdown to brain destruction.

cd-i__7th-guest.article:
**The 7th Guest** arrived on the Philips CD-i as a port of one of the most celebrated titles of the early CD-ROM era, and it stands among the strongest entries in the platform's catalog. The player wanders the abandoned mansion of toymaker Henry Stauf, where six guests gathered years ago and none of them ever left. The whole house is a connected set of puzzles: chess variants, piece-sliding challenges, mazes, word games, and logic puzzles that must be solved to unlock further rooms. Between them, the ghosts of the original guests appear in the air, gradually revealing what happened in the house.

The game was a technical sensation in its day, combining pre-rendered three-dimensional environments with smooth movement through the corridors and live actors inserted directly into the scenes. That is exactly what made it a showcase title for CD drives, and porting it to CD-i made sense: the platform was built around video played from disc and a home setup connected to a television. Cursor control via the controller is slower than a mouse, but for a game built on calm reasoning that hardly matters.
