The sound and music, including the famous theme and the eerie whispered voices, rank among the best the genre has ever produced.

The success of The 7th Guest fundamentally shaped what games looked like in the mid-nineties and kicked off a wave of titles built around live actors and extensive video sequences. Contemporary critics praised the inventiveness of the puzzles and the atmosphere, with complaints mostly aimed at the story being little more than window dressing between riddles. Today the game still works as a beautifully tuned horror experience for patient players: the puzzles have aged well because they are built on pure logic, and the empty house with its creaking wood and indistinct voices still creates unpleasant tension. Anyone wanting to try what games boasted about when CD media first arrived will find here one of the few titles that holds up as full-fledged entertainment, not merely as a technical demo.
cd-i__7th-guest.teaser: The famous puzzle adventure from the early CD-ROM era, set in an abandoned mansion full of puzzles and mysteries.

cd-i__myst.article:
**Myst** appeared on the Philips CD-i quite late, when the platform was already fading, yet it remains one of the most valuable titles ever brought to it. The player finds themselves on an abandoned island with no instructions, no goal, and almost no text. All that is available is an environment full of machines, libraries, pipes, and control panels that must be understood and set in motion. Gradually, further worlds open up from books, each with its own logic and its own mechanisms, and fragments of journals piece together the story of two brothers and their father. There is no enemy here, no time limit, no way to die — only curiosity and honest observation.

The game is built on pre-rendered images between which the player moves by clicking, which on CD-i shows up as longer loading times and a slower-moving cursor than on a computer. Visually, though, the island still holds up today: the static scenes are carefully composed and enhanced with subtle animation and, above all, sound. The audio side is crucial, since the quiet music, wind, waves, and the hum of mechanisms carry the entire atmosphere of solitude. The puzzles are not bolted on from the outside but grow out of the world itself, so the player is not guessing what the author wants but discovering how the machine in front of them actually works.

Myst became one of the best-selling games of the nineties and for a long time defined what a calm adventure game for a wide audience looked like. Critics praised its ideas and its technical execution, with reservations aimed at the static nature of the world and occasional aimless wandering. Today its influence is visible wherever a game tells its story through environment and lets the player explore at their own pace. The CD-i version is interesting mainly as proof that this phenomenon found its way even onto a console hooked up to a television — a setting where, unlike at a computer monitor, people mostly played in twos or threes. And it is precisely in pairs, with one person sketching diagrams on paper and the other handling the cursor, that Myst works best.
cd-i__myst.teaser: A late but valuable addition to the CD-i; a mysterious island with almost no guidance and no text.

cd-i__dragon-s-lair.article:
**Dragon's Lair** is a legend from the arcades that returned on the Philips CD-i in a form that finally made sense at home. The knight Dirk the Daring ventures into the castle of the dragon Singe to rescue Princess Daphne, and the whole game is essentially an animated film into which the player intervenes with short commands at the right moment. When doors open with tentacles reaching out, or the floor gives way underfoot, the player must instantly choose a direction or draw a sword. A mistake means instant death and one of dozens of carefully animated scenes in which the knight comes to a bad end. Progress therefore rests on memorizing the correct sequence of reactions, a principle as austere as it is addictive.

Technically, it was ideal material for the CD medium. The original arcade machine used LaserDisc and played back full animation drawn by professionals from the classic school of animated film, and the CD-i version builds directly on that: the picture is fluid, the music and sound effects come from the original, and the result feels like a Saturday-morning cartoon the player gets to reach into. Controlling it via the CD-i controller demands a certain tolerance for lag, since the window for the correct decision is short and imprecision is punished.

At the time, Dragon's Lair was seen both as a showcase of what the new medium could do and as proof that interactive film has its limits. The game offers a stunning spectacle but fairly shallow gameplay, something critics already pointed out back in the eighties. Today it's worth trying mainly for the animation, which hasn't aged a day, and for the peculiar kind of tension that arises when the player knows the scene by heart and their hand still trembles. It is a piece of history that still feels like a carnival attraction in the best sense of the term. At the same time, it's a title that influenced an entire generation of developers: the idea of a game as a film into which one intervenes only at precisely defined moments has returned in countless forms ever since, and it is still called the legacy of Dragon's Lair.
cd-i__dragon-s-lair.teaser: An arcade legend that plays like an animated film, into which the player intervenes with commands at the right moment.

cd-i__lemmings.article:
**Lemmings** also arrived on the Philips CD-i, bringing with it one of the smartest game ideas of its time. A procession of small creatures pours out of an opening at the edge of the screen and keeps walking straight ahead until they hit a wall or fall into a pit. The player cannot command them directly, only assign a role to individuals: digger, bridge-builder, climber, floater, blocker, or the one who sacrifices itself in an explosion. Out of a handful of roles and a limited number of uses for each, a surprisingly deep puzzle game emerges, in which the goal is to get a set proportion of the procession safely to the exit. Every level has its own trap, its own materials, and its own solution, which often looks obvious only after several failures.

The CD-i version benefits from the medium above all through sound: the music is recorded, and the well-known folk melodies ring out fuller than on older home computers. The visuals stay faithful to the original — tiny figures on colorful backgrounds — where, thanks to the television screen, one occasionally has to squint. The most delicate spot is the controls, because the game was designed for a mouse, and precisely clicking on one specific figure in the middle of the crowd is noticeably harder with a controller. Anyone who gets used to it, though, gets the complete experience, including levels that test one's patience.

The original ranks among the most influential games ever made: it defined an entire genre of puzzle games built around indirect crowd control, and its echoes still appear today. At the time it received enthusiastic reviews across every platform and became one of the titles bundled with the hardware. Today it works just as well as it did then, because its rules are simple, legible, and uncompromising. It is to the CD-i version's credit that it was not a shortchanged port but an honest rendition of a game that deserves attention even decades later. For CD-i owners it also represented a rare chance to play a classic their friends knew from the Amiga or from consoles, giving the platform's catalog a name it seldom got to carry.
cd-i__lemmings.teaser: The classic about directing a procession of little creatures using jobs like digger or bridge builder.

cd-i__mad-dog-mccree.article:
**Mad Dog McCree** brought a Western shooting gallery to the Philips CD-i that had crowds flocking to arcades in the early nineties. The game is shot entirely with live actors, and the player takes on the role of a gunslinger who must free the mayor and his daughter from the clutches of a gang of bandits led by the titular villain. A live-action scene plays out on screen, and the instant an opponent appears, the player must aim and fire immediately. Hesitate, and you take a bullet and lose a life. Besides shootouts in the street, in the saloon, or in the canyon, the game also offers practice duels and several branching paths, so progress is not entirely linear.

The original arcade machine used LaserDisc and a light gun, so porting it to CD-i came down to how aiming would be handled. The game can be controlled with a cursor via the controller, which is slower, but with the special light gun made for the platform the experience comes close to the original. Technically it's an impressive showcase of what the CD medium could do: the video runs smoothly, transitions between scenes are snappy, and costumed actors create a backdrop unheard of in home entertainment at the time. Music and sound effects lifted straight from classic film Westerns help build the atmosphere.

At the time, Mad Dog McCree was one of the best-known examples of the interactive shooting-gallery genre and set off an entire wave of titles built on the same recipe. Critics faulted its short playtime and the fact that once you learn the right sequence, playing becomes a matter of memorization, but praised the technical execution and its infectiously tongue-in-cheek tone. Today it's worth trying mainly with two people at one screen, where it becomes a fun social occasion. It's also a good record of the direction the game industry briefly took once it discovered video. The live-action Western styling — the hat, the dusty street, an actor staring straight into the camera at the player — carries a naive charm that today's realistic shooters simply cannot replicate.
cd-i__mad-dog-mccree.teaser: A western movie shooting gallery with live actors; hesitate on your aim and you'll pay for it.

cd-i__voyeur.article:
**Voyeur** is one of the boldest titles ever released for the Philips CD-i, and it also best shows what its creators had in mind by the term "interactive film." The player sits in an apartment facing the mansion of a powerful politician, Reed Hawke, and uses a camera to observe the windows of his house. The task is to record incriminating material before a murder takes place. The whole game runs in real time, divided into time slots during which scenes play out in various rooms. It is never possible to see everything at once, so progress means repeatedly going through the same evening and searching for moments that fit together. The footage gathered is then presented as evidence.

Technically, it's a grand showcase of what the disc could do: the game consists almost entirely of live-action video with professional actors, among whom Robert Culp stands out in the role of the main villain. The editing, the music, and the darkly lit interiors create the mood of an eighties thriller, with the one difference that the viewer themselves decides where to look. The video resolution is, understandably, low and the picture grainy, but that oddly reinforces the sense of secretly watching from a distance.

At the time, the game was much talked about because of its erotic and violent content, which clearly marked it as a title for adult audiences only. Critics praised its ambition and its cast, with reservations aimed at how repeatedly watching the same scenes drags on, and at how the interaction is limited to choosing a window. The game was later ported to computers and released for other systems. Today it is interesting above all as an attempt at a genuinely different format: a blend of detective story, espionage, and surveillance narrative that the game industry has rarely attempted since. The idea that the player pieces together the truth from fragments of other people's conversations and decides for themselves what to pay attention to at any given moment fully returned only many years later, in independent detective games.
cd-i__voyeur.teaser: A daring interactive movie about watching a politician through a camera before a murder happens.

cd-i__zombie-dinos-from-planet-zeltoid.article:
**Zombie Dinos from Planet Zeltoid** is a typical example of the educational discs Philips released in droves for the CD-i, only with a much bigger dose of humor than usual. The game runs on a wild premise: aliens have revived the dinosaurs and unleashed them on Earth, so it's up to the player to bring them back under control. To manage that, the player must learn something about each species, since the right approach always depends on how a dinosaur lived, what it ate, and how it moved. Facts are gathered from a database full of images, text, and spoken narration, and immediately put to use in action segments built around quick thinking and aimed reactions.

The target audience was school-age children, and the presentation reflects that. The graphics combine drawn environments with digitized models, the pace is brisk, and short animated interludes play between segments, narrated by a host who comments on the whole nonsense with a wink. Sound-wise, the disc makes full use of the CD, so the narration is voiced and the music continually shifts mood depending on whether the moment calls for reading or fighting. The educational content is solid and matches the state of knowledge at the time, even though today's picture of what dinosaurs looked like differs from the nineties version in many respects.

At the time, discs like this mattered for CD-i because Philips marketed the machine to families as a multimedia device, not just a games console. Educational discs were meant to prove the machine could do more than play games, and Zombie Dinos was among the more entertaining ones, since it never tried to pass itself off as school. Today what stands out most is its tone: it's learning material unafraid of being silly, loud, and colorful. For collectors it's an interesting record of how education and entertainment mixed together in the mid-nineties. For the kids who received such discs back then, they often left a stronger impression than many a big game, because the combination of spoken word, pictures, and fast action was a genuine novelty on a screen in the living room.
cd-i__zombie-dinos-from-planet-zeltoid.teaser: An educational disc about pacifying reanimated dinosaurs, where progress depends on knowing each species.

cd-i__sesame-street-numbers.article:
**Sesame Street: Numbers** belongs to the educational discs with which Philips defended the idea that the CD-i was not a games console but a multimedia device for the whole family, sitting under the television. The title uses the license of the famous children's show and its puppet characters, who guide preschoolers through their first steps in counting. The content is divided into short activities: finding a specified number of objects in a scene, ordering digits, simple addition using pictures, and recognizing shapes and sounds. Everything is designed so a child can handle the controls alone, using slow cursor movement and a single confirm button, and so no mistake leads to punishment, only a new attempt and encouragement.

Technically, the disc relies above all on sound and video. The characters speak and sing, the narration is voiced by the show's actual actors, and short songs and animated interludes play between tasks, giving the child a familiar setting even outside of television broadcasts. The picture combines drawn scenes with video, and today one notices the limited resolution of the era's format, though the coloring and editing rhythm still follow the same rules as the show itself. It was precisely this faithfulness to the source that was the main reason parents bought discs like this.

At the time, educational titles made up a large part of the CD-i catalog and were sold in stores alongside the machine as proof of its usefulness. Reviewers judged them differently from games, that is, by whether they engaged children and whether they carried genuine educational content, and by that measure the Sesame Street series held up better than average. Today the disc is interesting mainly as a record of one path home entertainment could have taken: slow, gentle, non-competitive software for the very young, of a kind that almost vanished from game consoles in later years. Anyone who runs such a disc today sees a piece of the era's vision of family electronics, one in which the television was meant to serve learning just as much as play, and in which a preschooler first got a controller in their hands.
cd-i__sesame-street-numbers.teaser: An educational game for preschoolers featuring Sesame Street; counting and ordering digits.

vectrex__mine-storm.article:
**Mine Storm** was the game every Vectrex owner played first – whether they wanted to or not, since it couldn't be removed. It was permanently burned into the console's memory and started up automatically whenever no cartridge was plugged into the slot. It's a loose variation on Asteroids: a small vector ship hovers in the middle of the screen, surrounded by a field of magnetic mines that the player must blast apart before they close in. But the mines don't behave like passive rocks. Each type has its own personality – some break into smaller pieces when hit, others actively hunt the player, others release shrapnel or split into swarms of small fighters. Progressing between waves means the mine types combine and their numbers grow, so what starts as a clear, open field quickly turns into a trap. The ship can rotate, thrust, and jump into hyperspace, which randomly teleports the player elsewhere – sometimes straight into a mine.

Technically, Mine Storm is a showcase for why the Vectrex existed in the first place. The built-in black-and-white vector monitor draws lines directly with the electron beam, so the screen knows no pixels or blurry edges: the ship and mines are sharp, glowing outlines that never break up even during fast movement. The ship's rotation is completely smooth, something raster consoles of the era couldn't manage, and explosions scatter into a delicate web of lines. The sound is spare, synthetic, and nervous; the beeps and buzzes exist mainly to ramp up the tension, and they succeed. The picture was also topped with a colored plastic overlay placed over the screen, which gave the black-and-white image a tint of color and highlighted the playing field.

Period reviews cited the game as proof that home vector graphics were no mere curiosity but a full-fledged arcade experience. There's also a well-known story about a bug in the later levels that led the manufacturer to offer a fixed version under the name Mine Storm II. Today, Mine Storm is above all a great introduction to the Vectrex aesthetic: simple, tough, and addictive arcade action where you can lose an entire evening chasing a better score without even noticing.
vectrex__mine-storm.teaser: A built-in variation on Asteroids that every Vectrex owner launched first.

vectrex__scramble.article:
**Scramble** was one of the most influential arcade games of the late seventies and early eighties, and the Vectrex counted it among its finest conversions. The player pilots a small fighter craft that constantly scrolls from left to right over a nastily uneven landscape, and must fight through six distinct sections to reach the enemy base. It fires forward while also dropping bombs downward, so two tasks are handled at once the whole time: shooting down missiles launched from the ground and incoming enemies, while also destroying fuel tanks. Fuel drains on its own, and the only way to refill it is to hit a tank below you. This creates a constant dilemma – play it safe and maneuver up high, or risk dropping into a narrow corridor for another tank.

The Vectrex version rewrites the original raster arcade game into pure lines and, surprisingly, loses nothing in the process. Cave ceilings, hills, and narrow tunnels are drawn as sharp angular lines, missiles launch as thin streaks of light, and explosions scatter into fleeting patterns. Thanks to the vector monitor, the picture is perfectly smooth, and in tight passages it's easy to judge exactly where the ship still fits. The sound is more sparse than in arcades, yet it has its own nervous rhythm: a constant engine drone, terse beeps of gunfire, and a loud crack on impact with rock.

The game was praised at the time as one of the titles that justified buying the whole console, since it offered an arcade experience with few compromises. Its structure – six sections of distinct character flowing into one another without a break – became a template for the entire horizontal shooter genre, and its influence can be traced through dozens of later games. Today Scramble works as a beautifully compact arcade game: a single run lasts a few minutes, but memorizing the entire route takes considerably longer. The game also has no dead spots where you can relax, so even a short session feels intense. Anyone wanting to show why a vector console made sense in 1982 usually reaches for this one.
vectrex__scramble.teaser: A conversion of an influential arcade game; a fighter jet shoots forward and drops bombs downward.

vectrex__berzerk.article:
**Berzerk** sends the player into an endless maze of electrified corridors inhabited by shooting robots. The concept is simple and merciless: each room has several exits, a character with a gun stands inside, along with a cluster of robots that move slowly and fire. There are three ways to kill them – with your own shot, by luring a robot into a wall, or by having the robots accidentally shoot each other. The walls themselves are electrified, so even a careless step means instant death. If the player lingers too long in a room, the bouncing smiley face Evil Otto appears – indestructible, able to pass through walls, and gradually speeding up. He isn't really an opponent; he's a countdown clock wearing a grin – and it's precisely him that turned Berzerk into a game about constant forward motion.

The Vectrex conversion takes advantage of the vector monitor drawing thin glowing lines: the maze looks like a shining wireframe blueprint, the robots are angular figures assembled from a handful of segments, and shots are short bright lines that are easier to track in motion than on raster systems. The Vectrex's analog stick lets you aim in eight directions while moving at the same time, which is essential for this type of game. The arcade cabinet was famous for its synthetically speaking robots; the home version has to make do with sparse electronic sounds, which nonetheless do a good job underscoring the oppressive atmosphere of the empty corridors.

Berzerk is often called the forefather of the arena shooter genre, and its legacy shows up anywhere a player fights through enclosed rooms full of enemies. At the time, the Vectrex conversion was well received precisely for its precise controls. Today it's appreciated as a pure game of spatial reasoning: deciding which exit to take is ultimately often more important than the aiming itself. Clearing a room doesn't mean success, because the next one is always a little more densely packed, and a single wrong step sends the player back to the start. It's exactly that combination of simple rules and zero tolerance for mistakes that keeps Berzerk alive today.
vectrex__berzerk.teaser: A merciless maze of electrified corridors full of robots that even shoot at each other.

vectrex__rip-off.article:
**Rip Off** is a game that was ahead of its time in something taken for granted today – genuine two-player cooperation. A pile of fuel canisters sits in the middle of the screen, and enemy ships fly in from the edges trying to drag them away. The goal isn't to survive or rack up points for kills, but to defend your property. Once the last canister is gone, the game is over. The opponents don't behave like mindless targets: some head straight for the loot, others hold back and shoot, others try to circle around behind the player. Once someone grabs a canister and heads for the edge with it, you have to chase them down and destroy them before they escape.

With two players, the game turns into something quite different from a score-chasing duel. Both ships are on the same side, share the same canisters, and have to coordinate who guards the center and who goes on the chase. Friendly fire doesn't kill, so there's plenty of room for chaos, and a match tends to come with constant shouting across the room. The Vectrex conversion of the Cinematronics arcade original is visually spotless: the ships are thin triangular outlines, the momentum of movement is finely balanced, and everything plays out on a black field free of any distracting detail.

At the time it was one of the most praised titles in the whole library, precisely because of the cooperation, which wasn't at all common in 1982. Its influence can be traced through the whole line of cooperative arcade games built around jointly defending a single spot. Today Rip Off holds up extremely well – the rules explain themselves in half a minute, a match lasts a few minutes, and the urge to play just one more is strong. On its own it's a decent game; with two people it's one of the best reasons to turn on a Vectrex at all. Solo play has a different flavor: without a partner, the player must constantly decide whether to defend the pile or chase down the thief, and doing both at once simply isn't possible. It's exactly that tension that gives the sense the game is thinking, even though there are barely a few dozen lines on screen.
vectrex__rip-off.teaser: Defending fuel canisters from ships in genuine two-player cooperation; ahead of its time.

vectrex__armor-attack.article:
**Armor Attack** puts the player in command of a light jeep crew fighting through a ruined city full of enemy tanks. The basic balance of power already sets the game's tone: the jeep is fast and nimble, but a single hit means instant death, while the tanks are slow, heavily armored, and hit hard. A direct confrontation is therefore suicide. The winning tactic is to use the grid of streets and rubble as cover, circle around opponents, shoot at their sides, and vanish around a corner between shots. A helicopter also occasionally appears over the city, and unlike the tanks it ignores buildings and flies straight over them – shooting it down is the single most valuable kill in the game.

The Vectrex suits a game like this almost suspiciously well. The city is drawn as a network of thin white lines seen from above, so the overview of the entire battlefield is perfect, and thanks to the sharp vector image you can judge precisely whether a shot will pass through the gap between buildings. The jeep's movement has noticeable momentum, and the analog stick allows for fine directional corrections. The sound design is sparse and terse – the deep rumbling booms of the tanks and the dry crack of your own shot are enough to make the empty streets feel dangerous.

Like Rip Off, the game offers a two-player cooperative mode, where two jeeps move through the same city and can cover each other or lure tanks into a better position. At the time it was among the respected arcade conversions and praised for a more tactical pace than the usual arcade shooter offered. Today Armor Attack feels like a forerunner of later top-down tank arcades: short, precise, and built more on patience than a quick trigger finger. Individual runs are tense precisely because the player can't afford a single mistake, yet the game never feels unfair – enemies move predictably, and a loss is always the result of a bad decision, not chance. That's a quality a lot of more modern games lack.
vectrex__armor-attack.teaser: A fast, fragile jeep against slow armored tanks; a direct fight is pure suicide.

vectrex__star-trek-motion-picture.article:
**Star Trek: The Motion Picture** was a major draw for Vectrex owners – a licensed game based on one of the best-known sci-fi properties, and also one of the few titles on the console that tries to be more than a purely arcade shootout. The player commands the Enterprise and follows the action from the bridge: ahead lies a view of space with incoming Klingon ships, and below is a panel of gauges. Besides firing photon torpedoes and phasers, you must monitor your shield status and energy reserves, which get consumed by absolutely everything – movement, shooting, and defense alike. When they run out, the game ends regardless of how many enemies you've shot down so far.

Resource management is really the heart of the game. Energy can be replenished at a space station, but docking with it is a delicate maneuver during which the ship is vulnerable, and the Klingons are waiting for exactly that moment. This creates a constant cycle: fight, watch your dwindling reserves, retreat in time to refuel, then head back out. On top of that come enemy shots that can be deflected with shields, and dangerous space obstacles. The vector image gives the whole thing surprising depth – Klingon ships grow from small outlines as they approach, and the drawn silhouettes look exactly the way people remember them from the movie screen.

At the time it was one of the most talked-about titles in the library, since it paired a famous license with unusually complex controls that took a while to get used to. In hindsight it's interesting mainly as evidence that, already in the early eighties, developers were attempting to simulate a command bridge rather than just shooting at targets. Today it plays slower and more deliberately than the rest of the Vectrex lineup – and that's precisely what makes it refreshing among the other titles. It takes some patience, and ideally a glance at the manual, since the controls aren't self-explanatory, but once you get the hang of it, a surprisingly absorbing rhythm of fighting and refueling emerges. It's a game that reminds today's player just how early developers were already trying for something more than pure reflexes.
vectrex__star-trek-motion-picture.teaser: Licensed space action from the bridge of the Enterprise against Klingon ships; more than just an arcade game.

vectrex__cosmic-chasm.article:
**Cosmic Chasm** holds an unusual place in gaming history: it's one of the few titles that first appeared on a home console and only later got an arcade version, exactly the reverse of what was customary at the time. The premise is dramatically catastrophic. The player descends into a huge fissure in a planet threatening to collapse, and must fight through a system of connected chambers to reach the core, which must be destroyed. The path isn't linear – tunnels connect the chambers, and the player chooses the direction, so every descent looks a little different and can't be memorized as a fixed sequence.

Gameplay alternates between two modes. In the chambers it's a fast-paced fight: the player moves, rotates, and shoots at glowing creatures that multiply quickly and try to surround them. Between chambers, the game switches to a corridor flythrough, which is mostly about precision and quick reactions. The deeper the player descends, the more aggressive the environment becomes and the less time there is to think. The vector graphics work superbly here, since the chamber walls are drawn as glowing outlines and the enemies appear against the black void as sharp shapes of light with no distracting visual clutter whatsoever.

The sound underscores the sense of descending into the depths: a low rumble, sharp beeps on firing, and a pronounced sting when transitioning between levels. At the time the game was seen as one of the technically most ambitious things released for the Vectrex, precisely because of its shifting pace and structure of interconnected rooms. Today it's worth trying not only for its gameplay but also as a curiosity: a game that made the journey from the living room to the arcade, and one that still demonstrates that a vector display could evoke an atmosphere raster systems of the day simply couldn't match. It plays fast and hard, individual attempts last a few minutes, and the urge to try the descent again and get one level deeper comes almost automatically. Anyone looking for a Vectrex title with real pace and a structure offering more than repeating a single screen should start right here.
vectrex__cosmic-chasm.teaser: A descent into a crumbling planet toward its core; a rare case of a console release before the arcades.

vectrex__spike.article:
**Spike** is a game that comes up every time the conversation turns to what the Vectrex could do beyond the competition. The reason is sound: the game uses digitized speech, played through the console's speaker without any extra accessory. The characters talk, comment on the action, and the intro even features a short spoken scene. In 1983, that meant a great deal on a home system, and it drew people to the screen just as much as the gameplay itself.

The game itself is a platformer with a story: the title character Spike sets out to rescue his Molly, kidnapped by a malicious villain. The path leads across a system of platforms and ladders, where you must jump between them, dodge falling boulders and thrown obstacles, and collect rocks, your only means of defense. The level isn't just an obstacle course – it's mainly about timing, because danger arrives in a rhythm, and the player has to wait for the right moment instead of charging blindly ahead. Threats gradually stack up, acting simultaneously, and the heights you can fall from keep growing too.

Visually the game uses the vector image differently than the shooters do: the characters are drawn with bold, cartoonish lines, and the animation has surprising personality even though everything is built from just a handful of segments. It's exactly this combination of spoken word, humor, and a recognizable hero that turned Spike into something like the platform's unofficial mascot – his likeness appeared in promotional materials and in later homebrew titles alike. Today the game is appreciated mainly as a likeable, short arcade piece with an exceptional technical backstory that can still surprise. The difficulty is honestly arcade-tough, and the game doesn't spare you punishment for a bad jump, so there's no shortage of challenge, but thanks to a quick restart you never get stuck for long. Of all the Vectrex titles, Spike is also the one that feels the most like an actual game with a character and a story, not just an abstract duel of lines on a black background.
vectrex__spike.teaser: A platformer famous for digitized speech played straight out of the Vectrex's speaker.

vectrex__web-wars.article:
**Web Wars** is the strangest and, at the same time, the most visually memorable game in the entire Vectrex library. The player controls a ship inside a giant web that stretches into the depth of the screen, moving forward and backward along its strands. The goal isn't just shooting — the core mechanic is colliding with space creatures that appear within the net. Each creature has its own point value, and while some are worth grabbing, others try to destroy the player. This creates a peculiar rhythm where shooting alternates with bold dives and retreats back to the safer part of the web.

Technically, it's a showcase piece. The web is drawn as a perspective tunnel of thin lines that rotates with the player's movement, and the creatures are detailed silhouettes — birds, fish, insects, and other shapes that have nothing to do with outer space, which is exactly why the game feels like a feverish dream. The cartridge came with a colored overlay that gave the scene a striking tint and further amplified the psychedelic impression. The sound is loud, raw, and nervous, fitting perfectly with the overall visual style.

Opinions were divided at the time: some reviewers praised the game as the most striking demonstration of what the vector display could do, while others criticized it for having thin gameplay beneath the flashy surface that grows repetitive quickly. Both assessments still hold up today. Web Wars plays out quickly and is more likely to surprise you than to hold your attention for long evenings. Still, it's one of the first things worth showing to someone who has never seen this console, because nothing quite like it existed on any other system of the era. The game's visual inventiveness also shows well where the vector display could have headed given more time: instead of yet another ship duel, the authors dove into a bizarre bestiary and a space that moves and changes shape. That's part of why Web Wars still shows up on every list of the strangest games of the eighties.
vectrex__web-wars.teaser: The strangest Vectrex game; flying through a web full of creatures you crash into.

vectrex__fortress-of-narzod.article:
**Fortress of Narzod** belongs among the Vectrex games that don't draw attention with flashy visuals but with unusually tactical gameplay. The player controls a warrior with a cannon fighting his way up through several floors of a stone fortress. Each floor is essentially a maze of walls, slanted surfaces, and openings, populated by enemies. The key to the game lies in how the projectiles behave: they bounce off walls. Direct fire is often impossible because the opponent is standing around a corner or behind an obstacle, so the player has to aim at a wall and calculate the angle of the ricochet. A simple shooter thus turns into something between billiards and a combat puzzle.

Enemies differ in behavior — some charge straight at the player, others fire from a distance, and others try to block the path. Each floor also has its own layout of obstacles, so the player must quickly get their bearings and find a spot from which they can fire safely. The advance grows steadily denser, the space narrows, and there's less time to think. The vector display serves the game well: the walls are clean lines, so the player sees exactly the geometry they need to exploit — absolutely essential in a game built around ricochets.

The sound is sparse and functional: dull thuds when a shot hits a wall, and a sharp beep on a hit. At the time, the game was received as something more unconventional than a typical arcade title, precisely because it rewards thinking before reflexes. Today it's one of the best-aging titles in the library — the ricochet mechanic works just as well as it did forty years ago, and individual levels can be cleared in many different ways, which tempts players into repeated attempts at a cleaner, faster run. The game is uncompromisingly hard, and the first playthrough typically ends right in the lower floors, yet failure never feels random: the player usually knows exactly which wall they should have used and where they wasted a shot. This kind of informed defeat keeps people coming back to the controller and makes Fortress of Narzod one of the most underrated titles on the console.
vectrex__fortress-of-narzod.teaser: Tactical action where shots bounce off the fortress walls; direct fire often doesn't work.

vectrex__vector-pilot.article:
**Vector Pilot** is the most frequently cited example of just how far the community managed to push a thirty-year-old console. It's a homebrew shooter inspired by the arcade game Time Pilot: the player pilots an aircraft in the center of the screen, turns in any direction, and the world rotates along with it, so the battlefield has no edges. The task is to shoot down a set number of enemies, survive waves of larger machines, and rescue parachuting survivors along the way. Each level plays out in a different era — from propeller planes through jet fighters to spacecraft — and both the pace and enemy behavior change with each one.

Technically, it's a showpiece. The game moves far more objects at once than was typical for period Vectrex titles, and does so without noticeable flicker or image tearing — remarkable on a vector display, where every additional object costs brightness and stability. It also adds elaborate music, cutscenes, and smoothly moving cloud-and-star backgrounds. The controls are precise and responsive, so combat maneuvers — pulling into loops and building speed against a wave of enemies — work just as well as they did in the original.

The game was released on real cartridges and is still prized among collectors as one of the high points of Vectrex homebrew. It illustrates well that the scene around this console never truly went to sleep, and that new authors knew how to use the hardware better than some of the original publishers had. For today's player, Vector Pilot is probably the best entry point into the platform: it looks more modern, plays more smoothly, and yet retains exactly the sharp vector aesthetic that still gives the Vectrex its dedicated fans. It also plays great in short bursts, since one round takes a few minutes and the difference between a bad and a good attempt is immediately obvious. Anyone who plays it without knowing the context will find it hard to believe it runs on 1982 hardware.
vectrex__vector-pilot.teaser: A homebrew shooter inspired by Time Pilot; the borderless battlefield rotates along with the aircraft.

vectrex__protector.article:
**Protector** is a homebrew title often cited as proof that the Vectrex had more in it than the original developers ever managed to extract. The inspiration is obvious: the player flies over a planet's surface much like in Defender, the screen scrolls sideways, and below, people are being abducted by enemy ships. Once an abduction is completed, the enemy transforms into a far more aggressive form, so rescuing people isn't just a side objective for points but a critical defensive duty. The player must constantly switch flight direction, watch the radar at the top of the screen, and decide which part of the planet needs help first.

The technical side is what pushed the game into the ranks of platform legends. It manages smooth horizontal scrolling of an extensive landscape, a considerable number of simultaneously active objects, and still keeps the image clear and stable. That's the hardest discipline on a vector display, since the more lines that get drawn, the more the image weakens and flickers. The game also comes with its own music and very precise controls that match the pace of the on-screen action. Alongside the main game, the cartridge includes a smaller bonus title in the style of classic space-invasion shooters, making the whole package feel like a full-fledged release.

Protector was released on real cartridges complete with box and manual, making it one of the first modern homebrew projects that could hold its own against commercial production. Among collectors it's one of the most sought-after items, and its name comes up every time people discuss just how much could be squeezed out of the console. Today it still plays superbly — it's fast, difficult in exactly the way a game of this type should be, and feels like a title that should have appeared on the Vectrex back in the eighties. The early going is demanding, since the player has to learn to read the radar and estimate how much time remains before the last person is abducted, but once that clicks, the game settles into a very satisfying rhythm. For introducing someone to the platform today, Protector, along with a handful of other homebrew gems, is the best possible calling card the Vectrex has.
vectrex__protector.teaser: A homebrew tribute to Defender, where abducted people turn into a much more aggressive form of enemy.

vectrex__patriots.article:
**Patriots** is one of the earliest swallows of Vectrex homebrew and is still cited today as the title that kicked off the modern-day scene around this console. The game follows the classic Missile Command formula: cities and missile batteries stand at the bottom of the screen, enemy missiles rain down from above, and the player must launch counter-missiles in time so they detonate at the right spot and intercept the incoming threats. You don't hit the target directly but rather the future meeting point, so the whole game rests on judging time and distance. Smart missiles that split appear over time, along with fast planes streaking across the screen, and with each wave there's less time to think.

On the Vectrex, this concept has one big advantage: the vector display draws missile trails as thin glowing lines that are gorgeously legible in a darkened room, and the explosions bloom outward as radiant circles. Clarity is markedly better as a result than in the raster versions of the era. The analog joystick lets you smoothly guide the targeting cursor across the screen, which matters a great deal in a game built on precision. The sound is simple but punchy — every explosion has its own response, and the escalating pace is easy to feel.

Historically, the game matters mainly because it was released on a real cartridge at a time when the Vectrex had long been a dead platform, proving that new material could still come out for it. It opened the door for other authors and for later, more technically ambitious projects. Today you'll appreciate it as an honest, quickly graspable arcade game that fits the console's character perfectly — and as a reminder that some platforms never truly end. Compared to later, more technically advanced homebrew projects it feels more modest, but that only makes it easier to come back to — everyone knows the rules, a round takes a few minutes, and the tension in the final waves, when more missiles fall than one person can target in time, works exactly the same as it did when the original was made.
vectrex__patriots.teaser: One of the earliest Vectrex homebrew pioneers, based on Missile Command.

x68000__final-fight.article:
**Final Fight** is one of the most iconic beat-'em-ups of the late eighties and early nineties, and its conversion for the Sharp X68000 still stands as a showcase of what a Japanese home computer could achieve once Capcom itself took the job in hand. Mayor Mike Haggar, street brawler Cody, and ninja Guy set out to clean the streets of Metro City of the Mad Gear gang and rescue the kidnapped Jessica. The whole game rests on a simple yet remarkably satisfying combat system where a few buttons and precise timing are all it takes. Each character, however, plays quite differently: Haggar relies on raw strength and wrestling throws, Cody on balance and work with a knife or pipe, and Guy on speed and jumping kicks. The progression is linear, but the levels are packed with detail, breakable barrels, food hidden in crates, and enemies arriving in increasingly nasty combinations.

Technically, the X68000 version is exactly the reason enthusiasts bought this computer. A machine built around the Motorola 68000 processor with hardware support for sprites and several scrolling layers managed to bring the arcade original across with minimal compromise, including large animated characters, smoothly moving backgrounds, and a color palette the consoles of the time couldn't match. Sound comes courtesy of a Yamaha FM synthesis chip supplemented by sampled drums and voice clips, so the rhythmic tunes accompanying each district of Metro City sound full-blooded and hits land with proper weight. Loading from floppy disks was the price paid for that fidelity.

At the time, this conversion was seen as one of the arguments for why the X68000 was the best home arcade machine in Japan, especially compared to the trimmed-down console version, which lost a character and an entire level. Final Fight's own influence on the genre is significant: it defined the pacing, the structure of enemy waves, and the bonus stages that dozens of later games would copy. Today the game feels short and to the point, which only makes it easier to return to, especially in two-player mode on a single monitor, where it turns into a classic half-hour ride full of disarming violence and eighties aesthetics.
x68000__final-fight.teaser: Capcom's iconic beat-'em-up; Haggar, Cody, and Guy clean the streets of Metro City of the Mad Gear gang.

x68000__strider-hiryu.article:
**Strider Hiryu** is one of those titles people still argue about — whether the arcade original or the Sharp X68000 version looks better. The player takes on the role of the futuristic ninja Hiryu, who cuts his way with the plasma katana Cypher through snowy Moscow, a flying fortress, Siberian forests, and an orbital station, all the way to the immortal Grandmaster. For 1989, the controls are extraordinarily free: Hiryu climbs walls and ceilings, slides down slopes, somersaults over chasms, and his attack sweeps a wide arc, so combat feels more like a dance than careful, measured jumping. He also has three robotic helpers he can collect and summon, and the game never lets you stand still, since the scenery moves, shifts, and crumbles beneath his feet.

The conversion for the X68000 is a textbook example of how ports were supposed to look. The computer had enough sprites and colors to sustain enormous bosses, like the serpent made of shifting segments or the mechanical centipede, and it handled multi-layered parallax backgrounds as well. The music uses FM synthesis to preserve the original's grimly epic tone with its pseudo-Russian motifs, complemented by sampled shouts and impact sounds. It's precisely the audio side that leads many collectors to consider this version the definitive home rendition, long before the game reached modern platforms as part of compilations.

At the time, this was the flagship of the Japanese computer scene, a game X68000 owners showed visitors as proof their expensive machine was worth having. Strider Hiryu's influence on the genre is still visible today: fast acrobatic action, an emphasis on fluid movement, and bombastic set pieces later resonated throughout a whole range of action platformers, and its lead hero became a fixture of Capcom's crossover fighting games. Today the game is still snappy and legible, only mercilessly short and difficult, as befits its arcade origins. It suits anyone who likes action that hits the ground running from the first minute and doesn't waste time on explanations.
x68000__strider-hiryu.teaser: A ninja of the future with the Cypher blade; wall-climbing was unheard-of freedom in 1989.

x68000__ghouls-n-ghosts.article:
**Ghouls 'n Ghosts**, released in Japan as Daimakaimura, is the sequel to the famous Ghosts 'n Goblins, and on the Sharp X68000 it appeared in a form uncomfortably close to the arcade machine. Knight Arthur once again sets out for his beloved, this time against the demon Lucifer, and once again faces a journey across graveyards, ice fields, windmills, and burning villages. The core of the gameplay hasn't changed: Arthur throws spears, daggers, scythes, or shields, survives only a single hit before losing his armor and being left in his underwear, and a second hit means death. New compared to the first installment is the ability to shoot up and down, and above all the golden armor, which, once charged, unleashes a spell that varies depending on the currently equipped weapon.

The X68000 version is, from a technical standpoint, one of the high points of home conversions of its era. The computer managed rotating platforms, rippling water, collapsing bridges, and enormous bosses without noticeable cutbacks, while retaining the color richness that keeps the game's gloomy world looking so charming. The sound relies on FM synthesis and reproduces the famous melodies with their marching rhythm so well that you'll find yourself humming them long after switching the machine off. The atmosphere is an odd blend of horror and comic-book exaggeration, where death arrives with a skeletal laugh and the enemies are more cute than scary — until they've killed you for the fifth time in a row.

At the time, the game was among the most sought-after titles available for Japanese computers, and critics praised precisely its faithfulness to the original. The series' influence on the genre is undeniable: it defined the notion of the honestly hard platformer with punishing yet fair difficulty, and its DNA is visible from Dark Souls to modern indie titles that openly cite it as an influence. Today the game demands patience and a willingness to memorize enemy placement, but the reward is beautifully crafted action where every screen of progress feels like a personal victory. A must for anyone who wants to understand where the cult of difficult games comes from.
x68000__ghouls-n-ghosts.teaser: A conversion strikingly close to the arcade original; Arthur again faces the demon Lucifer.

x68000__street-fighter-ii-champion-editi.article:
**Street Fighter II' Champion Edition** arrived on the Sharp X68000 at a time when the fighting game was already a worldwide phenomenon, and it became one of Capcom's last great achievements on this platform. Compared to the original version, Champion Edition adds playable bosses Balrog, Vega, Sagat and M. Bison, and above all allows mirror matches, where two identical fighters in different colors can face each other. The system is still a textbook example today: eight directions, six buttons of varying strength for punches and kicks, special moves input with quarter-circles and dragon motions of the joystick, and above it all a layer of timing, range and reading the opponent that made the game the first true competitive sport of the video game era.

The conversion to the X68000 had a difficult task, because the CPS arcade board had more memory and colors than the home computer offered. Nevertheless, the result preserves large, smoothly animated characters, recognizable backgrounds from an Indian shrine to a Chinese market, and above all the speed without which a fighting game wouldn't make sense. The music performed by the Yamaha FM chip sounds different from the arcade machine, but has its own sharp character, and the famous themes of the individual arenas are fully recognizable; sampled attack shouts then give the fights the needed punch. For comfortable play, a proper arcade joystick was recommended, of which there were plenty available in Japan for this computer.

At the time, this title marked the closing of the X68000's golden era as a home arcade machine, and Japanese players took it as proof that the machine could keep pace even after six years. The influence of the game itself on the genre cannot be overstated: Street Fighter II created the rules by which fighting games are still built today, from selecting characters with different fighting styles through the special attack system to the culture of tournaments and arcade challenges. Today this version is interesting mainly as a historical artifact and as a very solid way to play the classic on period hardware. The gameplay itself has aged remarkably well and even after decades can still split a room into two camps.
x68000__street-fighter-ii-champion-editi.teaser: Adds playable bosses and mirror matches of the same fighters; a textbook-balanced system.

x68000__gradius.article:
**Gradius** was one of the first major titles to appear on the Sharp X68000, and right from the start it set the bar for what a home conversion of an arcade game should mean. The player pilots the fighter Vic Viper against the Bacterion Empire, progressing through seven thematically distinct stages, from a volcanic planet with lava spewers, through a field of Moai statues, to the biomechanical guts of the enemy base. The key mechanic is the famous power-up gauge: shooting down red formations adds a capsule, which the player moves along the indicator and then decides for themselves whether to invest in speed, missiles, double shot, laser, Option satellites or a shield. It was precisely this freedom that set Gradius apart from the competition and turned every playthrough into a strategic decision.

On the X68000, the game showed why the computer was nicknamed the home arcade machine. Hardware sprites and several independently scrolling layers allowed smooth movement without noticeable slowdown even when the screen filled with swarms of enemies, and the color palette allowed the characteristic high-contrast backgrounds to be preserved. The sound uses FM synthesis to deliver the famous rhythmic tracks, among the most memorable melodies of the eighties, complemented by sampled explosion effects. The atmosphere is purely sci-fi, cold and stark, yet the game feels almost hypnotic thanks to the perfect rhythm in which the waves of enemies arrive.

At the time, this conversion was seen as clear proof of the quality of the new machine, and for many Japanese players it was the first game they ran on the X68000. Gradius's influence on the shooter genre is fundamental: the optional upgrade system, satellites mirroring the ship's movement, and the concept of memorizing enemy placement were all adopted by dozens of later titles, many of them made directly by Konami. Today the game is shorter and stricter than modern players are used to, but it offers clean, still-functional gameplay that rewards patience. For anyone who wants to understand the roots of Japanese shoot-'em-ups, this is where it begins.
x68000__gradius.teaser: It set the bar for home conversions; the famous power-up bar and seven planets of the Bacterion empire.

x68000__gradius-ii.article:
**Gradius II** on the Sharp X68000 is what's known as a dream conversion: an arcade hit from the late eighties arrived on the home computer in a form so close to the original that the differences are hard to find. Vic Viper once again faces the Bacterion Empire, but this time with a significantly expanded upgrade system, since the player now chooses from several preset gauge configurations before starting. One relies on classic missiles and laser, another on shots in all directions, another on mines or a split beam, and each choice changes the pace of the game and how you can handle specific sections. In addition, new stages were added, featuring fiery eruptions, ice crystals and the famous gallery of bosses from previous entries.

Technically, this is one of the most highly rated conversions on the platform. The computer handles an enormous number of moving objects, elaborate multi-layered backgrounds and effects that were unthinkable on the consoles of the time, all while maintaining the smoothness the genre depends on. The music ranks among the best Konami produced during the FM synthesis era, and the X68000 with its Yamaha chip suits it exceptionally well; the tracks accompanying each stage carry an epic charge and give the game the feeling of a great space campaign. Digitized voice clips and explosions round out the impression.

At the time, this version served as a trump card for the Japanese computer scene and as a reason fans of shoot-'em-ups bought the machine even years after its release. Gradius II's influence on the genre is visible mainly in how it handles weapon selection and difficulty escalation, with each stage introducing a new threat and forcing the player to change approach. Today, despite its age, the game remains excellently playable, clear and fair, if merciless; whoever manages the first playthrough usually comes back for a better score. It's one of the titles that make it worth trying X68000 emulation even for someone who has never heard of the platform.
x68000__gradius-ii.teaser: A dream conversion of the arcade hit; the differences from the original are hard to spot.

x68000__salamander.article:
**Salamander** is a side branch of the Gradius series that differs from the main line in several fundamental ways, and it received a conversion on the Sharp X68000 that matched the demands of contemporary fans. Above all, it alternates between horizontally and vertically scrolling stages, so the player moves from a classic rightward flight into vertical sections above a planet's surface and back again. The second major change is the upgrade system: instead of a gauge that needs to be charged, the player collects specific icons that immediately grant speed, a missile, laser or a satellite. This makes the game more accessible while also making it fiercer, since after dying the loadout can be recovered faster than in Gradius. There's also a full two-player simultaneous mode, which makes it an ideal title for a shared evening.

Visually, Salamander is famous for its organic, biological design, where pulsating tissue, fiery protuberances and giant creatures made of flesh and metal wind between metallic structures. The X68000 handles this aesthetic with colors that suit it well and maintains smoothness even when the screen fills with projectiles. The FM synthesis soundtrack is fast, rhythmic and driving, complemented by sampled effects, and together with the darker visual tone it creates the atmosphere of a journey into the guts of something living and hostile. Even today, it remains one of the most distinctive audiovisual identities in the genre.

At the time, this conversion was a respected entry in the X68000 catalog, though it stood in the shadow of the more famous Gradius II. Salamander's influence on the genre lies mainly in mixing horizontal and vertical sections and in its emphasis on two-player cooperation, which was a bold move at a time when most shooters assumed only a single pilot. Today the game feels brisk and readable, its difficulty somewhat friendlier than its sister series, and cooperative play gives it an energy the single-player mode lacks. For anyone who loves classic shooters, it's a very pleasant hour spent in the fiery guts of a space monster.
x68000__salamander.teaser: A spin-off of Gradius alternating horizontal and vertical scrolling, plus other ship upgrades.

x68000__parodius-da.article:
**Parodius Da!** is a crazy parody of Konami's own work and one of the most entertaining shoot-'em-ups ever made; its conversion to the Sharp X68000 was one of the titles that gave the computer a privileged status among genre fans. Instead of the Vic Viper fighter, you can choose a flying penguin, an octopus, a butterfly fairy or a miniature version of the ship from Gradius, and use it to fight your way through a world where the bosses are dancing choirs, giant cats, or Japanese cultural icons transformed into hostile machines. Yet the game system remains surprisingly serious: the upgrade gauge works exactly as in Gradius, only the set of bonuses differs depending on the chosen character, and the difficulty, despite the comedic facade, is fully legitimate.

Humor is the game's main asset and shows up in everything, from the music to the enemy designs. The soundtrack takes classic pieces of classical music and folk melodies and reworks them into an exuberant chiptune form, which the X68000's FM synthesis delivers with infectious energy. Visually it's an explosion of color, alternating between a carnival setting, sweet candy backdrops and an underwater world, and the computer handles the large number of moving objects without noticeable trouble. It's precisely this combination of high color count and smoothness that makes this version such a convincing home rendition of the arcade original.

At the time, Parodius Da! was something Japanese players bought as a counterbalance to series taken deadly seriously, and the series went on to spawn several sequels across platforms. Its influence on the genre lies in showing that you can preserve the mechanical depth of a classic shooter while laughing at yourself; without it, many of the comedic shooters of the nineties likely wouldn't exist. Today the game still works wonderfully, because its humor hasn't aged and its gameplay is as solid as its serious counterparts. Anyone looking for proof that Japanese shooters can be both cute and tough at the same time will find it here.
x68000__parodius-da.teaser: A crazy parody of Konami's own games; a penguin or an octopus instead of a ship, dancing bosses.

x68000__nemesis-90-kai.article:
**Nemesis '90 Kai** is a peculiar and highly regarded piece of the Sharp X68000 catalog: a completely reworked version of the classic Gradius that Konami prepared exclusively for this computer. The foundation remains familiar — the ship Vic Viper, the upgrade gauge, and progression through planets full of volcanoes, Moai statues, and biomechanical corridors — but everything underwent a thorough revision. The stages are rearranged and expanded with new sections, enemy placement differs, alternative paths were added, along with several bosses that weren't in the original at all. The result feels like both a remake and a sequel at once, offering enough new content to surprise even players who know the original by heart.

Technically, it's a title created with awareness of the target platform's capabilities, not merely a straight port. The graphics use a high color count and several scrolling layers, the backgrounds are more detailed than in the original, and the whole game runs very smoothly. The music, however, is what players remember most often: the Gradius tracks are rearranged for the X68000's sound chip and expanded with sampled drums, so they sound richer and punchier than their older versions. The atmosphere combines the stark solitude of space with the sense of relentless pressure typical of the series, and the new music gives it a surprisingly modern edge.

At the time, this was a gift to fans of the platform and one of Konami's last major achievements on Japanese computers. The title remained an exclusive, which gradually made it a collector's prized item and one of the main reasons to bother with X68000 emulation. Its influence on the genre is indirect but interesting: it showed that a classic can be reworked for stronger hardware without losing its essence, an approach we see today in countless remasters. For today's player, it's a very well-playable shooter that can be recommended even as a first introduction to the Gradius series.
x68000__nemesis-90-kai.teaser: A completely reworked Gradius exclusive to the X68000; rearranged stages and new sections.

x68000__akumajou-dracula.article:
**Akumajou Dracula** for the Sharp X68000 is one of the most significant entries in the Castlevania series, and also a game that remained practically unavailable to Western players for many years. Konami took Simon Belmont's original story and rebuilt it from the ground up: the castle is larger, the levels are newly designed, and in several places the player chooses which way to continue, so the path to Dracula isn't the same every time. The core gameplay remains true to the series' roots — slow, deliberate movement, a whip with three upgrade levels, and secondary weapons like holy water, an axe or a cross boomerang. Precise jumps and knowledge of enemy behavior are essential, since a hit player often falls into a pit before they can react.

Technically, it's one of the most beautiful games on the platform. The high color count allowed for detailed Gothic interiors, stained-glass windows, burning chandeliers, and the surfaces of underground lakes, and the game also plays with effects like rotation or shifting lighting. The soundtrack rearranges the series' classic themes for the FM chip and adds new tracks that rank among the best ever heard in Castlevania; the combination of grim melody and rhythmic drive gives the castle its characteristic atmosphere of horror with a Gothic melodramatic edge.

At the time, the title was seen as the pinnacle of what Japanese computers had to offer, and its later reworking for the Super Famicom helped spread awareness of it beyond Japan. Its influence on the genre lies mainly in showing that a classic Castlevania could be richer, longer and visually more ambitious without losing its harsh core, and a direct line runs from here to later entries in the series. Today the game is still demanding and requires patience, but it rewards players with excellent level design and an atmosphere that holds up against anything from the nineties. For lovers of Gothic action, it's a mandatory stop.
x68000__akumajou-dracula.teaser: Castlevania rebuilt from the ground up, long unavailable in the West; a larger castle.

x68000__space-harrier.article:
**Space Harrier** is among the most famous arcade machines of the eighties, and its conversion to the Sharp X68000 was seen in Japan as a small miracle. Playing a flying hero with a laser cannon, you rush into the depth of the screen across the surrealist Fantasy Zone, where flying dragons, stone heads, mechanical enemies and checkerboard-colored fields with scattered trees await. The gameplay is extremely simple, yet surprisingly demanding thanks to its speed and density: the hero can move across the entire screen, shoots forward, and must dodge projectiles and obstacles that approach from a distance at breakneck speed. Each stage ends with a boss fight, each with its own movement pattern.

The original ran on an expensive machine with a moving cabinet and hardware built for scaling giant sprites, which was a nightmare for home systems in the eighties. The X68000 had enough power and colors to pull off a convincing illusion of speed with large, smoothly scaling objects, and as a result this conversion stood out above all competing versions on the market at the time. The music is unmistakable, cheerful and driving forward, and in its Yamaha FM chip version it retains its infectiousness; together with the digitized voice clips at the start of the game, it rounds out the atmosphere of a colorful dream that makes no sense and doesn't intend to.

At the time, this conversion served as proof that the X68000 truly was a home arcade machine, and together with other conversions from the same publisher it defined the platform's reputation. Space Harrier's influence on the genre is fundamental: it stood at the birth of what came to be called super scaler games, influenced an entire generation of fast-paced action titles, and its aesthetic is still cited today in stylized indie games and in music. Today it's a short, intense experience you can play through in twenty minutes and then keep returning to for the score. It feels like pure distilled fun, nothing about it has aged a day.
x68000__space-harrier.teaser: Sega's legendary rail shooter; the X68000 port was seen in Japan as a small miracle.

x68000__out-run.article:
**Out Run** isn't a classic race but a joyride for its own sake, and that's exactly what made it one of the most beloved arcade machines of all time; the Sharp X68000 version was among the best home conversions available in Japan. The player sits behind the wheel of a red convertible, a co-pilot at their side, with an open road ahead running through coastlines, deserts, stone villages, and snowy mountain passes. The goal is to clear each section before the timer runs out, and at the end of every stage you choose whether to go left or right, so the track branches into five different endings. The handling emphasizes smooth cornering, braking technique, and overtaking slower cars that appear at inconvenient moments.

The conversion had to nail the hardest part: the illusion of speed in the pseudo-3D view behind the car, where the road rises, dips, and curves. Thanks to its power and color palette, the X68000 managed to keep up a decent pace along with detailed scenery — palm trees, rocks, and houses sweeping past — so the result felt far closer to the arcade on a home screen than competing versions on other computers. The music is legendary: before starting, the player picks from several tracks, and their sunny, tropical-flavored FM-synth melodies remain among the most cited soundtracks in gaming history.

At the time, Out Run was a symbol of carefree luxury, and its X68000 conversion helped cement the machine's reputation as the best home arcade platform. Its influence on the genre is enormous: it defined the category of arcade driving games built around the feeling of speed rather than simulation, spawned a whole line of sequels, and its legacy is still visible in modern games that embrace the sunset-and-open-road aesthetic. Today Out Run feels surprisingly fresh, because its charm was never rooted in technology but in mood. Just a few minutes in, and the urge to keep driving arrives on its own.
x68000__out-run.teaser: A ride for the joy of it, not a classic race; the X68000 version was among the best home ports.

x68000__after-burner-ii.article:
**After Burner II** puts the player in the cockpit of an F-14 fighter and won't let them out until they've survived dozens of waves of enemy aircraft; the Sharp X68000 conversion ranks among the most ambitious ports the platform ever received. The game is viewed from behind the aircraft, the screen tilts and rotates with every maneuver, and the player alternates between a machine gun and homing missiles carried in limited supply. The key to survival is constant movement, careful use of afterburner, and so-called manual braking, which lets you drop behind enemies and shoot them down from the rear. Between certain stages, mid-air refueling appears, acting as a brief breather before the next dose of chaos.

The original was one of Sega's famous "Super Scaler" arcade machines with a hydraulic cabinet, so the conversion's main goal was to preserve speed and the sheer number of scaled objects on screen. With its Motorola 68000 processor and strong graphics subsystem, the X68000 performed remarkably well for a home computer, even though it naturally couldn't match the arcade's full density. The sound, however, is an unambiguous triumph: the driving rock themes rendered through FM synthesis rank among the most energetic music any Yamaha sound chip ever produced, and combined with the missile-lock voice callouts they create the atmosphere of a late-1980s action blockbuster.

At the time, the game served alongside other Sega arcade conversions as proof of the X68000's exceptional standing among Japanese computers. After Burner's influence on the genre shows in how it set the pace for arcade flight action, where the point isn't simulation but adrenaline and pure reflex; its DNA is visible in dozens of later games and in modern titles that embrace retro aesthetics. Today it's a short, loud, and intensely thrilling affair that leaves your fingers aching and offers no room for thought. That's exactly why it still works.
x68000__after-burner-ii.teaser: Adrenaline-fueled action in the cockpit of an F-14; the X68000 port ranks among the platform's most ambitious.

x68000__cho-ren-sha-68k.article:
**Cho Ren Sha 68K** proves that a platform's best game doesn't have to come from a big publisher. This vertical shooter was created by a single Japanese author as a non-commercial title for the Sharp X68000, and it's still regarded as one of the best-tuned shoot-'em-ups of the 1990s. The player pilots a small ship fighting through waves of enemies in open space, built around a system of three main-weapon levels supplemented by satellites and smart bombs. One distinctive touch is how power-ups are collected: the icons change type depending on how long they stay on screen, forcing the player to choose between grabbing one quickly or waiting for a better variant, which adds pleasant tactical tension to otherwise straightforward action.

The gameplay is remarkably clean. The ship's hitbox is small and clearly readable, enemy projectiles are easy to see, and the wave patterns feel tuned down to the individual pixel. The visuals lean on a dark starfield backdrop, sharp colors, and smooth movement with no slowdown, so even when the screen fills with dozens of bullets, everything stays legible. The music is fast and melodic, and paired with sharp explosion sounds it underscores the focused pressure that a good shooter needs. The author also kept updating the game for years, which was far from common in the home-computer scene.

Because it was freely distributed, the game spread quickly among X68000 owners and built a reputation that reached beyond the platform's borders; a Windows version later followed, bringing it to players worldwide. Its influence on the genre lies chiefly in showing how high a single creator's work could reach, and it became a favorite reference point among fans of classic shooters. Today it remains one of the best ways to experience what the X68000 could do, and it's entirely approachable: short, demanding, but fair and addictive.
x68000__cho-ren-sha-68k.teaser: A non-commercial vertical shmup by a single author, praised as one of the best-tuned ever made.

x68000__thunder-force-ii.article:
**Thunder Force II** was first released on the Sharp X68000, and only later became one of the titles that helped launch the Mega Drive. That's where the series found the shape it has kept ever since: fast, loud, and technically punching above its era's standard. The game alternates between two entirely different level types. In an overhead view, the player flies over sprawling bases and must locate and destroy every designated target, moving freely in any direction, where exploration matters just as much as shooting. The classic horizontally scrolling missions, meanwhile, offer a more direct experience with waves of enemies and a boss at the end.

The core of the system is an arsenal you switch through on the fly. Each weapon has a different angle and range, so picking the right one for a given situation matters more than aiming precision; losing an upgrade after being hit also forces cautious play. On the X68000, the game benefits from high resolution and a rich color palette, giving backgrounds a more detailed, less jagged look than the console version, and the scrolling's smoothness was, in 1988, among the best a home computer could show. The FM soundtrack is classic Techno Soft: melodic, almost rock-driven, and memorable enough that players still recall it long after they've forgotten the level layouts. And it's more than mere backdrop: individual tracks carry a different character depending on the mission type, helping the player sense when a change of pace is coming — something rarely a given in shooters of that era.

It was precisely this music and technical audacity that turned the series into a brand shooter fans followed for the rest of the nineties. Thunder Force II sits as a transitional entry in that lineage, still finding its shape, and its overhead sections feel more sprawling today than the tight horizontal stretches later entries would perfect. Even so, it holds its own value: a readable, pleasantly short game that shows how one of the most respected shooter series of all time grew out of an ambitious computer title.
x68000__thunder-force-ii.teaser: Predecessor to the famous Mega Drive version; a fast shooter alternating top-down and side-scrolling.

x68000__genocide.article:
**Genocide** is one of the games that, in the late 1980s, proved the Sharp X68000 didn't need arcade source material to build an identity of its own. Studio Zoom built this side-scrolling action game around a combat suit the player fights through with, cutting across a range of environments from barren plains to the mechanical interiors of enemy bases. Combat isn't about mashing a button quickly: movement carries weight, attacks have noticeable wind-up, and opponents take up enough screen space that reading their movement and keeping your distance pays off. The result feels methodical rather than frantic, and punishes lack of focus.

Zoom had positioned itself from the start as a studio that made things on the X68000 look expensive. Genocide relies on large, carefully animated characters, drawn cutscenes, and a dark art direction blending fantasy motifs with military hardware.
