The color palette is subdued and cold, the environments feel abandoned, and the FM-chip music accompanies the action through mood rather than catchy hooks. It was exactly this combination that gave the game its period reputation as a title trying to feel more mature than console platformers and offering the player a believable world. Between missions, screens of text and artwork appear, framing the campaign and, in 1989, felt unusually cinematic for a home computer. The storytelling is spare but coherent.

At the time, this was a flagship of home-grown production for this computer, and above all proof that the Japanese computer scene had a shape of its own, distinct from consoles. Zoom followed the success with a sequel that refined the pacing and controls and is, among fans of the platform, better known today than the first entry. Now, Genocide is an experience for the patient: the controls take getting used to, the difficulty is unforgiving, and the level structure is sparer than modern standards. But whoever accepts its slower rhythm finds an atmospherically powerful game and a piece of history that underpins the X68000's reputation as a machine for original titles.
x68000__genocide.teaser: Side-scrolling action in a battle suit where every move has weight and attacks a real wind-up.

x68000__geograph-seal.article:
**Geograph Seal** is the boldest game ever released on the Sharp X68000, and also one of the most important blind alleys in the history of 3D action. Studio Exact put the player in the cockpit of a transformable mech and let them move through a fully polygonal space in first-person view. The key isn't shooting, it's jumping. The player springs into the air, tilts the view downward mid-flight, aims at the target below, and lands exactly where needed. That single idea turned the clumsy 3D action of 1994 into something intuitive to control, one that gave spatial awareness a purpose.

The levels are built as arenas with targets to destroy, platforms to capture, and enemy units that never let the player stop. The mech switches between movement and combat modes, so the game already works with the rhythm of weapon-swapping that later action titles would adopt. Technically, it was extreme: a fully rendered polygonal environment running on a home computer with no dedicated graphics card, at a readable frame rate and with surprisingly good spatial orientation. The audio side is sparser, leaning on atmospheric electronic accompaniment that underscores the feeling of a lonely mission in a sterile, artificial-feeling world. The controls are off-putting at first, since they combine movement, aiming, and jumping in a way no one in the mid-1990s was used to; but after a few missions they turn into a precise tool that lets you clear an arena in one continuous chain of bounces.

The game's historical significance is greater than its reach at the time would suggest. Exact went straight from it to Jumping Flash on the PlayStation, which carried the same look-down jump principle to a global audience and earned a reputation as a pioneer of 3D platforming. Geograph Seal stayed locked to a Japanese platform and long remained a title people read about more than played. Today it's fascinating precisely for how early it solved a problem the whole industry kept struggling with for years afterward.
x68000__geograph-seal.teaser: A bold mech FPS with a fully polygonal space; the key to progress is jumping, not shooting.

x68000__aquales.article:
**Aquales** is one of those titles Sharp X68000 owners loved to show off, because at first glance it looked like something that had no business running on a home computer. Studio Exact built a side-scrolling action game here around a combat suit that walks, jumps, slides, and shoots in every direction while multi-layered scenery of a future war zone scrolls past around it. Combat combines ranged fire with close attacks, and the player must watch not only their health but also their position relative to flying opposition attacking from both sides of the screen. The pace is brisk, the levels short, and the difficulty tuned so the game can be learned by heart.

What stands out most is the technical execution. The main mech's animation runs through an unusually high number of frames, so its movement feels heavy and mechanically convincing; the parallax background layers scroll smoothly, and the color palette holds a cold, metallic tone. This was exactly the X68000's home turf: it could display large moving objects without flicker or slowdown, something consoles of the era only managed with compromises. The FM music is fast and rhythmic, with prominent basslines that push the game forward, and the sound effects give the gunfire the volume it needs. The environments also aren't afraid of verticality, so some sections involve climbing and descending, which breaks up the monotony of running right and forces the player to think about where the next attack will come from.

At the time, it was one of the demonstrations that the Japanese computer scene could produce its own arcade-quality action games, and Exact built a reputation with this title as a studio that pushed the platform's technical limits. Not long after, the same team moved on to 3D experiments that eventually carried it all the way to PlayStation. Today, Aquales feels like a compact, honestly crafted piece of action without unnecessary flourishes: it isn't long, doesn't have a complex story, and doesn't try to impress with anything other than movement and style. As an introduction to what home-grown X68000 action production looked like, it's a great place to start.
x68000__aquales.teaser: Side-scrolling action in a battle suit with multilayer parallax, a beloved X68000 showcase.

x68000__rusty.article:
**Rusty** is a game one could easily mistake at first glance for a lost Castlevania entry, and that's exactly what its creators were going for. The heroine is a warrior armed with a whip who fights her way through a gothic world full of vampires, undead, and demons, across levels split into short sections capped by a boss fight. The basics are classic: walking forward, careful jumps, a whip strike with a noticeable delay, and collecting secondary weapons and attack upgrades. But the game adds its own touches, including more pronounced acrobatic movement and more aggressive opponents who force the player to keep their distance and work with the weapon's reach.

The atmosphere is markedly darker and more sensual than its inspiration. The art direction leans on blood, horror motifs, and an eroticized stylization of the main character, which clearly aimed Rusty at an older segment of the Japanese computer scene's audience. The Sharp X68000 obliges with its color palette and high resolution: the backgrounds are detailed, the characters large, and the animation smooth, so the game visually holds its own next to the best console platformers of the time. The FM accompaniment leans on dramatic, almost rock-flavored tracks that keep the pace and noticeably intensify during boss fights. The heroine also isn't limited to the whip alone: collected items expand her options and change the reach and power of her attacks, turning her equipment into part of the tactics against specific opponents.

Because the X68000 never left Japan, Rusty stayed outside the mainstream, and Western players long knew of it only by hearsay, as a game that dared to do its own take on Castlevania. Today, fans seek it out precisely for that combination: familiar, honestly functioning gameplay wrapped in a package that's noticeably harsher and more distinctive in style. The difficulty is tough and the controls demand patience, but anyone who likes classic whip-driven platformers will find here one of the most interesting titles this genre ever produced outside the major studios.
x68000__rusty.teaser: A gothic action platformer with a whip, openly inspired by Castlevania — and a well-disguised clone.

x68000__mad-stalker-full-metal-force.article:
**Mad Stalker: Full Metal Force** combines two genres that rarely mixed in 1994: level-based brawling action and one-on-one fighting games. The player controls a battle suit in a cyberpunk city, smashing through crowds of enemies using combinations of punches, kicks, and special attacks input with joystick motions, exactly like in arcade fighting games. Each level culminates in a duel against a rival mech with its own set of moves, and it's these duels that gave the game its reputation as a title demanding real skill from the player, not just mashing a button.

On the Sharp X68000, the game benefited from what the platform did best: large, richly animated characters and smooth movement without slowdown even when several robots swarm the screen at once. The visual style blends heavy machinery with a neon cityscape, and the FM-synthesized soundtrack goes for brisk, almost rock-inspired tracks that keep pace with the fights. The environments change quickly enough to keep things fresh, and the game's length is deliberately short, since the focus isn't on progression but on mastering the fighting system and repeated attempts at a better performance. Besides the main campaign, the game also offers a two-player duel mode where you can pick from the mechs encountered in the story, bringing it closer to classic fighting games and significantly extending its lifespan. It's this mode in particular that made it a favorite for get-togethers among X68000 owners.

Its success with Japanese players led to Mad Stalker being ported to other platforms including the PC Engine, FM Towns, and PlayStation, which was unusual for a game originally released for a home computer. Still, the X68000 version remains the reference edition for fans, since it was built directly for this hardware. Today it plays like a charmingly distinctive hybrid: direct enough to finish in a couple of evenings, yet deep enough to reward players who learn its timing and moves. For fans of mechs and beat 'em ups, it's a small but honest classic.
x68000__mad-stalker-full-metal-force.teaser: A beat-'em-up with level progression where each one ends in a one-on-one fighting-game duel.

x68000__asuka-120-burning-fest.article:
**Asuka 120% Burning Fest** is a fighting game built specifically for the Sharp X68000 at a time when the genre was dominated by arcades and consoles, yet it earned a reputation as one of the most fluidly controllable titles of its kind. The premise is deliberately lighthearted: the fight is over supremacy between school clubs, and the entire cast consists of schoolgirls, each with her own fighting style, from a straightforward power wrestler to fast, technical characters. Fights unfold at a brisk pace, emphasizing attack strings, interrupting the opponent's combos, and well-timed blocking, making the game feel more aggressive than most of its contemporaries.

The system is built on simple move inputs that are nonetheless deep in how individual attacks link together. A skilled player can keep an opponent under pressure for long stretches, and the gap between a beginner and a veteran is more noticeable here than in slower fighting games. On the X68000, the game benefits from high resolution and smooth animation: characters are large, their movements readable, and the controls responsive—exactly what matters most in a fighting game. The visual style leans on bright colors and anime stylization, the FM chip music is fast and catchy, fitting the game's carefree tone throughout. Characters have their own short pre- and post-match lines, so even a brief playthrough gives the cast personality and explains why the series earned a devoted following. Matches against the CPU mainly serve as practice for two-player duels on the same machine.

Success with Japanese players led to a string of sequels and ports to other platforms, turning what began as a computer-exclusive title into a small but lasting series with its own community. The X68000 version remains the starting point, and fans still credit it with a certain charm of directness that later entries traded for more complex systems. Today, Asuka 120% stands as a great example that fighting games didn't have to originate in an arcade cabinet to work, and that the Japanese computer scene could craft its own answer to the era's clash of major brands.
x68000__asuka-120-burning-fest.teaser: A fighting game about school clubs made exclusively for the X68000; known for unusually snappy controls.

x68000__granada.article:
**Granada** is a top-down action game in which the player pilots a futuristic battle tank through urban and industrial arenas full of enemy units. The key idea is simple and, in 1990, remarkably elegant: the turret aims independently of the vehicle's direction of travel, so you can reverse while firing forward, circle an opponent, or keep firing at one target while dodging. This turns what would otherwise be straightforward action into a game about positioning and controlling space. Levels have clearly defined objectives, time pressure, and bosses that demand different tactics from regular enemies, and the overall length is short but dense.

On the Sharp X68000, Granada looked exceptional for its time. Scrolling is fast and smooth, many objects move on screen at once, and explosions and environmental destruction carry the necessary weight; the game feels more like an arcade title than a home production. Wolf Team was building a reputation at the time as a studio that leaned on striking technical visuals and strong music, and Granada is a good example of that: the FM soundtrack is energetic, almost rock-inspired, and keeps up the tension even in moments when the player is just moving between targets. Visually, a cool industrial style dominates, matching the stark, militaristic premise. Enemies arrive in waves from the edges of the screen and use different types of fire, so the player must constantly reassess which part of the arena to hold and when it's worth falling back; precision of movement matters here more than raw firepower.

The game later made it to the Mega Drive, making it accessible to a wider audience, but the X68000 version remains the one fans cite as the original and technically cleanest. Today Granada is a one-evening experience: the controls can be learned within a few minutes, but the difficulty is set so that the first run is certainly not going to be trouble-free. For anyone curious about what Japanese computer action looked like at the turn of the decade, it's one of the best-playing and best-sounding examples.
x68000__granada.teaser: Top-down tank action with an independently aiming turret — an idea that turns combat into a game of positioning.

x68000__phalanx.article:
**Phalanx** is a horizontally scrolling shooter that studio Zoom built specifically for the Sharp X68000 as a showcase of what its computer could do. The player pilots a fighter craft blasting through a series of levels ranging from open space to the cramped corridors of enemy bases, collecting upgrades that change the character of their weapons. Weapons don't simply stack up without thought: each has a different spread and range, so choosing a loadout before every stretch is part of the game, and a poorly chosen arsenal can turn even a manageable level into an ordeal. Adding to that is the classic system where getting hit sends you back to the start of your progress.

Technically, Phalanx relies on smooth multi-layer scrolling, large bosses, and backgrounds that try to feel like part of a single world rather than interchangeable scenery. The X68000's color palette allowed for finer gradients than console players were used to, and the game makes the most of this especially in its space and cave sections. The FM soundtrack is more restrained and atmospheric, at times almost cold, matching the stark sci-fi tone. The game's rhythm alternates between open stretches and tight corridors where the level geometry itself is the main opponent. It's precisely in these confined sections that the game's precise controls shine, since the outcome often comes down to a single pixel of clearance between the ship and the wall. The pace is slower than in later shooters, which today reads as calm rather than dated.

Internationally, Phalanx became famous mainly for its Super Nintendo port, whose Western box art featuring an old man with a banjo became one of the most frequently mocked examples of nonsensical game covers. The original X68000 version stayed in Japan and has a reputation among platform fans as a solidly crafted shooter that doesn't aspire to surpass Gradius but does its job cleanly. Today it plays as a pleasantly short and readable representative of the genre: nothing groundbreaking, but well-built levels, a solid feel for control, and a reminder that Zoom was among the most active home developers on this computer.
x68000__phalanx.teaser: A horizontal shmup from Zoom, a showcase of the X68000's power with weapons tailored to each situation.

x68000__lagoon.article:
**Lagoon** is an action RPG that originated on the Sharp X68000 before becoming known through its Super Nintendo port. The player takes on the role of a young swordsman tasked with finding the cause of a blight spreading through the region's waterways, progressing through towns, caves, and towers along the way. The foundation is classic: conversations with townsfolk move the story along, better gear is bought in shops, and experience and keys to further progress are gathered in dungeons. Combat happens directly in the environment without switching to a separate screen, giving the whole progression a fluid rhythm and making the game feel brisker than most turn-based Japanese RPGs of the time.

Combat itself is simple but demands patience. The hero attacks at short range with a sword, enemies move unpredictably, and healing costs both money and time, so progress often slows to a cautious probing of every new room. The X68000 version benefits from high resolution and a richer palette: the map is more detailed, characters larger, and environments more colorful than in the later console version. The FM music leans on melodic, slightly melancholic tracks that support the world's mildly fairy-tale atmosphere of being threatened by something no one can see. The map is divided into several areas connected by paths, and the player regularly returns to previously visited locations, since new gear and information from townsfolk open up directions that were inaccessible before. This slows down navigation but also makes the world feel more interconnected than in purely linear action games of the era.

At the time, Zoom was one of the busiest Japanese developers for home computers, and Lagoon was its attempt to add something with a story and longer arc to its lineup of action titles. It was reasonably well received in its day, and its console version later divided players over the stiff combat and short weapon range. Today the original version is interesting precisely as a comparison: it shows how differently the same game could feel on more capable hardware. For fans of early action RPGs, it's a pleasantly intimate adventure for a few evenings.
x68000__lagoon.teaser: An action RPG that preceded its more famous Super Nintendo port; the story of a young swordsman.

x68000__cotton-fantastic-night-dreams.article:
**Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams** is a horizontal shooter that stands out right away by having you fly a young witch on a broomstick instead of a spaceship. Cotton doesn't take up arms against the dark forces for noble reasons but for the promise of candy, and this lighthearted tone runs through the entire game, including the drawn cutscenes and chatty characters. Attacks come both as a standard shot and as magic in three elements, obtained by collecting crystals; a crystal's color determines the type of spell, and gathering experience gradually strengthens the character, adding a light growth element to an otherwise purely arcade genre.

The gameplay hinges on managing magic wisely and reading enemy waves that arrive in readable formations. Bosses are large, visually distinctive, and require learning their patterns; the difficulty is nicely balanced to be challenging without being off-putting. The Sharp X68000 version is among those cited at the time as an example of how close a home computer could get to its arcade source: smooth scrolling, large moving objects, and a rich palette that shines especially in fairy-tale backgrounds full of castles, graveyards, and night skies. The FM-synthesized soundtrack works with bold melodies close to a fairy-tale musical. On top of that, collecting crystals forces the player to take risks and fly into spots they'd otherwise avoid, adding pleasant tension to an otherwise clear and readable game.

Cotton eventually became one of the best-known faces of the so-called cute'em up, shooters that traded military seriousness for colorful fantasy, and the brand went on to see a number of sequels and modern revivals. For X68000 owners, it was one of the titles that showed the platform could handle licensed arcade ports at a very high level. Today the game still feels fresh mainly thanks to its humor and visual style: it's short, clear, and ideal for anyone wanting to try the genre without the tough school of classic military shooters.
x68000__cotton-fantastic-night-dreams.teaser: A horizontal shooter on a broomstick; a witch fights for candy, not for heroism.

pc-98__policenauts.article:
**Policenauts** is a sci-fi detective adventure in which former police officer Jonathan Ingram returns among the living after twenty-five years in hibernation, and is immediately drawn into a search for his ex-wife's missing husband. The trail leads to the Beyond Coast orbital colony, which he once helped build, and what starts as a routine missing-person case ends up entangled with organ trafficking, corruption, and personal revenge. The story is told as a buddy movie: Jonathan reunites with his old partner Ed Brown, and their banter, arguments, and shared silences carry most of the emotion in the whole story.

The gameplay follows the classic Japanese point-and-click interface, where you use a cursor to search static screens, talk to characters, and pick topics from a menu. Conversations are unusually branching—you can ask most people about dozens of items—and the game rewards players who ask about things that don't directly relate to the case. Crime scene investigations and interrogations are supplemented by action interludes with target shooting and a few short minigames. The pace is driven by film-style cuts and long animated cutscenes, extraordinarily lavish for the time. Getting stuck is practically impossible, as the game tends to push the player forward; those who want to can spend hours asking about the colony's background and Earth's politics instead. It's precisely this optional layer of text that makes Policenauts feel more like an interactive novel than a puzzle-based adventure.

Technically, it was one of the most ambitious things ever released on the PC-98: the game spans a large number of floppy disks and bets on large hand-drawn character portraits and anime-style animation. The sound design combines voice acting with synthesized music that underscores the colony's cold, weary atmosphere. In Japan, Policenauts earned a reputation for mature, adult storytelling and later received ports to the 3DO, PlayStation, and Saturn. Today it stands above all as a fascinating record of how early Japanese adventure games worked with cinematic language, and thanks to a fan translation into English, it's finally accessible outside Japan as well.
pc-98__policenauts.teaser: Konami's sci-fi detective story about a policeman out of hibernation; the investigation leads to an organ trade.

pc-98__yu-no-girl-who-chants-love-at-bou.article:
**YU-NO: A Girl Who Chants Love at the Bound of this World** is among the most ambitious visual novels ever released on the PC-98. Student Takuya Arima searches for his missing father, an archaeologist and researcher, and comes into possession of a device capable of jumping between parallel worlds. What begins as an intimate story about a small seaside town gradually grows into a sweeping saga about time, loss, and responsibility, one that abandons its realistic setting in its second half and blossoms into pure fantasy.

The key to the whole game is a system its creators called A.D.M.S., a branching map of the story that the player navigates like a tree. At its nodes, you can save a so-called reflector device, return to an earlier decision, and play out a different branch, with knowledge and items from one storyline unlocking paths in another. The result is a puzzle where the goal isn't just reaching the right ending, but mapping out the entire space of possibilities. Between dialogues, you explore static scenes with a cursor, collect items, and solve logical obstacles. The branching is so dense that the game is hard to get through without notes or your own map, and part of the pleasure comes from gradually realizing that the diagram on screen isn't a helper tool but the very core of the design. Some branches lead to dead ends whose purpose only becomes clear in hindsight.

On the PC-98, the game served as a showcase for the machine's capabilities, with detailed hand-drawn backgrounds, striking portraits, and an extensive soundtrack that alternates calm urban themes with darkly mythic pieces. This music, alongside the writing, is often cited as the best thing ELF ever released. YU-NO became a benchmark for later visual novels dealing with time travel, and its influence is visible across a whole generation of titles that followed it. Today a modernized version and a fan translation both exist, making it accessible even without knowledge of Japanese; the pace is slow and the content aimed at adults, but its narrative ambition has aged remarkably well.
pc-98__yu-no-girl-who-chants-love-at-bou.teaser: The most ambitious visual novel on the PC-98; traveling between parallel worlds changes everything.

pc-98__eve-burst-error.article:
**EVE Burst Error** is a detective visual novel that built its reputation on a single idea: you play as two characters at once. On one side stands the weary private detective Kojiro Amagi, on the other the young government agent Marina Hojo. Each investigates a seemingly unrelated case — he a stolen work of art, she the protection of an important figure — and only slowly does it become clear that both threads lead to the same conspiracy.

The mechanic called "Multi Sight" lets the player switch between the two investigators at any point during the game, and this forms the central puzzle. Information Marina uncovers unlocks a new topic of conversation for Kojiro, and vice versa; some scenes simply won't progress until the other character reaches a certain point. The narrative is thus built by piecing together two perspectives on the same event. The investigation itself runs through a classic command menu — look, talk, think, move — supplemented by interrogations where the order of chosen topics matters. The game makes sure the switching is never just cosmetic: many twists only make sense because you've seen the same situation from both sides and know something neither character could know alone. Players who get stuck have usually just forgotten to switch and ask the right person at the right moment, which is at once the system's greatest weakness and its greatest charm.

Visually, the game benefits from sharp, comic-book-styled character designs and colorful static scenes that looked very crisp on the PC-98. The soundtrack is jazzy and tense, holding the tone of a hard-boiled thriller with a hint of conspiracy. EVE Burst Error became one of the most respected titles of its genre in Japan and kicked off a long line of sequels and remakes on other platforms. The dual-perspective structure later appeared in many adventure games and still feels surprisingly modern today; the game contains adult scenes, but the emphasis clearly lies in the story and in a solidly built detective plot.
pc-98__eve-burst-error.teaser: A detective visual novel played as two characters whose cases eventually intertwine.

pc-98__desire.article:
**Desire** is a mysterious visual novel set on a remote tropical island housing a private corporation's research facility. Journalist Albert and young Makoto arrive there each for their own reason, and gradually stumble upon experiments dealing with human memory and consciousness. The story unfolds across two scenarios, and only their combination reveals what really happened on the island — and why no one is meant to leave it.

The game builds on the dual-perspective principle later made famous by EVE Burst Error: you see one event from both heroes' points of view, and details that make no sense in one storyline gain meaning in the other. Interaction happens through a command menu and screen exploration, with emphasis on careful reading and on choosing the right moment to switch to the other character. Decisions are few but crucial, and the game expects you to play through it more than once before piecing together the full picture. The island itself acts as a closed setting with a limited number of locations and characters, so the player quickly gets oriented and can focus on figuring out who to actually trust. Tension doesn't come from action but from small inconsistencies between what individual characters claim, and from how the same scene differs depending on who is experiencing it.

On the PC-98, Desire was among the titles that showed a visual novel need not be just a sequence of images. It blends sci-fi thriller, melodrama, and horror, shifting tone depending on which character you're following. The graphics rely on large portraits and atmospheric island scenery, while the music offers calm, slightly oppressive themes. The title was ported to the Saturn, PlayStation, and other systems, and alongside the studio C's Ware's other games it helped establish the template for the Japanese story-driven adventure of the nineties. Today it plays slowly, and its strength lies in the gradual unveiling of its mystery; anyone who enjoys a slow-building secret will find one of the platform's classics here.
pc-98__desire.teaser: A mysterious visual novel on an island where memory experiments uncover a dark conspiracy.

pc-98__doukyuusei-2.article:
**Doukyuusei 2** followed up on a game that essentially invented the free-roaming dating-sim genre in Japan. The player once again takes on the role of a final-year high school student during summer break and has a few weeks to build relationships with dozens of characters. Nothing holds his hand — he's given only a town, a calendar, and a clock that keeps ticking.

That is exactly the core of the gameplay: every location has its own schedule, and characters appear only at a certain time in a certain place. Moving around the map costs time, so planning the day becomes essentially a logistics puzzle. Conversations run through an action menu, and individual storylines develop gradually across the whole summer — a missed meeting can close off an entire branch for good. The sequel expanded the system with more characters, a more elaborate calendar, and smoother dialogue handling, so players get lost considerably less than in the first game. There is no single correct path: the calendar is short and the characters numerous, so the player must decide who gets their time and let the rest slide. That's also where the urge to replay comes from, since every run looks different and many scenes only appear if you're in a specific place at a precise hour.

Technically, this represented the peak of what ELF could do on the PC-98: colorful backgrounds of the town at different times of day, animated portraits, and an extensive soundtrack carrying the light, summery tone that became the series' trademark. Doukyuusei 2 had an enormous impact in Japan, paved the way for later school romances, received an anime adaptation as well as console ports, and its structure of freely spent time still shows up in raising sims today. It's an adult title and, without knowledge of Japanese, a demanding one, but as a historical milestone it's impossible to overlook, and its open structure is more interesting today than that of many linear novels that followed it.
pc-98__doukyuusei-2.teaser: A sequel to the game that invented the Japanese dating sim, with free movement around town and time.

pc-98__sotsugyou-graduation.article:
**Sotsugyou: Graduation** is a raising sim in which the player takes on the role of homeroom teacher for a class of final-year female students, with one school year to guide them toward their final exams and toward the future they deserve. It sounds unassuming, but it's actually a surprisingly demanding management game built around a budget of time, fatigue, and moods that all affect one another.

Each week you draw up a schedule: how many hours go to which subjects, how many to sports, club activities, or rest. An overworked student starts losing motivation or falls ill; a neglected one slips in her tests and drags down the whole class's mood. Between blocks of lessons come short scenes and conversations that shape the relationships among the girls, and at the end of the year, accumulated statistics determine where each of them ends up — from university to entirely unexpected paths. It's precisely this number of endings and the need to optimize the game that make it a title built for repeated playthroughs. The system's beauty lies in the fact that the students differ in temperament, and their reactions to the same schedule are not identical; what strengthens one may break another. The player therefore isn't looking for a universal recipe but is learning several different people and adjusting the plan accordingly, sometimes sacrificing one ambition for the sake of another. Feedback arrives after every week, so it's always clear what just went wrong.

On the PC-98, the game looked clean and legible: large character portraits, well-organized statistics tables, and simple but memorable melodies. Sotsugyou became one of the most influential Japanese titles of the first half of the nineties, launching a wave of raising sims, receiving a sequel, console ports, and an anime adaptation, and its DNA can be traced in a whole series of later games where a human fate is assembled out of numbers and a schedule. Today it's a slow game, heavily dependent on tables, but mechanically still elegant and unusually calm.
pc-98__sotsugyou-graduation.teaser: A surprisingly demanding homeroom-teacher simulation, budgeting time and the moods of your students.

pc-98__dragon-knight-4.article:
**Dragon Knight 4** is the most ambitious entry in its series and also one of the rare cases where an erotic adventure turned into a full-fledged tactical strategy game. The story follows the fate of a hero trying to stop the expansion of a powerful empire, offering a notably more serious, adventurous tone than the previous entries, including a large cast of characters and a long campaign split into chapters.

Battles take place on a square grid, where squads made up of individual heroes and hired units face off against each other. Terrain, range, turn order, and even who you place next to whom all matter, since units boost one another. Between battles, the game returns to its adventure portion: you visit towns, recruit allies, hold conversations, and develop relationships with characters, which in turn affects their strength on the battlefield. The campaign offers several ways to bring the story to a close, so the player has to manage not just tactics but also who to devote attention to along the way. The difficulty leans toward planning rather than punishment; the game gives you plenty of room to reinforce and equip your army but won't let you finish the whole campaign with a single lineup. The recruitment system also means the same battle can be won in very different ways depending on who you managed to enlist earlier. The chapters are long enough for a real bond to form with individual characters.

On the PC-98, this was a lavishly produced title with hand-drawn portraits, animated scenes, and an extensive orchestral score lending the battles an epic feel. The game was later ported to consoles in a modified form and circulated in the West under an English title, which made it known even to audiences outside Japan. Dragon Knight 4 is still remembered as proof that adult titles could offer mechanics on the PC-98 comparable to Japanese console strategy games of the time, and its tactical layer holds up even after all these years.
pc-98__dragon-knight-4.teaser: The series' most ambitious entry; an erotic adventure that grew into a full tactical strategy game.

pc-98__kichikuou-rance.article:
**Kichikuou Rance** is an alternative entry standing outside the main Rance series, in which the picaresque adventurer becomes a king and the player takes control of an entire continent. It combines turn-based strategy with a story-driven adventure: you rule a state, wage wars, deal with vassals and hostile powers, all while following one of the most extensive scenarios Alicesoft ever wrote.

The game is divided into turns, in which you split a limited number of actions among diplomacy, construction, training, and military campaigns. Each province has its own commander, each commander has their own abilities and their own story scenes, and since resources are always scarcer than needed, it mostly comes down to choosing whom to sacrifice. Battles play out as clashes between squads, where their composition and the heroes' abilities decide the outcome. Hanging over all of this is time pressure: enemies advance on their own, and the game has a fixed ending regardless of how much you managed to accomplish. There are multiple endings depending on who you saved and what you let fall. Ruling the empire is never abstract, though: most decisions immediately take the form of a scene where you talk to someone, promote someone, or send someone to a certain death. It is exactly this link between the dry strategic table and concrete fates that turns every turn into a choice the player genuinely feels, rather than a mere click into a budget.

Visually, this is typical late PC-98 production, with colorful portraits, a clear strategic map, and many individually illustrated scenes. The soundtrack alternates marching themes with darker pieces, supporting a surprisingly grim tone not usually found in games of this type. Kichikuou Rance has a reputation among fans as the best entry in the series precisely because of how seriously it takes the consequences of the player's decisions. It is explicitly an adult game, with coarse humor and violence, but as a strategy with story it is unusually dense and still commands a devoted audience today.
pc-98__kichikuou-rance.teaser: A Rance spin-off in which the adventurer becomes a king ruling an entire continent.

pc-98__nobunaga-s-ambition-lord-of-darkn.article:
**Nobunaga's Ambition: Lord of Darkness** is another entry in Koei's flagship historical strategy series, and for many players the one where the series found its definitive shape. The player picks one of the daimyo of a fractured Sengoku-era Japan and tries to unify the country, whether through military force, economic strength, marriage politics, or intrigue. Every province has its own economy, its own garrison, and its own people who need looking after.

On the strategic level, you manage individual territories: planting rice, building levees, trading, recruiting and training soldiers, and keeping an eye on the population's satisfaction and the vassals' loyalty. A campaign then shifts into a battle mode on a grid, where terrain, weather, morale, and unit type all matter. A signature layer is espionage, since ninja can burn down warehouses, spread rumors, or lure an enemy general over to your side. Individual historical commanders each have their own stats and personality, so even dry tables end up telling a story. The game lets the player choose the scope of a match, from a single scenario with a small number of provinces to unifying the entire archipelago, so it can be played in one long evening or over several weeks. Progress is gradual, and a mistake in the economy only shows up several turns later, which forces you to plan ahead rather than bet everything on a single offensive.

On the PC-98, the game looked dignified and, above all, clear: portraits of the warlords, a map of Japan, and plenty of data that could all be handled quickly from the keyboard. The music is ceremonial, with a Japanese instrumental flavor, and together with the message screens it creates the impression of a chronicle the player is writing themselves. Lord of Darkness was released on a large number of platforms and, for many players abroad, served as a first gateway into Japanese historical strategy games. Today it remains an excellently balanced game, slower-paced but without unnecessary complexity, and its system of provinces and vassals can be grasped in a single evening.
pc-98__nobunaga-s-ambition-lord-of-darkn.teaser: An entry in Koei's flagship historical series that, many say, found its definitive form here.

pc-98__romance-of-three-kingdoms-iii-dra.article:
**Romance of the Three Kingdoms III: Dragon of Destiny** brings Koei's proven formula to China at the twilight of the Han dynasty. The player chooses one of the warlords known from the classic novel and tries to seize control of a map divided into dozens of cities, doing so by building up the economy, recruiting armies, and above all gathering capable people — without whom not even the richest province can defend itself.

The heart of the game lies in managing generals. Each has values for war, intelligence, charisma, and loyalty, and the game forces you to seek them out, persuade them, promote them, and watch that no one lures them away from you. A turn is divided into months, in which you issue orders: till the fields, repair the walls, distribute rice, send out spies, forge alliances, or march into the field. Battles unfold on a map with regard to supplies, terrain, and morale, and a clever general can outwit their opponent with fire, an ambush, or a ruse before it even comes to a direct clash. Diplomacy matters just as much as the army: marriages, gifts, prisoner exchanges, and plain bribery can all shift the balance of power without a single battle. And because the computer-controlled opponents do exactly the same, the player must constantly track who has just allied with whom and which of their borders is currently weakest. The yearly cycle of harvests and famines keeps the whole match locked in a steady rhythm.

On the PC-98, the game used its higher resolution to fit a legible map and tables onto the screen at once, complementing it with a series of painted portraits that still rank among the best Koei produced at the time. The music is rich and ceremonial, with a strong Chinese character. The third entry is often cited as the point where the series found the ideal balance between depth and clarity, and many players return to it even after later entries were released. The learning curve is gentle, a single match takes dozens of hours, and the human element — caring for your generals — makes it a compelling game even away from the battlefield.
pc-98__romance-of-three-kingdoms-iii-dra.teaser: Koei's proven formula transplanted to China; the game's core lies in managing generals, not armies.

pc-98__uncharted-waters-new-horizons.article:
**Uncharted Waters: New Horizons** is a maritime adventure and trading strategy in one, and it's among the most beloved games Koei ever made. The player picks one of several captains, each with their own story and goal — from treasure hunting through restoring family honor to purely explorative ambitions — and sails out into the world of the early modern era, where ports from Lisbon to Nagasaki lie open to be explored.

Gameplay rests on three pillars. The first is trade: you buy cheap, sail far, and sell dear, with prices reacting to what you've dumped on the market where. The second is combat — naval battles that take wind and distance into account, or switching to man-to-man combat on deck. The third is exploration, where clues from taverns and libraries send you searching for unknown capes, cities, and monuments. Above it all looms fleet management, supplies, wages, and crew morale, because hunger and disease sink an expedition more reliably than enemy cannons. Yet the game never pushes you anywhere: you can spend years dealing purely in spices, work as a cartographer for the royal court, or turn pirate and live off other people's cargo. Each captain's goals serve more as a guideline than an obligation, which is exactly why every playthrough tells a different story. Progress also unlocks naturally, with better ships and new maps.

On the PC-98, the game felt like a huge, open world map full of small details, with painted portraits of characters and ports alike. The soundtrack, with its distinctive themes for each region, ranks among Koei's most memorable work of all. New Horizons had an enormous influence in Japan and Korea, where the series eventually led to an online sequel, and it's still cited today as a model open game in which the player decides for themselves what to make a living from. Anyone who enjoys calm building and maps that slowly fill in will find one of the platform's very best games here.
pc-98__uncharted-waters-new-horizons.teaser: Naval adventure and trading strategy in one; among Koei's most beloved games.

pc-98__princess-maker-2.article:
**Princess Maker 2** is a raising simulation in which the player takes on the role of a warrior entrusted by the gods with a ten-year-old daughter, and has eight years to raise her into practically anyone. A queen, a priestess, a general, a merchant, or simply an ordinary woman who finds her own happiness. The game offers dozens of endings and doesn't mark any single one of them as the only correct one.

The year is divided into months, and each month you decide what your daughter will spend her time on: studying, training, working at a tavern or on a farm, going on expeditions into the wilderness, or resting. Earned money pays for tutors, clothes, and equipment. Beneath the surface run dozens of stats, from strength and intelligence to morale, stress, and reputation, all influencing each other, so that excessive drilling leads to exhaustion and rebellion, while too much freedom leads to spoiling. On top of that come random events, battles during expeditions, and yearly festivals where you're compared against others. Crucially, the game gives no clear instructions on where to aim: the stats relate to each other indirectly, and many endings require a combination of traits that's found more by feel than by calculation. Also at play is how you talk to your daughter in regular conversations, since your relationship with her as a father influences what she's even willing to do.

On the PC-98, the game relied on a clean, appealing art style with plenty of illustrations that change as the daughter grows and depending on the path you lead her down, together with a calm, gently fairy-tale-like soundtrack. It was precisely the pairing of studio Gainax with this genre that drew attention beyond its usual audience, and Princess Maker 2 became the series' best-known entry, with ports to numerous platforms and a long fan afterlife. Today it's striking how sensitively it can assemble tables of numbers into the feeling that you've genuinely raised someone, and how mercilessly it shows you when you've overdone it. Eight in-game years pass faster than you'd expect, and the final year tends to be a desperate scramble to make up for what you've neglected.
pc-98__princess-maker-2.teaser: A raising-sim with dozens of endings; your daughter can grow up to be a queen or an ordinary woman.

pc-98__power-dolls.article:
**Power DoLLS** is a near-future tactical strategy game in which colonists on a distant planet fight for independence from Earth, and the main strike force is carried entirely by an all-female unit of combat-mech pilots. The campaign leads the player through a series of missions, from diversionary strikes to open confrontations, and along the way develops a story about rebellion as well as the relationships within a small crew that has to rely on itself.

Combat takes place turn-based on a varied map, where each machine has a limited number of movement and action points. Terrain plays a key role, since hills, forests, and waterways affect both visibility and speed of advance, and it's just as important how you equip a machine before a mission. Weapons, sensors, and load capacity are chosen based on the assignment, and an overloaded mech barely moves. Pilots have their own experience and specializations, so losing a seasoned commander hurts. Missions also often have a goal other than destroying everything: reaching somewhere within a time limit, evacuating civilians, or simply surviving until reinforcements arrive. Because damaged machines have to be repaired between missions and experienced pilots can't be replaced overnight, the player manages the unit over the long term, and winning at any cost doesn't pay off. Careful advancement, reconnaissance, and use of cover prove more reliable here than a frontal assault, which sets the game apart from the faster mecha titles of the time.

On the PC-98, the game was among the most visually striking titles of its era, combining a clear tactical map with large anime-style character illustrations and animated cutscenes. The music is energetic and militaristic, with several distinctive themes that carry through the rest of the series. Power DoLLS went on to receive several sequels and earned a reputation in Japan as an honest mecha strategy game that relies on planning and logistics rather than big numbers. Today it stands out precisely for its emphasis on pre-mission preparation: whoever gets their loadout wrong loses before firing a single shot.
pc-98__power-dolls.teaser: A near-future tactical strategy game with an all-female unit of combat mech pilots.

pc-98__master-of-monsters.article:
**Master of Monsters** is a turn-based fantasy strategy game in which the player doesn't lead an army of humans into battle, but summons monsters instead. As one of the elemental lords, you occupy the map, gather energy from captured towers, and use it to create new creatures, from goblins and harpies to dragons and demons. The goal is to destroy the opponent's stronghold before they destroy yours, and the path there runs through slowly expanding your influence across a hex map.

Mechanically, this is a strategy game with simple rules and surprising depth. Each unit has its own movement, melee and ranged attacks, and resistance to different damage types, and crucially, it develops into stronger forms through combat experience. This creates the dilemma that defines the game: build many weak creatures quickly, or feed experience to a chosen few? Terrain affects movement and regeneration, towers can be captured and taken over, and since energy is limited, summoning each monster is an investment you can't take back. Battles resolve automatically once you designate an attacker and a target, so all the decision-making happens on the map, in unit positioning, and in the timing of attacks. The game also allows multiplayer matches on a single machine, which made it a popular title for shared evenings at the time of release. Individual maps also differ in the layout of their towers, and with it the whole pace of a match.

On the PC-98, the game looked sober, with a legible map, small unit icons, and brief combat animations, but that very clarity serves it well. The soundtrack consists of simple, catchy melodies in the style of Japanese wargames of the time. Master of Monsters also made it to consoles, where it found a Western audience, and together with other titles from studio SystemSoft it ranks among the foundations of Japanese turn-based strategy. Today it's among the best-aged games the platform produced: the rules can be grasped within a few minutes, a single match takes an hour or two, and the tactical decisions remain engaging.
pc-98__master-of-monsters.teaser: A turn-based fantasy strategy game where monsters, from goblins to dragons, are summoned instead of armies.

pc-98__ys-i-ancient-ys-vanished.article:
**Ys I: Ancient Ys Vanished** sends the red-haired adventurer Adol Christin into the cursed land of Esteria, where he must uncover what happened to the long-vanished civilization of Ys and gather the six sacred books scattered across the world. The game is played from a top-down perspective, but instead of a standard combat menu it offers the so-called bump system: you attack simply by having Adol run into an enemy off-center. It sounds like a simplification, but in practice it creates fast, almost rhythmic gameplay, all about angle of approach, timing, and knowing when to back off instead. Progression is more linear than in the computer RPGs of the time, and the player doesn't have to grind through hours of random battles just to move forward.

On the PC-98, the game made the most of high resolution and a legible palette, so the maps of Esteria, the Zemeth mine, and Darm Tower feel sharp and clear; the color-restrained yet strikingly stylized screens rank among the best Japanese computers offered at the time. The music remains the most-cited part of the game to this day — the Falcom Sound Team jdk built, on the FM synthesis of the sound cards, tracks that suit an action game rather than a slow fantasy adventure, and the boss themes burned themselves into the memory of an entire generation of players. The boss fights are, in fact, a discipline of their own: each one has a clearly readable movement pattern that must be read before the healing potions run out.

At the time, this marked a decisive break from the tough, slow dungeons that defined Japanese computer RPGs back then. Ys showed that an action RPG could be accessible, brisk, and still full of atmosphere, and it kicked off a series that continues to this day. Adol became an icon, and his first quest has since received a huge number of ports and remakes. Today it plays quickly, in one or two evenings, and while the bump system takes a moment to get used to, the reward is one of the cleanest adventures of its era. The short runtime is a virtue here rather than a shortcoming: the game never pads itself out, every location has a reason to exist, and the ending arrives before it would have had a chance to grow tiresome.
pc-98__ys-i-ancient-ys-vanished.teaser: An action RPG with a bump system — you attack simply by walking into the enemy; simple and effective.

pc-98__ys-ii-ancient-ys-vanished-final-c.article:
**Ys II: Ancient Ys Vanished – The Final Chapter** picks up exactly where the first game left off: Adol finds himself in the floating land of Ys, among its inhabitants and ancient temples, and completes the story that the first game only began. Both games were conceived as a single whole from the start, and the second part confirms it — the map is bigger, the story is more talkative, and the characters get considerably more room to breathe. The main new feature is magic: Adol acquires magical rings, the most important of which is fire magic, giving him a ranged attack for the first time. There's also a transformation into a demon, which lets him talk to enemies and reveal parts of the world that a player would otherwise simply have wiped out.

The bump combat system remains, but the addition of ranged shots changes the pace — the dungeons are more complex, full of multi-level mazes and switches, and the bosses demand a combination of quick dodging and careful magic management. On the PC-98, the game continues to make the most of high resolution and delicate work with a limited palette; the temple interiors and icy passages rank among the most visually striking places in the whole series. The music once again outshines much of the competition of the time, and several tracks from the second game have become a permanent part of Falcom's repertoire, which it still reworks to this day.

At the time, the second game was received as a more polished version of a proven concept, and together with the first, it became what fixed Ys in players' minds. Later compilations of both games, released across dozens of platforms, only confirmed that together they form a single story arc. Today Ys II feels like a natural climax: shorter than modern RPGs, but denser, and its final stretch ranks among the best-built payoffs of Japanese computer game-making at the end of the 1980s. Anyone who's finished the first game should practically continue right away — the transition between the two is seamless, and the second part assumes knowledge of the characters and places from Esteria. A newcomer, on the other hand, risks missing half the references, since the game doesn't bother recapping what happened before.
pc-98__ys-ii-ancient-ys-vanished-final-c.teaser: A direct sequel to the first, completing one story; a bigger map and new magic for Adol.

pc-98__brandish.article:
**Brandish** is a dungeon crawler that invented its own way to keep the player disoriented: the map doesn't rotate around the character — the entire world rotates around them instead. When the hero, mercenary Ares Toraernos, turns left, the whole screen turns with him, which turns orientation underground into a game in its own right. Ares falls into the ruins of a buried city and has to dig his way back up — so progress runs opposite to the usual scheme, climbing from the depths toward the surface, floor by floor, past traps, trapdoors, and locked passages.

Combat happens in real time directly on the map: you attack in the direction the character is facing, so a lot depends on whether the player manages to turn in time before the monster does. Equipment wears out, weapons break, keys get used up, and many floors are built as logic puzzles with sliding blocks and switches. On the PC-98, the game looks clean and legible, which matters a great deal given this design — the high resolution made it possible to render floors, traps, and level differences so they could be read at a glance. The accompanying music is darker and tighter than in Ys, and supports well the feeling of descending into something that should have stayed shut.

Brandish earned a reputation at the time as a game for the patient: it's demanding, unforgiving of mistakes, and without notes on paper it's easy to get lost in its floors. But it's precisely that combination of action, map puzzle, and resource-limited survival that created a memorable whole, and the series went on to receive sequels and console ports. Today Brandish is interesting for exactly the same reason it was back then — the rotating map remains a unique idea that nobody has really repeated, and anyone who gets used to it will get several dozen hours of honest dungeon-crawling. It's worth reaching for one of the later versions, though, or at least keeping your own sketches, since the original doesn't account for the player setting the game aside and coming back to it a week later — without notes, finding your way around the floors becomes a discipline all its own.
pc-98__brandish.teaser: A dungeon crawler where it's not your character that turns, but the world around them — disorientation as a mechanic.

pc-98__popful-mail.article:
**Popful Mail** is a lighthearted side-scrolling action RPG starring the elf bounty hunter Mail, who chases after an elusive criminal mainly because she's run out of money. The tone is comedic from the very first moment: characters bicker, plans fall apart, and the game regularly pokes fun at serious fantasy clichés. Alongside Mail, other heroes join the party and can be switched between, each with a different range and attack style, so choosing who to play changes how a given section can be tackled.

The gameplay rests on platforming action — jumping, slashing, dodging projectiles — combined with an RPG layer of shops, gear upgrades, and experience. Levels are built as short, tight expeditions ending in a boss fight, which keeps the game's pace up. On the PC-98, Falcom focused on bold, cartoon-style visuals with large, legible characters and color-coordinated backgrounds; portrait insets during dialogue give the whole thing the feel of an animated series. The music is more playful and melodic than in the studio's more serious titles, and together with the witty dialogue creates an atmosphere quite different from most Japanese output of the time.

At the time, the game won over an audience precisely through its lightness and by not going down the path of a punishing dungeon. It later received console remakes that also brought it to Western players, and its Sega CD version ranks among the best-known localizations of its kind. Today, Popful Mail makes for a pleasant counterpoint to the more serious RPGs of its day: it can be finished in a few evenings, the action has just the right bite, and the humor has aged surprisingly well, since it rests on the characters rather than on era-specific references. It's also worth noting how well-paced the game is: the difficulty rises gradually, shops appear just as your equipment starts running low, and no section drags on long enough to stop being fun. From today's perspective, it's one of the most enjoyable ways to sample what the PC-98 could do in the action genre, without having to fight the unforgiving difficulty typical of other titles of the era.
pc-98__popful-mail.teaser: A comedic action RPG with an elf bounty hunter who regularly tosses fantasy clichés aside.

pc-98__dragon-slayer-legend-of-heroes.article:
**Dragon Slayer: The Legend of Heroes** marks the point where Falcom stepped away from the action experiments of the Dragon Slayer series and wrote a classic turn-based JRPG with a strong focus on story. The player accompanies Prince Selios, who grows up in seclusion after his father's death and the usurpation of the throne, and gradually returns to reclaim his kingdom. The narrative is structured around the towns and kingdoms the party passes through, each bringing its own smaller subplot — creating the impression of a journey across an inhabited world rather than just a chain of dungeons.

The combat system is turn-based and semi-automatic: the player sets a general strategy and the characters carry it out, which speeds up ordinary encounters and saves time when moving across the map. Supplies, spells, and equipment are handled through clear menus, the difficulty is gentler than in the era's hardcore dungeon crawlers, and the game relies instead on drawing the player forward through the characters' fates. On the PC-98, the creators bet on richly colored towns and character portraits in dialogue; the high resolution let background details shine, and the interface remains legible even today. The music ranks among the most melodic Falcom produced at the time, and several themes return in arranged form in later games.

The significance of this game outgrew its own qualities: it founded the Eiyuu Densetsu line, which spawned a long series of sequels and eventually the Trails series, one of the most extensive narrative sagas in the genre. At the time it reached many Japanese platforms and is still remembered as the title that established Falcom's character- and world-driven approach. Today it plays comfortably and without unnecessary frustration — it's more a calm, long journey than a test of patience. One price it pays is predictability: anyone familiar with later Japanese RPGs will guess most of the twists in advance, because this very game helped invent some of them. Still, it remains honestly told, and its pacing — a few hours per kingdom, then onward — holds up well even today, even though the individual battles feel old-fashioned.
pc-98__dragon-slayer-legend-of-heroes.teaser: The point where Falcom left action experiments behind for a classic turn-based JRPG focused on story.

pc-98__emerald-dragon.article:
**Emerald Dragon** belongs to the titles that pushed Japanese computer RPGs toward cinematic storytelling. The story of a dragon hero who takes on human form, and the girl bound to him by an ancient promise, builds on relationships between characters and on long dialogue passages accompanied by large drawn portraits. The game doesn't try to be an open world to explore; it leads the player along a precisely defined path and rewards them with scenes that, at the time, felt closer to anime than to a computer game.

Battles take place on a separate combat screen and have their own quirk: the player directly controls the main character, while allies act according to their personalities and set instructions. This means less micromanagement and more attention to positioning and attack timing, but it also means the player has to learn what their companions understand and what not to ask of them. On the PC-98, the game mainly capitalized on its visual side — carefully drawn portraits and colorful backgrounds make full use of the high resolution and rank among the best the genre produced on this platform. The music is romantic and orchestrally styled, with distinctive themes tied to individual characters.

At the time it was praised precisely for its presentation and storytelling, and it became one of the reasons Japanese computer RPGs began to be compared with console competitors. It was later released in remade versions on consoles, which expanded the story scenes even further. Today Emerald Dragon is interesting as evidence of how early Japan embraced the idea of the RPG as a told drama — the gameplay is simpler than that of its dungeon-crawling rivals, but that's exactly why it can still be finished today without a major fight against the interface. Its weakness lies precisely in the limited control over the party, which can feel wilful in tougher encounters, and in its linearity, which leaves little room for personal discovery. But anyone coming for the story and the artwork will get one of the most visually accomplished games on the entire platform.
pc-98__emerald-dragon.teaser: A JRPG pushed toward cinematic storytelling; long dialogues with large drawn character portraits.

pc-98__xak-art-of-visual-stage.article:
**Xak: The Art of Visual Stage** is an action RPG built on a combination of a top-down view while traveling and direct action in combat. The player takes on the role of young warrior Latok Kart, whose homeland is threatened by demons that have broken into the world of humans, and gradually passes through towns, caves, and temples scattered across the land. The storytelling follows a classic pattern — talking to inhabitants, collecting items and keys, opening up new areas of the map — but the game tries to keep the player moving and not slow them down with unnecessary backtracking.

Combat happens in real time directly in the environment, without switching to a separate screen: it comes down to which way the character is facing, when they strike, and how quickly they pull back. Equipment that can be bought and found changes both the reach and power of attacks, and in later stretches progress is impossible without better gear. On the PC-98, the game looks bright and colorful, with striking drawn character portraits in dialogue that Micro Cabin used as its signature trait. The soundtrack uses the FM synthesis of sound cards and offers melodic, memorable tunes that give each area its own character.

The Xak series was one of the respected representatives of the action RPG on Japanese home computers and received sequels as well as versions for other platforms. At the time it was seen as an accessible alternative to tougher dungeon crawlers: action-packed enough to be fun, clear enough that the player wouldn't get lost. Today it plays briskly, its pace faster than one would expect from a title from the early nineties, and the aesthetic of the drawn portraits keeps the overall visual impression afloat. Its weakness remains the difficulty, which in later sections relies more on grinding than on skill — without patiently gathering experience and money, progress stalls. But if the player gets used to the rhythm of alternating battles and shopping, they'll get a tight adventure with good music and a world that left a visible mark on the Japanese computer gaming scene, thanks also to its sequels.
pc-98__xak-art-of-visual-stage.teaser: An action RPG combining top-down travel with direct-action combat against demons.

pc-98__rusty.article:
**Rusty** is an action platformer that openly borrows the structure and mood of gothic vampire-hunter adventures and transplants them onto Japanese computers. The main heroine is a girl who sets out against demonic forces, progressing through a series of self-contained levels ending in a boss fight. The core is a long-reaching melee attack, supplemented by secondary weapons picked up in the environment — and, as in the genre's models, it mostly comes down to precise attack timing, jump control, and not getting knocked off a ledge.

Levels are designed to alternate fast sections with cautious progress: among platforms, ladders, and repeatedly respawning enemies, the player learns the route by heart. Bosses have readable patterns and can usually only be beaten after several attempts, once you understand the rhythm of their attacks. On the PC-98, the game went for a dark, saturated palette, large character sprites, and plenty of background detail, making it visually one of the most striking action games on the platform — remarkable in itself, since the PC-98 wasn't built for smooth scrolling. The music is suitably dramatic and fits the gothic tone stylistically, the atmosphere occasionally slides toward the choral, and the game contains scenes intended for an adult audience.

At the time, Rusty found its audience mainly among players who missed a proper console-style action game on computers, and over the years it earned a reputation as a cult title, mentioned as one of the few genuinely successful platformers on the PC-98. Today it's short, hard, and to the point — it can be finished in one longer sitting and delivers exactly what it promises: good old-fashioned action without delay. Anyone looking on the PC-98 for something other than sprawling RPGs and text adventures will find here one of the few games that can be played on reflexes alone. The precision required is high, and without repeated attempts the final levels can't be cleared, but the satisfaction is all the greater when the route finally comes together the way it should.
pc-98__rusty.teaser: A gothic action platformer with a whip, carrying the mood of vampire adventures onto computers.

pc-98__alltynex.article:
**ALLTYNEX** is a vertical shooter from the doujin studio Siter Skain that achieved something not expected of an office computer on the PC-98 — smooth arcade action with a dense field of bullets and a mech that behaves differently in combat than an ordinary ship. The player controls a combat machine equipped, alongside regular fire, with a melee attack, so the game isn't just a matter of dodging: it's advantageous to let some enemies get close and finish them off up close, which requires the player to be brave enough to move into spots they'd otherwise avoid.

The structure is classically arcade-like — a handful of short levels, each ending in a fight against a striking boss, a scoring system that rewards risky play, and a length matching a single arcade credit. That's precisely why ALLTYNEX gets played over and over: the goal isn't to finish it, but to finish it better. Technically it's an impressive piece of work, since the game had to fit within the PC-98's capabilities while still maintaining high pace; the graphics are purely mechanical, metallic and cold, and the music uses FM synthesis to keep a sharp, mechanical rhythm that suits the theme.

The game was made outside commercial distribution, within the doujin scene, and mainly for that reason it remained known only to a narrow circle for a long time. Siter Skain followed up with more shooters, and ALLTYNEX eventually received a modern remake that brought it to Western players as well. Today it's interesting in two ways: as a solid, tough shooter that doesn't feel amateurish even after all these years, and as evidence of just how capable the Japanese independent scene on the PC-98 was even before the platform came to be dominated by the first Touhou games. For today's player it's a short but intense experience — a single run takes a few dozen minutes, and the game practically begs to be replayed. The melee attack also adds a dynamic that most vertical shooters of the time didn't offer, and it keeps attention alive even after running through the same levels several times.
pc-98__alltynex.teaser: A doujin vertical shmup with dense bullet patterns and a robot capable of close-range combat too.

pc-98__touhou-reiiden-highly-responsive-.article:
**Touhou Reiiden ~ Highly Responsive to Prayers** is the first game in a series that later became one of the biggest phenomena of the Japanese independent scene — and the only entry that isn't a shooter. The player controls shrine maiden Reimu Hakurei and bounces a magical ball to break blocks on screen, essentially a breakout variant. Reimu, however, can move across the entire bottom of the field, can jump, slide, and launch the ball with her own amulets, so the game leans closer to an action arcade game than a passive paddle bounce.

The levels are short, and boss fights wait in between, with bosses attacking in bullet patterns — here, for the first time, you can see where the series will head. After a few rounds the path splits into two branches leading to different worlds, extending the game's lifespan and encouraging replays. Technically it's a title built for the PC-98 with FM music that even then showed the author's knack for catchy melodies; ZUN, at the time a member of the student circle Amusement Makers, wrote and scored the game himself, and he kept this one-person approach throughout the rest of his career.

At the time it was a marginal doujin game distributed in a small run, and its real significance only became apparent in retrospect. The characters, musical themes, and basic mythology of the world of Gensokyo introduced here are still used in the series today, and fans return to it precisely to see where it all began. As a game, Reiiden is the hardest and least polished entry of the whole early pentalogy — the controls are rougher and the ball-bouncing can be frustrating — but as a historical document it's irreplaceable. It also plays differently from everything else in the series, so even a longtime Touhou fan runs into unfamiliar habits here and has to learn from scratch. It's precisely this distinctiveness that makes the first game one people return to more out of curiosity than for the gameplay itself — and yet you can already tell that the author knew exactly what mood he wanted to give his world.
pc-98__touhou-reiiden-highly-responsive-.teaser: The first, non-shooter entry of the legendary series — actually a variation on Breakout with Reimu.

pc-98__touhou-fuumaroku-story-of-eastern.article:
**Touhou Fuumaroku ~ Story of Eastern Wonderland** is the second game in the series and also the moment Touhou found its true form: a vertical shooter with bosses attacking in elaborate bullet patterns. This time Reimu Hakurei flies on the back of the old turtle Genjii, investigating who is sending a wave of supernatural visitors to the Hakurei Shrine. Before starting, the player chooses a type of armament, which changes both the width and power of the shots, and together with a limited number of magic attacks determines how well they'll handle the densest sections.

The structure is classically arcade — five levels ending in a boss fight, plus a bonus level for those who beat the game without using a continue. The bullet patterns are simpler than in later games, but faster and less forgiving, since the character's hitbox isn't yet as tiny as in later titles. On the PC-98 the game had to fit within the platform's modest capabilities while still keeping dozens of bullets moving smoothly at once, which it managed thanks to economical yet legible graphics. The music uses FM synthesis, and even here you can already hear themes the series would carry forward, ones fans still recognize decades later.

The second game is also the first to feature a cast of distinctive female opponents each with their own personality — this very principle is what turned Touhou into material for an endless stream of fan works. At the time it was still a doujin game distributed outside regular stores, but today it's one of the most-played titles in the entire PC-98 library. Anyone who wants to understand why the series became a phenomenon should start right here: this is the first true Touhou. Finishing it takes under an hour, but clearing it without losing a life is a matter of many attempts — and that's exactly where its greatest appeal lies: the game is short, can be picked up any time, and can always be played a little bit better. Today it's best treated as the historical foundation — later entries are more polished, but this is where the vocabulary the whole series still speaks was born.
pc-98__touhou-fuumaroku-story-of-eastern.teaser: The second entry, where Touhou found its true form: a shmup with bosses attacking in bullet patterns.

pc-98__touhou-yumejikuu-phantasmagoria-o.article:
**Touhou Yumejikuu ~ Phantasmagoria of Dim.Dream** is the most unusual piece of the early pentalogy: instead of a classic progression through levels, it offers one-on-one duels on a split screen. Each player has their own playing field, and the goal isn't to survive a path to a boss but to wear down the opponent before they wear you down. Destroying enemies and collecting items on your own side sends the opponent an additional wave of bullets and obstacles, so the game plays out like a race in efficiency — whoever clears their own field better swamps the other one more.

A wide selection of characters is available, each with different fire and different special attacks, and during a duel you can briefly power up, which layers the encounters even further. Two players can sit at one computer facing each other, or you can play through a story mode against computer opponents. On the PC-98 that meant rendering two full shooter screens at once, a solid feat on this platform; the compromise is a smaller playing field and coarser detail, but the smoothness was preserved. The music again builds on FM synthesis and ranks among the best heard in early Touhou.

Versus-style duels returned in the series a few more times, which shows how well the idea worked, but no later take ever had quite the same peculiar energy as this first attempt. At the time the game was a rarity, since a duel between two shooter fields wasn't a common discipline in the year it was released. Today, Yumejikuu is above all a great two-player game on one machine — chaotic, fast, and unexpectedly tactical once you understand how to pour bullets over to the other side of the screen. The solo campaign against the computer is noticeably less interesting and, in later encounters, rather unfair, so the game's value stands or falls on whether the player has someone to play with.
