With two players, though, it's still one of the most entertaining titles ever made for the PC-98, and the clarity of both fields holds up even after all these years, so the game can be picked up in an emulator without any trouble.
pc-98__touhou-yumejikuu-phantasmagoria-o.teaser: The most unusual entry of the early series — split-screen one-on-one duels.

pc-98__touhou-gensoukyou-lotus-land-stor.article:
**Touhou Gensoukyou ~ Lotus Land Story** is the fourth entry in the series and the first in which the player chooses between Reimu Hakurei and the witch Marisa Kirisame — a duo that has since become the face of the entire Touhou franchise. Each of them has different shot patterns and a different take on the magic attack, so the character choice changes not only the difficulty but also how each bullet pattern can be solved. The story leads the heroines to a lake and into the dreamlike world beyond it, with a tone that is more dreamy and calm than in the previous entries.

In terms of gameplay, it's a significant step forward: the bullet patterns are slower but denser and more deliberate, so for the first time the game truly plays out the discipline the series is famous for — finding the safe gap in a pattern that looks impassable. Boss fights consist of several phases with distinct characteristics, and there's even a hidden extra stage for the most hardened players. On the PC-98, the game pushes the platform to the edge of its capabilities with the number of bullets shown on screen at once and still keeps things smooth; the graphics are more polished than in its predecessors, and the color palette separates bullets from the background better, which is essential for this genre.

The music is among the most cited parts of the early pentalogy, and several tracks from here return in arrangements in later entries and in a vast amount of fan work. At the time it was a doujin title sold at events and online, but this is exactly where the series matured into the shape that the Windows entries would later refine. Today, Lotus Land Story is the best entry point into the PC-98 era of Touhou: it's readable, fair, and its difficulty can be managed even without years of training. Collecting point items near the top edge of the screen introduced a principle that stayed with the series, and combined with the character choice, it gives the game unexpected replayability. Even after all these years it doesn't feel dated — the bullet patterns are designed so well that they would hold up in a modern game, just at a coarser resolution and with fewer effects. Anyone coming to it through the later Windows entries will be surprised how little the game's core has changed since then.
pc-98__touhou-gensoukyou-lotus-land-stor.teaser: The fourth entry and the first to let you choose between Reimu and Marisa, the duo that became the series' face.

pc-98__touhou-kaikidan-mystic-square.article:
**Touhou Kaikidan ~ Mystic Square** closes out the Touhou era on the PC-98 and is also the most polished entry of the entire quintet. The player chooses from four characters — Reimu, Marisa, Mima, and Yuuka — and each has such different shot patterns and magic attacks that the game plays a little differently every time through. The plot sends the heroines into the demonic world of Makai to investigate the source of a supernatural disturbance, and the individual stages match that with a noticeably darker, temple-tinged journey.

Compared to the previous entries, several years of accumulated experience show: the bullet patterns are the most complex of the entire PC-98 era, bosses have more phases with clearly distinguished attack sets, and the game communicates what it wants from the player more clearly. The item-collection system rewards a bold push toward the enemies, so scoring isn't just cosmetic but a real reason to play more riskily. Technically, this is the peak of what could be squeezed out of the old platform — bullet density is high, movement stays smooth, and the graphics are more careful than in any earlier entry. The music again relies on FM synthesis and ranks among the most beloved soundtracks of the early series.

After Mystic Square, the creator went quiet, and the series returned only years later on Windows, where it became a globally known phenomenon. That's exactly why the fifth entry is seen as a bridge between two eras: it contains almost everything that defines Touhou, just in a technically more modest form. Today it's the best choice for a player who wants only one of the PC-98 entries — it offers the greatest depth, the best boss fights, and the strongest atmosphere. The difficulty is higher than in its predecessors, which might discourage a newcomer, but the choice of four characters makes it possible to find a style that suits the player, and the lower difficulty tiers offer a way through even for less experienced players. In the end, Mystic Square is a game that can be recommended even to people who otherwise don't care for shoot-'em-ups — it's short, clear, and its bullet patterns can be read more like a puzzle than a punishment.
pc-98__touhou-kaikidan-mystic-square.teaser: Closes out Touhou's PC-98 era as the most polished entry of the five, with a choice of four characters.

nes__kung-fu.teaser: An early NES beat-'em-up where you fight your way through the floors of a building toward a final rooftop showdown.
nes__kung-fu.article:
**Kung Fu** is among the earliest titles the Nintendo Entertainment System embraced in the console's early years. The game casts the player as a fighter who must battle through five floors of a building to rescue a kidnapped girlfriend – a premise that other genre legends would make famous a few years later. The controls are spare and direct: two attacks, a kick and a punch, combined with sideways movement and crouching, with no combo systems or special moves. It's precisely this simplicity that makes Kung Fu a textbook example of an early side-scrolling beat 'em up, where rhythm and well-timed strikes against overwhelming enemies attacking from both sides are what matter most.

The game's atmosphere is spare but effective – each floor of the building has its own set of enemies and visual style, which gradually intensifies toward the final rooftop showdown. The music and sound effects reflect the technical limits of the 8-bit era, yet they became an unmistakable part of the experience for a generation of players who ran the game on their first home console. Kung Fu shaped the direction of the entire beat 'em up genre on 8-bit systems and showed how powerful an impression a minimalist concept built on repetition and escalating difficulty could make.

Today Kung Fu is more of a historical curiosity than a game players return to for depth of systems – the frustration of endlessly respawning enemies and the short playtime are obvious at first glance. Even so, it offers a valuable look at the genre's origins and shows the foundation from which more elaborate beat 'em ups later grew.

**Why play it:** For fans of gaming genre history and retro console owners who want to experience firsthand what a beat 'em up looked like in 1985, tough and uncompromising difficulty included.

snes__mega-man-7.teaser: A classic action platformer where you blast through the Robot Masters' stages and collect their weapons.
snes__mega-man-7.article:
**Mega Man 7** arrived on the Super Nintendo in the mid-1990s, at a time when the series' 16-bit era already seemed to be winding down – yet it delivered a full-fledged sequel to the iconic action platformer with more striking visuals and bigger, more detailed character sprites. The player once again works through the stages of eight Robot Masters in any order, defeating them and acquiring their weapons, which are then used as a weakness against other bosses – a principle that has remained the series' core since its beginnings. The controls are precise and match what Mega Man fans expect: jumping, shooting, and quick reactions are key to handling the traps and enemies scattered throughout the stages.

Visually, the game benefits from higher sprite resolution and a more colorful palette, made possible by the SNES's more powerful hardware compared to the previous NES entries, giving characters and environments a more three-dimensional, detailed look. The soundtrack continues the series' established tradition – energetic tracks underscoring the pace of each stage and boss fight. Mega Man 7 also introduced new characters and elements that later enriched the series' lore, though in player and critic rankings it often ends up overshadowed by earlier entries due to its slower pace and longer animations.

The seventh installment is thus more a choice for players who already know and love the formula of previous Mega Man games and want to experience it in the SNES's graphical dress, rather than an ideal entry point into the series for complete newcomers.

**Why play it:** For players familiar with earlier Mega Man games who will appreciate the visual leap to the SNES and don't mind a slower pace compared to its 8-bit predecessors.

snes__super-bomberman-2.teaser: An explosive multiplayer brawl where you plant bombs and blow away opponents in a maze.
snes__super-bomberman-2.article:
**Super Bomberman 2** built on the success of the first SNES entry and expanded the explosive action concept with new elements that cemented the Bomberman-style party game genre as a staple of 1990s home consoles. The basic principle stays the same – the player lays bombs, destroys breakable blocks in the maze, collects power-ups, and tries to outsmart opponents by blowing them up at just the right moment. The controls are simple and accessible, making the game an ideal choice for quick multiplayer bouts where several players gather around a single screen.

The second installment added new arena types, upgrades, and mechanics that enriched the combat system and gave the game more tactical depth than the original – players had to consider not only bomb placement but also which power-ups to collect and when to risk using them. The visual style is colorful and cartoonish, typical of the series, and the music accompanying each arena has a brisk tempo matching the fast pace of the matches. Besides the multiplayer mayhem, the game also offers a single-player story campaign, though it serves more as a bonus alongside the main draw of multiplayer competition.

Super Bomberman 2 is among the titles that, even years later, still work primarily as a party game for several people around one screen, and it's precisely in this respect that it retains its charm to this day.

**Why play it:** For groups of players looking for accessible, chaotic multiplayer fun on one screen, rather than fans of deep single-player stories.

mega-drive__phantasy-star-ii.teaser: A sci-fi RPG from Sega with a dark story and notoriously unforgiving dungeon difficulty.
mega-drive__phantasy-star-ii.article:
**Phantasy Star II** is among the most ambitious RPG creations SEGA released for the Mega Drive as early as the late 1980s, at a time when the console RPG scene was still in its infancy and most attention was focused on computer and console titles from other manufacturers. The game abandons the fantasy setting of the first installment and moves the story a generation forward into the sci-fi universe of the planet Motavia, where a group of heroes gradually uncovers a dark conspiracy behind the facade of a seemingly perfect society. Battles use a turn-based system with random encounters, typical of the era, but with greater demands on managing the party, equipment, and individual characters' techniques.

The uncompromising difficulty of the dungeons is one of the game's most frequently cited traits – the vast, labyrinthine mazes without a map force the player to rely on their own notes and patience, which put off many players used to friendlier design both back then and today. This harshness was controversial at release, yet the combination of a dark sci-fi story, an elaborate world, and the courage to go against genre conventions still gives the game its reputation as one of the most significant early console RPGs. The music and visual style heighten the bleak atmosphere of a fading utopia that the player gradually uncovers.

Phantasy Star II thus remains an important milestone of the genre, though its demands on patience and navigating mapless mazes mean that today's player needs a good deal of determination.

**Why play it:** For fans of RPG history and players who don't crave comfort and want to experience an uncompromisingly hard, yet narratively ambitious, sci-fi adventure from the late 1980s.

zx-spectrum__poklad.article:
**Poklad** was created in 1984 as the very first game by sixteen-year-old František Fuka, later the legendary Fuxoft, making it one of the oldest surviving computer games made in Czechoslovakia. Fuka programmed it on a friend's computer, since he couldn't yet afford his own ZX Spectrum, and then distributed the game on cassettes among a small community of eight-bit owners of the time, who played and copied it back and forth among themselves. The player finds themselves in a magical land divided into a grid of rooms across three floors, tasked with finding five hidden treasures, communicating with the surroundings through simple text commands and gradually piecing together a map of the unknown world purely from room descriptions.

The controls are typical of the early text-adventure genre: the player enters short commands, examines room descriptions, and collects items that open the way forward, with the individual levels connecting logically and progress requiring systematic exploration of every corner. Graphics are either entirely absent or purely incidental, so the whole atmosphere rests on the text and the player's imagination — a common approach on the ZX Spectrum and its domestic clones in the mid-1980s, since writing a text parser was far more accessible to beginning programmers than drawing animated characters, and it also placed far fewer demands on memory.

At the time, the game circulated mainly within a narrow circle of friends and computer clubs; it was later officially released, already as a historical curiosity, by the Proxima publishing house as part of the Fuxoft uvádí collection. Today, Poklad's value lies mainly in documenting the very beginnings of one of the most prolific creators of the Czechoslovak scene, and in showing how a complete gaming experience could be built with the most modest means and no commercial backing whatsoever. For today's player it's more of a historical artifact than playable entertainment, since the text-adventure genre now demands a considerable dose of patience, but historically it remains unmissable as the first step of a famous authorial career.
zx-spectrum__poklad.teaser: The debut work of a sixteen-year-old Fuxoft, one of the oldest surviving Czechoslovak games.

zx-spectrum__poklad-2.article:
**Poklad 2** is not a continuation of the story but a reworked and expanded version of Fuka's debut Poklad, which František Fuka designed as early as 1985 — shortly after the first installment, by which point he already had more experience with his own ZX Spectrum. It wasn't officially released until much later, in 1992, when the Proxima publishing house included it in the retrospective Fuxoft uvádí collection alongside the author's other older works, to save them from being completely forgotten. The principle stays the same: the player moves through a grid of rooms in the magical land and searches for treasures, controlling the game via a text parser with simple commands, and progress requires matching found items to the right places.

Compared to the original version, Poklad 2 is larger, containing more rooms and more elaborate puzzles, which better shows how quickly Fuka's programming and game-design skills improved in the mid-1980s and how he gradually mastered the principles he would later build much more ambitious titles on. Technically it remains a purely text-based affair with no graphical elements, music and sound play virtually no role, and all the emphasis lies on the descriptions and the logic of the puzzles, so the atmosphere is created purely inside the player's head.

Within the context of the domestic scene, Poklad 2 is interesting mainly as a link between Fuka's early attempt and his later, considerably more ambitious text adventures such as Podraz or Indiana Jones, which show that with every new title the author grew more confident and unafraid to expand the scope and complexity of the puzzles. For players of the time it was accessible entertainment that just needed to be copied or dubbed from cassette among friends, since official distribution channels for domestic productions practically didn't exist. Today it's seen mainly as a historical record of the development of one of the key authors and as a small chapter in the story of Czechoslovak text-adventure creation, rather than a game today's player would return to for its playability or graphics, of which it essentially has none.
zx-spectrum__poklad-2.teaser: A reworked version of Fuk's Poklad, released only later in the Fuxoft uvádí collection.

zx-spectrum__podraz-3.article:
**Podraz 3** is one of the best-known text adventures by František Fuka, alias Fuxoft, created in 1986 and officially released in 1992 by Proxima – Software v.o.s. The player takes on the role of an unemployed programmer named Tim Coleman, whose task is to track down the password to a gang of thieves' account and transfer the money elsewhere — a plot Fuka delivers with the exaggerated humor typical of the whole series. Like Fuka's previous games, it's a purely text-based game in which the player moves through the world using short commands, examines the surroundings, and solves a series of connected puzzles, needing nothing more than a keyboard and patience.

Podraz 3's strength lies in the humor and exaggeration with which Fuka spiced up an otherwise simple plot framework, as well as the smoothness with which individual situations flow into one another — the player doesn't have to wander a sprawling map but rather progresses fairly linearly from one scene to the next, which made the game accessible even to less experienced text-adventure players. Technically the game requires nothing more than the ZX Spectrum's text mode, so the entire atmosphere rests on Fuka's writing, which his peers valued for its wit and irony, setting it apart from the drier foreign genre templates that rarely reached us at the time.

Within the Podraz series, part three is often cited as one of the high points, followed by the fourth and fifth installments, which together created one of the most recognizable domestic gaming brands of its time. In the context of the era, when importing Western ZX Spectrum games into Czechoslovakia was difficult, Fuka's text adventures represented one of the few domestic alternatives of comparable quality, and they were played by owners of Didaktiks and Spectrum clones across the whole country. Today Podraz 3 is remembered mainly as a showcase of the distinctive humor of nascent Czech game creation and as proof that even a modest text parser could tell a memorable story.
zx-spectrum__podraz-3.teaser: An ironic text adventure about a programmer trying to loot a gang of thieves' bank account.

zx-spectrum__podraz-4.article:
**Podraz 4** continues Fuxoft's successful series of text adventures and was created in 1986; shortly afterward the Slovak group Antok Software also distributed the game, which shows how quickly Fuka's games spread across Czechoslovakia on cassette among computer clubs and individual enthusiasts far beyond Fuka's own hometown. Like the other installments, it's a purely text-based adventure controlled with simple commands, in which the player advances through a sequence of connected situations and puzzles and has to remember the links between previously found clues.

Podraz 4 sticks to the same formula as the previous installment — the main character is once again a figure from society's margins, the plot is laced with the irony and black humor typical of Fuka's style, and the game requires no graphics or sound hardware beyond the ZX Spectrum's basic text mode. Precisely because of its modest hardware demands, it could spread easily even on domestic clones like the Didaktik, which had more limited capabilities than the original British machine, reaching a substantially wider audience than a purely graphical game would have.

The series' popularity grew over time partly because the individual installments were loosely connected in style and humor, so players who had grown fond of the third part were happy to pick up the fourth as well and looked forward to the next one, much like a book or film series. The fact that other groups besides the author himself picked up and further distributed the game shows how highly it was valued in the community of the time — official distribution was limited, so people simply copied good games and passed them on hand to hand on cassette, often even between the two republics. Podraz 4 thus remains an important piece in the mosaic of Fuka's work and in the memory of the generation that grew up on the Spectrum; for today's player it offers more of a nostalgic experience than a challenge comparable to contemporary foreign adventures, but as evidence of how inventively an entire game series could be built from one modest machine, it remains valuable to this day.
zx-spectrum__podraz-4.teaser: Another installment in the Podraz series, which spread across Czechoslovakia on cassette tapes at lightning speed.

zx-spectrum__podraz-5.article:
**Podraz 5** closes out the classic line of Fuxoft's text adventures, and besides František Fuka, Daniel Pražák also contributed to its creation. The game was released in 1988, distributed simultaneously by several groups – the Slovak Antok Software as well as the Czech AmSoft and Immortal Software – which only confirms how lively the unofficial distribution network was at the time among owners of the ZX Spectrum and its domestic clones, where quality titles spread faster than any official offering. The principle remains faithful to the previous installments: a purely text-based game where the player enters brief commands and progresses through a chain of connected situations and puzzles, where a wrong step often means having to backtrack a few moves.

Daniel Pražák's co-authorship brought a fresh perspective to the series, and together with Fuka they pushed the concept to what was conceivable within the possibilities of the 48K Spectrum at the time – the game does without graphics, with the entire impression created by text, humor, and pacing of the narration that follows the tried-and-tested style of the previous installments. As with the earlier entries, emphasis was placed on smooth continuity between scenes so the player wouldn't lose the thread or motivation to keep going, even as the puzzles gradually got tougher.

For many players, Podraz 5 marked a symbolic full stop to a series that accompanied the Czechoslovak ZX Spectrum scene for several years and became one of the most recognizable domestic gaming brands of the eighties, comparable at the time to imported foreign adventures. The fact that the individual installments were distributed independently through multiple publishing groups at once still stands today as evidence of how popular and sought-after Fuka's work was within a community that had no access to official Western distribution channels and relied on its own informal sharing network among computer clubs, schools, and individuals. From today's perspective, Podraz 5 is mainly proof of the consistency with which Fuka carried the entire series through to its conclusion – something that was far from a given in amateur creations of the time, since many similar projects were left unfinished after just the first or second installment.
zx-spectrum__podraz-5.teaser: The final installment of the classic Podraz series; the script was co-written by Daniel Pražák alongside Fuka.

zx-spectrum__indiana-jones-3.article:
**Indiana Jones 3** is another of Fuka's text adventures inspired by the popular film franchise, created in 1990 and officially released in 1992 by Proxima – Software v.o.s. as part of the Fuxoft Presents collection. Together with Indiana Jones 1 and 2, it forms a loose series in which Fuka retold the adventures of the famous film archaeologist in the form of a text parser controlled by simple commands, with the player progressing scene by scene and solving puzzles matching the situations the film character typically finds himself in.

The game sticks to the tried-and-tested scheme of Fuka's text adventures – no graphics, an emphasis on smoothly chaining scenes and puzzles, and a playful, ironic narrative tone with which Fuka enlivened even a borrowed premise, so the game doesn't feel like a mechanical transcription of the film but rather a distinctive story with its own rhythm. Unofficial adaptations of popular films and books were typical for the Czechoslovak scene of the time, because licenses were unavailable, so authors simply "appropriated" beloved characters and transplanted them into a text medium that required nothing more than imagination in writing the parser and knowledge of the film's source material.

According to Fuka himself, the Indiana Jones series ranks among his best-known works alongside Tetris 2 and Podraz 3, and to this day old-timers fondly return to it as an example of how inventively a fun game built on nothing but text could be squeezed out of the ZX Spectrum's limited resources. The third installment garnered the same acclaim as the previous two – players especially praised the witty dialogue and inventive puzzle solutions that played with the film's premise without slavishly copying it scene by scene. For today's player, Indiana Jones 3 is mainly a cultural curiosity, but in the context of its time it demonstrates just how strongly film blockbusters influenced even amateur, homegrown game development, and together with the Podraz games and Tetris 2 it forms the core of why Fuxoft is still mentioned today as one of the most distinctive names of the early Czechoslovak computer scene.
zx-spectrum__indiana-jones-3.teaser: Fuka's text-adventure parody of the famous movie archaeologist, continuing on from parts 1 and 2.

zx-spectrum__tetris-2.article:
**Tetris 2** was created by František Fuka in 1990 for the ZX Spectrum and its domestic Didaktik clones, and it became his internationally most successful work – even thirty years on, fans still cite it, especially from Eastern Europe, and enthusiasts have even taken on a modern remake for today's hardware and emulators. The basic mechanic follows the famous Tetris: the player arranges falling blocks into complete rows, which then disappear and make room for the next pieces at an ever-increasing pace, the goal being to survive as long as possible without letting the playing field fill up to the top.

Fuka's version, however, offered something that wasn't a given at the time – a two-player game on a single ZX Spectrum keyboard, a variant where two people could compete against each other without needing a second computer or expensive peripheral equipment. At the time, this was an idea that significantly boosted the game's playability and social dimension, because Tetris could now be played as direct duels between friends, not just as a chase for one's own high score. Technically, the game is lean and fast, with simple but functional graphics and music typical of the eight-bit Spectrum, which managed to set the game apart from a number of other domestic clones of the same concept.

Tetris 2 still ranks among the most cited works of Fuka's entire body of work and stands as proof that even a modest domestic clone could offer the local scene its own, originally conceived take on a world-famous concept. According to Fuka's own words, the game still brings him emails from fans, mainly from Eastern Europe, where people remember it as one of the first games on which they played against each other on a single machine, and enthusiasts have even taken on a modern remake for today's hardware to make it accessible to a new generation. For many old-timers it remains synonymous with playing Tetris on the Spectrum altogether, and it's a rare case of a Czechoslovak domestic game whose fame significantly exceeded the borders of the region where it was created.
zx-spectrum__tetris-2.teaser: Fuka's most internationally successful game; it still has fans today, mainly in Eastern Europe.

zx-spectrum__f-i-r-e.article:
**F.I.R.E.** is an action shooter that František Fuka created together with Michal Hlaváč in 1988; it was then commercially released in 1992 by Ultrasoft. The name is an acronym that can be loosely translated as fast, ingenious and risky elimination, and that is exactly what the game demands of the player – controlling a small rocket flying over the surface of an unknown planet, it must destroy waves of enemies without crashing into the terrain or getting hit by enemy fire.

The game is divided into four levels, each ending with a battle against a different large enemy – ranging from an enemy rocket, through a giant wasp and a space dragon, to a head with a propeller. This variety of bosses was unusual for domestic ZX Spectrum production and showed that even authors known mainly for text adventures could pull off fast action with smooth scrolling and clear graphics, where the player has to keep track of their own position, enemy fire, and the terrain's layout all at once. The music for the game was composed by Fuka himself, who devoted himself to music on eight-bit machines in parallel with his programming work and remained actively engaged with Spectrum chiptunes in later years as well.

F.I.R.E. demonstrates the versatility of Fuxoft's output, which wasn't limited to text adventures alone – it showed that the authors could also handle the fast action-shooter genre, popular among players who preferred reflexes over text puzzles and demanded a quick pace and clear feedback on every move from a game. The fact that the game only reached commercial release four years later through Ultrasoft shows just how long an amateur-made game could wait before one of the domestic publishers of the time officially took it under its wing. Within domestic production for the ZX Spectrum and its clones, F.I.R.E. ranks among the more technically accomplished achievements of the late eighties and still appears on lists of the most interesting Czechoslovak games of the period, often alongside Fuka's text adventures as proof that his output had a much wider range than one might expect from a single author.
zx-spectrum__f-i-r-e.teaser: An action shooter about a rocket blasting through waves of enemies above the surface of an alien planet.

zx-spectrum__rychle-sipy-zahada-hlavolam.article:
**Rychlé šípy: Záhada hlavolamu** (Fast Arrows: The Mystery of the Puzzle) is an adventure created in 1988 by the brothers Petr Mihula (programming and graphics, under the Májasoft label) and Ondřej Mihula (music, CIDsoft), and it was one of the first Czech text adventures to combine text with graphical illustrations of rooms and characters. Its source is the famous novel of the same name by Jaroslav Foglar, so the game leads the player into the world of the Rychlé šípy clubhouse and the mysterious district of Stínadla, where the task is to find a puzzle box hidden in a cage and bring it back to the clubhouse, solving a number of small puzzles and conversations with characters from the book along the way.

Control is done by entering one- or two-word commands such as wait, north, help, examine chronicle, or buy hammer, which felt natural to players of the time thanks to their experience with text adventures, but the graphics additionally added atmosphere that purely text-based games lacked, helping players better picture the world of Stínadla as it was known to readers of the book. The combination of a familiar Foglar-based premise, honestly crafted puzzles, and visual accompaniment made the game an exceptional experience that appealed not only to fans of text adventures but also to a wider circle of readers of Foglar's books who otherwise never played computer games at all.

The game became one of the most popular domestic adventures of its time, and in 1991 it was even re-released by the Slovak Ultrasoft, confirming its reach across the republic's borders and across generations of Rychlé šípy readers. The fact that two siblings dared to combine programming with their own music and graphics was, for amateur ZX Spectrum production, an unusually professional combination, thanks to which the game still stands out even among other domestic text adventures. Záhada hlavolamu is still considered one of the milestones of the Czechoslovak ZX Spectrum scene today – it showed that combining local literary classics with a computer game could work, and it still ranks among the titles worth trying even decades later, whether for nostalgia or for the story itself.
zx-spectrum__rychle-sipy-zahada-hlavolam.teaser: One of the first Czech text adventures with illustrations; based on the novel by Jaroslav Foglar.

zx-spectrum__jmeno-ruze.article:
**Jméno růže** (The Name of the Rose) is an adventure created under the pseudonym George K. by Jiří Koudelka and released in 1991 by Proxima – Software v.o.s. Despite its title, it does not literally adapt Umberto Eco's novel of the same name – the main character isn't Eco's monk William of Baskerville but the movie inspector Jacques Clouseau, known from the Pink Panther series, whom the plot sends to a monastery in Germany, home to a mysterious order of nuns called Posxtey, to investigate suspicious events hidden behind the monastery walls.

The game was unusually large for the ZX Spectrum, and because it couldn't fit entirely into 48 kilobytes of memory at once, individual parts had to be continuously loaded from the storage medium on the fly, which was a fairly unusual solution on eight-bit machines. Because of this, it was initially released only for computers connected to a Didaktik 40 floppy drive, and it wasn't until 1993 that a version was made for the 128-kilobyte Spectrum, which eliminated the need for on-the-fly loading and allowed the game to also come out on cassette, making it accessible to a much wider circle of players.

The combination of a parodic plot, a large world, and a technically demanding solution makes Jméno růže one of the more ambitious domestic adventures of the early nineties, a time when the domestic scene was no longer afraid to tackle larger and technically more complicated projects. The humor built on the contrast between a serious literary source and a grotesque film character gave the game a distinctive tone that set it apart from more seriously toned foreign adventures as well as from earlier domestic text adventures. It also shows how freely creators of the time worked with foreign source material and genre conventions, piecing together an original, distinctive story from various sources – a famous novel and a film comedy – tailored to the tastes of domestic players of the time. The technical demands the game's scope forced upon it make Jméno růže an interesting piece of evidence of just how far domestic amateur creation could be pushed at the twilight of the eight-bit era.
zx-spectrum__jmeno-ruze.teaser: Despite the title, it's not an adaptation of Eco; the hero is film inspector Clouseau from The Pink Panther.

zx-spectrum__xor.article:
**Xor** is a puzzle game created for the ZX Spectrum in 1990 by Marek Trmač from the group GCC; it was officially released in 1992 by Proxima – Software v.o.s. as part of the Tinny collection. Its source was the original commercial game Xor by Astral Software from 1987, available on a number of other platforms, but Trmač's Spectrum version wasn't a mere port – the author designed thirty entirely new levels for it, twice as many as the British original had, and adapted them to the capabilities and graphical style of the ZX Spectrum.

The gameplay resembles Boulder Dash, but follows its own, more complex rules: the player moves through a maze full of blocks that need to be pushed, destroyed, or bypassed in the right order to reach the goal, and a single wrong move can make a level impossible to finish, forcing the player to start the level over from the beginning. The emphasis on forward planning and patient trial of approaches makes Xor a typical representative of the puzzle-game genre, which was very widespread on the ZX Spectrum due to its low graphical demands and was popular even with players lacking fast reflexes.

Thanks to its expanded number of levels and local distribution, Trmač's version won its own audience among Czechoslovak players independent of the foreign original, and it still appears today in overviews of the most accomplished domestic puzzle games for this platform. It's also worth noting that this is an adaptation of an existing concept rather than an original idea – such reworkings of foreign games were common on the scene of the time, since license fees were unattainable for amateur authors, so they simply reworked interesting mechanics according to their own ideas. For genre fans, Xor remains a challenge even today, because its puzzles depend neither on reflexes nor on graphical execution but purely on the ingenuity of the solution, and it can be played just as well on the original machine as on a modern emulator.
zx-spectrum__xor.teaser: A Spectrum version of the commercial game Xor, but with thirty entirely new and harder levels.

zx-spectrum__krtek-auticko.article:
**Krtek a autíčko** (The Little Mole and the Car) is an action platformer created by the studio Kybersoft and released in 1990 by Proxima – Software v.o.s.; the music for the game was composed by Miroslav Hlavička. The game builds on the popularity of Zdeněk Miler's animated Little Mole, one of the most recognizable characters in Czechoslovak culture, and transplants it into a simple but inventive game framework understandable even to the youngest players, who were just starting out with computers.

The player's task, in the role of the Little Mole, is to load crates onto a truck, hindered along the way by a chaotic environment full of obstacles and quirky creatures called "springers." The Mole can actively interact with the surroundings – using a shovel to clear obstacles, or apples with which he can lure away or occupy the springers, which gives the game a mildly strategic dimension beyond simple item collecting and forces the player to think through the order of actions in each room. The game supports control via Kempston joystick as well as redefinable keys, which was standard at the time for more polished titles and made the game more accessible even to less experienced players.

Choosing such a familiar character from a series beloved by children was a smart move that won the game an audience even among younger players who otherwise never played text adventures or action shooters and approached the computer more as a toy. The graphical rendering of the characters and environment sticks to the source's charming style and, together with Miroslav Hlavička's music, creates an atmosphere noticeably lighter than that of the vast majority of action games of the time. Krtek a autíčko today ranks among the more charming chapters of domestic ZX Spectrum production – it shows that domestic studios could also work with locally rooted humor and characters that carried a completely different emotional resonance for the Czechoslovak audience than anything imported from abroad, and thanks to that the game still holds a special place among those who remember it.
zx-spectrum__krtek-auticko.teaser: A platformer starring Zdeněk Miler's popular Mole, aimed mainly at the youngest players.

pc-dos__quake.article:
**Quake** marked id Software's leap from the fast but flat graphics of Doom to a fully three-dimensional world with dynamic lighting and simple physics. The player finds themselves in a dark, gothic environment full of stone temples, lava, and organic biomechanical structures, fighting through traps, secret passages, and increasingly aggressive enemies across four thematic episodes. Compared to the studio's previous titles, it added freedom of movement along all three axes, jumping across chasms, and so-called rocket jumping, which quickly became part of player culture and later competitive multiplayer. The weapon arsenal, from the shotgun to the grenade launcher and nail gun, was complemented by grim, almost alien-looking locations blending fantasy and technological elements.

On an average DOS machine of the mid-1990s, Quake was extremely demanding – a fully textured 3D environment with its own software renderer and static lighting system required a powerful processor, and reducing the resolution to a minimum was often necessary for smooth play. The game's music was composed by Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails, giving the atmosphere an industrial, oppressive edge that stood in clear contrast to the metal-heavy production typical of FPS games at the time, playing more in ambient waves between battles than as a continuous backdrop. The dark, almost music-free passages heightened the sense of isolation in a hostile world, and the sounds of footsteps and monsters became a key part of the player's orientation.

Quake also pioneered internet multiplayer, giving rise to an extensive deathmatch scene, later competitive tournaments, and technologies such as the client-server model that other online games would later build upon. The game's engine inspired numerous other studios, and its later source code release enabled a wealth of mods, technological experiments, and entirely new genres, starting with the early team-based mod Team Fortress. Even today, Quake is considered one of the key milestones of the FPS genre, and its gameplay and gunplay still hold up years later.
pc-dos__quake.teaser: id Software's step from Doom's flat graphics to a full 3D world with dynamic lighting.

pc-dos__duke-nukem-3d.article:
**Duke Nukem 3D** pitted a brash, self-aware sense of humor and cinematic references to nineties action B-movies against the serious, dark aesthetic of Doom and Quake. The hero Duke fights his way through streets overrun by aliens, strip clubs, cinemas, and space stations, dropping lines lifted from films like Alien or Total Recall along the way, destroying interactive environments, and wielding weapons such as the machine gun, rocket launcher, laser rifle, and the shrink ray, which turns enemies into tiny targets that can be stomped flat. The game ran on an enhanced Build engine, which, unlike Quake, allowed even an ordinary DOS machine to run at high resolution and smoothly.

The Build engine brought interactive environments unusual for its time – the player could flush toilets, turn on televisions, break mirrors, operate elevators, and look up and down, none of which was a given for FPS games back then. The level design leaned on recognizable, civilian locations, from Los Angeles to a space base and a lunar colony, and the dense atmosphere was underscored by synthesizer music and a wealth of digitized one-liners that became iconic and were still quoted by players years after release. It also added a wealth of secret rooms and references to other games that rewarded thorough exploration of the levels, and the game supported a map editor, which gave rise to a huge amount of community-made level content.

The game achieved enormous commercial success and, together with Doom, defined the shape of nineties action FPS games, though its signature was humor, pop-culture exaggeration, and confident vulgarity rather than a horror atmosphere. Critics and players alike praised above all the feel of the guns, the fluidity of movement, and the unusually high degree of environmental interactivity, which briefly became a genre standard that other studios tried to imitate. Even years later, Duke Nukem 3D remains a beloved classic, followed by a string of sequels, expansion packs, and remasters, none of which, however, achieved the same combination of exaggeration, action, and the Build engine's technical finesse as the original from 1996.
pc-dos__duke-nukem-3d.teaser: Against the dark seriousness of Doom and Quake, it sets brash humor and one-liners from action B-movies.

pc-dos__hexen-beyond-heretic.article:
**Hexen: Beyond Heretic** followed up on Heretic with a modified Doom engine and took players into a dark fantasy world divided into large interconnected hubs that could be freely revisited, even after the player had left an area because of an inaccessible puzzle. Three character classes are available – the Fighter, the Cleric, and the Mage – each with its own set of weapons, combat style, and difficulty, making the game replayable and giving it an unusual degree of variety for its time. Instead of a linear progression from the start of a level to its end, the player must solve puzzles interconnected across several maps, seeking levers, keys, and triggers located levels away from where they are used, which was far more complex than in its predecessors and required keeping notes.

The graphics were built on the same technology as Doom and Heretic, but the level design moved toward a more vertical layout, and the atmosphere evoked dark castles, swamps, ice canyons, and necropolises. The music used MIDI compositions with a dark, medieval tone that complemented the game's grim mood well and changed depending on the specific area. On DOS machines, the game ran smoothly even on less powerful hardware, since it was still based on the proven 2.5D engine, so it remained accessible even to owners of weaker systems. Sound effects such as cracking ice or the distant rumble of gates further reinforced the feeling that the player was moving through a living, interconnected world rather than a sequence of separate arenas.

Hexen was praised specifically for its willingness to move away from straightforward shooting toward more elaborate level design and puzzles, which set it apart from most of the FPS competition of the time, even though some players found the difficulty of navigating between hubs frustrating. It is still regarded today as one of the most ambitious titles built on the Doom engine, and its hub-based level system inspired later action RPG titles.
pc-dos__hexen-beyond-heretic.teaser: A modified Doom engine and a fantasy world with interconnected hubs you can travel between freely.

pc-dos__descent.article:
**Descent** abandoned the flat corridor mazes typical of the shooters of its time and offered genuine movement with six degrees of freedom – the player's spacecraft could turn and fly in any direction, with no concept of up or down. The player infiltrates a network of underground mining complexes controlled by treacherous robots that have attacked mining facilities across the solar system, and must navigate winding tunnels, destroy enemies, collect key cards and hostages, and finally escape each level before the mine's self-destruct system detonates. This principle of free movement in space was completely new on DOS computers and disorienting at first, but it also opened up a type of level design entirely different from corridor shooters with a fixed sense of up and down.

The game used its own 3D engine with textured polygons, which was demanding on the hardware of the time but made the mine environments feel genuinely three-dimensional and maze-like, with corridors crossing in every direction. Ambient electronic music and sounds echoing through the metal corridors reinforced the claustrophobic atmosphere and disorientation the game deliberately built up. Controls combining keyboard, mouse, or a joystick with a throttle lever required practice and adjustment to flying without a fixed horizon, but the reward was an unusual freedom of movement that the shooters of the day did not offer. The gradual unlocking of new weapons and ship upgrades between mines also gave the game a certain sense of progression and reward for successfully completed missions.

Descent built a strong fanbase largely thanks to its innovative multiplayer, where battles in fully three-dimensional space demanded entirely different tactics than a classic ground-based deathmatch. Together with its sequel, it laid the foundation for the six-degrees-of-freedom space action subgenre, which remains fairly rare and prized to this day for its technical boldness and uncompromising approach to design.
pc-dos__descent.teaser: Instead of flat mazes, it offered flight with six degrees of freedom, with no up or down.

pc-dos__descent-ii.article:
**Descent II** expanded the concept of the first game with new weapons, enemies, and more varied environments, from ice caves to volcanic, organic, and alien complexes, softening the impression of repetitive metal tunnels that the first game occasionally could not avoid. The core gameplay remained the same – the player pilots a small spacecraft through the mazes of mining complexes with six degrees of freedom of movement, destroying robotic guards and seeking a way to escape, but thanks to an improved engine the environments looked more colorful and varied than in the original game. New secondary weapons were also added, such as guided missiles, a plasma cannon, and special mines, and a new type of enemy, including smarter robots, required different combat tactics. The game also featured so-called thief robots that stole the player's supplies and guide-bots that, on request, showed the way out of the maze, addressing one of the frequent orientation problems of the first game.

On DOS machines of the second half of the nineties, the game benefited from faster processors and offered smoother performance even at higher resolutions, though it still retained the dense, technical look typical of textured 3D polygons of its era. The sound design and atmospheric electronic music continued in the vein of the first game and supported well the feeling of lonely exploration of dangerous underground complexes full of traps and hidden passages. The game also expanded multiplayer options and offered a more elaborate set of maps designed specifically for multiplayer battles, including new game modes beyond the classic deathmatch.

Descent II is still valued today as a more mature and balanced sequel that developed the strengths of the original without changing its core identity built on free movement in space. Together with its predecessor, it defined the six-degrees-of-freedom action subgenre and remained a favorite target for fans looking for an alternative to the traditional corridor shooters of the time, even though this type of gameplay ultimately remained a rather niche corner of the genre.
pc-dos__descent-ii.teaser: It expands the first Descent with new environments, from ice caves to alien complexes.

pc-dos__blood.article:
**Blood** is among the darkest and bloodiest titles built on the Build engine, the same technology that powered Duke Nukem 3D. The player takes on the role of Caleb, an undead gunslinger seeking revenge on a cult called the Cabal that once betrayed and killed him, moving through cemeteries, abandoned mansions, circuses, sewers, and other horror-themed locations full of traps, hidden passages, and grotesque violence. Weapons such as dynamite, a shotgun, a chainsaw, and a voodoo hat firing spiritual energy, combined with victims falling apart in pieces and enemies set on fire, earned the game a reputation as one of the most brutal shooters of its generation, even compared to other Build engine titles.

Beyond the violence, Blood is also known for its black humor, its many film and literary references to classic horror movies, from Evil Dead to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, and its unusually atmospheric sound design, where creaking doors, distant laughter, and Caleb's sarcastic one-liners created a mood that was oppressive yet playful at the same time. The Build engine enabled detailed interactive environments on DOS computers, including destructible objects, collapsing floors, and dynamic lighting, which, despite the technical limitations of the era, made the game feel alive and unpredictable. The high difficulty the game offered, especially at the harder difficulty settings, was among the toughest in the entire genre and required careful planning of one's approach.

Although Blood could not match Duke Nukem 3D in commercial success, it still enjoys cult status among players today thanks to its difficulty, atmosphere, and horror treatment, which was fairly unusual for the FPS genre at the time. Many fans still consider it one of the high points of the Build engine, a game that brought a darker, rawer tone back to the genre after a wave of lighter titles, all without giving up its own distinctive sense of humor.
pc-dos__blood.teaser: One of the bloodiest titles on the Build engine; Caleb takes revenge on the cult that killed him.

pc-dos__shadow-warrior.article:
**Shadow Warrior** followed the success of Duke Nukem 3D using the same Build engine, this time with the protagonist Lo Wang, a former hitman for the Japanese arms corporation Zilla Enterprises, who turns against his employer after discovering its true intentions. The game combines firearms such as shotguns, rocket launchers, and explosive-tipped grenades with a katana for melee combat and a range of throwing weapons like shurikens, placing greater emphasis on melee combat within the FPS genre than most of the competition at the time. The environments draw on Asian aesthetics – temples, gardens, dragon statues, and industrial complexes are full of traps, secret passages, and interactive elements typical of the Build engine. Enemies also included supernatural foes and mythical creatures, giving the game a touch of supernatural horror alongside its action.

Like Duke Nukem 3D, the game reveled in self-aware, borderline politically incorrect humor and a wealth of one-liners from its hero, which drew criticism from some audiences but contributed to its popularity and cult status among others, similar to previous 3D Realms titles built on a similar type of humor. The graphics engine enabled high resolutions on DOS computers, sloped surfaces, and vertical viewing angles, so the level design could be clearer and more open than in older titles, with plenty of outdoor areas and changes in elevation.

Shadow Warrior is remembered today mainly as one of the last great Build engine titles from the era when the engine dominated the market, before it was ultimately overshadowed by fully 3D-accelerated technologies like Quake. A later remake and sequel revived interest in the original, which remains a favorite among connoisseurs of nineties shooters with an Asian action flavor and its unmistakable combination of melee and ranged weapons.
pc-dos__shadow-warrior.teaser: A Build-engine shooter featuring Lo Wang, who combines firearms with a katana.

pc-dos__redneck-rampage.article:
**Redneck Rampage** is another Build engine shooter, this time offering a parodic take on rural America – the player takes on the role of one of two brothers, Leonard or Bubby, who set out to rescue their pig Bessie, abducted by aliens, gradually uncovering a conspiracy involving the alien cloning of the residents of the small town of Hickston. Instead of sci-fi bases or dark temples typical of other FPS games of the time, the locations consist of farms, trailer homes, strip clubs, a church, and country roads, giving the game an unmistakable, unapologetically kitschy tone with an openly parodic take on rural America.

The weapons match the theme – alongside a shotgun and a pistol, there is also a chainsaw, dynamite, bottles of moonshine, and even a live chicken used as a weapon, and the soundtrack consists of country and bluegrass tunes, which are completely unusual in the context of the FPS genre and give the game a distinct identity. Enemies were also accompanied by digitized voice lines with a heavy Southern accent, further underscoring the game's overall caricature-like tone. As in other Build engine games, the player could partially destroy the environment and take advantage of the vertical layout of the maps, but the graphics were somewhat simpler and more repetitive in texture compared to Duke Nukem 3D, reflecting the lower production budget.

Thanks to its exaggerated, parodic approach, the game built a small but loyal fanbase and is viewed today more as a curiosity and a product of the nineties FPS fever than as a technical or gameplay milestone. Nevertheless, it remains an interesting testament to the variety of genre variations the Build engine allowed at the time, and it inspired the sequel Redneck Rampage: Suckin' Grits on Route 66, which continued in a similarly parodic spirit along America's Route 66, further developing the same world of rural clichés and alien conspiracy.
pc-dos__redneck-rampage.teaser: A parody Build-engine shooter about rescuing a pig abducted by aliens.

pc-dos__star-wars-dark-forces.article:
**Star Wars: Dark Forces** introduced the mercenary Kyle Katarn, who sets out for the Rebel Alliance to foil a secret Imperial project, the Dark Trooper — elite combat robots threatening the balance of power in the galactic civil war. Unlike many shooters of the era, the game featured its own advanced Jedi engine, which allowed multi-level maps with stairs, bridges, and platforms above and below one another, so the level design felt far more three-dimensional than in many competing titles built on a flat grid without true verticality.

The game combined straightforward action with jumping sections, lever-based puzzles, and the search for keycards, while environments ranging from Imperial bases to Star Destroyer docking bays and the sewers of the planet Anoat faithfully echoed the atmosphere of the film trilogy. Sound effects and musical themes were drawn directly from the films, including the well-known Imperial theme, giving players the feeling that they were truly moving through the Star Wars universe rather than a generic sci-fi backdrop with a borrowed license. On DOS computers the game was well optimized, running smoothly even on mid-range hardware, which helped make it accessible to a broad player base. Besides ordinary blasters, the player could use grenades, mortars, or thermal detonators, and gradually unlock upgrades for their suit, enriching the level design with optional tactical approaches.

Dark Forces became a commercial and critical success and kicked off the Jedi Knight series, which continued even after the shift to 3D-accelerated graphics and the introduction of lightsabers and Force powers. To this day it is regarded as one of the best licensed FPS titles of the 1990s and a demonstration of how a film license can be turned into a game with its own technical and creative identity, rather than a superficial adaptation of the source film.
pc-dos__star-wars-dark-forces.teaser: Kyle Katarn and the custom Jedi engine, with multi-level maps stacked above and below each other.

pc-dos__full-throttle.article:
**Full Throttle** is a point-and-click adventure set in the harsh world of biker gangs in the near future, in which the player takes on the role of Ben, leader of the Polecats gang, framed for the murder of a motorcycle manufacturer and forced to uncover the real conspiracy surrounding Corley Motors, the last American motorcycle factory. Compared to traditional LucasArts adventures, the game simplified inventory puzzles and the classic combining of dozens of items in favor of more direct storytelling and several action sequences, including biker brawls, chases, and highway riding, which broke up the purely point-and-click gameplay and gave the game a dynamic pace.

The game's visual style drew on comic-book aesthetics and the raw atmosphere of biker subculture, backed by a striking rock soundtrack from the band The Gone Jackals, which gave the story an energy unusual for the adventure genre, more accustomed to orchestral or synth-driven music. Tim Schafer, as writer and designer, helped craft a tight, cinematic story with strong characters and dark humor, though the actual playtime was noticeably shorter compared to other LucasArts adventures, which became a subject of debate at the time about value for money. The gruff yet charismatic voice acting of the main hero, together with the vivid supporting cast of the biker gang, formed the core of the entire narrative and lent it cinematic credibility.

Full Throttle is still cited today as one of the most atmospheric titles of the golden era of LucasArts adventures and an example of a successful fusion of storytelling, music, and visual style into a compact, tightly constructed whole. Its short playtime is often seen as intentional, ensuring the story never loses pace or wanders into unnecessary side detours, which sets it apart from the more sprawling adventures of the time.
pc-dos__full-throttle.teaser: A LucasArts adventure from the rough world of biker gangs, with simplified puzzle-solving.

pc-dos__discworld.article:
**Discworld** brings to the screen the world of Terry Pratchett's famous humorous fantasy novels, casting the player as the inept wizard Rincewind, who must solve a mystery involving a dragon threatening the city of Ankh-Morpork. The game is a classic point-and-click adventure with an extensive inventory and elaborate, often convoluted puzzles that became notorious for their difficulty and sometimes almost absurd logic, requiring unconventional thinking and frequent combining of seemingly unrelated items.

The graphics used characters animated with traditional techniques and then digitally transferred into the game, giving the world of the Discworld a distinctive, cartoonish look matching the illustrations from the source novels. Rincewind was voiced by Eric Idle of Monty Python, whose comedic delivery, together with the other voice actors, gave the game a strong humorous tone in keeping with the literary source and its typically British, dry humor. On DOS computers, the game required a CD-ROM drive because of the large amount of voiced dialogue and animation, which in 1995 was still a fairly new standard that not every computer owner met. Rincewind was accompanied by his loyal, if somewhat reluctant, Luggage, whose presence and comments on events added another layer of characteristic Pratchett-style humor to the game.

Discworld is still remembered as a faithful and witty adaptation of Pratchett's world, though its puzzles are often cited as among the hardest and at times unfair in the entire adventure genre, which led many players to resort to hints. Nevertheless, it remains a favorite among fans of the source novels and of classic 1990s graphic adventures, and it received a sequel, Discworld II: Mortality Bytes, which continued with similar humor and puzzle style, again returning to the world inspired by Pratchett's novels.
pc-dos__discworld.teaser: An adventure based on Terry Pratchett's comic fantasy, notorious for its difficult puzzles.

pc-dos__star-wars-rebel-assault.article:
**Star Wars: Rebel Assault** was among the first titles to fully exploit the capacity of CD-ROM media, and it became one of the best-selling games of the early CD-ROM era. The player takes on the role of a young Rebel Alliance pilot named Rookie One, whose journey from training on Tatooine to key battles of the saga, including the attack on the Death Star and the Battle of Hoth, is told through corridor-style flight and ground sequences with limited but effective freedom of movement, supplemented by digitized film footage and classic Star Wars sound effects.

The visual style combined hand-drawn and digitized footage with music and sound effects taken directly from the Star Wars trilogy, which, at a time when most games ran in low resolution with MIDI music, felt extraordinarily impressive audiovisually and, for many players, offered a first glimpse of what the CD-ROM format could do. The gameplay, however, was rather simple and linear, closer to an interactive movie with minimal actual player control over movement, which was a common compromise at the time for games built primarily around cinematic presentation and atmosphere. The player mostly just aimed the cursor and dodged obstacles or enemy fire, while the movement of the ship or character itself followed predetermined paths, resembling a ride more than a full-fledged flight simulation.

Rebel Assault is remembered today mainly as a technological showcase of the power of the CD-ROM format and as evidence of the early fascination with multimedia content in games, rather than as a deep gaming experience with elaborate mechanics. Nevertheless, it played a significant role in popularizing CD-ROM drives on personal computers and remains an interesting historical stop in the development of Star Wars games, later followed by the sequel Rebel Assault II with improved graphics and smoother controls.
pc-dos__star-wars-rebel-assault.teaser: One of the first titles to fully exploit the CD-ROM; on-rails flight through the saga's battles.

pc-dos__strife-quest-for-sovereign.article:
**Strife: Quest for the Sovereign** was built on a modified Doom engine but combined classic shooter action with elements that were utterly unusual for the FPS genre in 1996 — dialogue trees, quests, factions, and the ability to decide, in a world ruled by a totalitarian theocracy called the Order, whom to kill and whom instead to spare or recruit as an ally. The player becomes a member of the rebel organization known as the Front, fighting against the Order, and besides shooting must complete tasks for various characters in the city, buy equipment from merchants, and build reputation with factions, bringing the game closer to an action RPG than a pure arena shooter.

The graphics were based on the same technology as Doom and Heretic, but the level design was more open and interconnected, with a central city serving as a hub for quests, shopping, and conversations with non-player characters. The music and sound effects maintained a dark, industrial atmosphere fitting the theme of an oppressed world ruled by a religious dictatorship, and the voiced character dialogue gave the story unusual depth for the time, when most FPS games told their story only through text interludes. The player could also improve character attributes such as accuracy or stamina over the course of the game, bringing it even closer to a hybrid between an action game and an RPG.

Strife never commercially matched the success of Doom or Quake, partly because it was released at a time when players' attention was already turning to fully 3D-accelerated titles, but among connoisseurs it earned a reputation as a forerunner of later immersive sims and hybrid action games, such as the later titles from Looking Glass Studios, thanks to its ambitious blend of FPS and RPG elements. In hindsight, Strife is praised precisely for how early and how naturally it managed to incorporate elements into the FPS genre that would only become commonplace in action games many years later.
pc-dos__strife-quest-for-sovereign.teaser: The Doom engine combined with dialogue and factions - utterly unusual for the FPS genre in 1996.

pc-dos__terminal-velocity.article:
**Terminal Velocity** offered fast, arcade-style space action in which the player pilots a fighter craft defending the solar system against an invasion by an alien race called the Vinedians, who have attacked human colonies on several planets and moons. Unlike the more simulation-oriented space titles of its day, Terminal Velocity built on straightforward, pace-setting action closer to a fast arcade flier than an elaborate simulator, emphasizing spectacular explosions, fast-paced firefights, and flights through canyons and underground tunnels on various planets of the solar system, from Mars to Pluto.

The game used its own 3D engine with textured surfaces and hardware-undemanding yet visually impressive terrain rendering, which allowed it to offer sprawling, open environments instead of the enclosed corridors typical of other DOS shooters of the time. Electronic music and forceful sound effects underscored the fast tempo of the gameplay, and the game boasted one of the first supported interfaces for the nascent 3D graphics accelerators, which were only just beginning to make their way into the mainstream home computer market. The gradual unlocking of stronger weapons and ship upgrades between missions gave the gameplay a clear sense of progression without disrupting its otherwise straightforward, action-oriented nature.

Terminal Velocity earned its popularity mainly through its accessibility and brisk pace, which set it apart from more complex space simulators like Wing Commander or Descent that demanded a longer learning curve from the player. Today it is remembered as a solid, if less ambitious, representative of the space action genre from the mid-1990s, and as one of the early examples of games prepared for the coming era of 3D acceleration, which within the following few years completely transformed the look of computer games and definitively relegated software rendering to the past.
pc-dos__terminal-velocity.teaser: A fast, arcade-style space shooter, closer to flight arcades than a simulator.

pc-dos__ishar-legend-of-fortress.article:
**Ishar: Legend of the Fortress** is an action RPG from the French studio Silmarils that loosely follows on from their earlier title Crystals of Arborea and opens the eponymous trilogy. The player takes charge of a group of adventurers tasked with defending the fortress of Ishar against enemy raids, gradually discovering a sprawling island world full of towns, caves, and remote shrines.

The game combines first-person movement through the environment with a fairly simple combat system and party management, where each character has their own set of skills, equipment, and tasks. Heavy emphasis is placed on recruiting companions, trading, and gradually unlocking new areas of the map, while the player must often juggle time, since the defense of the fortress runs in the background throughout the game. On the PC systems of the time, the game presented itself in colorful VGA graphics with atmospheric music, which in 1992 was a fairly costly undertaking for a small European studio.

Ishar earned a reputation as a dense but rewarding game for fans of European RPGs looking for an alternative to the then-dominant American series such as Ultima or Might and Magic. The controls and density of text feel archaic today and the game demands patience, yet it remains an interesting example of how European studios of the nineties approached the RPG genre in their own way — emphasizing atmosphere and a richly developed world rather than action pacing. The game was also developed simultaneously for several platforms of the time, including the Amiga and the Atari ST, with the DOS version, thanks to broader sound card support, offering somewhat more atmospheric musical accompaniment and cleaner audio. Despite its limited technical means, the series managed to maintain its own visual identity thanks to hand-drawn character portraits and stylized landscapes, which made Ishar an easily recognizable brand among European RPGs of the era. It is also worth mentioning that the name of the fortress Ishar itself gave its name to the entire trilogy, a fairly unusual decision at a time when studios were only just beginning to look for ways to build their own game brands.
pc-dos__ishar-legend-of-fortress.teaser: An action RPG from Silmarils that opens the trilogy about defending the fortress of Ishar from raids.

pc-dos__ishar-2-messengers-of-doom.article:
**Ishar 2: Messengers of Doom** is the sequel to the European RPG from studio Silmarils, moving the action aboard a giant flying fortress heading toward an impending doom. The player once again assembles a group of adventurers and explores the vast, vertically structured environment of the ship and the surrounding islands, while trying to uncover the cause of the approaching catastrophe and find a way to prevent it.

Compared to the first installment, the game expands the possibilities for movement and interaction with the world, adds more elaborate puzzles tied to the ship's mechanisms, and offers a wider range of characters with their own abilities and equipment. The combat system remains simple, with the focus of the game lying more in exploration, gathering information, and solving related tasks than in pure action. The graphical presentation on DOS systems built on the first installment with colorful environments and accompanying music that nicely underscored the somewhat oppressive atmosphere of a dying airship full of strange inhabitants.

The second Ishar is ranked by fans among the high points of the series thanks to its imaginative setting and denser story dramaturgy. For today's player, the main obstacles are the austere controls and the absence of modern conveniences such as an automap, yet they will appreciate the atmosphere of a decaying world and the honestly elaborate, if demanding, design that rewards patient exploration of every corner of the ship. Like the first installment, this game was also released on several European platforms simultaneously, with the DOS version benefiting from more advanced sound cards and a wider color palette, which gave the music and sound effects a more pronounced presence. Silmarils maintained their characteristic visual signature in the second installment as well, with hand-painted portraits and backgrounds that set the series apart from competing RPGs and remain instantly recognizable to this day. The theme of the dying airship also gave the entire game a fairly unusual sense of urgency that open-world RPGs of the time usually lacked, contributing to Ishar 2's reputation as one of the most atmospherically powerful installments in the entire series.
pc-dos__ishar-2-messengers-of-doom.teaser: The sequel to Silmarils' RPG, this time aboard a giant flying fortress heading toward doom.

pc-dos__ishar-3-seven-gates-of-infinity.article:
**Ishar 3: The Seven Gates of Infinity** concludes the trilogy from studio Silmarils and moves the adventure into seven interconnected worlds, between which the player travels using magical gates. A group of heroes must journey through diverse environments, from desert plains to icy realms, and face a threat endangering the very existence of the game's universe.

The game's structure remains faithful to its predecessors — first-person movement, party management with individual skills, and simple but functional combat — but with significantly greater environmental variety thanks to the concept of the seven gates. This brought a more varied visual style and more types of puzzles and tasks, but also higher demands on orientation within a vast, sprawling world without modern navigation aids. The sound design and music on DOS underscored the distinct atmosphere of each world, which was seen as a step forward within the series.

Ishar 3 tends to be rated as a dignified, if not revolutionary, conclusion to the series — it rather expands the proven formula than fundamentally changes it. Today's player will appreciate the variety of the seven worlds and the closure of the story arc, less so the archaic controls and the density of systems that players of the nineties had to figure out without internet guides. Within the context of European RPGs, Ishar 3 remains an interesting testament to the courage of a small studio to build its own, distinctive fantasy worlds. Although Silmarils closed the series after this installment, their approach to RPGs — with an emphasis on travel, trade, and the atmosphere of unknown lands — influenced the perception of smaller European studios as full-fledged alternatives to the major American publishers. The trilogy as a whole thus today also serves as testimony to the diversity of the RPG genre on PC in the first half of the nineties, when several distinct schools of game design existed side by side. After finishing the trilogy, Silmarils moved on to other projects, but none of them ever achieved a reputation similar to the Ishar series, which remains their best-known legacy among retro RPG fans.
pc-dos__ishar-3-seven-gates-of-infinity.teaser: It closes the Silmarils trilogy with a journey across seven worlds connected by magic gates.

pc-dos__albion.article:
**Albion** is an RPG by the German studio Blue Byte, telling the story of the crew of the spaceship Toronto, who, after crash-landing on an unknown planet, discover a richly developed fantasy world inhabited by various races. The main hero, Tom Driscoll, finds himself in the middle of a conflict between the native inhabitants and a mining corporation, giving the game an unusual blend of sci-fi and fantasy.

The game alternates a top-down view while traveling across the world map with turn-based combat and extensive dialogue passages, through which the player gradually pieces together the political situation of the planet Albion. The world is divided into several distinct regions, each with its own culture, language, and architecture, which represented an unusually ambitious feat of world-building in the mid-nineties. On DOS and early Windows machines, the game benefited from detailed 2D graphics and atmospheric music that effectively supported the sense of discovering an alien world.

Albion is still valued today, especially by old-school RPG fans, for its dense story, morally ambiguous factions, and unusual combination of a sci-fi frame with a fantasy core, where technologically advanced humans colonize a world with its own magic and mythology. Its accessibility today is limited by a slower pace and a less clear interface, yet the game remains one of the most interesting German RPGs of the nineties and an inspiration for the later work of Blue Byte, which later became famous for the Battle Isle and The Settlers series. Special attention should also be paid to the fact that the planet's different factions and races hold differing views on colonization and technological progress, so the player gradually pieces together the conflict from multiple points of view rather than a clear-cut division into good and evil. This approach to storytelling, where no side is purely good or evil, was among the most interesting things European RPGs had to offer in the mid-nineties. Blue Byte also supported the game with a fairly extensive printed manual containing maps and descriptions of the individual cultures, which, in the era before widespread internet access, made it easier for players to find their way around the complex world and today serves as a valuable artifact for collectors.
pc-dos__albion.teaser: A Blue Byte RPG about the crew of a crashed spaceship in a world blending sci-fi and fantasy.

pc-dos__elder-scrolls-ii-daggerfall.article:
**The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall** is the second installment of Bethesda's legendary series and, at the time of its release, was one of the most expansive RPGs ever made — the game world of the provinces of High Rock and Hammerfell was procedurally generated and included thousands of towns, villages, and dungeons. The player creates their own character, choosing a race, class, and set of skills, and then sets out into an open world full of factions, quests, and political intrigue.
