The game offers unprecedented freedom of movement and approach to quests — it is possible to become a member of the thieves' guild, mages, fighting orders, or even vampires, with decisions affecting the further development of the story. Technically, it was a very ambitious project with a 3D environment, which placed heavy demands on the PCs of the time and was notoriously known for its technical flaws and bugs at launch. Despite this, it offered an unusual degree of simulation of the world, weather, and time of day.

Daggerfall is now regarded as a groundbreaking, if roughly polished, step toward open-world RPGs, one that influenced the direction of the entire Elder Scrolls series and the genre in general with its emphasis on player freedom. Due to its technical imperfections and lack of clarity, playing it today is mainly a matter for enthusiasts and historians of the genre, though community fixes and modern engines like Daggerfall Unity continue to extend its life and bring it closer to new generations of players. The scale of the game was truly unprecedented in 1996 — the game world included hundreds of thousands of individual locations and hundreds of side characters, which required an enormous amount of content generated partly procedurally and partly by hand. This scale became both a strength and a source of repetitive, generic content, a trade-off Bethesda was well aware of and gradually addressed in later installments of the series with a smaller but hand-crafted world. Nevertheless, Daggerfall remains to this day a reference point that Bethesda itself and the media repeatedly return to when discussing how large an open-world RPG should actually be.
pc-dos__elder-scrolls-ii-daggerfall.teaser: At the time of release, one of the largest RPGs ever; a procedurally generated world.

pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-star-trail.article:
**Realms of Arkania: Star Trail** is the second installment of the trilogy by the German studio Attic Entertainment, based on the rules of the tabletop game Das Schwarze Auge. The player leads a group of adventurers who set out across the vast continent of Aventuria on the trail of a mysterious threat, with the journey leading through mountains, forests, and underground passages full of dangers.

The game builds on Blade of Destiny with an elaborate character creation system featuring dozens of attributes and skills, tactical turn-based combat, and a strong emphasis on expedition logistics — the player must manage food supplies, heal wounds, and deal with party fatigue during the long journey. This simulation-heavy approach made Star Trail one of the most demanding and deepest RPGs of its time, rewarding careful planning. The graphics on DOS were solid, if no longer cutting-edge even at release, but the game was carried above all by the depth of its systems and its faithfulness to the Das Schwarze Auge source material.

Star Trail is still valued by European RPG fans today for its uncompromising depth and authentic translation of the Das Schwarze Auge rules into computer form. For today's player it is a very demanding, slow title with no forgiveness for mistakes, yet it offers a unique sense of a genuine expedition through an inhospitable landscape that more modern RPGs often lack. The Das Schwarze Auge rule system on which the game is built differs significantly from American systems like Dungeons & Dragons in its emphasis on more realistic injuries, illnesses, and fatigue, which made Star Trail a simulation with its own distinctive rules rather than a derivative of established genre templates. This very fidelity to the tabletop source is the reason the series still enjoys respect today, especially in German-speaking countries, where the DSA rules originate and where they have a long tradition. For players accustomed to American RPG templates, the sheer number of numerical attributes and modifiers can be confusing at first, but once they grasp the system's basic logic, they discover an unusually elaborate simulation of an adventuring expedition, where a failure in supply management can threaten the party just as much as direct combat with an enemy.
pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-star-trail.teaser: The second part of the trilogy based on the Das Schwarze Auge rules; an expedition across Aventuria.

pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-shadows-over-r.article:
**Realms of Arkania: Shadows over Riva** concludes Attic Entertainment's trilogy based on the Das Schwarze Auge system and shifts the action to the city of Riva, which faces a siege by hostile forces. The player once again leads a group of adventurers, but this time with a stronger emphasis on the urban setting, diplomacy, and preparing the defense rather than on long expeditions through the wilderness.

The third installment brought improved graphics and a clearer interface compared to previous entries, while retaining the complex character system and tactical combat that made the series famous. The game newly places greater emphasis on building relationships with factions inside the besieged city and on decisions that affect the course of Riva's defense. Even so, the game remains demanding and text-heavy, staying true to the spirit of the source material even in its technical execution on the DOS and Windows machines of the time.

Shadows over Riva is often seen by fans as a more accessible, yet still deep, conclusion to the series, one that moved away from pure exploration toward a more dramatic siege story. Today the game is mainly a matter for connoisseurs of the German RPG scene, whose complexity and slow pace will especially appeal to players seeking an authentic tabletop-game experience translated to the computer. The trilogy as a whole documents how the German gaming scene in the nineties tried to bring its own tabletop RPG tradition into computer form, independent of the American or Japanese take on the genre, and Shadows over Riva, as the final installment, capitalizes on this effort with the most elaborate, if also the most constrained, story of the entire series. For collectors of European RPGs, it is a mandatory item alongside Blade of Destiny and Star Trail. The conclusion of the trilogy also symbolically closed one of the last great waves of European RPGs built on their own, independent rule systems, before the genre on PC increasingly merged, in the second half of the nineties, with American and later console-inspired templates and more accessible, action-oriented gameplay.
pc-dos__realms-of-arkania-shadows-over-r.teaser: Concludes the Arkania trilogy with a focus on the besieged city of Riva and preparing its defense.

pc-dos__septerra-core-legacy-of-creator.article:
**Septerra Core: Legacy of the Creator** is a JRPG-style RPG from the American studio Valkyrie Studios, set on a fractured world divided into several concentric shells, between which one can travel using a giant elevator called the Core. The player leads a party of heroes led by a young girl from one of the lower shells, who set out to uncover the secret of their world's creation and face a threat endangering all of its layers.

The game combines turn-based combat inspired by Japanese RPGs with hand-drawn backgrounds and a fairly extensive, linearly told story full of twists. The combat system uses a timeline on which the player plans the actions of characters and enemies alike, bringing more tactics than classic menu selections. Visually, the game relied on detailed 2D backgrounds combined with 3D character models, which even after all these years gives it a distinctive look.

Septerra Core is praised especially for its imaginative world of divided shells and a story drawing on creation mythology, less so for its occasionally slower pace and lengthy dialogue. For fans of the JRPG style on PC, it is one of the few notable Western attempts at a genre then dominated mainly by the console Final Fantasy series, and it therefore deserves a place among the interesting, if lesser-known, titles of the late nineties. The game's publisher was Monolith Productions, which at the time was experimenting with various genres, and it was precisely this partnership with the smaller Valkyrie Studios team that allowed a title to emerge that was not afraid to draw openly on Japanese game aesthetics at a time when they were still relatively rare on Western computers. To this day, Septerra Core is therefore among the titles that fans of the genre discover belatedly, pleasantly surprised at how well its story and world have held up over the years. The main heroine also stood out as an unusual female protagonist for a genre that in the nineties on PC was still mostly built around male heroes, giving the game a still-appreciated, somewhat timeless dimension today.
pc-dos__septerra-core-legacy-of-creator.teaser: An RPG inspired by JRPG style, set in a shattered world of shells connected by a giant elevator.

pc-dos__outcast.article:
**Outcast** is an action-adventure by the Belgian studio Appeal, telling the story of a team of soldiers and scientists sent to the alien planet Adelpha to prevent a catastrophe threatening Earth. The main hero, Cutter Slade, explores vast, open areas inhabited by the alien race of the Talan, completes tasks, and gradually uncovers the conspiracy behind the catastrophe.

The game was technologically exceptional thanks to its own voxel engine, which in 1999 offered unusually expansive and colorful outdoor environments with a smooth horizon — a combination of action, adventure elements, and open exploration unique for its time. The Talan also communicated through fully voiced dialogue and had a well-developed culture of their own, giving the setting unusual depth. The hardware demands were enormous, and the game was among the most technically demanding titles of its time, which made it difficult for owners of older PC systems to access it.

Outcast is now seen as ahead of its time — its open world and emphasis on exploration anticipated later open-world games, but commercially it failed to succeed as it deserved due to its high performance requirements. Among players and developers it has a reputation as a cult classic and a technical marvel, still admired today by fans of unconventional game worlds and experimental graphics technology. The game's music was composed by a symphony orchestra, an unusually costly decision for game production at the end of the nineties, contributing to the overall cinematic impression of the journey to Adelpha. This is partly why Outcast is still remembered today as a game that dared a vision exceeding the technical and financial possibilities of most of its competition at the time, and partly because of that it became a legend more among connoisseurs than among the wider gaming public. Its exceptional standing is also evidenced by the fact that developers and players repeatedly returned to it in subsequent years through fan-made patches and, later, an official re-release that made it possible to run the game on modern computers.
pc-dos__outcast.teaser: An action-adventure built on its own voxel engine, technologically exceptional for its time.

pc-dos__normality.article:
**Normality** is a point-and-click adventure by the British studio Gremlin Interactive, set in the dystopian city of Neutropolis, where any creativity and individuality is harshly suppressed by the ruling corporation. The player takes on the role of a young city resident who, against his will, discovers an illegal resistance movement fighting for freedom of expression and gradually gets caught up in a conflict with the totalitarian regime.

The game combines classic adventure-style puzzle-solving and item collecting with a partially 3D-rendered environment, through which the player moves more freely than in the purely 2D adventures of the time. The game's humor draws on satire of consumer society and cultural suppression, with many puzzles set within the mundane, deliberately drab appearance of a city ruled by bureaucracy. On DOS machines, it presented itself with fairly good graphics, fully voiced characters, and a distinctive musical component that complemented the game's satirical tone well.

Normality did not achieve the same acclaim as other Gremlin Interactive adventures, yet it is valued for its unusual dystopian humor and unconventional setting. Today it is more of a curiosity for collectors and genre fans, who will appreciate the atmosphere of the drab city and the exaggeration with which the game comments on the suppression of individuality and creativity. In the mid-nineties, Gremlin Interactive was better known for sports and action titles, so Normality represented a rather bold departure toward a narrative-driven adventure with pronounced political exaggeration. This is precisely why today's players and genre historians see it as an interesting, if overlooked, experiment worth discovering alongside the more famous adventures of the nineties, such as those from LucasArts or Sierra. The shift toward a partially three-dimensional environment also showed where the point-and-click adventure genre would head in the following years, even though Normality itself remained more of a side stop on that road than one of its main milestones.
pc-dos__normality.teaser: Gremlin's adventure set in a dystopian city where a corporation harshly suppresses creativity.

pc-dos__little-big-adventure.article:
**Little Big Adventure** is an action-adventure game by the French studio Adeline Software International, in which the player takes on the role of the young Twinsen, fighting against the totalitarian dictator Dr. FunFrock on the planet Twinsun. The game combines exploration of an isometric 3D world, puzzle-solving, item collecting, and simple action combat into one cohesive whole.

Twinsen can switch between several behavior modes — normal, athletic, aggressive, and discreet — which affects his movement and his options for interacting with the environment and enemies. The colorful, fairy-tale visual style contrasted with a darker story about totalitarian rule, giving the game a distinctive identity. On DOS systems, the game ran on its own engine combining polygonal characters with pre-rendered environmental elements, accompanied by the striking, still-beloved music of Philippe Vachey.

Little Big Adventure is today considered one of the most original European action-adventure games of the nineties, valued for its inventive world, humor, and gameplay. It ranks among the titles that age very well even after all these years thanks to its timeless visual style and thoughtful design, and many players recommend it as an ideal entry point into the genre for newcomers. The game was designed by Frédérick Raynal, who had previously worked on the Alone in the Dark series, and this experience is reflected in the elaborate atmosphere and cinematic storytelling, which in Little Big Adventure combines fairy-tale exaggeration with more serious themes of dictatorship and resistance. The combination of accessible controls, clear puzzles, and unforgettable visual stylization still makes it one of the most welcoming gateways into the world of nineties action-adventure games. The game was also released under the alternative title Relentless: Twinsen's Adventure in the North American market, which shows how publishers in the nineties often adjusted the marketing of European titles for different audiences without touching the essence of the game itself.
pc-dos__little-big-adventure.teaser: An isometric adventure about Twinsen, who switches between a normal and an athletic mode.

pc-dos__little-big-adventure-2-twinsen-s.article:
**Little Big Adventure 2: Twinsen's Odyssey** continues the story of Twinsen, who, after his wedding, must once again spring into action to protect his planet Twinsun from a new threat arriving from space. The game expands the world of the first installment with new islands, underwater areas, and journeys into space, while retaining the proven mix of adventure, action, and platforming elements.

Compared to the first game, the sequel offers a larger and more varied world, more elaborate animations, and an improved system for switching between Twinsen's behavior modes. The puzzles are more interconnected, and the game places greater emphasis on traveling between islands using various means of transport. The graphics on DOS and early Windows systems built on the first game with an improved engine and once again featured the distinctive music of Philippe Vachey, which shaped the fairy-tale, occasionally melancholic atmosphere.

Twinsen's Odyssey is often ranked alongside the first installment as one of the pinnacles of Adeline Software International's work, though some fans consider the first game the somewhat purer experience. Today the game is valued for its relaxed atmosphere, humor, and timeless visual style, thanks to which it belongs among the adventure games that retain their appeal even after many years. The second installment also expanded the travel options to include a submarine and other vehicles, allowing the player to visit settings that the first Little Big Adventure did not offer at all, from underwater caves to distant planets. This variety, combined with a more mature, somewhat more melancholic story, makes Twinsen's Odyssey a natural, worthy sequel to the beloved Adeline Software International brand. The second game also retained the characteristic sense of humor of the first, where more serious plot lines regularly alternate with lighter, almost grotesque situations, which remains one of the main reasons the series is still remembered by the generation of players who grew up with it in the second half of the nineties.
pc-dos__little-big-adventure-2-twinsen-s.teaser: Twinsen returns to action after his wedding; the world expands to include islands, the ocean depths, and space.

pc-dos__might-and-magic-iv-clouds-of-xee.article:
**Might and Magic IV: Clouds of Xeen** is an RPG by the American studio New World Computing that brought the series to the world of Xeen and offered an expansive environment to explore with a party of up to six player-created characters. The goal is to uncover the mystery of strange phenomena threatening the world of Xeen, as the player gradually discovers a connection to a spaceship and technologies hidden beneath the surface of the fantasy world.

The game uses grid-based first-person movement and turn-based combat typical of the series, along with a deep system of classes, spells, and items. A special feature was that Clouds of Xeen could later be linked with its follow-up, Darkside of Xeen, into one shared, even larger adventure. On DOS systems, the game offered colorful, if technically undemanding, graphics, but the depth of its systems and the scope of its world were among the most ambitious in the genre.

Clouds of Xeen is still valued by old-school RPG fans for its generosity, amount of content, and inventive sci-fi and fantasy twist at the end of the story. For new players, entry is hampered by the dated interface and the need for manual mapping, yet it remains one of the high points of the Might and Magic series and an example of how well the linking of two separate games into one large whole could work. The series was created by Jon Van Caneghem, whose studio New World Computing was at the time among the most prolific creators of classic PC RPGs, while simultaneously building the strategy series Heroes of Might and Magic. Clouds of Xeen thus stands at the crossroads between the earlier games in the series, with their firmer, more linear story, and the later titles, which increasingly leaned toward open exploration of a vast world. Linking Clouds of Xeen with Darkside of Xeen into a single, unified World of Xeen was an unusual publishing move at the time, turning two separately sold games into one of the most extensive adventures that PC RPGs offered at the time, and it is still cited today as an example of thoughtful expansion of a game brand.
pc-dos__might-and-magic-iv-clouds-of-xee.teaser: An RPG with a party of up to six characters and a mystery linking a fantasy world to a spaceship.

pc-dos__ultima-viii-pagan.article:
**Ultima VIII: Pagan** transports the legendary Avatar to the dark world of Pagan, where he is cast without his usual abilities and must learn to control elemental magic in order to survive and find his way home. Compared to previous installments in the series, the game is more linear and places greater emphasis on platforming jumps and action combat than on open exploration and moral choices, which, given the series' reputation, was a fairly controversial decision.

The game introduced a new magic system based on combining elemental runes and brought a smoother, more action-oriented movement of the character, including jumping between platforms, bringing it closer to an action-adventure game. Technically, it was an ambitious title with elaborate isometric graphics and the dark, oppressive atmosphere of the inhospitable world of Pagan, but the game was plagued at release by technical problems and a feeling of incompleteness, partially remedied by a later expansion.

Ultima VIII remains one of the most debated installments in the series — fans of the RPG canon often criticize it for departing from the freedom and moral depth that made the series famous, while other players appreciate its dark atmosphere and faster pace. Even with the passage of time, it remains an interesting, if contradictory, experiment that shows how Origin Systems was searching for new directions for its flagship brand. The game was designed by a team led by Richard Garriott, the creator of the entire Ultima series, which only underscores how fundamental a departure from the series' established values Pagan represented — the guide of virtues disappeared, the ability to freely leave locations was simplified, and emphasis on moral dilemmas gave way to more linear storytelling. It is precisely this contrast that makes Ultima VIII a favorite topic of discussion among fans of the series to this day, whether they consider it a bold experiment or a departure from what made Ultima exceptional. The subsequent expansion Pagan: The Lost Vale attempted to restore some of the missing content and correct the impression of a rushed release, but it never fully succeeded, and Ultima VIII thus remains regarded to this day as the most controversial chapter of an otherwise highly respected series.
pc-dos__ultima-viii-pagan.teaser: The Avatar, stripped of his usual abilities, learns elemental magic; more linear than the series was known for.

pc-9x__unreal.article:
**Unreal** burst onto the first-person shooter scene in 1998 and immediately showed that technology could be just as important as level design. The custom Unreal Engine delivered a colorful, organic environment on the alien planet Na Pali, full of dense forests, caves, waterfalls, and ancient temples — a complete contrast to the dark, metallic bases and space stations then dominant in the genre. Playing as a prisoner who is the sole survivor of a crashed transport ship, the player gradually transforms into someone capable of standing up to the brutal Skaarj race and helping the oppressed native Nali people.

The gameplay was built on exploration, atmosphere, and a surprisingly varied arsenal of weapons, the most striking of which was the ASMD Shock Rifle with its devastating combo of primary and secondary fire. The level design often rewarded patience and attentiveness rather than just quick reflexes, which noticeably set the game apart from more dynamic competitors like Quake. On Windows 9x computers, Unreal was also notoriously demanding on hardware — truly smooth performance at high detail settings required a powerful graphics card and a fast processor, so for many players it became associated with the memory of a necessary system upgrade. The game also featured a multiplayer mode, which was later expanded into the standalone Unreal Tournament.

Contemporary reviews praised especially the visuals, music, and dense atmosphere of the alien planet, though enemy AI and the game's uneven pacing were occasionally criticized. The graphics engine subsequently became the foundation for a number of other games and cemented Epic and Digital Extremes as key names in the game industry for decades to come. Today, Unreal stands as an important milestone — a title that showed a shooter could also be a visually stunning and almost contemplative experience of discovering an alien world, not just combat in narrow corridors.
pc-9x__unreal.teaser: A graphics revolution of 1998; instead of metal bases, the colorful jungle of the planet Na Pali.

pc-9x__quake.article:
**Quake**, released in 1996, completed the revolution that Doom had started a few years earlier, bringing the action shooter into fully three-dimensional space. Instead of a flat map with height tricks, id Software offered real staircases, bridges, towers, and chasms through which the player moved in a dark, gothic world full of stone castles, lava caves, and technological bases. The story was minimalist — a soldier fighting his way through portals between dimensions against a mysterious entity called Quake — but the action itself and its pacing played the leading role.

The gameplay was built on brutal speed, precise aiming, and techniques such as bunny hopping and rocket jumping, which players mastered largely thanks to the huge multiplayer community. Online deathmatch, played over a modem or a local network, became one of the pillars of the emerging esports culture of the nineties. On Windows 9x machines, the game excelled thanks to support for accelerated 3D rendering through interfaces such as Glide, which on 3dfx Voodoo cards made it a visually stunning experience with smooth lighting and textures. The game also earned cult status thanks to the dark, industrial music of Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails, which defined the game's atmosphere just as strongly as its visuals.

Contemporary reception was enthusiastic, and Quake quickly became the reference title for the entire genre, with its engine serving as the foundation for dozens of other games and mods, including the legendary Team Fortress. The level design drew on gothic and Lovecraftian aesthetics, with heavy emphasis on dynamic lighting and shadows that seemed almost revolutionary at the time and defined the visual language of many later titles. Today the game functions as a historical milestone — raw, fast, and surprisingly playable even decades later, thanks in large part to an active community that keeps it alive through enhanced source ports and new maps.
pc-9x__quake.teaser: Doom got a third dimension; a dark gothic world of climbing, jumping, and falling into chasms.

pc-9x__serious-sam-first-encounter.article:
**Serious Sam: The First Encounter**, released in 2001, arrived with a simple but tremendously effective recipe — put the player up against hundreds of enemies at once and let them run and shoot their way across sprawling Egyptian deserts and ancient temples. The Croatian studio Croteam deliberately returned to the pure, straightforward action of early-nineties shooters, but went incredibly far for its time in terms of visuals and the scale of its battles. The protagonist, Sam "Serious" Stone, fights his way through a world inspired by Egyptian mythology to stop an alien invasion led by the tyrant Mental.

At the core of the gameplay were massive arenas where dozens to hundreds of enemies of various types would pour toward the player at once, from exploding clowns on unicycles to giant skeletons with cannons for arms. The level design deliberately favored open spaces over narrow corridors, allowing for circular movement, dodging, and tactical use of terrain. On Windows 9x computers, the custom Serious Engine offered surprisingly good scalability, so the game ran even on weaker systems, while also excelling at the number of simultaneously rendered characters, which was a technical rarity at the time.

The game was enthusiastically received, particularly for its humor, self-irony, and uncompromising intensity, which stood in contrast to the dark and realistic shooters fashionable at the time. The accompanying music and sound design further amplified the sense of an approaching apocalypse whenever the screen filled with an endless stream of enemies pouring in from all sides. Serious Sam helped revive interest in the "arena shooter" genre and inspired a number of later titles built around hordes of enemies. Even today, The First Encounter remains a popular choice for quick, uncomplicated fun and a reminder of just how entertaining a shooter can be without unnecessary padding, story detours, or cover-based combat.
pc-9x__serious-sam-first-encounter.teaser: Hundreds of enemies at once across vast Egyptian deserts; pure nineties-style action.

pc-9x__sacrifice.article:
**Sacrifice**, released in 2000 by Shiny Entertainment, is one of the most distinctive attempts to combine real-time strategy with action-based third-person controls. The player takes on the role of a young sorcerer learning to cast spells under the guidance of one of five eccentric gods, and must choose whom to devote their loyalty to — each deity offers different units, spells, and combat philosophy, from necromancy to elemental magic. Instead of classic base-building, the game relies on sacrificing your own units and converting enemy blood into mana, giving battles an unusually ritualistic feel.

The gameplay was more direct than that of contemporary strategy games like Command & Conquer — the player directly controlled their sorcerer, cast spells with the mouse, and only supplementarily commanded smaller groups of units, so battles unfolded at a much faster and more personal pace. The campaign, with five separate storylines depending on the chosen god, offered strong replayability and black humor woven throughout the script from beginning to end. On Windows 9x, the game stood out with colorful, stylized graphics and smooth action even on mid-range systems, meaning it did not feel as hardware-demanding as competing titles.

Contemporary reviews praised the originality of the concept, the humor, and the voice acting, although the multiplayer community remained smaller than the game deserved. The visual style of each god, from the bony necromancer to the fiery-colored god of war, gave each campaign its own identity, and players often grew so fond of a particular faction that they returned to it repeatedly. Sacrifice became a cult favorite rather than a mass hit, and it is still cited today as an example of a bold genre mashup that never quite caught on in the mainstream. Today it appeals mainly through its atmosphere, humor, and unusual combination of strategy with third-person action, a combination almost no one has really attempted to repeat since.
pc-9x__sacrifice.teaser: An unusual mix of RTS and third-person action; the player serves one of five gods.

pc-9x__giants-citizen-kabuto.article:
**Giants: Citizen Kabuto** from 2000 is one of the strangest and most original games of its time – an action adventure combined with strategy elements, in which the player gradually becomes all three warring factions of the story. First you play as the surfing adventurer Reznor, then as female warriors of the Meccaryn tribe controlled from a bird's-eye view similar to an RTS, and finally as a giant alien creature named Kabuto, who devours everything in his path and literally grows with every bite. This alternating view of the same conflict from different angles was utterly unique at the time of release, and players gradually pieced together the mosaic of the same island from three completely different perspectives.

Each of the three campaigns offered a different play style and pace – action shootouts, tactical unit command, and destructive environmental devastation by a giant monster – and the game managed to switch smoothly between them without losing cohesion. The graphics engine was very demanding for Windows 9x computers of its time, but it offered a colorful, tropical island setting and convincing animations, especially for the giant Kabuto. The game's humor was strikingly black and self-deprecating, with sharp dialogue and parody of gaming clichés.

Critics praised Planet Moon Studios' courage in experimenting with three genres in one game and the technical side of the title, though some players complained about uneven difficulty between the campaigns. The music and voice acting gave the whole story a cinematic feel that contrasted with the often grotesque and exaggerated action on screen. Giants: Citizen Kabuto never became a commercial smash, but it earned a reputation as a cult classic that fans remember as one of the most original games of the turn of the millennium. Even with the passage of years, its inventiveness and genre-bending daring feel surprisingly fresh.
pc-9x__giants-citizen-kabuto.teaser: Three distinct play styles in one game – a surfer, an RTS warrior woman, and the giant monster Kabuto.

pc-9x__messiah.article:
**Messiah** from 2000 by Shiny Entertainment is an action adventure built on an unusual concept of possession – the player controls a little angel named Bob, who can float above the levels and fly into characters' bodies, subsequently taking full control of them. Each possessed character has its own abilities, weapons, and social status, from ordinary guards to prostitutes and soldiers, which pushed the game into a dark, satirical narrative about a corrupt future city full of religious motifs and social decay.

The gameplay was built on puzzles solved precisely through taking over different bodies – the player had to figure out which character needed to be controlled to progress, open a door, or convince a guard. The graphics engine, which later also served Sacrifice, brought striking, fully 3D stylized graphics with smooth character animation to Windows 9x computers, although the game's development was unusually long and was accompanied by technical and production troubles that partly showed in the final result. The atmosphere was dark and grotesque at the same time, with black humor and social satire hidden beneath a layer of violence and vulgarity, which placed the game among the most controversial action adventures of its time.

Contemporary reviews were mixed – they praised the originality of the concept and the technical side, but criticized the uneven pacing and controversial content, which in some countries led to censorship interventions and edits of localized versions. Messiah never became a mass hit, but remains an interesting example of a bold design experiment from the turn of the millennium, when developers dared to take more risks than today's big-budget productions. Today it is interesting mainly as a curiosity and proof of how boldly the action adventure of that era could approach character-control mechanics.
pc-9x__messiah.teaser: The little angel Bob possesses characters' bodies and takes over their abilities in a dark satirical adventure.

pc-9x__divine-divinity.article:
**Divine Divinity** from 2002 by the Belgian studio Larian Studios is an action RPG that earned a reputation as one of the last great isometric adventures of its era. The player travels through the vast fantasy world of Rivellon as a chosen hero whose fate is linked to a fight against a dark force named Damian, and gradually discovers that their own identity is far more mysterious and complicated than it first seemed. The choice between three classes – warrior, mage, and hunter – influenced the play style and approach to combat and puzzles, while the game never tied the player down too much with rules, allowing experimentation with skill combinations.

The game combined fast, action-oriented click-to-fight combat with a surprisingly deep system of side quests, dialogue, and exploration, which set it apart from simpler action RPGs like Diablo. The world was densely packed with detail, witty text notes, and references that rewarded players for thoroughly exploring every corner, and almost every character could be approached to get at least a small piece of information or a quest. On Windows 9x and early XP computers, the game ran on an isometric 2D/3D engine that could handle even weaker rigs, offering colorful, fairy-tale-inspired settings from rural villages to dark dungeons.

Contemporary reviews praised the game for its scope, humor, and honest craftsmanship, which made it a surprise hit and helped launch the career of Larian Studios, which many years later created Divinity: Original Sin and Baldur's Gate 3. The music and the written humor in item and book descriptions gave the world of Rivellon a distinctive, slightly ironic tone that Larian's series became famous for in later installments too. Divine Divinity is still considered one of the best action RPGs of the turn of the millennium and is regarded by genre fans as required classic that is worth revisiting even after all these years.
pc-9x__divine-divinity.teaser: One of the last great isometric RPGs of its era; the vast fantasy world of Rivellon.

pc-9x__syberia.article:
**Syberia** from 2002 is a point-and-click adventure carrying the visual and narrative vision of Belgian illustrator and writer Benoît Sokal, whose atmosphere of melancholy and forgotten mechanical wonders made it one of the most cited adventure games of the new decade. The player steps into the role of American lawyer Kate Walker, who arrives in a remote French village to negotiate the sale of a mechanical automaton factory and gradually gets drawn into a journey across Eastern Europe all the way to Siberia, following the trail of the eccentric inventor Hans Voralberg, whose vanished trace forces her to reconsider her own life and priorities.

The gameplay was classic for the genre – solving item and logic puzzles, exploring the environment, and dialogue with vivid characters – but the game was set apart by an unusually strong visual style and sense of detail. Hand-painted backgrounds, mechanical automatons, and a train pulled by a mammoth created a unique, dreamlike world on the border of steampunk and old-world fairy tale. On Windows 9x and early XP setups, the game ran smoothly thanks to pre-rendered backgrounds combined with 3D characters, which allowed it to look visually rich even on ordinary hardware of the time.

Syberia received enthusiastic reviews especially for its atmosphere, music, and story about a journey for a lost childhood dream, and became one of the commercially most successful adventure titles of its generation at a time when the genre was generally fading into the background. The melancholic score, full of strings and gentle melodies, heightened the sense of a journey to the end of the world and became an inseparable part of the memory of the game for many players. The game helped prove that the classic adventure still had something to offer if it bet on a strong authorial signature. Today Syberia is considered one of the most beautiful and poetic adventure games ever released, and its charm has not aged.
pc-9x__syberia.teaser: Benoît Sokal's melancholic adventure game about forgotten mechanical wonders.

pc-9x__outcast.article:
**Outcast** from 1999 by the Belgian studio Appeal is among the most ambitious action adventures of its generation, even though it didn't fare too well commercially. The player takes on the role of former soldier Cutter Slade, who is sent to the parallel world of Adelpha to rescue scientists stranded after a failed experiment, and gradually becomes entangled in a conflict between the local Talan tribes and an occupying alien technology whose military dominance oppresses the native population. The world of Adelpha was remarkably alive – with its own language, religion, and social structure for the natives, who reacted to the player according to their actions.

The game was pioneering for its use of a voxel engine for vast, open outdoor environments combined with polygonal characters, which at the time of release allowed distant views and a sense of a truly open world unheard of on Windows 9x computers. The gameplay blended action shootouts, platforming sections, and conversations with NPCs who gave quests and provided information about the world, thereby foreshadowing later open-world adventures. Orchestral music recorded by the Moscow Symphony Orchestra gave the game an unusually grand, cinematic atmosphere.

Contemporary reviews praised the technical innovation, the scope of the world, and the music, but high hardware requirements and lacking marketing support meant the game didn't succeed commercially as much as it deserved. The dialogue with the native Talans, written with an emphasis on their own culture and manner of expression, was among the most elaborate that action adventures of the time had to offer. In the following years Outcast built a strong cult following and is remembered today as a forerunner of many ideas that later made other open-world titles famous. Its later remake only confirmed that the original had an extraordinarily forward-looking vision.
pc-9x__outcast.teaser: An ambitious action-adventure set in the parallel world of Adelpha; a commercial flop, now a cult classic.

pc-9x__brany-skeldalu.article:
**Gates of Skeldal** from 1998 is one of the most significant Czech games of the nineties and still enjoys the reputation of a cult classic of domestic creation. Studio Napoleon Games created a step-based dungeon crawler in a fantasy world where the player assembles a party of adventurers and makes their way through winding underground corridors, castles, and caves full of traps, puzzles, and monsters, with progress through the map requiring patience and careful mapping of branching corridors. The game drew on the tradition of Western RPGs like Might and Magic, but carried its own distinctly Czech atmosphere, sense of detail, and specific storytelling style, which still evokes strong nostalgia among players of the time.

The gameplay was built on turn-based combat, party management, and gradual character development, while also placing considerable emphasis on solving puzzles and discovering hidden parts of the map. The text descriptions and dialogue were written with care and humor, which set the game apart from many foreign competitors who couldn't take local context into account. On Windows 9x computers the game ran even on more modest hardware, which made it accessible to a wide range of Czech players of the time, for whom it was often their first serious RPG experience on a home computer.

Contemporary responses were warm, the game gained a loyal fanbase, and became one of the pillars of the nascent Czech gaming industry alongside titles like Fish Fillets. The vocabulary, character names, and small jokes referencing Czech reality gave the game an unmistakable domestic identity that foreign RPGs of the time logically lacked. Its influence persists to this day – the game received sequels as well as modern remastered versions that allowed it to reach new generations of players too. Gates of Skeldal remains a reminder of a time when Czech developers proved they could compete with the world's best even with limited resources.
pc-9x__brany-skeldalu.teaser: A cult Czech dungeon crawler; step-by-step movement through winding corridors full of traps and monsters.

pc-9x__brany-skeldalu-2.article:
**Gates of Skeldal 2: The Fifth Apprentice** from 2002 followed up on the success of the first installment, but chose a different path – instead of a step-based dungeon crawler, it delivered a point-and-click adventure enriched with turn-based combat. The player takes on the role of a student at a magic university in Engeor, who becomes a victim of dictator Wahargem's totalitarian regime, and gradually turns from a persecuted refugee into one of the key figures in the resistance against tyranny, having to choose between cautious tactics and open rebellion. Napoleon Games thus combined adventure storytelling with elements that fans knew from the previous game, offering more of a spiritual successor in a different guise than a direct sequel.

The gameplay combined classic adventure-style puzzle solving, item collecting, and conversations with NPCs with tactical combat, in which the player directed the movement and actions of characters on a turn-based basis. The story was darker and more politically engaged than in the first installment, with themes of oppression, resignation, and rebellion, giving the game an unusually serious tone for a fantasy setting. The graphics moved the series visually forward, while on Windows 9x and early XP computers the game ran smoothly even on ordinary hardware of the time, making it accessible to as wide a range of players as the first installment.

Contemporary reviews praised the story and atmosphere, though the genre shift from the first installment divided part of the fanbase, who had expected a continuation in the form of a dungeon crawler. The characters and their fates were drawn with an eye for detail, and players especially remembered the supporting characters of the resistance, whose motivations were not black and white. Nevertheless, the game took its place among the respected titles of the Czech gaming industry and expanded the world of Skeldal with another chapter of its history. Today it is seen as a bold, though not unreservedly accepted, experiment with a genre shift within a beloved domestic brand.
pc-9x__brany-skeldalu-2.teaser: The sequel took a different path – an adventure game with turn-based combat instead of step-by-step corridor crawling.

pc-9x__fish-fillets.article:
**Fish Fillets** from 1998 is a puzzle game from the Czech studio ALTAR Interactive that, despite its simple premise, became one of the most beloved domestic games ever. The player controls a pair of fish agents of a secret underwater organization who move through dozens of rooms full of objects that need to be moved, tilted, and stacked so that both fish can find their way out without either of them being crushed, stuck, or drowned. Beneath the seemingly naive visuals lay a surprisingly demanding physics-based puzzle construction that forced the player to think through every step and anticipate the chain reaction of their own actions.

The gameplay required alternating control of both fish and forward planning, since every movement of one object could affect the whole room as well as the fate of the other character. Humor and distinctive voice acting gave the game an unmistakable atmosphere, which won it fans across generations, including children, for whom it was often their first serious logic game on a computer. On Windows 9x computers the game ran without problems even on modest hardware, which, together with its low requirements, helped it achieve extraordinarily wide distribution in Czech households and schools.

Both contemporary and later reviews praised the game for the ingenuity of its puzzles, its humor, and timeless graphics, and Fish Fillets became one of the foundational titles of the modern Czech gaming scene. Thanks to the game's success, studio ALTAR was able to move on to more ambitious projects, but the pair of fish agents remained its best-known and most cited work both at home and abroad. Its success led to a sequel, Fish Fillets 2, and a modern remake, Fish Fillets NG, which made the game accessible to new platforms and generations. To this day the game is a symbol that clever game design and distinctive humor can overcome the limits of a studio's size or budget.
pc-9x__fish-fillets.teaser: A beloved Czech puzzle game; two fish work together to solve puzzles by moving objects around.

pc-9x__half-life.article:
**Half-Life** from 1998 by Valve fundamentally transformed the first-person shooter genre by never breaking the narrative with a cutscene or forcing the player to leave the protagonist's body. Physicist Gordon Freeman finds himself in the middle of a catastrophe at the underground research complex Black Mesa after an experiment with an unknown sample tears open a rift to another dimension, and he must fight his way out through alien creatures as well as soldiers sent to cover up the incident at any cost, including eliminating witnesses. The entire story unfolds seamlessly, from Gordon's own eyes, without a single loss of control.

The gameplay blended firefights with environmental puzzles, platforming sections, and scripted sequences that at the time felt completely natural and unforced, unlike many later games that used similar tricks far more clumsily. The enemy AI, especially that of the special-forces soldiers, was among the most advanced of its era and forced players to think tactically instead of simply charging in head-on. On Windows 9x machines the game ran on a modified GoldSrc engine derived from Quake, which delivered solid performance even on mid-range setups, and it also became the foundation for the phenomenal Counter-Strike modification.

Half-Life earned near-unanimous acclaim from critics and players alike and is still ranked among the most influential computer games of all time. The atmosphere was further amplified by dense, industrial music and sound design that could build tension even in moments when seemingly nothing was happening on screen. Its emphasis on uninterrupted storytelling influenced countless later titles and became a standard the shooter genre has kept returning to ever since. Even decades later, the game offers a surprisingly cohesive and gripping experience that has not aged the way one might expect from a title nearly thirty years old.
pc-9x__half-life.teaser: No cutscenes and no character switches; Gordon Freeman in one uninterrupted take.

pc-9x__starcraft.article:
**StarCraft** from 1998 by Blizzard Entertainment ranks among the most influential real-time strategy games ever made, largely thanks to its unprecedentedly balanced clash of three utterly distinct races. The human Terran Dominion, the insectoid Zerg, and the technologically advanced Protoss offered such different playstyles, tactics, and aesthetics that the game still serves as a textbook example of asymmetric yet fair game design. The campaign led players through a sprawling galactic conflict full of twists, betrayals, and unforgettable characters, told through well-acted video sequences.

The gameplay was built around base building, resource management, and unit command, with each race demanding a completely different approach to micromanagement and strategic planning. On Windows 9x machines the game ran smoothly even on modest hardware, which allowed it exceptionally wide adoption, and online play through Battle.net turned it into one of the first mass online multiplayer phenomena. In South Korea in particular, StarCraft became nothing short of a national sport and laid the foundations of modern esports with professional leagues and televised matches.

Contemporary reviews were nearly unanimous in their enthusiasm, and the game won numerous awards for design and balance, helped further by the successful Brood War expansion that broadened both story and content. Strong voice acting, cinematic video sequences, and a polished script pushed strategy game storytelling to a new level and showed that even the RTS genre could deliver an emotional and unforgettable story. StarCraft influenced an entire generation of strategy games, and its multiplayer scene stayed active for decades after release. Today it is regarded as one of the most important titles in the genre's history, and its influence is visible in every modern real-time strategy game.
pc-9x__starcraft.teaser: Three distinct races, perfectly balanced; a textbook example of asymmetric game design.

pc-9x__tajemstvi-osliho-ostrova.article:
**The Secret of Donkey Island** (Tajemství Oslího ostrova) is one of the best-known Czech adventure games of the nineties, and both its structure and humor place it firmly in the tradition of classic graphic adventures like Monkey Island. The player takes on the role of a hero who sets out for an island inhabited by strange characters in order to solve the mystery behind its name, solving a series of inventory puzzles, character conversations, and logical item combinations along the way. The genre's typical point-and-click controls were a common standard at the time of release, and the game handles them reliably, albeit with a certain stiffness typical of domestic productions of the era.

The visuals rely on hand-drawn backgrounds and simply animated characters, giving the game a distinctive, slightly naive look that nonetheless fits its overall comedic tone. The humor draws on a typically Czech range of jokes, wordplay, and parodic references to contemporary pop culture and local realities, which earned the game a strong fan base, especially among players who grew up on domestic productions of the nineties. The music and sound are modest but functional, and they nicely complement the atmosphere of the island adventure.

At the time of release the game stood out for offering an adventure that spoke the players' native language and referenced humor close to home, a striking difference in an era dominated by foreign titles. To this day, The Secret of Donkey Island is regarded as one of the icons of Czech game development in the nineties and a reminder of a time when domestic studios were still finding their own voice against major foreign publishers. For today's player the game holds mainly nostalgic value and offers an interesting glimpse into the early days of Czech game design, still the subject of nostalgic debates on fan forums. Many players return to it because its characters and their lines have become part of a generation's shared memory, with references to them still appearing in other domestic productions that pay tribute through quotes and homages.
pc-9x__tajemstvi-osliho-ostrova.teaser: A Czech adventure game in the spirit of Monkey Island; humor and inventory puzzles on Donkey Island.

pc-9x__draci-historie.article:
**Dračí Historie** (Dragon History) is a Czech fantasy game for DOS and Windows 9x that draws on the domestic tradition of the tabletop game Dračí doupě (Dragon's Lair) and transposes its world into an isometric computer adventure. The player traverses a sprawling game map, completes quests, fights monsters, and develops a character through battles with classic fantasy enemies, while the game combines action elements with simple RPG mechanics such as collecting items, upgrading equipment, and progressing through the story across several chapters. The combat and map-movement systems are simplified enough to be accessible even to players who were only just discovering fantasy RPGs through the tabletop original.

The technical execution matches that of a smaller domestic production from the late nineties — the graphics are simpler than those of foreign competitors in the same genre, but the game tries to compensate with its emphasis on a fantasy setting that was, thanks to Dračí doupě, extraordinarily popular in the Czech Republic. The game's atmosphere draws precisely on this domestic familiarity and fondness for the fantasy universe, which allowed it to reach an audience that might otherwise never have found its way to foreign RPGs, and the music aims to evoke a gloomy, adventurous mood.

At the time of its release Dračí Historie was not among the technically most ambitious titles, but thanks to its ties to a popular domestic brand it found its place in the memory of players who grew up on the books and tabletop game Dračí doupě. Today it is viewed more as a curiosity and evidence of how domestic studios tried to translate successful literary and gaming brands into digital form, rather than as a technically timeless title. For fans of Czech gaming history it nonetheless remains an interesting artifact documenting the diversity of domestic production at the time and the effort to connect computer games with the tradition of domestic fantasy literature and tabletop gaming, which formed an important part of Czech pop culture in the nineties.
pc-9x__draci-historie.teaser: A Czech fantasy RPG drawing on Dračí doupě (the Czech Dungeons & Dragons); an isometric action adventure.

pc-9x__polda.article:
**Polda** (Cop) is a Czech comedic adventure in which the player becomes a clumsy police officer solving a criminal case full of absurd situations and typically Czech humor, with the investigation leading him through a series of bizarre settings and encounters with eccentric characters. Built on the classic point-and-click principle, the game offers item combining, conversations with a colorful gallery of characters, and a series of funny, often parodic scenes poking fun at police work and the social realities of the time. The gameplay is straightforward and focuses mainly on wit and atmosphere rather than complex logical puzzles, so the game flows briskly and lets the dialogue and situational comedy of individual scenes shine.

The visuals match those of a smaller domestic production from the late nineties — hand-drawn environments and simply animated characters create a distinctive, cartoonish look that fits the game's overall humorous tone and gives each location a recognizable visual identity. Voice acting and sound play a key role in Polda, since much of the comedy rests precisely on the characters' vocal delivery and their catchphrases, many of which entered everyday speech among players of the time and still appear as quotes on fan forums and in the common speech of the generation that played it as children or teenagers.

At the time of its release Polda became one of the most popular domestic titles precisely because of its distinctive humor, easily understood by a Czech audience, which also earned it several sequels. The game is still remembered today as one of the icons of Czech game development in the nineties and an example that success need not rest on technical sophistication but rather on well-aimed humor and a solid understanding of the domestic audience. For many who remember it, Polda remains synonymous with the golden age of Czech adventure games, and it still appears in overviews of the most significant domestic titles of the nineties alongside other comedic classics of the era.
pc-9x__polda.teaser: A clumsy policeman and absurd cases full of typically Czech humor; a classic adventure game.

pc-9x__polda-2.article:
**Polda 2** continues the successful first installment and once again builds on the combination of a classic point-and-click adventure with a strongly comedic tone, this time with an expanded story and a greater number of locations for the player to explore while uncovering a new criminal case. The clumsy police officer once again finds himself entangled in strange cases and grotesque characters, while the gameplay stays faithful to the proven formula — the player combines items, holds conversations, and moves through a plot full of parodic references to the era's reality and social conditions, with several scenes deliberately parodying clichés from other popular adventure games and films.

Compared to the first installment, the sequel offers somewhat more polished graphics and more content, while retaining the same distinctive humor and voice acting that had been a key draw for fans of the first Polda and had contributed decisively to the overall impression of the game. The environments and characters are once again rendered in a cartoonish style that underlines the absurdity of the situations the protagonist repeatedly finds himself in through no fault of his own, and the music and sound design nicely complement the overall lighthearted atmosphere of the whole game, while individual locations offer a greater number of side interactions and jokes to discover.

Polda 2 confirmed that the first installment's success was no fluke and cemented the series' position as one of the most popular domestic gaming brands of the turn of the millennium. For players at the time it was a welcome continuation of beloved humor in a somewhat more varied guise; today it is seen as a natural part of the golden age of Czech adventure game creation alongside the first installment. Together with the other entries in the series it helped define what a successful domestic comedic adventure for a broad audience could look like, and it cemented the series' reputation as a reliable brand that players looked forward to with every new sequel.
pc-9x__polda-2.teaser: A continuation of the proven formula – more locations, more jokes, the same clumsy Czech detective.

pc-9x__horke-leto.article:
**Horké léto** (Hot Summer) is a Czech adventure game from the second half of the nineties that combines a detective plot with a lighter summer atmosphere, contrasting with the seriousness of the mystery the player must gradually unravel. Playing the main character, the player moves between several locations, interrogates characters, gathers clues, and solves classic adventure puzzles based on combining items and reasoning logically about the connections between individual leads, while the story gradually reveals the background of the mysterious event that gives the game its name, and the player must piece together fragmentary information from various characters to arrive at the case's resolution.

The game's presentation matches that of a smaller domestic production of the time — static, hand-drawn backgrounds and simpler character animations create an atmosphere that relies more on text and dialogue than on technical spectacle, so the player must rely mainly on careful reading and listening to the characters. The emphasis on domestic settings and local realities gives the game a distinctive flavor, one that made it easy for players to connect it with their own experience of summer holidays and vacations at home, in contrast to the exotic backdrops of foreign adventure games, whose settings were more distant and less intimately familiar to the domestic player.

Horké léto was not among the most commercially successful or most discussed titles of its time, but thanks to its distinctive, locally flavored storytelling it found a place among players seeking adventures with a domestic touch. Today the game is remembered mainly by fans of Czech gaming history as evidence of the diversity of domestic adventure game creation in the nineties, when alongside the big comedic hits there also emerged more intimate, more seriously toned stories with a detective undertone that focused more on atmosphere and local color than on grand plots.
pc-9x__horke-leto.teaser: A Czech detective adventure whose relaxed summer atmosphere contrasts with the seriousness of the mystery.

pc-9x__7-dni-7-noci.article:
**7 dní a 7 nocí** (7 Days and 7 Nights) is an adventure game from the late nineties whose title refers to a time-bound story unfolding over the course of a single week, during which the main character tries to uncover the true nature of a mysterious event that has turned her life upside down. The player moves through a series of locations, talks to characters, and solves tasks that gradually reveal the background of the central plot through a layered puzzle of partial information, while the game's structure, divided into individual days, gives the narrative a firm rhythm and a sense of passing time — a fairly unusual element in domestic adventure games of the era — lending the game a sense of urgency, as if the player had to solve the mystery before the allotted time ran out.

Technically speaking, it is a typical representative of smaller Central European productions of its time — the game relies on hand-drawn scenes, simple animations, and an emphasis on text and atmosphere rather than graphical spectacle, placing it alongside other more intimate regional adventure games. The story and dialogue carry the main weight of the experience, while the puzzles stick to the classic adventure framework of combining items and talking to characters scattered across the individual days, whose order follows the passing of the week in which the story is set.

In its time the game appealed to players seeking a more seriously toned alternative to the comedic titles that dominated at the time by offering a more earnest narrative with a clearly defined time structure. Today, 7 dní a 7 nocí is a rather peripheral yet still interesting memory for veterans of the domestic adventure scene, but it remains an interesting piece of evidence of how varied the approaches to storytelling could be in the production of the time, alongside the prevailing comedic genre of the era, and a reminder that the domestic scene was not limited only to parodies and humorous titles.
pc-9x__7-dni-7-noci.teaser: An adventure game set within a precisely defined week, during which the hero uncovers a hidden truth.

pc-9x__asmodeus-ukradeny-trun.article:
**Asmodeus: Ukradený trůn** is a Czech fantasy game combining elements of action RPG with a story about a usurped throne and the fight against the dark forces behind the seizure of power, with the main hero gradually becoming a key figure in the struggle to restore rightful rule. The player moves through a series of levels full of enemies, collects gear, and gradually develops the character's abilities and equipment, with the combat system and game progression following the then-popular top-down action RPG formula, similar to foreign titles of the same era, and the player gradually discovers stronger weapons and spells needed to progress into the deeper parts of the story.

The graphics match the capabilities of smaller domestic productions of the mid-1990s – the game environments are built from simpler sprites and textures, but the game tries to create a dark fantasy atmosphere fitting the story of a stolen throne and the malevolent forces threatening the entire kingdom. The music and sound effects complement the game's gloomier mood well and underscore the sense of an endangered fantasy world that the player must save with their own hands, while the gradual unveiling of the plot behind the usurped throne adds a narrative dimension to otherwise straightforward gameplay.

Within the domestic production of the time, Asmodeus was among the more technically and content-wise ambitious attempts at a homegrown fantasy RPG, and was seen as one of the proofs that even smaller Czech studios could try their hand at a genre then clearly dominated by major foreign titles. Today the game is viewed mainly as a historical curiosity and evidence of the early ambitions of domestic game development in the fantasy RPG field, even though it could not fully compete technically with foreign competitors that had far larger budgets and more experience with the action RPG genre.
pc-9x__asmodeus-ukradeny-trun.teaser: A Czech fantasy action RPG about fighting a throne usurper and the dark forces behind him.

pc-9x__legenda-o-zlatem-nezdaru.article:
**Legenda o Zlatém Nezdaru** is a Czech comedic adventure with fantasy themes, whose very title – a parody of classic legends about a golden treasure – hints at the ironic, self-deprecating tone that runs through the whole game, from the opening scene to the story's very resolution. Playing an unsuccessful hero, the player sets out on a quest full of grotesque situations, solves classic adventure puzzles based on combining items and conversations with odd characters along the way, and gradually uncovers a parodic version of the traditional fantasy treasure-hunt story, with many situations built around the hero's plans repeatedly failing to go exactly as expected.

The game's production matches the era's standard for smaller domestic productions – hand-drawn environments, simpler animations, and a strong emphasis on text and dialogue, through which the game achieves the vast majority of its comic effect. The humor relies on consistently mocking classic fantasy clichés and on typically Czech wordplay and exaggeration, placing the game alongside other domestic comedic adventures of the time, without trying to compete with major foreign productions on a technical level, focusing instead on making sure each individual scene delivers its own well-built comedic punchline.

Legenda o Zlatém Nezdaru was not among the most commercially widespread and well-known titles of its era, but thanks to its consistently parodic approach to the fantasy genre it found a place among players who appreciated self-deprecating humor similar to other domestic comedy games of the time. Today the game is remembered only marginally, as part of the broader wave of Czech comedic adventures of the late 1990s that offered an alternative to more seriously toned foreign fantasy titles and gleefully poked fun at genre clichés which they themselves also made abundant, happy use of.
pc-9x__legenda-o-zlatem-nezdaru.teaser: An ironically named Czech comedy adventure game about an unsuccessful hero and his quest.

pc-9x__belegost.article:
**Belegost** is a Czech fantasy game whose name refers to the dwarven city from Norse and Tolkienesque mythology, and the game's overall setting matches that reference – a dark, underground fantasy world where the player gradually uncovers the fate of a once-mighty dwarven civilization. The player moves through winding corridors and vast underground locations, fights monsters, and gradually develops their character, with the game combining action RPG elements with exploration of environments reminiscent of classic underground dungeons full of traps and hidden treasures, which the player must work through step by step to strengthen their character before more demanding battles.

Technically, it is a typical representative of smaller domestic productions of the late 1990s – the graphics are noticeably simpler, but the game tries to compensate with a dense, dark atmosphere of the underground world and an emphasis on exploration and battles of rising difficulty. The sound design and music nicely round out the grim, oppressive mood of the underground environment through which the player must fight their way toward the goal of their quest to save the endangered dwarven kingdom, while the growing strength of enemies on deeper levels forces the player to proceed cautiously and thoughtfully.

At the time of its release, Belegost stayed rather on the margins of players' attention compared to major foreign RPGs of the same era, whose budgets and development team sizes were incomparably larger, but for fans of domestic fantasy creations it represented further evidence of smaller Czech studios' efforts to create their own genre work. Today the game is viewed mainly as a historical curiosity and an interesting testament to the overall diversity of the domestic RPG scene of the time, which tried to draw even from internationally known fantasy mythology and transpose it into its own game production with limited but honestly used resources.
pc-9x__belegost.teaser: A dark underground fantasy RPG named after a dwarven city from Norse mythology.

pc-9x__ve-stinu-havrana.article:
**Ve stínu havrana** is a Czech fantasy game with RPG elements, whose grimly toned title hints at the darker atmosphere of the whole story, set in a fantasy world threatened by a mysterious force tied precisely to the motif of the raven, which becomes both a symbol of impending misfortune and a clue to averting it. Playing the main hero, the player moves through a story full of battles, conversations with characters, and the gradual development of their own character and abilities, with the game trying to offer a complete fantasy world with its own mythology and dark conflict background, gradually revealed to the player through conversations with characters and discovered text records.

The technical execution matches smaller domestic productions of the turn of the millennium – the graphics and animations are more modest than the foreign competition, but the game relies on atmosphere, story, and a musical score that underlines the darker tone of the whole narrative and accompanies the player even in the most tense moments of playing through the game. Emphasis is placed on the gradual, thoughtful revelation of the conflict's background and on building tension rather than on technical spectacle or extensive action sequences, which makes the game feel more intimate than many foreign fantasy RPGs of the same time.

Within the overall context of the offerings of the time, Ve stínu havrana thus remained a more intimate, less widely known title, known mainly among true fans of domestic fantasy creations, but it still represents an interesting and honest example of the ambitions of smaller Czech studios to create their own darkly toned RPG in an era dominated by major foreign productions in this genre. Today the game is remembered as a natural and integral part of the broader mosaic of domestic attempts at fantasy RPGs of the late 1990s and early 2000s, when small domestic studios honestly tried to find their own place alongside dominant foreign brands.
pc-9x__ve-stinu-havrana.teaser: A grim Czech fantasy RPG in which the raven is a symbol both of misfortune and of the path to averting it.

pc-9x__hidden-and-dangerous.article:
**Hidden & Dangerous** is a tactical action game from Illusion Softworks that puts the player in command of a small commando unit operating behind enemy lines during World War II, with individual missions requiring careful planning of both approach and loadout before deployment. The game combines direct control of a single soldier with tactical command of the entire four-member squad, careful route planning, the use of cover, and coordinating attacks from multiple directions, which at the time of release represented an unusually elaborate approach to the military action genre on Windows 9x computers.

Missions take place across large outdoor maps as well as inside buildings and demand thoughtful advancement from the player rather than uncompromising assault, since overwhelming enemy fire can quickly decimate a squad. The atmosphere of the World War II conflict is underscored by realistically depicted weaponry, period-accurate settings, and a musical score, while the graphics engine offered large outdoor spaces that were unusual among tactical action games at the time. Switching between soldiers allowed the player to direct each team member's movements individually, turning each mission into more of a tactical puzzle than a straightforward firefight.

Hidden & Dangerous achieved international success and ranks among the most significant Czech gaming achievements of the 1990s, which put domestic development on the world stage even before the same studio became famous for Mafia. The game influenced further work in the tactical war action genre and is still remembered today as one of the milestones that got people talking about the Czech game industry abroad. Even after all these years it remains playable thanks to its emphasis on tactics, which holds up well even next to newer titles, and many still consider it a harbinger of the later international success achieved by the creators who went on to make the Mafia series.
pc-9x__hidden-and-dangerous.teaser: Commanding a commando squad during World War II; tactics and cover instead of a headlong charge.

pc-9x__original-war.article:
**Original War** is a Czech real-time strategy game from Altar Interactive that brings an unusual narrative framework to the genre: time travel and a fight over a rare resource between American and Soviet factions in the middle of prehistory, where both superpowers sent expeditions with their own conflicting goals. The game combines classic RTS elements – resource gathering, base building, and real-time unit management – with a more elaborate system of individual characters, each with their own name, skills, and experience that develop over the course of the campaign and affect how successfully a unit can carry out assigned tasks.

This emphasis on individual units set Original War apart from most strategy games of the time, because losing an experienced soldier carried real weight and the player was motivated to protect their people instead of throwing them recklessly into battle. The story campaign, told through cutscenes and dialogue, gave the game an unusual degree of narrative ambition for the genre, while the graphics matched their era and handled both prehistoric landscapes and the bases of both rival factions well, with the variety of environments being one of the game's visible strengths.

Original War was praised at the time of release above all for its unconventional combination of a sci-fi story with a prehistoric setting and for its elaborate system of units with their own identity, which earned it a reputation as one of the most interesting domestic strategy games of the turn of the millennium. The game significantly influenced the overall perception of Czech strategy game development and is still cited today as an example of how an established genre can be enriched with an unconventional idea. For players interested in the history of the real-time strategy genre, Original War remains a playable and distinctive experience, set apart from most of the competition precisely by its emphasis on the fate of individual soldiers.
pc-9x__original-war.teaser: A Czech RTS with an unusual framework – time travel and a fight over resources in prehistoric times.

pc-9x__dostihy-sazky.article:
**Dostihy a sázky** is a Czech simulation of horse racing and betting, in which the player becomes both a stable owner and a bettor at once – training horses, taking part in races, and managing their capital through bets on individual races, with the choice of the right horse and the amount wagered determining the further growth of the stable. The game combines simple economic management of the stable with a visualization of the races themselves, in which the player watches how their charges perform against the competition and decides which horses and bets to invest further funds in, with the gradual growth of capital and improvement of the stable forming the main motivation to keep playing.

The game's presentation is fairly austere and matches the capabilities of smaller domestic productions of the late 1990s, with simple graphics of the racetrack and clear text menus for managing the stable and individual bets. But it was precisely this simplicity and clarity that counted among the game's main strengths, thanks to which it was embraced even by players who otherwise did not play computer games much, making it unusually popular across generations of players and non-players alike, who appreciated above all its easy entry point without the need to laboriously learn the controls.

Dostihy a sázky became an unexpected phenomenon in Czechia and ranks among the most widely played domestic titles of the late 1990s, played in many households often even outside the traditional circle of computer game players. Its success clearly showed that a simple, understandable game built on a popular theme can compete even with far more technically advanced titles, and the game went on to receive further sequels. Today it is regarded as a notable and unmistakable phenomenon of Czech gaming culture at the turn of the millennium and recalls a time when simple domestic simulations could compete even with far costlier foreign games.
pc-9x__dostihy-sazky.teaser: A Czech horse racing simulation; the player is both the owner of a stable and a bettor.

pc-modern__arcanum-of-steamworks-and-mag.article:
