**The Witcher** is an action RPG from the Polish studio CD Projekt RED, based on Andrzej Sapkowski's book series about the witcher Geralt of Rivia. Until then the studio had only localized other people's games, and no one expected it to build a sprawling RPG on a modified Aurora engine straight from Neverwinter Nights. In 2007 the result felt unusually mature: Geralt isn't a hero saving the world, but a hired professional moving between warring factions who almost never has a purely good choice available. Decisions also carry delayed consequences — the outcome often only shows up a chapter later, by which point the player barely remembers what exactly they decided.

Combat was built around rhythmic clicking in three styles — fast, strong, and group — which had to be switched depending on the type of opponent, on top of Signs (simple spells) and, above all, preparation. Before a fight the witcher brews potions from ingredients, oils his swords, and studies the bestiary, so a significant part of the game happens outside combat. The system was unusual and divided players, but it captured the logic of the source material: Geralt doesn't win through strength but by preparing for a specific monster. The setting of Vizima and the surrounding villages is muddy, poor, and hostile, Adam Skorupa's music blends Slavic motifs with dark ambience, and the whole thing feels more like a Central European legend than classic fantasy.

The game originally launched in a state marred by long loading times, clunky localization, and technical bugs; a year later the Enhanced Edition substantially fixed it and added new voice acting and missions. It was this version that found The Witcher its audience, selling over two million copies and turning a previously unknown Polish studio into a name a whole series could be built on. In hindsight it's the roughest entry in the trilogy, but also the one where it shows most clearly that the authors wanted to tell a story about moral grey areas before that was common in the genre.

**Why play it:** Pick up the Enhanced Edition and you get the roughest entry in the trilogy, but also the one where the drive to tell a story about moral grey areas — before that was common in the genre — shows through the most.

pc-modern__witcher-2-assassins-of-kings.teaser: CD Projekt RED's first game on the REDengine; an RPG about a king's murder and northern intrigue.
pc-modern__witcher-2-assassins-of-kings.article:
**The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings** is the second entry in the witcher series and the first CD Projekt RED game built on its own REDengine. The leap over the first game is immediately visible: character animation, lighting, and level of detail were among the best you could see on PC in 2011, and the game became notorious for how reliably it could max out contemporary graphics cards. This time Geralt is accused of murdering a king, and the story of political intrigue among the northern kingdoms is told from the perspective of someone with no reason to root for either side.

The major change is in how the campaign is structured. After the prologue, the story splits along one decision into two completely different branches that differ in locations, characters, and what the player learns about the plot — an extraordinarily costly solution for its time, since most players will never see half the content. Combat abandoned rhythmic clicking for more direct action with dodges, blocking, and Signs, a step that brought the series to a wider audience but was brutally difficult at first. Alchemy and preparation remained, just moved into meditation, so potions can no longer be drunk mid-fight.

The 2012 Enhanced Edition added hours of new scenes, a tutorial, and an arena, and that same year an Xbox 360 version arrived too — technically stripped down but content-complete. The second game is often called the least accessible entry in the series and, at the same time, the densest one — it's shorter than the third game, has no open world, and focuses on a handful of locations, giving each all the more room. Without it, though, Wild Hunt wouldn't exist: this is where the studio tested out its own technology, branching storytelling, and the tone that would make the series famous.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates a dense, more linear story focused on a few locations instead of an open world will find here the foundation of the technology and tone that Wild Hunt later built on.

pc-modern__witcher-3-wild-hunt.teaser: The peak of Geralt's trilogy; its side quests are still considered the best in the entire RPG genre.
pc-modern__witcher-3-wild-hunt.article:
**The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt** closes out Geralt's trilogy and is the game that fundamentally raised the bar for what side content in an open world should look like. Velen, Novigrad, and Skellige aren't scenery dotted with icons but places with their own problems, where even a minor contract to kill a drowner often ends in a family tragedy or the discovery that the real monster walks on two legs. The Bloody Baron side story is regularly cited as one of the best pieces of side narrative in the genre's history, despite having no direct connection to the main plot about finding Ciri and the Wild Hunt.

Mechanically it's a compromise between the realism of the earlier games and smoother flow: combat combines two swords, Signs, a crossbow, and dodges, potion and oil preparation remains but the game doesn't require it on the lowest difficulties. Witcher Senses guide the player along trails and turn investigation into a mechanic of its own. The open world is enormous and yet hand-built — there's no generated content on the map, and every question mark exists for a reason. Music by the Polish trio Percival draws on Slavic folk tradition, and together with dynamic weather and a changing day-night cycle it captures the atmosphere of the source material more faithfully than anything before it.

The base game was followed by two expansions that stand on their own as full-fledged titles: Hearts of Stone, with a narratively polished story about the Man of Mirrors, and Blood and Wine, which added an entire new, colorful region called Toussaint and gave the series a fitting close. Wild Hunt collected over two hundred Game of the Year awards, sold in the tens of millions of copies, and in 2022 received a PS5 and Xbox Series version with ray tracing and content inspired by the TV series. For a large part of the audience it remains the yardstick against which every other sprawling RPG is measured.

**Why play it:** For lovers of sprawling RPGs, it's the title against which all others are still measured — with hundreds of Game of the Year awards and two full-fledged expansions on top.

vfx1__descent.teaser: Six-axis fighter flight through mine tunnels; the disorientation this VR headset was built for.
vfx1__descent.article:
**Descent** was among the titles directly tied to Forte VFX1 already in the marketing materials, because its six-degrees-of-freedom movement through mining tunnels made the headset relevant to it like to few other games. The pilot of the Pyro-GX fighter is not limited to movement on a flat plane as in classic shooters, but crawls, spins, and flips along every axis through narrow mining corridors full of robots and mines, and this very spatial disorientation was exactly what the VFX1's stereoscopic display was meant to show off at full strength. The goal of each mission is to destroy the reactor of a mining base and manage to escape before the tunnels collapse, which keeps the game at a constant pace and forces the player to keep the map in their head even while floating upside down between robots and laser traps.

In practice, though, the headset ran into the hard limits of its low-resolution LCD panels, so the textured tunnel walls dissolved into blurry patches of color, and orientation in space actually became harder than on a regular monitor, even though orientation was exactly what stereoscopy was supposed to make easier. Head movement for looking around worked, but the lag between turning your head and the image redrawing, combined with the headset's tunnel vision, quickly induced nausea in more sensitive players, so long play sessions in the VFX1 were the exception rather than the rule, and most players returned to the mouse, keyboard, and joystick after a while.

The game itself, even without the headset, was one of the most significant titles of the mid-1990s, with a dense atmosphere, nerve-wracking music, and an innovative game system that inspired a whole generation of mining and maze shooters, from Forsaken to later entries in the series itself. Today, Descent is remembered above all as a game that showed just how demanding it was to bring six-axis freedom into virtual reality of that era, and it remains an interesting historical testbed for early VR peripherals, one that shows clearly why full movement freedom in VR only caught on many years later.

**Why play it:** For fans of early VR attempts and mining shooters, Descent is an interesting probe into why full movement freedom in virtual reality only caught on many years later.

vfx1__descent-ii.teaser: A sequel with six-axis flight through tunnels; bigger levels and the same adrenaline-fueled disorientation.
vfx1__descent-ii.article:
**Descent II** built on the success of the first game and brought larger, visually richer levels, new types of enemies and weapons, but the basic principle stayed the same - a robotic fighter's combat in a labyrinth of mining tunnels with six-axis movement, which made the game a natural candidate for Forte VFX1 support. The developers gave attention to headset support in the second installment as well, so players could put on the goggles and let themselves be surrounded by a space where up and down stopped having a fixed meaning, which was meant to enhance the feeling of actually piloting a small fighter through tight corridors.

Technically, it was a step forward thanks to more detailed textures, more colorful environments, and, newly, alien locations outside the mines, but this paradoxically made things harder for the headset, since the VFX1's low panel resolution could only turn the richer graphics into a blurry mush in which it was hard to make out distant details or the small indicators on the cockpit dashboard. The head-tracking latency and narrow field of view also again contributed to feelings of nausea, so even enthusiasts often put the headset on only for short demonstration segments, while the main play happened as usual on a monitor with a mouse or joystick.

Descent II is valued today as one of the high points of the 1990s mining-shooter genre, with a more elaborate story, new enemy factions, and technical improvements such as variable lighting and cinematic cutscenes. The music and sound design gave the mining complexes a claustrophobic, industrial atmosphere that, together with the pressure of a countdown before the reactor's explosion, gave the gameplay its characteristic tension, which became a hallmark of the whole series. In the context of the VFX1, it remains a demonstration of how that generation of VR hardware was too weak to handle even a slightly more demanding sequence than its predecessor, and of how much difference every extra step in visual complexity made for hardware that was already running at the edge of its capabilities with the first installment.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates the claustrophobic atmosphere of the mines and the tension of a ticking countdown will find in Descent II a high point of the genre from the 1990s, even though its VFX1 version shows the limits of the era's VR hardware.

vfx1__doom.teaser: The game that defined the first-person shooter; hell on Mars with a shotgun.
vfx1__doom.article:
**Doom** is a game that fundamentally defined the first-person action shooter genre and became a natural testbed title for early VR peripherals, including Forte VFX1, whose drivers and utilities let players replace the classic mouse-look with head movement. The setting of a Mars base and hellish dimensions, through which the player shoots their way through an army of demons using a shotgun, plasma rifle, or chainsaw, thus gained a new, more intense dimension thanks to the headset's stereoscopic display, even though the game itself was designed for movement on a flat plane, without any real vertical freedom and without the ability to look straight up or down.

With Doom on the VFX1, the contrast was most apparent between the engine's simplicity, which managed a smooth framerate even on the PCs of the time, and the limits of the headset itself. The low display resolution meant that the characteristic pixelated textures of walls and enemy sprites were even coarser than on a monitor, and the narrow field of view made orientation in complex levels full of secret rooms a frustrating experience. The fast turning typical of Doom, given its emphasis on action and close-quarters firefights, was also one of the main triggers of nausea for players with no experience of VR simulator sickness, so many took the headset off after just a few minutes.

Despite these limits, Doom remained in the memories of early VR enthusiasts as one of the first proofs that first-person action and a headset could work together, though not without sacrifices in comfort and clarity. The game itself still holds the status of an absolute classic, along with its influence on the entire genre, whether in terms of level design, networked multiplayer, or the dark industrial atmosphere heightened by Bobby Prince's music, while its VFX1 version remains mainly a curiosity for collectors and historians of early virtual reality gaming on PC.

**Why play it:** For collectors and historians of early VR, Doom in the Forte VFX1 headset is mainly a curiosity, but the game itself remains a timeless classic worth playing even without it.

vfx1__heretic.teaser: A fantasy shooter on the Doom engine; an elf fights with magic against D'Sparil and can even fly.
vfx1__heretic.article:
**Heretic** built on the Doom engine but wrapped it in fantasy scenery, magical weapons, and the ability to fly, which made it a somewhat more interesting candidate for a headset than its predecessor, since flying over the landscape gave the Forte VFX1's stereoscopic display a natural reason to exist. Playing as an elf warrior, the player fights D'Sparil's armies using weapons like the serpent staff, the fireball, or the magic bow, and the passage through gothic castles and dungeons tried to feel darker and more elaborate than shooters of the time usually offered, including elements like a potion inventory and quick transitions between connected levels.

On the VFX1, however, the game ran into the same technical limits as the whole generation of Doom-derived engines, namely the headset's low resolution, which turned the more detailed textures of castles and monsters into a blurry smudge, and a limited field of view that prevented the space from feeling as enclosed and claustrophobic as the authors intended. The ability to fly, even though it was only temporary in the game via a spell, also brought a risk of stronger disorientation, since the combination of vertical movement and stereoscopy was hard for the headsets of the time to handle without a feeling of nausea, so players tended to limit the flight spell on the VFX1 to short exploratory trips.

Heretic is seen today as an important stepping stone between purely sci-fi shooters and later fantasy action RPGs, with atmospheric music and an inventive system of magic items that also became the foundation for its sequel, Hexen. The choice between several types of weapons, each with a different effect against different kinds of monsters, brought a new layer of tactical decision-making to the Doom-derived genre, which players and reviewers of the time appreciated as a refresh of the established formula. In the history of the VFX1, it remains an example of a game where the ambitions of its level design ran into the hard reality of the era's hardware, with the headset serving more as a demonstration of possibilities than a fully viable way to play for the average player.

**Why play:** Anyone who appreciates tactical weapon choice and atmospheric music will find in Heretic an important stepping stone between sci-fi shooters and fantasy RPGs, even though the headset served more as a demonstration of possibilities.

vfx1__magic-carpet.teaser: Flying on a magic carpet over undulating terrain; spell combat combined with strategy.
vfx1__magic-carpet.article:
**Magic Carpet** was one of the most visually ambitious games of the mid-1990s thanks to its fully textured, smoothly undulating terrain, over which the player flies on a magic carpet and casts offensive and defensive spells against enemy sorcerers and their creatures. Besides combat, the player also has to build mana from sacred sites and expand their territory, which gives the game a strategy-genre dimension too, and it was precisely this aerial movement in every direction combined with open spatial freedom that made the game a natural candidate for the Forte VFX1, since the feeling of flying over a landscape was exactly the kind of experience stereoscopic headsets promised to deliver better than a monitor.

Reality turned out to be more complicated, however, because the game's smooth, technically demanding terrain engine combined with the headset's low resolution produced an image where landscape details were blurry and orientation over large maps was difficult, which also made basic territory management and spotting enemy towers at a distance harder. The combination of free flight along all three axes and a limited field of view also caused significant nausea in many players, since the brain had few visual reference points for judging speed and altitude, and the head-tracking latency only made the effect worse, so only the most tolerant players tended to stick with the headset.

Even without VR support, Magic Carpet earned a reputation as one of the technically most advanced games of its time and inspired later titles built on destructible terrain and ranged magical combat, including its own sequel, Magic Carpet 2. In the context of the VFX1, it remains proof that not every type of movement suited early headsets equally well, and that open flight, despite its appeal, was one of the most demanding scenarios for the stereoscopic technology of the time and its limited refresh rate.

**Why play:** Fans of destructible terrain and ranged magical combat will enjoy the technically advanced Magic Carpet, even though open flight was one of the most demanding scenarios for VR headsets of that era.

vfx1__system-shock.teaser: A sci-fi adventure on the Citadel station against the AI SHODAN; hacking and cybernetic implants.
vfx1__system-shock.article:
**System Shock** delivered an unusually elaborate simulated world for its time, the space station Citadel, where the player, as a hacker, wakes into a nightmare controlled by the insane artificial intelligence SHODAN, and must explore the space, hack systems, and fight mutants and robots using a combination of physical weapons, energy weapons, and cybernetic implants that enhance the character's senses and abilities. Free camera movement in every direction, including looking up and down through the station's multi-level decks, made it one of the titles for which Forte VFX1 support made sense, since the player could genuinely turn their head while examining the station's multi-level rooms and ventilation shafts.

On the VFX1, however, the headset's typical ailments showed up, namely a coarse resolution that turned the game's detailed, text- and visually dense interface into a barely readable mess, and a narrow field of view that prevented the station's complex layout from being perceived the way it was designed. Navigating menus, reading text and audio logs, and interacting with the sensitive interface that System Shock relied on heavily for storytelling and orienting in the plot, was practically uncomfortable in the headset, so players tended to treat VR support more as a technical curiosity than a practical way to play for longer stretches.

System Shock is regarded today as one of the founding titles of the immersive sim genre, and its influence is evident across a whole range of later games, from Deus Ex to BioShock, which openly builds on the theme of an insane artificial intelligence. The atmosphere, heightened by SHODAN's iconic voice and dark electronic music, made it an unforgettable experience even on a regular monitor, and its VFX1 version remains mainly proof of how difficult it was to bring a complex simulation with so much on-screen information into early virtual reality.

**Why play:** For fans of the immersive sim genre, System Shock with its iconic SHODAN is an unforgettable experience even on a regular monitor, while its VFX1 version demonstrates the limits of early virtual reality.

vfx1__quake.teaser: A fully 3D engine replaced Doom's sprites with real geometry; a revolution in level design.
vfx1__quake.article:
**Quake** brought a fully three-dimensional engine that replaced Doom's earlier sprite-based approach with real polygonal geometry, dynamic lighting, and real 3D enemy models, and that is precisely why it became one of the titles where support for headsets like the Forte VFX1 had genuine justification, since the player could for the first time look up, down, and sideways with full three-dimensional consistency across the gothic and industrial levels full of demons and robots, without running into sprites flatly facing the screen. The real revolution was the fully three-dimensional world itself, which let level designers build far more sophisticated and spatially legible architecture than previous engines allowed.

Practical use of the VFX1 with Quake, however, ran into hardware limits from both sides. Quake itself was demanding for mid-1990s processors, and running in stereoscopic mode, which had to render the scene practically twice, lowered the frame rate even further, which combined with the headset's low resolution and noticeable head-tracking latency created an environment ideal for the rapid onset of nausea. The fast action sequences, strafing, and jumping between platforms that are characteristic of Quake were among the worst possible scenarios for motion-sickness sensitivity in VR at the time, even for players who otherwise had no problem with the headset in slower titles.

Even so, Quake remains one of the most influential titles in the history of computer games, with its dark industrial design, music by Trent Reznor, and the foundations on which the entire genre of networked deathmatches and esports later grew, and its engine also became the basis for a number of other games from other studios. Within the VFX1's history it is remembered as a game that pointed the way toward where VR might move in the future thanks to fully three-dimensional spaces, even though mid-1990s technology was still nowhere near ready for that ambition, whether in processor power, display resolution, or head-tracking speed.

**Why play:** Anyone who appreciates dark industrial design and Trent Reznor's music will find in Quake one of the most influential titles in gaming history, whose VFX1 version hints at the direction VR could eventually take.

vfx1__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tiger.teaser: Cinematic sequences with Mark Hamill combined with space dogfights against the Kilrathi.
vfx1__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tiger.article:
**Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger** combined extensive filmed cutscenes with Hollywood actors, including Mark Hamill in the lead role of Captain Christopher Blair, with classic space dogfights in which the player, as a fighter pilot, battles the hostile Kilrathi race, and the player's decisions in dialogue scenes affect the further course of the story and missions. Space combat in open space with no fixed horizon made it a logical candidate for Forte VFX1 support, since looking around the cockpit and tracking enemies in every direction matched exactly the kind of experience stereoscopic headsets promised to deliver.

In practice, however, the game ran into the headset's usual limits, namely the low resolution that made it hard to make out distant fighters and cockpit instrument details, and a limited field of view that, paradoxically, made harder exactly what the headset was supposed to make easier, namely tracking enemies at the edge of vision during a dogfight against multiple opponents at once. The cutscenes, one of the game's main draws and taking up an unusually large amount of space on CD discs for the time, also didn't display in the headset's stereoscopic mode the way they were designed for a standard screen, so players often switched between the headset and the monitor depending on whether it was an action flight or a story segment.

Wing Commander III is remembered today as one of the most expensive and ambitious titles of its era thanks to its combination of interactive film and space simulator, and its influence on the genre is evident in a whole range of later games built on cinematic storytelling and branching narratives based on the player's performance. In the context of the VFX1, it remains an example of a game where the title's strengths, namely its cinematic presentation and acting performances, were at the same time exactly what translated worst into early virtual reality.

**Why play:** For fans of cinematic storytelling and space simulators, Wing Commander III is an ambitious combination of interactive film and action, even though its strong cinematic presentation translated worst into early VR.

vfx1__mechwarrior-2-31st-century-combat.teaser: A cockpit simulator of a BattleMech robot; managing heat, ammo, and machine damage.
vfx1__mechwarrior-2-31st-century-combat.article:
**MechWarrior 2: 31st Century Combat** put the player in the cockpit of a giant combat robot, a BattleMech, and offered a simulation full of heat management, ammunition, and damage to individual parts of the machine in battles against the Wolf and Jade Falcon clans in the world of the BattleTech universe. The cockpit perspective, full of instruments, and the need to rotate the mech's torso independently of the head's view so the player could aim weapons in a direction other than where their machine was moving, made it one of the most natural candidates for Forte VFX1 support, since tracking the radar, targets, and instrument panel with head movement made sense in the context of a cockpit simulator.

In the headset, however, a typical problem of that generation of VR showed up, namely that the more information the game needed to display at once, the worse the VFX1's low panel resolution handled it. The small readouts on temperature, ammunition, and damage to individual mech parts, to which the game gave much greater emphasis than classic shooters, were hard to read in the headset's stereoscopic display, and the mechs' slower, lumbering movement fortunately counted among the less demanding scenarios for motion sickness, so MechWarrior 2 was, compared to fast shooters, more tolerable, though not without difficulty when rotating the torso quickly to track an enemy.

MechWarrior 2 is regarded today as one of the most significant mech simulators of all time, with a dense atmosphere heightened by its metallic cockpit design and unmistakable orchestral score, and it became the foundation for an entire series of sequels and expansions, including standalone add-ons focused on individual warring clans. Its emphasis on tactics, choosing loadouts before a mission, and the gradual damaging of specific mech parts gave the game an unusually simulation-like character for its time. In the history of the VFX1, it belongs among the titles where the headset managed to at least partly fulfill its promise thanks to the slower pace of play, even though the readability of its small instruments remained a lasting weakness.

**Why play:** Fans of tactical mech simulators will enjoy MechWarrior 2 for its dense atmosphere and emphasis on loadouts and mech damage, and thanks to the game's slower pace, it's among the titles where the VFX1 headset worked relatively best.

vfx1__terminal-velocity.teaser: A fast space combat simulator through canyons and tunnels; the flight was accompanied by electronic music.
vfx1__terminal-velocity.article:
**Terminal Velocity** was a fast-paced space combat simulator in which the player pilots a fighter through canyons, tunnels, caves, and open stretches of space, battling enemy ships, guns, and defense bases, all accompanied by energetic electronic music. The combination of high-speed flight close to the surface and free movement along every axis made it a title that, at the time, counted among the interesting showcases for headsets like the Forte VFX1, since the fast sense of flight was exactly what stereoscopy was meant to highlight and what set the game apart from slower space simulators.

But it was precisely that speed that became the main problem on the VFX1, since the combination of high flight speed, the headset's low resolution, and head-tracking latency created ideal conditions for the rapid onset of nausea in more sensitive players. The detailed canyon and surface textures the game prided itself on, and by which it wanted to set itself apart from flatter space levels in other titles, also broke apart into blurry color streaks in stereoscopic display, which made it harder to accurately judge distance from walls while flying at high speed and increased the risk of collision.

Terminal Velocity earned a reputation as one of the faster and more accessible space shooters of the mid-1990s, praised for its smooth movement, large arsenal of weapons, and catchy soundtrack, and it became the foundation for its later sequel, Fury3. The game bet on straightforward, arcade-style fun without unnecessarily complicated controls and without the need to configure ship loadout before every mission, which won it players who were put off by the austerity and demands of other space simulators of the time. In the history of the VFX1, it is remembered as an example of a game whose greatest strength, namely the feeling of speed, was at the same time exactly the trait that made the headset least usable for longer play sessions.

**Why play:** Anyone looking for a fast, accessible space shooter without unnecessarily complicated controls will appreciate Terminal Velocity, even though its sense of speed made the VFX1 headset least suited to longer play sessions.

vfx1__star-wars-dark-forces.teaser: Kyle Katarn against the Empire in vertically rich levels full of stormtroopers.
vfx1__star-wars-dark-forces.article:
**Star Wars: Dark Forces** introduced agent Kyle Katarn and his fight against the Empire and the Dark Trooper project through extensive, vertically rich levels that, thanks to the custom Jedi engine, allowed jumping, swimming, and traversing spaces with height differences far more prominently than other shooters of the time. It was precisely this vertical complexity that made it an interesting candidate for Forte VFX1 support, since looking up and down through cargo holds, ducts, and Imperial bases full of stormtroopers had genuine justification in the headset.

In the end, however, the game ran into the same limits that accompanied the whole generation of engines derived from a principle similar to Doom's, namely the headset's low panel resolution, which made the more detailed textures of bases and ships blurry, and a limited field of view that specifically hampered the vertical orientation the VFX1 was supposed to highlight. The jumping sequences, swimming through flooded corridors, and quick transitions between floors also intensified, for some players, the sense of disorientation typical of early VR devices and their imperfect head-motion tracking.

Dark Forces is remembered today as one of the best-crafted action titles set in the Star Wars universe from the 1990s, with atmospheric music echoing the film score and level design that pushed the genre forward through its verticality, and it inspired later entries in the Jedi Knight series. Weapons, enemies, and vehicles faithfully drew from the film trilogy, and the story takes place in parallel with the events of the classic films, so the game managed to appeal even to Star Wars fans who otherwise didn't play action shooters, and that licensed authenticity was one of its main assets. In the context of the VFX1, it remains an example of a game where ambitious level architecture was at the same time exactly what made playing in the headset more difficult and harder to orient in than flatter titles.

**Why play:** Fans of Star Wars and action shooters alike will enjoy Dark Forces for its faithful license and vertical level design, which at the same time made playing in the VFX1 headset more difficult.

vfx1__hexen-beyond-heretic.teaser: A darker sequel to Heretic; three character classes and puzzles interwoven between levels.
vfx1__hexen-beyond-heretic.article:
**Hexen: Beyond Heretic** expanded on the fantasy world of its predecessor Heretic with a more interconnected, hub-based level design, three distinct character classes with their own weapons and abilities, and a darker, more gothic atmosphere full of puzzles linking levels together, requiring the player to return to places visited long before. As with Heretic, the verticality of the environment and the ability to look around freely made good use of Forte VFX1 support, while the more complex interconnection of levels meant that spatial orientation mattered even more to players than in the simpler shooter titles of the time.

This is precisely where the headset's limits showed up most acutely, since Hexen relied on the player remembering the look and layout of places they would later need to return to with a new key or item, and the VFX1's low-resolution panels made distinguishing individual parts of the levels a substantially harder task. The limited field of view also made it harder to read the navigational cues that the interwoven level design depended heavily on, so longer play sessions in the headset were impractical even for players who otherwise didn't experience much nausea with other titles.

Hexen is valued today as an ambitious and innovative title that tried to push the fantasy shooter genre toward more elaborate puzzle design and nonlinear progression between levels, even at the cost of demanding more from players and their sense of orientation. The choice of one of three characters, each with its own arsenal, playstyle, and distinct strengths and weaknesses in combat, also gave the title a degree of replayability that the simpler, more straightforward shooters of the time usually didn't offer. In the history of the VFX1, it remains an example of a game whose greatest quality — a complex, interconnected world — was exactly the trait the headset's technical limitations undermined the most.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates elaborate puzzles and three distinct characters with their own arsenals will find in Hexen an ambitious step forward for the fantasy shooter, even though its complex interconnected world was the biggest burden for the VFX1 headset.

virtuality__dactyl-nightmare.teaser: One of the first Virtuality titles; combat on platforms above a chasm and a dreaded pterodactyl.
virtuality__dactyl-nightmare.article:
**Dactyl Nightmare** is a title indelibly written into the history of virtual reality — it was one of the first games the wider public actually experienced on the Virtuality machine, and it is still cited today as a breakthrough moment for the games industry. Wearing the headset and holding a joystick, the player moved across a set of floating platforms and towers above an empty chasm, with the task of finding and shooting the other players connected to the same arena before they did the same to them. On top of that, a giant pterodactyl occasionally flew over the whole scene, capable of snatching an unlucky player in its claws and carrying them high into the air before dropping them back down — a moment that became an iconic memory for everyone who tried the game.

Technically, this was a very simple, fully polygonal environment with crude shading and a low frame rate, but combined with the enclosed headset, the overhead counterbalance arm, and the physical platform on which the player turned around, it created a then-unprecedented sense of immersion in three-dimensional space. The system could also link two or more such platforms into a single shared arena, so players really did see and shoot at each other in real time. The sound design was minimalist — the game was accompanied more by gunshot effects and the pterodactyl's roar than by elaborate music, but the atmosphere was well served by the sheer emptiness of the geometric world and the silence between firefights. In arcades and entertainment centers in the early nineties, this was an attraction people lined up for, because nothing like it had been experienced before.

Dactyl Nightmare is remembered today above all as proof that the idea of networked multiplayer VR worked three decades before the arrival of modern headsets, and many later attempts at location-based VR entertainment consciously return to its concept. The game became one of the most frequently cited examples in retrospectives covering the origins of virtual reality. Played today, it comes across mainly as a historical curiosity — graphically primitive, but conceptually surprisingly legible and still fun in its simplicity.

**Why play it:** For fans of VR history, Dactyl Nightmare is proof that networked multiplayer virtual reality worked three decades before today's headsets, and even now it charms with its graphically primitive but legible simplicity.

virtuality__dactyl-nightmare-2.teaser: A sequel to the famous arena above the chasm; more varied environments and the same dreaded pterodactyl.
virtuality__dactyl-nightmare-2.article:
**Dactyl Nightmare 2** built on the famous first installment and offered players an expanded version of the original idea of a combat arena full of platforms, towers, and falling platforms above a bottomless chasm. The basic principle stayed the same — several players linked over a network competed against each other in first-person shooting, while the dreaded pterodactyl kept circling overhead, ready at any moment to grab an inattentive player and carry them elsewhere on the map. The sequel, however, brought a modified, more varied environment with more levels and hidden corners, small rule tweaks, and a subtle recalibration of match pacing meant to make the game a bit more dramatic and give those who knew the first game a new reason to return to the arena.

Visually, the game was built on the same polygonal engine as the Virtuality system, meaning simple, fully shaded shapes rendered at coarse resolution inside a heavy headset, which was the ceiling of arcade VR's technical possibilities at the time. Still, the more varied environment of the second installment better emphasized the sense of height and the danger of falling platforms, something players often mention in reviews and memories as an improvement over the more straightforward first game. The sound design again stuck to effects and atmospheric backing, with music not playing a key role in the experience — the main draw was the very sense of presence in three-dimensional space and the tension of an invisible opponent somewhere around the corner of the same arena.

In Virtuality venues, the second installment served as a natural expansion of the offering for players who had grown fond of the original, and it helped cement the series' reputation as the system's flagship. From today's perspective, it is viewed mainly in the context of the first game, remaining its somewhat lesser-known but historically interesting expansion, one that shows how quickly early VR arcades tried to keep their visitors' interest with new content, and how seriously the creators of the time took the idea of a sequel to a proven concept.

**Why play it:** Anyone who knows the first game will appreciate Dactyl Nightmare 2 as a lesser-known but historically interesting expansion, showing how quickly early VR arcades tried to keep players' interest with new content.

virtuality__legend-quest.teaser: A fantasy adventure through a dark castle; slower and more cautious exploration than a pure shooter.
virtuality__legend-quest.article:
**Legend Quest** was among the founding titles of the Virtuality system and offered players a fantasy-themed adventure set in a dark castle full of enemies and traps. Playing a lone hero, the player moved through a polygonal maze of corridors and halls, clashed with skeletons and other fantasy opponents, and tried to push deeper before running out of time or lives. Unlike the Dactyl Nightmare arena, this was a game with a clearer goal and progression, one that wasn't just a fast reflex-driven firefight but a slower, more careful passage through unfamiliar space, making it a pleasant addition to the lineup alongside the purely combat-focused titles of Virtuality's first generation. The game thus gave players a sense of genuinely exploring a foreign place, not just repeatedly entering the same arena.

The visual foundation consisted of the same simple, fully shaded polygons as the system's other games, dressed up with a medieval fantasy backdrop — castle walls, statues, and dark corridors that, thanks to the headset and the ability to look around in space, felt surprisingly convincing, even though by today's standards it's very crude, untextured graphics. The sound again remained more functional than musically rich, emphasizing combat effects and footsteps in empty halls, which heightened the sense of loneliness in an unfamiliar environment and forced the player to proceed cautiously from one hall to the next.

Within the Virtuality arcade lineup, this was a popular alternative to action shooters, and it is still mentioned today as one of the titles that proved early VR could offer something other than pure action — namely a hint of the fantasy-adventure genre, with progression and a goal. To today's player the game inevitably feels archaic, but as evidence of an early attempt at a game world with atmosphere it has its historical value, and it shows how varied a lineup Virtuality tried to build from the very start for as wide a range of arcade visitors as possible.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the history of early VR, Legend Quest is proof that Virtuality offered something other than pure action, namely a hint of fantasy adventure, even though it inevitably feels archaic to today's player.

virtuality__grid-busters.teaser: Arcade action in a networked arena; survive waves of enemies and shoot down opponents in first person.
virtuality__grid-busters.article:
**Grid Busters** was an arcade action title on the Virtuality system that put players in the cockpit of a fast craft in the middle of an abstract networked arena and had them face waves of enemies as well as other players connected to the same match. The goal was to survive in an open space made of geometric structures and platforms while shooting down opponents before they shot you down — a principle close to the space shooter arcade games of the era, just experienced in first person inside the headset, with the ability to turn in literally any direction. The player could also move freely between the individual geometric platforms, which set the game apart from the strictly rail-based space shooters of the time.

Technically, the game used the same simple polygonal rendering system as the other Virtuality titles, meaning crude, fully shaded, untextured shapes, but combined with the moving platform and joystick they created a convincing sense of flying through space. The visual style leaned on neon-toned geometry reminiscent of a digital grid, which nicely masked the hardware's technical limitations and gave the game a distinctive, futuristic atmosphere without needing detailed graphics or elaborate music. The audio was limited to gunfire, explosions, and engine noise, in keeping with the minimalist approach typical of Virtuality titles.

In the arcades of the time, Grid Busters was among the titles meant to demonstrate that Virtuality could also deliver fast action in the style of classic arcade shooters, transposed into fully three-dimensional space. Today it is seen as a lesser-known but typical representative of the early era of location-based VR, interesting mainly as part of the broader picture of what the Virtuality system was in the nineties and how varied an offering it tried to present to its visitors right from its market launch.

**Why play it:** Anyone interested in the variety of Virtuality's arcade lineup will find in Grid Busters a typical, if today little-known, representative of the early era of location-based VR, bringing classic arcade action into 3D space.

virtuality__vtol.teaser: Aerial action in the cockpit of a VTOL craft; hovering in place gave a real sense of piloting.
virtuality__vtol.article:
**VTOL** put the player of the Virtuality system into the cockpit of a combat aircraft capable of vertical takeoff and landing, offering an aerial action game over a three-dimensional battle landscape. Joystick controls allowed climbing, descending, and hovering in place while the player shot down enemy targets on the ground and in the air — making it one of the few early Virtuality titles built on aerial rather than ground-based action, offering a different kind of movement through space than the on-foot arenas like Dactyl Nightmare. The craft's ability to hover in place and rotate around its own axis gave the player the feeling of truly piloting an aircraft, not just following a predetermined track the way many aerial arcade games of the era did.

The visuals again relied on a simple polygonal engine without textures, this time spread across an open landscape with terrain and distant targets, which heightened the sense of height and flight for players inside the headset. Looking down at tiny targets and structures on the surface, combined with the ability to freely look around inside the cockpit, was among the moments players remembered most from a Virtuality arcade visit. The sound design focused on engine roar and explosions, with music staying in the background — the emphasis was on the feeling of controlling a craft in space, still a novelty in early-nineties arcades and one that drew in even players who already knew Virtuality's on-foot combat games.

VTOL expanded the second generation of the Virtuality system's lineup with an aerial genre, showing that the concept of location-based VR could be applied beyond on-foot combat. From today's perspective, it is a technically modest but conceptually interesting demonstration of how early virtual reality imagined cockpit flight, and the title is often cited as evidence that Virtuality's creators didn't want to stick to just one type of experience and sought ways to apply the same technology to different genres.

**Why play it:** For fans of aviation themes, VTOL is an interesting, technically modest demonstration of how early VR imagined cockpit flight, and evidence of Virtuality's effort to expand its lineup beyond on-foot combat.

virtuality__zone-hunter.teaser: A shooter through industrial corridors; tension from limited visibility replaced player-versus-player rivalry.
virtuality__zone-hunter.article:
**Zone Hunter** was among the best-known titles of the Virtuality system's second generation, offering a first-person action shooter set in dark industrial and sci-fi corridors occupied by hostile creatures and machines. The player moved through the space, aiming and shooting at targets emerging from corridors and corners, and compared to the Dactyl Nightmare arena this was a more structured, corridor-based progression with a clearer sense of danger lurking around every corner. The game thus relied more on the tension of limited visibility and sudden encounters with enemies than on the open competition between players that characterized the older first-generation titles, giving matches a stronger feeling of a lone advance through hostile territory.

Visually, the game benefited from a darker tone to its environment, which even with crude, untextured polygons felt unexpectedly evocative inside the enclosed headset — shadows, narrow corridors, and sudden attacks created a tension that the open arenas of other Virtuality titles did not offer. The enclosed headset and limited field of view paradoxically worked in the game's favor, since the player never saw what lay around the nearest corner until they actually got close to it, forcing them to rely on hearing and intuition as well as sight. The sound design relied on footstep, gunfire, and enemy sound effects, which combined with spatial perception to contribute to the atmosphere of threat, even though music itself played only a supporting role.

Zone Hunter is often mentioned today as one of the titles whose corridor-based design came close to the early first-person shooters on personal computers, just rendered in a fully three-dimensional, immersive form. Within the history of arcade Virtuality, it is regarded as one of the most accomplished titles of the second series both technically and atmospherically, and it still draws collectors and retro-VR enthusiasts today to seek out working machines on which they could try it again.

**Why play it:** Fans of corridor-based first-person shooters will be drawn to Zone Hunter as one of the most accomplished titles of Virtuality's second generation, both technically and atmospherically.

virtuality__exorex.teaser: A one-on-one fighting game in robots; a first-person duel instead of a classic fighting game.
virtuality__exorex.article:
**Exorex** was a fighting game on the Virtuality system in which two players faced off in an arena as robots or armored figures equipped with various weapons and abilities. Unlike on-foot shooters like Dactyl Nightmare, this was a focused one-on-one duel where timing attacks, defense, and use of the arena's space were key, bringing the game close to the fighting titles of the time, just translated into an immersive first-person environment. The player thus didn't watch their character from a distance as in classic fighting games, but experienced the duel directly from the perspective of the fighting machine itself, a fundamentally different way of presenting the same genre compared to the arcade cabinets of the era, forcing the player to gauge distance to their opponent and timing far more intuitively than in flat-screen fighting games.

The technical execution again relied on simple, untextured polygonal models, this time emphasizing the robotic or armored figures of the opponents, which could be observed up close thanks to movement within the arena's space. Thanks to spatial tracking of the player, the system could recognize not just button presses but also, to some extent, how the player moved and turned on the platform, enriching the duel with a physical dimension compared to flat fighting cabinets. The sound design accompanied the duels with collision and gunshot effects, with music staying in the background — the main emphasis was on the feeling of a real opponent standing directly opposite the player in another headset of the same machine.

Exorex represented the Virtuality system's attempt to also offer the genre of direct combat duels, popular in arcades of the time, thereby expanding the palette of experiences offered by the second generation of machines. Today it is remembered as a lesser-known but interesting piece of evidence for how early VR tried to adapt popular arcade genres to its new spatial medium and its technical limitations, even in a genre that connects less naturally to virtual reality than pure shooters.

**Why play it:** Anyone seeking a curiosity from VR history will appreciate Exorex as evidence of Virtuality's effort to bring even the combat duel into a spatial medium, even though duels connect less naturally to virtual reality than shooters.

virtuality__boxing.teaser: First-person boxing; real movement and ducking made the match physically demanding.
virtuality__boxing.article:
**Boxing** was a sports title for the Virtuality system that brought the classic boxing duel into an immersive first-person ring environment. The player faced a virtual opponent and used movement and controls to block and return punches, with the goal of exhausting or knocking out the opponent before that happened to them – a simple, readable concept that made good use of the system's ability to track the player's position and orientation in space. The very fact that the player actually had to move, duck, and turn in the pod to avoid a hit turned the seemingly simple concept of boxing into a surprisingly physically demanding experience, after which arcade visitors were often noticeably sweaty and out of breath.

The visuals kept to the style of other Virtuality titles, meaning simple, fully shaded polygonal figures without textures, in this case reduced to a boxer figure of the opponent standing directly in front of the player in the ring. Despite the crude model, the system managed to convey the direction and speed of the opponent's attack precisely enough that the player had a real chance to recognize and react to a punch in time, which was a fairly solid achievement for the simple graphics of the era. The sound design focused on typical boxing sounds – punches landing, breathing, and crowd reactions in the background – meant to round out the sporting atmosphere without needing an elaborate musical score.

In the arcade lineup, Boxing served as an easily accessible sports title, distinct from Virtuality's predominant action and combat games, and appealing even to casual players who just wanted to try VR without having to learn complicated rules. From today's perspective, it is a modest but exemplary application of the era's technology to a simple sports concept, one that nicely complemented the varied lineup of the second-generation machines and demonstrated the versatility of the motion-tracking system used.

**Why play it:** For casual players who just wanted to try VR without complicated rules, Boxing was an accessible sports title, and it remains to this day a showcase application of the era's technology applied to a simple concept.

virtuality__buggy-ball.teaser: Football on buggies in an arena; the ball is pushed into the opponent's goal with a buggy.
virtuality__buggy-ball.article:
**Buggy Ball** combined driving small buggies with the principle of a sports game resembling football or hockey, where the goal was to use a buggy to push a large ball into the opponent's goal. The player sat behind the wheel of a buggy rendered in an arena space, maneuvered around the field, and tried to get the ball where it needed to go, which made the game one of the few sport-vehicle titles in the Virtuality lineup and set it apart from the predominantly on-foot action titles. The fight for the ball between the buggies also naturally led to collisions and jostling, which added another dimension to matches besides pure scoring and brought the game closer to contact sports than classic racing.

Technically, this was again a simple, textureless polygonal environment, this time bounded as an enclosed field with goals and a large ball in the middle, which, thanks to the cockpit view from the buggy, was easy to read even with the limited resolution of the helmets of the time. The clearly defined, enclosed playing field helped players quickly grasp the rules even without lengthy onboarding, which was an advantage for Virtuality titles, since a typical arcade visit lasted only a few minutes and no one wanted to spend a long time studying instructions. The sound design focused on the buggy's engine and ball impacts; music was again only supplementary, with the main attention directed at the dynamics of the game itself and the rivalry between players.

Buggy Ball expanded the second generation of Virtuality's sports offerings with a collective, at-a-glance easier-to-grasp concept, making it a suitable choice even for less experienced arcade visitors. In its historical context, it is now seen as an interesting example of an attempt to link VR with a traditional sports game concept as early as the beginning of the 1990s, long before similar attempts on modern headsets, and it is a reminder that the idea of virtual sport is nothing new in recent years.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for proof that the idea of virtual sport is nothing new in recent years will find in Buggy Ball an interesting attempt to link VR with a collective sports concept as early as the start of the 1990s.

virtuality__total-destruction.teaser: A vehicular twist on Dactyl Nightmare; armored machines destroy each other in an arena.
virtuality__total-destruction.article:
**Total Destruction** was built on vehicle arena battles, in which players controlled armored machines and tried to destroy each other in an enclosed space full of cover and obstacles. It was a direct vehicular variation on the principle known from on-foot arenas like Dactyl Nightmare – instead of moving on their own legs, the player maneuvered a vehicle, aimed weapons, and used the arena's terrain to take cover from the fire of opponents connected in the same match. Having to track both the vehicle's movement and the position of opponents in the space around them at the same time made the combat somewhat more demanding and tactical than in the series' purely on-foot titles, because the player had to think about the speed and direction of their own movement, not just aiming.

Visually, the game again drew on the simple, fully polygonal, textureless rendering typical of Virtuality machines, in this case applied to armored vehicles and the destructive effects of their hits. The arranged cover and obstacles in the arena also forced players to think about their route, which set the game apart from the more open, at-first-glance more straightforward arenas of other titles, adding an element of planning to the combat rather than just reflexive shooting. The sound design accompanied the battles with explosions and engine sounds; music played a secondary role to the basic feeling of tension from vehicle combat in an enclosed space full of cover.

Total Destruction was among the titles meant to show that Virtuality's arena rivalry could be successfully transferred to vehicles as well, expanding the range of experiences offered in the second generation of machines. Today it is seen as an interesting, if lesser-known, variant of the vehicle combat concept that became a common part of mainstream video games a decade later, and as proof that the idea of arena vehicle battles has roots as far back as early virtual reality arcades.

**Why play it:** Fans of vehicle combat will find Total Destruction an interesting early example of the arena vehicle battle concept, which did not become mainstream until a decade later.

cardboard__lands-end.teaser: A pilgrim's puzzle adventure from the creators of Monument Valley, controlled solely by head gaze.
cardboard__lands-end.article:
**Lands End** was among the titles that showed in 2015 that mobile VR on Google Cardboard could be more than a technical curiosity, and also a place for thoughtful game design. The game, from the British studio Ustwo Games, known above all for the hit Monument Valley, casts the player as an unknown wanderer walking through the ruins of a vanished civilization on a distant island floating somewhere above the sea. Instead of classic movement via joystick or touch, it relies exclusively on head-gaze tracking and a single button on the cardboard headset, which made it a showcase example of so-called gaze-based control, at the time the only sensible approach on hardware without controllers and without hand tracking.

The gameplay rests on simple but elegantly designed puzzles: the player activates a beam with their gaze, using it to push aside rocks, turn mechanisms, transfer energy between ancient artifacts, or gradually unlock the path to further parts of the island. The visual style is minimalist, with striking color gradients, clean geometric shapes, and low-polygon architecture, which helped the game run smoothly even on weaker phones slotted into a cardboard case. The atmosphere is rounded out by calm, ambient music, quiet sound design, and a complete absence of any rush, time pressure, or enemies.

Contemporary reviews praised above all how well the developers came to terms with the platform's limitations and turned them into part of the design rather than an obstacle, much as they had already done with touch controls in Monument Valley. Lands End became one of the reference titles for showing what Cardboard could do, and it is still cited today as an example of a game that targeted neither action nor adrenaline, but calm exploration of space through gaze. Even years later it plays surprisingly well, precisely because it never tried to pretend to be more than mobile VR could handle at the time, and focused on what the platform was genuinely good at.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for calm exploration of space through gaze rather than action will appreciate Lands End as a reference title of mobile VR that still plays well today, precisely because it never pretended to be more than Cardboard could handle at the time.

cardboard__incell-vr.teaser: An arcade race inside the human body; the bloodstream becomes a colorful track.
cardboard__incell-vr.article:
**InCell VR** took players into a fantastical environment inside the human body, where an ordinary cell became a racetrack. The game was made by the studio Nival, otherwise known more for turn-based and strategy projects, and was adapted for Cardboard as a fast arcade race in which the player steers a tiny organism flowing through a blood vessel or cellular structure full of colorful organelles, viral particles, and obstacles that flash by as if in a neon-lit tube.

Controls were based on turning the head, which the player used to dodge left and right, collect bonuses, and avoid infection, while the speed of the ride was set by the game itself and gradually increased with the length of the track. Visually, it was one of the more colorful and technically ambitious titles of the early Cardboard library, where illuminated organic shapes, pulsing structures, and smooth transitions between track sections nicely demonstrated how a stereoscopic image on a phone could create a sense of depth even in an abstract environment that had no real-world counterpart or precise scientific model.

At the time of release, it was one of the titles often cited as proof that mobile VR could handle genre entertainment as well, not just contemplative walks or brief demonstrations. Short play sessions, a clearly readable goal, and zero need to learn complicated controls made it an ideal showcase for new owners of cardboard headsets who wanted to show something off in a few minutes. Today InCell VR feels like a pleasant reminder of a time when developers were still experimenting with which genres could be translated at all into a space without a classic controller, and the solution of head-based navigation remains one of the cleaner examples of such an experiment. The game also frequently appeared in curated lists of recommended titles for new Cardboard owners, because within a few minutes it could demonstrate just how different the feeling of speed and depth is in a stereoscopic image compared to an ordinary flat screen, without requiring the player to have any prior experience with virtual reality or gaming in general.

**Why play it:** Fans of mobile VR's early days will enjoy InCell VR as a pure example of head-based navigation and a demonstration that cardboard headsets could handle genre entertainment too, not just contemplative walks.

cardboard__inmind-vr.teaser: A flight through the brain and nerves, where head gaze is used to target damaged synapses.
cardboard__inmind-vr.article:
**InMind VR** is the studio Nival's second excursion into the human body, but this time, instead of the bloodstream, it takes players into the brain and nervous system. The goal is to fly through a network of neurons and aim with head-gaze at damaged or overly active synapses, which the game frames as a mildly educational glimpse into how dopamine and other neurotransmitters work, though it mainly serves as a pretext for fast action and a simple scoring system that motivates the player to come back for a better result.

Mechanically, it is a typical on-rails shooter adapted for Cardboard: the flight path is fixed, the player only aims with their gaze and fires with a single button, so there is no need for movement in space, which would not have been comfortable or precise on a cardboard headset without controllers anyway. The environment of the brain is rendered as an abstract tunnel full of light discharges, pulsing fibers, and organic structures, which allowed the developers to work with visuals that were striking but computationally undemanding, suitable for weaker mobile chips.

The game fit into the wave of early Cardboard titles that tried to prove the on-rails action genre was naturally well suited to mobile VR, since it eliminates the problem of movement and orientation in space. Combined with the earlier InCell VR, it showed that Nival could recycle the same design formula into different thematic wrappers, from the circulatory system to neurons, while keeping the same accessible gameplay built around short sessions, which for the technological possibilities of the time was the maximum achievable in terms of comfort and smoothness without risking motion sickness. The two games together formed something like an informal pair and were among the titles that electronics store customers had demonstrated to them as proof that a phone slotted into a cardboard box could offer an experience otherwise associated only with expensive game consoles or computers.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the history of mobile VR who wants to see how Cardboard solved movement in space using on-rails action – ideally paired with InCell VR as its informal twin.

cardboard__sisters.teaser: A short, quiet horror set in a dark house; the tension is built on atmosphere, not action.
cardboard__sisters.article:
**Sisters** is a short horror experience from the studio Otherworld Interactive that was among the first to show that genuine fear could be evoked even on Cardboard, despite hardware without motion tracking. The player finds themselves in the role of a child in a dark house, gradually discovering traces of two sisters and an unpleasant presence that inhabits the house, with the whole experience built on the slow buildup of tension rather than action, violence, or being chased.

The game uses gaze-based navigation and relies primarily on sound design and lighting work, since the phone's limited computing power did not allow for complex effects or detailed character models. Jump scares are dosed sparingly, which gives them greater impact, and the short runtime, usually just a few minutes, places the game among the so-called VR vignettes – experiences designed to take only a moment but linger in the player long after taking off the headset.

Sisters was often cited as proof that a limited mobile VR platform need not be an obstacle for a genre built on atmosphere and psychological pressure rather than graphical fidelity or complex animation. In the context of Cardboard, it was one of the titles that deliberately exploited the player's isolation inside the headset, the feeling that they can see nothing outside and are left with only what the game itself shows and what they hear in the headphones. Even years later, it remains an example of how effectively an unpleasant, claustrophobic sense of threat could be evoked with minimal resources and without a single controller. Its short playtime in particular proved to be an advantage, since horror in a headset is a physically and psychologically exhausting experience, and many players replayed Sisters repeatedly to show it to friends and watch their reactions, turning it into one of the informal social rituals associated with the first cardboard headsets.

**Why play it:** For horror fans, for whom isolation inside a headset and a dark atmosphere are enough for tension instead of graphical fidelity – the short playtime here is more an advantage than a flaw.

cardboard__vanguard-v.teaser: A sci-fi rail shooter with robots and mechs; aim with your head, fire with a single button.
cardboard__vanguard-v.article:
**Vanguard V** is an on-rails action shooter from the Korean studio Wemade that took classic arcade rail shooters as its model on Cardboard and transplanted them into a sci-fi setting full of robots, defense turrets, and enemy mechs attacking from different directions. The player moves along a fixed path through an attack base or battlefield and aims with head-gaze, while firing is triggered by a single button on the headset, with no need for any other control.

Visually, the game relied on bright colors and readable enemy silhouettes so that targets were always easy to spot despite the limited resolution of phones of the time, projected through Cardboard's two lenses. The pace was fast, with short waves of enemies, a simple weapon upgrade system, and progressively harder sections, making it a typical representative of the so-called arcade shooters adapted for short play sessions, which mobile VR without controllers essentially required.

Within the early Cardboard library, Vanguard V was among the titles demonstrating that the shooter genre could be transferred to the platform if it were stripped of the need for free movement and replaced with a fixed rail and clearly readable targets. The game carried a similar design approach to a number of other on-rails titles of the time and still serves today as a reminder of how developers intuitively searched for genres that worked even with a single button and gaze as the only input, before headsets with full-fledged controllers and spatial hand tracking reached the market. For many players, it was their very first encounter with the idea that you could shoot in virtual reality like in a classic arcade hall, only instead of aiming a toy gun you aimed with your own head, which was still a fairly unusual feeling in 2015. Short missions made it possible to play the game for a few minutes between other activities and return to it again without losing track of progress, which proved to be a practical trait given how quickly a phone slotted into cardboard heats up and how limited battery life is when wearing a headset for longer periods.

**Why play it:** For collectors of mobile VR history who want to experience how early Cardboard titles tackled the shooter genre with a single button and gaze instead of free movement in space.

cardboard__chair-in-room-greenwater.teaser: A lightweight mobile version of the horror walking sim from Oculus Rift.
cardboard__chair-in-room-greenwater.article:
**Chair in a Room: Greenwater** is an atmospheric horror walking-sim adventure from British studio Wolf & Wood Interactive, which arrived on Cardboard as a lightweight mobile variant of the original experience built for positionally tracked headsets like the Oculus Rift. The player walks through an abandoned, decaying building resembling a former asylum, picking up story fragments along the way about the experiments that once took place within its walls.

For the mobile version, free movement through space had to be replaced with gaze-based navigation, where the player is transported between fixed points in the environment simply by looking at them. This meant the game lost some of the original's physical immediacy, but it kept the oppressive atmosphere created by the sound design, dim lighting, and the sense that in the dark corridors you never know what's around the corner or in the next room. Interaction is limited to simple object examination and solving minor puzzles, with classic combat essentially absent.

The game belonged to a small but distinctive group of horror titles on Cardboard that showed the tension-and-exploration genre could work even without full motion tracking or controllers. Critics and players alike saw it as proof that porting a more ambitious VR experience to more limited hardware was possible, albeit with necessary compromises in control and sense of presence. Today, Greenwater is an interesting example of how the same game could be adapted to very different tiers of VR technology of the time, from a full PC headset all the way down to a lensed piece of cardboard. It is precisely this contrast between versions that makes the mobile port a fascinating historical artifact, because it shows exactly what a horror game built on slow walking and careful listening loses when physical movement is taken away and replaced with mere gaze, and what it can still hold on to even under those conditions.

**Why play:** For the curious who want to compare exactly what a horror experience loses when ported from a full PC headset to a simple lensed cardboard box.

cardboard__bait.teaser: A portable fishing simulator with no demands on reflexes; just a rod, the water, and calm.
cardboard__bait.article:
**Bait!** from Swedish studio Resolution Games was one of the most accessible titles of early mobile VR, turning Cardboard into a portable fishing simulator that made no great demands on reflexes or understanding of complex mechanics. The player stands on a pier or a boat, watches the surface of a lake, and uses their gaze plus simple controls to cast a line, wait for a bite, and then reel in the fish, all while calming ambient sounds of water, birds, and rustling nature play in the background.

The game deliberately gave up any reflex-based challenge, instead building on a relaxing, meditative pace, which set it apart from most action-oriented Cardboard titles focused on fast reactions and short adrenaline bursts. The graphics were stylized and colorful, emphasizing the pleasant lake setting, changing weather, and calm water surface, which nicely masked the technical limitations of mobile rendering while giving the game its distinctive, gentle look.

Bait! became one of the examples showing that mobile VR could be used for genres beyond horror and action, and it later grew into a more successful series on more powerful platforms like Gear VR, Daydream, and standalone headsets with controllers. The Cardboard version, however, remains important as the first step that showed calm, low-demand gameplay could be just as suited to short VR sessions as adrenaline-fueled titles, perhaps even more so, given how quickly players tired in headsets of the era and how limited battery life was. In retrospect, Bait! is often cited as an example of a title built on patience and observing the environment, qualities that also appealed to people who otherwise deliberately avoided action or horror Cardboard games, thereby broadening the platform's audience to players seeking calm rather than tension. The short, self-contained play sessions also matched the real capabilities of the hardware at the time well, since a player could stop at any moment, take off the headset, and return later exactly where they left off, without feeling they had missed an important part of the experience or progress.

**Why play:** For players looking for calm, low-demand VR entertainment without adrenaline; patient fishing suited Cardboard better than most action and horror titles of the time.

cardboard__dreadhalls.teaser: One of the oldest VR horrors (2013, Rift DK1); endless dark corridors with no light.
cardboard__dreadhalls.article:
**Dreadhalls** is among the oldest and best-known horror experiences in virtual reality period, having originally been created back in 2013 for the Oculus Rift DK1; its later mobile version for Cardboard and Gear VR brought the same dread into pocket-sized form without needing a connected PC. The game was made by the small studio White Door Games and builds on a single principle: the player is trapped in an endless network of dark, procedurally generated corridors and must find a way out, feeling nearly blind along the way.

On Cardboard, movement was converted to automatic or gaze-controlled walking, while the main threat remains the sounds of footsteps, breathing, and distant growling that signal approaching, almost invisible enemies hidden in the dark. The absence of a map or a clear goal, together with oppressive silence broken by sudden sound effects, creates a permanent sense of disorientation that is characteristic of the game and that works even with the significantly reduced graphics of mobile phones compared to the PC version.

Dreadhalls is often mentioned as one of the titles that helped define what horror in VR even looks like, and its port to Cardboard showed that its key elements, dread, isolation, and sound, could be preserved even on far weaker hardware without spatial tracking or controllers. For many players it was their first genuinely unpleasant experience with a cardboard headset, and even today the game is referenced as an example of how little is needed to evoke a strong sense of threat when the sound design is handled well. The fact that the game could work across such different platforms, from a powerful PC with a motion-tracked headset all the way to a phone slotted into a box, made it one of the frequently cited arguments for the claim that horror is a genre naturally suited to mobile VR, since it doesn't require complex interaction, just environment and sound.

**Why play:** For VR horror fans who want to experience how little it takes to evoke dread and fear with well-executed sound design, whether on a powerful PC headset or in a cardboard box.

cardboard__cardboard-camera.teaser: Google's tool for creating your own VR photospheres with sound, not for playing games.
cardboard__cardboard-camera.article:
**Cardboard Camera** is an app straight from Google that turned Cardboard into a tool for creating your own VR content rather than just consuming it, setting it apart from the vast majority of other titles on the platform focused purely on entertainment. The user slowly rotates their phone around its own axis while the app stitches together a panoramic photosphere complemented by spatial audio recorded during the capture, producing a simple but functional 3D record of a specific place and moment.

The resulting images can be viewed directly in the headset with a parallax effect that gives the static photo a sense of depth, and can be shared further as VR photos compatible with other viewers supporting the photosphere format, including the viewer built into Google Photos. Technically, this was a clever use of an ordinary phone camera and gyroscope, without needing specialized hardware, which fit well with Cardboard's philosophy of being the cheapest and most accessible entry point into virtual reality.

Cardboard Camera wasn't a game, but it was one of the most frequently mentioned apps on the entire platform because it demonstrated a practical use of VR beyond entertainment, specifically as an alternative to family photo albums or a way to record travel and memories.
