At the same time, it ran into the limits of mobile VR photography, such as the lower resolution of the resulting sphere, sensitivity to hand movement during capture, and difficulty capturing moving objects. It is still remembered today as one of the most accessible ways to create your own memory viewable in stereoscopic space. Unlike most other apps on the platform, Cardboard Camera didn't require understanding any game rules or controls; all you had to do was turn the phone around its own axis, which made it understandable even to people who otherwise never considered gaming or virtual reality at all and only tried a headset once while visiting friends.

**Why play:** For anyone who wants to simply capture a memory in stereoscopic space without needing to learn any game rules or controls.

cardboard__cardboard-design-lab.teaser: Google's demo of VR interactions - an elevator, a tentacle, a swing, and a virtual panel.
cardboard__cardboard-design-lab.article:
**Cardboard Design Lab** was created by Google as an interactive demo and, at the same time, a guide for developers and ordinary users alike who wanted to try out what kind of interactions mobile virtual reality even allows and where its natural limits lie. The app offered a series of short scenes in which the player could try operating an elevator, controlling a tentacle, riding a swing, moving across platforms, or interacting with a virtual panel, each scene serving as a standalone demonstration of a different gameplay mechanism.

The goal wasn't to offer a continuous story or challenge but rather a catalog of possibilities that developers could use as inspiration when designing their own Cardboard apps, accompanied by brief commentary explaining the advantages and pitfalls of each approach, for instance why it's advisable to avoid fast virtual movement without corresponding physical movement of the body, in order to prevent motion sickness. Technically, the app was undemanding, since the individual scenes were minimalist and served a purely demonstrative purpose rather than being a full-fledged experience.

In the history of Cardboard, Design Lab holds a special place as one of the few apps aimed more at creators than end players, and many later Cardboard games unknowingly repeated exactly the patterns that this app was the first to systematically demonstrate and name. Today it stands as an interesting historical document of the early phase of mobile VR, when the entire field was still working out what was safe from a design standpoint and what already caused players motion sickness or a loss of spatial orientation. For many people, it was also their very first opportunity to get their hands on virtual reality for free, without having to buy a specific game, since the app was freely downloadable and all it required was the Cardboard itself and a phone they already had at home. Translating this idea into concrete, tangible scenes, such as riding an elevator or manipulating a virtual tentacle, proved to be a smart move, because it let both developers and casual onlookers quickly form their own idea of what was actually technically feasible on the given platform and what wasn't.

**Why play:** For anyone interested in the history of VR design, and for anyone who wanted to try, for free and without buying a game, how virtual reality actually works for the first time.

cardboard__anshar-wars-2.teaser: A space on-rails shooter; a fighter cockpit, head aiming, and fire with a single button.
cardboard__anshar-wars-2.article:
**Anshar Wars 2** is the sequel to a space action shooter from Norwegian studio Campfire Union, and it was one of the more technically ambitious titles in the early Cardboard library, following on from the first installment, which had originally been made for Gear VR. The player sits in the cockpit of a fighter ship and battles enemy fleets across a series of missions, aiming by turning their head and firing with the headset's single button, similar to other on-rails space shooters of the time.

The game relied on impressive space visuals, explosions, various types of enemy ships, and fast-paced firefights meant to demonstrate that even a mobile chip could deliver a visually striking sci-fi experience comparable to more powerful platforms. The controls were simplified to work without a physical controller, with an emphasis on the ship moving automatically along predetermined trajectories while the player's role was reduced purely to shooting and dodging enemy fire.

Within the Cardboard era, Anshar Wars 2 followed a similar path to Vanguard V or InMind VR, namely offering an action genre without requiring free movement through space, which was essentially the only workable recipe for an action game without controllers or hand tracking. The music and sound effects lent it an epic feel that contrasted with the simplicity of the mechanics itself, and the game remains an example of how the space rail-shooter genre adapted to the limits of early mobile virtual reality and its single input button. The fact that this was a sequel rather than an entirely new concept also showed that Campfire Union had built enough trust with its first installment to invest in improved graphics and expanded content for the second entry, made for a platform that was still a full generation younger than Gear VR. Fans of space shooters thus got a full-fledged sequel to a beloved concept even on the cheapest possible entry point into virtual reality, which only confirmed that developers of the time didn't associate Cardboard purely with short technology demos, but also with seriously designed games with their own identity and sequels.

**Why play:** For fans of space shooting arcade games who will appreciate the epic music and sound despite the simple on-rails mechanics limited by early Cardboard's single button.

cardboard__titans-of-space.teaser: A tour of the solar system with planets at real scale - a popular VR showcase ride.
cardboard__titans-of-space.article:
**Titans of Space** is an educational VR tour of the solar system from studio DrashVR, which on Cardboard became one of the most frequently recommended showcase experiences for new users, much as its original version had already done on early PC headsets. The player sits in a small capsule that gradually carries them past the Sun and each of the planets, with every body rendered at proportionally accurate size, meant to convey the true scale of the universe better than any image on a flat display or in a school textbook ever could.

Interaction is minimal; the experience runs almost automatically, and the player focuses on observing and listening to brief information about each planet, making it closer to a planetarium show or educational program than a traditional game. This simplicity was actually an advantage, since Cardboard without controllers and with limited processing power wasn't suited to complex interaction, while a slow, contemplative ride past the planets ran flawlessly even on weaker phones without risk of stutter.

Titans of Space was often cited as one of the first experiences that could explain to people new to VR why a stereoscopic view in a headset differs from watching a video on a monitor, specifically through the sense of the true size of planets standing in space around the player. It remains a frequently cited example that not every VR experience has to be a game in the traditional sense to be impactful, educational, and meaningful even for audiences outside the gaming crowd. Teachers and science communicators occasionally used it as a teaching aid when covering the solar system, since the feeling of standing next to a body many times larger than yourself could explain the almost unimaginable size differences between the planets of the solar system, and how small Earth is by comparison, better than any lecture.

**Why play:** For anyone who wants to understand why a view in VR differs from watching a video on a monitor; the sense of the true size of the planets works as a convincing teaching aid even for audiences outside gaming.

pc-vr__half-life-alyx.teaser: Valve's return to Half-Life, completely rebuilt for VR. The gravity gloves became the symbol of the game.
pc-vr__half-life-alyx.article:
**Half-Life: Alyx** marks Valve's return to one of gaming's most significant franchises, this time completely rewritten for virtual reality. The player takes on the role of Alyx Vance a few years before the events of Half-Life 2, in an occupied City 17 full of Combine patrols and mutated headcrabs. The entire game was designed from the ground up with VR interaction in mind: weapons are reloaded by hand, objects are picked up and thrown, puzzles are solved by manipulating the environment, and gameplay as a result feels far more physical than in classic shooters. The gravity glove, which lets you pull objects and ammunition toward you from a distance, plays an important role and became one of the most frequently mentioned elements of the controls.

Technically, it's one of the most visually accomplished VR games ever made, with detailed environments, convincing lighting, and carefully directed scenes that use the first-person perspective to build tension. The sound design and music continue the atmosphere of the original series, and the claustrophobic tunnels and quiet moments interrupted by sudden headcrab attacks feel considerably more intense in VR than on a flat screen. The game requires a powerful PC and a headset such as the Valve Index, HTC Vive, or Oculus Rift, and even years later it remains one of the most graphically demanding VR titles on the market.

Upon release, Half-Life: Alyx received extremely positive reception and is often described as the game that finally showed VR could deliver a full-fledged, long, and narratively rich experience rather than just a technology demo. Many developers now cite it as a reference point for movement, object interaction, and level design in virtual reality. Even years later it remains one of the most frequently recommended titles for anyone putting on a VR headset for the first time, and its influence can be seen in later games that adopted a similar approach to handling objects and weapons. The game also features an optional locomotion mode that lets players choose between teleportation and smooth walking based on their own sensitivity to VR motion sickness, which contributed to its broader accessibility.

**Why play:** For anyone putting on a VR headset for the first time and wanting to experience a full-fledged, narratively rich title that still serves today as a reference point for movement and object interaction in virtual reality.

pc-vr__beat-saber.teaser: Slicing cubes to the rhythm with two sabers; a simple rule with a huge skill ceiling.
pc-vr__beat-saber.article:
**Beat Saber** is a rhythm game in which the player uses two glowing sabers to slice colored cubes flying in time with the music, with each cube needing to be cut in the correct direction, and sometimes the player must also dodge obstacles or duck under an obstacle bar. The principle is simple and intuitive, yet it offers plenty of room for improvement – from slow songs for beginners to extremely fast maps that demand quick reflexes and precise coordination of both hands, so the game works as both fun and a form of physical training.

The game stands out with its purely stylized neon graphics, which don't tax the hardware and run smoothly even on weaker configurations, making it one of the most accessible VR titles on the market for owners of smaller gaming PCs. The original soundtrack combines electronic music and synthpop, and was later expanded with dozens of paid and community song packs, including collaborations with major music artists and popular film and game brands. The game's physical demands are a frequent argument for VR as a form of exercise, and many players use it directly as an alternative to classic cardio workouts.

Reception of the game has been exceptionally positive from the start, and Beat Saber quickly became one of the best-selling VR titles ever, often serving as the first VR demo for a new user. Thanks to its easy modifiability, a large community emerged creating custom maps for thousands of songs, giving the game practically endless lifespan. Today, Beat Saber is synonymous with VR fitness and fun at the same time, and remains one of the most-played titles on platforms like SteamVR even years after release. Gradually added difficulties and modes like One Saber or No Arrows also give the game an extra dimension for players who have already mastered the basic difficulty levels and want to keep refining their technique.

**Why play it:** For anyone looking for a first VR demo or wanting fitness fun with practically endless lifespan thanks to thousands of community maps.

pc-vr__superhot-vr.teaser: Time in SUPERHOT only passes when the player moves; dodging bullets becomes an action choreography.
pc-vr__superhot-vr.article:
**SUPERHOT VR** transforms the original concept of SUPERHOT – where time moves only when the player moves – into a fully immersive virtual environment. The player physically dodges bullets, ducks behind cover, catches enemy weapons in mid-air, and plans every movement like choreography, because any action sets time moving forward. The result is a feeling of becoming a movie action hero who has time to think through every step, making strategy at least as important as reaction speed.

The visual style with white environments and red, glass-like enemy figures has been preserved in the VR version and works very well, since the minimalist graphics reduce hardware demands while emphasizing movement and action. The conversion to VR controls – grabbing weapons, throwing objects, physical dodges – was critically praised as one of the best-executed conversions of a flat-screen game into virtual reality, since the original time-based-on-movement mechanic fit VR more naturally than classic keyboard-and-mouse controls. Short, intense levels give the game pace suited even to players unaccustomed to longer stays in a headset.

The game became one of the most frequently cited examples of how VR can amplify an already existing game mechanic, not just offer a new way of viewing a scene. Even years after release, SUPERHOT VR still appears on recommended lists for new headset owners as a demonstration of how physical activity and strategic thinking can be combined in one short but intense playthrough, one that differs noticeably from the classic flat-screen version in its sense of personal presence in the action. The game also consists of relatively short levels that can be replayed to find a more efficient way of dealing with the wave of enemies, which supports its long-term replayability even after completing the main campaign.

**Why play it:** For new headset owners and experienced players alike looking for short but intense gameplay, where physical activity and strategic thinking merge into an experience unattainable on a flat screen.

pc-vr__boneworks.teaser: A physics-based VR action game on a custom engine; your hands have weight, and walking on uneven terrain is a challenge.
pc-vr__boneworks.article:
**Boneworks** is a physics-based game built on its own engine that simulates every movement of the body and objects with an emphasis on realistic mass behavior. The player has a fully physical body – hands that actually hold objects with weight, legs and a body that collide with the environment, and weapons whose recoil and magazine handling correspond to real mechanisms. This approach was unusually ambitious at the time of release and required the player to get used to a non-intuitive but very convincing way of interacting, where even simple walking on an uneven surface can be a challenge.

The game combines combat with weapons and bare hands, solving physics-based puzzles, and exploring a dark, industrial environment full of robotic enemies. The atmosphere is cold and mildly unsettling, with a minimalist story told through recordings and notes scattered across the levels. Technically, Boneworks is demanding both on performance and on player adjustment, but its physics system was often described as groundbreaking for the VR action genre, since practically all objects in the game world react to touch and the weight-feel of the hands.

After release, the game gained significant attention among the core VR community as proof that physical interaction can be the foundation of an entire game, not just a supplementary feature. Boneworks influenced a number of later VR titles that adopted a similar approach to hands and object physics, and its sequel Bonelab built further on this foundation and expanded it with additional options. Thanks to a level editor and an open community, a range of unofficial maps and mods emerged that extended its lifespan. The sound design, where every impact of an object against a wall or a falling item produces a matching sound, further reinforces the feeling that the player is in a material, physically consistent environment. Stepping, squeezing through narrow spaces, and climbing over obstacles require genuine physical movement from the player, bringing Boneworks closer to later titles built on full, body-based VR control.

**Why play it:** For the core VR community craving a game where physical interaction with objects is the foundation, not an add-on – the sound design and tangible sense of environment make it a genre benchmark.

pc-vr__bonelab.teaser: The successor to Boneworks with swappable avatars - the character's weight and height change how you move.
pc-vr__bonelab.article:
**Bonelab** builds on the physics system of the previous game, Boneworks, and expands it with the ability to switch avatars mid-game, which affects the character's weight, height, and way of moving. The player moves through various environments full of puzzles, combat, and exploration, where each avatar change – from a light robotic figure to a heavy, slow one – changes how one interacts with the surroundings, giving the game a variety that most other physics-based VR titles lack.

The game retains the dark, industrial atmosphere of its predecessor, complemented by more colorful and stylized locations resembling test chambers and laboratory environments. Physical interaction with weapons and objects remains the core of the gameplay, with the developers further improving collision detection and hand behavior to feel more natural than in the previous installment. The soundtrack and sound design support the feeling of an isolated, semi-abandoned world that the player gradually uncovers while progressing through the chapters.

Bonelab was received as a solid sequel that develops the original game's unique physics mechanics and additionally offers extensive modification and custom-content creation options. Thanks to its open approach to mods, it became a popular platform for community creation of new levels and avatars, extending its lifespan far beyond the original campaign. A mod management tool built directly into the game made sharing community content easier and contributed to a long-term active player base. The sandbox mode, which allows free experimentation with objects, weapons, and avatars outside the main campaign, became one of the most frequently praised features, as it gives players room for their own creativity and improvisation without the constraints of the story line. The variety of avatars, from small and fast to large and slow, also shows how significantly changing one's own body can affect the sense of space, height, and physical strength during play, an experience a classic screen-based game cannot offer.

**Why play it:** For fans of the first game and newcomers alike who want to experiment in a sandbox and create custom content in addition to the campaign, thanks to extensive mod support.

pc-vr__lab.teaser: A collection of mini-games from Valve set in the Aperture Science lab; a showcase of roomscale VR.
pc-vr__lab.article:
**The Lab** is a collection of short games and technology demos created by Valve to showcase the capabilities of the HTC Vive and roomscale VR. The player moves through the virtual laboratory of Aperture Science, from which they enter individual mini-games – from shooting a bow at robotic targets, through taking care of a dog named Rychlík by throwing a disc, to a driving simulator or exploring the surface of another world. Each part focuses on a different form of VR interaction and serves as a gentle introduction to virtual reality for new users experiencing a headset for the first time.

Graphically, The Lab is stylized and undemanding, which fits its purpose as a demonstration title meant to run on a wide range of hardware, including weaker home PCs. The humor, drawing on the atmosphere of the Portal series – the AI's lines, references to Aperture Science – gives the collection a distinctive tone that pleasantly reminds many players of Valve's original games. Each mini-game is short but carefully tuned to showcase a different advantage of VR, such as spatial audio, physical distance estimation, or a sense of scale when looking down from great height.

At the time of release, The Lab was often recommended as a first experience for new VR headset owners, since it offered, for free, a varied and technically impressive showcase of what virtual reality makes possible. Even years later it remains a popular demonstration of roomscale VR capabilities, and several of its mini-games, especially the one with the dog Rychlík, became a frequently cited symbol of the early era of VR on PC. Its free distribution also helped spread awareness of VR among players who otherwise wouldn't have bought a paid game, and several of its mini-games are still cited today as examples of elegant, clear VR design that needs no complicated explanations or an extensive tutorial. Precisely because each mini-game lasts only a few minutes, The Lab is also often used when demonstrating VR at public events, where there's a need to quickly and reliably show various aspects of this technology to new people.

**Why play it:** For new VR headset owners looking for a free, technically impressive showcase of roomscale VR – just a few minutes are enough, even for the mini-game with the dog Rychlík.

pc-vr__job-simulator.teaser: A comedy about robots parodying human jobs; sandwiches and engines assembled blindly.
pc-vr__job-simulator.article:
**Job Simulator** is a comedic simulation game in which the player, in a fictional future where all work is done by robots, experiences a parody of four classic jobs – an office worker, a head chef, an auto mechanic, and a store cashier. Each environment is full of interactive objects that can be manipulated in ways that often lead to absurd and comical situations, such as throwing food into a blender, assembling nonsensical sandwiches, or building an engine from the wrong parts.

The game was one of the first to show how well VR can work for simple, playful interaction with objects without requiring precise physics simulation or a realistic story. Graphically it's stylized and colorful, which, combined with cartoonish robots and voice lines, creates a light-hearted atmosphere suitable even for complete VR beginners. During development, Owlchemy Labs put great emphasis on making every interaction intuitive and fun on its own, without the need for complicated instructions or tutorials, which proved key to its broad accessibility.

Job Simulator became one of the most frequently demonstrated VR titles at public events and electronics stores, since it managed to quickly and clearly show the magic of virtual reality even to people who had never tried VR. Its success helped studio Owlchemy Labs build a position as one of the leading developers focused on accessible, humorous VR experiences, and it paved the way for the sequel Vacation Simulator, which further built on a similar concept. The accuracy of hand detection and the ability to perform seemingly mundane activities, such as opening drawers or fidgeting with small objects on a desk, were unusually convincing at the time of release and contributed to the feeling that the player really was in a real office or kitchen. Each of the four environments also contains a number of hidden details and side interactions that reward players for thorough exploration, making the game play out differently even on a second or third playthrough.

**Why play it:** For anyone who wants to show the magic of virtual reality to people who have never tried VR – the accurate hand detection and mundane activities like opening drawers still feel convincing today.

pc-vr__vacation-simulator.teaser: The spiritual successor to Job Simulator; robots discover the concept of vacation at the beach and in the mountains.
pc-vr__vacation-simulator.article:
**Vacation Simulator** is the spiritual successor to Job Simulator, in which the same robots from the previous game get to know the human concept of a vacation. The player moves through three distinct environments – a beach, mountains, and a forest – where they can fish, grill, craft objects, paint, or simply relax, with each activity handled as a separate interactive experience with its own side tasks and unlockable content that motivates repeated visits to each location.

Compared to the previous game, Vacation Simulator offers a larger and more open environment to explore, more crafting options, and longer playtime, while retaining the same stylized, colorful visuals and robotic humor. Physical interaction with objects, pouring liquids, or combining ingredients while cooking are handled with great attention to detail, making simple experimentation with the environment the core of the fun. The game also allows crafting souvenirs and items that the player can bring back to their virtual home between locations.

The game was received as a successful expansion of the original concept, offering more content and longer lifespan for players who enjoyed Job Simulator. Thanks to its accessibility and gentle, relaxed atmosphere, it's often recommended as a good choice for players who just want to relax and experiment in VR rather than deal with tense action situations. Support for various headsets and undemanding graphics requirements also allowed the game to reach players with weaker gaming PCs. Robotic characters with their own personalities and voice lines give the individual locations character and playfulness, making the game a suitable choice for playing together with family or friends who have no prior VR experience. The expanded crafting system and the ability to store items in a virtual scrapbook also give the game a light collecting dimension that motivates repeated visits to already completed locations.

**Why play it:** For players who just want to relax and experiment in VR without tense action situations, ideally in the company of family or friends with no prior VR experience.

pc-vr__budget-cuts.teaser: A stealth VR action game with a portal that reveals a room before you step into it.
pc-vr__budget-cuts.article:
**Budget Cuts** is a stealth action game with a distinctive teleportation mechanic that lets the player look through a teleport portal into another part of the level before actually moving there. The player moves through an office building full of robotic guards, whom it's necessary to either avoid or eliminate using thrown knives, improvised weapons, or silent attacks from stealth, since being spotted usually means a quick end to the attempt and a return to the start of the level section.

The look-ahead teleportation mechanic is the game's main innovative feature and was critically praised as a clever way to solve movement in VR without the risk of nausea associated with classic smooth locomotion. The office-company setting is stylized, with slightly comically-toned robots and notes that contrast with the tense, quiet gameplay reminiscent of classic stealth games like Thief or Deus Ex. Each level requires careful route planning and use of the environment, including hiding in ventilation shafts or under desks.

The game was well received primarily thanks to the originality of its teleportation mechanic, which was described as one of the best solutions for locomotion in VR games in general. The sequel Budget Cuts 2 built on this foundation and expanded the original concept with additional weapons and levels, confirming that the teleportation stealth mechanic had long-term success with players. The game is also often cited as an example of how to solve movement in VR without requiring physical walking over a large space. The tense yet mildly comical atmosphere gives the game a distinctive tone that sets it apart from most more serious stealth titles, making it an accessible introduction to the genre even for players who would otherwise be wary of a serious stealth focus. The ability to preview the next room through the portal before deciding whether to move there gives the player a sense of control over risk that is rather the exception, not the rule, in other VR stealth games.

**Why play it:** For fans of the stealth genre and newcomers alike who will appreciate the original teleportation mechanic solving VR movement without requiring physical walking, wrapped in a tense yet mildly comical atmosphere.

pc-vr__lone-echo.teaser: A zero-gravity VR adventure on a mining station; moving by pushing off instead of walking is unique.
pc-vr__lone-echo.article:
**Lone Echo** casts the player as the android Jack, who works as technical support for astronaut Liv aboard a mining station orbiting Saturn. The game takes place in a weightless environment, where the player moves by grabbing surfaces and pushing off objects, creating a completely different feel of movement than most other VR titles. Interacting with objects, repairing equipment, and solving technical problems form the core of the gameplay, accompanied by a strong story and good voice acting for the main characters that keeps the player engaged throughout the game.

Visually, the game feels very convincing thanks to the richly detailed station and realistic space environment effects, with the absence of gravity simulated so well that it is among the most frequently praised elements of the game. The relationship between Jack and Liv, built through dialogue during shared problem-solving, gives the game an emotional dimension that was unusual for VR games at the time of release. The music and ambient sounds complement the atmosphere of isolation far from Earth and heighten the feeling of loneliness in space.

Lone Echo was, after release, received as one of the most ambitious and narratively rich VR games of its time, praised especially for combining a technically advanced simulation of weightless movement with quality storytelling. The game helped show that VR can carry a longer, emotionally grounded story, and it inspired other titles working with a similar sense of movement in a gravity-free space. The multiplayer successor Echo VR then expanded the movement system into a competitive sports format. The gradual unlocking of new areas of the station, and the associated repairs of damaged systems, also give the game the structure of a classic adventure, where each solved task moves the story a bit further and reveals another part of the mystery surrounding the station. The sense of cooperation between Jack and Liv, where one often advises the other over the radio while solving a technical problem, gives the game a human dimension despite the main character being an android, and contributes to the emotional impact of its ending.

**Why play it:** For players craving a longer, emotionally grounded story in VR – a technically advanced simulation of weightless movement gives the exploration of the space station the structure of a classic adventure.

pc-vr__asgard-s-wrath.teaser: A massive Norse action RPG in which you guide a hero as a deity and also fight yourself.
pc-vr__asgard-s-wrath.article:
**Asgard's Wrath** is an expansive action RPG set in Norse mythology, in which the player plays as a deity guiding a mortal hero, while at key moments being able to take direct control and fight with their own hands against mythological creatures and gods. This two-tier structure – guiding the hero from a deity's perspective while also personally taking part in combat – gives the game an unusually large scope both in environmental scale and in the intensity of the action, and allows for smoothly switching between the roles of strategist and fighter.

The game offers an expansive world full of puzzles, weapon-and-shield combat, and branching story lines, which at the time of release made it one of the longest and most content-rich VR games on the market. Both visually and audibly it is crafted with great attention to detail, featuring large boss fights against enormous creatures that use VR scale to heighten the sense of size and threat. Melee and shield combat was critically praised for its precision and physical sense of resistance, while guiding the hero from the deity's perspective feels more like a classic action adventure with puzzle elements.

Asgard's Wrath was, after release, described as one of the most ambitious and complex VR games of its generation, often compared to classic action RPGs on consoles and PC. Its length and depth of story exceeded the expectations of many players, who at the time associated VR mainly with shorter experiences, and the game thus significantly pushed the boundaries of what virtual reality is expected to offer. Subsequently released standalone expansions further extended the game's lifespan and expanded its story world. The combination of deep, character-development-based gameplay in the style of a classic action RPG with everything VR enables in direct combat made it one of the most frequently cited examples of what a truly expansive RPG built specifically for virtual reality can look like.

**Why play it:** For players who expected only short experiences from VR – an expansive action RPG comparable to console and PC classics shows how deep and long a virtual world can be.

pc-vr__elite-dangerous.teaser: A vast space simulation of an entire galaxy; VR adds a genuine sense of cockpit scale.
pc-vr__elite-dangerous.article:
**Elite Dangerous** is an expansive space simulation set in a realistically scaled-down replica of the entire Milky Way, in which the player trades, fights, explores, and builds their own career as a pilot. VR headset support was added shortly after the game's release and allows the player to sit in the ship's cockpit and look around the dashboard and surrounding space with a sense of scale that cannot be replicated on a flat screen, while the player can physically turn their head to check the radar and the view from the cockpit.

The game places great emphasis on simulation elements – piloting the ship requires managing power between engines, weapons, and shields, navigation is done using star maps, and docking at stations requires precise maneuvering through narrow spaces. VR adds a convincing sense of space and depth to this system, especially when approaching large space stations or flying through asteroid fields, where the player can physically turn their head for a better view of their surroundings. The sound design of the ship's systems and the music accompanying long-distance travel further heighten the feeling of genuine piloting.

VR support for Elite Dangerous was well received as one of the best ways to experience the game, and many long-time players say that after trying VR they don't want to go back to playing on a flat screen. The game is still regularly updated today, and its VR mode remains one of the most frequently recommended examples of how virtual reality can enhance the sense of scale and immersion in a space simulation that otherwise requires dozens or hundreds of hours of play. The large community of players, trading factions, and exploration expeditions organized directly by players also give the Elite Dangerous universe the feel of a living, collaboratively built world, which is experienced even more intensely in VR than on a monitor screen. The richly detailed dashboard, with dozens of switches and displays that can be directly touched and viewed from different angles in VR, is one of the elements that most often surprises players with its authenticity when first sitting down in the cockpit.

**Why play it:** For fans of space simulations who, after trying VR mode, no longer want to go back to a flat screen – it enhances the sense of scale and immersion over dozens or even hundreds of hours of play.

pc-vr__no-man-s-sky.teaser: An endless procedural universe to explore; VR adds landing and walking on planets.
pc-vr__no-man-s-sky.article:
**No Man's Sky** is a game about exploring a practically infinite, procedurally generated universe, in which the player flies between planets, gathers resources, builds bases, and upgrades their ship and equipment. VR support was added to the game via an update several years after its original release and allows players to experience landing on unknown planets, walking on their surface, and piloting the ship from a first-person view with the full sense of scale of vast landscapes and the starry sky overhead.

The VR mode converts most of the game's main mechanics – mining, combat, base building, and interstellar travel – into a format suitable for a headset, while preserving the original procedurally generated environments with their own flora, fauna, and weather phenomena. The transition between exploring a planet on foot and flying in space feels especially convincing in VR thanks to the sense of height and depth that a flat display cannot fully convey. Manipulating inventory and building bases directly with your hands also gives these activities a new, more tactile dimension.

The addition of VR support was well received as a significant expansion of an already existing and expansive game, making it accessible to players seeking immersive experiences. Thanks to continuously expanded content and regular updates, No Man's Sky in VR remains one of the most expansive exploration titles available on PC headsets, often praised for the sense of freedom and scale of the universe, which kept growing with each new update. The transition between exploring on foot and flying takes place in VR without loading screens, which reinforces the feeling of one continuous, uninterrupted journey from a planet's surface all the way into deep space. The ability to seamlessly switch between VR and the classic display also gives players the flexibility to choose their way of playing depending on their mood or the length of a planned gaming session, which is an unusual advantage for a title of this scale and sets No Man's Sky apart from other VR titles tied exclusively to a single mode of play.

**Why play it:** For explorers seeking a sense of freedom and an endless universe without loading screens between walking on a planet's surface and flying, with the option to switch back to the classic display at any time.

pc-vr__elder-scrolls-v-skyrim-vr.teaser: The whole vast Skyrim in VR; the view from a mountaintop carries a completely different weight.
pc-vr__elder-scrolls-v-skyrim-vr.article:
**The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim VR** brings the vast open world of the beloved fantasy RPG into virtual reality, while preserving most of the content of the original game, including the main and side story lines, crafting, magic, and both melee and ranged combat. The player can travel across Skyrim, watch dragons flying over the mountains, or make their way through dark dungeons with a sense of scale and depth that is substantially more intense in VR than on a flat screen, and looking at the landscape from a mountaintop feels especially impressive.

The conversion to VR controls lets you physically draw a bow, swing a sword, or cast spells with hand movements, giving combat a different, more physical character compared to the original keyboard-and-mouse or gamepad controls. Technically, it is the same world as in the original 2011 game, adapted for stereoscopic display, which brought increased hardware requirements but also allowed players to re-experience a well-known world in a new way. The atmosphere of the Nordic landscape, the music, and the sounds of wind in the mountains gain a new, stronger dimension in VR.

Skyrim VR was received with great interest after release as one of the first conversions of a truly vast, long-form RPG into virtual reality, and many players described it as one of the longest and most content-rich VR experiences available on PC. Thanks to support for community modifications, which expanded the VR version with further improvements and fixes, the game kept an active player base for several years after release, with many mods focusing directly on improving VR controls and interaction with objects. The view from towers, castles, or from the top of the Throat of the World over the vast landscape below is among the moments players most often cite as proof of how dramatically VR can change the experience of an otherwise well-known world. The chance to re-experience dozens of hours of well-known content, but with a new sense of spatial depth when viewing the landscape or dungeons, made Skyrim VR one of the most frequently recommended choices for players who want a long and content-rich VR experience.

**Why play it:** For fans of expansive RPGs who want to experience Skyrim's well-known world anew – the view from castle towers or from a mountaintop over the vast landscape is among the most frequently mentioned VR moments of all.

pc-vr__half-life-2-vr-mod.teaser: A fan-made VR mod of the legendary shooter; you hold the gravity gun directly in your hand.
pc-vr__half-life-2-vr-mod.article:
**Half-Life 2: VR Mod** is a community modification of the original Half-Life 2, which converts the classic 2004 shooter into a fully playable version for virtual reality, with support for hand controller movements, physical weapon aiming, and the ability to manipulate the legendary gravity gun directly with your hand. The mod includes both the base game and its episodic expansions, and tries to preserve the original level design while adapting the controls to the new way of playing, including adjustments to firefights and vehicle sequences.

Work on the mod took several years and required reworking animations, control schemes, and parts of the user interface so they would work naturally in spatial display. The result is an experience that lets you relive iconic locations such as Ravenholm or Black Mesa East from a completely new perspective, where the player physically ducks behind cover and manually reloads weapons, giving otherwise well-known scenes a new sense of tension. Vehicle control, such as driving the airboat or the buggy, also gained a different, more physical feel in VR.

After release, the mod was received very positively as one of the most ambitious and best-executed community conversions of a classic game into VR, which Valve subsequently supported through official distribution on Steam. For many long-time fans of the Half-Life series, the mod represented a chance to relive a beloved story in a way that the original game could not offer at the time of its creation, and it became proof of the vitality of community creation around older Valve titles even many years after their original release. The fact that volunteers, without official support from the studio, managed to convert such an extensive and technically complex game into a functional VR form was often cited as an example of how far a modding community can go when it has access to an open and well-documented game engine.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Half-Life series who want to experience a beloved story in a way the original could not offer at the time – proof of how far a modding community can go without official support.

pc-vr__pavlov-vr.teaser: A multiplayer tactical shooter with physical weapon reloading and aiming.
pc-vr__pavlov-vr.article:
**Pavlov VR** is a multiplayer tactical shooter that brings the tradition of online FPS games built around team firefights into virtual reality – players compete in modes inspired by classics like Counter-Strike, Search & Destroy, or battle royale, with the difference being that all weapon handling is done with your own hands. Loading a magazine, flipping off the safety, aiming through real sights, and running between cover – all of this is handled physically, which gives the game a tangibility that flat shooters cannot offer, and the player must learn the same skills as with a real weapon, just in a safe virtual environment.

The game began as a fairly modest project in Unreal Engine, but thanks to a long stay in Early Access on Steam it gradually grew to include dozens of weapons, maps, and game modes, including a cooperative zombie survival mode. Support for community mods and custom maps also plays a big role, thanks to which Pavlov built a loyal player base far beyond the typical VR audience. The sound design of combat, the echo of gunshots in enclosed spaces, and the necessity of communicating with the team create tension typical of competitive tactical shooters.

Within the PC VR scene, Pavlov has long been considered one of the most convincing proofs that physical interaction with a weapon can work not only in slow-paced adventures but also in fast, competitive multiplayer. The transition from Early Access to full release was accompanied by gradual improvements to the network code and optimization for weaker VR headsets, thanks to which the game retained playability even on less powerful computers. Even years later it remains one of the most-played VR shooters on PC and a reference title for anyone who wants to experience team combat with a genuine sense of a weapon in hand, and a number of later multiplayer VR titles openly cite its formula of physical weapon handling as their model.

**Why play it:** For fans of competitive multiplayer with a genuine sense of a weapon in hand, it is one of the most-played and most-referenced VR titles on PC, functional even on weaker rigs.

pc-vr__onward.teaser: A seriously intended tactical FPS with no health bars; only observation and communication decide the outcome.
pc-vr__onward.article:
**Onward** is among the games that defined what a seriously intended tactical shooter in virtual reality can look like. Instead of arcade-style action, it builds on a slower, more methodical pace – players are split into two opposing teams, communicate by voice, plan their approach, and must respect realistic ballistics as well as limited ammunition supplies. There are no classic health bars or a minimap in the corner of the screen, which brings the game closer to the authentic feel of a military operation, where the most important information comes from observing your surroundings, not from a game interface.

Weapon handling is treated with great attention to detail: the player physically inserts magazines, racks the charging handle, switches fire modes, and uses a radio to coordinate with teammates. It is precisely this layer of realism that made Onward a reference title for the tactically focused VR community and inspired a number of later games in the genre, including direct competition like Pavlov, with which Onward is still most often compared today. The game went through a long development period in Early Access, during which the maps, weapon arsenal, and game modes were refined before it reached full release.

Onward's atmosphere is built on quiet tension – rustling in the bushes, footsteps on gravel, or the sound of an opponent reloading around the corner can decide survival just as much as an accurate shot. The sound design is therefore minimalist and functional, with practically no background music, because silence itself is the most important piece of information on the battlefield. Due to the absence of artificial crutches, the game is uncompromising toward newcomers, but that is precisely what makes it so valued among players who want to experience a tactical shooter in VR without compromises. To this day, Onward remains one of the pillars of PC VR multiplayer and a benchmark against which new tactical titles in the genre are automatically compared, and its emphasis on communication and planning also influenced the design of later military VR simulators.

**Why play it:** Because of an uncompromising tactical shooter built on silence and communication, without artificial crutches for newcomers, Onward remains among the pillars of PC VR multiplayer to this day.

pc-vr__blade-and-sorcery.teaser: Combat driven by real physics; the strength and angle of your attack decide the outcome, not animations.
pc-vr__blade-and-sorcery.article:
**Blade & Sorcery** built its entire concept on physics-based melee combat – swords, axes, bows and spells aren't controlled through scripted animations but through the actual movement of your hands, with the game calculating in real time a weapon's weight, angle of impact, and the force needed to pierce or sever. The result is combat that never looks the same twice and whose outcome depends purely on how the player physically aims and strikes, setting the game apart from any scripted combat animation in ordinary action games.

The game began as a small one-developer project and, through Early Access on Steam, gradually grew to include an extensive magic system, firearms inspired by the fantasy world, ragdoll physics for enemy bodies, and later mod support, which made it one of the most moddable VR games ever – the community added its own weapons, environments, and entire game modes. The graphics are restrained, focused mainly on the functionality of the physics system, but it's precisely the raw and often graphically violent presentation of combat that gave the game a reputation as a technical showcase for physical interaction in VR. The absence of music and the emphasis on the sounds of impacts, metal scraping of weapons, and characters' breathing underscore the sandbox nature of the game, where the atmosphere is created above all by the player's own style of combat.

Blade & Sorcery became one of the most-cited examples of what virtual reality is capable of in melee combat, and it inspired numerous other titles that attempted a similar approach to physical combat. Even without a fixed story or goal, thanks to its endless combat variability and mods it remains one of the most-played sandbox VR games on PC and is often cited as the first title new headset owners use to demonstrate to others just how convincingly virtual reality can simulate physical combat.

**Why play:** For the endless variability of a physics-based combat sandbox and a rich modding scene, Blade & Sorcery is often the first demo headset owners show to others.

pc-vr__into-radius.teaser: A Stalker-like survival game in a frozen zone; every expedition risks both equipment and life.
pc-vr__into-radius.article:
**Into the Radius** places the player into a freezing, post-Soviet zone full of anomalies, mutated creatures, and supernatural phenomena, heavily inspired by the atmosphere of stalker-style survival games. As a lone stalker, the player must survive expeditions into the dangerous area, gather artifacts and materials, manage weapons and equipment at the base, and gradually unlock the zone's deeper mysteries without ever being sure what exactly awaits around the next corner – every expedition carries a real risk of losing equipment and life.

The game stands out for its elaborate weapon system – every piece must be physically disassembled, cleaned, reassembled, and maintained, turning mere shooting into a full-fledged game mechanic the player must think about long before the actual firefight. The combination of slow pacing, permanent resource scarcity, and dense sound design creates an oppressive atmosphere where even an ordinary distant sound can trigger tension and force the player to slow down and listen to their surroundings. Survival elements like hunger, fatigue, or limited backpack capacity force the player to plan every expedition carefully, setting the game noticeably apart from more action-oriented VR titles and bringing it closer to slow, deliberate survival simulations than to fast action.

Thanks to its depth and uncompromising atmosphere, Into the Radius built a reputation as one of the most elaborate survival titles on PC VR and became especially popular among players seeking a slower, more deliberate experience instead of fast action. The soundscape built on distant howling, crackling radio static, and the silence of the zone completes the sense of isolation that sets the game apart from louder action titles. Its success later led to the release of a sequel, confirming just how strongly this concept resonated with VR audiences and how well the stalker atmosphere blends with the physical interaction of virtual reality.

**Why play:** For players seeking a slower, more deliberate survival experience with a dense stalker atmosphere, Into the Radius ranks among the most elaborate PC VR titles, a fact confirmed by the release of its sequel.

pc-vr__walking-dead-saints-and-sinners.teaser: A survival horror set in zombie-infested New Orleans; weapons physically wear down and fall apart.
pc-vr__walking-dead-saints-and-sinners.article:
**The Walking Dead: Saints & Sinners** places the player in the flooded streets of New Orleans, overrun by zombies and warring factions of survivors, where every decision – who to save, who to rob, who to trust – affects the story's direction and relationships with the city's various factions. The game relies on physical interaction with everything around you: the player searches dead bodies, opens drawers, disassembles weapons, and improvises melee combat with whatever is at hand, from a kitchen knife to a baseball bat that, after a few hits, gets thoroughly battered and must be repaired or replaced.

Fighting zombies demands precision and caution – a single careless swing can end in a fatal bite, and the game punishes recklessness far more harshly than classic action titles. The crafting system, inventory management, and gradual gear upgrades give exploration purpose, while morally ambiguous side quests and decisions affecting the fate of individual factions give the story weight. The sound design, the muffled creaking of floors in flooded buildings, and sudden attacks from the dark create a dense horror atmosphere that virtual reality amplifies even further, and music appears only rarely, letting silence and the sound of sloshing water carry most of the tension.

Upon release, the game was hailed as one of the high points of the survival horror genre in VR, showing that a licensed zombie game could offer depth comparable to a full-fledged independent title. The later release of a sequel confirmed that the concept of physical combat against zombies in a flooded city has lasting appeal among players, and many players returned to New Orleans several more times after their first playthrough to try different decisions. To this day it remains among the titles often cited as proof that VR can tell an emotionally powerful story with real moral dilemmas, not just offer brief technical demos.

**Why play:** For its emotionally powerful story with real moral dilemmas and physical combat against zombies, this ranks among the high points of survival horror in VR, worth replaying for its different decisions.

pc-vr__arizona-sunshine.teaser: One of the first major zombie shooters for VR, also playable in co-op.
pc-vr__arizona-sunshine.article:
**Arizona Sunshine** was one of the first major zombie shooters designed specifically for virtual reality, and it's still counted among the titles that helped define what an action VR game with a hearty dose of humor and tension should look like, without ever taking itself too seriously. The player crosses a parched Arizona wasteland overrun by the undead, gathers weapons and ammo, and solves simple but effective puzzles while trying to survive the journey to the goal, either alone or in co-op with another player watching their back against hordes attacking from every side.

Shooting relies on physically manipulating weapons – reloading, aiming down sights, and having to keep track of ammunition give even ordinary zombie plinking a tension that flat-screen games can't offer. The humorous tone, combining a raw zombie apocalypse with the main character's lighthearted one-liners, gave the game a distinct identity apart from darker survival horrors. The two-player co-op mode was also a fairly unusual feature at the time of release and contributed to the game's long-lasting community, since clearing the wasteland of the undead together turned out to be one of the most enjoyable ways to experience virtual reality with a friend, even for players who otherwise prefer single-player experiences.

Arizona Sunshine became one of the most commercially successful early VR titles and helped prove that the zombie shooter genre could work just as well on the new platform as on classic consoles and PC, without having to sacrifice content scope for the sake of technological novelty. The parched desert scenery, abandoned gas stations, and overgrown cacti gave the game a visual identity players easily associated with the whole series. Its influence is visible in the sequel and a range of other VR shooters that adopted its basic formula of physical shooting combined with a light tone.

**Why play:** For a lighthearted zombie shooter with a striking desert atmosphere that proved the genre could work in VR just as well as on classic platforms, and influenced a whole line of successors.

pc-vr__star-wars-squadrons.teaser: Convincing space fighter cockpits in VR; you manage power, weapons, and shields.
pc-vr__star-wars-squadrons.article:
**Star Wars: Squadrons** brought the iconic space battles of the Star Wars universe into virtual reality, offering one of the most convincing piloting experiences PC VR had seen up to that point, thanks to a maximum emphasis on detailed cockpits and controls that are approachable yet complex. The player sits in the cockpit of a New Republic or Imperial starfighter and, with full head and hand tracking, operates onboard systems, redistributes power between weapons, shields, and engines, and tracks opponents by looking around the cabin, creating a sense of genuine presence in combat that flat flight simulators can barely replicate.

The game combines a short single-player campaign told from the perspective of pilots on both sides of the conflict with a full multiplayer mode, where teams clash in team battles and large-scale fleet engagements. Detailed cockpit models, reworked control panels, and the need to physically watch the displays inside the cabin make the VR mode a far more intense experience than playing on a flat monitor, even though the game was designed to work equally well in both modes.

The sound design of engines, blaster fire, and pilot voice communication, together with music continuing the film series' tradition, rounds out an atmosphere that appealed both to Star Wars fans and fans of aerial action. Transitions between starfields, damaged ships, and laserfire in the dark of space also stand out especially well in VR thanks to the natural perception of depth and distance, which is crucial for judging distance to a target. Star Wars: Squadrons is still cited today as one of the best proofs that a major licensed game can fully and equally support virtual reality rather than treating it as a mere add-on, and many players consider it the most convincing starfighter piloting simulation they could try within the Star Wars universe.

**Why play:** For Star Wars fans and aerial action fans alike, it offers one of the most convincing starfighter piloting simulations the universe has ever gotten, thanks to the natural perception of depth in VR space.

pc-vr__iracing.teaser: A respected racing simulator with laser-scanned tracks; VR enhances your ability to judge corners.
pc-vr__iracing.article:
**iRacing** is one of the most respected racing simulators ever made, known for its emphasis on precise vehicle physics, laser-scanned circuits, and an organized online league structure in which players are ranked into divisions by performance and cleanliness of driving, much like a real racing ladder. Virtual reality support added another dimension to an already demanding simulator – a natural sense of distance into a corner, checking mirrors by turning your head, and a more sensitive perception of braking points, which is much harder to judge on a flat monitor and comes almost instinctively in VR.

The simulator is aimed primarily at players who want an experience as close to real motorsport as possible, including the need to track tire wear, fuel, and changing track conditions such as rain or shifting surface temperature. In VR this demand is heightened even further, since the player genuinely feels the car's position in space and must rely on peripheral vision just like a real driver, which also changes how they judge gaps between rivals during risky overtakes. Combined with supported wheels and pedal sets, the VR mode becomes one of the most faithful available ways to experience professional-level driving without real risk, and a number of professional drivers actually use the simulator for real training.

Thanks to a regularly updated car roster, seasonal series, and an active community, iRacing remains one of the pillars of PC sim racing, and VR support only strengthened its reputation as a simulator aimed at players willing to invest time in mastering every detail of driving. The absence of music during a race and the emphasis on the authentic sound of engines, tires, and collisions rounds out the pursuit of as faithful a motorsport experience as possible, in which VR is just one more step toward perfect simulation.

**Why play:** For players willing to invest time in mastering every detail of driving, iRacing remains one of the pillars of PC sim racing thanks to its car roster and active community, with VR only heightening the authenticity.

pc-vr__assetto-corsa.teaser: A precise simulator with licensed cars and tracks; VR sharpens your judgment of braking points.
pc-vr__assetto-corsa.article:
**Assetto Corsa** built a reputation as one of the most accurate racing simulators thanks to its finely modeled vehicle physics and licensed circuits and cars from real-world motorsport, on which the effort to recreate real car behavior as faithfully as possible clearly shows. Virtual reality support let players sit in the cockpit in a genuinely authentic way – tracking speed through the dashboard display with peripheral vision, naturally judging braking points through depth perception, and turning their head to check mirrors, none of which ever felt as natural on a flat monitor and which noticeably changed how the player perceives speed and the proximity of rivals.

The game offers a wide range of cars, from road models to full-blooded racing specials, and a set of tracks faithfully matching real circuits, which, combined with a VR headset and a supported controller or wheel, makes it one of the most popular titles among the sim-racing community, one willing to invest even in costly hardware. The modding scene has also added hundreds of additional cars and tracks over the years, helping Assetto Corsa maintain an active player base long after its original release, even after the arrival of newer competing simulators it still competes with today for the sim-racing community's attention.

The sound design of engines and tires, combined with a precise feel for driving, helped Assetto Corsa become a reference point for later sim-racing titles, including its own sequel. In VR mode, the difference between driving on smooth asphalt and a broken road surface stands out noticeably as well, since the player perceives the car's jolts spatially, not just through a screen. In VR it then offers one of the most convincing feelings of speed and control over a vehicle that the PC platform can offer in the racing simulator genre.

**Why play:** For its precise feel of driving and the noticeable difference between smooth asphalt and broken road surface, Assetto Corsa offers in VR one of the most convincing feelings of speed in the racing simulator genre.

pc-vr__microsoft-flight-simulator.teaser: A faithful reconstruction of the entire planet; in VR the pilot turns their head and judges distance.
pc-vr__microsoft-flight-simulator.article:
**Microsoft Flight Simulator** is one of the most ambitious simulators ever made – thanks to satellite data and cloud-based terrain processing, it offers a faithful reconstruction of the entire planet, which the player flies across in dozens of civilian and smaller aircraft, from small sport planes to airliners. Virtual reality support added a key dimension to this already exceptional project: a pilot can physically turn their head, track the instrument panel with peripheral vision, and judge the distance to the runway through natural binocular vision, which is far more intuitive for precise landings than looking at a flat monitor and significantly reduces the need to rely solely on instruments.

The depth of the simulation, from realistic weather through airport traffic to the finely modeled cockpits of individual aircraft, makes the VR mode an extremely demanding yet immensely satisfying experience for aviation fans, who find a far more natural way of controlling flight in VR. Watching the sky, clouds, and shifting lighting throughout the day feels far more convincing in virtual reality, since the player perceives the depth and scale of the landscape naturally rather than through a flat image, and the view down onto real cities and rivers reconstructed from real-world data, unfolding beneath the aircraft's wings on an unexpected scale, is just as powerful.

The addition of VR support was welcomed by the player community as one of the most significant steps in the simulator's history and cemented its reputation as the technological flagship of the genre, even though its high performance demands required players to have powerful computers to run the simulation smoothly in VR. Microsoft Flight Simulator in VR shows just how well large, data-driven simulations can combine with the immersion of virtual reality, and it remains a reference title for anyone interested in flying in virtual space.

**Why play:** For anyone interested in flying in virtual space, it is the genre's technological flagship, provided you have a powerful computer able to smoothly render the simulation in VR.

pc-vr__google-earth-vr.teaser: A three-dimensional map of the entire planet; a single hand gesture and you're flying over the landscape.
pc-vr__google-earth-vr.article:
**Google Earth VR** brought the well-known three-dimensional map of the entire planet into virtual reality, letting users literally stand on the summit of Mount Everest, fly around the Eiffel Tower, or look down on their own street from a bird's-eye view without ever leaving the living room. Instead of classic mouse-and-keyboard controls, the player physically reaches out to zoom in on a location, or uses simple gestures to fly over the landscape, turning the experience of browsing maps into genuine travel through space, where the user sets both the route and the speed of movement.

The application uses the same photogrammetric and satellite data as the desktop version of Google Earth, offering realistic three-dimensional models of cities, mountains, and oceans at a scale that feels far more intense in VR than on a flat screen, with a precision that photos or videos simply can't convey. The sense of height when looking down from a mountain summit or from a skyscraper window was, at the time of release, one of the most powerful demonstrations of what virtual reality can achieve even without traditional game content, and many users described their first experience as an almost physical feeling of vertigo, even though they were standing safely on the ground in their own living room.

Google Earth VR quickly became one of the most frequently recommended titles for new VR headset owners precisely because of its accessibility and immediate wow factor – it requires no gaming knowledge and can show within a few minutes why virtual reality is a unique medium. The absence of music, with only ambient environmental sounds present, further supports the impression that the player is truly standing in that place rather than merely watching a visualization, which holds equally true for the street noise of a big city and the silence of a high-mountain landscape. Even years later, it remains a symbol of how well VR suits the visualization of the real world.

**Proč hrát:** Because of its immediate wow factor and zero barrier to entry, it's one of the titles most often recommended to new headset owners, and a symbol of how well VR suits visualizing the real world.

pc-vr__tilt-brush.teaser: VR painting in space; you can walk around the artwork from all sides like a sculpture.
pc-vr__tilt-brush.article:
**Tilt Brush** turned virtual reality into a three-dimensional painting canvas – instead of a brush on paper, the user paints directly into the space around them using the controllers, with dozens of brushes available ranging from a classic watercolor stroke to light, animated, or particle effects that behave in space almost like living things. The resulting works can be walked around from every side and viewed from entirely new angles, which is fundamentally different from any traditional drawing experience on a flat screen, where perspective is forever fixed to a single viewpoint.

The tool quickly became one of the most iconic showcase titles of the early PC VR era, because within a few minutes it could convince complete newcomers of the point of virtual reality – creating a three-dimensional image with a mere movement of the hand felt magical and yet intuitive, without the user needing any prior artistic experience. The color palette, stroke transparency, and the ability to set your own reference photos as a backdrop gave the program professional uses beyond mere experimentation, from architectural sketching to character design. Artists around the world began using Tilt Brush to create presentations, concept sketches, and standalone works of art, which they then shared online, giving rise to an active community around VR creation.

Tilt Brush significantly influenced the perception of virtual reality as a creative tool rather than merely a gaming platform, and inspired a range of similar applications focused on 3D creation and sculpting in VR. The absence of any game objective or score paradoxically contributed to its popularity, since every user could set the pace and purpose of their creation entirely for themselves. Even after years, it remains one of the most frequently cited examples of how VR can serve artistic self-expression outside traditional gaming genres.

**Proč hrát:** For creative self-expression free of any gaming objective or score, Tilt Brush ranks among the most influential examples of how VR serves as a tool for 3D creation, not just a gaming platform.

psvr__astro-bot-rescue-mission.teaser: A first-person platformer in VR; turning your head reveals hidden paths.
psvr__astro-bot-rescue-mission.article:
**Astro Bot Rescue Mission** is a first-person platformer in virtual reality in which the player becomes both an observer and an active participant in the adventure of a small robot named Astro. The camera is fixed to the player's viewpoint, so instead of classic camera rotation, the player looks into the game's levels as if into miniature dioramas, and by turning their head reveals hidden paths, enemies, or collectibles tucked around a corner or overhead. Astro himself is controlled with a classic DualShock 4 controller, running, jumping, and gaining various abilities depending on the environment, from rocket boots through a grappling hook to a water jet used to put out fires or reveal invisible platforms. The individual worlds are thematically distinct – jungle, desert, icy plains, and volcanic terrain – and in each one the player gradually rescues scattered robot friends who hide behind the scenery or directly behind the player's back, turning the level design into a constant game of hide-and-seek.

The game arose as a full sequel to the smaller tech demo Robot Rescue and fully demonstrated how well traditional platformer design can be combined with the spatial awareness of VR. The graphics are colorful, clean, and technically very well polished, so the game ran smoothly even on a base PS4 without noticeable frame-rate drops. At the end of each world awaits a boss fight against a distinctive character, requiring a combination of classic controls and physically dodging attacks by moving the head. Cheerful music and sound effects round out a playful, relaxed atmosphere, providing a pleasant counterpoint to the more demanding and darker action titles available on the platform.

At release, the game was received by critics and players alike as one of the most convincing proofs that virtual reality doesn't have to be just a technological attraction but can be a full-fledged gaming medium with its own advantages. It laid the groundwork for the later Astro's Playroom, bundled free with the PS5, and subsequently for the standalone title Astro Bot. It still ranks today among the titles recommended to new headset owners as a first showcase of what PSVR can do, thanks to its accessible controls, thoughtful level design, and complete absence of any feeling of motion sickness.

**Proč hrát:** For accessible controls, thoughtful level design, and a complete absence of motion sickness, it's a title recommended to new PSVR owners as a first showcase of what the headset can do.

psvr__resident-evil-7-biohazard-vr.teaser: The entire Resident Evil 7 game, no shortcuts, in VR; the enemy could be anywhere around you.
psvr__resident-evil-7-biohazard-vr.article:
**Resident Evil 7: Biohazard VR** brings the entire main game into virtual reality without any compromises or cuts – the player can experience Ethan Winters's whole story from start to finish in first person directly in the headset. The game takes place in the dilapidated house of the Baker family in Louisiana, where the player explores dark corridors, solves simple puzzles, manages a limited supply of ammunition and healing herbs, and faces mutated family members and fungal monsters. In the VR version, all the tension is amplified by the fact that the player physically turns their head to see around corners, and enemies can appear literally anywhere in their field of view. The slower pace of the first hours, when the player mostly explores the house cautiously and conserves resources, feels much heavier in VR, since the distance provided by a screen no longer protects them, and the feeling of physical presence in the Bakers' house is almost constant.

Technically, this was an extremely demanding undertaking, because Capcom had to adapt not just the camera but also movement, combat, and environmental interactions so they would work in a full game packed with detail and stressful situations. The game offered several movement and aiming options, from smooth walking to teleportation and head-aimed targeting, so every player could adjust the settings according to their own tolerance for motion sickness. The sound design plays an even bigger role here than on a regular television – creaking floorboards, distant footsteps, or the character's breathing literally surround the player from every side, multiplying the atmosphere of gloom and claustrophobia.

After release, the VR mode became one of the reasons many players bought a PSVR headset at all, and it's still cited today as one of the most intense horror experiences virtual reality has to offer. The game significantly influenced how VR is approached for big-budget titles – it showed that a complete transfer of an entire game, not just a short demo, is both technically possible and desired by players. Even years later, Resident Evil 7 in PSVR remains a showcase of how strongly spatial perception can amplify fear and tension.

**Proč hrát:** For one of the most intense horror experiences VR has to offer, worth buying an entire headset just for it – it shows how strongly spatial perception can amplify fear and tension.

psvr__blood-and-truth.teaser: A linear action adventure set in the London underworld; weapons are held and reloaded physically.
psvr__blood-and-truth.article:
**Blood & Truth** is a linear action adventure set in London's criminal underworld, where the player, as former soldier Ryan Marks, tries to save his family from a gangster conspiracy. The game combines cover-based shootouts, stealth sections, and movement sequences, with the player's movement between positions handled through a quick teleport that minimizes the risk of motion sickness while preserving cinematic pacing. Weapons are held and reloaded physically using the Move motion controllers, so drawing a pistol from its holster or reloading a shotgun is just as important a skill as aiming itself. Between firefights, the player also passes through small puzzle sequences, such as manually picking locks, bypassing security systems, or piecing together torn documents, which momentarily slows the pace and lets the intricately modeled environments shine.

The London Studio team, previously known for series like SingStar, built a reputation with this title as the creator of one of the most cinematic VR experiences on PSVR. The story is told in the form of an action film with characters played by real actors, and the game moves smoothly between shootouts, chases, and calmer narrative passages. The graphics were among the technically most advanced on the platform at release, and the detailed depiction of London along with well-executed facial animation helped maintain the illusion that the player is truly part of an action movie. Short interludes in which the player assembles a firearm from individual parts with their bare hands became one of the most frequently mentioned tactile details of the game.

Critics and players alike praised above all how naturally the handling of weapons and cover in space translated into tense firefights, demonstrating that even a linear, heavily scripted action title can work better in VR than looser open-world concepts. Blood & Truth is today seen as one of the high points of the action-adventure genre on PSVR and a showcase of how cinematic storytelling can be combined with active gameplay.

**Proč hrát:** For a cinematically told, linear action story with natural handling of weapons and cover in space, it's one of the high points of the action-adventure genre on PSVR, where linearity works in the game's favor.

psvr__tetris-effect.teaser: Classic Tetris in a hypnotic audiovisual show that surrounds the player from all sides in VR.
psvr__tetris-effect.article:
**Tetris Effect** combines the classic gameplay of arranging falling blocks with a hypnotic audiovisual show that reacts to the player's every move. The basic rules of Tetris remain unchanged, but around them arises a world of colorful visuals, music, and sound effects that synchronize with the rotation and placement of pieces so closely that the game ends up feeling more like an audiovisual experience than a purely logical puzzle game.
