In the PSVR version, spatial perception amplifies this effect further – the player is surrounded by cosmic scenery, underwater worlds, or desert landscapes unfolding in every direction around the playing field. Every cleared line and every falling piece triggers its own sound and light effect, so the player is gradually building not just towers of blocks but the musical piece itself that accompanies a given level.

The creative team behind the game is led by Tetsuya Mizuguchi, known for music-driven action titles like Rez, which is evident in how strongly mechanics are tied here to rhythm and color. The game offers several modes, from classic survival to timed challenges to meditative modes focused on relaxation. It's precisely in VR that this meditative aspect shows through most strongly, since the feeling of immersion in the space around the playing field can induce an almost trance-like state of concentration, in which the player stops focusing on score and lets themselves be carried by the combination of music and colorful scenery.

Tetris Effect was received at release as one of the most original ways to revive a decades-old concept, and the VR mode was frequently mentioned as the best way to experience the game, since spatial immersion in music and light gave even the famously familiar seven pieces an entirely new meaning. The title proved that even an extremely simple game mechanic can gain a completely new dimension in virtual reality if supported by thoughtful audiovisual design. It's still considered one of the most pleasant and most relaxing puzzle experiences on PSVR.

**Proč hrát:** For the most relaxing and audiovisually richest way to experience a notoriously familiar puzzle mechanic, the VR mode is, according to many players, the best variant of Tetris Effect.

psvr__beat-saber.teaser: Slicing cubes with lightsabers to the rhythm of the music; an icon of VR as a real physical activity.
psvr__beat-saber.article:
**Beat Saber** is a rhythm game in which the player uses two light sabers, colored blue and red, to slice through blocks flying toward them in time with the music, while respecting the direction each block must be struck from and simultaneously dodging obstacles or ducking under walls. The game requires real physical movement of the arms, hands, and sometimes the whole body, so it quickly became one of the most frequently mentioned titles when it came to VR as a form of physical activity. On PSVR, controls are handled via Move controllers, whose position is tracked by a camera, which works reliably, though with somewhat less precision than later solutions on other platforms. The game offers several difficulty levels, from a slow pace for complete beginners to expert modes where blocks come at high density and the player must combine precise hits with quick full-body dodges.

The game originally emerged as a smaller project from an independent studio, and thanks to the viral spread of short gameplay clips became one of the best-known VR titles of all, even before it arrived on consoles. The soundtrack combines electronic music created specifically for the game with later expansions of licensed songs, which allowed the song library to keep expanding and kept the community active. The visual style is simple but effective – neon colors, pulsing environments, and precise synchronization with the music create the impression that the player is part of a music video, and even small deviations in hand movement are immediately visible in how precisely the saber slices the block.

Beat Saber became one of the few VR titles to cross over beyond the gaming community and be perceived as a fitness activity as well, evidenced by the fact that many players described real fatigue in their arms and back after longer play sessions. On PSVR, it let a large number of players experience a phenomenon they had previously only known from PC, and helped cement the headset's reputation as a device suited not just for sitting, but also for active movement in the living room.

**Proč hrát:** Thanks to rhythm-based action that also works as a real fitness activity and can properly tire out your arms and back after a longer session, Beat Saber ranks among the titles that made PSVR most famous.

psvr__moss.teaser: An adorable platformer in which you help the mouse Quill overcome obstacles as an invisible deity.
psvr__moss.article:
**Moss** casts the player as a silent guardian who, from a first-person perspective, watches over and influences the adventure of a tiny mouse named Quill in a fairy-tale, hand-painted world. Quill herself is controlled with an analog stick like in a classic third-person platformer, while the player simultaneously acts as a kind of invisible deity who can, using the Move controller, manipulate levers, move platforms, or temporarily control magical objects in the environment. This combination of two layers of control – direct control of the character and indirect influence over the world around her – is the core of the game's originality. Quill handles combat against goblins and other enemies herself with her own sword and acrobatic jumps, but the player often helps from behind by pinning an enemy in place with a magic field or opening the way to further progress, turning combat into the shared work of two participants.

The dioramas through which Quill moves are designed so the player feels they are looking into a real, tangible model of a medieval fantasy landscape full of moss, stone ruins, and glowing mushrooms. The visual style is detailed and cozy, the music supports a fairy-tale, at times melancholic atmosphere, and Quill's animation ranks among the most distinctive characters VR offered on PSVR – her expressions and gestures could evoke strong empathy in players, even though she doesn't speak a single word throughout the whole game. The player can also pet or greet Quill with a hand gesture at any time, and she reacts to these small gestures, which deepens the relationship between character and player in a way classic on-screen controls can hardly offer.

Moss was praised at release as one of the best proofs that VR need not be limited to first-person action experiences, but can also work as a thoughtfully designed narrative platformer with puzzles. Studio Polyarc built a reputation through the game as one of the most capable smaller teams in the scene, and the title became a model for later games that combine direct character control with spatial puzzles solved from an observer's perspective.

**Proč hrát:** For a thoughtfully designed narrative platformer with puzzles solved from an observer's perspective, Moss offers proof that VR doesn't have to be just about first-person action.

psvr__moss-book-ii.teaser: A continuation of the mouse Quill's story with new abilities, including slowing down time.
psvr__moss-book-ii.article:
**Moss: Book II** picks up directly from the story of the little mouse Quill and expands the original concept with new mechanics without abandoning the basic principle of the game, in which the player, viewing events as an observer, influences what happens in the diorama world while controlling the character herself with a classic gamepad stick. New, stronger magical abilities are added to the game, letting the player more actively intervene against packs of goblins and other enemies, move larger objects, or work together with Quill to solve more complex spatial puzzles that make even greater use of the diorama's height and depth than in the first game. A new time-slowing ability lets the player better coordinate helping Quill in the more hectic fights against multiple opponents at once, which, together with the more elaborate puzzles, raises the cooperation between player and character to a higher level than in the first game.

Visually, the game continues the cozy, hand-painted style of its predecessor, but the environments are more varied and technically demanding, which on PSVR meant noticeably higher hardware requirements than in the first title. The narrative continues in the same silent, gesture- and expression-led style, with Quill and the supporting characters communicating without words, and the player, as an invisible companion, gradually uncovering the broader context of a world that the first game only hinted at. The new environments also take the player into more expansive outdoor locations and towns, giving the series a sense of a bigger, more elaborate world.

Book II was received as proof that the concept from the first game still had room to grow, and the expanded gameplay mechanics were praised as a natural continuation of what the first Moss had suggested. On PSVR it was one of the last big exclusive titles to arrive still on the first generation of the headset, which places it in the role of a dignified conclusion to one of the platform's most beloved series and a demonstration of how far a combination of direct and indirect control can be taken in virtual reality.

**Why play:** For expanded mechanics that naturally build on the first game, this is a dignified conclusion to one of the most beloved series of the first generation of PSVR headsets.

psvr__farpoint.teaser: A sci-fi shooter with a rifle-shaped controller and smooth locomotion instead of the then-common teleportation.
psvr__farpoint.article:
**Farpoint** places the player on an unknown planet, sent to search for a missing research expedition, and has them face swarms of alien insects as well as small puzzles in more open, though still linearly guided, environments. The game was designed alongside a special peripheral controller shaped like a rifle, which combines two Move motion sensors into a single body, so aiming and reloading the weapon feels natural, much like real shooting. The player's movement across the planet is handled through smooth walking, which was a relatively bold step at the time of release, since many VR titles of that era relied on teleportation out of concern for motion sickness. The player gradually finds upgrades and alternative weapons, so the fight against swarming insects steadily gains tactical depth, even though the core of the game remains primarily action-focused and direct.

The visual side relied on expansive outdoor vistas with desert canyons, cave systems, and stormy skies, which was a demanding task for the VR hardware of the time, and the game therefore occasionally struggled with lower texture sharpness. The soundscape and tense music focused on building an oppressive atmosphere of loneliness on an alien planet, where the player never knows from where the next wave of enemies will emerge. Occasional detours from the main storyline lead to diary entries from the missing expedition, which gradually fill in the picture of what happened on the planet before the player arrived.

At the time of release, Farpoint was viewed primarily as a showcase title for the new controller, but it was also among the first larger sci-fi shooters to offer smooth movement on PSVR without significant motion-sickness issues for most players. The game helped show that specialized hardware can markedly improve the feel of aiming in VR, and it became one of the titles frequently mentioned in connection with the early era of shooting genres on PSVR.

**Why play:** For smooth movement without significant motion-sickness issues and a demonstration of how a specialized controller improves aiming in VR, Farpoint ranks among the first larger sci-fi shooters on PSVR.

psvr__rez-infinite.teaser: A cult music-action shooter where every hit forms part of the track; in VR it takes on a new dimension.
psvr__rez-infinite.article:
**Rez Infinite** is a modern reworking of the cult music-action shooter Rez from the early 2000s, in which the player flies through an abstract, wireframe digital space and shoots geometric enemies in time with electronic music, with every hit and sound becoming part of a track the game generates in real time. In the PSVR version this concept gains a new dimension, because the spatial perception of the wireframe world and the feeling of flying through abstract tunnels feel far more intense thanks to the headset than on a regular screen. The avatar character controlled by the player gradually transforms and expands along with the progress of the track, which visually symbolizes the connection between human consciousness and the digital space the player moves through.

Infinite additionally adds a brand-new, exclusive stage called Area X, created specifically for virtual reality, which further develops the original game's synthetic, minimalist aesthetic into a fully three-dimensional space. The visual style combines simple geometric shapes with intense color effects that react to the music, and it is precisely this synesthetic combination of sound, light, and movement that is the main reason the game is still cited today as one of the platform's strongest sensory experiences. The game also includes a special mode in which the Move controller in the player's hand vibrates in time with the bassline, so the sensation of the music literally passes through touch as well.

At release, Rez Infinite was received as proof that old, seemingly abstract game concepts can find entirely new justification in VR. Critics repeatedly praised how naturally the music-action mechanic connected with the headset's spatial perception, and the title became one of the reference points for discussions of how virtual reality can elevate a game's artistic side beyond a mere technical attraction.

**Why play:** For the way the music-action mechanic connects with the headset's spatial perception, it stands as proof of how VR can elevate a game's artistic side beyond a mere technical attraction.

psvr__wipeout-omega-collection-vr.teaser: A free VR expansion for the Wipeout racing series; from the cockpit it amplifies the sense of insane speed.
psvr__wipeout-omega-collection-vr.article:
**Wipeout Omega Collection VR** is a free expansion of the Wipeout Omega Collection that lets players race selected tracks of the futuristic anti-gravity series directly from the cockpit of their craft in the PSVR headset. The game retains the series' extremely high pace and demanding controls, where the player balances speed, collecting energy for weapons and shields, and precisely navigating turns on tracks that run through canyons, cities, and futuristic complexes. In VR mode, the cockpit view further heightens the sense of real speed and depth, as peripheral vision catches the blurring surroundings alongside the craft. Players can choose from several ships with different acceleration, handling, and durability characteristics, which, combined with the weapon- and defense-collecting mode, gives what looks at first like a purely racing game a tactical dimension of combat between pilots.

The collection combines remastered tracks and ships from several previous entries in the series, which on PSVR meant that players could for the first time experience a decades-old concept of anti-gravity racing in a fully stereoscopic spatial form. Technically it was one of the more demanding VR ports of its time, since the game's extreme speed placed high demands on frame-rate smoothness to avoid motion sickness, and the resulting solution was often cited as one of the best technically tuned on the platform. The series' characteristic electronic music accompanies the races in the VR version as well, and together with the feeling of sitting directly in the cockpit it creates the impression that the player is truly piloting a futuristic machine pushed to the limits of its capabilities.

Wipeout Omega Collection VR was received as one of the most convincing proofs that fast racing games can work better in VR than expected, provided the technical execution is up to standard. The title became a favorite showcase for demonstrating the headset's capabilities thanks to the combination of an iconic series, distinctive electronic music, and an intense sense of speed that cannot be fully replicated on a regular screen.

**Why play:** For the intense sense of speed, electronic music, and iconic series that a regular screen can never fully replicate, Wipeout Omega Collection ranks among the best showcases of what PSVR can do.

psvr__until-dawn-rush-of-blood.teaser: A rail shooter from a roller-coaster car through an amusement park; the rails spare your stomach.
psvr__until-dawn-rush-of-blood.article:
**Until Dawn: Rush of Blood** puts the player in the seat of a roller-coaster cart riding through a dark amusement park and the surrounding woods, with the player shooting from a first-person perspective at monsters and other threats emerging on either side of the track. It is a so-called rail shooter, where movement happens automatically along a predetermined track and the player focuses purely on aiming and survival, a concept that proved to be exceptionally well suited to early VR hardware thanks to minimizing the risk of motion sickness. The player shoots using Move controllers, and besides regular weapons can also collect upgrades and unlock alternative paths for the cart by managing to hit hidden targets placed along the track, which gives even this linear rail shooter a reason for repeat playthroughs.

The game loosely follows on from the atmosphere of the survival horror Until Dawn, borrowing its dark setting, masks of deranged clowns, and horror motifs, but instead of a branching story with decision-making it offers a purely action-driven, adrenaline-fueled ride full of sudden jump-outs and jump-scare moments. Sound design and the play of light and shadow are key to building tension, with spatial audio in the headset heightening the sense that danger can appear from any direction. The individual sections of track gradually move from an abandoned fairground into dark forests and underground spaces, so the game's atmosphere keeps sharpening as the ride progresses.

At the time of release, Rush of Blood was among the most frequently recommended titles for new PSVR owners who wanted to show the headset off to friends, since the combination of short, intense segments and simple controls made the game an ideal showcase experience. Even today it is cited as one of the best examples of how effectively a rail shooter can use VR to build a horror atmosphere without needing a complex movement system.

**Why play:** Thanks to short, intense segments and simple controls, it was a favorite choice for showing off PSVR to friends, and it remains one of the best rail shooters at building a horror atmosphere.

psvr__batman-arkham-vr.teaser: A detective spin-off from Rocksteady; instead of combat, you solve a mystery as Batman using gadgets.
psvr__batman-arkham-vr.article:
**Batman: Arkham VR** puts the player in the role of Batman himself, letting them explore, from a first-person perspective, a detective mystery tied to the disappearance of two close associates, with the game, instead of the classic combat of the Arkham series, focusing on slower, exploration- and puzzle-driven passages. The player uses Batman's gadgets, such as the batclaw or the forensic scanner, to analyze the crime scene, gather evidence, and uncover connections, which overall creates more of a detective experience than the action-driven, adrenaline-fueled ride the series was previously known for. Playing as Bruce Wayne, the player moves between several iconic locations well known to fans of the previous games, gradually gaining the ability to fire a Batarang or use the batclaw for quick movement, even though movement in the game itself is handled mainly through safe teleportation.

The short playtime is offset by an exceptionally strong sense of presence – the player can, for the first time, look into a mirror and see themselves as Batman, examine the Batmobile in detail, or the interior of the Batcave, moments that reviewers repeatedly praised as emotionally powerful precisely because of the virtual reality medium. The visual and sound design continues the dark, gothic aesthetic of the Arkham series, and the voice acting maintains the high quality fans were used to from previous entries. It is precisely this connection between a familiar world and a new first-person perspective that makes exploring even simple rooms an unusually powerful experience.

At release, Batman: Arkham VR was received as one of the best pieces of proof that licensed characters and worlds can offer an entirely new type of experience in VR – not just playing as the hero, but literally being the hero. The title became a frequently cited example of how even a short, seemingly modest game can leave a strong impression thanks to thoughtful work with space and first-person perspective.

**Why play:** For a short but powerful experience where you don't just play as the hero but literally are him, Batman: Arkham VR ranks among the most cited examples of what licensed characters can achieve in VR.

psvr__superhot-vr.teaser: Time in the game only passes when you move; a principle that feels perfectly natural in VR.
psvr__superhot-vr.article:
**Superhot VR** brings to virtual reality the original concept in which time in the game moves only when the player moves – stand still and the world around you freezes too, including flying bullets and attacking enemies. This mechanism, which on a regular screen worked as a clever puzzle of timing, becomes, in VR, a perfectly natural tool: the player physically leans away from bullets, dodges an enemy's fist, or catches a flying weapon in real time, with their own bodily movement directly dictating the pace of the action. Weapons are not limited to firearms – the player can also take down opponents with fists, katanas, or thrown objects, and after an enemy is hit, their weapon remains floating in the air, waiting for the player to physically take it in hand.

The visual style stays true to the original – purely white environments, red polygonal enemies, and black weapons create a minimalist yet unmistakable aesthetic that also turned out to be very easy on the eyes and undemanding on hardware in VR. The game is divided into short, intense segments in which the player gradually faces increasingly complex situations with more opponents and weapons, which, together with the slow-motion mechanic, creates the feeling of a filmic choreography of action scenes. After completing a level, the player can also replay a recording of their playthrough as a smooth action scene, one in which the slow motion disappears and everything they previously did step by step plays out at real speed.

At release, Superhot VR was almost universally received as one of the best proofs that mechanics originally designed for a flat screen can find a second, even stronger life in VR. The title became one of the most frequently cited examples of how well-connected player-movement design and game mechanics can create an experience that simply cannot be fully replicated in any other medium.

**Why play:** For a mechanic where time only flows with the player's movement and found an even stronger form in VR than on a flat screen, Superhot VR is one of the most frequently cited examples of flawless design.

psvr__persistence.teaser: A sci-fi horror on a degenerated ship with roguelite elements; the corridors are reshuffled after death.
psvr__persistence.article:
**The Persistence** places the player aboard a spaceship whose crew has been genetically degraded by unstable cloning following a crash, and sends them through dark, procedurally generated corridors, collecting upgrades and either avoiding or directly confronting mutated creatures. The game combines elements of survival horror with a roguelite structure – with each death, the ship's layout is partially rearranged, which keeps tension high even across repeated runs and prevents relying on a memorized route. The player can defend against the mutants not only with weapons but also through stealth and distraction tactics, gradually finding genetic samples and materials that let them upgrade their character's abilities at the ship's vending machines, from movement speed to resistance to attacks.

The player's movement around the ship is handled through a combination of smooth walking and teleportation depending on preference, which was a relatively advanced approach to solving VR motion sickness for its year of release. The cramped, oppressive corridors of the ship, full of flickering lights and metallic sounds, create a strongly claustrophobic atmosphere, heightened by spatial audio – footsteps and the breathing of enemies must be tracked by ear as well as by sight, since they often approach from behind or from the sides, outside direct field of view. The main antagonist, who relentlessly pursues the player throughout the ship, additionally cannot be killed by ordinary means, forcing the player to rely on hiding and fleeing rather than direct confrontation.

The Persistence was received as one of the more ambitious horror titles on PSVR thanks to combining roguelite elements with a full-fledged sci-fi story, a combination that was relatively unusual for VR games at the time. The game was later also released on traditional non-VR platforms, which only confirmed that the core game system was strong enough even outside the headset, but the PSVR version remains cited as the most intense and atmospheric way to experience the ship Persistence.

**Why play:** For fans of sci-fi horror with a roguelite structure, where you never know what's lurking around the corner – the experience is most intense in VR, though the game works well outside the headset too.

psvr__statik.teaser: You solve puzzles by feeling a box you can only see in VR; from the creators of Little Nightmares.
psvr__statik.article:
**Statik** is one of the most unusual puzzle games for PlayStation VR, because it combines virtual reality with a physical box-shaped controller that the player holds in hands cuffed behind their head. In the headset, they see a virtual version of this box, but they manipulate it with their real hands – searching by touch for switches, dials, panels, and locks that are often not directly visible, forcing the player to uncover them blindly or by rotating the whole box. This principle, which studio Tarsier Studios, later known primarily for Little Nightmares, built on the contrast between what the player sees and what they feel in their palms, makes Statik an experience that couldn't be replicated without VR.

The game is divided into a series of standalone box puzzles, each with its own mechanics and visual style – from simple combination locks to more complex spatial puzzles requiring simultaneous rotation of the box and watching the image in the headset. The atmosphere is restrained and somewhat melancholic, accompanied by quiet music and a subtle narrative about the main character trapped in a strange institution, whose story is gradually revealed between levels. Technically, it was a modest but precisely tuned production that ran stably on PSVR without major demands on the console's performance.

At release, Statik attracted attention as proof that PSVR could offer game ideas that simply aren't possible outside virtual reality, because the necessity of tactile searching for switches whose location the player can only guess creates a tension that ordinary puzzle games could never achieve through a controller in hand. The shorter playtime is offset by the intensity of the experience and the feeling that the player is truly discovering the solution with their hands, not just their eyes, and that every solved box is a small personal victory over an unknown mechanism. To this day it remains among the titles frequently cited as an example of the original use of a physical peripheral controller in combination with a VR headset, and as a reminder that sometimes a simple idea taken to its logical conclusion is enough to create an experience that can't be confused with any other game on the platform.

**Why play:** For players seeking original puzzle experiences where you feel around for unknown switches with your hands – the shorter playtime is offset by the intensity and the sense of genuine discovery.

psvr__thumper.teaser: The creators call it rhythm violence; a metal beetle on rails where every impact creates the music.
psvr__thumper.article:
**Thumper** is a rhythm action game that its creators at studio Drool describe as rhythm violence – the player steers a metal beetle hurtling along a curved track and must, in precise time with the music, perform dodges, slams into turns, and jumps over obstacles, or else crash and lose energy. Unlike classic rhythm games, where the player reacts to a notation displayed on screen, here the music is generated almost in sync with what's happening on the track – every impact, turn, and jump creates a sound and bass accent, so the game and soundtrack merge into one continuous stream of tension. The tempo gradually accelerates and the levels grow in complexity until the game demands an almost meditative concentration and learned reflexes.

In the PSVR version, this already-intense game gains an additional dimension, because the spatial perception of the rapidly approaching track and the dark, metallic aesthetic amplify the sense of real speed and pressure. The visual style is dark, industrial, and minimalist, with sharp contrasts of light and shadow that feel far more urgent in a headset than on a flat screen. The audio – deep bass, metallic grinding, and wailing effects – is the core of the whole experience, and the game deliberately uses it to evoke physical tension, almost discomfort, which the creators described as part of the intended impression.

Thumper was received at launch as one of the most original attempts to combine a rhythm game with intense action and a test of reflexes, and the VR version was often cited as the most powerful way to experience the game, precisely because of the spatial immersion in speed and dark atmosphere that a classic screen can't match with the same physical urgency. The game influenced later rhythm titles by showing how deeply music can be organically tied to game mechanics, and it is still cited today as an example of how VR can amplify even seemingly simple game rules, provided the entire audiovisual design is built from the start with the player's spatial perception in mind.

**Why play:** For fans of rhythm games craving adrenaline, where music and reflexes merge into one – spatial immersion in VR gives the pace a physical urgency that a flat screen can't offer.

psvr__firewall-zero-hour.teaser: A tactical 4v4 shooter with no respawns; a single death ends the round for that player.
psvr__firewall-zero-hour.article:
**Firewall Zero Hour** is a tactical multiplayer shooter designed specifically for PSVR and the Aim controller, in which two teams of four players face off in short, intense rounds – one team attacks and tries to hack a computer, the other defends it. Each round is one-shot and without respawns, so a single death means the end of a player's participation in that round, forcing players toward cautious advances, slow movement between cover, and careful listening for the footsteps and sounds of enemies hidden around the corner. The rifle-shaped Aim controller, which can be swapped for various models of long and short weapons, gives aiming a physical precision that standard Move controllers never offered, and became one of the main reasons the game felt so convincing.

Maps set in warehouses, office buildings, or city streets are designed with an emphasis on multiple access routes and hidden nooks, which encourages tactical play based on communication between teammates and correct positioning of forces. Technically, it was one of the most ambitious multiplayer shooters on the platform – the game had to handle synchronization of movement, aiming, and voice communication among four to eight players in real time, which places high demands on the VR hardware of the era. Audio plays a key role, since the spatial sound of footsteps and gunfire often decides who survives the first exchange of fire.

Firewall Zero Hour was received at launch as one of the most convincing proofs that a full-fledged competitive multiplayer could work in VR, provided it's supported by a quality peripheral controller. The game maintained an active player community after release thanks to regular updates and new maps, and it remains frequently cited as one of the best tactical experiences PSVR has to offer, even though its tense, slow pace isn't for everyone.

**Why play:** For players seeking a serious tactical multiplayer in VR with an active community and regular updates, even though the slow, tense pace suits more patient team players.

psvr__ghost-giant.teaser: As a ghost giant, you help a lonely boy in an adorable, miniature seaside town.
psvr__ghost-giant.article:
**Ghost Giant** places the player in the role of a huge, invisible ghost who becomes friends with a lonely boy named Louis in a small coastal town full of adorable inhabitants wrestling with their own worries. In the game world, the player is literally a giant – seeing the town and its inhabitants as a miniature diorama that they reach into with their hands, lifting little houses, moving objects, opening doors, or helping Louis solve small tasks and overcome everyday troubles. The interactions are designed to feel gentle and playful – the player can literally lift the town closer to their eye to examine a detail, or lean down to chat with the little characters at their level.

The visual style combines a fairy-tale, soft art design with a sensitive story about loneliness, loss, and family relationships that gradually unfolds as the player progresses through the town. The voice of the giant ghost, who advises and encourages Louis, gives the game an emotional center of gravity that goes beyond mere puzzle mechanics, and gentle music accompanies the calm, contemplative pace of the game. Interactions based on physical hand movement using Move controllers feel surprisingly natural, and the player quickly learns to perceive the town as a living, tangible object that they can handle carefully or playfully, depending on the situation.

Ghost Giant was praised at launch primarily for its sensitive story and unusual sense of scale, in which the player acts as a huge but kind guardian of a small world, whose tiny gestures of care carry real weight within the story. The game became one of the examples of how VR can serve calmer, emotionally focused stories rather than just action or horror experiences, expanding the idea of which genres can work on a headset. To this day it is praised as one of the warmest and most welcoming games on PSVR and is often recommended even to players who are wary of typical action VR titles.

**Why play:** For players craving a calm, emotionally driven story instead of action or horror – the unusual sense of scale and the kind care for a tiny world make it one of the warmest games on PSVR.

psvr__marvel-s-iron-man-vr.teaser: Flight and combat controlled by hand movement as repulsors; one of the best flight systems in VR.
psvr__marvel-s-iron-man-vr.article:
**Marvel's Iron Man VR** gives the player the feeling of truly becoming Tony Stark in his armor, because the game's flight and combat system is designed precisely around the movement of the Move controllers, which the player holds in outstretched arms like repulsors. Tilting and rotating the hands controls flight speed and direction, pulling the trigger fires energy blasts, and combining both movements allows for acrobatic maneuvers while evading enemy missiles and drones. This control scheme, which initially requires some getting used to, becomes remarkably convincing once mastered and is often cited as one of the best flight systems in VR altogether.

The story follows the film mythology of Iron Man but is told through its own original plot set after the events in which Tony Stark left the weapons industry, pitting him against a new threat tied to his own past. Missions take place in various environments, from open ocean areas to dense urban canyons, alternating between fast action battles and slower passages of exploration and gathering upgrades for the armor. The visual presentation is top-notch on PSVR, with generous vistas and explosive effects that feel very cinematic during intense battles against multiple opponents.

The game was received at launch as one of the best exclusive titles of PSVR's late lifecycle and is often cited as proof that a superhero experience can work better in VR than on a classic screen, precisely thanks to the physical sensation of flight and aiming with one's own arms. Studio Camouflaj, previously known mainly for the smaller title Republique, built a reputation through Iron Man VR as the creator of one of the most ambitious and elaborate VR experiences on the platform. Even years later, the game remains frequently cited as one of the titles that best demonstrates why motion controllers can be more convincing for the feeling of flight than any analog joystick.

**Why play:** For superhero fans craving the feeling of true flight and aiming with your own arms, which a classic screen never achieves with the same conviction.

psvr__sairento-vr.teaser: Ninja action with katanas and bullet-time jumps between rooftops; teleportation as parkour.
psvr__sairento-vr.article:
**Sairento VR** is a fast-paced action shooter inspired by ninja and cyberpunk aesthetics, in which the player moves through the environment using a combination of shooting, katana combat, and acrobatic parkour – double jumps, wall-running, and slowed-down bullet-time falls. Movement is based on teleporting between points in the environment, but unlike ordinary, static teleportation, here the player often jumps or leaps from rooftop to rooftop, creating a sense of dynamic, acrobatic movement rather than mere point-to-point hopping. Combat combines firearms held in both hands with katanas and shurikens, and the game actively rewards an aggressive, fast play style with precise headshots and combinations of dodges and counterattacks.

The environments draw on a futuristic, neon-lit city full of robotic and human opponents, and the level design is built to encourage vertical movement – rooftops, walkways, and high platforms require the player to actively use jumps and parkour abilities. The visual style is stylized, with an emphasis on striking effects during slowed-down time, which the player activates during a jump in order to aim more precisely at multiple targets at once. This slowed-time system combined with acrobatic movement is the core of the game's identity and sets it apart from most of the more static VR shooters of the era.

Sairento VR started as a smaller, independent project, but thanks to its inventive combination of movement and combat, it earned attention as one of the most action-packed and fastest games PSVR has to offer. The game showed that even with limited resources, a full-fledged action experience with its own distinctive identity can be built on console VR, and it is still sought out today by players who want to experience virtual reality with a sense of speed and martial arts that most slower, more cautious titles don't offer. For players seeking an intense challenge, Sairento VR remains one of the few titles on the platform where near-constant movement and acrobatics are a necessity, not just an optional embellishment of gameplay.

**Why play:** For players seeking intense, fast action with acrobatics and martial arts instead of slower, more cautious titles – an independent project that proved a full-fledged VR experience can be built with limited resources.

psvr__job-simulator.teaser: A comedic parody of past jobs played by robots; a classic for VR newcomers.
psvr__job-simulator.article:
**Job Simulator** is a comedic simulation in which the player, in a future run by robots, experiences a parody of everyday jobs of the past – working in an office, in fast food, in a store, or in a garage – with the robots performing these professions as a museum-style reconstruction with a thoroughly exaggerated, comedic take on human behavior. Using the Move controllers, the player manipulates objects with complete freedom – they can staple papers, mix coffee, serve burgers, or repair cars, and the game almost always allows for a completely absurd, nonsensical use of objects without blocking progress. It is exactly this freedom and tolerance for experimentation that made the game one of the most frequently demonstrated titles for new VR users, since simple physical interactions like grabbing a cup or throwing a paper ball made immediate sense without any need for instructions.

The game's humor is based on an exaggeratedly grotesque take on office and service environments, with robots commenting on the player's behavior parodying clichés about work life with exaggeration and self-indulgent playfulness. The visual style is colorful, simple, and stylized so that in-game objects are easily recognizable and graspable, which also helped the game run smoothly on the PS4 hardware of the time. Short tasks in each environment can be repeated freely without strict goals, so the game functions more as a playful sandbox for experimentation than as a linear challenge.

Job Simulator was received at launch as one of the most accessible and most entertaining introductions to virtual reality altogether, thanks to which many people tried a VR headset for the first time. Studio Owlchemy Labs built a reputation through the game as a creator of intuitive, humorous VR experiences, and the title was long used as a standard demo game to showcase PSVR's capabilities to newcomers to virtual reality.

**Why play:** For anyone just discovering virtual reality – an accessible, humorous, and intuitive introduction that was long used as the standard demo for PSVR's capabilities.

psvr__everybody-s-golf-vr.teaser: The friendly Clap Hanz golf series, where swinging the Move controller genuinely controls the ball's flight.
psvr__everybody-s-golf-vr.article:
**Everybody's Golf VR** brings the relaxed, friendly golf series by Clap Hanz into virtual reality and lets the player physically mimic a golf swing using the Move controller, which functions as a virtual club. The swing of the arm, the speed of the stroke, and the angle of impact directly affect the ball's flight, so the game requires genuine movement coordination rather than just pressing a button at the right moment, as was typical of the series' previous entries on classic screens. The player plays through several courses with varying terrain, weather, and difficulty, while the series retains its typically lighthearted, welcoming tone without requiring deep knowledge of golf rules.

In its VR form, the game gains authenticity from the fact that the player watches the ball from their own eyes directly at the tee or on the green, which helps in better estimating distances and terrain slope than a classic on-screen view. The visual style continues the series' colorful, friendly aesthetic with distinctive characters and sunny, relaxing course environments, complemented by soothing music that underscores the game's non-aggressive, laid-back atmosphere. At the same time, the physical arm movement with every swing gives playing golf in VR an unexpectedly active, almost sporty dimension, distinct from more passive sports titles on a classic console.

Everybody's Golf VR was received as one of the most accessible sports titles on PSVR, suitable both for experienced fans of the series and complete newcomers, who appreciated that the physical arm swing works intuitively without lengthy learning and without frustration from inaccurately read movement. The game showed that even a traditionally calmer sports genre can offer a refreshing, physically active experience in virtual reality without losing its original, undemanding and welcoming character. For many players it became a favorite casual game they return to for short, relaxed rounds between more demanding action titles on the headset.

**Why play:** For players seeking a short, relaxed round of golf between more demanding action titles – the intuitive arm swing works without lengthy learning and appeals to experienced players and complete newcomers alike.

psvr__dreams.teaser: Media Molecule's creation tool, where in VR you sculpt games and worlds directly in the air around you.
psvr__dreams.article:
**Dreams** is above all a creative tool and platform for making games, animations, and interactive experiences, in which players can use Move controllers to sculpt their own models, program game logic, and assemble complete levels without writing a single line of code. PSVR support adds a new dimension to this creative process — the creator can step directly into a work-in-progress world, sculpt objects at real-world scale around themselves, and judge spatial compositions in a way a classic screen view could never offer. In this mode the Move controllers act as the sculptor's virtual brushes and tools, letting the player shape forms directly in the air with a movement of the hand.

Outside of creation mode, Dreams also offers a vast library of games and experiences made by the community, many of which can likewise be played in PSVR, meaning that the content available for the headset keeps expanding through the players' own work rather than the developer studio's alone. Media Molecule, previously known for the LittleBigPlanet series, built on its long tradition of shared-creation tools and, in Dreams, brought it to an exceptionally open and technically ambitious result. It is precisely this openness of the system and the ability to share and play others' creations that makes the scope of content practically unlimited, dependent only on the community's activity.

Upon release, Dreams was hailed as one of the most ambitious attempts at democratizing game creation, and its VR support was seen as a natural extension that brings the creative process closer to the feeling of actual sculpting and building. Given the practically unlimited amount of user content, playtime in Dreams is a matter of how much community creation a player is willing to explore, and the title remains one of the most open and longest-lasting tools PSVR has to offer. Even years later, Dreams is cited as an example of how far you can go when a game-creation tool is designed with full regard for spatial perception and the physical movement of the creator's hands.

**Why play it:** For creative players willing to spend dozens of hours sculpting and building in VR — the practically unlimited amount of community content makes Dreams one of the most open tools on PSVR.

psvr__concrete-genie.teaser: You bring wall paintings to life with a magic brush; the VR mode pulls you directly into the picture.
psvr__concrete-genie.article:
**Concrete Genie** is a story-driven adventure about a boy named Ash who uses a magic brush to bring paintings to life on the walls of the decaying harbor town of Denska, and with their help drives back the darkness that has spread through the city. The core game is played on a standard screen, but PSVR offers a separate, supplementary game mode in which the player finds themselves directly inside one of Ash's paintings and can freely interact with the colorful creatures from his artwork in a fully three-dimensional, painted space. In this mode, the player uses the Move controllers to paint strokes of light and color directly into the air around them, bringing to life small, playful beings reminiscent of the adorable creatures from the main game.

The visual style continues the bold, colorful art design of the core game, where dark, gray wall surfaces contrast with vivid, fantastical paintings full of animal and plant shapes. The VR portion is deliberately designed as a calmer, contemplative addition to the more action-oriented main story, focusing chiefly on free-form creative play and observing the creatures' reactions to the player's brushstrokes. The music and sound design evoke a dreamlike, fairy-tale atmosphere that matches the game's overall gentle and optimistic tone.

The VR mode of Concrete Genie was received as a pleasant, if brief, extension of the experience of the core game, one that showed how even a non-essential, supplementary VR passage can let a player physically look around and experience an artistic world they would otherwise only observe from a distance on screen. For fans of the main game, it's a welcome bonus that underscores the whole title's creative, artistic theme and lets the player briefly become part of the painting they had previously only watched. PixelOpus, Sony's internal studio focused on experimental projects, used this add-on to show that even a smaller VR passage can meaningfully enrich a game's storytelling without needing to offer dozens of hours of its own content.

**Why play it:** For fans of the main game looking for a welcome bonus on top — the short VR mode lets you physically explore an artistic world you'd otherwise only watch from the sidelines of the screen.

psvr__no-man-s-sky.teaser: A procedural galaxy played entirely in VR - base building and walking on alien planets.
psvr__no-man-s-sky.article:
**No Man's Sky**, since the update that brought PSVR support, offers the ability to explore a practically unlimited, procedurally generated universe directly from a first-person view in the headset, including landing on alien planets, gathering resources, building bases, and piloting spacecraft. VR support isn't limited to a brief demo but covers the entire game — a player can complete the main story campaign in virtual reality, build extensive colonies, and pilot ships and exosuits, with all controls adapted for either the Move motion controllers or the standard DualShock, according to preference. The feeling of standing on the surface of an unknown planet and observing alien flora and fauna at a one-to-one scale is often cited as one of the strongest reasons to try the game in VR, even though it's the same content the game offers outside the headset as well.

Technically, this was an extremely demanding transition, because No Man's Sky was designed as a vast, open game with long play sessions, which for VR brought challenges related to maintaining a smooth frame rate and comfort during extended play. Hello Games offered several movement options, including teleportation as well as smooth walking, so players could choose an approach suited to their own tolerance for motion sickness. Space combat, ship landings, and walking on planetary surfaces in the headset create a sense of scale and depth that, on a regular screen — even though the game looks visually the same — simply cannot be fully replicated.

After VR support was introduced, No Man's Sky was cited as proof that even an extremely vast, previously controversially received game can gain a second wind thanks to later updates and a new platform. Given the procedurally generated, practically endless universe, playtime remains open-ended and depends on how long a player is willing to keep exploring, which has made No Man's Sky VR one of the most expansive and ambitious VR experiences available on PSVR.

**Why play it:** For players willing to lose themselves in a procedurally generated universe for dozens or even hundreds of hours — VR support gave a once controversially received game a second wind.

psvr__star-wars-squadrons.teaser: Fighter duels from the cockpit of both an X-wing and a TIE fighter; a campaign told from both sides of the conflict.
psvr__star-wars-squadrons.article:
**Star Wars: Squadrons** is a space combat simulator in which the player sits in the cockpits of iconic Star Wars starfighters, such as the X-wing or the TIE fighter, and with full PSVR support experiences battles from the pilot's point of view, surrounded by control panels and a view of the surrounding chaos of battle. The game offers a campaign told from the perspective of both warring sides of the conflict, the New Republic and the Imperial remnants, and supplements it with an extensive competitive multiplayer mode, in which teams of pilots fight in large-scale, tactical battles that require managing power between weapons, shields, and engines. Controls can be handled with a standard controller or a flight stick, while VR adds the ability to physically look around the cockpit and track opponents with peripheral vision, which significantly improves situational awareness during fast maneuvers.

The visual and audio presentation faithfully follows the aesthetic of the film series — the sound of proton torpedoes, the roar of laser cannons, and the characteristic beeping of onboard systems create an exceptionally authentic sense of presence in a starfighter's cockpit within the headset. The cockpits of the individual ships are modeled in detail and are functional, so the player can track damage, shield status, and power distribution directly on the onboard displays in front of them, which in VR reinforces the feeling of actually piloting the machine. Battles take place across varied environments, from open space to fields full of asteroids and ship wrecks, which add visual depth and tactical hiding opportunities to the combat.

At launch, the game was hailed as one of the best space simulators of recent years, and its full VR support on console, not just on PC, was praised as an unusually generous move for a budget-priced title. Star Wars: Squadrons has become one of the reference points in discussions of how well VR can enhance the feeling of sitting in a cockpit and physically piloting a spacecraft, and for Star Wars fans it was one of the most authentic ways to become a pilot in the galactic conflict.

**Why play it:** For fans of Star Wars and space simulators craving the feeling of sitting in a starfighter's cockpit — full VR support on console is an unusually generous move for a budget-priced title.

psvr__borderlands-2-vr.teaser: The complete Borderlands 2 in VR; aiming weapons with your own hand adds a new dimension.
psvr__borderlands-2-vr.article:
**Borderlands 2 VR** brings the complete content of the beloved loot shooter Borderlands 2, including the main campaign and most of its expansions, into virtual reality on PSVR, with the player moving through the planet Pandora in first-person, collecting ever more powerful weapons with procedurally generated properties, and fighting hordes of bandits, mutants, and robotic enemies. Firefights gain intensity in VR thanks to physically aiming weapons with the Move controllers and the ability to freely look around the battlefield, which adds a new tactile dimension even to routine skirmishes in a game with such a strong emphasis on collecting and upgrading an arsenal. The game systems remain faithful to the original — the player chooses from several distinct characters with specific skills and abilities and progresses through a lengthy story full of the series' characteristic, sarcastic humor.

Converting such a large game to VR required adjustments to both movement and the user interface — inventory and weapon-stat menus are displayed on virtual panels in front of the player, and movement through the world can be handled with either smooth walking or teleportation, according to preference. The visuals were only slightly adjusted compared to the original game, so the title retains the series' characteristic hand-drawn, comic-book style, but it was technically challenging to keep a stable frame rate during more hectic battles with many enemies and effects at once. Pandora's expansive world, with dozens of hours of side quests, remains complete in the VR version, making it one of the most content-rich titles available for the headset.

Borderlands 2 VR was received as an ambitious, if technically demanding, attempt to bring a full-length, long game with a vast world into virtual reality, rather than a shorter experience tailor-made for VR. For fans of the series, it was a way to experience the beloved world of Pandora from a completely new perspective, and the title still ranks among the most extensive action games that can be played on PSVR from start to finish.

**Why play it:** For fans of the series wanting to experience the world of Pandora from a new perspective — a technically demanding but ambitious port of a vast, long game rather than a shorter experience tailor-made for VR.

psvr__doom-vfr.teaser: A fast VR spin-off from Doom (2016); teleport movement and brutal close-range finishers.
psvr__doom-vfr.article:
**Doom VFR** is a standalone VR spin-off of the rebooted 2016 Doom, set in the same complex of the UAC Martian mining facility shortly after the outbreak of the demonic invasion, in which the player takes on the role of a digitized consciousness of a facility employee and faces hordes of demons with fast, aggressive gunplay. Movement is handled mainly through teleportation between points in the environment, which was a common approach to addressing motion sickness at the time of release, but the game supplements it with the ability to quickly close the distance to enemies for effective close-range finishers, similar to the brutal execution animations from the core game. The pace of combat remains fast and aggressive, with an emphasis on constant movement between cover and switching weapons depending on enemy type, though overall combat is somewhat slower and more cautious than in the non-horror version of the game outside VR.

Visually, the game draws directly on the environments and enemy design of the core Doom game, with a bloody, dark aesthetic of Martian complexes and hellish portals, which feels considerably more intense and oppressive in the headset thanks to spatial awareness of attacks coming from multiple directions. The sound design relies on heavy, aggressive music and noise effects characteristic of the series, which in VR further heighten the tension while advancing through the facility's dark corridors. The shorter playtime compared to the core game is offset by the intensity of individual encounters and the need to decide quickly whom and how to attack, since VR lacks the easy overview that a classic screen offers.

At release, Doom VFR was received as a solid, if more intimately scaled, attempt to bring the iconic series' fast, aggressive action into virtual reality, and it was especially praised for how well the combination of teleportation with close-range finishers worked to keep the game's pace up. For Doom fans, it was a way to experience the Martian facility and the hordes of hell from a completely new, immediate perspective, and the title is still cited as one of the more technically accomplished attempts to bring fast FPS action to VR on PSVR.

**Why play it:** For Doom fans wanting to experience the Martian facility and the hordes of hell from an immediate perspective — a more intimately scaled but technically accomplished port of fast FPS action to VR.

psvr2__horizon-call-of-mountain.teaser: The PSVR2 launch showcase from Guerrilla Games; free climbing on rocks and archery.
psvr2__horizon-call-of-mountain.article:
**Horizon Call of the Mountain** was a launch title for PlayStation VR2 and from day one served as the flagship showcase of what the new headset can do. The player doesn't take on the role of Aloy, but rather a former prisoner named Ryas, who journeys across overgrown ruins, mountain ridges, and valleys inhabited by mechanical creatures from the world of Horizon. The core of the gameplay is free climbing across rock faces, overhanging structures, and old ruins, where the player decides for themselves where to reach with a hand and how to find the next handhold, giving movement a physical sense of effort and height. The second pillar is archery — arrows are physically pulled from a quiver on the back, nocked onto the bow, and drawn by the player's own hands, making combat against the mechanical enemies one of the most natural-feeling shooting experiences virtual reality has to offer.

On the technical side, the game fully leverages the high resolution and HDR of the PSVR2 display to showcase expansive landscapes full of vegetation, bodies of water, and the series' characteristic mechanical monsters. Haptic feedback in both the headset and the Sense controllers rounds out the atmosphere — the player feels vibrations while climbing a rock face, when an arrow hits its target, or in the proximity of a dangerous creature, and the adaptive triggers create real resistance when drawing the bow. The music follows the tone of the main series, and together with the sweeping vistas it creates a sense of genuine adventure, not merely a brief technological demo.

At launch, the game was praised by critics and players alike as proof that a full-fledged AAA VR experience on console is possible, and many reviews recommended it as the very first title for new headset owners. To this day it holds its position as one of the best introductions to PSVR2 — offering a satisfying length, varied environments, and a sense of epic scale without requiring prior knowledge of the main Horizon games, and it remains a beloved showcase of what climbing and archery can be in virtual reality.

**Why play it:** For new PSVR2 owners looking for a first title to try out the headset — a satisfying length, varied environments, and climbing combined with archery require no knowledge of the main Horizon games.

psvr2__gran-turismo-7.teaser: A free VR mode turned GT7 into the feeling of sitting in a cockpit among hundreds of cars.
psvr2__gran-turismo-7.article:
**Gran Turismo 7** received a free update shortly after the launch of PlayStation VR2 that added a full-fledged VR mode to the extensive racing simulation, with no need to buy a separate game. The player sits in the cockpit of one of several hundred licensed cars and, for the first time on console, can genuinely look around the track, turn their head into a corner, or catch oncoming rivals out of the corner of their eye. The core of the game remains the same as in the regular mode — collecting and tuning cars, the career mode, the GT Café with gradually unlocked challenges, and online races — VR mode primarily concerns the driving itself, where the sense of speed and spatial depth increases dramatically.

Technically, this is one of the most demanding VR titles on PSVR2, because Polyphony Digital had to adapt the finely detailed cars and tracks from the regular game to stereoscopic rendering and the high frame rate needed for comfortable VR driving. The reward is an unusually strong sense of presence in the cockpit — the dashboard, rearview mirrors, and steering movements all feel convincing, and together with support for wheels and pedals it creates one of the most realistic racing experiences on the market. The engine sound and surrounding traffic, heightened by the headset's spatial audio, give even well-known tracks a new dimension.

Gran Turismo 7's VR mode was received at launch as one of the strongest arguments for buying a PSVR2, because it combines the content depth of a full racing game with the immediate feeling of driving from a first-person perspective. Reviewers and players frequently noted that this mode was the first time they truly felt the real scale of the track and the speed of driving in a way a flat screen never could, even though longer VR sessions can be limited for more sensitive players by eye strain. Even with the passage of time, this mode remains valued as an example of how well an existing, extensive game can be complemented with VR without any compromise to content, and it ranks among the titles recommended to new headset owners as a first stop.

**Why play it:** For racing fans craving the feeling of real speed and track scale from a first-person perspective — the content depth of a full game with no compromises, even though longer sessions can tire the eyes of more sensitive players.

psvr2__resident-evil-village-vr-mode.teaser: The whole Village free in VR; turning your head around corners cranks up the tension a notch.
psvr2__resident-evil-village-vr-mode.article:
**Resident Evil Village VR Mode** brings the entire main story of Resident Evil Village into virtual reality as a free update for PSVR2 owners, without shortening the plot or the playtime. Players once again step into the skin of Ethan Winters, who is trying to save his daughter from a cult worshipping a mutated entity in a snowy Central European village surrounded by castles and underground complexes. In VR, exploring the village, Lady Dimitrescu's castle, and the underground laboratories becomes a much more personal experience — the player physically turns their head to see around corners, aims weapons with their own hand, and enemies can appear literally anywhere in their field of view, which significantly heightens the tension compared to playing on a screen.

Capcom adapted movement, aiming, and environmental interactions for the VR mode so they would work in the brand-new perspective without losing the pace of the more action-heavy sections for which Village is known compared to the series' previous entry. It offers several movement options, from smooth walking to teleportation, so every player can adjust the settings to their own tolerance for motion sickness. Spatial audio plays an even bigger role here than on television — creaking floorboards, distant growls, or a sudden roar from around a corner surround the player from every side, making the village's dark, gothic atmosphere feel much heavier.

After release, the VR mode became one of the main draws for PSVR2 owners and was cited as one of the most intense horror experiences on the platform. It showed that even a large, more action-oriented game full of boss fights can work just as well in VR as more intimate titles, and many players reported replaying the game through the VR mode even though they had already finished it on a screen. To this day it remains one of the most cited reasons to get the headset in the first place, and together with the Resident Evil 4 VR mode forms a pair of titles recommended to new PSVR2 owners as the first choice for trying out the horror genre.

**Why play:** For horror fans and those who have already finished the game on a screen — the VR mode offers one of the most intense experiences on PSVR2 and is among the first choices for trying out the headset.

psvr2__resident-evil-4-vr-mode.teaser: The famous RE4 remake free in VR; reloading and aiming for weak points is now down to your own hands.
psvr2__resident-evil-4-vr-mode.article:
**Resident Evil 4 VR Mode** is a free update to the Resident Evil 4 remake that brings agent Leon Kennedy's entire long campaign into virtual reality on PSVR2. Players once again make their way through the eerily quiet Spanish village infected by the Las Plagas parasite, fight fanatical villagers and mutated bosses, and escort Ashley Graham to safety — but now with their own hands instead of an on-screen controller. Reloading weapons, opening the inventory case, or aiming at enemies' weak points become physical actions in VR, which makes the famous merchant system and the legendary battles with villagers in the opening village feel even more intense than in the original remake.

Technically, this was a very demanding conversion, since Capcom had to adapt a remake designed for classic controls and camera framing into a full stereoscopic perspective without losing the atmosphere or the pace of its action sequences. The game offers several movement and aiming modes so players with varying tolerance for motion sickness can handle it. The intricately modeled village, chapel, and underground laboratories feel far more claustrophobic in VR thanks to spatial perception, and spatial audio — from a distant bell tolling to an enemy's breath around the corner — amplifies the tension the Resident Evil series is known for.

After release, the VR mode was received as one of the most ambitious efforts on PSVR2, since it offered a complete, dozens-of-hours-long game instead of a short demo, and it was free to everyone who already owned the remake. Reviewers and players alike called it one of the most intense ways to experience the remake, since physically reloading and manipulating the inventory add a fresh sense of tension even to scenes players already knew by heart. It is still cited today as proof that even a large action game with many fights and boss battles can work completely naturally in VR, and together with the Resident Evil Village VR mode it stands among the flagship demonstrations of what PSVR2 can do in the survival horror genre.

**Why play:** For remake owners who want to experience it again as a complete, dozens-of-hours-long VR game for free — physically reloading and handling the inventory add fresh tension to scenes you already know by heart.

psvr2__synapse.teaser: Telekinesis instead of running – one hand shoots, the other lifts enemies and hurls them around.
psvr2__synapse.article:
**Synapse** is a PSVR2-exclusive action shooter built on an unconventional idea — instead of controlling the character's movement in the classic way, the player uses telekinesis to lift enemies, the environment, and projectiles into the air and manipulate them directly with their hands. The character, an agent trapped inside his own mind, fights his way through a surreal, fragmented landscape made of shattered memories, and combat plays out with the player shooting a weapon with one hand while lifting cover, barrels, or the enemies themselves with the other, hurling them at the ground or into each other. This combination of two simultaneous actions — aiming and telekinetic manipulation — creates gameplay that would be difficult to realize outside of VR.

The game makes heavy use of the Sense controllers' adaptive triggers and haptic feedback, letting players feel the difference between a light release of telekinetic force and full concentration needed to lift a heavier object. The visual style combines dark, industrial environments with abstract, dreamlike passages that reflect the protagonist's disintegration, complemented by intense electronic music underscoring the tension of each encounter. The level design is structured as a sequence of compact arenas where the player must quickly switch between taking cover, lifting objects, and shooting, making the game a fast, intense experience rather than a sprawling adventure.

Synapse was among the first exclusive titles built specifically for PSVR2 and was praised for its original use of the motion controllers in a way that goes beyond ordinary aiming and grabbing objects. Reviewers highlighted that controlling shooting with one hand and telekinetic manipulation with the other simultaneously demands an unusual level of focus and coordination, setting the game apart from most classic VR shooters where the player mainly works with a weapon. Studio nDreams, which has a number of VR titles to its name, used it to show how the console's new hardware opens up mechanics impossible on classic flat screens, and the game earned a reputation as one of the technically most interesting showcases of both the headset's capabilities and the Sense controllers' adaptive triggers.

**Why play:** For players looking for an unusual challenge for both hands at once — simultaneously shooting with one hand and manipulating telekinesis with the other demands a level of coordination classic VR shooters don't offer.

psvr2__firewall-ultra.teaser: The sequel to Firewall Zero Hour; tactical 4v4 shootouts with a single life per round.
psvr2__firewall-ultra.article:
**Firewall Ultra** is a PSVR2-exclusive tactical multiplayer shooter and a direct sequel to the popular Firewall Zero Hour from the headset's previous generation. Players split into two four-person teams, attackers and defenders, where one side tries to capture and hack a secured laptop while the other defends it for the entire round — rounds are short and tense, since a single fatal hit means that player is out until the next round. The emphasis on a slower, tactical approach, team communication, and using cover instead of running blindly makes the game more of a thoughtful take on classic tactical shooters than fast arcade action.

In the PSVR2 version, the game uses precise Sense controller tracking for realistic weapon handling and aiming, including physically looking down a sight or leaning out from behind cover, and the adaptive triggers provide different resistance depending on the weapon type. The map environments, from abandoned industrial zones to dockside warehouses, are designed with plenty of narrow corridors, windows, and hidden paths that encourage cautious movement and ambushes. Spatial audio plays a key role — footsteps, doors opening, or a weapon being unholstered can be heard from every direction, and experienced players use them to gauge an opponent's position before they even see them.

Firewall Ultra continued its predecessor's reputation as one of the most seriously crafted VR shooters and was received as proof that even a competitive multiplayer genre can work on PSVR2 with enough depth for long-term play. Players who spent dozens of hours in Firewall Zero Hour and were looking for a smoother, more technically advanced sequel especially appreciated the improved visuals and more precise controller tracking compared to the first generation of the headset. The combination of tactical pacing, physical weapon handling, and well-designed maps makes it one of the top choices on the platform for players seeking a competitive experience with a higher degree of strategic demand than faster arcade shooters.

**Why play:** For Firewall Zero Hour veterans looking for a smoother, more technically advanced sequel with more precise controller tracking — the tactical pace suits players with strategic patience.

psvr2__kayak-vr-mirage.teaser: A calm rowing simulation; a paddle in both hands drives your kayak through fjords and whitewater alike.
psvr2__kayak-vr-mirage.article:
**Kayak VR: Mirage** is a calm sports simulation in which the player sits in a kayak and propels themselves forward with genuine, physical paddling motions held in both hands via the Sense controllers. The game offers free-roaming trips through landscapes full of fjords, caves, and quiet lakes, as well as racing courses with gates and time limits, and whitewater sections where you need to angle the kayak correctly and use the current's power instead of fighting against it. The paddling itself is designed to match real technique — the player alternates strokes on each side, brakes with a reverse stroke, and leans their body to keep balance, making the game a mild form of physical activity at the same time.

On PSVR2, the game benefits from sharp visuals and a wide field of view to bring out the intricately crafted landscapes — from calm Nordic fjords to tropical lagoons — and reflections of light on the water's surface that change smoothly with the time of day and weather. Haptic feedback on the controllers simulates the paddle stroke hitting the water as well as impacts against rocks or rapids, which helps sell the feeling that the player is actually steering the vessel rather than watching an automated motion. The audio side relies on ambient nature sounds, splashing water, and distant birdsong, together creating a meditative, relaxing atmosphere distinct from most of the more action-oriented titles on the platform.

Kayak VR: Mirage was received as a pleasant demonstration that PSVR2 doesn't have to serve only adrenaline-fueled and horror experiences, but also calmer, almost wellness-oriented activities. Many players also appreciated the game as a form of light exercise, since repeated paddle strokes over a longer session genuinely work the shoulders and back, which is rather the exception among console games. Thanks to its simple yet physically satisfying paddling controls, it became a popular choice for relaxed play as well as a showcase of movement simulation that can be picked up in VR almost without any learning curve, and it is often recommended to people who are just starting out with virtual reality and looking for an easy, low-stress way into the platform.

**Why play:** For players looking for a calm, almost wellness-like activity instead of adrenaline — the simple paddling works as light exercise and makes for an easy entry into VR even for complete beginners.

psvr2__no-man-s-sky.teaser: The entire No Man's Sky universe in VR; scanning plants by hand and a cockpit view while flying.
psvr2__no-man-s-sky.article:
**No Man's Sky** offers full virtual reality support on PSVR2 for the game's entire vast universe, from exploring procedurally generated planets and building bases to piloting your own ship, interstellar travel, and multiplayer expeditions with other players. Players can physically look up at a sky full of unknown constellations, reach out a hand to scan plants and creatures, or glance over their shoulder in the cockpit while flying through a planet's atmosphere, adding an entirely new dimension to exploration even years after the base game's release. Mining resources, crafting equipment, trading at stations, and fighting pirates in space remain unchanged, but the spatial perception of the scale of planets, ships, and stations in VR greatly strengthens the feeling that the player is truly present in a huge, living universe.

On PSVR2, the game uses improved resolution and eye tracking to deliver sharper visuals of distant objects and smoother transitions between menus and the game world, which matters a great deal in such a vast game with so many systems. The Sense controllers' adaptive triggers and haptics respond to mining with a laser, firing handheld weapons, and the impact of a ship landing, making the routine activities a player performs for dozens of hours feel less repetitive. Ambient music and the sounds of different biomes, from stormy wastelands to calm ocean planets, together with a sense of spatial depth, heighten the feeling of solitude and exploratory excitement the game is known for.

VR support on PSVR2 was received as one of the most natural expansions of the game, since it requires no separate version or content restrictions — players can switch between VR and standard play at any time. No Man's Sky therefore stands among the titles that demonstrate how well an existing large-scale game can be complemented by full VR support without compromise, and it remains one of the most extensive experiences available on the platform.

**Why play:** For PSVR2 owners wanting a vast space experience without compromise — smoothly switching between VR and standard play makes No Man's Sky one of the most extensive offerings on the platform.

psvr2__star-wars-tales-from-galaxy-s-edg.teaser: Droid ND-3 on Batuu straight from the Disney parks; blaster, lightsaber, and both episodes in one edition.
psvr2__star-wars-tales-from-galaxy-s-edg.article:
**Star Wars: Tales from the Galaxy's Edge - Enhanced Edition** casts the player as the droid ND-3, who tries to help the local inhabitants of the outlying planet Batuu — familiar from Disney's theme parks — while avoiding the First Order and other dangerous factions. Gameplay combines exploration of atmospheric locations, simple puzzles, handling a blaster and a lightsaber, and interacting with characters and creatures well known to Star Wars fans, from porg-like critters to bounty hunters and stormtroopers.
