Its short playtime goes hand in hand with the high replayability of individual attempts, so players easily find reasons to return for another and another run in pursuit of a cleaner, more precise performance, and this replayability is the main reason the title is still talked about in the score-chasing community today.

**Why play it:** If you're looking for a less hectic but precisely tuned vertical shooter with fluid action and a moody electronic soundtrack, Shienryu is a solid choice even today.

saturn__guardian-force.teaser: A horizontal shmup where the ship can aim in multiple directions; run-and-gun elements and multi-phase bosses.
saturn__guardian-force.article:
**Guardian Force** is a horizontal shooter whose Saturn port arrived on the console late in its life as a conversion of an arcade original. The game departs from the classic shmup formula in that the player's ship can aim in multiple directions at once and carries hints of run-and-gun action, requiring careful reaction to enemies approaching from various angles of the screen, not just from the front, and quick switching between several weapon types depending on the situation. Levels are punctuated by massive bosses with several combat phases, placing emphasis on memorizing patterns and gradually refining strategy across repeated playthroughs, with some sequences even requiring the destruction of smaller parts of a boss's body separately before its vulnerable core can be exposed.

Technically, Guardian Force ranks among the more solid genre conversions on Saturn — the action stays smooth even with large numbers of enemies and projectiles on screen, the graphics are detailed and richly colored, with striking explosions and mechanical enemies. The soundtrack rounds out the intensity of the battles with an energetic, electronically tinged score typical of the late 1990s. The game had a limited release and remained practically unknown outside Japan, which today makes it a sought-after collector's title among import players. Among genre fans it is prized specifically for its unconventional multi-directional aiming system, which lends an otherwise genre-traditional shooter a distinctive strategic dimension rarely seen in competing titles, and it still plays today like an interesting, lesser-known departure from the established formula. The combination of carefully designed boss fights and the need to think about multiple directions of fire at once makes Guardian Force a title that rewards patience and repeated play just as much as quick reflexes, and even after all these years it offers an experience that a typical horizontal shmup usually doesn't.

**Why play it:** For collectors of import titles and shmup fans alike, thanks to its unconventional multi-directional aiming system, which lends the game a distinctive strategic dimension beyond the genre average.

saturn__gokujou-parodius.teaser: A comedic Gradius spin-off from Konami; parody characters and bosses spoofing other games.
saturn__gokujou-parodius.article:
**Gokujou Parodius** is a Saturn port of Konami's popular arcade shooter, which builds its parodic, comedic tone on the Parodius series, itself a spin-off of the seriously-toned space shooter Gradius. The player chooses from a colorful cast of characters and craft — from traditional fighters to parody forms of animals, mascots, and even a mermaid — and makes their way through colorful, humorously conceived levels full of references to other games and pop culture. The core gameplay, however, remains honestly shmup-based: collecting power-ups from the iconic capsule menu, building a formation of support objects called Options, and battling outlandishly designed bosses that parody enemies from the studio's more famous games and beyond.

The Saturn version handled the technically demanding, color-and-effect-packed arcade original reliably, with smooth action and a faithful reproduction of the cheerful visual style and catchy, melodically varied soundtrack that draws on classic Konami motifs as well as parodic nods to other musical genres. Reception in Japan, where the game was released, was warm — the Parodius series has long enjoyed popularity among Japanese players precisely because of its combination of solid gameplay and lighthearted humor that never slides into cheap parody at the expense of playability. It remains a beloved demonstration that a demanding, readable shmup doesn't have to be seriously toned, and among collectors and genre fans, Gokujou Parodius holds a reputation as an entertaining, accessible title that works even for players who otherwise don't care for classic shooters. Funny animations, exaggerated sound effects, and a constant stream of visual gags make it a great choice for two-player sessions as well, where the humor only multiplies, and many players still recommend it as the ideal first introduction to both the Parodius series and the shmup genre in general, since it's readable and never feels frustrating.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its cheerful visuals, catchy parodic soundtrack, and lighthearted humor that never comes at the expense of playability, it ranks among Konami's beloved, entertaining shmups.

saturn__raystorm.teaser: A vertical shmup from Taito; a combination of direct fire and homing lock-on lasers.
saturn__raystorm.article:
**RayStorm** is a vertical shooter from Taito and spiritual successor to the earlier-released Layer Section, whose Saturn version arrived in 1997 as a port of the arcade original. The player controls one of the fighters equipped with both direct fire and homing lock-on lasers capable of hitting multiple targets at once, including enemies on the ground beneath the aircraft — combining both types of attack is key to efficient progress as well as to a high score, since properly splitting fire between direct targets and locked laser targets can significantly cut down the time needed to clear the screen. Levels alternate classic vertical scrolling with passages in 3D perspective, where the player flies into the depth of the screen among industrial structures and giant enemy vessels.

The Saturn port had to contend, in technical terms, with demanding 3D sequences that pushed the hardware of the time to its limits, and the result is solid, if not flawless — in more hectic moments there's a noticeable slight drop in frame rate. Visually the game combines a stark, futuristic aesthetic with dense, electronic music that nicely underscores the pace of the action and lends the battles with giant bosses appropriate drama. It was released only in Japan, and among genre fans RayStorm is prized as one of the important milestones in the history of modern shmups, since it was here that the lock-on laser system, later widely copied by other titles, showed itself in its refined and balanced form. Even today it's considered one of the most technically and design-wise ambitious shooters of the 32-bit console generation, comparable to the parallel-released PlayStation version, and its influence can be seen both in the studio's later Taito titles that continued experimenting with the lock-on mechanic and in a whole range of other vertical shooters that later adopted a similar homing-fire system as a standard part of the genre's repertoire.

**Why play it:** For fans of genre history, RayStorm is an important milestone thanks to its refined lock-on laser system, even though its technically demanding 3D passages come with occasional slight slowdown.

psp__fight-night-round-3.teaser: The boxing series became famous for Total Punch Control — punches and blocks controlled by moving the stick.
psp__fight-night-round-3.article:
Fight Night Round 3 became famous mainly for its Total Punch Control system, in which attacks and blocks were controlled by moving the right analog stick instead of pressing buttons – this feature gave boxing bouts on home consoles a smoother, more physical feel than the button-based controls of earlier entries in the series and forced players to think about the direction and speed of a punch just as much as its timing, while the career mode offered a fighter's gradual rise from lower weight classes to title bouts, with training minigames between fights and a steady unlocking of new opponents and gear.

However, the PlayStation Portable version had to rework this cornerstone of the gameplay, because the PSP had only one analog control and no second stick needed for full motion-based punch control. EA Chicago therefore moved the controls back to buttons and the screen's face buttons, which brought the combat closer to the traditional scheme of older boxing games than to the system that made Round 3 famous on home consoles. The graphics were adapted to the handheld's lower power, with simpler textures, fewer arena details, a smaller crowd, and more limited facial damage animation suited to the handheld's small screen.

In terms of content, this was a simplified version with a smaller selection of modes and boxers, without the full online multiplayer that the home consoles offered via Xbox Live, since the PSP's networking capabilities were considerably more modest by comparison and it wasn't possible to play against opponents on other platforms. Still, for players on the go it was a solid way to play boxing away from home, albeit knowing it was more of a lightweight variant than a portable equivalent of the PS3 or Xbox 360 version with the same control system and the same depth of career mode, if with noticeably more modest audiovisual presentation matching the handheld's small screen.

**Why play it:** For players on the go, it's a solid way to play boxing away from home, even though it's more of a lightweight variant without the home consoles' full online multiplayer.

psp__burnout-dominator.teaser: The last Burnout before the open-world Paradise; a return to classic races and crashes.
psp__burnout-dominator.article:
Burnout Dominator from 2007 was the last entry in the series before the move to the fully open-world Burnout Paradise, and it returned to the classic structure of separate races, chases, and stunt sequences that Burnout grew up on. The game from Criterion Games built on crash battles with oncoming traffic, scored drifting, and the so-called Burnout mode, where accumulated energy temporarily boosts the car and triggers its own chain of destruction in heavy traffic. Compared to the previous entry, Burnout Revenge, the series returned to a somewhat more sober, less chaotic ride, but retained the series' typical emphasis on risk and reward for driving into oncoming traffic.

The PlayStation Portable version launched alongside the PlayStation 2 edition, but it had to account for the handheld's considerably weaker hardware and the lack of a second analog stick, which the PSP doesn't have – the camera and cornering therefore used a control scheme adapted to the single analog nub and buttons. The smaller screen and lower performance required simplified vehicle models, sparser traffic on the track, shorter draw distance, and more modest smoke and spark effects on impact, so the spectacular chain crashes typical of Burnout feel somewhat more contained on the PSP than on the PlayStation 2. On the plus side was portability – the game could be played anywhere, without a television and without connecting to a home console.

Content-wise, the PSP version stayed faithful to the original – the same cars, tracks, and game modes, just adapted to the handheld. Collecting points, unlocking new cars, and progressing through the individual race series worked the same as on the home console, so players effectively lost none of the game content. That made it one of the few entries in the series that players could take with them on the road and play, say, on a train or during a school break, before EA and Criterion abandoned portable versions of the series entirely with the arrival of Burnout Paradise.

**Why play it:** Anyone who wants classic Burnout on the go gets the same cars, tracks, and game modes on PSP as on the home console, without losing any game content.

psp__flow.teaser: Jenova Chen's meditative evolutionary arcade game based on flow theory; it arrived on PSP from PS3.
psp__flow.article:
flOw is a meditative game about a microscopic creature that dives ever deeper down a water column, devouring smaller organisms, avoiding larger predators, and gradually evolving into a more complex form. The game was designed by Jenova Chen as a student project at the University of Southern California, inspired by psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's theory of the state of flow, after which the game is named. In 2007, his new studio, thatgamecompany, reworked it into a downloadable form for the PlayStation 3, where it launched as one of the first titles on the then-new PlayStation Network. A year later, the same concept also appeared on the portable PSP console.

The PSP version keeps exactly the same core principle of the game – tilting the creature, descending into deeper and more dangerous layers, and transforming based on the food gathered – but it had to deal with the fact that the handheld has no motion sensors or vibration, on which the PS3 version's alternative control scheme built by tilting the SIXAXIS controller. On the PSP, only the classic analog stick remained, the visuals were adapted to the console's smaller screen, and the music and sound effects received minor adjustments due to the weaker speaker. Trophies were also missing, which the PS3 version later gained through a firmware update. Still, the overall feel of playing remained very similar – it's a short, visually clean experience that can be completed in under an hour, but one players liked to return to for its hypnotic pace and calming atmosphere.

The PSP release expanded the game's audience beyond the PlayStation Network environment on PS3 and showed that a simple, elegant concept holds up even on more modest hardware without the need for powerful graphics. For handhelds, it was an unusually artistic and non-commercial effort, the likes of which had barely appeared on the PSP before then. Together with the later ports to PS Vita, iOS, and eventually PC in 2013, the PSP release confirmed that flOw managed to reach players across platforms without having to give up its minimalist character.

**Why play it:** Fans of minimalist, meditative games will appreciate that the simple concept holds up even on the handheld's more modest hardware and delivers an experience just as elegant as the original.

psp__littlebigplanet.teaser: A platformer with the motto Play, Create, Share; Sackboy and levels made of cardboard, fabric, and string.
psp__littlebigplanet.article:
LittleBigPlanet is a platformer in which the main character, Sackboy, makes his way through colorful, hand-crafted levels built from real materials – cardboard, fabric, wood, string, and buttons. The character can be dressed in dozens of costumes and decorated with stickers collected while going through the campaign, and the physics engine gives jumping and swinging on ropes a pleasantly tangible feel. Alongside the campaign itself, the game offers a sophisticated level editor in which players can build their own levels, from simple jumping courses to complex machines, and share them with others – this made it a unique combination of game and creative tool for its time, summed up by the motto "Play, Create, Share." The entire campaign is also accompanied by warm, witty narration voiced by actor Stephen Fry, which gives an otherwise quiet platformer a distinctive English atmosphere.

The PSP version launched a year after the original on the PlayStation 3 and had to adapt the whole concept to a portable console with a single screen and considerably weaker hardware. It lacks four-player co-op on a single screen, since that couldn't reasonably fit on the handheld's small display – a fellow player joins only via a local wireless ad-hoc connection between two handhelds. Levels and gameplay elements relying on controller tilt via Sixaxis were also dropped, since the PSP has no motion sensor, so the controls rely purely on buttons and the analog stick. The level editor was retained, including the ability to build and upload custom levels, but in a more limited form matching the handheld's memory and performance, and the graphics were reworked for the smaller screen resolution. Despite these limitations, it was a functional and playable port that let fans take the creative platform with them on the road, albeit with a noticeably smaller scope than on the home console. Custom levels could also be uploaded and shared online from the handheld, so community creations were connected to some degree between PSP and PS3, even though both versions remained separate software with their own level catalogs.

**Why play it:** For players who want LittleBigPlanet on the go too, the portable version offers a preserved level editor, albeit without the four-player co-op and controller tilt of the PS3 original.

psp__echochrome.teaser: A minimalist puzzle game inspired by Escher — rotate the camera to connect impossible paths.
psp__echochrome.article:
echochrome is a minimalist puzzle game built on optical illusions in the style of M. C. Escher's drawings. The player rotates the camera around a featureless wireframe figure walking along impossible staircases, bridges, and corridors suspended in empty white space, and must find the viewing angle from which seemingly broken paths visually connect into a single walkable route. The game has no combat or time pressure; it's purely about gradually discovering how perspective can trick the eye and turn an impassable structure into a path to the goal. Visually, the game relies on complete minimalism – a purely white background, simple wireframe structures, and a quiet, meditative atmosphere without music that might distract the player from thinking.

The PSP version launched alongside the release on PlayStation 3 in 2008, so it's not a later port but a simultaneous release for both platforms from the very start. The key difference is in the controls – the PS3 version allowed the player to rotate the camera around the scene by tilting the Sixaxis controller too, which gave the game a pleasantly physical feel of connecting hand movement to camera movement, while the PSP has no motion sensor, so the player controls the camera solely with the analog stick and directional buttons, which, despite the lack of tilt, remains precise and quick to master. The graphics were adapted to the handheld's smaller screen and lower chip performance, but the puzzles themselves, the levels, and their order remained the same between both versions. For a game whose core rests purely on thinking about perspective and viewing angle, the absence of controller tilt removes one control input and changes the feel of playing, but it has no major impact on the actual difficulty and solving of the puzzles. Thanks to the PSP's portability, the game also suited occasional play in shorter sessions, while on PS3 it was more of a settled-in session in front of the TV with the controller in both hands. Both versions also share the same system of unlocking further sets of levels based on how many puzzles the player has already solved, so progression through the game remains equally structured on both platforms.

**Why play it:** Puzzle fans will be pleased that the PSP version launched alongside the PS3 version and offers the same puzzles and levels, just with the camera controlled purely by the analog stick instead of controller tilt.

psp__silent-hill-shattered-memories.teaser: A psychological reinterpretation of the first Silent Hill; therapy sessions change the game on the fly.
psp__silent-hill-shattered-memories.article:
Silent Hill: Shattered Memories (2009) was one of the series' most distinctive entries – it wasn't a remake of the first Silent Hill in the usual sense, but a psychological reinterpretation of it, in which the player underwent sessions with a fictional therapist between chapters, and the game dynamically adjusted the characters' appearance and the story's tone based on the player's answers and behavior. Instead of fighting monsters, the main emphasis was on fleeing and solving puzzles in a snowy alternate version of the town of Silent Hill, into which the player would slip each time they got closer to uncovering another part of the truth about the protagonist's missing daughter. The atmosphere was further shaped by the music of the series' longtime composer, Akira Yamaoka, who remained true to the series' characteristic industrial sound even in this reinterpreted take on the story.

The portable version for the PlayStation Portable arrived in early 2010, alongside the release for the PlayStation 2, a few months after the original Wii version. It had to do without the Wii Remote's motion controls, which were used on Wii to aim the flashlight and examine objects – on the PSP, this was replaced with controls via the analog stick and buttons, which meant the game lost some of the immediacy of the original controls, though it remained just as smoothly playable.

Due to the handheld's performance, the PSP version was the graphically most modest of all releases – lower screen resolution, simplified textures, and somewhat longer loading times were the price for letting players go through the whole story away from home, on the road, or without a connection to a TV. However, the key mechanic of tracking the player's behavior and the nonlinear narrative with the same possible endings were preserved, so despite the technical compromises, the PSP version offered the same psychological experience as the other versions. The escape sequences from monsters in the dark "other world" were also preserved, albeit with slower controls on the handheld's small analog nub than what motion-based aiming offered on Wii.

**Why play it:** Despite being the graphically most modest of all versions, the PSP version offers the same psychological experience and nonlinear storytelling as at home on the big screen.

ps2__ace-combat-04-shattered-skies.teaser: One of the first major aerial action games on PS2; the legendary rival Yellow 13 remains iconic to this day.
ps2__ace-combat-04-shattered-skies.article:
**Ace Combat 04: Shattered Skies** is one of the first major aerial combat games on the PlayStation 2, and it made full use of the new generation's graphical leap to render clouds, reflections on a fighter's fuselage, and vast combat zones stretching from the sea to mountain ranges. The player takes on the role of a pilot codenamed Mobius 1 and, across a series of missions over the fictional continent of Usea, fights on the side of the Federation of Ellador against the independent ISAF forces, gradually facing off against a legendary rival named Yellow 13, whose yellow fighters became an iconic symbol of the series. The gameplay is built on an arcade-style take on aerial combat: the player collects special weapons, completes side objectives for financial bonuses, and between missions spends earnings on new aircraft and upgrades, from more powerful engines to more accurate missile armaments.

The game's strong point is its storytelling, which doesn't unfold through classic command-briefing dialogue but through diary entries from a girl living in a country ravaged by war — the contrast between her civilian perspective and the player's role as an unnamed ace gives the campaign an unusual emotional dimension that aerial combat games of the time rarely offered. The orchestral score amplifies the sense of massive air battles and became a series hallmark carried into later entries, along with an emphasis on dramatic mission narration and wingmen chatter over the radio.

Contemporary reviews praised above all the smoothness and intensity of the air battles and the careful crafting of individual missions, which made this entry the foundation that Project Aces built all its later PS2 sequels on. This was the game that decisively moved the series away from its more modest beginnings on the original PlayStation and established it as one of the console market's flagship aerial action franchises. Even years later, the game holds up as an accessible, well-balanced arcade aerial action title that requires no knowledge of simulators, yet still delivers a satisfying feel of flying, maneuvering, and dueling an opponent still counted among the most memorable rivals in the entire series.

**Why play it:** For players wanting accessible, well-balanced aerial action without needing to know simulators, Shattered Skies is a great entry point — it offers smooth combat and an unforgettable rival that the creators built every subsequent PS2 entry upon.

ps2__ace-combat-5-unsung-war.teaser: Aerial action with command over your wingmen in battle; a strong focus on the politics and propaganda of war.
ps2__ace-combat-5-unsung-war.article:
**Ace Combat 5: The Unsung War** expanded the series' concept with an emphasis on teamwork — the player, a pilot codenamed Blaze, flies with the Wardog squadron and during missions issues radio commands to their wingmen, directing formations, assigning attack targets, and deciding whether they should cover the player's own aircraft or independently eliminate enemy targets. The story takes place in a conflict between Osea and Yuktobania and places greater emphasis on the political backdrop of the war, propaganda, and relationships between squadron members than earlier entries, as the player gradually discovers that the real enemy may not be where they first looked.

The gameplay stays arcade-style but adds deeper wingman management and more varied mission types, from escorting bombers to defending bases and night-time raid operations. The visuals pushed the series further with more detailed aircraft models and larger battle scenes featuring dozens of enemy and allied units in the sky at once, which on PS2 hardware required careful optimization to keep the frame rate stable even with large formations. Radio communication between pilots in flight gives the missions a cinematic pace and the atmosphere of a real war operation.

Upon release the game was received as one of the peaks of the series on PS2 and reinforced Ace Combat's reputation as a brand that can combine accessible arcade action with an elaborate story. This was helped by the scope of the story's cast and their fates, which make the campaign feel more like a war drama with airplanes than a sequence of isolated missions. The orchestral music again ranks among the game's strongest points, and many of its themes have remained fan favorites for years. Even now the game feels like one of the generation's most comprehensive aerial titles, though squadron control and the opening tutorial may initially feel less welcoming to today's players than more modern entries in the genre.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for aerial action with an elaborate story and an orchestral score whose themes have stuck with fans to this day will find Unsung War one of the peaks of the series on PS2, even though squadron control initially demands more from the player.

ps2__ace-combat-zero-belkan-war.teaser: A prequel to Ace Combat 04 with a moral choice between Knight and Mercenary that reshapes the story's fate.
ps2__ace-combat-zero-belkan-war.article:
**Ace Combat Zero: The Belkan War** serves as a direct prequel to Ace Combat 04 and tells the story of the Belkan War, which in the series' fictional world precedes the events of the first PS2 entry and is referenced there as a dark chapter of history. The player takes on the role of a mercenary pilot, and over the course of the campaign, through their behavior in combat and dialogue choices, aligns with the approach of either the Knight, who follows the rules of engagement and spares civilians, or the Mercenary, who pursues profit regardless of the consequences — this affects other characters' reactions as well as the story's ending, making it one of the few entries in the series with such a pronounced element of moral choice.

The combat system introduces what's called Ace Style, which gradually leans toward one of several styles based on the player's approach to combat — precise hits, defensive maneuvers, or aggressive close-range fire — unlocking different bonus abilities and special weapons. Visually, this is one of the most advanced entries on PS2, with a dense atmosphere driven by a darker narrative tone than earlier episodes, complemented by a striking orchestral score that heightens the drama of battles over the mountainous terrain of Belka and the tragedy of a civil war between former allies.

Within the series, Belkan War is often cited as one of the best-written entries thanks to its elaborate supporting cast of pilots and their fates, which retroactively tie into later games set in the same world. The narrative framework, in which journalist interviews with ace pilots from both sides of the conflict punctuate the individual missions, gives the whole campaign the feel of a genuine historical retrospective. For players coming from earlier entries, it offers a natural culmination of the storyline and stands among what pushed the PS2 generation of Ace Combat furthest in terms of storytelling, which is why it's still often recommended as one of the series' absolute peaks.

**Why play it:** For fans of the series, Belkan War is recommended as one of its peaks thanks to its elaborate cast of pilots and the journalistic narrative framework that gives the campaign the feel of a genuine historical retrospective.

ps2__naval-ops-warship-gunner.teaser: An action game where you design your own battleship yourself, from hull to armament; salvage upgrades your next mission.
ps2__naval-ops-warship-gunner.article:
**Naval Ops: Warship Gunner** is an action game from Koei in which the player doesn't just command a crew, but literally builds their own battleship — from the type of hull, through the propulsion system, to the placement of main turrets, secondary guns, and anti-aircraft armament on deck. The campaign takes place in an alternate history reminiscent of World War II, and the player goes through a series of naval battles where materials and technology salvaged from sunken enemy vessels feed directly into upgrading their own ship before the next mission, linking the combat and construction sides into a single loop.

This system of building and customization is the game's main draw — it combines real-time action control of the ship, where the player maneuvers between torpedoes and air strikes, with an almost RPG-like approach to managing equipment, which was a fairly unusual combination for a naval combat title on PS2. The graphical treatment of the sea surface, hit explosions, and the massive models of battleships lent the battles appropriate grandeur, even though the controls themselves remained more arcade than simulation, focusing on combat clarity rather than realistic sailing physics.

The game built a reputation among genre fans as a curious but enjoyable title precisely because of the freedom it gave in designing your own vessels to suit your playstyle, and it became the foundation for the sequel Naval Ops: Commander. The sheer range of available components also earned praise, letting players experiment with very different ship concepts, from fast patrol vessels to slow but extremely armored hybrids of battleship and aircraft carrier. Today it feels like an unusual but functional mix of building set and action that has few direct competitors on PS2, and it still appeals to players with a fondness for building and upgrading machinery between battles.

**Why play it:** Anyone with a fondness for building and upgrading machinery between battles will appreciate Warship Gunner as an unusual but functional mix of ship-building set and action that few other PS2 titles rival.

ps2__naval-ops-commander.teaser: A sequel to Warship Gunner with command of an entire fleet instead of a single ship; tactics over action.
ps2__naval-ops-commander.article:
**Naval Ops: Commander** follows up on Warship Gunner and shifts the emphasis from directly controlling a single ship toward commanding an entire fleet. The player builds and upgrades multiple vessels at once, plans their deployment across individual battles, and handles tactical decisions at the level of a whole squadron rather than focusing on a single battleship, pushing the game closer to tactical strategy with pronounced action elements instead of the pure action of the first title.

The ship customization system remains the core of the experience — the player still chooses weapons, armor, and technological upgrades for individual vessels according to the style they want to bring to the fleet, whether that's fast torpedo boats built for scouting and raids or heavy battleships built for long-range gun duels. The alternate-history war setting and monumental sea battles remain a constant of the series both visually and atmospherically, complemented by a broader strategic layer of decisions between missions, where the player must weigh what types of ships to even deploy for a given battle. Multiple ships fighting at once also demand more from the console's performance, so the game at times opts for a compromise between battlefield size and individual model detail, keeping the action readable even with a full fleet on screen.

For fans of the previous title, Commander offers a natural expansion of the concept toward a larger scale of warfare, though it moves somewhat away from the purely action-focused core of the first title and places greater demands on planning between missions. The shift from a single heroic ship to an entire fleet also changes the pace of play — individual battles take longer, and the player has to return to the fleet overview menu more often than to the action itself. Within the PS2 library it remains a more niche but distinctive entry for players who took a liking to combining shipbuilding with tactical decision-making at sea, and it can still be recommended today as a natural sequel for fans of the first game.

**Why play it:** For fans of the first game who want the combination of shipbuilding and tactical decision-making on a larger scale, Commander is a natural sequel, even though the pace slows due to more frequent planning between missions.

ps2__sky-odyssey.teaser: A flight adventure without emphasis on combat; rescue missions and precise landings amid scenic vistas.
ps2__sky-odyssey.article:
**Sky Odyssey** is an arcade flight adventure from Cross Company that sets itself apart from typical combat simulators by emphasizing exploration and scenery rather than combat. The player pilots historical propeller aircraft through varied environments inspired by real-world locations around the globe, completing tasks such as rescue operations, precision landings on hard-to-reach strips, or navigating through canyons and mountains, rather than shooting down enemies, of which the game features only a handful.

The emphasis on atmosphere and freedom of flight makes Sky Odyssey more of a meditative experience akin to later flight games like Pilotwings than a classic action flight simulator of its era. The graphical treatment of the landscape, weather, and lighting effects, such as sunlight glinting off water or fog drifting between mountain peaks, was among the ways the game demonstrated the graphical capabilities of the new console at launch, even though the actual range of available missions and gameplay options remains fairly limited, making the game more of a short but intense experience. The aircraft controls are simplified so as to convey the feeling of flight even to players with no experience of the genre, meaning the game can be played practically without a tutorial.

The game earned a small but loyal fanbase who appreciated its unconventional, non-confrontational take on a flying game on a console full of combat titles focused on war and rivalry. A scoring system for landing precision and smoothness of flight gives even seemingly free-form flying a clear goal and motivation to revisit individual sections again and again until the player manages to fly through them flawlessly. Today it plays as a pleasant, relaxed-paced diversion that shows the flight game genre on PS2 wasn't confined solely to military action, and it offers an interesting alternative for players looking for something different from Ace Combat.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for a calm alternative to combat flight games like Ace Combat will find in Sky Odyssey a pleasant, relaxing experience with a flight-precision scoring system that motivates you to revisit individual sections again and again.

ps2__secret-weapons-over-normandy.teaser: A World War II action flight game from LucasArts; aerial dogfights alternate with ground bombing missions.
ps2__secret-weapons-over-normandy.article:
**Secret Weapons Over Normandy** is a World War II action flight game from LucasArts, a follow-up to the earlier titles Battle of Britain and Secret Weapons Over Europe, this time brought to consoles with an emphasis on cinematic presentation and accessibility for a wider audience. The player takes on the role of pilot Chris "Wildcard" Wilson, and the campaign combines classic aerial dogfights with ground bombing and reconnaissance tasks, giving the missions greater variety than pure aerial combat alone, as the player gets to fly different types of aircraft within a single mission.

The game leans on accessible arcade controls and a fast mission pace, complemented by a narrated story with cinematic cutscenes that give the campaign a structure close to an adventure film about wartime pilots over World War II Europe. Models of historical aircraft, such as Spitfires, Messerschmitts, or bombers, as well as European battlefield environments, were rendered on PS2 with an emphasis on action clarity and smoothness even in moments when several enemy planes appear in the sky at once and the player has to quickly assess target priorities. Switching between aircraft mid-mission also forces the player to adapt their playstyle to the specific type of machine, from nimble fighters to slow but sturdy bombers.

Within the genre of wartime flight action games, the title was a solidly received entry that benefited from the LucasArts license and from Totally Games' experience with previous entries set in the same historical period. The sound design, with period ground-crew chatter and radio news broadcasts between missions, helped build the atmosphere of wartime Europe and was among the details reviewers praised at the time. Today it's an accessible entry point into the theme of World War II in the air for players who don't want to reach for a full-fledged flight simulator, and it still offers solid entertainment even with the passage of time.

**Why play it:** For players who don't want to reach for a full-fledged flight simulator, Secret Weapons Over Normandy offers an accessible and atmospheric entry point into World War II aerial combat action.

ps2__top-gun-combat-zones.teaser: Arcade flight action based on the Top Gun film; flashy maneuvers straight off the carrier deck.
ps2__top-gun-combat-zones.article:
**Top Gun: Combat Zones** is an action flight game built on the Top Gun film license, in which the player takes control of modern fighter jets and completes missions inspired by the atmosphere of the movie, from basic training aboard an aircraft carrier to full-on combat deployment in war zones around the world. The emphasis is on fast arcade aerial combat, where the player earns points for flashy maneuvers, precise hits on enemy aircraft, and completing secondary mission objectives, which helps them climb through the ranks of the squadron.

The game tries to carry over the film's distinctive atmosphere — the pilots' cocky one-liners, the rivalry over who's the top ace at the base, and fast, flashy dogfights full of maneuvering — into a playable form, even though the technical scope and mission variety reflect a more modest budget than the big flight series of the era, such as the rival Ace Combat. The controls stay simple and accessible even to players with no experience of flight games, and the game doesn't try to simulate real flight but instead offers a short diversion in the style of the movie's aerial chases.

In period reactions, the title was received as an average genre entry that traded mainly on the popularity of the movie brand rather than technical or gameplay ambition, and compared to the competition it felt more modestly produced, whether in terms of aircraft models, mission environments, or the more limited number of available planes. For many players it was nonetheless a gateway into the flight action genre, since the name Top Gun instantly evoked specific expectations, and the game tried to deliver on them at least in broad strokes. Today its value lies mainly as a curiosity for fans of the Top Gun film and collectors of licensed PS2-era games who want to see how a movie identity fared as a flight arcade game on a console a generation younger than the film it was based on.

**Why play it:** As a curiosity, Top Gun: Combat Zones will appeal mainly to fans of the film brand and collectors of licensed PS2-era games who want to see how the movie's identity translated into a more modestly produced flight arcade experience.

ps2__burnout.teaser: Racing where risk decides the outcome; oncoming traffic and drifting fill the Boost meter for turbo speed.
ps2__burnout.article:
**Burnout** was released on PlayStation 2 in 2001 and, from the very first moment, built on a simple but addictive idea: the more recklessly the player drives, the faster they reach the finish line. Instead of collecting weapons, money for engine upgrades, or licensed cars, the game offered pure driving on the edge — rewarding driving against oncoming traffic, close near-misses with cars coming the other way, and long drifts through corners. Every such risky moment filled the Burnout meter, and emptying it triggered a burst of turbo speed, letting the player overtake rivals in places ordinary driving never would. The game offered classic races, time-trial competitions, and one-on-one duels where courage and precision of driving mattered above all else.

On the PlayStation 2 hardware of the time, Criterion Games managed to conjure a strong sense of speed even without photorealistic graphics — blurring scenery, fading silhouettes of oncoming cars, and convincing-looking crashes gave the game a cinematic tension. Tracks ran through city highways, mountain switchbacks, and country roads, and were always laced with traffic that represented both the main threat and the main source of points. Engine sound, thumping music, and the commentator's voice heightened the sense of a rushed, nervous drive where a single mistake could turn a leading position into a pile of wreckage in an instant.

At the time of release, Burnout positioned itself as a fresh alternative to simulation-leaning racing series and showed that arcade racing could be built on risk instead of collecting upgrades. Although it was soon overshadowed by more polished sequels, it laid the groundwork for the principles Criterion kept building on for the whole decade that followed — reward for daring, an emphasis on flow and tension over car specs. Today the game will mainly appeal to players interested in the roots of a series whose fame arrived with its later entries, or to those who want to see what the arcade racing genre looked like right on the threshold of the new console generation.

**Why play it:** Anyone interested in the roots of the Burnout series will find in the first game a fresh arcade foundation built on risk instead of collecting upgrades, even though it was soon overshadowed by more polished sequels.

ps2__burnout-2-point-of-impact.teaser: The Burnout sequel debuts the Crash mode — smash as many cars as possible at an intersection.
ps2__burnout-2-point-of-impact.article:
**Burnout 2: Point of Impact** arrived on PlayStation 2 in 2002 and, compared to the first game, significantly sped up the pace and refined the system of rewards for risky driving. The Boost meter now filled up not only from drifting and driving against traffic, but also from close near-misses with rivals, which pushed the player to constantly probe the line between caution and reckless daring. A new addition that became one of the series' signature features was the standalone Crash mode, in which the player drove into busy intersections aiming to cause the biggest possible chain-reaction pile-up and rack up points for wrecked cars — a mechanic straddling the line between racing and a destructive toy that quickly became a beloved pastime in its own right.

Technically, the game pushed the series forward — a faster and smoother feeling of speed, more convincing collision physics, and more varied tracks, from coastal highways to snowy mountains. The graphics engine on PlayStation 2 handled high speed and dense traffic without major compromises, which was no small technical achievement at the time. The music and sound design continued to build the series' signature nervous atmosphere, where driving on the edge of a crash was rewarded rather than punished. Compared to the first game, it also added a wider selection of cars and tracks, making it feel richer and more varied in content.

Critics and players alike received Burnout 2 as a marked improvement over the first game, one that finally showed the full potential of a concept built on risk. The Crash mode became so popular that Criterion kept developing it in later sequels, and thanks to the second game the series itself began to establish itself as a distinctive alternative to Gran Turismo and Need for Speed. Even today, Point of Impact stands as a playable and entertaining proof that arcade racing doesn't necessarily need weapons or an open world to be fun — all it takes is daring, well-balanced risk, and a few busy intersections you can barrel into at full speed.

**Why play it:** For players craving arcade racing without weapons or an open world, Point of Impact is a playable proof that all it takes is daring, well-balanced risk, and busy intersections — this was the entry where the series fully showed its potential.

ps2__medal-of-honor-frontline.teaser: A World War II shooter that brought the Allied Assault style to consoles; the landing at Normandy.
ps2__medal-of-honor-frontline.article:
**Medal of Honor: Frontline** was released on PlayStation 2 in 2002 and was among the titles that brought console players a World War II first-person shooter experience similar to what Medal of Honor: Allied Assault had done on PC. The game guided an American soldier through several key moments of the Western Front, from the landing at Normandy through the French countryside to the fortifications of the occupied coast. The player advanced through linear, scripted levels, destroying machine-gun nests, taking out soldiers dug in behind cover, and completing sub-objectives such as sabotaging guns or rescuing allies, with the game placing more emphasis on cinematic pacing and atmosphere than on freedom of movement.

Technically, it was one of the more visually impressive titles of the early PlayStation 2 era — a richly detailed battlefield, dense gunfire, and explosions gave the battles a very convincing weight for the time. The music by composer Michael Giacchino deserved special mention, its symphonic, dramatic motifs heightening the sense of pathos and heroism, and it was among the most highly praised aspects the game offered. The controls were adapted for the gamepad, and despite the absence of the analog aiming typical of later shooters, the game played smoothly and clearly. The individual missions were also interwoven with short cinematic sequences that added urgency and drama to the story.

Frontline was very well received critically at the time of release and helped establish the war shooter genre as a solid fixture of console offerings, paving the way for further entries in the series as well as rival titles like Call of Duty. Today the game feels more like a linear, guided experience with an emphasis on atmosphere and music rather than a technically demanding shooter, but as a historical milestone of the genre and a reminder of the early era of console FPS games, it still holds value, mainly thanks to its unmistakable music and cinematically constructed missions.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for a historical milestone of the war-shooter genre with unmistakable music and cinematically constructed missions will appreciate Frontline as the title that paved the way for Call of Duty and other rivals.

ps2__medal-of-honor-rising-sun.teaser: The series heads to the Pacific for the first time; the war against Japan from Pearl Harbor to island jungles.
ps2__medal-of-honor-rising-sun.article:
**Medal of Honor: Rising Sun** arrived on PlayStation 2 in 2003 and, unlike previous entries in the series, shifted the story from the European battlefield to the Pacific theater of World War II. The player took on the role of an American soldier and moved through key moments of the war against Japan, including the attack on Pearl Harbor, jungle combat, and landings on islands occupied by the Japanese army. The gameplay stayed true to the concept of the previous entries — linear progress through scripted missions, destroying fortified positions, and completing sub-objectives — this time complemented by new environments such as dense tropical vegetation or ship decks. The series thus offered, for the first time, a look at the war in the Pacific, which was rather the exception amid the flood of Europe-focused World War II shooters of the era.

Technically, the game benefited from the experience EA Los Angeles had gathered on the previous entries — battlefields felt densely populated with enemies, the explosions and firefights had a brisk pace, and the music once again gave the individual missions a cinematic, dramatic edge. The Pacific theater's environments, from jungles to coastal bunkers, gave the series a visually distinct atmosphere compared to the European settings of earlier entries, setting the game apart from the rest of the competition, which was focused mostly on the Western Front. Even the sound effects of weapons and Japanese equipment tried to keep pace with the distinct character of the Pacific battlefield.

Rising Sun was received somewhat more mixed than the older entries in the series, with critics pointing to a smaller step forward compared to previous games and a certain repetitiveness in the missions, yet it still became a commercially successful title that expanded the series' thematic scope to the Asian theater. For players interested in early PlayStation 2-era war shooters, it remains an interesting glimpse into a period when the genre was still finding its footing on consoles, and a reminder of a time when Medal of Honor was among the genre's leaders, before it was dethroned by faster-evolving rival series.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the early era of war shooters on PlayStation 2, Rising Sun is an interesting glimpse into a period when the genre was still finding its footing, even if critics pointed to repetitive missions and a smaller step forward compared to previous entries.

ps2__onimusha-warlords.teaser: Feudal horror with fixed cameras à la Resident Evil, but with sword-based action instead of survival.
ps2__onimusha-warlords.article:
**Onimusha: Warlords** brought Japanese feudal horror to PlayStation 2, blending the combat system of action games with puzzles and survival-horror atmosphere. The player steps into the role of the samurai Samanosuke, who battles demons that have taken over a castle amid the civil war in 16th-century Japan, in order to rescue an abducted princess and uncover the fortress's dark secret. The combination of pre-rendered backgrounds, fixed camera angles, and a fluid combat system immediately evoked Resident Evil, though with a far more action-oriented, sword-based approach to combat, where enemies could be dramatically cut to pieces. The castle's claustrophobic corridors, dark courtyards, and underground dungeons created a sense of an enclosed, dangerous space where another wave of demons could be waiting around every corner.

The game is built around collecting the souls of defeated enemies, which the player uses to upgrade weapons, armor, and magical abilities, as well as solving simple puzzles while making their way through the castle and its surroundings. The graphics were among the best at the time of release — detailed characters set against painted backgrounds felt cinematic, and the atmosphere was rounded out by dense orchestral music and a tense sound backdrop full of distant screams and creaking. Onimusha: Warlords became one of the early major hits of the PlayStation 2's early era and kicked off a long-running and commercially successful series.

Period reviews praised above all the atmosphere and the blend of action with horror elements, even though the game itself was fairly short and could be finished in just a few evenings. Today the title holds up nicely as a showcase of the early PS2 generation, and its influence is evident even in later Capcom action games, including Devil May Cry. A later remaster showed that the concept still holds up even with the passage of time and can still pull the player into its dark feudal world full of demons and intrigue. The short playtime also means even a player just wanting a taste of how the acclaimed series began can easily find the time for it today.

**Why play it:** For an atmospheric blend of action and horror from the early PS2 era, which thanks to its short playtime you can easily finish in just a few evenings, getting a taste of how Capcom's celebrated series began.

ps2__onimusha-2-samurai-s-destiny.teaser: A sequel with allies you recruit, whose trust affects side quests and even the ending.
ps2__onimusha-2-samurai-s-destiny.article:
**Onimusha 2: Samurai's Destiny** followed up the series' successful debut with a new hero, the young samurai Jubei Yagyu, and expanded the combat system with deeper weapon customization and companion mechanics. The player once again battles hordes of Genma demons during Japan's feudal civil wars, but unlike the first game, this one lets you recruit allies who accompany you, help in combat, and influence the outcome of side quests and even the final shape of the story depending on how much trust you build with them. Side characters stopped being mere set dressing and became a full part of both strategy and storytelling, a fairly unusual approach for action games of the time.

The combat system stayed faithful to its predecessor — fast sword slashes, blocking, and special attacks unlocked by collecting the souls of fallen enemies — but new weapons, blacksmith upgrades, and the ability to combine different fighting styles gave the game noticeably more depth than its predecessor had. Visually, the game benefited from the proven combination of pre-rendered backgrounds and detailed character models, which the PlayStation 2 handled without trouble, and the atmosphere was rounded out by dark, at times almost melancholic orchestral music accompanying the journey through a devastated land.

At release, Onimusha 2 was received as a full-fledged and in many ways improved sequel that broadened the series' story and gameplay scope, giving far more room to its side characters and their fates. The companion system and story branching based on player choices were among the things that set the game apart from other action titles of its generation. Today it's viewed as one of the series' high points and a demonstration of how Capcom, in the PS2's early years, managed to blend atmosphere, action, and story into a cohesive whole that still plays well today. Fans of the series still remember it as the entry where the potential of story branching within an action game first came fully into its own.

**Why play it:** For a more elaborate sequel with loyal allies and a story that branches based on your choices — many fans rank it among the high points of the entire Onimusha series.

ps2__time-crisis-3.teaser: A light-gun shooter with pedal-controlled cover; it truly comes alive with the GunCon 2 peripheral.
ps2__time-crisis-3.article:
**Time Crisis 3** brought to the PlayStation 2 an arcade light-gun shooter that made the Time Crisis series famous for its cover mechanic — the player presses a foot pedal to duck behind obstacles and reload, then releases it to pop up and fire at enemies. This simple but tense loop made the game an ideal experience both in arcades and at home with the GunCon 2 peripheral, which Namco released for the home version to recreate the arcade feel as faithfully as possible. You could also play with a regular controller, but it was with the light-gun peripheral that the game truly showed its qualities and brought the arcade atmosphere into the living room.

The game offers a linear progression through several missions full of soldiers, vehicles, and standout boss fights, with the story following a pair of mercenaries fighting against a fictional dictatorship threatening a small island nation. Besides the main campaign, Time Crisis 3 also includes additional modes focused on timed shooting and scoring, which extend the otherwise fairly short game's playtime, and unlockable content motivated players to replay it on higher difficulties. The graphics were clean and action-packed for their time, with an emphasis on smooth environmental motion and precise hit registration — a key parameter for the genre.

In reviews, the title was praised especially for faithfully bringing the arcade experience home and for the polished cover mechanic that became synonymous with the whole series. Without a light gun, the game loses some of its charm and plays worse with a standard controller, but it still stands as an example of precise genre design. Time Crisis 3 ranks among the high points of light-gun shooters on the PS2 and is a reminder of a time when arcades and home consoles still worked closely together on shared titles. The series continued even after leaving arcades, but this particular entry is still remembered as one of its most balanced and most playable.

**Why play it:** For a precisely tuned arcade shooter with a cover system — ideally with a light gun, since without one the game loses a bit of its charm, but it still ranks among the high points of the genre on PS2.

ps2__socom-u-s-navy-seals.teaser: A pioneer of voice-based online multiplayer on consoles; tactical command of a SEALs squad.
ps2__socom-u-s-navy-seals.article:
**SOCOM: U.S. Navy SEALs** marked a breakthrough for the PlayStation 2 in console online multiplayer — the game let players communicate by voice through a bundled headset and fight in team firefights over the internet, which was an almost unheard-of novelty on consoles in 2002. The single-player campaign was built around tactical command of a SEALs squad, where the player issues orders to teammates through a quick command menu and advances carefully through environments full of enemies and snipers. Missions took the player through dense vegetation, abandoned villages, and military compounds, where a mistake in your approach usually meant an instant mission failure.

The gameplay emphasized realism and tactics over action pacing — a quick death from a single well-aimed shot forced the player to think about cover, movement, and cooperation with AI teammates, which set the game noticeably apart from the more arcade-like shooters of the time. Controlling the squad via a contextual menu was unusual at first, but once mastered offered satisfying tactical depth. The graphics were in line with the PS2's early years and weren't the main draw — the emphasis was placed above all on tension and cooperation in the online environment.

The need to additionally buy a network adapter and headset meant that the game was best appreciated by players willing to invest in the console's nascent online infrastructure. SOCOM became one of the best-selling and most influential online titles of its generation, laying the foundation for the entire series and for the concept of console online play with voice chat, which was later adopted by other platforms and genres as well. Today the game mainly serves as a historical reminder of what the beginnings of organized console multiplayer looked like, and as one of the pillars of the reputation Zipper Interactive built among tactical players around the world. Even years later, it remains an example of how a single title could define an entire genre of tactical online shooters on consoles.

**Why play it:** For a historical look into the beginnings of console online gaming with voice chat — you'll appreciate it mainly as a reminder of a time when that required a network adapter and a headset.

ps2__socom-ii-u-s-navy-seals.teaser: An expansion of SOCOM with bigger maps, soldier classes, and the option to play as the terrorist faction too.
ps2__socom-ii-u-s-navy-seals.article:
**SOCOM II: U.S. Navy SEALs** expanded its predecessor's successful concept with bigger maps, more elaborate soldier classes, and a more stable online infrastructure, which made it one of the most-played multiplayer titles on the PlayStation 2 throughout the whole generation. The game kept its predecessor's tactical pacing, where a careless approach meant a quick death, and added new game modes, destructible environmental elements, and the option to play as either the SEALs or the terrorist faction, each with their own gear. The mission environments expanded to include urban areas, ports, and mountain terrain, which required players to take a different approach depending on the type of surroundings.

The single-player campaign again focused on commanding a small squad and advancing tactically through the environment, but the heart of the experience was online multiplayer with headset support, which enabled real team communication during firefights and remote coordination of tactics. An expanded selection of maps and weapons, along with an improved player rating system featuring stats and leaderboards, gave the game long-term appeal and built a loyal, competitive community around it that kept coming back months after release. An improved communication system between players and more stable servers eliminated many of the first game's shortcomings and made it easier for less technically savvy players to get into.

SOCOM II is often described as the high point of the series on PS2 and one of the titles that proved consoles could offer a full-fledged, long-lasting online experience comparable to PC shooters of the time. Its influence on later tactical online shooters on consoles was noticeable, and a number of its mechanics later appeared in other series focused on team-based tactical play. Today it's a reminder of the golden era of the PS2 online community built around the network adapter and headset. For many players it still literally evokes the scent of early console multiplayer, when checking leaderboards and arranging matches became part of the daily routine.

**Why play it:** For a look back at the golden era of the SOCOM online community and the high point of the series on PS2, which proved consoles could handle a full-fledged tactical multiplayer experience comparable to PCs.

ps2__getaway.teaser: A cinematic gangster London with no HUD and a gritty, raw take on the underworld.
ps2__getaway.article:
**The Getaway** took players to a faithfully recreated London, where the story unfolds from two points of view — Mark Hammond, a former gangster searching for his kidnapped child, and detective Sam, pursuing the criminal world from the inside. The game combined open-city driving with third-person on-foot action and had no traditional in-game HUD, which was meant to heighten the cinematic, raw feel of a London gangster underworld inspired by British crime cinema. Realistically portrayed characters, gritty dialogue, and a naturalistic depiction of violence pushed the game closer to a mature gangster drama than to lighthearted action entertainment.

Firefights relied on a cover system and manual aiming, while the driving sections used realistically modeled streets of the British capital that could be driven through with near-documentary accuracy based on the city's actual layout. The absence of a map and HUD indicators was a bold design choice meant to deepen immersion in the story, but it also made the game harder for many players and complicated orientation. The atmosphere was rounded out by dark music close to British action films, voice acting with pronounced accents, and terse, hard-edged gunfight sound design.

At release, The Getaway was praised especially for its technical rendering of London and its cinematic atmosphere, though its raw difficulty, stripped-down controls, and confusing navigation drew more mixed reactions from critics and players alike. The title from Team Soho showed Sony's ambition to create its own answer to Grand Theft Auto-style gangster action games, with an emphasis on realism instead of open freedom and humor. Today the game is an interesting reminder of London's underworld as captured by the technology of the PlayStation 2's early era. It's still talked about as a bold, if not flawless, attempt to offer an alternative to the American open-world action games that dominated at the time.

**Why play it:** For a cinematically rendered London and a bold, if not flawless, attempt by Sony at its own gangster alternative to Grand Theft Auto — just expect stripped-down controls and higher difficulty.

ps2__freedom-fighters.teaser: Alternate history: a Soviet occupation of New York, and the resistance of ordinary plumbers against it.
ps2__freedom-fighters.article:
**Freedom Fighters** places the player into an alternate history in which the Soviet Union, rather than the USA, brought down Nazi Germany and subsequently occupied New York, where a group of ordinary plumbers becomes the core of a resistance movement against the occupation. The game, from Danish studio IO Interactive — later known for the Hitman series — combined a third-person shooter with command of a small group of rebels, whom the player gradually recruits, arms, and leads into battle for key points across the city. The gradual growth of the resistance network from a handful of people in a basement into an organized militia gave the story a clear sense of escalation and rising hope.

A key element is the charisma system — successful actions such as freeing civilians or destroying propaganda symbols increase the player's authority and let them recruit more allies, who then fight alongside them, provide cover, and seize strategic points across the city. Battles for New York thus felt like small-scale military operations rather than solo firefights, and the atmosphere of an occupied city was underscored by Soviet propaganda, flags, street patrols, and a grim soundscape. The music and sound design effectively evoked the tense atmosphere of resistance in an occupied metropolis, where even ordinary subway streets and housing blocks bore the marks of a long occupation.

Freedom Fighters received positive reviews for its original premise and for the tactical depth of squad command, even though the game itself wasn't especially long and the story unfolded in a fairly straightforward manner. It ranks among the quality, if today less remembered, titles of the PS2 generation that offered a well-thought-out mix of action and light strategy. Its concept of recruiting and commanding allies later influenced a number of other action games built around a similar theme of resistance against an occupying force. That's partly why discussions still occasionally return to games that deserve a more modern sequel, or at least a remaster for a new audience.

**Why play it:** For a well-thought-out mix of action and light command strategy, where you recruit and lead fellow fighters in a resistance against occupation — the pace is brisk and the game never drags.

ps2__red-dead-revolver.teaser: A western tale of revenge with Dead Eye aiming, which later became the trademark of the Red Dead series.
ps2__red-dead-revolver.article:
**Red Dead Revolver** brought a third-person western action game to the PlayStation 2, in which the player, as gunslinger Red Harlow, sets out on the trail of the men who murdered his family during his childhood, gradually getting caught up in a web of betrayal, revenge, and his own past tied to guns that once belonged to his father. The game combined fast-paced firefights with the iconic slow-motion Dead Eye aiming mode, which let the player mark multiple targets at once and take them out with a single swift motion — a mechanic that later became the trademark of the entire Red Dead series.

Besides the linear campaign, the game also offered arena battles in Showdown mode and the option to play as several different characters, each with their own weapons, stats, and fighting styles, adding variety to an otherwise straightforward western-shooter concept. Dusty towns, saloons, mines, and desert landscapes were rendered with a real feel for the genre, accompanied by music inspired by classic spaghetti westerns, which, together with the exaggeratedly stylized characters, rounded out the distinctive, unmistakable atmosphere of Red Dead Revolver's western world.

The game had a turbulent development history — it was originally started by Capcom in collaboration with Angel Studios, before Rockstar San Diego took over the project and finished it with its own, more distinctive vision. The result was received as a solid, atmospheric western action game, though it would take its sequel, Red Dead Redemption, several years later to show the full potential of an open-world western concept. On the PS2, Red Dead Revolver remains a well-regarded predecessor to the later major series and a demonstration of Rockstar's shift toward more distinctive action games. For fans of the later, bigger series, it's interesting in hindsight to see just how many ideas and motifs from this smaller title actually carried forward into the future.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Red Dead series, it's interesting as an atmospheric, if smaller, predecessor in which you can retroactively spot a number of ideas that Red Dead Redemption would later develop to their full potential.

ps2__gungrave.teaser: From the creator of Trigun; a dead gangster fights with two pistols and a giant coffin as a weapon.
ps2__gungrave.article:
**Gungrave** was created in collaboration with Yasuhiro Nightow, creator of the manga and anime series Trigun, bringing his distinctive visual style into a third-person action shooter about a dead gangster named Beyond the Grave, who returns from the grave as a silent hitman settling scores with his former underworld allies, the ones who once betrayed him and left him for dead. The gameplay was built on a simple but effective principle — massive firefights against waves of enemies, combining two pistols and a giant coffin that serves both as a melee weapon and as the source of devastating special attacks.

The game leaned on style and pure action fun rather than complex mechanics: the levels were linear, clearly laid out, and full of flashy animations and explosions, which made Gungrave feel like an interactive anime action film set in factories, docks, and skyscrapers of the criminal underworld, where the main hero gradually fights his way up to the very top of the organization that once betrayed him. The striking character designs, atmospheric electronic and rock music, and a charismatic protagonist who barely speaks a single line of dialogue all created an unmistakable atmosphere that set the game apart from other action titles of its generation.

Although the game's length and system depth were fairly limited and it could be finished quite quickly, Gungrave built up a cult status thanks to its stylish presentation and was successful enough to get a sequel as well as its own anime series. Today it's seen as an example of collaboration between the video game and manga industries, and as one of the titles that proved even a simple action loop can work thanks to a strong visual identity. For fans of stylized action games, Gungrave remains a pleasant nostalgic treat that can easily be finished in a single afternoon, yet still leaves behind an unforgettable visual impression.

**Why play it:** For a stylish action ride, easily finished in one afternoon, with an unforgettable visual identity that earned the title cult status and its own anime series despite its simplicity.

ps2__twisted-metal-black.teaser: A dark, horror-tinged turn for the series; asylum patients fight to the death to have a wish granted.
ps2__twisted-metal-black.article:
**Twisted Metal: Black** took the vehicular combat series into darker, rawer waters than fans were used to — instead of the lighter tone of previous entries, it offered a grim, at times downright horror-inflected story set in an insane asylum, whose patients fight to the death in their armed vehicles in exchange for having one wish granted, be it revenge, redemption, or some other, far darker goal. Each character had their own dark backstory and unsettling cutscenes shot in a grotesque, comic-book aesthetic, which made the game an unusually bleak experience set against otherwise arcade-style action.

The gameplay itself stayed true to the series' core principle — players destroy opponents across enclosed arenas scattered across a fictional city using weapons mounted on their vehicles, collect power-ups, and make use of each machine's special abilities, from rocket barrages to teleportation, with the choice of vehicle significantly changing both the tactics and pace of individual fights. Compared to earlier entries, Black brought improved physics, more detailed destructible environments, and a darker visual style that made good use of the PlayStation 2's capabilities. The music and sound effects reinforced the bleak, unsettling atmosphere of the whole game and its nighttime city, through which players fight their way from one bizarre arena to the next.

Twisted Metal: Black was received by critics and players alike as a return to the series' roots and one of the best entries ever, praised for its atmosphere, well-balanced multiplayer, and the boldness to push a previously lighthearted brand in a significantly darker direction. To this day it's considered the peak of the vehicular combat series on the PlayStation 2, and its grim tone went on to inspire later entries in the series. For fans of the genre, it remains one of the must-play titles of the entire console generation. The combination of dark humor, unflinching brutality, and stylish presentation still makes it an exceptionally distinctive experience today.

**Why play:** For a darker, rawer return to the roots of vehicular combat games that, thanks to its well-balanced multiplayer and dark humor, still stands as the peak of the entire series on PS2.

ps2__dead-or-alive-2-hardcore.teaser: A fast fighting game from Team Ninja built on strike-throw-guard; arenas have multiple levels and traps.
ps2__dead-or-alive-2-hardcore.article:
**Dead or Alive 2: Hardcore** brought to the PlayStation 2 an expanded version of the successful arcade and Dreamcast fighting game from Team Ninja, renowned for its fast, technical combat system built around striking, throwing, and blocking, where every action has its clear counter-action, making fights resemble a rapid game of rock-paper-scissors in which knowing your opponent's style matters as much as raw reflexes. The battlegrounds, too, were more than flat arenas — they were multi-level environments with drops, traps, and interactive elements able to turn around even a fight that seemed already decided.

The game offered a wide roster of fighters with distinct styles, from fast striking techniques to grappling moves inspired by real martial arts, and put emphasis on precise defensive timing rather than memorizing long combos as in rival titles. The Hardcore version for PS2 added new characters, costumes, and game modes over the original release, and made use of the new console's power for more detailed character models, smoother animation, and more elaborate environments, making it, at the time of release, one of the visually most impressive fighting titles on the market — evident too in the detailed rendering of each arena and its lighting.

Dead or Alive 2: Hardcore was praised for the depth of its combat system and for graphics that stood among the most technically advanced showcases among early PlayStation 2 games. Alongside rival series like Tekken and Virtua Fighter, it helped define the 3D fighting genre at the turn of the millennium and set the bar for animation fluidity. Today it's regarded as one of the most technically and mechanically accomplished fighting titles of its console generation. Many players still cite the Dead or Alive series as their first encounter with more technically demanding fighting games beyond traditional arcade machines.

**Why play:** For a technically advanced, nimble 3D fighter that, alongside Tekken and Virtua Fighter, helped define the genre at the turn of the millennium and was many players' first taste of more demanding combat.

ps2__guilty-gear-x2.teaser: A technical anime fighter with a rock soundtrack and the Roman Cancel combo system.
ps2__guilty-gear-x2.article:
**Guilty Gear X2** brought to the PlayStation 2 a fast, technically demanding 2D fighting game from Arc System Works, renowned for its striking anime visual style, energetic rock soundtrack, and a deep combat system full of combos, cancellable attacks, and special maneuvers like the Roman Cancel, which let skilled players extend and vary their attack sequences almost indefinitely. The Guilty Gear series built its reputation precisely on this combination of high difficulty for newcomers and enormous depth for players willing to invest the time to master its mechanics. A system of defensive barriers and combo interruptions also gave even players under pressure a chance at a dramatic last-moment comeback.

The series' characters were defined by bold, exaggerated designs and fighting styles of their own that reflected their personalities, from fast swordfighters through wrestlers to slower but devastating brawlers wielding giant weapons. The hand-drawn sprite animation reached a high level of quality and fluidity on PS2, and together with the energetic metal and rock music, it created a distinctive atmosphere the series has kept across all its sequels ever since. The game also offered local multiplayer for competitive players craving fast, evenly matched fights.

Guilty Gear X2 was prized above all by the hardcore fighting-game community for its technical depth and visual style, even though its steep learning curve put off casual players looking for something simpler. The title cemented the series' reputation as one of the most respected in the 2D fighting genre and paved the way for later entries that still compete in tournaments around the world today. On PS2, Guilty Gear X2 remains one of the most technically impressive 2D fighting games of its generation. The series' unmistakable visual identity also made it a recognizable brand well beyond the narrow circle of competitive players.
