**Why play it:** Without Xbox Live connectivity and with a smaller online community via PlayStation Network, it was a somewhat lonelier experience than on Xbox 360, even though the actual racing and tracks stayed the same.

ps3__portal.teaser: A short, brilliant puzzle game about portals and GLaDOS; one of the most talked-about games of its time.
ps3__portal.article:
Portal is a short but extraordinarily inventive puzzle game built around the portal gun, which Valve packaged into The Orange Box compilation together with Half-Life 2, both of its episodes, and Team Fortress 2. In it, the player moves through a series of test chambers under the guidance of the artificial intelligence GLaDOS and solves puzzles based on opening two linked portals in space and using momentum-based movement - despite its short length, it became one of the most discussed titles of its time. On PlayStation 3, Portal launched as part of The Orange Box compilation on December 11, 2007, roughly two months later than the PC and Xbox 360 versions, which arrived already in October. The delay had a clear reason - the PlayStation 3 port wasn't created directly by Valve but by a hired external team, and the result was noticeably weaker technically by the standards of the time, with a lower frame rate and longer loading times than on rival platforms, which a number of period reviews noted.

The game itself - the sequence of test chambers with the portal gun and the story about the controlling artificial intelligence GLaDOS - remained unchanged in content; it's an identical experience to the PC or Xbox 360 versions, with the same puzzles, the same pacing of story revelation, and the same closing song Still Alive. The difference lay mainly in the fact that the PlayStation 3 version lacked comparable achievement support and online features on release day, because the PlayStation Network was only at the start of its development in the fall of 2007 and was missing a number of services that Xbox Live players were used to.

Valve took players' dissatisfaction with the quality of the port to heart and, in the following months, took over care of the PS3 version of The Orange Box itself, including updates and later Steamworks support on this console - a unique move on PlayStation 3 at the time that showed how seriously Valve took its reputation on this platform, and fans still remember it today as an example of an unusually accommodating publisher response to a flawed port.

**Why play it:** For Portal fans, it's interesting to see how Valve, after a weak start, took the quality of the PS3 version to heart and was the first to bring full Steam integration to this console - a unique move for its time.

ps3__tales-of-vesperia.teaser: An action JRPG with real-time battles on a 2D axis; the story of mercenary Yuri Lowell.
ps3__tales-of-vesperia.article:
Tales of Vesperia launched in 2008 as an Xbox 360 exclusive and became one of the last major JRPGs that owners of Microsoft's console could enjoy at the time without having to resort to a Japanese version. The game from the famous Tales of series offers an action battle system that plays out in real time along an imaginary 2D axis, an elaborate story about the mercenary Yuri Lowell and his journey across the world of Terca Lumireis, and the typical mix of humor, friendship, and darker themes the series has long been known for. Characters gradually join the party during the journey, each with their own arsenal of spells and combos that can be fluidly chained together in battle.

A year later, in September 2009, the game also arrived on PlayStation 3 - but only in Japan. This wasn't a simple rewrite: developers at Namco Tales Studio expanded the version with two new playable characters, Flynn Scifo and Patty Fortune, added several hours of extra story plus new animated cutscenes from studio Production I.G., and adjusted the balance of the battle system, including new abilities for existing characters. Paradoxically, though, the PS3 release lost its English voice acting - it was dubbed only in Japanese, which effectively locked it out for players outside Asia without knowledge of the language, even if they managed to physically obtain an import copy.

The Xbox 360 version thus remained for many years the only one fans outside Japan could play without a language barrier, while the richer content of the PS3 release long remained the privilege of the Japanese market and an object of envy for foreign fans following events only from afar through internet forums and videos of imported copies. The expanded content reached international players only a decade later in the form of the separately released Definitive Edition, which, however, represents a different, newer title built on more modern hardware and with full English voice acting for the new content.

This discrepancy between versions is still cited today as an example of how Japanese publishers approached regional differences in that era - while they prepared an expanded version for the domestic audience, foreign players had to wait years before they could access the same content through official channels and in a language they understood.

**Why play it:** For JRPG fans, it's an interesting example of how Japanese publishers approached regional differences in that era - foreign players had to wait many more years for the full content.

ps3__castle-crashers.teaser: Four-player co-op mayhem with Tom Fulp's hand-drawn art style.
ps3__castle-crashers.article:
Castle Crashers conquered Xbox Live Arcade in August 2008 and quickly became one of the digital platform's most beloved titles. This colorful brawler about knights hacking their way through armies of monsters with friends to rescue kidnapped princesses combines simple but addictive enemy-bashing with RPG elements - characters level up, collect weapons, and unlock dozens of playable heroes with distinct abilities. Co-op play for up to four players on one screen was a major draw from the start, and combined with creator Tom Fulp's distinctive hand-drawn art style, it helped the game stand out from the rest of the XBLA lineup.

On PlayStation 3, the game arrived via PlayStation Network in November 2010, more than two years late. Studio The Behemoth used the version to include content that Xbox 360 players had to unlock gradually through updates and downloadable add-ons - the PS3 release offered it all right out of the box, including additional playable characters and the Photo Booth minigame, where players could photograph their characters in goofy poses. Controls were adapted for the DualShock 3, and the game fully used trophies instead of achievements, with online multiplayer running free over the PlayStation Network.

Despite the later start, it paradoxically offered a more complete and content-rich experience than the original Xbox 360 version at launch, which quickly earned it a loyal following among Sony console players and kept it popular for years after release.

The situation was thus the exact opposite of many other ports of the era, where a later release on another platform usually meant more of a technical compromise - with Castle Crashers, the wait instead meant PS3 players got the most complete version of the game right away, without having to follow the gradual rollout of paid content the way early Xbox 360 owners did.

**Why play it:** Anyone picking up Castle Crashers on PS3 gets the most complete version of the game with all the content at once, without having to follow the gradual release of paid expansions like the first Xbox 360 owners did.

ps3__saints-row-2.teaser: Gangster open world pushes absurdity further than GTA; the campaign can be played co-op too.
ps3__saints-row-2.article:
Saints Row 2 launched in October 2008 simultaneously for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, continuing from the first game as an open world full of gangster anarchy, dark humor, and nearly unlimited freedom in how the player enjoys the game - from the main story through dozens of side activities to extensive character customization, letting players design literally any look for their gangster. Compared to the rival GTA series, the game pushed absurdity even further and offered a full two-player co-op mode running through the entire main campaign.

The PS3 version launched the same day as the Xbox 360 release, but technically fell behind - reviewers and players complained about a lower frame rate, longer loading times, and noticeably worse optimization compared to Microsoft's console, especially in more densely populated parts of the city of Stilwater. Content-wise, both versions were identical; the difference was purely in engine performance on different hardware, which was fairly common for multiplatform titles of this generation and affected quite a few other games of the time as well.

Still, the PS3 release found its audience and, alongside the Xbox 360 version, helped the Saints Row series establish itself as a freewheeling, self-aware alternative to more seriously toned open-world games of the era, which the even more over-the-top third and fourth entries later built on.

The performance gap between the two consoles at the time sparked wider discussion about how difficult it was for smaller studios like Volition to efficiently optimize large open worlds on the PlayStation 3's architecture, which was generally considered harder for developers to work with compared to the Xbox 360.

Reviewers at the time consistently recommended that players who owned both consoles pick the Xbox 360 version instead, where the game ran more smoothly and without such pronounced frame rate drops while driving through Stilwater's busier districts, even though the game's actual content remained completely identical on both platforms.

**Why play it:** The same open-world chaos content-wise as on Xbox 360, but with more noticeable frame rate drops in Stilwater's busier districts - if you have the choice, go for the smoother Xbox 360 version instead.

ps3__battlefield-bad-company.teaser: Mercenary dark humor and environmental destruction on the Frostbite engine go hand in hand.
ps3__battlefield-bad-company.article:
Battlefield: Bad Company launched in June 2008 simultaneously for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, bringing a new approach to DICE's series - instead of a purely serious military conflict, it offered the story of a squad of mercenary soldiers with dark humor and a bombastic singleplayer campaign the series had previously lacked on consoles. The game's key selling point remained extensive environmental destruction built on the Frostbite engine, which let players shoot through building walls, level entire structures, and change the tactical situation on the battlefield on the fly.

Both console versions launched the same day and were very close in both content and technical terms - Battlefield: Bad Company was in fact developed as a console title with no planned PC version, which was unusual for the Battlefield series, since up to that point it had primarily positioned itself as a PC affair with titles like Battlefield 1942 or Battlefield 2. Differences between the Xbox 360 and PS3 releases were minimal and mainly involved small technical details, loading time length, and the use of trophies instead of achievements.

Only the sequel Bad Company 2, two years later, brought the series back to PC, while the first game remained an exclusively console affair of the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 generation and is still only available on those two platforms today.

The lack of a PC version was unusual at the time especially because Battlefield had a strong historical fan base of multiplayer battles on computers - but DICE decided to focus Bad Company purely on a console audience with a simpler, more accessible campaign centered on a buddy squad of characters.

The console release thus functioned more like an experiment in how the series could behave outside its traditional PC home - the emphasis on destruction and the B-movie humor of the mercenary squad proved to be a successful direction that DICE went on to further develop in the subsequent Bad Company entries, this time with a full PC version alongside both consoles.

**Why play it:** For its emphasis on destructible environments and the B-movie humor of the mercenary squad, which proved to be a successful direction developed further in later entries, Bad Company is worth trying as a console experiment outside of PC.

ps3__race-driver-grid.teaser: Less simulation-heavy driving, flashy damage, and cinematic replays; one of the generation's hits.
ps3__race-driver-grid.article:
Race Driver: GRID launched in May 2008 simultaneously on Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, and PC, and became one of the best-reviewed racing titles of its generation. Codemasters combined a rawer, less simulation-focused driving model than in previous TOCA/Race Driver entries with flashy vehicle damage and cinematic camera work and replays, making the game feel more dramatic than most of the competition at the time, whether in circuit races, drift challenges, or street battles.

The PlayStation 3 version launched the same day as the Xbox 360 release and offered practically identical content - the same tracks, cars, and game modes, including a career mode taking the player across several continents from Europe through America to Japan. Differences were minimal and mainly involved the use of trophies instead of achievements and small technical variations due to the different hardware of the two consoles. The game drew criticism at the time for lacking a cockpit view, but this was shared equally across all platforms, so PS3 players were at no disadvantage compared to others in this regard.

The PS3 release helped GRID reach a broad audience across both of the generation's main consoles and reinforced Codemasters' reputation as a studio capable of competing with established series like Gran Turismo or Forza Motorsport even outside its home platform of Xbox.

The success of the simultaneous release across both consoles and PC later convinced Codemasters that a multiplatform strategy was worth sticking with for the series, and the studio repeated the same approach for the follow-up GRID 2 and further sequels.

The PlayStation 3 version was thus no second-rate add-on - it contributed to GRID becoming one of the titles that helped Codemasters build a reputation as a studio capable of delivering a quality racing experience across all the generation's main platforms without major compromises on any of them.

**Why play it:** For racing game fans, it's a guarantee of enjoying just as good an experience on PlayStation 3 as on other platforms of that generation, without technical compromises.

ps3__midnight-club-los-angeles.teaser: Illegal street racing in a faithfully rendered Los Angeles with deep car tuning.
ps3__midnight-club-los-angeles.article:
Midnight Club: Los Angeles launched in October 2008 simultaneously for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, bringing Rockstar Games' series of illegal street races to a faithfully rendered Los Angeles with an open map including the surrounding highways. Compared to previous entries, it offered denser traffic, more elaborate vehicle damage, and deeper tuning and personalization options for both cars and motorcycles, making it one of the most technically advanced arcade racing games of its generation.

The PS3 version launched the same day as the Xbox 360 release and was identical in content - the same Los Angeles map, vehicle roster, and race modes, including online multiplayer for up to sixteen players simultaneously active in one city. Differences between the platforms were minimal, mainly showing up as small frame rate variations and the use of trophies instead of achievements. Later downloadable content, such as the South Central expansion adding new cars and routes, also released on both consoles simultaneously, so neither platform had a content lead.

The game never released on PC, which was the exception rather than the rule for Rockstar Games at the time - the studio then focused primarily on console releases and didn't consider a PC version a priority for smaller series like Midnight Club compared to flagship series like Grand Theft Auto.

Midnight Club: Los Angeles thus became the series' final major entry - Rockstar San Diego never released another sequel after it, and the series remained closed out with the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 pairing.

For street racing fans, that means only these two equal versions of the game exist to this day - no later remaster or port to newer hardware was ever made, so both console releases remain the only way to play Midnight Club: Los Angeles in its original form.

**Why play it:** Since no remaster or port was ever made, this is the only chance to play Midnight Club: Los Angeles in its original form - an ideal choice for street racing fans.

ps3__sonic-unleashed.teaser: By night a powerful Werehog, by day a fast platformer; the journey spans seven continents.
ps3__sonic-unleashed.article:
Sonic Unleashed launched simultaneously on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in November 2008, bringing a key new twist to the series - Sonic the Hedgehog turns into a werewolf-like Werehog at night, with slower, power-based combat gameplay featuring stretchable arms, while during the day the game returns to the traditional fast 3D/2D platforming sections that made the series famous back in the Sega Mega Drive days. This version was developed directly by the in-house Sonic Team and graphically ranked among the series' most ambitious entries on the hardware of the time, with a journey across seven stylized continents inspired by real places on Earth.

The PlayStation 3 version launched the same day as the Xbox 360 release and was practically identical to it - same settings, levels, and length, with only minimal technical differences due to the different hardware of the two consoles, such as small variations in loading times. This pair of versions offered the full, graphically most polished Sonic Unleashed experience, while the simultaneously released Wii and PlayStation 2 versions from a different studio were designed quite differently, with a different level structure and engine.

The Werehog sections split players and critics at the time - many reviews praised the fast daytime sections full of acrobatic running and jumping but criticized the slower, repetitive nighttime combat sections, which made up a substantial part of the total playtime.

Still, the Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 versions remain the ones players return to most often today, precisely thanks to the best balance of graphical quality and smoothness among all four simultaneously released platforms.

The difference between the Xbox 360 and PS3 releases was minimal even technically - both versions ran on the same Hedgehog Engine that Sonic Team developed for this entry, so players had essentially a free choice of platform without worrying about a noticeable compromise on either console.

**Why play it:** For Sonic fans it doesn't matter which console they pick - both the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions run on the same Hedgehog Engine and offer a practically identical experience.

ps3__prince-of-persia.teaser: A series restart with painterly graphics; companion Elika saves the prince instead of a game over.
ps3__prince-of-persia.article:
The 2008 Prince of Persia marked a restart for the series - Ubisoft Montreal abandoned the dark tone and more linear structure of the previous Sands of Time trilogy and offered a more open world, a strikingly stylized cel-shaded look reminiscent of a painting, and an immortal main hero accompanied by his companion Elika, thanks to whom the game almost entirely did away with classic game over screens - falling into a chasm simply had the prince rescued and the game continued. The game launched in December 2008 simultaneously on Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3.

Both console versions launched the same day and were very close in both content and visuals - the same open world divided into several themed areas, the same acrobatic movement system enabling fluid wall-running and rope traversal, and combat mechanics based on timing dodges and counterattacks. Differences between the Xbox 360 and PS3 releases were minimal, limited to small technical details due to the different hardware and the use of trophies instead of achievements.

The downloadable Epilogue expansion, which later concluded the story and offered new areas to explore, also released simultaneously on both consoles, so PlayStation 3 players didn't miss out on any content or face delayed availability compared to Xbox 360 owners.

Simultaneous release on both consoles was standard practice for Ubisoft at the time for its major first-party franchises, reflecting an approach where the publisher didn't want to alienate either main platform with a later or reduced release for its flagship titles.

The cel-shaded graphics also aged very well on both consoles - unlike the photorealistically styled games of that generation, the stylized, painterly look didn't date as quickly, which holds equally true for both the PS3 and Xbox 360 versions to this day. Neither platform offered any exclusive content that would put the other at a disadvantage, so the choice between PS3 and Xbox 360 remained purely a matter of personal controller and game library preference.

**Why play it:** Thanks to the stylized cel-shaded graphics, which have aged much better than the photorealism of the era, it's a pleasantly timeless experience on both PS3 and Xbox 360 alike.

ps3__command-and-conquer-red-alert-3.teaser: An absurd alternate Cold War with live-action cutscenes and three factions.
ps3__command-and-conquer-red-alert-3.article:
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 brings an absurd alternate history of the Cold War between the Soviets, the Allies, and the Empire of the Rising Sun to a real-time strategy game featuring live-action cutscenes, over-the-top comic-book units, and a two-player co-op campaign that can be played as any of the three factions, each with its own story and its own take on military technology, from classic tanks to giant walking machines. The game became especially famous for its live-action cutscenes with real actors, whose bizarre plot about a fight for world domination gives it a lighthearted, campy quality that has helped the series stay popular among players to this day.

The PlayStation 3 version arrived only in 2009, a year after the PC and Xbox 360 releases, and is content-wise based on them - it brings the same campaign, the same factions, and the same live-action cutscenes with actors unchanged, including the ability to play through the whole campaign in two-player co-op. Controls were adapted for the DualShock 3 similarly to the Xbox version, using radial menus controlled with the analog sticks instead of a mouse; the PS3 version also didn't offer native keyboard and mouse support, which the PC version had for players who preferred more precise controls. The one-year gap from the other platforms meant PlayStation 3 players could watch PC and Xbox 360 owners enjoy the game well before they got to play it themselves. Compared to the PC release, this means purely gamepad-based control of the strategy game, which makes it more accessible to console players but also strips away the precision of unit selection and micromanagement that the RTS genre is accustomed to on PC. Despite these limitations, the PS3 version offers the complete campaign for all three factions as well as online multiplayer over the PlayStation Network with the same maps and game modes the PC and Xbox 360 versions had a year earlier, so PlayStation 3 players ultimately didn't end up with a lesser experience, just a delayed one.

**Why play it:** Anyone who prefers gamepad controls will appreciate that, despite the year-long delay, the PS3 version offers the same campaign and two-player co-op as the PC and Xbox 360 versions, just without keyboard and mouse support.

ps3__far-cry-2.teaser: Malaria, jamming guns, and wind-driven fire turn Africa into an unpredictable trap.
ps3__far-cry-2.article:
Far Cry 2 offers a vast open Africa, where the player, playing a mercenary, hunts for the arms dealer known as the Jackal, all while contending with malaria afflicting the main character, weapon wear and jamming, and fire that can spread on its own across the landscape depending on wind direction, becoming a weapon just as dangerous as firearms themselves. This is complemented by weapons that wear down as the game progresses and can jam at the least convenient moment, and a wounded buddy who can be rescued mid-firefight, making every encounter an uncertain and unpredictable experience. The open world, split into two vast regions, is also not traversed via any fast-travel map — the player genuinely drives by car, boat, or on foot, which makes traveling between missions part of the gameplay experience itself.

The PlayStation 3 version launched simultaneously with the PC and Xbox 360 releases in 2008 and features the same open world, the same campaign, and the same side activities as the other platforms released that same day. Like the Xbox version, it runs at a fixed resolution and frame rate tuned to the console's performance rather than the scalable graphics settings available on PC, and the controls are adapted for the DualShock 3 instead of mouse and keyboard, which particularly changes long-range aiming and camera turn speed during firefights. Compared to the PC version, it thus lacks mod support and the finer graphics tuning based on hardware performance, but in terms of content it is an entirely identical game with the same storyline, the same factions, and the same side activities across the open world. Online multiplayer runs over the PlayStation Network with the same game modes as on other platforms, so PS3 players missed out on neither the cooperative nor the competitive experiences found on the other versions — they simply controlled them with a DualShock 3 instead of a mouse and keyboard, making the game more accessible to players who prefer a console over building a gaming PC.

**Why play it:** For players without a PC, this is a full-fledged variant with the same open world and campaign as on other platforms, albeit without mod support and finer graphics tuning.

ps3__assassin-s-creed.teaser: The series debut built on observation and assassinations; the sci-fi frame with the Animus defined the format for a long time.
ps3__assassin-s-creed.article:
Assassin's Creed from 2007 was the first installment of Ubisoft's series to build its gameplay around observation, stealth, and targeted assassinations within vast recreations of medieval cities. Playing as the assassin Altaïr, the player moved through Jerusalem, Damascus, and Acre, climbed buildings using a free-running movement system, and completed side tasks before proceeding to the main target. The entire story was also framed by a science-fiction plot involving a device called the Animus, through which the modern-day protagonist Desmond Miles relived the memories of his ancestor — this dual narrative went on to become a hallmark of the entire series. The game drew attention at the time particularly for its handling of crowds and cities, though it was criticized for the repetitiveness of the side missions that preceded the main assassinations.

The PlayStation 3 version launched alongside the Xbox 360 release in November 2007, so the two console versions barely differed from each other in content or technically — it was essentially the same game with the same content, just with a different controller button layout. The difference only showed up after launch: trophy support on the PlayStation 3 didn't exist yet at the time, and Sony only introduced it in mid-2008, so PS3 players had to wait for an additional update for the ability to collect trophies in Assassin's Creed, while Xbox 360 players had access to achievements from day one. For achievement hunters, the launch PS3 version was thus an incomplete experience for several months, though this had no effect on the gameplay itself, and the game ran at the same frame rate and resolution on both consoles.

Before the game arrived on PC a year later, both console versions remained the main reference for how Assassin's Creed was meant to look and play — the PC version was accompanied by discussions about its then-controversial copy protection requiring a constant internet connection. The console editions thus retained their reputation for a long time as the most convenient way to enjoy the series without such complications.

**Why play it:** Anyone wanting to avoid the then-controversial PC protection requiring a constant internet connection found a more convenient, trouble-free way to enjoy the game in the console version.

ps3__beatles-rock-band.teaser: A musical biography of The Beatles with period footage; singers will appreciate the three-part harmonies.
ps3__beatles-rock-band.article:
The Beatles: Rock Band from 2009 was an exceptional project — a musical rhythm game that, instead of a generic playlist, offered a complete musical biography of The Beatles, complemented by archival photographs, period recordings, and stylized 'dream' visual scenes inspired by the band's individual eras. Players on drums, guitar, bass, and vocals moved chronologically through the discography, from the early years at the Cavern Club to the later studio albums, so the game functioned simultaneously as an interactive documentary and as an entertaining multiplayer party game. For singers, it also offered a system of up to three-part harmonies that could reward the accuracy of individual vocal lines, not just the main melody.

The PlayStation 3 version launched on the same day as the Xbox 360 and Wii editions and offered the same content and the same songs. Compared to the Wii version, however, it had a full-fledged online multiplayer mode — the Wii of the time didn't allow online play for Rock Band titles to the same extent as the HD consoles, so PS3 players could compete and cooperate with remote teammates, which wasn't possible on Wii. The graphical presentation of the 'dream' interlude scenes was also more detailed on PS3 thanks to the more powerful hardware, with sharper textures for the archival photographs and smoother animation.

Instrumental peripherals (guitar, drums, microphone) were only partly compatible between platforms due to the different connectors on each console, which was a common complication throughout the Rock Band series for owners of multiple systems — players often had to buy a separate set of instruments for each console. Even so, the content and musical experience on PS3 remained identical to the other HD versions of the game, and after completing the career mode, players could freely replay any unlocked song in any order, whether solo or with a full four-member band.

**Why play it:** Beatles fans will appreciate that the musical content and experience on PS3 are identical to the other HD versions of the game, even though instruments from other consoles won't carry over due to different connectors.

ps3__dead-space-extraction.teaser: A light-gun prequel to Dead Space, set aboard the Ishimura before the first game.
ps3__dead-space-extraction.article:
Dead Space: Extraction from 2009 was an on-rails light-gun shooter that expanded the space horror of the Dead Space series with a prequel narrative set before the events of the first game aboard the mining ship Ishimura. The player followed a fixed path full of Necromorph monsters, aiming and shooting off enemy limbs just like in the main series, and followed the story from the perspective of a group of survivors whose fates intertwined with the later installments. Besides the shooting itself, the game also made room for exploring the surroundings, gathering resources, and reading text logs that fleshed out the atmosphere of the dying space station, setting it apart from other quick, disposable light-gun titles.

The original was made exclusively for Wii, where aiming was done by pointing the Wii Remote directly at the TV screen — this control style suited the on-rails shooter genre well and was one of the reasons the game received better reviews from critics than reception from the wider player base, which, partly due to its association with Wii, was slower to warm to it. The game didn't arrive on PlayStation 3 until 2011, when EA offered it as bonus content with the limited edition of Dead Space 2 and later also separately via the PlayStation Network, with precise aiming now handled by the PlayStation Move controller, offering similar accuracy to the Wii Remote.

The PS3 version also benefited from more powerful hardware — it offered sharper textures, higher resolution, and a more stable frame rate compared to the original, and it also gained trophy support, which the Wii lacked by design. For players without a PlayStation Move controller, the game was also playable with a standard gamepad, albeit with less precise aiming than with motion controllers, so most players seeking the full on-rails experience ultimately opted to get a Move controller. Thanks to its bundling with the Dead Space 2 edition, the game also reached a significantly wider audience than it had on Wii two years earlier.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its bundling with the Dead Space 2 edition and sharper graphics compared to the Wii original, this is the most accessible way to try this well-crafted on-rails shooter, ideally with a Move controller.

ps3__assassin-s-creed-ii.teaser: Ezio Auditore in Renaissance Italy; the installment that elevated the series into a grand open world.
ps3__assassin-s-creed-ii.article:
Assassin's Creed II tells the story of Ezio Auditore da Firenze, a young Venetian nobleman who, after the murder of his father and brothers, transforms into a master assassin pursuing a Templar conspiracy across Renaissance Italy, from Florence through Venice to Rome. Compared to the first installment, the game significantly expanded its repertoire of movement and combat, adding city economies, purchasing and upgrading equipment, swimming, hidden assassin tombs full of acrobatic puzzles, and flight using Da Vinci's flying machine. Dozens of side quests, collecting codex pages and feathers scattered across the map gave players a reason to explore the open world far more thoroughly than in the original game, which is why the second installment became one of the most significant titles of the entire console generation.

On PlayStation 3, the game launched on the same day as the Xbox 360 version, in November 2009, and it was identical in content — no platform got a different story, different main quests, or different endings. The differences in 2009 mainly concerned technical performance: at launch, the PS3 version ran with somewhat less stable frame rates in larger crowds of characters in cities than the competing Xbox 360, something reviewers at the time also noticed, though Ubisoft later partially evened out the differences with updates. The controls were adapted to the DualShock 3 button layout, but otherwise it was exactly the same experience as on Xbox, including the same music and the same voice acting.

More interesting was the fate of the downloadable content: the Battle of Forlì mission, which added a story episode featuring Caterina Sforza, was for a time a timed exclusive on PlayStation 3, while Xbox 360 owners had to wait somewhat longer for it. This practice of timed DLC exclusives was common among publishers at the time, and Assassin's Creed II was one of its notable early examples within a single console generation, though it had no effect on the main campaign, which players on both platforms ultimately experienced as essentially identical.

**Why play it:** PlayStation 3 owners also had temporary exclusive access to the Battle of Forlì mission, even though the main campaign remains essentially identical and equally excellent on both consoles.

ps3__borderlands.teaser: The founder of the looter shooter genre; cel-shaded comic-book style, randomized weapons, four-player co-op.
ps3__borderlands.article:
Borderlands combines a first-person shooter with RPG elements and loot mechanics typical of games like Diablo — as one of four treasure hunters, the player traverses the desert planet of Pandora, fires dozens of types of procedurally generated weapons with randomized attributes, supplements their loadout with grenades and shields, and gradually levels up their character according to a chosen specialization, whether that's a sniper, a mercenary, a siren with magical abilities, or a hunter with a robotic companion. Its distinctive cel-shaded comic-book visual style with bold black outlines gave the game a look unlike the realistic war shooters of the time, and combined with four-player co-op and dark humor, it made Borderlands one of the founders of the entire looter-shooter genre.

The PlayStation 3 version launched simultaneously with Xbox 360 and PC in autumn 2009 and was completely identical in content — the same campaign, the same weapons, the same four playable treasure hunters, and the same world of Pandora with the same side quests. The main difference showed up in the technical execution: reviewers and players at the time pointed out that the PS3 version suffered from somewhat worse frame rate stability and longer loading times between areas than the competing Xbox 360, something that was fairly common among multiplatform titles from the first half of the PS3/360 generation due to the console's different architecture.

Four-player co-op worked on PS3 the same way as elsewhere, over the PlayStation Network, and it also supported local split-screen for two players on a single console, just like on Xbox. Content-wise, the PS3 version thus offered exactly the same experience as its counterparts on other platforms, just with a noticeably rougher technical side, which players noticed most during more demanding firefights with lots of enemies and effects on screen at once. Nevertheless, it was a fully content-complete version of the game, with all the same weapons, enemies, and side quests as the other platforms offered, so PS3 players didn't come away with a diminished experience — just a technically somewhat rougher one.

**Why play it:** For buddies craving a cooperative looter shooter, the PS3 version offers the same content as elsewhere, including split-screen, just with a somewhat rougher technical side during demanding firefights.

ps3__wolfenstein.teaser: B.J. Blazkowicz against occult Nazis; the Shadow dimension gives the action a supernatural twist.
ps3__wolfenstein.article:
Wolfenstein from 2009 returns players to the role of agent B. J. Blazkowicz fighting against a Nazi occult program, this time in the fictional city of Isenstadt, where German scientists are attempting to harness a paranormal energy called Vril. The game continues the classic series' combination of straightforward action shooting with supernatural elements — Blazkowicz gains the ability to shift into a shadow dimension that lets him slow down time, pass through invisible walls, heal faster, or see hidden enemies and objects, so the game blends classic gunplay with a supernatural twist and a more open take on the city between missions.

The PlayStation 3 version launched simultaneously with Xbox 360 and PC in August 2009 and offered exactly the same campaign, the same shadow dimension, and the same weapons and their upgrades as on the other platforms — no version received exclusive content. The controls were adapted to the DualShock 3 with analog sticks instead of mouse and keyboard, a standard compromise for console versions of first-person shooters at the time, and aiming also included mild magnetic target snapping to make aiming with a gamepad easier.

Technically, the game ran on PS3 at the same resolution and with similar frame rate stability as on Xbox 360, without significant differences that reviewers at the time would highlight — both console versions were perceived as essentially equal. The main difference compared to the PC version thus lay not in the campaign content but purely in the controls and in the lack of the ability to set custom key bindings or play at a higher resolution, which PC players with more powerful hardware were used to. The game also included online multiplayer, which on PS3 ran over the PlayStation Network with the same maps and game modes as on Xbox 360 via Xbox Live, so no content difference could be found between the consoles in this part of the game either.

**Why play it:** Console players get an equally stable and content-complete version on PS3 as on Xbox 360, including online multiplayer with the same maps and modes.

ps3__dirt-2.teaser: Colorful, accessible rallycross fun with Ken Block instead of a dry rally simulation.
ps3__dirt-2.article:
DiRT 2 is a racing game focused on rallycross, buggies, trucks, and other off-road disciplines, in which the player, as a member of a fictional rally team, races exotic tracks from London through Croatia to Malaysia and Morocco. Compared to the first DiRT game, the series shed some of its seriousness and added a colorful, energetic presentation with commentary, a musical score, and friendly rivalry among drivers, including real rally star Ken Block, making it feel more accessible to a wider audience and less like a pure rally simulation aimed only at a narrow circle of fans.

The PlayStation 3 version launched simultaneously with Xbox 360 and PC in late 2009 and offered the same tracks, the same vehicles, and the same career mode as the other platforms — no version received exclusive extra content or different disciplines. The controls were adapted to the DualShock 3, including the ability to use the analog sticks' sensitivity for fine throttle and brake control, which is crucial in a racing game for handling slides on gravel, mud, or sand.

Technically, the PS3 version ran at a comparable resolution to Xbox 360, online multiplayer ran over the PlayStation Network instead of Xbox Live, but otherwise it was an equivalent experience without noticeable differences that reviewers would highlight. Compared to the PC version, the PS3 version naturally lacked the option for custom graphics settings beyond what the console offered, and players were limited to a gamepad instead of the optional steering wheel and pedals that PC owners could connect to their computer for a more precise feel of the track. The career mode, with its gradual unlocking of new disciplines, vehicles, and sponsors, was just as long and just as structured on PS3 as on Xbox 360, including the same voice-over theme and driver conversations between races.

**Why play it:** Rallycross fans will be pleased that the career mode on PS3 is just as long and structured as on Xbox 360, just with multiplayer over the PlayStation Network instead of Xbox Live.

ps3__skate-2.teaser: Flick-It controls replace buttons with tilting the sticks; you build ramps in a broken-down city.
ps3__skate-2.article:
Skate 2 is a skateboarding game that follows the first installment and its acclaimed Flick-It control system, in which tricks are performed by tilting both analog sticks to mimic the real movement of feet on a board, instead of the simple button-mashing typical of the rival Tony Hawk's series. The game is set in the fictional city of San Vanelona, which was partially destroyed by an earthquake, and the player can build and modify ramps, rails, and other obstacles directly in the open world using objects scattered around the streets, placing skateboarding in a more believable and interactive urban environment than before.

The PlayStation 3 version launched simultaneously with Xbox 360 in early 2009 and was completely identical in content - the same city of San Vanelona, the same tricks, the same custom obstacle-building system, and the same story mode following a skater's career from nothing to fame. The controls remained built on the same principle of tilting the analog sticks adapted for the DualShock 3, which, thanks to the controller's sensitivity for this game, didn't need the Sixaxis feature or any other motion control at all, unlike some other PS3 games of the time.

Unlike other multiplatform games of the era, Skate 2 never came to PC at all - the series remained exclusively a console affair for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, so PC owners never got to play this game in any form. There were also no significant technical differences in framerate or graphics recorded between the two console versions, so choosing between PS3 and Xbox 360 was essentially a matter of personal platform preference and possibly your online friends' community, not the quality of the game's execution itself. Online multiplayer and uploading custom trick videos worked identically on both consoles, just through different networks - PlayStation Network on PS3 and Xbox Live on Xbox 360 - with the same ability to share your own gameplay clips with the player community.

**Why play it:** Because the game never came to PC, the PS3 console version is the only choice for fans without an Xbox 360 - technically on par and with the same ability to share your own trick videos.

ps3__lost-planet-extreme-condition-colon.teaser: Giant Vital Suit mechs against insectoid Akrid on a frozen planet; without heat you freeze to death.
ps3__lost-planet-extreme-condition-colon.article:
Lost Planet: Extreme Condition took players to the frozen planet E.D.N. III, where giant mech suits called Vital Suits battle insectoid Akrid for the thermal energy needed to survive in extreme cold. Capcom built the game on the MT Framework engine and combined a third-person action shooter with the pressure of constantly replenishing heat, without which the character would die of cold, forcing players to keep pushing forward and switch between on-foot action and piloting giant mechs against equally giant enemies.

The game arrived on PlayStation 3 roughly a year after the original on Xbox 360, under the expanded title Colonies Edition, which hints that this wasn't a simple port. The PS3 version added new missions and characters tied to the story compared to the original game, along with an expanded multiplayer offering with additional maps and split-screen game modes not found on Xbox 360, giving players more ways to spend time outside the main campaign than the original Xbox 360 version offered. The graphics engine stayed the same, so the visual difference between the consoles wasn't dramatic, but in terms of content this was the richest version of the game Capcom offered at the time.

The release fit into the early phase of the PlayStation 3's life cycle, when publishers were still testing how to differentiate the console from the competition - for Lost Planet, that meant added extra content rather than a technical edge, since both systems handled the game at comparable graphical quality, and Capcom bet that players would appreciate more content rather than a technical advantage the console could hardly deliver anyway. For players picking up Lost Planet for the first time specifically on PS3, Colonies Edition thus represented a more complete experience than the original Xbox 360 version, even though it arrived a year late and without a simultaneous release on both consoles, which PlayStation-preferring players had to wait longer for than Xbox 360 owners.

**Why play it:** For players picking up Lost Planet for the first time on PS3, Colonies Edition offers a more complete experience thanks to the added extra content compared to the Xbox 360 version, albeit with a year's delay.

ps3__resistance-2.teaser: The campaign leads through a devastated America; giant bosses give the game unprecedented scale.
ps3__resistance-2.article:
**Resistance 2** follows the opening chapter of the trilogy and pushes the alternate-history invasion of the alien Chimera into even more epic proportions. The player once again takes on the role of soldier Nathan Hale, whose body has been infected by the Chimeran virus and is gradually turning into something between human and the enemy he's fighting. This time the campaign leaves Europe behind and leads through devastated American cities from San Francisco to Chicago, where the player gradually learns how catastrophically the invasion struck the United States and how desperate the defense of humanity's remnants has become. The player also faces giant bosses that give the series a genuine sense of threat and scale rarely offered by shooters of the time, and the fights against them are among the game's most memorable moments.

The gameplay rests on a classic FPS foundation enriched by a more limited weapon loadout at any one time, which pushes the player toward more tactical decision-making than the more open-ended first game. The arsenal combines earthly weapons with strange Chimeran technologies that enable unconventional ways to eliminate enemies, such as shooting around corners or slowing down time. Great emphasis was placed on an eight-player cooperative mode with its own campaign running parallel to the main story, and on an extensive online multiplayer supporting up to sixty players, an unusual scale for consoles at the time, showing where online play on PS3 could head. Insomniac Games leveraged the console's power to render sprawling battlefields and mass battles with many enemies on screen at once without the game losing smoothness.

The atmosphere draws on a grim vision of an occupied America and industrial, oppressive music underscoring the hopelessness of the resistance against overwhelming odds, while the visuals alternate between ruined metropolises and dark underground complexes. Contemporary reviews particularly praised the boss fights, the variety of environments, and the multiplayer component, although some fans of the first game missed the split-screen co-op that the sequel replaced with an online-only format. In the context of the genre, this was one of the more ambitious console shooters of its generation, showing that even an exclusive console series could rival the scale of major multiplatform hits. It's still remembered today as a technically and content-wise solid sequel that knew how to work with the large scale of its world and offer players a rich mix of action, atmosphere, and teamwork.

**Why play it:** Fans of grim sci-fi shooters will be drawn in by the dark atmosphere of an occupied America, elaborate boss fights, and an extensive multiplayer, although fans of the first game may miss the split-screen co-op.

ps3__armored-core-4.teaser: A restart of the mech series for a new console generation; you pilot the advanced Next machine.
ps3__armored-core-4.article:
**Armored Core 4** marked a restart of FromSoftware's long-running series of mechanized combat simulators for a new console generation. The game casts the player as the pilot of a so-called Next, a highly advanced combat mech, and follows a story set in an era when the world is recovering from a large-scale conflict and power is held by multinational corporations controlling giant flying fortresses called Cradles. The conflict between these corporations and resistance forces forms the backdrop for a series of missions in which the player gradually rises among elite pilots and uncovers the political intrigue behind the war.

Compared to earlier entries in the series, the fourth Armored Core focused on faster, more airborne combat - mechs can fly longer and more fluidly using boosters, which fundamentally changes combat tactics and gives the game a brisker, more arcade-like pace than the previous, more ground-oriented installments. The player still assembles their own robot in detail from dozens of parts affecting weight, speed, armor, and weaponry, while needing to balance weapon power against the machine's mobility, and this depth of customization remains the core of the series even in this restart. The graphics engine leveraged the PS3's power to render sprawling arenas, destroyed cities, and spectacular fights against giant bosses that test both the player's reflexes and the thoughtfulness of their build.

The music and sound design underscore the industrial, mechanical atmosphere of the battles, while the story is told rather sparsely, through terse text supplemented by briefings, which is typical for the series and leaves more room for the player's imagination. Contemporary reception was mixed to positive - the speed and intensity of the combat, along with the boldness of reworking the series' established formula, were praised, while criticism targeted the steep difficulty, poor accessibility for newcomers, and a relatively short campaign. For fans of the mech genre, this was an important restart that paved the way for the series' further installments on PS3 and is still ranked among the genre's respected, if demanding, titles focused on building and piloting your own combat machine.

**Why play it:** Mech fans craving fast and demanding action will enjoy the series' bold restart, though the steep difficulty, poor accessibility for newcomers, and short campaign require patience.

ps3__armored-core-v.teaser: The most ambitious entry in the mech series, with emphasis on online battles for territory.
ps3__armored-core-v.article:
**Armored Core V** is the fifth numbered entry in FromSoftware's mech series and in many ways the most ambitious attempt to bring the series to a wider audience and to modern online play. The player once again sits in the cockpit of a war mech called an Armored Core and fights on behalf of one of the factions in a world devastated by an earlier conflict, where individual corporations, mercenary units, and resistance groups compete for control over the remaining resources and territory both on the surface and underground, where humanity has partly retreated following the previous catastrophe.

Compared to previous entries, the game placed a stronger emphasis on teamwork and tactics - it introduced a command system allowing the player to issue orders to allies controlled by AI or by other players, and missions often require capturing and defending control points rather than the purely straightforward action runs of older entries. Mech customization remained as deep as before, with a wide range of parts affecting weaponry, mobility, and defense and the ability to finely tune every aspect of the machine, and the game placed greater emphasis on cooperative and competitive multiplayer, which became one of the main pillars of content, including an extensive team-based base-capture mode outside the main campaign.

Technically, the game offered more detailed environments and more elaborate explosion and damage effects on PS3 than earlier entries, although the series' engine was, even at this point, still recognizable by its distinctive, technical, and deliberately heavier controls that the series traditionally maintains and that demand patience and practice from players. The atmosphere remains dark and war-torn, with electronic and industrial music accompanying the battles and minimalist storytelling through text messages and briefings. Contemporary reviews praised the ambition of the shift toward more tactical, team-based play and the sophistication of the multiplayer modes, while also pointing out that the game moved away from some traditional elements of the series and that the single-player campaign felt secondary compared to the online component. For players interested in mechs and tactical action combat, this is an interesting, if polarizing, entry with its own identity within the series, one that experimented with a direction the series could have taken.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates a more tactical, team-oriented multiplayer and more elaborate machine damage will find an interesting shift in the series here, even though the single-player campaign feels weaker by comparison.

ps3__silent-hill-homecoming.teaser: A survival horror about a soldier returning home who searches for his missing brother.
ps3__silent-hill-homecoming.article:
**Silent Hill: Homecoming** tells the story of soldier Alex Shepherd, who returns home wounded to the fictional American town of Shepherd's Glen and discovers that his younger brother has vanished without a trace. The search leads him through fog-shrouded streets into a parallel, dark Silent Hill, where reality falls apart and turns into a nightmare full of twisted monsters and rusted industrial spaces. The game emphasizes a personal, family drama that gradually unfolds through memories and fragments, typical of the whole series.

Homecoming was developed by the American studio Double Helix Games, making it one of the first entries in the series entrusted primarily to a Western developer, and it shows - the combat system is more action-oriented and fluid than in previous Japanese-developed entries, with the ability to dodge and chain attacks, but at the same time it lost some of the slow, oppressive pace that fans loved about the series. Visually, the game relies on dark, rain-soaked interiors and grotesque enemy designs, and the atmosphere remains dense despite the faster-paced action.

Critics and fans received Homecoming with mixed feelings: they praised the combat system but criticized the game's smaller openness, shorter playtime, and a story that at times slides toward simpler jump-scare horror at the expense of the psychological depth of previous entries. Even so, it remains a respected attempt to modernize the series for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 generation of consoles.

**Why play it:** For fans of more action-oriented survival horror who appreciate smoother combat than in older Silent Hill entries but don't expect the psychological depth of the original trilogy.

ps3__silent-hill-downpour.teaser: A survival horror about an escaped convict; rain signals the shift into a darker world.
ps3__silent-hill-downpour.article:
**Silent Hill: Downpour** puts escaped convict Murphy Pendleton in the lead role, spat out by a dark forest somewhere near the town of Silent Hill after a transport crash. A more open, partially sandbox-style environment lets you walk the streets in any order, complete side objectives, and stumble upon fragments of Murphy's past that gradually reveal why he ended up in prison and what he regrets. The key gameplay element is rain - once it starts, the town transforms, streets crumble, and a more aggressive variant of enemies attacks the player, setting the game apart from its more linear predecessors.

Development was handled by the Brno-based studio Vatra Games, for whom this was their first major foreign project, and the game carries the mark of a smaller team that tried to bring the series back closer to the slower, exploratory pace of the first entries. The combat system is deliberately clunky and weapons break quickly, so the game pushes the player toward fleeing rather than fighting, matching the spirit of classic Silent Hill. The sound design and the grim urban atmosphere rank among the strongest things Downpour has to offer.

Technically, the game suffered from period-typical performance issues and frame-rate drops, which reviewers criticized, even as they praised the courage to return to a slower pace and a more open structure. Among series fans, Downpour still has a mixed reputation today - to some it's an underrated return to the roots, to others a technically unpolished entry.

**Why play it:** For players who prefer exploration and atmosphere over action and can forgive technical flaws in exchange for a return to the slower pace of classic Silent Hill.

ps3__silent-hill-hd-collection.teaser: A remastered collection of Silent Hill 2 and 3 for one console generation.
ps3__silent-hill-hd-collection.article:
**Silent Hill HD Collection** bundles together remastered versions of the second and third installments of the series, namely Silent Hill 2 and Silent Hill 3, which many players and critics consider the peak of the whole brand. The aim of the collection was to make both titles accessible to a new generation of players on PlayStation 3 at an upgraded resolution, with reworked lighting and minor control tweaks, without touching the story structure or puzzles themselves.

Unlike similar remasters of other series, however, the collection wasn't met with a warm reception. The port wasn't handled by the original Japanese studio but by an external team, which lost part of the source files during the process and had to partially reconstruct the game - the result was missing sound effects, altered music compared to the original, and noticeably worse fog effects, which had been key to the atmosphere of both games. Fans thus criticized the collection for offering a degraded version of iconic games instead of a faithful remaster.

Even so, the HD Collection remains, for many players, the only convenient way to play both games together on a PlayStation 3 console, and despite its technical shortcomings it still offers the core of what makes Silent Hill 2 and 3 genre classics - psychologically dense stories, iconic enemies, and music whose atmosphere still works despite the degraded sound quality.

**Why play it:** For players without access to the PS2 originals who want to experience Silent Hill 2 and 3 on one console and can accept that the sound and visuals are noticeably weaker than the originals.

ps4__yakuza-kiwami.teaser: A remake of the first Yakuza game with Kazuma Kiryu; a yakuza drama of honor and betrayal in Kamurocho.
ps4__yakuza-kiwami.article:
**Yakuza Kiwami** is a remake of the first game in the famous Japanese Yakuza series from 2005, reworked by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio on a modern engine with new story tangents and characters from later entries added in. The player once again steps into the shoes of Kazuma Kiryu, a former yakuza who served ten years for a murder he didn't commit to cover for his friend, and after his release returns to the fictional Tokyo district of Kamurocho to find out where ten billion yen vanished from the clan's coffers, along with the daughter of his late colleague. It's told as a yakuza drama full of honor, betrayal, and family bonds, one that regularly swings into moments of almost soap-opera excess.

The core of the gameplay is a linear story interspersed with cinematic sequences and an open district packed with side activities - from karaoke, batting cages, and hostess clubs to collecting cats and the original Majima Everywhere minigame, in which rival Goro Majima can ambush the player at any moment while walking the streets, forcing them to keep sharpening their combat skills. Combat offers four distinct fighting styles with their own skill trees and makes heavy use of the surrounding environment, from trash cans to motorcycle wheels. On PlayStation 4, the remake runs smoothly at high resolution and noticeably improves the controls and graphics over the PlayStation 2 original, while preserving the original voice cast, which gives the characters weight and credibility.

Critics and fans alike embraced Kiwami as the ideal entry point into the series for players put off by the dated look of the first game; thanks to the reworked controls and dubbing, it remains playable today. The neon streets of Kamurocho and the melancholic music round out an atmosphere that can turn from serious to outright comedic within minutes, and that very combination is part of why the Yakuza series earned a loyal fanbase even outside Japan. The remake also works as a safety net for newcomers who want to enter Kazuma Kiryu's long story chronologically and without compromises in controls, and many players discovered the whole series through Kiwami and stayed with it for years.

**Why play it:** For newcomers who want to enter the Yakuza series through a reworked, playable introduction full of Kamurocho's neon streets and unexpected humor.

ps4__yakuza-kiwami-2.teaser: A remake of the second game on the Dragon Engine; the first seamless transition between combat and exploration.
ps4__yakuza-kiwami-2.article:
**Yakuza Kiwami 2** is a remake of the second entry in the series from 2006, this time built on the Dragon Engine, which for the first time brought a seamless transition between combat and exploration with no visible loading screens. Kazuma Kiryu once again heads to Kamurocho and to the newly designed Osaka district of Sotenbori to prevent a war between the yakuza and a Korean organization and to uncover a conspiracy reaching all the way to the leadership of the Tojo clan. The story ranks among the most emotionally powerful in the whole series and also introduces a side plotline about detective Kaoru, which functions as a smaller, self-contained campaign with its own character arc.

The gameplay is built around exploring two large districts full of side quests, minigames, and businesses the player can build up to earn money, from a hostess club to their own cabaret, with the business management growing into a standalone economic minigame complete with its own staff and competitors. Combat is faster and smoother than in previous entries thanks to the new engine, which allows for fluid animations and larger crowds of opponents at once. On PlayStation 4, the game benefits from sharper graphics, better lighting, and significantly shorter loading times, so even years later it still feels surprisingly modern, and the new Sotenbori district with its own minigames and shops gives players a reason to explore beyond the main storyline.

Contemporary reviews praised above all the storytelling and tension of the main plot, which many players and journalists called one of the series' high points. The music and the nighttime city's soundscape support an atmosphere that's half melodrama, half action thriller, and the cinematically staged final battles are part of what the Yakuza series has long been known for. Kiwami 2 still stands today as proof that a remake can be more than a technical polish - it can be a full-fledged return to a story that holds up even years later and offers new players one of the best introductions to the world of Kazuma Kiryu.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Yakuza series craving one of its narrative highlights, where melodrama blends with cinematically staged battles and tension that holds up all the way to the end.

ps4__yakuza-5-remastered.teaser: The most sprawling entry in the series - five playable characters and five cities across Japan.
ps4__yakuza-5-remastered.article:
**Yakuza 5 Remastered** is a PlayStation 4 version of the series' sprawling fifth entry, adapted from the original PlayStation 3 game to run at a higher resolution and with steadier framerates. The game stands out for its sheer scope - the player gradually takes control of five playable characters, including Kazuma Kiryu, young boxer Taiga Saejima, hostess Haruka Sawamura, and others, and the story unfolds across five different cities throughout Japan, including Sapporo and Fukuoka, which otherwise don't appear in the series.

Each character has their own play style - Kiryu fights with classic fisticuffs, Saejima relies on brute strength, Haruka pursues a singing career instead of combat and unlocks rhythm minigames, while the other protagonists offer different approaches to both combat and spending free time in the city. This makes Yakuza 5 one of the most content-packed entries in the series in terms of sheer volume and playtime. The PS4 remaster doesn't add new mechanics, but it makes the game accessible without needing an older console and removes technical rough edges from the original, such as framerate drops in crowded streets or longer loading times between districts.

At its original release, Yakuza 5 was praised in Japan especially for its bold structure with five main protagonists and its finely detailed cities, though it arrived in the West later and with less attention than other entries, which for a long time earned it a reputation as the series' overlooked installment. Today fans see it as a hidden gem of the series that offers an unusually wide range of play styles in a single package and serves as a bridge between the classic trilogy and the modern entries built on the Dragon Engine. Thanks to the PS4 remaster, new players could also catch up on story threads before the arrival of Yakuza 6 without having to hunt down an old PlayStation 3, making it easier to piece together the full continuity of Kiryu's story within a single console generation.

**Why play it:** For series fans who want to fill in the full continuity of Kiryu's story without an old PS3, the remaster offers a hidden gem with an unusually wide range of play styles in one package.

ps4__yakuza-6-song-of-life.teaser: The final chapter of Kazuma Kiryu's story; the first entry built on the new Dragon Engine.
ps4__yakuza-6-song-of-life.article:
**Yakuza 6: The Song of Life** closes out Kazuma Kiryu's long-running story and is the first entry in the series built on the new Dragon Engine, which replaced the older technology and delivered seamless open cities with no transition screens between combat and walking around. The story picks up directly after the previous entries - Kiryu is released from prison and learns that his adoptive daughter Haruka is in a coma after a car accident and has a son whose existence no one knew about. The search for the boy's father takes Kiryu from Kamurocho to the new, quieter coastal district of Onomichi, where instead of yakuza he mostly encounters fishermen, farmers, and local small-time troublemakers.

The combat system was simplified down to a single style instead of the earlier multiple variants, making the game more approachable for newcomers, while also adding a more detailed injury system and contextual fights that make use of the surroundings, from street furniture to vehicles that can be used to throw opponents across the street. The new Onomichi district contrasts with the noisy Kamurocho through its slower pace and smaller community, which is also reflected in side quests focused on local residents and the fishing community. On PlayStation 4, the game showed off the full graphical power of the Dragon Engine - densely populated streets, realistic faces, and smooth transitions between cutscenes and gameplay, all of which make Kamurocho and Onomichi feel more alive and cohesive than in earlier entries built on the previous technology.

Critics praised above all the emotional culmination of Kiryu's story and the technical leap forward, though the simplified combat system sparked discussion among part of the fanbase about whether the series was losing some of the depth of its earlier fights. The musical score and cinematic final sequences rank among the strongest in the series and round out a farewell to a character players had followed through many previous entries. Yakuza 6 today stands as both a dignified, emotional conclusion to one of the longest-running game sagas and as the technological foundation on which all later entries in the series were built, including the spin-off Judgment.

**Why play it:** For players who followed Kiryu through the previous entries, it offers an emotional and technically accomplished conclusion to one of the longest-running game sagas, even if the simplified combat system trimmed some of its complexity.

ps4__judgment.teaser: A darker, noir-tinged Yakuza spin-off about detective Takayuki Yagami in Kamurocho.
ps4__judgment.article:
**Judgment** is a detective spin-off from the creators of the Yakuza series, set by Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio in the same fictional district of Kamurocho, but with a new protagonist - former lawyer Takayuki Yagami, who becomes a private detective after losing a court case. The main plot revolves around a series of brutal murders tied to both the yakuza and the police, and Yagami has to combine investigative work with fistfights to see the case through to the end. The tone of the game is darker and more noir than the main series, though it keeps its trademark humor in the side activities.

The gameplay expands the proven Yakuza formula with detective mechanics - tailing suspects through crowds, photographing evidence, squeezing through small spaces like a rat, or hacking locks using a drone. The combat system is built around two styles, power and acrobatic, and offers elaborate combos and finishers that make use of the environment. Kamurocho feels more alive in Judgment than ever before thanks to new side cases and activities, from escape rooms to drones and playing tabletop games at an arcade, and many of them work more like small detective puzzles than typical Yakuza-style side content.

On PlayStation 4, the game uses the same Dragon Engine as Yakuza 6 and offers one of the most detailed renditions of Kamurocho in the whole series, with smooth transitions between street investigations and cinematically staged fights. Critics praised above all the strong story with unexpected twists and a fresh perspective on a familiar setting, which earned Judgment a reputation as one of the series' best spin-offs and convinced many players that Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio can tell a story outside the established framework of yakuza drama too. Due to later licensing issues involving one of the actors, the game disappeared from digital storefronts, so the PS4 version remains one of the few reliable ways to play it in its original form as intended.

**Why play it:** Because of licensing issues it vanished from digital storefronts, so the PS4 version remains one of the few reliable ways to experience a strong detective story in one of the Yakuza series' best spin-offs.

ps4__lost-judgment.teaser: The sequel to the detective spin-off; a school bullying case across two connected cities.
ps4__lost-judgment.article:
**Lost Judgment** is the sequel to the detective spin-off Judgment, in which Takayuki Yagami and his colleagues from the Yagami Detective Agency head to two cities at once - Kamurocho and the new district of Isezaki Ijincho, based on the real city of Yokohama. The main story revolves around a school bullying case that gradually uncovers a much wider and darker web of motives reaching into one character's past. The game isn't afraid to tackle sensitive topics like bullying or suicide and treats them more seriously than most entertainment titles from the same studio.

The combat system builds on the first game and adds a third style focused on fighting multiple opponents at once with a weapon resembling a bo staff, giving the player three distinct approaches to combat depending on the situation. New detective mechanics include motorcycle chases, diving, and an extensive school club system, in which Yagami helps students with their extracurricular activities, from dance to a detective club. Both cities are densely packed with side quests and minigames, so the game offers dozens of hours of content beyond the main story, including separate smaller narrative branches tied to individual school clubs.

On PlayStation 4, Lost Judgment runs somewhat more demandingly than its predecessor due to the greater density of detail across two cities at once, yet it remains smooth and on par graphically with other titles built on the Dragon Engine, with striking cinematic cutscenes during key fights. Critics praised especially the ambition of the storytelling and the willingness to tackle serious topics, as well as the level of detail in both game cities, which places the game among the high points of the entire spin-off series. Like the first game, Lost Judgment later disappeared from digital storefronts due to a licensing issue, so a physical or previously purchased PS4 copy remains one of the sure ways to get hold of it.

**Why play it:** For fans of ambitious storytelling and two intricately detailed cities, Lost Judgment is the high point of the spin-off series, and after being pulled from stores, the physical PS4 version remains one of the sure ways to get hold of it.

ps4__yakuza-3-remastered.teaser: Kiryu briefly trades the yakuza life for an orphanage in Okinawa; the series' calmest story.
ps4__yakuza-3-remastered.article:
**Yakuza 3 Remastered** brings the series' third entry from 2009 to PlayStation 4, in which Kazuma Kiryu temporarily steps away from yakuza life and moves from Kamurocho to Okinawa to run the Morning Glory orphanage. The peace doesn't last long, though - local land disputes and old ties to the Tojo clan gradually pull him back into a conflict that links the idyllic island setting to darker themes of organized crime and corruption. The contrast between sunny Okinawa and old Kamurocho is one of the biggest things that sets the third entry apart in the series, and it was the first time the series showed it could also tell calmer, less action-heavy stories.

The combat system builds on previous entries but adds new techniques and smoother animations; the remaster also restores several content pieces that were cut from the Western PlayStation 3 release during localization, including some side quests. The game still centers on fistfights in an open environment, collecting side activities, and taking care of the children at the orphanage, which gives the story an unusually family-oriented and calmer tone compared to the surrounding entries, especially in contrast with the darker nighttime Kamurocho the player regularly returns to.

The remastered PS4 version offers higher resolution and steadier framerates, making the game more playable than ever, although the old control scheme and camera betray its origins from the end of the PlayStation 3 era. Contemporary reviews of the third entry were more mixed than for its predecessors, mainly due to the slower pace and reduced action in the game's second half; the remaster, however, gave players and critics a chance to revisit it and appreciate its unconventional story about family in the middle of a criminal underworld. Thanks to the restored content, the remaster today offers a more complete and faithful version of the story than the one players knew from the Western PlayStation 3 release.

**Why play it:** Thanks to the remaster and restored content, the PS4 version offers a more complete and playable take on an unconventional story about family amid the criminal underworld than the one players knew from the older PS3 version.

ps4__call-of-duty-modern-warfare.teaser: The 2019 series reboot; a raw take on modern warfare, including a controversial mission.
ps4__call-of-duty-modern-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty: Modern Warfare** from 2019 was a reboot of the legendary series that returned to a raw, darker take on modern warfare while also serving as a new platform for long-term multiplayer support on PS4. The campaign follows the intertwined fates of CIA operatives, British special forces, and rebels from the fictional Middle Eastern country of Urzikstan, and the game isn't afraid to portray war in a rawer, more uncomfortable way than players of the series were used to, including a controversial mission inspired by an attack on the London Underground.

Gameplay-wise, it's a pure-blooded action shooter focused on pace, cover-based firefights, and cinematic action sequences, but Infinity Ward also added slower, tense sections in a horror-like or stealth-infiltration style. Multiplayer introduced a completely reworked weapon system with a deep customization tree, along with the new Special Ops co-op mode, which linked smaller story missions with procedurally generated challenges for multiple players. The graphics engine on PS4 rendered realistically lit environments and detailed character models, though it required some framerate compromises on the base console compared to more powerful models.
