That atmosphere is indeed one of the game's main strengths — misty Victorian streets, an oppressive soundscape of a disease-ravaged city, and dark gothic aesthetics create a dense mood that few other RPGs achieve. Contemporary reviews praised the original moral system and story but criticized the technical side and repetitive combat. Despite these flaws, Vampyr remains a respected title for players seeking an RPG with a strong atmosphere and genuinely difficult moral decisions that carry lasting consequences for the world around the character.

Each district of London is populated by its own set of characters with a name, occupation, family relationships, and personal secrets that the player uncovers through conversation and investigation, making decisions about life and death far more personal than in other vampire games. If the player chooses the path of killing, the district grows poorer, shops disappear, and disease spreads faster, while a more merciful approach means a harder but morally cleaner playthrough with a weaker character. This interconnection of systems gave Vampyr a reputation as a thoughtful, if technically imperfect, work that, thanks to its strong theme and atmosphere, still holds onto devoted fans today.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for a thoughtful, if technically imperfect, vampire RPG will appreciate Vampyr for its personal moral dilemma — killing impoverishes a district and spreads disease, while the gentler path means a harder but cleaner playthrough.

xbox-one__dragon-s-dogma-dark-arisen.teaser: Action RPG famous for climbing giant monsters; Pawns learn from their own experience.
xbox-one__dragon-s-dogma-dark-arisen.article:
**Dragon's Dogma: Dark Arisen** is an action RPG from Capcom that arrived on Xbox One as a remastered version of the original 2012 game, expanded with the Dark Arisen content. Playing as the Arisen, whose heart was torn out by a dragon, the player sets off across an open fantasy world accompanied by a party of Pawns, AI-controlled companions who learn from experience and can be shared with other players online. The combat system is famous for its physicality, with the player literally climbing onto giant monsters such as griffins or cyclopes and attacking their weak points, which remains one of the most striking combat experiences in the genre to this day.

On Xbox One the game ran at a smoother resolution and frame rate than the original release, while retaining all the depth of its vocation system, crafting, and nighttime survival, when the world turns into a far more dangerous place after dark. The atmosphere is heightened by dark fantasy aesthetics and orchestral music that underscores the epic scale of battles with giant beasts. Both contemporary and retrospective reviews praise above all the originality of the combat system and the AI companions, which has given the game a loyal fanbase even years after release. Dark Arisen is still regarded today as a cult classic and one of the most distinctive action RPGs of its generation.

The Dark Arisen expansion adds the vast underground area of Bitterblack Isle, full of particularly dangerous enemies and powerful gear, which functions as a kind of endgame content for players for whom the already lengthy main campaign wasn't enough. Pawns also carry knowledge of enemy weaknesses and can be hired from other players online, so even a solo player effectively benefits from the experience of the whole community. The unusual emphasis on physical interaction with the world, where the character can carry heavy objects or grab a giant monster's fur and climb it to reach its vulnerable spot, still stands out as one of the most distinctive combat systems in the genre and inspired a number of later games.

**Why play it:** For players craving the genre's most distinctive combat system, where you can climb a giant monster's fur to reach its vulnerable spot, Dark Arisen also offers the Bitterblack Isle endgame area and pawn knowledge shared with the whole community.

xbox-one__ni-no-kuni-ii-revenant-kingdom.teaser: JRPG from Level-5 with fairy-tale visuals; for the first time without Studio Ghibli and with action combat.
xbox-one__ni-no-kuni-ii-revenant-kingdom.article:
**Ni no Kuni II: Revenant Kingdom** from Level-5 is a JRPG sequel to the successful first game, this time without direct involvement from Studio Ghibli, though its visual style retains the fairy-tale, colorful aesthetic reminiscent of an animated film. The player takes on the role of young King Evan, who after losing his throne sets out to build a new kingdom and gather allies across a vibrant fantasy world. The combat system abandons the previous game's turn-based approach in favor of real-time action combat with the ability to switch between characters, complemented by tactical command of small sprites called Higgledies in a separate mode.

A major part of the game is building and managing your own kingdom, where the player takes in new citizens, constructs buildings, and develops technologies, giving the game a distinct management dimension beyond a traditional RPG. On Xbox One the game ran technically without major issues and offered a colorful, fairy-tale world accompanied by music from an experienced composer who carried forward the melodic quality of the first game. Contemporary reviews praised the variety of content and pleasant atmosphere, though some players missed the deeper emotional connection offered by its predecessor thanks to the collaboration with Studio Ghibli. Even so, Revenant Kingdom remains one of the most accessible and visually pleasant JRPGs of its generation, ideal even for players less familiar with the genre.

A smaller side mode featuring battles of the Higgledies sprites, resembling simplified real-time strategy, adds variety beyond the main combat system and unlocks its own progression independent of the main characters' level. Travel between kingdoms takes place on a stylized world map, where the player encounters random battles and hidden treasures, so the game's structure alternates between free exploration and a regular return to developing your own kingdom. The colorful, almost childlike aesthetic contrasts with fairly serious themes of betrayal and a ruler's responsibility, giving Ni no Kuni II a distinctive tone among the JRPGs of its time.

**Why play it:** For fans of JRPGs with a childlike, colorful aesthetic and more serious themes of betrayal and responsibility, Ni no Kuni II also offers a diversion in the form of Higgledy sprite battles and building your own kingdom.

xbox-one__yakuza-like-dragon.teaser: The series swaps action for turn-based combat inspired by Dragon Quest for the first time; hero Ichiban.
xbox-one__yakuza-like-dragon.article:
**Yakuza: Like a Dragon** marked a major turning point for Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio's long-running series, as it swapped the traditional action combat for a turn-based RPG system inspired by classics like Dragon Quest for the first time. The player takes on the new lead character Ichiban Kasuga, a former yakuza who, after sixteen years in prison, discovers his clan betrayed him and sets out through the city of Yokohama in search of the truth and his own place in the world. Battles play out as party-based turn-based fights, where characters use vocations resembling everyday jobs, from cook to homeless person, with bizarre yet functional abilities.

The game retains the series' signature mix of a serious crime story and utterly absurd humor, side activities, and minigames that the series is famous for, from karaoke to a business simulator to bizarre side quests. On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and offered an extensive, richly detailed urban setting full of life, complemented by striking music alternating emotional melodies with energetic battle themes. Contemporary reception was very positive, with critics and fans alike praising the boldness of changing the established combat system while still keeping the series' characteristic spirit. Yakuza: Like a Dragon became one of the best-received entries in the series and successfully opened the brand up to new players beyond traditional action fans.

Unlike earlier protagonists in the series, Ichiban isn't a cold-blooded brawler but rather a naive dreamer inspired by Dragon Quest heroes, which is reflected in how, in his own imagination, he perceives fights with street gangs as epic RPG battles against monsters. The vocation system, which can be changed almost anytime between battles, allows players to experiment with different playstyles, from dancer to detective to a classic brawler, and each vocation has its own set of abilities and weapons. Yokohama's extensive substories and side activities, from a management simulator to absurd side quests, add dozens of extra hours of content beyond the main story.

**Why play it:** For anyone who wants to experience Yakuza as a naive RPG adventure inspired by Dragon Quest, the flexible vocation system, from dancer to detective, and dozens of hours of Yokohama's absurd side activities are a real draw.

xbox-one__disco-elysium-final-cut.teaser: An RPG with no combat, just dialogue and the character's inner voices; this version comes with full voice acting.
xbox-one__disco-elysium-final-cut.article:
**Disco Elysium: The Final Cut** brought the console version of ZA/UM's critically acclaimed RPG to Xbox One, enriched with full voice acting for every character and additional political content. The player wakes up as an amnesiac detective in the decaying port city of Revachol and must investigate a murder while gradually piecing together their own past, identity, and political beliefs. Instead of traditional combat, the game relies almost entirely on dialogue and a skill system, where twenty-four inner voices of the character, ranging from intellect to empathy to physical prowess, comment on situations and influence the player's available choices.

The writing is exceptionally rich and literary, full of dark humor, existential musings, and political satire examining ideologies from communism to ultranationalism without offering easy answers. On Xbox One, gamepad controls work surprisingly naturally thanks to a clear quick-selection system, and the voice acting adds a new layer of character to the cast. The atmosphere is completed by melancholic music and a visual style reminiscent of an oil painting. The game was showered with awards for its writing and originality at launch, and the Final Cut only confirmed that this is one of the most ambitious and literary RPGs of recent years, one that redefined what a dialogue-driven RPG can be.

The world of Revachol carries traces of a fictional but deeply developed history full of failed revolutions and colonial injustices, which the player gradually uncovers through conversations with residents, newspaper clippings, and the detective's own memories. The skill system doesn't function as mere passive bonuses but as active inner voices that can tempt the detective into impulsive acts, self-destruction, or unexpected flashes of intuition, portraying the protagonist's fractured psyche in an unusually literal way. The added Final Cut political quests further deepen the ideological spectrum the player can choose for their character, from communism to fascism, without the game ever painting any direction as unambiguously right.

**Why play it:** For players who want an RPG with a deeply developed world and skills that function as active inner voices, the Final Cut also offers expanded political quests and a spectrum of ideologies from communism to fascism.

xbox-one__middle-earth-shadow-of-war.teaser: The sequel to Shadow of Mordor expands the Nemesis system with fortresses and an orc army.
xbox-one__middle-earth-shadow-of-war.article:
**Middle-earth: Shadow of War** from Monolith Productions is a sequel to Shadow of Mordor that expands its Nemesis system with a much larger open world, fortresses to conquer, and more complex relationships between orc captains. The player once again controls the ranger Talion, bound to the spirit of the elf Celebrimbor, and builds their own army of orcs in Mordor, using it to defend conquered fortresses and attack enemy ones. The combat system loosely follows the style of the Batman: Arkham games with fluid chains of attacks, dodges, and stealth takedowns, enriched with the ability to enslave defeated captains and turn them against their own faction.

On Xbox One the game offered a sprawling world divided into several regions, each with its own fortresses and unique orc captains whose personalities, strengths, and weaknesses are procedurally generated, so no playthrough is ever the same. The game was surrounded by controversy at launch over microtransactions tied to the time-consuming fortress-siege system, which the studio later partially eased and eventually removed the microtransactions entirely. The atmosphere is completed by Tolkien's dark fantasy aesthetic and epic music accompanying the great battles for the fortresses. Despite the initial controversy, Shadow of War is valued today above all for its Nemesis system, which remains one of the most original gameplay mechanics of recent years.

Every orc captain remembers previous encounters with the player, can be scarred, get promoted, or flee the fight like a coward, and this memory turns every battle into a unique, personal story that never plays out the same way twice. Conquering a fortress unfolds as a large-scale siege battle in which the player assembles their own army from subjugated orcs and plans the attack based on the strengths and weaknesses of the enemy captains defending the castle. Compared to Shadow of Mordor, the larger world also offers several distinctly themed regions, from swamps to volcanic wastelands, adding greater visual and tactical variety to the overall journey through Mordor.

**Why play it:** Thanks to the Nemesis system, where orc captains remember every encounter and carry its scars, and larger siege battles with your own orc army, Shadow of War offers a more varied and personal Mordor than its predecessor.

xbox-one__way-out.teaser: A cooperative prison-break adventure playable only by two; it cannot be completed solo.
xbox-one__way-out.article:
**A Way Out** from Hazelight Studios is a cooperative action adventure designed exclusively for two players, whether locally on a split screen or online, and the game cannot be completed solo. The story follows two convicts, Leo and Vincent, who together plan an escape from prison and then flee both justice and old debts, while an unexpected friendship gradually develops between them. The gameplay constantly shifts genres and perspectives, from stealth and puzzle-solving to car chases to shootouts, and the screen is split between both players for almost the entire game, who often tackle different but interconnected tasks at the same time.

On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and made use of the Friend's Pass feature, which let one player buy the game and invite a friend to play together for free, an unusually generous move for its time. The cinematic direction, following both heroes in split screen like an action thriller, gives the game a distinctly filmic feel, supported by atmospheric music that accentuates both the tension of the escape and the quiet moments between the characters. Contemporary reviews praised above all the inventiveness of the cooperative design and the emotional ending of the story. A Way Out became a celebrated example of how an entire game can be built around a shared experience between two players, and it inspired other cooperative titles that followed it.

Throughout the game the players maintain two completely different perspectives on the same situation, with one proceeding impulsively through force while the other prefers to outwit the guards through cunning, and the game uses this contrast even in moments when their paths temporarily split on screen and they need to cooperate remotely through communication outside the game. The short playtime is deliberately compressed so that no passage grows stale, with the developers choosing to sacrifice length in favor of pacing and constantly surprising the player with new gameplay situations. As a result, A Way Out became a reference point for discussions of how much a shared experience between two players can deepen the emotional impact of a story about betrayal and friendship.

**Why play it:** For players seeking a cooperative experience with real emotional impact, A Way Out stands out for the contrasting perspectives of two convicts and its deliberately compressed pacing that never lets a single passage grow stale.

xbox-one__what-remains-of-edith-finch.teaser: A short, inventive adventure; each family story is told through a completely different gameplay mechanic.
xbox-one__what-remains-of-edith-finch.article:
**What Remains of Edith Finch** from Giant Sparrow is a short but remarkably inventive adventure in which young Edith returns to her family's house on the coast to go through the history of her cursed family and find out how each of her relatives died. The game is structured as a collection of small vignettes, with each family member's story told through a completely different gameplay mechanic, one moment a surreal walk through childhood fantasy, another a tense sequence in a canning factory, elsewhere an abstract vision of approaching death, making every chapter a unique experience.

On Xbox One the game ran flawlessly, as it's fairly undemanding on hardware, focusing above all on atmosphere and storytelling rather than action challenges. The visual style combines a realistically rendered yet oddly extended family house full of improvised additions with poetic, dreamlike sequences for each individual memory, and the music sensitively underscores a melancholic, though never outright frightening, mood. Contemporary reception was extraordinarily positive, with the game collecting awards for storytelling and innovative design, and it's often cited as one of the finest examples of how gameplay mechanics can be used to tell an emotional story. Even years after release it remains a benchmark title of the walking-sim adventure genre and a demonstration of how powerfully a game can function as a literary medium.

The Finch family house itself functions as a narrator, with the bricked-up rooms of deceased relatives turned into small memorial shrines, through which Edith symbolically walks back into the present after experiencing each memory. Every vignette adopts a form suited to that character's nature and fate, so the player is never bored by repeating the same mechanic, and the transitions between the different styles are smooth and unforced. The short playtime is paradoxically one of the game's greatest strengths, as it never lets any idea grow stale, keeping the whole experience dense and emotionally focused from beginning to its moving conclusion.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates a short but dense narrative experience will find in What Remains of Edith Finch a house that functions as a narrator and vignettes that change form to match the fate of each member of the Finch family.

xbox-one__fifa-17.teaser: The football series runs on the Frostbite engine for the first time; smoother movement, livelier stadiums.
xbox-one__fifa-17.article:
**FIFA 17** marked a major turning point for the series – EA Sports moved the football simulation onto the Frostbite engine for the first time, which until then had mainly served action games like Battlefield. The result was a noticeably more realistic presentation: players moved more fluidly, had more distinct individual characteristics, and thanks to better lighting and crowd animations the stadium atmosphere felt far livelier than in previous installments. The football on the pitch itself stayed true to the series, but the new engine allowed for finer physical interactions between players and the ball, most noticeable in duels for possession and set pieces. A more sophisticated dribbling and one-on-one dueling system was also added, bringing the game a step closer to the authentic feel of real football.

The most striking new feature, however, was The Journey game mode, which brought a full-fledged story mode with voiced dialogue, career decisions, and a personal life storyline for young talent Alex Hunter to a football game. The player progressed from a youth academy through a first professional contract to a starting spot on an English club, blending cinematic cutscenes with classic matches against real Premier League clubs. It was a bold move by which EA Sports tried to reach players who don't much seek out classic sports management or online career modes, bringing the football simulation closer to the kind of storytelling more familiar from big action games.

On Xbox One the game ran stably, using the console's power for a smooth sixty frames per second even with full stadiums, which was still exceptional in sports production at the time. Contemporary reviews praised above all the visual leap forward and the inventiveness of The Journey, while players returned to traditional modes like Ultimate Team or Online Seasons out of habit, keeping the series' loyal fanbase intact. Today, FIFA 17 is mainly an interesting reminder of the era when the series was still getting used to its new technological foundation, and as such it works more as a nostalgic memory than a current-day experience.

**Why play it:** For players interested in a period reminder of the series' shift to a new technological foundation, FIFA 17 offers a stable sixty frames per second even with full stadiums and the inventive story mode The Journey.

xbox-one__nba-2k17.teaser: One of the most sophisticated basketball simulations of the generation, with realistic AI and atmosphere.
xbox-one__nba-2k17.article:
**NBA 2K17** was among the most sophisticated sports simulations on the market at the time of its release, and on Xbox One it demonstrated just how far basketball games had come from their arcade roots. The game relied on precise movement animation, realistic ball physics, and an AI system that tried to mimic the real tactical behavior of NBA teams – from set plays through screens to defensive rotations. Visually, it was one of the best-looking sports games of the generation, with detailed player models and arena atmosphere that changed depending on the importance of the match, including crowd reactions to key moments of the game.

The MyCAREER mode again benefited from cinematic production, this time with a story called Livin' Da Dream, which cast real actors and musicians and interspersed matches with longer cinematic scenes off the court. Players created their own character and progressed from college basketball to a professional NBA career, with off-court decisions affecting relationships with teammates, coaches, and sponsors. Alongside this, the game offered an extensive MyGM mode with full club management, where you could negotiate trades and plan seasons years in advance, and the endlessly popular MyTEAM with collectible player cards.

On Xbox One the game ran smoothly, using the console's power mainly for detailed lighting and crowd animations in the stands, which varied depending on the type of arena and the importance of the match. Reviews at the time ranked it among the best sports titles of that season, thanks partly to the depth of its game mechanics and the amount of content that offered entertainment for months. The NBA 2K series is still nicknamed the most sophisticated basketball simulation ever, and the 2016 installment was one of the steps that cemented this reputation – even years later it's clear why the game earned such a broad fan base.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for one of the most sophisticated basketball simulations ever will appreciate NBA 2K17's depth of game mechanics, detailed lighting, and crowd animations that still uphold the series' reputation today.

xbox-one__madden-nfl-17.teaser: The official NFL simulation with a new Ball Carrier Balance system for smoother ball-carrying runs.
xbox-one__madden-nfl-17.article:
**Madden NFL 17** continued EA Sports' long-standing tradition of the official American football simulation, and on Xbox One it introduced an improved running system called Ball Carrier Balance, which gave players greater control over jukes, dodges, and staying balanced under defensive hits. This one change had an impact on the overall feel of the game – battles at the line of scrimmage and runs into the defense felt more dynamic and less predictable than in previous years, something appreciated especially by veteran series players who had spent hundreds of hours with earlier installments and were very sensitive to fine differences in the controls.

The game again offered the full range of modes typical of Madden: a franchise mode with team management spanning several seasons ahead, online leagues against other players, and the collectible Ultimate Team mode, where cards were used to build dream lineups of NFL stars. Match presentation stuck to a TV-broadcast style with commentary and graphic transitions meant to give viewers the feeling of watching a real broadcast, which had long been a signature trait of the whole series and one reason why even casual sports fans sought the game out, appreciating its accessible presentation.

On Xbox One the game benefited from the console's power especially when simulating a larger number of players on the field and in the more detailed animations of trench battles, where most of the match's decisive moments took place. Reviews at the time rated it a solid, if not revolutionary, installment that moved the series forward through incremental improvements rather than a major overhaul, and players explained this conservative approach as an effort not to risk tampering with a well-tuned system. For American football fans, however, it was the only truly official option on the market, and Madden NFL 17 still serves today as an interesting glimpse of what sports simulations looked like in the mid-2010s.

**Why play it:** For American football fans with no other official option on the market, Madden NFL 17 offers a solid, well-tuned system and detailed animations of trench battles, even if it's more of an incremental improvement than a revolution.

xbox-one__f1-2019.teaser: The pinnacle of Codemasters' F1 simulation; Formula 2 races as a career springboard for the first time.
xbox-one__f1-2019.article:
**F1 2019** is considered one of the high points of Codemasters' official Formula 1 game series, and on Xbox One it offered a sophisticated combination of realistic handling and an accessible sporting experience. The game faithfully modeled all the season's tracks and factory teams of the time, including newcomers, and for the first time in the series added Formula 2 races, which served as a career springboard for a rookie driver and offered their own season with rivals striving to move up to the top class. The physics model tried to capture the behavior of real single-seaters, from tire wear through aerodynamics to pit-stop strategy, and players had to adapt these decisions to the current course of the race.

The career mode was among the most extensive in the series – the player progressed from F2 to their dream F1 team, negotiated contracts, oversaw car development, and faced politics within the team, including comparisons with their teammate. There was also multiplayer with leaderboards and a so-called esports environment, which in the following years became an important part of the official F1 scene. The game also offered scalable difficulty and driving aids, which made it accessible to both simulation enthusiasts and casual players who mainly wanted to experience the atmosphere of the top racing category without years of practice on the wheel.

On Xbox One the game ran stably and used the console's power for detailed car and track models as well as realistic weather that changed during the race, including showers affecting tire choice. Reviews at the time often called F1 2019 the best installment of the series to date, emphasizing the depth of the career mode and its fidelity to the real sport. Even years later it's a title that represents well what the peak official Formula 1 simulation looked like at the end of the Xbox One generation.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for the peak official Formula 1 simulation from the end of the Xbox One generation will appreciate F1 2019's depth of career mode, realistic dynamic weather, and fidelity to the real sport.

xbox-one__dirt-4.teaser: A rally simulation with the Your Stage system, which procedurally generates an endless number of tracks.
xbox-one__dirt-4.article:
**DiRT 4** continued the successful line of rally simulations from Codemasters, and on Xbox One it introduced, among other things, the Your Stage system, which could procedurally generate a practically endless number of rally tracks based on specified parameters. Players could set the length, terrain type, and weather, and the game would then assemble a unique route on its own, a significant step up from the traditional limited number of hand-designed stages that genre fans were used to and had eventually memorized by heart. Thanks to this, no two runs through the same location were ever quite the same, which heightened the tension even on repeat playthroughs.

The game returned to a more demanding, more simulation-oriented driving model after the criticism that had accompanied the previous, more arcade-like installment DiRT Showdown, and offered a wide range of vehicles from classic rally specials through rallycross to buggies and American-style trucks. The career mode guided players through various motorsport disciplines, while a dedicated Joyride mode was used for free driving and stunts away from the pressure of racing against the clock. Vehicle sound design and co-driver pace notes announcing upcoming corners had long been strengths of the series, and DiRT 4 didn't disappoint in this regard.

On Xbox One the game visually benefited from richly detailed environments, from muddy forest tracks to dusty desert stretches, and dynamic weather that changed surface grip in real time and forced players to adapt their driving style on the fly. Reviews at the time praised mainly the generated-track system and the return to more demanding handling, though some players complained about the lower overall number of hand-designed locations compared to older installments. Today, DiRT 4 remains a popular choice for rally fans who appreciate the combination of a simulation-oriented approach and near-endless replayability.

**Why play it:** For rally fans wanting a combination of a simulation-oriented approach with near-endless replayability, DiRT 4 offers a generated-track system and dynamic weather that changes surface grip mid-drive.

xbox-one__dirt-5.teaser: A shift from simulation toward arcade fun; festival effects, a commentator, and varied disciplines.
xbox-one__dirt-5.article:
**DiRT 5** marked a significant shift for the series away from pure simulation toward more arcade-like, visually spectacular fun aimed at a broader audience. Codemasters decided to build the game around show elements – fire effects at the start, a commentator accompanying the races, and stylized graphics with bold colors were meant to evoke a festival-style motorsport spectacle rather than a serious rally simulation. A number of disciplines were on offer, from classic rallycross through ice circuits to freestyle jumps, which set the game apart from its narrowly focused predecessors and also attracted players who had skipped earlier installments of the series because of their difficulty.

The career mode was accompanied by a story told in podcast form, which commented on the player's journey through the world of motorsport and tied individual races together into a more coherent whole, supplemented by interviews with both fictional and real motorsport personalities. The game offered split-screen for local multiplayer as well as online races, an increasingly uncommon approach for racing titles at the time, appreciated especially by players who preferred playing on one screen with a friend. The vehicle roster included a wide range of cars, from rally specials through buggies to iconic off-road machines, with a physics model tuned more for a flashy, accessible driving style than the hardcore simulation the series had offered before.

On Xbox One the game ran with slightly reduced graphical quality compared to the newer consoles, yet it retained its distinctive visual style with bold sky color transitions and flashy replays capturing the best moments of the race. Reception at the time was mixed – reviewers praised the fun factor and variety of content but criticized technical shortcomings and less refined handling compared to earlier installments of the series. Even so, DiRT 5 found an audience among players looking for a lighter, visually appealing alternative to traditional rally simulations.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for a lighter, visually appealing alternative to traditional rally simulations will appreciate DiRT 5's colorful style and variety of content, even though technical shortcomings and weaker handling are noticeable.

xbox-one__need-for-speed.teaser: The series reboot combines nighttime street racing with cinematic scenes and real tuning-scene stars.
xbox-one__need-for-speed.article:
**Need for Speed** from 2015 was a reboot of the long-running arcade series, and on Xbox One it tried to combine the nighttime street racing scene with a cinematic presentation full of live-action actors. The player took on the role of a newcomer trying to make a name for himself among five legends of underground racing in the fictional nighttime city of Ventura Bay, watching live-action sequences between races featuring real actors and real personalities from the automotive and tuning scene, such as Magnus Walker or Ken Block, which gave the game an authentic feel and set it apart from purely animated competitors.

The game placed heavy emphasis on visual style and car customization – players could not only upgrade cars' performance but also modify their looks using an extensive editor for paint, decals, and body kits, which made it possible to create a practically unique car reflecting the player's personal style. The open world was designed to run in near-constant dusk and nighttime, giving the game its characteristic neon atmosphere inspired by classic entries in the series like Underground, to which the game openly paid homage. Races were divided into five styles based on the individual legends, from drifting through speed duels to free roaming the streets, with each style carrying its own leaderboard and rewards.

On Xbox One the game visually ranked among the best-looking racing titles of the generation, thanks to its detailed lighting model and reflections on wet asphalt, further accentuated by the constant nighttime darkness. Reviews at the time praised the atmosphere and customization but criticized the requirement of a constant online connection even for offline play, as well as excessively aggressive police chases. Even so, the game became a popular choice among arcade racing fans and is still remembered today as a worthy, if not flawless, return to the core of the series and its nighttime spirit.

**Why play it:** For arcade racing fans craving the series' nighttime spirit, Need for Speed offers atmosphere and customization on par with the best-looking titles of the generation, even though the constant online requirement annoyed offline players too.

xbox-one__crew-2.teaser: An open world where you switch seamlessly between cars, planes, and boats across a map of the USA.
xbox-one__crew-2.article:
**The Crew 2** expanded the ambitious concept of its predecessor with an entirely new dimension – on Xbox One, players could freely switch not only between cars but also motorcycles, boats, and planes, all within one giant open-world map, a scaled-down replica of the United States. This transition between elements happened practically without interruption, so it was possible to set off from a car race, fly over a canyon in a plane a few seconds later, and land directly on the water for a powerboat race, which was a unique gaming experience at the time of release that no other title of a similar scale offered.

The game structured its content around the concept of motorsport disciplines and so-called Live families – street racing, off-road, freestyle, and pro racing, each with its own specific vehicles and racing styles as well as its own sets of rewards and upgrades. Career progression was tied to the player's follower count on fictional social networks within the game world, meant to motivate trying out as wide a range of disciplines as possible before gaining access to the most prestigious races. Over the following years, the game also received extensive free updates that added new vehicles, seasonal events, and other content, turning it into a long-running live service rather than a one-off title.

On Xbox One the game benefited from a vast, richly detailed map featuring iconic locations from New York to the Grand Canyon, although smooth framerate had to give way to the size of the open world and the amount of displayed detail. Reviews at the time praised the scope and variety of content, though some players complained about a less refined driving feel compared to more specialized racing games. The Crew 2 thus remains an interesting demonstration of how far one can push the concept of a single giant interconnected motorsport world, one the player could return to at any time in any vehicle without a single loading screen.

**Why play it:** Anyone wanting to drive across a giant interconnected world from New York to the Grand Canyon in any vehicle without a loading screen will appreciate The Crew 2's scope and variety of content despite its less refined driving feel.

xbox-one__project-cars.teaser: A racing simulation developed with the player community; dynamic weather and day-night transitions.
xbox-one__project-cars.article:
**Project CARS** came about in an unusual way – Slightly Mad Studios developed it partly with the financial support and feedback of a player community, who could test the game and influence its development years before official release through a paid-access system to development builds. It thus arrived on Xbox One as one of the most ambitious racing simulations of the generation, emphasizing a faithful physics model, dynamic weather changing in real time, and transitions between day and night that had a direct impact on track grip, visibility, and the choice of the right strategy.

The vehicle roster included hundreds of licensed cars across categories, from classic historic specials through GT cars to open-cockpit prototypes, and the game offered an elaborate career mode that guided players through progression across several motorsport disciplines, from single-seaters to endurance racing. The controls were designed primarily for players with a racing wheel, but also worked with a standard gamepad, albeit demanding greater feel and patience when searching for the limit of tire grip. It was precisely this difficulty and authenticity of the physics model that set the game apart from the more accessible arcade racers available on the same console.

On Xbox One the game visually impressed with its detailed rendering of weather and lighting, though the technical side suffered from occasional framerate dips in more demanding conditions with a larger number of cars on track. Reviews at the time praised the depth of the simulation and the scope of content, while also pointing out a less polished user interface and a steeper learning curve that could discourage genre newcomers. Nevertheless, Project CARS established itself as one of the most significant simulation titles of the early Xbox One era and paved the way for sequels that further developed and refined this concept, bringing it closer to a wider audience.

**Why play it:** For players seeking the depth of a racing simulation with detailed weather and lighting, Project CARS remains a significant title of the early Xbox One era, even though its steeper learning curve could discourage newcomers.

xbox-one__farming-simulator-19.teaser: The most ambitious entry in the series to date; a new engine and licensed machinery like John Deere.
xbox-one__farming-simulator-19.article:
**Farming Simulator 19** brought the most ambitious installment yet of the long-running farming simulation series to Xbox One, this time powered by a completely reworked graphics engine that significantly improved the visual quality of fields, machinery, and weather compared to previous entries. Players managed their own farm from the ground up — a sown field had to be plowed, seeded, tended, and finally harvested, with the whole process interwoven with raising animals, growing various crops, and gradually expanding a fleet of machinery featuring dozens of licensed agricultural brands such as John Deere or Case IH, each machine with its own specifications, performance, and behavior in the field.

Unlike action-oriented racing titles, the game relied on a calm, deliberate pace and managerial decisions — when to sow, which crop to choose based on market demand, or how to efficiently invest earnings into new machines and buildings. Multiplayer let players manage a farm together with friends, which proved to be a surprisingly popular way to spend time, and the game also offered, for the first time in the series, a more elaborate system of seasonal weather changes affecting crop growth and the need to plan work ahead, including preparing machinery for winter.

On Xbox One the game ran stably, and the new engine showed especially in the more detailed rendering of fields, forests, and machinery, even though it was primarily a title built on content and depth of systems rather than technical showmanship. Contemporary reviews praised the scope of the simulation and its accessibility for newcomers and veterans of previous entries alike, who appreciated the smooth transition to the new visual style. Farming Simulator 19 confirmed that the farming simulator genre has a solid and surprisingly broad audience on consoles, one that seeks a different kind of relaxation than action or racing titles and enjoys returning to the long-term building of its own farm.

**Why play:** For fans of farming simulators who want to relax through the long-term building of their own farm instead of action or racing, and who will appreciate its accessibility for newcomers too.

xbox-one__powerwash-simulator.teaser: Washing away grime with a pressure washer, of all things, became an unexpectedly relaxing and addictive game.
xbox-one__powerwash-simulator.article:
**PowerWash Simulator** managed to turn what seemed like a dull activity at first glance — washing grime off with a pressure washer — into one of the most relaxing and beloved games of its time, and on Xbox One players could try it for free from day one as part of Game Pass, which greatly helped its reach. The premise was simple: the player took hold of a spray gun and gradually cleared grime from houses, garden furniture, playgrounds, or entire streets, and the visual and audio satisfaction of vanishing dirt turned out to be an unexpectedly strong hook that drew in even people outside the usual gaming audience who otherwise didn't play games at all.

The game gradually unlocked increasingly extensive and varied locations, from a modest family house to thematic maps inspired by science fiction or horror motifs, each offering its own layout of grime and hidden details to discover that rewarded thorough players. There was also cooperative multiplayer, in which multiple players could clean the same location at once, which proved to be a surprisingly addictive social experience, and many players sought it out as a shared evening activity. The absence of time pressure, combat, or any kind of stress made the game an ideal title for switching off the mind after a demanding day.

On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and was technically undemanding, matching its focused, minimalist concept without unnecessary graphical showmanship. Contemporary reviews and the player community embraced the game enthusiastically, thanks in part to the combination of a meditative game loop and unexpectedly satisfying feedback from removing grime. PowerWash Simulator became one of the most surprising successes of its generation and showed that even a seemingly boring everyday activity can be remarkably addictive in game form and accessible even to people who otherwise don't play video games at all.

**Why play:** For anyone who wants to try an unexpectedly addictive and meditative game loop, accessible even to people who otherwise don't play video games at all.

xbox-one__crash-team-racing-nitro-fueled.teaser: A remake of the go-kart classic from the nineties; the same controls and powerslide drift in a new coat of paint.
xbox-one__crash-team-racing-nitro-fueled.article:
**Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled** was a complete remake of the beloved kart racing game from the late nineties, and on Xbox One it arrived with significantly reworked graphics while preserving the exact feel of the original's controls, including the series' signature powerslide drifting and combat system of power-ups on which the series built its identity. Studio Beenox focused on making the game play identically to the PlayStation classic, only in a modern visual coat with detailed character models and environments inspired by the Crash Bandicoot universe, which worked well even for players who knew the series only by reputation or from later games featuring Crash.

The game also included tracks and characters from the sequel Crash Nitro Kart, offering the most extensive content collection in the series' history in one place and giving players a reason to explore even its lesser-known installments. A career mode guided players through a story inspired by the original, while online multiplayer and regular seasonal updates with new characters, tracks, and cosmetic items kept the game alive long after release. The weapon combat system, from rockets through mines to protective masks, remained faithful to the original and still ranks among the best-balanced and most demanding in the kart racing genre.

On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and was visually among the most attractive remakes of its generation, with a colorful, clear style matching the Crash Bandicoot series and its long-standing visual identity. Contemporary reviews praised the remake for its faithfulness to the original and its quality craftsmanship, making it one of the best-received remakes ever. Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled thus successfully appealed to both fans of the original game and a new generation of players encountering this kart classic for the first time, who quickly understood why it's still called one of the most demanding kart games of all time.

**Why play:** For Crash Bandicoot fans and newcomers alike looking for one of the best-crafted remakes and, at the same time, one of the most demanding kart games ever made.

xbox-one__team-sonic-racing.teaser: Kart racing built on teamwork, not a solo fight for first place.
xbox-one__team-sonic-racing.article:
**Team Sonic Racing** set itself apart from classic kart racers by emphasizing teamwork — instead of a purely individual fight for first place, the game rewarded players for helping teammates, whether by passing along power-ups, drafting trailing racers in a slipstream, or blocking opponents before the finish line. This concept, building on the earlier Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, required players on Xbox One to think not just about their own position but about the overall result of a team made up of three characters, setting the game apart from the genre's typical, purely individualistic approach.

The game offered a varied selection of tracks inspired by classic zones from the Sonic the Hedgehog series, accompanied by an energetic soundtrack from the series' long-standing sound team. The Team Adventure career mode led players through a story about rival teams — Team Sonic, Team Rose, and Team Dark — gradually unlocking new vehicles, upgrade parts, and game modes designed for quick, repeated play. A vehicle customization system let players combine bodies, wheels, and add-ons to suit their driving style, from speed and handling to the power of power-up use.

On Xbox One the game ran smoothly and colorfully, with the series' signature style translated into modern visuals and familiar characters from Sonic's television and gaming adventures. Contemporary reviews praised the team-based concept in particular as a refreshing change in an often individualistic genre, even though it was a somewhat more modest title in terms of content compared to the direct competition. Team Sonic Racing still found a loyal audience among series fans and genre enthusiasts looking for an alternative to established big names, who appreciated the emphasis on cooperation and a friendlier, less mean-spirited take on weapon-based combat.

**Why play:** For fans of the Sonic series and players looking for an alternative to established kart racers, thanks to a refreshing emphasis on teamwork and friendlier combat.

xbox-one__watch-dogs.teaser: An action adventure with hacking as your main weapon; Aiden Pearce controls an entire city remotely.
xbox-one__watch-dogs.article:
**Watch Dogs** is an open-world action adventure that took players to a fictional version of Chicago controlled by a central operating system called ctOS. The main character, Aiden Pearce, a skilled hacker, sets out on a path of revenge after a tragic incident he is responsible for, while also uncovering the dark practices of corporations and government agencies with access to the private data of every resident of the city. The game combines cover-based shooting, car chases, and above all hacking — the player can remotely control traffic lights, bridges, security cameras, and even the phones of passersby, which factors into both combat and the solving of side missions.

On Xbox One the game served as one of the first major next-gen titles meant to showcase the power of the new generation — in reality, though, the graphics didn't match the previously shown footage, sparking discussions about what became known as a downgrade. Even so, gameplay remained varied thanks to online elements, where other players could covertly enter the world and hack Aiden himself, which at the time felt like an innovative blend of singleplayer and multiplayer. Chicago's dark, rainy atmosphere, underscored by an electronic soundtrack, complemented the game's themes of surveillance and loss of privacy well.

Reception was commercially very successful, even though reviews were more mixed than the hype had suggested. Watch Dogs launched a new Ubisoft franchise, and the theme of hacker surveillance became all the more relevant thanks to real-world cases surrounding data monitoring. Today the game feels like an interesting snapshot of a time when open worlds were still learning to work with modern technology as a core gameplay mechanic.

**Why play:** For players interested in open worlds with a hacking theme, and anyone curious to look back at a time when data surveillance was just entering pop culture.

xbox-one__nier-automata.teaser: An unconventional action RPG from PlatinumGames based on a concept by Yoko Taro; the android 2B fights for the meaning of existence.
xbox-one__nier-automata.article:
**NieR: Automata** is an action RPG from PlatinumGames based on a concept by Yoko Taro, and it ranks among the most unconventional major games of its generation. It takes place in the distant future, where humanity has fled to the Moon and, on the abandoned Earth, android units of YoRHa face off against machines of alien invaders. The player controls the android 2B, later joined by the scout 9S, and gradually discovers that the divide between "friendly" and "enemy" machines makes less and less sense.

Combat is handled by Platinum, so it's fast, fluid, and built around alternating light and heavy attacks, last-moment dodges, and supporting fire from the flying companion Pod. But the game constantly shifts genres: the camera switches to a side view, then to a top-down view reminiscent of an old-school shooter, and elsewhere the action turns into a text-based interface. Crucially, one playthrough isn't the end — the story unlocks over several playthroughs, each showing the same events from a different perspective, and only together do they form the complete picture. Anyone who stops after the first ending misses most of what the game is actually about.

The strongest aspect is the music by Keiichi Okabe, which combines a choir singing in an invented language with piano and electronics, and which shifts according to setting and situation. Critics highlighted precisely this combination of top-tier action with a narrative unafraid to ask questions about the meaning of existence, without becoming overly self-serious. On Xbox One the game arrived later than on other platforms, in the Become as Gods edition, technically improved over the original release. Today it is considered one of the most important Japanese games of the past two decades.

**Why play:** For players craving top-tier action combined with a deep narrative about the meaning of existence and an unforgettable score by Keiichi Okabe.

xbox-one__subnautica.teaser: A survival game on an alien planet with no weapon and no map; just an escape pod, a scanner, and the depths of the ocean.
xbox-one__subnautica.article:
**Subnautica** is a survival game from Unknown Worlds in which, after a spaceship crash, the player finds themselves alone in the ocean of an alien planet. They have no weapon, no map, and the only thing they have is an escape pod and a scanner. From there the whole experience unfolds: gathering resources, building a base on the seabed, crafting better gear, and above all gradually descending into depths where it's dark, the pressure is immense, and the creatures are considerably bigger than you.

The game deliberately avoids classic enemies to defeat — most of the tension comes from the environment itself. Oxygen is counted in seconds, the Seamoth submersible has a limited depth range, and going deeper first requires finding the materials to upgrade it, which means exploring an area the player hasn't seen yet. The fear of the depths is done honestly here: it's not about jump scares, but about sound, visibility of only a few meters, and the awareness that the way back is long. The story is revealed through found logs, explaining why the ship crashed and what happened on the planet before that.

Visually the game is built on colorful coral reefs in the shallows that gradually give way to increasingly inhospitable biomes. On Xbox One it arrived some time after a lengthy PC early access period and was well received precisely for how it manages to tie survival mechanics to exploration. The sequel, Below Zero, later carried the same principle into polar waters. Subnautica is often recommended even to people who don't normally play survival games — and, conversely, not recommended to those who have a problem with deep water.

**Why play:** For players who want to explore a colorful underwater world by combining survival with exploration — but definitely not for those who have a problem with deep water.

switch__slay-spire.teaser: A card-based roguelike that essentially founded the entire deckbuilding roguelike genre.
switch__slay-spire.article:
**Slay the Spire** combined a card game with a roguelike structure and essentially defined the entire deckbuilding roguelike genre, which after its success flooded the market with dozens of followers. The player climbs a tower full of enemies, and with each floor builds a deck of cards representing attacks, defense, and special abilities for four distinct characters, each offering its own playstyle and synergies. After each battle the player chooses a new card or relic, creating tension between immediately strengthening the deck and keeping it lean in the long run — a bloated deck full of unusable cards can kill just as reliably as a lack of power. There's also a choice of path between floors, so the player decides for themselves whether to risk an extra fight for a reward or head instead to a merchant or a rest site.

The Switch version arrived with a slight delay after the PC release and carried the game over without major compromises — controlling cards with Joy-Cons or the touchscreen feels intuitive, and the game is a great fit for handheld play in short sessions. The visuals are austere but functional, and the music underscores the atmosphere of a freezing, dangerous tower without unnecessary filler. Procedurally generated maps ensure no run is ever the same, and permadeath forces players into careful planning of every step — one poorly chosen card in the middle of a run can mean having to start the whole tower over again from floor one.

Both critics and the player community embraced the game enthusiastically already during its Early Access release, and the Switch port only expanded its fan base among handheld players. Slay the Spire is still considered one of the most influential titles of its decade — it taught the genre how to elegantly combine chance with deep strategic decision-making, and it remains the reference point against which every new deckbuilder is measured. Its building blocks, from relics to interlinked cards, have become the vocabulary used to describe dozens of genre followers to this day.

**Why play:** Anyone wanting to experience the title that taught an entire genre how to combine chance with deep strategic decision-making will find in Slay the Spire the reference point against which every new deckbuilder is still measured today.

switch__balatro.teaser: Poker recast as an addictive roguelike loop of joker cards; one combo can rack up millions of points.
switch__balatro.article:
**Balatro** takes the rules of poker and wraps them in an endlessly addictive roguelike loop where the player builds poker hands with the help of jokers that alter the scoring rules in fundamental ways. The goal of each round is to reach a set score before the hand of cards runs out, and as the antes progress the pressure mounts, forcing the player to build ever more extreme synergies between jokers, the deck's cards, and their upgrades. A simple card game thus turns into a deep optimization puzzle, where one well-built combo can generate scores in the millions. Between rounds the player also shops for new jokers, card decks, or tarot cards, so the strategy keeps developing beyond the dealing and scoring of hands itself.

On Switch the game launched on the same day as on other platforms, and handheld mode proved to be the ideal setting for its signature "just one more round" pacing. Minimalist pixel art with bold colors and simple but catchy sound effects create the atmosphere of a cozy casino that, beneath the surface, turns into an increasingly deranged mathematical system. The Switch's portability reinforces the sense that this is the perfect game for waiting rooms, train rides, and short breaks, since a quick round can be paused at any time and picked back up later.

Balatro became one of the most widely praised indie titles of its era after release and quickly earned a reputation as a game that redefines what a card-based roguelike can look like. Its influence shows in how it is discussed as a title that managed to win over both card-game fans and players who had previously passed on the roguelike genre. Even with time's distance it remains a reference example of elegant game design built on a single idea taken to perfection, and its success confirmed that even a seemingly exhausted theme like poker can hide unexpected depth.

**Why play it:** For elegant game design built on a single idea taken to perfection, one that managed to win over both card-game fans and people previously indifferent to the roguelike genre, Balatro is a clear choice for anyone looking for an addictive card game.

switch__inscryption.teaser: Card duels that gradually turn into a dark, multi-layered horror full of twists.
switch__inscryption.article:
**Inscryption** is a card game that, under the guise of a seemingly ordinary dueling system, gradually turns into a dark, multi-layered horror full of mysteries and unexpected twists. The player sits at a table across from a mysterious figure and plays card duels where animal cards with their own stats and abilities fight for survival - sacrificing each other, gaining power from the bones of previously fallen allies, with their value shaped by rules the player gradually learns for themselves. It soon turns out, however, that the game also operates outside the cards themselves, with escape-room elements, manipulation of the file system, and references to the author's earlier works. Being divided into several distinctly different chapters gradually changes the rules and visual style so much that the player never knows what comes next - a peaceful card match can transform without warning into an entirely different kind of game.

The game arrived on Switch somewhat later than on PC, but the port preserved the original's nervous, claustrophobic atmosphere - dim lighting, the creaking sounds of a wooden cabin, and the narrator's voice watching the player work just as evocatively on the handheld as on a large monitor. Controlling the cards is clear both on the touchscreen and with the Joy-Cons, even though the game wasn't primarily designed for consoles, and playing in the dark with headphones only heightens the oppressive atmosphere.

Inscryption received very positive reviews on release, especially for its boldness in constantly subverting player expectations and for its thoughtful blending of card mechanics with horror storytelling. It became an example of how the card-game genre can be pushed toward an authorial, strongly narrative experience, and thanks to the Switch version it also found an audience among players who don't normally seek out horror but were lured in by its unconventional concept. To this day it's discussed as a game best played without any prior knowledge of what awaits.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates card mechanics interwoven with thoughtful horror storytelling that constantly shatters expectations should play Inscryption without any prior knowledge of what's coming.

switch__monster-train.teaser: A deckbuilder turned inside out: instead of defending against a raid, you defend a hellish train across three decks.
switch__monster-train.article:
**Monster Train** is a deckbuilder that flips the classic "defend against a raid" formula inside out - here the player defends a runaway hellish train from angels trying to seize it floor by floor, with battles taking place simultaneously across three vertically connected decks, forcing the player to constantly shift units between them depending on where the greatest danger looms. Combining two monster factions with distinct abilities lets players build decks with dozens of different synergies and strategies, from mass-poisoning enemies to a single enormously powered giant around which the whole deck is built. A damage-multiplier system also lets even seemingly weak cards generate astronomical numbers by the end of the game, which motivates players to experiment with unconventional combinations instead of relying on proven safe bets.

The Switch version arrived with the complete game, including content that was added gradually on PC, and the handheld's portability suits the genre just as well as it does other card-based roguelikes. The graphic style combines a dark, flame-lit palette with clear card icons, so even on a smaller display the game stays readable in the most hectic moments with dozens of effects on screen at once. The music supports the feeling of inevitably rising pressure as the train climbs toward the final battle against the heavenly triumvirate itself.

Critics especially praised the depth of its strategic options and the boldness of building the game around the unconventional spatial concept of three floors at once, which set it apart from the wave of similar titles that followed Slay the Spire's success. Monster Train became one of the titles cited as an example of how to push the deckbuilder genre further, and the Switch version opened it up to a wider handheld audience that appreciated being able to play long strategic sessions away from the living room as well.

**Why play it:** For its bold spatial concept of three floors at once, which pushes the deckbuilder genre further beyond the Slay the Spire template, Monster Train is a great choice for long strategic sessions away from home too.

switch__vampire-survivors.teaser: The character attacks on its own, the player just collects experience; a defenseless hero becomes an army within minutes.
switch__vampire-survivors.article:
**Vampire Survivors** is an action roguelike in which the player's character automatically attacks swarms of enemies, while the player's job is simply to move around the arenas, collect experience, and choose between the weapons and upgrades on offer. From this simple concept, in which the screen gradually fills with hundreds to thousands of enemies, an unexpectedly deep system of synergies between weapons and passive items emerges, turning a defenseless little character into a force that wipes out the entire screen within a few dozen minutes. Unlockable characters, maps, and secret weapon combinations also give the game very high replayability even after clearing the first run. Between expeditions the player also spends collected gold on permanent upgrades, so even an unsuccessful run contributes to progress on the next attempt.

The Switch version kept the low price and fast pace that made the game famous, and the handheld's portability proved to be a natural fit for short, addictive sessions squeezed between other obligations. The retro pixel art with its limited color palette runs smoothly even when the screen is literally overflowing with enemies and effects, which is technically impressive given the number of simulated objects at once. The chiptune music rounds out the nostalgic, arcade atmosphere, a deliberate contrast to the modern, deeper mechanics underneath.

On Switch and elsewhere, the game kicked off a wave of so-called "bullet heaven" titles that flipped the classic bullet hell formula - instead of dodging bullets, the player floods the screen with their own barrage. Vampire Survivors became a phenomenon thanks to the combination of its low price, immediate accessibility, and enormous replayability, and it's still cited today as the title that founded its own subgenre, whose influence is visible in the dozens of games that followed it.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its low price, immediate accessibility, and enormous replayability, Vampire Survivors founded its own bullet heaven subgenre and remains a clear choice for anyone who wants to see where it all began.

switch__cult-of-lamb.teaser: Combines action-roguelike combat with running your own cult; a cute style with dark themes.
switch__cult-of-lamb.article:
**Cult of the Lamb** combines action-roguelike combat with building and managing your own cult, creating an unusual mix of two very different gameplay loops. In the dungeons, the player, as a sacrificed lamb resurrected by a dark god, makes their way through procedurally generated levels with a simple but snappy combat system full of dodges and combo attacks, while between expeditions they take care of a village of followers - building structures, meeting their needs, earning their devotion, performing rituals, and expanding the cult's influence over the surrounding world. The cute visual style contrasts with dark themes of sacrifice, manipulation, and religious fanaticism, giving the game a distinct identity of its own that sets it apart both from pure action roguelikes and classic sim titles. Steadily accumulating dungeon gear, new spells, and weapon upgrades give the player a sense of constant growth even between individual dungeon runs.

On Switch the game launched alongside other platforms, and the handheld's portability suits managing the village between dungeon expeditions especially well, when the player assigns tasks, resolves disputes among followers, and decides on the cult's future direction. The colorful, cartoonish graphics run smoothly and clearly on the console, and the music accompanying both the dungeons and the calmer village scenes nicely underscores the game's shifting mood.

Cult of the Lamb received very favorable reviews on release for its inventive genre combination and distinctive atmosphere, which turns religious symbolism into a darkly comic gag without giving up the tension and a certain moral unease over the player's growing power over their own followers. It became one of the standout indie successes of its season and showed that combining roguelike action with sim management can work as a complete, mutually reinforcing whole rather than two separate games stitched together, inspiring a number of titles that tried to repeat a similar recipe.

**Why play it:** For its inventive fusion of roguelike action and cult sim management, its darkly comic tone, and the moral unease of growing power over your own followers, fans of both genres will fall for it.

switch__baba-is-you.teaser: A puzzle game where you don't move a character - you move the rules of the game itself, written as sentences.
switch__baba-is-you.article:
**Baba Is You** is a puzzle game whose central mechanic is manipulating the rules of a level itself - the player moves not just characters but the word blocks forming sentences like "Baba is you" or "Wall is stop" directly, and rearranging them changes what counts as a playable character, what blocks movement, what leads to winning, or what transforms into what. Breaking apart one sentence and building a new one can thus solve a puzzle that initially seemed physically unsolvable. This concept lets the designers build puzzles where the solution often lies in completely reconsidering what the player took to be the level's immutable laws of physics, and as the game progresses ever more unexpected rule combinations arise, forcing the player to forget learned gaming conventions and think, quite literally, outside the usual categories.

The Switch version preserved the original's stark, pixel-art aesthetic, where simple shapes and clear colors serve pure readability of the rules rather than visual flourish, and the console port lost none of the precision needed to track how the words on screen behave. Controlling it with the Joy-Cons or buttons is precise, and the game suits handheld play excellently thanks to its short, self-contained puzzles, which can be tackled in sessions of any length, whether that's a few minutes or a longer, focused evening. Minimalist music leaves room for the quiet thinking that is the heart of the experience.

Baba Is You was repeatedly praised by critics on release as one of the most original puzzle concepts of its generation, because it offers an entirely different definition of what it means to "solve a puzzle" - the player here doesn't manipulate objects in a world according to rules, but manipulates the rules themselves. The game is still cited today as an example of bold, purely mechanics-driven design, and it inspired a number of successors working with a similar idea of programmable rules, though none of them has ever managed to fully match it.

**Why play it:** For puzzle fans craving a truly original challenge, one where you don't solve the world according to the rules but change the rules themselves - you won't find anything else quite like it.

switch__return-of-obra-dinn.teaser: A detective puzzle about reconstructing a ship's crew's fates using only observation and logical deduction.
switch__return-of-obra-dinn.article:
**Return of the Obra Dinn** puts the player in the role of an insurance investigator who, in 1807, walks through an abandoned trading ship that has mysteriously returned to port without its crew. Using a pocket watch with the ability to send the player back to the moment of each character's death, they must piece together fragments, frozen scenes, and snippets of conversation to reconstruct the fates of every crew member - who died, how, by whose hand, and when - based purely on observation, listening, and logical deduction, with no additional hints. The game never tells the player whether their conclusion is correct until they've verified enough irrefutable evidence themselves, which makes it one of the most demanding detective games of its kind, where the main tools are a pencil, paper, and patience.

Visually the game uses striking monochrome graphics inspired by old computer monitors, which on Switch look sharp and legible despite the low resolution of the retro style, while also giving the whole ship an unmistakable, slightly eerie look. The Switch version arrived somewhat later than on other platforms, but carried the game over without changes to the mechanics, and handheld mode proved pleasant for focused, longer investigation sessions, letting the player re-examine already visited scenes at any time. The sound design - the creaking of the ship, snippets of conversation, and atmospheric music - plays a key role in reconstructing each individual scene and uncovering the connections between them.

Return of the Obra Dinn was praised by critics on release as an exceptionally original detective experience, and its creator built on his existing reputation as a maker of unconventional mechanics. The game is still considered one of the high points of the logic-adventure genre and an example of how an entire game can be built on trust in the player's ability to observe closely, listen, and piece the facts together themselves, without ever being led by the hand.

**Why play it:** For detective-story lovers who want to piece a case together from nothing but observation, listening, and their own judgment, without any hand-holding whatsoever.

xbox-series__diablo-iv.teaser: The dark, gothic Sanctuary in full glory; fast ability-clicking and endless builds.
xbox-series__diablo-iv.article:
**Diablo IV** continues Blizzard Entertainment's long-running action-RPG series, bringing the dark, gothic world of Sanctuary in full glory to Xbox Series X/S. The player chooses from several classes - Barbarian, Sorcerer, Necromancer, Rogue, or Druid - and makes their way through an open world full of side quests, strongholds to capture, dungeons, and world bosses that other players passing by can spontaneously join in on. Combat is built on fast, tactical ability-clicking and build combinations, placing the game among the most refined representatives of the hack-and-slash genre, while an item system with a wealth of affixes offers room for experimentation even after dozens of hours of play.

On Xbox Series X/S the game runs smoothly at high resolution, and the fast SSD noticeably shortens loading times between the open world and instanced dungeons or boss fights. Gamepad controls are precisely tuned and offer a fully viable alternative to traditional mouse-and-keyboard control, without losing precision in fast fights against dozens of enemies on screen. The atmosphere is rounded out by grim music and sound design that carry on the tradition of the previous entries; rain-soaked backdrops and darkly toned cutscenes reinforce the sense of a hopeless, dark fantasy world that has been the hallmark of the Diablo series from the very start.

Diablo IV was received on release as a return to the series' roots after the controversial mobile spin-off, though its online elements and seasonal content sparked debate among players used to the purely offline play of earlier entries. The game offers a solo campaign as well as co-op play for up to four players, and regular seasons with new content, temporary mechanics, and character resets keep the community active long after launch. Today it ranks among the most-played RPGs on Xbox Game Pass and serves as an entry point into the genre for a new generation of players unfamiliar with the series' earlier entries, while also being a place series veterans regularly return to with each new season.

**Why play it:** With a solo campaign, co-op for up to four players, and regular seasons of new content, it serves as an ideal entry point into the genre as well as a place series veterans love to return to.

xbox-series__diablo-ii-resurrected.teaser: A remaster of the 2000 classic; switch between new and original graphics with a single button.
xbox-series__diablo-ii-resurrected.article:
**Diablo II: Resurrected** is a modern remaster of the cult classic from 2000 that brings the complete original game plus the Lord of Destruction expansion to Xbox Series X/S in reworked graphics. The visuals have been completely rebuilt in high resolution, while the player can switch back to the period-accurate graphics at any time with a single button press and compare just how far the isometric world of Sanctuary has come. Seven classes, an elaborate system of runes and items, build crafting around specific sets, and endless replayability thanks to randomly generated dungeons and the Nightmare and Hell difficulties remain untouched and still work exactly as they did in the original from the turn of the millennium.

On the new generation of consoles the game benefits from fast loading and stable performance, which for a title dependent on smooth item farming and quick transitions between areas means a noticeably more pleasant experience than on older hardware or on a period PC. The controls have been adapted to the gamepad and offer clear quick slots for spells and potions, which for a game designed primarily for mouse and keyboard was managed without major compromises in clarity. The audio side, including Matt Uelmen's iconic music and the atmospheric sounds of the catacombs and desert temples, has been preserved almost unchanged and still ranks among the most atmospheric scores of the entire action RPG genre.

The remaster was received by fans as a respectful and technically accomplished tribute to the original, which at its time defined the entire action RPG genre and influenced countless later games including Diablo III and IV themselves. On consoles it allowed the series to reach an audience that would otherwise never have gotten to the 2000 PC version, and cross-region online multiplayer also helped revive the community around trading rare items. Even years later Diablo II remains one of the most influential titles of the genre, and Resurrected is still considered one of the best ways to play it on modern hardware.

**Why play it:** For fans who want to experience the title that defined the action RPG genre on modern hardware, Resurrected remains one of the most respectful and technically accomplished remasters out there.

xbox-series__persona-3-reload.teaser: A reimagining of the 2006 JRPG classic; school and social bonds by day, the Tartarus tower by night.
xbox-series__persona-3-reload.article:
**Persona 3 Reload** is a complete reimagining of the classic 2006 JRPG that combines modern visuals on Xbox Series X/S with the story of a group of high schoolers fighting supernatural beings called Shadows during a mysterious hour between days.
