Head Over Heels is still considered one of the high points of the isometric action-adventure genre of the 1980s, and its well-thought-out design, in which both the gameplay and the puzzles grow directly out of the two-character-merging mechanic, influenced a number of later games of this type. The game demands patience and systematic mapping of its world, but rewards the player with the feeling of elegantly solving complex spatial puzzles. Even decades later it remains among the titles regularly cited as proof of the creative peak of the British game scene of the 1980s and as an inspiration for the later genre.

**Why play it:** For players who enjoy elegantly solving spatial puzzles, Head Over Heels is one of the high points of 1980s isometric action-adventures, even though it demands patience and systematic mapping.

c64__renegade.teaser: A conversion of the Japanese beat-'em-up that popularised the street-brawler genre in the West.
c64__renegade.article:
**Renegade** arrived on the Commodore 64 in 1987 in a conversion by Ocean Software of the arcade machine by Japanese studio Technōs, which popularised the beat-'em-up genre in the West. The player, in the role of a young man named Mr. K, moves through a series of scenes — from a subway station through the street to the docks — facing rival gangs he must defeat with punches, kicks and grapples before advancing to the next area and eventually facing the boss of each level, while also having to deal with attacks from multiple directions at once along the way. Besides straightforward attacks, the game also offered the option to throw an enemy to the ground or hurl them into others, which was fairly sophisticated for its time and gave the fights a tactical dimension.

On the C64, the basic principle of successive combat against waves of enemies was successfully carried over while keeping the graphics legible, if simplified compared to the arcade original, with characters large enough and their movements clear enough that this remained essential for the fighting gameplay. The audio was economical, focused on hit sound effects that underscored the pace of the fights well, while the music played more of a supporting role. The game's difficulty was seen as fairly high, in keeping with the title's arcade origins, geared toward short, intense sessions full of combat.

Renegade was among the first notable representatives of the street-brawler genre on 8-bit home computers, and its success helped pave the way for a number of later games of this type, including more famous sequels and rival titles such as Double Dragon. Although the C64 conversion didn't match the quality of the arcade original, it was seen at the time of release as a solid, playable home port of a popular concept. Today the game holds mainly historical value as evidence of the early days of the brawler genre on 8-bit home platforms.

**Why play it:** Anyone interested in the early days of the street-brawler genre on home computers will find Renegade offers a solid port of a popular arcade concept, though today it holds mainly historical value.

c64__krakout.teaser: A polished ball-and-paddle game with power-ups that alter the paddle's and ball's properties.
c64__krakout.article:
**Krakout** was released by Gremlin Graphics in 1987, and on the Commodore 64 it was one of the most polished games in the brick-breaking genre made famous earlier by Breakout and later by Arkanoid. The player controls a paddle moving along the bottom of the screen, bouncing a ball upward to destroy bricks arranged across the top of the play field, with different brick types requiring different numbers of hits or hiding power-ups that alter the paddle's or ball's properties, from slowing the ball down to multiple simultaneous bounces in a single round. Some levels also introduce moving obstacles that further complicate the ball's path.

Compared to many simpler clones, Krakout was distinguished by a very elaborate power-up system and a fairly large number of varied levels that gradually raised the demands on the player's precision and reflexes. On the C64 the game excelled with smooth ball movement and clear, colour-contrasted brick-field graphics, which was essential for this type of game, since even a slight delay in paddle control could mean losing the ball and ending the round. The soundtrack, by a leading composer of the scene, complemented the game's brisk pace well and, together with the bounce sound effects, created a pleasantly hypnotic atmosphere for long play sessions in front of the screen.

Krakout was ranked in contemporary reviews among the best titles of its genre on 8-bit platforms and was praised precisely for the richness of its power-up system, which managed to squeeze surprisingly long-lasting gameplay out of the simple ball-bouncing concept. The game still works today as an excellent example of how even a seemingly exhausted arcade concept can be revitalised through clever level and power-up design. For today's player it's a brisk, easy-to-grasp yet still addictive piece of entertainment that holds its own even next to the more famous Arkanoid on the same platform.

**Why play it:** For brisk, easy-to-grasp yet addictive arcade entertainment, Krakout is an excellent choice on the C64 thanks to a rich power-up system that holds its own even next to the more famous Arkanoid.

c64__sanxion.teaser: A wild vertical shmup from newcomer studio Thalamus; a tougher second lap awaits after completion.
c64__sanxion.article:
**Sanxion** was released in 1986 by the newly formed studio Thalamus and, on the Commodore 64, was one of the most striking vertically scrolling shooters on the whole platform. The player pilots a fighter craft flying through the defense lines of an enemy base, destroying waves of opponents and collecting power-ups that change the type and strength of the ship's fire, from faster projectiles to area-effect weapons, and after completing the first set of levels the game offers a second, tougher lap through the same scenes but with a new enemy layout, extending the title's life beyond a single standard playthrough.

Technically, the game became famous above all for its spectacular opening diagonal scrolling star-field effect, with which the game begins and which, at the time of release, showed just what the VIC-II chip on the C64 was capable of, even though the actual playing fields then shifted to more standard vertical scrolling. The gameplay was fast-paced and demanding, with dense enemy fire requiring quick reflexes and a good knowledge of attack patterns. An absolutely essential part of the experience was the music by Rob Hubbard, one of the most respected composers of the C64 scene, whose energetic score for Sanxion is still, to this day, among the most cited musical works on the whole platform and has been remixed many times over.

Sanxion is still remembered above all for its combination of a strong technical impression, fast-paced action and unforgettable music, thanks to which it was, at the time of its release, among the titles demonstrating just what could be achieved on the C64 both visually and sonically. The game helped establish Thalamus's reputation as a publisher of technically ambitious games, and its soundtrack influenced how important a role a game's music could play, even in titles focused purely on action. Sanxion remains a well-regarded representative of the genre even today, worth trying just for the phenomenal audiovisual impression of the game's opening alone.

**Why play it:** Anyone wanting to experience the phenomenal audiovisual impression the C64 could deliver in the mid-1980s should try Sanxion just for its unforgettable music and technical achievement.

c64__ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny.teaser: The peak of Garriott's series; the C64's open world tackles the morality of freedom and tyranny.
c64__ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny.article:
**Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny** ranks among the high points of Richard Garriott's entire series, and its 1988 Commodore 64 version proved that even an eight-bit machine could carry a sprawling open world with dozens of towns, castles, islands, and branching underground complexes. The player returns to Britannia, where in the Avatar's absence the tyrannical Order of the Shadowlords has seized power and imposed a strict, outwardly just but actually oppressive regime built on suppressing the people's free will. The game thus goes deeper into moral gray areas than its predecessors, forcing the player to consider what freedom truly means and what price they are willing to pay for order.

The gameplay is built on top-down exploration, text dialogue with characters that respond to specific keywords, recruiting a party of eight companions, and tactical combat on its own screen, where unit position and terrain matter. On the C64 the world was spread across many floppy disks, and frequent disk swapping was part of the price for its scope, but the game still offered an elaborate day-and-night system, the need for food and light underground, shop opening hours, and a believably living town economy where characters kept their own daily routines. The graphics were more modest than the PC versions and the color palette more limited, yet the atmosphere was well supported by spare but functional music accompanying the journey across the land.

At release Ultima V was received as one of the most ambitious RPGs on the market and is still ranked among the best entries in the whole series. It influenced a whole generation of open-world RPGs with its emphasis on a simulated world with its own rhythm, one that doesn't just wait for the player's steps but keeps living on without them. Today the game will appeal mainly to players interested in the genre's history who have patience for period controls and constant disk swapping — but as a piece of design it remains remarkably readable even decades later, and many of its ideas still turn up in RPGs today.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the genre's history with patience for period controls and disk swapping, Ultima V offers a remarkably readable design and a simulated world whose ideas still turn up in RPGs today.

c64__bard-s-tale-ii-destiny-knight.teaser: Even larger mazes than the first game; turn-based combat with striking monster portraits.
c64__bard-s-tale-ii-destiny-knight.article:
**The Bard's Tale II: The Destiny Knight** followed up Interplay's successful first-person dungeon crawler in 1986, offering players even larger and more treacherous mazes spread beneath the city of Skara Brae and beyond it. The goal for the party of adventurers is to find the legendary Destiny Wand, the only thing that can stand against the dark mage Lagoth, who threatens the whole world's balance between good and evil. The structure stays faithful to the first game — building a party of up to six characters from several classes and races, step-based first-person movement through the maze, and turn-based combat against monsters drawn in large, striking portraits that gave the battles a distinctive visual identity.

The second game adds an emphasis on puzzles, teleporters, dark corridors, and traps that often demand precise mapping and patient experimentation — the game is notorious for its difficulty and its lack of mercy toward careless adventurers who don't keep their own paper maps of each level. On the Commodore 64 the game ran smoothly even with plenty of monsters on screen and used a distinctive, atmospheric soundtrack that reinforced the sense of descending into ever more dangerous and darker depths of the maze. Importing characters from the first game let players continue the story with their already battle-hardened, experienced heroes and all their gear.

In the mid-1980s The Bard's Tale II was among the best-selling RPGs on the Commodore 64 and cemented the series' reputation as one of the most demanding and elaborate on the platform. Today's players may find it inaccessible due to the lack of an auto-map and the terse text interface with little guidance, but it remains an important reminder of what the dungeon crawler genre looked like before the graphical improvements and conveniences of the 1990s.

**Why play it:** Anyone who wants to see what the dungeon crawler genre looked like before the graphical conveniences of the 1990s will find in The Bard's Tale II a demanding but historically important experience without an auto-map.

c64__wasteland.teaser: The spiritual predecessor of Fallout; key paragraphs are read from the included book.
c64__wasteland.article:
**Wasteland** from 1988 by Interplay is rightly considered the spiritual predecessor of the Fallout series and one of the most influential post-apocalyptic RPGs ever made. The player commands a squad of Desert Rangers crossing a parched America destroyed by nuclear war, resolving moral dilemmas, building a reputation with individual factions, and facing mutants, robots, and desperate survivors fighting over the last remaining resources. On the Commodore 64 the game used a top-down map view and tactical, turn-based combat, complemented by the iconic system of numbered paragraphs from the included book — at key moments the game would refer the player to a specific number in the manual, which at the time got around the machine's memory limitations while also serving as copy protection.

Wasteland stood out for its nonlinear design: the world can be explored in different orders, decisions have permanent consequences, and the game remembers destroyed or resolved locations even after reloading a saved position. Character skills ranged from firearms through piloting and repairing equipment to unconventional fields like trap demolition or talking to animals, encouraging genuinely varied approaches to solving individual tasks. The atmosphere was rounded out by spare but functional graphics and a dark, raw tone that was unusual for RPGs of the time and set the game apart from more fairy-tale-like fantasy titles.

Contemporary critics praised the game for its ambition and originality, even though the controls and the extensive text passages in the book could be demanding and less accessible for some players. Wasteland fundamentally shaped the genre's direction toward morally ambiguous, open worlds with lasting consequences for decisions, and its legacy is still visible today not only in Fallout but in many other modern RPGs. Today the game is mainly a historical curiosity, but its system of choice and consequence still feels surprisingly modern and timeless.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the roots of Fallout and morally ambiguous open worlds, Wasteland offers a system of choice and consequence that still feels surprisingly modern years later, even though the controls remain demanding.

c64__zork-i-great-underground-empire.teaser: A foundational text adventure; the advanced Infocom parser understood even complex sentences.
c64__zork-i-great-underground-empire.article:
**Zork I: The Great Underground Empire** is one of the founding works of the text adventure genre, and its Commodore 64 version brought the legendary Infocom parser to owners of the eight-bit machine as well. With no graphics at all, the player explores a vast underground empire full of traps, puzzles, trolls, and treasures, communicating with the game through typed commands processed by an advanced text parser that understood relatively complex sentences rather than just simple verb-noun pairs, which was common among competitors at the time.

The gameplay rests on carefully examining the surroundings, collecting items, solving logical puzzles, and gradually building a mental map of the world, since the game offers no auto-map or hints of any kind. It's also famous for its dry English humor and its occasional merciless killing of the player who doesn't proceed carefully enough — saving and frequent backups of one's position were as much part of an experienced player's basic toolkit as pencil and paper for drawing the map. On the Commodore 64 the game ran from disk with no major changes compared to other platforms, since all the content was textual and independent of the graphical power of any particular machine, relying only on a virtual machine called the Z-machine.

Zork I was both a commercial and a critical phenomenon at release and helped define the entire genre of interactive fiction on personal computers for years to come. Its influence is visible across a whole generation of later text and graphic adventures, which borrowed both its puzzle structure and its distinctive narrative style and dry humor typical of Infocom's output. The game was, after all, the first entry in a loose trilogy, and many of its puzzles, locations, and solutions have stayed in players' memory to this day as a widely shared cultural legacy of the whole genre. Today the game will appeal mainly to players interested in the history of game storytelling and puzzle design — without knowledge of English and patience for the period parser, though, access to it is fairly difficult, even if the reward of a well-thought-out world is worth it.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the history of game storytelling and puzzle design, Zork I is a defining work that shaped the entire text adventure genre, though it demands English and patience with the period parser.

c64__hobbit.teaser: A text adventure with static location illustrations; it faithfully follows Tolkien's story of Bilbo.
c64__hobbit.article:
**The Hobbit** from 1982 by Melbourne House was one of the first text adventures to add static but atmospheric illustrations of individual locations to its spare text parser, and on the Commodore 64 it became one of the most successful and most talked-about titles of its time. The game faithfully follows the story of Bilbo Baggins from J. R. R. Tolkien's book — from meeting Gandalf and the dwarves, through the journey across the Misty Mountains, the encounter with Gollum, all the way to the final confrontation with Smaug — and the player must proceed in broad strokes true to the source material, though with room for their own improvisation and detours.

The key innovation was an advanced text parser and, above all, a system of characters driven by their own simple artificial intelligence — Gandalf, Thorin, and other companions moved and acted independently, sometimes actively helping the player in a fight or with a puzzle, other times complicating the whole situation, for instance by falling asleep in the middle of danger or wandering off elsewhere. This unpredictability made every playthrough a uniquely different experience, but it also led to frustrating, seemingly unsolvable situations caused by bugs and the technical limitations of the era.

The Hobbit became one of the best-selling titles for eight-bit computers in Britain, and its combination of text, static images, and simulated independently acting characters was genuinely groundbreaking for its time. The Tolkien license itself also contributed to its popularity, winning over the game even players who otherwise had little experience with text adventures. Contemporary critics praised its ambition and atmosphere, while also noting its technical flaws, occasional unsolvable situations, and the need to patiently wait for the game to process longer commands. Today the game is an important reminder of an early attempt to simulate a living, reactive world in an adventure game, and it remains an interesting historical artifact for fans of Tolkien and of interactive fiction in general.

**Why play it:** For anyone who wants to experience an early attempt at simulating a living, reactive game world combined with the Tolkien license, The Hobbit remains a fascinating historical artifact despite its period technical flaws.

c64__planetfall.teaser: Infocom sci-fi with an emotional story; the little robot Floyd is one of the genre's best characters.
c64__planetfall.article:
**Planetfall** from 1983 is one of Infocom's most beloved text adventures, and on the Commodore 64 it offered players a well-crafted sci-fi story combined with unusually emotional storytelling for its time. Playing a rank-and-file, rather lazy member of the space patrol, the player is stranded on an abandoned planet and must gradually uncover what happened to its once-advanced civilization, with the key companion along the way being the little robot Floyd — one of the most memorable digital characters of its era, playful, loyal, and, later in the game, tragically important to the story's emotional climax.

The gameplay relies on the traditional Infocom text parser, exploring a vast abandoned science base, solving time-sensitive puzzles, and cooperating with Floyd, who helps the player with tasks and comments on events with his own, often comic remarks that lighten the mood. The game deftly alternates lighthearted humor with more serious, melancholy tones, going further than most adventures of the time, which focused purely on puzzle logic without any deeper emotional dimension. On the C64 the game ran smoothly, since like other Infocom titles it didn't depend on graphical power, only on the text engine, the Z-machine, shared across all platforms.

Planetfall was highly praised at release for an originality and emotional depth unusual in the genre of purely text-based games up to that point, and it's still cited today as an example that even a game without a single picture can evoke a powerful emotional experience comparable to literature or film. Its influence on later storytelling in game adventures is undeniable and still cited today, whether in the combination of humor with more serious themes or in the figure of a companion who not only helps the player but also builds an emotional bond with them. Today's player will mainly appreciate the story and the character of Floyd, though the period parser demands considerable patience and a decent command of English to bring out all the nuances of the storytelling.

**Why play it:** For players who appreciate a strong story and emotional depth even without a single picture, Planetfall, thanks to the character of Floyd, remains one of the genre's most moving experiences — though it demands English and patience with the parser.

c64__deja-vu-nightmare-comes-true.teaser: A noir detective story controlled with a mouse rather than typed commands; amnesia and Chicago gangsters.
c64__deja-vu-nightmare-comes-true.article:
**Deja Vu: A Nightmare Comes True** brought a noir detective story to the Commodore 64 from ICOM Simulations, a studio known for its MacVenture system — an adventure controlled with a mouse and drop-down menus instead of traditional typed commands. The player wakes up as an amnesiac man in the men's room of a bar, blood on his hands and a corpse nearby, and must gradually reconstruct his own forgotten past, entangled with the gangster underworld of 1930s Chicago.

The gameplay is built on combining found items, thoroughly searching the environment, and choosing from a menu of actions such as Take, Use, Open, or Look, which was an unusual and intuitive solution on eight-bit platforms compared to the purely text parsers of the competition. The game also ran in real time, so the player was under constant pressure — long hesitation or bad decisions could gradually worsen the character's health or lead to other unpleasant consequences. The C64 version featured spare but functional graphics evoking a dark, cinematic atmosphere well suited to the hard-boiled detective genre and its typical clichés.

Deja Vu was praised for its atmosphere and innovative controls, and it helped popularize the so-called point-and-click adventure control scheme even before its later mass adoption by studios like LucasArts and Sierra On-Line. On the Commodore 64 it was one of the less common, and all the more interesting, ports of what was then a very popular graphic adventure genre, retaining a substantial part of the original versions' atmosphere on an eight-bit machine. The story also skillfully uses the theme of memory loss as a narrative device, letting the player uncover the character's past gradually, just as the character does themself. Today the game will appeal mainly to fans of noir detective stories and adventure genre history, though the pacing and period controls may feel somewhat archaic.

**Why play it:** For fans of noir detective stories and adventure genre history, Deja Vu offers an atmospheric tale of memory loss and an early point-and-click control system, though the period pacing calls for patience.

c64__pawn.teaser: An ambitious British text adventure; it showed that even outside the US, one could match Infocom.
c64__pawn.article:
**The Pawn** from the British studio Magnetic Scrolls was one of the most ambitious text adventures of the mid-1980s, and on the Commodore 64 it convincingly demonstrated just how far a text parser could go outside the dominant American studio, Infocom. The player finds themself in a fantasy land called Kerovnia, which they must thoroughly explore, understand its intricate politics, and solve a series of interconnected puzzles in order to finally reach the mysterious ruler named Kronos and uncover his intentions.

The game's parser was among the most advanced then available on the market — able to handle complex sentences, pronouns, and contextual references to previously entered commands, making communication with the game feel more natural and fluid than in competing titles. The puzzles in The Pawn require careful examination of the environment and patient experimentation, with the game rewarding creative solutions and offering the player more than one possible path to reach certain goals. On the C64 version, the text was further complemented by static illustrations of individual locations, which helped set the fantasy world's atmosphere without relying purely on verbal description.

At release, The Pawn was received by critics as one of the best text games outside Infocom's output and launched a successful series of further adventures from Magnetic Scrolls, which built a solid name for themselves on the strength of it. It helped show that European studios could compete with the American leaders in the text adventure genre both technically and in content, despite a smaller team and budget. The world of Kerovnia also feels surprisingly coherent and believable, with its own politics, humor, and cast of characters who respond distinctively to the player's commands. Today the game is of interest mainly to fans of classic text adventures and genre history; a modern player, though, will inevitably be tested by their patience with the period style of controls and command typing.

**Why play it:** For anyone who wants to see that European studios could compete with the American leaders in the text adventure genre, The Pawn offers the coherent world of Kerovnia with its own politics and humor, though the period control style remains demanding for a modern player.

c64__guild-of-thieves.teaser: A sequel to The Pawn; layered puzzles of a thieves' guild on the island of Kingdom.
c64__guild-of-thieves.article:
**Guild of Thieves** followed up on the success of The Pawn in 1987 and became one of the most acclaimed text adventures from Magnetic Scrolls on the Commodore 64. The player travels to an island called Kingdom to become a member of a prestigious thieves' guild, which requires completing a series of daring heists and convincingly proving their skill, ingenuity, and capacity for logical reasoning within an elaborate, interconnected world full of layered puzzles.

The game builds on the same advanced text parser as its predecessor, refined even further this time, and offers a more open structure where many tasks can be solved in different orders or even in several different ways depending on the player's preference. The puzzle design is renowned for its elegance—solutions often require attentiveness to small details in the environment descriptions rather than randomly trying commands. On the Commodore 64, the text was accompanied by high-quality illustrations of key locations, which visually set the game apart from starker American competitors and gave it a distinctive fantasy-adventure atmosphere with a touch of humor.

Guild of Thieves was received very favorably by contemporary critics and is often ranked among the very pinnacles of British text adventures of the 1980s, frequently rated even higher than The Pawn itself. Together with other titles from Magnetic Scrolls, it proved that the text adventure genre still had room to grow even after the rise of graphical adventures from rival studios, thanks to witty writing, a well-thought-out world, and puzzles built on logic rather than guessing the right verb. At the same time, the game doesn't take itself too seriously and approaches the adventure with a generous dose of exaggeration, giving it a distinctive, easily recognizable character. Today's player will appreciate the ingenuity of the puzzles and the dense atmosphere, though navigating the world without available hints can be fairly demanding for an unaccustomed player.

**Why play it:** For ingenious, logic-based puzzles and an atmosphere full of English humor, ideal for players who don't mind drawing a map on paper and thinking hard about every command.

c64__wizardry-proving-grounds-of-mad-ove.teaser: Founder of dungeon crawlers; a six-member party faces Werdna in a ten-level dungeon.
c64__wizardry-proving-grounds-of-mad-ove.article:
**Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord** from Sir-Tech is one of the founding titles of the dungeon crawler genre, and its later port for the Commodore 64 brought this classic to owners of the eight-bit machine several years after its original release. The player assembles a party of up to six adventurers from several races and classes and sends them into a ten-level maze hidden beneath the castle of the mad wizard Werdna, tasked with recovering a legendary stolen amulet.

The game plays out entirely in first-person view with simple wireframe 3D graphics depicting the dungeon corridors, while combat is static, accompanied by text descriptions of actions and striking monster portraits. Wizardry is famous for its high difficulty and permanent character death—a fallen hero can theoretically be resurrected, but a failed resurrection attempt means their definitive, irreversible loss, forcing the player to caution and careful planning of every expedition. Mapping each level of the maze was entirely up to the player, so paper and pencil were as essential a part of the kit as the party members' swords and armor.

Wizardry became both a commercial and critical success, defined the basic mechanics of the entire genre for years to come, and inspired countless successors, including early Japanese RPGs, where its influence was especially strong and long-lasting, still visible today in series such as Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy. On the Commodore 64, despite the simplified graphics, the game faithfully carried over the core of this dense, uncompromising yet rewarding gameplay, where every descent to a deeper level brings a genuine sense of accomplishment. The maze world offers no story in the modern sense; all the tension comes purely from the uncertainty of what lurks around the next corner. To today's player it may seem cruel and unforgiving of mistakes, but as a historical milestone of the genre it is utterly unmissable.

**Why play it:** For fans of uncompromising dungeon crawlers and anyone interested in the roots of Japanese RPGs, this is a historically pivotal experience, though today it remains mercilessly difficult and shows no mercy for mistakes.

c64__phantasie.teaser: A more accessible alternative to Wizardry; a party faces the mage Nikademus in a vast world.
c64__phantasie.article:
**Phantasie** from Strategic Simulations, Inc. was among the most popular RPGs on the Commodore 64 in the mid-1980s, offering a somewhat more accessible alternative to the dominant, considerably more demanding dungeon crawlers of the time, such as Wizardry. The player leads a party of adventurers through a vast fantasy world full of towns, caves, graveyards, and wilderness, ultimately facing the evil mage Nikademus, whose dark plans threaten the entire land and its inhabitants.

The game combined a top-down map view with textured mazes and turn-based combat, in which an entire row of monsters could face the party at once, depicted with simple but distinctive, easily recognizable icons. A notable asset of Phantasie was the included paper map of the game world, which helped players orient themselves far more easily than in many competing titles with no automap or hints at all. The experience system, character progression, and equipment management were clear and well balanced, making the game feel overall less merciless than, say, the aforementioned Wizardry, without sacrificing gameplay depth and strategy.

Phantasie earned praise on release for both its accessibility and its content, and it kicked off a successful series of sequels in the following years that retained a loyal following throughout the 1980s. On the Commodore 64 it was among the best-selling RPGs and helped popularize the entire genre with a wider audience beyond the core of hardcore players who had until then made up the bulk of the community around such titles. The sound was solid for its time of release and, combined with colorful, clear graphics, gave the game a pleasantly cozy adventure atmosphere. Today the game is interesting mainly as a reminder of an era when computer RPGs were still searching for the balance between systemic depth and accessibility for the average player.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the balance between depth and accessibility in early RPGs, where cozy graphics and sound make playing a pleasant reminder of the genre's search for its roots.

c64__simcity.teaser: Will Wright's legendary sandbox simulation; no goal, just building and disasters.
c64__simcity.article:
**SimCity** is one of the most significant simulation games of the 1980s and 1990s, and it arrived on the Commodore 64 as a port of the famous title by Will Wright and Maxis. In it, the player doesn't earn points for shooting enemies but for building and maintaining a functioning city—placing residential, commercial, and industrial zones, building roads, power lines, police and fire stations, and trying to keep the budget in the black. The game has no fixed goal or ending; it's more of an open sandbox simulation where the player decides for themselves whether to build a metropolis or experiment with disasters such as fires, earthquakes, or a giant monster invasion. Advisors are also available to warn the player about rising crime, traffic jams, or power shortages, so the player gradually learns to read the map as a living organism, where every intervention affects neighboring districts.

On eight-bit hardware, the game had to contend with graphics and memory limitations, so the visual style is simplified compared to later versions, but the basic mechanism—linking zones, traffic, and tax revenue—remained functional and legible. Control via joystick and keyboard replaced the mouse the game was accustomed to on other platforms, which slowed play down somewhat but didn't stop SimCity from finding its own audience and community of players on the C64. The sound is sparing, focused more on short effects for construction, traffic collapse, or disaster than on an extensive musical backdrop, reflecting how Brøderbund adapted the game to the constraints of the eight-bit platform.

The game's significance extends beyond the platform itself—SimCity founded the entire city-building simulation genre and inspired dozens of later titles, from competing city builders to later entries in its own series and other Maxis simulations. Even on the Commodore 64, it still attracts players who want to experience the genre's roots on period hardware, although smoother and graphically richer experiences are offered by the Amiga or PC versions. Precisely because it is a port of a truly influential game and not a derivative work, the eight-bit version of SimCity remains an interesting stop for collectors and genre historians alike.

**Why play it:** For collectors and genre historians who want to experience the roots of city-building simulations directly on eight-bit hardware, even though smoother versions are offered by the Amiga or PC.

c64__balance-of-power.teaser: Chris Crawford's Cold War strategy game; a direct clash of superpowers ends the game immediately.
c64__balance-of-power.article:
**Balance of Power** is a political strategy game by Chris Crawford in which the player takes on the role of the President of the USA or the General Secretary of the USSR during the Cold War era. The goal isn't military victory but maintaining and expanding global influence without triggering a nuclear apocalypse—any escalation of a crisis that turns into a direct armed clash between the superpowers ends the game immediately in defeat for both sides. The player invests in allies around the world, responds to uprisings, coups, and diplomatic crises, and negotiates wherever possible to maintain the fragile balance of power. The game also continuously evaluates a so-called prestige score for both superpowers, so the player feels the consequences of their actions even without open conflict, simply through a comparison of global influence.

On the Commodore 64, the game works with a clear world map and text reports on events in individual countries, placing emphasis on thinking and decision-making rather than action or visual flair. The pace is slow and deliberate, close to a board game, and the game actively punishes aggressive or reckless moves—an unusual approach to the topic of nuclear confrontation in the mid-1980s that was much debated within the player community. The atmosphere is rounded out by terse, matter-of-fact diplomatic reports that give the player the feeling of sitting in on a real briefing rather than playing an action game.

Balance of Power is often remembered as one of the first games to seriously engage with the political and diplomatic dimension of strategy instead of pure military expansion, and it is still cited today as a pioneering title of the genre. On the C64, it still offers an interesting look at how games of the 1980s managed to treat the serious topic of the Cold War without reducing it to a mere military shooter, which is why it's still talked about today as one of the first truly serious political simulations for home computers.

**Why play it:** Worth trying for its fresh, seriously handled treatment of the Cold War without reducing it to a military shooter, as one of the first serious political simulations.

c64__seven-cities-of-gold.teaser: Colonizing the New World; trading with native tribes or plundering them is up to the player.
c64__seven-cities-of-gold.article:
**Seven Cities of Gold** casts the player as a conquistador exploring and colonizing the New World during the age of exploration. The game combines a sea voyage across the Atlantic, exploration of an unknown continent, contact with native civilizations, and the building of settlements and trading posts—the player decides for themselves whether to trade with the native tribes and build peaceful relations, or to exploit and plunder their gold. How the player treats individual tribes also affects how easily they will later replenish supplies, find new allies, or learn the location of the legendary golden cities the game is named after.

On the Commodore 64, the game offers a procedurally generated continent map, so every expedition is different, and it weaves several distinct layers of gameplay—from sailing a ship to overland expeditions to settlement management—into one cohesive whole. The graphics are simple but functional, and the game prides itself on a sense of discovering unknown territory, where the player never knows in advance what they'll find beyond the next hill or river. Switching between views from the ship's deck, an overland expedition, and founding a settlement gives the game a pace that's unusually varied for an eight-bit computer.

The game was created by Ozark Softscape, centered around Danielle Bunten Berry, known for her emphasis on player freedom and an open decision-making system with moral consequences. Seven Cities of Gold is often ranked among the pioneering titles of the open-world strategy simulation genre and influenced later games about exploration and colonization, including the studio's own Pirates! series, which the authors followed up with a few years later. Even decades later, it's clear the game emphasized freedom of decision over linear progression, setting it apart from the more common strategy games of the time with fixed objectives. On the Commodore 64, the game also showed that even relatively modest hardware could carry a simulation with several interconnected systems at once, without falling apart into a series of isolated minigames.

**Why play it:** For lovers of open-ended strategy games that emphasize freedom of decision over linear progression, you'll also appreciate how modest hardware managed to carry several interconnected systems at once.

c64__lords-of-conquest.teaser: Territorial strategy for up to four players; the map is generated differently every time.
c64__lords-of-conquest.article:
**Lords of Conquest** is a strategy game for one to four players, in which the goal is to fight for control of territory on a map made up of continents and seas. Players take turns occupying territory, building armies, ships, and resource mines, trying to dominate as much of the map as possible both militarily and economically—the game somewhat resembles board strategy games like Risk, but with its own rules for resource extraction and unit construction. The map is also generated differently every time, so players can't plan their starting positions in advance and must react to whatever continents and resources chance assigns them. Resources such as iron, horses, or wood determine which units a player can afford to build, so managing territory is just as important as the combat clashes themselves.

On the Commodore 64, the game relies on a clear map and simple, quickly understood controls, which made it popular as a game for multiple players taking turns at a single computer. The turn-based system leaves room for planning, but a match doesn't lose pace, since individual rounds are short and focused on key decisions about expansion and territorial defense. It was precisely the combination of simple rules and a changeable map that made the game a popular choice both for quick matches among friends and for longer tactical duels, in which the border between individual players gradually took shape.

The Ozark Softscape team, again led by Danielle Bunten Berry, was in the mid-1980s one of the few studios systematically dedicated to multiplayer strategy games for home computers. Lords of Conquest is remembered today mainly as a carefully tuned multiplayer title that showed even an eight-bit computer could offer deep strategic fun for a group of players at a single screen, without requiring a complicated manual or lengthy learning curve, making it easy to return to even years later without detailed knowledge of the rules.

**Why play it:** If you're looking for a deep yet easy-to-grasp multiplayer strategy game for a group at one screen, it plays without needing to study a thick manual even years later.

c64__ancient-art-of-war.teaser: Tactical warfare with infantry, archers, and cavalry; also includes a scenario editor.
c64__ancient-art-of-war.article:
**The Ancient Art of War** is a strategy game set in fictional ancient battles in which the player commands armies made up of infantry, archers, and cavalry. On a tactical map, the player deploys units, plans movement and attacks, and must take terrain, troop morale, and supply into account—classic elements that helped lay the foundation for an entire generation of later turn-based war games. The player can also modify the battlefield terrain itself and build simple scenarios, giving the game a certain constructive dimension beyond just commanding pre-made battles. It also includes an editor in which the player can assemble their own army and unit deployment before engaging in an actual clash with the opponent.

On the Commodore 64, the game offers a clear, easily readable interface with unit icons and a map across which armies move in real time, interrupted by pauses for issuing orders. The campaigns are designed as a series of separate scenarios, which makes the game accessible even to players who don't want to invest dozens of hours into one long continuous campaign. Short, clearly readable unit animations give the player quick feedback on how their army is faring in combat, without having to decipher tables of numbers. The musical accompaniment is minimalist; the game relies more on sound effects of marching and combat, which underscore the clarity of the action on screen.

The game was developed by Evryware and published by Broderbund, and it was precisely its accessibility and elegant design that earned it a good reception even beyond the narrow circle of wargame fans. The Ancient Art of War is often mentioned as one of the games that managed to make tactical command accessible to a wider audience, and on the Commodore 64 it still offers a pleasantly legible and quickly understood entry point into the genre of historical strategy games, without burdening it with an excess of rules, which is why it's still recommended today as a suitable first step for players who want to get into the turn-based strategy genre.

**Why play it:** For players who want to get into the turn-based strategy genre for the first time, it offers a legible, quickly understood entry point without an unnecessary excess of rules.

c64__nato-commander.teaser: An early Sid Meier game; NATO defends Central Europe against the Warsaw Pact.
c64__nato-commander.article:
**Nato Commander** is one of Sid Meier's early games, in which the player commands NATO forces in a hypothetical conventional conflict in Central Europe against the forces of the Warsaw Pact. The game is built on a hexagonal map across which infantry, armor, and air force units move, and the player must weigh the balance of forces, terrain, and supply lines to defend key territories against an attacker's superior numbers. The game offers several scenarios with different force ratios, so the player can try both balanced battles and hopeless-looking defensive actions, where the main task is to delay the enemy's advance for as long as possible. At the same time, the player must decide when to deploy air power to support ground units and when to hold it back for the later, decisive phase of the battle.

On the Commodore 64, the game benefits from a clear hexagonal interface and a relatively fast pace to each turn, making it more accessible and quicker to grasp than some of the more complex wargames of the time. Both the opponent's AI and the game's pacing were designed so that a session wouldn't eat up an entire afternoon, which was rather the exception in the turn-based wargame genre. The spare, functional graphics clearly distinguish the various unit types and terrain, so even after several turns the player easily keeps track of the overall situation on the front. The sound is restrained, limited to short movement and firing effects, signaling that the game's focus is tactical decision-making rather than audiovisual spectacle.

Nato Commander was made at MicroProse during the period when Sid Meier was still establishing himself as a designer of war simulations, before he later became famous for his civilization and flight titles. Today the game is interesting mainly as evidence of the early phase of his career and as an illustration of how the turn-based wargame genre, in the early 1980s, was searching for a way to reach a wider home-computer audience, well before Meier became one of the best-known names in the games industry.

**Why play:** Worth attention mainly for its historical value as an early work by Sid Meier, before his civilization and flight hits, and especially for fans of the wargame genre's development.

c64__kampfgruppe.teaser: Turn-based war on the Eastern Front; the interplay of tanks, infantry, and artillery decides the day.
c64__kampfgruppe.article:
**Kampfgruppe** is a turn-based war strategy game from Strategic Simulations, Inc., set amid the fighting on the Eastern Front of World War II. The player commands battalions and regiments of the German or Soviet army at the tactical level, directing the movement of tanks, infantry, and artillery across a hexagonal map, and must account for supply, morale, and the interplay between the different branches of the military. The game contains several historical scenarios, from smaller raids to larger battles that decide the fate of an entire stretch of the front. The player must constantly balance the speed of an armored advance against the need to keep infantry and artillery within mutual supporting range, or risk their own formation falling apart.

On the Commodore 64, the game offers an elaborate combat system, detailed for its time, which takes into account the properties of specific types of equipment and units — so the player doesn't feel like they're merely shuffling abstract tokens around, but genuinely commanding a combined-arms formation. The interface is text-and-graphics based, with a clear map and menus for issuing orders, matching the standard of SSI's wargames of the era. The pace of the game is slow and deliberate; individual turns require weighing cover, visibility, and firing range, which lengthens matches but also adds to the tension. The audio is sparse by today's standards, with the game focused primarily on clear map-reading and on making sure the player always has a clear picture of the positions of their own and enemy units.

Kampfgruppe belongs to a series of historical war simulations with which SSI built its reputation in the 1980s as a specialist in depth and historical fidelity at the expense of accessibility. The game was praised by genre fans for its precision and is still remembered today as one of the representative examples of turn-based wargames from the golden age of eight-bit computers, which relied on elaborate rules rather than flashy visuals.

**Why play:** For fans of historically faithful turn-based wargames who prefer elaborate rules over visual flair, it ranks among the representative examples of the genre's golden age.

c64__ogre.teaser: An adaptation of Steve Jackson's board game; the more damaged the giant Ogre tank gets, the more vulnerable it becomes.
c64__ogre.article:
**Ogre** is a strategy game from Origin Systems based on Steve Jackson's board game of the same name, set in a future dominated by giant walking tanks called Ogres. The player usually commands the defenders, who use smaller tanks, infantry, and anti-tank units to try to stop, or at least damage, the attacking Ogre before it reaches their command center. The progressive damage to the giant machine is reflected in the gameplay itself — as the Ogre loses weapons and mobility, the defenders' chances improve, so even a seemingly lost battle can turn around in the final turns. The defending player must also sacrifice some units purely to slow the Ogre's advance and buy time for concentrated fire from other squads.

On the Commodore 64, the game translates the board game original onto a hexagonal map with a turn-based system that preserves the tension of the original — the defender has more units at their disposal, but the Ogre is enormously tough and its weapons gradually wipe out the defense one unit at a time. The graphics are spare and functional, fully subordinated to the clarity of the tactical situation, which was a common approach for board game conversions at the time. The short length of a single match also makes it easy to replay with a different defender setup and try out a different tactic. The sound effects of gunfire and explosions are economical but expressive — every unit lost can be heard, and the player keenly senses how the balance of power on the map gradually shifts.

Ogre is valued above all for its fidelity to the original and for the purity of its concept — one large, uneven battle whose prospects for both sides shift from one turn to the next. On the Commodore 64, the game remains interesting as an example of how a successful board game design can be carried over to an eight-bit computer without losing its tension, especially since the Ogre concept later inspired several follow-up releases and expansions of the board game itself, to which the player community still returns today.

**Why play:** Worth trying for the purity of its one-big-uneven-battle concept and its fidelity to the board game, as an example of just how well a board game's tension can carry over to an eight-bit computer.

c64__war-in-middle-earth.teaser: A strategy game based on The Lord of the Rings; you simultaneously direct the battle for Middle-earth and Frodo's secret march.
c64__war-in-middle-earth.article:
**War in Middle Earth** is a strategy game from Melbourne House that adapts Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings into a war strategy played out on a map of Middle-earth. The player simultaneously directs two storylines — the military campaign, in which the armies of Rohan, Gondor, and their allies face the forces of Mordor, and the journey of Frodo's fellowship carrying the Ring toward Mount Doom, which must be kept hidden from the enemy. The longer the player manages to keep Frodo's group out of the sight of Sauron's hostile forces, the greater the chance of finally destroying the Ring, while the military front meanwhile keeps Mordor's attention and forces occupied elsewhere. The player is thus constantly thinking on two levels at once — where to strengthen the military defense, and at the same time by what route to safely lead a handful of heroes through territory full of enemies.

On the Commodore 64, the game combines a strategic map showing the movement of armies with separate screens for tracking the Ring-bearer's progress, attempting to carry over the dual tension of the book — the military resistance and the secret mission on which the outcome of the entire war depends. The graphics use portraits and maps that looked impressive for their time, and the game ranks among the more ambitious licensed adaptations of its era. The vast map of Middle-earth and the number of units, towns, and characters mean the player has to learn to switch between a strategic overview and closely following the fate of individual heroes. Text messages and character portraits add to the atmosphere, giving the player, even on limited hardware, the sense of watching a truly epic, bookish story unfold.

War in Middle Earth is valued precisely for its effort to translate the very essence of the book's plot into game mechanics — linking open military confrontation with the quiet, vulnerable journey of the heroes in the background. On the Commodore 64, it is one of the more expansive Middle-earth-themed strategy games of the eight-bit era, and it still attracts Tolkien fans and collectors of licensed titles alike, who appreciate that the game didn't settle for merely a superficial use of names and places from the book.

**Why play:** For Tolkien fans and collectors of licensed titles who will appreciate that the game doesn't treat the names and places superficially, but genuinely weaves together the military and the quiet storyline.

c64__populous.teaser: The founder of the god-games genre from Bullfrog; you shape the land and gather your followers' faith.
c64__populous.article:
**Populous**, from Bullfrog Productions, is regarded as the founding title of the god-games genre, in which the player, as a deity, shapes the landscape to allow their followers' civilization to grow, while also battling a rival tribe's god for the souls of the inhabitants. The player raises and lowers terrain to create flat land for new settlements, sends down disasters such as floods or volcanic eruptions, and in the later stages of the game can also call down direct military strikes against the enemy. As the inhabitants' faith in the player's deity grows, stronger powers unlock, from earthquakes all the way to a spectral Armageddon, pushing the game from quiet building toward open confrontation with the rival. The followers themselves are the key source of power — the more densely settled and well-developed the land, the greater the might available to the player's deity.

On the Commodore 64, the game was ported with the limitations of eight-bit hardware in mind — the isometric view of the landscape is preserved, albeit with simpler graphics and slower response than on the 16-bit platforms the game was primarily designed for. Even so, it managed to keep the core gameplay loop of shaping terrain, growing settlements, and the gradual escalation of the conflict between the two deities. Players used to the smoother versions will appreciate that the eight-bit port, despite its technical limitations, kept the controls clear and the map legible. The music is more modest than in the versions on more powerful computers, yet it still manages to evoke the calm, meditative atmosphere of shaping the land that the game offers during its quieter stretches.

Populous is still cited today as the game that founded an entire genre, later popularized by titles such as Black & White or Dungeon Keeper. The Commodore 64 version can't compete with the smoothness of the original on the Amiga, but it allowed the god-games genre to reach players limited to eight-bit hardware, and so it remains an interesting historical chapter in the development of both the series and the entire genre of divine simulations.

**Why play:** For anyone interested in the roots of the god-games genre later made famous by titles like Black & White or Dungeon Keeper, it's worth playing despite being less smooth than the Amiga version.

c64__wargame-construction-set.teaser: Both an editor and a game at once; build your own turn-based battles and rules however you like.
c64__wargame-construction-set.article:
**Wargame Construction Set** is a unique tool from Strategic Simulations, Inc. that, instead of offering one specific battle, gives the player the ability to design their own turn-based war scenarios. The player defines the map, terrain, units, and their properties, and can then play through the created scenario themselves or hand it off to another player — the game thus functions as both an editor and a full-fledged game system at once. Not only the maps and units can be configured, but also the basic combat rules, so more experienced players could build scenarios matching almost any historical period or fictional conflict. The program thus worked more like a rules construction kit than a single specific game, which was a fairly unusual approach for home computers in the mid-1980s.

On the Commodore 64, Wargame Construction Set offers clear tools for editing the hexagonal map and setting unit parameters, which made it a popular tool among genre enthusiasts who wanted to create their own historical or fictional battles without needing to program. The included sample scenarios also served as a guide to working with the system, as well as being full-fledged games in their own right. The text-and-graphics interface is just as spare as in other SSI wargames, but the editor's controls are designed to accommodate less experienced users with no programming knowledge. Working with the editor is step-by-step and clear, so even building a larger scenario could be managed gradually, across several shorter sessions.

At a time when wargames were a genre with a fairly narrow but devoted fan base, Wargame Construction Set gave that community a creation tool similar to the game editors of later years. On the Commodore 64, it remains an interesting example of how SSI approached the genre not just as a series of individual titles, but also as an open platform for custom scenarios that the player community could shape to fit its own vision.

**Why play:** For players interested in period game editors who want to see how SSI gave wargame fans a tool for creating their own scenarios instead of yet another closed-off title.

c64__pole-position.teaser: A conversion of the famous Atari/Namco arcade game; a qualifying lap and the race itself on the Fuji Speedway circuit.
c64__pole-position.article:
**Pole Position** was one of the first big arcade hits to find its way onto home computers, and it arrived on the Commodore 64 in the mid-1980s as a conversion of the legendary Atari and Namco machine. The player sits behind the wheel of a Formula car, and the task is first to drive a qualifying lap in order to earn a spot on the starting grid, then to run the actual race on the Fuji Speedway circuit against computer-controlled rivals. The controls are simple — accelerator, brake, and steering left and right — but the game demands precise avoidance of other cars and the track barriers, since every collision costs precious seconds and, at worst, causes the car to explode, followed by a brief animation and a loss of valuable time.

The graphics on the C64 use the familiar view from behind the car and a smoothly rushing track lined with advertising billboards, which was a notable technical feat for its time, even though a conversion to an eight-bit computer logically couldn't fully match the smoothness of the original arcade machine. The music and engine sounds are spare but functional, lending the game an arcade pace whose main goal was to faithfully recreate the feel of the arcade hall, where players at the time would go to play the real cabinet machine for a few coins. The time limit, which extends as the player passes checkpoints, forces constant pushing on the accelerator and risk-taking, while points awarded for placement at both the start and the finish motivate repeated attempts at a better result.

Pole Position helped popularize the racing game genre on home computers and became the benchmark against which later titles were measured, whether for the behind-the-car viewpoint or for the very principle of qualifying before the race. Today the game feels more like a historical curiosity — simple, short, and repetitive — but it holds an irreplaceable place in understanding the development of the racing genre on eight-bit machines, and it still offers brisk, easily grasped fun for a few minutes, ideal for a quick play without a long learning curve.

**Why play:** For its brisk, easily grasped fun that lasts a few minutes and its irreplaceable place in the history of the racing genre, it's worth a quick play even today.

c64__stunt-car-racer.teaser: Original elevated tracks full of jumps; a bad landing shatters your car to pieces.
c64__stunt-car-racer.article:
**Stunt Car Racer** from 1989, by programmer Geoff Crammond, is one of the most original racing games of the eight-bit era. Instead of classic tracks, the game offers insane elevated courses full of jumps, guardrail-less turns, and long drops into empty space — landing badly after a jump is enough to shatter the car to pieces, accompanied by a dramatic animation of the bodywork breaking apart. Duels are always one-on-one within a tournament ladder, where the player gradually climbs from the weakest opponents to the league's champions, while a wrecked car can only be repaired to a limited degree between laps, and a damaged car handles worse, pushing the player toward more cautious, yet still fast, driving.

On the Commodore 64, the game runs in fast wireframe 3D graphics that, despite the hardware limitations, feel surprisingly smooth and give the player a clear sense of speed and height above the track, as the course winds high above the ground with no safety rail whatsoever. The car's physics, the bouncing over track irregularities, and the need to brake before jumps create a tension that racing games of the time mostly didn't offer, since a single miscalculation of the distance to the next track segment can mean an instant fall. The engine and crash sound effects are spare, but the music between laps rounds out the atmosphere of a tense tournament, where the player faces increasingly skilled opponents one after another and must adapt to their aggressive driving style in tight duels to advance further.

At the time of its release, Stunt Car Racer was highly praised by critics precisely for its bold concept and technical execution, and it still ranks among the titles recommended for trying on the C64 as a showcase of what the machine was capable of in the hands of a skilled programmer. Its influence can be seen in later stunt-racing games as well, and the game retains a fresh, addictive feel even decades later, because the combination of simple rules and merciless physics works regardless of the title's age and can still get the player to try just one more run.

**Why play:** For fans of merciless physics and simple rules that, even after all these years, keep tempting you into one more try, it's among the titles showing what the C64 was capable of in a skilled programmer's hands.

c64__test-drive.teaser: Driving exotic sports cars; the main enemy is the police radar.
c64__test-drive.article:
**Test Drive** from 1987 by Distinctive Software was one of the first computer games that tried to offer a genuine feel of driving exotic sports cars on public roads. The player could choose between several legendary cars, such as the Ferrari Testarossa, Porsche 911, or Lamborghini Countach, and take them along a winding mountain road, where the main enemy wasn't rival racers but police patrols and heavy traffic that had to be dodged — getting caught by the radar meant a chase and the end of the ride if caught.

On the Commodore 64 the game offers a view from inside the car's cabin with a visible steering wheel and dashboard, which felt unusually authentic at the time, and the individual cars differed from each other in acceleration, top speed, and cornering behavior, so choosing a car had a real impact on driving style. The gearshift lever and the need to shift gears correctly added a simulation dimension to the game that set it apart from purely arcade racers, and a bad downshift could slow the car down at the worst possible moment. The road also changes according to weather and visibility, so fog or darkness can make orientation harder and force the player to slow down even where they could otherwise floor it, while rain reduces the car's grip in corners.

Test Drive became a commercially successful title and kicked off a long series of sequels that later moved to newer platforms and became famous for further entries focused on specific car models. Within the C64 library it represents one of the most ambitious attempts of its time at simulating road driving, and even today it's interesting as proof of how a simple concept of dodging traffic can be built into an atmospheric drive along mountain switchbacks, where it's a joy to watch the landscape around the road gradually change and the tension of an approaching police patrol build with every passing mile.

**Why play it:** For fans of atmospheric drives along mountain switchbacks, where the tension rises with every mile and every approaching police patrol, it still offers a functional slice of early road-racing simulation.

c64__grand-prix-circuit.teaser: A Formula racing simulation inspired by F1; car setup decides both speed and stability.
c64__grand-prix-circuit.article:
**Grand Prix Circuit** from 1988, made for Accolade by Distinctive Software, brought the world of Formula racing inspired by the Formula 1 season of the time to the Commodore 64. The player goes through a world championship on a series of real and fictional circuits, and before each race adjusts the car's gear ratio, suspension stiffness, and other parameters that affect its behavior on track, so a compromise must be found between speed on the straights and stability through the corners. A practice lap is used to fine-tune the setup and qualify for a starting position, which brings the game closer to a simulation than an arcade racer, where the order on the starting grid wouldn't matter.

The graphics on the C64 offer a view from behind the single-seater and decently animated rivals who behave convincingly in the corners and are capable of both overtaking the player and being overtaken, which gave players of the time a real sense of battling for position on track. Driving requires braking before corners and smoothly steering into the apex, otherwise the car easily runs off the track or spins out, and even a small mistake in the racing line costs precious tenths of a second. The seasonal points standings and championship motivate the player to complete the whole series of races, not just a single lap, much like in a real championship season where points add up and the final races decide everything.

At the time of release, Grand Prix Circuit was among the more sophisticated racing titles on eight-bit computers and showed that even the C64 could offer elements of a genuine motorsport simulation, albeit with the simplifications the machine's power demanded. Today it's interesting mainly as an example of an early effort to combine car setup with arcade-style play, and as a companion to Accolade's later Formula 1 series, which built on this foundation and expanded it with new circuits and car setup options.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the early combination of car setup with arcade racing, it's worth a look as the foundation on which Accolade's entire Formula 1 series later built.

c64__kikstart-2.teaser: Physics-based motocross with a track editor; body lean decides how you land off a jump.
c64__kikstart-2.article:
**Kikstart 2** from 1987 by Mastertronic followed up on the successful motocross game Kikstart and brought physics-based racing through obstacle courses full of bumps, ramps, and jumps to the Commodore 64. The player controls a motorcyclist from a side view and must constantly balance the body's lean forward and backward so as not to lose balance and fall after landing a jump, which is the core of the whole gameplay — a single misjudged distance between ramps means a crash to the ground and the loss of precious seconds. The addition of a track editor let players design their own circuits and share them with each other, an unusual feature for its time, thanks to which the community could keep producing ever more demanding and inventive tracks.

The controls are deceptively simple — throttle and body lean — but mastering the rhythm of jumps and landings requires a considerable amount of practice and patience, because the ideal technique differs slightly for every ramp depending on its slope and length. The graphics are economical but legible, and the rider's little figure is animated fluidly enough that the player can see exactly when a crash is coming and when the lean is still fine. The music between laps is short and simple, with the main emphasis placed on the ride itself and the tension of every jump, which can end in a successful landing or a painful crash to the ground and the need to restart the attempt at the best possible time.

Kikstart 2 became a popular title in Britain thanks to its low price and accessibility, and it's often remembered as one of the games where players spent hours trying the same ramp over and over until they managed to clear the whole track without crashing. On the Commodore 64 it's a pleasantly distinctive representative of the genre, since it combines a motocross race with elements of a balance-based platformer, and even today it offers an addictive, easily understood game loop that lures players into chasing ever better times on the same, well-known track.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its unusual combination of a motocross race with a balance-based platformer, and its addictive chase for better times on a familiar track, it's a pleasantly distinctive title in its genre.

c64__chase-h-q.teaser: A port of the Taito arcade machine; a timed chase ends by ramming the criminal's car.
c64__chase-h-q.article:
**Chase H.Q.** from 1989, ported to the Commodore 64 by Ocean Software based on the original Taito arcade machine, casts the player as police officer Tanner, who pursues fleeing criminals in an unmarked sports car. Each level has a time limit to catch up with the fleeing car, and once it's reached, a short but intense phase of ramming into it follows, until it stops — the game thus combines pure racing with an action element of collisions, where the criminal's car must be repeatedly rammed so that its bodywork falls apart and the chase ends in an arrest.

On the C64 the game offers a view from behind the car and heavy traffic that must be dodged at full speed, while the timer counts down relentlessly and forces the player to take risky passes between vehicles at the edge of what's possible, because failing to reach the suspect's car within the limit means the end of the mission and having to try it again. A distinguishing feature is the turbo button, which can briefly catapult the player forward and save an almost lost run to the scene, though its use is limited and needs to be saved for the most critical moment. The briefing at the start of each mission and the energetic music give the game a strong atmosphere of an action police series, further underlined by a short animation of getting into the car before the chase starts and a quick display of the map marking the pursuit route.

Chase H.Q. was among the successful arcade conversions to eight-bit machines, and its simple but adrenaline-fuelled concept — catch up, reach, ram — proved successful enough to spawn several sequels on other platforms that developed the same principle of short, escalating chases against the clock. On the Commodore 64 the game is praised for its fast pace and directness, thanks to which it still works today as a short, intense gaming session without the need to learn complicated rules, making it a good choice even for players who just want to try a retro game for a few minutes between other activities.

**Why play it:** If you want a short, adrenaline-filled chase without having to learn complicated rules, it works as a quick gaming session even today, ideal for a few minutes between other activities.

c64__lotus-esprit-turbo-challenge.teaser: A fast Gremlin Graphics racing hit; two-player cooperation on a single joystick.
c64__lotus-esprit-turbo-challenge.article:
**Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge** from 1990 by Gremlin Graphics was among the fastest and graphically smoothest racing games to appear on the Commodore 64. The game offers a choice between several versions of the Lotus Esprit with different performance, and offers both solo races against rivals and a cooperative two-player mode, where one player steers and the other operates the turbo and shifts gears — an unusual idea for the genre that required good coordination between the two players sharing a single joystick and keyboard, and turned an otherwise solo discipline into a team experience.

Technically the game impressed with the smooth scrolling of the track and a sense of speed that few titles managed to achieve in a rear view on the C64, and even with the years that have passed, driving feels surprisingly brisk and free of noticeable animation stutter, which was far from a given for games on this machine. The tracks lead through varied environments and contain junctions with traffic as well as short branches that force the player to quickly choose a direction, where a wrong decision can mean drifting off the ideal line, losing precious seconds, and dropping to the back of the field. The controls are sensitive to precise braking before corners, while the open feeling of speed rewards players who take risks at the edge of the car's capabilities and aren't afraid to take corners nearly flat out, even at the cost of a slight slide at the edge of the track.

Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge received a warm reception from both reviewers and players precisely for its speed and playability, and it kicked off a small series of sequels on the Commodore 64 that further developed the same concept on new tracks. It's still cited today as an example of just how far the illusion of high speed could be pushed on this computer within simple 2D graphics, without the game losing playability or clarity for both players sharing a single keyboard.

**Why play it:** Fans of fast racing will appreciate just how far the illusion of high speed could be pushed on this computer within simple 2D graphics, even with two players sharing a single keyboard.

c64__kick-off-2.teaser: The most influential football simulation of the eight-bit era; direction and button hold length control passes.
c64__kick-off-2.article:
**Kick Off 2** from 1990 by Anco Software is among the most influential football simulations of the eight-bit era, and on the Commodore 64 it offered fast, seemingly chaotic, but immensely refined gameplay. The player controls only one footballer with the ball at a time, and passes, shots, and crosses are performed with a combination of direction and how long the button is held, requiring far more feel and practice than rival games with automatic passing, where it was enough just to aim toward the next teammate and let the game handle the rest.

The physics of the ball, which bounces and rolls across the pitch independently of the players, was unusually realistic for its time and gave rise to a generation of players who practiced precise crosses and free kicks to absolute perfection, because a correctly timed and aimed shot could send the ball flying straight into the top corner, while a rushed attempt usually ended up wide of the goal. The game offers league and cup modes, squad editing, and the option to play against the computer or against a second player, which made it a popular choice at parties and tournaments among friends, where it quickly became clear who had truly practiced the controls and who was just blindly hoofing the ball forward. The graphics are austere, but the top-down view of the pitch remains clear even during fast ball exchanges and quick counterattacks, so the player always has a sense of where best to send the ball.

Kick Off 2 is still mentioned today as one of the best football games on home computers, and its control system influenced a number of later sports titles that moved from simple arcade football toward greater simulation depth. On the Commodore 64 the game remains playable even after all these years, although it requires patience while getting used to the unintuitive, but ultimately very satisfying, controls that, once mastered, offer a real sense of control over every movement of the ball on the pitch.

**Why play it:** For fans of football simulations who stick with the initially unintuitive controls, it ultimately offers a satisfying sense of real control over the ball on the pitch.

c64__winter-games.teaser: The winter sequel to Summer Games, with different precise timing for each event.
c64__winter-games.article:
**Winter Games** from 1985 by Epyx followed up on the success of Summer Games and brought the sports-Olympics concept to the Commodore 64's wintry setting.
