Players choose between events such as luge, speed skating, ski jumping, biathlon, or figure skating, and each of them has its own control scheme based on quick and precise joystick presses at just the right moment, so success in one event doesn't guarantee success in another, and a well-rounded player must be able to switch between entirely different movement patterns.

The game stands out with carefully animated athlete figures and the atmosphere of a real winter Olympics, underlined by opening ceremonies with the flags of participating countries and anthems during the results announcements, which at the time counted among the details that turned playing into a genuine experience. Some events, such as ski jumping, place emphasis on precisely timing the takeoff and holding body posture in the air, while others, like speed skating, are purely about the speed of alternating direction on the joystick and the endurance of fingers, which must keep a steady rhythm for the whole length of the race. The option for several players to take turns at one computer was a big draw for game nights with friends at the time, when they competed for the best overall placement across all events, and the final standings were often decided by just a fraction of a point.

Winter Games was among Epyx's most successful sports titles and cemented the format in which the player goes through a series of minigames connected by a shared Olympic theme, a model the studio went on to develop further in later entries of the series. On the Commodore 64 the game remains a pleasant example of what we'd now call a party sports game, and its individual events are still fun even years later thanks to simple but demanding control mechanics that reward hours of practice in each discipline.

**Why play it:** For a group of players looking for simple but demanding sports minigames tied together by a shared Olympic theme, it still holds up after years of practicing each individual event.

c64__world-games.teaser: Unusual sporting events from around the world — sumo, log rolling, tug of war.
c64__world-games.article:
**World Games** from 1986 by Epyx expanded the series of Olympic sports games with events from around the world that weren't part of the classic Olympic Games, and brought them to the Commodore 64 in a spirit similar to the earlier Summer Games and Winter Games. Players can try sumo wrestling, cliff diving into the sea, log-cutting lumberjack contests, tug of war, weightlifting, or barrel jumping, with each event having its own characteristic controls and requiring a different combination of speed, strength, and precise timing.

The game's presentation places emphasis on the cultural context of each sport, with stylized backgrounds from various countries and short animations before each event that give the game a sense of traveling around the world and set it apart from the somewhat plainer feel of the series' earlier entries, making the game feel more colorful and varied. The controls remain true to Epyx's style — quick sequences of joystick presses at just the right moment — but some events, such as sumo, add an element of direct one-on-one competition between two players, where the goal is to push the opponent out of the ring before they do the same to you. The character graphics are detailed for their time and the individual sports are easily recognizable at a glance, which also helps players who weren't familiar with a given event beforehand.

World Games was well received as a colorful mix of unconventional sports that offered players more than just a repeat of the classic Olympic events, and it became a popular choice for playing with a group. On the Commodore 64 it's among the titles that are still fun today, especially in a group, where competing for the best result in exotic events works just as well as it did decades ago, and the unusual selection of sports still makes for a refreshing change of pace even after all these years, compared to ordinary Olympic games and their established events.

**Why play it:** For playing with a group, you'll appreciate the unusual selection of exotic events, which even after all these years makes the game a refreshing change of pace compared to ordinary Olympic games and their established events.

c64__leaderboard.teaser: One of the first golf simulations with a three-stage swing instead of a single button.
c64__leaderboard.article:
**Leaderboard** from 1986 by Access Software was among the first golf simulations that tried to emulate a real golf swing instead of simply hitting the ball with a single button. The player sets the power and accuracy of the shot using a three-stage system – starting the swing motion, reaching the top of the backswing, and the moment of impact with the ball – where even a slight timing error causes a slice or a hook and sends the ball off the fairway into the rough or straight into the water, forcing the player to play the next shot from a much worse position.

On the Commodore 64, the game offers several professional eighteen-hole courses with varied terrain, water hazards, and bunkers, and the player has to pick the right club for the distance and the conditions on the green, since choosing a weaker or stronger club drastically changes the ball's trajectory and landing. Accounting for wind strength and the slope of the green added strategic depth to the game, since reading the hole correctly was often more important than the power of the shot itself, and experienced players could save strokes through smart shot planning. The sound of the club striking the ball and the crowd's applause after a good shot round out the tournament atmosphere and reward the player for a precisely executed stroke, while a botched shot is met with the crowd's quiet disappointment.

At the time, Leaderboard was considered one of the most accurate golf simulations on home computers, and its swing system influenced many later golf games, which adopted and further developed the same three-stage principle. On the Commodore 64, the game is still appreciated for its faithful handling of golf rules and can still keep players entertained by hunting for the ideal strategy on every hole, though today's players need patience with its slower pace and fewer visual effects than they're used to from newer sports titles - but anyone willing to spend a little patience will still enjoy its take on golf even after all these years.

**Why play it:** For patient golf fans who don't mind a slower pace and fewer effects than newer titles, offering an honestly crafted three-stage swing and the search for the ideal strategy on every hole.

c64__exolon.teaser: An action platformer by Raffaele Cecco; a flamethrower with unlimited ammo and grenades to use sparingly.
c64__exolon.article:
**Exolon** is an action platformer by Raffaele Cecco, released in 1987 by Hewson Consultants for the Commodore 64. Playing a mercenary named Chubby, the player fights through six planets full of alien enemies, robots, and traps, armed with a flamethrower with unlimited ammo and a limited supply of grenades that must be carefully saved for tougher opponents, locked doors, and obstacles blocking the way forward across the hostile landscape. Crates scattered around also hide additional weapons and ammo pickups, so part of the game involves systematically searching for them.

The game is a typical example of the British style of 1980s action platformers - fast, unforgiving, and built around memorizing enemy and trap placement, where a single mistake often means instant death and a return to the start of the level. Despite the C64's technical limitations, the graphics offered detailed backdrops for each planet with its own atmosphere and color palette, while smooth scrolling gave the game a sense of dynamism and real progress across enemy territory. Sound effects and music rounded out the tense atmosphere of constant danger, typical of Hewson's output as a whole.

Exolon was both a commercial and critical success for Hewson and cemented the studio's reputation as one of Europe's leading developers of action games for 8-bit machines. The game is still valued today for its balanced yet demanding design and is often mentioned alongside Cecco's other work, such as Cybernoid or Stormlord, as an example of how sophisticated British programmers could get with the C64's limited hardware to squeeze the maximum graphical and gameplay impact out of it. The game also got a sequel, Latex, and is still regularly mentioned among the best action platformers on the whole platform, mainly thanks to its unforgiving yet fair difficulty.

**Why play it:** For an unforgiving but fairly tuned action platformer by Raffaele Cecco that still ranks among the highlights of the C64 catalog and rewards patience with precise controls.

c64__sentinel.teaser: An original 3D strategy game about absorbing the landscape and facing off against the watching Sentinel.
c64__sentinel.article:
**The Sentinel** is an original strategy-puzzle game, one of the most distinctive and unconventional on the whole platform, made by British programmer Geoff Crammond and released in 1986 by Firebird for the Commodore 64. The player moves through a series of three-dimensional landscapes rendered in solid color surfaces, and the goal is to absorb the surrounding objects, convert them into energy, and use that energy to climb higher and higher, until finally taking the place of the watching Sentinel at the top of the landscape and ultimately absorbing it as well, thereby completing the level and moving on to the next, harder landscape.

At the time, the game was completely unconventional - it combined no action or reflexes at all, relying instead purely on spatial reasoning, careful forward planning of moves, and judging the field of view of enemy guardians, who turn the player back into a harmless rock upon detection and force them to start over. It placed non-trivial demands on the hardware of the time with its pseudo-3D rendering of tens of thousands of uniquely, algorithmically generated landscapes that varied in difficulty, size, and the number of objects available to absorb and convert into valuable energy. As a result, progressing through the game never looked quite the same twice, and the player had to rely on their own judgment rather than on learned patterns.

The Sentinel is still regarded today as one of the most original and influential games of the 8-bit era - it inspired later creators in their approach to spatial puzzles and procedurally generated worlds, and it received highly favorable reviews in the contemporary press for its originality. Its abstract, meditative atmosphere, underscored by sparse electronic sound, makes it a title that fundamentally differs from most of the C64's action output, and it is still sought out today precisely for its uniqueness and the unrepeatable, almost contemplative feel of playing it, something few other games on the 8-bit platform ever offered.

**Why play it:** For a meditative, entirely unhurried puzzle game with no equal on the C64 - an ideal choice for players seeking originality and atmosphere over action.

c64__skool-daze.teaser: A classic of school simulations; steal your report card before someone catches you.
c64__skool-daze.article:
**Skool Daze** is an adventure game with simulation elements, today regarded as a classic of the school-simulation and open-world game genre, made by Microsphere and released for the Commodore 64 by David Reidy and Keith Robinson in the mid-1980s, shortly after the successful and influential ZX Spectrum version. The player takes on the role of a mischievous schoolboy who has to sneak through a sprawling British school full of teachers, prefects, and classmates, steal his report card from the locked headmaster's office, and change the bad grades in it before someone catches him red-handed and sends him back to class as punishment.

The game combines free movement through the sprawling school building with simple but thoughtfully designed tasks - the player has to keep track of the class schedule, avoid the watchful eyes of individual teachers each with their own personality and weaknesses, cooperate with classmates in exchange for small favors, and handle situations using a catapult or stink bombs placed under enemies' feet. This approach to an open, socially oriented game world was completely unusual in the mid-1980s and in many ways foreshadowed later simulation-adventures with open worlds, free play, and character interaction. Every character in the school has their own daily schedule and behavior, which gives the game a surprisingly lively feel of a functioning micro-world.

Skool Daze is still regarded today as one of the most imaginative British titles of its time, strongly marked by a distinctive sense of humor and gentle satire aimed at the British school system of the day, its authorities, and its typical schoolyard characters. Even decades later, it's often cited as a pioneering game that showed a simulation of everyday life and social relationships could be just as engaging as a classic action or adventure game, and it inspired a direct sequel, Back to Skool, with an even larger game world and new characters.

**Why play it:** For its distinctive British humor and imaginative simulation of school life, which still works as a fresh alternative to the C64's usual action fare.

c64__x-out.teaser: An underwater shoot 'em up where you assemble your own submarine from modules before every mission.
c64__x-out.article:
**X-Out** is a horizontal shoot 'em up with an unusual underwater setting and a ship-building system, released for the Commodore 64 in 1990 by the German studio Rainbow Arts. The game takes place underwater, and its distinctive feature is a phase before each mission where the player assembles their own submarine from various available modules - hull, engines, armor, and weapons - and only then heads into action against enemy forces hidden in the ocean depths and its underwater bases bristling with defense turrets.

This emphasis on carefully tailoring the ship before each mission set X-Out apart from most competing space shooters and made the player think as much about equipment combinations as about the actual shooting, dodging, and recognizing individual enemies' weak points. The graphical depiction of the underwater world, with richly drawn backgrounds full of coral, wrecks, and sea creatures, together with the music, gave the game a distinctive atmosphere, noticeably different from the space themes then common among competing titles in the genre. A poorly assembled submarine could sink even an otherwise experienced player as early as the first half of the game, so it paid to carefully think through the choice of weapons and armor before heading into action.

X-Out was among the more technically and creatively ambitious products of the German scene at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s and confirmed the reputation of Rainbow Arts, already built by earlier titles like Katakis or Turrican, as a publisher with a knack for imaginative genre design and quality craftsmanship. The game is still valued today, mainly by genre fans, for its unconventional take, ship upgrade system, and musical score, even though even at the time it was one of the more demanding and less forgiving entries in the vertical and horizontal shooter genre, aimed at advanced and patient players.

**Why play it:** For fans of vertical shooters looking for an unconventional ship-upgrade system - but expect higher, less forgiving difficulty than in competing titles.

c64__xenon-2-megablast.teaser: A vertical shmup by The Bitmap Brothers with a shop for upgrading your ship between missions.
c64__xenon-2-megablast.article:
**Xenon 2: Megablast** is a vertical shoot 'em up, a sequel to the successful 1988 Xenon by the British studio The Bitmap Brothers, whose Commodore 64 conversion was published by Image Works at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s. The player pilots a combat ship that can be upgraded between missions in an in-game shop with new weapons, auxiliary modules, and engine upgrades, then progresses through a series of organically and technically themed levels full of enemies, hazards, and massive bosses at the end of each one that demand a well-considered choice of loadout.

The game became famous above all for its music - the original version featured a distinctive adaptation of the track "Megablast" by Bomb the Bass, and the Commodore 64 version also tried to reproduce this unmistakable electronic sound on the 8-bit SID chip as faithfully as possible, which was considered a remarkable technical feat at the time and was widely covered in contemporary magazines. Visually, the game benefited from the detailed artwork typical of The Bitmap Brothers, though the port to the significantly weaker C64 hardware necessarily meant some simplification compared to the 16-bit Amiga and Atari ST versions, which became the series' reference standard. Even so, the conversion retained a fast pace and clarity that kept it playable and enjoyable even on this noticeably weaker machine.

Xenon 2 is still seen today as one of the more ambitious European shooters of its era, an example of the effort to carry the audiovisual qualities of the groundbreaking 16-bit Amiga over to older, technically weaker 8-bit machines. The Commodore 64 version doesn't reach the quality of the original, but it's still among the interesting and honestly executed conversions that demonstrate just how far 8-bit hardware could still be pushed at the twilight of its life, when an experienced, seasoned team of converters set out to do it.

**Why play it:** For players curious how far the 8-bit C64 could be pushed converting an ambitious Amiga shooter - more an honest technical showcase than an experience on par with the original.

c64__1985-day-after.teaser: A modern demoscene game for the C64 with a post-apocalyptic, atmospheric story of survivors.
c64__1985-day-after.article:
**1985: The Day After** is a Commodore 64 game, a showcase of what the modern demoscene can achieve today with thirty-year-old hardware, released in 2018 by the demoscene group Genesis Project, whose output includes significant contributions from Czech creators. The game places the player in a post-apocalyptic 1985, where the world struggles with the ruins of civilization and a shortage of resources after a nuclear war, and combines slower-paced exploration of a devastated environment, simple action sequences, and strongly narrative, atmospheric storytelling about survivors in this harsh, inhospitable world.

The title is a demonstration of what the Commodore 64 is capable of more than three decades after its market launch - it uses advanced graphics and music techniques that demoscene creators gradually developed and refined on the platform over that time, offering a visually and aurally much richer experience than was typical for the hardware in its original 1980s era full of technical limitations. The atmosphere of destruction, silence, and hopelessness is underpinned by quality, carefully composed music and thoughtfully constructed locations within the devastated, silent world. The emphasis on story and atmosphere rather than reflex-based action is characteristic of the modern Commodore 64 homebrew scene, and Genesis Project is among its most notable creators in this respect.

1985: The Day After is among the most acclaimed modern homebrew titles for the Commodore 64 and is proof that the platform still has an active, creative community today, in which the Czech demoscene, gathered around groups like Genesis Project, plays a significant role. The game drew attention from the retro community worldwide and is often cited as an example of how modern demoscene know-how and decades of accumulated technical tricks can push the capabilities of a thirty-year-old home computer far beyond its original purpose.

**Why play it:** As a showcase of what modern demoscene know-how can squeeze out of thirty-year-old hardware - an ideal choice for players interested in today's C64 homebrew scene.

amiga__birds-of-prey.teaser: An Electronic Arts flight simulator more accessible than the competition, without a flood of switches.
amiga__birds-of-prey.article:
**Birds of Prey** is a combat flight simulator from Electronic Arts that put players in the cockpits of modern fighters like the F-15, F-16, F-14, MiG-29, or Su-27, offering a series of fictional conflicts scattered across various corners of the world, from desert skirmishes to Cold War tension over northern Europe. Compared to the competition, the game aimed to be more accessible - the controls weren't as cluttered with switches and checklists as in rival simulators, yet it still offered decent depth in weapon selection, tactics, and various mission types, from patrol flights to complex strikes on ground targets and bomber escort.

On the Amiga, the game ran in vector 3D graphics with filled polygons, where the terrain, sky, and aircraft models looked simple but, thanks to smooth rendering, managed to convey a convincing sense of speed and altitude. The Commodore hardware naturally couldn't compete with the powerful PC rigs the game also shipped for, so the developers had to limit scenery detail and the number of rendered objects to keep the frame rate playable even during fast maneuvers and close-range dogfights. The sound design - engine roar, radar warning tones, and menu music - rounded out the atmosphere of modern aerial combat and helped players stay oriented amid the hectic moments of a firefight.

In period reviews, Birds of Prey was praised especially for the sheer scope of content - the number of aircraft, missions, and game modes - which made it one of the more comprehensive offerings in the genre on the Amiga. Many players saw it as a more accessible alternative to the more elaborate but demanding Falcon-type series, and that balance earned it popularity even among less experienced pilots. Today the game stands as a typical representative of the early generation of 3D flight simulators, when studios were still searching for the balance between realism and playability on limited home hardware, and as such it deserves a place in the history of the genre on the Amiga.

**Why play it:** For players who want a more accessible alternative to demanding series like Falcon — a comprehensive flight simulator with a wide range of aircraft and missions, suitable even for less experienced pilots.

amiga__knights-of-sky.teaser: A MicroProse flight simulator set in the skies of World War I; a career from rookie to ace.
amiga__knights-of-sky.article:
**Knights of the Sky** is a flight simulator from MicroProse set in the aerial battles of the First World War, where the player becomes a fighter pilot for one of the warring sides and gradually builds a career from an inexperienced rookie to a respected ace. The game combined a career mode with gradual promotions, medals, and a shifting reputation with the enemy, alongside period biplanes and triplanes including famous machines like the Fokker or Sopwith Camel, each with its own flight characteristics, climb rate, and maneuverability that had to be learned and used to advantage.

The Amiga version carried a flight model that was fairly sophisticated for its time, reflecting the slower, more fragile two-winged fabric aircraft - a different dynamic from modern jet simulators, where split seconds and high speed decide everything. The graphics used simple but legible 3D wireframe and filled models, while the landscape below the plane, the clouds, and the smoke from downed aircraft lent the battles above the front line an appropriate sense of trench-war atmosphere. The music and sounds of machine-gun fire, cracking wing timber, and engine drone heightened the tension typical of aerial duels of the time, where survival often hinges on a split-second decision.

The game continued MicroProse's beloved tradition in the genre of historical simulators and was praised for combining historical authenticity with an addictive career system that made players want to survive one more flight and climb further in rank and reputation. In the context of the Amiga, it was one of the few simulators focused specifically on the First World War, and even today it draws retro-game collectors with its unusual, slower, more tactical take on aerial combat compared to more modern jet-focused series that emphasize speed and missile armament. This unique perspective on a historically distant chapter of aviation is exactly what makes the game a valuable reminder of how differently people flew and fought before aircraft had radios, radar, and gun sights.

**Why play it:** For fans of aviation history, it offers a rare look at the First World War instead of the more common World War II or jet-age settings — a slower, more tactical take on aerial combat with an addictive career system.

amiga__wings.teaser: A Cinemaware flight adventure combining dogfights with cinematic cutscenes and personal drama.
amiga__wings.article:
**Wings** is a flight action-adventure from Cinemaware that follows the career of a British pilot from training through the battles of the First World War to his return home, blending direct aerial combat with cinematic cutscenes, dialogue, and decisions that affect the course of the story and relationships with the rest of the squadron's crew. This emphasis on narrative and atmosphere, typical of Cinemaware, set Wings apart from purely simulation-focused competitors - the player experiences not just combat in the air, but also the personal drama of a soldier caught up in war, including the loss of comrades and the weight of the decisions he carries.

The game was made primarily for the Amiga and fully exploited its graphical and sound capabilities - cinematic transitions, detailed character portraits, and atmospheric music that, combined with dynamic flight sequences, created the impression of an interactive war film. The flight sections themselves offered a solid, if not extremely complex, flight model for biplanes, complemented by a system of injuries, aircraft damage, and gradually building an ace's reputation, while between missions the player walks the base, talks with colleagues, and follows the development of his own story. Alternating action with storytelling kept the game's pace fresh and distinct from the purely simulation-focused titles common at the time.

Wings received very positive reviews on the Amiga and is still considered one of the high points of Cinemaware's catalog - an example of how the flight simulator genre can be enriched with cinematic storytelling and emotional weight. Its influence can be seen in later games that tried to combine action gameplay with narrative, and even after all these years Wings offers players a unique experience that goes beyond merely racking up kills, remaining one of the most memorable games on the Amiga. The combination of sensitively told story, striking music, and solid flight sections makes it a title remembered longer than many technically more ambitious but emotionally colder simulators of the same era.

**Why play it:** For players who want more from a flight simulator than just racking up kills — cinematic storytelling, emotional weight, and music that make it one of the most memorable titles in Cinemaware's catalog.

amiga__silent-service-ii.teaser: A sequel to MicroProse's submarine simulator with a more elaborate sailing and battle model.
amiga__silent-service-ii.article:
**Silent Service II** is a sequel to the popular submarine simulator from MicroProse, putting the player in command of an American submarine operating in the Pacific during the Second World War. Compared to the first installment, it brought a more advanced sailing model, a more elaborate torpedo-attack system, crew management, and convoy tracking, and it expanded the number of missions and historical scenarios in which the player must contend with Japanese anti-submarine defenses and patrol ships hunting for enemy submarines.

The Amiga version offered improved 3D graphics for the periscope and map views, letting players track the movement of enemy ships and plan an attack based on speed, heading, and depth. The game's tension rested on patient waiting, silently closing in on the target, and then delivering a torpedo strike, where a wrong estimate could lead to a retaliatory depth-charge bombardment and hull damage that had to be repaired underway. Sonar sound effects, the hull creaking under water pressure, and crew reports rounded out the claustrophobic atmosphere of combat beneath the waves, where every decision is a matter of the whole ship's survival.

The game was praised for the depth of its simulation and the authenticity of its period campaigns, which made it one of the most respected submarine-warfare simulators on the Amiga. For players interested in tactics and history, it offered long-lasting play through a campaign with many patrols, and even with the years it remains a valued example of a genre that, unlike fast action simulators, was built above all on patience, observation, and a carefully considered tactic of gradually closing on the target. For many players, Silent Service II represented the counterpart to the hectic flight and helicopter simulators, where cold, systematic reasoning by a commander was valued over reflexes. It's precisely this slower, more contemplative rhythm that still makes the game a sought-after title today among fans of historical war simulators who appreciate a realistic take on submarine warfare in the Pacific.

**Why play it:** For patient tacticians who prefer observation and a carefully considered approach to the target over reflexes — one of the most respected submarine simulators on the Amiga.

amiga__gunship-2000.teaser: A MicroProse helicopter simulator in AGA graphics; a demanding title for the Amiga 1200.
amiga__gunship-2000.article:
**Gunship 2000** is the sequel to the successful helicopter simulator Gunship, and it arrived on the Amiga in a version using the AGA graphics chipset, making it one of the more technically demanding titles for the Amiga 1200. The game puts the player in command of an attack helicopter, primarily the AH-64 Apache, in fictional and historically inspired conflicts, with an emphasis on tactical mission planning, weapon selection, and cooperation with other units on the battlefield, including coordination with ground forces and other helicopters in a flight.

Compared to the previous installment, Gunship 2000 expanded the range of controllable aircraft, refined the helicopter flight model and damage system, and added more detailed maps with varied terrain, where using cover and low-flying tactics to evade anti-aircraft defenses was essential. The graphics on the AGA Amiga could display more detailed scenery and explosion effects than older simulators, though the resolution and frame rate still reflected the limitations of a home computer compared to the powerful PC rigs of the time. The sound design, onboard computer callouts, and rotor noise added to the tension of low-level reconnaissance flights over enemy territory, where the player has to rely on using terrain for cover.

The game continued MicroProse's tradition of thoroughly crafted military simulators and was praised for combining tactical depth with accessibility for a wider audience. On the Amiga, it was one of the late and most ambitious simulators, showing how far the platform could push the complexity of military simulations in the AGA era, and it remains today an interesting showcase of early-1990s helicopter combat, especially valued by fans of tactical simulators. For owners of more powerful Amigas, it was one more proof that the platform, even at this stage of its life cycle, could still deliver ambitious, graphically demanding military simulations comparable to contemporary PC output.

**Why play it:** For fans of MicroProse's military simulators, it offers tactical depth combined with accessibility and is one of the most ambitious helicopter simulations of the AGA era on the Amiga.

amiga__epic.teaser: A futuristic flight simulator from Digital Image Design about fighting off an alien invasion.
amiga__epic.article:
**Epic** is a futuristic flight simulator from Digital Image Design, published by Ocean Software, that combines fast-paced combat between piloted craft with a storyline set in the distant future amid an alien invasion. The player takes on the role of a pilot fighting against a hostile race, progressing through a series of missions in which, besides shooting down enemy aircraft, they also handle defending ground targets, escort duties, and reconnaissance flights over unknown territory.

On the Amiga, the game benefited from a smooth 3D engine with filled polygons that, compared to Digital Image Design's earlier titles, offered smoother animation and more detailed models of aircraft and scenery, with the speed and agility of the craft higher than in traditional military simulators. The combination of brisk action with a military sci-fi theme and cinematically staged cutscenes between missions gave the game an atmosphere close to that of space action films, supported by dramatic music and explosion and laser-fire sound effects. The controls were somewhat more accessible than in the studio's purely simulation-focused titles, which opened the game up to a wider audience that didn't want to spend a long time learning complicated cockpits.

At launch, Epic was praised for its graphical quality and pace, which set it apart from slower, more technically demanding simulators like TFX from the same studio. Within the Amiga's catalog, it stands as an example of how Digital Image Design managed to adapt its technological base to a more action-oriented, less simulation-focused audience, and it's still remembered today as one of the visually most striking flight titles of its time on the platform, recalled even by players with no interest in pure simulators. Its sci-fi framing and faster pace made it a good entry point into the genre for those wanting to move from World War II or Cold War aircraft toward more fantastical, action-packed scenarios.

**Why play it:** For players who want a faster, sci-fi-flavored entry point into flight simulators without needing to master the full realism of titles like TFX — visually one of the most striking flight games of its time on the Amiga.

amiga__fighter-bomber.teaser: Multirole bomber simulator from Digital Integration; bombing runs and dogfights.
amiga__fighter-bomber.article:
**Fighter Bomber** is a flight simulator from Digital Integration, a studio that specialized in modern combat aircraft simulations during the second half of the 1980s. The game puts the player in the cockpit of a multirole bomber and offers a series of missions focused on attacking both ground and aerial targets, requiring the player to combine precise bombing with defense against enemy fighters and anti-aircraft defenses, where weapon selection and approach tactics significantly affect mission success.

On the Amiga, the simulator used simple but functional vector 3D graphics typical of Digital Integration's output at the time, with cockpit instruments, radar, and the target-lock system rendered with an emphasis on clarity even on older hardware. The flight model was simpler compared to later simulators, but still required the player's attention to speed, altitude, and fuel, especially during longer raids over enemy territory full of anti-aircraft batteries. The music was minimalist, but the sounds of anti-aircraft fire, explosions, and onboard system announcements did a good job of underscoring the tension of each mission.

Fighter Bomber fit into the broader line of military simulators through which Digital Integration made its name on the Amiga and other eight-bit and sixteen-bit platforms, alongside titles like F-16 Combat Pilot. Although it wasn't among the most complex simulators of its time, it was valued for its accessibility and fast mission pace, which didn't require hours of studying the manual. Today it's a typical example of early flight simulators from the late 1980s, when the emphasis was placed more on action and immediate playability than on the detailed realism of later series. For collectors and genre fans, it remains a pleasant reminder of a time when even a modest studio could establish its own line of military flight simulators.

**Why play it:** For fans of early flight simulators, it offers accessible, fast-paced missions without hours of manual-reading — a pleasant reminder of a time when action came before the detailed realism of later series.

amiga__f-16-combat-pilot.teaser: F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter simulator in a fictional Cold War conflict.
amiga__f-16-combat-pilot.article:
**F-16 Combat Pilot** is a flight simulator from Digital Integration that focuses on one of the best-known modern multirole aircraft, the F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet, offering the player a series of missions ranging from patrol flights and bomber escort to direct combat against Soviet aircraft in a hypothetical Cold War conflict over the Central European front. The game was a typical representative of the genre, which tried to bring players closer to the controls of a modern combat aircraft without the extreme technical complexity of later professional simulators.

The Amiga version depicted the world using vector 3D graphics with simply filled surfaces, where terrain, sky, and enemy aircraft models were rendered economically but functionally, with an eye to the performance of the available hardware. The cockpit with its instruments, radar, and weapon-targeting system formed the core of the gameplay, and the player had to keep track of fuel, altitude, and damage during longer missions over enemy territory guarded by missile batteries. Engine sound effects, gunfire, and radar warning tones lent the game suitable tension even without an extensive musical score, which was only minimally common for similar titles at the time.

At release, F-16 Combat Pilot was ranked among the solid, accessible simulators that expanded the range of military flight games on the Amiga alongside MicroProse's output. Although it couldn't technically compete with later, more elaborate simulators, it played a role in popularizing the genre on the platform and is still remembered today as one of the first accessible F-16 simulators for home computers, one that opened the genre to a wider circle of players. Compared to later competition, its take on flight and combat is more modest, but that's precisely what makes it a good introduction for players who want to understand how flight simulators on the Amiga evolved in their early years.

**Why play it:** For players who want to understand the early steps of flight simulators on the Amiga, it's a more modest but accessible introduction to the genre of F-16 simulations, one that helped open the subject to a wider audience.

amiga__tfx.teaser: Demanding AGA simulator of fictional prototype fighters from Digital Image Design.
amiga__tfx.article:
**TFX** (Tactical Fighter Experiment) is a flight simulator from Digital Image Design, published by Ocean Software, which on the Amiga was released in a version requiring the AGA graphics chipset and was among the most technically demanding titles on the platform in the early 1990s. The game offered the piloting of three fictional but realistically conceived next-generation combat aircraft prototypes and put the player through missions of varying difficulty, from reconnaissance to complex bombing and fighter operations within a broader war campaign.

The Amiga version benefited from Digital Image Design's advanced 3D engine, which was able to render more detailed terrain, shading, and weather effects on the AGA Amiga 1200 than older simulators on the same platform, though this demanded powerful hardware and thus put the game out of reach for owners of base Amiga 500 models. The flight model was elaborate and emphasized realistic aircraft behavior, fuel and weapons management, and tactical mission planning, which set the simulator apart from the more action-oriented titles of the same studio, such as Epic, and placed it closer to the professional simulators available at the time only on PC.

TFX was valued especially among simulation enthusiasts for its technical ambition and depth, even though its hardware demands limited the number of players who could enjoy it in its full glory on the Amiga. Within the Amiga catalog, it represents one of the last great flight simulators before the platform's decline, and it's still remembered today as an example of just how far AGA Amiga graphics could be pushed in the hands of an experienced studio with years of simulator expertise. For today's players and collectors, TFX is an interesting testament to how the Amiga, even at the twilight of its commercial era, tried to keep pace with the rapidly growing demands of the military flight simulation genre, even though it was already clear at the time that the PC platform would soon definitively take the lead in this field.

**Why play it:** For simulation enthusiasts with a powerful Amiga, it offers one of the platform's last and most technically ambitious flight simulators — a showcase of just how far AGA graphics could be pushed shortly before the Amiga's decline.

pc-dos__command-and-conquer.teaser: The game that, alongside Warcraft, defined the RTS genre; GDI against Brotherhood of Nod over Tiberium.
pc-dos__command-and-conquer.article:
**Command & Conquer** from 1995 by Westwood Studios stood at the birth of the real-time strategy genre in the form players know it today, and together with Warcraft it defined the rules of the genre for years to come. The player sides with one of two factions — the military organization GDI or the mysterious Brotherhood of Nod — and across a series of interconnected missions builds bases, mines the mysterious mineral Tiberium, and commands units in a battle for control of a world plagued by this alien substance. Both factions' campaigns offer a different perspective on the same war, which in 1995 was an unusual and highly praised approach to storytelling in a strategy game, and the missions also shift settings from urban areas through forests to desert regions affected by Tiberium.

The gameplay is built on a simple but functional system of base-building, resource mining, and mouse-driven unit control, complemented by a clear interface that became a model for entire generations of RTS titles. Units of both factions had a distinct character — GDI relied on heavy machinery and air strikes, Nod on speed, sabotage, and stealth — so playing as either side felt genuinely different. Live-action cutscenes were inserted between missions, with characters addressing the player directly from the screen — at the time a complete novelty that gave the game a cinematic atmosphere and helped tell a gripping story about a global conflict. The music was composed by Frank Klepacki, whose energetic electronic tracks are among the most recognizable in gaming music history and still evoke the atmosphere of nineties war strategy games.

Command & Conquer became a commercial and critical hit and launched one of the most successful game series of the nineties and 2000s. Its influence on the RTS genre is fundamental — it established conventions later adopted by dozens of other games, and multiplayer over network or modem showed just how much fun it could be to measure yourself against a live opponent. The game later also received a remastered version that made the original experience accessible to modern players, and it remains a mandatory stop for anyone interested in the history of strategy games.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the history of strategy games — the title that established the RTS genre's conventions and, with network multiplayer, showed how much fun it is to measure yourself against a live opponent.

pc-dos__command-and-conquer-red-alert.teaser: Alternate history where Einstein removed Hitler and cleared the path for a Soviet superpower.
pc-dos__command-and-conquer-red-alert.article:
**Command & Conquer: Red Alert** from 1996 is an alternate-history spin-off from Westwood Studios that, instead of the Tiberium War, tells the story of a great conflict between the Allies and the Soviet Union in a far more dangerous twentieth century. According to the opening story, Albert Einstein decided to erase Hitler from history by traveling back in time, but in doing so unintentionally allowed the Soviet Union to grow into an enormous military superpower — and the player thus finds themselves in the middle of a war where Tesla towers, heavy tanks, and battleships fire at each other instead of the ordinary weapons of the Second World War.

Gameplay-wise it builds on the first Command & Conquer but adds a range of new units and structures — from spies and trained dogs that reveal enemy cloaking to submarines and battleships in naval missions — and, in many respects, a more balanced and faster pace of play, which earned it a reputation as one of the best multiplayer RTS titles of its time. The Allied and Soviet campaigns again combine classic missions with live-action FMV cutscenes, this time even more self-aware and full of exaggeration — the game is conscious of its own absurdity and plays with it, whether it's generals in uniform or dramatic speeches from Soviet commanders. The music was again composed by Frank Klepacki, whose track Hell March became one of the most iconic melodies in the history of strategy games and still appears at game-music concerts today.

Red Alert was received very warmly and in many respects surpassed its predecessor in popularity, especially thanks to its balanced and addictive multiplayer over network and modem. It founded its own long-running sub-series, kept alive for many years after release through expansion packs and sequels, and is still remembered today as one of the most entertaining strategy games of the nineties — a game that managed to be both tense and funny at once without losing its edge in combat balance.

**Why play it:** For lovers of balanced, addictive multiplayer and a strategy game that manages to be tense and funny at the same time — one of the most entertaining RTS titles of the nineties.

pc-dos__dune-ii-building-of-dynasty.teaser: The game that essentially invented the RTS genre; three houses fight over spice on Arrakis.
pc-dos__dune-ii-building-of-dynasty.article:
**Dune II: The Building of a Dynasty** from 1992 is the game with which Westwood Studios essentially defined the real-time strategy genre as we understand it today — base-building, resource mining, research, and direct real-time unit control were first combined by this very title, inspired by Frank Herbert's Dune universe. The player picks one of three noble houses — Atreides, Harkonnen, or Ordos — and on the desert planet Arrakis fights for control of deposits of the rare spice, the key resource of the entire universe, which the imperial court also longs to obtain in the background of the story.

The core of the game consists of gathering spice with harvester vehicles protected from giant sandworms, building a base with limited space, and gradually unlocking more advanced units and technologies through research buildings. Each house has its own set of units and special abilities — the Atreides rely on infantry and reconnaissance, the Harkonnen on brute military force, the Ordos on speed and sabotage — which gives the game a certain tactical variety despite the still-simple mouse controls of the time, which lacked more advanced features like group orders. The graphics and sound were of very high quality for their time, and the atmosphere of the parched, dangerous planet was supported by austere but functional music as well as the sounds of hissing sand and the deep rumble of an approaching worm.

Dune II became a direct inspiration for both Warcraft and Command & Conquer and is generally recognized as the game that established the RTS genre as such — earlier titles contained similar elements, but this was the first to combine all the key elements into a single coherent form, which the entire genre then adopted. Even more than three decades later, Dune II is valuable as a historical milestone, though its pace and controls are naturally slower and less comfortable than in later strategy games, and players used to more modern RTS titles will need to lower their expectations of smoothness.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the roots of the RTS genre who's willing to lower their expectations of smoothness and controls — Dune II is a historical milestone from which both Warcraft and Command & Conquer descend.

pc-dos__warcraft-orcs-and-humans.teaser: Blizzard's debut, which brought Dune II's model to the fantasy world of Azeroth; humans versus orcs.
pc-dos__warcraft-orcs-and-humans.article:
**Warcraft: Orcs & Humans** from 1994 was the first title from what was then a still little-known studio, Blizzard Entertainment, and opened one of the most successful fantasy series in video game history. The game clearly builds on the model set two years earlier by Dune II, but transplants it into the fantasy world of Azeroth, where the human kingdom of Stormwind must face an invasion of bloodthirsty orcs arriving from another world through a portal.

The player chooses one of two campaigns — human or orc — and across a series of missions builds bases, mines gold and lumber, trains units from foot soldiers to mages and orcish shamans, and commands battles in real time. Between missions, the game was accompanied by illustrated screens with dialogue that gradually revealed the story from the chosen side's perspective and gave the conflict a clearer motivation than mere territorial conquest. Compared to Dune II, the game placed a much stronger emphasis on units with special abilities and magic, such as healing priests or shamans' fire spells, foreshadowing the direction other Blizzard strategy games would later take. Visually and audibly it was an engaging, colorful production with a strong dark-fantasy atmosphere, supported by atmospheric music and unit voices reacting to orders, though technically the game was still limited by a slower engine, minor shortcomings in unit control, and the absence of multiplayer over the internet — players could only face each other over a local network or modem.

Warcraft: Orcs & Humans was received as a promising debut and a solid competitor to Dune II and Command & Conquer, even though it was later overshadowed in fame by the far more successful Warcraft II. For the series and the entire Blizzard studio, it was a key first step that laid the foundations of the Warcraft world, its factions, and its visual style, opening the way to its later enormous success, both in the strategy genre and later in the MMO genre, where it became one of the most influential game worlds of all.

**Why play it:** For Warcraft fans curious where it all began — a solid, if now surpassed, debut that laid the foundations of the world, factions, and visual style of a later gaming legend.

pc-dos__wing-commander-ii-vengeance-of-k.teaser: Sequel to Origin's space simulation; pilot Blair faces treason charges amid the war.
pc-dos__wing-commander-ii-vengeance-of-k.article:
**Wing Commander II: Vengeance of the Kilrathi** from 1991 by Origin Systems continues the first installment's space combat simulation and picks up the story of pilot Christopher Blair, who, following the events of the previous game, faces charges of treason and must once again earn the trust of human command amid the ongoing war with the Kilrathi race. The game combines action-packed aerial dogfights in space with a fairly branching story, where the outcome of individual missions influences which missions and twists the player experiences next, and a failed mission can even lead to a permanently different, worse-off war situation.

Gameplay-wise, it's a refined version of the first Wing Commander — better graphics, smoother combat, a wider selection of fighter and bomber craft and weapon systems, and a more elaborate system of conversations between missions aboard the mothership, where the player talks with fellow pilots and superiors and watches how the personal relationships between characters gradually evolve. The game also offered the option to eject from a damaged fighter and wait for rescue, adding another layer of tension to individual missions. It was precisely these between-mission sequences that gave the game an unusually strong sense of connection to its characters for its time and strengthened the emotional impact of the story, whether it involved the loss of a comrade or tense moments before a decisive battle. The music and sound effects supported the tension of the space dogfights well, which were among the technically most demanding scenes that DOS computers with sound card support could display and play back at the time.

Wing Commander II was received by critics and players as a significant improvement over the already successful first installment and cemented the series' position as the flagship of the space simulator genre. Its emphasis on story, characters, and the consequences of player decisions influenced later installments of the series as well as the competition, and it's still remembered today as one of the peaks of Origin Systems' early era and as a stepping stone toward the even more cinematic sequels.

**Why play it:** For fans of space simulators who appreciate a strong emphasis on story, characters, and the consequences of their own decisions — one of the peaks of Origin Systems' early era.

pc-dos__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tige.teaser: Space simulation with live-action full-motion video cutscenes; Mark Hamill as pilot Blair.
pc-dos__wing-commander-iii-heart-of-tige.article:
**Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger** from 1994 by Origin Systems took the space simulator series a big step further through its extensive use of live-action full-motion video cutscenes that linked the individual missions into a cohesive, cinematically told story. The lead role of pilot Christopher Blair was played by Mark Hamill, best known as Luke Skywalker from Star Wars, which was an unusual and heavily promoted move toward film production for the gaming industry of the time; other roles featured additional experienced actors who lent the scenes a credibility that games of the era rarely offered.

The game continues the raw, more serious narrative of the ongoing war with the Kilrathi and offers a branching story in which the player's choices and performance in individual missions influence which direction the plot takes and how the conflict ends - the game even allowed the story to be completed with the war lost, an unusually bold approach for its time. The space combat itself remains true to the previous entries - fast, action-packed dogfights between starships with an emphasis on managing energy, weapons and formations - but visually and technically it represented a major leap thanks to full use of CD-ROM media for video and sound, plus an improved 3D engine for the combat itself. Production was costly by the standards of the time, and it showed in every detail, from costumes to set design, and the game also demanded a more powerful computer than players had been used to until then.

Wing Commander III is often remembered as one of the high points of the so-called interactive movie era of computer games in the mid-1990s, when studios experimented with live actors and high production budgets. Even years later, the game remains an interesting example of where game storytelling could go with the arrival of CD-ROM, and for fans of the series it remains one of the most striking and ambitious entries in the entire franchise.

**Why play it:** For players curious about the era of interactive film with live actors and high production budgets — one of the most ambitious and striking entries in the entire Wing Commander series.

pc-dos__wing-commander-armada.teaser: Strategic spin-off from Origin; a turn-based fleet map instead of the series' linear campaign.
pc-dos__wing-commander-armada.article:
**Wing Commander Armada** from 1994 is a spin-off from Origin Systems' main series that, instead of a linear story-driven campaign, focuses on a multiplayer, strategy-oriented take on space battles between Humans and the Kilrathi. The game combines a turn-based strategic map, on which players deploy and move fleets, with action-based ship combat in the style of the classic Wing Commander games, triggered whenever units clash on the map.

This hybrid approach was unusual at the time of release - the player has to handle both tactical decision-making at the level of the entire war, deciding where to concentrate forces and how to defend key systems, and the space combat itself in real time, switching from the fleet commander's view down into the cockpit of a specific fighter. The game supported two-player play against each other over modem or serial cable, which in 1994 was the main reason many fans of the series bought the title - the chance to face a live opponent was still rare at the time, and Armada was among the first titles in the brand to deliberately bet on it. Besides human players, it was also possible to play against a computer-controlled opponent, so the game could also serve as a standalone tactical challenge. The graphics and combat controls were based on the previous entries in the series, so players used to Wing Commander II and III quickly found their bearings in combat, even though the map interface itself was rather plain and more functional than elaborate.

Wing Commander Armada was received as an interesting, if smaller and less ambitious, side product of the main series, aimed primarily at fans who wanted to try multiplayer combat without waiting for a full-fledged sequel with a big story. Today it is mainly remembered as a curiosity showing how, in the mid-1990s, studios experimented with combining strategy and action genres within a single established brand, before similar hybrid concepts became more common in the genre.

**Why play it:** More for series fans craving fast multiplayer combat without a big story than for newcomers — an interesting curiosity that combines strategy with action within an established brand.

pc-dos__silent-service.teaser: One of the first credible submarine simulations; the foundation of the entire war game genre.
pc-dos__silent-service.article:
**Silent Service** is one of the first truly credible submarine simulators on PC, and together with other MicroProse titles from the mid-1980s it laid the foundations of the entire war simulation genre for home computers. The player commands an American submarine in the Pacific during World War II and must handle planning a voyage on the strategic map, searching for Japanese convoys, closing in on the target, and finally the torpedo attack itself using the periscope or sonar. The commander's career progresses from simpler patrols to more demanding missions, where both the number of enemy vessels and their ability to detect the player increase.

At the core of the game is careful work with angle on the bow, speed and distance to the target - a successful torpedo hit requires a genuine understanding of attack geometry, not just pulling the trigger. This is followed by the risk of a counterattack from escort vessels, when the submarine must dive to a safe depth, cut engine power, and wait out a wave of depth charges. The graphics are austere by today's standards but readable for their time, and the sonar and explosion sounds build tension typical of underwater combat well, even though DOS hardware at the time offered only limited sound and graphics capabilities. The game also rewards patience and planning more than quick reflexes, which set it apart from the more action-oriented titles of its era.

In the mid-1980s the game was praised precisely for a depth and authenticity that could not be found in any other home title at the time, and it became a model for later submarine simulators, including its own sequel. It also influenced how other developers approached modeling torpedo attacks and convoy behavior. Today, Silent Service is interesting mainly as a historical milestone of the genre - the pace is slow and the controls archaic, but the principle of tactically hunting convoys still works, and for players willing to accept the pace of the era it offers an authentic taste of underwater warfare that few other games of the time could match.

**Why play it:** For players willing to accept a slow pace and archaic controls in exchange for an authentic taste of tactical convoy hunting that no other home title offered in the mid-1980s.

pc-dos__silent-service-ii.teaser: Sequel with a more detailed 3D view of the submarine's deck, bridge and periscope.
pc-dos__silent-service-ii.article:
**Silent Service II** is a direct sequel to the successful submarine simulator that uses the improved graphics and sound of the late 1980s to make the action in the depths of the Pacific feel more believable than in the first game. The player again commands an American Gato- or Balao-class submarine against Japanese convoys and warships, but now has access to a more detailed 3D rendering of the deck, bridge and periscope, as well as a more elaborate damage model and submarine handling. There is also now the option to view your own submarine from an external perspective, which helps better judge its position relative to the surface and the enemy.

Mechanically, the game expands the original concept with a choice between historical missions and a freer campaign, while retaining the emphasis on tactical attack planning - calculating angle on the bow, target speed and distance remains key to the effective use of torpedoes. It also adds improved artificial intelligence for escort vessels, making it harder to escape after a successful attack, so the player has to think through not just the hit itself but also the escape route and behavior during a depth-charge counterattack. The sound effects of engines, sonar and explosions round out the tense, anticipatory atmosphere typical of the whole genre, and together with a more elaborate weather model they also affect how well a convoy can be seen through the periscope.

Compared to its predecessor, Silent Service II feels like a more mature and accessible title that retained its respect for authenticity while easing navigation thanks to better overview screens and a clearer interface. In its contemporary context it held up as a worthy sequel to one of the genre's foundational simulators and broadened the circle of players willing to take on more elaborate underwater tactics. To this day, it is valued by collectors of DOS war games as a more balanced and visually friendlier variant of the same game philosophy already offered by the first title, just with a higher degree of comfort and a better feel to the controls.

**Why play it:** For those who want the same authenticity as the first game but with a clearer interface and more comfortable controls — a more balanced and visually friendlier variant of the same underwater tactics.

pc-dos__aces-of-deep.teaser: The pinnacle of DOS submarine simulators; you command a U-boat against Allied convoys.
pc-dos__aces-of-deep.article:
**Aces of the Deep** is one of the pinnacles of the submarine simulator genre on DOS, putting the player in the role of the commander of a German U-boat during World War II carrying out patrols in the Atlantic against Allied convoys. Compared to earlier titles, it offers a substantially more detailed model of the submarine, weather and convoy behavior, so every voyage takes place in a differently configured and less predictable environment. The player also has to monitor the state of their own crew and equipment, since damage from a counterattack affects how long the submarine can stay on patrol.

The game combines a strategic map, on which patrols are planned and fuel and torpedo consumption tracked, with an elaborate combat mode in which the player controls diving, sonar, the periscope and even fire from the deck gun. The career mode lets the player follow the commander's progress from the start of the war into later phases, when Allied countermeasures improve significantly and survival becomes much harder - the game thus does a good job simulating the real course of the Battle of the Atlantic, from the successful early years of the German U-boats to their later heavy losses. The sound design, with engine noise, sonar pings and tense silence while evading depth charges, was among the best DOS simulators offered at the time of release, and together with the fairly detailed 3D depiction of the deck, bridge and torpedo tubes it creates a strongly evocative atmosphere of long hours spent below the surface waiting for the right moment to attack.

Aces of the Deep was received after its release as one of the most authentic war simulators of its generation, and for a long time served as a reference point for later submarine games that tried to offer a similar degree of simulation. Even years later, thanks to the depth of its systems and its atmosphere, it remains a title that still holds up as one of the best examples of what the genre achieved at the end of the DOS era, and for fans of submarine war games it remains a mandatory stop.

**Why play it:** For fans of submarine war games seeking maximum system depth and atmosphere — one of the best examples of what the genre achieved at the end of the DOS era.

pc-dos__harpoon.teaser: Extensive naval warfare simulation based on Larry Bond's board game; you command an entire fleet.
pc-dos__harpoon.article:
**Harpoon** is an extensive simulation of modern naval warfare, based on the professional board wargame of the same name designed by Larry Bond. Unlike submarine simulators focused on a single ship, Harpoon puts an entire fleet of ships, submarines and aircraft into the player's hands and lets them run large-scale Cold War weapons operations - from patrol frigates to guided missiles and anti-submarine helicopters. The scenarios cover various geographic theaters and various hostile factions, so the player gradually gets to know the full breadth of possible modern conflicts at sea.

The game works with a semi-professional model of weapon systems, sensors and tactics that was unusually detailed at the time of release even for enthusiasts of military simulators, let alone for casual players. The user plans the movement of units on the tactical map, sets rules of engagement, and has to handle combat at long range, where the opponent often shows up first only as a signal on radar before being visible physically, and a wrong decision about firing can mean the loss of an expensive ship within moments. This abstraction makes Harpoon more of a wargame with military precision than an action simulation, which was appreciated especially by players interested in the Cold War and modern naval strategy, even though it demanded patience and a willingness to study extensive documentation from them.

Harpoon earned a reputation after release as one of the most authentic computer treatments of modern naval warfare and spawned a whole series of expansions and sequels that further developed the system. For today's player it is demanding due to its complexity and DOS text interface, but as a historical record of what professional wargaming looked like when transferred to a home computer, it still carries weight and is often mentioned as one of the most ambitious projects of its kind, as well as evidence of how close computer and tabletop wargaming could be to each other at the end of the 1980s.

**Why play it:** For patient players interested in professional wargaming who aren't put off by the DOS text interface — one of the most ambitious transfers of modern naval warfare to the computer.

pc-dos__red-storm-rising.teaser: Based on the novel by Clancy and Bond; you command a nuclear submarine against the Soviet fleet in the Atlantic.
pc-dos__red-storm-rising.article:
**Red Storm Rising** is based on the novel of the same name by Tom Clancy and Larry Bond and brings the player into a fictional third world conflict, in which they command an American Los Angeles-class nuclear submarine against the Soviet fleet in the North Atlantic. Unlike World War II simulators, here the player works with modern technology - guided torpedoes, sonar with both passive and active modes, and combat at much greater ranges, where visual contact with the enemy is the exception rather than the rule, and patient analysis of sensor data plays a decisive role rather than quick reaction to what's visible on screen.

The game skillfully combines a tactical map with a three-dimensional view of the deck and submarine controls, with sonar work and recognizing contacts by their acoustic signature playing a key role before the player ever sees the enemy at all. The campaign follows a broader military conflict in Europe, so individual missions have context, and the player has to weigh not just the immediate engagement but also the strategic impact of their actions on the whole war and the course of the Allies' ground and air operations. The sound design of the sonar and the tense, silent duels with an opponent who can be heard but not seen were among the most atmospheric passages of the genre at the time of release and captured the nervousness of real underwater combat well.

Red Storm Rising was praised on release as one of the most elaborate simulators of modern underwater warfare, and thanks to its connection to a popular novel it also reached players outside the traditional circle of war simulation fans. To this day it is considered one of the best DOS submarine titles, and its emphasis on sonar and long-range tactics influenced later simulations of modern submarines, including later games focused on the nuclear-era Cold War, and it is often mentioned as one of the best adaptations of Clancy's literary world into game form, one that managed to combine a gripping story with an honest simulation core.

**Why play it:** For fans of both Tom Clancy and elaborate submarine simulations — it combines a gripping Cold War story with an honest emphasis on sonar and long-range tactics that influenced later titles in the genre.

pc-dos__gato.teaser: Early World War II Pacific submarine simulator; sonar, diving and torpedo attacks.
pc-dos__gato.article:
**Gato** is one of the early submarine simulators for home computers, putting the player in the role of the commander of an American Gato-class submarine fighting against Japanese convoys and warships in the Pacific during World War II. For its time, the game offered a relatively detailed submarine model, in which the player monitors sonar, controls diving and surfacing, and plans torpedo attacks based on the target's speed and course, while also having to account for a limited supply of fuel and torpedoes on board, which leads to weighing when it's worth attacking and when it's better to end the patrol and return to port.

The gameplay is built on a simple but functional cycle: locating a convoy on the map, closing in either submerged or on the surface, calculating the angle on the bow for the torpedo tubes, and then dealing with the countermeasures of escort vessels. The graphics are necessarily simple given the year of release, with simple outline renderings of ships and instrument panels, but the overview map and indicators give the player enough information for sound tactical decisions even without modern visual bells and whistles. The sound design is limited to basic sonar signals and explosions, yet it still manages to convey a sense of tension during the long wait before firing.

In the mid-1980s, Gato was among the first titles to show that even limited DOS hardware could support a convincingly functioning war simulator, and it earned a reputation as an honest, if undemanding, submarine game. Today the game is interesting mainly as a historical exhibit and a stepping stone toward later, more elaborate submarine simulations like Silent Service, alongside which it belongs among the genre's foundational titles by concept, even though it lacks the later degree of detail, graphical polish and atmosphere that newer titles brought at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

**Why play it:** For those interested in the genre's history rather than modern comfort — an honest, undemanding stepping stone toward more elaborate submarine simulations like Silent Service, even though it now lacks the detail and atmosphere of later games.

pc-dos__sub-battle-simulator.teaser: Submarine simulation letting you command a German U-boat too; more accessible controls than the competition.
pc-dos__sub-battle-simulator.article:
**Sub Battle Simulator** is a submarine simulator from the late 1980s that, unlike competing titles, lets the player command not only an American submarine but also a German U-boat, offering a chance to experience the underwater war from both sides of the World War II front. The player plans patrols, hunts for convoys, and leads torpedo attacks, with the game emphasizing relatively accessible controls compared to the more complex simulators of the same era, making it a good entry point for less experienced genre fans who didn't want to immediately grapple with the lengthy manuals and dozens of instruments offered by the more elaborate competing simulators from major publishers like MicroProse or Sierra.

The combat system builds on the classic model of calculating angle of approach and target speed, complemented by the risk of retaliation with depth charges when, after firing torpedoes, the submarine must dive quickly and wait for the enemy to lose the trail. The graphics are simple, with a schematic display of the deck and instruments, but thanks to their clarity they let the player get oriented quickly even without a long learning curve, which was an advantage at the time over more complicated competing titles. The option to choose sides also gives the game a degree of replay value, since each side has differently set priorities and risks, from aggressive convoy hunting to cautious defense of one's own routes.

Sub Battle Simulator wasn't as widely discussed at release as the genre's flagship titles from MicroProse, but thanks to its accessibility and the option to play as either side of the conflict, it found its place among fans of DOS submarine simulators. Today it's interesting mainly as an alternative take on a theme other titles approached from just one side of the front, and as a reminder that the genre also had simpler, more accessible entries that could offer fun without requiring hours of studying a manual, without unnecessarily oversimplifying the subject of undersea warfare.

**Why play it:** For players who want to try submarine warfare from both sides of the front without hours of studying a manual — a more accessible, simpler alternative to MicroProse's flagship simulators.

pc-dos__688-attack-sub.teaser: Cold War nuclear submarine simulation; combat fought by sonar, not visual contact.
pc-dos__688-attack-sub.article:
**688 Attack Sub** puts the player in command of a modern American Los Angeles-class nuclear submarine, offering a simulation of undersea combat set in a fictional Cold War conflict. Unlike World War II-era simulators, here the player works with torpedoes capable of tracking a target, sonar distinguishing between passive and active modes, and combat that's often fought at ranges where the enemy is just a blip on the sonar display, long before it's even visually confirmed — so the player has to rely on experience reading sonar data and patiently tracking changes in the acoustic picture of the surroundings.

Gameplay focuses on tactical decision-making — when to use active sonar and risk detection, how to interpret the acoustic signatures of other vessels, and how to maneuver so the submarine evades anti-torpedo countermeasures. The game offers several scenarios of varying difficulty and types of opponents, from patrol ships to enemy submarines, giving the player room to adjust the pace from simpler patrols to demanding one-on-one duels in the depths. The visual and audio presentation of the sonar and the submarine's interior was a solid standard for the genre at the time of release and complemented the sense of an enclosed, claustrophobic space beneath the surface.

At release the game was praised for its relatively accessible take on modern undersea warfare, which didn't demand as deep a commitment as competing titles, and it became one of the more popular simulators of its kind in the late 1980s. For today's player it remains an interesting showcase of how DOS simulators approached the era of nuclear submarines and missile armament shortly before the end of the Cold War, when the subject was still current and appealing to a wide range of war-simulation fans looking for tactics rather than action.

**Why play it:** For war-simulation fans who want tactics rather than action and will appreciate a more accessible take on the era of nuclear submarines and missile armament at the tail end of the Cold War.

pc-dos__great-naval-battles-north-atlant.teaser: First entry in SSI's series about the battles of the North Atlantic, including the hunt for the Bismarck.
pc-dos__great-naval-battles-north-atlant.article:
**Great Naval Battles: North Atlantic 1939-1943** is the first installment in SSI's series of naval strategy simulations, recreating key battles of the North Atlantic during World War II — from the hunt for the battleship Bismarck to clashes between convoy escorts and German surface raiders and U-boats. The player commands individual vessels or entire task groups and decides on course, gunnery, and maneuvers both in real time and in an overview tactical mode that lets you watch the whole battle from a bird's-eye view while still stepping in to control individual ships when needed.

The game combines historically grounded scenarios with a fairly detailed model of gunnery ballistics, armor, and ship damage, so battleship duels feel more like a thoughtful long-range contest than an action-packed shootout. Besides individual battles, it also offers a broader campaign perspective on the war in the Atlantic, where the player follows the impact of individual clashes on the overall course of the conflict and has to manage limited forces across multiple operations. The graphics, with views of the sea and ship silhouettes, were solid for their time and supported strategic decision-making well without unnecessary clutter, whether the player was watching the battle from the map or from a closer view of individual vessels.

Great Naval Battles: North Atlantic was received as a thoroughly crafted and historically faithful simulation that appealed to players more interested in naval warfare than in action, and it launched a beloved series of further installments covering other World War II theaters. Today it's valuable mainly as a detailed reconstruction of specific historical battles that other titles in the genre only touched on in passing, and as a reminder of how SSI approached historically accurate war simulations straddling the line between board game and computer game.

**Why play it:** For fans of World War II naval history — a detailed, historically faithful reconstruction of specific battles that other titles in the genre only touched on in passing.
