pc-dos__task-force-1942.teaser: Sequel to Great Naval Battles set in the Pacific; command carrier task forces at Midway and Coral Sea.
pc-dos__task-force-1942.article:
**Task Force 1942**, the second entry in the Great Naval Battles series, moves the setting from the Atlantic to the Pacific and lets the player command American and Japanese carrier, cruiser, and destroyer task forces in key battles such as Coral Sea or Midway. Compared to the first installment, the game puts greater emphasis on aircraft carriers and their air wings, so combat isn't limited to gunnery duels between surface ships but also includes complex management of a fleet's air component, where the player must coordinate reconnaissance, combat air patrols, and strikes against enemy ships without losing track of the rest of the fleet out on the open ocean.

The player moves the fleet on the tactical map, launches scouting and strike squadrons, and has to weigh aircraft range, weather, and the risk of the enemy group's anti-aircraft defenses before committing to a full strike. Surface ship combat remains as detailed as in the previous installment, with a model of armor and gunnery ballistics, but now the player also has to fold air operations into the overall battle strategy, including the risk of a carrier being left without air cover. The historical scenarios let the player replay key moments of the Pacific War knowing how they actually turned out, and try to find a different, perhaps better solution than the one real commanders chose in history.

Task Force 1942 was praised as a successful expansion of the Great Naval Battles concept to include the air component of the Pacific war, and it cemented the series' position among the most elaborate naval strategy games on DOS. Even today it remains an interesting example of how the genre managed to combine historical accuracy with accessible strategic gameplay without overwhelming the player with micromanagement unrelated to actually commanding the fleet, and it remains a pleasantly readable strategy game even for players with no prior experience with the series.

**Why play it:** For Great Naval Battles fans and newcomers alike with no prior experience with the series — an accessible strategy game that combines historical accuracy of the Pacific War with an air component, without unnecessary micromanagement.

pc-dos__ssn-21-seawolf.teaser: One of the most detailed submarine simulators on DOS, close to professional training simulations.
pc-dos__ssn-21-seawolf.article:
**SSN-21 Seawolf** ranks among the most detailed submarine simulators released for DOS, putting the player in command of the most modern American attack submarine of its day, set in fictional conflicts of the late Cold War and its aftermath. The game continues the tradition of realistic undersea combat simulators but pushes the level of detail in the sonar model, weapon systems, and enemy behavior to the maximum for its time, aiming to come close to the professional training simulations used by the navy itself — reflected in the sheer amount of detail in the submarine's individual systems.

The player has to master a complex interface for passive and active sonar, identify targets by their acoustic signature, and make tactical decisions about when to stay hidden and when to risk detection for a more precise fix. The campaign offers a series of missions of increasing difficulty, in which the player faces not only enemy submarines and ships but also the limits of their own equipment — sensor range, torpedo endurance, and how the submarine behaves during fast maneuvers at depth. The sheer number of tracked parameters and menus makes the game more a tool for patient planning than fast action, where every maneuver decision is counted in minutes, not seconds.

SSN-21 Seawolf was praised on release precisely for its technical depth and was regarded as one of the most demanding and authentic simulations of modern undersea warfare on computers at the time, comparable to other seriously intentioned military simulations. For today's player it's demanding due to its complexity and text full of technical jargon, but as an example of just how far the submarine simulator genre could go by the end of the DOS era, it still has value and is often mentioned among the pinnacle works on the theme of modern undersea warfare on personal computers of the 1990s, whose footsteps later, even more elaborate simulations would follow.

**Why play it:** For players craving maximum technical depth and expert authenticity in modern undersea warfare, who won't be scared off by dense text and complex controls — a pinnacle title of the late DOS era.

pc-dos__wolfpack.teaser: Simulation of a German U-boat attacking in wolfpacks; coordinate with other submarines in action.
pc-dos__wolfpack.article:
**Wolfpack** is a submarine simulator from the early 1990s that puts the player in command of a German U-boat operating in wolfpacks against Allied convoys in the Atlantic during World War II. Unlike simulators focused on a single submarine, Wolfpack at least partially highlights the tactics of group attacks typical of real German wolfpack operations the game is named after, so the player also has to think about coordinating with other submarines instead of hunting a lone vessel by themselves, as older simulators focused on just one submarine offered, regardless of the rest of the pack operating in the same area.

The gameplay combines positioning relative to the convoy, tracking patrol vessels, and the classic calculation of torpedo attack parameters with reacting to countermeasures, when the submarine has to dive after an attack and evade depth charges. The graphics are appropriate for their time — a simple but functional display of the deck, periscope, and overview map gives the player enough information for sound tactical decisions without burdening them with excess detail. Sonar and explosion sounds add to the atmosphere, even if technically it's not the most ambitious presentation in the genre compared to flagship titles from major publishers who could afford more elaborate graphics and sound.

Wolfpack wasn't as widely discussed at release as the genre's flagship titles, but thanks to its focus on convoy-attack tactics from the German side, it found its place among fans of DOS submarine simulators. Today it's interesting mainly as an alternative perspective on the same theme of undersea warfare that competing games often approached from the Allied side, and as a reminder of the diversity the genre offered back then, one that didn't settle for a single point of view on the Battle of the Atlantic and offered various ways to experience the same historical subject.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience the Battle of the Atlantic from the German side — an alternative perspective on convoy-attack tactics of undersea warfare that competing titles approached from the Allied side.

pc-dos__north-atlantic-86.teaser: Hex-based naval wargame from SSG about a fictional clash between NATO and the Warsaw Pact in the Atlantic.
pc-dos__north-atlantic-86.article:
**North Atlantic '86** is a hex-based naval wargame from the Australian studio Strategic Studies Group that simulates a fictional conflict between NATO and the Warsaw Pact in the North Atlantic in the mid-1980s. The player commands fleets of surface ships, submarines, and aircraft, and has to manage contact recognition, fire control, and the deployment of anti-submarine forces across a vast ocean map divided into hexagonal fields, typical of board wargames converted to computer form without losing their analytical depth or the emphasis on carefully considered force deployment over the vast expanse of the North Atlantic.

The game is built on a turn-based system, where the player gradually moves units, sends out reconnaissance patrols, and decides on engaging in combat based on limited and often uncertain information about enemy positions, which nicely reflects the uncertainty of real naval warfare. Combat plays out more abstractly than in simulators with a three-dimensional view of the deck, but thanks to that the game covers a much broader strategic scope of the fictional superpower conflict, including logistics and the deployment of air support from coastal bases. Overview screens and text reports on the outcomes of engagements gave the game the feel of an expertly run war game rather than an audiovisually lavish simulation.

In the mid-1980s the game was praised by war-game fans as a well-considered and historically grounded speculation on what a clash of superpowers at sea might look like, and it became one of SSG's standout titles for DOS. Today it's interesting mainly as evidence of the era's genre of hex-based war games applied to the theme of the Cold War at sea, rather than as a simulator offering an immediate action experience, and it will be appreciated mainly by patient players interested in military history and the planning depth of classic wargames, who don't mind the slower pace of a turn-based system.

**Why play it:** For patient fans of military history and turn-based hex wargames who don't mind a slower pace — a well-considered speculation on what a clash of superpowers at sea might have looked like during the Cold War.

pc-dos__gunship-2000.teaser: Helicopter combat simulation from MicroProse; career progression from rookie to more modern equipment.
pc-dos__gunship-2000.article:
**Gunship 2000** is a helicopter combat simulation from MicroProse, a sequel to the earlier Gunship title from the mid-1980s, bringing a much more detailed campaign system and more modern graphics. The player sits in the cockpit of American combat helicopters, primarily the AH-64 Apache, OH-58 Kiowa, or AH-1 Cobra, and carries out campaign missions ranging from terrain reconnaissance and convoy escort to direct attacks on tank columns and air-defense systems. The game offers career progression, where the pilot gradually earns higher ranks and access to more modern equipment and weaponry, and the individual campaigns are set in various geographical scenarios, including a hypothetical conflict in Central Europe, the Middle East, and the South American jungle.

The controls combine fairly realistic flight physics with a clear interface that's manageable even for players without an air-simulator background — various difficulty levels are available, along with the option to turn off more complex avionics systems and automatic radar target acquisition. Full-color VGA graphics and smooth terrain animation with hills, rivers, and settlements were cutting-edge for the genre in 1991, complemented by convincing sound effects of explosions, warning alarms, and engine roar. The overall atmosphere captures well the tension of flying low over enemy territory, where any hesitation can mean the loss of an expensive machine and its entire crew, and the game reinforces that pressure by making lost helicopters genuinely missed in the career mode.

Gunship 2000 became one of the most commercially successful simulators of its time and is still mentioned today as an important milestone in the genre of helicopter combat games, one that also inspired later titles such as Comanche: Maximum Overkill. Even decades later it remains surprisingly playable thanks to its clear mission structure, the satisfying feeling of gradually upgrading equipment, and the variety of its campaigns, even though its controls and graphics inevitably feel dated today and the enemy AI is noticeably simpler compared to later games.

**Why play it:** For fans of helicopter combat simulators — a clear mission structure and satisfying equipment upgrades keep the game playable today, even though the graphics and enemy AI have noticeably aged.

pc-dos__lhx-attack-chopper.teaser: Simulation of the then-in-development LHX helicopter; choice of arcade or fully simulation mode.
pc-dos__lhx-attack-chopper.article:
**LHX Attack Chopper** is a helicopter combat simulation from Electronic Arts, set in the near future, that casts the player as the pilot of the experimental LHX attack helicopter, at the time genuinely under development for the US Army as a successor to an older helicopter type. The game combines individual missions with a broader campaign in which the player carries out tasks ranging from reconnaissance and convoy escort to destroying enemy vehicles with guided missiles, unguided rockets, and the onboard cannon, with choosing the right weapon for a given target type being key to mission success. The choice between a simpler arcade mode and a fully simulation mode made the game accessible both to less experienced players and to flight enthusiasts who wanted to manage fuel, individual system damage, and limited ammunition.

Technically, the game benefited from colorful VGA graphics and digitized sound, which in 1990 were among the better standards on DOS, although the terrain was still rendered rather schematically, with limited detail depth and simpler textures than later titles on similar themes. The music and sound effects nonetheless supported the feeling of low-altitude combat over the landscape well, including at night, when the game used thermal imaging and other sensors simulating modern cockpit equipment. Missions were designed to gradually increase the demands on tactics, route planning, and managing limited weapons and fuel.

LHX Attack Chopper was among the popular simulators of its time and helped popularize the theme of combat helicopters on personal computers even before the arrival of more advanced titles like Gunship 2000 or the later Comanche: Maximum Overkill. Today it serves as an interesting historical glimpse into the early phase of helicopter simulators, even though its controls, graphics, and enemy AI are clearly marked by their era and appear simplistic compared to later games, which does not diminish its historical significance.

**Why play it:** For fans of the early history of helicopter simulators who will appreciate the game's pioneering status despite its simplified controls and graphics typical of its era.

pc-dos__10-tank-killer.teaser: Simulation of the American A-10 Warthog; destroying tanks by flying low between hills and valleys.
pc-dos__10-tank-killer.article:
**A-10 Tank Killer** is an air combat simulation from Dynamix that focuses on the American attack aircraft A-10 Thunderbolt II, nicknamed the Warthog, designed primarily to destroy ground vehicles and provide close air support to ground forces in combat. The player carries out missions focused on supporting friendly troops, destroying tank columns, bridges, and air defense systems, with the game emphasizing choosing the right weapon for a specific target type and the tactic of flying low between hills and valleys, where the terrain makes the aircraft less vulnerable to enemy anti-aircraft fire.

The simulation offered a higher level of detail than many competing titles, including damage modeling for individual aircraft parts, various levels of control difficulty from simplified to a demanding simulator mode, and an elaborate mission-planning system before the aircraft even took off. The graphical treatment of the terrain, with hilly landscapes, valleys, and rivers, was imaginative for its time and supported gameplay focused on low-altitude flight, where actively using terrain cover against radar lock-on was necessary. The sound design, with engine roar, cannon fire, and explosions, complemented the feeling of combat at low altitude over enemy territory well.

A-10 Tank Killer is often cited as one of the first simulators specifically devoted to an attack aircraft designed for fighting ground vehicles, and it foreshadowed later specialized simulators of this aircraft type as well as the sequel A-10 Tank Killer II, released a few years later by the same studio. Today it is interesting primarily as evidence of how the genre gradually specialized in specific aircraft types and their tactical roles, instead of the generic model of a universal fighter with unlimited weapons and all-purpose equipment. Anyone trying the game today will appreciate above all its clear mission structure and clearly defined objective for each flight.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the beginnings of specialized flight simulators, who will appreciate the clear mission structure and clearly defined objective of each flight.

pc-dos__their-finest-hour-battle-of-brit.teaser: Flight simulation of the Battle of Britain in 1940; dynamic campaign shaped by mission outcomes.
pc-dos__their-finest-hour-battle-of-brit.article:
**Their Finest Hour: The Battle of Britain** is a flight simulation from Lucasfilm Games that takes the player into the air battles over southern England during the summer and autumn of 1940, a critical period in British history. The game lets you fly for the British RAF in aircraft like the Hawker Hurricane and Supermarine Spitfire, or for the German Luftwaffe in Messerschmitts and bombers, and offers a dynamic campaign in which the course of the battle also unfolds according to the outcomes of the player's individual missions, so no two campaign playthroughs are quite the same and the outcome of the battle can vary depending on the player's performance.

The game was praised at the time for the careful modeling of each aircraft's flight characteristics and for its effort to capture the historical context of the battle, including the various phases of the German campaign, from attacks on airfields and radar stations to the widespread bombing of London during the so-called Blitz at the end of the year. The graphics used advanced texturing of 3D aircraft models for its time, giving the dogfights a more convincing look even years later, and the music and sound effects of engines, machine guns, and anti-aircraft fire evoked the atmosphere of period air battles over the English countryside and industrial targets well.

Their Finest Hour is today considered one of the significant flight simulators focused on the Second World War, and it paved the way for the later title Secret Weapons of the Luftwaffe from the same studio, with which it shares core technology and mission design philosophy. Even years later, players appreciate above all its historical authenticity and the ability to experience the battle from both sides of the conflict, which was unusual at the time and gave the game added value compared to purely America-centric simulators focused on only one side of the battlefield. It is precisely the ability to experience the famous battle from the Luftwaffe's perspective as well that makes the game a valuable historical experience for those interested in aviation history to this day.

**Why play it:** Thanks to the ability to experience the Battle of Britain from both sides of the conflict, including the Luftwaffe's perspective, it remains a valuable historical experience for those interested in aviation history.

pc-dos__secret-weapons-of-luftwaffe.teaser: LucasArts on experimental Luftwaffe aircraft from the end of the war, including the jet-powered Me 262.
pc-dos__secret-weapons-of-luftwaffe.article:
**Secret Weapons of the Luftwaffe** is a flight simulation from LucasArts that focuses on experimental and groundbreaking aircraft of the German Luftwaffe from the end of the Second World War, including early jet aircraft such as the Messerschmitt Me 262 or the rocket-powered Me 163 Komet. The player progresses through a campaign of fictional and historically inspired missions, gradually gaining access to more advanced aircraft, and the game also allows choosing among Allied aircraft to compare the performance of both sides and their differing tactics against bombers and escort fighters.

The simulation stood out for its elaborate mission editor, which let players create and modify their own scenarios, weapon loadouts, and combat conditions — uncommon at the time of release and one that considerably extended the game's lifespan even after completing the main campaign. The graphical treatment of the aircraft models and landscape was above average for DOS in the first half of the 1990s, and the game worked well with the difference between classic propeller aircraft and the newly introduced jet-powered machines, which was also reflected in different flight characteristics, speeds, and dogfighting tactics between generations of technology.

Secret Weapons of the Luftwaffe is still valued today for its focus on the late phase of aviation development in the Second World War, a theme other simulators covered far less, and for its tools enabling custom content creation and scenario sharing among players via disk copies and later the internet. Within the genre of historical flight simulators, it remains one of the technically and content-wise most ambitious titles of its generation and a reminder of the creative boldness of the studio then known as Lucasfilm Games, later LucasArts. The combination of a historical theme with open tools for custom content makes it a title that draws many players back to explore again even years later.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its focus on the late phase of wartime aviation and its open tools for creating custom content, players gladly return to it for further exploration even years later.

pc-dos__chuck-yeager-s-advanced-flight-t.teaser: A training simulator with legendary pilot Chuck Yeager as your instructional guide.
pc-dos__chuck-yeager-s-advanced-flight-t.article:
**Chuck Yeager's Advanced Flight Trainer 2.0** is a flight simulator from Electronic Arts that, unlike combat-focused titles, emphasizes pilot training and mastering the flight characteristics of various aircraft, from small civilian planes to supersonic fighters capable of breaking the sound barrier. The legendary pilot Chuck Yeager also appears in the game, helping the player improve their flying skills through commentary and challenges and complete a series of training tasks focused on flight precision, landing, and maneuvering in various conditions, including reduced visibility and strong wind.

The game focuses primarily on a realistic flight model and clear instrumentation, thanks to which it was praised both as an educational tool and an entertaining simulator for players who wanted to understand the basics of aerodynamics and how an aircraft behaves at various speeds and angles of attack, including phenomena such as spin stalls. The graphics were simpler than competing action-focused combat simulations, but clear and functional, and the sound design focused mainly on the engine, instrument warning tones, and the instructor's voice commentary accompanying each exercise. The gradual increase in the difficulty of individual tasks gave the player a sense of real progress in piloting skills, similar to actual flight training.

Chuck Yeager's Advanced Flight Trainer 2.0 is seen today as one of the first popular simulators to combine entertainment with real aviation know-how and a famous figure of American aviation, and it recalls a time when the flight simulation genre was still relatively young and experimented with various approaches to teaching flight rather than pure combat against an opponent. For many players, it was their very first encounter with real aerodynamics in game form and an inspiration for an interest in aviation in general, without a single shot or guided missile ever being fired.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience real aerodynamics in game form without firing a single shot, it's a pleasant and instructive introduction to flying from a legend of American aviation.

pc-dos__b-17-flying-fortress.teaser: Simulation of the B-17 bomber; commanding the whole crew, gun turrets, and a precise bombing run.
pc-dos__b-17-flying-fortress.article:
**B-17 Flying Fortress** is a flight simulation from MicroProse that puts the player in the role of crew commander of an American B-17 bomber during raids over Germany in the Second World War. Unlike fighter simulators, the game focuses on managing the whole crew, operating individual machine gun turrets, maintaining the bomber formation, and precisely targeting objectives with the bombsight, with the player able to take control of different crew members depending on the current situation and the urgency of the threat from enemy fighters.

The game was praised for its realistic depiction of the bombing campaign, including the risk of losing friendly aircraft from the formation, damage to the player's own plane from anti-aircraft fire and fighters, and the need to deal with a possible engine fire or wounded crew members during the long return flight to the base in England across the English Channel. The graphical rendering of aircraft formations and anti-aircraft fire was impressive for its time, and the tension was heightened further by the need to fly long stretches over enemy territory without being able to immediately intervene in the plane's own defense, when the player can only watch as enemy fighters approach and the formation slowly thins out from damaged aircraft.

B-17 Flying Fortress is still mentioned today as one of the few simulators devoted to the perspective of a bomber crew rather than a lone fighter pilot, which gives it a specific and fairly rare place within the genre among titles of the same era. This different perspective, the emphasis on teamwork inside the aircraft, and the palpable risk of losing the plane and crew make it a game that remains interesting beyond a purely nostalgic view of period Second World War simulators. It is precisely the tension of the player not having full control over the mission's outcome, having to rely also on the formation of other bombers, that gives the game its distinctive atmosphere.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its unusual bomber-crew perspective and the tension of the mission's outcome depending not just on the player but on the whole formation, it still offers a distinctive experience today.

pc-dos__knights-of-sky.teaser: Flight simulation of World War I on biplanes; a career from rookie to ace of the skies.
pc-dos__knights-of-sky.article:
**Knights of the Sky** is a flight simulation from MicroProse set in the First World War, in which the player, as a fighter pilot, flies historical biplanes over the Western Front and other battlefields of that global conflict. The game combines individual dogfights with a career campaign in which the pilot gradually builds up a reputation, earns decorations, and can move between different aircraft types, as aviation technology evolved rapidly during the war, from slow observation planes to faster and better-armed fighters.

The simulation tried to faithfully capture the specifics of aerial warfare of the period, including the limited armament of propeller-synchronized machine guns, slower speeds, and the need to rely on the maneuverability of wood-and-canvas aircraft rather than modern sensors or guided missiles from later 20th-century conflicts. The game also featured a campaign system that tracked the progress of the entire war, including changes in the weaponry of both sides, so the player could experience firsthand how quickly aviation technology developed during this period. The graphical rendering of the biplanes and landscape was appropriate for its year of release, and the atmosphere was well complemented by music and sounds matching older piston-engine types and period field airfields with primitive facilities.

Knights of the Sky is valued today above all as one of the few flight simulators focused on the First World War, a period that remains relatively rarely covered in the genre compared to the Second World War or modern conflicts fought with jet aircraft. As a result, even years later it retains a certain uniqueness and historical value for fans of early aviation and for those interested in the military history of the First World War in general, who will find it hard to find this theme treated with comparable care in other simulators.

**Why play it:** For those interested in the First World War, a theme rarely covered in flight simulators, it's a unique and still valuable glimpse into early aviation.

pc-dos__f-15-strike-eagle-iii.teaser: Third installment of MicroProse's series on the F-15E Strike Eagle; choice of arcade or simulation mode.
pc-dos__f-15-strike-eagle-iii.article:
**F-15 Strike Eagle III** is an air combat simulation from MicroProse, the third installment in the series focused on the multirole fighter-bomber F-15E Strike Eagle of the US Air Force. The game offers campaigns set in several different world conflict regions, and the player carries out missions ranging from dogfights through destroying ground targets to suppressing air defenses, choosing weapons according to the type of task and able to switch between simplified arcade and more demanding simulation controls depending on their own experience and appetite for detailed planning before each takeoff.

This installment brought significantly improved 3D graphics compared to its predecessors, with textured aircraft and terrain models, which noticeably advanced the visual side of the series, and it also offered a more elaborate briefing, mission planning, and a clearer battlefield map before takeoff. The sound design, with control tower voice callouts, radar warnings, and weapon system sounds, supported the feel of modern 1990s air combat well and gave individual missions a cinematic pace and tension. The series as a whole long maintained a reputation as a simulator that offers enough depth for more experienced players while not discouraging anyone with control complexity right from the start, which made it a natural entry point into the genre for many home computer owners of the time.

F-15 Strike Eagle III is considered the culmination of its series on DOS and an example of how MicroProse's accessible, more arcade-oriented flight simulations managed to advance technically and content-wise alongside more demanding competing titles like Falcon 3.0. Today it represents a solid example of a popularizing approach to the genre that also attracted players without a deeper interest in fully realistic flight simulators and their complex navigation and fire-control systems, while still offering enough varied missions for repeated play even after finishing the main campaign.

**Why play it:** If you're looking for an accessible, more arcade-style flight simulation with plenty of varied missions for repeated play, this is the culmination of MicroProse's series on DOS.

pc-dos__aces-over-europe.teaser: The successor to Red Baron from Dynamix, moving aerial combat to World War II Europe.
pc-dos__aces-over-europe.article:
**Aces Over Europe** is a flight simulator from Dynamix, following up on the successful Red Baron and moving the theme of aerial combat to World War II Europe. The player can choose between several Allied and German fighter aircraft and flies a campaign following the key phases of the air war over Europe, from the defense of Britain during the Blitz to Allied bombing raids over the continent in the later years of the war, with an emphasis on historically grounded scenarios, specific opponents, and the evolution of tactics throughout the conflict.

The game built on technology similar to that used by Dynamix in Red Baron, but adapted to the more modern World War II aircraft with higher speed, stronger armament, and different combat tactics compared to the slower World War I planes. The graphical rendering of the 3D aircraft models and terrain was of good quality and clarity for its time, and the game also offered the option to watch the dogfight from various camera angles, including a replay of the fought battle, which was not entirely common at the time and, according to available reviews, was appreciated by players. The campaign also responded to the player's performance, unfolding somewhat differently depending on how they fared in key missions, which increased motivation to play carefully even in less important tasks.

Aces Over Europe is today seen as a worthy continuation of Dynamix's line devoted to historical aerial conflicts and as one of several quality World War II simulators released in the first half of the nineties. Its contribution lies primarily in an accessible yet historically grounded treatment of the subject, which appealed to both demanding and more casual players of flight simulators of its era. For players who came to love Red Baron, it represented a logical and welcome expansion of the theme into a new historical era with faster aircraft and more intense combat.

**Why play it:** For fans of Red Baron who want to move aerial combat to World War II with faster aircraft and more intense dogfights, this is a logical and welcome expansion of the theme.

pc-dos__microsoft-flight-simulator-5-0.teaser: Microsoft's civilian flight simulator; free flying without missions all around the world.
pc-dos__microsoft-flight-simulator-5-0.article:
**Microsoft Flight Simulator 5.0** is a civilian flight simulator developed by the Bruce Artwick Organization for Microsoft, representing a significant step in the long history of this series, which dates back to the early eighties and several previous versions. Unlike combat simulators, the game focuses on free flying, instrument flight practice, and completing journeys between airports around the world, offering several civilian aircraft including small sport planes as well as larger airliners, and the player can freely view the landscape, coastlines, and urban development as they see fit, without needing to complete specific tasks.

Version 5.0 brought significantly improved graphics with textured terrain, bodies of water, and buildings, which was a noticeable leap forward compared to earlier installments, and it also expanded the range of sceneries and airports around the world, including more detailed surroundings of major cities and significant landmarks that players could use for orientation even without fully relying on instruments. The simulation focused on precise modeling of flight characteristics and instruments, thanks to which it was also used as an informal training tool for people interested in real flying, not merely as a purely entertaining pastime with no further connection to the real world of aviation.

Microsoft Flight Simulator 5.0 is still mentioned today as a key milestone in the history of civilian flight simulators, one that showed the genre could exist outside a military and combat framework, and it laid the foundation for further installments of the series, which to this day rank among the longest-running game franchises of all. Its open approach to flying, its emphasis on freedom of movement, and the absence of any combat remain an inspiration for modern simulators of this type on today's computers, which still build on similar principles of free world exploration.

**Why play it:** Because of its open approach to flying without combat and its emphasis on freedom of movement, it is a key milestone of civilian simulators whose principles live on today in the series' modern successors.

pc-dos__f-14-fleet-defender.teaser: A simulation of the carrier-based F-14 Tomcat; defending aircraft carriers and working the radar at long range.
pc-dos__f-14-fleet-defender.article:
**F-14 Fleet Defender** is an aerial combat simulation from MicroProse focused on the carrier-based F-14 Tomcat fighter, serving the United States Navy in defending aircraft carriers and escort formations against aerial and missile threats on the open sea. The player carries out missions ranging from patrol flights and intercepting enemy aircraft to more complex operations involving cooperation with other units of the fleet, with the game emphasizing radar management, long-range target identification, and choosing suitable guided missiles based on the type and behavior of the opponent on the radar screen.

The simulation offered a detailed model of the F-14's cockpit and systems, including the specifics of its two-seat configuration with a pilot and weapons systems officer, and the player could switch between both roles depending on the chosen difficulty level and personal preferences when planning a mission. The graphical rendering of ocean sceneries, aircraft carriers, and escort vessels was convincing for its time and complemented well the feeling of operating from the deck in the middle of the open sea, where returning to the carrier's short landing strip is its own separate challenge requiring precise adherence to the landing corridor.

F-14 Fleet Defender is valued for its thorough treatment of naval air warfare and the specifics of a carrier-based aircraft, which sets it apart from simulators focused purely on land bases and classic fighter duels over the continental mainland. It remains an interesting example of how MicroProse expanded its range of flight simulators to include increasingly specific types of aircraft, crews, and operational environments typical of a modern navy and its air forces. For fans of carrier aviation, it remains to this day one of the few simulators to cover the subject in such detail, including the need to account for the ship's limited supplies of fuel and ammunition on board.

**Why play it:** For fans of carrier aviation who appreciate a detailed treatment of naval air warfare, including the need to watch limited fuel and ammunition aboard the ship, this is one of the few simulators covering it in such detail.

pc-dos__jetfighter-ii-advanced-tactical-.teaser: A more arcade-style fighter jet simulation than competing titles from MicroProse or Dynamix.
pc-dos__jetfighter-ii-advanced-tactical-.article:
**JetFighter II: Advanced Tactical Fighter** is an aerial combat simulation from Velocity Development studio that aims for a more accessible, arcade-style take on modern air combat than competing titles of the same era. The player flies powerful fighter jets and carries out missions involving both aerial dogfights and attacks on ground targets, with the game trying to offer fun even to players who don't want to work through the complicated simulation systems typical of titles from MicroProse or Dynamix, focusing mainly on smooth, quickly accessible action.

The game focused on a smooth feel of flying and clear controls, complemented by colorful graphics and simpler but functional models of aircraft and terrain that did not place heavy demands on the performance of the home computers of the time with their limited memory. The emphasis on fast pace, easy entry into combat without lengthy planning, and straightforward mission objectives made it a popular choice for players looking for fun action rather than a detailed simulation requiring the study of an extensive manual and cockpit instrument layout before every flight. Through this approach, the JetFighter series built its own audience distinct from fans of more demanding competing titles.

JetFighter II: Advanced Tactical Fighter is remembered today as one of the more accessible representatives of the flight genre on DOS from the early nineties, standing in contrast to the more demanding simulators from MicroProse or Dynamix mentioned above. Its value lies precisely in the fact that it opened the genre to a wider audience without requiring deep knowledge of aviation systems and lengthy training before the first mission flown in the virtual cockpit, and even after all these years it remains a pleasant example of a lighter take on flight simulation that still finds an audience among players who prefer quick fun over long study of a manual.

**Why play it:** If you want a flight simulator without the need for lengthy training and manual study, this is a pleasantly lighter and more accessible alternative to the more demanding competitors from MicroProse or Dynamix.

pc-dos__x-com-ufo-defense.teaser: The legendary combination of base strategy and turn-based combat against aliens.
pc-dos__x-com-ufo-defense.article:
**X-COM: UFO Defense** was released in 1994 by Mythos Games studio in cooperation with publisher MicroProse, and in Europe it was released under the title UFO: Enemy Unknown. The game combines two layers of play: on the strategic world map, the player runs the international organization X-COM, builds and expands bases, funds research and equipment production, negotiates with the supporting governments of individual countries, and decides where to send a squadron to intercept and shoot down alien craft, while the tactical layer moves the action to a turn-based battlefield, where individual soldiers with their own equipment, injuries, and morale face alien life forms amid the destructible terrain of cities, countryside, and downed craft.

The turn-based system with action points, the ability to fire both on command and reactively (so-called reaction fire), hidden areas outside line of sight, and the permanent consequences of losses gave the game a tension that was unusual in any previous strategy game — the death of an experienced soldier was irreversible, and the player grew emotionally attached to the named characters, their statistics, and their experience. On the PC hardware of the time, the game ran in VGA graphics with an isometric view; the music and sound effects (explosions, screams, sounds of alien weapons) supported well the atmosphere of paranoia and constant escalation of the threat, as more dangerous types of aliens, civilian abductions, and the need to dissect and research captured technologies were added as the game progressed.

The game was immediately received by critics and players alike as an exceptionally original and deep experience, and it is still considered a foundational work of the turn-based tactical strategy genre with base management. It influenced dozens of later titles (from the official remake XCOM: Enemy Unknown from 2012 to independent projects inspired by its system), and even more than thirty years later, thanks to community ports and modern interfaces, it remains playable and serves as an example of how to connect strategic decision-making with emotionally demanding tactical combat, where every single decision carries weight and no mission is entirely without risk.

**Why play it:** For fans of turn-based strategy, this is a foundational work of the genre that, thanks to community ports, still works today and offers tense decision-making where no mission is without risk.

pc-dos__x-com-terror-from-deep.teaser: The X-COM sequel moved beneath the ocean surface; underwater bases and combat below the waves.
pc-dos__x-com-terror-from-deep.article:
**X-COM: Terror from the Deep** followed up in 1995 on the success of the first installment and moved the fight against the alien threat from land beneath the surface of the oceans, where, according to the story, the defeated invasion force had withdrawn. The game preserves the proven structure of its predecessor — on the strategic world map, the player builds underwater bases, directs research and equipment production, and sends submarines to intercept enemy craft, while tactical engagements take place on a turn-based battlefield where this time soldiers fight both underwater and on land, with different physics of movement, visibility, and weapon effects underwater, where harpoons and torpedoes behave differently from classic firearms.

The new setting brought its own set of enemies, weapons, and technologies inspired by ocean themes and Lovecraftian horror of the depths, shifting the game toward a darker and more anxious atmosphere than the original installment had. The game is also much harder due to more aggressive enemies, tougher opponents even in the early stages, and a less balanced pace of technological progress, so players often had to resort to more thorough mission planning and a more cautious approach than in UFO Defense. On the technical side, the game ran on the same engine as its predecessor, in VGA graphics with an isometric view, complemented by atmospheric music and sounds that evoked well the claustrophobic and oppressive feeling of the deep-sea environment and the isolation of bases on the ocean floor.

Terror from the Deep was received at the time of release as a worthy, if substantially harder, sequel, which, thanks to its high difficulty and new setting, earned itself a loyal fan base. Today it is seen as a respected, if less balanced, sister to the first installment, interesting especially for players who came to love the X-COM system and want to experience its darker, more demanding variation with a unique underwater atmosphere still rather uncommon in the genre.

**Why play it:** For players who loved the first X-COM and want to experience its darker, harder variation with a unique underwater atmosphere, this is a respected, if less balanced, sister to the first installment.

pc-dos__ultima-ii-revenge-of-enchantress.teaser: Time travel appears in the series for the first time; battles with Minax take place directly in real time on the map.
pc-dos__ultima-ii-revenge-of-enchantress.article:
**Ultima II: The Revenge of the Enchantress** follows up on Richard Garriott's debut and sends the player across time and space — from ancient Egypt through the distant future to the streets of New York. The sorceress Minax is taking revenge for the defeat of her master Mondain from the first installment, and the player must travel through several historical periods and parallel worlds to stop her before she destroys the Earth itself. The game keeps the top-down view, turn-based combat, and open traveling structure of the first installment, but adds a much more varied environment and, for the first time in the series, time travel as a game mechanic. Combat takes place in real time directly on the game map; the player moves between dozens of towns and locations and acquires ships, horses, and even spacecraft to reach places inaccessible on foot, which gave players of the time an unprecedented sense of freedom of movement across interconnected worlds.

On the technical side, it is still a roughly drawn world with simple colored tiles typical of the early eighties, but on the DOS computers of the time the game seemed impressive in its scope and the number of places one could visit. Music was practically absent; the atmosphere was instead built up through text descriptions and the occasional beep of the PC speaker. Contemporary reception was largely positive, the game sold well and cemented the reputation of the Ultima series as an ambitious pioneer of the genre, although reviewers even then pointed out unbalanced difficulty, frequent bugs, and confusing puzzle structures that required out-of-game hints.

From today's perspective, Ultima II is playable mostly as a historical curiosity and evidence of how quickly the series evolved in its early years — the third installment already fixed many of its shortcomings. Still, it is an important milestone: it showed that a computer RPG need not be confined to a single world, and it foreshadowed the later epic journeys across Britannia with which the Ultima series is associated to this day. For collectors and historians of the genre, it remains an interesting testament to how tentatively yet boldly the creators of the time were still searching for the language of the computer RPG.

**Why play it:** For collectors and historians of the genre, it is an interesting testament to how tentatively the creators of the time were still searching for the language of the computer RPG, even though the third installment quickly fixed many of its shortcomings.

pc-dos__ultima-iii-exodus.teaser: The first installment with a full party of four characters and tactical combat on its own screen.
pc-dos__ultima-iii-exodus.article:
**Ultima III: Exodus** marked a major leap forward for Richard Garriott's series. For the first time, the player could assemble an entire party of up to four characters instead of a single hero, combat moved to a separate tactical screen with visible unit positions, and the world of Sosaria gained a much more elaborate structure of towns, dungeons, and quests. The story revolves around a mysterious entity named Exodus, half machine and half demon, created by the sons of the defeated villains from the previous installments, who threatens the entire world. The player gradually pieces together information from NPCs, solves puzzles, and builds up the strength of their party before daring the final confrontation. Characters can also upgrade their equipment with merchants, and the game offered, for the first time in the series, a class system with different abilities, which gave party building a much more tactical dimension than in the previous installments.

The graphics used colored tiles and simple animations, but compared to its predecessors it appeared much more polished and clear, which also applied to the DOS version, which became the reference platform for later ports and conversions to other home computers. The music on the PC speaker was sparse, but the atmosphere was well carried by detailed descriptions and the feeling of a genuinely open world, where almost every building hid its own small story or a useful character. Critics and players received Exodus enthusiastically, and it is still considered a title that defined many conventions of the CRPG genre — party-based combat, an elaborate economic system, and an emphasis on freedom of choice in progressing through the story.

The influence of Ultima III on later games is hard to overstate; it inspired both its own sequels and competing series such as Might and Magic or Wizardry. Even today the game is playable thanks to its logical structure and clear rules, although the controls and pace of the game demand a good deal of patience from the modern player and acceptance of the era's conventions, such as manually mapping dungeons and terse text-based communication with the surrounding world.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its logical structure and clear rules, the game is playable even today, though its controls and pace demand a good deal of patience from the modern player with the terse text-based communication and manual dungeon mapping.

pc-dos__ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny.teaser: A darker Ultima: the true villain here is a tyrannical ideology, not a monster.
pc-dos__ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny.article:
**Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny** pushed the series toward a much darker and morally more complicated narrative. This time Britannia is threatened not by a magical monster but by an ideology - a tyrannical order called the Fellowship, which, under slogans of harmony and enlightenment, effectively oppresses the population and has imprisoned Lord British himself. Playing as the Avatar, the player must return to a world that appears to be prospering but is in fact suffering under a subtle dictatorship, and must learn to distinguish truth from propaganda. The game expanded the virtue system from the previous installment with a deeper ethical dilemma and, for the first time, offered a day-and-night cycle affecting character behavior and shop opening hours. Players could also resort to less heroic methods such as theft or deception, pushing the game closer to genuine moral ambiguity than RPG players of the time were used to.

Technically, this was one of the most extensive and detailed worlds DOS had seen up to that point - with elaborate interiors, a full VGA color palette in its later versions, and music that, thanks to sound card support, gave the game a truly epic atmosphere. Reviewers particularly praised the depth of the story and the freedom with which players could approach resolving conflicts, from diplomacy to open rebellion against the Fellowship. Ultima V is still cited today as one of the high points of the entire series and an example of how a political and philosophical theme can be brought into a fantasy RPG without feeling contrived or cheaply moralistic.

Even decades later, the game holds up as a remarkably mature piece of storytelling, though its text-command controls and the need for manual mapping today require a considerable amount of patience. For genre fans it remains a clear must-play title and a key point in the history of the Ultima saga, followed by the equally esteemed Ultima VI. Thanks to it, the series cemented its reputation as a maker of games unafraid to let players think about the consequences of their own decisions instead of just collecting experience and better gear.

**Why play:** For genre fans this is a clear must-play title and a key point in the history of the Ultima saga, though its text-command controls and manual mapping today demand a considerable amount of patience.

pc-dos__wizardry-proving-grounds-of-mad-.teaser: One of the founders of the CRPG genre; a merciless dungeon crawler with permadeath.
pc-dos__wizardry-proving-grounds-of-mad-.article:
**Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord**, together with Ultima, stood at the birth of the entire computer RPG genre and was one of the first to bring the spirit of tabletop games like Dungeons & Dragons into the form we now call a dungeon crawler. The player builds a party of up to six adventurers from several races and classes, descends with them into a ten-level maze beneath the wizard Werna's castle, and fights for survival in turn-based battles depicted only as simple enemy icons on a black background. The goal is to obtain a legendary amulet and confront the mad overlord himself, but the path there leads through brutally unforgiving mapping and the constant risk of permanent character death, after which the player must visit a temple and pay a hefty sum of gold to save the unfortunate victim's soul.

The graphics were limited to wireframe first-person views of corridors and a bare-bones text menu, and music was practically absent, yet the game still managed to evoke intense tension simply through how mercilessly it punished carelessness and poor combat decisions. Its contemporary reception was extraordinary - Wizardry became one of the commercially most successful early titles for personal computers and, in Japan, fundamentally shaped the birth of the entire JRPG genre, from Dragon Quest to Final Fantasy, where its traces remain visible to this day. The DOS version from the mid-1980s brought the game to a wider circle of PC platform players and helped it maintain commercial success even years after its original release on other systems.

Today, Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord is playable more as an archaeological artifact - its harsh difficulty and the need to manually draw maps on paper are extremely uncompromising for a modern player. Yet the game's historical significance is undeniable, and without it, dungeon crawlers and Japanese RPGs alike would look completely different, as would later generations of games inspired by its turn-based, permadeath-driven combat system.

**Why play:** Without this title, dungeon crawlers and Japanese RPGs alike would look different, though its harsh difficulty and the need to manually draw maps on paper are extremely uncompromising for a modern player.

pc-dos__wizardry-iv-return-of-werdna.teaser: A series unique - the player controls the defeated villain; notoriously brutal difficulty.
pc-dos__wizardry-iv-return-of-werdna.article:
**Wizardry IV: The Return of Werdna** turned the entire series' concept on its head - instead of a heroic party, the player controls Werdna, the defeated villain from the very first installment, who as a ghost tries to claw his way back up from the deepest level of the maze, regain his power, and take revenge on the adventurers who once defeated him. The game is notorious for its extreme difficulty and a design full of traps, ambushes, and the need to control summoned monsters and enemy agents instead of a classic balanced party. Progressing often requires descending deeper than one would expect, since the only path to power paradoxically leads further from the surface. The player must also handle battles against entire groups of enemies at once while distinguishing which of them are genuine opponents and which are merely traps set by former allies.

Visually, the game continues the bare-bones style of the previous installments - wireframe corridor views and a text menu, with no major graphical ambitions even by the standards of the late 1980s. Precisely because of this, all of the game's difficulty rested on thoughtful yet unforgiving puzzle and trap design, not on audiovisual presentation or a musical score, which the game practically lacked. Contemporary reviews praised the originality of the concept, but the game also earned a reputation as one of the most difficult CRPGs of all time - a reputation it still carries today and which discouraged a considerable portion of even experienced series veterans.

The fourth Wizardry installment is remembered today mainly as a curiosity and an extreme challenge for old-school genre enthusiasts - its steep learning curve and uncompromising design make it more of a historical oddity than a game for the average player. Even so, it earned respect as a bold experiment that was not afraid to view an otherwise seriously maintained fantasy dungeon crawl series from an unexpected angle, showing that even an established series can sacrifice one installment to a risky idea.

**Why play:** For old-school genre enthusiasts, this is a bold experiment and a historical oddity whose steep learning curve and uncompromising design are certainly not for the average player.

pc-dos__wizardry-v-heart-of-maelstrom.teaser: A return to the traditional party after the experimental fourth installment; old characters can be imported.
pc-dos__wizardry-v-heart-of-maelstrom.article:
**Wizardry V: Heart of the Maelstrom** returned the series to the traditional concept of a balanced adventuring party after the experimental fourth installment. This time the player faces a wizard named Rentaur, who threatens to gain control over a powerful magical vortex at the center of the maze, and must fight through a labyrinth full of traps, puzzles, and monsters with a party of characters to prevent this. The system of character creation, races, and classes builds on the previous installments, but with an improved interface and a somewhat friendlier, though still demanding, difficulty curve. The game also allowed importing characters from previous installments in the series, so loyal players could bring a party built up over the first three games into the new adventure and continue developing it.

Graphically, it was still bare-bones wireframe first-person views, but the DOS version benefited from better support for the graphics cards of the time and clearer menus than earlier installments in the series. The music remained minimalistic; the atmosphere was created more by a sense of permanent threat and the need for careful expedition planning, including supplies of food and light. Reviewers praised the return to thorough, thoughtful dungeon design and the more welcoming accessibility for new players, without the game losing the series' reputation as one of the most demanding on the market.

Heart of the Maelstrom is regarded today as one of the more mature installments of the classic Wizardry saga, one that shows well how the dungeon crawler genre gradually softened in the second half of the 1980s without abandoning its uncompromising core. For old-school RPG fans it remains a valuable and influential title of its era and a natural bridge to the later, even more elaborate installments of the series. Even years later, it's evident how carefully the labyrinth was designed to reward patient exploration and systematic recording of the clues found.

**Why play:** For old-school RPG fans this remains a valuable and influential title, whose carefully designed labyrinth rewards patient exploration and systematic recording of clues.

pc-dos__f-15-strike-eagle-ii.teaser: An accessible flight simulator with a choice between arcade and more realistic flight models.
pc-dos__f-15-strike-eagle-ii.article:
**F-15 Strike Eagle II** expanded and modernized the successful concept of an accessible flight simulator that MicroProse had launched back in the mid-1980s. The player takes the controls of an F-15E strike fighter and flies missions over several real-world conflict zones, from the Middle East to Vietnam, with the goal of destroying designated targets and returning safely to base. Compared to the first installment, the second offered a substantially more elaborate campaign structure, a wider selection of weapons and missions, and an improved choice between a more arcade-like and a more realistic flight model, which made the game accessible to both impatient players and fans of more detailed simulations. The campaign gradually unlocks more demanding missions and new aircraft; the player collects decorations for successfully completed tasks and can watch their pilot career gradually expand to include further conflicts and scenarios around the world.

The graphics used the vector 3D environments typical of MicroProse flight simulators of the time - flat colored polygons, but with smooth movement and a solid sense of speed and altitude. On the DOS platform, the audio benefited from support for the sound cards of the time, which delivered engine roar and radar warning tones convincingly by the standards of the day, noticeably heightening the tension during evasive maneuvers against enemy missiles. Contemporary reviews praised the game's balance between accessibility and authenticity, and it became one of the commercially successful titles of the genre at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s, helping MicroProse cement its reputation as a leading name in flight simulators.

Even years later, F-15 Strike Eagle II demonstrates how MicroProse managed to make flight simulators fun even for players who didn't want to study thick manuals. Its accessible difficulty and emphasis on action made it an ideal entry point into a genre that, in the 1990s, was further developed by titles like Falcon 3.0 or Aces of the Deep - games with substantially higher demands for simulation realism.

**Why play:** Thanks to its accessible difficulty and emphasis on action, it was an ideal entry point into the flight simulator genre, even though it was later surpassed by more demanding titles like Falcon 3.0.

pc-dos__might-and-magic-ii-gates-to-anot.teaser: Beneath the surface of a fantasy kingdom hides a sci-fi mystery; a party of up to six heroes.
pc-dos__might-and-magic-ii-gates-to-anot.article:
**Might and Magic II: Gates to Another World** followed up on Jon Van Caneghem's successful debut, taking players to the world of CRON, where beneath the surface of a fantasy kingdom lies a sci-fi mystery about the planet's extraterrestrial origins. The player once again assembles a party of up to six adventurers, explores an expansive map of towns, caves, and dungeons from a first-person perspective, and completes tasks for local rulers and mysterious machines that gradually reveal the true nature of the world. Compared to the first installment, the second offered a substantially larger and more varied map, more classes and races, and a more elaborate magic system divided among several spell schools. The player could also import characters from the first installment, allowing them to continue developing them, and the game offered a more elaborate economy with the purchase of ships and other equipment needed to explore more remote parts of the map.

Visually, the game stuck to the simple but functional wireframe corridor views and colored tile maps typical of dungeon crawlers of its time; the DOS version benefited from support for the graphics modes available at the time. The music was sparse, but the atmosphere was well built by the sense of discovering a vast and surprisingly interconnected world, where fantasy elements gradually gave way to the sci-fi twist that arrived with the revelation of the true nature of the planet CRON. Contemporary reviews particularly praised the scope of content and the depth of the character system, thanks to which the Might and Magic series began establishing itself as a serious competitor to Wizardry and Ultima in the dungeon crawler space.

Gates to Another World is still valued today by old-school CRPG fans as the installment that gave the series a clear identity, combining classic fantasy adventure with an unexpected sci-fi twist. The game's difficulty and scope make it a title more for patient players willing to map a vast maze step by step, but its influence on later installments in the series is undeniable.

**Why play:** For patient players willing to map a vast maze step by step, this is the installment that gave the series a clear identity combining fantasy adventure with an unexpected sci-fi twist.

pc-dos__king-s-quest-iv-perils-of-rosell.teaser: Princess Rosella takes the lead role for the first time; fairy-tale motifs and adventure puzzles.
pc-dos__king-s-quest-iv-perils-of-rosell.article:
**King's Quest IV: The Perils of Rosella** was the first in the series to place a female character in the lead role - Princess Rosella, daughter of King Graham, who sets out on a rescue mission after her father falls ill with a mysterious disease. To save him, she must obtain a magical fruit from a distant enchanted island, facing witches, fairies, and other fairy-tale creatures along the way while solving classic adventure puzzles based on collecting items and cleverly using them in the right place. The game continued the series' tradition of weaving European fairy-tale motifs into one cohesive fantasy world. Talking animals and magical helpers accompany Rosella on her journey; the player must correctly time many actions and combine items in a way typical of Sierra's adventure games of the era.

Technically, this was one of the first Sierra titles to fully take advantage of the capabilities of the era's 16-color EGA graphics cards and the emerging VGA cards, offering a significantly more colorful and detailed environment than previous installments. On DOS computers with sound card support, the game also offered digitized music and sound effects, considerably enhancing the fairy-tale atmosphere compared to the earlier beeps of the internal speaker. Contemporary reviews praised the game for its visuals, atmosphere, and the boldness of building a story around a female heroine, which was still an exception in adventure games of the time, though there were also objections to the overly unforgiving traps leading to the character's dead-end death.

King's Quest IV is regarded today as one of the high points of Sierra On-Line's early era and evidence of how rapidly graphic adventure games evolved visually and narratively in the second half of the 1980s. For genre fans it remains a pleasantly playable fairy-tale classic, albeit with the typically merciless adventure-game dead ends of the time, which today's player will probably appreciate better with the help of a walkthrough.

**Why play:** For genre fans, this is a pleasantly playable fairy-tale classic from Sierra On-Line's peak era, albeit with the typically merciless adventure-game dead ends that today's player will probably appreciate better with a walkthrough.

pc-dos__sid-meier-s-civilization.teaser: The turn-based strategy that founded the 4X genre; hooks you with 'just one more turn'.
pc-dos__sid-meier-s-civilization.article:
**Sid Meier's Civilization** established, in 1991, the entire turn-based strategy genre on a new principle: you lead a single civilization from its first settlements in the Stone Age to a space launch, with every decision - where to found a city, what to research, with whom to make peace - having an impact dozens of turns ahead. The design combined city building, a technology tree, diplomacy, and warfare into a single whole where nothing functions in isolation: a strong economy feeds the army, the army protects trade routes, trade finances science. The game ran even on hardware from the XT to the 486 with limited memory and graphics, because its turn-based nature forgave slower processors - the player only waited for the computation of opponents' turns, not for smooth animation.

Controls are purely mouse and keyboard, across a map divided into tiles, city menus, and a technology tree that lies behind the turn-based game like an invisible skeleton of progress. The game became famous for its ability to keep players glued to the screen long past when they'd planned to stop - the turn-based loop is designed so that after completing one round, it always tempts you to resolve just one more unfinished task, found just one more city, or complete one last invention. This "just one more turn" effect became synonymous with the entire 4X genre (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate), and Civilization didn't just define it in words but mechanically as well - victory can be achieved militarily, technologically, culturally, or diplomatically, offering players several parallel paths to the goal.

The game's influence on the industry is hard to overstate: it founded a series that continues to this day, inspired dozens of competing 4X titles, and its concept of balanced civilization development is still studied today. On period PCs it required only modest performance, so a huge number of people played it even on older machines, and it became one of the reasons the strategy genre expanded so rapidly on computers.

**Why play:** For anyone who wants to experience the birth of the turn-based 4X strategy genre in its purest form and has the patience for hours of planning instead of instant action.

pc-dos__simcity.teaser: An endless simulation without victory; it laid the foundations of the city-builder genre.
pc-dos__simcity.article:
**SimCity** from 1989 by Maxis turned the logic of games of that era upside down: instead of offering a fight for victory, it offered an endless simulation in which the player, as mayor, establishes zones for residential, industrial and commercial use, builds roads, power plants and water systems, and watches an empty map turn into a living metropolis. The game grew out of a fascination with urban planning and simulation models, and the result was a title with no fixed ending and no opponent - the only adversary is your own inability to keep the budget, traffic and residents' satisfaction in balance. On XT through 486 computers, SimCity ran smoothly even on modest hardware thanks to its simple 2D graphics and tile-based system, controlled with the mouse through a toolbar menu and a map divided into zone squares.

A key element is feedback: a poorly placed power plant raises pollution and lowers land values, missing roads cripple traffic and residents move away, excessive taxes slow growth. The game thus gently teaches systems thinking and long-term planning without ever explaining anything explicitly - the player learns the connections by watching graphs and advisor reports and experimenting. The game also featured random disasters like fires, earthquakes or the arrival of a giant monster, which added unpredictability and humor to the simulation.

SimCity founded the entire city-builder genre and became a template for later simulation games. It showed that a game doesn't need a victory or an ending to hold a player's attention for dozens of hours, and it is still cited today as one of the first truly successful city-management simulators.

**Why play it:** Ideal for players who enjoy building and systems planning more than combat - a classic that showed a meaningful game doesn't need a victory or an ending.

pc-9x__command-and-conquer-tiberian-sun.teaser: A darker sequel with a day-night cycle and mutated Brotherhood of Nod units.
pc-9x__command-and-conquer-tiberian-sun.article:
**Command & Conquer: Tiberian Sun** continued the famous strategy series and moved the conflict between GDI and the Brotherhood of Nod into a near future devastated by a mysterious substance called tiberium, which had turned entire landscapes into a dangerous yet valuable resource. The game expanded the proven mechanics of resource gathering, base building and unit control with new elements such as a day-night cycle affecting visibility on the battlefield, aircraft units capable of rapid redeployment, and cyborgs and genetic mutants in Nod's ranks that gave the faction a darker and more menacing character. Both sides' campaigns were again tied together with live-action cutscenes that gave the story about the fight for tiberium a cinematic feel and were among the era's draws for the whole real-time strategy genre.

Technically, this was an ambitious step. The game ran on an upgraded engine that allowed more complex and varied terrain, more units on screen at once, and more elaborate visual effects for explosions and fires, which took a toll on performance on the era's Windows 9x machines and meant the game shipped with a number of technical problems that required follow-up patches. The atmosphere was rounded out by music from Frank Klepacki, the series' longtime composer, who combined electronic and rock elements into Command & Conquer's signature sound and created melodies players still remember today.

Despite its early shortcomings, Tiberian Sun became a beloved part of the series and expanded the story of the tiberium war with another, darker chapter, later extended by the Firestorm expansion. Today it is seen as a transitional game between the classic style of the first Command & Conquer and the more modern approach of later strategy titles, and for fans of late-1990s RTS games it remains a nostalgic experience remembered with respect for its scope, ambition and sci-fi atmosphere plagued by tiberium. The combination of a grim narrative and morally ambiguous factions gave the series themes that later entries built upon, and many players still consider this the title where Command & Conquer became a larger sci-fi saga with its own mythology.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Command & Conquer series who want to experience a darker continuation of the tiberium war, sitting between the classic first game and the more modern strategy titles that followed it.

pc-9x__command-and-conquer-red-alert-2.teaser: An exaggerated, comic-book tone - dog units, bear weapons and commanders with one-liners.
pc-9x__command-and-conquer-red-alert-2.article:
**Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2** took players back into an alternate history in which the Cold War between the Soviets and the Allies escalated into an open conflict over the territory of the United States itself. Instead of Tiberian Sun's dark tone, the game embraced an openly exaggerated, at times almost comic-book style - whether it was dog units, bears as a Soviet weapon, or overly patriotic American commanders delivering witty one-liners. In terms of gameplay it's classic base building, ore harvesting and rivalry between two distinctly designed factions, where the Soviets rely on brute force, heavy machinery and psychic weapons, while the Allies bet on advanced technology, mobility and precision.

The game excelled in clarity and well-balanced pacing, which made it one of the most-played strategy titles of its era on Windows 9x computers, both in the campaign and especially in online multiplayer. Live-action cutscenes with real actors gave the campaign a cinematic atmosphere and humor, the music was again composed by Frank Klepacki, whose tracks are among the most recognizable themes of the whole series and remain associated with the image of a Soviet invasion of America to this day. The graphic style combined an isometric view with colorful effects and clearly readable units, which made the game accessible to less experienced players and simplified orientation even in larger battles.

Red Alert 2 received the Yuri's Revenge expansion, which added a third faction and new units, and to this day many fans consider it one of the high points of the classic Command & Conquer era. Its easy accessibility, distinctive factions and exaggerated story made it a game the community keeps coming back to even decades later, including modern fan modifications, community servers and an active online multiplayer scene. It was precisely the accessibility with which the game combined fast pacing, understandable units and an over-the-top story that made it an ideal gateway into the real-time strategy genre for a whole generation of players encountering Windows 9x for the first time, and many still remember it as one of the first truly big games on their computer.

**Why play it:** For players looking for an accessible, fast-paced RTS with distinctive factions and an over-the-top story - Red Alert 2 remains playable today thanks to its active community and mods.

pc-9x__age-of-empires.teaser: Founder of historical RTS games; leads civilizations from the Stone Age to the Iron Age.
pc-9x__age-of-empires.article:
**Age of Empires** moved real-time strategy out of fantasy and sci-fi settings into ancient civilizations and became one of the founding titles of the historical RTS genre on Windows 9x computers. The player progresses gradually through historical eras from the Stone Age to the Iron Age, builds settlements, gathers resources such as wood, food, gold and stone, and leads one of several ancient civilizations, for example the Egyptians, Greeks, Babylonians or Phoenicians, each with its own units, buildings and small in-game bonuses reflecting its historical character.

The game placed emphasis on historical atmosphere and education - individual campaigns followed real historical figures and events, from Egyptian pharaohs to the Greek wars, which was fairly unusual for the genre at the time and gave the game an educational dimension without detracting from its entertainment value or strategic depth. On Windows 9x computers the game ran smoothly even on less powerful hardware, the graphics were clear and units easily distinguishable by type and civilization, which made it easier to keep track of larger battles with many units on the map. The sound design and orchestral music helped create the impression of a journey across ancient empires and their rise and fall.

Age of Empires from Ensemble Studios laid the foundation for the Genie engine, on which the much more famous Age of Empires II was later built, and kicked off an entire series that remains among the best-known historical strategy games in the world to this day. Even years later, the game is valued as a pioneering title that managed to turn history into accessible and addictive strategic entertainment and inspired numerous other historical strategy games that followed it. The Rise of Rome expansion then added further civilizations and campaigns and showed that there was lasting interest among players in the format of a historical strategy game with real nations, something fully confirmed just two years later by the second installment, which perfected the concept.

**Why play it:** For fans of historical strategy games who want to discover the roots of the engine on which the much more famous Age of Empires II was later built.

pc-9x__age-of-empires-ii-age-of-kings.teaser: One of the most significant RTS games ever; campaigns about Joan of Arc and Genghis Khan.
pc-9x__age-of-empires-ii-age-of-kings.article:
**Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings** moved Ensemble Studios' historical strategy into the Middle Ages and became one of the most significant real-time strategy games ever made. The player builds settlements, develops an economy and leads one of many civilizations, from the Britons and the French to the Mongols or the Japanese, each with its own units, technologies and playstyle derived from historical reality.
