**Why play it:** Armor fans will appreciate its emphasis on the platoon's team tactics instead of the lone heroism of a single tank, even though commanding several vehicles at once takes a bit of getting used to.

pc-9x__steel-beasts.teaser: A tank combat model so faithful that a real army later used it for training.
pc-9x__steel-beasts.article:
**Steel Beasts** was created with the ambition of offering a maximally faithful model of modern tank combat, so much so that the game was later adopted as a training tool by real army units, which is exceptional among domestic simulators of the nineties. The player could pilot modern main battle tanks, monitor crew behavior, work with a thermal sight, rangefinder, and various types of ammunition, and take part in large-scale scenarios in which they cooperated with other vehicles and infantry against enemy forces on an open, terrain-varied battlefield.

The game calmly built on an elaborate model of ballistics, visibility, and target recognition, where the player had to correctly identify the type of enemy vehicle before choosing the appropriate ammunition and firing, and an error in estimating distance or terrain slope could mean a miss even on what seemed like an easy shot. The graphical presentation was functional and clear, emphasizing the readability of the battlefield and the tank's instruments over flashy visual detail, and the audio, with the rumble of the engine, the turning of the turret, and the deep sound of the main gun firing, nicely conveyed the ponderous yet powerful presence of armored vehicles on the battlefield.

Steel Beasts is still remembered today as one of the most authentic tank simulators ever made for personal computers, and its continued development and professional use by armed forces prove that the game's basic model has held up even after many years. For fans of truly thorough armor simulation, the game remains nearly unrivaled, even though its austere controls and technically oriented interface require newcomers to put in considerable effort to learn them. The fact that a domestic simulator gradually evolved into a tool used even in the training of real tank units is quite exceptional among games of this period and lends the title a special historical weight.

**Why play it:** For fans of truly thorough armor simulation, this is a nearly unrivaled title, whose later professional use by armed forces lends it special historical weight, even though its austere interface requires considerable effort to learn.

pc-9x__panzer-elite.teaser: A Second World War tank campaign following a single crew across years and positions inside the tank.
pc-9x__panzer-elite.article:
**Panzer Elite** took players into tank battles of the Second World War on the Western Front, where they could fight on the side of either the German Wehrmacht or the Allied forces, and offered a campaign following the crew of a single tank across several years of the conflict, with a gradual upgrade of equipment matching the historical development of armored vehicles. The player could move between different positions inside the tank, from commander to gunner to driver, which gave the game a distinctive sense of connection with the crew and their fate over the course of the long campaign.

The game relied on a fairly realistic model of ballistics and damage, where the outcome depended on the type of ammunition, the angle of impact, and the specific spot hit on the hull or turret of the enemy vehicle, and the open battlefields allowed players to choose between a cautious advance using terrain cover and a more aggressive, direct approach. The graphical rendering of the terrain, villages, and vehicles was decent for the turn of the millennium, with clearly recognizable silhouettes of individual tank types, and the audio, with crew reports in the national languages of both sides, nicely underscored the authenticity of whichever front the player found themselves on. Switching between positions inside the tank also forced the player to alternate between the roles of observer, gunner, and driver depending on what the specific battlefield situation required at the moment.

Panzer Elite won favor among tank simulator fans through its combination of a personal view of the crew with an elaborate model of the armored vehicles of both warring sides, and through the length of its campaign, which followed the war's development from its early years to its conclusion. Today the game is interesting especially as one of the few titles of its time to offer a symmetrical view of the conflict from both sides of the front line, similar to what flight simulators focused on the Battle of Britain had done a few years earlier. It is precisely this two-sided perspective and the personal bond with one particular crew that give the campaign an emotional dimension usually missing from purely tactical titles.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its symmetrical view of the conflict from both warring sides and the personal bond with one particular crew, it offers a campaign with an emotional dimension usually missing from purely tactical tank simulators.

pc-9x__im1a2-abrams.teaser: A modern M1A2 Abrams with laser rangefinder and thermal sight for night and fog.
pc-9x__im1a2-abrams.article:
**iM1A2 Abrams** belonged to the line of titles published by Interactive Magic, recognizable by the distinctive lowercase i in their names, and focused on the modern American M1A2 Abrams tank in hypothetical conflicts of the nineties. The player sat both behind the main gun and behind the wheel of the tank, handled target acquisition using a laser rangefinder and thermal sight, and had to account for limited visibility in poor weather or at night, when combat tactics differed markedly from a clear day with good terrain visibility.

The game offered a solid damage and ballistics model matching the genre's demands of the time, placing emphasis on choosing the correct ammunition type for the target and on using terrain as cover against enemy fire, which was generally true of all tank simulators of that era, but iM1A2 Abrams handled this principle with an honest effort at accuracy. The graphical rendering of the terrain and vehicles matched the standard of the late nineties, and the sound design, with the rumble of the engine, turret rotation, and crew callouts, nicely rounded out the feel of operating heavy armor on a modern battlefield. The campaign gradually put the player up against more varied opponents and terrain, forcing adaptation of tactics from open desert country to more densely built-up areas.

iM1A2 Abrams is remembered today mainly by fans of the Interactive Magic series as one of the more thorough attempts to capture the M1A2 Abrams tank at a time when it was still a relatively new and technologically advanced weapon. For collectors and enthusiasts of nineties tank simulators, the game remains an interesting entry in the broader lineup of similarly focused titles from the publisher of the time, which specialized specifically in military simulations of various kinds of hardware. Together with the other titles in the series, it rounds out the picture of an era when one publisher built its reputation precisely on the serial production of military simulators gradually covering different kinds of weapons and combat equipment.

**Why play it:** Collectors and enthusiasts of nineties tank simulators will enjoy it as an interesting entry in Interactive Magic's broader lineup of military titles, even if today it's more of a collection filler than a must-play.

pc-9x__destroyer-command.teaser: The Battle of the Atlantic from the other side of the periscope; a destroyer hunts submarines with sonar and depth charges.
pc-9x__destroyer-command.article:
**Destroyer Command** was created as a companion piece to the then-new Silent Hunter II and turned the view of the Battle of the Atlantic around to the other side of the periscope, with the player now commanding an Allied destroyer whose job was to protect convoys from German submarines. The game combined patrolling around merchant ships with the active use of sonar and depth charges, requiring the player to estimate a hidden submarine's position from sound traces and react quickly before a U-boat could launch torpedoes at one of the escorted convoy ships. Besides the direct hunting role, the player also had to manage coordination with other escort vessels and decide when it was more advantageous to split forces into a wider patrol and when to instead concentrate the defense close to the most threatened cargo ships.

Technically, the game benefited from the same engine as Silent Hunter II, offering a convincing depiction of a stormy ocean, burning ships, and nights lit by flares while searching for an enemy submarine. The sound design, with active sonar pings, crew reports of detection, and the rumble of depth charges, nicely built the tension of a chase in which the roles of hunter and hunted could flip at any moment. The campaign offered a sequence of patrols of increasing difficulty, matching the evolution of anti-submarine tactics over the course of the war, and the player could thus watch how the technical means of detecting submarines gradually improved on both sides of the conflict.

Destroyer Command is seen today as an interesting complement to the classic submarine series, offering a contrasting perspective that let players experience the Battle of the Atlantic from the hunter's side rather than the hunted submarine. Although the game never achieved the same popularity as its companion Silent Hunter II, among genre fans it is valued precisely for this rare opportunity to see the same conflict from the opposite side of the surface. Bundling both games together also let players experience the very same battle both from a submarine's viewpoint and from that of its pursuer, a unique approach within the genre to a single historical subject.

**Why play it:** Fans of submarine simulators will be drawn in by the rare chance to experience the Battle of the Atlantic from the hunter's perspective rather than the hunted submarine's, especially combined with Silent Hunter II as two sides of the same conflict.

pc-9x__panzer-commander.teaser: A tank simulation of both fronts of WWII from the position of commander, gunner, and driver alike.
pc-9x__panzer-commander.article:
**Panzer Commander** took the player through tank warfare on both the Eastern and Western fronts of the Second World War in the form of two separate campaigns, one for the German Wehrmacht and the other for the American army, following the fate of one particular tank commander from the early battles through to the later stages of the conflict. The player could switch between the positions of commander, gunner, and driver, direct the movement of the whole unit within a smaller formation, and carry out missions ranging from reconnaissance and defending key points to breakthrough attacks against fortified lines.

The game worked with fairly open battlefields where using terrain, forests, and villages as cover mattered, and it offered a damage model that distinguished individual parts of the tank, so that even a seemingly survived hit could knock out the crew or the main weapon. The graphical rendering of the terrain and vehicles was solid for the end of the nineties, and the sound design, with the rumble of engines, the crack of turrets, and crew callouts in the appropriate language, nicely conveyed the atmosphere of armored combat on an open front, whether it was the snowy plains in the east or the French countryside in the west. The differing climate and terrain conditions of the two theaters also called for a different approach to tactics, which gave the campaigns some welcome variety.

Panzer Commander is remembered today as one of the more ambitious tank simulators of its generation thanks to its two full-fledged campaigns from different points of view on the war and its emphasis on the personal story of a tank commander making his way through the conflict. For fans of World War II armor, the game remains an interesting choice even today, especially thanks to the variety of environments between the two theaters and the honest tank-combat model fitting for its era. The ability to experience the war from both the German and the American crew's perspective also gave players a more complete picture of how armament, tactics, and deployment conditions differed for armored units on both sides of the front.

**Why play it:** Thanks to two full-fledged campaigns from the German and American perspectives and an honest tank-combat model, it will appeal to fans of World War II armor who value seeing both sides of the front.

pc-9x__grand-theft-auto.teaser: The foundation of the famous series, still seen from a bird's-eye view; the freedom to do evil was groundbreaking back then.
pc-9x__grand-theft-auto.article:
**Grand Theft Auto** laid the foundation for one of the most successful game brands of all time, in a form that differs fundamentally from later installments. The game is played from a top-down view, across three loosely connected cities named Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City, whose names the franchise later borrowed for its three-dimensional sequel. The player takes on the role of a small-time criminal who picks up jobs from various gangs via street payphones and gradually climbs the underworld hierarchy. It was precisely this openness and the option to either complete missions or simply drive around the city causing minor mischief that felt unusual at the time of release and foreshadowed the later sandbox genre.

The core of the gameplay is stealing and driving vehicles, shootouts with the police, and completing missions such as delivering goods, eliminating a target, or a chase. The player's behavior is tracked by a star-rating system indicating the level of police attention, which deploys increasingly tougher units, up to military forces, as violence escalates. The graphics consist of small but legible sprites viewed from a fixed isometric camera, accompanied by radio stations playing music and parodic DJ segments that rounded out the atmosphere of a satirical metropolis. It was precisely this humorous detachment that set the game apart from the raw impression its content alone might suggest, and a number of hidden bonuses and jokes rewarded players for thoroughly exploring the streets.

Grand Theft Auto caused considerable controversy after release over its violence and the way it rewarded criminal behavior, and in some countries it faced censorship or an outright sales ban, which paradoxically only increased its media coverage. Even so, it became commercially successful and kicked off a series that remains among the most significant in the games industry to this day. Today the controls and graphics feel archaic, navigating the city without a map is demanding, and the gameplay feels stiff compared to later titles, but its historical significance as a pioneer of the open-world genre is undeniable.

**Why play it:** As a pioneer of the open-world genre it holds undeniable historical significance, even if the archaic controls, graphics, and mapless navigation today make playing it more of a curiosity than a comfortable experience.

pc-9x__grand-theft-auto-2.teaser: A top-down sequel with gang reputation; favor with one gang means war with another.
pc-9x__grand-theft-auto-2.article:
**Grand Theft Auto 2** carries on from the first game with the same top-down view, but moves the action to an unspecified future and offers a larger, more elaborate city divided into three districts, each with its own character. The novelty is a reputation system with the individual gangs, where completing a gang's jobs builds the player's trust with that group while possibly making an enemy of another. This element added a layer of tactical decision-making, since friendship with one gang could mean hostility from another and turn the player's own surroundings into dangerous, watched territory that had to be approached with caution from then on.

The gameplay remains faithful to the proven formula of stealing cars, completing missions, and fleeing the police, with the star system indicating the level of pursuit expanded and tightened with new stages of security-force deployment. New weapons, vehicles, and even machines offering bonuses directly on the street were added, including temporary character upgrades. The visual style stayed true to the first game's isometric view, but with a higher level of detail and a more colorful, futuristically toned palette evoking gritty industrial districts. The sound again drew on radio stations parodying period pop culture and advertising, giving the game the same ironic tone as its predecessor.

By the time of its release, Grand Theft Auto 2 already stood in the shadow of the series' upcoming three-dimensional leap, so it didn't feel as groundbreaking as the first game, even though it was rated as a successful refinement of the core concept that offered more content and systemic depth. The gang reputation system became one of the elements that returned, in altered form, in later installments of the series. Today it's viewed mainly as the last stop of the old two-dimensional era of GTA — still playable and functional, but overshadowed by the revolution that arrived the very next year with the move to 3D and, with it, the series' worldwide breakthrough.

**Why play it:** For series fans, it's a gameplay-wise still functional last stop of the old two-dimensional GTA era, even if it's now overshadowed by the revolution the move to 3D brought a year later.

pc-9x__x-com-apocalypse.teaser: The series moves into a single megacity; strategic management combined with detective investigation.
pc-9x__x-com-apocalypse.article:
**X-COM: Apocalypse** is the third installment of the cult series about defending Earth against an alien invasion and is the first to set it within a single enormous futuristic city, Mega-Primus, divided into dozens of separate districts each with its own administration and public mood. The player again runs the X-COM organization, builds and equips bases, recruits and trains agents, and leads investigations into strange incidents that gradually reveal a network of infiltration by alien cults as well as corporations operating directly within the city. The game's structure thus combines strategic resource management with a detective thread of tracking down the source of the threat and those truly behind it.

The tactical battles that form the core of the series here for the first time offer a choice between the classic turn-based system and a newly introduced real-time mode with the ability to pause the game at any point and issue orders, which was a significant novelty for the genre and remains a debated change to this day. The combat takes place in densely built urban environments with civilians, traffic, and destructible architecture, where every rocket hit can bring down an entire building along with unprotected bystanders, raising both the tension and the tactical demands. Base management, technology research, and equipment manufacturing remain as complex as in previous installments, complemented by trading and shifting diplomatic relations with the various factions within the city.

Apocalypse was received with respect for its ambitious scope at the time of release, even though part of the player base criticized it for its complexity, bloated systems, and the technical demands it placed on computers of the era. Within the series it is valued today precisely for its bold urban setting and choice of combat system, even though it departed in many ways from the raw atmosphere of the first two games. For fans of turn-based strategy it remains a demanding but rewarding experience that still shows the depth and systemic ambition the genre was capable of reaching in the nineties.

**Why play it:** For fans of turn-based strategy who don't mind a steep learning curve and bloated systems, Apocalypse offers some of the most ambitious and deepest battles the genre produced in the nineties.

pc-9x__worms-2.teaser: Turn-based warfare of worms on destructible terrain; a richer and more polished successor to the first game.
pc-9x__worms-2.article:
**Worms 2** expands the proven concept of turn-based artillery combat with harmless-looking worms into a more polished and content-rich whole. The principle remains the same as in the first game: two to four teams of worms take turns on a destructible 2D map, trying to use a wide arsenal of weapons — from the bazooka through the holy hand grenade to a sheep carrying a timed charge — to wipe out the opposing units before those units wipe them out. The terrain can be blasted apart and craters form from the explosions, making every round a unique tactical puzzle where judging distance, power, and wind's effect on a projectile's path is what matters. Movement across the map is aided by tools such as the rope or the parachute, mastering which opens up room for bolder maneuvers and escapes from enemy fire.

Compared to the first game, a range of new weapons and tools was added, along with improved graphics with more colorful and detailed environments and an expanded editor allowing players to build their own maps and scenarios to their own liking. Humor remains a key part of the experience, whether in the absurd sound effects, the overly theatrical deaths of the worms, or the contrast itself between the adorable look of the little characters and the devastating arsenal at their disposal. Local multiplayer for several players on one computer was the main reason the game became a beloved party pastime in schools and among friends, where a single round could easily eat up an entire afternoon.

Worms 2 was received at the time of release as a marked improvement over the first game and cemented the series' position as one of the most enjoyable turn-based combat games on PC. Its influence is still evident in the artillery-strategy genre today, where it remains a frequently cited and referenced model. Short, intense matches full of unexpected twists keep the game feeling fresh, even though two years later it was partly overshadowed by its own improved sequel subtitled Armageddon.

**Why play it:** Thanks to its short matches full of unexpected twists and its place in the history of the artillery genre, Worms 2 is worth returning to even today, even though in many ways it was surpassed by its own sequel, Armageddon.

pc-9x__worms-armageddon.teaser: The peak of the Worms series; the most extensive weapon arsenal and a community still alive today.
pc-9x__worms-armageddon.article:
**Worms Armageddon** is widely regarded as the pinnacle maturation of the whole series and remains among its most-played installments to this day thanks to an active community and Team17's endless support. The basic principle of a turn-based battle between teams of worms on destructible terrain remains unchanged, but the game delivers the most extensive weapon arsenal in the whole series, from the classic bazooka and holy hand grenade to extravagances like the Sheep Launcher cannon, a teleporting banana bomb, or the good old dagger for close combat. Each weapon has its own style of use and forces the player to think about angle, power, and wind's effect on a projectile's path, turning every round into a small tactical calculation where even a slight inaccuracy can decide the fate of an entire team.

Compared to its predecessor, the game fine-tuned weapon balance, added new game modes, and significantly expanded the possibilities of the scenario and map editor, which over the years turned it into a living platform for creating custom content and hosting tournaments. The visual style stays true to the cartoonish, colorful aesthetic with a strong dose of black humor, backed by the iconic sound bites of the worms, which became an inseparable part of the series' identity and an unmistakable memory for an entire generation of players. The multiplayer experience, whether local or online, remains the core of its appeal, with the game able to flip an entire match's outcome on a single lucky or unlucky turn.

Upon release, Worms Armageddon received widespread acclaim as the definitive version of the concept and became the reference point for every subsequent installment of the series. Thanks to its unceasing community, mods, and organized tournaments, it remains playable and active even decades later, a rare feat for a title from the end of the nineties. Even today it's among the titles well suited to firing up for a few quick rounds with a group of friends without losing any of its infectious fun along the way.

**Why play it:** Thanks to an active community, mods, and tournaments that keep the game alive to this day, Worms Armageddon is an ideal choice for a quick round of turn-based combat with friends, even decades later.

pc-9x__delta-force.teaser: A tactical shooter with vast outdoor terrain instead of Doom or Quake's narrow corridors.
pc-9x__delta-force.article:
**Delta Force** was made by NovaLogic and released for PC in 1998 as a military tactical shooter that stood apart from the competition of the time mainly through the sheer scale of its playing space. The player takes on the role of a member of an elite US special forces unit and moves through missions set in deserts, mountains, and urban areas around the world, alternating stealthy advances with long-range firefights in the open. Instead of the narrow corridors typical of Doom or Quake, the game offered sprawling outdoor terrain, so a sniper rifle and tactical planning of your approach based on the landscape actually made sense, including choosing weapons and equipment before each mission according to how the objective was meant to play out.

Technically, the game was powered by NovaLogic's own voxel-based terrain rendering (Voxel Space), which made it possible to render huge open landscapes with a long draw distance — something no polygon engine of the time could match. The player could spot enemies at great range and choose between a close-quarters assault and a cautious flanking maneuver through the terrain. The price for this was blockier, less detailed character and object graphics that looked somewhat dated even for their time. The sound and atmosphere leaned on a plain, matter-of-fact portrayal of armed conflict without pathos, which fit the emphasis on weapon realism and character vulnerability — a couple of hits could quickly end a mission, setting the game apart from the more arcade-like shooters of the era.

Delta Force was well received, especially thanks to its multiplayer, where the sprawling maps allowed for a different style of play than the arena-based approach of contemporary shooters, and it became the foundation of a long-running series of sequels from NovaLogic that returned again and again to its theme and its commitment to realism. In the history of the genre, it ranks alongside Rainbow Six among the pioneers of tactical military shooters emphasizing realism and open space over corridor-based action. Today it looks visually dated, and the controls and pacing are noticeably a product of their era, but as one of the first truly open outdoor battlefields in a shooter, it still holds historical significance and remains an interesting stop for anyone curious about the roots of the genre.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the roots of tactical military shooters and their shift toward open outdoor battlefields, Delta Force still holds historical significance, even though it looks dated today both graphically and in its controls.

pc-9x__swat-3-close-quarters-battle.teaser: A tactical shooter where your weapon is the last resort — commanding a team and negotiating with hostage-takers.
pc-9x__swat-3-close-quarters-battle.article:
**SWAT 3: Close Quarters Battle** was released in 1999 under the Sierra label, and unlike the action shooters of its time, it built on a slow, tactical approach to violence in which the weapon is only the last resort for resolving a situation. The player commands a SWAT police tactical unit, and the job isn't just to shoot but above all to manage the team — splitting up teammates, issuing orders to breach a room, negotiating with detainees, or using non-lethal means such as batons or tear gas wherever the situation allows. Missions include hostage rescues, actions against armed suspects, and negotiations, and an incorrect or hasty approach often means the death of a hostage, a teammate, or the needless killing of a civilian, all of which count as a mission failure in the scoring.

The game placed extraordinary emphasis on the AI of civilians and opponents alike, and on how the player communicates with their team — a detailed command system was available for movement, clearing rooms, opening doors with cover, and handling detained persons, so success often depended more on patience and communication than on aim. Visually, it consisted of dark, cramped building interiors, warehouses, apartments, and public spaces, which, combined with quiet, tense music and the constant awareness that a single wrong step could end the mission, created an atmosphere much closer to a real police operation than a B-movie shootout full of flashy animations.

Contemporary reception ranked the game among the best tactical shooters of its generation, praising above all the depth of its missions, the behavior of its AI, and its sensitive treatment of the subject of tactical police units. SWAT 3 influenced later tactical titles focused on police and counter-terrorist operations and is still mentioned today as one of the important forerunners of modern tactical games of this type, including newer titles built on a similarly slow and deliberate pace. Even with today's dated graphics, it remains a tense experience for players who enjoy careful, deliberate progress more than reflexes and fast shooting.

**Why play it:** Anyone who prefers deliberate progress and the tension of a realistic operation over reflexes and fast shooting will find SWAT 3 a tense experience, even with its now-dated graphics.

pc-9x__tom-clancy-s-rainbow-six-rogue-sp.teaser: A tactical shooter built on careful preparation, where a single hit often means death.
pc-9x__tom-clancy-s-rainbow-six-rogue-sp.article:
**Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear** was released by Red Storm Entertainment in 1999 as a sequel to the first Rainbow Six, expanding on its recipe for a realistic tactical shooter built as much on preparation as on the action itself. Before each mission, the player draws up a plan of advance for multiple teams, sets routes, entry points, loadouts, and precise timing of actions, and only then watches how that plan plays out in the actual operation — a single hit is often enough to kill the character, so caution and thorough preparation carry more weight than reflexes and quick reactions. The missions are drawn from both fictional and realistically inspired counter-terrorist operations around the world, from rescuing hostages on a plane or a ship to disarming explosives and apprehending suspects.

Compared to the first game, Rogue Spear offered improved graphics, more missions, a wider selection of weapons, and expanded options for configuring the team's equipment before an operation, letting the player tailor tactics to a specific situation in much greater detail. The game later received several expansion packs adding more missions, weapons, and environments, showing just how strong a player base it managed to build. Its multiplayer, which pitted small teams of players against each other in a one-life mode with no respawns, was one of the things that kept the game alive over the long term within the community of tactical-shooter fans and competitive clan matches of the era.

At the time, Rogue Spear was received as a successful improvement over the original Rainbow Six, and together with SWAT 3 it shaped the tactical military shooter genre at the end of the nineties, when the emphasis on planning and realism stood in direct contrast to fast-paced action shooters. Today it is seen as one of the cornerstones of the entire Rainbow Six series, which years later led to the massively popular Rainbow Six Siege, and as proof that thorough planning could be just as tense in a shooter as the firefight itself.

**Why play it:** As one of the cornerstones of a series that later led to Rainbow Six Siege, Rogue Spear shows just how tense thorough mission planning could be, even before the firefight itself begins.

pc-9x__everquest.teaser: A groundbreaking 3D MMORPG with thousands of players; without a reliable group, you won't survive in Norrath.
pc-9x__everquest.article:
**EverQuest** marked a leap for the MMORPG genre in 1999 similar to what Doom had done a few years earlier for first-person action games — suddenly there was a three-dimensional world in which thousands of players moved simultaneously, not just a handful of text commands like the earlier MUD games. The player created a character from several races and classes, set out into the sprawling world of Norrath, and spent hours killing monsters, collecting loot, and completing quests, but the main focus of the game was really about building a group — without reliable allies, it was hard to survive in the more dangerous areas. Progress was deliberately slow and grueling, forcing players to spend entire evenings in a single location and rely on strangers they met right there in the game.

Technically, the game ran on an engine capable of rendering vast outdoor areas as well as dark underground dungeons, which placed considerable demands on the hardware of the time — new players often complained about long loading times and the need to upgrade their graphics card and internet connection. The atmosphere was reinforced by melancholic music and a persistent sense that the world existed and carried on living even without a logged-in player, including the risk that after death a character would lose experience and have to run back into the dungeon to recover their own corpse, which placed the game among the noticeably harsher experiences of its time.

EverQuest quickly became a phenomenon and for several years defined what a subscription-based online RPG should look like — competitors like Asheron's Call followed just a few months later. The player community around it also created some of the first extensive fan databases, guides, and discussion forums, which became a model for later online games. Today the game is mostly remembered by MMO veterans who miss the slower, more dangerous, and more social take on the online world that modern titles no longer offer, and many still call it one of the founding cornerstones of the genre.

**Why play it:** For MMO veterans who miss the slower, more dangerous, and more social take on the online world, EverQuest remains one of the founding cornerstones of the entire genre.

pc-9x__asheron-s-call.teaser: EverQuest's rival, with free-form character development and body-part targeting instead of fixed classes.
pc-9x__asheron-s-call.article:
**Asheron's Call** was released in 1999 under Turbine Entertainment and became one of the first serious rivals to EverQuest, even though it went its own way in many respects. Instead of rigidly fixed classes, it offered a free-form character development system where the player put together skills according to how they wanted to fight and play, and instead of densely populated cities, it built on the feel of a vast, sparsely settled continent called Dereth, full of ruins, magic, and dangerous monsters. The combat system also offered optional targeting of individual body parts, which wasn't common in the genre at the time.

The game also stood out for its technical handling of the world — instead of switching between separate zones with loading screens, Dereth ran as a single seamless map that could be traveled on foot, through portals, or with the help of levitation and speed spells. The developers also regularly added new content through story events that permanently changed the world and that players could take part in directly, which was a fairly bold move at a time when online games were still finding their identity. The darkly toned graphics and atmospheric music supported the feeling of a lonely journey through a harsh landscape full of forgotten ruins and ancient curses. A system of portals connecting distant locations also helped players get around the map, so they didn't have to rely solely on long treks on foot.

Although the game never managed to surpass EverQuest in popularity, among genre fans it earned a reputation as a title with a more thoughtfully designed and player-friendlier character system, a gentler difficulty curve for beginners, and less harsh punishment for character death. It's still cited today as proof that the MMORPGs of the late nineties didn't have to copy a single proven formula and could offer their own distinctive take on online adventure, emphasizing freedom, exploration, and a living, changing story of the world.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for proof that late-nineties MMORPGs didn't have to copy a single proven formula will find in Asheron's Call a more thoughtfully designed character system and a gentler entry point for beginners.

pc-9x__meridian-59.teaser: One of the very first graphical MMORPGs from 1996; a world seen through a first-person view.
pc-9x__meridian-59.article:
**Meridian 59** is remembered today as one of the very first graphical MMORPGs ever made — it came out all the way back in 1996, years before EverQuest, and together with Ultima Online it paved the way for the entire genre. Players found themselves in a fictional university campus, from which a magic portal took them into a dark fantasy world where, unlike later MMOs, they experienced the action from a first-person view, similar to the action games of the time like Doom. This visually set the game apart from everything else on the market at launch and remained one of the title's defining quirks throughout its entire run.

The game, made by Archetype Interactive, combined real-time combat with a simple but functional system of magic and items and ran on relatively modest graphics, which let it run even on the weaker hardware common among home computers of the time connected over slow modems. Its business model was also significant — Meridian 59 was among the first titles to charge for play through a monthly subscription, setting the direction that nearly the entire online gaming genre would later follow. The world was divided into smaller, interconnected areas, and the atmosphere was reinforced by a dark, gothic aesthetic and music that underscored the sense of danger around every corner, as well as the need to cooperate with other players to complete tougher quests.

At the time of release, only a modest number of people played the game compared to the later giants of the genre, but Meridian 59's historical significance is undeniable — without it, the path to EverQuest and the later major MMORPGs would have looked different. The game also received further updates even after competing titles arrived, which speaks to a surprisingly loyal core community. Today it's more of a curiosity for game-industry historians than a playable experience for the average player, but as a milestone it remains unmissable and a reminder of how tentatively and experimentally the online RPG genre once began, before the rules we now take for granted had settled into place.

**Why play it:** For game-industry historians, Meridian 59 is an unmissable stop — it shows how tentatively and experimentally the online RPG genre once began, even if today it serves as a playable experience for very few.

pc-9x__subspace.teaser: A mass multiplayer real-time space shooter for dozens of players at once.
pc-9x__subspace.article:
**SubSpace**, later renamed Continuum, brought something in 1997 under the Virgin Interactive publishing label that had few equivalents at the time — a mass multiplayer real-time space shooter for dozens of players at once on a single server. Instead of the gradual character-building of the MMORPGs of the era, it was about fast, skill-based combat between small spacecraft, where players split into teams and fought for control of territory, bases, or flags. Between matches, they could choose from several types of ships with different armaments and different roles within the team, from fast fighters to slower but tougher support ships.

The game's graphics were deliberately simple, two-dimensional, and viewed from above, but that actually suited the dial-up modem connections of the era well — the game ran smoothly even on slow internet, where competing 3D titles would stutter or simply weren't reasonably playable at all. Central to it was ship movement physics reminiscent of the classic Asteroids, joined by dozens of types of weapons and upgrades, and above all an emphasis on teamwork and tactics, which helped build a loyal community of players who organized their own leagues, tournaments, and specialized game modes run on private servers that the community itself more or less managed.

SubSpace never became a mass hit comparable to the MMORPG hits of its time, but among the pioneers of online multiplayer it holds a firm place as one of the first titles that managed to bring together a large number of players in one action-packed world without requiring expensive hardware or a fast connection. Its legacy is visible in later online action games built on a similar model of mass but accessible multiplayer for a broad player base, and thanks to its dedicated community, the game itself kept playable servers running long after its official end.

**Why play it:** As one of the first titles to bring together a large number of players in one action-packed world without demanding expensive hardware, SubSpace still holds a firm place among the pioneers of online multiplayer today.

pc-9x__king-s-quest-i-quest-for-crown.teaser: The game that started Sierra's fairy-tale series; a remake with colorful VGA graphics.
pc-9x__king-s-quest-i-quest-for-crown.article:
**King's Quest I: Quest for the Crown** is the game with which Sierra On-Line's entire series of fairy-tale adventures actually began — this particular version from 1990, however, is a remake of the original 1984 game, graphically and technically upgraded for the new SCI engine from blocky AGI images to more colorful VGA graphics. The player takes on the role of the knight Graham, whom King Edward sends to find three lost treasures of the kingdom of Daventry — a magic mirror, an invisible shield, and a chest that fills itself with gold. Moving the character is handled with the arrow keys, while the surroundings are dealt with using text commands or simple keyboard shortcuts, which was still a standard approach for Sierra titles at a time when mice were only just becoming common in adventure games. The game leaves the player free to roam the open map of the kingdom without any fixed order of tasks, so the three treasures can be sought in any order — an unusual approach to adventure-game structure back in 1984.

The game world is assembled from fairy-tale motifs — a giant, dwarves, a witch, and the three bears all meet here within a compact, easy-to-navigate map of locations that can be finished in a few hours if the player knows the solutions to the puzzles; without a walkthrough, though, the game can frustrate with sudden deaths and dead ends typical of early Sierra adventures. The music and sound were modest given the standard PC hardware of the time, so the atmosphere was carried mainly by the graphics themselves and by a fairy-tale story that skillfully wove familiar fairy-tale characters into one consistent world. The game's historical significance is nonetheless undeniable — King's Quest laid the foundation for the entire genre of graphical adventures with free character movement around the scene and influenced dozens of later games.

Today it plays more like a museum piece than a smooth experience — the controls and puzzle logic are archaic and can easily frustrate without patience or a walkthrough. Still, for understanding the development of the genre and the legacy that later Sierra adventures built on, King's Quest I remains an unmissable milestone that players and genre historians alike keep coming back to.

**Why play it:** Anyone wanting to understand the roots of the graphical adventure genre and the legacy that later Sierra games built on will appreciate King's Quest I as a milestone — even knowing it plays today more like a museum piece.

pc-9x__king-s-quest-ii-romancing-throne.teaser: King Graham rescues Valanice in a new fairy-tale adventure through a magic portal.
pc-9x__king-s-quest-ii-romancing-throne.article:
**King's Quest II: Romancing the Throne** builds on the success of the first installment from 1984 and sends King Graham, now ruler of Daventry, on a new fairy-tale adventure – this time tasked with freeing the beautiful Valanice, imprisoned by the evil witch Hagatha in a distant land. The game runs on an improved version of the AGI engine and offers a somewhat larger world than the first game, divided into several areas connected by magic doors that the player gradually unlocks using items collected along the way. The path to completing the quest also leads through a portal into an entirely different, fairy-tale-flavored realm, which was an imaginative way at the time to expand the series beyond a single kingdom.

The gameplay remains true to the Sierra style: a text parser for interacting with the surroundings, arrow keys for movement, and plenty of random deaths if the player doesn't proceed carefully or save often enough. Graham's journey leads through graveyards, caves, and enchanted castles, with some puzzles requiring unconventional logic that the era's player community solved more by sharing tips in magazines than by pure deduction. Technically it's still modest sixteen-color graphics, but for the mid-1980s it was an above-average presentation of a fairy-tale world on PC, complemented by simple melodic music that accompanied transitions between locations.

Among fans of the series, King's Quest II is often seen as somewhat weaker than the first and third installments due to the illogical nature of some puzzles and the strictness of timed situations, yet it holds an irreplaceable place in the genre's history as a direct successor to the formula Sierra gradually refined. Today's player will mainly find a nostalgic glimpse into the early stage of graphic adventures rather than a smooth, trouble-free gaming experience, and it will be appreciated above all by those interested in the development of the series as a whole.

**Why play:** Anyone interested in the development of the series as a whole will appreciate King's Quest II as a nostalgic glimpse into the early stage of graphic adventures, even though illogical puzzles and strict time limits will test their patience.

pc-9x__king-s-quest-iii-to-heir-is-human.teaser: A slave secretly completes tasks under the watch of an evil wizard; one mistake means instant death.
pc-9x__king-s-quest-iii-to-heir-is-human.article:
**King's Quest III: To Heir Is Human** from 1986 shifts the focus from King Graham to a young slave named Gwydion, held captive by the evil wizard Manannan, who forces him to gather ingredients for magic potions. The game is unique in that the first third takes place in the wizard's house, where the player must secretly complete tasks while keeping track of where Manannan has gone – if he catches him disobeying, the game quickly ends in death. Only later is it revealed that Gwydion is actually Prince Alexander, King Graham's lost son, which ties the story into the rest of the series and gives meaning to the fate we follow in later installments.

The second half of the game opens up into freer exploration of islands and towns, where the player gathers materials for potions against a running limited game clock – a mechanic that was unusually tense for its time and frustrating for many players due to the strict time limits and the need to plan routes ahead, since a wrong decision can consume precious turns. The player can also control a dragon that Gwydion frees along the way, bringing an unexpected element into an otherwise earthbound adventure. The graphics and controls follow on from the second installment, meaning the AGI engine with arrow-key movement and a text parser, but the level design is considerably more elaborate and branching than in previous entries in the series.

Thanks to its more elaborate story and bolder mechanics, King's Quest III is still regarded by players today as one of the better early installments in the series, even though its pacing and time limits can still test patience after all these years. It also holds key significance for the series as the first game to hint at the wider mythology of Daventry and to connect Graham's family line with the main hero, a thread later installments built upon, and it is still mentioned today as one of the bolder experiments of the early era of Sierra adventures.

**Why play:** Thanks to its more elaborate story and bold mechanics that first develop the mythology of Daventry, King's Quest III ranks among the better early installments of the series, even though its pacing and time limits will test your patience even today.

pc-9x__king-s-quest-iv-perils-of-rosella.teaser: First installment with playable Princess Rosella; the new SCI engine brought a day-night cycle.
pc-9x__king-s-quest-iv-perils-of-rosella.article:
**King's Quest IV: The Perils of Rosella** from 1988 was a milestone for Sierra in several respects at once – it was the first game to run on the new SCI engine, which brought smoother animation, a day-night cycle, and more elaborate sound, and at the same time the first installment in the series with a playable heroine, Princess Rosella, who sets out to save her dying father King Graham using a magic potion from the enchanted land of Tamir. Her journey takes her, among other places, beneath the surface of the sea, where she must deal with a mermaid – an unusually varied setting for adventures of that time – and further into darker corners of the realm, where the evil Lolotte and her servants lie in wait.

The gameplay sticks to the formula of previous installments – arrow-key movement, a text parser for interaction, and plenty of puzzles built around collecting and combining items – but the world is visually richer and more atmospheric, with a good fairy, the evil witch Lolotte, and a mermaid as key characters in the side plotlines. The day-night cycle also changes the behavior of some enemies and opens up different paths through the game, an unusual dynamic layer for an adventure of this type in 1988 that gave the experience a distinct sense of passing time. The game also introduced more elaborate character animations and smoother transitions between scenes, which made the world of Tamir feel more alive than the flat locations of previous installments.

King's Quest IV is often ranked among the highlights of the series' early era thanks to the combination of a stronger story, a playable female heroine, and technical improvements from the SCI engine, which Sierra later used in its other adventure games as well, including later King's Quest installments and other series of its own. Even years later, the game shows well how quickly the graphic adventure genre evolved in the second half of the 1980s, and fans of classic Sierra games still rank it among the titles worth rediscovering.

**Why play:** The combination of a stronger story, playable heroine Rosella, and technical improvements from the SCI engine makes King's Quest IV one of the highlights of the series' early era, well worth rediscovering.

pc-9x__comanche-2.teaser: A helicopter simulator built on the remarkable Voxel Space voxel technology.
pc-9x__comanche-2.article:
**Comanche 2** followed up on the first installment of NovaLogic's helicopter simulator in 1995 and offered players another batch of missions in the cockpit of the RAH-66 Comanche battle helicopter, built on the then-remarkable Voxel Space voxel terrain rendering technology, thanks to which the game could display vast, smoothly undulating landscapes without classic polygon models. Compared to the first installment, Comanche 2 brought an improved selection of missions and somewhat more varied environments in which they took place, from desert areas to mountainous regions.

The player carries out a series of military missions – destroying convoys, defending bases, reconnaissance, and escort operations – with an emphasis on tactical use of terrain, where the helicopter can hide behind a hill and expose only its sensors before launching a guided missile at the target. The controls were more accessible than in the harder flight simulators of the time, so the game won over players who normally avoided the sim genre, while joystick and HOTAS enthusiasts appreciated the depth of difficulty settings and more realistic flight physics compared to the competition. Missions could also be adjusted for simulation difficulty, so players could choose between a more arcade-like and a more demanding approach to controlling the machine.

The voxel graphics gave the game an unusually smooth feel of flying over hilly terrain on the PC hardware of the time, though at the cost of detail on individual objects, and the music along with engine and gunfire sounds heightened the tension of the combat missions. Comanche 2 cemented NovaLogic's position as a specialist in accessible helicopter action and paved the way for the commercially more successful Comanche 3, released two years later, which built further on the same technology and expanded the series with additional missions and capabilities. Even today, Comanche 2 remains an interesting example of how, in the mid-1990s, developers sought alternatives to what was then still costly polygon rendering.

**Why play:** Thanks to the unusually smooth flying feel brought by the voxel graphics, Comanche 2 is an interesting example of how alternatives to costly polygon rendering were sought in the mid-1990s.

pc-9x__grand-prix-2.teaser: One of the most accurate recreations of 1990s Formula 1; the 1994 season plus a track editor.
pc-9x__grand-prix-2.article:
**Grand Prix 2** from 1996 was the second installment in Geoff Crammond's renowned racing simulation series, published under the MicroProse label, and in the mid-1990s it was considered one of the most accurate recreations of a Formula 1 season the PC had to offer at the time. The game featured the complete starting grid of the 1994 season with period-accurate teams, drivers, and tracks, and the player could complete both individual races and an entire championship season, including qualifying, practice sessions, and car setup. A track editor was also available, allowing the player community to create their own circuits and expand the game's offering beyond the official content.

At the core of the game was elaborate driving physics that responded to downforce, gearbox, tire, and weather settings, so success depended not just on reflexes but also on understanding how the car behaved in corners and under braking. The AI of the opponents ranked among the best on the market for its time and could react to the player's mistakes as well as changing track conditions, setting the game apart from more arcade-oriented competitors, such as the racing titles of the time focused more on action than simulation. The graphics were detailed for 1996, with smoothly animated cars and grandstands full of spectators, though the hardware demands meant that smooth performance required a decently equipped computer with a sufficiently fast processor.

Grand Prix 2 is still mentioned among racing sim fans today as one of the gold standards of the genre in the 1990s, and its influence is evident in the later Grand Prix 3, which further built on the same approach to simulating Formula 1. For players seeking an authentic F1 experience from that era, Grand Prix 2 remains a very playable choice even after all these years, though the controls require a bit of patience while getting used to the period interface and car setup, which offered dozens of parameters to tune.

**Why play:** For players seeking an authentic 1990s Formula 1 experience, Grand Prix 2 remains a very playable choice even today – all it takes is a bit of patience with the period interface and car setup.

pc-9x__command-and-conquer.teaser: The game that defined the RTS genre for years to come; the fight between GDI and the Brotherhood of Nod over mysterious tiberium.
pc-9x__command-and-conquer.article:
**Command & Conquer** by Westwood Studios from 1995 ranks among the games that defined the entire real-time strategy genre for many years to come. The player chooses between the GDI faction, defending world order, and the Brotherhood of Nod led by the mysterious Kane, with both campaigns telling the story of a struggle for control over the mysterious substance tiberium, which transforms the landscape and the people who come into contact with it. Both sides also offer a different perspective on the same conflict, so the player effectively goes through two interconnected yet separate storylines.

The gameplay was built on gathering resources via harvester vehicles, base building, and choosing between a defensive or offensive strategy, and the game became one of the first to massively popularize real-time base building and unit micromanagement, following the model of the earlier Dune II. Live-action cutscenes with actors were inserted between missions, an unusual and highly impressive way of storytelling in 1995 that set the game apart from the drier strategy titles of its time and gave the campaign a cinematic atmosphere. Multiplayer over a local network and modem also opened the way for the game to have a long life among players who wanted to compete against each other directly.

Frank Klepacki's music, full of electronic and rock motifs, became an inseparable part of the atmosphere and is still remembered by fans today as one of the best game soundtracks of the 1990s. Command & Conquer had an enormous influence on the development of the entire RTS genre, inspired countless successors, and founded a long-running series whose later installments Tiberian Sun and Red Alert 2 remain beloved classics to this day. Even with the passage of time, strategy fans regard it as a mandatory entry in the genre's history and as one of the reasons real-time strategy became such a popular genre on PC.

**Why play:** Because of Frank Klepacki's unmistakable music and its role as founder of the entire RTS genre, Command & Conquer ranks among the mandatory entries in the history of strategy games on PC.

pc-9x__command-and-conquer-red-alert.teaser: An alternate history where Einstein prevents Hitler and opens the way for Stalin's army.
pc-9x__command-and-conquer-red-alert.article:
**Command & Conquer: Red Alert** from 1996 was originally conceived as a prequel to the story of the Tiberium saga, but Westwood Studios ultimately turned it into an alternate history in which Albert Einstein travels back in time to prevent Hitler's rise – thereby inadvertently opening the way for Stalin's Soviet Union to unleash war against the Allies. The player thus chooses between the technologically more advanced Allies and the numerically stronger, more brutal Soviet Army, each with a different set of units and strategic approach to the same conflict, allowing players to experience the war from two completely different perspectives.

The game expanded on the foundations laid by the first Command & Conquer with new units such as Tesla coils, dogs as scout units that reveal spies, and naval battles, offering more varied tactical options than its predecessor. The campaigns were again interspersed with live-action cutscenes, this time with an even greater dose of deliberate exaggeration and dark humor, which became characteristic of the Red Alert series and set it apart in tone from the more serious Tiberium saga. Expanded multiplayer and more varied maps further supported the game as a favorite choice for competitive players who wanted to test their strength against each other, not just against computer-controlled opponents.

Frank Klepacki's soundtrack, again with distinctive electronic-rock motifs, remains among the most frequently mentioned game music of the 1990s, and together with a distinctive art style it helped Red Alert build its own loyal fanbase independent of the main Tiberium series. Commercial and critical success led to a long line of sequels, including the already-released Red Alert 2, and Red Alert still ranks among the most popular and most-played titles of the early era of real-time strategy on PC, one that players gladly return to, aided also by later remastered releases.

**Why play:** Thanks to its distinctive art style, iconic Frank Klepacki soundtrack, and its own loyal fanbase, Red Alert still ranks among the most popular and most-played titles of the early era of RTS on PC.

pc-9x__midtown-madness-2.teaser: Open-world racing through London and San Francisco with no rules and no penalties for crashes.
pc-9x__midtown-madness-2.article:
**Midtown Madness 2** is an arcade racing title from Angel Studios that in 2000 followed up on the first installment and brought open-world city racing to London and San Francisco. Players could drive through streets, parks, tram tracks, and even inside subway stations in any order they liked, knocking over traffic cones, scattering pedestrians, and ramming into oncoming cars, without the game punishing reckless driving in any way beyond bodywork damage. Compared to the first installment, a motorcycle vehicle category was added along with the ability to freely switch between cars, which heightened the sense of freedom in an open world that was still a fairly unusual concept at the time. Alongside time-based races, the game also offered free-roaming drives through the city with no set goal.

Technically, the game benefited from colorful, clear graphics and a smooth sense of speed, though the models of both cities were, understandably, heavily simplified and served mainly as a backdrop for spectacular chases. The sound design was rounded out by roaring engines, screeching tires, and opponent voice lines, which made the game feel lively even in one-off practice sessions outside of career mode. The behavior of other traffic and pedestrians, who tried to dodge out of the way of the speeding car, contributed to the chaotic but entertaining feel of driving through the city. Network or internet multiplayer was one of the features valued at the time and contributed to the impression that this was entertainment meant more for competing with friends than for a perfect driving simulation.

At the time, the game was seen as a successful sequel that expanded the successful formula of the first installment with new settings and vehicles without fundamentally changing its character. In the arcade city-racing genre it left its mark as one of the titles that foreshadowed later open-world racing games, even though it itself remained more lighthearted fun than a technological milestone. Many players still remember the series today as a pioneer of open-world city racing. Today, Midtown Madness 2 feels like a pleasant retro reminder of a time when an open city, a handful of cars, and no rules were all it took for a game to entertain for hours on end.

**Why play:** As a pleasant retro reminder of a time when an open city, a handful of cars, and no rules were enough for fun, Midtown Madness 2 still entertains today, even though it was more lighthearted fun than a technological milestone.

pc-9x__nascar-racing-2.teaser: A deep NASCAR oval-racing simulation from Papyrus, favoring detail over arcade driving.
pc-9x__nascar-racing-2.article:
**NASCAR Racing 2** from 1996 by Papyrus followed up on the first game in the series and deepened the developer's reputation as specialists in realistic oval racing simulation of the American NASCAR championship. The game offered a season with real tracks and cars and put emphasis on the physics model of car behavior, tire wear, and chassis setup, making it a far more demanding and technical title than the arcade racing games of its time. Players could fine-tune their car setup down to the smallest detail according to track type and weather conditions, which was especially appreciated by players looking for a genuine simulation rather than just flashy driving. It also included a track editor and the ability to adjust opponent parameters, which extended the game's lifespan through community-made content.

The opponents' artificial intelligence was among the most highly rated elements of the game at the time, as the computer-controlled drivers reacted to events on track, drafting, and collision situations more believably than the competition. The graphics remained within the bounds of what was possible at the time, but smoothness and readability at high speeds were exemplary for their era. The audio side relied on roaring engines and pit radio communication, deepening the sense of a genuine race weekend. The game also supported multiplayer, which made it popular in early online racing leagues, where players gathered for regular races following the real NASCAR calendar.

NASCAR Racing 2 is remembered today as one of the titles that defined the genre of computer racing simulations and influenced later entries in the series as well as competing simulators. Papyrus cemented its reputation through it as a studio capable of offering depth without sacrificing playability. For today's player it is mostly a historical curiosity due to its dated graphics, but fans of the simulation genre still find in it an honest foundation of mechanics that have essentially remained unchanged to this day and on which later entries in the series were built.

**Why play it:** Fans of the simulation genre still find in NASCAR Racing 2 an honest foundation of mechanics that have essentially remained unchanged to this day, though today's player will mostly see it as a historical curiosity due to its dated graphics.

pc-9x__tomb-raider-iii-adventures-of-lar.teaser: Acrobatic jumping and puzzles across four continents; the level order was selectable for the first time.
pc-9x__tomb-raider-iii-adventures-of-lar.article:
**Tomb Raider III: Adventures of Lara Croft** was released in 1998 by Core Design and sent Lara Croft on a journey across four continents in pursuit of fragments of a mysterious meteorite, from Indian jungles through London sewers to Pacific islands and Antarctic bases. The game retained the proven combination of acrobatic platform jumping, solving spatial puzzles, and shootouts with wild animals and human opponents, but unlike previous entries it let the player choose the order in which to visit the individual regions, bringing a greater sense of freedom into an otherwise linear narrative. It also featured vehicles such as a quad bike or a small submarine, which could be used in some sections to cross larger areas more quickly.

Level design went in many passages toward greater complexity and difficulty than earlier entries, with branching paths and tougher jumps, which earned mixed reactions - some players appreciated the challenge, others found it frustrating. Technically the game ran on an improved version of the engine from previous entries and offered more varied environments and weather, including storms and snow, which affected visibility and the atmosphere of individual levels. The music and sound design continued to build on the mysterious, adventurous atmosphere the series was famous for, though without as striking a surprise effect as in the first game. The controls remained faithful to the grid-based movement style of previous entries, requiring patience and precision from players when judging jumps.

In the context of its time it was another commercially successful addition to the series, though it also suggested that the pace of one entry per year was starting to wear the series thin in terms of ideas. Even so, Tomb Raider III remains a significant milestone of the action-adventure genre of the nineties, and for fans of the series it remains a playable reminder of an era when Lara Croft was among the most iconic characters in computer games and her adventures defined the entire third-person genre.

**Why play it:** For fans of the series, Tomb Raider III remains a playable reminder of an era when Lara Croft was among the most iconic characters in games and defined the entire third-person action-adventure genre.

pc-9x__simcity-3000.teaser: An iconic city-building game about planning, construction, and the growth of your own city.
pc-9x__simcity-3000.article:
**SimCity 3000** followed up on the successful predecessor SimCity 2000 and in 1999 reconfirmed that city building can be just as addictive as an action game. The player founds a new town literally on a green field, divides plots into residential, industrial, and commercial zones, builds roads, power plants, and waterworks, and watches as a handful of houses gradually grows into a metropolis. Budget, taxes, demand for individual types of development, and citizen satisfaction are constantly changing, forcing the player to think in long-term horizons and react to their own mistakes - overcrowded traffic, pollution, or crime can quickly bring even a thriving city to its knees.

Compared to the second entry, the game added more elaborate relationships between neighboring cities within a region, the ability to make agreements on sharing electricity, water, or landfills, and expanded the range of special buildings and disasters that can spice up even the most carefully planned development. The isometric graphics with finely drawn terrain and buildings felt very fresh at the time of release, and together with calm, atmospheric music created the impression of a living, breathing city growing according to the player's decisions. Mouse controls, clear panels, and advisors pointing out problems made the game accessible even to people who had until then avoided strategy games.

SimCity 3000 became one of the best-selling titles of the genre and for many years defined what a serious city-building simulator should look like - its influence is visible in dozens of later games that tried to offer similarly deep city management. On a period PC running Windows 9x the game still runs smoothly today, and thanks to its modest system requirements it is one of the easiest ways to find out why the city-builder genre was so successful in the nineties.

**Why play it:** An ideal choice for anyone who enjoys thoughtful planning and wants to see the results of their own decisions grow building by building, without the pressure of a time limit.

pc-9x__medieval-total-war.teaser: A turn-based strategy game with grand real-time battles; the pioneer of the Total War series.
pc-9x__medieval-total-war.article:
**Medieval: Total War** from 2002 by The Creative Assembly developed the concept outlined two years earlier by Shogun: Total War, and brought battles of thousands of units into the setting of medieval Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. The game combines a turn-based strategic map, on which the player manages provinces, builds structures, collects taxes, and plans diplomacy or religious policy, with real-time battles where infantry, cavalry, and siege engine formations clash on open terrain. It is precisely this hybrid of turn-based empire management and tactical combat that became the hallmark of the entire series, and Medieval refined it significantly.

The player chooses one of the European factions and tries to expand their territory, keep their subjects satisfied, and at the same time face raids from neighbors, crusades, or internal revolts. Battles are clear thanks to legible formations and the ability to micromanage individual units, yet they still manage to convey the feeling of a truly great medieval campaign - especially when the battlefield shifts to a castle siege with towers, battering rams, and catapults. The atmosphere is enhanced by the emphasis on historical detail, the diversity of units by region, and the religious dimension of the game, where Christian and Muslim factions each have their own specifics.

Medieval: Total War cemented the series' position as one of the most influential strategy concepts of its era and paved the way for later entries that remain among the best-selling PC strategy games to this day. Although the graphics and controls bear the marks of their time, the core gameplay - a battle of well-thought-out strategy on the map combined with tense battles in the field - still works without any loss of quality even years later, and the game runs without trouble on an ordinary period PC with Windows 9x.

**Why play it:** A great choice for fans of historical strategy games who want to experience battles of thousands of units in real time while also immersing themselves in the turn-based management of a medieval empire, without having to reach for the simplifications of later entries in the series.

pc-modern__polda-4.teaser: The most seriously toned entry in the Pankrác series; a case about a professor and his time machine.
pc-modern__polda-4.article:
**Polda 4** continues the beloved Czech series of point-and-click adventures about the quirky policeman Pankrác and delivers the most seriously toned entry in the series, in which the detective investigates a case involving Professor Santus and his dangerous invention — a time machine. Compared to earlier entries, simple jokes take a back seat and the story gets a more elaborate, if still lighthearted, treatment featuring themes of time travel and the paradoxes that come with it. The gameplay stays classic — the player moves through locations, collects and combines items in an inventory, and talks to characters whose lines carry the series' signature voice acting, featuring several well-known Czech actors who lent their voices to the other entries as well.

Technically, Polda 4 marked a major turning point for the series — instead of static drawn scenes, it used 3D graphics for the first time, which felt unusual to players used to years of the hand-drawn style of earlier entries. The game's settings range from a classic police station to more fantastical locations tied to the professor's invention, marking the series' first partial departure from a purely realistic Czech setting. The audio still relies on full voice acting, which was and remains the series' main draw, complemented by music that fleshes out the atmosphere of each location. The switch to 3D graphics split the audience — some appreciated the modernization and the attempt to move the series forward, while others missed the hand-drawn backgrounds typical of the earlier entries.

At launch the game was embraced mainly by loyal fans of the series, who watched with interest how Polda handled both the technological and the narrative shift. Today, Polda 4 is seen as a transitional entry between the older and newer forms of the series — an important step showing that the Czech team Zima Software was willing to change an established formula, even at the cost of a mixed reception among part of the audience, and it paved the way for the sequels that followed.

**Why play it:** For loyal fans of the series it's an interesting transitional entry showing how Zima Software dared to change an established formula, even at the cost of a mixed reception.

pc-modern__polda-5.teaser: Made over three years on essentially no budget; the humor and Luděk Sobota's voice acting stay true to the series.
pc-modern__polda-5.article:
**Polda 5** was made over three years on essentially no budget with a minimal team, which is noticeably reflected in the finished game, but it still gave the series about policeman Pankrác another humorous case in the spirit of the earlier entries. The player returns to the classic point-and-click formula — exploring the environment, collecting and combining items in an inventory, and conversations full of trademark one-liners, whose main draw since the first game has been Luděk Sobota's voice acting as Pankrác. The story again mines parody of the crime genre and references to Czech reality of the mid-2000s, while keeping the typical exaggeration and absurd twists fans had come to expect.

The limited production resources also show in the technical execution — the graphics and animation feel more modest compared to the previous entry, individual locations are less detailed, and the overall production bears the marks of both haste and a lack of funding. Even so, the production tried to preserve the series' distinctive visual style and keep the recognizable characters from earlier entries. The audio remains built on voice acting and light music that give the game the atmosphere fans were used to from before. The lower production quality was seen by players and the contemporary press alike as a weakness, one the game only partly offset with the loyalty of its fanbase and the ongoing popularity of its main character.

Looking back, Polda 5 is generally considered the weakest entry in the series, yet it remained an important stepping stone after which the creators at Zima Software decided to give the brand a more substantial overhaul in later entries. For collectors and loyal series fans the game mainly carries nostalgic value, standing as evidence of the difficult conditions in which domestic adventure games were made at the time, and as a reminder that even a small studio managed to keep the series alive.

**Why play it:** More for collectors and loyal series fans, for its nostalgic value — as evidence of the difficult conditions in which domestic adventure games were made at the time — than as a fully rounded experience.

pc-modern__polda-6.teaser: A return to the older, more popular entries after a weaker fifth installment; once again with Luděk Sobota.
pc-modern__polda-6.article:
**Polda 6** brought the series about policeman Pankrác back into the spotlight after years of silence, when Zima Software, working with another team, decided to return to the older, more popular entries and appeal above all to longtime fans who, after the weaker fifth game, were unsure whether continuing the series still made sense. The gameplay again relies on the tried-and-tested point-and-click foundation — collecting and combining items in an inventory, moving through locations, and dialogue full of wordplay, complete with Luděk Sobota's signature voice acting as the main hero along with other familiar voices tied to the series since earlier entries. The creators' goal was to return to what fans had enjoyed about the first entries and experiment less with the more serious tone of the earlier episode, bringing back in full the series' typical humor built on exaggeration and puns.

Technically the game grew noticeably compared to Polda 5 — the graphics and scene design feel more elaborate, locations are more detailed, and the production visibly tried to respond to the criticism aimed at the weaker previous entry. The setting again combines everyday Czech reality with exaggeratedly comic situations that Pankrác stumbles into during his investigations. The audio remains built on voice acting and light music that round out the comedic atmosphere typical of the whole series since its beginnings.
