Visually and musically it was one of BioWare's most ambitious projects at the time, featuring extensive voice acting and cinematic cutscenes.

Inquisition received numerous awards after release, including Game of the Year honors, and became the series' most commercially successful entry. Despite criticism from some players over the sprawl of the open world, it remains valued to this day for its breadth of content, well-crafted party characters, and political intrigue, making it one of the significant representatives of fantasy RPGs of its generation. The Trespasser expansion later closed out the Inquisition storyline and hinted at the direction the series would take in its next entries.

**Why play it:** Its breadth of content, well-crafted party, and political intrigue make Inquisition one of the significant representatives of fantasy RPGs of its generation, despite the sprawl of its open world.

pc-modern__pillars-of-eternity-ii-deadfi.teaser: The spiritual successor to Baldur's Gate sails onto the seas of the Deadfire archipelago for the first time.
pc-modern__pillars-of-eternity-ii-deadfi.article:
**Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire** continues the story of the Watcher from the first game, who, after the awakening of the ancient god Eothas, sets sail across the Deadfire archipelago to prevent the threat this god poses to the entire world. The game from Obsidian Entertainment retains the systemically deep approach of classic isometric RPGs like Baldur's Gate, but this time sets the story in a more open space that the player explores aboard their own ship among islands, factions, and pirates. The game was preceded by a successful crowdfunding campaign, much like the first entry, and a number of companions from the previous game, such as Eder and Aloth, return in Deadfire with their own continuing personal stories.

The combat system offers a choice between turn-based and fluid real-time-with-pause modes, allowing players to adjust the game's pace to their own preferences, while character and party creation offers a wide range of classes, races, and subclasses with many possible combinations. The world of Deadfire is politically divided among several factions vying for control of trade and power in the archipelago, and the player's decisions about alliances impact how the story and the game's ending unfold. Visually, the game builds on the hand-painted environments of its predecessor, complemented by naval combat between ships.

Deadfire was received very positively by critics for the depth of its systems, its writing, and the freedom it gives players in resolving conflicts, even though it did not sell as strongly as the studio had hoped. For fans of classic, dialogue-rich RPGs, it remains one of the most complex representatives of the genre on PC today and a demonstration of how a traditional isometric RPG can be expanded toward a more open world. The turn-based combat mode, originally added as an optional update only after release, became the preferred way to enjoy the game for many players.

**Why play it:** For fans of dialogue-rich isometric RPGs, Deadfire remains one of the most complex representatives of the genre on PC, especially with the later turn-based combat mode.

pc-modern__dragon-age-ii.teaser: Hawke's story told across three acts, narrated retrospectively through Varric's interrogation.
pc-modern__dragon-age-ii.article:
**Dragon Age II** shifted the series from a classic party-based RPG toward a more action-oriented style that placed greater emphasis on fast combat and a dynamic camera. The player takes on the role of Hawke, a refugee from Ferelden, whose story unfolds over ten years in the city of Kirkwall and is told retrospectively through a conversation between the dwarf Varric and a templar investigating his role in the events that shook the entire city. This narrative framework gave the game an unusual three-act structure, over which political conditions and relations between the mage and templar factions gradually shifted, culminating in an open conflict between Knight-Commander Meredith and First Enchanter Orsino. Unlike the silent protagonist of Origins, Hawke was for the first time in the series fully voiced, lending the dialogue a more personal, cinematic tone.

The combat system was faster-paced and more visually flashy than in Origins, with an emphasis on ability combos and quick switching between party members, which drew mixed reactions – some fans appreciated the fluidity, while others missed the tactical depth of its predecessor. The game also reused a number of environments, just with different decorations and waves of enemies, which was criticized at the time due to the shorter development cycle forced by the publisher. On PC the game ran smoothly even on mid-range configurations of the time and offered detailed visuals of Kirkwall's environments along with strongly voiced characters, including the return of companions like Varric, Merrill, and Aveline, joined by new faces such as Fenris and Anders.

Despite its mixed reception, Dragon Age II remains an important milestone for the series – it showed that BioWare was willing to experiment with narrative structure and with a morally ambiguous ending in which no side of the conflict is unambiguously in the right. To this day it retains a following of fans who appreciate its more personal, intimate story focused on a single city and a single family, in contrast to the more epic scope of its predecessor and successors.

**Why play it:** Anyone who appreciates a more personal, intimate story focused on a single city and family rather than the epic scale of the surrounding entries will find here a bold experiment in narrative structure.

pc-modern__dragon-age-veilguard.teaser: The latest Dragon Age after ten years; more action-focused combat against two elven gods.
pc-modern__dragon-age-veilguard.article:
**Dragon Age: The Veilguard** is the latest entry in the series, arriving ten years after Inquisition and bringing significantly more action-oriented, fluid combat with less emphasis on tactical pausing and controlling the whole party from the outside. Playing as Rook, the player leads the Veilguard, a group whose goal is to stop two ancient gods of the elven pantheon, Elgar'nan and Ghilan'nain, who were accidentally released from their prison at the end of the Trespasser expansion and now threaten all of Thedas. The story unfolds across new and familiar locations, including Minrathous and Weisshaupt, and places emphasis on personal relationships with companions like Neve, Bellara, Davrin, Emmrich, and Lucanis, as well as on the consequences of decisions from previous entries, reflected through a so-called Decision Tome rather than a direct import of saved playthroughs.

Visually, the game leans into a more stylized, colorful look than the darker Inquisition, runs on the Frostbite engine, and on PC offers support for modern performance-scaling technologies and high resolutions, including ultrawide monitors. The combat system was designed to be more fluid and accessible, with an emphasis on ability combos between the three playable characters in combat, which sparked discussion among longtime fans used to the series' more tactical approach.

Reception was mixed – some players and reviewers praised the quality of the storytelling, the companions, and the technical execution, while others regretted the departure from the series' isometric roots, the simplification of RPG mechanics, and the reduced emphasis on the moral ambiguity the series was previously known for. The Veilguard thus remains a much-discussed attempt to modernize the brand for a new audience without fully abandoning the characteristic humor and personal stories that made Dragon Age famous. On PC, the game also came with support for higher frame rates and modern display technologies, making it the most technically advanced entry in the series at the time of release.

**Why play it:** If you don't mind the departure from the series' isometric roots and simplified RPG mechanics, you'll appreciate the quality storytelling, companions, and the most technically advanced production in the series to date.

pc-modern__mass-effect.teaser: The foundation of the trilogy; Commander Shepard hunts the traitor Saren and uncovers the Reaper threat.
pc-modern__mass-effect.article:
**Mass Effect** introduced a universe where humanity discovered the remnants of ancient technology and joined a galactic community of races overseen by the Citadel. As Commander Shepard, the player sets out aboard the ship Normandy to hunt down the rogue Spectre Saren, who is collaborating with the mechanical Geth, and uncovers the threat of the ancient Reaper race hidden beyond the edges of the galaxy. The game combined third-person action shooting with a dialogue wheel and a Paragon/Renegade morality system that influenced relationships with the crew and the story's development, complemented by a choice of one of six character classes ranging from soldier to biotic.

Exploring the galaxy also involved the ground vehicle Mako and scanning planets, which lent a sense of vastness to the universe, even though the environments themselves were fairly sparsely populated. The PC version, which arrived several months after the Xbox 360 release, brought higher-resolution textures and mouse-and-keyboard support, though the controls still felt clearly designed primarily for a gamepad. Technically, the game, built on Unreal Engine 3, suffered from long loading times and a cumbersome inventory screen, something frequently mentioned in reviews, though the atmosphere was well served by Jack Wall's striking music and extensive voice acting for characters like Garrus, Wrex, and Liara.

Mass Effect became the foundation of one of the most significant sci-fi series of the modern era and showed how to combine cinematic storytelling with player choices that carry over between installments. Today it is seen primarily as an introduction to a much larger story, whose full impact only comes into focus with its sequels, but even on its own it offers a strongly atmospheric sci-fi story with a richly developed world and its codex. Choices such as the fate of the Rachni species or the decision about the Council also carried over into the sequels, which at the time was among the most ambitious attempts at continuity across several separately released games.

**Why play it:** As an introduction to a sprawling sci-fi story with choices that carry into the sequels, it offers an atmospheric world with a rich codex, especially for players planning to play through the whole trilogy.

pc-modern__mass-effect-legendary-edition.teaser: A remaster of the whole trilogy in one package; the biggest beneficiary is the technically dated first game.
pc-modern__mass-effect-legendary-edition.article:
**Mass Effect Legendary Edition** bundled all three games of the original trilogy into a single package, including most of the additional content such as Bring Down the Sky or Omega, and unified them visually and mechanically for modern hardware. The remaster reworked lighting, textures, and character models, significantly improving the first game, which was technically the most dated with its slow movement and unwieldy inventory screen, while preserving the original voice acting, music, and the key gameplay decisions carried over between episodes via the save-file system.

Beyond the visual overhaul, the developers also unified some gameplay systems, such as shooting, cover controls, and inventory in the first game, to better match the standards players had grown used to in the sequels, without fundamentally altering its distinct, slower, more exploration-focused identity. The multiplayer mode from the third game, on the other hand, was not included in the release, as the edition focused purely on the story campaign. On PC, the edition offered support for ultrawide monitors, high frame rates, and modern resolutions, a significant step up from the original versions from the late 2000s, complemented by small bonuses like a concept-art gallery.

Legendary Edition allowed a new generation of players to experience the complete story of Commander Shepard in one package and was received as a sensitively made remaster that respects the original without unnecessarily rewriting it. For many fans it remains the best way to experience the trilogy today, whether for the first time or on a replay, thanks to a balanced blend of nostalgia and modernization that loses none of what made Mass Effect special, including its distinctive atmosphere and music. The release also came at a time when BioWare was working on the next entry in the series, so Legendary Edition also served as a reminder and rediscovery of the Mass Effect universe for a wider audience ahead of the franchise's return.

**Why play it:** For new and returning players alike, it remains the best way to play through Shepard's entire trilogy today, in one balanced and sensitively made remaster.

pc-modern__icewind-dale-ii.teaser: A tactical D&D adventure on the Infinity Engine, focused more on combat than story.
pc-modern__icewind-dale-ii.article:
**Icewind Dale II** followed up on the successful first game with an updated set of Dungeons & Dragons 3rd Edition rules, built on the Infinity Engine, which at the time also powered titles like Baldur's Gate and Planescape: Torment. Unlike Black Isle Studios' more story-rich games, the Icewind Dale series focused primarily on tactical combat and exploring the icy region around Icewind Dale, where the player's party of up to six characters — built entirely from scratch with no pre-made companions — sets out to face a goblin invasion and a darker conspiracy lurking behind it.

The updated ruleset brought expanded character-creation options, more classes, subraces like Aasimar or Half-Orc, and prestige classes available only after meeting certain conditions, pushing the game closer to a more tactical RPG that emphasizes assembling an effective party rather than branching dialogue and choices with moral weight. On PC, the game demanded fairly solid hardware at the time to run its isometric visuals smoothly, with plenty of effects and units fighting simultaneously in large-scale battles, which was technically demanding for its era and made the game one of the more difficult representatives of the genre.

Icewind Dale II is today valued mainly by players seeking purely tactical combat and a deep knowledge of D&D rules rather than those expecting a story as elaborate as Baldur's Gate. It represents one of the last major titles built on the Infinity Engine, after whose release Black Isle Studios ran into trouble with publisher Interplay, closing out an era of classic isometric RPGs at the turn of the millennium before the genre briefly gave way to more action-focused games and was revived a decade later by titles like Baldur's Gate 3. The Enhanced Edition, later released by Beamdog alongside other remastered Infinity Engine titles, let the game run smoothly on modern operating systems and brought minor interface improvements.

**Why play it:** Fans of purely tactical combat and D&D rules, rather than those looking for a story on the level of Baldur's Gate, will enjoy one of the last titles built on the Infinity Engine, still playable today thanks to the Enhanced Edition.

pc-modern__neverwinter-nights-2.teaser: A new Electron engine and a reworked party system; you lead up to three companions at once.
pc-modern__neverwinter-nights-2.article:
**Neverwinter Nights 2** followed up on the 2002 original with the new Electron engine, which brought more modern visuals along with a reworked party system in which the player controls up to three companions at once, with the option to pause time for more tactical decisions in combat. The story takes the player to the region around Neverwinter, where they face an invasion by the King of Shadows and gradually uncover the connection between their own fate and an artifact called the Silver Sword of Gith, accompanied along the way by memorable companions such as the dwarf Khelgar, the tiefling thief Neeshka, and the paladin Casavir.

The game was built on the Dungeons & Dragons 3.5 edition ruleset and offered an extensive editor for creating custom modules and campaigns, continuing the beloved community-made content of the first game and enabling the creation of numerous persistent multiplayer worlds run by the fan community for years afterward. On PC it required above-average performance at the time due to more demanding visual effects and expansive outdoor environments, which was noted in reviews as a weakness alongside technical shortcomings and bugs at launch. The campaign was supplemented by two expansions, Mask of the Betrayer and Storm of Zehir, the first of which is particularly praised for its unusually dark and philosophical story about a curse of hunger for souls.

Neverwinter Nights 2 is remembered today mainly for its expansions and its community's modular creations, which expanded the game with hundreds of custom campaigns and adventures. Even though the base game itself had a rougher reception than its predecessor, it cemented Obsidian Entertainment's reputation as a studio capable of telling deep, morally ambiguous RPG stories, a reputation it built on a few years later with Pillars of Eternity. The Electron Toolset, bundled directly with the game, allowed players not only to script their own dialogues and quests but also to build extensive exteriors and interiors, making the game a popular platform for homebrew campaigns played among friends over a network.

**Why play it:** For fans of morally ambiguous D&D stories and custom-made adventures thanks to the Electron Toolset editor, even though the base campaign feels rougher today than later Obsidian RPGs.

pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik.teaser: The founder of modern World War II flight simulators; the Eastern Front and the Il-2.
pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik.article:
**IL-2 Sturmovik** from 2001 is one of the founding titles of modern World War II flight simulators and the first entry in the legendary series from 1C:Maddox Games. The game focuses on the Eastern Front and the Soviet air force, with the player primarily taking the cockpit of the Il-2 ground-attack aircraft the title is named after, though a range of other Soviet and German aircraft are also available. The campaign guides the player through key battles on the Eastern Front and combines scripted historical scenarios with dynamically generated missions, a fairly unusual combination of approaches for its time. The game also included a mission editor, which let players build their own scenarios and share them within an early but active online community.

The gameplay was built on a detailed flight model that aimed to faithfully simulate the behavior of individual aircraft types, including their strengths and weaknesses, structural damage, and engine behavior. Players could choose a level of realism ranging from a more arcade-like approach to a full simulation with manual propeller pitch control, engine cooling, and navigation without any assists. The visual presentation of the terrain and aircraft models was exceptionally detailed for its time, and the game became a benchmark for the visual quality of flight simulators in general, though this level of detail also demanded fairly high hardware requirements for the era.

The sound design of engines and both onboard and anti-aircraft gunfire contributed to the overall authentic atmosphere of combat over the front, as did the carefully rendered cockpit models of each aircraft. The game earned strong renown within the community of aviation history enthusiasts and became the foundation on which later entries were built, including Forgotten Battles and Pacific Fighters, which shared the same engine and design philosophy. Even years later, it's clear how significantly it influenced the direction of military flight simulators going forward and how it set the bar for flight-model authenticity, even though from today's perspective the graphics and interface are naturally dated.

**Why play it:** For enthusiasts of World War II aviation history who appreciate authentic combat sound design and carefully detailed cockpit models, even though the graphics and interface feel dated today.

pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-forgotten-batt.teaser: Expanded the first game with more fronts and aircraft; the foundation for the whole expansion series.
pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-forgotten-batt.article:
**IL-2 Sturmovik: Forgotten Battles** built on the success of the first game and broadened its scope with a range of additional World War II fronts and aircraft, including fighting in Finland and other sections of the Eastern Front. It substantially expanded the roster of German, Soviet, and Finnish types and added new campaigns built on a more refined flight and damage model. This installment became the foundation for the entire subsequent line of expansions, including the Aces Expansion Pack and Pacific Fighters, which gradually turned IL-2 Sturmovik into a sprawling platform rather than a single game.

Compared to the first game, Forgotten Battles improved the visuals, fixed a number of shortcomings in the flight modeling, and added a more complex dynamic campaign that responded more effectively to the player's successes and failures in individual missions. The multiplayer component became one of the pillars of the game's popularity, as it allowed large-scale online battles with dozens of players on both sides of the front and also supported organized flying squadrons with a stable membership base. It was precisely these community servers and organized squadrons that gave the game a long lifespan well beyond a typical game's cycle — an unusual feat for simulators at the time — and many such communities kept running for years afterward.

The audio design and the atmosphere of combat over European battlefields stayed true to the spirit of the previous game, only with a higher degree of detail and authenticity in the engines and onboard weapons, including recognizable sounds for individual types of machine guns and cannons. Forgotten Battles is still cited today as one of the high points of the classic IL-2 Sturmovik era, meaning the period before later installments moved to a new game engine. For enthusiasts of World War II aviation history, it represented — and still represents — one of the most comprehensive simulation experiences of its time, even though the controls and interface feel archaic today and require a degree of patience to learn.

**Why play it:** For fans of aviation history looking for one of the most comprehensive simulation experiences of the classic IL-2 Sturmovik era, even though the controls and interface now demand patience.

pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-cliffs-of-dove.teaser: A new engine and the Battle of Britain; for the first time you can also control anti-aircraft defense on the ground.
pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-cliffs-of-dove.article:
**IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover** moved the series from the Eastern Front to the Battle of Britain and at the same time introduced an entirely new graphics engine meant to replace the aging technology of the earlier games. The game focuses on aerial combat between the RAF and the Luftwaffe over southern England and the Channel, offering iconic aircraft such as the Spitfire, Hurricane, Messerschmitt Bf 109, and bombers like the He 111 and Junkers Ju 87. In addition to flying missions, it also lets players control ground and naval anti-aircraft defenses, an unusual added feature for its time that lets the battle be seen from the defenders' perspective on the ground as well.

The release was accompanied by a considerable number of technical problems, performance drops, and bugs that damaged the game's initial reception and led to a long series of fixes lasting many months after launch. At the same time, the flight and damage model was among the most sophisticated of its era, offering a very detailed simulation of how aircraft behaved under various kinds of structural and powerplant damage. Visually, even after years of patches, the game offered impressive views of the southern English countryside and the sea surface of the Channel, which in many respects surpassed the earlier games in the series.

Through successive updates and later unofficial community modifications, stability and playability improved significantly, and the game eventually found a solid core of fans who appreciated the depth of its simulation. Cliffs of Dover is viewed today as an ambitious but troubled release, whose technological foundation nonetheless later served as a springboard for the new generation of the series — Battle of Stalingrad and the titles that followed it. For anyone interested in the Battle of Britain, it remains, despite its flaws, one of the few detailed simulators devoted to that particular subject, and its development is still followed by later community patches that keep adding aircraft and fixing remaining shortcomings.

**Why play it:** For those interested in the Battle of Britain who will appreciate one of the few detailed simulators on the subject, even though it took later community patches to bring the game to stable playability.

pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-battle-of-stal.teaser: A new generation of the famous series; a modern engine and dynamic weather over Stalingrad.
pc-modern__il-2-sturmovik-battle-of-stal.article:
**IL-2 Sturmovik: Battle of Stalingrad** launched a new generation of the famous series and became the foundation of a modern, still-expanding simulation ecosystem set amid the fighting for Stalingrad on the Eastern Front. The game runs on a reworked engine that significantly improved terrain detail, aircraft models, and damage simulation compared to the older games, and it also features dynamically changing weather and seasons that affect visibility. It offers both Soviet and German aircraft typical of the Battle of Stalingrad and focuses on a highly refined, modern flight model that tries to capture the aerodynamic behavior of individual types as accurately as possible.

Since its release, the game has become a living platform onto which further campaigns set in other periods and fronts of World War II have gradually been added, sold as standalone expansions sharing the same engine and a connected Eastern Front game map. The multiplayer component offers large-scale online warfare with a sophisticated dynamic campaign system that responds to the outcomes of battles fought by individual player communities, thereby changing the course of the virtual war. Visually and audibly it ranks among the most sophisticated World War II simulators, with a very detailed cockpit environment, convincing weather and lighting modeling, and carefully recorded engine sounds for each type of aircraft.

Battle of Stalingrad is now generally regarded as one of the technically most advanced flight simulators devoted to World War II and is often recommended as the entry point into the whole series for new players, since it contains the most developed tutorial and assistance tools. Its long lifespan and constant expansion with new campaigns and aircraft show just how well its underlying technological and gameplay framework was designed. Even years later, it remains a reference title of the historical flight simulator genre and an inspiration for other simulation projects focused on flight-model authenticity.

**Why play it:** For both new and experienced flight simulator players, thanks to the most developed tutorial and assistance tools in the IL-2 Sturmovik series and still-reference-level technical execution.

pc-modern__lock-on-modern-air-combat.teaser: The predecessor of DCS World; detailed avionics simulation for the Su-27 and A-10 of its time.
pc-modern__lock-on-modern-air-combat.article:
**Lock On: Modern Air Combat** arrived in early 2003 as one of the most sophisticated modern combat aviation simulators of its time and became the predecessor of the later DCS World platform. The game, from studio Eagle Dynamics, let players fly selected contemporary combat aircraft, including the Su-27 and A-10, and focused on a detailed simulation of their avionics, weapon systems, and flight behavior. The campaign and individual missions took place in modern conflict scenarios that combined aerial dogfights with ground support and attacks on land and naval targets.

The flight model was among the most realistic on the market at the time, and the game let players choose between simplified and fully simulation-level controls, making it accessible both to newcomers and to demanding flight simulation enthusiasts. The detailed rendering of cockpits, radar systems, and weapon loadouts stood in contrast to the more arcade-like flight games of the era and marked a significant step toward an authentic simulation of modern aerial combat. The graphical treatment of the terrain and aircraft was above standard for its time and contributed to the overall sense of credibility, as did the elaborate sound effects for engines and fired weapons, including the realistic behavior of heat-seeking and radar-guided missiles.

Lock On became the foundation on which Eagle Dynamics later built the expansive DCS World platform, whose individual aircraft modules still build today on principles laid down by this very title, including its modular approach to individual aircraft. For the simulation enthusiast community of the time, it represented a significant step toward modern combat aviation, as opposed to the World War II simulators that had until then clearly dominated the market. Today it is seen mainly as a historically important precursor to today's DCS World and as one of the first seriously intentioned simulators of modern aviation on personal computers.

**Why play it:** For anyone interested in the history of modern combat aviation on PC and in the roots of today's DCS World, whose foundation Lock On laid at a time when the market was dominated by World War II simulators.

pc-modern__dcs-world.teaser: A free platform with purchasable modules; the Su-27, F/A-18, and historic aircraft alike.
pc-modern__dcs-world.article:
**DCS World** is a free platform from studio Eagle Dynamics onto which individually sold, extremely detailed simulation modules for specific combat aircraft, helicopters, and ground vehicles are gradually added. The base platform is free and includes training maps and a handful of basic aircraft, while full-fledged combat planes such as the Su-27, F/A-18 Hornet, F-16, or Mi-24 are purchased individually as paid modules, each with its own depth of cockpit and systems simulation. Over the years, the module lineup has also grown to include historic World War II aircraft, so the platform today covers several distinct historical periods.

A defining feature of DCS World is its almost study-level degree of detail in individual cockpits, where nearly every button and switch functions according to the real documentation of the aircraft in question, including complete engine start-up procedures and onboard system settings. This makes the platform a popular tool not only for entertainment but also for serious aviation enthusiasts and, in some cases, even for training purposes. The maps depict real regions, including the Caucasus, Normandy, and the Persian Gulf, and allow both historical and modern combat scenarios depending on the modules selected.

The multiplayer component allows large-scale cooperative and competitive missions that combine different types of hardware into a single battle, making DCS World one of the most complex war simulation platforms on the market. High performance requirements and a fairly steep learning curve are the price of its extraordinary simulation depth, which many players acquire gradually, system by system, often with the help of community guides and tutorials. Even today, DCS World is considered the technological and simulation pinnacle of the genre and is regularly expanded with new maps, aircraft modules, and graphics engine improvements that steadily raise the platform's overall visual quality.

**Why play it:** For players seeking one of the most complex war simulation platforms on the market, willing to master a steep learning curve in exchange for extraordinary depth and an ever-growing range of aircraft and maps.

pc-modern__microsoft-flight-simulator.teaser: Satellite data render the whole Earth; civilian flying with real weather and traffic.
pc-modern__microsoft-flight-simulator.article:
**Microsoft Flight Simulator**, from 2020, revived the brand's long history and delivered a civilian flight simulator that, thanks to satellite data and cloud processing, renders the entire surface of the Earth at very high quality. The game, from studio Asobo Studio, lets players fly a wide range of civilian aircraft, from small sport planes up to airliners, while focusing on maximum visual and meteorological authenticity of the environment. Real weather, current air traffic, and precise terrain models make it an experience close to actual civilian flying, including a simulation of turbulence and airflow over different types of terrain.

The core of the game is a refined flight model together with a detailed simulation of each aircraft's systems, though the level of detail varies by aircraft type and by third-party add-ons. Players can choose between simpler assisted modes and fully manual controls, making the title accessible to both casual players and flight simulation enthusiasts. Another strength is the extensive support for mods and add-ons from the community and third parties, which keep adding further aircraft, airports, and scenery with a high level of detail, often matching specific real-world locations.

The game's visual and technical execution was praised enormously at launch and became a new benchmark for civilian flight simulators, especially thanks to the combination of real satellite data with machine-generated buildings and vegetation that together create a convincing picture of the landscape and cities. Through successive updates, the game has expanded its content with further world regions and new aircraft, and improved both the performance and the detail of existing areas. Today, Microsoft Flight Simulator is regarded as the modern flagship of civilian flying on PC and the successor to a long-running series that has existed on computers since the 1980s, making it one of the longest-running game brands of all.

**Why play it:** For lovers of civilian flying seeking the most convincing image of the real Earth PC simulators have ever offered, thanks to the combination of satellite data and machine-generated landscape.

pc-modern__microsoft-flight-simulator-x.teaser: The last classic entry in the series before the 2020 generation; thousands of airports to explore.
pc-modern__microsoft-flight-simulator-x.article:
**Microsoft Flight Simulator X** was for a long time the pinnacle, and also the last classic installment, of the traditional series of civilian flight simulators from Microsoft, before it was replaced years later by the new generation launched in 2020. The game offered an extensive, if by today's standards simplified, model of the entire planet's surface, with thousands of airports and a wide range of civilian and smaller sport aircraft, from small training planes up to airliners. Free flight, in which players could choose their own route, aircraft, and conditions, was complemented by a challenges mode and individual missions focused on specific flying skills.

The flight model was very credible for its time, and the game supported a broad range of control devices, from a simple gamepad up to full joysticks and simulator cockpit setups with physical switches. Another strength was its remarkably developed support for mods, add-on aircraft, scenery, and community tools, which kept the game's active player base alive long after release, in some cases right up until the arrival of the new generation of the simulator. The graphical treatment of the landscape and aircraft was at the top of the genre at launch, though it naturally aged over the years compared to newer simulators.

FSX's release was demanding on the hardware of the time for many players, sparking discussion about optimization, but it also confirmed the title's ambition to push as far as technically possible toward a detailed rendering of the entire planet, including thousands of smaller airports. After Microsoft ended its support, the fan and modding ecosystem kept caring for the game, allowing it to remain playable and expandable for many more years, including through unofficial modifications enabling it to run on newer hardware. Today, FSX is seen as the last great representative of the classic era of civilian flying on PC before the rise of modern simulators.

**Why play it:** For fans of the classic era of civilian flying on PC who will appreciate thousands of finely detailed airports and the active modding community that keeps FSX playable even on modern hardware.

pc-modern__x-plane-11.teaser: Aerodynamics computed from a physical model, not from tables; also popular for pilot training.
pc-modern__x-plane-11.article:
**X-Plane 11** is a civilian flight simulator from studio Laminar Research that stands apart from competing titles primarily through its use of so-called blade element theory to calculate aerodynamics, meaning aircraft behavior is derived from a physical model of their construction rather than from pre-programmed tables. This makes the flight simulation especially credible even for unusual or non-standard damaged aircraft, which has won it favor not only among enthusiasts but also among part of the professional flight training community, which uses the simulator as a supplement to conventional training.

The game offers a wide range of civilian aircraft, from small sport planes to airliners, and allows detailed simulation of systems, weather, and ground traffic at airports, including realistic behavior in strong wind or crosswind conditions. Scenery covers the entire surface of the planet, though the level of detail across regions is uneven and is significantly expanded by an active community creating add-on scenery, aircraft, and flight planning tools. The user interface and settings are fairly technical and less approachable than in competing titles, reflecting the game's focus on simulation accuracy over friendliness, and newcomers may need a while to find their way around the settings.

The sound design and flying atmosphere are subordinated primarily to the credibility of the simulation rather than to visual stylization, and the game therefore comes across as matter-of-fact and technical, more like a professional tool than an entertainment product aimed at a broad audience. Thanks to its openness to modification and its certification for part of flight training, X-Plane 11 earned respect as a serious simulation tool, not just an entertainment title. Even after the release of its successor, X-Plane 12, the eleventh installment remains popular thanks to its lower performance requirements and the extensive library of existing community add-ons, which are not yet fully available for the newer version.

**Why play it:** For players who prefer a matter-of-fact, technically credible flight simulation over visual stylization, and who benefit from the extensive library of community add-ons still missing from the newer X-Plane 12.

pc-modern__war-thunder.teaser: Free-to-play title combining planes, tanks and ships in battles spanning history since the interwar era.
pc-modern__war-thunder.article:
**War Thunder** is a free-to-play online war game from studio Gaijin Entertainment that combines air, ground and naval combat units in shared battles spanning historical periods from the interwar era to early post-war technology. The player gradually unlocks tech trees for individual nations, including the USA, Germany, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and Japan, and can choose between several levels of realism, from more arcade-like battles to a demanding simulator mode with full cockpit controls and no on-screen assists.

The game's air component offers hundreds of historical aircraft from early fighters through bombers to the first jet-powered machines, with their performance and armament based on historical documentation and gradually adjusted as new findings emerge. Battles often take place in combined engagements where aircraft cooperate with or fight against tanks and anti-aircraft defenses on the ground, an unusual and refreshing combination compared to purely aerial simulators. The game's free-to-play model is supplemented by premium vehicles and a subscription, which has sparked discussions about progression balance, especially at higher tiers, where advancement without paid content is noticeably slower.

Visually and audibly, War Thunder ranks among the technically advanced titles of its genre, and regular updates expand the roster of vehicles and maps with newer, more modern machines, including modern jet aircraft and missile systems. Thanks to its combination of accessibility for new players and depth for enthusiasts of historical technology, it has become one of the most-played online war games ever and has built a long-term active community. For those interested in historical aircraft and ground vehicles, it offers an unusually broad and still-growing database of machines from many countries and eras, complemented by detailed information on their history and armament.

**Why play it:** For fans of historical and modern vehicles across countries and eras who will appreciate its accessibility for newcomers as well as its depth for enthusiasts, plus a constantly growing database of machines.

pc-modern__ace-combat-7-skies-unknown.teaser: Arcade aerial combat in the fictional Strangereal, cinematically staged and spectacular.
pc-modern__ace-combat-7-skies-unknown.article:
**Ace Combat 7: Skies Unknown** brought PC players the long-awaited continuation of the arcade aerial combat series that combines spectacular, cinematically staged dogfights with a fictional wartime story set in the world of Strangereal. As a fighter pilot, the player progresses through increasingly demanding missions filled with enemy fighters, huge aircraft carriers and futuristic weapon systems, while the plot combines political intrigue with the personal story of the main character, whose past is gradually revealed.

The gameplay builds on an accessible yet satisfying flight model that focuses on smooth maneuvering, target locking and the spectacular use of special weapons rather than full simulation accuracy. The missions offer great visual variety, from storm fronts through mountains to space elevators and other grandiose structures, lending the series its typically spectacular character and sense of drama. Virtual reality support for part of the content further heightens the feeling of immersion in aerial battles and flying the aircraft from the cockpit, a rather rare feature for purely arcade aerial combat.

The musical score and cinematic cutscenes have long been among the series' strongest points, and Skies Unknown continues this tradition, with bombastic orchestral pieces accompanying key battles and dramatic story turns. At release, the title was well received as a return to the series' roots after detours into more realistically styled spin-offs, and it is often cited as one of the best entries in the series, comparable to the franchise's earlier high points. For fans of arcade aerial combat, it offers one of the most cohesive and visually striking experiences of the genre on PC, thanks in part to its engaging audiovisual treatment of individual missions and their carefully constructed dramaturgy.

**Why play it:** For fans of arcade aerial combat craving bombastic music, cinematic cutscenes and a return to the series' roots after detours into more realistic spin-offs.

pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-h-w-x.teaser: Arcade aerial combat with Enhanced Reality View assistance for easier target runs.
pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-h-w-x.article:
**Tom Clancy's H.A.W.X** is an arcade aerial combat game set in the near future, in which the player, as a pilot in a mercenary air unit, takes part in conflicts tied to the universe of Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon and other brands carrying the author's name. The game focuses on fast, spectacular aerial combat with modern and futuristic aircraft, complemented by a system called Enhanced Reality View, which displays a recommended flight path to the player and eases orientation during complex maneuvers and target runs. The roster of aircraft includes real current and upcoming fighters and bombers, among which the player gradually unlocks access to more powerful machines.

Missions combine fighter-versus-fighter combat with ground unit support and convoy protection, and between missions the player can also switch between several aircraft with different characteristics and specializations, from fast fighters to heavy bombers. The emphasis on accessibility and smooth action makes H.A.W.X a typical representative of the arcade approach to aerial combat, aimed at a broader audience rather than simulation enthusiasts, making it easy to pick up even for players with no experience of more demanding simulators. Visually, the game offered nicely rendered views of cities and landscapes during low-altitude flights, which was frequently mentioned as a positive in contemporary reviews, along with dynamic camera work following the action from several angles.

The storyline connecting the game to other titles from the Tom Clancy universe gave the campaign broader context, even though the script itself remained rather in the background in favor of action and spectacular maneuvers. H.A.W.X received a sequel, H.A.W.X 2, which further developed the same arcade approach to modern aerial battles and expanded the available roster of vehicles. Today, the title is seen as a typical, well-made representative of accessible arcade aerial combat from the late 2000s, even though the genre is now dominated by newer titles such as Ace Combat 7.

**Why play it:** For players seeking accessible arcade aerial combat with spectacular maneuvers and ties to the world of Tom Clancy, even though the script stays mostly in the background behind the action itself.

pc-modern__strike-fighters-2.teaser: A more accessible Cold War combat aircraft simulator; an alternative to the demanding DCS World.
pc-modern__strike-fighters-2.article:
**Strike Fighters 2** is a flight simulator from the small studio Third Wire Productions, focused on the Cold War era and modern combat aircraft of the second half of the twentieth century. The game emphasizes a combination of relatively accessible controls with credibly rendered avionics and armament for each aircraft, which made it a popular choice for players who wanted deeper simulation than arcade flight games but without the extreme demands of full-fledged study simulators like DCS World. The roster of aircraft covers both the Western and Soviet blocs, allowing a range of fictional and historically inspired Cold War conflicts to be simulated.

The base game was gradually expanded with numerous paid and unofficial add-ons that added further aircraft, maps and conflicts, from Middle Eastern wars to fictional Cold War scenarios set in Europe. It was precisely this openness to modification and the ease of community content editing that gave the game an unusually long lifespan well beyond its original release, aided by tools for creating custom missions and campaigns. The graphics were solid for their time, though not on the level of major simulator productions, a shortfall made up for by the breadth of content and the variety of scenarios and available aircraft.

The sound design and modeling of individual aircraft reflected the studio's many years of specialization in this type of simulator, dating back to even older entries in the series from the late nineties. Thanks to its low performance requirements and extensive modifiability, Strike Fighters 2 has kept an active community for many years after release, despite being a product of a small independent studio without a major publisher's budget. For those interested in Cold War and modern-era aircraft, it still offers today one of the few more detailed simulation alternatives outside the big commercial series, with a very open and friendly modding community.

**Why play it:** For those interested in Cold War and modern-era aircraft outside the big commercial series, who will appreciate low performance requirements and an open, friendly modding community.

pc-modern__silent-hunter-iii.teaser: The definitive submarine simulation: periscope, TDC targeting computer and war in the Atlantic from 1939.
pc-modern__silent-hunter-iii.article:
**Silent Hunter III** cast the player as the commander of a German Type VII U-boat during the Second World War, and for many genre fans it became the definitive embodiment of the submarine simulator on PC. The player plans voyages from French ports, tracks merchant convoys through the periscope and hydrophone, manually calculates torpedo firing angles using a simulated TDC targeting computer, and must manage limited fuel, torpedoes and crew patience during long patrols in the Atlantic. The career mode carries the player through the entire war from 1939 onward, with the success of individual patrols affecting decorations, promotions and gradual upgrades to the submarine.

The game combines detailed simulation with tense moments of evading depth charges from escort vessels, dynamic hull damage, and modeling of crew experience and morale that directly affects the submarine's performance. The range of realism settings spans from a more accessible arcade approach to fully manual control without helper indicators, so the game could be tailored by both newcomers and seasoned simulation enthusiasts alike. The graphics engine felt unexpectedly convincing for its time — the rippling surface, weather and lighting gave the game a strong atmosphere, underscored by oppressive music and the sounds of sonar, engines and distant explosions. Extensive community modifications, especially the GWX package, later deepened the game's realism and content and became almost a mandatory addition for many players.

Upon release, Silent Hunter III earned praise for its simulation depth and atmosphere, and to this day fans of the genre still rank it among the best submarine simulators ever made. It significantly influenced later entries in the series as well as competing naval warfare titles and set a benchmark that later simulators long measured themselves against. Even with today's hindsight, it works as an exceptionally tense and well-thought-out simulator, though it demands patience and a willingness to learn its complex systems from the player.

**Why play it:** For fans of submarine simulators seeking an exceptionally tense and well-thought-out experience, still ranked among the best of its kind today, though it requires patience to master its complex systems.

pc-modern__silent-hunter-4-wolves-of-pac.teaser: The proven submarine simulation moves to the Pacific; choose between the American and Japanese side.
pc-modern__silent-hunter-4-wolves-of-pac.article:
**Silent Hunter 4: Wolves of the Pacific** moved the proven submarine warfare simulation from the Atlantic to the Pacific and gave the player the choice of commanding an American or Japanese submarine across a vast Pacific theater. Instead of convoys sailing through cold northern waters, the player deals with long transits across open ocean, hunting for enemy merchant and warships, and deciding when to risk an attack and when to dive and wait for a safer opportunity instead. The choice of side also fundamentally changed the perspective on the war itself, since the Japanese campaign put the player in the role of defending their own supply lines.

The game builds on the mechanics of the previous entry — manual torpedo targeting, crew management, submarine damage and changeable weather — and expands them with a dynamic campaign following the key points of the Pacific front from the attack on Pearl Harbor onward. The rendering of the ocean and lighting conditions under tropical sun or during a storm was among the best of its time, and together with atmospheric music it heightened the sense of loneliness on long patrols far from the home port. The length of individual voyages and the need to monitor fuel and crew oxygen supplies also added an element of logistical planning that other simulators of the time did not emphasize as much. Community modifications once again pushed the game toward greater realism and filled in a number of missing details, including more historically accurate ship models.

The game was received as a worthy expansion of the series into a new setting, though some players had reservations about period technical shortcomings. Even so, it became a popular choice for those who wanted to experience the naval war from both the Japanese and American perspectives. Today it is valued above all for the atmosphere of the vast Pacific and for its long, meditative patrols that contrast with the tense moments of torpedo attacks.

**Why play it:** For players wanting to experience the naval war from both the Japanese and American perspectives, who will appreciate the atmosphere of the vast Pacific and the contrast between long patrols and tense torpedo attacks.

pc-modern__silent-hunter-5-battle-of-atl.teaser: A return to the Atlantic with a first-person walk through the submarine and control of every station.
pc-modern__silent-hunter-5-battle-of-atl.article:
**Silent Hunter 5: Battle of the Atlantic** returned to the European theater and gave the player command of a German submarine in a new graphical form, including the ability to walk through the interior of the submarine in first person and personally operate individual crew stations, from navigation through sonar to the torpedo tubes. The basic principle remained the same as in previous entries — voyages from French ports, hunting for convoys, manual torpedo targeting, and trying to survive countermeasures from escort vessels and aircraft protecting Allied ships throughout the Battle of the Atlantic.

Compared to earlier entries, the game simplified some simulation elements and placed greater emphasis on visuals and direct crew control, which produced mixed reactions among the series' hardcore fans, since the beloved manual TDC targeting computer was retained but was surrounded by more action-oriented, accessible elements. A new engine technically brought more detailed submarine and ocean models and more impressive interiors, but the game launched burdened with bugs and a controversial always-online verification system that made offline play or play without a stable internet connection difficult for many players. The atmosphere was rounded out by music and interior sounds, such as the hull creaking under pressure or crew shouts when hit, which heightened the claustrophobic feeling of a long stay beneath the surface, far from the home port.

Upon release, the game faced criticism mainly for its technical problems and copy protection, but subsequent updates and community modifications significantly improved it over time and filled in missing content. Today, Silent Hunter 5 is seen as the weakest of the main trio of modern entries in the series, yet thanks to patches and mods it has found its own circle of fans who appreciate above all its visual side and the ability to personally walk through the submarine's interior.

**Why play it:** For series fans willing to overlook the weaker reputation of the youngest entry in exchange for the ability to personally walk through the submarine's interior, especially after fixes and mods filled in the missing content.

pc-modern__dangerous-waters.teaser: The most demanding military simulator: command a submarine, ship or aircraft based on sonar detection.
pc-modern__dangerous-waters.article:
**Dangerous Waters** ranks among the most demanding and detailed military simulators ever made for PC, as it lets the player command not only a submarine but also a surface ship or an anti-submarine aircraft, all within one interconnected system of modern naval warfare. Instead of an arcade approach, it offers gameplay based on genuine sonar and radar detection, where the player must analyze acoustic traces, distinguish target types by their acoustic signature, and only then decide whether to fire or evade based on that data.

The simulation's depth is also reflected in its controls — the number of switches, displays and stations resembles a real combat information center, and the game makes practically no compromises in favor of accessibility, even for newcomers, who must first work their way through extensive training missions before understanding how the individual sensors and weapon systems work together. Missions range from hunting Cold War Soviet submarines to more modern scenarios involving guided missiles and air defense, while multiplayer allowed multiple players to split the individual posts on a single vessel among themselves, with each focusing on their own station — a unique approach at the time to cooperation and team coordination within a single combat unit. The sound design of the sonar, the rumble of turbines and radio communication were among the elements that defined the game the most and gave it an almost documentary tone.

Due to its extreme difficulty and austere user interface, Dangerous Waters remained the domain of a narrow but dedicated community of tactical simulator enthusiasts rather than a mass-played title. Even today it is considered one of the most authentic attempts to simulate underwater and surface combat, and regardless of its age it still serves as a reference point for every later project attempting a similar degree of realism and complexity.

**Why play it:** For dedicated tactical simulator enthusiasts seeking one of the most authentic attempts to simulate underwater and surface combat, even at the cost of extreme difficulty and an austere interface.

pc-modern__battlestations-midway.teaser: A hybrid of strategy and action: command the fleet at Midway while switching into the cockpit or onto the deck.
pc-modern__battlestations-midway.article:
**Battlestations: Midway** offered an unusual combination of strategic command over a naval fleet with direct, action-based control of individual ships and aircraft, making it a hybrid between a tactical simulator and arcade action. In the campaign, the player follows the key battles of the American-Japanese war in the Pacific, deploys ships and squadrons on the map, and at crucial moments can switch into the cockpit of a torpedo bomber or onto the deck of a battleship to fight from the perspective of a single unit, before returning to the overall battle overview to decide the fleet's next move.

This link between the two layers of gameplay gave battles a dynamism that purely tactical simulators of the time didn't offer — the player could personally pilot a fighter squadron covering their own bombers, or directly man a battleship's anti-aircraft guns during a Japanese air raid and repel a wave of torpedo bombers before they could reach the player's own carriers. The graphical rendering of giant battleships, aircraft carriers, and dozens of simultaneously flying planes was impressive for its time, underscored by bold music that emphasized the epic character of the Pacific clashes. The campaign followed historical milestones from Pearl Harbor to the Battle of Midway, after which the game is named, with the player gradually working their way from early defeats to the decisive victories of the American navy.

Battlestations: Midway was received as a fresh and accessible take on naval warfare that managed to appeal even to players who would normally shy away from a typical strategy simulator. It's still valued today for its inventive genre mix and visually spectacular battles, even though it leans more toward fun action than deep simulation. For many players it was their first encounter with the subject of the Pacific naval war and served as an accessible gateway to the less arcade-like simulators of the same period. The quick switching between the strategic and action viewpoints also became a hallmark of the whole series and inspired the sequel, Battlestations: Pacific.

**Why play it:** For players who'd be put off by a classic strategy simulator but will appreciate an inventive mix of action and strategy, plus visually spectacular Pacific battles, as an accessible gateway into the subject.

pc-modern__battlestations-pacific.teaser: A sequel with a campaign for the Japanese navy; a second perspective on the war in the Pacific.
pc-modern__battlestations-pacific.article:
**Battlestations: Pacific** built on the successful concept of the 2007 predecessor and expanded it primarily with the option to play a campaign as the Imperial Japanese Navy, which gave the Pacific conflict a second, previously unused perspective. The player again switches between commanding the entire fleet on the strategic map and directly controlling individual ships and aircraft in an ongoing battle, whether a destroyer, a submarine, or a fighter squadron protecting its own carriers, and can jump between units at any time depending on where the battle is currently heating up.

The Japanese campaign let players experience an alternative version of the war, where they try to counter growing American superiority, offering a different pace and different tactical choices than the offensive American storyline, where the player is instead pushed toward rapid expansion and exploiting overwhelming material superiority. This contrast between defensive and offensive strategy was one of the biggest differences between the sequel and the original. The game broadened its roster of units and battle scenarios, improved the graphics and the explosion and fire effects on decks, and kept the bold, cinematically styled music accompanying the great clashes between the fleets of both sides of the conflict. Multiplayer modes let players face off against each other in these very same spectacular battles of carriers, battleships, and submarines, offering entertainment even after finishing both single-player campaigns.

Battlestations: Pacific was received as a successful expansion of the core idea, bringing more content and variety through playable Japan. Today it's seen as the more mature and content-richer of the series' two entries, and remains a popular choice for fans of an accessible take on the Pacific naval war even years later, particularly thanks to the chance to experience the conflict from both sides of the front line.

**Why play it:** For fans of an accessible take on the Pacific naval war who will appreciate the richer content and the chance to experience the conflict from both sides of the front line through playable Japan.

pc-modern__ship-simulator-extremes.teaser: The civilian counterpart to war simulators: steering tankers and tugboats into ports around the world.
pc-modern__ship-simulator-extremes.article:
Unlike most titles in this selection, **Ship Simulator Extremes** doesn't focus on war but on civilian shipping, offering the player the chance to take the helm of a tanker, a container ship, a tugboat, or a rescue vessel across a range of ports and waterways around the world. The goal of each mission is to bring the ship safely and precisely to its destination, back it up to a pier, or carry out a rescue operation at sea, which in practice means mastering the physically modeled inertia of giant vessels, currents, wind, and limited visibility, where a single misjudged distance can mean a collision with a pier or another ship.

The game emphasizes authentic controls of the kind a player would find on the bridge of a real ship, including radar, GPS navigation, and communication with port control, and rewards patient, precise maneuvering rather than fast reflexes, a key difference from the more action-oriented titles in this selection. The graphical rendering of ports, weather, and the water surface was solid for its time and gave the simulation the atmosphere it needed, though neither the sound nor the music was ever what defined the game most. The range of different vessel types, from small tugboats to giant tankers, let the player experience just how differently individual ships behave, from nimble rescue boats to slow-reacting giant container ships.

Ship Simulator Extremes was received as a solid, if niche, simulation for players looking for an alternative to war and action titles. Today it remains an interesting choice for those who want to experience the calmer, meditative side of sailing the seas, even though it lacks the tension and drama of military simulators. It's precisely this calmer, more accessible nature that still makes it a suitable choice for players just getting acquainted with the ship simulation genre.

**Why play it:** For players seeking a calmer, meditative alternative to war and action titles, and an accessible introduction to the ship simulation genre, even without the tension of military simulators.

pc-modern__naval-action.teaser: An 18th-century sailing ship MMO with genuine sailing physics; turning into the wind takes forever.
pc-modern__naval-action.article:
**Naval Action** transports players to the era of sailing ships of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, the age of great naval wars between European powers, offering an open multiplayer world where ships are governed by genuine sailing principles — the need to track wind direction and strength, trim sails, and plan maneuvers dozens of seconds ahead, because turning into the wind takes a long time and can't be rushed. The player gradually builds a career from a small schooner up to giant ships of the line, trades, builds ships, and takes part in battles between national factions and independent players, with the choice of historical faction affecting both port access and the types of vessels available.

The combat system rewards patience and a thorough knowledge of sailing both with and against the wind, because a poorly angled ship can lose speed at exactly the moment it needs to escape or attack from an advantageous position, and regaining lost speed can take whole minutes. The game's economic layer ties production, trade, and warfare between players into a single living world, where losing a ship in battle has real consequences for further play and forces the player to weigh the risk before setting sail. The graphical rendering of the sea, sails, and detailed damage to wooden hulls was among the best the genre had to offer, reinforcing the illusion of genuine sailing-ship warfare, where you can watch sails gradually tear and rigging snap under fire.

Naval Action was praised above all by players seeking an authentic sailing model that other games lacked, though its steep learning curve and focus on multiplayer combat put off some casual would-be players. It remains one of the few titles that devote themselves so thoroughly to the physics of sailing, and for naval history enthusiasts it represents a one-of-a-kind experience.

**Why play it:** For naval history enthusiasts craving an authentic sailing model that other games don't offer, even though the steep learning curve and focus on multiplayer combat will put off casual players.

pc-modern__atlantic-fleet.teaser: Tactical war at sea: the hunt for the Bismarck and Atlantic convoys under two flags.
pc-modern__atlantic-fleet.article:
**Atlantic Fleet** is a turn-based and real-time tactical game focused on the surface naval battles of the Second World War in the Atlantic, where the fate of convoys supplying Britain was decided, in which the player commands a British or German fleet of battleships, cruisers, and destroyers and must exploit the strengths and weaknesses of each vessel type. The campaign follows key historical clashes, from the hunt for the Bismarck to long convoy battles in the harsh waters of the North Atlantic, forcing the player to decide on ship positioning, firing angles, and target priority before the gun battle itself even breaks out, one where how quickly the player can react to the enemy's opening salvos also matters.

Made by the same studio behind the later Cold Waters, the game builds on a clear yet honest model of ballistics and ship damage, where individual hits gradually knock out turrets, the rudder, or the engine room, changing the tactical situation as the battle progresses, so that even a badly damaged ship can still decide the outcome of an engagement. Clean 3D graphics with the option to watch the duel from various angles made every exchange of fire a visually legible and tense experience, even though the game aims more for accessibility than maximum simulation depth. The sound effects of the guns and the music accompanying the battles gave the games a dramatic tone matching the historical events they depict, whether it's the chase after a lone battleship or defending a convoy against overwhelming odds.

Atlantic Fleet was well received as an accessible yet honest alternative to larger, more demanding simulators, ideal for players who wanted to experience great battleship battles without having to master complex controls. It's still counted among the favorite titles for fans of Second World War surface naval warfare and serves as a good introduction to the subject before tackling more demanding simulators.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience great battleship battles without mastering complex controls, ideal as an accessible introduction to Second World War surface naval warfare.

pc-modern__cold-waters.teaser: Cold War submarine warfare inspired by Red Storm Rising; more accessible, but still tactical.
pc-modern__cold-waters.article:
**Cold Waters** draws inspiration from classic titles like Red Storm Rising and lets the player command an American submarine in hypothetical Cold War conflicts that, fortunately, never escalated into open war, facing off against submarines, surface ships, and patrol aircraft of the Soviet navy in a tense environment where a single mistake can mean a quick end to the patrol. Rather than the extreme complexity of the most demanding older simulators, it relies on more streamlined, but still tactically demanding controls, where the correct use of depth, speed, angle, and silent running decides whether the submarine remains undetected until the right moment for an attack or a quiet escape arrives.

The campaign ties individual missions into a broader story of an escalating conflict that, in a different turn of the Cold War, could easily have grown into open war, and rewards cautious, deliberate play over rash aggression — a single mistake in estimating the enemy's position can mean getting hit by a torpedo or a depth charge. Clear, legible graphics and an intuitive interface let the game appeal even to players who'd be put off by text-heavy simulators like Dangerous Waters, without sacrificing the tension of hunting submarines beneath the waves. The sound design of the sonar and the music underscoring the tense moments before firing a torpedo are among the strongest things the game has to offer, and together with the crew's callouts they create a powerful atmosphere of undersea tension.

Upon release, Cold Waters was very well received by both critics and players as a successful revival of the genre of modern submarine simulators, one that had been neglected for a long time. It's still considered one of the most accessible, yet still tense entry points into the genre of Cold War submarine simulators, even for players with no prior experience with hardcore simulators.

**Why play it:** For players with no experience with hardcore simulators who are looking for an accessible, yet still tense way into the long-neglected genre of Cold War submarine simulators.

pc-modern__uboat.teaser: Silent Hunter enriched with crew management; a top-down cutaway of the submarine like in a management sim.
pc-modern__uboat.article:
**UBOAT** combines classic Second World War submarine warfare simulation, similar to the older entries in the Silent Hunter series, with elements of crew management and survival, where the player not only plans voyages and convoy attacks, much like in classic Silent Hunter titles, but also handles the submarine's daily operation — assigning shifts, monitoring the crew's fatigue and morale, repairing damaged systems, and deciding how to use the limited space for supplies, ammunition, and other equipment needed for a long voyage far from the home base. The top-down cutaway view of the submarine, similar to management simulators, gives the player direct control over what's happening in every part of the hull, from the engine room through the torpedo tubes to the galley and crew quarters.

The combat sequences themselves preserve the tension typical of the genre — manually aiming torpedoes, evading depth charges, and having to decide when to risk surfacing and when to stay at a safe depth and wait for a patrol plane or destroyer to lose interest and sail off elsewhere. The crew-survival element, however, gives the game a different dynamic than the older Silent Hunter titles, because even a successful voyage can end badly if the player neglects the crew's rest or training. The game was released gradually in early access, during which it expanded with new mechanics and content before reaching its full release, changing and deepening significantly compared to its early form.

UBOAT was praised specifically for combining two genres that had rarely crossed paths before, and it built its own audience among fans of both submarine simulators and survival management games. Today it represents one of the more modern and accessible alternatives for players who want to experience submarine warfare from an unusual angle, one where keeping the crew strong and in good spirits matters just as much as hitting a convoy.

**Why play it:** For players wanting to experience submarine warfare from an unusual angle, where hitting a convoy matters just as much as keeping the crew strong and in good spirits, thanks to its blend of simulation with survival management.

pc-modern__sea-power-naval-combat-in-mis.teaser: A rare simulator of the guided-missile and radar era; commanding an entire naval battle group at once.
pc-modern__sea-power-naval-combat-in-mis.article:
**Sea Power: Naval Combat in the Missile Age** simulates modern and Cold War naval battles of the guided-missile, radar, and air-defense era — territory that few simulators have covered so far — with the player commanding entire groups of surface ships, submarines, and aircraft and having to master electronic warfare just as well as classic maneuvering, because an overlooked radar contact can mean losing the entire group. Instead of a single ship, the game emphasizes command of an entire battle group, where radar coverage, missile defense, and offensive assets must be coordinated across several vessels at once, much as a real task-force commander would do.

The game follows in the tradition of older tactical simulators focused on modern naval warfare and tries to model just how fundamentally guided missiles and electronic warfare transformed the character of naval battles compared to the artillery duels of the past. Engagements are often decided the moment the enemy is detected and the threat correctly assessed, not only once direct contact is made, giving the game a different pace than classic Second World War submarine or battleship simulators, where combat is far more visual and direct. A clear tactical map combined with a detailed 3D view of individual ships lets you follow the battle on both levels at once, from the global deployment of forces down to the launch of a single missile.

Upon release, Sea Power was received as an interesting and technically ambitious attempt to fill the gap between historical Second World War simulators and the shortage of games focused on the era of missiles and modern electronics. For fans of the genre, it represents one of the few current titles that treat modern naval warfare with the same seriousness as a classic like Dangerous Waters, and as such it's winning an ever-growing circle of fans.

**Why play it:** For fans of seriously crafted naval simulators who missed a game devoted to the era of missiles and modern electronics with the same care as the classic Dangerous Waters.

pc-modern__world-of-warships.teaser: Wargaming's World of Tanks brought to the sea; historic battleships in team-based battles.
pc-modern__world-of-warships.article:
**World of Warships** takes Wargaming's successful formula, known from the tank-based World of Tanks, out to sea, offering players battles between dozens of historic battleships, cruisers, destroyers, and aircraft carriers from the first half of the twentieth century, modeled after real vessels from around the world. Matches take place in teams on relatively small maps full of islands and narrow straits, where the player must consider their own ship's armor angle against the enemy, choice of ammunition, gun range, and when to reveal their position with an attack versus staying hidden behind a smokescreen while waiting for a more advantageous moment to strike.

The free-to-play model, with gradual unlocking and upgrading of ships using in-game and real-world resources, motivates players to progress through the tech tree across several naval powers, from Japan to the United States and Germany, with each nation's line of ships having its own characteristic playstyle, from precise but slower Japanese cruisers to durable American battleships. Clear, colorful graphics and fairly accessible controls allowed the game to reach a broad audience that might otherwise be intimidated by more complex historical simulators, without entirely abandoning respect for the historical accuracy of the vessels' designs. Regular updates brought new ships, maps, and game modes, keeping the player community active for many years after release, and the game remains among the longest continuously supported online titles of its genre to this day.

World of Warships became one of the most successful modern naval-themed games ever and introduced a wide generation of players to the subject of battleships and cruisers who might otherwise never have encountered the genre. It remains a living, regularly updated game with an active community to this day, and represents a completely different, more arcade-like approach to the subject than most other titles in this selection.

**Why play it:** For players who want battleships and cruisers in an accessible, arcade-style form with a lively, regularly updated online community, rather than a hardcore simulator.

pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-iii.teaser: First brought the series into 3D; the 2002 port showed PC gamers open-world at a new scale.
pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-iii.article:
**Grand Theft Auto III** brought the series into a genuinely three-dimensional world and arrived on PC in 2002 as a port of the console version, published by Rockstar Games. The player finds themselves in Liberty City, a fictional metropolis inspired by New York, in the role of a silent criminal named Claude, who fights his way up the mob hierarchy to power after a botched heist and betrayal.
