The game combined a third-person action shooter with an open world that could be freely explored, cars that could be stolen, and linear as well as side missions completed at the player's own pace and preference — a concept that, in 2002, hardly anyone on PC had seen at that scale.

The core of the gameplay is a combination of vehicle driving, shooting, and completing missions assigned by characters scattered around the city, complemented by radio stations with their own hosts, ads, and music spanning multiple genres, which lend the world a surprisingly authentic atmosphere of a crime-ridden metropolis. The PC version offered higher resolution and better draw distance compared to the consoles of the time, and it also became the foundation for an extensive modding scene, thanks to which the game still maintains an active community of creators adding new vehicles, missions, and technical improvements to this day. Mouse and keyboard controls brought more precise aiming, making the game even more accessible on computers to a wider audience of players used to other genres than action-adventures.

Upon release, GTA III received extraordinary acclaim as well as controversy over its violence and the ability to commit crimes without immediate punishment, sparking public debates about the influence of video games on society and attempts to ban it in some countries. It fundamentally defined the open-world action genre and influenced dozens of later titles that adopted its formula of a free city full of opportunities and side activities. Even years later it remains playable and historically significant, though its controls, camera, and artificial intelligence feel archaic today compared to the sequels it itself helped launch and define for years to come.

**Why play it:** For anyone curious where the modern open-world genre was born — but expect archaic controls, camera, and AI compared to later entries.

pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-vice-city.teaser: Neon-lit eighties Miami; Tommy Vercetti builds a crime empire among gangs and cartels.
pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-vice-city.article:
**Grand Theft Auto: Vice City** arrived on PC in 2003 and transported players to the sunny Vice City, a caricature of 1980s Miami full of neon lights, palm trees, convertibles, and synthesizer music that saturates the entire city with its atmosphere. Main character Tommy Vercetti, after being released from prison and a drug deal gone wrong, tries to rebuild his own criminal empire and gradually finds himself in conflict with local gangs, cartels, biker gangs, and corrupt politicians and police officers alike. Compared to the third installment, the game significantly expanded the world, added the ability to buy properties and businesses that generate income, and offered a more elaborate story with distinctive, well-written characters.

The gameplay builds on its predecessor but refines the shooting, driving model, and vehicle variety, including motorcycles, boats, and helicopters, opening up even more ways to move around the city. The 1980s stylization is also reflected in the soundtrack, where dozens of licensed songs playing on fictional radio stations, combined with neon graphics and bold colors, create an unmistakable atmosphere of the disco, new wave, and rock era. The PC version benefited from higher graphical quality and also became a very popular platform for modifications that extended the story, vehicle roster, and technical capabilities of the engine far beyond the game's original intended limits.

Vice City was met with enthusiastic acclaim from critics and players alike upon release and remained one of the most successful and best-selling games of its generation for years, even though it too faced criticism for its depiction of violence and stereotypical portrayal of certain communities. Its emphasis on atmosphere, music, and the personality of its protagonist influenced the direction of the entire series as well as competing open-world games for years to come. Today it is regarded as one of the high points of the early era of three-dimensional GTA games, one that players return to both for nostalgia and for gameplay that remains functional and fun.

**Why play it:** For its unmistakable atmosphere, eighties soundtrack, and charismatic protagonist, which make Vice City fun and functional even today, not just a nostalgic memory.

pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-san-andreas.teaser: Three cities, desert, and mountains in one world; Carl Johnson faces the collapse of his family and gang.
pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-san-andreas.article:
**Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas** was released on PC in 2005 and offered an unprecedentedly vast world made up of three cities inspired by Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Las Vegas, along with the countryside, desert, and mountains between them. The story follows Carl Johnson, who returns home to Los Santos after years away to face the collapse of his family and gang, as well as the schemes of corrupt police officers exploiting his past for their own gain. The game expanded the series' concept with a gang territory system, character training, appearance, clothing, and vehicle customization, as well as flying planes and skydiving.

The scope of content was staggering for its time: the player could go to the gym, eat at fast food restaurants, play pool, or get tattoos and haircuts, creating a sense of a truly lived-in world rather than just a backdrop for missions. Technically, the game ran on an improved version of the Vice City engine, and the PC version enabled higher resolution and modifications, among which a controversial modification unlocking a cut sexual scene stood out, leading to the game's rating being subsequently changed in some countries and its withdrawal from sale. A hip-hop, funk, and rock soundtrack from the nineties gave the world a distinctive period identity tied to West Coast culture.

San Andreas became one of the best-selling and most influential titles of its generation and set the benchmark against which the ambitions of open-world games were measured for years afterward. Critics and players praised the scope of content, the freedom, and the number of parallel activities the game offered alongside the main storyline, as well as its distinctive characters and dialogue full of period slang. Even today it is considered one of the high points of the series thanks to its wealth of activities and nostalgic mid-nineties atmosphere, though some of its mechanics, animations, and graphics now clearly show their age and require a bit of tolerance from a modern player.

**Why play it:** For fans of a huge amount of side content and the nostalgic atmosphere of the mid-nineties, even though outdated mechanics and graphics today require a bit of tolerance.

pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-iv.teaser: A darker Liberty City powered by Euphoria physics; Niko Bellic seeks a fresh start and revenge.
pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-iv.article:
**Grand Theft Auto IV** arrived on PC in 2008 and brought the series into a new generation thanks to the switch to the RAGE engine with the Euphoria physics system, which gave the movement of characters and vehicles a significantly more realistic and natural feel than previous entries. The story is set in Liberty City, modeled after New York, and follows Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant with a dark military past, who is looking for a fresh start in America as well as revenge for a betrayal from the past. The tone of the game is darker and grittier than its predecessors, placing greater emphasis on characters, moral dilemmas, and the consequences of violence.

The open world was denser and more visually detailed than earlier entries, with elaborate modeling of traffic, pedestrians, and weather, as well as a mobile phone system through which the player arranges meetings, manages contacts, and decides on side activities with friends. The PC version had technical problems with optimization and copy protection at launch, which drew criticism from players and journalists alike, but thanks to later fixes, modifications, and high resolution it became a popular choice for players wanting the best available graphical quality. Multiplayer modes expanded the game with cooperative and competitive activities set in the same city.

GTA IV was received by critics upon release as a significant artistic and technical step forward, praised especially for its storytelling, voice performances, and atmosphere of a decaying American dream full of corrupt characters. Although its PC version had an inglorious technical start, it is now appreciated as one of the technically most demanding titles of its time, and complemented by the expansions The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, it offers rich and varied content. The game's influence on storytelling in open-world games, as well as the series' reputation as a vehicle for social commentary, remains apparent long after its release, and many later titles consciously referenced its melancholic tone.

**Why play it:** For players who appreciate strong storytelling and the melancholic atmosphere of a decaying American dream, further enriched by the expansions The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony.

pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-v.teaser: Three intertwined protagonists and a satire of America; heists staged as cinematic set pieces.
pc-modern__grand-theft-auto-v.article:
**Grand Theft Auto V** arrived on PC in 2015, a year after the console versions, bringing the series' most expansive and detailed world yet, spread across the fictional Los Santos and the surrounding countryside, mountains, and desert. For the first time, the game centers on three main protagonists, between whom the player switches in real time, and their intertwined fates form the backbone of a story about heists, betrayals, and satire of the American way of life and showbusiness. Heist missions become the game's set-piece highlights, combining planning, choice of approach, shootouts, and police chases.

The PC version stood out for its support of high resolution, denser traffic, improved weather, and other graphical enhancements beyond the console versions, which for a long time made it a standard benchmark for graphics card performance. Besides an extensive single-player campaign, the game also offered the online multiplayer Grand Theft Auto Online, which over the years grew into an independent living world with regularly added content, vehicles, and activities, becoming an extraordinarily long-term profitable product for the publisher. Humor, music, and a satirical view of modern California gave the game an unmistakable and recognizable tone.

Grand Theft Auto V is among the most successful and most discussed video games ever made, and its PC version, thanks to modifications, high frame rates, and a persistent online community, remains alive to this day, more than ten years after its initial release. Critics praised the scope of the world, the quality of the storytelling, and the technical execution, even as the game repeatedly became a target of debates about the depiction of violence and microtransactions in the online mode. As a must-play title, it still serves as an entry point into the entire series for a new generation of players who never experienced the earlier entries, and its longevity on PC has virtually no equal in the open-world genre.

**Why play it:** For newcomers and series veterans alike — thanks to modifications, high frame rates, and a lively online community, the PC version remains current even ten years after release.

pc-modern__max-payne-2-fall-of-max-payne.teaser: A noir story about detective Max Payne; rain, neon, and a bitterly sarcastic inner monologue.
pc-modern__max-payne-2-fall-of-max-payne.article:
**Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne** was released in 2003 by the Finnish studio Remedy Entertainment and followed up the successful first game with a darker, more intimate story about detective Max Payne, entangled in a murder and a conspiracy connected to his past, as well as a striking new character, hired killer Mona Sax, with whom he shares a complicated emotional relationship. The game retained its noir atmosphere full of rain, shadows, and neon signs, along with a sarcastic inner monologue that gives the action a literary, almost melancholic edge typical of the entire series.

The core of the gameplay remains the slow-motion bullet time, allowing for elegant cascades of shootouts with diving through cover and a floating camera on the final kill, complemented by the improved Havok physics engine, thanks to which objects in the environment react to explosions and gunfire much more convincingly and dynamically than in the first game. The level design is more compact and linear, but denser with action sequences and cinematic moments, including sequences styled as comic book panels that replaced some parts of the narration between chapters. The PC version offered full mouse and keyboard support as well as, for its time, advanced graphical effects, including dynamic lighting, reflections, and realistic rain on windows.

Critics praised the storytelling, atmosphere, and technical execution, although the game also drew criticism for its shorter overall length compared to the first installment. Despite its more modest commercial results, Max Payne 2 is now considered one of the high points of the noir action shooter genre and a model for later games working with the bullet time mechanic and cinematic storytelling. Its tone, music, and narrative style inspired numerous successors, and the game still retains a loyal fanbase after all these years thanks to an active modding scene and its reputation as one of the best-written action titles of its time.

**Why play it:** For fans of noir storytelling and bullet time action, though expect a shorter length than the first game — the atmosphere and music more than make up for it.

pc-modern__max-payne-3.teaser: Max Payne relocated to a scorching Sao Paulo; a breakdown told through cinematic flashbacks.
pc-modern__max-payne-3.article:
**Max Payne 3** was released on PC in 2012 under Rockstar Games, which took over development of the series from the Finnish studio Remedy, and moved the title character from cold, snowy New York to the scorching and dangerous Sao Paulo in Brazil, where Max works as private security for a wealthy family of businesspeople. The story follows his gradual moral and physical breakdown amid kidnappings, gang wars, and police corruption, told through nonlinear flashbacks and cinematically edited sequences with a striking, high-contrast visual style.

The game retained the beloved bullet time mechanic, expanded with smoother cover, combined shooting while moving and jumping, and elaborate kill-cam animation slowing down the final kill in a room for cinematic effect, complemented by visual artifacts like film grain and chromatic aberration evoking an action movie. The graphics engine delivered, for its time, very advanced lighting, environmental destruction, and smooth cinematic transitions between chapters without loading screens, which made the game a technical showcase for the studio. The PC version offered full high-resolution support and multiplayer modes using the same slow-motion mechanics in competitive matches with multiple players at once.

Max Payne 3 received praise on release for its storytelling, atmosphere, and technical execution, although some voices missed the raw original noir stylization of the first two installments set in New York. As, so far, the final chapter of the series, it closes Max Payne's story in a dignified and gritty way and is still valued today for its cinematic direction of action sequences as well as its excellent musical score by the band Health. For fans of third-person action shooters, it remains an important reference point of the genre and a demonstration of how to move an older franchise in a new direction without betraying what made Max Payne Max Payne.

**Why play it:** For fans of third-person action shooters who appreciate cinematic direction of the shootouts and excellent music from the band Health in a dignified conclusion to Max's story.

pc-modern__hitman-absolution.teaser: Agent 47 moves closer to cinematic storytelling; a new Instinct ability helps read the environment and blend into crowds.
pc-modern__hitman-absolution.article:
**Hitman: Absolution** is the entry in which IO Interactive tried to push Agent 47 closer to linear, cinematic storytelling and move away from the purely sandbox levels of the earlier games. The story deals with a betrayal inside the ICA agency and the Agent's effort to protect a young girl, Victoria, giving Agent 47 an unusually personal motivation the series had not offered to that degree before. The gameplay rests on the familiar foundation – disguises, silent takedowns, improvised accidents – supplemented by a new Instinct ability that highlights guards and interactive objects and helps the player read the environment, or even stay briefly invisible within a crowd. Alongside the main campaign, the game offers a Contracts mode in which players can create and share their own targets and kill conditions, which partly made up for the lost freedom of the large sandbox levels.

Technically it was a noticeable leap forward thanks to the improved Glacier 2 engine, which delivered more detailed environments, more striking lighting effects, and a darker, almost noir atmosphere spanning American cities and countryside. The music and sound design underscored the story's grim tone, which was rawer and more personal than in earlier entries, with a stronger emphasis on cinematic camera sequences between missions. Contemporary reception was mixed: some players and reviewers praised the craftsmanship of individual missions and the visual side, while others criticized the shift away from sandbox openness, the guards' artificial intelligence, and the heavy reliance on scripted sequences.

Despite the mixed reception, Absolution played an important role as a transitional entry between the older and newer eras of the series – many of its ideas, including the emphasis on richly detailed locations and individual kill opportunities, were later put to good use by the 2016 reboot. Today it's played more as an interesting detour than as the series' high point, but as an action stealth title with striking visuals and a strong story it still holds up.

**Why play:** If you're looking for a transitional chapter between the series' older and newer eras with striking visuals and a strong story, Absolution still holds up well despite its mixed reception.

pc-modern__hitman.teaser: An episodic return to sandbox gameplay; a living Sapienza and Paris full of NPCs with their own routines.
pc-modern__hitman.article:
The 2016 **Hitman** returned the franchise to the formula that made it famous – sprawling sandbox levels full of side paths, disguises, and opportunities to eliminate a target unnoticed. The game launched episodically, gradually adding locations such as a Paris fashion show, the Italian town of Sapienza, or the Moroccan markets of Marrakesh, building each one as a living, densely populated space full of NPCs with their own behavior and routines that could be observed, eavesdropped on, and turned to the player's advantage. The Opportunities system subtly nudges the player toward interesting ways to complete the objective without taking away the freedom to choose one's own, purely improvised path, and the time-limited Elusive Targets added the tension of one-off, unrepeatable tasks where a mistake meant an irrecoverably lost opportunity.

Technically it was a significant step forward – crowds of characters, detailed interiors and exteriors, and elaborate lighting gave Agent 47 the most believable environments in the series' history. The sound and music sensitively underscored the tension and dark humor the series is famous for, and the overall atmosphere combined luxurious locations with the raw brutality of the assassin's trade. Critics and players alike embraced the return to the sandbox concept enthusiastically, and the game is now generally considered one of the high points of the whole series and of the stealth sandbox genre, even though the episodic release schedule initially raised concerns among part of the audience.

Thanks to its later merger into the World of Assassination collection, this entry remains playable and relevant today, with content expanded over further years and linked to its sequels, together forming one of the genre's most extensive sandbox trilogies. For new players it works as an ideal entry point into the series, and for the stealth-action genre it demonstrates how to give systemic freedom to a large number of possible solutions for a single mission.

**Why play:** Thanks to its merger into World of Assassination, this entry is an ideal gateway for new players into one of the genre's most extensive sandbox trilogies.

pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-ch.teaser: Considered the high point of the series by fans; light and shadow as the key stealth mechanic.
pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-ch.article:
**Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory** is the entry many fans and reviewers consider the high point of the whole series and one of the best stealth titles of its generation. NSA agent Sam Fisher once again moves through the shadows, using multispectral goggles, sticky cameras, and other espionage gear to reach his objectives without unnecessary violence, though the game also offers a harder, more direct approach for players who prefer action. The key element remains the elaborate light-and-shadow system – the player constantly assesses where they can and cannot be seen, extinguishes lamps, hides bodies, and listens for footsteps behind doors, and the game rewards a stealthy, nonviolent completion of the mission.

On PC the game offered the most refined presentation of all the versions available at the time, with improved lighting, smoother animation of Sam Fisher's movement, and support for the era's modern graphics cards, which made details like dynamic shadows and light reflections on wet surfaces stand out. Sound played an irreplaceable role in Chaos Theory – footsteps, echoes, and guards' voices are just as important as what the player sees, and the tense, quiet atmosphere, permeated by a sensitive musical score, gave every mission a cinematic edge. The game also introduced the popular cooperative and asymmetric multiplayer mode Spies vs. Mercs, which pitted spies against heavily armored mercenaries with different abilities and long stood as one of the most original online modes of its time.

Contemporary reviews were nearly unanimously enthusiastic, and Chaos Theory is still cited today as a textbook example of what an elaborate stealth system should look like, where every player decision has a visible impact on how the mission unfolds. The game's influence is noticeable in later series entries and in competing titles that borrowed its light-and-shadow mechanics, and even after all these years it still plays surprisingly well.

**Why play:** As a textbook example of an elaborate stealth system where every decision has a visible impact on the mission, Chaos Theory remains surprisingly playable even after all these years.

pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-do.teaser: Sam Fisher infiltrates a terrorist cell; the terrorists' trust grows at the expense of his relationship with the NSA.
pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell-do.article:
**Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Double Agent** puts Sam Fisher in an unusual position – after his daughter's death, the NSA agent goes undercover to infiltrate the JBA terrorist cell and must balance the trust of his new comrades against loyalty to his own government. The game thus adds moral decision-making to the traditional level-by-level infiltration: completing tasks for the terrorists raises their trust but damages his relationship with the NSA, and vice versa, giving the missions a more personal and psychologically tense dimension than series fans had been used to so far. Fisher also has to move among civilians at the terrorists' base, where a single suspicious gesture can blow his entire cover identity.

The game was released in two noticeably different versions for different platforms, with the PC getting a variant close to the new console generation of the time, featuring settings ranging from a New York skyscraper to an Arctic base to a terrorist training camp. Technically it built on the visual style of previous entries, though with a darker, more civilian atmosphere fitting its setting in a more realistic world after the New York tragedy, and it offered new menus and interface tailored to this particular release. The music and sound design again worked with silence and tension, though at times the game felt less polished than the preceding Chaos Theory, particularly in the guards' artificial intelligence and the smoothness of the controls.

Reception was noticeably more mixed than for the series' high point; players appreciated the bold story and moral dilemmas but criticized the technical shortcomings and the sense that the game had drifted from Chaos Theory's perfectly tuned stealth system. Even so, it's an important and imaginative detour in Sam Fisher's history that showed the series was willing to experiment with storytelling beyond its proven formula, and it's still worth attention today precisely for its unusual narrative framework.

**Why play:** For Sam Fisher's bold story and moral dilemmas, Double Agent is worth a look as an imaginative detour, despite its technical shortcomings and less polished stealth system.

pc-modern__metal-gear-solid-v-phantom-pa.teaser: An open world for the stealth series; Venom Snake builds a private army at Mother Base.
pc-modern__metal-gear-solid-v-phantom-pa.article:
**Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain** moves the series into an open world – playing as the scarred Venom Snake, the player plans and carries out military operations in Afghanistan and later East Africa, building and expanding his own private army at the floating Mother Base between missions. The core of the game remains stealth – spotting patrols, using terrain, disguises, and improvised decoys to draw enemies away – but the open world allows a much freer approach to objectives than the earlier linear entries, including nighttime movement, vehicles, and companions such as the dog D-Dog or the silent sniper Quiet. The system for recruiting captured enemies at Mother Base further links the individual missions into one ongoing economic and personnel cycle.

The game ran on the proprietary Fox Engine, which on PC delivered excellent technical execution with high frame-rate stability, detailed textures, and convincing weather and time-of-day modeling, making it one of the best-handled technical ports of a major Japanese production of its time. The atmosphere was rounded out by Ludvig Forssell's score together with a selection of licensed period songs the player could listen to via a cassette player, and the overall tone combined military realism with the series' typically Kojima-esque contemplativeness and dark humor. Critically the game was received as one of the best stealth sandboxes of its generation, though the story side remained unfinished – a planned third chapter was cut, leaving the game to end without full narrative closure.

Phantom Pain is also the last entry Hideo Kojima directed for the Metal Gear Solid series before leaving Konami, which is part of why it holds a special, almost symbolic place in the genre's history. To this day it's played as a demonstration of how to spread systemic stealth gameplay across an open world without losing tension and depth, and many of its game systems have become a reference point for later open-world action games.

**Why play:** For the symbolic status of the last entry directed by Hideo Kojima, and as a demonstration of how to spread systemic stealth gameplay across an open world without losing tension.

pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell.teaser: A pioneer of the light-and-shadow mechanic; Sam Fisher extinguishes lamps and sneaks quietly past guards.
pc-modern__tom-clancy-s-splinter-cell.article:
**Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell** introduced players to Sam Fisher, an NSA veteran and agent of the secret Third Echelon unit, and along with him the emphasis on light and shadow as a key gameplay mechanic that no other major action game offered to that degree at the time. The story deals with a crisis around Georgia and the threat of nuclear conflict, but really serves mainly as a framework for a series of carefully designed missions in which the player sneaks through shadows, extinguishes lights, hangs from pipes, and decides whether to merely bypass guards or quietly take them out. Gear like an optic cable for spying through doors or thermal vision gave the player's progress a believable espionage feel.

On PC the game stood out for its then very advanced lighting and shadow rendering, which created a tense, almost claustrophobic spy-thriller atmosphere – the player must constantly monitor their own visibility via a light meter and adjust their approach accordingly. The music and sound design underscored a sense of isolation and risk typical of Cold-War-flavored spy stories of the time, and the individual locations, from Russian prisons to Tokyo skyscrapers, gave the game variety despite its linear structure. At the time the game was received as a serious rival to the Metal Gear Solid series and classic titles like Thief, and on both PC and consoles it earned a reputation as a technically and design-wise ambitious project.

With its emphasis on realistic light manipulation, the first Splinter Cell laid the foundation on which all later series entries built, and even with the years of hindsight it's clear how great an influence it had on shaping the modern stealth genre. Today it feels a bit slower and less forgiving than its sequels, with less sophisticated guard AI and a simpler movement repertoire, but as a historical milestone it remains a game worth returning to.

**Why play:** As the historical milestone that laid the foundation of the modern stealth genre through its emphasis on light manipulation, even though it feels slower today and has simpler guard AI than its sequels.

pc-modern__diablo-iv.teaser: A return to the series' dark, gothic roots in a sprawling, explorable open world.
pc-modern__diablo-iv.article:
**Diablo IV** returns the series to its dark, gothic roots and combines them with an open world the player explores between the main storyline and a wealth of side quests. The story takes place in Sanctuary as it is gripped by the return of the demoness Lilith, and the player chooses one of several classes – Barbarian, Sorceress, Necromancer, Rogue, or Druid – each with its own combat style and branching skill tree. The world is divided into several regions with distinct climates and visual moods, from snow-capped mountains to parched wastelands, and the player moves between them on horseback or via fast travel between discovered waypoints.

The core of the game remains the proven hack-and-slash gameplay: collecting gear, upgrading equipment, building a character build, and gradually strengthening the character through difficulty tiers up to an endgame with dungeons, seasonal mechanics, and world bosses. The open world brings shared spaces with other players, random events, and strongholds to conquer, so the game combines a solo story experience with online elements without forcing the player into full multiplayer. Technically the game runs on a modern engine with an emphasis on atmospheric lighting, weather, and detailed environments, which stands out especially in dark interiors and stormy landscapes on powerful graphics cards; the game also offers scalable graphics settings for a wider range of configurations.

The audiovisual presentation builds on the dark aesthetic of previous entries, the music reinforces the sense of decay and threat that made the series famous, and the sound design of combat gives weapon and spell strikes appropriate weight. Diablo IV launched to a somewhat more mixed reception than the pre-release expectations suggested, particularly over questions of monetization and character balancing, but the core game underwent substantial changes in seasonal updates after release, gradually altering the endgame content and item economy. Its influence on the genre is evident in how the game repopularized the combination of an open world with the collection-focused core of action RPGs. Today it represents a sprawling game with dozens to hundreds of hours of content for players who want to endlessly improve their character and hunt for better gear.

**Why play:** For the dark atmosphere, striking music, and dozens to hundreds of hours of seasonally refreshed endgame content, even though questions of monetization and character balancing come with it.

pc-modern__diablo-ii-resurrected.teaser: A faithful remaster of the 2000 classic; press a key to switch to the original pixelated look.
pc-modern__diablo-ii-resurrected.article:
**Diablo II: Resurrected** is a faithful remaster of the classic 2000 action RPG that preserves the original gameplay mechanics, balancing, and mission structure, but offers reworked graphics in high resolution with the option to switch back to the original pixelated look at any time with a single keypress. The player chooses one of seven classes – Amazon, Barbarian, Necromancer, Paladin, Sorceress, Druid, or Assassin – and moves through five acts full of a dark fantasy story about fighting ancient evils, from the barren steppes of the first act to the hellish scenery of the game's finale.

The gameplay rests on collecting items, building a character via a skill tree, and fighting hordes of enemies as well as unique bosses, including the legendary Diablo, with the system of randomly generated items and their properties remaining unchanged at its core. The remaster added support for higher resolutions, shared storage between characters, modern online services, and cross-play between platforms, making it more accessible for new players and an enjoyable revisit for veterans returning to their favorite builds. On a modern PC the game runs smoothly even on low-end hardware, since at its core it's a title from the early 2000s with a new graphical coat of paint, which owners of older hardware will appreciate too.

The game's atmosphere remains dark and gothic, accompanied by iconic music that ranks among the most recognizable in the genre and still evokes strong nostalgia today. Diablo II was groundbreaking in its time and significantly shaped the entire action RPG genre along with its loot and build systems, so Resurrected is seen as both a reverent and functional way to revisit that influence without having to fight against outdated technology. For today's players it offers dozens of hours of gameplay with a single character and much more when building multiple builds and farming items in the game's later stages, where players often return to the same areas for better gear.

**Why play:** For a reverent and functional return to a groundbreaking action RPG classic with iconic music and dozens of hours of item hunting and character building, without having to fight outdated technology.

pc-modern__xcom-2.teaser: Humanity lives under alien occupation; XCOM wages a guerrilla war from the flying base Avenger.
pc-modern__xcom-2.article:
**XCOM 2** moves the series into a darker reality where humanity has surrendered to alien occupation, and the player leads the guerrilla organization XCOM, operating from a mobile base — the Avenger aircraft, which itself functions as a relocatable strategic base moving across the world map. Unlike the previous game, you're now the attacker rather than the defender: missions run under time pressure, the player must steal technology, sabotage enemy projects, and gradually build a resistance across the world's regions, all while negotiating with regional resistance factions for support.

Turn-based combat remains the core of the game: hit-percentage chances, critical hits, cover, and positional tactics, enriched with new elements like concealing units in the shadows, timed mission objectives, and permanent death of soldiers, which gives every decision weight and forces the player to plan each step and the order of actions within the squad. Between missions, the player manages research, equipment production, and the strategic world map, where they compete against the alien's growing control, represented by the so-called Avatar Project. On a modern PC, the game demands a bit more performance than its predecessor due to more detailed models, environments, and procedurally generated maps, but it remains accessible even on mid-range machines.

The visual style and music continue the series' tradition, but the tone is rawer and more tense, matching the role of rebels fighting underground and defending the last remnants of human resistance. XCOM 2 was received by critics as a worthy and in many ways bolder sequel than Enemy Unknown, especially thanks to its higher difficulty and the constant pressure of time limits that curbs overly cautious play. To this day it's considered one of the best modern representatives of turn-based strategy, and players still remember it thanks to its extensive modding community, which expanded the game with new missions, units, and entire campaigns.

**Why play it:** For fans of tense turn-based strategy with high difficulty and constant time pressure, still expanded to this day by a rich modding community adding new missions and campaigns.

pc-modern__xcom-chimera-squad.teaser: A cheaper spin-off set in a post-war city; a mixed team of humans and aliens holds a fragile peace.
pc-modern__xcom-chimera-squad.article:
**XCOM: Chimera Squad** is a lighter, cheaper spin-off set shortly after the events of XCOM 2, at a time when humans and aliens are trying to live side by side in a single city run by a provisional administration tasked with maintaining fragile post-war order. The player leads a mixed team of human and alien agents investigating rising violence and trying to hold together a fragile peace among factions competing for influence in a post-war metropolis full of tension between the different species.

The game abandons permanent unit death in favor of a fixed but diverse roster with unique abilities and personal backstories, and introduces a split-turn system where the actions of the player and enemies interleave instead of strictly alternating rounds. Missions often begin with a breach through a door, after which the player decides how best to handle the tactical situation, or deploys a different tactic for a different group of enemies. A shorter, more accessible campaign combined with a lower price makes Chimera Squad a good entry point for players who were wary of the full complexity of XCOM 2, and it's technically undemanding even on older hardware, so even a weaker laptop can run it.

The tone of the game is lighter, with an emphasis on the individual agents' personalities, their distinct gear, and their relationships with one another, which is reflected in a more humorous storytelling style between missions through comic-book-style cutscenes interspersed with conversations at the base. Reception was mixed to positive — players appreciated the new mechanics and the lower time commitment, though some missed the tension of permanently losing units that defined earlier entries. Today, Chimera Squad is remembered as an interesting experiment that showed the series that XCOM's turn-based system can be changed more substantially than just cosmetically, without losing the tactical depth and tension typical of this type of strategy game.

**Why play it:** For players who want to try a lighter, faster variant of XCOM's turn-based system with strongly defined agent personalities, even at the cost of less tension from permanent unit losses.

pc-modern__unreal-tournament-2004.teaser: The peak of arena shooters; vehicles and the Onslaught mode brought battles for dozens of players.
pc-modern__unreal-tournament-2004.article:
**Unreal Tournament 2004** is among the pinnacles of classic arena shooters, expanding on its predecessor's concept with new vehicles and sprawling maps built for large battles with dozens of players at once, whether against bots or in online matches. The game offers a wide range of game modes, from classic deathmatch and capture the flag through team variants to Onslaught and Assault, where players move between control points in tanks and other vehicles and complete sequential objectives, or Bombing Run, which resembles a team sport with a ball.

The shooting is fast, precise, and movement-based — dashing, double jumps, and specific weapons like the Flak Cannon or Shock Rifle defined the game's style, demanding reflexes, spatial awareness, and thorough knowledge of individual maps. Thanks to the Unreal Engine 2, the game ran very smoothly with low system load, both on hardware of its time and today, which made it a favorite choice for online tournaments and competitive play over more demanding but slower rivals. An extensive modding scene, a map editor, and tools for creating custom content extended the game's life for many years after release and gave rise to a number of popular community mods and custom game modes.

The atmosphere was energetic and sporty, accompanied by electronic music that gave matches their pace and underscored the feeling of fast, adrenaline-fueled action on screen. Unreal Tournament 2004 was received by critics as one of the best titles of the genre of its time, and it's still cited today as a reference point for arena shooters, alongside its rival Quake III Arena. Even years later, the game feels fresh thanks to its straightforward, skill-demanding gameplay free of unnecessary complications, and it still holds a small but loyal community of players who return to it regularly even many years after release.

**Why play it:** For lovers of straightforward, skill-demanding arena action without unnecessary complications, which is still kept alive today by a loyal community of players.

pc-modern__unreal-tournament-3.teaser: A graphical leap thanks to Unreal Engine 3; arena combat complemented by vehicles and a story campaign.
pc-modern__unreal-tournament-3.article:
**Unreal Tournament 3** followed up on its successful predecessors and brought a graphical leap by deploying Unreal Engine 3, which was at the time among the most advanced available technologies and was used in a number of other major games across genres. The game kept the core of arena combat — fast movement, jumps, and the series' characteristic arsenal of weapons — and complemented it with vehicles and a more elaborate campaign mode, set within a conflict between humans and the robotic Necris race, told from the perspective of a mercenary team.

Multiplayer modes included classic deathmatch, capture the flag, Warfare as the successor to Onslaught, and other variants of team battles on sprawling maps full of vehicles and strategic points that had to be progressively captured and defended. Visually, the game looked significantly better than its predecessors thanks to advanced lighting, detailed character models, and more elaborate environment textures, which at the same time raised the hardware requirements and demanded a fairly powerful computer at the time of release. Partly because of this, the game failed to reach the same popularity as UT2004, also partly due to strong competition in the online shooter market at the time of its release.

The sound design and electronic music continued the series' style, and the atmosphere remained fast-paced and competitive, though the overall tone was somewhat more serious than in previous entries. Critics praised the technical execution, the clarity of the combat, and the movement system, but at the same time saw the game as less groundbreaking than its predecessor and less innovative compared to the competition on the market at the time. Looking back, Unreal Tournament 3 is remembered as the series' last major entry and a showcase of what the peak of Epic Games' technology looked like before the rise of free-to-play shooters, which later came to dominate the online market and reshaped the genre.

**Why play it:** For fans of fast arena combat who will appreciate a technically polished movement system and clarity, even though it's more the series' last major entry than a genre breakthrough.

pc-modern__unreal-ii-awakening.teaser: A departure from arena multiplayer toward a linear campaign about a conspiracy surrounding mysterious artifacts.
pc-modern__unreal-ii-awakening.article:
**Unreal II: The Awakening** departs from its predecessor's arena multiplayer, offering instead a linear single-player campaign with an emphasis on story and atmosphere set among distant space colonies at the edge of civilized space. The player controls Captain John Dalgliesh, a member of a border patrol who gradually uncovers a conspiracy connected to mysterious artifacts scattered across remote planets, visiting a number of different worlds along the way to their discovery.

The gameplay combines a first-person shooter with exploration of varied environments — from tropical jungles through icy plains to space stations and underground complexes — and between missions the player chooses the next objective aboard their ship, where conversations with the crew also take place and relationships between the supporting characters develop. Weapons offer alternative firing modes, giving combat a certain tactical depth despite the more linear structure of the game compared to the series' more open arena entries. Technically, the game, built on a modified Unreal Engine 2, looked very high quality at the time of release, especially thanks to carefully designed environments, particle effects, and dynamic lighting.

The music and sound design support a calmer, more contemplative tone compared to the series' more action-oriented entries, though the combat itself remains intense and often requires tactically switching weapons. Reception was mixed — players expecting multiplayer experiences like the earlier Unreal titles were sometimes disappointed by the missing network mode, while fans of story-driven shooters appreciated the atmosphere, the visuals, and the elaborate space setting. Today, Unreal II is seen as a bold, if not unreservedly successful, attempt to push the Unreal brand toward a story-driven sci-fi adventure, and for fans of the series it remains an interesting detour from its arena-based core.

**Why play it:** For players craving an atmospheric sci-fi story with an elaborate space setting, though not for those who expect the series' traditional multiplayer.

pc-modern__worms-w-m-d.teaser: A return to 2D roots after 3D experiments; worms once again wreck the terrain with the sheep bomb and grenades.
pc-modern__worms-w-m-d.article:
**Worms W.M.D.** brings the series back to its roots of 2D turn-based action with a hand-drawn art style, after the 3D experiments in earlier entries that didn't win over part of the fanbase. Players once again manage a team of worms fighting each other on destructible terrain, aiming to eliminate the opponent's units using a bizarre arsenal of weapons, from the sheep bomb to holy hand grenades and other iconic, over-the-top absurd tricks the series was built on.

Newly, the game adds vehicles such as tanks and motorboats, plus building elements that let players construct improvised fortifications and structures out of crates of materials on the map, opening up new tactical options for defense and attack for the whole team. The turn-based system remains faithful to the classic formula — the player has a limited time to move and attack, while the terrain keeps changing due to weapon destruction and affects the rest of the match, so no two games look the same. The game supports local and online multiplayer for several players, which even years later makes it a popular choice for quick, chaotic matches among friends, and it runs undemandingly on a modern PC thanks to its simple but inventive 2D graphics.

Humor remains a key part of the atmosphere, from the worms' one-liners to the absurd weapons and their sound effects, which the series has been famous for since the nineties and which reappear in W.M.D. in refreshed form. Worms W.M.D. was received as a successful return to the series' traditional style after the mixed reception of its 3D attempts, appreciated by both longtime fans and newcomers looking for fun turn-based strategy. To this day it remains a solid representative of the genre for those who want lighthearted but strategically interesting fun for one sitting or many, ideally in the company of friends around one screen or over the internet, where matches often end in raucous laughter.

**Why play it:** For a group of friends looking for lighthearted but strategically inventive turn-based fun full of absurd weapons and the worms' legendary humor.

pc-modern__medal-of-honor-allied-assault.teaser: War from a soldier's point of view, from Normandy across Europe; cinematic storytelling instead of a bare-bones simulation.
pc-modern__medal-of-honor-allied-assault.article:
**Medal of Honor: Allied Assault** is a war shooter that throws the player into the role of an American soldier fighting on key fronts of the Second World War, from the landing at Normandy through the North African desert to the trenches of occupied Europe. The game is built on linear missions full of scripted moments, where the player shoots their way through villages, bunkers, and fortified positions, with stealth passages, sabotage missions behind enemy lines, and defending positions against repeated waves of attacking enemies along the way. The weapon arsenal matches the standards of the period — rifles, submachine guns, grenades, and machine guns — and the game emphasizes the atmosphere of battlefield chaos and cinematic storytelling rather than a bare-bones military simulation.

Technically, the game ran on a modified version of the Quake III Arena engine, which allowed it to offer, for its time, impressive visuals with more open spaces, smoke effects, and dense action on screen, with dozens of enemies attacking the player at once. The sound design was among the best PC games had to offer at the time, with weighty gunfire and explosion sounds along with emotive orchestral music that heightened the pathos of the war scenes. The game's most famous and most-cited sequence remains the landing on Omaha Beach, which clearly drew inspiration from the film Saving Private Ryan and became a model for many later war games that tried to imitate a similar moment.

After release, the game received a very positive reception from both players and reviewers, who praised the cinematic direction, the intensity of the action, and the engaging, well-constructed campaign. Allied Assault is today considered one of the founding titles of the modern war-shooter genre and is associated with the beginnings of Infinity Ward, whose founders worked on the game before creating their own Call of Duty series. Even years later, the game works as an engaging and surprisingly dynamic campaign, though its technical execution and the rather basic enemy AI naturally bear clear marks of their time of origin.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the roots of the modern war-shooter genre, still driven today by a dynamic and cinematically directed campaign, even though the technology and enemy AI reveal their age.

pc-modern__medal-of-honor-pacific-assaul.teaser: The war series moves to the Pacific; a greater emphasis on story and relationships within the unit.
pc-modern__medal-of-honor-pacific-assaul.article:
**Medal of Honor: Pacific Assault** moves the war series from the European battlefield to the Pacific, following a young American soldier from the attack on Pearl Harbor through amphibious landing operations on Pacific islands to hard-fought battles in dense jungles against the Japanese army. Compared to previous entries in the series, the game puts significantly greater emphasis on story and on the relationships between the members of the unit the player accompanies throughout the campaign, making the war feel more personal, more emotional, and less like a sequence of isolated combat missions without context.

In terms of gameplay it's still a linear action shooter, but with several new features, such as simplified squadmate commands, dramatic sequences of defending positions against waves of Japanese soldiers, and an intense atmosphere of fighting in dense vegetation, where the enemy attacks from hiding and is hard to spot, creating tension different from the series' European entries. Technically, the game used an improved version of the engine from earlier entries in the series and offered denser vegetation, more pronounced lighting, and more detailed environments across Pacific islands and ships. The sound design was again one of the game's strong points, with the tense atmosphere of the tropical jungle and dramatic music accompanying key battle scenes, including naval and aerial engagements.

At release the game was seen as a worthy continuation of the series, though it already had to face growing competition from a new genre rival in the form of the Call of Duty series, whose first entry had come out just a year earlier and was quickly winning over both players and reviewers. Pacific Assault is remembered today mainly as one of the last major single-player titles of the classic Medal of Honor series before its later transformation, and for fans of the Pacific front of the Second World War it still offers an engaging, emotionally told, atmosphere-laden story about the horrors of fighting in the jungle.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Pacific front of the Second World War, who will appreciate the emotionally told, atmosphere-laden story of one of the last major single-player entries in the classic series.

pc-modern__medal-of-honor-airborne.teaser: Every mission begins with a parachute drop; the player chooses both the landing spot and the route to the objective.
pc-modern__medal-of-honor-airborne.article:
**Medal of Honor: Airborne** brings a distinct gameplay innovation to the series, putting the player in the boots of a paratrooper from the 82nd Airborne Division, with every mission literally beginning with a parachute jump over the battlefield. The player chooses the landing spot and the direction to head toward the objective, which affects where the mission starts, which enemies are encountered first, and what route through the battlefield is ultimately taken, giving the game noticeably more freedom than the series' earlier, strictly linear entries. The campaign takes the player through key airborne operations of World War II, from the invasion of Sicily through the liberation of the Netherlands to the final battles in Germany.

The weapon system was enriched with gradual weapon upgrades during play, where frequent use of a particular rifle or submachine gun unlocks better sights, magazines, or other modifications, encouraging players to stick with a favorite piece of gear throughout the campaign. The game ran on Unreal Engine 3, which gave it a very solid visual coat for its time, with nice lighting effects and partially destructible environments, though the level design remained fairly compact and enclosed despite the freedom offered by the jump. The audio side maintained the series' high standard, with quality battlefield sound and cinematic orchestral music underscoring the dramatic moments of the jumps and the subsequent battles for villages and bridges.

Airborne received a more mixed reception from critics and players than earlier entries; the fresh idea of the optional jump was praised, but the somewhat shorter and less tightly constructed campaign was criticized compared to previous titles in the series. Historically, Airborne is interesting as one of the last major single-player titles of the classic Medal of Honor era before the series stepped away for several years and later returned in the form of a reboot focused on more modern conflicts. Today, the game is best appreciated by players looking for an alternative perspective on wartime operations through the eyes of a lone paratrooper dropping into the unknown.

**Why play it:** For players seeking an alternative perspective on wartime operations through the eyes of a lone paratrooper, even though the campaign is shorter and less tightly constructed than previous entries in the series.

pc-modern__medal-of-honor.teaser: A reboot of the series set in present-day Afghanistan; a grittier tone and the perspectives of several soldiers at once.
pc-modern__medal-of-honor.article:
The 2010 **Medal of Honor** marked a fundamental reboot of the series, moving it from the historical context of World War II into the present day and having the player fight alongside American special forces in the mountains of Afghanistan. The campaign alternates between the perspectives of several soldiers, from ground operators of a Tier 1 unit to pilots of aircraft providing air support to ground forces, thereby trying to show the contemporary conflict from several angles at once instead of a single heroic narrative thread. The game's tone is deliberately grittier, harsher, and less heroic than in earlier entries, with an emphasis on tension, uncertainty, and the psychological toll of modern asymmetric warfare.

In terms of gameplay, it's a fairly traditional corridor shooter emphasizing cover, tactical advancement of small squads of soldiers, and intense mid-range firefights, complemented by the harsh mountainous terrain of Afghanistan as a distinctive and authentic backdrop. The game ran on a modified version of the Unreal Engine 3 and looked technically solid, though not groundbreaking, with functional lighting, decently animated characters, and believably rendered villages. The audio was one of its stronger points, with realistically depicted gunfire, authentic radio communication, and darker, less bombastic music than in the series' historical entries.

The reboot met with a more mixed critical reception; the ambition to show a contemporary conflict more rawly and believably was praised, but the campaign's brevity and a certain similarity to the competing Call of Duty series, against which the game competed directly on the market during the same period, were criticized. Despite the mixed reception, this reboot remains an interesting historical stop in the series, showing how Medal of Honor tried to find its identity again at a time when the modern military shooter genre was clearly dominated by other brands.

**Why play it:** For those interested in the series' history who will appreciate the attempt at a rawer, more believable take on the conflict of the time, despite the shorter campaign and the shadow of stronger competition from Call of Duty.

pc-modern__call-of-duty.teaser: The first entry in the famous series; three national perspectives on World War II and loyal squadmates.
pc-modern__call-of-duty.article:
**Call of Duty** is the first entry in what is today a huge series, and at the time of its release it represented a clear attempt to push war shooters a step further than the then-dominant competition led by the Medal of Honor series. The campaign is split into three storylines following an American, a British, and a Soviet soldier, letting the game show World War II from several national perspectives at once, from the landings in Normandy through the North African battlefield to the crushing Battle of Stalingrad and the crossing of the Rhine into Germany itself. Emphasis is placed on a sense of unit camaraderie, as armed squadmates accompany the player for most of the game, reacting to their surroundings, taking cover, and giving each other orders.

The game was built on a modified Quake III Arena engine, which allowed it to offer dense, chaotic action with large numbers of enemies and allies on screen at once, a fairly novel and gripping experience at the time compared to the then-established, calmer styles of war shooters. The level design emphasized scripted moments and cinematic storytelling, with missions like the defense of Stalingrad with noticeably limited ammunition still ranking among the most memorable passages of the genre's early era. The audio was excellent, with dense gunfire, soldiers shouting amid the chaos of battle, grenade explosions, and epic orchestral music underscoring the pathos and horror of the war scenes.

Call of Duty was received extremely positively after release and quickly established itself as a full-fledged competitor to the then-dominant Medal of Honor series, which was all the more remarkable given that it was the debut of a newly founded studio. From today's perspective, the first installment is key mainly because it laid the foundation for one of the most successful game franchises of all time and defined many elements still used in the war shooter genre today, including an emphasis on cinematic quality and pacing. Despite its age, the game still offers a surprisingly intense, well-told, and often surprisingly challenging campaign.

**Why play it:** For players interested in the roots of the genre, who will appreciate the surprisingly intense and well-told campaign of the debut title that laid the foundation for one of the most successful game franchises of all time.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-2.teaser: A sequel with more polished level design; again three fronts and three World War II soldiers.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-2.article:
**Call of Duty 2** builds on the success of the first installment and once again tells the story of World War II through three storylines, this time following a Soviet soldier defending Stalingrad, a British soldier fighting Rommel's forces in the North African desert, and an American paratrooper taking part in the Normandy landings and the subsequent campaign across Europe. The mission-by-mission structure remains similar to the first game, but it brings significantly more polished level design, smoother pacing, better balanced action, and less frustrating checkpoints, making the campaign feel more accessible to a wider audience.

One of the main innovations is a system of automatic health regeneration, which replaced earlier health packs and later became the de facto standard for nearly the entire action shooter genre for years to come. The game ran on a new engine with improved lighting, destructible environments, and better character animation, allowing it to look significantly better than the competition and showcase monumental battle scenes such as the siege of the El Alamein fortress or the dramatic defense of Pegasus Bridge during the paratrooper landings. The audio was among the absolute best of its time, with intense battle sound, thundering explosions, and unmistakable orchestral music composed by Michael Giacchino.

Call of Duty 2 received near-unanimous critical acclaim upon release and is still considered one of the high points of the entire series and of the war shooter genre in general. The game helped cement Call of Duty's dominance in the market and set a bar that competing series, including Medal of Honor itself, had to catch up to, its later entries responding to that pressure. Even with the passage of years, the campaign remains an intense and well-constructed experience that many players today still rank among the very best individual entries in the entire long-running series.

**Why play it:** For war-shooter enthusiasts looking for one of the high points of the entire series, whose intense and well-constructed campaign holds up even after many years.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-world-at-war.teaser: The series' return to World War II with a harsher, rawer tone than earlier entries.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-world-at-war.article:
**Call of Duty: World at War** brings the series back to World War II after the previous installment, Modern Warfare, moved the action to the present day, and focuses on two exceptionally brutal fronts of the conflict, the Pacific battlefield against Japan and the bloody Soviet campaign toward Berlin. The campaign is deliberately rawer and more violent than earlier series entries, openly depicting the cruelty of war on both sides of the front, pushing the game toward a harsher, darker, and less romanticized narrative tone than players were used to from previous installments.

In terms of gameplay, the game builds on the proven foundation of Modern Warfare, including regenerating health and intense scripted sequences, but adds its own elements such as a flamethrower for clearing Japanese bunkers or emotionally intense defensive missions against overwhelming enemy numbers. The game ran on a modified version of the series' engine and looked technically very good, with impressive fire, smoke, and explosion effects amid the dense jungle environment and the ruined streets of besieged Berlin. Besides the campaign, World at War also became famous for its cooperative Nazi Zombies mode, which grew from a bonus surprise for loyal players into one of the franchise's most popular and enduring game modes, as well as a quality multiplayer building on the successful Modern Warfare formula.

The game was received very positively upon release, with praise for the intense campaign, the convincing atmosphere of the Pacific and Eastern fronts, and the surprisingly addictive and engaging zombie mode, which quickly built its own loyal community of players. World at War is now seen as an important milestone for the series, since it was the zombie mode that kickstarted a trend that became a lasting part of the Call of Duty brand for many years to come. Even today, the game offers an intense and emotionally powerful experience of some of the toughest and bloodiest battles of the entire Second World War.

**Why play it:** For players craving an intense campaign from the Pacific and Eastern fronts, as well as the addictive zombie mode that launched a lasting series tradition.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-2.teaser: A controversial mission made the game famous for sparking debate about violence in games; a gripping espionage plot.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-2.article:
**Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2** builds on the groundbreaking first Modern Warfare and expands its story with a gripping plot full of twists, conspiracy, and global conflict, taking players from snow-covered mountains through Brazilian favelas to the streets and suburbs of Washington itself. The campaign again alternates between the perspectives of multiple characters, including soldiers of the elite Task Force 141 unit and American marines, and became famous for several controversial and extremely emotionally charged missions that, at the time of release, sparked a wide societal debate about the depiction of violence in video games and the limits of interactive storytelling.

In terms of gameplay, the game improves on the previous installment's proven foundation with fast pacing, cinematic scripted sequences, and a wide range of modern military weapons and equipment, from sniper rifles to portable rocket launchers. The multiplayer also drew great attention, introducing an elaborate reward system called killstreaks, allowing players to call in air support, reconnaissance satellites, or other bonuses for a series of kills without dying, which became one of the genre's most influential and most-copied elements for many years to come. Technically, the game ran on an improved version of the series' engine and offered detailed environments and solidly animated characters, complemented by quality sound and dramatic, tense music underscoring the growing chaos of the global conflict.

Modern Warfare 2 became a commercially extremely successful title upon release, breaking sales records of the time, and is still considered one of the most influential entries in the entire series, one that defined the shape of online multiplayer shooters for an entire following generation of consoles and computers. Both its campaign and its multiplayer are still cited today as models for what a modern military action game should look like, and many of its elements, from killstreaks to mission structure and narrative pacing, continue to influence the genre today.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience the title that defined the shape of online multiplayer shooters for an entire generation - from killstreaks to narrative pacing, it still influences the genre today.

pc-modern__battlefield-1942.teaser: A pioneer of large-scale vehicle battles; infantry, tanks, and aircraft on a single map.
pc-modern__battlefield-1942.article:
**Battlefield 1942** set a grand vision of wartime chaos against the backdrop of World War II in a way no other shooter offered at the time. Instead of closed corridors, it came with sprawling maps like Wake Island, El Alamein, or Battle of the Bulge, across which players move on foot, in tanks, jeeps, boats, and aircraft. It was precisely this freedom of movement and the interconnection of infantry with vehicles that defined the game and became the foundation the whole series still stands on today. Up to 32 players on a server split into two teams and classes - assault, medic, engineer, sniper, tank crewman, and pilot - each fulfilling a different role within the broader tactical whole.

Technically, the game ran on the proprietary Refractor engine and felt generous for its time: open spaces, noticeable explosions, and dense smoke gave the battles a dramatic edge, though the graphics themselves were more functional than flashy. The audio, with battlefield noise and soldiers' voices, only underscored the atmosphere, while the music stayed more in the background, mainly accompanying the menus. The expansion packs Road to Rome and Secret Weapons of World War II expanded the roster of fronts, vehicles, and weapons and kept the community active for years to come. The main game mode was Conquest, where teams control points on the map and gradually deplete the opposing team's ticket count of lives, which became a standard later adopted by subsequent entries in the series.

The contemporary reception was extremely positive - Battlefield 1942 became one of the most-played multiplayer titles of its time and founded the genre of large-scale vehicular shooters that was later developed further by other entries in the series as well as competing brands. Today the game is naturally dated in both graphics and controls, but its legacy is evident in every subsequent Battlefield - from the classes to the vehicles to the emphasis on team coordination on large maps. For those interested in the genre's history, it's an essential stop, even though active play today is kept alive mainly by community servers and fan projects. It's also worth noting that the popular Desert Combat modification, transposing the game into modern desert warfare, partly inspired the direction Battlefield 2 later took.

**Why play it:** For those interested in the history of the vehicular shooter genre, whose legacy is visible in every later Battlefield, even though the game is kept alive today mainly by community servers and fan projects.

pc-modern__battlefield-vietnam.teaser: The 1942 formula transposed into the Vietnamese jungle; Huey helicopters play a key role.
pc-modern__battlefield-vietnam.article:
**Battlefield Vietnam** transposed the proven formula of large vehicular battles from 1942 into the jungles of Southeast Asia and the Vietnam conflict. Players split into the American army and the forces of North Vietnam with the Viet Cong, fighting on maps full of rice paddies, dense vegetation, and rivers, where Huey helicopters play a key role in troop movement. The class system carried over from the previous installment got a Vietnamese coat of paint, including each side's distinctive weaponry and the asymmetry between the technologically equipped American army and the guerrilla tactics of the Viet Cong, who relied on tunnels and ambushes. As in the previous game, it builds on a territorial conquest mode where teams clash over control points scattered across the sprawling map, and here too, coordination between infantry and vehicles plays a key role.

The game ran on an improved version of the Refractor engine and, compared to its predecessor, added smoother vehicle handling as well as a somewhat livelier jungle environment with denser vegetation that changes combat tactics. A quirk that earned the game attention was its in-game radio player featuring period music from the 1960s, which fleshed out the atmosphere of wartime Vietnam much like period films did - players could turn on the radio directly in vehicles while driving. This combination of sound and setting gave the game a distinctive atmosphere that many players still remember today.

Critically and commercially, the game was received solidly, though it never reached the phenomenon status of Battlefield 1942 - many reviewers praised the atmosphere and the new setting but criticized the relatively small number of new features compared to its predecessor. In the history of the series, it's an interesting detour that showed the formula of large vehicular battles works outside of World War II too, and it paved the way for the later shift to a modern battlefield in Battlefield 2. Today it's more a matter for collectors and genre history enthusiasts than for casual players, though it occasionally turns up as a favorite pick at retro gaming events devoted to older multiplayer titles.

**Why play it:** More for collectors and genre history enthusiasts than casual players - a solid detour that showed the formula of large vehicular battles works outside of World War II too.

pc-modern__battlefield-2.teaser: Moves the series into the present day and introduces the commander mode that reshaped multiplayer tactics.
pc-modern__battlefield-2.article:
**Battlefield 2** moved the series away from historical wars into the modern era and became one of the most influential multiplayer shooters of its generation. Players fight as fictional factions - the US military, the Chinese military, or the loosely defined MEC coalition - on large maps combining infantry, armored vehicles, and aircraft. The key innovation was the commander system, where one player coordinates the team from a bird's-eye view, calls in artillery strikes, places supply points, and issues orders to individual squads, pushing the game from chaotic firefights toward deliberate tactical cooperation.

The game introduced a detailed system for unlocking weapons and abilities based on experience with a given class, and placed heavy emphasis on communication between four-person squads via voice chat and a map-marking system. On the Refractor 2 engine the game looked very good for its time, with impressive explosion and destruction effects, and despite its higher demands it ran smoothly on hardware of the era. The sound design, with realistic battle noise and clear commander callouts, was among the best the genre offered at the time, and maps like Karkand or Mashtuur City became legendary arenas of the esports scene, hosting tournaments in both team and clan play.

Battlefield 2 received exceptionally positive reception and became a reference point for the entire genre of large multiplayer shooters - its class, commander, and squad systems were adopted by many later entries in the series as well as competing games. It also had an enormous impact on the modding scene, which produced expansions like Project Reality that pushed combat simulation even closer to realism. Today the game officially no longer works because its servers have been shut down, but the community keeps it alive through unofficial servers, and for veterans it remains one of the most significant titles in the genre's history.

**Why play it:** For veterans of large multiplayer battles, whose class, commander, and squad systems are still kept alive today by unofficial servers and the modding scene around Project Reality.

pc-modern__battlefield-4.teaser: Frostbite 3 and Levolution - a collapsing skyscraper changes the whole battlefield on the fly.
pc-modern__battlefield-4.article:
**Battlefield 4** continued the modern military conflict from Battlefield 3 and brought it to the new Frostbite 3 engine, which enabled a fundamentally more destructible environment. The key new feature was so-called Levolution - scripted, massive changes to the environment during a match, such as the collapse of a skyscraper on the Siege of Shanghai map, which alters the topography of the battlefield and forces players to adapt their tactics on the fly. The game offers both a single-player campaign following a squad of American soldiers caught up in a conflict between the US and China, and a large-scale multiplayer for dozens of players featuring infantry, armored vehicles, helicopters, and aircraft. The team commander system known from Battlefield 2 also returned, this time controllable from a tablet or mobile app, meant to let players command the battle even outside the main game.

Technically, it was one of the most graphically ambitious titles of its time - destructible environments, dynamic weather, and detailed water models gave the battlefields a credibility no competing title offered at the time. The rough launch, however, was accompanied by extensive technical problems with multiplayer and servers, which haunted the game for a long time and which the developers addressed over months of patches after release. The sound design of weapons and explosions remained a traditional strength of the series and reinforced the feeling of massive battles.

Despite its launch problems, Battlefield 4 built a loyal community that still plays the game today, thanks to its extensive content, expansion packs like China Rising or Naval Strike, and long-term support. In the wider context of the series, it is seen as a transitional entry between the more modern era of Battlefield 3 and the large historical entries that came later. The Second Assault expansion also brought remastered fan-favorite maps from Battlefield 3, which players welcomed as a nostalgic touch. Even years later, it remains one of the most technically accomplished multiplayer titles of its generation, still maintaining an active online community.

**Why play it:** For players seeking a technically accomplished multiplayer experience with extensive content and expansion packs like China Rising or Naval Strike, which even after years still has an active community.

pc-modern__battlefield-1.teaser: World War I in a shooter is a rarity; the giant Behemoths can turn a battle around.
pc-modern__battlefield-1.article:
**Battlefield 1** moved the series into the setting of World War I, portraying a conflict that had long remained almost untouched in video games. Players fight on fronts from Europe to the Middle East, operate period vehicles such as early tanks, biplanes, or armored trains, and can take part in cavalry charges on horseback. A unique new feature was the so-called Behemoths - giant units such as an airship, an armored train, or a battleship, which appear during a match as a powerful reinforcement for a struggling team and can turn the tide of battle.
