The War Stories campaign offers several short standalone stories from the perspective of different soldiers and nations, aiming to show the human side of the global conflict instead of a single linear story.

On the Frostbite engine, the game looked exceptionally good - dynamic weather, sandstorms limiting visibility, and destructible environments created atmospheric moments the genre had not seen before. The sound design, with heavy music and authentic period weapon sounds, reinforced the grim atmosphere of trench warfare, including the effect of dense fog of war, where smoke and dust make it impossible to get one's bearings on the battlefield. Multiplayer maps like Verdun Heights or Amiens were among the most striking environments the series had offered up to that point, and the orchestral score gave the battles a gravity and dramatic weight the military shooter genre had not really known before.

Battlefield 1 received exceptionally positive reception from critics and players and was praised above all for its courage to tackle a less common historical period and for its strong atmosphere. Many players and critics still rank this entry among the best in the entire series precisely because of its combination of an unusual setting, visual style, and accomplished sound design. Even years later, Battlefield 1 remains one of the most atmospheric military shooters ever released, and expansions like In the Name of the Tsar later added the Eastern Front and the Russian army to the offering.

**Why play it:** For fans of atmospheric military shooters who appreciate the courage to tackle a less common historical period, the strong atmosphere, and the accomplished sound of World War I.

pc-modern__battlefield-v.teaser: A return to World War II with a less flashy take; stories from lesser-known episodes of the conflict.
pc-modern__battlefield-v.article:
**Battlefield V** brought the series back to World War II and aimed for a rawer, less flashy portrayal of the conflict than earlier entries offered. The War Stories campaign continued the concept from the previous entry with several shorter stories, this time focused on lesser-known episodes of World War II, while multiplayer again offered large maps with infantry, tanks, and aircraft, and a new Grand Operations mode simulating the front's advance across several days of fighting. The game also introduced the Companies system, letting players customize the look and loadout of individual military specializations and vehicles throughout their career.

On the Frostbite engine, the game once again excelled with destructible environments and dynamic weather, complemented by an emphasis on physically accurate projectile behavior and the ability to build makeshift fortifications and trenches directly in combat, giving players greater control over defending positions. The sound design remained a traditional strength of the series, with an emphasis on authentic period weapon and vehicle sounds. However, the game was criticized at launch for a lack of content in the first months and for the absence of a battle royale mode, which was added only later under the name Firestorm and played out on a large standalone map for dozens of players.

Initial reception was more mixed than for the previous entry - the game was dogged by discussions about the pace of post-launch support, even though its content grew significantly over the following years. Over time, the community's rating improved as developers added further fronts and content. Today, Battlefield V is seen as a solid, if not flawless, entry in the series, praised especially for its atmosphere and battlefield sound design, and later updates added a Pacific theater with further fronts and vehicles, gradually bringing the game closer to the scope players had expected from a major Battlefield title at launch.

**Why play it:** For patient players willing to wait for the game to gradually gain further fronts and content - today it offers a solid battlefield strong on atmosphere and sound, even though its launch was mixed.

pc-modern__bioshock-2.teaser: You play as a Big Daddy in Rapture; clunkier but more powerful combat, and a new rival - the Big Sister.
pc-modern__bioshock-2.article:
**BioShock 2** returns players to the underwater city of Rapture, this time in the role of one of the iconic Big Daddies named Delta, searching for his lost Little Sister. Compared to the first game, it offers clunkier but more powerful combat with a drill as the primary weapon, the ability to wield a weapon and a plasmid simultaneously in each hand, and the mechanic of adopting or harvesting Little Sisters, which affects the ending similarly to the previous game. The new adversaries are Big Sisters, fast and dangerous beings protecting the orphaned girls, and fights against them are among the most tense moments in the game; the story also, for the first time, extends beyond Rapture itself into the adjacent district of Pauper's Drop and other parts of the city.

The game runs on an improved version of the first game's engine and visually continues the dilapidated yet still strikingly stylish look of Rapture with its water-drenched art deco architecture. A multiplayer mode set before the city's fall was added, but it left little impression on critics or players. As in the first game, the atmosphere is enhanced by period music from the 1940s and 1950s playing from gramophones and radios, combined with the oppressive industrial sound of the environment.

Critically, BioShock 2 was received positively, though without the same enthusiasm as the first game, which it struggled to match in terms of contribution to the genre. Especially praised was the Minerva's Den add-on, a short but emotionally powerful standalone story that many consider one of the best pieces of content in the entire series. Today the game stands as a solid sequel that perhaps didn't dare take as many risks as the original, but offers a faithful expansion of the world that defined the entire immersive sim shooter genre, and the theme of personal responsibility and manipulation, explored through Delta and his relationship with his Little Sister, gives the story an emotional dimension the first game lacked.

**Why play it:** For fans of Rapture craving a faithful expansion of the immersive sim shooter world, especially for the Minerva's Den add-on, one of the best pieces of content in the entire series.

pc-modern__bioshock-infinite.teaser: The flying city of Columbia instead of Rapture; Elizabeth and tears between realities.
pc-modern__bioshock-infinite.article:
**BioShock Infinite** leaves behind the underwater Rapture and moves players to the flying city of Columbia, a utopia built on nationalism and religious fanaticism in the early twentieth century. The player takes on the role of former agent Booker DeWitt, tasked with rescuing a mysterious girl named Elizabeth, who has the ability to open tears between parallel realities - a mechanic that becomes central to both the combat and the storytelling. The relationship between Booker and Elizabeth gradually deepens over the course of the game, and Elizabeth also acts as an active companion in combat, tossing the player ammo, health, or money, and opening tears that summon weapons or cover.

Combat combines firearms with so-called Vigors, an equivalent of the plasmids from previous games, and movement around the city is enabled by Skyhooks and rail lines called Sky-Lines, along which the player zips between the floating buildings. Visually, it is one of the most distinctive titles of its time thanks to its bright colors and sunny, seemingly idyllic atmosphere of Columbia, which contrasts with the darkness of the story hidden beneath the surface. The musical side combines period songs adapted for the era with an original atmospheric score and is among the most highly praised elements of the game.

BioShock Infinite received exceptionally positive reception and was praised above all for its story, its way of conveying themes through the environment, and its unexpected, complex ending exploring the idea of parallel worlds. Many players and critics rank it among the best story-driven games of its generation, and its impact on how video games are perceived as a storytelling medium was felt even outside the gaming community. Even today, Infinite remains a frequently cited example of how an action game can combine gameplay with an ambitious philosophical and social theme, and the later Burial at Sea add-on additionally connected the story with the world of the original Rapture.

**Why play it:** For players seeking a story-driven game that combines action gameplay with an ambitious philosophical theme and an unexpected, complex ending about parallel worlds.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-black-ops.teaser: The Cold War, a CIA agent, and a story that plays with the player's memory and identity.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-black-ops.article:
**Call of Duty: Black Ops** took the seventh entry in the series into the dark days of the Cold War, where the player, in the role of CIA agent Alex Mason, gets caught up in a story full of interrogations, conspiracies, and operations across Cuba, Vietnam, and the Soviet Union. After Modern Warfare 2, Treyarch took the reins and delivered a narrative that plays with the main character's memory and identity, a fairly bold storytelling move for a mainstream action series at the time. The campaign alternates fast-paced action sequences with quieter interrogation moments and keeps the typically Hollywood-style pacing full of twists that made the series famous starting with Modern Warfare.

Gameplay-wise, the game builds on the proven foundation of FPS action with regenerating health, scripted events, and carefully directed battles, while adding varied sequences such as a motorcycle chase, jungle combat, or defending a base against waves of enemies. Multiplayer introduced the Create-a-Class system with a custom selection of perk combinations and emblem options, as well as the Zombies mode, which grew from a mere bonus extra into one of the main pillars of the entire brand and still has loyal fans returning for further maps today. On PC the game ran smoothly and technically built on previous entries running on a similar engine, though not every version launched without issues, requiring several patches over time.

The atmosphere is reinforced by tense music and authentic period props, weapons, and uniforms, which evoke the Cold War era better than most contemporaries set in more modern conflicts. Critically and commercially, Black Ops was highly successful and cemented Call of Duty's position as the dominant action series of its decade, attracting millions of players every year. Today the game stands as a solid landmark in the brand's history, thanks above all to its Zombies mode and its bold narrative structure, which returns in various forms in later entries of the series and has become one of its recognizable trademarks.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Cold War and a bold approach to storytelling, who will also appreciate the legendary Zombies mode, which became one of the recognizable trademarks of the entire series.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-black-ops-ii.teaser: The series' first entry with a branching story and multiple endings, plus a bold leap to the year 2025.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-black-ops-ii.article:
**Call of Duty: Black Ops II** was the first entry in the series to dare set a large part of its story in the near future, specifically the year 2025, while also continuing the events of the original Black Ops from the Cold War era. The player once again takes on the roles of both Alex Mason and his son David Mason, moving through a branching story where choices and actions during the campaign affect subsequent events and lead to several different endings. This approach was a genuine innovation for the series at the time and clearly set the game apart from its linear predecessors, which had guided players along a single fixed path with no way to influence the direction of the story.

The futuristic setting introduced new gameplay elements such as controlling robotic units, exoskeletons for movement, or remotely piloted aircraft, and expanded equipment that was further developed in later entries of the series. Multiplayer gained the Pick 10 system, giving players greater freedom in building their own loadout instead of a fixed set, and the Zombies mode again grew with new content, characters, and maps that became very popular among players and still have loyal fans today. On PC the game made good use of contemporary hardware without major issues, offering stable performance even in large, chaotic multiplayer battles with many players at once.

The sound design and score reinforced a tense atmosphere alternating between the dark mood of a political thriller and forceful, tension-filled action narrative. Black Ops II was praised above all for its courage to experiment with a branching story in a mainstream series and for expanding the Zombies mode, which became one of the main reasons players still return to this entry even years after release. Within the series as a whole, it is often regarded as one of its peaks, because it combined narrative ambition with a finely tuned and balanced multiplayer that retained a large player base long after release and inspired later futuristic entries in the brand.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience the courage to experiment with a branching story in a mainstream series and a finely tuned multiplayer that retained its player base long after release.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-3.teaser: Closes out the trilogy around Soap MacTavish and Captain Price with a fast, cinematic pace.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-modern-warfare-3.article:
**Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3** closed out the trilogy centered on Soap MacTavish and Captain Price, bringing to a close the global conflict begun in the previous Modern Warfare titles. The game takes players through major cities like New York, London, and Paris, where large-scale military clashes unfold between the Russian army and allied forces while the world teeters on the brink of all-out war. The narrative keeps the series' signature style of fast cuts between different acts and characters, which lets the conflict be shown from multiple angles and keeps the pace high throughout the relatively short but intense campaign.

The new studio Sledgehammer Games contributed more significantly to development for the first time alongside Infinity Ward, leading to an even greater emphasis on cinematically directed sequences and striking scenery of ravaged European and American cities. Gameplay-wise, the game stays true to the series' established FPS formula of linear levels, scripted moments, and intense firefights, occasionally broken up by short driving or flying sequences over the battlefield. Multiplayer introduced the Strike Packages point-reward system in place of classic killstreaks and further developed the competitive side, which at the time was among the most-played online experiences of all, drawing in millions of players worldwide.

Technically, the PC version ran on a proven engine similar to previous entries, offering smooth performance even on then-common configurations without requiring expensive upgrades. Reception at the time was very positive, mainly thanks to the combination of familiar, tried-and-true gameplay and the grandeur of the trilogy's conclusion, though critical voices pointed out a certain repetitiveness compared to earlier entries in the series. Today, Modern Warfare 3 is regarded primarily as a fitting conclusion to one of the most significant storylines in the entire Call of Duty series, one that defined modern military shooters for years to come and influenced numerous other games in the genre.

**Why play:** For series fans looking for a fitting conclusion to one of Call of Duty's most significant storylines, even though the gameplay repeats the tried-and-true formulas of previous entries in places.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-advanced-warfare.teaser: Private armies instead of nation-states; Kevin Spacey in a lead role gave the campaign unusual drama.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-advanced-warfare.article:
**Call of Duty: Advanced Warfare** moved the series into a near future where private military corporations take over the role of classic armies, and the player, as soldier Jack Mitchell, finds himself in the middle of a conflict with the powerful Atlas Corporation. The campaign's main star was actor Kevin Spacey in a prominent role as the corporation's boss, which gave the game an unusually strong acting component and a greater emphasis on cinematic storytelling and character drama than most previous entries in the series. The story explores questions about what influence private capital can have on the conduct of wars, and repeatedly confronts the player with difficult moral decisions.

The key new feature was the exoskeleton, which gave the player double jumps, quick sideways dodges, and faster movement across the battlefield, noticeably changing both the pace and the vertical dimension of combat compared to its more grounded predecessors. This element also influenced the design of the multiplayer maps, which now accounted for multi-level movement, jumps between rooftops, and new tactical options for both attack and defense. Sledgehammer Games sought to bring a fresh visual style with thoroughly detailed future technology, from combat drones to advanced weapons and equipment, which set the game apart from the series' previous, more contemporary-set entries.

On PC, the game used a new graphics engine and offered significantly improved visuals and more detailed character models compared to earlier titles, although optimization at launch wasn't entirely flawless and required subsequent fixes. Reception at the time was mixed to positive; players appreciated the new movement and cinematic production, but part of the fanbase missed a return to more grounded, realistic action. Advanced Warfare kicked off the exoskeleton and higher-tempo trend that the series then followed in several later entries before returning to a more grounded style of combat a few years later. For many players, it therefore remains a symbol of the period when Call of Duty tried to find a new direction and distinguish itself from ever-similar military shooters.

**Why play:** For players who want to experience the moment when Call of Duty experimented with exoskeletons and a faster combat pace, even at the cost of not-quite-polished optimization at launch.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-wwii.teaser: A return to World War II after years of futuristic entries; an emphasis on camaraderie among soldiers.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-wwii.article:
**Call of Duty: WWII** marked the series' return to its original World War II setting after years of futuristic, contemporary-styled entries, which many longtime fans welcomed with relief. The story follows a squad from an American infantry division from the landing in Normandy through the campaign across Europe toward Germany, placing emphasis on camaraderie among the soldiers and the human dimension of the war rather than the grand technological effects of the previous futuristic entries. The narrative also tries to capture the darker, rawer sides of war, giving the campaign a heavier weight than had been typical for the series in recent years.

Gameplay-wise, the game returned to a more grounded pace without double jumps or an exoskeleton, while also introducing a squad-leader system that let the player ask squadmates for extra ammo, medkits, or grenades right in the middle of a firefight. Multiplayer offered the War mode, where one team attacks and the other defends a sequential set of objectives on the map, as well as the social space Headquarters, where players could meet and chat outside of combat. With this entry, Sledgehammer Games proved that even a return to a classic World War II setting could deliver clean, well-tuned mechanics for a broad audience.

On PC, the game technically benefited from richly detailed European battlefields, ruins, and villages, as well as atmospheric orchestral music that effectively underscored the serious tone of the wartime narrative. Both critical and player reception was very positive, praised mainly for the return to the series' proven fundamentals and for an emotionally powerful campaign with a human dimension. Within the modern part of the series, WWII is considered one of the more successful attempts at a return to its roots, one that also showed World War II still has plenty to offer new generations of players in today's games industry. The multiplayer community around the game stayed active for several years after release, confirming that the classic World War II setting has a firm place alongside the series' more modern and futuristic entries.

**Why play:** For fans of World War II stories who'll appreciate the series' return to more grounded combat, an emotional campaign, and atmospheric orchestral music.

pc-modern__call-of-duty-warzone.teaser: Free-to-play battle royale for one hundred fifty players; the Gulag gives fallen players a chance to return to the fight.
pc-modern__call-of-duty-warzone.article:
**Call of Duty: Warzone** brought the series into the world of battle royale games and quickly became one of the most-played free-to-play titles of its time, available standalone without needing to own the full game. It uses the sprawling map Verdansk and, later, other locations, where up to one hundred fifty players fight for survival in a gradually shrinking radioactive zone, with the key distinguishing feature being the Gulag system, which gives fallen players a chance to return to the match through a one-on-one duel against another fallen player.

The game builds on the proven shooting foundation known from the contemporary Modern Warfare entries, so weapon handling, recoil, and character movement feel familiar even to players of the series' classic parts. Warzone adds elements typical of the battle royale genre on top of that, such as looting gear from crates, completing contracts for rewards, and stockpiling in-game cash that can be used to buy equipment or revive fallen teammates at buy stations directly on the map. The Plunder mode additionally offered an alternative without elimination mechanics, focused purely on collecting and safely banking cash before time runs out.

On PC, the game required more powerful hardware due to the large open map and the high number of players in a single session at once, which over time also led to a fairly large installation size on disk. Warzone became a massive commercial success and significantly expanded the Call of Duty player base beyond traditional fans of individual entries, becoming part of a broader Warzone platform interlinked with other contemporary titles in the series. Today, the game stands as an important example of how a large, traditionally linear action brand managed to adapt successfully and quickly to the era's battle royale trend. Gradual updates, new maps, and seasonal content kept the player community active for a long time and cemented Warzone as a lasting part of the wider Call of Duty platform.

**Why play:** For players craving massive battle royale action with regular new content, ideally on a more powerful PC with plenty of disk space.

pc-modern__hearthstone.teaser: An accessible digital card game set in the Warcraft world; the game handles the rules for you.
pc-modern__hearthstone.article:
**Hearthstone** is a digital collectible card game from Blizzard Entertainment set in the Warcraft universe, released in 2014 as a free-to-play title for PC and later for mobile platforms as well. The player picks one of the hero classes, builds a thirty-card deck, and in turn-based duels tries to bring the opponent's health down from thirty points to zero using minions, spells, and the hero's power. Unlike classic paper CCGs such as Magic: The Gathering, Hearthstone removes most of the administrative burden – cards are played according to the rules automatically, minion combat is calculated by itself, and the game guides the player with clear visual cues, making it extremely accessible even for complete newcomers who would get lost in the rules of the paper version.

This accessibility was key to its massive success: Hearthstone became one of the most-played digital card titles of all time and, together with other titles, kicked off a wave of digital CCGs that capitalize on the computer handling complex card interactions without errors or delays. The game regularly receives expansions with new packs, alternates between the Standard and Wild formats, and offers alternative modes like Arena, the autobattler Battlegrounds, or solo adventures with story bosses and unique rules.

Visually, it builds on stylized, comic-book graphics and a humorous tone that contrasts pleasantly with the darker tone of the main Warcraft series, complemented by fully voiced card lines and music that changes according to the setting of each expansion. Hundreds of thousands of viewers regularly watch the game on streaming platforms, and for many years an organized esports scene with top-level tournaments has operated around it. Despite its age, thanks to regular support, low hardware requirements, and a well-thought-out free-to-play model, Hearthstone remains one of the most accessible gateways into the world of digital card games, and it still ranks among the most-watched and most influential titles in its genre, one whose design inspired practically the entire wave of card games that followed it.

**Why play:** Thanks to low hardware requirements, a well-thought-out free-to-play model, and comic-book graphics, it remains one of the most accessible and most-watched digital card games of all time.

pc-modern__magic-gathering-arena.teaser: The official digital Magic from Wizards of the Coast; sets release simultaneously with the paper editions.
pc-modern__magic-gathering-arena.article:
**Magic: The Gathering Arena** is the official digital implementation of the world's oldest and most widespread collectible card game, run by Wizards of the Coast itself since 2019. Unlike earlier attempts at digital Magic, it's a full-fledged platform with its own client, ranked ladders, draft tournaments, and regularly released expansions that mirror the paper editions almost simultaneously with their physical release. Players open packs, draft cards, or build sixty-card decks from their own collection, and face off in turns where victory is decided by a combination of mana curve, card types, and the complex synergies among the thousands of existing spells and creatures.

Arena's main strength lies in the fact that the computer can flawlessly resolve even extremely intricate chains of effects that would require an experienced judge in the paper game – the stack, priority, and the interactions between abilities are all handled automatically, letting the player focus their full attention on strategy. Economically, Arena is built on a free-to-play model with virtual currency, card packs, and a seasonal mastery system, which, compared to the costly hobby of collecting paper cards, makes it a significantly more accessible entry point into the world of Magic.

Visually, it sticks to the illustrations and style of the paper original; cards come to life with subtle animations and sound effects that underscore the atmosphere of the various factions and worlds Magic has passed through over its decades of existence. Besides the classic Standard and Historic formats, Arena also offers the streamlined Alchemy format with digitally rebalanced cards that wouldn't make sense in paper form, and it has extended the game to mobile devices as well. Arena has become the primary platform for competitive Magic play and for watching professional tournaments, and today represents the most active and most vibrant way to enjoy this classic, over-thirty-year-old card game without needing a physical collection and without risking damage to rare paper cards.

**Why play:** For Magic fans who want to play Standard, Historic, and the experimental Alchemy without needing a physical collection, with the option to watch and play professional tournaments as well.

pc-modern__magic-gathering-duels-of-plan.teaser: The first serious attempt at digital Magic; an ideal entry point for newcomers.
pc-modern__magic-gathering-duels-of-plan.article:
**Magic: The Gathering — Duels of the Planeswalkers** was Wizards of the Coast's first serious attempt to bring Magic in digital form to a broad audience on PC and consoles, developed by Stainless Games and released in 2009. Unlike the later Arena, it didn't offer free deckbuilding from the entire card collection – the player progressed through a campaign against a series of AI opponents, gradually unlocking pre-built decks and could only upgrade them to a limited extent by adding cards from a small pool of rewards. This simplified approach made the game an ideal gateway for newcomers who wanted to learn Magic's basic mechanics – mana, card types, creature combat – without having to study the extensive rules of the paper game.

The game emphasized clarity and fast matches, and its controls were adapted for gamepad use as well, enabling releases on consoles alongside the PC version. Duels of the Planeswalkers came out as a series of yearly titles (2009 to 2015), each bringing a new set of decks, a campaign, and online multiplayer, similar to sports series released every year. The series was eventually replaced by Arena, which offered a more open and deeper approach to deckbuilding.

Both audibly and visually, the game benefited from classic Magic card illustrations complemented by simple animations and atmospheric music that underscored the fantasy tone of the various factions, while the campaign took the player through a series of duels against the planeswalkers the series is named after. Each yearly entry gradually added new sets of pre-built decks corresponding to the paper editions releasing at the time, so the game also served as a clear showcase of what Magic had to offer that particular year. Although titles in the series are no longer available for purchase today, at the time of release they played a key role in bringing to Magic a generation of players who otherwise might never have gotten into the paper version of the game, and they showed that a complex card game could be successfully made accessible even outside specialized game stores and player community hubs.

**Why play:** A historically interesting pick for those who want to see how Magic brought new players into the series in the era before Arena, even though the entries are no longer for sale today.

pc-modern__slay-spire.teaser: The fusion of deckbuilder and roguelike founded an entire new subgenre of games in 2019.
pc-modern__slay-spire.article:
**Slay the Spire** combined two genres that seem far apart at first glance – deckbuilding and roguelike – and the result is a title that in 2019 practically founded an entire new subgenre of games. Instead of facing another player, it's a solo climb up a procedurally generated tower full of enemies, elite fights, and bosses, where the character (one of four, each with different decks and strategies) gradually expands their deck with new cards and grows stronger with relics. Cards represent attacks, defense, and abilities paid for with energy points, and the key lies in combining them into combo chains that let you take down even seemingly unbeatable enemies.

Unlike classic collectible card games, there's no collecting cards for real money here, nor any competing against other players – all the depth comes from the decisions made during a single playthrough (a run): which card to add to the deck, which to remove instead, which path through the tower to choose. Permadeath and random generation ensure high replayability and force the player to adapt each run to the cards on offer, which sets the game apart from the fixed archetypes of classic CCGs. It's precisely this model, where risk management and building synergies matter more than reaction speed, that makes Slay the Spire a textbook example of how well card mechanics work on a computer without the need for physical components.

Visually, it's modest, hand-drawn graphics and a spare interface which, thanks to their clarity, let players focus on strategy, and the game is rounded out by atmospheric, minimalist music underscoring the grim journey up the tower. The game spent a long period in early access, during which developers at the small studio Mega Crit Games continually fine-tuned it based on community feedback before it reached full release in 2019, later joined by an expansion adding a fourth playable character. Both critics and the player community embraced the game enthusiastically, and Slay the Spire became the reference point against which every other roguelike deckbuilder is still measured today, including several other titles on this list.

**Why play:** For fans of roguelike deckbuilders, this is an essential classic against which the entire genre is still measured, thanks to its clear design and well-thought-out strategic depth.

pc-modern__inscryption.teaser: A seemingly ordinary card game that gradually turns into a dark psychological horror.
pc-modern__inscryption.article:
**Inscryption** is a card game that, under the guise of a seemingly ordinary combat CCG, gradually transforms into a dark, psychological horror full of metagame twists, characteristic of the work of Daniel Mullins (Pony Island). The player finds themselves locked in a dark cabin across from a mysterious figure and must play card duels for their own life — creature cards are crafted right at the table by sacrificing other cards and adding blood and bones, which sets the game apart from standard CCGs where cards are fixed and purchased. As the game progresses, both the rules and the aesthetics change dramatically several times; the game abandons simple card combat and incorporates elements of escape rooms, hacking, and exploration, shattering any notion of what a card game can even be.

It's precisely this structural unpredictability that is Inscryption's main draw — the player never knows whether another layer of reality or an entirely different game system is hiding around the corner, and the creators play with the expectations of experienced card game and horror fans alike. The atmosphere is enhanced by an oppressive soundscape, the ticking of analog devices, and the narrator's voice, which constantly makes the player uncertain about who is actually in control of the game.

After its release in 2021, Inscryption received exceptionally positive reviews for its originality and boldness in experimenting with form, and today it is considered one of the most striking indie titles of its decade — one it's deliberately better to know as little as possible about beforehand, so the element of surprise stands out. On PC it works ideally thanks to precise mouse control necessary for manipulating cards and objects on the virtual table, searching drawers, and typing on the keyboard for puzzles, and thanks to its modest system requirements it is accessible on practically any computer. It's a typical example of a game that can't be pigeonholed into a single category — it combines card duels, a horror adventure, and elements of a computer simulation, and it's precisely this unpredictability that makes it one of the most original experiences the card game genre has offered in recent years.

**Why play it:** For players open to unpredictable experiences that are best known as little about in advance as possible — the combination of card duels, horror adventure, and gameplay experiments works flawlessly on PC.

pc-modern__balatro.teaser: Poker as a roguelike deckbuilder; jokers with their own effects push the score into the billions.
pc-modern__balatro.article:
**Balatro** takes ordinary poker as its foundation and builds on it an original roguelike deckbuilder that became one of the most successful indie titles of recent years in 2024. Instead of competing against other players, the player forms poker hands from a deck of cards, but multiplies and modifies the resulting score using so-called Jokers — special cards with their own effects that are collected, combined, and made to synergize with one another over the course of a run. The goal in each round is to beat an increasing target score before running out of hands, and to gradually build ever more bizarre and powerful combinations of effects that can turn a simple pair or straight into a combo worth billions of points.

Unlike classic card games, there is no opponent here and no negotiation — all the depth lies in how the player builds synergies between Jokers, Tarot and Planet cards, consumable items, and modifications to the deck itself, whether that means adding special suits, multipliers, or removing weak cards. Progress through the game is divided into so-called Antes, and within them a sequence of rounds called Blinds, where the last, hardest round in each Ante forces the player to keep searching for more efficient combinations. This purity of mechanics, combined with short, addictive rounds, makes Balatro a textbook example of so-called "one more run" design, where a single failed attempt immediately leads to another.

Visually the game relies on simple but striking retro pixel-art graphics complemented by minimalist yet infectious sound design and music that underscores the casino atmosphere with stylized cards and a game table. Balatro was essentially created by a single developer under the pseudonym LocalThunk, and its unexpected commercial and critical success, amplified further by its release on consoles and mobile devices, showed that even a seemingly exhausted genre like card deckbuilding still has plenty to offer if it comes with a sufficiently elegant and legible idea, such as linking poker hands with roguelike progression.

**Why play it:** The elegant combination of poker hands with roguelike progression and an infectious retro visual style make Balatro one of the most addictive card titles of recent times.

pc-modern__monster-train.teaser: Combat takes place on the floors of a train carrying hell's last flame; enemies attack from below.
pc-modern__monster-train.article:
**Monster Train** builds on the wave of roguelike deckbuilders kicked off by Slay the Spire, but adds its own key mechanic — combat doesn't take place on a single plane, but across several floors of a vertical train carrying hell's last flame to safety. The player builds their deck from two different clans (demons, reptiles, gravediggers, and others) whose cards can be combined into unexpected synergies, and must decide which of the train's floors to station their units on, since enemies advance from the bottom floor toward the core, which must be protected at all costs.

This spatial layout of the battlefield gives Monster Train a unique extra tactical layer compared to standard one-card-versus-one-card card combat — the player must consider not just the strength of the cards, but also exactly where on the train to place them in order to take advantage of terrain bonuses, protect vulnerable units in the back, and still prevent the enemy from breaking through to the heart of the flame. Each clan also brings a powerful champion unit around which an entire deck synergy can be built, and the combination of two clans at once allows for an enormous variety of different builds and strategies, which, together with the permadeath mechanic, ensures the high replayability typical of the entire roguelike deckbuilder genre.

The game also excels visually thanks to its striking, darkly stylized graphics and atmospheric music that reinforces the hellish setting of the story about the last spark of hell's flame carried by the train upward to the surface, where a variety of bosses with their own special combat rules await the player. The game also includes a system of difficulty levels (Covenant), which gradually adds handicaps and forces the player to seek out ever more effective strategies even after completing the base campaign. After its release in 2020, Monster Train was received exceptionally well by critics, and it convinced a number of players and reviewers that it could compete with — and in some respects even complement — the genre's established pioneer, which made it one of the most acclaimed titles of its kind on PC and later on consoles as well.

**Why play it:** For fans of roguelike deckbuilders looking for a worthy rival to the genre's pioneer, with a striking dark atmosphere and a difficulty system for long-term replayability.

pc-modern__gwent-witcher-card-game.teaser: Standalone Gwent from The Witcher 3; unit strength adds up across three rows instead of mana.
pc-modern__gwent-witcher-card-game.article:
**Gwent: The Witcher Card Game** originated as a standalone expansion of the popular minigame from The Witcher 3, and in 2018 CD Projekt Red released it as a full-fledged free-to-play title with ambitions to rival the genre's biggest names. Unlike typical CCGs built around spending mana, here players play cards into three separate rows (melee, ranged, and siege combat), where unit strength simply adds up, and the winner is whoever has the higher total after winning two of three rounds — so the player must also think strategically about when it's advantageous to concede a round and save cards for the next one.

This row system, the absence of mana constraints, and the emphasis on card effects that change turn order or wipe out entire rows make Gwent a mechanically distinct experience from Hearthstone or Magic, even though it shares the basic CCG framework of collecting cards and building decks from factions like the Northern Kingdoms, Nilfgaard, Skellige, Scoia'tael, or Monsters. The cards draw on the rich universe of The Witcher, and their artwork is among the most striking in the genre, with animated portraits and atmospheric music that continues the series' tradition.

After release, Gwent underwent several major reworks of both balance and visuals, including a complete overhaul of the card artwork into fully 3D form, reflecting the studio's long-term effort to find the ideal shape for the game in the competitive world of digital card games. The game also included a system of optional leader abilities for the factions, activated once per match, capable of fundamentally changing the course of a duel. Although it never achieved Hearthstone's mass success, it built a loyal community of players who appreciated its different approach to the genre, the tactical depth of the row system, and its deep roots in the respected fantasy world of the Witcher saga, whose atmosphere it managed to carry over to PC even outside the main series of games from CD Projekt Red. The game also featured regular tournaments and seasonal ladders, through which the studio worked long-term to keep Gwent alive as an active competitive platform alongside its classic player base.

**Why play it:** For players seeking tactical depth and a different approach to the card game genre, set in the atmosphere of the Witcher world, even if it never surpassed Hearthstone's mass success.

pc-modern__thronebreaker-witcher-tales.teaser: Gwent's system set within a full RPG featuring open exploration and moral choices.
pc-modern__thronebreaker-witcher-tales.article:
**Thronebreaker: The Witcher Tales** is a unique hybrid that places Gwent's card system within a full, story-driven RPG featuring open exploration, decisions with moral consequences, and a branching plot. The player takes on the role of Queen Meve of Lyria and Rivia, moves through a semi-isometric world, gathers resources, solves side quests, and leads her army into battles fought precisely through Gwent-style card duels — three rows, unit strength adding up, special card abilities.

Unlike standalone Gwent, however, the card duels in Thronebreaker are not competitions against other players but part of a linear, carefully balanced story — many of the battles feature unique puzzle-like victory conditions, special rules, or scripted situations that function more like thoughtfully designed puzzles than a classic card duel. The player builds their deck gradually from cards found while exploring and rewards for completing quests, so the game links RPG progression with a gradually deepening card strategy.

Visually and narratively, Thronebreaker draws fully on the grim, morally ambiguous atmosphere of the Witcher series, complemented by quality voice acting and music from composers associated with the series, and the decisions the player makes along Queen Meve's journey have a real impact on which characters and locations appear later in the story. Critics especially praised the story's unexpected depth, the quality of the writing, and the boldness of combining two seemingly incompatible genres — turn-based card strategy and a sprawling fantasy RPG with moral dilemmas — which is why Thronebreaker remains to this day one of the most interesting and most underrated experiments with card mechanics within a larger RPG whole. Although it was built on the same engine and set in the same world as standalone Gwent, it works entirely on its own, and no prior experience with the competitive card title is needed to play it.

**Why play it:** For fans of the Witcher series and players craving a fresh combination of turn-based card strategy with a sprawling fantasy RPG full of moral dilemmas and quality storytelling.

pc-modern__legends-of-runeterra.teaser: Riot Games' entry into CCGs set in the League of Legends universe; unused mana carries over to the next round.
pc-modern__legends-of-runeterra.article:
**Legends of Runeterra** is Riot Games' entry into the digital CCG genre, set in the League of Legends universe, released in 2020 as a free-to-play title with an emphasis on a player-friendly economy and deep strategic gameplay. Duels take place on a single board, where players alternate between the roles of attacker and defender — the attacker deploys units, the defender decides which cards to block them with, creating constant tactical tension around when it's advantageous to attack and when it's better to hold back. The key innovation is a mana system split into regular mana and so-called spell mana, where unused mana carries over into the next round and allows spells to be cast even outside the player's own turn.

Decks are built from two regions of the universe (Demacia, Noxus, Piltover and Zaun, the Shadow Isles, and others), each with its own playstyle, and their combination allows for a wide range of archetypes. Champion cards play a special role, capable of evolving (leveling up) into more powerful versions once certain conditions are met during a game, which brings a narrative arc to matches similar to a character's progression in a story-driven game. Economically, Riot bet on a generous free-to-play model without loot boxes, where players unlock cards through play and targeted crafting, which was viewed positively at the time in contrast to the practices of competing titles.

Visually the game benefits from beautifully animated cards and atmospheric music that ties into the broader League of Legends universe, and it also offers a solo mode called Path of Champions, in which the player goes through a series of challenges against AI, similar to roguelike deckbuilders. Although it never managed to significantly dent Hearthstone's dominance, it earned the respect of critics and players alike for its thoughtful design, the tactical depth of its attack-and-block system, and its player-friendly approach to monetization without aggressive purchase pressure. The game was also released on mobile devices with the same account progression as on PC, making it one of the first truly full-fledged cross-platform digital CCG titles of its time.

**Why play it:** For players who want a tactical card game with player-friendly monetization free of aggressive purchase pressure, and full gameplay across both PC and mobile.

pc-modern__yu-gi-oh-master-duel.teaser: A digital rules simulator for the Yu-Gi-Oh! TCG with thousands of cards from the start of the game.
pc-modern__yu-gi-oh-master-duel.article:
**Yu-Gi-Oh! Master Duel** is the official digital rules simulator for the Yu-Gi-Oh! Trading Card Game, released by Konami in 2022 as a free-to-play title with an enormous scope — from launch it contained thousands of cards spanning decades of the franchise's history, including the newest archetypes. The game faithfully carries over the complex, at-first-glance intimidating rules of the paper original: Fusion, Synchro, Xyz, and Link Summoning of monsters, intricate chains of effects activated in response to an opponent's moves, and a specific turn-phase structure — all of it evaluated by the computer flawlessly and far faster than any human referee could manage at a physical table.

It's precisely this ability to manage extremely complicated card interactions flawlessly and quickly that is the main reason Master Duel works better on a computer than any previous attempt to bring Yu-Gi-Oh! into digital form — players who previously avoided the paper rules because of their complexity can now enjoy the game's depth thanks to automation, without having to study hundreds of exceptions. Cards are obtained through crafting using in-game currency as well as through packs, a ranked ladder provides a competitive backdrop, and the game regularly adds new archetypes synchronized with the release of physical sets.

Visually it relies on a clear 3D interface for the duel table with impressive animations for summoning monsters and their attacks, complemented by music that continues the series' long tradition, and it also offers a solo mode with a tutorial that walks newcomers through the game's basic principles step by step. The game supports international play across PC, consoles, and mobile devices, connecting a community that used to be fragmented across several unofficial simulators. Following its release, Master Duel received very positive reception, especially from fans of both generations, and became the main platform for competitive Yu-Gi-Oh! play worldwide.

**Why play it:** For fans of both generations of Yu-Gi-Oh! who will appreciate the clear 3D interface, a solo tutorial for newcomers, and the leading platform for competitive play across all platforms.

pc-modern__papers-please.teaser: Bureaucratic border control turns into a tense moral drama about money and family.
pc-modern__papers-please.article:
**Papers, Please** puts the player behind the border-control window of the fictional totalitarian republic of Arstotzka, and turns bureaucratic routine into a surprisingly tense and morally charged game. The task is to check the passports, visas, and other documents of arriving travelers, detect forgeries and discrepancies, and decide who to let through and who to detain. Every decision has a cost — literally, since the salary depends on the number of people processed per day, and it's from that salary that rent, food, and medicine for the family that depends on the player are paid.

The gameplay rests on gradually increasing rule complexity: at first it's enough to verify a name and photograph, later fingerprints, metal detectors, changing lists of banned countries, and ever more elaborate forgeries are added. The game skillfully combines mechanical precision with moral dilemmas — refugees with invalid papers, smugglers offering bribes, secret-service agents demanding exceptions. Visually the game relies on a stark pixel-art aesthetic and a gloomy color palette that perfectly matches the atmosphere of Cold-War-era bureaucracy and omnipresent surveillance.

The game also includes a hidden plotline involving an underground organization called EZIC, which gradually contacts the player through messages smuggled between the documents and offers them the chance to actively rise up against the ruling regime — one of a total of twenty different endings the game offers. Government propaganda on posters in the background, gloomy music, and the cramped composition of the window only reinforce the feeling that the player is merely a cog in an enormous state machine.

After its release the game received an exceptionally positive response for the originality of its concept and for how it manages to extract genuine tension and ethical questions from what at first glance looks like dull administrative work. It became one of the most frequently cited examples proving that video games can tell powerful stories through purely systemic gameplay without a single cutscene. Even years after release, it is still referenced as a pioneering work of the "bureaucratic simulator" genre and has inspired numerous successors. Even after all this time, it still functions as a chilling reminder of how easily an ordinary person can become a tool of a repressive system.

**Why play it:** For players open to unconventional storytelling, it's a chilling reminder of how easily an ordinary person can become a tool of a repressive system, built entirely on administrative gameplay.

atari-st__powermonger.teaser: Spiritual successor to Populous set in a more earthbound world; subdue provinces through diplomacy as well as war.
atari-st__powermonger.article:
**Powermonger** built on the success of Populous, transplanting the god-view strategy concept into a more earthbound, historically flavored setting. The player takes on the role of a warlord whose army has been shipwrecked in an unknown land divided into dozens of provinces, and must gradually subjugate the local population - through diplomacy, trade, or military force. Each province has its own rulers, economy, and units, so the player is constantly balancing between building alliances and waging open campaigns.

The Atari ST version preserved the smooth top-down view with the ability to rotate and zoom the map, which, combined with units that could be controlled individually or in groups, created a genuine sense of commanding a vast territory. Individual characters in the world have their own needs - they eat, age, and react to how the player treats them, an unusually elaborate detail for 1990 that made Powermonger's world feel more alive than most strategy games of the era. The campaign consisted of many interconnected missions and offered considerable freedom in how the player chose to subdue each region. Seasons also affect harvests and unit movement, so a campaign planned for winter requires a different approach than a summer expedition.

Powermonger confirmed Bullfrog's reputation as a creator of imaginative strategy simulations and expanded the audience that had grown fond of Populous to include players looking for a deeper, less abstract system. For its time, it was a technically and content-wise ambitious title that showed how far the strategy genre could push on eight-bit successor platforms, offering a considerably longer and more varied campaign than its predecessor. Today the game will appeal especially to those who love early Bullfrog and want to see how the principles that later evolved into titles like Dungeon Keeper or Theme Park first took shape.

**Why play:** For fans of early Bullfrog who want to see how the principles behind later titles like Dungeon Keeper or Theme Park took shape, in a deeper and less abstract strategy game than Populous.

atari-st__midwinter.teaser: Open-world action strategy with dozens of controllable characters, from foot soldier to hang-glider pilot.
atari-st__midwinter.article:
**Midwinter** is a sprawling action-strategy simulation in which the player leads a resistance movement on a frozen island invaded by a hostile army. Instead of linear missions, the game offers an open world with dozens of characters, each with their own skills and equipment and each directly controllable by the player - from foot soldiers and skiers to hang-glider pilots. The goal is to organize the resistance, coordinate its individual members, and gradually drive the invaders off the island, with the method of achieving that largely left up to the player.

Technically, this was an exceptionally ambitious project for 1989: the entire island was rendered as a continuous 3D landscape with no loading between areas, traversable by snowmobile, skis, or air. On the Atari ST the game ran in both wireframe and filled 3D graphics, which, despite the platform's hardware limitations, managed to convey a sense of a vast, open world. Controls for individual characters and vehicles differed by type, requiring the player to adapt to different control schemes within a single game. Characters also had their own morale and fatigue, so long marches or repeated combat could take resistance members out of action just as effectively as a direct clash with the enemy.

At release, Midwinter was praised above all for the scope and freedom it offered players - the concept of an open world with character choice was thoroughly unusual in 1989 on the eight-bit successor generation. The game was well ahead of its time and is often cited as an early example of what later became standard in open-world games; its success later earned it a sequel, Midwinter II: Flames of Freedom. Today Midwinter is interesting chiefly as a historical milestone - its ambition, combined with the hardware of the era, still commands respect, even though the controls and pacing feel archaic by modern standards.

**Why play:** For lovers of gaming history who will appreciate just how far ahead of its time the game was with its open-world concept and character choice - even though the controls and pacing feel archaic today.

atari-st__starglider.teaser: Space combat sim with a fully filled 3D polygon world - a technical marvel of 1986.
atari-st__starglider.article:
**Starglider** combines a space simulator with action shooting and ranks among the most technically impressive titles of the early Atari ST era. The player pilots the fighter craft Egron and defends the planet Novenia from an invasion of hostile robotic machines, switching between a cockpit view and a tactical map of the surrounding area. Combat takes place in a fully rendered 3D space with filled polygons, which in 1986 was an exceptionally demanding and ambitious feat for a home computer. The player must switch between flight mode, maneuvering among the mountains and canyons of the surface, and direct combat against enemy robots such as the Egg Fighter, Walker, or Mine, each of which demands a different tactic.

The game was developed by Argonaut Software and, on the Atari ST, used the power of the 68000 processor to render smoother and faster 3D scenes than eight-bit machines could manage. The gameplay was built around fighting waves of enemies of various types, spiced up with occasional dialogue from the enemy commander that lent the game a good dose of humor and personality. Gradually destroying enemy forces and defending the planet's key points formed a clearly readable, if not especially long, gameplay loop that motivated players to replay for a better score and deeper penetration into the enemy's defenses.

At release, Starglider was praised chiefly for its technical execution of 3D graphics, which ranked among the best home computers had to offer, and helped establish the Atari ST as a platform capable of competing with more demanding simulations. The game later received a sequel, Starglider 2, with an even more elaborate world. Today Starglider is interesting mainly as a demonstration of just how far programmers could push vector and polygon graphics on mid-1980s hardware, and as a reminder of the early days of Argonaut.

**Why play:** For anyone interested in the history of 3D graphics on home computers - it shows just how far programmers could push vector graphics as early as the mid-1980s.

atari-st__defender-of-crown.teaser: Medieval England, jousting tournaments, and castle sieges; a Cinemaware classic with a cinematic touch.
atari-st__defender-of-crown.article:
**Defender of the Crown** casts the player into a medieval England divided among rival noble houses, offering a mix of strategy, tournaments, and action mini-games. As the leader of one of the houses, the goal is to gradually gain control of as much territory as possible, using diplomacy, military campaigns, castle sieges, and the abduction of noble ladies, around whom a side plot unfolds. The strategic map of England shows the balance of power among the various factions, and the player decides where to direct their army and with whom to form alliances, with the choice of one of four playable noble families giving each playthrough a slightly different starting point.

The game from studio Cinemaware set itself apart from other strategy titles through its emphasis on cinematic presentation - between turns on the map, animated sequences play out for jousting tournaments, sword duels, or castle sieges, each functioning as a self-contained action mini-game. On the Atari ST the game benefited from more colorful and detailed graphics than eight-bit platforms could offer, allowing a more faithful rendering of the chivalric aesthetic on which Cinemaware built its reputation. Catapult assaults on castle walls, jousting duels, and archer skirmishes looked more colorful and fluid on the ST than in the older eight-bit versions, accompanied by period music underscoring the chivalric theme.

Defender of the Crown became one of the standout titles of the mid-1980s precisely because it combined a strategic layer with striking animated scenes, and for years it served as a showcase of what home computers were graphically capable of. The concept of alternating between a strategic map and action sequences influenced other Cinemaware games as well as later strategy titles with cinematic presentation. Today the game appeals more as a historical artifact and a showcase of the era's artistic style than for the depth of its strategic layer, which is fairly simple compared to later games.

**Why play:** For fans of period strategy games who will appreciate the visual and atmospheric presentation more than the depth of the strategic layer, which is fairly simple compared to later games.

atari-st__balance-of-power.teaser: Cold War geopolitical strategy; excessive aggression ends the game in war.
atari-st__balance-of-power.article:
**Balance of Power** is a geopolitical strategy game in which the player, leading either the USA or the Soviet Union, manages a network of allies around the world in the Cold War era. The goal is not military victory but maintaining and expanding influence through diplomacy, economic aid, and covert operations, and the game explicitly punishes excessive aggression - escalating a conflict all the way to nuclear war ends the game immediately, announcing with ironic commentary that nobody won. This design element made Balance of Power a unique experience among strategy games of its time, forcing the player to seek sustainable long-term solutions to conflicts rather than simple military escalation.

The game was designed by Chris Crawford, and on the Atari ST it was played via a clear world map on which the player tracks the political situation in individual countries and reacts to crises triggered by the opponent as well as local conflicts. Decisions are made through simple menus and diplomatic choices, so the game emphasized weighing consequences rather than fast reaction times or graphical action. After each turn the game also offers a brief explanation of why the opponent reacted the way it did, helping the player understand the system's logic and learn from their own mistakes.

In the mid-1980s, Balance of Power was seen as an intellectually demanding and unusually serious attempt to bring the real political reality of the Cold War into a computer game, and it earned respect beyond the traditional gaming audience, including among commentators concerned with education and international relations. The game is still cited today as one of the first examples of so-called serious games - titles that aim not only to entertain but also to teach about the real world. Even decades later it remains interesting as evidence that the strategy genre could already, in the 1980s, transcend the mere conquest of territory.

**Why play:** For players interested in politics and Cold War history - one of the first titles that wanted not just to entertain, but also to teach about the real world.

atari-st__centurion-defender-of-rome.teaser: Build the Roman empire from warlord to emperor, with sea battles and gladiator combat in the arena.
atari-st__centurion-defender-of-rome.article:
**Centurion: Defender of Rome** puts the player in the role of a Roman warlord tasked with expanding and maintaining the empire's dominance over the entire Mediterranean. The game combines a strategic map, on which provinces are managed, taxes collected, and campaigns planned, with tactical battles on land and sea and gladiator arena combat that functions as self-contained action sequences. The political layer also includes the relationship with the Roman Senate and the emperor, whose favor can boost or end the player's career, and over the course of the game the player can rise from a mere warlord all the way to the title of emperor.

On the Atari ST the game offered colorful, clear rendering of both the empire's map and the individual battle and arena scenes, which played out in real time with the ability to command units directly. The alternation between calmer strategic management of provinces and dynamic combat kept the game's pace lively and prevented it from shrinking into mere resource counting. Gladiatorial combat in the arena also serves a practical role - a successful fighter earns extra resources that can be reinvested into building the empire, while also boosting popularity among the Roman people.

Centurion: Defender of Rome was praised at release for how accessibly and enjoyably it combined empire management with action elements, without either component overshadowing the other. The game followed in the tradition of titles like Defender of the Crown and further developed the genre of historical strategy games with cinematic presentation, clearly understandable controls, and a fast pace accessible even to less experienced strategy players. Today Centurion is interesting as one of the more accessible entry points into the genre of historical strategy games and as evidence of how strongly themes of ancient Rome resonated across the games industry at the end of the 1980s.

**Why play:** For players looking for an accessible entry point into historical strategy games - its fast pace and clear controls make it a pleasant choice even for less experienced strategists.

atari-st__falcon.teaser: F-16 flight simulator with a functional cockpit and an emphasis on realistic aircraft handling.
atari-st__falcon.article:
**Falcon** is a flight simulator for the F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet, which on the Atari ST offered one of the most elaborate flight models of its time. The player pilots a modern fighter jet, handling takeoffs, landings, navigation, and air combat against enemy aircraft, with the game placing emphasis on relatively realistic aircraft behavior - reacting to speed, altitude, fuel, and damage - in contrast to the simplified arcade flight games of the era. The cockpit offers functional instruments including radar, an onboard computer for firing missiles, and a warning system for enemy lock-on, so a successful flight requires monitoring several gauges at once.

On the Atari ST the game ran in vector 3D graphics with filled surfaces, made possible by the platform's more powerful processor, and offered a clear cockpit view with functional instruments. The game also included a mission editor that let players build their own scenarios and objectives, significantly extending the title's lifespan beyond the pre-built missions. Players could also choose the simulation's difficulty level, from a simplified flight model suitable for beginners to a more demanding setting closer to the real behavior of the aircraft, making the game accessible to both newcomers and more experienced flight-sim enthusiasts.

Falcon, from studio Spectrum HoloByte, helped establish the Atari ST as a platform suitable for more demanding flight simulations, which had previously been the domain of more powerful computers. The game's success led to several sequels and expansions and helped popularize the genre of military flight simulators among the broader home computer audience, which had previously seen this type of game as the domain of specialized and considerably more expensive platforms. Today Falcon is interesting mainly as a reminder of an era when simulators were still finding the balance between accessibility and realism, and as one of the more technically demanding titles in the Atari ST's early catalog.

**Why play:** For those interested in the history of flight simulators, who will appreciate how the genre was still finding the balance between accessibility and realism on 1980s hardware.

atari-st__f-18-interceptor.teaser: Atari ST launch title with then-unheard-of smooth 3D; action missions flying the F/A-18 Hornet.
atari-st__f-18-interceptor.article:
**F/A-18 Interceptor** was one of the flagship titles Atari released alongside the launch of the ST line, and it demonstrated then-unheard-of smooth real-time 3D rendering on a home computer. The player takes the controls of an F/A-18 Hornet fighter and completes a series of missions ranging from flight training and aircraft-carrier defense to direct combat against enemy planes, with the game emphasizing action pacing over simulation depth. Missions often connect into a broader scenario, so successfully landing on the aircraft carrier and refueling and rearming is just as important as the aerial combat itself.

The game's graphics used filled polygons instead of mere wireframe models, a remarkable feat for 1987 and one of the main selling points Atari used to market the ST as a more powerful alternative to both the eight-bit machines of the time and competing sixteen-bit systems. The controls combined a joystick with keyboard shortcuts for managing weapons, radar, and the aircraft's tactical systems, and the player could switch between the cockpit view and an external camera, which made orientation easier during carrier landing maneuvers. The colorful texturing of sea and sky, along with smooth animation of other aircraft, ranked among the best home computers offered in this category at the time of release.

F/A-18 Interceptor served first and foremost as a technological showcase for the new platform and played a significant role in how the Atari ST was perceived at launch - as a machine capable of delivering graphical experiences earlier computer generations could not manage. Although the game feels today more like a simple arcade title than a full simulator, historically it remains valuable as evidence of the ST's launch lineup and as one of the first titles to show the direction flight games on the platform would take, as well as how quickly the graphical execution of home computer simulators would continue to improve.

**Why play:** For collectors and historians who want to see the technological showcase of the Atari ST at its launch - by today's standards the game feels more like a simple arcade title than a full simulator.

atari-st__lotus-esprit-turbo-challenge.teaser: An iconic ST racing classic with an adrenaline-fueled sense of speed and a split-screen for two.
atari-st__lotus-esprit-turbo-challenge.article:
**Lotus Esprit Turbo Challenge** is among the most beloved racing games ever released for the Atari ST, and one of the reasons why many players associate this computer with a feeling of speed and adrenaline. The game puts players behind the wheel of a Lotus Esprit sports car and offers a series of tracks full of curves, oncoming traffic, and hazards that must be mastered within a time limit. The controls are straightforward and forgiving, so players quickly learn to hit the racing line, use the nitro boost on straights, and avoid collisions that can slow them down enough to miss a checkpoint. The game also offered a split-screen two-player mode, which was not a given for racing titles on eighteen-bit computers at the time and contributed to the game's popularity at gaming get-togethers.

Technically, the Atari ST version benefited from smooth scrolling backgrounds and legible graphics that felt fast and dynamic despite the platform's limitations. The atmosphere was strongly enhanced by energetic music accompanying the menus and the individual track sections, which became an inseparable part of the experience and which many players still remember today. The game relied on a simple but addictive game loop – the further a player progressed through the series of tracks, the more demanding and faster the races became. The game gave the player a limited supply of time, which could be extended by passing through checkpoints, keeping the tension high throughout the ride and forcing players to risk faster but more dangerous routes.

At the time of release, the game received very positive reception and became one of the most commercially successful titles for both the Atari ST and the competing Amiga. It launched a series of sequels and influenced numerous other arcade racing games on sixteen-bit platforms. Even today it is considered a prime example of how the simple principle of driving from point A to point B can be turned into maximum fun, and it remains among the titles retro gaming fans love to revisit, appearing on modern retro compilations as well.

**Why play:** For arcade racing fans who appreciate how the simple principle of driving from point A to point B can be turned into maximum fun — a title worth returning to.

atari-st__lotus-turbo-challenge-2.teaser: An improved sequel to the beloved Lotus racing formula, with more varied tracks.
atari-st__lotus-turbo-challenge-2.article:
**Lotus Turbo Challenge 2** followed up on the successful first installment and brought an improved version of the beloved Lotus racing formula to the Atari ST. Compared to its predecessor, it offered more elaborate tracks, new gameplay elements, and the ability to compete against another player, which increased replayability and made the game a popular choice for shared gaming evenings. The principle remained similar – the player must complete the track within a time limit, avoid traffic, and use the nitro boost at the right spots – but the tracks were more varied and offered more visual variety of environments, from city circuits to country roads. The player could choose between several difficulty levels and game modes, which made the game accessible to both newcomers and more experienced players looking for a challenge.

On the Atari ST, the game again benefited from smooth animation and legible graphics that made good use of the platform's capabilities, accompanied by catchy music continuing the successful sound style of the first installment. The sense of speed was reinforced by small details such as screen shake on impact or changing scenery along the track, which set the game apart from many simpler competing racing titles of the time. The split-screen two-player mode was retained, and together with the improved selection of tracks, it was one of the main reasons the game became so sought-after on both the Atari ST and the Amiga, even though the core principle remained typically arcade-like and easily accessible.

Lotus Turbo Challenge 2 was well received at launch by both critics and players, who appreciated that virtually every aspect of the first installment had been improved. The game further cemented the series' position as one of the most popular racing brands on sixteen-bit home computers, and it is still remembered today as one of the high points of the arcade racing genre on the Atari ST, one that also inspired other creators of automotive arcade games of the era.

**Why play:** For fans of the first installment and newcomers to arcade racing alike — it improves on virtually every aspect of its predecessor and ranks among the high points of the genre on the Atari ST.

atari-st__super-cars-ii.teaser: Top-down view, car upgrades between races; an addictive progression system across the championship.
atari-st__super-cars-ii.article:
**Super Cars II** is a top-down racing title that, on the Atari ST, followed up on the successful first installment and expanded it with new tracks, cars, and gameplay options. The player races small, nimble vehicles along tracks full of turns, jumps, and obstacles, and can invest earned points and winnings into upgrading their car – a faster engine, better tires, or a sturdier chassis. This progressive upgrade element gave the game a sense of continuity across individual races and motivated players to keep going through the championship series. The tracks ran through varied environments from city streets to country roads and contained shortcuts that could be discovered through repeated play and used to gain an advantage over opponents.

The game's graphics on the Atari ST were colorful and clear, with a well-readable track despite the top-down view, which demanded quick orientation. The controls were straightforward, but mastering drifts and racing lines in corners required practice, giving the game a pleasant learning curve and rewarding players who practiced the tracks repeatedly. The game also featured weapon-based duels between cars, which brought it closer to zany arcade fun than to a serious racing simulation. It also supported two players competing at once, which, together with the car upgrade system, made it a popular choice for repeated gaming sessions with friends, who could also compare their accumulated winnings and upgraded cars.

Super Cars II was well received at launch for its fun factor and variety of content, and it was among the popular titles of its genre on sixteen-bit computers. It is still seen today as an enjoyable example of top-down arcade racing, combining speed, car-upgrade strategy, and a bit of chaotic fun from the combat elements, which is why it retains its playability even years after release.

**Why play:** For fans of lighthearted arcade racing with car upgrades and a bit of chaotic combat fun that has held up well even years after release.

atari-st__hard-drivin.teaser: An ambitious 3D racing simulation with a loop and a jump ramp, faithful to its arcade original.
atari-st__hard-drivin.article:
**Hard Drivin'** was, for its time, an unusually ambitious attempt at a realistic 3D racing simulation that brought the essence of the famous arcade cabinet to the Atari ST. Instead of flat sprites and simple track scrolling, the game offered a genuinely three-dimensional environment rendered in wireframe and solid polygon graphics, through which the player moved with physics accounting for steering, braking, and collisions. The track included a loop, a jump ramp, and other elements that were a real rarity on home computers of the time. Besides the classic race-against-the-clock mode, the game also offered a duel against a rival car, which required the player to master overtaking in technically demanding sections of the track.

On the Atari ST, hardware performance was a noticeable limitation – the frame rate was lower than on the arcade machine, and the game placed high demands on the processing time needed to render the 3D scene, which affected smoothness.
