Its free-to-play model with ads was unobtrusive in this case and didn't hinder quick repeated play, which, together with links spreading virally on social media, helped the game reach a much wider audience than its purely gaming qualities alone would have attracted.

**Why play it:** Suitable for nostalgics who want to be reminded of the internet humor of the turn of the 2000s and 2010s, wrapped in a simple, addictive arcade game.

mobil__secret-of-monkey-island-2-special.teaser: A remaster of the classic LucasArts adventure with new graphics and the option to switch to the original.
mobil__secret-of-monkey-island-2-special.article:
**The Secret of Monkey Island 2: Special Edition** brought the classic LucasArts point-and-click adventure to touchscreen phones with reworked graphics and new voice acting, while keeping the original pixel-art version just one tap away — the player could switch between the modern and retro look at any time and watch the same scene transform between two decades of game graphics development. The controls translated the classic point-and-click mouse scheme to touch: tapping moves the character, double-tapping examines things, gestures open the inventory — and it all worked surprisingly naturally even without a physical cursor.

LucasArts released this remaster in 2010 as part of the wave of classic adventure remasters kicked off by the first Monkey Island, and the mobile version let a new generation of players discover the story of the pirate Guybrush Threepwood and his search for LeChuck's treasure without needing to dig up an old computer or an emulator. The humor, dialogue trees full of absurd puzzles, and the unmistakable music remained untouched, just wrapped in a more modern shell.

The port succeeded above all thanks to a well-thought-out adaptation of the controls to touch, which didn't shortchange the precision the adventure genre needs, and the ability to switch to the original graphics worked as a nice nod to players who already knew the game from the nineties. Unlike many other retro remasters, you could also switch between the old and new look at any moment during play, not just at the start of the game, letting the player compare what's on screen scene by scene.

**Why play it:** An ideal choice for fans of classic adventure games and newcomers alike, since it offers comfortable touch controls without losing the spirit of the original.

mobil__sonic-cd.teaser: A port of the Sega classic with time-travel mechanics between past and future.
mobil__sonic-cd.article:
**Sonic CD** brought one of the most elaborately designed entries of the early Sonic era to mobile phones, built around a time-travel mechanic – at select points in a level, the player could jump between the past, the present, and two versions of the future, good and bad, depending on how they acted at that moment. This unique layer on top of the classic ring-collecting and level-running gameplay made Sonic CD a more deeply crafted title than was typical for Sega's platformers of the nineties.

SEGA released the mobile port of Sonic CD in 2011 with updated high-resolution graphics and the option to choose between the Japanese and American soundtracks, a welcome detail for fans who had long argued over both versions of the score. Controls relied on on-screen virtual buttons, which for a fast platformer built on precise jump timing represented a noticeable compromise compared to a physical controller, even though the port tried to keep the layout as thumb-friendly as possible.

Translating precise platforming sequences to a touchscreen will never be perfect, but Sonic CD was among the better-executed ports of its era thanks to solid emulation of the original game and the care given to both graphical and audio details, rather than just a retitled repackaging of the same code. For many fans, it was also the first chance to try the game at all, since the original on the Sega CD had been a niche release with limited availability in Europe at launch.

**Why play it:** Fans of classic Sonic will appreciate the inventive time-travel mechanic, but should expect that virtual buttons can't replace the precision of a physical controller.

mobil__tiny-tower.teaser: A tower-building simulator full of Bitizens; a pioneer of mobile freemium games.
mobil__tiny-tower.article:
**Tiny Tower** from studio NimbleBit was released in 2011 and is one of the first titles to show on a mass scale what a freemium simulator tailored to a touchscreen phone looks like. The player builds a vertical skyscraper, floor by floor, fits it out with shops, restaurants, and apartments, and populates it with characters called Bitizens, each with their own name, dream, and favorite job. Controls rely on simple tapping – you choose the type of floor, move the elevator up and down between levels, and take on new tenants who look for work themselves based on their interests and skills.

The whole game keeps running even in the background of the phone: materials for building the next floor accumulate over time, shops need regular restocking, and profits grow slowly but surely even when the player doesn't have the app open. Anyone who doesn't want to wait for construction to finish or for stock to be restocked can buy off their impatience with the virtual currency TowerBux, purchased with real money. Tiny Tower is among the games that popularized this model on a mass scale and essentially defined it for an entire generation of mobile titles, and it also inspired its own sequel, the casino-themed Tiny Tower Vegas.

Visually, it's cute pixel art in pastel colors, complemented by light humor in the Bitizens' lines and their small personal stories that unfold as time passes. The game's appeal rests on gentle, unobtrusive progress without stress or time pressure – ideal for a few minutes between other activities, exactly as mobile gaming at the start of the decade was starting to call for.

**Why play it:** suited to players who enjoy calm building games running in the background of their phone and don't mind the waiting mechanics typical of free-to-play titles of that era.

mobil__superbrothers-sword-and-sworcery-.teaser: An adventure with striking pixel-art visuals and Jim Guthrie's atmospheric soundtrack.
mobil__superbrothers-sword-and-sworcery-.article:
**Superbrothers: Sword & Sworcery EP** from 2011 by the Canadian studio Capybara Games is among the works that proved a mobile game could be an artistic experience on par with the independent computer adventures of its time. As the Scythian, the player travels through a stylized landscape full of ancient mysteries, solves simple puzzles by touching the screen, and watches the moon's phases influence events in the game – a mechanic tied to the actual phases of the real Moon was one of the production's most distinctive and widely discussed ideas.

The controls are minimalist, based on tapping and dragging a finger across the screen, which suits the slow, contemplative pace of the game well, along with a story that unfolds more through mood and imagery than dialogue. The bold, angular pixel-art visuals with long shadows and hazy color gradients create the atmosphere of a dreamlike fairy tale, heightened by Jim Guthrie's soundtrack – one of the most quoted and acclaimed pieces of mobile game music of its time, later also released as a standalone album.

The game became a symbol of the rising wave of artistically ambitious mobile titles and, alongside other independent projects, helped show that iOS and Android could be a fully-fledged platform for auteur projects, not just quick arcade distraction. The pace is deliberately slow and meditative, which some players will welcome as a refreshing change, while others may initially find its unusual structure jarring.

**Why play it:** a good choice for players seeking a short, atmospheric, and visually unforgettable experience, rather than those expecting fast action and clear rules from a mobile game.

mobil__battleheart.teaser: An action RPG with a party of heroes controlled by finger swipes; tactical depth in a small package.
mobil__battleheart.article:
**Battleheart** from the two-person studio Mika Mobile was released in 2011 and is among the games that showed how elegantly an action RPG with several characters at once could be controlled on a touchscreen. The player assembles a party of four heroes from different classes – warrior, mage, healer, or archer – and by dragging a finger sends them into battle against waves of enemies in neatly designed small arenas full of traps and positional advantages.

The combat system is built on simple gestures: dragging a finger sets the target of an attack or the direction of a character's movement, while tapping an icon activates that class's special ability. Beneath the friendly, cartoonish look with bold colors hides surprising tactical depth – correct unit placement and class combinations decide success just as much as the player's quick reflexes. As they gain experience, characters gradually improve, unlock new abilities, and change the appearance of their gear, keeping the game interesting even after many hours of repeated play.

Battleheart became one of the reference titles of the early App Store era, still cited today as an example of how to bring the complexity of a traditional RPG to a small screen without unnecessarily simplifying its mechanics. The studio followed up its success with the more expansive sequel Battleheart Legacy, but it's the first game that remains prized for its compactness, purity of idea, and straightforward, honest controls.

**Why play it:** recommended for players who want a tactical RPG playable in short sessions and who appreciate controls designed specifically for a touchscreen rather than carried over from consoles.

mobil__dungeon-raid.teaser: A match-3 puzzle combined with RPG progression; a forerunner of the puzzle-RPG hybrid genre.
mobil__dungeon-raid.article:
**Dungeon Raid** from the small studio Fireflame Games was released in 2011 and is among the first games to successfully combine match-3 symbol-matching mechanics with the progression system known from RPGs. The player drags a finger across a grid of icons representing swords, shields, spells, or gold, and by connecting longer chains defeats enemies, collects treasure, heals the character, and replenishes the supply of mana for stronger spells.

With experience gained, the character grows, gains new abilities, and gets stronger gear, so each subsequent expedition into the dungeon is more demanding due to stronger enemies, but the character is also better prepared for it thanks to prior progress. This hybrid of puzzle mechanics and RPG progression was far from a given in 2011, and Dungeon Raid is now looked back on as one of the titles that helped kick-start this later hugely popular genre mix on mobile platforms and show it the way.

Visually, it's a plain, purely functional look with no great visual ambitions – the game's strength lies entirely elsewhere: in the addictive pull toward one more round and in gradually building an ever stronger and tougher character. Controls via dragging a finger across the grid are intuitive and quickly learned even without instructions, making the game suitable both for short breaks and for longer play sessions before bed. The fight for the longest possible chain also forces the player to think ahead about the grid, rather than just reacting to the first available connection.

**Why play it:** suitable for puzzle-game fans who also want a sense of long-term progress and character development, not just a repeating round without lasting consequences.

mobil__contre-jour.teaser: A physics puzzle platformer with silhouette visuals and a melancholic atmosphere.
mobil__contre-jour.article:
**Contre Jour** from studio Mokus Games was released in 2011 and is among the mobile games that proved a physics platformer could also be a fully-fledged visual work of art. The player controls a small creature named Petit and, by touching the screen, deforms the terrain itself – stretching and compressing the landscape like a rubber membrane to get him safely past chasms, spikes, and other obstacles to the end of the level.

Controls consist solely of dragging fingers across the screen, changing the shape of the ground beneath and above the character's head, which calls for feel and patience rather than the quick reflexes typical of classic platformers. The puzzles gradually introduce new elements – gravity fields changing the direction of falling, moving platforms reacting to touch, beams of light and shadows – maintaining a smooth difficulty curve from simple early levels to noticeably tougher later chapters.

The visual side rests on silhouette graphics with striking sunsets and soft color gradients between sky and landscape, accompanied by a melancholic ambient soundtrack underscoring the main character's loneliness. This combination creates a contemplative, almost dreamlike atmosphere, placing Contre Jour alongside other art-minded mobile titles of its time, such as the aforementioned Sword & Sworcery. The game was also released on other platforms beyond mobile, but touch controls suit its principle of terrain deformation most naturally.

**Why play it:** recommended for players seeking a calm, aesthetically captivating puzzle platformer rather than fast action or a tough challenge to reflexes and precision.

mobil__final-fantasy-tactics-war-of-lion.teaser: A mobile port of Square Enix's acclaimed tactical RPG classic from the PSP era.
mobil__final-fantasy-tactics-war-of-lion.article:
**Final Fantasy Tactics: The War of the Lions** arrived on mobile platforms in 2011 as a port of an acclaimed tactical RPG classic that Square Enix originally released for the PSP as an expanded version of the legendary title from PlayStation in the nineties. The player commands a group of mercenaries on isometric battlefields divided into a grid, where unit positioning, terrain height differences, and the turn order of individual fighters based on their speed all matter.

Bringing a complex tactical system to a touchscreen was no small challenge – the game offers both touch controls and a virtual D-pad with buttons, though precise unit placement on a phone's relatively small display in particular takes some getting used to and care. The extensive job system with dozens of classes, the elaborate work system for gradually improving characters, and the dark, politically charged story from the fictional kingdom of Ivalice all remain preserved in full in the mobile version, without cuts.

It's one of the most substantial and demanding titles of its time on mobile, aimed more at players willing to invest dozens of hours in careful strategy than those looking for quick entertainment on a commute. The port made this respected game accessible to a new generation of players who never owned a PSP and knew the classic only by reputation. The English localization of War of the Lions also brought a reworked, more literary translation of the dialogue compared to the original PlayStation version, something appreciated even by players familiar with the older game.

**Why play it:** ideal for fans of deep tactical RPGs willing to adapt to touchscreen controls in exchange for one of the best-written strategy games of its era.

mobil__another-world-20th-anniversary-ed.teaser: An anniversary remaster of Eric Chahi's cult cinematic platformer from 1991.
mobil__another-world-20th-anniversary-ed.article:
**Another World: 20th Anniversary Edition** was released in 2012 as an anniversary remaster of a cult cinematic platformer created in 1991 by French author Eric Chahi, which was ahead of its time in the way it told its story. The player takes on the role of scientist Lester Knight Chaykin, transported after an experiment accident into a hostile alien world, where he must survive through careful movement, dodges, and only a few, but well-measured actions.

The mobile version adapts the originally keyboard-based controls to virtual buttons and an on-screen stick, which for a game built on precise timing of jumps, dodges, and shooting requires some patience to get used to, though functionally the controls play surprisingly well. The remaster brings reworked graphics with smoothed vector shapes and more fluid animation, while also offering the option to switch back at any time to the original angular pixel look from the nineties for a direct comparison of both versions.

The game is still valued today for its cinematic storytelling without a single line of text, smooth transitions between individual scenes, and the atmosphere of solitude in a thoroughly hostile environment that defined the entire genre of so-called cinematic platformers at the time. Twenty years after the original, it showed that its minimalist design still holds up on a touchscreen phone. The short playtime and clear structure also make the remaster a suitable introduction for players who want to experience Another World for the first time.

**Why play it:** suitable for players interested in gaming history and atmospheric storytelling, less so for those who don't enjoy mobile controls for action sequences with precise jump timing.

mobil__bard-s-tale.teaser: A humorous action RPG full of self-irony that pokes fun at genre clichés.
mobil__bard-s-tale.article:
**The Bard's Tale** from inXile Entertainment arrived on mobile in 2012 as a port of an action RPG that openly mocks itself and the entire fantasy genre. The player takes on the role of a cynical wandering bard whose only real weapon is a sharp tongue and cunning, moving through a parody fantasy world full of deliberately broken clichés about brave knights, kidnapped princesses, and saving the world from a dark lord.

Combat plays out in real time with simple touch controls — attacks, dodges, and special abilities are triggered by tapping virtual buttons placed around the screen's edges, while a virtual joystick on the left side of the display handles movement. The humor rests mainly on richly voiced narrator and character lines that constantly comment on genre clichés, the player's greed, and the game's own mechanics, which remain among the title's most quoted and funniest moments to this day.

The mobile version is noticeably more modest in scope than the 2004 console and PC original, but it carries over the humor, voice acting, and core gameplay fairly faithfully and without major compromises. It was precisely this self-mocking, at times almost absurd tone that made The Bard's Tale an exception among the earnestly-toned fantasy RPGs of its generation, and that holds true for the mobile port as well. Progress through the game also comes with gradual weapon and ability upgrades, so battles keep changing as the hours add up rather than staying the same throughout.

**Why play it:** recommended for players who enjoy a parody of the fantasy genre and don't mind a somewhat simplified action RPG controlled by touch instead of a classic gamepad.

mobil__draw-something.teaser: Draw and guess with friends; a social hit that Zynga bought at the peak of its fame.
mobil__draw-something.article:
**Draw Something** from OMGPOP studio launched in 2012 and became one of the fastest-growing social hits of the early smartphone era, spreading literally from hand to hand among friends. The premise is simple: one player picks from a choice of words and must draw it with a finger on the touchscreen, while the other player tries to guess what it is, then the roles swap — each round plays out asynchronously between two friends on their phones without needing to play at the same time.

The drawing controls are deliberately limited to a handful of colors and brush thicknesses, so even a complete drawing novice with no talent whatsoever could manage it, and it was precisely those clumsy, often funny attempts to convey the given word that formed the game's main appeal and the material shared among friends and on social media. The game was free to download with ads and the option to buy coins with real money to unlock more colors, which was at the time a still relatively new but rapidly spreading model for such a massively popular game.

The popularity was so meteoric that Zynga bought OMGPOP just weeks after launch for hundreds of millions of dollars — a deal that later turned out to be one of the most discussed in mobile gaming industry history, since player interest in the title dropped off fairly quickly and the acquisition's value never fully paid off.

**Why play it:** the game is no longer actively supported at its original scale, but as a historical reminder of viral social gaming and simple drawing with friends, it still holds its charm.

mobil__spaceteam.teaser: A chaotic party game where you shout nonsensical technical commands at each other.
mobil__spaceteam.article:
**Spaceteam** from independent developer Henry Smith launched in 2012 as a local co-op party game that works best when you're sitting in one room loudly shouting instructions at each other. Each player sees their own control panel on their phone, full of knobs, levers, and sliders, but the commands that appear on screen usually belong to a teammate's panel — the goal is to read the instruction aloud as fast as possible and find whoever at the table has that control, so they can execute it before time runs out.

The controls rely on quickly tapping, dragging, and turning virtual elements scattered across the entire screen, while a relentless time limit ticks down on every command and the spaceship around the players gradually changes shape and color depending on how well or badly the crew is doing during the flight. Chaos, confusion, and loud shouting are a deliberate part of the fun here, not a design flaw or a technical shortcoming of the game.

The game became a beloved example of how mobile phones can serve as a party game for a whole room full of people, not just a device for one player staring at a screen, and it inspired a number of other local party titles using multiple interconnected phones at once. Part of the experience is also the visual state of the growing spaceship, which changes, gets damaged, and changes color as the flight progresses depending on how many mistakes the crew made along the way.

**Why play it:** ideal for a group of friends looking for loud, chaotic fun at a party or celebration, considerably less suited to quiet or solo play.

mobil__hill-climb-racing.teaser: Physics-based 2D racing with a single gas-pedal button; a huge mobile hit with countless clones.
mobil__hill-climb-racing.article:
**Hill Climb Racing** from Finnish studio Fingersoft launched in 2012 and became one of the biggest mobile hits of its generation thanks to its near-artless simplicity of control. The player drives a vehicle across a hilly 2D landscape using just one button for the gas and another for the brake, while a physics model determines how the car tilts in the air, bounces on impacts, and lands on a markedly uneven terrain full of steep hills and deep drops.

The goal is simple — drive as far as possible without crashing on your head or running out of fuel halfway through the course, while the coins earned go toward gradually upgrading the vehicle and unlocking entirely new machines, from a motorbike through an off-road car and a tank all the way to a monster truck. It was precisely the combination of easy-to-grasp controls and surprisingly demanding, unpredictable physics that created an addictive gameplay loop, which spread the game among players worldwide practically without any major marketing.

The success of Hill Climb Racing kicked off an entire wave of similar physics-based racing titles on mobile platforms and brought Fingersoft a direct sequel of its own. The chosen model was free-to-play with ads and the option to buy coins with real money, which was by 2012 already an established but still fairly sensitively received approach to mobile game monetization. Two simple buttons and unpredictable terrain kept the game playable even on the smallest displays and without needing any tutorial.

**Why play it:** suited to anyone wanting undemanding but addictive fun for a few minutes a day, with the understanding that ads and microtransactions are an integral part of the whole experience.

mobil__pou.teaser: A Tamagotchi-style virtual pet that children around the world fell in love with.
mobil__pou.article:
**Pou** from Zakeh studio launched in 2012 as a virtual pet following in the Tamagotchi tradition, just carried over to the touchscreen of a modern smartphone. The player takes care of an alien creature resembling a potato with big eyes — feeding it, bathing it, putting it to sleep, and playing with it through simple minigames, while Pou itself gradually grows, ages, and changes mood depending on how well and regularly it is cared for.

The controls are fully adapted to touch and require no reading at all: feeding happens by dragging food straight into its mouth, washing by dragging a sponge across its whole body, and individual minigames are controlled by simple tapping or tilting the phone from side to side. The simplicity and cute, universally understandable look with no need for text made Pou a hit across age groups and language regions alike, especially among small children and their parents.

The game was free to download with ads and offers of cosmetic add-ons, outfits, or room upgrades for real money, which was by then an already fairly common model for this type of constantly-returned-to virtual pet simulator. Despite its apparent simplicity, Pou maintained a long-term loyal player base thanks to regularly added content and new minigames. The absence of text and its language neutrality also let the game take root practically all over the world without needing localization.

**Why play it:** suited especially to younger players and fans of simple pet simulators who accept ads as a natural part of the free-to-play experience.

mobil__10000000.teaser: A match-3 puzzle combined with a dungeon crawler; one of the first puzzle-RPG hybrids.
mobil__10000000.article:
**10000000** combines turn-based match-3 symbol matching with the progression of a classic dungeon crawler — the player drags a finger across a grid of tiles, forms rows of three or more, and depending on the type of symbols connected, attacks monsters, opens chests, or moves the character down the corridor toward the exit. Each round runs on a short time limit, forcing quick, instinctive decisions rather than long deliberation over moves, while still keeping the clarity of purely touch-based controls.

The game launched in 2012 from small studio EightyEight Games at a time when mobile stores were flooded with countless Bejeweled clones. Instead of merely racking up score, it gave every connected row a concrete in-game consequence — damage to an enemy, an unlocked door, a resource gained for crafting equipment. Between puzzles, the character progresses through a dark tower, collects items, and improves their stats, creating a reward loop that felt unusually elaborate for mobile at the time. Crafting better equipment also ran on real time, one of the earliest hints of how free-to-play mechanics would later creep into the genre.

Visually, **10000000** goes for austere pixel art and a gloomy underground tower setting that contrasts with the puzzle's colorful icons. The game's success showed that combining two established genres could work better on mobile than yet another straight copy of a tabletop classic, and it inspired a later wave of puzzle-RPG hybrids that today form a distinct, well-populated category in mobile stores. The controls stay clear throughout and require no complicated gesture combinations, making the game accessible even to players just starting out with the puzzle genre.

**Why play it:** for players who enjoy match-3 puzzles but also want a sense of progression, equipment, and meaningful decisions alongside them, it offers one of the best-tuned early entries in the puzzle-RPG genre.

mobil__waking-mars.teaser: A gentle exploration platformer about cultivating an alien ecosystem on Mars.
mobil__waking-mars.article:
**Waking Mars** is a gentle exploration platformer in which the player, as a trapped scientist, makes their way through a cave system beneath the surface of Mars, bringing its long-dead ecosystem back to life. The controls are entirely touch-based — the character jumps and glides in gravity lower than Earth's, while tapping plants lets the player harvest seeds, plant them in new spots, and watch how different species of plants and spores react to each other and spread further through the caves.

The game was released in 2012 by Tiger Style, a studio that had already made a name for itself with the earlier game Spider: The Secret of Bryce Manor, and just as with that game, the focus here was mainly on atmosphere and a calm pace rather than combat or time pressure. Instead of enemies, the player faces ecosystem puzzles — figuring out which plants need light, which feed on other organisms, and how to link their chain together so the biosphere sustains itself and opens a path forward. This approach made the game feel more like meditative gardening than action exploration, which was unusual for mobile in 2012.

The visual style combines dark cave shadows with the vivid colors of blooming flora, underscoring the contrast between dead rock and life coming back to it. The music and sound design likewise deepen the sense of loneliness and discovery on an alien planet, even in moments when the game gives the player no specific task and just lets them wander and watch the ecosystem develop on its own. At release, the game was well received by critics, who praised precisely the boldness of building an entire title around a nonviolent cultivation mechanic instead of combat.

**Why play it:** for players seeking a calm, contemplative mobile alternative to action titles who don't mind a slower pace, Waking Mars offers a unique experience of growing alien life.

mobil__hundreds.teaser: A minimalist puzzle where you inflate circles with your finger to sum to 100 without letting them touch.
mobil__hundreds.article:
**Hundreds** is a minimalist puzzle whose rule fits in a single sentence: you touch circles on the screen, they start to inflate, and you must bring their sum to exactly one hundred without letting any two enlarged circles touch each other or hit the edge of the playing field. The slightest slip — holding a finger down a fraction of a second too long, or picking the wrong order — and the round ends in failure, making every level a short but intense exercise in concentration.

The game launched in 2013 from Semi Secret Software and belonged to a wave of mobile puzzle titles that deliberately returned to pure, geometric simplicity instead of colorful characters and story frameworks. As the game progresses, further mechanics are added — circles that move, that need to be kept active longer, or that react to multiple fingers at once — so a surprisingly wide range of puzzles can be built from this simple principle. Multi-finger touch control also makes good use of what touchscreens can do that a mouse and keyboard cannot.

The visual style is deliberately spare — black background, colored circles, minimal text and interface, so all attention goes to the mechanic itself. This cleanliness helped the game stand out in a crowded store full of visually louder titles and also gave it long-lasting appeal, since this kind of minimalism doesn't age the way period-specific graphics do. It's precisely this reduction to a single mechanic without distracting elements that makes Hundreds a title that holds up well even after years, without feeling dated.

**Why play it:** anyone who likes short, elegant puzzles without unnecessary trimmings and wants a game that can be played in short breaks will find exactly that kind of title in Hundreds.

mobil__flappy-bird.teaser: Infamous one-tap difficulty; the creator pulled it from stores at the height of its fame.
mobil__flappy-bird.article:
**Flappy Bird** is a short arcade game with a single control — tapping the screen makes the bird flap its wings and rise a little, otherwise gravity mercilessly pulls it back down. The goal is to fly between pipes reminiscent of Super Mario Bros without touching a single one, and it's the extremely unforgiving timing that turned what looks like a childish game into one of the hardest mobile arcade games ever made.

The game was created in 2013 by a Vietnamese developer under the name dotGears and initially went unnoticed, before becoming a viral phenomenon a year later thanks to shared scores and frustrated player reactions on social media. At the height of its popularity, when the game was earning significant money from ads, the creator himself pulled it from both the App Store and Google Play — stating that the popularity and addictive nature of the game had grown beyond what he was comfortable with and that he didn't want to build on it further. Since then, the original Flappy Bird has officially been unavailable, and the market is flooded only with countless unofficial clones and imitations trying to capture the same feeling of frustration.

Visually, it's deliberately simple pixel art reminiscent of older Nintendo games, which only heightened the contrast between the harmless look and the brutal difficulty. This very contrast — a childish appearance versus frustrating, near-impossible difficulty — became the central theme of countless internet jokes and memes that accompanied the game at the peak of its fame, even more so than the gameplay itself.

**Why play it:** Anyone wanting to experience a legend of mobile gaming has to accept that the original is no longer officially available and is left with clones — but historically, Flappy Bird remains an important reminder of how fast a simple idea can explode and disappear just as quickly.

mobil__badland.teaser: A darkly poetic physics-based platformer; one of the first showcases of Unity graphics on mobile.
mobil__badland.article:
**BADLAND** is a darkly poetic, physics-based platformer in which a furry alien creature flies through a forest full of traps, gears, and hazards, while the player controls its wing-flapping against gravity with a single tap on the screen. The controls stay extremely simple, but the combination of physics, speed, and multiplying copies of the player's own character — the game can multiply the player's character into dozens of simultaneously flying copies — creates surprisingly demanding and chaotic moments where you need to react to narrow gaps and falling boulders within a split second.

The game was released in 2013 by the Finnish studio Frogmind, and at the time of release it was one of the most visible showcases of what the Unity graphics engine was capable of on mobile devices — dense, solid black silhouettes of the characters against a richly textured, almost photorealistic forest background looked unusual on phone displays. The game also offered local multiplayer for up to four players on a single device, either cooperatively or against each other, which was a rarity on mobile at the time.

The atmosphere is completed by an almost wordless, silent story and a dense, dark ambient soundtrack, which makes the game feel more like an art experience than a classic arcade title. BADLAND kept this tone and visual style in its sequel BADLAND 2, which expanded the same principle with new environments and new gameplay elements without abandoning the original simplicity of one-tap controls.

**Why play it:** For players who want a visually striking mobile platformer with atmosphere and undemanding but tense one-finger controls, BADLAND is still worth it today.

mobil__my-talking-tom.teaser: A virtual cat that repeats whatever you say. The founder of the Talking Tom franchise.
mobil__my-talking-tom.article:
**My Talking Tom** is built on a simple but extremely addictive principle — the virtual cat Tom repeats words recorded in your own voice in a comically sped-up or slowed-down form, and the player also has to take care of him like a real pet: feeding him by tapping on food, petting him by swiping a finger across the screen, putting him to bed, or playing with him in small minigames scattered around the apartment.

The game was released in 2013 by the Croatian-Cypriot studio Outfit7 as part of the expanding Talking Tom series, which started as an app without much of a game layer and gradually turned into a full-fledged virtual pet simulator with its own economy of coins and diamonds. The game is free to download but relies on ads between activities and in-app purchases of virtual currency, which can be spent on clothes, furniture for the apartment, or speeding up progress — a model that most similar pet simulators have copied ever since. The huge commercial success of My Talking Tom in particular helped build Outfit7 into one of the largest mobile game studios in the world, and it also became the springboard for the follow-up animated series Talking Tom and Friends.

Simple, colorful graphics and exaggeratedly comic cat animations make the game accessible even to the youngest children, which was the main target audience from the very start.

**Why play it:** Parents of young children looking for harmless entertainment for a few minutes will find the game suitable, but they need to expect ads and pressure toward in-app purchases, which are an almost inseparable part of the experience in this series.

mobil__zombie-tsunami.teaser: An endless runner with an ever-growing horde of zombies that sweeps away everything in its path.
mobil__zombie-tsunami.article:
**Zombie Tsunami** is an endless runner in which the player swipes a finger up and down to make a horde of zombies jump over obstacles, drop into underground tunnels, or collect bonuses, while the horde itself grows with every person it absorbs and rolls through the city like a literal human — or rather undead — tsunami. The bigger the horde, the more destruction it can wreak on buildings and vehicles, giving the game a satisfying sense of growing power.

The game was released in 2013 by the French studio Mobigame, previously known for the title Edge, and Zombie Tsunami quickly became one of the most successful representatives of the endless runner genre on mobile alongside Temple Run and Subway Surfers. Controls using one or two finger swipes are maximally accessible, yet the game gradually adds new environments, special zombie abilities, and coin collecting to unlock them, so a short round can keep you entertained for long minutes. The game is free to download and is monetized through ads along with virtual currency purchases, a model that lets players get by without paying but forces them to accept interruptions.

Colorful, cartoonish graphics and black humor — the game doesn't take the zombie apocalypse theme seriously at all and plays it purely for laughs — give the title a lighthearted atmosphere free of any horror anxiety. Gradually unlocking new zombies with their own abilities also gives the player motivation to keep coming back even after clearing the basic levels.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for an undemanding, humorously toned take on the endless runner genre for quick breaks between other activities will find Zombie Tsunami a reliable choice, albeit with ads as the price for being free.

mobil__trivia-crack.teaser: A trivia wheel of fortune that spread at lightning speed thanks to social sharing.
mobil__trivia-crack.article:
**Trivia Crack** turned the classic quiz into a turn-based party game where players take turns answering questions from six categories, trying to be the first to spin the wheel of fortune and collect all the badges. The principle is simple — tap to choose an answer from four options — but the social dimension, where a player waits for a friend's turn and can have several games going at once through notifications, turned the game into a phenomenon that spread mainly through friends sharing challenges with each other.

The game was released in 2013 by the Argentine studio Etermax and scored especially well in Latin America, from where it quickly spread to the rest of the world and briefly topped download charts worldwide. The game is free but runs on a lives system — after a few wrong answers you have to wait, watch an ad, or buy more attempts and wheel spins with real money, a model that kept the game freely available but at the same time clearly pushes it toward small purchases for impatient players.

Colorful mascots for each category and simple, clear graphics made the game accessible entertainment for a broad audience, not just hardcore gamers. It was precisely the combination of simple rules, short rounds, and easy sharing of results on social media that made it one of the most prominent mobile phenomena of the first half of the decade.

**Why play it:** For people who want a light, social trivia game for taking turns with friends, Trivia Crack still works — you just need to expect the lives system and pressure toward small payments if you want to play without waiting.

mobil__quizup.teaser: A real-time trivia contest against players from around the world on hundreds of topics.
mobil__quizup.article:
**QuizUp** built its identity on a single promise — an instant real-time duel against a random opponent from anywhere in the world on a topic you chose, ranging from movies and history to narrowly focused categories like a specific TV show or sports club. Both sides received the same questions at the same time, and speed as well as accuracy of answers decided the winner, creating a tension that turn-based quizzes like Trivia Crack didn't offer, which made the game feel closer to an online duel than a classic questionnaire.

The game was released in 2013 by the Icelandic studio Plain Vanilla, and shortly after launch it was among the fastest-growing apps ever — helped by the huge selection of topics and the social element of profiles and leaderboards by individual category. Still, the studio failed to find a long-term sustainable business model based only on ads and cosmetic purchases; the game passed to publisher Glu Mobile in 2016, and a few years later the online service was permanently shut down, so today QuizUp no longer works in its original form and can no longer be downloaded or played.

A simple, clean visual style emphasizing large topic photos and a clear interface made the app a very pleasant experience during its heyday even for casual players, who appreciated being able to compete only in topics they genuinely enjoyed instead of a generic, undifferentiated quiz.

**Why play it:** Historically, QuizUp is an interesting reminder of the early era of real-time mobile trivia, but no one can play it today since the service was shut down and the game disappeared from stores.

mobil__dumb-ways-to-die.teaser: A collection of absurd minigames born from a public-safety song about railway safety.
mobil__dumb-ways-to-die.article:
**Dumb Ways to Die** is a collection of lightning-fast minigames in which the player taps, swipes, or tilts the phone within a few seconds to save an adorable little character from an absurdly grotesque death — from sticking a hand into a blender, to jumping onto railway tracks, to pulling stingers out of a hornet. Each minigame lasts only a few seconds, and the pace picks up with each round, so the game works like a reflex test similar to the minigame parades made famous by the WarioWare series.

It was created in 2013 as a companion app to a public-safety campaign by the Australian company Metro Trains Melbourne, whose same-titled viral song about safety around trains and tracks had previously become a worldwide hit thanks to its cute but darkly humorous animation. The game carried this tone over into interactive form and became just as popular as the video itself, even though its original purpose was to remind commuters of basic safety rules around trains. It's free to download and monetized through ads and small purchases of new characters and minigames, but the base content remains playable without paying.

Colorful, round character graphics and a catchy jingle make the game accessible entertainment for all age groups, even though it's secretly a safety campaign funded by a transit company rather than a classic game publisher.

**Why play it:** Anyone looking for a short, funny reflex-based game for a few minutes and who doesn't mind dark humor will appreciate Dumb Ways to Die as a great example of how even a public-safety campaign can be turned into a genuinely fun game.

mobil__injustice-gods-among-us.teaser: A superhero card-collecting game with turn-based fights; the mobile spinoff of NetherRealm's console brawler.
mobil__injustice-gods-among-us.article:
**Injustice: Gods Among Us** brought the world of the same-named console fighting game by NetherRealm Studios to mobile, but instead of direct button-based fight controls it relied on collecting cards of DC Comics characters and deploying them in fast, largely automated battles, where the player triggers special attacks with a tap and watches the outcome of the animated clash. Cards are obtained in packs for both in-game and real currency and can be upgraded and combined into stronger versions, placing the game among the early mobile card-collecting fighters with gacha mechanic elements.

The game was released in 2013 by NetherRealm Studios as a companion app to the console game Injustice: Gods Among Us, and it also functioned as a promotional tool — unlocking certain characters and rewards in the mobile version could be linked to the console title. The game is free to download but runs on an energy system limiting the number of fights per time period and on purchasing card packs with real money, making it a typical example of the free-to-play model, where progress without paying is possible but noticeably slower.

The graphics use the same 3D character models as the console version, so visually the game looks better than one would expect from a mobile title of that era, even though the fights themselves are simplified down to a few taps.

**Why play it:** Fans of DC Comics characters will enjoy collecting their favorite heroes and villains, but anyone expecting a full-fledged fight like on console will be disappointed by the simplified, tap-based controls and the pressure to purchase card packs.

mobil__pixel-gun-3d.teaser: A blocky Minecraft-style shooter with multiplayer and an endless supply of weapons and skins.
mobil__pixel-gun-3d.article:
**Pixel Gun 3D** brings the blocky, Minecraft-style aesthetic into the first-person shooter genre — the player moves with a virtual analog joystick on one side of the screen and aims and shoots with the other finger on the other side, a solution that became the standard for touchscreen FPS games. The game offers both a singleplayer campaign against zombies and other enemies, and online multiplayer in arenas for multiple players at once.

The game was released in 2013 by studio Cubic Games and from the start relied on a huge selection of weapons, skins, and cosmetic add-ons that let players customize their character and gear — from classic rifles to fantasy laser weapons to costumes inspired by pop culture. The game is free to download, but a large part of the content, especially the more striking weapons and skins, is locked behind in-game currency that can be earned slowly by playing or bought quickly through in-app purchases — a model that has kept the game among the highest-grossing mobile shooters for years. Over the years, new game modes, maps, and seasonal content were added, so the game functions more like a live service than a closed title.

The visual style remains true to its blocky aesthetic, but the animations and effects gradually received more modern treatment than one would expect from a 2013 game, which helped the title keep its player base even a decade later.

**Why play it:** For players who want a Minecraft-style multiplayer shooter on mobile and don't mind gradually unlocking content with in-game currency or small purchases, Pixel Gun 3D offers a solid, long-term updated choice.

mobil__township.teaser: A farm-and-city-building combo from Playrix; harvest crops and build your own metropolis.
mobil__township.article:
**Township** combines two popular mobile schemes into one working whole — the farming loop of harvesting and processing crops with building and expanding a city. The player taps to harvest fields, drags a finger to build houses, factories, and later mines or a zoo, and switches between the game's various layers (farm, production, trade, train transport to other regions) with a single gesture. The controls are designed purely for touchscreens — no menu is more complicated than dragging an icon with a finger — which made Township accessible from the start even to people who, on a smartphone, had previously played little more than solitaire.

Playrix released the game in 2013, at a time when the genre of Facebook farming simulations was already fading and publishers were looking for ways to bring the same gameplay to a pocket device. Unlike pure farming games, Township added a second layer — genuine city building with residents, public buildings, and the gradual unlocking of new areas — earning it its own place alongside competing titles. The game is free-to-play with an energy system and a premium currency for speeding up construction, but the main loop can be played without paying, just more slowly.

Its long lifespan is one of the main reasons Township is still talked about — Playrix has expanded the game for years with new content, seasonal events, and game mechanics, so today's version is substantially richer than the one from 2013. The combination of a relaxed pace, clear graphics, and the gradual unlocking of new layers of gameplay also made it a title favored by players outside the traditional audience for mobile simulators, and Playrix later built its other titles in the same style on this success.

**Why play it:** Township suits players who want an easygoing building loop for a few minutes a day and don't mind that faster progress is tied to purchases or waiting.

mobil__deus-ex-fall.teaser: A mobile sequel to the cyberpunk Human Revolution; stealth action shrunk into your pocket.
mobil__deus-ex-fall.article:
**Deus Ex: The Fall** brings the cyberpunk world of Human Revolution to the touchscreen and tries to preserve the core of the gameplay — the choice between a silent playthrough, hacking, and direct confrontation. The controls rely on a virtual joystick and contextual buttons for cover, hacking terminals, and using weapons, a compromise that works better in the slower stealth sections than in firefights. The player takes on the role of mercenary Ben Saunier and moves through smaller, enclosed locations whose atmosphere and visual style — neon streets, augmentations, corporate darkness — clearly reference the larger console/PC installment.

The game came out in 2013 as a paid title, but later built in microtransactions for the in-game currency needed to upgrade augmentations, which drew criticism from both players and reviewers — the game's pacing sometimes felt designed to make the payments make sense. The story also isn't self-contained and ends mid-plot with a reference to a sequel that was never released, so the experience remains permanently unfinished.

Even with these caveats, it's one of the more ambitious attempts to bring a large action RPG series to mobile without changing the genre into a simpler arcade experience, and for Deus Ex fans it remains an interesting detour thanks to a visual quality that wasn't a given on mobile devices at the time. The sound design, voice acting, and overall production level also matched a console game more than a typical mobile title of its day, which visibly set the game apart from its surrounding competition.

**Why play it:** Fans of Human Revolution who want to sample the same atmosphere on the go will appreciate it, but should expect a cut-off ending to the story and microtransactions for augmentations.

mobil__8-ball-pool.teaser: A multiplayer pool game that turned mobile into a virtual pool hall with token tournaments.
mobil__8-ball-pool.article:
**8 Ball Pool** turned billiards into a social multiplayer game that can be started anytime against a random opponent or a friend. The controls are simple — dragging a finger sets the power and direction of the shot, another gesture applies spin to the ball — and this very simplicity let the game work equally well on a small phone and on a tablet. Instead of a single game mode, Miniclip offers leaderboards, tournaments with stakes, and the gradual unlocking of fancier pool tables, turning the virtual pool hall into a genuine ecosystem with seasonal events.

The game came out in 2013 and quickly became one of the most-played sports titles on mobile, partly because it combines a low entry barrier (almost everyone knows the rules of pool) with enough depth for players who want to practice shot precision. The game's economy is built on in-game currency and tournament tokens, which can be both earned by playing and bought with real money — a classic free-to-play model with optional payments.

The long-term popularity of 8 Ball Pool showed that even such an old-fashioned sport as billiards can work as a live service with a community, clans, and regular updates, which was a less common approach for mobile sports games at the time. The social dimension — the ability to challenge a specific friend, compare leaderboards, or follow other people's matches — keeps the game alive even for players who otherwise don't follow billiards.

**Why play it:** A good choice for anyone who wants quick matches against real opponents without having to learn complicated controls, though be prepared for pressure to spend on tournament tokens.

mobil__leo-s-fortune.teaser: A visually gorgeous platformer about a fox searching for stolen gold; fairy-tale style.
mobil__leo-s-fortune.article:
**Leo's Fortune** is a platformer built on the contrast between a fairy-tale, hand-painted world and surprisingly demanding jumping sections. The touchscreen controls use virtual arrows or device tilt and a single action button for jumping, with the core mechanic being the inflation and deflation of the round fox-like character, which controls the height of the jump and the fall. The level design alternates classic jumping with puzzle sections that use physics and destructible environments, so the game never feels like a simple coin collector but rather like a well thought-out platforming whole.

It was released in 2014 by the small studio 1337 & Senri and quickly drew attention mainly for its visual side — a softly shaded, storybook-styled world with striking colors was among the most beautiful things to appear on mobile at the time, and the game won awards at gaming ceremonies for it. It's a paid title without ads or microtransactions, which was not entirely typical for a mobile platformer at the time and reinforced the impression of a premium product.

The story about a fox searching for stolen gold is simple, but it mainly serves as an excuse to connect the various, visually distinct worlds the player progresses through. The short but dense playtime and well-paced difficulty also mean the game never feels artificially padded just to extend its length.

**Why play it:** Ideal for platformer fans who want a compact experience without extra payments and who appreciate the artistic side as much as precise jump controls.

mobil__best-fiends.teaser: A match-3 puzzle with an army of cute bugs; an easygoing puzzle with distinctive characters.
mobil__best-fiends.article:
**Best Fiends** is a match-3 puzzle game that wraps its puzzle skeleton in distinctive, cute bug characters and a light story framework about defending a garden from an army of ants. The controls involve dragging a finger between neighboring tiles and matching the same colors into rows, while gradually adding special abilities of the collected characters, which can be upgraded and combined into a team. The level design keeps adding new rules and obstacles, so even after dozens of levels the game never feels stale.

Seriously released the game in 2014 and built it from the start on a standard free-to-play model with an energy system that limits how many levels can be played in a row, along with common microtransactions for speeding up collecting and upgrading characters. The distinctive visual style and cute characters helped the game stand out from a flood of similar puzzle titles and find a loyal community of players who appreciated the atmosphere more than puzzle difficulty.

Best Fiends grew into spin-off titles in the following years and remains actively maintained, which isn't entirely common for a puzzle game from 2014. The studio gradually added new characters, environments, and story chapters, so the game still feels like a living, continually updated product rather than a long-abandoned title.

**Why play it:** Good for players looking for an easygoing match-3 with pleasant graphics for short sessions, keeping in mind that energy limits and time-limited events push toward occasional payments.

mobil__wayward-souls.teaser: A Rocketcat Games roguelike dungeon crawler; permadeath and several distinctly playable classes.
mobil__wayward-souls.article:
**Wayward Souls** is a roguelike action game from Rocketcat Games that offers a surprisingly elaborate combat system on a small screen, with several characters that play quite differently — a knight, a thief, a mage, and others. The controls rely on a virtual joystick for movement and a set of buttons for attacking, dodging, and special abilities, with the game designed to work even without physical buttons, which was no small feat for an action roguelike on mobile at the time. Each run through the dungeon is procedurally generated, and death means returning to the start, so the game is built mainly around mastering combat and gradually improving player skill.

It was released in 2014 as a direct successor to the studio's earlier titles (Mage Gauntlet, Punch Quest) and is a one-time paid game without ads or microtransactions — a model on which Rocketcat Games built its long-term reputation as an independent studio focused on control quality. This emphasis on making sure the touch controls of an action game never feel like a compromise is part of what earned the game recognition from reviewers and players who prefer more demanding titles.

Permadeath and unlockable characters give the game solid replayability despite being a smaller, focused project without ambitions to be a long-term live service. Each character also offers its own playstyle and its own storyline, so repeated runs through the dungeon never feel entirely the same.

**Why play it:** Suits players who want a genuinely demanding action game on mobile with honest controls and don't mind repeated deaths as part of the progress.

mobil__toy-blast.teaser: A match-3 puzzle where colorful toys pop instead of gems, chaining bonuses together.
mobil__toy-blast.article:
**Toy Blast** belongs to the family of puzzle games where, instead of classically swapping tiles, you tap groups of same-colored blocks, which then disappear and trigger a chain reaction of bonuses. The controls are purely touch-based and built around a single gesture — tapping — which makes the game accessible even to complete newcomers to the genre, while deeper strategy comes from planning which bonus to trigger when and how to meet the level's limited goals, such as knocking down a certain number of specific toys. Visually, the game relies on a colorful, toy-like world that works well on small displays.

Peak Games released the title in 2015 and built it from the start on a free-to-play model with lives that refill over time or can be bought, along with the usual microtransactions for power-ups and progress. Toy Blast still retains a large player base even a decade later, placing it among the most successfully long-running mobile puzzle titles ever, and the studio continues to expand it with hundreds of new levels and seasonal events.

The similarity to the later sister title Toon Blast is no coincidence — both games share a similar game skeleton, just with a different visual wrapper, and Peak Games effectively became one of the most successful puzzle publishers on mobile. Regular daily rewards and short, clearly bounded levels also make the game a typical example of a title built for day-to-day player retention.

**Why play it:** A good choice for fans of simple puzzles for short moments between other activities, although long-term progress without paying tends to be slow due to limited lives.

mobil__agar-io.teaser: A browser hit brought to mobile; devour smaller cells and grow, or be devoured yourself.
mobil__agar-io.article:
**Agar.io** brought to mobile the principle that made it famous in web browsers – the player controls a cell, moves around the map by dragging a finger or using a virtual joystick, and tries to devour smaller cells while avoiding larger opponents. The simplicity of the rules – no story, no levels, just real-time growth and survival against other players – made it an ideal candidate for a pocket-sized transfer, since the entire gameplay fits onto a single touch surface without the need for a complex menu.

The game was originally created by developer Matheus Valadares, who brought it to mobile platforms in 2015, where it quickly rode the wave of popularity that Agar.io had earned on YouTube and Twitch as a widely watched multiplayer phenomenon. The mobile version runs on a free-to-play model with ads between matches and microtransactions for cosmetic cell skins, though money doesn't affect the gameplay itself.

It was precisely this type of game – a massively multiplayer arena with minimalist rules – that, after Agar.io, inspired an entire wave of similar ".io" titles, though the mobile version of the classic remains one of the genre's best-known representatives. The absence of any tutorial or complex menu also means you can jump into the game literally within a few seconds of opening the app.

**Why play:** Good for moments when you want a quick, uncomplicated match against live opponents without having to learn anything extra, though the ads between rounds need to be accepted as part of the package.

mobil__prune.teaser: A meditative puzzle about pruning a tree toward the light; minimalism from an ex-Apple designer.
mobil__prune.article:
**Prune** is a meditative puzzle in which the player, with a single swipe of a finger, prunes the branches of a growing tree to guide it toward the light and help it bloom. The controls are reduced to the bare minimum – no buttons, no menu during play, just a swipe gesture across the screen that trims unwanted branches and opens up space for new growth – and this simplicity is the foundation of the entire experience. The visual style is as austere as the controls: black silhouettes of trees against a single-color background that changes as the game progresses, completing the atmosphere of each level.

The game was created in 2015 by Joel McDonald, who had previously worked as a designer inside Apple, which shows in the thoughtful minimalist presentation and in how precisely the game doles out new mechanics. It's a one-time paid app with no ads or microtransactions, conceived more as a short contemplative experience than a game meant for dozens of hours – Prune can be finished in a matter of a few hours, but leaves a strong visual impression.

It's precisely the combination of game mechanics with visual artistry that made Prune a frequently cited example of how even a minimalist mobile title can come across as a work of art, not just a time-killer. The absence of text and language barriers also means the game works just as clearly for players anywhere in the world.

**Why play:** Recommended for players looking for a short, calm, aesthetically strong experience rather than a challenge – it's a paid game without aggressive monetization, but also without a long playtime.

mobil__lumino-city.teaser: A hand-crafted paper town photographed as a scene; a loose sequel to Lume.
mobil__lumino-city.article:
**Lumino City** is an adventure game built on a unique production technique – the entire game environment, buildings, mechanisms, and characters are hand-made from paper, cardboard, and wood and then photographed, so the player moves through a real, tangible miniature city instead of digital 3D graphics. The controls are simple touch point-and-click: tapping moves the camera and interacts with objects, while the main content of the game is logic puzzles based on mechanical devices – pulleys, elevators, gears – scattered throughout the city.

State of Play released the game in 2015 as a loose sequel to the earlier title Lume, continuing the same approach: the story about searching for a kidnapped grandfather serves mainly as a pretext for exploring the city's individual districts and solving their puzzles. It's a one-time paid game with no ads, which fits its character as a self-contained authorial work rather than a live service with long-term content.

The hand-made environment set the game apart from the vast majority of both mobile and console competition and earned it awards for its visual side, even though the puzzles themselves are rather classic and undemanding. The sound design and overall atmosphere of the city feel more like a stroll through a cozy, slightly melancholic place than a classic logic challenge.

**Why play:** Will appeal to players who appreciate an original visual technique and a calmer adventure pace more than puzzle difficulty; it's also a compact paid title with no need for further spending.

mobil__mortal-kombat-x.teaser: A card-based fighting game tying in with the console entry; iconic killers in collectible form.
mobil__mortal-kombat-x.article:
**Mortal Kombat X** on mobile is not a direct port of the console fighting game, but a standalone card game that turns the series' iconic killers – Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden, and others – into collectible cards grouped into teams. Fights play out semi-automatically: the player triggers attacks and characters' special abilities by tapping, while deeper strategy comes from choosing a lineup, upgrading cards, and their faction composition, not from classic manual combos like on console.

The game was released in 2015 by NetherRealm Studios alongside the big console entry and also worked as its promotional companion – players could unlock characters tied to the console version and follow the same story framework from a different angle. The model is free-to-play with an energy system, collecting cards from packs similar to gacha, and microtransactions to speed up progress, which is fairly typical for mobile fighting games derived from big brands.

Transferring the series' brutal aesthetic and fatalities into a card format was, at the time, an unusual experiment that showed big fighting franchises can be adapted to mobile even outside the classic one-on-one genre. Regularly adding new cards tied to the console game's current content also kept players in the loop between the series' major releases.

**Why play:** Will appeal more to fans of the Mortal Kombat brand than to players looking for a classic fighting game; they should expect progress to depend heavily on collecting cards and waiting times.

mobil__marvel-future-fight.teaser: An action RPG about collecting Marvel heroes into a team; a huge roster of characters from comics and films.
mobil__marvel-future-fight.article:
**Marvel Future Fight** is an action RPG in which the player assembles teams from an extensive roster of Marvel heroes and villains and sends them into real-time battles on the touchscreen. The controls combine a virtual joystick for movement with buttons for basic attacks and each character's special abilities, while the depth of the game lies mainly in collecting, upgrading, and combining heroes into functional lineups, not in the technical difficulty of the battles themselves.

Netmarble released the game in 2015 and built it on a gacha model – new heroes and gear are obtained mainly through random draws from packs, which can be bought with real money or slowly earned by playing, and the game has long been among the highest-grossing mobile titles ever thanks to the huge amount of licensed content from comics and films. The roster of playable characters has grown over the years to hundreds of names across the entire Marvel universe, turning the game into a practically endlessly expandable collecting project.

It's precisely the breadth of the license and the regular tie-ins with current films that keep the game alive even ten years after release, even though new heroes come accompanied by increasingly aggressive gacha mechanics. For fans of the comic universe, it's also appealing that characters from completely different corners of Marvel mythology can meet on a single team.

**Why play:** Good for Marvel fans who want to collect favorite characters into a team, but they should expect gacha monetization where full progress without paying takes considerably longer.

mobil__hitman-sniper.teaser: A sniper puzzle from the creators of Hitman GO; precise hits and clever chain combos.
mobil__hitman-sniper.article:
**Hitman Sniper** builds on the proven principle of previous mobile titles from Square Enix Montréal – the game is derived from the Hitman GO mini-series, but instead of turn-based strategy on a board-like layout, it offers pure sniper action from a fixed position. The player watches the scene through a rifle scope, tracks the movement of guards and civilians, and looks for the moment when a hit won't raise the alarm. The controls are adapted for the touchscreen – aiming with a finger across the display, zooming with a drag, and a single tap to fire – and work surprisingly precisely even without physical buttons, although the game is played exclusively in landscape orientation.

The game's charm lies in chain combos: taking out multiple targets in a single instant, detonating a barrel of explosives so it takes out further enemies, or dropping a chandelier onto a passing guard's head. Each level can be finished within a few minutes, but replaying for a higher score and to fulfill bonus conditions gives the game a lifespan far beyond its short story – leaderboards and unlockable weapons motivate you to return even to levels you completed long ago. Visually, it's austere, stylized graphics that emphasize the scene's readability over detail, which ultimately benefits the game – the player focuses on tactics, not on the surrounding scenery.

The game is paid with optional microtransactions for weapons and upgrades, which at the time was more of an exception in a genre of mobile shooters dominated by ads. It's still available for download today, though publisher support has gradually faded and no new content has been added for a long time.

**Why play:** Ideal for players who want short, well-thought-out pocket sniper puzzles without the aggressive monetization typical of free-to-play competitors.

mobil__grand-theft-auto-liberty-city-sto.teaser: A mobile port of a 2005 PSP original; a prequel to GTA III set in Liberty City.
mobil__grand-theft-auto-liberty-city-sto.article:
**Grand Theft Auto: Liberty City Stories** arrived on mobile phones as a port of a game already ten years old from the PlayStation Portable, and this shows at every turn – it's a full-fledged open-world title with cars, weapons, missions, and an overview of mafia factions of a kind that didn't commonly make it onto touchscreens in 2015. The player takes on the role of Tony Cipriani and goes through a story that chronologically precedes the events of GTA III, including a return to the well-known Liberty City in its older, more densely populated form, with its own set of locations and characters.

The controls were reworked for touch devices – a virtual joystick for movement and buttons for shooting and entering vehicles are placed around the edges of the screen and can even be adjusted to finger size and the player's habits. Playing with support for a physical controller is also possible, which brings the game closer to a console experience than a mobile pastime for a few minutes between other activities. Transferring such an extensive world into a smaller format naturally brings compromises – textures are simplified and object pop-in is more noticeable than on the PSP, but the actual feel of driving, shooting, and completing missions remains functional and enjoyable to play.

The game is paid, with no ads and no microtransactions, which places it among the more honest mobile ports of big brands – compared to later titles in the series, it relies on a one-time payment instead of a free-to-play model with add-on purchases.

**Why play:** Fans of the series will appreciate a complete GTA experience with clear touch controls for a one-time price without aggressive microtransactions.

mobil__coin-master.teaser: Slot spinning combined with village building; spread virally through friend invites.
mobil__coin-master.article:
**Coin Master** is among the most successful free-to-play titles of its generation, even though its core mechanic is surprisingly simple – the player spins a virtual slot machine that yields coins, attacks on other players' villages, or shields to protect their own base. The coins earned are then invested into building and upgrading one's own village, so the game combines the randomness of a slot machine with the sense of gradual growth familiar to players of building simulations, and regularly offers new themed maps as motivation to keep progressing.

Viral social spread played a crucial role in the game's success – a system of rewards for inviting friends and integration with social networks allowed Coin Master to grow at a rate that outpaced most of its contemporary competition. The controls are purely touch-based and reduced to the bare minimum of tapping and dragging, so anyone can handle the game regardless of gaming experience, which was one of the keys to its mass reach across age groups and beyond the traditional circle of mobile gamers.

Monetization is aggressive and built on buying spins and coins, an energy system limiting the number of free moves available, and regular event campaigns pushing players to spend. The game still runs on regular updates with new themed maps to this day, but the economy is clearly designed so that paying players progress considerably faster than those who play for free.

**Why play:** Suitable for players looking for undemanding, socially connected fun for a few minutes a day, but you need to expect pressure to spend for faster progress.

mobil__slither-io.teaser: A snake-shaped answer to Agar.io; grow by eating glowing pellets and avoid collisions.
mobil__slither-io.article:
**Slither.io** arrived on mobile as a response to the browser hit Agar.io of the time, with which it shares the core principle – the player controls a gradually growing creature on a shared online map full of other real players. Instead of a cell you control a snake that collects glowing pellets, lengthens, and tries to make opponents crash into its body, while it must itself avoid the same fate and watch both its own tail and the surrounding players at once.

Touchscreen controls are based on a simple drag principle – the snake heads wherever your finger points, while a second tap triggers a short speed burst at the cost of body length. This simplicity is also the game's main strength: it needs no tutorial, works on older hardware and slower connections, and a match lasts exactly as long as the player manages to survive among dozens of other snakes on the same map. The atmosphere is deliberately minimalist, the colorful map on a dark background serves purely for orientation, no graphical showiness has a place here, so the player's attention stays where it belongs – on movement and tactics.

The game is free-to-play with ads and cosmetic add-ons for purchase, without any real pay-to-win element affecting the actual gameplay. It was precisely this undemanding monetization combined with simple rules that helped the title keep its player base for years after the initial wave of popularity around .io games.

**Why play it:** A great choice for quick sessions between other tasks – you'll grasp the rules in a few seconds, and the ads are more of a minor toll than an obstacle.

mobil__her-story.teaser: A detective game searching a video-clip archive; keywords piece together a murder story.
mobil__her-story.article:
**Her Story** is one of the most distinctive adventure games of its time – instead of a classic dialogue tree or moving through locations, the player searches a large archive of short video clips from police interviews, with the only tool being a search field. By entering keywords, the player gradually uncovers fragments of testimony from a woman suspected in her husband's disappearance and pieces together for themselves what actually happened – the game never offers a linear sequence of events, only fragments from which the player must assemble the story themselves, with the order in which clips are discovered differing from playthrough to playthrough.

On a touchscreen the controls work surprisingly naturally – typing keywords on the virtual keyboard and tapping search results mirrors the experience of the computer version without any change to how the game is approached. Author Sam Barlow proved with this format that an adventure game doesn't have to rest on an inventory and item puzzles, but can work purely as a detective puzzle about human memory and language. The acting performance in the recorded footage carries the entire atmosphere of the game and gives it an unusual rawness for a mobile title.

It's a one-time paid game with no ads or microtransactions, completable in one to two longer sessions. After release it received exceptionally positive critical acclaim and became a frequently cited example of how well a purely narrative experience can work on mobile.

**Why play it:** For players looking for a thoughtful detective story without action and without free-to-play elements – all it takes is patience and a willingness to piece the fragments together yourself.

mobil__lords-mobile.teaser: A kingdom-building strategy game with real PvP and alliances of players from around the world.
mobil__lords-mobile.article:
**Lords Mobile** belongs to the family of mobile kingdom-building strategy games that dominated ad space on social networks and beyond in the mid-2010s. The player manages their own castle, mines resources, builds an army, and gradually joins a larger world full of other real players, with whom they can form alliances or, conversely, wage open conflicts over territory, heroes, and resources.

Controls are adapted to the touchscreen through a clear map and menus – most decisions happen outside of direct action, in the form of planning buildings, research, and troop movements that continue even in the background when the player doesn't have the app open. This model allows the game to be played in waves of short checks several times a day, making it more of a long-term commitment than a title for a single sitting. The social dimension of the game – guilds, alliances, and rivalry between servers – is one of its main draws and sets it apart from purely single-player strategy games, where the player competes only against the computer.
