Monetization is built on a free-to-play model with a strong offering of speed-ups, special units, and subscription packages, so paying players advance noticeably faster than those who invest only time. The game still runs on regular updates, new heroes, and seasonal events, and remains among the longest-running, highest-grossing mobile strategy games ever.

**Why play it:** Suitable for players fond of long-term building and social strategy, who accept that faster progress often calls for payment.

mobil__gardenscapes.teaser: Match-3 combined with garden renovation; the game that kickstarted the whole genre.
mobil__gardenscapes.article:
**Gardenscapes** combined two previously separate mobile traditions – match-3 puzzles and gradual building or beautifying of a space – into one whole that became the template for the entire later genre. The player goes through levels matching identical symbols on the board, and the stars or coins earned are then invested into renovating a neglected garden around an old mansion, cared for by a narrator named Austin, with every decoration decision permanently changing the garden's appearance.

It's precisely the linking of two loops – puzzle and building – that gives the game motivation to keep going, even though the match-3 levels themselves are often simpler than in dedicated puzzle games. Touch controls are maximally intuitive, dragging a finger across the board to connect symbols can be managed by anyone without training. Visually the game builds on a warm, fairy-tale-like aesthetic with a gradually transforming garden that visibly shows the player where their effort is heading, which was an unusually strong motivational element at the time of release.

The game is free-to-play with an energy system limiting the number of attempts and microtransactions to top up lives or special booster items that ease harder levels. Playrix later built an entire series of similar titles on Gardenscapes' success, and the model combining puzzle and renovation became one of the most copied in the entire mobile gaming industry.

**Why play it:** Ideal for casual players who want a relaxing puzzle with visible progress, keeping in mind that the energy system eventually pushes toward spending for faster progress.

mobil__crashlands.teaser: A crafting action RPG full of humor and surprisingly deep character gear.
mobil__crashlands.article:
**Crashlands** took the proven crafting formula of survival and base-building and brought it to the touchscreen with controls designed directly for fingers, not as a compromise port. The player character Flux Dabes crash-lands on an unknown planet, where she must gather resources, craft tools and weapons, and gradually work her way through a story full of absurd humor and distinctive dialogue that sets the game apart from most similarly themed titles on the market.

The combat system combines real-time dodging and attacking with a fairly deep gear system – weapons and armor can be combined and upgraded, giving the game surprising depth for a mobile title. Controls are handled by a virtual joystick for movement and buttons for actions positioned so they don't cover the action on screen, and it works just as well on a small phone as on a tablet. The visual style, with bold colors and exaggerated character proportions, gives the game a fairy-tale lightness that contrasts with the fairly demanding crafting system underneath.

It's a one-time paid game with no ads, which was rather the exception among mobile RPGs in its release year. With this approach, Butterscotch Shenanigans built a reputation as a studio that relies on honest content rather than monetization, and the game remains a celebrated example of how a full-fledged RPG can work on mobile without a single paid upgrade offer.

**Why play it:** For players craving a deep crafting RPG with humor, with no worries about ads or pressure toward microtransactions.

mobil__titan-quest.teaser: A well-made mobile port of the classic 2006 action RPG.
mobil__titan-quest.article:
**Titan Quest** brought to mobile phones one of the most distinctive action RPGs of the mid-2000s, which in its day rivaled Diablo with its own take on mythology and an extensive system of hero classes. The player travels through an ancient world inspired by Greek, Egyptian, and other mythologies, wipes out crowds of enemies, and gradually combines two skill trees into their own unique character build according to their own playstyle.

HandyGames handled the transfer to the touchscreen with a virtual joystick for movement and buttons for skills, supplemented by an auto-attack option by tapping an enemy, which makes longer play sessions on a small display easier. The scope of the original game – including expansions and gear management mechanics – has been preserved almost unchanged, which makes the mobile version a full-fledged replacement for the computer original rather than just a stripped-down variant. The graphics were slightly adjusted for smaller screens compared to 2006, but the basic atmosphere of ancient landscapes, temples, and the underworld remains untouched.

The game is a one-time paid purchase with no ads or microtransactions, placing it among the more honest mobile ports of major computer titles. Thanks to its large amount of content, saveable progress, and solid controls, it remains among the recommended choices for players looking for a genuine action RPG in their pocket.

**Why play it:** A great choice for fans of Diablo-like games who want an extensive action RPG with dozens of hours of content for a one-time price.

mobil__baldur-s-gate-ii-enhanced-edition.teaser: The legendary CRPG from 2000, finally in your pocket; one of the best games of the genre.
mobil__baldur-s-gate-ii-enhanced-edition.article:
**Baldur's Gate II: Enhanced Edition** brought to touchscreens one of the most acclaimed RPGs in the history of computer gaming, originally released in 2000. Beamdog prepared an enhanced version with bug fixes, expanded content, and an adjusted interface that tries to preserve the depth of a classic isometric RPG even on a screen significantly smaller than the one it was originally designed for, including the entire branching campaign and companions to recruit.

Touch controls are handled by a combination of tapping for movement and target selection with context menus for party commands; a complete interface overhaul was necessary due to the originally very dense layout of controls on a computer screen. The result is functional, though it requires patience – this is a game with pausable real-time combat, an extensive inventory, and dozens of hours of dialogue, which places greater demands on orientation on a small display than action titles do. That's precisely why a tablet or a connected physical keyboard and mouse are often recommended for playing today.

It's a one-time paid game with no ads, with a price matching the scope of the content rather than typical mobile titles. Baldur's Gate II is still considered one of the best RPGs ever, and the mobile version allows access to this legacy even without a computer, albeit with controls that take some getting used to.

**Why play it:** For players willing to invest time in a deep classic RPG with a rich story, ideally on a tablet or with a keyboard connected for clarity.

mobil__fifa-mobile.teaser: A lightweight free-to-play football series from EA adapted for phones.
mobil__fifa-mobile.article:
**FIFA Mobile** brought Electronic Arts' football license to phones in a lightweight form, adapted for shorter play sessions than the full console entries in the series. The player builds a team from cards of favorite players, manages matches with simplified controls, and gradually upgrades the squad through seasonal events and competitions against other players online worldwide.

The matches themselves work on a principle of simplified touch controls – dragging a finger determines the direction of a pass or shot, while a large part of the tactical decisions happens automatically, which makes the game accessible even to players without experience with classic football simulations. This compromise between depth and accessibility is also what sets the mobile version apart from console FIFA – it's more of a collectible card game with a football overlay than a simulation of the sport itself. Regular season updates and ties to real football competitions keep the game in line with current events on the pitch, including period-accurate lineups and player transfers.

Monetization is free-to-play with player card packs, season passes, and microtransactions that noticeably speed up building a strong team. The game has been substantially reworked several times over the years, and the older 2016 version differs from the current offering, though the core model based on collecting and upgrading cards has stayed the same.

**Why play it:** Suitable for football fans who want to collect favorite players and play quick matches, keeping in mind that competing at the top usually requires payment.

mobil__honkai-impact-3rd.teaser: Action RPG from miHoYo that foreshadowed the later success of Genshin Impact.
mobil__honkai-impact-3rd.article:
**Honkai Impact 3rd** introduced in 2016 the visual style and approach to action RPGs that the studio miHoYo later developed into the much more famous Genshin Impact. The player controls a group of heroines fighting against a mysterious entity called Honkai, moving through anime-styled environments and combining fast attacks, dodges, and each character's special abilities in clearly structured missions and story chapters.

Touchscreen controls rely on a virtual joystick for movement and buttons for attacks and abilities; combat is fast and visually impressive, with an emphasis on fluid combo chains and switching between characters in the team. The visual presentation, with its striking anime character designs and elaborate combat animations, was among the best mobile action RPGs had to offer at the time of release, and thanks to this the game quickly built a loyal player base even outside Asian markets.

It is a gacha title – characters and their upgrades are obtained through random draws paid for with in-game or real currency, a model players should be aware of before deciding whether to try the game. The free-to-play core of the game is playable without spending money, but obtaining stronger characters without paying requires significantly more patience. Honkai Impact 3rd remains an actively supported title with regular content updates.

**Why play it:** For fans of anime action RPGs and gacha systems who accept that fully unlocking favorite characters comes with patience or payment.

mobil__homescapes.teaser: Another match-3 home-renovation game from Playrix; sibling of Gardenscapes.
mobil__homescapes.article:
**Homescapes** builds on the proven engine of Gardenscapes, just swapping the garden for an old family house that needs to be gradually repaired and furnished. The player goes through match-3 levels where swiping combines colored tokens into triples and higher combinations, and the money earned is then spent on renovating individual rooms – wallpaper, furniture, floors, small decorations. A light comic-style story unfolds between rounds about the butler Austin and his family trying to save the family estate, and this narrative framework gives meaning to what would otherwise be a purely mechanical matching of tokens, motivating the player to progress from room to room.

Playrix chose the same recipe that worked for its garden predecessor Gardenscapes and simply repackaged it in a different setting, which proved to be a reliable strategy for retaining a player base across multiple titles from the same studio running in parallel. The controls are purely touch-based – swiping a finger across the grid, no complex button combinations or extra gestures – so the game works equally well on phone and tablet and is accessible even to people who otherwise don't normally play mobile games. Visually everything is tuned to warm, cozy colors that underline the feeling of a neglected house gradually turning into a home, and with every completed room comes the motivation to see what the next one will look like.

Like the vast majority of Playrix titles, Homescapes is free-to-play with monetization that gradually intensifies – energy for playing runs out fairly quickly, extra moves, boosters and special items cost real money, and the pressure to spend noticeably increases with rising levels. The game nevertheless remains free to download on both major platforms and, even years after release, is regularly updated with new content and events.

**Why play it:** For fans of relaxed match-3 puzzles with a story sauce and house decorating, who should nonetheless expect that smooth progress without paying gets slower and slower and energy runs out faster than they might expect.

mobil__toon-blast.teaser: Colorful match-3 arcade game from Peak Games with simple addictiveness.
mobil__toon-blast.article:
**Toon Blast** belongs to the wave of colorful blast-puzzle games that, after the Candy Crush phenomenon, showed the genre still had plenty of room for variation and improving the basic mechanic. Instead of traditionally moving tokens into rows, the player taps groups of same-colored blocks stuck together, and the bigger the cluster the player finds and removes, the stronger a bonus power-up is generated as a reward right on the game board. Peak Games added cheerful cartoon characters with distinct personalities and level art that connects the environments, giving the player a sense of traveling between themed scenes and worlds, not just plain repetition of the same screen endlessly.

The simplicity of the controls – a single finger tap on a group of blocks – makes the game an ideal candidate for short play sessions between other everyday activities, and this accessibility was key to its massive success on both major mobile platforms shortly after release. The level design gradually adds obstacles like ice, chains, crates or special blocking tiles, so despite the ostensible simplicity of the basic mechanic, the game manages to keep the player at the screen much longer and at much higher levels than anyone might expect at first glance.

Monetization follows the classic free-to-play model: a limited number of lives that refill either gradually over time or instantly for real money, plus offers of boosters and special items that noticeably ease harder and more frustrating levels. The aggressiveness of monetization is comparable to most competitors in the genre, so not extreme, but definitely noticeable and hard to overlook in the higher tiers of the game.

**Why play it:** Suitable for anyone looking for undemanding but visually pleasant and colorful blast-puzzle fun for a few minutes a day, keeping in mind that without regular spending the pace of progress noticeably slows down over time.

mobil__wordscapes.teaser: Crossword puzzles combined with finding words in a letter grid; an addictive word puzzle.
mobil__wordscapes.article:
**Wordscapes** combines two long-popular word game genres into one cohesive package – classic word search in a letter grid and crossword assembly, where found words are gradually written into empty squares forming a simple pattern. The player connects adjacent letters into a word with a finger swipe, and if that word actually exists in the crossword, it automatically snaps into place; remaining letter combinations that make sense as a valid word but don't belong in the specific grid are also recognized by the game as bonus words and rewarded with extra points.

From studio PeopleFun, this is a title aimed primarily at players who love language puzzles and a calmer, more contemplative pace of play without the time pressure typical of many other casual games on the market. The graphics are deliberately simple and soothing – backgrounds with natural scenery like forests, beaches or mountains, gentle animations upon completing a level – so the game feels more like meditative vocabulary practice than adrenaline-fueled fun. It is precisely this combination of simplicity, calm pace and mental challenge that secured its long-term popularity across a very wide range of age groups, from students to retirees.

Monetization-wise, it is a free-to-play model with ads shown between individual levels and the option to purchase hints or permanently remove ads for a one-time fee; the overall pressure to spend is significantly milder compared to match-3 competitors, because the game lacks the classic system of gradually depleting lives that would force the player to wait or pay.

**Why play it:** Ideal for players who want an undemanding word puzzle without stress and time limits, whether as a regular evening routine before bed or a short distraction during the day.

mobil__golf-clash.teaser: Real-time multiplayer golf that turned the genre into a competitive hit.
mobil__golf-clash.article:
**Golf Clash** took an outwardly calm and slow sport and turned it into an exciting competitive experience against real opponents, though not exactly in real time but through asynchronous turns. Shots are controlled with a simple swipe gesture, where the player sets the power, direction and spin of the ball by dragging a finger across the screen and watching an accuracy meter, which proved to be a surprisingly precise and tangible way of simulating a golf swing on a phone's touchscreen. Individual duels against live opponents last only a few minutes per round, so the game fits perfectly into short free moments during the day, on the commute to work, or during a break.

Playdemic built the title's success precisely on multiplayer competitiveness – leaderboards, regular tournaments and clan battles gave the otherwise undemanding golf mechanic a new layer of tension and social dimension that earlier mobile golf titles had lacked until then. Gradually unlocking better clubs, balls and player characters motivates long-term play and tracking one's own progress through individual seasonal leagues, and the game has been regularly enriched with new courses and limited-time events since its release.

As a typical free-to-play title, it combines ads, premium equipment packs and an energy system limiting the number of matches that can be played without waiting or paying; in higher leagues, competitive pressure is noticeably reflected in the need to invest in better equipment just to keep pace with others.

**Why play it:** Recommended for players who want fast, competitive contests with a clearly readable and satisfying shot mechanic, even though they will inevitably run into the advantages of long-term paying players in the higher leagues.

mobil__efootball-pes.teaser: Konami's football series on mobile, eternal rival of FIFA Mobile.
mobil__efootball-pes.article:
**eFootball PES** was the mobile offshoot of Konami's long-running football series, which for years competed with FIFA Mobile for the favor of football fans directly on the phone. The controls were adapted for the touchscreen – a virtual joystick for moving players around the pitch and a set of buttons for passing, first-touch passing and shooting – and the game tried to preserve at least some of the tactical depth and emphasis on positioning for which the series had long been famous on home consoles. Collecting and gradually upgrading individual players through training and cards formed the core of long-term progression, similar to competing mobile football titles of the time.

Konami brought licensed teams, leagues and a number of real players into the mobile version, giving the game an authenticity that football fans had long valued, even though the graphics, animation smoothness and overall control responsiveness never quite reached the level of the series' console entries at the time. Seasonal updates, live events tied to real football tournaments and the regular addition of new player cards tried to copy the model that had already proven successful for the competing FIFA on mobile.

Monetization went the route of buying player packs similar to collectible cards, i.e. a gacha mechanic built directly into the football package, combined with a free-to-play approach and ads between matches; the desire for better and rarer player cards was the main driver of repeated spending in the store.

**Why play it:** Suitable for fans of Konami's football brand looking for a mobile alternative to FIFA, though they should factor in the gacha-based player-collecting system as a central and unavoidable part of the entire gameplay.

mobil__empires-and-puzzles.teaser: Match-3 combat system combined with castle building and RPG hero progression.
mobil__empires-and-puzzles.article:
**Empires & Puzzles** showed how elegantly two seemingly completely unrelated genres can be combined – classic match-3 token matching and turn-based RPG combat. Battles work by having the player charge their heroes' special abilities by matching colored tokens on the board, after which the heroes attack a row of enemies; the color of the tokens directly corresponds to the element of the given hero, so even classic matching of triples and quadruples at once gains a deeper tactical dimension and requires thoughtful turn planning. Between individual battles, the player also builds and gradually upgrades their own castle, giving overall progress a tangible and visible visual foundation.

Small Giant Games struck gold with this combination – the game managed to appeal both to longtime fans of the puzzle genre and to players craving character collecting and upgrading with genuine RPG depth and a strategic dimension to combat. The diversity of dozens of available heroes, elemental battles based on a rock-paper-scissors principle, and regularly added special events kept the player community active for many years after the original release, which is a rarity in this oversaturated genre.

Monetization is based on a gacha system of drawing new heroes for in-game or real currency through so-called challenges and portals, a typical and honestly acknowledged way of earning money for this type of game; collecting rare and legendary heroes is also the main driving force of long-term playability and repeated player spending.

**Why play it:** Suitable for players who want a proven puzzle mechanic enriched with genuine strategy and RPG hero collecting, with the understanding that the strongest and rarest heroes are firmly tied to random gacha draws.

mobil__merge-dragons.teaser: Merge puzzle where dragons and tiles combine into higher and higher forms.
mobil__merge-dragons.article:
**Merge Dragons!** is one of the titles that massively popularized the so-called merge genre – that is, combining two identical objects on the game board into one higher and more valuable whole. In the limited space of a garden, the player merges eggs, flowers, stones and even the dragons themselves, gradually unlocking rarer and much stronger forms while also healing and reviving the devastated landscape around them, which pushes the game closer to the genre of relaxed building games. Touch controls consist of simply dragging one object onto another and merging them, which is intuitive even for completely new players who otherwise don't regularly play strategy or puzzle games.

Gram Games came up with a mechanic that at first glance seems simple, even childlike, but offers surprising depth in planning how to most efficiently use the limited space of the game board and in what order to merge individual objects so the player doesn't lose valuable resources. Dragons as the central visual motif give the game a strong fantasy flavor and distinguish it from later similar merge titles that entered the market and drew heavily on its proven success.

It is a free-to-play game with an energy system limiting the number of actions per unit of time and offers of special themed packs; the pressure to spend grows gradually as the player reaches more demanding and expansive levels and wants to unlock rarer dragon types faster than purely free play would allow.

**Why play it:** Recommended for players with a soft spot for calm, thoughtful building puzzles, ideal for unwinding after a hard day, even though full progress without paying takes considerably longer than many would like.

mobil__getting-over-it-with-bennett-fodd.teaser: The infamous hammer-climbing-up-a-mountain game; a patience tester.
mobil__getting-over-it-with-bennett-fodd.article:
**Getting Over It with Bennett Foddy** is a deliberately cruel game built on a single idea – climb as high as possible up a mountain of assorted junk as a man sitting in a cauldron, using nothing but a single hammer, where one careless mistake can sweep the player back down dozens of minutes of accumulated progress. The controls are purely one-fingered: dragging across the touchscreen moves the hammer, which the player braces against rocks, debris, and all manner of objects to push upward. The apparent simplicity of this single input hides an extremely unforgiving physics system, where almost every movement demands maximum precision, patience, and a cool head even after repeated failure.

Bennett Foddy designed the game as an open tribute to older, frustrating titles that shaped his own gaming experience, accompanying it with his own philosophical commentary that reflects on frustration, perseverance, and the meaning of repeated failure as you play. This combination of brutal difficulty and unexpectedly introspective narration made it a genuine phenomenon on streaming platforms, where viewers were immensely entertained by players' emotional outbursts after an unlucky fall from a nearly reached summit.

It's a paid game with no ads or microtransactions whatsoever, which is more the exception than the rule in the world of mobile titles, and it gives the player the assurance that all the frustration experienced stems purely from the game's own difficulty, not from artificially created monetization pressure.

**Why play it:** For players with genuinely steady nerves seeking an extreme challenge and an introspective experience for a one-time price – definitely not for anyone who plays mobile games mainly to unwind and relax.

mobil__grid-autosport.teaser: Feral's mobile port of a solid racing game with realistic handling.
mobil__grid-autosport.article:
**GRID Autosport** proved that a more demanding and honest racing simulation can work even on a phone's touchscreen without losing what mattered most about the original console and PC experience. Feral Interactive brought the game to mobile platforms with several optional control schemes – tilting the device itself, an on-screen virtual steering wheel, or classic touch buttons – letting players freely choose whichever variant suited them personally best. The driving model stayed closer to realistic handling than the arcade racing typical of most mobile platforms, which was especially appreciated by longtime genre fans coming from PC and consoles.

The mobile port included a wide range of tracks, licensed cars, and competitive disciplines straight from the original game, meaning it wasn't a lightened or trimmed-down version, but an honest transfer of a full-fledged racing title into a pocket format. Feral Interactive already had rich experience porting graphically and technically demanding games to mobile devices at the time, and GRID Autosport ranked for a long time among their most successful and best-rated efforts in this specific regard.

It's a paid game with no ads or any microtransactions, which was essentially the standard across Feral's entire portfolio – the player buys the title once and gets the complete content without further pressure toward additional spending.

**Why play it:** Suitable for fans of more realistic racing simulations who appreciate being able to freely customize their control method and pay just once for the whole honest content package with no hidden surprises.

mobil__rise-of-kingdoms.teaser: A strategy game with real civilizations and large-scale empire building.
mobil__rise-of-kingdoms.article:
**Rise of Kingdoms** ranks among the more ambitious mobile strategy games, combining careful city building with a vast map shared by thousands of other players around the world. At the start, the player picks one of the historical civilizations, constructs buildings, chooses a direction for technological research, and leads armies commanded by real historical generals such as Richard the Lionheart or Zhuge Liang, giving the game a pleasant educational touch combined with a genuinely massive multiplayer environment. Controls are fully adapted to the touchscreen through clear menus and a sprawling map that the player navigates with simple swipe and pinch gestures.

Lilith Games bet on long-term alliances and diplomacy between individual players, where cooperation as well as open conflicts between rival clans form the core of the whole social experience, similar to other large-scale MMO strategy games on mobile. The huge scope of available content and regularly released updates have kept the game alive for many years since its original release and given it a stable and loyal player base across many countries around the world.

Monetization combines a free-to-play approach with strong pressure to speed up construction, research, and troop training through payment, which is entirely common for this type of large-scale strategy game and becomes a noticeable and almost unavoidable part of competing with other players and clans in the later stages of the game.

**Why play it:** Recommended for players who have enough time and desire to build a long-term community within a strong alliance, keeping in mind that without regular investment, competing with paying players becomes considerably harder and slower.

mobil__helix-jump.teaser: A simple falling arcade game from Voodoo; a typical hyper-casual hit of its time.
mobil__helix-jump.article:
**Helix Jump** is a pure distillation of the whole hyper-casual principle – a single control gesture, instant understanding of the rules within seconds, and a game loop addictive enough that the player reaches for another attempt almost without thinking. A small ball falls through a long spiral of colorful platforms with holes, and the player rotates the entire structure by dragging a finger across the screen to find a free opening, while any collision with a solid platform immediately ends the current attempt. Zero entry barrier and completely instant feedback make the title an ideal example of why the whole hyper-casual genre spread so rapidly among hundreds of thousands of players worldwide around 2018.

Voodoo was at the time one of the most significant and prolific publishers of exactly this type of game, and Helix Jump ranked among their most successful titles ever, defining the visual style of minimalist colorful geometric shapes and simple yet satisfying physics typical of the whole genre. Short play sessions lasting mere seconds to minutes made it an ideal filler for spare moments between other everyday activities, whether on the go, in line, or during a short break.

Monetization rests almost entirely on ads shown between individual attempts at progress, while the game itself is completely free to download with no need to pay to continue or unlock content, which exactly matches the typical and widespread model of the whole hyper-casual segment of that era.

**Why play it:** Suitable for moments when you just need a few minutes of undemanding fun without learning anything new, keeping in mind that ads are an integral and unavoidable part of the whole experience.

mobil__old-school-runescape.teaser: The classic 2007 version of RuneScape finally on mobile phones too.
mobil__old-school-runescape.article:
**Old School RuneScape** brought to smartphones a version of the legendary MMORPG frozen in the form it had in 2007, that is, before a number of later changes that the player community itself democratically voted down as undesirable and preferred to return to the original take on the game. The mobile version preserves the complete game world of Gielinor, including all the skills, quests, and the open economy tied to trading with other players, just with controls sensitively adapted for the touchscreen – simple tapping on the movement target, clear contextual menus, and an adjusted interface for the inventory and skill panel.

With this step, Jagex allowed players to continue characters created perhaps many years earlier directly from a pocket device anywhere on the go, which was a major milestone for many longtime fans, since RuneScape had traditionally been perceived as a purely browser-based and later desktop affair requiring a mouse and keyboard. Transferring the complex system of dozens of skills and a sprawling open world onto a small phone screen turned out surprisingly well and without major compromises, even though touch controls never quite match the precision and speed of a classic mouse and keyboard in more demanding combat.

The game is free-to-play, with limited content available for free and a paid monthly membership that unlocks the vast majority of the game world, skills, and quests; the mobile title adopted this membership model directly from the original PC version without any changes.

**Why play it:** Ideal for longtime RuneScape veterans as well as entirely new players craving a classic MMORPG experience on the go, though keep in mind that genuinely full content requires a regular paid subscription.

mobil__gacha-life.teaser: Character creation and gacha mechanics; a popular storytelling tool for young players.
mobil__gacha-life.article:
**Gacha Life** is a character and story creation tool that built a cult following among young players, largely thanks to its endless combinations of hairstyles, outfits, and accessories in an anime style. The player assembles their own characters from dozens of pieces and then places them into a studio, where static comics or short videos are created – this is also the source of the game's enormous popularity on YouTube, where creators publish their own stories complete with voice acting and music. Controls are purely touch-based and simple, dragging elements and selecting from menus, so even a small child can handle the game.

Despite the name, gacha here isn't a classic pull-for-real-money system – items are unlocked with in-game currency that the player earns by playing minigames, so the game functions as free-to-play without aggressive monetization, setting it apart from most gacha titles on the market. This very accommodation of a young audience without spending pressure was key to its success and gave rise to an entire community of amateur creators who tell their own series using the game. Lunime followed up on this success with the sequel Gacha Life 2 and the related titles Gacha Club and Gacha Studio, which expand the range of costumes and backgrounds.

The game has no story or objective of its own – it's a purely creative sandbox where the player supplies the meaning themselves, whether that's drawing a comic, filming a video, or just putting together outfits. The visual style with big eyes and pastel colors clearly targets fans of anime and Japanese pop culture, even though the game itself was made outside Japan.

**Why play it:** Ideal for children and young anime fans who want to create their own characters and stories without spending money and share them further.

mobil__donut-county.teaser: A puzzle about a hole that swallows an entire town; short, funny, and original.
mobil__donut-county.article:
**Donut County** is a short but unforgettable puzzle adventure in which the player controls not a character but a hole in the ground that grows larger with every object it swallows. By dragging a finger across the screen, you move the hole beneath keychains, bushes, cars, and even entire buildings of a Californian suburb, and the more things it swallows, the bigger the hole gets and the even larger chunks of scenery it can devour – the principle recalls the famous Katamari Damacy, just turned inside out and reduced to a single touch gesture. Developer Ben Esposito refined it to complete clarity, so the game controls just as well on a small phone as on a tablet.

The story follows a raccoon named BJ, who inadvertently – actually because of a smartphone app controlling mysterious holes – swallows the entire small town along with all its neighbors, and the game then returns in lighthearted dialogue to how it all actually happened. The humor is gentle, text-based, and American, full of absurd characters and awkward moments, which makes the game feel more like an interactive sketch than a classic platformer. The visual style with flat colors and simple shapes keeps the game low-cost yet visually distinctive.

The campaign is deliberately short, completable in a single afternoon, and this brevity is one of its greatest strengths – the game never starts to bore or repeat the same trick. The reward for finishing is a bonus mode where you can keep swallowing things after the story ends. On mobile it's a paid game with no ads or microtransactions, which matches its tone as a one-off artistic experience rather than an ongoing service.

**Why play it:** Suitable for anyone who wants to experience an original and funny idea in just a few hours without any unnecessary padding or spending pressure.

mobil__dandara.teaser: A metroidvania with unusual wall-and-ceiling movement instead of jumping.
mobil__dandara.article:
**Dandara** ranks among the metroidvanias unafraid to challenge the genre's basic rules – the main heroine can't walk or jump normally at all, but instead teleports between illuminated surfaces and can attach herself to the ceiling, a wall, or the floor depending on where the player aims. This unconventional movement system also changes the logic of combat and exploration, since the player must constantly think in terms of every side of a room, not just left to right. On touch controls this initially demands more from the player, but once you've mastered the basics, it makes Dandara one of the freshest platformers of its kind.

The Brazilian studio Long Hat House built a world called Salt as a crumbling civilization full of oppression and forgotten corners, which the player gradually unlocks by collecting new abilities – the classic metroidvania principle, just delivered in a black-and-white, high-contrast visual style with bold color accents. The atmosphere is heavier and more melancholic than in most genre touchstones, which sets the game apart visually too and gives it a distinctive tone.

The game was released first on consoles and PC, and the mobile version then brought the same content adapted for touch controls, including the option to connect an external gamepad for more precise teleportation control. The port succeeded, with the game retaining its pace and difficulty, only requiring a bit more patience when playing purely on a phone display.

**Why play it:** A tip for metroidvania fans looking for a genre entry with a genuinely different movement core, not just a cosmetic tweak, even though mastering the touch controls takes a bit of practice.

mobil__what-golf.teaser: An absurd parody of golf where anything but the ball goes flying.
mobil__what-golf.article:
**What the Golf?** borrows only the word from the rules of golf and then knocks them down one by one - in one level a house flies instead of the ball, in another it's the golfer himself, elsewhere a basketball hoop or a flock of birds, and the player never knows in advance what will happen on the next shot. Studio Triband built the entire game on a principle of constant surprise, so the sports genre here quietly morphs into a platformer, a logic puzzle, and a parody of other video games within a few seconds of play, and the player never knows what awaits on the next shot.

The controls remain deliberately primitive - just stretch the rubber band with your finger like in classic mini-golf and let go, with the power and direction of the shot governed by the gesture on the screen. It's exactly this simplicity that lets the game pile up dozens of bizarre ideas without an overly complicated tutorial, so new players understand the game instantly and the surprise comes only from the level design, not from the control scheme, which stays the same throughout and never requires new menus or settings.

Short levels and a constant stream of new gags make the game an ideal title for a break between other activities, with the humor also targeting players who've never played golf in their life and never got closer acquainted with the rules of the real sport. References to other genres and games - from platformers to rhythm titles - work as a witty wink for more experienced audiences without putting off casual players just looking for a bit of quick fun between other duties of the day.

**Why play it:** A great choice for anyone who wants a game for a few minutes a day full of funny surprises without having to take anything seriously or learn complicated rules.

mobil__grindstone.teaser: A puzzle game from Capybara Games combining turn-based battles with colored chains.
mobil__grindstone.article:
**Grindstone** combines turn-based chaining of same-colored enemies with the temperament of action brawling, which makes this game from the Canadian studio Capybara Games one of the smartest puzzle titles on mobile. The player drags a finger across adjacent monsters of the same color, and with each additional link in the chain both the attack's power and the amount of resources gained grow, so deciding when to end the chain and strike forms the core of the whole strategy. At first glance it's a simple mechanic, but as the tower's floors add up it quickly gains depth and tactical demands, since one bad decision can end the expedition.

The isometric world full of colorful monsters, axes, and magic potions has a lighthearted comic-book style that contrasts with the fairly merciless difficulty of the higher floors - the player can genuinely lose progress here if they misjudge a chain, which sets the game apart from more laid-back mobile puzzlers with no risk of failure. Between expeditions the player upgrades their gear and unlocks new characters with their own abilities, so progression feels like real growth and opens up new tactical options for the floors still to come.

Grindstone was among the launch titles of the Apple Arcade subscription service, meaning no ads and no microtransactions, just one-time access as part of the subscription. That let it afford higher difficulty and pacing without any pressure to monetize, which helped it earn a reputation as one of the finest titles on the whole service and an example of what an honest mobile game without ulterior motives should look like.

**Why play it:** Recommended for players who want a puzzle game with genuine strategic thinking and don't mind having an active Apple Arcade subscription to play it.

mobil__sneaky-sasquatch.teaser: A harmless stealth adventure of a sasquatch among humans; light and funny.
mobil__sneaky-sasquatch.article:
**Sneaky Sasquatch** puts the player in the fur of a shaggy sasquatch who earns a little extra among tourists in a national park by stealing snacks, taking on odd jobs, and even owning a car he can freely drive around the open world. The game from studio RAC7 Games combines stealth elements - hiding from park rangers and camping families - with a relaxed simulation of everyday life, where the sasquatch spends his earned money on upgrading his little house, clothes, or a better car, gradually building his own small lifestyle among humans.

The game's tone is deliberately harmless and funny, with no violence whatsoever - the biggest risk is getting spotted and chased off, not losing in the sense of a classic action game. The open world gradually grows with new locations, minigames like golf or fishing, and side quests, so the game also works as a laid-back collection of small activities rather than a linear story with a clear ending and a closing credits roll, which makes it suitable for playing without any long-term planning.

Controls are purely touch-based, with a virtual stick for movement and contextual buttons for stealing, driving, and interacting with characters, so the game stays legible on a small display even for younger or less experienced players. Sneaky Sasquatch is one of the titles in the Apple Arcade lineup, so it's played without ads or in-app purchases - it's a game with a steady supply of free content as part of the subscription, which sets it up for long-term, undemanding play in short bursts, ideally as an evening wind-down.

**Why play it:** Ideal for players looking for a relaxing game without stress or violence who have access to Apple Arcade, where it can basically be played endlessly.

mobil__human-fall-flat.teaser: A physics-based platformer with a clumsy little character; humor from chaotic controls.
mobil__human-fall-flat.article:
**Human: Fall Flat** brings a physics-based platformer to mobile in which the controlled character, Bob, has no fixed animations or precise jumps - every hand movement, body lean, or object pickup comes out of a physics simulation, so the result tends to be clumsy, unpredictable, and often outright comical. The player solves puzzles in dreamlike environments such as a castle, a factory hall, or a giant construction site by lifting crates, swinging on ropes, or pushing heavy objects, with controlling one's own body being just as big a challenge as the surrounding puzzles.

The mobile version was made by studio Curve Digital as a port of the original game from PC and consoles, and it tried to preserve the characteristic feel of loose, wobbly controls even on a touchscreen - virtual sticks control walking and the camera, while separate buttons control each hand individually. It's precisely the need to coordinate several controls at once that makes the mobile version a tougher experience than on a gamepad, but once you get used to it, it works surprisingly well and without major compromises, even though it takes a bit longer to get the hang of than on a physical controller.

The game began as a simple physics experiment by a Swedish developer that grew into a surprise hit thanks to funny videos shared from multiplayer sessions, and the mobile port only helped that popularity along - it made it possible to play practically anywhere. The content stays the same as on the major platforms, including online co-op for multiple players.

**Why play it:** A great choice for players who enjoy humor born from chaotic controls and don't mind juggling several controls at once on a touchscreen.

mobil__toca-life-world.teaser: A digital dollhouse with no goals or rules; just free-form play for kids.
mobil__toca-life-world.article:
**Toca Life World** is a digital dollhouse with no quests, points, or losing, in which children build their own stories out of characters, houses, shops, and towns from the Swedish studio Toca Boca. The player moves characters around the scene with a finger, opens doors, dresses up little figures, or prepares food in a virtual kitchen, and the whole interaction works as free-form play with no clear goal, much like classic play with dolls and figures, just in digital form and with the endless patience of a scene that never scolds anyone for a mistake.

The app merges together older standalone titles from the Toca Life series (school, hospital, office, and others) into one shared world that players can freely move between, which was a fairly novel approach to children's mobile games at the time of release. The base version is free to download and includes a limited selection of locations and characters, with further environments and items then purchasable as paid in-app content, and the range of new locations kept growing over the years.

The visual style is colorful, rounded, and friendly, with no violence or competitiveness whatsoever, which clearly aims the game at the youngest audiences and at parents looking for a safe digital alternative to physical toys. The absence of ads within the game itself is balanced out by exactly this system of purchasable content, which parents should keep in mind before getting the game for their children, since the individual location packs can gradually add up to a considerable sum.

**Why play it:** Suitable for parents of young children who want a safe, creative toy without violence or competition, though they should factor in paid add-ons within the app.

mobil__kingdom-two-crowns.teaser: Strategic kingdom-building in 2D; simple controls, a deep system.
mobil__kingdom-two-crowns.article:
**Kingdom Two Crowns** is a sequel to the minimalist strategy game about building a kingdom that fits on a single screen, yet hides a surprisingly deep game about deciding where to invest every coin earned. The player controls a single character, rides a horse left and right across a two-dimensional map, tosses coins to hermits so they become archers, carpenters, or wall-builders, and as night falls defends the walls against waves of monsters called Greed, which grow stronger and attack in greater numbers as the days go by.

The controls are deliberately spare - movement, dismounting from the horse, and tossing coins - yet out of that emerges a complex system of deciding on priorities, where every poorly spent coin can spell the kingdom's downfall. The pixel-art visual style paired with calm, atmospheric music creates a contrast between the peaceful daytime pace and the tension of the nighttime attacks, which gradually intensify and force the player to plan their defense ahead of time.

The mobile version carries over the same game as on consoles and PC, just with touch controls adapted for a smaller display, and the port works without major compromises, since the game was built on a simple control scheme from the very start. New environments and mechanics have also been added compared to the first game, including a boat for sailing between islands and new unit types that expand the kingdom's defensive options.

**Why play it:** Recommended for players who like strategy games with simple controls but deep decision-making, and who will appreciate that the game plays well even in short sessions during the day on mobile.

mobil__bloodstained-ritual-of-night.teaser: A metroidvania from Castlevania creator Koji Igarashi, in a full-fledged mobile release.
mobil__bloodstained-ritual-of-night.article:
**Bloodstained: Ritual of the Night** brings a full-fledged metroidvania to mobile phones, designed by Koji Igarashi, creator of the legendary Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and funded by fans through a crowdfunding campaign. Miriam makes her way through a vast gothic castle full of demons, collects dozens of weapons and magic items, and gradually unlocks new abilities that open up previously inaccessible parts of the map - following exactly the pattern that Igarashi himself helped define.

The game retains the same content as on consoles and PC, including an extensive combat system, item crafting, and dozens of hours of content in a single playthrough, making it one of the most substantial titles ever to reach mobile. Control via virtual buttons on the touchscreen works surprisingly precisely, though players used to a physical gamepad may still appreciate the option to connect an external controller for the tougher boss fights, where it often comes down to split-second timing.

The mobile port also manages to preserve the atmosphere - dark, gothic music and detailed environments - so the game doesn't feel like a stripped-down version for travel, but a full-fledged experience comparable to the major platforms. It's a paid title with no ads or microtransactions, matching its scope and production values, and it takes up a fairly large amount of storage space on a phone's display.

**Why play it:** A recommendation for fans of metroidvanias and Castlevania who want a large-scale, honestly crafted game on mobile with no compromises on content, just a higher purchase price.

mobil__alien-isolation.teaser: A claustrophobic horror game with an indestructible alien on your heels; only running and hiding, no combat.
mobil__alien-isolation.article:
**Alien: Isolation** is a claustrophobic survival horror game in which Amanda Ripley searches for the fate of her mother Ellen aboard the space station Sevastopol and soon discovers she isn't alone there - an indestructible alien prowls the station, one that can't be killed, only avoided. The mobile port from studio Feral Interactive carries over the same game that came out on consoles and PC, with all the same tension and pacing, where every sound of footsteps or the creak of a vent can signal danger nearby and forces the player to proceed with the utmost caution.

The game sticks to the visual aesthetic of the 1970s, as set out by the original Alien film - retro-futuristic screens, analog instruments, and dim lighting create an atmosphere that makes this horror game more of a slow game of hide-and-seek than an action shooter. The alien's artificial intelligence adapts to the player's behavior, so the same hiding tactic can't be repeated indefinitely, which keeps the tension high throughout the several-hour campaign and forces the player to change their approach from one chapter to the next.

On a touchscreen the game is controlled via a virtual stick and contextual buttons, which takes some getting used to at first but works precisely after a few chapters and doesn't spoil the game's carefully built pacing. It's an extensive, fully paid title with no ads, fairly demanding on both the phone's performance and its storage, so it suits newer and more powerful models better.

**Why play it:** Recommended for fans of horror and the Alien film who can handle a slow, nerve-wracking pace with no direct combat and don't mind paying full price for a large-scale mobile experience.

mobil__fantasian.teaser: A JRPG from Final Fantasy creator Sakaguchi featuring handmade diorama scenes instead of backgrounds.
mobil__fantasian.article:
**Fantasian** is a JRPG by Hironobu Sakaguchi, creator of the Final Fantasy series, that sets itself apart from most of its genre peers primarily through its backgrounds - instead of digitally painted sets, the game uses hundreds of handmade dioramas, physical models that the team scanned and turned into environments for individual locations. The result is a visually distinctive game full of depth and textures that are hard to achieve with purely digital graphics, giving the world an almost tangible atmosphere.

The combat system combines classic turn-based JRPG elements with a practical solution to random encounters - the player can "collect" enemies from a distance using a special mechanic and deal with them all at once later, which spares the game from annoyingly interrupting exploration while walking through the dioramas. The music was composed by Sakaguchi's longtime collaborator Nobuo Uematsu, giving the story and battles a characteristic orchestral feel familiar from Final Fantasy.

The game was released exclusively for Apple Arcade, split into two parts, with the first part available for free as part of the subscription and the second requiring a one-time additional payment - an unusual solution that combined a subscription model with a premium expansion. The game later received a release on other platforms under a new name, showing that reaching beyond a mobile audience was intended from the start and that Mistwalker treated the game as a full-fledged title.

**Why play it:** A tip for fans of the JRPG genre and of Hironobu Sakaguchi's work who will appreciate the unique handmade dioramas, but must reckon with an Apple Arcade subscription and an extra payment for the second half of the story.

mobil__stumble-guys.teaser: A mobile take on Fall Guys; a chaotic obstacle-course battle royale for crowds of players at once.
mobil__stumble-guys.article:
**Stumble Guys** puts up to thirty-two players at the start of an obstacle course full of flip platforms, swinging pendulums, rotating cylinders and slides, where they race for the last remaining spots all the way to the final round, and where a single mistimed jump means elimination. The controls are built purely for touch - a virtual joystick on the left, a jump button on the right, with a dash added later - and the game works as quick rounds lasting a few minutes, ideal for a bus ride or a spare moment between meetings. Visually it's colorful, round characters with dozens of costumes that can be unlocked by playing or by purchase, which makes cosmetics the main driver of further spending, while the courses themselves remain free for everyone.

The game emerged at a time when Fall Guys was still exclusive to consoles and PC and wasn't available in many countries at all, so Stumble Guys quickly filled the empty space on phones and became, for a large share of players, their first contact with the obstacle-course battle royale genre. The base game is free with ads and purchases of skins and a battle pass, which has kept the game alive for years after release thanks to regular seasons, new maps and crossovers with well-known brands from films and other games. Despite occasional criticism of recycled maps and unbalanced server matchmaking, the game's pace remains brisk and accessible even to players who otherwise don't play mobile games and are just looking for a short dose of fun.

**Why play it:** Suits anyone who wants fast, chaotic fun with friends in short, free play sessions, while accepting that cosmetics and the battle pass are the developers' main source of revenue.

mobil__uma-musume-pretty-derby.teaser: A gacha simulator of racehorses reimagined as girls, a huge hit in Japan from studio Cygames.
mobil__uma-musume-pretty-derby.article:
**Uma Musume: Pretty Derby** turns famous racehorses of the past into anime girls with their own personalities, whom the player trains over weeks of in-game time to bring them to the top of Japan's horse racing calendar. The game combines a training simulation - scheduling stamina, speed, power and intelligence, planning rest periods and special events tied to a particular character's story - with a racing portion, where results play out semi-automatically based on the set strategy and chosen starting position in the field. Controls are simple, taps and swipes through menus, so the game's core lies more in careful planning and reading each heroine's constructed story than in fast reflexes.

Cygames released the title in Japan in 2021, and it quickly became one of the most profitable gacha titles in the country, thanks in part to a license for real legendary racehorses and the extraordinary care put into the music, animation and emotionally charged stories of individual characters. International players waited a long time for the global English version, which arrived with a significant delay after the Japanese launch, so many fans knew the game for years only through imports, community patches or fan translations. Monetization relies on a gacha system for characters, support cards and costumes, which typically requires a lot of time or money to assemble a competitive team.

**Why play it:** Appreciated by fans of gacha simulators and the horse racing setting who are willing to invest time in long-term training and accept gacha monetization as a natural part of the game.

mobil__royal-match.teaser: A match-3 puzzle game with a king and a castle; one of the highest-grossing mobile titles ever.
mobil__royal-match.article:
**Royal Match** builds on the classic match-3 principle, but connects individual levels into a single continuous map around a castle that gradually gets repaired, furnished and decorated according to the player's progress, giving otherwise isolated levels a meaningful shared goal. Controls are purely touch-based - moving pieces across the grid, combining them into bonus power-ups like a rocket or a bomb - and the game skillfully paces its difficulty so that the player regularly runs into a limited number of lives and offers for real money at exactly the moments of greatest frustration. The character of King Rollo, who guides the player, encourages them and comments on their progress, gives the game an unusually distinct identity in a crowded market of similar titles.

Dream Games released the game in 2021, and thanks to aggressive marketing with short ad clips as well as a sophisticated live-ops system of gradually unfolding events, weekly happenings and seasonal passes, Royal Match climbed among the absolute highest-grossing mobile games in the world, even competing against much older and more established puzzle series. The success showed that even in a genre that looks mined to the last detail, it's possible to earn enormous amounts just through precise tuning of the sense of progress, rewards and social comparison with friends. It's free to download, but key progress is often accelerated precisely by microtransactions and purchases of extra lives, moves or special boosters for hard levels.

**Why play it:** Suitable for fans of relaxed puzzle games who want a nicely tuned match-3 experience with a narrative framework and can ignore the constant purchase offers.

mobil__pokemon-unite.teaser: A MOBA with Pokémon from studio TiMi; faster and more accessible than classic MOBA titles.
mobil__pokemon-unite.article:
**Pokémon Unite** brings the MOBA concept into the world of Pokémon, but simplifies it into matches lasting around ten minutes, where instead of destroying the opponent's base, players score points at central scoring points scattered across the map. Touchscreen controls use a virtual joystick and contextual buttons for attacks and abilities, so the game can be handled even without prior experience with classic PC MOBAs, where the entry barrier tends to be much higher. The selection of Pokémon divided into roles - attacker, defender, support, all-rounder or ranged attacker - gives players clearly readable archetypes they're used to from other team games, while also allowing a balanced five-person team to be assembled.

Developer TiMi Studio Group, which has extensive experience with mobile action titles for the Chinese market, released the game in 2021 simultaneously for mobile devices and the Nintendo Switch console with full cross-play between platforms, an unusual step for licensed brands at the time. Monetization runs on a battle pass, cosmetics and unlockable held items, which can also be obtained just by playing, placing the game among the more accessible forms of free-to-play compared to purely gacha competition dependent on chance. For longtime Pokémon fans, this was the brand's first official venture into the MOBA genre, opening it up to an entirely new group of players who until then had only known the series from its main RPG entries on game consoles and handhelds.

**Why play it:** Recommended for Pokémon fans as well as complete newcomers to the MOBA genre who want shorter and more accessible matches than classic PC MOBA games.

mobil__diablo-immortal.teaser: A mobile/PC MMO ARPG set between Diablo II and III; notorious for its controversial monetization.
mobil__diablo-immortal.article:
**Diablo Immortal** sets its story in the period between Diablo II and Diablo III and deals with what happened to the shards of the Worldstone after the fallen angel Tyrael's fall, linking familiar characters and locations with a new plot tailored directly for a mobile audience. The game offers a full-fledged action RPG with the same feeling of hacking through enemies, collecting loot and upgrading a character as the PC entries, transferred onto a touchscreen directional pad and automatic attack with special abilities on buttons, making it comfortable to play even with one hand. Multiplayer elements, clans, an open world and shared boss fights against world bosses make the game a living shared environment, not just a solo dungeon crawler.

Blizzard released the game in 2022 simultaneously on mobile and PC, and from day one it faced enormous criticism over monetization built on a gacha system of legendary gems, where the path to the strongest possible gear without paying was measured in months to years of intensive play. Analyses shortly after launch showed that fully gearing a character could require hundreds of thousands of dollars, which quickly made the game a symbol of aggressive mobile business practices even outside the gaming community and sparked discussion about regulating such systems. Despite the controversy, the game has a loyal core of players who appreciate the combat system, the open world and the atmosphere of a well-established dark fantasy universe with regular seasonal updates.

**Why play it:** Suits Diablo fans who want story connections between the entries and the series' proven combat system, but should factor in the harsh gacha monetization of endgame gear in advance.

mobil__goddess-of-victory-nikke.teaser: A gacha shooter with anime heroines from studio Shift Up; emphasis on characters as well as cover-based action.
mobil__goddess-of-victory-nikke.article:
**Goddess of Victory: Nikke** combines gacha collecting of anime heroines with a cover-based action shooter, where characters rotate in trios, each with their own weapon, special ability and role in the team, and success in a mission depends on the right combination of squad. Touchscreen controls simplify aiming to automatic targeting with manual triggering of special attacks and dodges, so the main emphasis falls on assembling and upgrading the team rather than pure player reflexes. The visual side and character design from studio Shift Up, which is also behind other notable action titles, is among the things that earned the game considerable attention soon after release, along with an elaborate post-apocalyptic atmosphere.

The game came out in 2022 and quickly established itself among successful gacha titles thanks to a combination of an elaborate story about humanity's downfall on the surface of the Earth and its retreat into underground shelters, together with regular events bringing new characters and story chapters. Monetization relies on a gacha system for characters, weapons and costumes, while the game deliberately works with its striking character design as part of its marketing and community presence. For players familiar with the gacha shooter genre, this is one of the technically most polished and graphically most ambitious entries on the market, with regular major story updates and accompanying music from multiple composers.

**Why play it:** An interesting choice for fans of gacha games and anime styling looking for a more action-oriented alternative to turn-based gacha RPGs, keeping in mind the need to invest in collecting characters long-term.

mobil__star-wars-knights-of-old-republic.teaser: A cult Star Wars RPG from Obsidian with darker morality and the mentor Kreia.
mobil__star-wars-knights-of-old-republic.article:
**Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II** brings to mobile the darker sequel to the cult RPG that studio Obsidian created in 2004 as the spiritual successor to the first entry from BioWare, this time with a markedly bleaker view of the Jedi Order and the war that scarred it. The story follows a lone Jedi cut off from the Force, guided by the mysterious mentor Kreia, who questions the very moral foundations of both the Jedi and the Sith, which still ranks the game among the most philosophical and ambitious RPGs in the Star Wars brand. Studio Aspyr Media released the mobile version, redesigning the controls into a virtual joystick and contextual buttons for combat and inventory, and the original's basic turn-based combat system adapted to touch surprisingly well.

The 2022 port is a paid game without ads or gacha elements, which places it in a minority but very welcome category among fans - that of full ports of older computer games - within the offering of mobile RPGs. Fans long called for a fix to the extensive unfinished content from the original release, caused by the deadline pressure of the time, for which community mods exist on PC, but the mobile version is based on the standard, officially released form of the game. Even so, it's one of the few ways to play this acclaimed entry directly on a phone without needing emulation, older hardware or hunting down a physical disc.

**Why play it:** Ideal for fans of Star Wars and classic RPGs who want a darker and more thought-provoking story and don't mind an older control scheme adapted for touch.

mobil__monopoly-go.teaser: Digital Monopoly with events and sticker collecting; a hit among mobile games of recent years.
mobil__monopoly-go.article:
**Monopoly GO!** turns the classic board game into solo digital entertainment, where instead of playing against live opponents, short rounds against virtual opponents take turns, and the main focus becomes collecting stickers for themed albums, completing time-limited events, and building your own empire of buildings on the game map. The controls are simple screen taps – you roll the dice, watch the movement animation around the classic checkerboard map, and deal with whatever the landed tile brings – so the game targets short, frequent sessions spread throughout the day rather than long, continuous play sessions.

Scopely released the game in 2023, and within a few months it climbed among the highest-grossing mobile games in history, thanks in part to a massive advertising campaign and a system where players send each other dice through social connections and compete in short-term event leaderboards. Monetization is built on purchasing dice with real money, which directly speeds up progress in events, and on collectible albums whose completion without paying can take a very long time and requires patience as well as trading duplicate cards. The game's success showed how powerfully a combination of a decades-old nostalgic brand with modern free-to-play design based on collections, leaderboards, and time pressure can work, and it inspired a number of similar titles from other publishers trying to repeat the same success with their own brands.

**Why play:** Suitable for players who enjoy short daily rituals and collectible events and don't mind that faster progress is closely tied to buying dice.

mobil__whiteout-survival.teaser: Strategic city-building in an icy apocalypse, with alliance wars over resources and territory.
mobil__whiteout-survival.article:
**Whiteout Survival** sets city-building in a frozen world after a climate catastrophe, where the player manages a settlement, mines resources, recruits heroes with their own abilities, and must constantly upgrade buildings and units to survive worsening frost, monsters, and attacks from other players. Alongside solo building, alliance membership plays a key role – shared research, resource sharing, and coordinated wars over territory against other alliances give the game a strong social and competitive dimension that goes beyond the individual player. The controls are touch-adapted, built around menus, map overviews, and construction queues typical of strategy games with long-term progression rather than fast reflex action.

Century Games released the title in 2023, and it quickly ranked among the highest-grossing mobile strategy games, helped along by an omnipresent advertising campaign featuring animated scenes set in the game's icy world. Monetization combines a free-to-play base with the purchase of construction speed-ups, special event bundles, and a battle pass, and while free progression is possible, it is noticeably slower than for paying players, especially in the later stages of the game. The genre relies on the proven strategy-game formula of long-term engagement through daily tasks, timed events, and alliance camaraderie, which players often keep alive in separate chat groups outside the game itself.

**Why play:** Will appeal to fans of slower-paced strategy games with a social alliance dimension who accept that faster progress will require time or money.

mobil__last-war-survival.teaser: A survival strategy game set after a zombie apocalypse; notorious for aggressive ads featuring famous actors.
mobil__last-war-survival.article:
**Last War: Survival** builds on a similar foundation to other mobile survival strategy games – after a zombie apocalypse, the player builds a base, recruits heroes with unique abilities, and leads alliances into battles over resources, territory, and strategically advantageous map positions. The gameplay combines resource management, upgrade research, and tactical unit deployment on the map, with controls remaining a simple touch menu without particular demands on reflexes or fast real-time decisions. What sets it apart is mainly its massive presence in mobile advertising, appearing in an incredible number of video spots with live-action scenes and famous faces that have little to do with the actual gameplay.

FirstFun released the game in 2023, and it quickly became one of the highest-grossing titles in the genre, largely thanks to an advertising budget that far exceeds typical mobile strategy games and flooded video ad space across apps. Monetization relies on speed-ups, a battle pass, and event bundles – the genre's standard model, just backed by substantially more aggressive new-player acquisition than the rest of the genre's competition. The game is a typical example of how marketing in this segment of the mobile market often drifts away from the actual game content, yet it has managed to retain players thanks to a steady stream of new events, heroes, and game seasons with their own storylines.

**Why play:** More for fans of survival strategy games who can filter out the exaggerated ads and accept the standard free-to-play pace with paid speed-ups.

mobil__sonic-mania-plus.teaser: A return to classic 2D Sonic from the pens of fan developers; a celebrated comeback.
mobil__sonic-mania-plus.article:
**Sonic Mania Plus** returns the series to its roots as a two-dimensional platformer in the style of Sega Genesis games, with pixel-art graphics, fast pacing, and levels inspired by classic zones from the nineties, supplemented with new original sections and surprising boss fights. Mobile controls use virtual buttons for movement, jumping, and spin dash, which, with a bit of practice, works surprisingly accurately even without a physical gamepad, though the more demanding platforming sections noticeably benefit from support for an external controller connected via Bluetooth. The Plus version additionally adds the playable characters Mighty the Armadillo and Ray the Flying Squirrel with their own abilities, as well as a new Encore mode, which rearranges zones, changes the music, and adds extra lives.

The original 2017 game was created by a team of fan developers who had previously made a name for themselves modding old Sonic titles, and SEGA gave them the room to build an official continuation of the classic series with deep respect for the original design. The mobile port of the Plus version didn't arrive until 2023 as a paid app without ads, placing it alongside classic full-fledged ports rather than the modern free-to-play model common on mobile. Critics and fans alike embraced it as one of the best returns of the brand to its origins after years of experimenting with less successful 3D entries, and the mobile version let people without an old console rediscover this comeback too.

**Why play:** A great choice for fans of classic 2D Sonic who want an honest platformer without ads and can manage playing on touch buttons, ideally with a controller.

mobil__resident-evil-village.teaser: A survival horror featuring the castle of vampire Lady Dimitrescu, one of the series' most iconic characters.
mobil__resident-evil-village.article:
**Resident Evil Village** brings survival horror to mobile, in which the main hero Ethan Winters finds himself in a village ruled by four mutated lords, among whom the giant vampire countess Lady Dimitrescu stands out, residing in her castle full of traps and ghostly daughters. The game combines first-person shooting, puzzle solving, and careful management of limited ammunition and healing supplies with moments of pure horror tension, where the player flees from practically invulnerable enemies through narrow corridors. The mobile port is natively optimized for newer iPhones and iPads with powerful chips, uses advanced image scaling and touch controls supplemented with virtual joysticks, though the game officially recommends connecting a physical controller for more comfortable and precise play.

Capcom released the port in 2023, several years after the original release on consoles and PC, and it is a paid, full-fledged version without microtransactions or ads, with the entire story and all modes from the console version. Technically, it is one of the most ambitious attempts to bring a graphically demanding modern game to a phone without changing the content, which largely succeeded thanks to the power of the latest Apple chips and clever graphics optimization. For players, it's a way to go through the entire story with all its iconic moments straight from their pocket, though the comfort of longer play without a physical controller has its noticeable limits.

**Why play:** Recommended for owners of powerful iPhones and iPads who want a full-fledged modern horror game on the go and don't mind buying a physical controller for more comfortable controls.

mobil__hades.teaser: An acclaimed roguelike about escaping the underworld; the story moves forward with each death, not in circles.
mobil__hades.article:
**Hades** arrived on mobile phones only several years after its debut on PC and Nintendo Switch, but even with the delay, it remains one of the best-rated roguelike titles of the past decade. Playing as Zagreus, son of the god of the underworld, the player repeatedly tries to fight their way from the realm of the dead to the surface, with each failed attempt pushing the story, relationships with characters, and mythological background a bit further – death here isn't a punishment but part of the narrative, which the game handles much more cleverly than most of its genre peers. On the touchscreen, the game offers a virtual controller and buttons for attack, dodge, and special abilities; the controls work surprisingly precisely and the layout can be adjusted in the settings, though players used to a physical gamepad will appreciate the option to connect an external controller via Bluetooth and play the phone more like a small console.

Visually, the game relies on a strong comic-book style and richly animated characters with full voice acting, while the music draws on Greek motifs and builds dynamically according to the situation in battle. The system of weapons, divine boons, and permanent progression unlocks new build options with each run, so even after dozens of hours the game still offers new combinations and the player keeps learning something new about the relationships between the gods of Olympus and the underworld. On mobile, the game is available through Netflix Games, meaning as part of a Netflix subscription with no additional payments and no ads, which is a pleasant exception compared to common practice on mobile platforms, but also a limitation for those who don't use Netflix.

**Why play:** For players with an active Netflix subscription who want to experience one of the best roguelike titles of the past decade on the go, without ads or microtransactions.
