mobil__wuthering-waves.teaser: An open-world gacha action RPG emphasizing a fast combat system; a Genshin Impact competitor.
mobil__wuthering-waves.article:
**Wuthering Waves** is among the most ambitious action RPGs that competed for gacha game players' attention in 2024, alongside the dominant Genshin Impact. Studio Kuro Games builds the game on an open world full of exploration, platform jumping, and combat that emphasizes fast combos, well-timed dodges, and switching between characters mid-battle – the pace is noticeably brisker than the competition, and combat here feels more like a console action game than a turn-based strategy. On the touchscreen, the controls rely on a virtual joystick and a set of buttons for attacks and abilities, and the layout can be customized in settings; the game also supports controller connection, which players moving from console action RPGs to a phone screen will appreciate.

Characters are obtained through a gacha system with random draws and paid in-game currency, which, just like in other titles of the genre, is set up to encourage repeated spending on the strongest and rarest heroes and their weapons. The game is free to download, but full progress without patient grinding usually requires an investment of either time or money. The story takes place in a post-apocalyptic world afflicted by a mysterious disease called Tacet Discord, the atmosphere combines melancholy with grand orchestral scores, and the game is regularly expanded with new regions, characters, and time-limited in-game events.

**Why play:** Fans of action gacha RPGs looking for a snappier combat system than Genshin Impact, but who must expect the need to invest time or money into progress.

mobil__zenless-zone-zero.teaser: An action gacha RPG from the creators of Genshin Impact, this time set in a stylized urban environment.
mobil__zenless-zone-zero.article:
**Zenless Zone Zero** is HoYoverse studio's third major title after Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail, this time set in a stylized urban environment instead of a fantasy landscape. Instead of a vast open world, the game combines city exploration in the form of isometric streets with expeditions into so-called Hollow zones, which the player reaches through a screen resembling a TV menu. Combat is fast, built on combo-style attacks, last-second dodges, and flashy switching between three characters in the team; on touch controls, this works surprisingly smoothly thanks to simple gestures and large buttons.

The visual style draws on anime and streetwear aesthetics, characters have distinctive designs and voice acting, and the music blends electronic and hip-hop elements that match the game's urban atmosphere. Like its sister titles, Zenless Zone Zero is built on the gacha model – the game is free to download, but the strongest characters and their upgrades are tied to draws paid for with in-game or real money, and the game actively encourages regular logins and spending during time-limited in-game events and banners.

**Why play:** Players who like the distinctive visual style and fast combat of HoYoverse titles but are looking for an urban setting instead of fantasy and have made peace with gacha monetization.

mobil__call-of-duty-warzone-mobile.teaser: Warzone battle royale in mobile form; an attempt to bring full-fledged Call of Duty into your pocket.
mobil__call-of-duty-warzone-mobile.article:
**Call of Duty: Warzone Mobile** is Activision's attempt to bring the sprawling battle royale experience from consoles and PC, without changing its format, straight into your pocket. On a map where dozens of players fight for survival, controls run through virtual joysticks and buttons scattered across the screen, though the game also supports external controllers and offers a fairly wide range of sensitivity and layout settings — without them, precise aiming on a touchscreen is hard to come by. The game shares weapons, gear, and part of its progression with the series' major entries on other platforms, so players can carry their pool of unlocked items across devices.

The graphics try to keep pace with console Warzone, which takes its toll on older phones in the form of frame rate drops and high demands on storage and data connections. The game is free to download and funds itself through a battle pass and cosmetic microtransactions, similar to the parent game on PC and consoles — standard practice for battle royale titles, but still an extra expense for players who want to unlock looks quickly instead of patiently earning free content.

**Why play it:** For Call of Duty fans who want a battle royale experience close to the console version on their phone too, though they should expect it to be demanding on phone performance and data usage.

mobil__squad-busters.teaser: A casual action game collecting units from Clash Royale, Clash of Clans, and Brawl Stars.
mobil__squad-busters.article:
**Squad Busters** is Supercell's attempt to bring together popular characters from Clash of Clans, Clash Royale, Brawl Stars, and its other in-house titles into a single lightweight casual game. The idea is simple: the player collects characters scattered across the map, builds a growing squad from them, and competes with other players in real time for treasure and survival, with a stronger and larger lineup usually winning out. Controls are stripped down to the bare essentials — just tap where you want your character to move, while everything else, attacks and collecting included, happens automatically, making the game an ideal pick for short play sessions between other activities.

Visually, the game continues the colorful, cartoonish style that Supercell made famous with Clash of Clans and Clash Royale, and fans of the earlier titles will appreciate the many references and familiar faces spanning the company's game universe. The game is free to download, with monetization resting on purchases of in-game currency and chests containing characters and upgrades — a model traditional for Supercell, but decidedly not free of cost if a player wants to keep pace with others progressing faster in the arena.

**Why play it:** For players who want lightweight, quickly understood fun from the Supercell universe for a few minutes a day, without needing deep strategic planning.

pico-8__jelpi.teaser: A sample game by the creator of PICO-8; the fantasy console's unofficial 'hello world'.
pico-8__jelpi.article:
**Jelpi** is the official sample game that Zep, the creator of the PICO-8 fantasy console, bundled directly with the engine to demonstrate its graphical and audio capabilities. For much of the community, it became the very first game they launched after installing PICO-8, and it still serves as the system's unofficial "hello world" today. The player controls a colorful little character who jumps across platforms, collects items, and dodges simple enemies across small, clearly laid-out levels. It's not a sprawling adventure, but a compact demonstration of how, within PICO-8's constraints (128×128 pixel resolution, sixteen colors, a tiny memory limit), you can build a playable and visually legible platformer without the design having to make major compromises in clarity.

Technically, Jelpi demonstrates the genre's basic building blocks: smooth jumping, collision detection with the environment, and a simple musical loop that accompanies the player through the levels. Controls are deliberately minimalist, so the game can be grasped within a few seconds, making it popular material for tutorials and the first steps of beginning developers who want to dig through the source code and learn how PICO-8 works under the hood — Jelpi's code is often one of the first examples newcomers try tweaking, whether to change character behavior or add their own levels. The chunky-pixel, bright-color visual style became something of a visual template for much of the later work on this platform, and many later games consciously or unconsciously build on it.

Today, Jelpi is played more for nostalgia and its historical significance than for gameplay depth — it's a short, undemanding experience that can be finished in a few minutes and never aspired to be a full-fledged commercial title. Even so, it remains an important point in PICO-8's history: it showed that the fantasy console could deliver genuinely playable content and inspired hundreds of independent creators to try their own platformers and action games on the limited platform. For new players, it's still a recommended first step before diving into the larger body of titles the PICO-8 community has amassed since 2015.

**Why play it:** More for collectors of PICO-8 history than for gameplay depth — a short, undemanding title that stood at the fantasy console's birth and inspired hundreds of other creators to make their own platformers.

pico-8__jasper-s-journeys.teaser: A classic 90s-style platformer squeezed into PICO-8; precise controls and legible level design.
pico-8__jasper-s-journeys.article:
**Jasper's Journeys** is an action platformer that brings the traditional recipe of classic console platformers from the nineties to PICO-8 — the player moves through a series of carefully designed levels, collects items, dispatches enemies with a jump on the head or a simple attack, and looks for the way out of each map. The game relies on precise controls and legible level design, where every screen offers its own combination of platforms, enemies, and obstacles, forcing the player to learn to recognize patterns and react to them in real time. Rising difficulty adds new enemy types and more complex jumping sequences, giving the game, despite its simple foundation, a proper learning curve.

The graphics use PICO-8's typical palette and simple but distinctive sprites, so even at low resolution it's clear what's an enemy, what's a platform, and what's a collectible. The music keeps the game's pace brisk and supports a sense of smooth progress through the levels without overwhelming the player. The platform's limitations show in that the author had to weigh trade-offs between the number of enemies on screen and animation smoothness — typical for PICO-8 development — yet still managed to keep the game legible even when several moving objects appear on screen at once.

Within the PICO-8 community, Jasper's Journeys is among the titles often recommended as a demonstration of how well the feel of a classic platformer in the style of early console games can be replicated on an eight- to sixteen-color console. The level structure, free of unnecessary narrative, lets movement and jumping themselves take center stage, which is exactly what players value most about the genre. Today the game is appreciated mainly by players with a soft spot for retro aesthetics and a straightforward challenge without unnecessary crutches — it's a title that can be played in short bursts and still deliver the satisfying feeling of clearing a level, without requiring knowledge of any complicated story context.

**Why play it:** For players with a soft spot for retro aesthetics and a straightforward challenge without unnecessary crutches — clean jumping and movement without distracting narrative, playable in short bursts with a satisfying feel.

pico-8__chibi-knight.teaser: Zelda in a PICO-8 nutshell; gradually unlocking abilities opens up previously inaccessible paths.
pico-8__chibi-knight.article:
**Chibi Knight** is an action-adventure inspired by classic games from The Legend of Zelda series, translated into PICO-8's minimalist garb. The player takes on the role of a small knight who moves through a series of interconnected locations, fights enemies with a sword, collects upgrades, and gradually unlocks new abilities that open up previously inaccessible paths. This principle of gradually unlocking the world is the core of the gameplay, and despite its short length it gives the game the feel of a small but full-fledged adventure, in which the player repeatedly returns to previously visited areas with new abilities and discovers corners that were off-limits on the first pass.

The combat system is simple but functional — the player swings a sword, dodges attacks, and must judge the right moment for a counterattack, especially in fights against larger enemies and bosses, who form the climax of individual sections of the game and require learning specific behavior patterns. Visually, the game works with a cute "chibi" take on its characters, which contrasts with the darker environments the player passes through, and the music rounds out the atmosphere of an adventure in a small but dense world, where playful design meets the more serious tone of the story itself, about a knight venturing into the unknown.

Chibi Knight is among the titles often cited in the PICO-8 community as proof that even on such a limited platform you can build a structured adventure with a sense of progress and discovery, not just a short arcade interlude. Thanks to its combination of combat, exploration, and gradual ability unlocking, the game remains a recommended entry point today for players who want to experience something close to a classic action-adventure on PICO-8, without having to reach for larger and more time-consuming titles, while its own length is still long enough for the player to experience a genuine sense of adventure with its own character development arc.

**Why play it:** For players who want to experience a structured adventure on PICO-8, with a sense of progress and discovery, instead of a short arcade interlude — combat and ability unlocking offer a genuine character development arc.

pico-8__doko-roko.teaser: Combat with a weight and feel rarely seen on PICO-8; an interconnected world full of hidden paths.
pico-8__doko-roko.article:
**Doko Roko** builds a surprisingly smooth and tactile combat system on top of PICO-8's constraints. The player controls a character with a melee weapon and must master the timing of attacks, dodges, and blocks in fights against a variety of enemies scattered across an interconnected world full of hidden paths and optional areas. The emphasis on how combat feels — the weight of hits, an enemy's reaction to being struck, the ability to combine movement with attacks — places the game among the technically most ambitious action titles on this platform, since combat this refined is rarely seen in small fan-made PICO-8 productions and requires careful tuning of reaction time and hitboxes so that fighting stays fair and still tense even after dozens of battles.

The level design supports freer exploration: the player gradually discovers new areas, finds upgrades, and learns to use the environment in combat, which brings the game closer to the metroidvania style than to a linear action platformer. Visually, Doko Roko works with a darker, rawer palette and spare but striking pixel art, accompanied by atmospheric music that heightens the feeling of a lonely journey through a hostile world full of uncertainty and hidden threats around every corner, without holding the player's hand with unnecessary text or map markers.

Within the PICO-8 community, Doko Roko is often cited as an example of how far a combat system's sophistication can be pushed even within an extremely limited engine with sixteen colors and low resolution. Today the game is appreciated mainly by players looking for something on PICO-8 deeper than short arcade fun — it's a title that rewards patience, carefully reading enemy patterns, and a willingness to explore every corner of the map, rather than relying on fast reflex-based action, and it rewards players who take the time to repeatedly try tougher fights.

**Why play it:** For patient players willing to read enemy patterns and explore every corner of the map instead of relying on fast reflexes — a sophisticated combat system even within an extremely limited engine.

pico-8__squareboy-vs-bullies-arena-editi.teaser: Fast arenas that shrink as difficulty rises; aggressive and precise play pays off here.
pico-8__squareboy-vs-bullies-arena-editi.article:
**Squareboy vs Bullies: Arena Edition** is a fast action platformer in which a small square-headed hero must defend against waves of bullying opponents across a series of enclosed arenas. The core of the gameplay is close-quarters combat combined with dodging and using the environment — the player must track where attacks are coming from and react with quick movements, since the game punishes hesitation and rewards aggressive but precise play. Successive waves of opponents force the player to constantly change position and never rely on a single safe tactic, because the arenas gradually shrink as difficulty rises, offering less room to dodge. The player thus has to learn to read which direction the next wave is coming from and reposition to a more advantageous spot in advance.

The game arose as an expanded version of an older concept, and the Arena edition adds a structure built around progressively clearing arenas of enemies, which brings it closer to an arena brawler than a classic linear platformer. The visual style is deliberately simple and legible — clearly distinguished colors for the player, enemies, and projectiles let you instantly tell what's happening on screen even at fast pace, which is crucial at such a low resolution. The sound design underscores every strike and hit with short, punchy effects that give combat tangible feedback.

Squareboy vs Bullies is among the titles that showed even a small action game built on a single clear premise — can you defend yourself in an enclosed space? — can work as full-fledged arcade fun on PICO-8. Thanks to its directness and brisk pace, the game holds a place among the community's favorite action pieces, and it still works today as a fast, intense gaming session without unnecessary complications, ideal for moments when the player doesn't want to deal with a sprawling story but just wants to test their own reflexes across several quick attempts in a row, which also makes the game well-suited to repeated returns after a longer break.

**Why play it:** For moments when you just want to test your own reflexes in a fast, intense gaming session without unnecessary complications — straightforward arcade fun built on a single clear principle of defense.

pico-8__pico-kombat.teaser: A fan-made 1v1 fighting game squeezed into 128×128 pixels; the spirit of the fighting game golden age in a pocket format.
pico-8__pico-kombat.article:
**Pico Kombat** is a fan-made fighting game inspired by classic one-on-one duels from the genre's golden age, transferred onto PICO-8's 128×128 pixel canvas. Players face off on a confined battlefield, combining punches, kicks, and special moves, and must track their opponent's dwindling energy as well as their own. Despite the platform's drastic technical limits, the game manages to preserve the basic feel of one-on-one combat that the fighting game genre has stood on for decades, including the need to judge distance and the timing of the opponent's lunges and to watch your own position relative to the battlefield's edges, since retreating into a corner here means losing room to dodge.

Implementing a fighting system at such low resolution and with a limited color palette is itself a technical feat — character animations must stay legible despite very few pixels available per frame, and yet the game still manages to distinguish individual attacks and their range. The sound design uses simple but punchy effects that give combat the dynamism and hit feedback it needs, which is absolutely essential to how a fighting game feels regardless of resolution — without strong audio feedback, even the best-animated strike wouldn't feel convincing.

In the PICO-8 community, Pico Kombat is often cited as proof that even the fighting game genre — traditionally dependent on detailed animation and large sprite sets — can be reduced to its essence and still remain fun. Today it's more of a curiosity and technical showcase than a game with the deep combat system of modern titles, but for fans of the genre and of PICO-8 history it represents an interesting stop and a reminder of how much can be squeezed out of extremely modest technical resources, provided the developer takes care with the genre's basic principles and doesn't neglect the feel of each individual strike.

**Why play it:** More a technical curiosity than a game with a deep combat system, but an interesting stop for fans of the genre and of PICO-8 history, showing how much can be squeezed out of extremely modest resources.

pico-8__hyperspace-dogfights.teaser: A classic shmup with readable bullet patterns; rewards the courage to fly as close to danger as possible.
pico-8__hyperspace-dogfights.article:
**Hyperspace Dogfights** is a fast-paced space shooter in which the player pilots a small ship against waves of enemy machines, dodging dense bullet fire while sniping targets at the same time. The game builds on the classic shmup principle — readable enemy fire patterns, gradually escalating difficulty, and a reward for precise and daring maneuvering as close to danger as possible without getting hit. Advancing waves of enemies introduce new ship and projectile types, forcing the player to constantly adapt to changing threats and adjust their dodging style to newly introduced foes. The movement space is limited and the density of fire grows faster than the player expects, so even experienced players must stay fully focused throughout the run.

Visually, the game uses a dark space background with bold color accents for projectiles and ships, which — even within PICO-8's limited palette — lets the player instantly recognize what's dangerous and what to avoid, even in hectic moments. The music keeps a tense, dynamic pace that reinforces the constant sense of threat typical of this action subgenre, and together with the fast sound effects of shots and explosions it builds the atmosphere of a life-or-death space battle, where a single second of inattention can mean the end of the run and a return to the start of the level.

Hyperspace Dogfights is one of the titles that show the shoot 'em up genre keeps its essence even on an extremely limited fantasy console — reflexes, pattern reading, and the tension of narrow dodges. Today the game is best appreciated by players looking for a short but intense arcade session focused mainly on their own score and gradually improving reactions, not on storytelling, gradual equipment gathering, or extensive content, which makes it a welcome choice for the moments between longer sessions of other, more demanding titles on the same console.

**Why play it:** For players looking for a short but intense arcade session built on reflexes, pattern reading, and chasing their own score — a welcome choice for the moments between longer sessions of other titles.

pico-8__squidasteroids.teaser: Asteroids with squids instead of boulders; humorous graphics, classic arcade screen pressure.
pico-8__squidasteroids.article:
**Squidasteroids** is an arcade shooter inspired by the classic concept of Asteroids, which the author enriched with his own, humorously toned visual theme featuring squid-like enemies instead of the traditional rocky fragments. The player controls a small ship, fires at approaching opponents, and must dodge their onslaught at the same time, while the difficulty gradually increases as more and more targets pile up on screen, forcing the player to prioritize which ones to destroy first so as not to be overwhelmed from all sides at once.

The game sticks to the genre's tradition of free movement in a vacuum — the ship has inertia, so the player must account for gradual acceleration and braking, which gives the battles a distinct rhythm different from typical shmups with fixed directional movement — a misjudged flight path can punish just as harshly here as a direct enemy hit. The graphical presentation is simple and clear, with bold enemy outlines against a dark background, keeping the game readable even when a larger number of objects accumulate on screen, and small humorous details in the enemy design give this otherwise purely arcade game a pleasant sense of levity without taking away from the tension of a growing number of opponents.

Squidasteroids is a typical example of how PICO-8 creators often take a familiar genre foundation and add their own personality to it without needing complicated mechanics. Today the game is a popular quick pastime for moments when the player just wants a short arcade session built on reflexes and chasing a higher score, without needing to learn anything complex or devote long, uninterrupted stretches of time to it, and the chase for a personal record easily pulls the player right back into starting another round the moment the previous one ends, hoping that this time they'll last a few waves longer than last time.

**Why play it:** For moments when all you need is a short arcade session without learning anything complicated — the chase for a personal record easily pulls the player right back into starting another round.

pico-8__mokoshka.teaser: A calmer, more exploratory platformer set in Slavic folklore; the terrain itself hints where to go next.
pico-8__mokoshka.article:
**Mokoshka** is a smaller platformer with exploration elements that takes the player into a stylized world inspired by Slavic mythology and folklore. The player moves through forest and underground scenery, jumps between platforms, avoids dangers, and searches for a way deeper into the game's world, with a pace that is calmer and more exploratory than in purely arcade platformers — patient observation of the environment is often enough to progress, rather than lightning-fast reflexes, which makes the game accessible even to players who usually skip classic action platformers because of their high demands on reflexes. The environment itself acts as a guide — the shape of the terrain and the placement of dangers hints at where it's safe to proceed, leading the player to read the screen more attentively than in a typical arcade platformer.

The game's visual style relies on a softer palette and atmospheric backgrounds that, even within PICO-8's constraints, manage to evoke a mysterious, fairy-tale-like environment. The music accompanying the levels supports the game's more contemplative tone and sets it apart from noisier action titles on the same platform, though there's no shortage of moments requiring a quick reaction to an approaching danger and a precisely timed jump between platforms, so the game manages to alternate calm passages with brief moments of tension.

Within the PICO-8 community, Mokoshka is an example of a smaller, atmospherically driven project that shows the platformer genre on this console doesn't have to be just about speed and reflexes, but can also be about mood and visual style. Today the game is appreciated mainly by players looking for a calmer, more exploratory experience on PICO-8 among more hectic action and arcade titles, who value that even a short game can build a distinctive, memorable atmosphere without needing an extensive story, a combat system, or dozens of hours of content.

**Why play it:** For players looking for a calmer, more exploratory experience on PICO-8 among more hectic action titles — the atmosphere and visual style carry the game even without an extensive story or combat system.

pico-8__ultra-business-tycoon-iii.teaser: A surrealist mix of business simulation and adventure by Zep, the creator of PICO-8 itself.
pico-8__ultra-business-tycoon-iii.article:
**Ultra Business Tycoon III** is one of the strangest and most distinctive games ever made specifically for PICO-8 — created by Zep, the creator of the fantasy console itself, and the result is a surrealist mix of business simulation, adventure, and bizarre storytelling. The player takes on the role of an employee of a strange corporation and gradually moves through a series of seemingly unrelated minigames and scenes that come together into a strangely moving, dreamlike story about work, alienation, and the meaning of existence. The game's structure resists classic genre pigeonholing — instead of a clearly defined goal, it offers exploration, experimentation, and the gradual uncovering of further layers of its absurd world.

Technically, the game demonstrates how flexible PICO-8 can be when its limits are approached creatively: it switches between different visual styles and game mechanics, from simple simulation screens to moments reminiscent of old-school adventure games. The musical accompaniment builds a melancholic, at times almost oppressive atmosphere that sets the game apart from typical action or platforming titles on this platform. It's precisely the combination of humor, absurdity, and sincere melancholy that makes Ultra Business Tycoon III an experience that's hard to categorize but leaves an all the stronger impression on the player.

Within the PICO-8 community, the game has long been regarded as a cult item — not necessarily for wide popularity, but for how inventively it uses the fantasy console's capabilities to tell a distinctive story. To this day it serves as a reminder that even a platform with such strict technical limits can host deeply auteur-driven works unafraid to experiment with both form and content, placing it more among interactive experiences than among traditional games in the narrow sense of the word. That's exactly why it's regularly cited as an example of the authorial freedom the fantasy console's creator allowed himself within his own tool, outside the expectations of the genres PICO-8 players are usually accustomed to.

**Why play it:** For players open to inventive, freely authorial works rather than traditional games in the narrow sense — a cult-status showcase of how even a strictly limited fantasy console can carry deeply personal storytelling.

pico-8__adventures-of-elena-temple.teaser: Tomb Raider in the spirit of PICO-8; pseudo-3D temples full of traps without a single actual polygon.
pico-8__adventures-of-elena-temple.article:
**The Adventures of Elena Temple** is an action-adventure game inspired by the early 3D adventure genre of the nineties — games like Tomb Raider or Prince of Persia — but transposed into PICO-8's extremely constrained environment. Playing as the archaeologist Elena Temple, the player moves through ancient temples full of traps, lever-and-platform puzzles, and dangerous creatures, and the game cleverly simulates a sense of three-dimensional space using an isometric-to-pseudo-3D perspective, even though PICO-8 doesn't natively support any real 3D graphics. The character's movement is stiffer and more deliberate than in typical platformers, matching the style of the games it draws inspiration from — the player must precisely judge jumps, turns, and interactions with the surrounding environment.

It's precisely this technical solution for the pseudo-3D effect on such limited hardware that has earned the game attention within the PICO-8 community — it shows that even with a resolution of 128×128 pixels and a small color palette, it's possible to evoke the illusion of deeper space and build puzzles on it based on perspective and room layout. The atmosphere is rounded out by spare but effective music and a visual style reminiscent of old adventure titles, making the game feel like a loving tribute to a genre that has almost disappeared from mainstream platforms today.

Among PICO-8 players, The Adventures of Elena Temple is valued precisely for this technical elegance and for its honest craftsmanship in puzzle and level design. Today the game works as a pleasant, compact reminder of a time when adventure games were built on a slower, more deliberate pace, and at the same time as a demonstration of how creatively one can work within the fantasy console's limitations. The short playtime here is more of a strength than a shortcoming — the puzzles and temple sections are designed to be completed in one focused sitting, without unnecessarily padding out the content.

**Why play it:** For fans of the slower, more deliberate pace of adventure games and honestly designed puzzles — the short playtime here is a strength, letting you get through the temple sections in one focused sitting.
